title: A Bloodsmoor Romance
author: Joyce Carol Oates
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A BLOODSMOOR ROMANCE By Joyce Carol Oates.  615 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $16.95.    WHEN we learn on the first page of ''A Bloodsmoor Romance'' that one of the five heroines has just been abducted ''in an outlaw balloon of sinister black silken hue,'' we know that Joyce Carol Oates - as well as the heroine Deirdre - has embarked on a perilous course. ''Well may you blink and draw back in alarm at that crude word abducted: and yet, I fear,'' remarks the narrator, a maiden lady of a certain age, ''there is no other, to be employed with any honesty.'' And some there may be who will blink and draw back from the whole enterprise: the long, fanciful adventures of the five Zinn sisters of Bloodsmoor, Pa., circa 1870. But the reader who has no aversion to abductions and balloons and the rest will be conveyed in a manner both pleasurable and instructive (the aim, some have said, of art) through more than 600 pages of an antiromance that provides the satisfactions of a romance too.
headline: BALLOONS AND ABDUCTIONS

title: This Strange New Feeling
author: Julius Lester
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THIS STRANGE NEW FEELING By Julius Lester.  149 pp. New York: The Dial Press. $10.95.  (Ages 12 and Up) By MAUREEN HOWARD   This is an attractive but uneven book by Julius Lester, a professor of Black Studies at the University of Massachusetts, who wrote ''To Be a Slave,'' which was a Newbery Honor Book in 1969. In each of its three tales ''This Strange New Feeling'' tries to be a fictionalization of history and a love story at once. The material, taken from 19th-century accounts of American slavery, is so strong that readers of any age will find the stories sharply instructive.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Namesake
author: Michel Goldberg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
NAMESAKE By Michel Goldberg.  Illustrated. 192 pp. New Haven, Conn.: Yale University Press. $13.95. 

WHEN World War II ended, an 8-year-old French schoolboy, Michel Cojot, began learning some unsettling things about himself. He learned that Cojot wasn't his name at all, but Goldberg. He learned that during the war his father had been deported from France ''to be resettled in the East'' - that is, destroyed at Auschwitz. He learned that his mother, eager to avoid offense in the anti-Semitic environment of France - apparently as overpowering after the war as before and during it - had been delighted, upon remarrying, to take the unambiguously non-Jewish name Cojot and impose it on her son. ''I was stripped of my private though very common surname,'' Michel Goldberg (as he calls himself now) writes in this memoir. ''It was like killing the father a second time.''

At school after the war, he recalls, ''I too became anti-Semitic.'' He embarked on a virtual career of self-hatred and as a result found himself unable to love. He found that ''self-hatred impels one to conquer by admiration what can really be conquered only by affection - 'I'm going to show them what I'm worth!' '' He hurled himself into the pursuit of competitive ''success'' - banking was the theater of these exertions - only to find that ''From success to success, I felt only defeat. I always needed to achieve more.''
headline: CHOOSING NOT TO KILL

title: Obasan
author: Joy Kogawa
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
OBASAN By Joy Kogawa.  250 pp. Boston: David R. Godine. $12.95.

AFTER Pearl Harbor, Canada's government, like that of the United States, abrogated the rights of its citizens who had Japanese ancestors. These Canadian Japanese forfeited their property, and, after being interned, the men were impressed into forced labor and the women and children transported to ghost towns and abandoned mining camps in the interior of the country to fend for themselves.  The avowed purpose of this national exercise in pernicious lunacy was patriotic: to discourage any overwhelming urge among people of Japanese origin to turn into spies. But since there is no evidence that Japanese Canadians were more inclined to treason than Canadians of German or Italian or, for that matter, any other derivation, and since discrimination against them continued for years after the war, one may be forgiven for suspecting that they were the victims of racism.
headline: UNNECESSARY PRECAUTIONS

title: A Little More Than Kin
author: Ernest Hebert
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A LITTLE MORE THAN KIN By Ernest Hebert.  224 pp. New York: The Viking Press. $13.95. By NICHOLAS DELBANCO   N his second novel, Ernest Hebert returns to the scene of his acclaimed first work: ''A Little More Than Kin'' takes place in the town of Darby, N.H., as did ''The Dogs of March.'' Mr. Hebert offers a continuity as well as a return. Ollie Jordan, head of the decrepit Jordan clan, and his idiot son, Willow, were ancillary characters in ''The Dogs of March''; they move stage center here. Howard Elman, brave, fumbling protagonist of the earlier novel, plays a supporting role in ''A Little More Than Kin''; he starts a dump-truck business and offers Ollie work. The summer with which the first book ends is the summer with which the second begins; the first concludes in fire, and the second, ice.
headline: AN ICY ENDING

title: A Midnight Clear
author: William Wharton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A MIDNIGHT CLEAR By William Wharton.  242 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $12.95.   DECEMBER 1944, the Ardennes Forest: An under-strength American Intelligence and Reconnaissance squad unenthusiastically mans a quiet observation post in a remote, deserted chateau. From the standpoint of military history, with the Battle of the Bulge impending, this is a bad situation. It is, however, a good situation for a war novel. In ''A Midnight Clear,'' William Wharton (the pseudonymous author of the much admired ''Birdy'' and ''Dad'') gives us both a gripping tale of military action and a perhaps less successful account of the human stakes in war.
headline: YOUNG AT WAR

title: Sassafrass, Cypress & Indigo
author: Ntozake Shange
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
SASSAFRASS, CYPRESS & INDIGO By Ntozake Shange.  225 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $10.95.

TOZAKE SHANGE'S first novel reads like it is the product of a collaboration among a gifted poet, a trendy revolutionary and a social director at a California resort. Sassafrass, Cypress and Indigo, the three sisters of the title, are introduced as young girls, and the reader is charmed by them as well as by the gracefulness of the introduction. Miss Shange's language is rich and economical and the three characters are compelling both as individuals and as personifications of black culture and the feminist spirit. But as their world begins to widen, the writing starts to deteriorate. When the sisters leave the protection of their mother - the best-drawn character in the book - they drift into relationships so banal they seem no more substantial than mist over a redwood hot tub.
headline: THREE SISTERS

title: The Second Stage
author: Betty Friedan
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SECOND STAGE. By Betty Friedan. (Summit Books, $5.95.) An ''uneasy sense'' that something had gone wrong with the women's movement led the author of ''The Feminine Mystique'' to re-examine it, and she discovered that it has entered its second stage. Her prescription here calls for ''a joint effort by men and women to redefine what is meant by success at home and on the job so that the needs of both sexes for achievement, intimacy and nurturance can find adequate expression.'' Our reviewer, Hilda Kay observed that ''it is possible to applaud this strategy without embracing the reasoning that produced it.''   MEMOIRS OF AN ANTI-SEMITE. By Gregor von Rezzori. (Penguin, $4.95.) The protagonist of this ''novel in five stories'' is an upper-class European living in a world that regards Jews as alien, threatening and despicable. ''Gregor von Rezzori's book does not recant or justify these views,'' Stanley Kauffmann wrote in his review. ''It is the straightforward yet imaginative, often discomfiting, always enthralling 'novel' of a life in which such attitudes provide the chief dynamics.''
headline: PAPERBACKS: NEW AND NOTEWORTHY

title: End-Game
author: Michael Gilbert
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: END-GAME By Michael Gilbert.  247 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $13.50. MR.CALDER & MR.BEHRENS By Michael Gilbert.  256 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $12.95.   MICHAEL GILBERT is now 70 and has, to mark the occasion, published his 22d crime novel and his 5th collection of stories. I have known and admired his work for many years. All who read detective fiction read it compulsively, but the compulsions vary: Some addicts are omnivorous, devouring all that comes to hand; others read a few authors intensely, insistent upon a concatenation of certain qualities. W.H. Auden confessed to being an addict of the first kind; I belong to the second group. The difference is this: The first group does not reread crime fiction, discarding books already encountered like empty cigarette packages, while the second group honors that fiction which not only withstands but welcomes rereading. It is not surprising that we members of the second group have a small number of favorite authors, all of whose works are as familiar as old friends but, like true friends, capable of surprising us. We return to their company because we are rewarded by being in their presence.
headline: WHO DID IT? MICHAEL GILBERT AND P. D. JAMES

title: Camus
author: Patrick McCarthy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CAMUS By Patrick McCarthy.  359 pp. New York: Random House. $17.95.   THE fate of Albert Camus's reputation since his death in 1960 has been curious. Consecrated as a classic in France by the publication of his complete works in the Pleiade series, he has nonetheless been passed over in embarrassed silence by most critics and younger writers there. In the United States his name is famous, but one suspects that his readers are mainly college freshmen. Camus's humanism - the message of revolt and fraternity that made him the most famous and emblematic intellectual figure to emerge from the Resistance movement of World War II and the political ferment that followed the Liberation - seemed even before his death to have become a trap: Camus le juste, the conscience of postwar Europe, became more and more an imitation of himself, caught in a noble but rather hollow moral rhetoric as he tried to hold his course between the totalistic thought of both right and left. Jean-Paul Sartre accused Camus (during their notorious feud following publication of ''The Rebel'') of always carrying with him a ''portable pedestal.'' There was some truth in the jibe.
headline: FROM ALBERT CAMUS TO ROLAND BARTHES

title: Monsignor Quixote
author: Graham Greene
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MONSIGNOR QUIXOTE By Graham Greene.  221 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $12.95.   IN recent years Graham Greene has been availing himself of the special prerogative of an old master. With many triumphs behind him, he can now turn his hand to whatever catches his fancy without feeling obliged to make a major statement or to advance his career in some striking way. The results of this freedom have ranged considerably in subject matter, tone and intensity. If none has been first-rate Greene, all have been interesting as latter-day reflections of the master's long-standing preoccupation with doom, pity and the inscrutability of God's will. In ''The Human Factor'' (1978) Greene once again stacked the deck against his protagonistvictim, a mediocre but kindly man trapped in a barbed-wire tangle of spying and betrayal. This novel was followed by ''Dr.  Fischer of Geneva, or The Bomb Party'' (1980), a chilling, even repellent story of a rich man who sadistically plays God with the poor toadies who strive to please him, tormenting and humiliating them for the sport of it. And now - again shifting course - Greene presents us with ''Monsignor Quixote,'' the gentlest and most amiable of his books since ''Travels with My Aunt.''
headline: AN AMIABLE GRAHAM GREENE

title: Selected Poems
author: Galway Kinnell
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SELECTED POEMS By Galway Kinnell.  148 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Co. $12.50.   AT the Donnell Library in Manhattan some 10 years ago, I witnessed a poetry reading so charged with high emotion and bardic intensity it left me both excited and exhausted. I could only imagine how it left the poet, Galway Kinnell, who, scarcely looking down at the page, had chanted his way through the whole of ''The Book of Nightmares,'' his book-length Rilkean sequence that remains one of the most ambitious works in contemporary poetry. This book, which exemplified Mr.  Kinnell's belief that it is ''the dream of every poem to be a myth,'' used material from his own life, such as the birth of his children, in ways that transcended autobiography and seemed to confront directly the rhythms of existence from birth to death. Especially as read aloud in one fell swoop, the poem gave powerful expression to the hopes and fears of a parent, husband and lover adrift in his own sense of mortality.
headline: IMPACT AND TRIUMPHANT

title: The Torch In My Ear
author: Elias Canetti
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE TORCH IN MY EAR By Elias Canetti.  Translated by Joachim Neugroschel.  372 pp. New York: Farrar Straus Giroux. $16.50.   ELIAS CANETTI had not even been considered a dark horse when he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1981. He did have a certain European reputation based on two very solid and unusual books. One is an extraordinary and very somber novel, ''Auto-Da-Fe,'' which relates the overcoming of a pathetically bookish and solitary scholar by evil minds; it was read as a political parable when it was published in 1935, two years after Hitler took power. The other is ''Crowds and Power'' (1960), which attempts the most systematic analysis imaginable of crowds as phenomena and of the effect of crowds on the sensations of daily living.   The cosmopolitan and polyglot influences in Canetti's life are remarkable. Born in 1905 in a Bulgarian town on the lower Danube in the old Ottoman Empire, he grew up speaking four languages at home.  He was educated in England, Switzerland and Germany but mainly in the Austro-Hungarian Empire. He has lived in England for many years, and he writes in German. Yet his books do not remind one in the least of the work of James Joyce, Ezra Pound or Vladimir Nabokov, those 20th century virtuosi in the witty crossing of languages and the invention of linguistic novelties. Canetti is a grimly serious thinker and sometimes ingenuous stylist.
headline: A BOOK MAN'S BOOK OF HIMSELF

title: Family Happiness
author: Laurie Colwin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FAMILY HAPPINESS By Laurie Colwin.  272 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $12.95.   POLLY SOLO-MILLER DEMAREST is one of those heroines of American fiction who appear to have everything. She is married to a large, handsome, usually amiable husband, Henry; she has two sweet children, Pete and Dee-Dee; she lives in a Park Avenue apartment; she has graduated from a good school and holds down a high-level job, as Coordinator of Research in Reading Projects and Methods for the Board of Education (''This job combined some of the things Polly held most dear - service, children, and books'').
headline: FOR THE WOMAN WHO HAS EVERYTHING

title: The Loser
author: George Konrad
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LOSER By George Konrad.  Translated by Ivan Sanders.315 pp. New York and San Diego: A Helen and Kurt Wolff Book/Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $14.95.   To a recent conference on writing and political censorship, the exiled Russian poet Joseph Brodsky remarked that writers in repressive societies are forced to take words more seriously than writers who have the luxury of saying anything. A diet of torture and prison may not be the healthiest way to feed a writer, but Mr.  Brodsky's observation contains a certain truth. In the last 20 years terrifying political power has produced a body of superb writing in Eastern Europe. Some writers, like Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, directly address politics; others, like the Czechoslovak novelist Jiri Grusa, engage passionately in formal experiments condemned as ''decadent'' by state censors. The effort to give a complete picture of enslaved life has prompted writers like the Yugoslav novelist Danilo Kis to cross and recross the frontier between fiction and reportage, while the cunning tactic of getting around censorship by writing allegory, as Aleksandr Zinoviev does, has given new vigor to that literary genre.
headline: A DARK NOVEL OF EASTERN EUROPE

title: Victorian Sculpture
author: Benedict Read
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: VICTORIAN SCULPTURE By Benedict Read.  Illustrated. 414 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $60.   THIS is one of the last books on earth that I ever expected to see. It is produced on a scale and with a physical splendor that would be appropriate to Donatello or Bernini. It is published for the Paul Mellon Centre for Studies in British Art by a great university press. It is written by one of the sons of Herbert Read, who for half a century upheld the cause of modernist sculpture in England. It is neither a hoax nor a polemic but a careful and reasoned account of a subject in which everyone is by now presumed to take a benevolent interest.   Yet the time is not long past when almost every good judge thought of Victorian sculpture as the most awful thing he had ever seen, without exception. Even in Victorian times John Ruskin, for instance, once said that ''the state of modern sculpture in England, as compared with that of the great Ancients, is literally one of corrupt and dishonorable death, as opposed to bright and fameful life.'' And this was the same John Ruskin whose ''Modern Painters'' erred if anything on the side of enthusiasm.
headline: ARTISTIC REAPPRAISAL

title: The White Plague
author: Frank Herbert
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WHITE PLAGUE By Frank Herbert.  445 pp. New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons. $14.95.   FRANK HERBERT'S latest novel is surprising in almost every way. To begin with, he has chosen not to return to the scene of his bestselling science-fiction series, the ''Dune'' tetralogy. After creating an immense far-future drama that mixed ''Star Wars''-type derring-do with ecological and eschatological concerns, Mr. Herbert has reined in his imagination and set it a much grimmer task. The time is today. The theme is the End of Civilization as We Know It.  The agent of destruction is the White Plague, a genetically engineered disease that kills only women.
headline: MADMAN'S REVENGE

title: The Burning House
author: Ann Beattie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BURNING HOUSE By Ann Beattie.  256 pp. New York: Random House. $12.95.   This is Ann Beattie's third collection of stories in eight years; it follows two novels, ''Chilly Scenes of Winter'' and the recent ''Falling in Place.'' By anybody's standards, this is a huge output, but Miss Beattie shows no signs of slackening.
headline: STORIES FROM THE AMERICAN FRONT

title: Cloak Of Darkness
author: Helen MacInnes
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CLOAK OF DARKNESS By Helen MacInnes.  342 pp. San Diego and New York: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich.  $13.95.   IN Helen MacInnes's novels - ''Cloak of Darkness'' is her 20th - every cafe and konditorei in Europe is a launching pad for terrorist activity, funded, encouraged and often directly organized by that source of all global evil, the K.G.B. The hand that brushes the Sacher torte crumbs off a lapel may shortly be carrying a Russian grenade. For many years Miss MacInnes has been the Claire Sterling of fiction; not even detente thawed her cold-war message. In ''Prelude to Terror'' (1978), the heroine, a Western agent, summed up the prevailing attitude: ''There's a job to be done, a necessary job.  Someone has to do it; we can't all sit back and watch the totalitarians take over.'' She goes on, ''I know it has to be done.  Or else we'll all end up regimented nonentities, scared to death to step out of line or raise our voices. Everything and everyone in place according to the book of Marx.''

title: Grace Abounding
author: Maureen Howard
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GRACE ABOUNDING By Maureen Howard.  175 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Co. $13.95.   THE term ''women's writer'' is usually one of dismissal. Women's writers are those who turn out the heavy-breathing romances, the gothics, the Harlequins, the standardized female fantasies. Maureen Howard once contemptuously summed up the whole genre, describing the techniques used by the author of a book someone gave her in college: ''How bathetic - the old girl's skill in uniting the witless young lovers. Here the tears. There the sighs.''   Mrs. Howard is herself a women's writer - but not in the dreary sense suggested above. Nor is she in the other sense of having written any kind of conventional feminist fiction, freeing her women from witless male dominance. Here the anger. There the career.

WE carry our history within us, in our habits, our language, our country, our names, our mores, our memories. To write from within that timescape is the prime function of the novelist whose subject is the past. The historian is concerned with facts, the archeologist with physical objects, but the novelist must find that universal center that is both contemporary and historically true if the novel is to transcend romance and create its own present. THE CAGE By Susan Cheever.  180 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Co. $11.95.

BOTH of these novels have as their focus the disintegration and sudden end of a long marriage. The wives are in their 40's, with grown children, and have never worked outside the home; the husbands are hard-driving and preoccupied professionals in their early 50's.  The women share other common ground: Each has an intense attachment to her past and in particular to her father. Their childhoods were so filled with, in one case, riches, in the other, affection, that it seems their present lives can never compare. But here, except for the skill that both authors employ in rendering the descriptive, intricate (and occasionally boring) details that make up the moments of domestic life, the novels part ways. Their considerable differences are due mostly to content and emotional depth.

SHADOW By Blaise Cendrars.  Translated and illustrated by Marcia Brown.  Unpaged. New York: Charles Scribner's Sons.  $12.95. (Ages 5 to 9)

As in Marcia Brown's other books (such as ''Once a Mouse'' and ''Cinderella,'' both of which won the Caldecott Medal) the illustrations in ''Shadow'' are splendid. Her unusual - and unusually vibrant - palette and bold images evoke an Africa whose mystery is riveting.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Reagan,
author: Lou Cannon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: REAGAN, By Lou Cannon.  Illustrated. 464 pp. New York:   NEAR the end of his splendid biography, ''Reagan,'' Lou Cannon writes, ''Most of the time, President Ronald Reagan was intuitively keen but intellectually lazy.'' This theme -that Mr. Reagan's career represents a triumph of personality and intuition over ignorance - runs through the book, supported by rich anecdotes and detail.   ''Reagan'' is a worthy successor to Garry Wills's ''Nixon Agonistes'' and James Wooten's biography of Jimmy Carter, ''Dasher.'' Those books are by journalists who rely on hard reporting rather than drugstore psychoanalysis to explain the inner forces that propel men into the White House. Mr. Reagan is the product of a simple place and time - Dixon, Ill., in the era when radio was king and the gang gathered at Fulf's Confectionary. It was, for Mr. Reagan, an age of innocence that imbued him with the boundless optimism that characterizes his activities today. ''Life,'' Mr. Reagan wrote more than 50 years ago in a bit of doggerel for his school yearbook, ''is just one grand sweet song, so start the music.''
headline: THE STYLE OF THREE PRESIDENTS

title: The Real Anti-Semitism In America
author: Nathan Perlmutter and Ruth Ann Perlmutter
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE REAL ANTI-SEMITISM IN AMERICA By Nathan Perlmutter and Ruth Ann Perlmutter.  303 pp. New York: Arbor House. $15.50.   ANTI-SEMITISM is a subject that makes smart people stupid. It comes from such disparate sources (the right and the left), embraces such contradictory ideas (the Jew as subversive, the Jew as exploiter), shows itself in so many guises and hides itself in so many pious rationalizations that it confounds our usual political categories. As a result, no other social issue has inspired less reasonable, nuanced argument or more blatant oversimplification, evasion and denial. If gentiles tend to resist recognizing any form of anti-Semitism more subtle than neo-Nazi ranting (that is, any form of which they themselves might be accused), Jews too often allow their political loyalties and preconceptions to determine which brands of anti-Semitism they will attack and which they will tolerate or explain away. Such double standards insure that our understanding of anti-Semitism remains fragmented and shallow, our opposition to it spasmodic and ineffective.
headline: ADVICE FOR SURVIVAL

title: Acceptable Losses

ACCEPTABLE LOSSES By Irwin Shaw.  303 pp. New York: Arbor House. $14.95.

LITERARY agent Roger Damon is sleeping peacefully in his Manhattan apartment, when at 3 in the morning he gets a mysterious telephone call from a stranger named Zalovsky. ''You've been a bad boy,'' Zalovsky says, ''and you're going to have to do something about it.'' By the end of the conversation Zalovsky has hinted that Damon will have to pay with his life for whatever he's done wrong. Is it just a call from another New York crank, pestering Damon because after years his squalid but scrupulously honest literary agency has finally come up with a huge best seller? Or is Zalovsky for real? Is he hunting Damon?
headline: TOO GOOD TO BE TRUE

SECOND HEAVEN By Judith Guest.  320 pp. New York: The Viking Press. $14.95.

''NEAT and orderly are out,'' says the suicidal boy in Judith Guest's first novel, ''Ordinary People.'' ''Rapturous. Passionate.  Use those. Pleasant and neat do not make it.''

In her second novel, ''Second Heaven,'' Judith Guest brings her own passionate moral concerns to a fine, old-style, high-drama confrontation with evil. Neat and orderly have now turned fanatic: A fundamentalist Christian father brutally beats his son for minute infractions of rules. Gale Murray, the 16-year-old abused boy, keeps running away, but the authorities bring him back. The father has convinced them that he is an upright family man who happens also to be a strict law-and-order disciplinarian. Nothing wrong with that, the authorities reason. We are, Miss Guest is careful to let us know, in the Middle West.
headline: THE WOUNDED HEALING THE WOUNDED

title: A Thousand Pardons
author: Katinka Loeser
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
A THOUSAND PARDONS By Katinka Loeser.  181 pp. New York: Atheneum. $12.95.

THE only mystery in this delightful book is its title: A thousand pardons for what? Katinka Loeser is not an apologetic person, nor is she (as Queen Victoria advised her granddaughter to be) humbleminded. She can't mean ''Excuse me for living'' when she gives unassailable proof that she has found a way to live the good life in a tottering world. Perhaps it's something she says when she steps on a cat. Perhaps she asks forgiveness for enjoying herself so much.
headline: LIFE WITH BETSY

title: The Good Son
author: Craig Nova
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GOOD SON By Craig Nova.  436 pp. New York: Delacorte Press/Seymour Lawrence. $15.95.   POP MACKINNON - ''a coarse, charming man, a lawyer, and a good one'' - wants his sons to follow his path: to be lawyers who know how to hunt and marry well; to be gentlemen who join that unassailable aristocracy which is earned by tough, no-nonsense cleverness and is protected by money. Son John disappoints Pop; he is killed in World War II. So son Chip - a fighter pilot who was shot down in the war but survived as a P.O.W. - becomes the title character of ''The Good Son,'' Craig Nova's fourth novel. In this dark, deep story of a father and son who love (and love to fight) each other, the good son is the one who will defeat, or even kill, his father with the father's own weapons.   I've read no better, no more bitter and ironic understanding of professional cunning and ambition since Joseph Heller's ''Something Happened.'' I've read no fuller mixture of human frailties, no more deft revelation of the chinks in moral armor since Robertson Davies's ''Leaven of Malice.'' I've read no more comic and painful exploration of the disasters of loneliness since Nabokov's ''Laughter in the Dark.'' As a virtuoso handling of first-person narration, ''The Good Son'' is as marvelous as Andre Brink's recent ''A Chain of Voices.''
headline: DESIRE, AMBITION AND FATHER

title: Heritage
author: Peter Driscoll

pull_quote: HERITAGE By Peter Driscoll.  437 pp. New York: Doubleday & Co. $17.95. MAX By Howard Fast.  395 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Co. $15.95.   PROFESSIONAL historians, having fragmented their subject into ever narrowing areas of special interest, are lately wondering aloud if there shouldn?ot be a return to what some of them call narrative history. After reading Peter Driscoll's latest novel, ''Heritage'' - a powerfully dramatic, sometimes lurid, always compelling story of the Algerian people's struggle against French rule from 1945 to 1962 - my sentiment is that the professors could take a lesson from someone like Mr. Driscoll, who apparently knows what history and narrative are all about.
headline: ALGERIA AND THE MOVIES

title: The Names
author: Don DeLillo
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE NAMES By Don DeLillo.  339 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.   AMERICA is an irresistible theme for American writers. This preoccupation is not usually patriotic; indeed it has nothing much to do with a country at all. America, in this context, is not a place or a nation but a condition of the soul tied to a habit of the possession of power.   Don DeLillo's first novel was called ''Americana.'' ''The Names,'' his seventh, is a dense, brilliant, ultimately rather elusive meditation on the relation of this half-mythological America to the historical world. A series of discreet markers gives us the time: ''This summer ... was the period after the Shah left Iran, before the hostages were taken.'' The principal settings of ''The Names'' are Greece and India, but the Americans in this novel mainly live in their own time and place, a sealed compartment, a subculture. They are executives of banks and insurance companies; they live in Athens, have lived in Teheran, Beirut, Cairo, Cyprus. They travel constantly to Turkey, Kuwait, Pakistan, Jordan, Zaire. ''It is like the Empire,'' one of them says. ''Opportunity, adventure, sunsets, dusty death.'' It is like tourism, another says: ''Errors and failings don't cling to you the way they do back home.'' Later we read: ''Americans used to come to places like this to write and paint and study, to find deeper textures. Now we do business.''
headline: AMERICANS ON THE PROWL

title: The Swan Villa
author: Martin Walser
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SWAN VILLA By Martin Walser.  Translated by Leila Vennewitz.  247 pp. New York: Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $14.95.   GOTTLIEB ZURN, the hero of this brief but brilliant novel, is a product of the German economic miracle, a lawyer who switched to real estate and rode the postwar boom to moderate affluence. Having done his bit to help develop the once grassy slopes of Lake Constance into high-rise condominiums, now in midlife he feels depressingly underdeveloped himself, obsolete and disposable, a banal character trapped in a banal dilemma. All Martin Walser does, in limpid prose and with the sure touch of a compassionate surgeon, is to bare the man's heart and trace the pathways of his pain. But in the process he evokes a life in our time, distinct from any other and yet subject to the same laws of supply and excessive demand that govern the lives of the multinational middle class throughout today's global village.   Like most young authors of the postwar German renaissance, Mr.  Walser - born in 1927 - made his debut under the aegis of Group 47, an association of veterans turned writers. The group fostered and facilitated the emergence of a stunning array of talent - from Hans Werner Richter, Alfred Andersch, Heinrich Boll and Gunther Grass to Hans Magnus Enzensberger, Ilse Aichinger, Hans Erich Nossack, Peter Handke and Uwe Johnson.
headline: THE EMPTY SUCCESS OF HERR ZURN

title: No Place On Earth
author: Christa Wolf
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
NO PLACE ON EARTH By Christa Wolf.  Translated by Jan van Heurck.  130 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $11.95.

CHRISTA WOLF is an East German novelist, essayist and scriptwriter whose prolific output has appeared in Germany over the past 30 years. Only three of her works, all novels, have been published in the United States. Yet I think of her as a poet - indeed, as the poet of starvation. This starvation can take many forms; it can be a hunger for food, for love, for mental grist, for truth. It springs from a deprivation of something essential, a basic nutrient of the spirit - room for the limbs to move, the mouth to speak and the heart to be free. At root, her theme is the lack of freedom.

Christa Wolf writes in a style that embodies her subject - spare, restrained, yet dotted like a trellis with budding flowers - about the difficulties of even finding one's own heart, mind and will in societies in which so much is controlled; and about the difficulty, once this self is found, of deciding on an expressive course of action.
headline: HEINRICH VON KLEIST COULD NOT LAST

title: Growing Up
author: Russell Baker
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GROWING UP By Russell Baker.  Illustrated. 278 pp. New York: Congdon & Weed. $15.   AS we all know from reading the higher fan journalism, funny people are really deeply unhappy. They had childhoods that make Charles Dickens's blacking factory seem like Charles Ryder's golden summer with Sebastian at Oxford.   And so I approached Russell Baker's autobiography, ''Growing Up,'' with high anticipation, expecting a heartening read about someone more miserable than I am. Alas, I was deeply disappointed. To come straight out with it, Russell Baker, who writes funny stuff three times a week for his Observer column in The New York Times, ruined my day. This is not the kind of book one can put down with a contented sigh: ''That poor son of a bitch.'' Instead of being a grim tale of drunken stepmothers and battered stepfathers, ''Growing Up'' is touching and funny, a hopeless muddle of sadness and laughter that bears a suspicious resemblance to real life.

title: Spacewar
author: David Ritchie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SPACEWAR By David Ritchie.  Illustrated. 224 pp. New York: Atheneum. $14.95.   EVER since the German army took over the German civilian rocket program before World War II, much of the world's military establishment has seen space as the ultimate battlefield. According to ''Spacewar'' by David Ritchie - a long essay, really, considering its brevity, tightness and selectivity -that view is expanding. The book may be too sketchy in the beginning, where Mr. Ritchie manages to telescope the early days of rocketry, from Tsiolkovsky to Goddard to von Braun, into 20 pages. However, that period has been written about exhaustively elsewhere, and the fact that we would still very likely be living in the pre-space age if it weren't for the German High Command is not news.   What is news, to me at least, is the manner in which the world's military has continued to dominate space in the 37 years since World War II ended; and it is this situation that Mr. Ritchie, a freelance science writer, outlines well.
headline: WHAT AND WHO IS UP IN SPACE

title: Anger
author: May Sarton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ANGER By May Sarton.  223 pp. New York: W.W. Norton & Co. $12.95.   IT seems natural to discuss May Sarton's 17th novel, ''Anger,'' in the context of the work that immediately preceded it - her remarkable book ''Recovering: A Journal 1978-1979'' - so linked, at times so nearly identical, are their major themes.   ''Anger'' is the story of a marriage of opposites: between the opera singer Anna Lindstrom, half-Italian, half-Swedish, artistic, passionate and verbal, and Ned Fraser, a Boston bank president who insists on making love with the lights out and achieves tender communication only with his dachshund. These two characters are the medium through which Miss Sarton voices her concern about intimacy, repression and self-knowledge. ''Anger'' sets out to prove the truth of a Rilke quotation initially invoked by Anna with her husband in mind: ''Perhaps everything terrible in us is in its deepest being something helpless that needs help.'' It would be a dense reader who failed to see that Ned's coldness has its roots in a protective reaction against early loss and guilt and that he ''needs help''; but the resolution of his problems and the reaching for this truth are too facile to have much impact.
headline: SOMETHING HELPLESS THAT NEEDS HELP

title: Deadeye Dick
author: Kurt Vonnegut
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DEADEYE DICK By Kurt Vonnegut.  240 pp. New York: Delacorte Press/ Seymour Lawrence. $14.95.   ''DEADEYE DICK'' is the life story, told by himself, of one Rudolph Waltz, born in Midland City, Ohio, in 1932 and now residing in Portau-Prince, Haiti, where he's the chef and co-owner (with his older brother) of a well-known hotel. Like many other books from the pen that brought us ''Jailbird,'' ''Slapstick'' and ''Welcome to the Monkey House,'' it's a riot of randomness. At age 12 young Rudy, schoolboy, fires off an unaimed round from a rifle belonging to his father's gun collection and accidentally kills a pregnant woman named Eloise Metzger, who's vacuuming her living room several blocks away when hit. Jailed for the deed, both Rudy and his eccentric father are viciously beaten by the police. (The cops bathe Rudy in ink and display him in a cage to selected visitors, who are encouraged to punch him out a little: ''I was regional theater.'') Lawsuits from the bereaved Mr. Metzger ruin the Waltz family financially (Rudy's father is heir to a drugstore chain fortune), and Midland Cityites bestow a mocking nickname on Rudy - the nickname that gives this work its title.
headline: A RIOT OF RANDOMNESS

title: Bech Is Back
author: John Updike
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BECH IS BACK By John Updike.  195 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.   SINCE 1970 Henry Bech has been one of John Updike's several alter egos. In ''Bech: A Book,'' Bech was the author of three novels and a miscellany and was beginning to find that leading the literary life was easier than writing. He was also a bachelor afraid to commit himself to marriage, and the fact that in this respect he was the opposite of Updike may have made him all the dearer to his creator.  But in ''Bech Is Back'' his dry period has stretched to 13 years, and though the descriptions of poor Bech's collisions with rare book collectors, Third World cultural attaches and sexual hostesses in the Commonwealth countries may be funnier than ever, they are sadder. He is running out of stalling tactics. At last he relinquishes his timidities, marries his mistress, finishes a long-awaited, bestselling book called ''Think Big'' and exchanges his shyness for disillusion, thereby becoming a formidable literary figure.  Henceforth if Bech gets into serious trouble he will be in the news, not merely quietly extinguished as a man or as an artist. And in accomplishing this ambiguously welcome transition, he is like Updike, which - though Updike evinces no undue interest in the books Bech writes -should keep him available for the future.
headline: A NOVELIST'S NOVELIST

author: Susanna Moore
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MY OLD SWEETHEART By Susanna Moore.  211 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Co. $12.95.   THERE is something fascinating about those elderly little children you see taking care of mothers who have never grown up, and most fascinating of all is the question of what becomes of the children after they themselves are grown. Do they ever get a second chance at the childhood they missed? What sort of parents do they make? In ''My Old Sweetheart'' Susanna Moore examines one such child - both as child and as adult - and the result is a first novel of considerable skill.

VEDI By Ved Mehta.  Illustrated. 258 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $16.95.
A FAMILY AFFAIR India Under Three Prime Ministers.  By Ved Mehta.  166 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $14.95.

MORE than a decade ago, Ved Mehta embarked on a project of extended self-location - in history and society as well as in family - and his family biographies (beginning with ''Daddyji'' in 1972) are reflections of larger themes. Access to metaphor has become Mr.  Mehta's great strength as a writer; what distinguishes his later work from his precocious early autobiography, ''Face to Face,'' is its ability to resonate beyond mere recitation.

title: In The City Of Fear
author: Ward Just
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN THE CITY OF FEAR By Ward Just.  291 pp. New York: The Viking Press.$14.95.   NOVELIST and short story writer Ward Just, a former reporter for The Washington Post, writes fiction from the standpoint of the idealistic generation that was summoned, as if by a clarion call, to the national capital by the election of John F. Kennedy to the Presidency in 1960, and then had to suffer over the next two decades such traumas, disappointments and disillusionments as the two Kennedy assassinations; the death of the Great Society dream with the huge, pointless expansion of the war in Southeast Asia; the bizarreries and scandals of the Nixon years - from carpet bombings and Cambodian incursions to the Presidential impeachment and the hasty pardon. At 46, having seen it all, Mr. Just bids to be considered the political novelist of his generation. He may even be considered for a rarer title, that of national novelist (have we had one since Henry Adams?), provided one believes that the capital and the nation are still in touch with each other these days for any essential purposes.
headline: MAKING IT IN WASHINGTON, AND NOT

title: Groundrush
author: Greg Barron
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GROUNDRUSH By Greg Barron.  309 pp. New York: Random House. $13.50. By MICHAEL MALONE   Is there a Montana novel? Perhaps. The middle-aged horse-training hero of Thomas McGuane's ''Nobody's Angel'' lives alone in Montana with his eccentric rancher grandfather; his pregnant sister commits suicide; his dad, a divorced test pilot, has died in a plane crash; he has love troubles and is full of ''sadness-for-no-reason.'' In Greg Barron's ''Ground-rush,'' the adolescent, football-playing hero, Beowolf Bailey, lives with an eccentric rancher grandfather; his mom died in childbirth; his dad, a smoke jumper, sky-dived to his death; Beowolf has love troubles (with his pregnant girlfriend) and is also victimized by an amorphous moroseness: ''His life was mired in thinking,'' in worrying about the future, about cancer, about President Nixon's Minuteman missiles in Condition Three Alert next door to his Rawlings, Mont., home.

title: Schindler's List
author: Thomas Keneally
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SCHINDLER'S LIST By Thomas Keneally.  Illustrated. 398 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $16.95.   WHEN the German Army invaded Poland in 1939, a swarm of carpetbaggers trailed after it, eager for the spoils of empire. They were the black marketeers and middlemen, the young sharks who knew how to get a general drunk and leave with a contract in their pockets. Among them was a young Sudeten German named Oskar Schindler, who had a reputation for womanizing and giving lavish parties for his influential friends.  Schindler knew how to make a bureaucrat happy, and he was rewarded with one of Cracow's plums. He was appointed Aryan treuhandler -read plunderer - of a prosperous Jewish-owned enamelware factory.
headline: A GOOD MAN IN A BAD TIME

title: The Four Wise Men
author: Michel Tournier
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE FOUR WISE MEN By Michel Tournier.  Translated by Ralph Manheim.  255 pp. New York: Doubleday & Co. $14.95.   IN his first novel, ''Friday,'' the highly regarded French novelist Michel Tournier reversed the relationship between Robinson Crusoe and Friday, with Friday, who is less limited than Crusoe, emerging as the ascendant figure. The novel, which transcended the cleverness of its idea, reimagined Defoe's fable into a resonant fable of its own.  In ''The Four Wise Men,'' Mr. Tournier again shows himself to be a philosophic novelist who likes to work with received material - the story of the Magi in this case -and play ironic variations on his subject, a writer for whom paradox and irony become a source of vision.
headline: BUT TAOR HAD A SWEET TOOTH

title: The Life Of John Berryman
author: John Haffenden
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LIFE OF JOHN BERRYMAN By John Haffenden.  451 pp. Boston: Routledge & Kegan Paul. $22.50.   ON Jan. 7, 1972, the poet John Berryman committed suicide by jumping off the Washington Avenue Bridge between St. Paul and Minneapolis. It was the second time that week he had resolved to kill himself . On Jan. 5 he left a note for his wife, Kate - ''I am a nuisance'' - and went off to do the deed. But he came back and wrote a poem about the episode, beginning, ''I didn't. And I didn't,'' and ending, after a dismal account of his life and job, ''Kitticat, they can't fire me.''
headline: SUICIDE WAS IN THE SCRIPT

title: The Crystal Child
author: Barbara Wersba
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE CRYSTAL CHILD By Barbara Wersba.  Illustrated by Donna Diamond.  36 pp. New York: Harper & Row/ Charlotte Zolotow.  $9.50. (Ages 9 to 12)

For this strange, cool little book, Barbara Wersba has dipped into what Tolkien calls the ''Cauldron of Story'' from which the Sleeping Beauty was drawn, as well as Snow White in her glass coffin and perhaps Maurice Sendak's ice baby -characters frozen in time, waiting for love to revive them.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Golden Hill
author: Shirley Lord
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GOLDEN HILL By Shirley Lord.  544 pp. New York: Crown Publishers. $14.95.   While some novels come to reviewers emblazoned with the label ''soon to be a major motion picture,'' ''Golden Hill'' arrives with the news that Shirley Lord, director of special projects for Vogue, is ''soon to be one of our most dazzling author/celebrities.'' After reading her novel, I can only conclude that author/celebrities are different from you and me. For one thing, they inhabit a world defined entirely by cliches. Their characters do things ''out of the blue'' when ''minutes passed like hours,'' ''legs turned to jelly'' or ''to water,'' and they ''racked their brains'' (sometimes they ''wracked'' them).
headline: FICTION IN BRIEF

title: The Joke
author: Milan Kundera
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE JOKE By Milan Kundera.  Translated by Michael Henry Heim.  267 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $14.95.   THE ever vigilant Party has already noted Ludvik Jahn's individualist deviations: ''You smile as though you were thinking to yourself.'' A student in Prague during the 1950's, Ludvik is a staunch Communist with but one chink in his ideological armor: He has a sense of humor. Irritated with his politically orthodox girlfriend - the kind called ''goodthinkful'' in Orwell's Newspeak - Ludvik sends her a teasing postcard: ''Optimism is the opium of the people!  A healthy atmosphere stinks of stupidity! Long live Trotsky!''   A boyish prank? An innocent joke? Not on Ludvik's life. He is soon brought up on charges at his Party cell and slyly excoriated by a friend and comrade, Pavel. Party and university expel poor Ludvik, and he is shipped off, for ideological rectification, to work as a penal laborer in the mines. On his occasional leaves from the mines, Ludvik has a frustrated love affair with a frightened, almost speechless girl named Lucie. It comes, like everything else in his life, to nothing.
headline: RED RULERS AND BLACK HUMOR

title: Blues For Charlie Darwin
author: Nat Hentoff
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BLUES FOR CHARLIE DARWIN By Nat Hentoff.  203 pp. New York: William Morrow & Co. $11.50. GOOSEFOOT By Patrick McGinley.  251 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $13.95. THE KINDNESS OF DR.AVICENNA By John Pearson.  265 pp. New York: A William Abrahams Book.  Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $15.50.   According to a recent Gallup poll, nearly half of all Americans believe God created man in his present, questionable form within the last 10,000 years. Considering that Charles Darwin's ''The Origin of Species'' was published in 1859, that's real blues for Mr. Darwin, to say nothing of the rest of us. But what Nat Hentoff suggests with the title of his latest novel - a police procedural about some particularly seamy goings-on in Greenwich Village - is, if anything, even worse news. One of his tough cops thinks that a form of social Darwinism might lead to a fascist state if the ''mad dogs'' are allowed to continue roaming our streets, leaving some 2,000 corpses in their wake each year.
headline: FICTION IN BRIEF

title: The Monster's Ring
author: Bruce Coville
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE MONSTER'S RING By Bruce Coville.  Illustrated by Katherine Coville.  87 pp. New York: Pantheon Books.  $8.95. (Ages 8 to 11)

Russell Crannaker is tired of running from the school bully, not getting a word in edgewise with his father, being babied by his mother.
headline: CHILDRENS'S BOOKS

title: Screenplay
author: MacDonald Harris
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SCREENPLAY By MacDonald Harris.  249 pp. New York: Atheneum. $12.95   ''IF you are like most people,'' the narrator tells us at the beginning of MacDonald Harris's new novel, ''you probably don't regard Los Angeles as a very enchanting city.''   We first hear from Alys as he reminisces about his cloistered youth as an only child, born of parents improbably named Dirk and Astree, growing up in St. Albans Place, a locked, private ''wonderland'' between Wilshire and Olympic Boulevards. His parents are beautiful, charming, curiously flat. At the end of Chapter One, on Alys's 18th birthday, they drive off on an excursion: ''As they disappeared down the street I saw them kissing, framed in the small rear window of the car.'' This happy ending to a charming short subject is punctuated by a fiery crash. Alys is left to his own devices, which create a very sophisticated feature picture indeed.
headline: ILLUSIONS OF ILLUSIONS

title: Terrorists And Novelists
author: Diane Johnson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TERRORISTS AND NOVELISTS By Diane Johnson.  257 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $14.50.   REMARKS aren't literature, Gertrude Stein famously remarked to Ernest Hemingway, and everybody more or less agrees. But good remarks - witticisms, epigrams, aphorisms, what you will - are luxuries no smart reader of verse or prose likes doing without. One strength of ''Terrorists and Novelists,'' a collection of reviews and reviewessays by a novelist and critic whose writing appears often in this journal and The New York Review of Books, is that it's jammed with good remarks. Miss Johnson observes - reviewing Norman Mailer on Gary Gilmore - that so-called true-life novels ''encourage ...  literary ambulance chasing.''
headline: INTELLIGENCE AT WORK

title: George Mills
author: Stanley Elkin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GEORGE MILLS By Stanley Elkin.  508 pp. New York: E.P. Dutton. $15.95.   IS there a writer anywhere more exasperating or whom we read with more delight and dismay than Stanley Elkin? None has such an ear for the language as we speak it or a readier, raunchier wit or a greater feel for the heart-rending vulgarities of our culture; at the same time, no writer I know of is so consistently undone by the unrestrained exercise of his own inherent gifts.   Arguably, his three finest works are ''The Living End,'' ''The Bailbondsman'' and ''The Franchiser.'' The protagonist of each is a middle-aged man, perhaps Jewish, certainly metropolitan (from Minneapolis, St. Louis or, in the case of the franchiser, any one of a dozen homogenous cities), though none is defined by his sex, region, religion so much as by his profession, his station in life.  Indeed, no comic writer since Dickens has portrayed so convincingly the way work shapes character, the way the routines of a job penetrate every action, every waking and even sleeping thought.
headline: GENERATIONS OF HORRIBLE FUN

title: Mozart
author: Wolfgang Hildesheimer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MOZART By Wolfgang Hildesheimer.  Translated by Marion Faber.  Illustrated. 408 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $22.50.   LET us put down our Mostly Mozart coffee mug with its copyrighted logo and enameled musical phrase, turn our eyes from stationery inscribed with the ''Elvira Madigan'' theme, remove the T-shirt graced with the bewigged profile, turn off the stereo playing one of the three dozen recordings of the ''Jupiter'' Symphony and imagine, for one moment, the man himself. Christened Johannes Chrysostomus Wolfgangus Theophilus. Born 1756. Died 1791.   As Wolfgang Hildesheimer reminds us again and again in this unusual biography, it is not so easy to visualize him. Can we imagine the composer of the Requiem playing billiards? (A billiard table with 5 balls and 12 cues was in the catalogue of his estate.) Can we imagine the composer of ''Cosi fan tutte'' writing scatological canons?  (Stefan Zweig even sent copies of Mozart's letters to Freud for consideration of their ''infantilism and coprophilia.'')
headline: DO ANGELS PLAY MOZART FOR GOD?

title: Leaders
author: Richard Nixon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LEADERS By Richard Nixon.  Illustrated. 371 pp. New York: Warner Books. $17.50.   WITH the one exception of Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew of Singapore, all the principal characters in Richard Nixon's new book were dead before the time of writing. Paul Freund has shrewdly observed that descriptions of the deceased often tell more about the author than about his subjects. And this reviewer, at least, found the book's reflection of Mr. Nixon's character and views no less interesting than what he tells us about the great and near-great whom he parades.    He has selected as his main subjects Winston Churchill, Charles de Gaulle, Douglas MacArthur and Shigeru Yoshida (considered jointly), Konrad Adenauer, Nikita Khrushchev and Zhou Enlai. Twelve other men, including David Ben-Gurion, Anwar el-Sadat and the Shah of Iran, and one woman, Golda Meir, are dealt with in a single chapter entitled ''A New World: New Leaders in a Time of Change.'' In theme and structure, therefore, ''Leaders'' is not unlike Winston Churchill's ''Great Contemporaries'' (1937). But there is no similarity of style or thought.
headline: A PRESIDENT ON HIS PEERS

title: Courier From Warsaw
author: Jan Nowak
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: COURIER FROM WARSAW By Jan Nowak.  Illustrated. 477 pp. Detroit: Wayne State University Press. $24.95.   DURING the summer of 1943, my wife and I were living, or rather hiding, in Jozefow, a small town near Warsaw. It was not the best of places. The Warsaw Ghetto had already been liquidated, and every few days SS units would appear, hunting for Jews to load on trucks or shoot on the spot. Needless to say, we were quite alarmed when one evening an unexpected knock was heard on the door. The unscheduled visitor turned out to be Zdzislaw Jezioranski, a young economist and one of my closest friends. We had graduated from the same Gymnasium in Warsaw in 1932 but had lost contact with each other before the war. I was a Jew, and he had come to see if he could help me. There was no time for a long conversation, our guest had to hurry into Warsaw before the curfew. We exchanged news about friends: the dead and the living. About himself, he said only that he belonged to the Underground, that we would not soon meet again and that his name was now Jan Nowak. Our meeting took place between his first and second mission as courier to Sweden for the underground Home Army. But, about this, Jezioranski-Nowak revealed nothing at the time.
headline: THE POLISH CONNECTION

title: A Lifetime Burning
author: Ellen Douglas
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
A LIFETIME BURNING By Ellen Douglas.  212 pp. New York: Random House. $13.95.

ELLEN DOUGLAS's fifth novel is a sad book about an intelligent, humorous, competent, sensual woman. If there were a checklist to count the blessings one's later life could bring, Corinne, the protagonist of ''A Lifetime Burning,'' could tick off every item: job (she's a professor of English literature at a small Southern college), husband (he's a doctor specializing in emergency medicine), children (three, all of whom have grown into admirable adults), psyche (no notable neuroses).
headline: NOT GOING GENTLE AT ALL

title: Summer Crossing
author: Steve Tesich
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SUMMER CROSSING By Steve Tesich.  373 pp. New York: Random House. $14.95.   STEVE TESICH wrote the screenplay of ''Breaking Away,'' one of the rare movies of recent times to delight us with a funny, touching, original tale of true-to-life terrestrial creatures coming of age in America. Now he has written ''Summer Crossing,'' which has to be counted a commercial and critical risk in today's supercharged literary marketplace. Mr. Tesich has committed a wholly traditional first novel. It is about a young man coming of age, feeling the joy and loss of first love, leaving his drab Middle Western home and going out into the world to become a writer. One can almost hear the ho-hums of certain sophisticated commentators programmed to respond to such subject matter by asking, ''So what else is new?''
headline: GROWING PAINS AND JOYS

title: The Almighty
author: Irving Wallace
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE ALMIGHTY By Irving Wallace.  403 pp. New York: Doubleday & Co. $15.95.

AT 58 Edward Armstead inherits ''the mines in Utah and Nevada. Oil wells in Oklahoma and Texas. The chain of markets. The New York real estate. The merchant ships. The art works.'' In all, his father's will leaves him a tidy $1 billion. But Edward is not happy, because he has not been left The New York Record, the newspaper his father built and ran autocratically. And Edward wanted that newspaper.
headline: NEWSPAPER STORY

title: The Twofold Vibration
author: Raymond Federman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE TWOFOLD VIBRATION By Raymond Federman.  175 pp. Bloomington, Ind.: Indiana University Press. $10.95.   Raymond Federman has long been associated with the literary avantgarde both as an editor and expounder of Samuel Beckett and as a coterie novelist. Idiosyncratic typography has been one of the trademarks of his fiction. Each page of his first novel, ''Double or Nothing'' (1971), for instance, was designed as an independent visual image, and his later ''Take It or Leave It'' (1976) not only employed various emblematic devices such as swooping or sagging lines but also omitted page numbers in order to emphasize that the sequence is arbitrary. As a result of Mr. Federman's studied refusal to succumb to the lures of sustained narrative, these earlier novels soon became tedious going. ''The Twofold Vibration'' is more conventional and more successful. Here Mr. Federman's wit and intelligence, his humor and sense of verbal play combine with his acute awareness of the problems of fiction to produce a mildly avant-garde cream puff with a science-fiction flavor.
headline: THE TIME IS NEW YEAR'S EVE, 1999

title: The Hite Report On Male Sexuality
author: Shere Hite
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE HITE REPORT ON MALE SEXUALITY. By Shere Hite. (Ballantine, $4.50.) Shere Hite rewrote portions of her 1981 best seller to produce this shorter version, which includes a new preface. Although her sample population - 7,239 men aged 13 to 97 - is not representative and her findings won't be news to therapists, our reviewer, Roger L. Gould, credited the book with pulverizing any remaining myths about ''normal'' male sexuality. The general reader, he said, might find it ''an eye opener in the tradition of the original reports of Alfred Kinsey.'' (Wardell B. Pomeroy's 1972 biography, DR. KINSEY AND THE INSTITUTE FOR SEX RESEARCH, has now been reissued by Yale University Press at $10.95 in paperback. It's a vivid and informative but not entirely objective portrait of Kinsey by a man who was his closest collaborator for 13 years.)

A PASSING SEASON By Richard Blessing.  201 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Co.  $11.95. (Ages 11 to 15)

It is to the credit of Richard Blessing, a published poet from Seattle, that his sports novel remains true to the traditional formula for fast pace and tension while at the same time focusing on a high school quarterback's complexity of character.

A PASSING SEASON

title: Goodbye, Mickey Mouse
author: Len Deighton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
GOODBYE, MICKEY MOUSE By Len Deighton.  337 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $14.95.

WHEN Len Deighton is in his usual good form, he makes it difficult for a reviewer to do his job properly. The narrative moves along so smoothly I forget to take notes, and once the action begins I don't want to stop to take any. After finishing ''Goodbye, Mickey Mouse,'' I felt as if I were back in school trying to fake a book report for Mr. Suitor's English class - ''I liked this book a lot. I learned many things I didn't know before, and it was very exciting.''
headline: PILOTS AND LOVERS

title: Rabbis And Wives,
author: Chaim Grade
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RABBIS AND WIVES, By Chaim Grade.  Translated by Harold Rabinowitz and Inna Hecker Grade.  307 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.   THE death in New York City in June of this year of the Yiddish writer Chaim Grade at 72 sparked a storm that seemed to rise straight from the pages of his novels. His widow, who is also the cotranslator of ''Rabbis and Wives,'' his latest English publication, did not inform anyone of her husband's death and had him buried privately in the presence of less than a handful of witnesses. The management and staff of The Jewish Daily Forward, the Yiddish paper in which Grade published most of his important work, reacted to what they felt was a deliberate slight and combined their praise for the dead writer with outbursts of injured honor. Meanwhile the bereaved readers, who would never have the concluding installments of the novel he left unfinished, mourned one of their favorite authors even as they marveled at the furor his death provoked.
headline: RELIGIOUS IMPERATIVES AND MORTAL DESIRES

title: Herbert Rowbarge
author: Natalie Babbitt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
HERBERT ROWBARGE By Natalie Babbitt.  216 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux.  $11.95. (Ages 14 and Up)

SOMEONE ought to start spreading the word that Natalie Babbitt is not only a children's writer. Granted, her books have the firmly defined story line that children love - as anyone knows who's watched a youngster sit mesmerized by ''Knee-Knock Rise'' or ''The Eyes of the Amaryllis.'' They're certainly plotted in a way that will lure the most phlegmatic young reader. But the style is so fine and subtle that grownups too will take real pleasure. ''Tuck Everlasting,'' for instance, is one of the best books ever written - for any age. You can picture a child rereading it every year or so, on into adulthood, and appreciating it at a deeper level each time.
headline:
CHILDREN'S BOOKS;
GOOD THINGS COME IN TWOS

title: The Golem
author: Isaac Bashevis Singer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE GOLEM By Isaac Bashevis Singer.  Illustrated by Uri Shulevitz.  85 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $10.95.

ISAAC BASHEVIS SINGER'S retelling of the legend of the golem is magical and compassionate, redolent with the warmth and philosophical wisdom for which this Nobel laureate is celebrated.  Economically stated, and accompanied by velvety black-and-white illustrations by Uri Shulevitz that sensitively complement the tone of the text, the legend shows the Jews of Prague in an imperiled situation. They are then offered, presumably by one of the 36 hidden saints, a chance to draw on their special chosen relation to God.  Rabbi Leib, combating the longstanding prejudice against the Jewish community, saves Reb Eliezer Polner from death by creating a golem who proves the false accusers wrong: The Jews have not put the blood of the child Hanka into their matzohs - only flour and water. Hanka is alive and well, simply sequestered by her father, Count Bratislawski, so that he could inherit her fortune and pay his debts.
headline:
CHILDREN'S BOOKS;
LONELY MONSTER

title: A Cry In The Night
author: Mary Higgins Clark
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
A CRY IN THE NIGHT By Mary Higgins Clark.  317 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $13.95.

JENNY MACPARTLAND is a soft touch. She gives her ne'er-do-well exhusband money even though she can barely afford the shabby one-room apartment in which she and her two small daughters live. Then one day happiness strikes: A rich and famous artist falls in love with her and after a whirlwind courtship, marries her, adopts the kids and whisks them all away to his luxurious but isolated family estate in Minnesota. Inevitably, as in all of Mary Higgins Clark's tales of horror, things soon begin to go slightly, then massively, awry.

title: Sweet Whispers, Brother Rush
author: Virginia Hamilton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SWEET WHISPERS, BROTHER RUSH By Virginia Hamilton.  215 pp. New York: Philomel Books. $10.95.  (Ages 11 to 15)   ''THE first time Teresa saw Brother was the way she would think of him ever after. Tree fell head over heels for him. It was love at first sight in a wild beating of her heart that took her breath. But it was a dark Friday three weeks later when it rained, hard and wicked, before she knew Brother Rush was a ghost.''
headline: FAMILY VISIONS

title: Regina
author: Leslie Epstein
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: REGINA By Leslie Epstein.  251 pp. New York: Coward, McCann & Geoghegan. $13.95.   WE know from Leslie Epstein's previous fiction - two novels and a collection of stories - that he has both a social conscience and masterly skills. We also know, especially from his last novel, ''King of the Jews'' (1979), set in a Jewish ghetto in Poland during World War II, that he has an imagination of catastrophe.   His new novel, ''Regina,'' is set in New York City in the 1980's, where inner catastrophes confront their external counterparts. One counterpart is the weather. It's midsummer; there's a heat wave and a drought. ''The sky above was white, blank, blazing.'' Water is rationed, but in any case the pipes only gurgle. Tempers are short.  People are out of work. They gather at night for vigils along the banks of the Hudson, ''perhaps like lemmings.'' They build bonfires, and they fish for eels. Somebody in the neighborhood (the Upper West Side) is killing women who, as it turns out, remind him of his mother. He stabs each of his victims exactly 27 times. Relations between the sexes and among parents and children are awry. ''It was a place as wicked as Babylon.''
headline: PARALLELS ARE EVERYWHERE

title: Confessions Of A Single Father
author: Jim Covington
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
CONFESSIONS OF A SINGLE FATHER By Jim Covington 181 pp. New York: The Pilgrim Press. $13.95.
FATHER AND SON By Darrell Sifford.  168 pp. Philadelphia: Bridgebooks/The Westminster Press. $9.95.
FROM the shelves of a modest private library I draw down some books: "My Father and Myself" by J. R. Ackerley, "Father and Son" by Edmund Gosse, "Photographs of My Father" by Paul Spike, "A Letter From My Father" (edited by Ward Smith's son, Page), "Best Father Ever Invented" by Mark Harris (and, ironically, about himself), "The Old Man and Lesser Mortals" by Larry L. King (collected essays, the title piece heart-stopping) and "Forgive the Father" by Howard Wolf, creator of the ultimate title in this genre. I recall Vladimir Nabokov's portrait, toneperfectly tough and tender, of his assassinated father in "Speak, Memory" and Frank Conroy's exactly befuddled memory of his in "Stop-Time." I call to mind Michael J.  Arlen's memorial to his father in "Exiles," and his exclamation in "Passage to Ararat": "Ah, fathers! How hard it is to be a father!"
headline: HOW HARD TO BE A FATHER

title: The Haunting
author: Margaret Mahy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE HAUNTING By Margaret Mahy.  135 pp. New York: Atheneum/ Margaret K. McElderry.  $8.95. (Ages 10 to 14)

When I started reading ''The Haunting,'' I had to reach for a pencil. There were passages to be noted, phrases neatly turned, descriptions that took one's breath away. Pause, if you will, over a ghost who swings ''from side to side, like an absent-minded compass needle searching for some lost North,'' and an old woman whose ''wrinkles were untidy - even wild as if time had played a careless game of tic-tac-toe all over her.'' Consider Barney, who ''felt Saturday sink into his bones even before he woke up properly,'' and Tabitha, who had the ''important, excited look of a person swollen out with secrets.''
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Cadillac Jack
author: Larry McMurtry
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CADILLAC JACK By Larry McMurtry.  395 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $15.95.   BY his own account, Cadillac Jack McGriff, 6 feet 5 inches of Texas manhood without his boots or Stetson, 35 years old and twice divorced, is a natural scout and a natural womanizer. Having done a stint as a bulldogger on the rodeo circuit, he retired to roam the country in his big pearl-colored Caddy with peach velour interior.  He now spends his days scouting - exploring back roads for antiques and collectibles, buying and selling what strikes his fancy, ''too curious, too restless, too much in love with the treasure hunt'' to specialize.
headline: A CAST OF AMERICAN ORIGINALS

title: The Literary Underground Of The Old Regime
author: Robert Darnton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE LITERARY UNDERGROUND OF THE OLD REGIME By Robert Darnton.  258 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press.  $16.50.

The French Enlightenment nursed prurient tastes as well as refined ones, and the literature that satisfied the former was more popular and more influential in prerevolutionary France than Rousseau's ''Social Contract.'' It, too, was called philosophy, but it featured such works as ''Venus in the Cloister, or the Nun in a Nightgown.'' There was a teeming literary underworld of pornographic fantasies about court and clergy. The history of that underworld lay unobserved in the commercial correspondence of a Swiss publishing house (the Societe typographique de Neuchatel). In 1965 Robert Darnton discovered the correspondence and his book gives us not only a history of 18th-century publishing but a notion of how the lower orders of literature contributed to the fall of the Old Regime.
headline: NONFICTION IN BRIEF

title: Shiloh And Other Stories,
author: Bobbie Ann Mason
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHILOH AND OTHER STORIES, By Bobbie Ann Mason.  247 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $12.95.   FOR several years short stories by Bobbie Ann Mason have been turning up - rather improbably, it seemed - in The New Yorker and The Atlantic. The improbability lay in the fact that Miss Mason writes almost exclusively about working-class and farm people coping with their muted frustrations in western Kentucky (south of Paducah, not far from Kentucky Lake, if that helps you), and the gap to be bridged empathically between her readership and her characters was therefore formidable. But formidable also is Miss Mason's talent, and her craftsmanship. ''Shiloh and Other Stories,'' her first collection, shows not only how good she can be but how consistently good she remains. The most improbable thing about this volume is that not a single page lags, hardly a paragraph fails, not one among 16 stories is less than impressive.
headline: PLAIN FOLKS AND PUZZLING CHANGES

title: The False Messiah
author: Leonard Wolf
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE FALSE MESSIAH By Leonard Wolf.  278 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Co. $13.95.   IN the spring of 1665, a Turkish Jew named Shabbatai Zevi proclaimed himself the Messiah, the promised redeemer who would usher in the apocalypse and gather the tribes of Israel in ecstatic union with God. He was neither the first nor the last to make such claims, but what distinguished Shabbatai Zevi from a host of other pseudo-Messiahs was the scope and tenacity of his influence. From Amsterdam to Budapest, from Jerusalem to Baghdad, whole communities were caught up in a sort of millennial hysteria, a mass movement with sufficient momentum to survive its leader's apostasy and death.
headline: ONE DAY HE SPOKE THE NAME OF GOD

title: Promise The Earth
author: Clive Irving
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PROMISE THE EARTH By Clive Irving.  402 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $15.95. A QUIVER FULL OF ARROWS By Jeffrey Archer.  189 pp. New York: Linden Press/Simon & Schuster. $9.95.   SET in the Middle East during World War I, ''Promise the Earth'' dramatizes the events that were to shape the politics of the area for the next seven decades and that have resulted - directly or indirectly, depending on one's bias - in the violence that convulses Lebanon and Israel today. Originally a journalist, Clive Irving maintains a confident grasp of facts while using fiction to explore the wider implications of events. His technique is to establish a more or less accurate historical context, then to populate it with real and imagined characters.
headline: A NOVEL AND SOME STORIES

title: Graven Images
author: Paul Fleischman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
GRAVEN IMAGES By Paul Fleischman.  Illustrated by Andrew Glass.  85 pp. New York: Harper & Row/ Charlotte Zolotow.  $9.95. (Ages 10 to 13)
By ANN CAMERON

The three stories in ''Graven Images'' concern characters who are deeply affected, maybe even possessed, by sculpted figures. In the lightest of these tales, ''Saint Crispin's Follower,'' a young shoemaker's apprentice lets his search for a servant girl's love be guided by the saint's figure on a broken weathervane. A series of comic misunderstandings leads him to his goal.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Loitering With Intent

IT'S heartening that after all these years the United States still has the capacity to bewilder Englishmen. ''There is a frozen supermarket dough which divides up by itself in the oven into small buns,'' Edmund Fawcett and Tony Thomas soberly report by way of beginning the last chapter of their pleasant and stimulating new portrait of American society, and they experience other odd epiphanies throughout their text. They see television soap operas as affirmation, for all the evil goings-on, of traditional family values; they see newspaper life-style sections as attempts to get people ''to recreate a manner of living that passed with the Gilded Age.'' They find American vacations ''astonishingly short'' and are amazed that Ronald Reagan could have been elected to the Presidency of a vast postindustrial nation in 1980 with a poster that depicted him as ''a ranger, a herd boss, a wagonmaster, or a cavalry captain,'' complete with Stetson hat.

''WE had fun doing it,'' Howard Hawks said of ''Scarface,'' the classic gangster movie he made in 1930, and ''fun'' would be a favorite word of his during his more than 40 years as an outstanding Hollywood director. Another favorite word was ''story.'' ''All I'm trying to do is tell a story,'' Hawks would insist whenever an earnest interviewer sought to dissect his talent. His films, Gerald Mast writes in ''Howard Hawks, Storyteller,'' went about ''their cheerful business of telling lucid stories.'' There was ''something uniquely American about the artistic aspirations'' of this director, whose ''urge was not to do something difficult (both for the artist and his audience) but something apparently easy, something fun.'' He built stories ''to accomplish the task that entertaining stories are supposed to accomplish in a democratic culture: not to exclude all except the specially equipped but to include as many as possible.''

author: Edward Shorter
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A HISTORY OF WOMEN'S BODIES By Edward Shorter.  398 pp. New York: Basic Books. $24.95.   Up till now women's bodies have had a good press.  Artists have nearly always thought well of them.  Initially their reproductive and nurturing potentialities were stressed, but more recently the emphasis has been upon the erotic aspects of the female nude.  This is hardly surprising, given the human male's hair-trigger response to visual stimuli.  Biologists have been equally flattering about women's bodies as reproductive machines that turn out children in such numbers that today man has crowded most other mammals off the face of the earth, leaving only the insects to compete.  Demographers have found that women's bodies last longer than those of men, that their life expectancy at birth is higher.  The economic historians, when they stop to think about the matter, also have nothing but praise for women's bodies, which have adapted remarkably to the long, backbreaking bending work in the fields imposed by postneolithic agriculture.
