By CATHLEEN SCHINE   EDITORS pull Maalox from drawers in scarred desks; reporters down Valium with bitter coffee gulped from Styrofoam cups; copy boys buzz about the latest staff suicide. In Bernard Weinraub's first novel, the newsroom of The Star, a failing New York daily, swarms with the sort of cliches no work of the power-and-passion school should be without. outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
CHRONICLE OF MY MOTHER By Yasushi Inoue.  Translated by Jean Oda Moy.  164 pp. New York : Kodansha International. $14.95.

ALTHOUGH Yasushi Inoue is one of the most respected novelists in Japan, he is not well-known outside his country. He is mainly a writer of historical fiction, but in ''Chronicle of My Mother'' he gives a factual account of his mother's long decline into senility.  The book demonstrates the differences between Japanese and Western attitudes towards old age; but it is also a remarkable witness to the fact that these differences are finally without the slightest importance. Aging and loss renders us all, both those who suffer it and those who, for the moment, merely observe it, equally helpless and universally stripped of some of our more comfortable assumptions.

title: How He Saved Her
author: Ellen Schwamm
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HOW HE SAVED HER By Ellen Schwamm.  274 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.   ELLEN SCHWAMM'S first novel, ''Adjacent Lives'' (1978), was a welcome addition to its kind, the novel of adultery. Its stylish New York milieu provided the setting for a scrupulous, subtle examination of an adulterous pair - appealing characters of literate energy and reflectiveness, each existing as fully in the real world of family and profession as in the urgent temporary universe of the love affair. ''Adjacent Lives'' asked hard questions about love, death and the death of love; it introduced Miss Schwamm as a writer of ripe sensibility and intelligence.   ''How He Saved Her'' has much in common with the earlier work, but it considers the end of a marriage, a woman's passage from the safety of her own chic and her husband's money to a life of curious selfrealization instigated by her lover. It is a somewhat longer and considerably more ambitious novel than ''Adjacent Lives,'' if not an entirely likeable one. Its wide social and psychological range provides many opportunities for Miss Schwamm to exercise her mordant subtlety, and she has taken many more risks than she did in her first novel.

EGION,'' a sequel to Mr. Blatty's enormously successful novel, ''The Exorcist,'' is a tightly written supernatural police procedural set in Washington. title: Shenfan
author: William Hinton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHENFAN By William Hinton.  Illustrated. 785 pp. New York: Random House. $25.   DURING the two and a half years I lived in Peking, I frequently saw specters from China immemorial. Here and there in Peking, in the city's broad avenues and narrow alleys, were sturdy, dusty, padded and patched visitors from the countryside. They wore black jackets and thick pants, carried plastic satchels on staves slung over their shoulders and appeared suspicious of the city's traffic, commercialism and noise. Many of these rural folk were there to petition the Government to correct wrongs - beatings, firings and seizures of property - that they said had been done by provincial officials. They were living reminders of the existence of a little-known China stretching for thousands of miles beyond the largely urban zones to which foreigners are restricted.   It is not that China's rural areas are entirely off-limits.  Journalists, diplomats, scholars, even tourists can pay brief visits to selected collective farms, where they get statistics-laden briefings by local leaders and are allowed to look for a few hours at schools, clinics, workshops, fields and a home or two. But such visits, always brief, fall far short of a prolonged, intensive study of conditions in China's countryside, where life has been changed by three decades of uninterrupted revolution. The foreigner who is allowed to live among the peasants is rare indeed.

pull_quote: FLASHBACKS By Timothy Leary.  Illustrated. 397 pp. Los Angeles: J.P. Tarcher/Distributed by Houghton Mifflin Co. $15.95.   The dawning of the age of Aquarius provided a new career for Timothy Leary. A researcher and teacher of psychology at Berkeley, then at Harvard, he became the LSD guru of the 1960's. His slogan ''Turn on, tune in, drop out'' answered the ethical and metaphysical needs of part of a generation. His image is fixed in the history of the period - that handsome smile on posters, that ardent manipulation of the media, that assumption of the dual role of genial cutup and philosopher to the Youthquake. author: Michael Novak

pull_quote: CONFESSION OF A CATHOLIC By Michael Novak.  221 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $12.95. By RICHARD GILMAN   CONTEMPORARY confessional books, a thriving industry, most often comprise selected revelations by celebrated personalities and are either flamboyant cautionary tales or sly incitements to envy.  Michael Novak's book is in a rather older and nobler tradition, that of an avowal of faith or account of its vicissitudes. The exemplary works are, of course, St. Augustine's ''Confessions'' and Cardinal Newman's ''Apologia pro vita sua.'' If I put Mr. Novak in that line, I mean it as a technical description, not praise. He's neither a tortured, eloquent soul nor a compelling expositor of reasons for belief, but a conventionally pious, less than moderately charitable and more than professionally pompous spokesman for a politicalreligious credo.

PINOCCHIO'S NOSE By Jerome Charyn.  384 pp. New York: Arbor House. $15.95.

author: Iris Murdoch

pull_quote: THE PHILOSOPHER'S PUPIL By Iris Murdoch.  576 pp. New York: The Viking Press. $17.75.   IN Plato's allegory of the cave, men are imagined as dwelling underground, necks and legs fettered so that they cannot look around to see the source of light but are condemned to see only passing shadows, to which they give various names and meanings. This is our commonly experienced reality. If an individual was freed of his shackles and forced to confront the source of light, he would be dazzled and blinded and might respond by preferring the shadows he had seen before, believing them to be clearer. Only by force can the shadow-enthralled be awakened to the genuine source of light -for Plato, the idea of the good, for Platonists of more recent times, God.

author: Jorie Graham
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EROSION By Jorie Graham.  83 pp. New Jersey: Princeton University Press.  Cloth, $12.50. Paper, $6.95.   ORIE GRAHAM'S second book brings the presence of poetry into the largest question of life, the relation of body and spirit, a relation more often considered by theologians and philosophers these days than by poets. Miss Graham's subject is the depth to which the human gaze can penetrate, the opening in reality into which the poet can enter.  Under the clothed she seeks out the naked; over the soil, the air; inside the integument, a kernel; through the cover of the grass, the snake; from the bowels of the earth, the disinterred saint. Against writers who press against the opacity and resistance of the material world, she suggests its profundity and penetrability - though there seems to be no stopping place for that penetration.

AN interesting scene or two in the 65-year history of relations between the United States and the Soviet Union has been played by an extraordinarily affluent group of Americans, namely Armand Hammer, Averell Harriman, Cyrus Eaton, David Rockefeller and Donald Kendall.  (Mr. Kendall, the youngest and the only one who could conceivably require identification, is the man who brought Pepsi-Cola to the Russians in exchange for a variety of more stimulating intoxicants for the American market.) These men have had much closer relationships with the Soviet leadership than run-of-the-mill diplomats, foreign policy specialists or politicians. ''Red Carpet'' by Joseph Finder takes up the history of their Russian relationships.
headline: MOSCOW'S FAVORITE CAPITALISTS

title: Doctor Blues
author: Mark Smith
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
DOCTOR BLUES By Mark Smith.  428 pp. New York: William Morrow & Co. $15.95.

LIKE those mythic heroes of unknown lineage who come from the sea, the major character and narrator of Mark Smith's sixth novel is found as an infant at the ocean's edge. "Dr. Blues," then, is a contemporary retelling of that most familiar of fictional journeys - a hero's quest for identity. To carry his story along, Mr. Smith depends upon three conventional types of narration: the comedy of manners, the mystery story and the adventures of a man on the road.  The only other ovel I know of that uses these narrative devices for the same purpose is Henry Fielding's "Tom Jones." But if "Tom Jones" and "Dr. Blues" seem to have something in common in terms of structure, they are antithetical in nearly every other respect.

In Fielding's novel, Tom's seemingly random movement from inn to inn leads him to his rightful heritage and happiness with his beloved. In "Dr. Blues," however, the hero, George Montrichard, gains nothing. Mr. Smith uses the three types of narrative to raise conventional expectations so that he can demolish them. His point seems to be that, in our more dangerous and ambiguous age, society cannot provide us with identity. Today, a search for identity must carry beyond our social environment, back all the way to our human beginnings.
headline: THE PAST INSIDE US

title: Short Flights
author: Barbara Probst Solomon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHORT FLIGHTS By Barbara Probst Solomon.  313 pp. New York: The Viking Press. $18.75.   HIGH up in her New York apartment with a perfect view of Central Park, a woman in her middle 40's is visited by a seductive Spanish novelist. He is not the first one she has known, nor will he be the last. ''My attitude concerning European men,'' Barbara Probst Solomon writes in this second volume of her engrossing memoirs, ''always has been: serve them three perfect meals a day; keep the steam heat shut off, bottled water in the refrigerator, and the blinds drawn tight across the windows at night. After that, I expect them to clue into my needs. Well, there is one more thing. Never ask too many questions.''
headline: SEDUCED BY SPAIN

title: August
author: Judith Rossner
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AUGUST By Judith Rossner.  376 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Co. $15.95.   LIKE Parisians, shrinks leave town in August. If they're New York shrinks, they flock to the Hamptons, where for one brief month no patients interrupt their lives. The patients, meanwhile, must fend for themselves. Along with the shorter breaks at Christmas and Easter, the recurrence of the August hiatus lends a rhythm to both sides of the psychoanalytic relationship. Enduring it or delighting in it, patient and analyst must somehow come to terms with August - the ritualized intrusion of time into the timeless world of the analytic session.   Judith Rossner's new novel takes its title and form from this fact of psychoanalytic sociology. Famous as a clinician of disordered minds - most memorably in ''Looking for Mr. Goodbar'' and ''Emmeline'' - Mrs. Rossner now turns her attention to the scene where disorders are supposed to get rectified. In meticulous detail, she narrates the five-year analysis of Dawn Henley by Dr. Lulu Shinefeld, the one a blond New England teen-ager, the other a fortyish Jewish Manhattanite. In the ordinary course of things, two such different women would never meet, but there's nothing ordinary about analysis, and as the two women grow and change, they make permanent marks on each other's lives.Walter Kendrick, who teaches English at Fordham University, is the author of ''The Novel Machine.''
headline: THE ANALYST AND HER ANALYSAND

title: The Montgolfier Brothers And The Invention Of Aviation, 1783 1784
author: Charles Coulston Gillispie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MONTGOLFIER BROTHERS AND THE INVENTION OF AVIATION, 1783 1784 By Charles Coulston Gillispie.  Illustrated. 210 pp. Princeton, N.J.: Princeton University Press. $35.   LONG ago, back when Johnny Carson was Jack Paar, the producers of ''The Tonight Show'' found a guaranteed laugh-getter in a compilation of early silent films of would-be aviators doing their best to get off the ground. It was impossible not to laugh as, one by one, the eager birdmen attempted without success to flap or leap or furiously peddle them-selves into the air - until you realized that real spines were snapping, real skulls were breaking. The struggle to fly has been a deadly serious business from the very first, as ''The Montgolfier Brothers and the Invention of Aviation, 1783-1784'' makes clear, but it has always been accompanied by unintended comedy.
headline: DREAMY JOSEPH AND BUSINESSLIKE ETIENNE

title: The Fashion System
author: Roland Barthes
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE FASHION SYSTEM By Roland Barthes.  Translated by Matthew Ward and Richard Howard.  303 pp. New York: Hill & Wang. $20.50.

FOR more than two decades, the late Roland Barthes was the glass of Parisian intellectual fashion, a sort of literary Dior who could spin out theories, myths and aphorisms to suit every occasion.  Wrestling matches, soapsuds, Garbo and steak all found their way into his work. He had the knack of seeing such things as woven into a seamless web of significance. In Barthes's writings, it often seems that the medieval doctrine of signs, according to which each flower and leaf is a little message from God, has been transplanted from the natural to the social world.
headline: SPEAKING THROUGH OUR CLOTHES

title: Widows
author: Ariel Dorfman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WIDOWS By Ariel Dorfman.  Translated by Stephen Kessler.146 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $11.95. SOUTH OF NOWHERE By Antonio Lobo Antunes.  Translated by Elizabeth Lowe.  154 pp. New York: Random House. $11.95.   ''WIDOWS'' is the first work of fiction by the prolific Chilean exile Ariel Dorfman to be published in this country, and it has a curious publishing history. As Mr. Dorfman explains in a brief dedicatory statement, he wanted to write a novel about the plight of the ''missing'' of Chile and the other southern cone countries of Latin America and about the torturous life of their distraught families. Had he written such a story with its true setting, he explains, it would never have been published in his native land. So he invented a Danish author named Eric Lohmann, a member of the anti-Nazi resistance in occupied Denmark in World War II who was supposed to have written this ''masked'' novel about Denmark by setting the story in what appears to be Greece during a similar moment of political oppresssion.
headline: THE 'DISAPPEARED' AND THE JETTISONED

title: Good Thunder
author: John Solensten
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GOOD THUNDER By John Solensten.  214 pp. Albany: State University of New York Press. $12.95. BABY SWEET'S By Raymond Andrews.  Illustrated by Benny Andrews.  212 pp. New York: The Dial Press, $15.95.   "GOOD THUNDER" is the co-winner of this year's Associated Writing Programs novel contest, and it proves that academia is not always the kiss of death. It is, in fact, a wonderful novel of the rituals of growing up. The characters are vivid, and the story is profoundly moving. The language at its best is honest, tough and as simple as headstones chiseled from rough rock.
headline: AMONG INDIANS AND GEORGIANS

title: Children Without Childhood
author: Marie Winn
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
CHILDREN WITHOUT CHILDHOOD by Marie Winn 224 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $13.95

MARIE WINN'S "Children Without Childhood" is a big concoction of complaints about the way we raise our children today. The author, a journalist whose last book was "The Plug-in Drug: Television, Children, and the Family," argues that childhood, which since the late Middle Ages has ideally been a period of happy innocence and protected nurturance, has become an "Age of Preparation" for the grim realities of adult life. We used to shelter our children, Miss Winn writes, from the "knowledge of sexuality...suffering, injustice, deceit, sorrow, death." Nowadays, she argues, most American parents not only let their children know about their grief, but also use their children as counselor/confessors from whom both consolation and absolution are sought. What she terms a "truly new parental style" - one in which adults seek to relate to their children as equals - is robbing the current generation of children of their childhood.

Some of the issues she raises (teen-age sexuality, the effects of television, the easy availability of drugs) merit a balanced discussion, but Miss Winn, unfortunately, never supplies a serious analysis of the real problems parents face in raising their youngsters in today's complex world. Instead, she has filled her book with misreadings of the work of psychoanalytic thinkers and child-development experts.
headline: CHILDREN AS VICTIMS

title: Winter Music
author: Karen Rile
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WINTER MUSIC By Karen Rile.  293 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Co. $15.95.   ONE of the most agreeable fringe benefits of reading novels is the visit to someone else's milieu. ''Winter Music,'' Karen Rile's excellent first novel, admits us to the small world of classical musicians in Philadelphia during the late 70's. Like many other professional worlds, it is a complicated network of ambitions and adjustments, past histories and present dramas, loves and friendships both current and lapsed. Miss Rile's cast of characters is very large. A brief attempt at charting all the connections resulted in a page of crisscrossed lines of force (it might be more appropriate to express the connections as recurrent musical phrases, themes and leitmotifs).
headline: HARMONIES AND DISCORDS

title: Out Of The Forties
author: Nicholas Lemann
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OUT OF THE FORTIES By Nicholas Lemann.  Illustrated. 147 pp. Austin, Tex.: Texas Monthly Press. $21.95.   HOW comforting it would be to go and live in the safely defined past if we were not certain that it led obstinately to the chaotic present. Books involving the national memory, especially those containing pictures, inspire a reverie whose satisfaction with the past has a quality of unspoken misery, full of a longing for youth and promise that we associate with a perspective just this side of the grave. In this antidote to sentimental memoirs, Nicholas Lemann manages to mingle nostalgia with bitterness, anger with pride in a fashion reminiscent of Michael Lesy's now semiclassic ''Wisconsin Death Trip.''   ''Out of the Forties'' proceeds like a series of mystery stories.  With the modest assumption that the old, if properly excavated, can tell us something we need to know about the new, Mr. Lemann combines arresting photographs of the 1940's with his own inspired detective work of the 1980's. The photographs are clues; Mr. Lemann's stories become the solutions. Beginning with 85,000 photographs shot for Standard Oil under the supervision of the photo-documentarian Roy Stryker, Mr. Lemann's first task was to winnow them down to a few score that could represent the period. He then indulged a fantasy we have all had when we see a gripping snapshot: Whatever happened to that steelworker or schoolgirl? He went and found out.
headline: TIME EXPOSURES

title: Tender Prey
author: Patricia Roberts
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TENDER PREY By Patricia Roberts.  263 pp. New York: Doubleday & Co. $13.95. SPEAK, ANGEL By Mary Elsie Robertson.  210 pp. New York: Atheneum. $12.95.   IS it mere coincidence, or can it be a sign and portent for our times that the two crime novels under review, ''Tender Prey'' by Patricia Roberts and ''Speak, Angel'' by Mary Elsie Robertson, follow parallel courses?
headline: IN THE ORBIT OF MENACE

title: Some Tame Gazelle
author: Barbara Pym
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOME TAME GAZELLE By Barbara Pym.  252 pp. New York: E.P. Dutton. $13.95.   ''IF only one could clear out one's mind and heart as ruthlessly as one did one's wardrobe,'' Belinda Bede muses toward the end of ''Some Tame Gazelle.'' But, of course, one can't, and her words sum up her situation in Barbara Pym's first novel, originally published in England in 1950 but not previously issued here. Belinda is a spinster in her mid-50's who since college has been fruitlessly in love with Henry Hoccleve, now an archdeacon and the vicar of her local church. Miss Pym doesn't treat Belinda's thought as a summation; it's just a single sentence dropped into the middle of a conversation with her sister, Harriet, about whether or not to get rid of an old green dress. All the big moments in this novel are like that - quiet, offhand realizations presented without a trace of bravado, as if they were accidents. They astonish only when one steps away from them and sees how deftly they are woven into and illuminate the uneventful surface of the narrative. A big scene, confrontation, consummation of any kind - all are un thinkable. Yet Miss Pym's restraint isn't an evasion but precisely the point.
headline: RESTRAINT IS THE POINT

title: Century French Literature
author: Germaine Bree
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
CENTURY FRENCH LITERATURE By Germaine Bree.  Translated by Louise Guiney.  390 pp. Illinois: The University of Chicago Press. $25.

SIXTY pages into her nimble, if promiscuous, study of literary history, and Germaine Bree is writing what I took to be a suicide note: ''From 1920 on ... actual literary life bore no resemblance to the ordered sequences presented by studies of literary history,'' she writes. To which one is bound to rejoin, ''Did it ever?'' Miss Bree cannot be accused here of having reduced French literary life after 1920 to ''ordered sequences''; rather the reverse, but she is writing literary history, so that it is a mite defeatist of her to confide such doubts about the genre.
headline: LITERATURE TO WRITING

title: Moon Deluxe
author: Frederick Barthelme
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MOON DELUXE By Frederick Barthelme.  240 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $15.95.   "MOON DELUXE" is a first collection of stories by Frederick Barthelme, and it can be said at the outset that it's impossible to conceive of any writer doing what he does any better than he does it. Part of what he does consists of delineating the malaise of the unattached middle-class male. The other part is sheer technique. His textures are impeccable: Rich, brightly colored, they seem to float on an underlying vacancy like mirages, leaving the reader dizzy and a little sunstruck. He has a hard, shiny, many-faceted insect's eye for the surfaces of things - seedy, greasy, plastic-coated things or lush, expensive, meretricious things - second only to Raymond Chandler's. His dialogue is faithful to the vernacular, totally believable, and at the same time it seems to have been bounced at an odd angle off some wall the reader can't see. If Mr. Barthelme hasn't been spotted as a brilliant screenwriter-in-embryo yet, he will be soon.
headline: MALE AND LONELY

title: Lead Time
author: Garry Wills
pull_quote: LEAD TIME: A Journalist's Education.  By Garry Wills. 389 pages. Doubleday & Company. $18.95.   WITH his talent for the new journalism and his taste for the new politics, Garry Wills fitted naturally among the writers who enlivened the pages of Esquire in the late 1960's and into the 70's. A few of his articles from those years are reprinted in ''Lead Time'' along with later contributions to The New York Review of Books, New York magazine, The New York Times Magazine, Playboy and other publications.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Nuclear Hostages
author: Bernard J. O'Keefe,
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NUCLEAR HOSTAGES By Bernard J. O'Keefe, 252 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Co. $14.95.    MOST books on nuclear strategy are the work of academics who feed on each other's writings, few of whom have seen a battlefield or the explosion of even a conventional bomb. The ''taking out'' of towns and cities, of command posts and airfields, in such books has become a cliche devoid of human content. Now at last we have a book written by someone who appreciates from firsthand experience the limitless destructive power of the forces that hold together the subatomic particles of matter. ''Nuclear Hostages'' pulls one up with a jolt.
headline: INVENTING ANNIHILATION

title: Moscow Women. Thirteen Interviews
author: Susan Jacoby
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MOSCOW WOMEN Thirteen Interviews.  By Carola Hansson and Karin Liden.  Translated by Gerry Bothmer, George Blecher and Lone Blecher.  Introduction by Gail Warshofsky Lapidus. Illustrated. 194 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. Cloth, $16.95. Paper, $7.95.   IN 1969 the November issue of the well-known Soviet magazine Novy Mir was held up by official censors while they decided what to do about a novel that was already set in type. Problems with the censors were nothing new for the magazine, which had published Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's ''One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich'' in 1962 and whose editor, the late Aleksandr Tvardovsky, continued to fight cultural restrictions as the political climate grew more repressive in the late 60's.
headline: By SUSAN JACOBY; Susan Jacoby is the author of "Inside Soviet Schools.'' Her ''Wild Justice: The Evolution of Revenge'' will be published this fall.

title: The Collected Poems, 1945-75
author: Robert Creeley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE COLLECTED POEMS, 1945-75.  By Robert Creeley.  671 pp. Berkeley: University of California Press. $28.50.   BUT for the size of this book, I would not believe that Robert Creeley is 57 now. ''All that was in print is here,'' Mr. Creeley says in his preface: everything printed in book or magazine or broadside during a 30-year span ''like some ultimate family reunion!'' There is ''a sense of increment, of accumulation,'' he writes. He's pleased by the three decades' continuum:    ONE THING done, the rest follows.
headline: ROBERT CREELEY'S CONTINUUM

title: A Journey In Ladakh
author: Andrew Harvey
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A JOURNEY IN LADAKH By Andrew Harvey. 236 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Co. $13.95.   THE journey in the title of Andrew Harvey's book has a double meaning that reflects the dual nature of the work itself. Mr. Harvey, a young poet and Shakespearean scholar, has on one level written a travel book of the sort in which the English have specialized since the early days of the Empire: an account of a trip to a remote corner of the world, with the expected descriptions of scenery and customs and the equally expected anecdotes concerning not only the natives but eccentric fellow-travelers encountered along the way. More urgently, however, ''A Journey in Ladakh'' records a spiritual quest that culminates in the author's instruction in the techniques of esoteric meditation by a Tibetan guru of great local renown.   Like the secular travel book, the spiritual odyssey from West to East (which may or may not involve a physical journey) has developed certain conventions of its own. We can observe them in the writings of such diverse seekers as Aldous Huxley and Christopher Isherwood or, more recently, in Paul Zweig's account of his involvement with the late Swami Muktananda in ''Three Journeys.''
headline: TRAVELING AND SEEKING

title: Overdrive. A Personal Documentary
author: William F. Buckley Jr. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OVERDRIVE, A Personal Documentary. By William F. Buckley Jr. Illustrated. 262 pp. New York: Doubleday & Co. $16.95   I CANNOT imagine that anyone who reviews this book will fail to mention the part about the limousine, so I may as well begin with it. Only a few pages into ''Overdrive,'' William F. Buckley Jr. gets into his limousine with Jerry the driver, Rebeca the Guatemalan, Olga the Ecuadorian and Rowley the dog, and the occasion inspires him to reveal the circumstances under which he had the car custom built. ''What happened,'' he writes, ''was that three years ago, when it came time to turn in my previous car, which had done over 150,000 miles, the Cadillac people had come up with an austerity-model limousine, fit for two short people, preferably to ride to a funeral in. The dividing glass between driver and driven was not automatic, there was no separate control for heat or air conditioning in the back, and the jump seats admitted only two. . . . This simply would not do: I use the car constantly, require the room, privacy, and my own temperature gauge. . . . There was, as usual, a market solution. You go out (this was in 1978) and buy a plain old Cadillac. You deliver to a gentleman in Texarkana. He chops it in two, and installs whatever you want. Cost? Interesting: within one thousand dollars of the regular limousine, and I actually don't remember which side.''
headline: EIGHT RICH AND BUSY DAYS

title: In Praise Of What Persists
author: Stephen Berg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN PRAISE OF WHAT PERSISTS Edited by Stephen Berg.  289 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $14.95.   Stephen Berg is a poet and one of the founders of The American Poetry Review.
headline: NONFICTION IN BRIEF

title: The Kingfisher
author: Amy Clampitt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE KINGFISHER By Amy Clampitt.  149 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf.  Cloth, $11.95. Paper, $6.95.  PERU    By Herbert Morris.  80 pp. New York: Harper & Row.  Cloth, $14.50. Paper, $6.95.    THE ISLAND-MAKER    By Roy Marz.  100 pp. Ithaca, N.Y.: Ithaca House. Paper, $6.     AMERICAN literary circles are fascinated by young poets (even, as in the Yale series, ''younger poets''). Although the attention is valuable for recognition and encouragement of promise, it often means that poets who have been at it for some time and who are thus more likely to turn out finished work are ignored. A recent and noteworthy trend, then, is the appearance of first books by poets who, for better or worse, cannot be described as young.   Here are three such first books. While Roy Marz no longer writes poetry (his active career as a poet was roughly from 1948 to 1963), the foreword by Baxter Hathaway to his ''Island-Maker'' announces it as a book ''that should be considered one of the minor classics of our time.'' The poems of Herbert Morris have been admired by readers of poetry journals for 25 years but now have been collected for the first time. And Amy Clampitt, with the publication of her brilliant first book, ''The Kingfisher,'' immediately merits consideration as one of our most distinguished contemporary poets.
headline: NATURE, FANTASY, ART

title: Short Circuit,
author: Michael Mewshaw
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHORT CIRCUIT, By Michael Mewshaw.  306 pp. New York: Atheneum. $13.95.  THE real mark of a muckraking journalist's success is having his work lead to changes in the system he exposed. Michael Mewshaw is no Lincoln Steffens or Seymour Hersh, and corruption in professional tennis is hardly as consequential as corruption in city government or duplicity in foreign policy. But it is unlikely that very many investigative reporters ever saw their writing spawn changes as swiftly as Mr. Mewshaw has.   Last June, shortly after a long excerpt from this book appeared in Harper's and before the book itself was even published, Guillermo Vilas, one of the top five players in the world, was suspended from tournaments for a year for accepting $60,000 to appear in a tournament in Rotterdam. It was the first time tennis officials had cracked down on a player for violating a fundamental rule of the tour: the prohibition against accepting a guaranteed payment just for entering a tournament. A main theme of Mr. Mewshaw's book is that guarantees are routinely paid, and tour officials, who winked at the practice for years, were undoubtedly reacting to his findings.
headline: UNDER-THE-TABLE TENNIS

title: Landscape Turned Red. The Battle Of Anti
author: Stephen W. Sears. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LANDSCAPE TURNED RED, The Battle of Antietam.  By Stephen W. Sears.  Illustrated. 431 pp. New Haven & New York: Ticknor & Fields. $17.95.   IF you had to choose a quintessential American township, Sharpsburg, Md., with its white frame houses set in pleasant and vigorously farmed downlands, would serve even today. But as Stephen W. Sears recounts in his compelling and exhaustive ''Landscape Turned Red,'' it was within Sharpsburg's folksy purlieus - in the corn fields, orchards, wood lots and country lanes between the town and a nearby creek called Antietam - that the most ruinous slaughter in all American history was consummated. For by the time the sun went down behind Sharpsburg and the Potomac on Wednesday, Sept. 17, 1862, 22,719 casualties had been inflicted, brother upon brother, in scarcely more than 12 hours.
headline: WHERE THE SOUTH'S FORTUNES TURNED

title: A Tiger For Malgudi
author: R K Narayan
pull_quote: A TIGER FOR MALGUDI. By R. K. Narayan. 176 pages. Viking Press.  $14.75. THE protagonist of R. K. Narayan's new novel is Raja, a splendid tiger who creates and loses a family, frightens the villagers in the south Indian territory he roams, becomes a star of the circus and a potential movie star and receives wisdom. Along the way, he also comes to understand a couple of the languages employed by humans as well as some antic aspects of the way they behave toward ''dumb'' animals and toward each other.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Beautiful Women: Ugly Scenes
author: C D B Bryan
pull_quote: BEAUTIFUL WOMEN; UGLY SCENES. By C. D. B. Bryan. 374 pages. Doubleday & Company. $16.95.  WHEN it comes to depictions of marital strife and domestic discord, we tend to think of several contemporary literary models: Edward Albee's play ''Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf'' and such novels as John Updike's ''Couples,'' Philip Roth's ''My Life as a Man'' and Richard Yates's ''Revolutionary Road.'' C. D. B. Bryan's new novel ''Beautiful Women; Ugly Scenes'' possesses a similar visceral impact. The book is unwieldy, its prose at times opaque, but its portrait of a man and his collapsing marriage is also powerful and disturbing, and it invests the familiar banalities of upper-middle class life with seriousness and art.   Confessional in tone, seemingly ingenuous in design, Mr. Bryan's book tells the story of the narrator's ongoing ''war with women.'' At the age of 42 the unnamed narrator realizes that he has ''never yet had a truly loving relationship with a woman.'' He says he wants to be ''a good lover: strong but tender, thoughtful though sure - a Gary Cooper or a Jimmy Stewart instead of a Clark Gable or John Wayne,'' and yet he is constantly mistaking passion for love, domesticity for security.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Dangerous Edge
author: Robert Daley
pull_quote: THE DANGEROUS EDGE. By Robert Daley. 411 pages. Simon and Schuster.  $16.95.  One of the many satisfying things about Robert Daley's new mystery, ''The Dangerous Edge,'' is the sly choice it offers the reader of identifying with either good or evil. You can just as easily lend your sympathy to Lambert, who robs the Banque de Nice, or to Bellarmine, the detective assigned to apprehend him.
headline: Books of The Times; Cop and Robber in Nice

title: Slouching Towards Kalamazoo
author: Peter De Vries
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
SLOUCHING TOWARDS KALAMAZOO 

By Peter De Vries.  241 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Co. $13.95.  

BY now, Peter De Vries must be getting a little bit weary of reading extravagantly favorable reviews of his books in which he is once again hailed as America's pre-eminent comic novelist. And of then seeing his novels achieve respectable but nonetheless relatively modest sales while the best-seller lists, big-bucks paperback deals, six-figure advances and even the more prestigious literary awards go to writers who are frequently far less talented than he. Of course, Mr. De Vries is scarcely a flower blushing unseen in the desert - he is a member of the American Academy and Institute of Arts and Letters and has long been recognized in intellectual circles as one of this country's finest contemporary novelists. Still, it seems somehow unfair that a writer of his abilities shouldn't be more widely known and read than such popular humorists as, say, Erma Bombeck or Andy Rooney.
headline: TRAVELS OF A LOVESICK BEAST

title: Lusts
author: Clark Blaise
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CLARK BLAISE prefaces ''Lusts'' with the familiar disclaimer that any resemblance between his characters and persons living or dead is purely coincidental. But when Mr. Blaise's protagonist, Richard Durgin, takes a writing course at the University of Iowa, the instructor bears more than a coincidental resemblance to a person very much alive: ''My teacher was Philip Roth, only twenty-eight that year, himself a presence.'' Since it has become fashionable for novelists to place real celebrities in imaginary gardens, one can easily suspend one's disbelief. Raymond Chandler and Hannah Arendt also make guest appearances.   The question of the novel's fictional heroine, though, is more problematic. Rachel Isaacs is a Holocaust-obsessed poet who, at the height of her powers and fame, kills herself, leaving behind 40 ''suicide poems,'' 20,000 pages of unpublished manuscript and her husband, Richard, himself still an aspiring writer. She soon becomes a cult figure. The novel is composed of Richard's intimate letters to Rachel's biographer, in which he attempts to illuminate his wife's background, her work and, most crucially (and most effectively), his own culpability in her death.
headline: THE CULT FIGURE'S WIDOWER

title: Rosenberg File, The. A Search For The Truth
author: Alan M Dershowitz
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE ROSENBERG FILE 

A Search for the Truth.  By Ronald Radosh and Joyce Milton.  608 pp. New York: Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $22.50.  

WERE Julius and Ethel Rosenberg guilty of transmitting American atomic secrets to the Soviet Union in the 1940's, or were they scapegoats of the cold war whose execution was a grave miscarriage of justice? That both are true is the intriguing argument of Ronald Radosh and Joyce Milton in their definitive account of the controversial case, ''The Rosenberg File: A Search for the Truth.''
headline: SPIES AND SCAPEGOATS

title: Final Dress
author: John Houseman

MIDWAY through this third volume of his memoirs, the producer and director John Houseman recounts how, in 1964, he began talking into a tape recorder in an effort to connect ''my childhood memories and the personal and professional events of my adult life.'' When the miles of tapes were transcribed, he says, he had a pile of 680 triple-spaced pages, much of which was ''repetitious, self-pitying and useless.''   Out of those pages, however, came ''Run-Through,'' a bright, chatty piece of reminiscence published in 1972, which documented the metamorphosis of a European grain merchant named Jacques Haussmann into John Houseman, a scrappy novice in American show business. Whereas that volume achieved vitality through its evocation of a vanished era in American theater and through its sprightly portraits of such figures as Orson Welles, the result in ''Final Dress'' is less felicitous. Though rarely self-pitying, the book is frequently repetitious and boring, and its lacks the verbal charm Mr. Houseman has demonstrated in the past.

FOUNDATIONS OF SPACE-TIME THEORIES    Relativistic Physics and Philosophy of Science.  By Michael Friedman.  Illustrated. 385 pp. New Jersey: Princeton University Press. $35.     AUGUSTE COMTE, the 19th-century social theorist and philosopher, confidently said in 1825 that one thing scientists would never know is the chemical composition of stars. It was a reasonable but false proposition. At the time Comte made the remark, Joseph von Fraunhofer in Germany was taking the first steps toward modern spectroscopy - the analysis of light in terms of the chemical composition of its source. In 1859 Gustav Kirchhoff proved the existence of sodium in the sun through spectroscopic methods. Thirteen years later at his observatory in Hastings-on-Hudson, N.Y., Henry Draper, dean of the medical school of New York University, photographed the light spectrum of Vega, a star 26 light-years from Earth, and became the first person to prove that the chemistry of distant stars was essentially the same as that on Earth.

THERE is something serendipitous about the recent spate of books about William J. ''Wild Bill'' Donovan, the World War I hero who became Washington's spy master during World War II and laid the foundations for the Central Intelligence Agency. It is not that the books reduce the Donovan legend to more human dimensions, although that was long overdue and ''The Shadow Warriors'' performs the historical refinement without disrespect for Donovan's accomplishments. Nor is it some new insight into how the Office of Strategic Services, which Donovan created and directed, made the Government more receptive to the establishment of a centralized intelligence organization, though that too is amply explained in Bradley F. Smith's book. The unexpected dividend is the pertinence of the story to current foreign policy and intelligence issues, particularly the Reagan Administration's extensive use of covert activities as an instrument of foreign policy.

Paper, $695 AYDEN CARRUTH'S ''Sleeping Beauty'' is a complex sequence of 15-line rhymed lyrics that conducts an impassioned inquiry into the spirit of romance. The fairy tale ''The Briar Rose'' by the Grimm brothers serves well as the narrative spine of the poem. Mr. Carruth's wife, Rose Marie Dorn, the    Dornr"oschen    (brier rose) to whom the poem is an offering of reconciliation, is a mature woman, though the memory of her as a slender girl of 17 also haunts the poet. Along his meandering (''northfaring'') route, the shy petitioner, contrite for transgressions against his lady, does not encounter the monsters and wizards, the damsels in distress and evil knights, of medieval romance; his adventures are in ternal and hallucinatory. As if he were an actor in a condensed allegory, he slips into the protean figures of a dreamer's fantasies, all of whose names begin with the letter H: poets (Homer, Hesiod, H"olderlin), philosophers (Heraclitus, Hegel), political leaders (Hannibal, Herod, Hitler), literary figures (Hamlet, Harlequin, Heathcliff), social types (Husband, Householder) and others.

IT'S now just a little more than two years since William Saroyan died at the age of 72. Stories, novels, plays and reminiscences poured from him in a spate, and two of the plays, ''The Time of Your Life'' and ''My Heart's in the Highlands,'' have a permanent place in the theater. He was a seemingly inexhaustible writer. He rose, in the great American tradition, from poverty to money, and then kept falling, again in the tradition, but this time of writers, into near-poverty - because drinking and gambling seemed as necessary to him as writing. His prose depended heavily on family, and yet his relationship with his children was tangled and tenuous. The one thing he did consistently was to keep writing, although, as he once said, ''I may not die a writer, I'm a cinch to die Saroyan.''

Its power is all the more impressive because nothing in Bernard Mac Laverty's first novel, ''Lamb'' (1980), quite prepares one for the beauty of this novel, for the delicacy and poise of its account of a teen-age boy's futile attempt to stay clear of the Troubles in Northern Ireland. pull_quote: LITERARY THEORY     An Introduction.  By Terry Eagleton.  244 pp. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.  Cloth, $29.50. Paper, $9.95.  URING the last 15 years, the nature of literary criticism in American and British universities has been profoundly altered by a series of foreign, primarily French, invasions. It is no longer possible for an academic critic merely to point out the beauties in Wordsworth or Tennyson. Now he must decide whether his point of view will be structuralist, semiotic, deconstructionist or psychoanalytical, whether he will take a Levi-Straussian, Jakobsonian, Derridan or Lacanian approach. In any case, he must give up the idea of simply responding to a poem; simple response is hopelessly passe. The modish thing is to insert works of literature into some vast, abstract formula that makes them symptoms of Western metaphysics, the post-Miltonic tradition or the dynamics of the human unconscious. Various as these approaches are, they all exhibit the same urge toward grandiose generalization. They all, that is, practice literary criticism as a springboard to ''theory.''

IT would probably take a novel stamped with the   surrealistic genius of a Gabriel Garcia Marquez   to render all the madness, perverse magic and tragedy of Juan Domingo Peron and his Argentina. But Joseph A. Page has come up with the next best option. His ''Peron'' is a clearly written, definitive study, the first biography that traces the legendary    caudillo    from birth to power to exile and back to power and death. This is a considerable feat of historical writing because the passions aroused by Peron in his nation are so great. For 30 years, Argentines have tended to define themselves as Peronists or anti-Peronists and to view recent history from the same perspective. How can a historian trust news accounts from the Peronist eras, when newspapers were so muzzled? The large number of Argentine books on Peron are clearly colored by their adulation or hatred of the man, as are the memories of people who lived under his rule. During my three years as a foreign correspondent in Argentina - coinciding with Peron's return from exile, his death and the overthrow of his wife, Isabelita, who succeeded him as President - I did not meet a single Argentine who could talk about the    caudillo    with dispassion.

He was born in Salt Lake City in 1869 and died 59 years later in Moscow, a hero to some, a renegade to others. The Soviets buried half his ashes beneath the Kremlin Wall and shipped the rest to Chicago, there to be interred near a monument to the Haymarket anarchists. As Peter Carlson makes clear in ''Roughneck,'' a well-told biography of William ''Big Bill'' Haywood, the apportionment of his remains suited the man's contradictory allegiances. He was ''as American as Mark Twain,'' Mr. Carlson writes, yet he ''seemed the very personification of proletarian rage, a capitalist's nightmare come to life.''   Founder of the radical ''Wobblies'' (International Workers of the World), a little union with big dreams, Haywood was able to challenge the hegemony of Samuel Gompers's conservative craft unions. ''Something in him moved people,'' notes Mr. Carlson. ''Women sat at this feet; children scampered into his lap as if he were Santa Claus.'' In 1912 in Lawrence, Mass., Haywood's energy and charisma converted a timorous strike by immigrant textile workers into a brilliant victory: ''Day and night Haywood scurried around the city, walking picketlines, leading marches, addressing rallies, chairing meetings. Expansive, optimistic, and charming, Haywood captivated the crowds. Strikers followed him wherever he went.''

WHEN, in 1966, Louis Leakey chose Dian Fossey to carry out a long-term study of gorillas in the wild, she was in her mid-30's and an occupational therapist in Louisville, Ky. Three years before, she had been to Africa, where she spent a hefty bank loan on a safari that included a trip to see the mountain gorillas and a visit to Louis and Mary Leakey's archeological excavation at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania. At Olduvai she dashed down a hillside to see a new find, fell, and she tells us, ''as the ankle cracked, the sudden pain induced me to vomit unceremoniously all over the treasured fossil.''   Three years later, when Leakey came to lecture in Louisville, Miss Fossey reintroduced herself and expressed once again her interest in animals in the wild and her longing for Africa. On the spot, it seems, and in spite of their unpromising first encounter, Leakey decided that she was the person he'd been looking for to study the nearly extinct mountain gorilla of central Africa. He advised her to have her appendix out and set about raising funds for her work. That Leakey was absolutely right in his intuitive choice is made clear by ''Gorillas in the Mist,'' Miss Fossey's memoir of her extraordinary 13 years in the field.

ARRIVING late at an elegant London dinner party, the narrator of ''Tamar,'' a short story in Mark Helprin's ''Ellis Island, and Other Stories,'' is seated at the ''children's table,'' as a kind of genteel punishment. EVERYTHING about the story that Anka Muhlstein tells in ''Baron James'' is outsize. The upward movement of the Rothschilds in the first half of the 19th century is the equivalent in financial and social terms of a blastoff at the Kennedy Space Center. The sums of money are colossal. The negotiations make one's head spin. The houses make Newport, R.I., look like Tobacco Road. The names dropped - however lightly - are an honor roll (and occasionally a dishonor roll) of 19th-century Europe.   In fact, the only thing about ''Baron James'' that is not outsize is the book itself. Anka Muhlstein is that rare thing in the 1980's - a biographer who travels light. Where others have trouble coming in under 700 pages, Miss Muhlstein's life of Queen Victoria had the proportions, give or take a whisker, of Lytton Strachey's slender masterpiece. Her new book ranges the length and breadth of Europe. It has to do with the waxing and waning of vast fortunes, the making and breaking of kings and queens and governments and the evolution of a distinctive ''Rothschild taste'' in the decorative arts. Yet it goes barely above 200 pages.

So were many others, including James Tate, who is about to leave behind the slightly patronizing rubric ''younger poet,'' patented by the Yale Series. When his first book was chosen for that series in 1966,    ''youngest    poet'' was the operative phrase, and perhaps ''war baby'' was another, with a brand new war beginning to escalate.   Since that time, as book after book of his has appeared, Mr. Tate has often seemed as plausible a standard-bearer as any for a generation dislocated and made permanently restless by the Vietnam War. No younger poet writing then wanted to negotiate with the middle-minded military-industrial society that got us into that mess. And not just Vietnam, but other conflicts; maybe America was just too violent. ''The Lost Pilot,'' the title poem of Mr. Tate's first book, concerns the death of his father in World War II. It is still one of his best poems, and one can infer that that early misfortune had something to do with his becoming a poet.

title: Angels
author: Denis Johnson
pull_quote: ANGELS. By Denis Johnson. 209 pages. Throwaway Lives Knopf. $12.95.  Bored with their successes, Americans are beginning to love their failures. This is especially true in our fiction, because writers of novels and stories seem to get bored faster than other people. Everybody in Denis Johnson's ''Angels,'' for example, is a failure. It's as if we were proud of having evolved a way of life in which you can fail more absolutely, more definitively or finally, than anywhere else. Because we haven't got an ancient culture, we seem to preen ourselves on having all the latest disabilities.   When we first meet Jamie, the heroine shall we say, of ''Angels,'' she's sleeping in a bus, dreaming about men dying in a cloud of poison. We read that ''she wished she could smother her baby,'' one of two children she seems to have conceived for the sole purpose of extending her indecisiveness. Jamie is running away from her husband because his conviction that ''one moment goes to the next'' strikes her as a very limiting way of looking at things.

THE trivializing habit of calling biographies by the first names of their subjects - usually their female subjects - is particularly inappropriate for Willa Cather, who was among the most masculine (or, in the current phrase, ''male-identified'') of women writers. In some ways, it would have been more to the point to call this book ''William: The Life of Willa Cather.'' From her high school days in Red Cloud, Neb., in the 1880's until halfway through her studies at the University of Nebraska, Willa Cather dressed as a boy, cut her hair like a man's and called herself William Cather. (Sometimes she added ''M.D.'') Her friends called her Willie or Dr. Will. She wanted to be a doctor. She practiced dissection, scandalizing her conservative hometown with her unfeminine enthusiasms. She taunted her hometown in return, casting herself in the role of defender of science and experiment, speaking in favor of vivisection at her high school graduation.

THE LIFE OF MAXWELL ANDERSON. By Alfred S. Shivers.  Illustrated. 397 pp. New York: Stein & Day. $25.

ARISTIDES, called the Just, was a great Athenian statesman. Once, unrecognized, he met a poor man who had voted against him. When asked why, the man said, ''It irritates me to hear him called always the Just.''

Was the great playwright Maxwell Anderson another Aristides the Just? Were his themes too sober? Was his style too conservative? Why is Eugene O'Neill better known today, although Anderson was on his heels for years? Why is O'Neill revived and not Anderson? Why do we who bought theater tickets through the 1920's and 30's and 40's know and revere him, while the equally passionate playgoers of today say, ''Maxwell who?''

title: Cathedral
author: Raymond Carver
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CATHEDRAL. By Raymond Carver.  228 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.   THERE are artists who reach the strange by staying with the ordinary. Maurice Utrillo paints European streets that narrow into enigmatic space and Edward Hopper American houses that seem laden with disquiet. How they do this only a very good art critic can explain, but that it happens everyone who looks at pictures must know.   Raymond Carver, an American writer now in his mid-40's, has been writing stories for some years that, on a smaller emotional scale, create similar effects. His settings are American towns, semi-industrial and often depressed. His characters, plebeian loners struggling for speech, now and then find work as factory hands and waitresses. His actions skid across the troubles of daily life and then, through some eerie turn of chance or perhaps a darker cause, collapse into failed marriages and broken lives. Familiar enough on the surface, these stories leave one with tremors that resemble the start of a breakdown. The familiar controls guiding daily life fall apart; panic takes over.

LANGSTON HUGHES. Before and Beyond Harlem.  By Faith Berry.  376 pp. Westport, Conn.: Lawrence Hill & Co.  Cloth, $19.95.; paper, $12.95.

WHEN the 75th anniversary of Langston Hughes's birth was celebrated in 1977 at the City College of New York, the historian John Henrik Clarke reminded the audience that Hughes had been a cultural hero, one of America's outstanding authors who was better known to black people than any other writer of this century. A leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920's, Hughes wrote 10 volumes of poetry, 9 works of fiction and 9 full-length plays. He was a librettist, translator, journalist, song lyricist and scriptwriter. But he is best remembered for his poetry, , as well as his 1935 play, ''Mulatto,'' and his comic character, Jesse B. Simple . In fact, Hughes's literary reputation rests primarily on his poetry, which is generously cited in this biography. He was among the first Americans successfully to use everyday speech patterns and a colloquial voice in his poetry as well the first to express the spirit of the blues.

Hughes also wrote two autobiographies - ''The Big Sea'' in 1940 and ''I Wonder As I Wander'' in 1956 - but both dealt with the details of his personal life in carefully measured prose. Leafing through those volumes, readers must have wondered: Was Hughes in fact as uncomplicated as his testimonies suggest?

In undertaking this biography of Harold Lloyd, the least remembered of the three great masters of silent film comedy, Tom Dardis was faced with translating into words comic effects whose genius lies in their being wordless. THE life's work of the poet Stephan Hermlin, born in Chemnitz (now Karl-Marx-Stadt) in 1915, consists of a few slim volumes of finely crafted poems, essays, novellas and radio plays. Despite his small output, Mr. Hermlin enjoys a literary reputation on both sides of the border dividing his country as one of the foremost living East German writers.   In 1976, he attracted international attention beyond the confines of the poetry-reading public when he initiated and helped draft a petition that was signed by a small number of East German artists and intellectuals asking the Government to reverse its decision to exile the poet and singer Wolf Biermann, who had begun to establish himself as a gadfly somewhere to the left of the authorities. The Government's response was to force some of the signers (not Mr. Hermlin) to join Mr. Biermann in the West. Two years later, Stephan Hermlin was the only member of the Writers' Union who objected to the threatened expulsion of a few mildly dissident authors from that organization (expulsion would make it impossible for their work to be published in East Germany).

Illustrated. 256 pp. New York: Random House. $17.95 *RED ARMY officer and scholar of German literature, Communist Party member and Jew, Lev Kopelev was imprisoned by his Government at the end of World War II for protesting against the looting, rape and murder of German civilians by Soviet soldiers. He was charged with the crime of ''bourgeois humanism.'' When he was sent to the gulag, his dossier was stamped ''TO BE PRESERVED FOREVER,'' a phrase he employed to fine purpose as the title of his book on his wartime experiences.   In ''Ease My Sorrows,'' he treats his life in a forced labor camp as a kind of work-study period in which the scholars also happened to be prisoners living at the site of their laboratories. Deploying his talents in linguistics and mathematics, together with a literary critic's knowledge of language and cultures, he devised methods of protecting codes and deciphering voices that the secret police hoped to use in developing ''voice prints'' and so make their wiretaps more effective.

author: V S Pritchett
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ''THERE in the absurdities or pathos of the private imbroglio has been my story,'' V. S.  Pritchett once wrote, ''the drama has lain in the sight of (people) floundering amid their own words, and performing strange strokes as they swim about, with no visible shores, in their own lives.'' A talented critic as well as one of the finest living writers of short stories, Mr. Pritchett sums up his own approach to the art of fiction with his usual concision. Comic in design, moral in vision, Mr. Pritchett's short stories are grounded in and preoccupied with the individual life. Noisy public events rarely intrude in his work; for him, more than enough drama is to be found in the inner lives of his characters; and taken together, those characters - so richly endowed with fantasies and illusions - make up a populous and distinctive fictional world.   Certainly ''More Collected Stories'' has its share of engaging characters: a pianist's jaunty lover who discovers that their sexual intimacy pales next to the dull, shared routines of the pianist's marriage; a foppish interior decorator who falls in love with a fat, ruddy-faced lady farmer; and a nouveau riche couple who find that their posh new home comes equipped with its previous tenant.

MILL Written and illustrated by David Macaulay.  128 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Co.  $14.95. (Ages 10 and Up) By D. J. R. BRUCKNER 

The New England cotton mills of the last century, mostly abandoned in the rush to new technologies, will never really be gone as long as David Macaulay's ''Mill'' has readers. His imaginary mills in an imaginary town in Rhode Island, and the generations of people who built and ran them, come to life in the mind and refuse to leave long after one has put his historical re-creation down. He reveals in detail the secrets of this man-made world but leaves one with the sense that it is part of nature, and just as surprising.

The first wooden mill of this book is begun in 1810 by a group of enterprising businessmen. One designs the mill, another its machinery; a third surveys land for the site. As workers cut a channel parallel to the river to divert a stream to turn the mill's great wheel, others build the structure to hold the machinery that is being made out of iron and wood on the site. When the mill begins to operate, we see how the raw cotton is prepared for the machines that card it, draw it into long strong fibers and finally twist and spin it into thread for sale to cloth weavers.

title: Newspaperman

pull_quote: NEWSPAPERMAN S. I. Newhouse and the Business of News.  By Richard H. Meeker.  Illustrated. 294 pp. New York and New Haven: Ticknor & Fields. $17.95.     S. I. (SAM) NEWHOUSE told the story on himself. He asked his wife, Mitzi, if she wanted anything as he was leaving his Park Avenue apartment for a stroll one Sunday: ''She asked for a fashion magazine, and I went out and got her Vogue.''   The year was 1959, the story apocryphal. But it characterizes Newhouse's style at the zenith of his remarkable, joyless, heroic, exhilarating, monomaniacal career, one as eccentric as any in the annals of American capitalism. At the time of his death in 1979, the Newhouse empire included 29 newspapers, a string of radio and television stations and the Conde Nast magazines (Glamour, Madamoiselle and House & Garden, in addition to Vogue). In 1920, Newhouse bought his first newspaper, The Fitchburg (Mass.) News, for $15,000. In his last deal, more than six decades later, he acquired the eight Booth papers in Michigan and the Sunday supplement Parade for a total of $305 million. In ''Newspaperman,'' Richard H. Meeker declares that that purchase is ''likely to remain the biggest newspaper deal of the twentieth century.''

Linder Professor of Social Science at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, N.J., has emerged as a name to reckon with. By profession, he is an anthropologist. D. Laing, Noam Chomsky or Fernand Braudel - about whom the public feels the need to be informed.

THEY fell in love in the ninth grade while holding hands in a movie balcony, and so ''Theme From 'A Summer Place' '' always was their song. After their wedding, someone remarked that the all- American girl had married the all-American boy. Jeffrey MacDonald was handsome and athletic, president of the student council, most popular, most likely to succeed. title: The Dangerous Edge
author: Robert Daley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE DANGEROUS EDGE, By Robert Daley.  411 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $16.95.

''The Dangerous Edge'' by Robert Daley is not only a non- stop thriller but also a story of surprising depth. The place is the grimy side of the French Riviera. The time is 1954, too soon for France to have recovered from the physical and moral devastation of the World War II, and this fact plays an important part in the narrative. The crime is the robbery of the safety deposit boxes of the Bank of Nice where the value of the loot in cash, gold and jewelry, not to mention incriminating personal documents and pornographic photos, is incalculable. And the master criminal who plans the robbery and organizes a mixed bag of toughs to carry out the plan is Lambert, an American who remained in France during the war.

Lambert is what would have been known by psychiatrists of that period as a psychopathic personality. He is attractive, clever, utterly unprincipled, and lives only for the excitement of the moment. He is drugged, in fact, by any kind of adverture that puts him one-up on the rest of the world. Playing the game is what matters to him, not the reward, and Mr. Daley depicts his complexities convincingly, even evoking a sense of pathos.

title: A Personal History

DISRAELI said that everyone has a right to be conceited until he is successful - in which case A. J .P. Taylor forfeited the right a long time ago. Mr. Taylor is a man of great gifts; he has put those gifts to good use, and everybody knows it. I have never met anyone, even among those who have been most exasperated by him, who has seriously tried to deny he is a major historian. To his more fastidious academic critics, not the least exasperating thing about him is that he has also been far more productive than most of them, productive on a positively 19th-century scale. He must be the most widely read English historian since G. M. Trevelyan, quite possibly since Lord Macaulay, and with good reason. He writes with a verve which will insure that books like his study of dissent in foreign policy, ''The Trouble Makers,'' or ''English History 1914-1945'' (in my opinion, his masterpiece) will survive on their literary merits even when they have been overtaken by subsequent research.

Perhaps this title should have been translated as ''The Master of Turning,'' which would have been more literal and also a proper tribute to its distinguished author, who is a master of metamorphoses. But perhaps this book, first published in 1974, ought not to have been translated at all. It is a very unpleasant work, without any redeeming esthetic merit or humane quality. Singer's best book, retroactively worthy of the Nobel Prize he won in 1978, was his ''Collected Stories,'' published last year. ''The Penitent,'' a failed attempt at a Swiftian diatribe against the contemporary world, is his worst book, and yet it does expose limitations that are not Singer's alone, and so it sadly defines much that is uneasy and probably insoluble in the dilemmas of Jewish culture at this time.

Soon after the 1929 stock market crash, Earl Browder, general secretary of this country's Communist Party, ordered that black people be placed ''in the foreground'' of the party's attempts to organize unemployed workers. pull_quote: They dazzle the eye, delight most who see them and command top prices in galleries and at auctions of American Indian art. These are what are called ''eye-dazzlers,'' the visually arresting blankets and rugs woven by Navajo women between 1870 and 1920 that are regarded as the precursors of the Op Art paintings of the 1960's. Explosive in their colors and dynamic in their designs, these weavings date to the period when aniline dyes transformed blankets into color-pulsing designs devised by the most skilled of the Navajo artisans.   Over the past 15 years, ever since artists and other collectors began seriously acquiring ''eye-dazzlers,'' these stunning weavings have been studied, written about, exhibited and acquired with mounting enthusiasm. The Navajo blanket exhibition of a decade ago focused national attention on quality examples in its coast-to- coast travels from the Los Angeles County Museum of Art to the Brooklyn Museum. It included works on loan from such artists as Jasper Johns, Donald Judd, Georgia O'Keeffe, Frank Stella, Kenneth Noland and Anthony Berlant. Mr. Berlant organized the show and, together with Mary Hunt Kahlenberg, wrote the catalogue, ''The Navajo Blanket,'' still unsurpassed as the textbook of this field.

pull_quote: SIX decades ago, it seemed to many observers that the era of realism was finished. Virgina Woolf boldly denounced the old-fashioned materialist novel by arguing that in the experience of ordinary consciousness, there can be no plot, no comedy, no tragedy, no love interest or catastrophe in the accepted style. Her pronouncement of 1919 has long since become famous as a manifesto of sorts in defense of a new and revolutionary art: ''Life is a luminous halo, a semi-transparent envelope surrounding us from the beginning of consciousness to the end. Is it not the task of the novelist to convey this varying, this unknown and uncircumscribed spirit, whatever aberration or complexity it may display, with as little of the alien and external as possible?''   Eva Figes's luminous prose poem of a novel, ''Light,'' like her earlier ''Waking,'' is clearly descended from Woolf's great experimental novels. Technique is all or nearly all in this fastidiously wrought narrative of a day in the life of Claude Monet in the summer of 1900. The reader is a witness to a remarkable variety of modulations of light - sunlight - beginning in the darkness preceding dawn and ending in night, ''as it gradually became impossible to distinguish leaf from branch, water from rock, even the house from the hillslope behind it.''

WHY have some American minorities climbed the ladder of economic success more readily than others? The simple answer - thay they encountered differing degrees of discrimination - does not seem wholly adequate. Like blacks, Chinese and Japanese immigrants to the United States were targets of extreme racism. Although never enslaved, they were subjected to segregation, discrimination and mob violence. Yet today their descendents have substantially higher average incomes than blacks and are proportionately much better represented in the elite professions. Asians, in fact, do better in the aggregate than Americans who are designated as Anglo-Saxon in origin. Similarly, Jewish immigrants and their children moved upward much more rapidly than Italians arriving about the same time, although it would be a tossup as to which group faced greater initial hostility from old-stock Americans.

THIS volume of 25 stories, chosen by the author, reflects his work from 1950 to the present, and it admirably represents his special achievement. Bernard Malamud has produced seven novels, beginning with ''The Natural,'' published in 1952, but none of the others has the verve of that first book, as none of the later novels has the steady conviction of his second novel, ''The Assistant'' (1957), and none of his longer fictions has the absolute rightness of tone and invention of his best short stories.   His real gift is for the short story, for the spare, rigorous etching of solitary figures caught in the stress of adversity. When Malamud translates such figures into the novel, whose ampler dimensions lead us to expect development, he has difficulty in making his personages go anywhere except deeper into disaster. The plots of his novels tend to devolve into extended fantasies - sometimes lurid, sometimes just depressing - of mutilation and interment. By contrast, his stronger stories exhibit exquisite artistic tact, a remarkable intuition for saying a great deal with the most minimal narrative gestures, and a delicacy of feeling about the characters that cannot be reduced to any simple technique.

I GOT so much pleasure out of Joseph Epstein's collection of essays, ''The Middle of My Tether,'' that I fell to wondering why such collections are not more popular, why it should be a maxim among publishers that most collections won't sell. It seems to me that form for people who buy ''collectibles,'' who read more magazines than anybody else in the world and who have fallen in love with the boutique. After all, what is a good collection but a boutique of ideas, collectible ideas or a superior kind of magazine?   Nonetheless, if I were to hazard a theory, I would say that readers resist collections because, consisting as they do of many pieces, they require a continual adjustment. One can't just settle down with a single theme but must keep changing direction with the author. Since collections are like an author talking to himself, readers may feel that they're on the receiving end of a monologue, that they're getting too much of someone else's personality. Even more than the poem or the novel, an essay can be the most personal of all literary voices.

THIS is the book that gives the lie to Tolstoy's belief that ''happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.'' The truth is just the opposite. Unhappy families are alike in highly predictable ways: The partners quarrel relentlessly, one bullies or tyrannizes the other, both put their selfish interests above their mutual interests as a couple. They have affairs, they disagree about power, they care about transient values, such as beauty, more than enduring ones, such as commitment. It's happy couples who differ, each in its own way. Some fight all the time, others rarely; some don't have sex very often, others do frequently; some are traditional, others egalitarian; some are possessive, others aren't.  But you won't see this overall pattern in ''American Couples'' at once. Like most survey researchers, Philip Blumstein and Pepper Schwartz, sociologists at the University of Washington, describe hundreds of tiny stars and few constellations. The reader who looks here for hot new findings on the state of the American couple will be disappointed. Indeed, the reader who seeks a summary may be surprised at how little has changed in the last 20 years of social turmoil.

Her study attempts not only to trace the shifting relationship between revenge and the idea of law, but also to define those forms of revenge which are consistent with the values of a civilized society.

PHILIP ROTH, recalling a visit to Prague in 1971, said he was struck by the contrasting situation of writers in a country that is not free and in the United States. Here, it seemed to him, ''everything goes and nothing matters''; there, ''nothing goes and everything matters.'' It is this concern that seems to underlie the trilogy that Roth began with ''The Ghost Writer,'' continued with ''Zuckerman Unbound'' and now concludes with ''The Anatomy Lesson.''   Certainly, Roth's fictitious novelist, Nathan Zuckerman, faces neither censorship nor imprisonment in his rapid journey up the freeway of American literary notoriety. What Zuckerman does face is an ambitious and egocentric self, strong on nerve and stomach, weak in empathy - an impoverished self that is at once his only resource and his major stumbling block. In ''The Ghost Writer,'' Zuckerman is a young beginner who tastes critical approval without the popularity that is the dream of artists no less than of politicians and other performers. A few years later, in ''Zuckerman Unbound,'' Zuckerman attains fame with the publication of ''Carnovsky,'' a novel not unlike Roth's own ''Portnoy's Complaint.'' But Zuckerman gains his renown at the expense of his family, who feel betrayed by his apparent caricatures of them in ''Carnovsky,'' and despite the critics, who consider the novel sensational and shallow.

Beethoven had one. So did Liszt and Mendelssohn, and their endorsements helped seal the Broadwood reputation as a maker of fine pianos, as did the British Royal Warrant, which the company has held for most of its existence. But as musical fashions have changed, the fortunes of piano makers have faded and flourished. In ''Broadwood by Appointment,'' David Wainwright, a journalist and amateur pianist, documents the highs and lows of the British piano manufacturer John Broadwood and Sons, which began in the early 1800's as a London harpsichord workshop with three employees. The book, though densely written, makes fascinating reading. And the text is enhanced by color reproductions of instruments that are lavishly decorated with inlaid wood, intricate carving and ornamental brass fittings and by several examples of the company's best seller, the square piano.  When the public demanded a smaller instrument with a full- bodied sound, Broadwood developed the upright, a teetering eight-feet-high instrument in which the grand piano's sounding board was placed on end. During the two World Wars, when materials and labor were scarce, the company made parts for airplanes and entered into joint ventures with other piano makers to stay in business. Along with these interruptions in piano making came the slow but steady challenge to the piano as a staple of entertainment and culture in the home. During the last 50 years, with the advent of television and such diversions as video games, Broadwood has encountered lean times, but consolidation and careful management have kept the company in the black.

HAT are we to make of a writer in the 20th century who lingered for months in Douglas, Ariz., drinking in the local bar with traveling salesmen and attending the policemen's ball; who had the benign look of a small-town dentist; who ''claimed his special table by the window'' in the New Haven Howard Johnson's? Didn't Thornton Wilder know that writers hung out in Greenwich Village or Montemartre, went about with a rumpled air suggestive of seedy escapades and dissipation, would no more have set foot in Hojo's than in their local Elks lodge? There are novelists who aspire to record the lives of ordinary citizens, to know the common man; but Wilder in many ways    was    a common man, and his reputation has suffered for it. Modernism has made mandatory the image of the artist as sickly and self-destructive, an outcast condemned to dwell on the difference between himself and a Philistine society. It has no place for a writer who wanted to be known as Everyone's Uncle.

 TWO years ago a 34-year-old Indian Moslem named Salman Rushdie published ''Midnight's Children,'' an astonishing novel that attempted nothing less than to create a fantastic fictional counterpart to the convulsive, often tragic events that have rocked the Indian subcontinent during the past 60 years. It was highly praised, both here and in England. In its fecundity, extravagance and scope, ''Midnight's Children'' reminded me of some vast Hindu temple, a multilayered structure intricately embellished with carvings of gods, demons, heroes, lovers and beasts.

Such an achievement casts a long shadow from which its successor must struggle to escape if it is to find light and space for its own development. Aware of this, Mr. Rushdie has moved the setting of his new novel from India proper to the somewhat thinner soil of a country that is ''not quite Pakistan'' and has erected a less imposing, though equally fantastic, edifice. ''Shame'' is a lively, amusing and exasperating work that will present certain problems for an American reader.
