His plays, divided between distancing dramas designed to make the audience think and didactic stage lessons designed to make the audience believe, leave conflicting clues, behind which their author escapes. We know that Brecht was what we may call, rather simplistically, an antifascist; but, beyond an implacable hatred for Hitler, the precise place on the political spectrum at which he wanted to locate himself remains obscure. Even after embracing Communist causes, he left escape routes open. And the autobiographical jottings of his late years are little better than calculated bits of self-dramatization, presenting a young Brecht single-minded, consistent and responsible - none of which he was.

The painstaking facsimile of ''Jazz'' by Henri Matisse takes the prize. How could it be otherwise when ''Jazz'' is a classic of our century and great pains have been taken with this edition? ''Jazz'' began as a book, and although individual pages from it are now often sold separately, it still makes most sense as a book.   First published in 1947 after a long period of gestation, ''Jazz'' consists of a series of images in cut and colored paper and a text by Matisse inserted among them. It seems to me that Donald Barthelme also intends these interludes to function as footnotes to the stories, like T. S. Eliot's notes for ''The Wasteland.''   The first interlude opens with, ''They called for more structure,'' and my hopes rose in anticipation of those antic structures for which the author is already famous. The speaker in this passage proposed to build a new city - ''Oh radiant city!'' - which would ''make architects stutter.'' For architects, perhaps we should read literary critics. Mr. Barthelme appears to be hinting at his esthetic.

WORKING CLASS HERO 

 A New Strategy for Labor.  By Stanley Aronowitz.  229 pp. New York: The Pilgrim Press. $18.95.

SCHOLARLY and intellectual interest in the American trade unions has been at a low ebb since the 1960's. Economists apart, such concerns have largely stemmed from prolabor views. The working class has long been identified by the intellectual left as the major source of political support for a movement dedicated to egalitarian, hopefully socialist, objectives. But from the 60's, the left intelligentsia, more concerned with domestic social issues and international relations than economics, has developed a disdain for labor as a conservative political force.

Stanley Aronowitz, a professor of sociology at the City University of New York, is an old-fashioned socialist. He retains the classic Marxist belief that at the center of the struggle for social progress there must be a strong working-class movement. He is, therefore, interested in analyzing, and helping to reverse, the decline of trade unions as a political and social force since ''the fundamental condition for the emergence of a progressive agenda in American national politics (is) the revival of the labor movement in the 1980's.''

He was editor of the college paper at Princeton and a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford, and then rose from private to captain as a marine in the Pacific during World War II. Since then he has held a number of plum jobs in journalism, was an aide to Gov. Chester Bowles of Connecticut and Gov. W. Averell Harriman of New York, and he is a professor of journalism at Columbia University. He has never been divorced or arrested and, until now, has never caused a scene in a public place.   About the only thing you can say against Penn Townsend Kimball is that he had a shaky grasp of the mechanics of self-advancement. Every time one of his jobs began to look like the beginning of a serious career, he quit - generally for something doubtful but interesting, like trying to elevate The New Republic into a liberal rival of Time and Newsweek, or trying to rescue Collier's magazine. THE literature of conscience is ultimately about the bewilderment of the naive. Why do men carry guns and build prison camps, when the nurturing earth is made for freedom? A conventional, medium-size, studious young man from an upper- middle-class Denver family, Mr. Conover thought that learning how to cope with certain kinds of fundamental difficulties might be a useful introduction to adult life.   ''Rolling Nowhere'' is an account of his travels on freight trains through the West and Middle West, from as far south as El Paso and north to Seattle. As we might expect, much of his book is naive, and that's all to the good. The reader, too, is naive about the life of a tramp, and the author's candor raises and answers the kinds of questions that might be overlooked by a more sophisticated approach.  Where do you sleep? RICHARD COBB is the most idiosyncratic contemporary historian of modern France. Always suspicious of authority and of political history written from the viewpoint of the rulers, he has looked at events - particularly the French Revolution - from the perspective of the underdogs and the misfits. Sir No"el Coward, playwright, actor, director, composer, novelist, diarist and for 30 years a short- story writer, was nothing if not a temperament, and for the better part of a generation, with eyes shaded by gesticulant hands trained in a posture of disciplined Tory salute, he faced great avalanches of limelit factual event in peace and war without once facing the fact of the end of the ''modern'' world. ONE of the frustrations of writing serious nonfiction is that good books almost always take a long time to produce. A writer who would treat the topical finds himself in a bind. If he takes the time to write a thorough, thoughtful book, public interest may wane, and subsequent events may render his thesis suspect. If, on the other hand, he rushes to judgment, he may end up producing something devoid of the insight and craftsmanship that differentiates literature from instant publications churned out by batteries of reporters and editors. She lived, as Robert Giroux says in his introduction to ''The Collected Prose,'' in such dissimilar places as ''Nova Scotia and Paris, Ouro Preto and Worcester, London and Key West, Poughkeepsie and Cape Cod, Petropolis and San Francisco, Mexico and Boston, North Haven and Greenwich Village, Seattle and Rio de Janeiro.'' Her books of poems bear geographical titles: ''North & South,'' ''Questions of Travel'' and ''Geography III.''   It's only natural to ask what she was looking for on the edges of those places, and I think that Helen Vendler has suggested an answer in her splendid essay on Miss Bishop's poems called ''Domestication, Domesticity, and the Other Worldly.'' Miss Bishop lost her father when she was 8 months old and her mother, after five years of pathological mourning, disappeared into a mental hospital. The child's and the woman's life after that was a search for domesticity, or for the exotic as a denial of the need for domesticity. Benson pictures him in his interminable biography, ''The True Adventures of John Steinbeck, Writer,'' Steinbeck appears to have been awkward, half-educated, sentimental and naive, a man who wrested an insecure fame for himself out of his determination, his unalloyed sincerity, his belief in himself and his immersion in time and place. In other words, he had all the virtues traditionally associated with the term American by those critics, like Mary McCarthy, for example, who disliked his work.   Born in Salinas, Calif., in 1902, Steinbeck was a ne'er-do-well, drifting from job to job and trying to find his natural voice in a fog of grandiloquence until ''Tortilla Flat,'' his first success, came out in 1933. A series of loosely strung sketches of the ''paisanos'' or outcasts on the fringes of Monterey, it was just the sort of book he needed. THE subject of femininity is at once instantly familiar and surprisingly unexplored. Like its relative, female sexuality, it has been for the most part discreetly ignored, put aside by men who disarmingly admit their inability to solve this riddle and passed over by women adhering to the conventions of female innocence. While the reasons for this restraint are legion, including the impossibility of an objective position and the fact that a woman who speaks about femininity disqualifies herself by the act of speaking, this restriction on knowledge renders women mysterious in the eyes of both sexes.

Although somewhat muted by its period trappings, ''The Proprietor'' by Ann Schlee is an elegant, absorbing and evocative novel. The proprietor, Augustus Walmer, is born into a banking family in 1806, in the midst of the Industrial Revolution. He belongs to the class that has decided to set the country right. At 30, he purchases a group of islands off the coast of England and settles there ''to devote his life to the conducting of an experiment to restore the islands' economy along utilitarian principles and to promote the greatest happiness among the greatest number of his people.'' Mrs. Schlee does all the things one enjoys in Victorian novels. Nature reflects or counters human action; dialogue is concise, description lavish; the marital and spiritual trials of several generations are sorted out. Reconstructing the story from journals and letters, she follows Walmer through a quarter-century, from an austere, idealistic youth to an old age in which, unchallenged and alone, he rules his property like some feudal lord. All the elements of this tale are familiar, but Mrs. Schlee has handled them very well, adding detail and narrative subtlety; there is also a haunting, coda-like final chapter. Her stately writing conveys the island's severe, desolate beauty and the social distinctions of city and country life. I couldn't help wondering why such skill should be devoted to reinterpreting 19th-century life and literature.  OUR 37th President has written another book.  The subject, of course, is foreign policy, Richard Nixon's abiding passion. In summary form, Mr. Nixon's argument is this. War between the superpowers, whether nuclear or conventional, would result in disaster for both sides. Dostoyevsky paid homage in fiction to Sonya's devotion to Raskolnikov, a thief and ax-murderer. But how much greater was the prestige of those innocent women who suffered for the criminals, when the crime was the pursuit of liberty, equality, fraternity.   Among the most famous female martyrs in Russia were the heroic wives (and occasionally lovers) of the Decembrists, named for an abortive military revolt of December 1825. Czar Nicholas I was threatened less by this poorly organized mutiny than by the secret discussion groups from which it sprang (schemes for freeing the serfs and introducing parliamentary democracy were intolerable to the new absolute monarch). With the severity that became his dubious hallmark, he sentenced 120 idealistic young men to death or hard labor, exile and the loss of property and titles. Reluctantly, he eventually allowed their wives to join them in frigid climes, provided they too gave up their positions in Russian society.

But the war had now begun to change its nature, and its proportions had swollen. The stakes on these days of late summer were much higher. George McClellan, at once theatrical and pedantic, had failed to take Richmond by his campaign up the Peninsula, and a new Northern army, under John Pope, had been formed. Fiery and bellicose, he was waiting by the Rappahannock River until McClellan's cumbersomely moving Army of the Potomac could be merged with his.  ''BURR'S life, take it altogether, was such as in any country of sound morals his friends would be desirous of burying in profound oblivion.'' So wrote America's most upright statesman, John Quincy Adams, after the death of his nation's greatest political reprobate. Adams's judgment neatly summarizes Americans' first image of Aaron Burr, that of an unprincipled political opportunist, dueling murderer and filibustering traitor. A second, often complementary image of Burr as the sober young republic's premier romantic adventurer is nearly as old. Indeed, so close are the facts of his ''colorful life . . . to the inventions of a novelist,'' in the words of the editors of this first major collection of his correspondence, that they have inspired several novelistic biographies and one fine novel, Gore Vidal's ''Burr.'' Paule Marshall's muses, she tells us, are ''the poets in the kitchen,'' West Indian immigrants like her mother who spent their days ''scrubbing floor'' for white housewives and then came home and talked away all silence, spinning language into richly patterned quilts. Invisible by race and invisible by sex, these women ''fought back, using the only weapon at their command: the spoken word.'' If their new country denied them, they would remake it in their own words: ''In this man world,'' they told each other, ''you got to take yuh mouth and make a gun!'' Like her muses, Paule Marshall lives in language; she retells the world in order to make it new. Her three novels span the last 25 years; the current collection - five short stories, an autobiographical essay and a novella, ''Merle,'' based on her superb 1969 novel, ''The Chosen Place, The Timeless People,'' Miss Marshall's finest book - is something of a sampler, offering an uneven but always rewarding introduction to her work. Unlike so much modern fiction, which often seems to be inscribed on the inside of a skull, Miss Marshall's tales are panoramic; her carefully detailed portraits are framed by restless social landscapes. In my favorite story, the autobiographical ''To Da-Duh, In Memoriam,'' a 9-year-old Brooklyn girl visits her grandmother on Barbados. The old woman, awed and terrified by rumors of New York, points out breadfruit, mangoes, fields of cane and asks triumphantly, ''Tell me, have you got anything like these in that place where you were born?'' When the child insists that New York has a building taller than the island's tallest palm or highest hill, the old woman and the old world are defeated.

 IF Modernism in the novel is understood to involve

radical or ''difficult'' experiments in language and

form, then the movement has indeed, like abstract

painting, fallen upon hard times. There is, however, another aspect of Modernism that, despite widespread cheapening and abuse, has retained much of its elan - the fiction of Surrealism or Magic Realism. While the two terms are not interchangeable, they are closely related, concerned as they both are with dreamlike distortions of what we like to think of as ordinary, waking reality. RICHARD HUGO, widely considered the pre- eminent poet of Western America, proclaimed, ''those words you can own . . . by right of obsessive musical deed.'' His subject was the American orphan, himself, refracted by scenes, people, weather, objects and creatures. Reading him is like browsing through secondhand shops with Wallace Stevens and Ernest Hemingway, chanting the mute histories of each cracked mirror and dented spittoon. Hugo felt and voiced the unprivileged, inarticulate world. His poems, although they are rarely outright narratives, tell the tale of the American search for identity and knowledge from the underbelly. One might say of him what he wrote about President Kennedy: ''He was not afraid of what we are.'' His is sometimes clunky, plodding poetry, but his collected work is a surprising, remarkable song of courage that penetrates inner landscapes. In ''Making Certain It Goes On'' - a welcome, stubby, wandering, and final collection - Richard Hugo, like Thoreau, earned the right to look any man in the face.

This slender volume, appearing midway through his second senatorial term, continues Mr. Moynihan's tradition of elegant and original thinking on the big questions of the day. The Senator puts three subjects under scrutiny, all of them having to do with America's role in the world and all of them related to the concept of loyalty - to nation, to good sense, to immutable principle - that the Senator sees his fellow citizens and politicians abandoning at our great peril.   Mr. Moynihan begins with nuclear arms, particularly last year's Senate decision to authorize funds for the MX missile, a decision that the Senator, with no apologies for hyperbole, calls ''probably the most fatal mistake in our history.'' Mr. Moynihan is no dove on defense. He believes that the massive buildup of nuclear arms by the Soviet Union has imperiled the American capacity to deter an attack. pull_quote: WRITING IN A STATE OF SIEGE. By Andre Brink. 256 pages. Summit Books. $15.95.   THERE is a well-known parable told by Garcia Lorca about a rich man and his peasant neighbor. As the two men stroll through the lovely countryside, the rich man exclaims, again and again, ''How beautiful!'' The poor man, however, merely clutches his stomach and cries, ''I am hungry, I am hungry, I am hungry.'' Such parables are commonly cited by those who argue that art is useless in the face of social problems, that artists and intellectuals are impotent when it comes to implementing political change. NIGEL HAMILTON remarks of Air Marshal Sir Trafford Leigh-Mallory that his ''pompous Englishness'' put off Gen. Omar Bradley and by implication other Americans. The phrase certainly fitted Field Marshal Sir Bernard Law Montgomery equally well, although Mr. Hamilton often seems not to realize it. Not only Montgomery's ego and eccentricities in themselves but the utter Britishness of manner and expression in which they were wrapped kept American soldiers from perceiving his merits.   In this huge second installment of what will be a three-volume biography, Mr. Hamilton may succeed as well as any writer can in lowering the barriers to American understanding of the field marshal. As a boy and young man, Mr. Hamilton was virtually adopted by Montgomery and came to observe him at close range. He has had complete access to his papers, and his questions were welcomed by Montgomery's friends. He disavows any intent ''to exonerate Montgomery from his grave failures as a soldier-statesman.'' The circumstances of men in battle - gratuitous violence, ambivalence, frustration and anger, divided loyalties - are all to be found in Rob Riggan's first novel, ''Free Fire Zone.'' They are handled remarkably well once Mr. Riggan gets a hold on his material. The characters are medics at an evacuation site, or free fire zone, in Vietnam, caught between the war itself and the hospitals several hours away. It's hard to think what would be worse - being on the battlefront or within the medical unit, mopping up the gore. On a visceral level, this novel horrifies, though not simply because of the blood and guts. As the story progresses, it moves away from the medics themselves to the effect of our presence upon individual Vietnamese. In one of the many powerful scenes in the second half of the novel, the pregnant Vietnamese wife of one of the medics comes to the evacuation unit to claim the body of her husband, only to learn that it has been shipped to America to his ''family.'' Back in the States, Jon O'Neill, the narrator, reflects upon all these events as he sleeps next to a girl he has picked up for the night. He realizes that his inability to feel for anyone or anything is an extension of his drugged-out state during the war. (''They sent them home in hermetically sealed steel boxes, and the living smuggled dope inside the same boxes; that was the reality - the dope, the callousness, the refusal to grasp what we were confronting, had in fact created.'')

By Russell Banks    WILLIAM McPHERSON'S first novel is an extraordinarily intelligent, powerful and, I believe, permanent contribution to the literature of family, childhood and memory. On the order of Frank Conroy's ''Stop-Time'' and Russell Baker's ''Growing Up'' (and, like them, no mere disguised autobiography or memoir), ''Testing the Current'' is a fully realized book that creates an entire, utterly believable world for us, immersing us wholly in Grande Rivi ere, Wisconsin, 1939, the ninth year of Tommy McAllister's life, the 25th year of his parents' marriage and the last year of what comes to feel like America's Age of Innocence.   Despite its careful, deliberate fix on the details of a 9-year-old boy's perceptions - of himself, of his close- knit, privileged Midwestern family and of their equally privileged friends and relations - the book has history in it, a coherent vision of America before World War II. An unstated but significant theme of the novel is that when the war began, everything changed forever.  We view Mr. McPherson's prewar world as if through amber. Consequently, the adults and children in it, with all their parochialism and pride, their hypocrisy, materialism and complacency, look sadly, almost tragically, innocent to us.We know what none of them knows, that soon, in a matter of months, their world will be swept away. It's not unlike Robert Musil's classic, ''The Man Without Qualities,'' but with a brilliant, observant child for the protagonist instead of a disengaged intellectual, and a mill town in Wisconsin in 1939 as setting instead of Vienna before World War I.

LINDA GALBRAITH was 26 years old and six months pregnant when she learned that she had acute myelogenous leukemia, a cancer of the blood that her doctors said gave her 18 months to live at best. Back in the 1950's Sloan Wilson wrote a novel, ''The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit,'' that caught the essence of what was then becoming known as the rat race. It was the story of a chronic worrier, Tom Rath, whose desire to be himself could not be reconciled with his ghostwriter's trade. A paratrooper in World War II, Tom hoped for peace as a Westport, Conn., commuter. But there were the usual money demands of a growing family, the need for a bigger house and the strain of a marriage to a woman who had grown up in a wealthy family expecting everything. There was also the lurking secret of the illegitimate son Tom had fathered in Rome in the war. The novel had a happy conclusion. Tom inherited grandma's big house, and his wife, Betsy, forgave his wartime infidelity. But now, a quarter-century later, we learn in a sequel that the Raths' contentment was momentary. Tom Rath, as the new novel picks him up in his middle age, is just the same old worrier. He still loathes writing for other people, he still frets because his paycheck can't meet occasional extravagances. Moreover, his teen-age children present a whole new set of exasperations. His relationship with his wife is outwardly calm, but he is ready for a fling. The fling, with a good-humored woman who is not a worrier, makes the story.

After a few tours as a professional wrestler, he returns to his home town of Union City, Ohio, where football memories are long and he is still a minor local hero. He marries, opens a bar and settles into a life of vague dissatisfaction, plagued by his regret over the stardom he never achieved. As his 40th birthday approaches, he is not willing to admit that at some stage of his life    too late    becomes a simple truth and not a fear. He prepares to make a comeback with a local football team, leaves his wife and has an affair with an old lover. Amid this spate of irresponsible behavior, his lover's son is arrested for a murder he did not commit and Roscoe, not knowing quite why, determines to ferret out the truth of what happened. In so doing, he recognizes the cowardice and lying endemic to the declining black community of Union City and begins to assume greater responsibility for reversing that decline. Roscoe will always dream big dreams, but with the ghost of his own murdered father looking over his shoulder, he begins to devote his fantasies to family and unity and quieter heroics. Mr. McCluskey relates these events quietly; there are no fireworks here, and little of the self-conscious cleverness that often mars the work of newer novelists.

SINCE morality makes awkward demands on us, and we appeal to it in making demands of each other, we have natural interest in the sources of its authority, if any. Is there hope for an objective standard which can settle some of the violent moral disagreements that surround us? Contemporary philosophers disagree as to whether the content of morality is universal - not whether everyone accepts the same morality (obviously they do not ) but whether it makes sense to look for principles that everyone ought to accept. many philosophers have agreed with Kant that it belongs to the essence of morality to discover standards for the conduct of life on which all rational beings can agree. Working the tradition of Jack London and Richard Adams, Donald McCaig, author of ''The Butte Polka,'' has produced an adult novel for animal lovers that does justice to both its human and canine characters. The plot involves the abduction of Nop, a noble Border collie in Virginia, by villainous rednecks, dog dealers and scientists, and his dramatic rescue by his owner, a Virginia sheep farmer. All this may sound more than a bit obvious, but Mr. McCaig, himself a Virginia sheep farmer, writes with an authenticity and crispness that bring a surprising liveliness to the story. At times, ''Nop's Trial'' assumes an insider's point of view. In one instance, Mr. McCaig writes that ''anyone who's ever seen a red fox slipping up behind an unsuspecting young groundhog has seen Nop's delicacy.'' Yet we might add that anyone who hasn't seen such a thing will still experience a keen sense of Nop's ''dog wisdom,'' so convincing is the novel's rendering of canine thoughts, sensations and even dreams. As for the human realm, it is captured with admirable economy, especially the violent, inbred world of junk cars and mobile homes into which Nop vanishes. ''Four families lived in the Gap and they were all more or less kin and though some hated the others' guts, they closed ranks against outsiders and their mouths against the law.'' The only jarring note in this entertaining novel is its preposterous dog talk, replete with ''thees'' and ''thous,'' which requires these otherwise dignified creatures to say things like, ''Nop, thou must be wary of cows with new young.'' Mr. McCaig would have done well to follow the advice of one of his epigraphs (quoted from John Holmes's ''The Farmer's Dog'') - ''A dog is not 'almost human' and I know of no greater insult to the canine race than to describe it as such.''

WHILE ''Adieux'' is a moving portrait of Jean-Paul Sartre in the last 10 years of his life, it is not a flattering one. Sartre was chronically ill during that time and half blind, unable to read, toward the end. The prospect of dying did not seem to concentrate his mind. Rather, he appears to be more diffuse, as if in his philosophy of engagement, or commitment, he felt the approach of death to be a disengagement or remitting.   In ''Adieux,'' Sartre sounds as if that is, in fact, what he is saying. He observes that his illness and near blindness robbed him of what he calls style. ''I've done what I had to do,'' he says. ''I've written, I've lived, there's nothing to regret.'' Not many men can look back on such a full, satisfying and influential life, and Sartre seems content to leave it at that. He's not trying to go further, just ruminating over the past and adding a few inconsequential footnotes.

''I AM bored by narrative,'' Virginia Woolf wrote in her diary in 1929, thus suggesting how the novel has been kept alive in our century by novelists' assaults on its conventions. Writers have chosen to write novels without plots or characters or the illusion of time passing. They have disdained to represent real life, as the painters did a half century before them. They have compacted their given languages, or invented their own, or revised the idea of composition entirely by assembling their books as collages.   Appearing noticeably in the United States 15 or 20 years ago was the disclaimed fiction in which the author deliberately broke the mimetic spell of his text and in sisted that the reader should not take his story to heart or believe in the existence of his characters. Disclaiming had the theoretical advantage of breaking through to some approximation of the chaos and loss of structure in life. The subject of these fictions became the impossibility of maintaining them, and the author by his candor became the only character the reader could believe in. John Barth is one writer who comes to mind as having explored the possibilities of this strategy, and the distinguished Czech novelist Milan Kundera in his new book, ''The Unbearable Lightness of Being,'' continues to find it useful.

pull_quote: TO LIVE AND DIE IN L.A.  By Gerald Petievich. (Arbor House, $14.95.) Susan Sontag once remarked that, for escape, ''I love to    read    the way people love to watch television.'' With ''To Live and Die In L.A.,'' reading is just like watching television; its characters and plot are straight out of an amiable, time-killing made-for-TV movie. Ace counterfeiter Rick Masters rules Southern California, but two treasury agents (among many others) are determined to put him behind bars. Richard Chance is a kamikaze cop who owes more than a little of his personality to Hicks in Robert Stone's ''Dog Soldiers.'' He's not above stealing money as well as classified evidence in order to assure that Masters gets his comeuppance. Also on the case is Jim Hart, a diligent, burned-out treasury officer who plugs away despite remorse over his wife's death. What    does    distinguish the story from a television melodrama is its liberal dose of sexual activity, some of it kinky. ''To Live and Die In L.A.'' is very much a male-dominated narrative. Men reflect on the mean streets they walk down; at one point a doomed crook muses, ''If there was anything he'd learned, it was that one simply could not be too cautious when dealing with the scum-of-the-earth.'' The bottom line here is that in Lotusland the good guys and the bad guys get all mixed up in the scum, and this world view makes Gerald Petievich's final resolution decidedly ambivalent.

Paper, $9.95.     ''CRIPPLE'' is a dirty word, to be avoided by all public speakers, as James Watt, the former Secretary of the Interior, found out. When the possessor of an intact body says ''cripple,'' he cannot help evoking the attitude of sneering condescension and cheap sympathy that the physically sound, in fear and self-defense, have traditionally adopted toward the lame. Like other ugly, guttural shorthand, ''cripple'' has a very different sense when it is used by a member of the group it brutally designates. It becomes a fighting word, a bitter emblem of anger and pride. This is how Lorenzo W. Milam uses it in ''The Cripple Liberation Front Marching Band Blues'': It stands emblazoned across the book's cover in inch-high capitals, runs boldly down its spine and, sometimes shortened to ''crip,'' slaps the reader in the face from every page.

HOW people feel about childbirth may tell us more about them than their politics does, or their philosophy - particularly now, when having children is no longer a matter of course, but of choice. When Francis Bacon said ''He who hath a wife and children hath given hostages to fortune,'' he did not seem to recognize that women shared the same predicament.   While Nancy Sorel neglects to mention this particular notion in ''Ever Since Eve,'' having children may be one of our principal articles of faith in a relatively faithless world. The thought of a child often seems to dissolve our skepticism. Even pessimists may regard a child as a symbol of rebirth. This says a lot about the irrational, as well as the rational, appeal of having children. It's a pity that for many parents the novelty wears off as the child grows up and vague hope turns into a hard fact.

 ''ON NATIVE GROUNDS'' (1942), Alfred Kazin's dazzling survey of the American prose literature of the previous half-century, brought him acclaim while he was still in his 20's. Further books defined his talent and temper: sensuously eager intelligence, a pride in America (for which he set demandingly high standards), and a special feeling for New York City. ''A Walker in the City'' (1951), for example, beautifully evoked a boyhood in Brownsville. He sought out kindred spirits among the offspring of Russian immigrants - precocious Our- Gang literati such as Isrolik, reading aloud T. S. Eliot's ''Waste Land'' ''with breathless adoration. . . . I seemed to see him sucking on each phrase like a lozenge he could not bear to swallow.''

Now, with ''An American Procession,'' Alfred Kazin confirms a reservation in the front tier of the reviewing stand, next to his eminent predecessors Van Wyck Brooks and Edmund Wilson. His title comes from a line in Whitman. I suspect Mr. Kazin fastened upon it mainly because most of the obvious titles have already been pre-empted, some by himself.

A CONCORDANCE, a reprise, a summary, all the old themes and obsessions hauled up by a single tough rope - does there come a time when, out of the blue, a writer offers to decode himself? Not simply to divert, or paraphrase, or lead around a corner, or leave clues, or set 
Cynthia Ozick's most recent books are ''Cannibal Galaxy,'' a novel, and ''Art and Ardor,'' essays.  out decoys (familiar apparatus, art-as-usual), but to kick aside the maze, spill wine all over the figure in the carpet, bury the grand metaphor, and disclose the thing itself? author: William Cronon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CHANGES IN THE LAND     Indians, Colonists, and the Ecology of New England.  By William Cronon.  241 pp. New York: Hill & Wang/Farrar, Straus & Giroux.  Cloth, $15.95. Paper, $6.95.       THE study of history, like history itself, runs an ever-shifting course. Indeed, the two are tightly linked. In a sense their course is the same. Always and inevitably, current history molds the interests, the questions, the values that historians bring to the life of the past. Thus the civil rights movement of the 1960's seeded a flowering of research in black history. And feminism yielded a new women's history. Moreover, the process is reciprocal. Black history and women's history serve, in their turn, to inform and invigorate the social movements that gave them rise.    Behold, then, ecological history, spawned by today's environmental concerns. Here is the newest of the new things under the historians' sun - newest, and quite possibly brightest - or, at any rate, most full of promise for advance in understanding. Black history and women's history bring new actors to the scholarly stage; ecological history changes the stage itself. For this is a history, William Cronon writes, ''which extends its boundaries beyond human institutions . . . to the natural ecosystems which provide the context for those institutions.''

ANY review of Mary Cunningham's ''Power Play'' must come to grips with the single most important issue regarding her much publicized relationship with William M. LIKE her earlier book, ''Psychoanalysis: The Impossible Profession'' (1981), Janet Malcolm's ''In the Freud Archives'' somewhat transcends what it appears to be: superb reportage. Both books are essays in personality, and in the broad sense deserve to be called ''fictions'' of the Age of Freud and Proust, in which we still live. But Miss Malcolm's main characters, this time, seem worthy of the grotesque cosmos of the novelist Thomas Pynchon. One is Jeffrey Moussaieff Masson, former Sanskrit scholar, former psychoanalyst, former Projects Director of the Sigmund Freud Archives, author of a current and rather dubious book, ''The Assault on Truth: Freud's Suppression of the Seduction Theory.'' Another is Peter Swales, follower of the mystic Gurdjieff and self-described ''punk historian of psychoanalysis.'' On the other or High Freudian side are Kurt Eissler, founder of the Freud Archives, eminently orthodox psychoanalyst, and the late Anna Freud, true daughter of the inventor of what remains our dominant theory of the psyche.

SCIENTISTS and philosophers concerned with the structure and nature of consciousness have traditionally assumed that there must be some absolute difference between humans and other animals. For thousands of years, there have been quarrels about exactly what this difference is, but there have not been many loud voices arguing that such an a priori assumption might cloud reason and observation both.   Instead of engaging this issue directly in ''Animal Thinking,'' Donald R. Griffin, who teaches at Rockefeller University and is the author of ''The Question of Animal Awareness'' and other books about animal behavior, wonders how we might find ourselves interpreting animal behavior - including that of insects and amoebas - if we were to suspend judgment about the currently dominant scientific theories, which hold that animals do not think. Instead of doing what science teaches us to do - that is, mostly, studying behavior that can be duplicated in controlled situations - what if we just observe and then tell speculative anecdotes about what we see?
headline: TALKING ANTS AND OTHER UNORTHODOXIES

But Schumann, who may have been in the late stages of syphilis, was hearing angelic voices in his head; gradually they turned hellish and drove him insane. As for Brahms, his music is more troubled than idyllic - filled with voices not just of nightingales but vultures.

That was the decade of the Japanese conquest of Manchuria, the Sino-Japanese War and the ''united front,'' which cloaked the basic conflict between Chiang Kai- shek's Nationalist Government and the Communists for ultimate power in China. It was a time of patriotic fervor, courage and sacrifice, mass exoduses from eastern to western China, of ''good guys'' and ''bad guys.'' author: Ken Ledbetter

pull_quote: FICTION    TOO MANY BLACKBIRDS. By Ken Ledbetter. (Beaufort, $14.95.) Reading ''Too Many Blackbirds'' is like sitting through a long criminal trial in which everyone takes the witness stand except the accused. The natural courtroom in Ken Ledbetter's first novel comprises the general store, barbershop and street corners of Poplar Springs, Kan., sites where gossip and speculation fly about a newcomer Morgan Ballard. Ballard dresses oddly, wears an unheard of Vandyke beard, is said to be rich and wanders down from his house on the hill to spew maxims that befuddle the locals, like ''it takes one hell of a lot of living just to get through life.'' The things that make Ballard an object of rabid gossip, though, are the tragedies that mark his brief life in Poplar Springs. A small boy drowns in Ballard's well; his first wife disappears, but then he is seen burying her; his second wife is burned to death in a fire in which he and his freakishly bright daughter, Ophelia, also die. These horrors, rendered by a third-person narrator, take place in the first chapter of the novel; the remaining 16 chapters are a series of monologues - testimonies, really - given by the residents of Poplar Springs. The librarian comments on Ballard's reading habits, the minister on his spiritual powers, the coffin maker on the casket and funeral procession of his first wife. Though some of these monologues are convincingly rendered, many suffer from a heavy dose of folksy philosophizing on such topics as the nature of storytelling, the difficulty of knowing another person and the benefits of deductive reasoning (there's even a discussion of ''Moby- Dick,'' though Faulkner's ''As I Lay Dying'' seems to be the elusive paradigm to which this novel aspires).

By Joyce Carol Oates    PRODIGIOUS Gore Vidal - the author, with this massive and carefully researched volume on Lincoln's Presidency, of some 25 books (19 novels, five collections of essays, one collection of short stories) and five plays; so kaleidoscopic in his interests, his energies and the remarkable range of his talents, the Vidal voice is as readily discernible in the comic masterpiece ''Myra Breckinridge'' as in the somber meditation upon mortality ''Two Sisters,'' as fully present in those critical essays in which, out of habit perhaps, he routinely excoriates experimentation in fiction, as it is in an experimental attempt of his own, last year's ''Duluth.''   So zestfully does Mr. Vidal contradict himself in his practice as a writer, one is not surprised to read, as long ago as 1967, that he has all but given up on prose fiction (''three centuries is quite long enough for any literary form'') while being told that he is at work on a ''chronicle'' of novels dealing with American history. If Mr. Vidal the polemicist is frequently at odds with, and not particularly nourishing to, Mr. Vidal the writer of fiction, one should not hold it against him. Consistency, as Whitman knew, is one of the minor American virtues.

SINCE the middle of the 19th century, a majority of social scientists and a substantial minority of historians have believed that a search for laws of history would be fruitful. The most impressive efforts along these lines (whether or not one agrees with them) have been those that have been broadly comparative. Karl Marx and Arnold Toynbee, otherwise unlikely bedfellows, belong together, at least in this regard. Such efforts are implicitly or explicitly anthropological; they recognize that the theorist who relentlessly focuses on a few cultural forms will never see the forest for the trees. At their best, the more comparative efforts give us a view of the sweep of social forces in history that seems as obedient to laws as, say, most of biology. They offer at least the prospect of a view of human nature that is more orderly and meaningful than the picture of endless foibles that emerges from more typical works of history.

The protagonist of this first novel by the Off Broadway playwright Anthony Giardina is Jack Henna - a 43-year-old insurance salesman with a house in the suburbs, a wife of 18 years, two sons and a life that, except for his older son's lack of interest or talent in sports, has epitomized the American dream at its most prosaic. Henna wants it that way, has ''worked hard to keep his life small.'' But when he learns that a colleague is having an affair, something is apparently triggered in his mind. He sees flaws in his life, and the first woman he meets thereafter becomes an object of exotic possibility and rampant fantasy. She is a ''beneficiary,'' the widow of a man who has committed suicide and left her on an isolated, unworked farm with a young, athletic son and few skills with which to confront the ''real world.'' Through Mr. Giardina's clever imagery, the reader understands long before Henna does that the woman and the boy and the farm are uncharted territory, waiting to become his ''garden,'' just as his own family has been. That the woman and her son may wish to clip and shape their own lives does not occur to him for some time. Mr. Giardina's experience as a playwright is evident in his scene-like approach to this psychological drama. He has an exquisite sense of the nuances of gesture and voice, the clamor of things unsaid.

Just as abrupt shifts occur between levels in the buildings Escher drew, abrupt semantic shifts occur in Mr. Ashbery's poems. Non sequiturs spin off in various directions; phrasings of inspired concision telescope with prolix, prosier ones. pull_quote: PILGRIMS IN THEIR OWN LAND    500 Years of Religion in America.  By Martin E. Marty.  Illustrated. 500 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Co. $25.      By Michael Kammen    FROM the beginning, religion has been a major element in the very marrow of American life. In the beginning were the settlers, the settlers knew the words, and they knew the words meant them - Chosen People. Ever since, religion has either been prominently onstage or else briefly in the wings making a change - from fundamentalist to modernist (or back again), from reformist to quietist, from seeking to self-satisfied and from privatist to what Abraham Lincoln labeled ''the political religion of the nation.''    In 1984 religion's role is once again at center stage. The issue of school prayer, presumably settled by the Supreme Court more than 20 years ago, has recently polarized millions, and it does so in a way that cuts across party, class and denomination. A constitutional amendment that would permit voluntary prayer in the public schools has been hotly contested in Congress and is likely to be an issue in many campaigns this fall.
headline: FAITH AMONG A RESTLESS PEOPLE

title: Fiction    Lizzie
author: Evan Hunter
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FICTION    LIZZIE. By Evan Hunter. (Arbor House, $16.95.) Late one August morning in 1892 in Fall River, Mass., someone murdered Andrew Jackson Borden and his wife, Abby. The unsolved crime has inspired more than a dozen books, several plays, two television treatments, even a ballet. Like many of those before him who have been fascinated by the case, Evan Hunter comes away from his research with a theory, a handful of facts rounded out with supposition and the zealous conviction of the amateur sleuth who's cracked an elusive nut. Widely known for the police novels he has written as Ed McBain, Mr. Hunter is a keen analyst of criminal motive, and his reconstruction in the last chapter of Lizzie Borden's actions on the day her parents were slain is an intriguing piece of speculative history that makes for the best reading in the book. Unfortunately, the platform on which that final scenario is played seems rather wobbly at times. In the factual chapters - courtroom scenes for which Mr. Hunter relied on actual transcripts from the trial - we are given reams of testimony that provide a measure of realism. The fictional chapters, which alternate with the factual, send Lizzie on a trip to Europe, where she is seduced into a lesbian affair by a woman she meets in London. Curiously, these episodes, based entirely on conjecture, are more important than those rooted in fact when it comes to shoring up Mr. Hunter's ultimate argument.

As he puts it, ''Rilke was perhaps more exclusively a poet than anyone before him or since.'' The implication is that the poet crowded out the man.

author: Yevgeny Yevtushenko
pull_quote: WILD BERRIES. By Yevgeny Yevtushenko. Translated by Antonina W. Bouis. 296 pages. Morrow. $15.95.  Wild Berries,'' Yevgeny Yevtushenko's first novel, is the Soviet equivalent of a potboiler. It consists of action, sex, landscape and elementary discussions of Russian life and literature. The descriptions of landscape are the best part; Mr. Yevtushenko is, after all, a well-known poet. Here and there, he manages a nice vignette or two, but generally the writing and the plotting are slapdash. In fact, it's remarkable that such an experienced poet should be so clumsy even in his first novel.   It's hard to say whether he's careless or disorganized or whether he's attempting to borrow the loose, associational structure of modern Western fiction. Whatever the case may be, it doesn't work. In one chapter, the book leaps from Siberia to Chile to show President Salvador Allende Gossens having his portrait painted. The sole link here seems to be that there are politics everywhere. Another chapter introduces a California rock group called the Tails, and here the cross-reference is the fact that a member of the group had visited the Soviet Union as a high school student.

title: Ulysses
author: James Joyce
pull_quote: The publication last week of a corrected version of James Joyce's ''Ulysses'' has been a major topic of conversation among Joyceans, some of whom have already ordered the $200 three-volume edition produced by Garland Publishing. But other Joyce enthusiasts have asked how soon they will be able to buy a low-cost edition that also corrects the 5,000 or so omissions, transpositions and other errors in existing editions.    The answer is not for a while. The agreement between Garland and the original publishers of ''Ulysses,'' Random House in the United States and the Bodley Head in Britain, specifies that those two publishers are not to bring out a revised-text edition for at least two years. A Random House spokesman said, ''We hope to issue the revised edition as soon as we can.''

It's as if they can't find their way back to the beginnings of words.

pull_quote: THE MIRROR MAKERS     A History of American Advertising and Its Creators.  By Stephen Fox.  Illustrated. 383 pp. New York: William Morrow & Co. $17.95.     ADVERTISING has always been the Peck's Bad Boy of American business. Unlike most goods and other services, which tend to be taken seriously, its products are words and pictures, urging us to buy things we probably don't need and often can't afford. (Nor is advertising necessarily a ''service.'' After all, we don't request its presence, as we do a plumber's.) Even so, it is impossible to visualize an America without it. And many of us secretly enjoy the sassier commercials and elegant layouts, not to mention being told of impending sales.    Stephen Fox has written a fascinating account of what may well be this country's most characteristic institution. ''The Mirror Makers'' moves from the earliest print shops to international agencies, with sources ranging from scholarly archives to personal interviews. The book is fun to read, but then the subject is a natural; advertising is an industry where egos loom large and methods verge on the outrageous. At the same time, the author is a trained historian, concerned with the power of advertising as a social force. His thesis, about which more momentarily, makes a great deal of sense.

author: Jane Somers

pull_quote: Caroline Seebohm is a freelance writer and critic.  IF THE OLD COULD . . .     By Jane Somers.  250 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.     THIS novel has an extremely courageous premise - the first love of a 50-year-old career woman.  Many women wonder what happens when the flesh begins to fail, the breasts begin to sag, the hair begins to thin and the body begins to lose all semblance of form - what happens, I mean, if a woman of middle years falls in love in the all-consuming, obsessive way that is normally the lot of a 17-year-old. The protagonist of ''If the Old Could . . .'' finds herself facing precisely this problem when she encounters love at first sight with a handsome American in London. The heroine's and the author's names are one and the same (though in fact the ''real-life'' Jane Somers is the pseudonym of a British journalist). The Jane of the novel is a top editor of a successful fashion magazine, a widow with no children, financially and professionally secure. But when she falls in love with Richard her world is turned on its heels.

title: Technostress
author: William Stockton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: William Stocktonby Everett M. Rogers and Judith K. Larsen. (Basic, $19.95.) By Scott Cohen. (McGraw-Hill, $14.95.)
pull_quote:
William Stockton is assistant to the Executive Editor of The New York Times. 



COMPUTERSSILICON VALLEY FEVER: Growth of High-Technology Culture. 

By now nearly everyone must know that high technology is the way of the future and that the cradle of high tech is a wonderful and mysterious place in California (where else?) named Silicon Valley. Silicon, of course, is the stuff rocks and sand are made of. It's also used to make microchips, ceramic gadgets the size of a little finger which contain thousands, even millions, of electronic circuits. Without them, there would be no video games, home computers, automobiles that talk back in monotones or navigational brains that enable a nuclear-tipped missile to hit the head of a pin 10,000 miles away.  Silicon Valley, located at the southern end of San Francisco Bay, is a feverish place where brilliant young engineers working in a friend's backyard garage invent the electronic marvels of our age. They spin off new companies at breakfast, grow into multimillionaires after lunch and lose their fortunes or have their companies shot out from under them before the evening's prime-time television sitcoms are finished. Hovering about are the venture capitalists, known locally as ''vulture capitalists.'' Everett M. Rogers and Judith K. Larsen, both Silicon Valley professionals, he a Stanford University professor and she a consulting engineer, interviewed many of the valley's leading lights, culled everything they could find about the place in the media and fashioned a literary stew.
headline: THINKING MACHINES AND THEIR PEOPLE

pull_quote: Grace Glueck is an art critic for The New York Times.  DIANE ARBUS     By Patricia Bosworth.  Illustrated. 366 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.     IT'S not too often, even these days, that photographers achieve the distinction of popular biographies. Though the camera now creates our most universal visions, those who have mastered it professionally are still not accorded the culture-hero status of actors, artists, writers and politicians. Their lives are left to gleam fitfully through their work. But the late photographer Diane Arbus (1923-1971) was something of an exception. A Park Avenue princess, she grew up to make freaks and misfits the subject of her art. Successfully teamed with her husband in fashion photography, she broke away to the rebellious new ground of 60's photojournalism. Then, well en route to the status of legend for her haunting camera confrontations, she committed suicide at the age of 48.

title: Fat Of The Land
author: Fred Powledge
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Bryan Miller is a reporter and restaurant columnist for The New York Times.  FAT OF THE LAND     By Fred Powledge.  287 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $15.95.     WHY is it so difficult to find a flavorful tomato at a supermarket, even in midsummer? Why do breakfast cereal boxes contain up to 37 percent air? Why do chicken breasts taste like cardboard? These and a score of other troubling questions are addressed by Fred Powledge in ''Fat of the Land,'' a lucid, disturbing account of America's biggest business - food. Mr. Powledge, the author of ''Water: The Nature, Uses and Future of Our Most Precious and Abused Resource'' and other books, cites Government statistics showing that of the nearly $300 billion Americans spent in 1982 on domestically produced food at the retail level, about one- fourth went to farmers. The rest went to middlemen - wholesalers, truckers, advertisers, packagers and retailers.  Mr. Powledge points out that Americans are becoming increasingly removed from their food sources, and the result, he says, is higher prices for lower quality. We are locked into a system that unnecessarily transports food thousands of miles and encourages concentration in food retailing to the detriment of consumers, he contends. For example, New York City, which is surrounded by major tomato growing regions (New Jersey, Long Island and upstate New York), depends on California and Mexico for most of its tomatoes year- round. Even in midsummer, he says, New York City is committed to a system that brings in nearly half its tomatoes from California.
headline: TOO FAR FROM THE FARM

title: The Only Problem
author: Muriel Spark
pull_quote: THE ONLY PROBLEM. By Muriel Spark. 179 pages. G. P. Putnam's Sons. $14.95.   IN her very first novel, ''The Comforters,'' written some two and a half decades ago, Muriel Spark explored the relationship between life and fiction, between God's intercession in our lives and a novelist's manipulation of his characters' fates. In the author's own fiction, nasty murders, suicides and other swift, unforeseen blows of fate proliferate with such abandon that questions about God's - not to mention, Mrs. Spark's - rather high- handed dispensing of justice are naturally raised. Now, in her 17th novel, Mrs. Spark, herself, has attempted to address the question of whether or not human suffering is justified. ''The Only Problem'' features a scholar- hero, obsessed with the Book of Job, and it also uses that biblical story as its central metaphor.

pull_quote: FICTION    THE COMPLETE KNOWLEDGE OF SALLY FRY. By Sylvia Murphy. (Putnam's, $13.95.) The problem with ''The Complete Knowledge of Sally Fry,'' an otherwise clever British novel written in the form of a dictionary, is that Sylvia Murphy has sacrificed the reader's sympathy for the sake of a good laugh. Sally Fry, a social worker and unwed mother, goes to her mother's peaceful Cornwall cottage in order to find a quiet place to finish her thesis. The sudden disappearance of her teen-age boy and the ill-timed arrival of every conceivable relative make work impossible and drive Sally to a ''self-therapy'' of her own invention - an alphabetical list of random words and the thoughts she associates with them. Her real concern, the dictionary reveals, is not work or family or romance but her son, Sebastian, an introverted, emotionally disturbed boy. But while Sally berates herself for not having done more for him, Sebastian's odd behavior is the comic trump card played time and again throughout the novel. This humor seems misplaced, especially since Sally's rather egocentric life and emotional neglect of her son are clearly to blame, at least in part, for his illness. Such apparent callousness mars an otherwise authentic, colorful portrait of a woman and her life, in which a funny and even moving voice may be heard.-    Jodi Daynard

FOREIGN BODIES 

 By Barbara Grizzuti Harrison.  348 pp. New York: Doubleday & Co. $16.95.  

THE self-harried heroine of Barbara Grizzuti Harrison's ''Foreign Bodies'' chooses men who do not or cannot love her. Angela, a journalist, is in love - besotted, really - with their rejection. Yet masochism is just Angela's starting point, almost an organizing principle. Intoxicated by her obsession, hung up in a sexual and spiritual purgatory, she is wildly self-destructive. She is just intelligent enough to keep finding literary or philosophical reasons to ''love'' Devi, a waspish Pakistani homosexual painter. Alas, he loathes her flesh and - as far as I could see - doesn't much care for her mind either.

title: On The Yankee Station
author: William Boyd
pull_quote: ON THE YANKEE STATION. By William Boyd. 217 pages. William Morrow and Company. $12.95.   AT age 32, William Boyd has already emerged as one of Britain's brightest new talents. The comic brio of his first novel, ''A Good Man in Africa'' - and the creation of Morgan Leafy, perhaps the funniest English bumbler since Lucky Jim - established him as a worthy heir to Waugh and Amis. And ''An Ice-Cream War'' - his ambitious second novel, which related the intertwined stories of several ordinary folk caught up in the madness of the Great War - not only ratified his easy grasp of irony and satire, but also enlarged his fictional terrain, demonstrating his capacity to also write with seriousness and compassion. Indeed Mr. Boyd seems singularly blessed with both an innate love of storytelling and the talent to render those stories in swift, confident prose.

LAURENCE BERGREEN must be the first person to have written about James Agee without any particular degree of emotional commitment or admiration. But perhaps this well-researched book is the dispassionate biography we need.

When Agee died on May 16, 1955, at the age of 45 after a heart attack in a Manhattan taxi, he had a minor reputation as a poet (a slim 1934 volume in the Yale Younger Poets series), a movie critic (for Time and The Nation) and a screenwriter (the scripts for ''The African Queen'' and a five- part study of Lincoln for the CBS arts program, Omnibus). In New York literary circles, however, this tall, handsome Southerner had become a legendary character for his attractive personality, extravagant behavior and unrealized genius. In Mr. Bergreen's words, he was ''a cult figure to the cognoscenti, respectably disreputable and roguish.''

pull_quote: FICTION    SEVEN SILENT MEN. By Noel Behn (Arbor House, $16.95.) The author of ''Big Stick-up at Brink's!'' and ''The Kremlin Letter'' again demonstrates his skill at believable suspense in this story of a bank robbery in a small Missouri city. The robbery is accomplished through a confusing network of tunnels, natural and man-made, which make it comparatively simple for the robbers to drill up through the floor of the bank's vault and provide them with an escape route as well. The reader observes the break-in, then watches the local F.B.I. office attempt to justify its involvement in solving the crime, which was committed against a bank without Federal insurance. When justification does come, the longtime senior resident agent is unaccountably transferred by direct order of his old friend and supporter, J. Edgar Hoover; thereafter the investigation is marred by confusion. Much detail is given about the background of several of the characters, but there are so many characters that it is difficult to keep track of who is who. The book has over 500 pages, and the last 150 do move quickly, suspensefully and involvingly - for one thing we find out for whom we should be rooting. Up to that point, nobody seems to have any clear idea of what's really going on except for the seriously bad guys, and we don't know who they are or what they are truly after. Descriptions of the layout of the tunnels and how they are used, together with the welter of characters, may well diminish the enjoyment of impatient readers, particularly those who do not easily visualize complicated diagrams.

title: The Only Problem
author: Muriel Spark
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE ONLY PROBLEM 

 By Muriel Spark.  179 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $14.95.  

THE only problem for Muriel Spark, it would seem, is that there are many questions for few answers.  This is the theme of her new novel, as it may well have been of all her others. Her devoted readers have always been aware that there is a metaphysical component to her fiction, and it is something of a relief that it has at last broken cover in the present work, which is both an extremely sophisticated account of the perils that surround our unsuspecting lives in the world today and a disputation on the subject of the Book of Job, which she calls ''the pivotal book of the Bible.'' Job and his disconcerting predicament challenge every optimistic belief one yearns to accept, lodging like a hard mass of contention in the consciousness of the hopeful believer. The same sort of existential distress is experienced by Mrs. Spark's current protagonist, Harvey Gotham, yet Mrs. Spark is too wise a writer to impose this metaphor on her readers, and her narrative is as seamless, as unnerving, and as expert as her readers have come to expect from this most excellent of storytellers.  
Anita Brookner's most recent novel is ''Providence.''

IN 1966, at the age of 24, the Austrian playwright   Peter Handke achieved the kind of    succ es de scandale    every ambitious young writer dreams of: At a   performance of his play ''Offending the Audience,'' the audience obligingly stormed the stage. Within a year, his play ''Kaspar'' was hailed as the most important since ''Waiting for Godot,'' and Mr. Handke became the    enfant terrible    of the European avant-garde, denouncing all social, psychological and historical categories of experience as species of linguistic fraud. author: Norman Mailer

pull_quote:
TOUGH GUYS DON'T DANCE 

 By Norman Mailer.  229 pp. New York: Random House. $16.95.  

THE first question is, Did Tim Madden, drunk and drugged, murder Jessica Pond? If not, who did? And in any case, how did Jessica Pond's severed head turn up in Madden's marijuana patch in Truro?

Norman Mailer's new novel is a murder mystery. The scene is Provincetown, Mass., on Cape Cod - ''And for fall, winter and spring, nothing is superior to little old P-town'' - the time is November, all the visitors have gone. Madden, an ex-bartender, is a writer of sorts. He has also done three years in jail for drug-running. His wife, Patty Lareine, has left him, so he is hitting the bottle in The Widow's Walk bar. Things get blurred when he blunders into a conversation between a California lady and her sexually ambiguous escort. In no time at all another female head turns up, severed and blond - ''Any lady who chooses to become a blonde is truly blonde,'' according to one of the novel's more charming passages. Two hundred pages later we have assembled, by my count, seven corpses, not including Madden's dog, Stunts, killed by Spider Nisseh's knife.

title: Fiction    Good King Harry
author: Denise Giardina
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FICTION    GOOD KING HARRY. By Denise Giardina (Harper & Row, $16.50.)    Denise Giardina makes a promising debut with this richly imagined historical novel told in the first-person voice of England's King Henry V. During his nine-year reign, from 1413 to 1422, Henry of Monmouth transformed an ailing England, fraught with internal dissension and civil rebellions, into the strongest kingdom in Europe. In telling the tale, Miss Giardina departs from the Elizabethan model of Shakespeare's debauched Prince Hal, profiting from later, less biased accounts, such as the Oxford scholar E. F. Jacob's 1947 history, ''Henry V and the Invasion of France.'' She rejects as well Henry's beloved sidekick, Falstaff, in favor of that famous sot's historical antecedent, Sir John Oldcastle, the Lollard reformer and eventual rebel against the king. There has been much speculation among historians about why the bawdy prince, a favorite of tavern keepers and whores, suddenly developed both a conscience and the habit of chastity. Miss Giardina also invents a character, a Welsh peasant girl named Merryn, as the mystery's solution and as a love to which Henry becomes completely devoted. The unfolding of this unlikely romance, in a setting of political intrigue and royal family squabbles, is as satisfying as the best of BBC's Masterpiece Theater series, and as tear-jerking as any novel by Dickens. It is no mean feat to invent a diction in modern English that is perfectly readable while capturing the flavor of an older language. With only occasional lapses, Miss Giardina succeeds in this.

title: Indian Country
author: Peter Matthiessen
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
INDIAN COUNTRY 

 By Peter Matthiessen.  338 pp. New York: The Viking Press. $17.95.  

ALMOST every book about the American Indian in recent decades, no matter how broad or narrow its historical perspective and no matter what nationality its author may be, is a combination of accusation and lament. The balance between anger and sorrow shifts according to the writer's viewpoint, but those two emotions seem unavoidable when the subject is any aspect of Indian life since the advent in North America of white settlers, traders, missionaries, miners, railroad men, the United States Cavalry, the Army Corps of Engineers, cattle and lumber barons, oil men, real estate developers, fast shufflers of treaties and other strange pieces of paper, the Bureau of Indian Affairs and preliterate foes such as deputy sheriffs and James Watt.

Peter Matthiessen's ''Indian Country,'' an eloquent and painful look at the past and present situations in many Indian territories where social unrest and injustice have turned into open confrontation, is no exception. But what makes this book most unusual and most valuable is its effort to infuse the inevitable anger and sorrow with a sense of immediate urgency, with prophetic warnings.
headline: 'SOMEBODY'S GOT TO HANG ON'

author: Nadine Gordimer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
SOMETHING OUT THERE 

 By Nadine Gordimer.  203 pp. New York: The Viking Press. $15.95.  

GREAT white sharks, killer bees, werewolves, devils, alien horrors bursting from the chests of movie spacemen: The popular culture of our fearful times has provided us with so many variations on the ancient myth of the Beast, the ''something'' lurking out there that hunts us and is hunted by us, as to make it one of the defining metaphors of the age. In the jungle of the cities, we live among our accumulations of things behind doors garlanded with locks and chains, and find it all too easy to fear the unforeseeable, all-destroying coming of the Ogre - Charles Manson, the Ayatollah Khomeini, the Blob from Outer Space. Clearly, many of these forebodings are the product of affluence and of power. The haves and the powerful, fearing the uprising of the have-nots and the powerless, dream of them as monsters.

title: London Fields
author: John Milne
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FICTION   LONDON FIELDS. By John Milne. (Hamish Hamilton/David & Charles, $14.95.) Take ''The Friends of Eddie Coyle'' and transport them to London and its environs and you get an idea of the milieu in which John Milne, author of the well-received novel ''Tyro,'' operates. But that's not to say that he is a carbon copy of George V. Higgins. Like Mr. Higgins, he is masterly in evoking the bleak world of small-potatoes thieves and penny-ante scam artists with dialogue that takes up most of this slim novel; the narrative passages are unusually graceful. Mr. Milne leads his Cockney protagonist Elf Hicks through a series of misdemeanors and felonies that result in the police collaring Hicks, then releasing him, hoping he will help them set a trap for his more wanted cohorts, which he does. But Hicks finds it increasingly hard to live with himself after his double-dealing precipitates his best friend's murder. His rage boils over and he strikes out brutally and senselessly. And here the author seems to be saying that rage is the sole engine of destruction and that further psychological explanations are pointless. Mr. Milne is incisive and convincing, but I have one caveat about the novel - the underworld slang might prove forbidding even to American readers who are usually comfortable with English colloquialisms. - Randy Hogan

author: Elinor Langer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: JOSEPHINE HERBST By Elinor Langer.  Illustrated. 374 pp. Boston: Atlantic/Little Brown & Company. $19.95.     FOR understanding what it was like to live to the full the turbulent American literary life of the 1920's and 30's as it moved from bohemianism to radicalism, there could be no more revealing figure than Josephine Herbst, a novelist who, strange as it seems now, was ranked in the 30's with Ernest Hemingway and John Dos Passos. She knew everyone and was in all the right places at the right historic moments - Greenwich Village, the Left Bank, Russia, Germany, Cuba and Spain. She captured the times in her fiction, her reporting and what Alfred Kazin called her ''incomparable letters, of the sort no one even thinks of writing any more.''   After 1940, when her reputation and income shrank almost to nothing, Herbst went obsessively back to the past in notes, journals and constantly revised memoirs, of which only three fragments were published. She was still working on them a few hours before her death, in 1969, at the age of 77.
headline: A LIFE OF PASSIONATE COMMITMENTS

title: Modus Vivendi
author: Deirdre Levinson
pull_quote: Here is Queenie Quesky addressing her students - or so she recalls - on the occasion of their immersion in Shakespeare's sonnets.    ''Inasmuch as we are undoubtedly among the last representatives of the posterity that wears this world out till the ending doom,'' she says, ''and inasmuch as it must follow that even the poet's pow'rful rhyme, eternal lines, black ink, virtue of pen cannot outlive all life, it behooves us, as among his last readers, therefore to read him well.''   So literature is the real heroine of this fiercely eloquent, ironic first novel about a woman trying to put herself together again after the death of her baby son. Queenie would drown her students in literature just as she once nearly drowned herself in water when, growing up as part of a tiny Jewish minority in a Welsh village, she devised for herself ''a training course in adamantine endurance, inflexible courage'' to distinguish herself from her three sisters, ''docile little girls, undifferentiated, undifferentiable, sifting and pouring and whisking and stirring and bowing and scraping in abject servility.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Art Dealers
pull_quote: Art dealing, as someone once said, is like conducting an orchestra. The only way to learn it is to do it. Among the books to read, there are the memoirs of great European dealers of the recent past like Ambroise Vollard and Daniel- Henry Kahnweiler. There is S. N. Behrman's immensely diverting life of Duveen. Among American growths, there are Julien Levy's ''Memoir of an Art Dealer'' and John Bernard Myers's recent and hugely mischievous ''Tracking the Marvelous.'' It probably helps to have been to business school. It is also a help to have family money, if you know how to use it, and to have served an apprenticeship with the best dealer who will take you on. But fundamentally, like the aspirant conductor, you just have to stand up in full view of the public. If you're no good, they'll tell you.     This was much in my mind a few weeks ago, when the 100th anniversary came around of the birth in Mannheim, Germany, of D. H, Kahnweiler. Kahnweiler lived to be a very old man indeed, and to the day of his death his gallery in Paris was the first one to go to if you were interested in Picasso. But he was known and admired above all for the fact that by the time he was 25 he had had the exclusivity of Picasso, Braque, Derain and Vlaminck. (Juan Gris came later, but not much later.)
headline: A BOOK THAT SHOWS ART DEALERS TO BE HUMAN, TOO

title: On The Third Day
author: Michael Delahaye
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FICTION    ON THE THIRD DAY. By Michael Delahaye. (Macmillan, $15.95.) Confronted by an American President's demand that Israel hand back the West Bank, the Israeli Government produces evidence of a stupendous archeological find - the first-century skeleton of a crucified man in his 30's lying in an ossuary inscribed ''Jesus the Nazirite.'' Soon the Vatican has joined Washington and the Palestine Liberation Organization in a mission to purloin the bones. Michael Delahaye presses the plot to a heart-racing conclusion. But ''On the Third Day'' is something more than a summer read. It is also a political novel of some insight. Career politicians, those ''self-serving apparatchiks,'' are dangerous not simply because they lack integrity, an aging Ben-Gurion-like figure tells Israel's prime minister, but because they lack ''the quality that distinguishes the statesman from the politician: vision - the ability to think in decades, not days; to look beyond the cluttered foreground to the distant horizon, the mountain peaks ahead, not the puddle at your feet.'' In ''On the Third Day,'' in fact, Mr. Delahaye, a former BBC reporter, has written a novel about political vision. It is that vision that determines the outcome of the novel's bone-snatching scheme, and also determines the future of Israel and the Roman Catholic Church. Indeed, it is a tribute to the book that its politics do not interfere with the suspense and that its elements of suspense do not detract from its political insight. The book has flaws - all the Americans are editorial-page cartoons and the love interest is laughable - but even so it is not too much to say that ''On the Third Day'' is everything a novel should be.

title: The Life And Death Of Liam Faulds
author: Hugh McCleave
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FICTION    THE LIFE AND DEATH OF LIAM FAULDS. By Hugh McCleave. (Joan Kahn/St. Martin's, $13.95.) With some clever turns and comic charm, the Scotsman Hugh McLeave's 10th novel tells the story of a novelist who decides to pump new life into his tired career by writing a novel under a nom de plume and is destroyed in the process. Graeme Baldwin, a once-bright star on the London literary scene, is now aging, weary and cynical. One night, while watching ''The Treasure of the Sierra Madre'' on television, he begins to contemplate the legends surrounding the mysterious identity of its author, B. Traven. Baldwin creates Liam Faulds and, under that name, writes ''A Common Grave,'' a star- crossed lovers' tale of a Catholic and a Protestant in Northern Ireland. The novel, of course, becomes a runaway best seller and the mysterious Faulds generates more curiosity and attention than might J. D. Salinger and Thomas Pynchon combined. Mr. McCleave's caricatures of high-powered Fleet Street publishers and authors are, if not poison-penned, enjoyably acidulous, and the elaborate plotting to create and sustain the myth of Liam Faulds has, at times, the exhilaration of a sturdily constructed mystery. But the book is on shakier ground in the more complex characterization of Martin Gilchrist, a young freelance writer whom Baldwin employs to impersonate Faulds's agent, and in the depiction of Anne, Martin's wife. Anne becomes the novel's pivotal character, but her motives for out-plotting Baldwin and turning her husband into Britain's hottest literary property - a plot that involves theft, arson and murder - are both vague and improbable.

pull_quote: HOLLYWOOD DYNASTIES LODZ By Stephen Farber and Marc Green.  Illustrated. 365 pp. New York: Delilah/Putnam Publishing Group. $16.95.     Since the Census Bureau has yet to compile industry-by-industry statistics on nepotism, it is hard to say if blood is thicker in Hollywood than anywhere else. But Stephen Farber and Marc Green make a convincing anecdotal case for the proposition that being born (or marrying) into the movie business is a high-benefit/high-risk affair.    When Carl Laemmle Jr. turned 21, his father gave him a birthday present - the post of head of production at Universal Studios. Carl Jr. did a creditable job for a while, turning out three triumphs of the early sound era, ''All Quiet on the Western Front,'' ''Dracula'' and ''Frankenstein.'' Then the ink turned red, and ''Junior,'' as he was known to one and all, had to endure the double indignity of being fired by his old man and replaced with his brother-in-law. He did not endure well. Junior Laemmle never again did any work to speak of, and he never married. He proposed once - to the actress Constance Cummings - but his father nixed the choice on the grounds that she was a gentile.

Literary modernism has been divided between romanticism, or the desire to grasp the infinite, and nihilism, the impulse to trash - to punish - that desire (this last having become the ''postmodernist'' specialty). The modernist question, as Octavio Paz's brilliant manifesto of 1956, ''The Bow and the Lyre,'' provided the terms for seeing - is whether man, who ''wants to be another,'' has the wherewithal ''to go beyond himself.'' TOWARD the end of World War II, John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern, in a long, highly mathematical treatise, launched a novel type of economic analysis called game theory. It differed from traditional theory in its focus on the strategic interdependence of a few actors, called players, each partially aware of the nature of their interdependence. The abstraction stripped away the details, color and personalities involved in political, military, business and family conflicts and isolated, with great clarity, underlying mathematical and strategic considerations. The two books under review deal with the application of these ideas to such ''games'' - a misnomer - as the arms race and inflation.
