pull_quote: LUCIFER: The Devil in the Middle Ages. By Jeffrey Burton Russell. (Cornell University, $24.95.) Jeffrey Burton Russell, who teaches at the University of California, Santa Barbara, knows the trickiness of his subject: ''The history of the concept of the Devil reveals all that can be known about the Devil, and it is the only way that the Devil can be known.'' Some history! The Devil has been around next to forever. But Mr. Russell is undaunted. In ''The Devil'' (1977), he tracked old Nick from antiquity through the New Testament; in ''Satan'' (1981), he followed him through the fifth century; ''Lucifer'' brings him up to the 16th, and a fourth volume is in the works. Mr. Russell begins ''Lucifer'' with the speculations of a sixth-century Serbian monk who opens the door onto Byzantine diabology. Byzantine devils were interesting but tame. It was in the West that they got really vicious - and sometimes comic. In this account they romp through plays, poetry and legends, belch brimstone from pulpits and torture saints and witches in ingenious hells. But it is the devil in the mind that is important to Mr. Russell. He recounts theolo-gians' arguments with an economy and clarity that makes them exciting. And his conclusion is a surprise - the Devil was sidelined not by skeptics but by St. Anselm of Bec and St. Thomas Aquinas who argued that Christ's death is not a ransom of captive sinners but an act of satisfaction to God for mankind's original sin; their resolution of the problem of evil and salvation in a world ruled by a just God made Lucifer a bit irrelevant in theology.

ANNA BANANA AND ME By Lenore Blegvad. Illustrated by Erik Blegvad. Unpaged. New York: A Margaret K. McElderry Book/Atheneum. $9.95. (Ages 4 to 8)


 WERE you one of those timid kids, like me - afraid of your own shadow? When my mother wouldn't let me see the movie ''The Thing'' because she said it would give me nightmares, it gave me nightmares anyway. Years later, when I did see the movie, I realized that my imagination had created a far worse monster than the film maker's. ''Anna Banana and Me,'' the dust jacket copy tells us, stems from Lenore Blegvad's childhood experiences and so the emotions it evokes have a quality of authenticity. Did her mother allow her to see ''The Thing''? Or did she have a friend like mine? Ellen's ability to make up real daytime horror stories far exceeded mine, and in the course of our friendship, my nighttime imagination was overworked. But Ellen was an irresistible friend, just like Anna Banana. She was braver than I, just as Anna Banana is braver than the little boy who tells this story. Anna leads him into places and games ''where,'' he says, ''I never go'' - into dark places under trees in the park, upstairs and down dark halls in his own apartment house, to the sandbox to build birthday cakes and castles, and finally to the lap of a stone statue like the one of Hans Christian Andersen in Central Park.

pull_quote: MUSIC IN TEREZIN 1941-1945 By Joza Karas. Illustrated. 223 pp. New York: Pendragon Press/Beaufort Books. $16.95.   TEREZIN, in Czechoslovakia, was one of the most enigmatic concentration camps. The Nazis groomed it to ''model'' status, at first permitting and later encouraging musical composition and performance there. Several concerts were literally command performances, immortalized on film by the Germans as evidence that Jewish prisoners were being treated well. The occurrence of several musical events in a single day at Theresienstadt - the camp's German name - was commonplace, and the performances often featured original works by more than 10 composer-inmates. At least four concert orchestras flourished there, and as many chamber groups, featuring musicians of the highest professional caliber. Operas, both original and classic, were performed by artists from wartime Europe. During a four-year period (1941-45), the finest music came soaring from what was, essentially, a halfway house to the Auschwitz inferno. Most puzzling was Terezin's schizophrenic origin - Nazi indulgence and defiant Jewish creativity.

THIS enthralling autobiographical fragment by Stuart Hood, a World War II British intelligence officer, tells of his escape from a prisoner-of-war camp in Parma and his life on the run with Italian partisans in the Resistance. Mr. Hood, formerly the head of the BBC World Service and responsible for scheduling programs at BBC Television, is now a freelance producer of documentaries and a scriptwriter for the BBC and ITV networks, and his skills as a writer are much in evidence here.   Mr. Hood's story begins a few weeks after the coup detat that overthrew Mussolini's dictatorship. On Sept. 8, 1943, the new Government suddenly announced Italy's breach with her Axis partner and the signing of an armistice with the Allies. In the confusion that followed, hundreds of Allied prisoners of war escaped, including Mr. Hood, who was then an army captain. In the ensuing days thousands of young Italians, acting out of a variety of motives, began to flee into the mountains to organize resistance against the Germans and the Italian Fascists.

MINIMALISM has its uses, and can achieve surprisingly varied effects: it can allude and expand, as well as leave out and compress.   At its most reductive or repetitive, it can induce corresponding states of boredom or trance. There is a kind of writing that masks a lack of substance by itself posing as substance. Rushing to fill that void, a reader must project his own meaning, or assume the presence of some meaning that eludes his grasp. At its worst, minimalism is a kind of fraudulent tic that serves to hide a vacuum or defend against feeling. At its best it can, with economy and restraint, amplify perception and force meaning to leap from the page. In most of the stories that make up this first collection, Amy Hempel has succeeded in revealing both the substance and intelligence beneath the surface of a spare, elliptical prose.

IMAGINE a writer with the prolific versatility and discipline of, say, John Updike - but an Updike who was forced to store a dozen years' worth of manuscripts in a drawer and then to publish them all within an extremely short time. This is the problem a reader faces in responding to ''Surplussed Barrelware,'' the third substantive work published in English translation during the past 18 months by the Russian emigre writer Vassily Aksyonov.   Mr. Aksyonov, perhaps the most gifted member of the post-Stalinist generation of Soviet writers, was rarely published in his native land during the repressive period between the 1968 Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia and his enforced emigration in 1980. The impressive body of novels, short fiction and plays published since his departure attests to the steadiness of purpose that kept Mr. Aksyonov writing under conditions much more likely to crush creativity than to act as the spur envisioned by some Western romanticizers of ''Russian suffering.''

author: Jimmy Carter

pull_quote: THE BLOOD OF ABRAHAM By Jimmy Carter. 257 pp. New York: Houghton Mifflin Company. $15.95.   WHEN an ex-President or other former holder of high political office writes a book about a major issue in which he was personally involved, we do not look for the precision and analytical depth of the scholar, nor for the immediacy and expository skills of the journalist. If we find them, we are grateful, and perhaps surprised; if we do not - as in this volume - we cannot reasonably complain. In such a book, we look for two things, facts and insights. The first may perhaps consist of the revelation of new facts, perhaps of the confirmation or denial of rumors and reports. The second, insights, may give us some new and deeper understanding of the problem itself, or, alternatively, of the perceptions and sentiments which shaped the author's own participation. It is for this last that President Jimmy Carter's new book on the Arab-Israeli conflict will chiefly be valued.

This is a bombast world: fig-trees,      Snow, macacos, ocean's hurl      And surf and surge, on applebough      As crag whose cave holds kraken or      With comb of coral mermaid cuddles. THIS slim volume descends upon the endless debate over the future of the welfare state as if out of a time warp. Today the focus in America has shifted to society's minimal obligations to the needy, to restoring incentives and promoting efficiency. And here is Michael Ignatieff, a young, highly regarded Canadian historian, asking such questions as whether any society deserving to be called decent can be satisfied with meeting its citizens' material needs while ignoring their requirements for ''fraternity, love, belonging, dignity, and respect.''   At the same time, not since the 1920's has American politics been so filled with talk of things spiritual, with one hope standing out - that a shared morality can reunite a country whose differences are threatening to overwhelm and paralyze it. Mr. Ignatieff does not directly address the modern American political and social agenda. His often beautifully written essay, however, is a much-needed reminder that the common purpose for which Americans profess to hunger will not be restored by political advertisements showcasing ethnic weddings or idealized suburban neighborhoods.

NAZI GOLD 

By Ian Sayer and Douglas Botting with the London Sunday Times. Illustrated. 423 pp. New York: Congdon & Weed. $21.95.

SINCE 1945, treasure-hunters have dug up most of Bavaria looking for Nazi gold. Coming late to the scent, through an entry in ''The Guinness Book of World Records,'' Ian Sayer and Douglas Botting calculate that some $2.5 billion (at present values) in bullion, coin and currency went missing from the Reichsbank's reserves that year in what the Guinness book calls the ''Robbery: Biggest Unsolved'' of all time. Mr. Sayer, a transportation executive, and Mr. Botting, the author of several books on World War II, also feel we might as well hang up our shovels now, for it looks as if the whole lot was safely pouched long ago by the Russians, by runaway war criminals, thieving ex-Nazis and United States military personnel in the American zone of Germany - arguably, on this evidence, the stickiest-fingered army of occupation since Attila dismantled the Roman Empire.

author: Roger Starr

pull_quote: THE RISE AND FALL OF NEW YORK CITY By Roger Starr. 258 pp. New York: Basic Books. $17.95.   THE New York that Roger Starr recalls - and would restore - was a place of ''civil peace'' and ''moral order.'' He has written a courageous and controversial book about a city he once loved but that no longer captures his affections. He speaks out strongly on race and class, levels charges of arrogance and cowardice and offers little solace for citizens who have mainly themselves to blame. There was hardly a page on which I did not find myself arguing with ''The Rise and Fall of New York City,'' which is probably why I enjoyed it as much as I did.   If New York's rise began when Peter Minuit bought Manhattan for a bargain price, the first half of the current century was really its golden years. By 1900, Mr. Starr reminds us, ''an unprecedented level of civil order seemed to have been achieved.'' The violence of earlier years had abated; even the poorest streets were surprisingly safe. People accepted whatever work and housing they could get; despite a diverse population, there was a tacit consensus about the goals and rules of urban life. Roger Starr was raised during this era, when a ''social distance between classes'' was still discernible. Like many members of his generation, he feels it is no longer his city.

On the one hand, we have the young, brainy but socially backward biochemist Jeremy Singer, a homunculus with an oversize, prematurely balding pate, whose ability to score with women ranks with Quasimodo's. MARY McCARTHY'S new book comprises uncollected reviews and criticism, obituary pieces on her friends Philip Rahv, Nicola Chiaromonte, Hannah Arendt and F. W. Dupee, political reporting, several prefaces and afterwords to other people's books, a retelling of ''La Traviata'' commissioned by the Metropolitan Opera and one biographical sketch, all culled from the last 15 years or so of her distinguished writing career.
headline: YOU PAY ATTENTION, YOU LEARN SOMETHING

title: Beyond The Chocolate War
author: Robert Cormier
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BEYOND THE CHOCOLATE WAR By Robert Cormier. 278 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $11.95. (Ages 12 and up)      NO one who has read Robert Cormier's young adult novel ''The Chocolate War'' can forget the anguish of that final fight under the spotlights at the Trinity School. The freshman Jerry, who alone has tried to challenge the corrupt power at the school, is beaten by the beastlike bully Janza, with the student body screaming for Jerry's blood. The confrontation was rigged by Archie, the leader of the school's secret Vigils society, with the tacit approval of the authorities. Worse than the physical and official brutality is Jerry's moral breakdown - he discovers his own pleasure in violence, and in his defeat whispers to the friend who betrayed him: ''play ball. . . . Don't disturb the universe.''   Eleven years after its publication, ''The Chocolate War'' continues to be controversial for its pessimism. While critics study its literary quality, it remains a favorite with teen-age readers. It has spawned nihilistic imitators, but, like most current young adult novels, they focus on the individual struggle to work things out with family, friends and lovers. Mr. Cormier is almost unique in his powerful integration of the personal, political and moral.
headline: No Headline

title: Around The World In 78 Days
author: Nicholas Coleridge
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AROUND THE WORLD IN 78 DAYS. By Nicholas Coleridge. (McGraw-Hill, $14.95.) If Phileas Fogg could dash around the world in 80 days, why shouldn't Nicholas Coleridge be able to duplicate the feat? There is no reason why not, it turns out, except for discontinued shipping routes, idiotic taxi drivers, even more idiotic bureaucrats, monsoons and the British Empire, the dissolution of which has divided one visa into at least 19.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Choosing Elites
author: Robert Klitgaard
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CHOOSING ELITES By Robert Klitgaard. 267 pp. New York: Basic Books. $19.95.   IT is good to go to Harvard. It is so good that about 13,000 apply for just over 2,000 places in the entering class. Ninety percent of the applicants could do solid academic work if admitted. At Stanford, where the numbers are virtually the same, 4,000 applicants had perfect A averages in high school. But from the deans of admissions' point of view, this much talent is a problem.   ''Choosing Elites'' provides a framework for thinking about admissions at elite universities; an extensive discussion of the problems of using quantified achievement scores to predict academic success and success in later life; and a case study of admissions at Harvard, where Robert Klitgaard, an economist, is an associate professor of public policy.
headline: LUCKING INTO HARVARD

title: Nowhere
author: Thomas Berger
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NOWHERE    By Thomas Berger. 190 pp. New York: Delacorte Press/ Seymour Lawrence. $14.95.   IMAGINE a playwright and private eye who is shipped off to a nation called Saint Sebastian - it is bordered on the north by Gezieferland, on the southeast by Swatina - where people with blond hair are scapegoats to those with brown (and where everyone is born a blond). As stand-up comics, literary parodists (like Rabelais) and satirists (like Swift) might say: swallow the premise, and you buy the whole routine.
headline: SEBASTIANI Terror

title: All Our Yesterdays
author: Natalia Ginzburg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ALL OUR YESTERDAYS    By Natalia Ginzburg. Translated by Angus Davidson. 300 pp. New York: Carcanet. $14.95.   NATALIA GINZBURG has been publishing since the 1930's, when she was in her teens.   But the list of her books is not long - perhaps a dozen titles - and it gives only a partial idea of her significance in the Italian cultural panorama. She has also been a critic, a successful dramatist, a valued translator (Proust and Flaubert) and she is now a member of Parliament. She grew up in Turin, and in the prewar years began working for the new publishing house of Giulio Einaudi, who introduced not only Mrs. Ginzburg but also Cesare Pavese and Elio Vittorini and, a little later, Elsa Morante and Italo Calvino. In addition to being vigorous anti-Fascists, these writers were alert to those foreign cultures that Fascist provincialism was trying to keep out of the country. Mr. Pavese translated ''Moby-Dick'' and works of Sherwood Anderson, and Leone Ginzburg, Natalia's first husband, helped introduce Russian literature into Italy.
headline: WAR IN A CLASSICAL VOICE

title: The Oxford Book Of Children's Verse In America
author: Donald Hall
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE OXFORD BOOK OF CHILDREN'S VERSE IN AMERICA    Edited by Donald Hall. 319 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $18.95.      THE new ''Oxford Book of Children's Verse in   America'' is not just one more collection of poetry for the young. Though it includes many of the poems that children today enjoy, it also contains many that older readers will recall from their own youth, and also some that our parents, grandparents and great-grandparents knew best. The content of children's anthologies and magazines changes dramatically over time, and the favorite verses of your childhood are very likely to have been forgotten in later collections. This volume does not forget them. It does not address itself principally to the contemporary child; rather, in the words of its editor, the gifted American poet Donald Hall, it contains ''work that represents a place, a time, or a genre.'' Because of this, it provides a fascinating historical record of how both poetry and childhood have been viewed from ''The Bay Psalm Book'' to Shel Silverstein and Nancy Willard.
headline: POETRY AND ITS SMALLEST Audience

title: Alice Through The Needle's Eye
author: Gilbert Adair
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ALICE THROUGH THE NEEDLE'S EYE    By Gilbert Adair. Illustrated by Jenny Thorne. 186 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $11.95.   SOME people are convinced that our greed for more of the same is a disaster when it comes to literature. Varieties of kisses or chocolate may promise a limitless pleasure without affecting the original commodity. But a fiction is a fiction, it is argued, and its elements are not, by some inherent structural rule, extendible beyond the self-defining bounds of the original. But alas, we do crave more Falstaff, more Sherlock Holmes, more James Bond, more Alice. We plead that a loved character's behavior may be repeated in infinite contexts that do not violate the authenticity of the fictions from which they derive. And, according to the law of supply and demand, our craving is sometimes satisfied. The fat knight is put through his paces; the lean detective survives the Reichenbach Falls; Alice dreams again.
headline: LEWIS CARROLL IS STILL DEAD

title: The Penguin Rhyming Dictionary
author: Rosalind Fergusson
pull_quote: THE PENGUIN RHYMING DICTIONARY. By Rosalind Fergusson. 530 pages. Viking. $20. ''The Penguin Rhyming Dictionary'' comes into the world trailing clouds of technological glory. At long last, as Rosalind Fergusson explains in her preface, mere human contrivance has given way to the clinical efficiency of a computer. In compiling the ''Dictionary,'' she began by extracting a list of words and their phonetic transcriptions ''from a standard dictionary data base.'' Then the computer took over, having been programmed to sort the words into phonetic order, ''working from the end of the phonetic transcription back to the beginning.''   It all sounds impressive, and Miss Fergusson is in no doubt as to the advantages her method enjoys over the hit-or-miss handiwork of the past: ''With its ability to scan through a complete list of phonetic transcriptions in a matter of minutes, the computer is an incomparably more versatile rhymester than the live poet with his dying brain cells and deteriorating memory.''
headline: Books of The Times;   Rhyming Computer

author: Tom Sharpe
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WILT ON HIGH. By Tom Sharpe. (Random House, $13.95.) title: Sweet Justice
author: Jerry Oster
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A man in a subway car shoots a punk and disappears. The news media make a big thing of it. The Mayor of New York demands that the killer be brought to justice. But public opinion is strongly on the side of the killer. Sound familiar? It should. You read about it in Brian Garfield's ''Death Wish,'' published in 1972, and then millions saw the film starring Charles Bronson. But those two were make-believe. In the case of Jerry Oster's SWEET JUSTICE (Harper & Row, $13.95), life seems to have imitated art. The book was written before Bernhard Goetz shot those youths in a New York subway car when he thought, or claims he thought, he was being threatened.   ''Sweet Justice'' starts with three punks in a subway car molesting a young woman. A bystander tells them to stop. When they start dragging the woman from the train, he shoots and kills the leader. Then he vaults from the train, which is pulling out of the station, and disappears.

author: Peter Niesewand

title: Days Between Stations
author: Steve Erickson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DAYS BETWEEN STATIONS. By Steve Erickson. (Poseidon, $15.95.) Sometime in the not too distant future, the planet Earth is rapidly going to the dogs. Los Angeles is swept by sandstorms that darken the sky and send dunes crawling up the buildings. A pall of smoke hangs over Paris, where the lights have gone out and bonfires burn out of control. The canals of Venice have inexplicably dried up, and the streets, smelling of garbage, are periodically plunged into deep fog. The landscape is fabulous, bleak; the lovers who travel through it, Michel and Lauren, are just the opposite - romantically alienated and drunk on their own eroticism. There is a healthy dose of cinematic surrealism in the Los Angeles writer Steve Erickson's moody first novel, along with a decidedly unhealthy dose of overwrought ''Fleurs du Mal'' bad dreams. Lauren, wife of a Vietnam veteran and world-class cyclist named Jason, stumbles into an adventure with the estranged, degenerate Michel (or Adrien - a victim of amnesia, he isn't sure which). Tortured by the past he cannot remember, with only a reel of film for a clue, he makes a voyage via flashbacks to Paris of the 1920's, where his grandfather is filming an epic of the death of Marat. With the magical ease of a movie that floats back and forth in space and time, the author at one point sets Lauren adrift on a houseboat from the Seine out onto the Atlantic, through the straits of Gibralter to meet Jason in the desiccated Venice.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Betsey Brown
author: Ntozake Shange
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BETSEY BROWN By Ntozake Shange. 207 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $12.95.   GROWING up isn't easy for the 13-year old heroine of Ntozake Shange's second novel, ''Betsey Brown'': ''Gosh, she wished her mother understood there was so much in the world to feel and see.'' Miss Shange writes, ''A girl had to get out of the house and into the thick of life, the heat of it, not knowing what all one could do with whoever you happened to be.'' Betsey happens to be a black girl coming of age in St. Louis in 1959, the year that city began to integrate its schools. The thick and the heat of life are the very fabric of this novel, which revolves around an eccentric and marvelous black family. Betsey's father, Greer, is a doctor. He wakes the children with conga drums in the morning and quizzes them on black history. His wife, Jane, a social worker, is trying to raise four of her own children and one of her sister's, run the household, and sort out her own identity - ''be who she was when Greer first courted her, a lady of intellect, mystery and surprises.'' While the parents make love in the morning, the grandmother frets about the children. ''Four chirren and God only knew how many more. Please, Lord, no more. Thy Bounty is Mightily Received.''
headline: LIFE ABOUNDING IN ST. LOUIS

title: The Half-Mother
author: Emma Tennant
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE HALF-MOTHER By Emma Tennant. 176 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $14.95.   THIS is Emma Tennant's eighth novel and, although short, it is complex and ambitious. She uses the first person to tell her story of strange passions. But that often most limiting technique is here moved so boldly through time and memory and the reader's changing perceptions that the effect is many-layered. In this way, ''The Half-Mother'' is immediately reminiscent of Ford Madox Ford's masterpiece, ''The Good Soldier,'' in which the final picture is only perceived at the very end.

author: Lawrence Badash
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: KAPITZA, RUTHERFORD, AND THE KREMLIN By Lawrence Badash. Illustrated. 129 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $20.   IN 1934 Peter Kapitza, a distinguished Soviet physicist who had lived in England for 13 years, was forcibly detained in the Soviet Union after he returned there for a visit with relatives. The sorrow of his friends and colleagues was matched by the anger of British science administrators, for only a little more than a year earlier Kapitza had been named director of the Mond Laboratory of Cambridge University, which had been constructed and equipped with expensive instruments designed for Kapitza's personal research.
headline: IVORY TOWER WITH ELECTRIC FENCE

title: The Call
author: John Hersey
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE CALL By John Hersey. 701 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $19.95.

JOHN HERSEY has a well-deserved reputation not only for writing on a wide variety of subjects, but also for managing to confront his readers with moral problems in a nondidactic way. Mr. Hersey does not don the mantle of preacher or prophet; he is a novelist and essayist first, last and always. But he seems aware, throughout his writing, that - as Christopher Fry puts it in ''A Sleep of Prisoners'' - ''Affairs are now soul size.'' I doubt Mr. Hersey would be comfortable with Mr. Fry's next line: ''The enterprise / Is exploration into God,'' but he would surely affirm that exploration into the heights and depths of the human spirit is proper to his craft. For whether he is confronting us with the genuinely sensitive and good-hearted Major Joppolo in ''A Bell for Adano,'' the magnitude of human evil in ''Hiroshima,'' the juxtaposition of Jewish greatness and Nazi depravity in ''The Wall'' or the unquenched yearning for a center of meaning in ''A Single Pebble,'' a cameo set in the China of his childhood, Mr. Hersey lays before us the quests, bafflements, frustrations and modest triumphs of the human spirit in ways that leave our minds sometimes ennobled and always stretched in new directions.
headline: ALL HIS LOSSES WERE HIS GAIN

title: Minds, Brains And Science
author: John Searle
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MINDS, BRAINS AND SCIENCE By John Searle. 107 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $10.   THE rumor is rapidly spreading, fanned by the devotees of the hallucinated discipline known variously as cognitive science and artificial intelligence, that the mind is nothing more than the computational humming of its programmed parts. Or, put more succinctly: man is a computer - of all things! In ''Minds, Brains and Science,'' his bluff and lucid little book, based on his 1984 Reith Lectures on the BBC, John Searle, a professor of philosophy at the University of California, Berkeley, tries to knock this picture of the mind into a cocked hat.
headline: IN THE CHINESE ROOM

title: The House Of The Spirits
author: Isabel Allende
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE HOUSE OF THE SPIRITS By Isabel Allende. Translated by Magda Bogin. 368 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95. WITH this spectacular first novel, Isabel Allende becomes the first woman to join what has heretofore been an exclusive male club of Latin American novelists. Not that she is the first contemporary female writer from Latin America (I think immediately, for instance, of Luisa Valenzuela and Cristina Peri Rossi) - but she is the first woman to approach on the same scale as the others the tormented patriarchal world of traditional Hispanic society and to argue that the enraged class violence in Latin America is a debate among men who are not only deaf but who have fixed and unalterable ideas on all subjects. And she has done all this in an absorbing and distinguished work that matches her predecessors' in quality as well as scope.
headline: RECONCILIATION AMONG THE RUINS

title: Hitler In History
author: Eberhard Jackel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
HITLER IN HISTORY By Eberhard Jackel. 115 pp. Hanover, N.H.: University Press of New England. $11.95. IMAGINING HITLER By Alvin H. Rosenfeld. 121 pp. Bloomington: Indiana University Press. $15. HITLER has been dead for 40 years, and yet he is alive - in the debates of historians and in the conscience and fantasy of people everywhere.

And no wonder: he was the most dramatic exemplar of demonic power in our century, a mass murderer, a genius without a trace of moral scruple. He found accomplices everywhere. We have to live with this memory; we live, moreover, in a world that was fashioned on the ruins of his empire. He remains a presence. Historians still grapple with the puzzles of his career, while most of the public seems to be endlessly fascinated and titillated by a mythic Hitler, a fabricated ghost that stalks the world.

''Hitler in History'' and ''Imagining Hitler'' attest the continuing curiosity about Hitler. They complement each other; one discusses aspects of the historic Hitler and the other explores the posthumous and fictionalized Hitler. Scholars argue about the causes of his success and the nature of his rule; others have an unappeasable hunger for vulgar, pornographic Hitleriana. The appearance of fraudulent Hitler diaries in 1983 was a striking example of the greed with which even responsible journals and individual scholars will exploit this mass appetite. As Alvin Rosenfeld notes. ''the marketing of Adolf Hitler has become big business.''
headline: EXORCISING THE 20TH CENTURY

title: Selling Out
author: Dan Wakefield
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SELLING OUT By Dan Wakefield. 300 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $16.95.   READ this book and you'll never again look at a television movie without thinking of Perry Moss and his descent into the seventh level of the Hollywood hell reserved for ''honest'' writers. A professor of literature at a small Vermont college and author of several prize-winning short stories, Perry is summoned to the Coast to bring quality and culture to Tinseltown television. He leaps at the chance to write a script honest and true, assuring himself and his wife that he will never ''sell out'' - never write a line that he knows to be meretricious and false.

RED BAKER By Robert Ward. 202 pp. New York: The Dial Press/ Doubleday & Company. $14.95.

WINTER in Baltimore, and the freezing cold reflects the despair of men laid off from the Larmel Steel works. It is 1983. The 60 percent of the work force that has been thrown out of work has little hope of ever getting its jobs back. The workers read in a local newspaper that their skills are ''nontransferable,'' but when Red Baker, the narrator and central character of Robert Ward's third novel, reaches the unemployment line, it doesn't take him long to realize the truth is bleaker still.

title: Inventing Ivanov
author: Roberta Smoodin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: INVENTING IVANOV By Roberta Smoodin. 295 pp. New York: Atheneum. $15.95.   SOME novels are so clever they're exhausting, like the glorious garden (blue roses! honeysuckle!) that turns out upon inspection to be an impassable maze. Intrepid hikers may someday find the center, the reflecting pool or sunny heap of stones, but they arrive toting maps and compasses, leveling rods and astrolabes. If they don't get lost in the labyrinth's dizzying spirals - ''Twirl follows twirl,'' writes Nabokov, ''and every synthesis is the thesis of the next series'' - their survival gear litters the lawn and crushes the flowers.

title: Sarah, Plain And Tall
author: Patricia MacLachlan
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SARAH, PLAIN AND TALL By Patricia MacLachlan. 58 pp. New York: A Charlotte Zolotow Book/Harper & Row. $8.95. (Ages 8 to 10) THIS is an exquisite, sometimes painfully touching little tale of a lonely, widowed late 19th-century prairie dweller, his two children and the laconic Sarah Elisabeth Wheaton, who comes from Maine to share their life.   It is the simplest of love stories expressed in the simplest of prose. Embedded in these unadorned declarative sentences about ordinary people, actions, animals, facts, objects and colors are evocations of the deepest feelings of loss and fear, love and hope.
headline: SARAH,PLAIN AND TALL

title: What The Light Was Like
author: Amy Clampitt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WHAT THE LIGHT WAS LIKE By Amy Clampitt. 110 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. Cloth, $14.95. Paper, $8.95. THE acclaim that has greeted Amy Clampitt's work is the more surprising in that its special characteristics are among those routinely disparaged by mainstream contemporary taste. Instead of ''natural speech'' and Hemingway terseness she gives us baroque profusion, the romance of the adjective, labyrinthine syntax, a festival lexicon. She is as ''literary'' and allusive as Eliot and Pound, as filled with grubby realia as William Carlos Williams, as ornamented as Wallace Stevens and as descriptive as Marianne Moore. Moore's Socratic tone, her appetite for fact and abrupt leaps of association have shaped Miss Clampitt's talent, and so has Hopkins - the accumulation of sensory ecstasies, the Saxonism of his diction and syntax, the multiplied coinages. All of this amounts to saying that Miss Clampitt is found among the famous eccentrics of style, like Milton, Dickinson, Mallarme and Stevens who write in a special poetic dialect of their own confection.
headline: CANDLE IN AN ICY DRAFT

title: Heat
author: William Goldman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HEAT By William Goldman. 244 pp. New York: Warner Books. $15.50. FINALLY, the wonderful thing about William Goldman's novels is this: they create a world in which we would like to live. That world is the world of Invention. This stuff is satisfying. Here in his new novel, ''Heat,'' we have a Tale of America. We have The Glider, a hit man from Tahoe who is a double for Fred Astaire; Baby, ruler of the Vegas Combination; Rainbeaux Wylie, ambitious woman; Cyrus Kinnick, computer millionaire from Boston; Ashley and Darryl Paxton, two media evangelists who've now turned to God.   And we have Shootouts, Punchouts, Rape and Revenge, a Gambling Binge written in the galloping style of Count Vronsky's steeplechase. We have changes of fortune, identity and sex. We have the American language written with the glorious vitality of the self-taught: ''The accent was so heavily British it made you want to break something.''
headline: LAS VEGAS, LOVE IT OR LEAVE IT

title: The Prick Of Noon
author: Peter De Vries
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PRICK OF NOON By Peter De Vries. 233 pp. Boston: Little Brown & Company. $14.95.   IT'S getting harder to be funny these days, especially in the comedy of manners of which Peter De Vries is such a master. De Vries's splendid precocity has always consisted, in the past, of a deeply serious, even puritanical attack on the morals and living styles of the gracious set, or the mob that in this story he calls the ''bohemian bourgeoisie.'' His famous puns (''It's the tale that dogs the wag'') and tricks of language habitually are at the service of a genuinely old-fashioned sensibility. Even his most Keystone Cop-like capers, such as ''The Tunnel of Love'' or ''Comfort Me With Apples,'' have a touch of John Knox preaching to fat-bellied sinners.
headline: PARONOMASIAMANIA

title: The Pork Butcher
author: David Hughes
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PORK BUTCHER By David Hughes. 123 pp. New York: Schocken Books. $11.95.   DAVID HUGHES'S ninth novel, a small, tightly constructed book, is rooted in the author's preoccupation with the continuing effects of this century's two major wars. Set in present-day Europe, ''The Pork Butcher'' deftly explores the inescapable burden of the past on the present, and has much to say about the nature of love in our times.
headline: A TASTE FOR RISK

title: Her First American
author: Lore Segal
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HER FIRST AMERICAN By Lore Segal. 287 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.   MORE than 20 years ago Lore Segal published a brilliant novel in the form of a memoir, ''Other People's Houses,'' which recounts the life of a Viennese refugee child who is boarded in a series of English families for seven years. Eventually her parents managed to leave as well, and are employed as servants in another series of houses. These members of a comfortable middle-class Jewish family are now treated as objects of charity, subject to the whims of various employers and bureaucrats. Lore manages to triumph over these vicissitudes with the help of the sharp analytic eye of a born writer. (One wonders if any of the English families so deftly anatomized in ''Other People's Houses'' ever read the book and felt any pangs other than the nip of the serpent's tooth. One meanly hopes so.) The memoir goes on to tell of Lore's three years in the Dominican Republic before she and her mother are finally admitted to the United States in 1951, and they have their own house at last. Ten pages from the end of the book a character called Carter Bayoux is introduced, a member of Lore's class in creative writing at the New School. He is ''a middle-age Negro . . . who dominated the class with his powerful presence and silence.'' He invites Lore to dinner the following week. ''We will go to a jazz place and give you an introductory course in Americana,'' Carter says.

author: Sol Stein
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE TOUCH OF TREASON. By Sol Stein. (St. Martin's, $15.95.) This terse thriller flies like a bullet to its inevitable conclusion: winning, whether it concerns a court of law or a raison d'etat, takes precedence over justice.

title: The Heart Of The Dragon

pull_quote: Published to coincide with a Public Broadcasting Service television series of the same name, THE HEART OF THE DRAGON (Houghton Mifflin, $29.95) succeeds admirably in explaining China, past and present, to a wide audience. pull_quote:
COME SING, JIMMY JO By Katherine Paterson. 197 pp. New York: Lodestar Books/ E. P. Dutton. $12.95. (Ages 10 and up) DURING the late 1930's, the best thing about a family visit to my cousin Mary Louise's house in Goldthwaite, Tex., was her mother's poems. Aunt Virginie grew up in West Virginia and had memorized old rhyming stories. One was about a little boy whose father died. The boy wrote him a letter in care of heaven, put a stamp on it, ran out to mail it and was hit by a carriage and killed. The poem concluded, amid a heavy flow of tears from little listeners, that the letter was getting special delivery.

Katherine Paterson's new novel has that same kind of direct, no-nonsense approach to grabbing a reader's emotions and wringing out the tears. Her subject is a family of country singers, and the quality of the prose in this story is much like the lyrics of their songs. These include such numbers as ''My Momma Is a Angel Up in Heaven'' and ''In the Sweet Bye and Bye.''

title: Low Tide
author: Fernanda Eberstadt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOW TIDE By Fernanda Eberstadt. 173 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.   FERNANDA EBERSTADT's first novel is something of an original. It starts like a send-up of a bodice-ripper. Told in a cloying gush, the opening scene presents us with a precocious 10-year-old, Jezebel, locked in the dream of a rotting Southern mansion and flirting with an Oxford University professor under the dining room table. (''I love you better than anything in the world,'' she tells him. ''Better than your daddy?'' he asks.) It ends in a tight-lipped splatter of blood and Raymond Chandler.

author: Pamela Alexander
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NAVIGABLE WATERWAYS By Pamela Alexander. 75 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. Cloth, $12.95. Paper, $5.95. THE LAMPLIT ANSWER By Gjertrud Schnackenberg. 83 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $12.95. ASSUMPTIONS By Marilyn Hacker. 92 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. Cloth, $14.95. Paper, $8.95. IT is characteristic of Pamela Alexander's book (the latest in the Yale Series of Younger Poets) that its title, ''Navigable Waterways,'' turns out to refer to flower stems. She is a poet of such shifting perspectives. A poem is a kaleidoscope in her hand, a ''brief incident / and running commentary.'' The images are designed illuminations - water birds whose ''cries sound / like miniature wine-glasses breaking / against the crusty earth.'' But she knows that images don't decorate experience so much as organize it.

title: Fiskadoro
author: Denis Johnson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FISKADORO By Denis Johnson. 221 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $14.95 POSTNUCLEAR literature often springs from ambiguous impulses. We all understand the big fear that propels it; what is more difficult to acknowledge is the element of wish fulfillment often present in fantasies of a world that has been swept clean of everything we know, and can therefore return to a pastoral innocence. In ''Fiskadoro,'' which joins the growing ranks of novels set beyond the end of the world, the poet and novelist Denis Johnson attempts something much more daring and provocative. He doesn't entirely avoid the millenarian impulse. But his startlingly original book is an examination of the cataclysmic imagination, a parable of apocalypse that is always present and precedes redemption in a cycle of death and birth, forgetting and remembering.
headline: POSTAPOCALYPTIC FASOTRAL

title: The Last Romance
author: Erica Abeel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LAST ROMANCE By Erica Abeel. 277 pp. New York: Avon Books. Paper, $6.95.   GENRE books have been so successful for publishers in the last few decades it is not surprising that potentially lucrative subgenres would occasionally be tested. Crucial elements of the standard Gothic romance, are, of course, an earnest, impoverished virgin, a brooding lord and a mysterious manor house. In the new subgenre, Manhattan Gothic, of which Erica Abeel's ''Last Romance'' is a case in point, the mysterious manor house becomes the untidy offices of a weekly New York City paper; the brooding lord an authoritarian senior editor, and the earnest, im-poverished virgin a freelance reporter who has been around the block a few times and is seeking not to lose her virginity but, as Madonna croons, to regain it.
headline: MANHATTAN GOTHIC ON NEWSPRINT

title: The Cider House Rules
author: John Irving
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CIDER HOUSE RULES. By John Irving. 560 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $18.95. BY turns witty, tenderhearted, fervent and scarifying, ''The Cider House Rules'' is, for me, John Irving's first truly valuable book.   The storytelling is straightforward - not the case with his huge commercial success, ''The World According to Garp'' (1978). The theme is in firm focus - not the case with ''The Hotel New Hampshire'' (1981). The novelist's often-deplored weakness for the cute and trendy, although still evident, is here less troubling.   Far more important, ''The Cider House Rules'' has a public dimension - could, indeed, play a significantly assuasive role in an American social conflict that is now dangerously exacerbated. The book is, to be sure, a novel (the author's sixth), not a tract; it follows several human lives from youth to maturity, gripping our attention as chronicle rather than argument.
headline: GUILT AND COMPASSION

title: A Vietcong Memoir
author: Truong Nhu Tang
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A VIETCONG MEMOIR By Truong Nhu Tang. With David Chanoff and Doan Van Toai. Illustrated. 350 pp. New York: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $17.95.   THE torrent of books about the Vietnam War brings to mind King Richard II's woeful invitation, ''Let us sit upon the ground and tell sad stories of the death of kings.'' If there are any but sad stories about those 30 years of strife between Westerners and Asians, they are yet to be told. The literature is a litany of death - deaths of men, women and children; of governments and reputations; of ideals and morals; of buddies and innocents, heroes and poltroons. ''A Vietcong Memoir'' by Truong Nhu Tang is about the death of a dream, a dream of an independent, peaceful and democratic Vietnam.
headline: DEFEATED BY VICTORY

title: Mountbatten
author: Philip Ziegler
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MOUNTBATTEN By Philip Ziegler. Illustrated. 784 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $24.95.      ''DICKIE'' MOUNT=   BATTEN - Earl Mountbatten of Burma - was one of Britain's wartime heroes. When he was a leader of a destroyer flotilla in 1940, his own ship was hit by a torpedo while in pursuit of a German U-boat, and 27 men were killed. Much to Mountbatten's chagrin, his courage during the action did not win him any decoration. But it made a considerable impression on Britain's new Prime Minister, Winston Churchill.   Almost exactly a year later, during the savage battle for Crete, Mountbatten was again in command of a destroyer flotilla. This time, under a German dive bomber attack, his own ship was sunk. Exhausted, bruised, half blinded by oil, Mountbatten was rescued from the sea.
headline: HE WORE HIS MEDALS GRACEFULLY

SHALL we take seriously the distinction Hortense Calisher makes between short stories and the ''little novels'' that constitute ''Saratoga, Hot''? What does a novel - even a novel manque - have or want that a story doesn't aspire to or leaves open or unexamined? And - the first question, perhaps - does it matter?

title: The Ghostway
author: Tony Hillerman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: It has been about three years since the last Tony Hillerman book about Jim Chee, the sergeant in the Navajo Tribal Police. Mr. Hillerman's new entry, THE GHOSTWAY (Harper & Row, $13.95), maintains the high standard of its predecessors, starting with ''The Fly on the Wall'' in 1971.   Mr. Hillerman supplies a good deal of cultural anthropology, and Jim Chee's racial heritage allows him to see and interpret symbols to which the white man is blind. Basic to ''The Ghostway'' are Navajo burial customs. Chee may be a liberated Indian with a college degree, but he is not so liberated that he does not feel the cumulative weight of his ancestors where religious rites are concerned.

title: Love Always
author: Ann Beattie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOVE ALWAYS By Ann Beattie. 247 pp. New York: Random House. $16.95. ANN BEATTIE has claimed her fictional territory with cool, clever prose and a brilliant eye for detail. In her short stories and two previous novels, ''Chilly Scenes of Winter'' and ''Falling in Place,'' her stance is that of a witty reporter charting the manners of the civilized and the chic among the post-60's generation. Her elegant aloofness alternately charms and maddens, and in the ironically titled ''Love Always,'' her most comic novel thus far, she poses some hard questions about her own art within a structure drolly modeled on the soap opera.

title: Last Letters From Hav
author: Jan Morris
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LAST LETTERS FROM HAV By Jan Morris. 203 pp. New York: Random House. $14.95. LIKE the current modes of poetry, travel writing is an art that necessarily partakes of fictional elements but is not supposed to. The great originals, like Herodotus and Marco Polo, freely interpolated whoppers into their travel chronicles. Our contemporaries are less at liberty to spin tales of ''Anthropophagi, and men whose heads / Do grow beneath their shoulders,'' but there are still ways to spice up the raw data of topography without overstepping the bounds of documentary. One simply offers hearsay evidence, as in this poker-faced account -from Jan Morris's most recent travel book, ''Last Letters From Hav'' - of the salt trade that for centuries has been the economic basis of the city's anomalous existence:   ''It is said to have been the Greeks who first discovered that salt extracted from the Hav marshes had aphrodisiac qualities: shiploads of it, they say, were sent to Attica, and according to Schliemann it was the salt that led Achilles to set up his base on Hav's western shore. By the Middle Ages the power of Hav salt was so well-attested that some scholars think it the first reason for the Arab seizure of the peninsula.''
headline: WITH A SHIPLOAD OF SALT

title: A Perfect Peace
author: Amos Oz
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A PERFECT PEACE By Amos Oz. Translated by Hillel Halkin. 374 pp. New York: A Helen and Kurt Wolff Book/ Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $16.95. THIS, the Israeli writer Amos Oz's most powerful work, is his fourth novel and ninth book to be published in the United States in English translation. The events of ''A Perfect Peace,'' which appeared in Israel in 1982, unfold between 1965 and 1967, from the news of skirmishes near the Syrian border to the Six Day War. The reverberations of these events permeate the book, lending it an atmosphere of continual unease and anticipation, but the clashes Mr. Oz evokes are more of the domestic variety - a generational conflict over the meaning of the Israeli experience itself. In ''A Perfect Peace,'' he examines the disjunctions of history and the ways in which a people -and finally it is more than just the Israeli people to whom he speaks - transcend such divisions.
headline: FICTION THAT IS WORLDS APART

title: The International Garage Sale
author: Stefan Kanfer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE INTERNATIONAL GARAGE SALE By Stefan Kanfer. 224 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $13.95. THE United Nations -what a subject for a great satire! At its founding strong men wept, spoke glowingly of beating weapons into plowshares and vowed never to wage war again. Forty years and umpteen million deaths later, the United Nations is a sputtering travesty. The chance for a spoof of modern peacekeeping, for a ''Dr. Strangelove'' or a ''Catch-22'' of bad faith, terrorism and idiot oratory would seem golden.   But Stefan Kanfer's comic thriller, ''The International Garage Sale,'' muffs the opportunity. Granted, Winston Churchill's worst fears were realized, and the United Nations (here called the World Body) is a Tower of Babel; the trouble is that Mr. Kanfer's diction tries to match the cacophony. People are forever screaming and bellowing, bombs exploding, buildings collapsing. Nor does anything simply happen: if a character repeats a phrase he does so ''numbly''; Beethoven wafts ''flawlessly''; glasses are drained ''morosely''; and New York glitters ''malignantly.''

title: Captain Maximus
author: Barry Hannah
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CAPTAIN MAXIMUS By Barry Hannah. 101 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $11.95.   BARRY HANNAH'S fiction - four novels, a volume of stories called ''Airships,'' and now this collection - read as though written by a good ol' boy become self-conscious. His lead characters, most of whom (like Mr. Hannah) have erupted from the Deep South, are defiantly what they are, but they are not so sure they like it. ''The Deep South might be wretched, but it can howl,'' says one of them. ''I sensed the smallness of myself, my petty desires, my murky ratlike aggression,'' says another. Mr. Hannah's protagonists, who usually narrate their own stories, tend to be randy, violent, hard drinkers, good haters and intermittently psychopathic, but they suffer from remorse and an outraged sense of style. They value grace under pressure, but lose their balance in thinking about it, in their fury at the moral pipsqueaks and ''monsters of piety'' around them. (''The only thing was to get drunk and fire at will.'') Of the many American short-story writers who have recently won acclaim, Mr. Hannah is the most invigorating: he does not write in the prevailing style of scrupulous meanness, and the desperation of his characters is anything but quiet.

title: Skeleton Crew
author: Stephen King
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SKELETON CREW By Stephen King. 512 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $18.95.   STEPHEN KING'S fiction, at its best, is equivalent to the post-Expressionist art found in the tiny galleries of Manhattan's East Village, where painters, sculptors and collagists often turn to the aggressive headlines of tabloid newspapers for inspiration. What erupts in their work is an apocalyptic world, at once magnetic and repulsive, in which good howls at evil, nature runs headlong into technology, humor provides life's one grand escape and ''control'' is a word with little meaning.
headline: DON'T TURN YOUR BACK ON THIS BOOK

title: Islands Of History
author: Marshall Sahlins
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ISLANDS OF HISTORY By Marshall Sahlins. 180 pp. Illinois: University of Chicago Press. $22.50.   THE general point of ''Islands of History'' is that historical process - social and cultural continuity as well as social and cultural change - is ''structural'': it is organized in terms of cultural programs. At the same time, structure (or culture) is historical; that is, it is not a set of transcendental and virtually immutable forms, but a historically generated and socially changeable system. Finally, Marshall Sahlins, a professor of anthropology at the University of Chicago, argues that one cannot understand the events or the structures, or their mutual interactions, without giving central place in one's analyses to the intentions and actions of real human beings, without whom there is neither history nor culture. (Social scientists sometimes forget that.) ''Islands of History'' contributes to the most important trends of current social thought. Those trends include the move toward a more historical anthropology, seen also, for example, in Eric Wolf's ''Europe and the People Without History''; the interest in understanding historical process as itself culturally shaped, as exemplified in Clifford Geertz's ''Negara'' and Michel Foucault's ''History of Sexuality''; and the growing awareness of culture as not only historically produced, but even sometimes consciously constructed, a point developed most recently in a provocative collection called ''The Invention of Tradition,'' edited by Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger.
headline: ACTING OUT CULTURE

title: Lonesome Dove
author: Larry McMurtry
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LONESOME DOVE By Larry McMurtry. 843 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.   THE practice of trail-driving herds of beef cattle over long distances from ranch to railhead flourished for just a moment after the Civil War and before the widespread use of barbed wire. It was the tiniest fraction of our national experience and did not directly involve more than a few thousand people. But maybe more than anything else - more than wars, more than slavery, more than urbanization or immigration - it has animated a part of our imagination out of which flows a vital branch of popular culture. Cowboyana in the form of dime fiction and stage shows flourished even before the short era of the trail drives ended. It nourished movies and television when they were young. Even today, it seems to be everywhere: in clothing, in advertising, in political rhetoric.   Unlike other themes that have obsessed us, though, the trail drive has not made the transition from low art to high art very well. The South has ''Gone With the Wind'' but also Faulkner; the cowboy has ''Red River'' and J. Frank Dobie. It seems mysterious that so rich a subject has not produced a great novel - perhaps it has become so stylized that there is no juice left in it.
headline: TALL IN THE SADDLE

title: A Matter Of Principle
author: Ronald Dworkin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A MATTER OF PRINCIPLE By Ronald Dworkin. 425 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $25.      MANY reviewers of   Ronald Dworkin's last book of essays, ''Taking Rights Seriously,'' hailed it as the finest contribution to the philosophy of law yet made by an American writer. In this new volume, ''A Matter of Principle,'' Mr. Dworkin, who teaches jurisprudence at both New York University and the University of Oxford, has collected a philosophical feast of 19 essays touching on a broad range of topics - from affirmative action, freedom of the press, civil disobedience and nuclear protest to the relationships between law and politics, law and economics, law and literary criticism, liberalism and justice, and principle and policy. Sixteen of the essays have been previously published; two are unpublished lectures and one essay is new but draws on previously published material. Mr. Dworkin's introduction tries to tie them all together.
headline: RIGHTS VS. GOALS

author: Richard Kennedy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AMY'S EYES By Richard Kennedy. Illustrated by Richard Egielski. 437 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $13.50. (Ages 8 and up) EVEN coastal sailors who cruise only in local waters know the feeling, upon letting go the mooring line, that anything might happen. The sea holds in wait for us not only its magnificence and fateful changes of weather but also our own capacity for wonder - for magic and mystery - and vulnerability as well. This is the feeling out of which Richard Kennedy has created ''Amy's Eyes,'' his 17th work for young readers. But the book is not just for the young - this rich, exuberant story wittily draws together several different literary traditions in ways that are pleasing to an adult.

title: Balanchine's Tchaikovsky
author: Solomon Volkov
pull_quote: Among the books concerning George Balanchine that have been published since the great choreographer's death two years ago, the most curious and most interesting is ''Balanchine's Tchaikovsky'' by Solomon Volkov (Simon and Schuster. $19.95) Mr. Volkov, a Soviet musicologist who emigrated to the United States in 1976, ran into a certain degree of controversy in 1979 with the publication of''Testimony: The Memoirs of Dimitri Shostakovitch.'' His claim that these memoirs were based on fresh conversations by himself with the late Soviet composer was doubted in some quarters and their authenticity as such was not accepted by Shostakovitch's son when he too arrived in the West a few years ago.   Now Mr. Volkov has presented a book based on what he says were 33 interviews in New York with Balanchine in 1981 and 1982. Conducted in Russian, the conversations have been translated for the book by Antonina W. Bouis. The subtitle is, in fact, ''Interviews with George Balanchine'' and in this case, the claim seems substantiated. Those of us who have had interviews with Balanchine over the years will recognize his views and his voice here. In fact, some of the material that Mr. Volkov considers as new - such as a debunking of the glamour surrounding the Diaghilev era - is consistent with Balanchine's publshed opinions in the past.

author: Frank Herbert

I gazed around the kitchen. Dingy, poor. I was just another mouth to feed - what did they need me for?''

title: Counsels Of War
author: Gregg Herken
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: COUNSELS OF WAR By Gregg Herken. 409 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95.   AFTER most wars soldiers plan how to fight the next one. In the United States since World War II, however, civilians too have pondered the next global conflict, arguing about how to avoid it. The appearance of nuclear weapons prompted a rethinking of the canons of military strategy, a task largely undertaken by people outside the armed forces. Civilians had the advantage of not being wedded to beliefs and institutional procedures left over from the period before 1945. They were frequently at odds with the military (and just as often deeply divided among themselves). These civilian experts and their disputes are the subjects of ''Counsels of War,'' by Gregg Herken, an associate professor of history at Yale University and the author of a previous book on American nuclear weapons policy.

outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN THE ATTIC By Hiawyn Oram. Illustrated by Satoshi Kitamura. Unpaged. New York: Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $10.95. (Ages 3 to 5) WHAT'S INSIDE? The Alphabet Book. By Satoshi Kitamura. Unpaged. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $11.95. IN 1942 the Vichy Government sent its first convoy of French Jews to the German death camps. More than 75,000 were deported during the next two years; most did not come back. The children who were left behind in hiding learned quickly not to talk about the deportations, never to ask why they occurred or when their parents would return. For most the silence has been endless, the French psychiatrist Claudine Vegh writes. As adults they do not discuss the war: ''It is taboo.''

''I Didn't Say Goodbye,'' published in France in 1979, is an extraordinary collection of interviews with 17 French men and women who lost one or both parents in the deportations - and never talked about it. They agreed to be interviewed by Mrs. Vegh because she is one of them. Her father was deported, and talking to her was like ''giving blood to a friend,'' as one man explains. But most could only tell their stories in darkened rooms; they spoke in monotones and whispers, often with their backs to her. These interviews, which have been gracefully translated by Ros Schwartz, are like monologues. Talking about their war experiences for the first time, these people seem to be talking to themselves, exorcising memories they have never been able to share.

BEYOND a certain vogue, as I remember, for ''Bonjour Tristesse'' and Albert Camus, a pious regard for Proust and Flaubert, and an occasional attempt at something almost-English, like the fussy, Gothic work of Michel Tournier, Americans on the whole do not get on with the French novel, and certainly not with the French experimental writers with whom Marguerite Duras is most often linked. It is true that in much of her work, Miss Duras uses obscurity - or at least manner and formal control - to combat or disguise her tendency to be melodramatic and sentimental. But in her small, perfect, new novel, she has found in reworking material she has used before - material evidently full of personal meaning - a felicitous and masterly balance between formalism and powerful emotional effect. ''The Lover,'' in this fine translation by Barbara Bray, is accessible the way Thomas Mann's ''Death in Venice'' or D. M. For example, in London, her phenomenally long-running play ''The Mousetrap'' is in its 34th year. There have been many discussions, ranging from the cynical to the stunned, about what has led to this unparalleled success. But the explanation lies surely in the enormous pleasure and excitement that generations of readers have derived from the Christie books. People jump at the chance of finding the same mixture served up to them in the theater - where they don't generally expect it.

title: Shanghai
author: Christopher New
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHANGHAI. By Christopher New. (Summit, $19.95.) ''So this is China,'' the Englishman John Denton thinks as he approaches Shanghai for the first time. We hope so. After all, this is no ordinary city he is entering. It is Shanghai at the turn of the century, a city with about as strong a romantic and mysterious resonance as one can find - it even gave its name to a form of kidnapping. This is the city we expect to find, reflecting the atmosphere of Josef von Sternberg's film ''Shanghai Express.'' The massive novel follows Denton's career as it ebbs and flows and intertwines with 50 years of Shanghai's turbulent political and economic history. On the surface, it would appear that Christopher New has provided enough color to sustain his nearly 900 pages. Among other things, Denton takes a gorgeous Chinese mistresss; gains, loses and regains a fortune; marries an American socialite; gets elected to the city council; races ponies; and even, at one point, hides Zhou Enlai in his kitchen. There is also an assorted cast of British and Chinese characters from the straitlaced to the devious, the most vivid of whom is Denton's Chinese mistress, the worldly-wise singsong girl Su-mei. But ultimately what is lacking in this book is not the right character types or even the correct street names but passion. Mr. New seems unwilling, or perhaps unable, to throw himself into this teeming world. Although we learn something about the ways and means of this city, particularly about the British Customs Service, these are just facts.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The New Kgb
author: William R Corson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE NEW KGB: Engine of Soviet Power. By William R. Corson and Robert T. Crowley. (Morrow, $19.95.) Despite its title, this book is mainly a history of the Soviet security and intelligence apparatus, rounded out by a retelling of some of the organization's more notorious exploits in Britain and the United States. The chapters on the methods employed by Soviet agents in ferreting out the West's industrial and military secrets are particularly timely, what with recent arrests of a number of Americans accused of spying for Moscow. But the book's message lies elsewhere. The authors, who claim a combined 70 years' experience in military intelligence, contend that the K.G.B. has taken over control of the Soviet Communist Party and ''now operates the U.S.S.R.'' They concede that this view puts them at odds with many ''traditional'' American scholars who see the party as still firmly in charge, and they provide little real evidence in support of their own opinion. Their conclusions are more a matter of interpreting Soviet political dynamics as holding out little hope for any improvement in East-West relations. American ventures in detente, trade and scientific exchange are dismissed as delusions that have made it that much easier for the K.G.B., beefed up before his death last year by the Soviet leader Yuri Andropov, to carry out his ukase -massive filching of Western high technology to modernize and expand the Soviet armed forces. Soviet professions of reasonableness are pretense, a smokescreen behind which Russia under its new K.G.B. masters reverts to harshest Stalinism.

title: Carpenter's Gothic
author: William Gaddis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CARPENTER'S GOTHIC By William Gaddis. 262 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $16.95.   THIS is William Gaddis's third work of fiction in 30 years. That sounds like a sparse stream, and misrepresents absolutely. Mr. Gaddis is a deluge. ''The Recognitions,'' his first novel, published in 1955, matches in plain bulk four or five ordinary contemporary novels. His second, ''JR,'' a burlesquing supplementary footnote appearing two decades later, is easily equivalent to another three or four. For those whom tonnage has kept away, ''Carpenter's Gothic'' - a short novel, but as mazily and mercilessly adroit as the others - should disclose Mr. Gaddis's terrifying artfulness once and for all. ''Carpenter's Gothic'' may be Gaddis-in-little, but it is Gaddis to the brim.   With fewer publications so far than he can count on one hand, Mr. Gaddis has not been ''prolific'' (that spendthrift coin); instead he has been prodigious, gargantuan, exhaustive, subsuming fates and conditions under a hungry logic. His two huge early novels are great vaults or storehouses of crafty encyclopedic scandal - omniscience thrown into the hottest furnaces of metaphor. Mr. Gaddis knows almost everything: not only how the world works - the pragmatic cynical business-machine that we call worldliness - but also how myth flies into being out of the primeval clouds of art and death and money.

WHO has not asked - if only when depressed - ''How should I live, and how can I find out?'' To read this book is to be taken through one of the most sophisticated discussions available of such questions by an engaging, skeptical, often wryly witty and extraordinarily subtle professional.   Bernard Williams, who teaches philosophy at Cambridge University, is something of an Establishment iconoclast - not an outsider, but a naughty boy of philosophy. In ''Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy,'' he attacks the main schools of moral philosophy after Aristotle, arguing that the goal of building a system of morality on the basis of universal and fundamental ethical truths is misguided. His advice to his fellow philosophers is to make a strategic retreat.

pull_quote: FORMS OF ATTENTION By Frank Kermode. 93 pp. Illinois: The University of Chicago Press. $9.95.   RECENT literary criticism has produced an almost medieval luxuriance of schools. This has encouraged what might be called a kaleidoscopic style of writing, in which the author seems constantly to be speaking to three or four people at the same time. Although ''Forms of Attention'' consists of only three lectures - given at the University of California, Irvine, by Frank Kermode, a fellow of King's College, Cambridge - it is kaleidoscopic. HOLDEN CAULFIELD, the hero of what was the coming-of-age novel for several generations, had a little sister named Phoebe, of whom he was touchingly proud. She was only 10 years old, but already she was writing books - which she never finished - and seemed an appealingly quirky little kid. Phoebe Desmond's mother took ''The Catcher in the Rye'' so to heart that it determined her first child's name. And this first novel is that child's own coming-of-age story, told in a voice one could easily imagine as the precocious Phoebe Caulfield's own. At least there is something more than faintly reminiscent of Holden's voice, with the achingly sensitive passivity replaced by a confident activism. But there is the old Caulfield impatience with phoniness, which, together with an adolescent awkwardness and gaucheness, provide much of the humor of this very funny book.

title: Foul Ball!
author: Alison Gordon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FOUL BALL! Five Years in the American League. By Alison Gordon. (Dodd, Mead, $14.95.) As a sportswriter for The Toronto Star, Alison Gordon covered the Toronto Blue Jays for five years, from spring training of the third year of the baseball franchise's existence (1979) until the end of the 1983 season. Watching an inept and luckless expansion team grow into a pennant contender, she got to know, as she puts it, ''a raft of fascinating people,'' and describing those people is what Miss Gordon does best. Of course, she is obliged to include stories about what it is like to be a woman working in the macho world of baseball, particularly doing the locker room interviews essential to a sportswriter's job. She tells these tales but gathers them into one token chapter, as if she got bored, the way most female sportswriters eventually do, with voyeuristic questions about the locker room. ''No one wanted to talk about what the job was like, what the real challenges were,'' she writes. ''They didn't want to talk baseball. All they wanted to know was whether I saw lots of naked men.'' But her job amounted to much more than that, and ''Foul Ball!'' is about what it is like to cover baseball, not about what it is like to be a woman covering baseball. Some might argue that the author herself - a woman who turned 40, got married and pursued various nonsports interests during the time that she covered the Blue Jays - is a more interesting subject than the people she has written about.

Tony Fraser, the district attorney, will have none of this. He wants a verdict of guilty, and he wants the killer sent away for life. What makes the book memorable is the legal knowledge the author brings to the case without ever becoming pedantic or sententious about it. title: Pindar
author: D S Carne-Ross
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PINDAR. By D. S. Carne-Ross. (Yale University, Cloth, $25. Paper, $7.95.) It was long the fashion among scholars to say Pindar was the greatest Greek lyric poet but he could only be understood by scholars. He is a tough case: his chosen vehicle, the victory ode presented in elaborate public ceremony, did not survive him, nor did the musical and choreographic components of his poems. But D. S. Carne-Ross, who teaches classics at Boston University, assumes that a reader who can comprehend poetry at all can understand Pindar, and he opens up the work of the great Theban more clearly than anyone has yet done in English. The challenge was great. Mr. Carne-Ross's ''Pindar'' is one of two inaugural volumes (the other is Paolo Vivante's ''Homer'') in a new series, Hermes Books, intended to make the ancient writers available to readers with little or no Greek or Latin. And if the author had not succeeded so well one would have said it could not be done with Pindar. First he draws on the best recent scholarship to describe the structure of the odes, which he compares to classical sonatas. Then, in close readings of a handful of the 45 surviving odes - readings considerably enhanced by his translations and his use of a tremendous range of reference to modern poetry - he makes the reader familiar with Pindar's dramatic instinct, his exuberance, his love of wit and surprise, his sense of humor and his incomparable technical skill. Mr. Carne-Ross doesn't make Pindar easy, but he does make him understandable, even natural.

title: The Trick Of The Ga Bolga
author: Patrick McGinley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE TRICK OF THE GA BOLGA By Patrick McGinley. 288 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $14.95. IT'S been 50 years now since Beckett, in praising O'Casey's homages to ''the principle of disintegration,'' gave us a phrase for the Irish comic vision. In its world disintegration seems purposive though impersonal; the universe, whatever parish priests choose to say, was created to insure the utter neatness of any local unraveling. All names are double, all meanings are double, all experience is disquietingly double.   For the Irish are not a ''poetic'' people; no, a ruthlessly logical people, who invent whole worlds to fit new kinds of reason. Patrick McGinley is quick at inventing such worlds (four novels in seven years). His newest, ''The Trick of the Ga Bolga,'' is dedicated ''To Myles,'' and if that's Myles na Gopaleen, alias Flann O'Brien -author of ''At Swim-Two-Birds'' and ''The Third Policeman'' - then Mr. McGinley invokes the shade of the most relentless comic logician since the longtime Irish head of state, Eamon De Valera. ''Dev'' designed the knockabout dream called Ireland Today. As for Myles, he invented, among other universes, one in which people slowly turn into bicycles by molecular exchange. The price of living in that one is being dead, and many have preferred ''life'' in De Valera's.
headline: A DEEP AND LASTING MAYONNAISE

title: The Jews Of Islam
author: Bernard Lewis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE JEWS OF ISLAM By Bernard Lewis. Illustrated. 245 pp. New Jersey: Princeton University Press. $17.50.   IT has been 30 years since the late S. D. Goitein wrote ''Jews and Arabs: Their Contacts Through the Ages.'' Summing up the nature of the Jews' encounter with their Arab neighbors, he confirmed the view that the lot of the Jews in the lands of Islam, although unenviable, had on the whole been more tolerable than in the European Diaspora. In his view, the position of the Jews was at its height in the early Middle Ages, when the emergence of a ''Jewish-Arab symbiosis,'' resting on basic affinities between the two cultures, had created a pluralistic interfaith coexistence. But after that, there was a long and steady deterioration. The results of further research, published in a series of four volumes entitled ''A Mediterranean Society,'' gave an economic and social dimension to this emphasis. Drawing on a cache of 11th-to-12th-century fragments found in the old Cairo genizah - in accordance with Jewish practice, discarded scraps of paper had been set aside in the synagogue's storeroom - he was able to attribute this decline to the transition from an international free-trade economy encouraging tolerance of religious differences to a more authoritarian regime moving in the direction of less cultural interaction.

If many English-speaking readers remain puzzled by the spell Poe cast over the intelligence of Baudelaire, Mallarme and Valery, so the French tend to be equally perplexed by the cult status accorded Laforgue by such talents as Joyce, Pound, Eliot, Crane and Stevens. Although his work and influence have been the subject of important studies in English, Laforgue has long been dismissed in his native land as a relatively minor fin de siecle figure, worth only a passing mention in standard literary histories. The announcement of a forthcoming Pleiade edition of his work suggests that Laforgue's French reputation is in the process of revision, but it is unlikely that he will ever reacquire the seductive glamour he held for the young Eliot or Pound.

Since his death in 1972, a penumbra of somber dignity has descended over his reputation. There is Alfred Kazin's memorable portrait of him in ''New York Jew,'' an austere, patrician figure striding the beach at Wellfleet, Mass., in Bermuda shorts and a white dress-shirt; the curmudgeonly, hard-drinking aristocrat of Richard Hauer Costa's memoir, ''Edmund Wilson: Our Neighbor From Talcottville''; the worldly intellectual depicted in the Festschrift edited by John Wain; the highhanded polemicist whose contentious correspondence with Vladimir Nabokov fills a hefty volume. By the end of his life, Wilson was more than our pre-eminent literary critic; he was the symbol of a vanished world, a world of grace, civility and moral rectitude, of devotion to the best that has been thought and said - a world in which literature was a high, perhaps the highest, calling.
