Hermeneutics, which refers to the systematic interpretation of texts, is conceived by Mr. Gadamer as a quest for ''agreement between reasonable beings'' who are divided by ''a multiplicity of . . . languages.'' Mr. Gadamer has written a text that, like other texts, contains the possibility of disclosing more than its author had intended.   His chronicle covers a deeply troubled period of German history, and a reader will naturally wonder how a mind steeped in many of the richest traditions of reflection upon the human condition has employed its skills to interpret a darkened world. A reader might also expect to learn how the university, organized by the mind, fared and responded when the surrounding society took to organizing itself as anti-mind.

''One Last Mirror,'' a novel portraying a Westerner's search for truth in the East, is a far cry from the once ''insightful'' tales based on Somerset Maugham's model, ''The Razor's Edge.'' Maugham produced a hero, Larry, scarred in World War I, fleeing from the hopeless and self-destructive West to find answers in the Himalayas. What Larry did there exactly Maugham never said, for he didn't know - he never pursued the Eastern path himself. Whatever happened, the hero returned purified. Buddhism is an ancient but effective method for breaking the human shell of ignorance. How? Well, never mind.

Call it Beat or Hip or Cool, it was the first anti-establishment sensibility anybody under 50 has personally experienced.

The combined political and esthetic spirit of that ''quiet'' decade had a home in the rebellious weekly newspaper The Village Voice (though many incorrectly locate The Voice as a 60's phenomenon). The typically American journey of the people who created, edited, rose and fell with The Voice, from rebellion to suc-cess and beyond, is the story Mr. Blum tells in his spirited roman a clef, which adheres loosely to character and event.

THE suspense novel - as Richard Lourie's ''First Loyalty'' is billed - is a tricky business these days, but more for its authors than for its readers. Readers can see most of the outcomes in advance, and, besides, the facts on the television news are usually more astonishing, the suspense often a real cliffhanger. So the thriller writer must dig ever deeper for new veins. THE trouble with anniversaries, as President Reagan now has reason to know, is that they tend to call forth ghosts. Whatever his intentions in going to the military cemetery in Bitburg, West Germany, that gesture only confirmed how much more difficult it is to bury the memory of the past than its victims. Ironically, though, the visit to Bitburg appears to have crowded out another specter that was hovering around the edges of our consciousness only a few months ago - the ghost of Yalta. The 40th anniversary of that conference moved the President himself to proclaim, this past February, that Yalta symbolized ''the dividing line between freedom and repression,'' a boundary that ''can never be made legitimate'' and that ''I do not hesitate to say . . . we wish to undo.'' President Carter's national security adviser, Zbigniew Brzezinski, seized upon the occasion to condemn Yalta in the pages of Foreign Affairs as ''a synonym for betrayal,'' and to call for a new effort to undo - peacefully, to be sure - the division of Europe. Both men thereby revived the tradition, once much in vogue among American politicians, of Yalta bashing.

THE stories in Mary Morris's new collection, ''The Bus of Dreams,'' have a light touch, and all give the appearance of looseness. Whether depicting life near Cape Canaveral in the early days of the space program, a day in the bedroom suburbs of Chicago, an American tourist in the slums of Lima, Peru, or a Caribbean vacation going sour, the stories have a deliberately sketchy quality, especially as Miss Morris evokes her characters' psychology. In fact, what these short fictions call to mind more than anything are newspaper clippings or news flashes, bits of familiar this and that whizzing by. Most of the 15 stories are topical to the core.

They also, as is fashionable, employ various narra-tive techniques of an extremely evident sort - for example, stories are related in the present as well as the past tense (though none in the future tense). This, combined with their topicality, keeps them as engrossing as a first-rate magazine article. Perhaps the best example is ''Shining Path,'' with its vivid evocation of Peruvian poverty. Similarly, in ''The Typewriter,'' the surfaces of several intersecting worlds flash before the reader's imagination in no time: the urban newspaperman, his script-writing second wife and the ways in which they disconnect, sounding like so many familiar reports from the therapist's couch. No contemporary reader is likely to lose his or her bearings here.

title: Afro-American Folktales
author: Roger D Abrahams
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AFRO-AMERICAN FOLKTALES: Stories From Black Traditions in the New World. Edited by Roger D. Abrahams. (Pantheon, Cloth, $22.95. Paper, $11.95.) In this sequel to his 1983 volume, ''African Folktales,'' Roger D. Abrahams has culled stories from American and Caribbean collections. Taken together, these tales reveal a world view marked by a gritty sense of realism. The good do not often triumph; the bad are inevitably more interesting character types. From creation myths to coded tales in which plantation masters are outwitted, the stories range across the heritage of an African past planted and tilled in the minds of slaves and their descendants. Mr. Abrahams's introduction traces the history of the tale collectors themselves, paying special tribute to Joel Chandler Harris, whose Uncle Remus and Brer Rabbit tales, he concedes, had racist undertones. Nevertheless, Harris rendered the exploits of animals with human qualities in a literary style quite close to the oral traditions out of which they came. Mr. Abrahams is not romantic about how the tales changed in their passage through the years and from Africa to the New World. Praise songs, epics and long genealogical recitations did not transplant. Perhaps this accounts for the more entertaining qualities of the previous collection; the immediacy of the mother culture gave the African folk tales more vivid moments. These Afro-American stories evince a survivor's sensibility, not without humor. The ones from urban America crackle with raw emotion. I was particularly struck by ''The Signifying Monkey,'' a trickster tale cast as a long tone poem.

Lessons abound for 20th-century warriors in this instructive study of the personal and military conduct of the enlisted men in the Union Army in the middle of the 19th century. Joseph T. Glatthaar, who teaches history at the Command and General Staff College's Combat Studies Institute in Fort Leavenworth, Kan., assembles the story of Gen. William T. Sherman's troops in their own words as they drove through Georgia and South Carolina and destroyed the Confederacy. Some of the main lessons are from Sherman himself: war is total and death-defying, an enemy's industry and property should not be spared, forget chivalrous conduct toward civilians. But the major lesson to be gained from the book concerns what integrates a soldier into a fighting unit. According to the quotations here from diaries and letters, the answer is not saluting but experience, mutual respect and camaraderie with officers. ''At first glance,'' the author writes, ''the men looked more like a mob than an army. They were an unkempt, boisterous, seemingly unruly lot, in no way resembling the stereotypical professional army. But Sherman's men took pride in their ability to endure all hardships and still achieve in battle.'' Officers and soldiers fraternized; generals were called by their first names. Mr. Glatthaar also covers whites' attitudes toward blacks in Union blue (they were generally admired but there were pockets of prejudice); the wartime election (the soldiers were overwhelmingly for President Lincoln); the destruction in the South (unsparing).

title: Cavour
author: Denis Mack Smith
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CAVOUR By Denis Mack Smith. 294 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95.   ''HISTORY is a great improviser,'' Count Camillo di Cavour used to say. After reading Denis Mack Smith's extraordinary saga of deception, ruthlessness, blunders and turns of fortune in the life of the man who more than anyone else brought about the unification of Italy in 1861, one feels the remark could easily have been Cavour's own epitaph. Lord Clarendon, the British Foreign Secretary, paid him the perhaps suspect compliment of being among the ''few foreigners I know who is like a practical well-educated English gentleman.'' Sir James Hudson, the British Minister in Turin, was his friend and admirer. Others had quite different opinions. To Disraeli, Cavour was ''utterly unscrupulous,'' and to John Daniel, the American Minister, he was an ''arch intriguer,'' domineering and grasping. He was criticized by some colleagues and compatriots for being vain, inscrutable, tyrannical and too much the aristocrat. King Victor Emmanuel II - whose prime minister Cavour was in Piedmont-Sardinia and who became king of Italy as a result of Cavour's efforts to drive Austria out of the north, unify north and south and take over the Papal States - never liked him, and was never grateful to him. Nevertheless, in that most romantic decade of Italian history - the 1850's - Cavour was one of the outstandingly successful and astute politicians - the wisest of his century, ''if not of all times,'' Mr. Mack Smith quotes the historian G. M. Trevelyan as having said, though that does seem a little rash.

pull_quote: STRINDBERG By Michael Meyer. Illustrated. 651 pp. New York: Random House. $24.95.   REAL superiority,'' Delacroix wrote, ''admits no eccentricity. . . . The great genius is simply a being of a more highly reasonable order.'' He remarked, however, that the opposite view seemed to prevail at the time, 1855. If only he had seen ''Amadeus'' or read Allen Ginsberg or had known that Sartre would describe Jean Genet, with only partial irony, as a saint. Since Delacroix's day, we have lived under the sign of one of his immediate successors, Arthur Rimbaud, who wrote that the poet, albeit a sage, was the great Sick Man, the great Criminal, the great Accursed. This conception, for a while startling, is by now a received idea. By the standards of the modern man on the street, a Dylan Thomas is obviously a poet while a William Carlos Williams is not. To justify his men or women, the biographer has to go back to the detail of their lives and discover the sinister, or at least the scandalous, element. THE valuable core of Anthony Hyde's first novel, ''The Red Fox,'' is its meditation on idealistic Westerners who spy for totalitarian governments. The author unhesitantly defines such idealism as treason - not pure and simple, perhaps, but shameful all the same. To read that lesson in ''The Red Fox'' is a refreshing experience, given the proliferation of books and films - for example, Robert Littell's novel ''The Amateur'' or ''The Jigsaw Man,'' starring Laurence Olivier and Michael Caine - where the fact is in various ways obfuscated. Stripped to its essentials, the argument of such works goes that some British lord or American intellectual was disappointed with democracy (or even with some Government agency), saw the light from Moscow and acted for the enemy in good faith - therefore he can and should be exonerated.

Such aristocratic and middle-class spies required a long series of eye-openers to recognize where their ideals had led them - the Hitler-Stalin pact, the East Berlin workers' uprising, the Gulag revelations, oppression in Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Poland, in Cambodia, Afghanistan and Ethiopia. The eyes of some have remained closed even after these spectacles, but ''The Red Fox'' is the story of a traitor whose eyes finally are opened and who, having acquired knowledge by bitter experience and self-examination, says many wise things on the subject of ideological spying.
headline: ON THE SCENT OF TREASON

title: Return Trips
author: Alice Adams
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RETURN TRIPS By Alice Adams. 195 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $14.95. NOBODY writes better about falling in love than Alice Adams. The protagonists of her stories, almost always women, often professional women - lawyers, art historians, illustrators, journalists - with a number of years and a good deal of experience behind them, know exactly what is about to happen: no nitwits, never victims or too gaga, they have been there before. They fall with eyes open, knowing full well that the man in question might be inappropriate - married or too self-involved ever to commit totally. Such women think they should know better. They do know better. That is the glory of an Adams heroine, she is that smart and still goes on. ''Ah,'' she says to herself, sighing, ''this again: love.'' And plunges in.
headline: WOMEN WHO DO KNOW BETTER

title: Borderline
author: Janette Turner Hospital
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
BORDERLINE By Janette Turner Hospital. 287 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $15.95.

ERASING the borders that define our lives has fascinated Janette Turner Hospital. In her first novel, ''The Ivory Swing'' (1982), a liberal Western family confronts traditional India and discovers what can happen when one set of beliefs is imposed on another. ''The Tiger in the Tiger Pit'' (1983), her second novel, teases apart a family's long-held assumptions about themselves and one another as they travel into new territory. According to Mrs. Hospital, disintegrating borderlines cause combustion and, literally, death.
headline: A QUALITY OF ABSENCE

title: Chin Music
author: James McManus
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CHIN MUSIC. By James McManus. (Crown, $14.95.) In his second novel James McManus plays dark games with a sports metaphor. ''Chin Music'' involves the last hours of Chicago and Gamma Ray Zajak, a pitcher for the Chicago White Sox, who wakes up in the hospital with amnesia and a monstrous headache, with the nuclear holocaust close at hand. Known for throwing at batters' heads - playing ''chin music,'' as it were -Gamma Ray has himself been laid up by a lethal fast ball to the cranium. Gradually he learns who he is and the novel follows him home through streets where murder, suicide, ground zero interviews for television and all manner of doomsday madness is transpiring. At one point Gamma Ray stumbles into a nightclub where sex and death abound and a handcuffed cheerleader is being punished for the patrons' enjoyment. Mr. McManus toys with images meant to shock - splattered brains, a dismembered body, eroticized suicide -shows some obliquely, shuffles others as though in a deck of cards and then flips them at the reader. He is clearly a talented writer, but his experiment seems naked and calls too much attention to itself. It may be ''that a syntactical series can swoop and leap like a mother and still retain deep intact structure,'' as he writes. But swooping to what end? ''Out of the Blue,'' Mr. McManus's first novel, about kidnappers who steal the wrong child, was more conventional. Composed of spare, snapshotlike segments, it was occasionally like trying to watch a banquet through a keyhole, but a vital tension kept it coherent.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: A Traveller's Room
author: Elspeth Davie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A TRAVELLER'S ROOM. By Elspeth Davie. (Hamish Hamilton/David & Charles, $15.95.) ''Where does it come from?'' demands a character in one of the 19 stories in this collection, ''the idea of order - this unknown, perfect state of things that makes us feel askew. Can you get some sense of it?'' In studiously measured prose, the Scottish writer Elspeth Davie conveys a sense of the repressive power of that idea of order. Almost all of her plots turn on the characters' feelings of ambivalence about their circumspect lives. In the title story a girl imagines that a mysterious traveler is an exotic explorer, only to meet the drab man and discover ''how all adventures can be flattened at one blow, how heroes are simply tired men.'' Several stories suggest that women are particularly likely to be trapped in flat, stiff lives; yet in the end Miss Davie often liberates them. ''It would do you good to let the whole house go crooked for a change,'' one woman is advised and, goaded by thoughts of her gallivanting suitor, she abandons her orderly ways. In ''The Return'' a wife with odd, emerald-green streaks in her hair also deserts a cramped life; she disappears back to her home in the sea. Green hair grows in one other overtly fantastic story, ''Green Head,'' in which a young man sprouts flowers from his scalp. Here the idea of order, gleaned from the known, imperfect state of nature, is robust rather than repressive: ''He was lucky, he realized, to have a rooted season of steady flowering and steady withering.''
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The English Room
author: Michael Pick
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Though not a soul is to be glimpsed in the 100 interiors in THE ENGLISH ROOM (Harmony Books/Crown, $19.95), it is the servants who seem to have just stepped discreetly aside after polishing the muzzles of the heraldic beasts on the newel posts or straightening the stadium-size Oriental rugs. Derry Moore, who took the evocative photographs, and Michael Pick, who emphasizes English history, designers and architects in his witty text, include two cozy country cottages, a swatch of town houses and a London flat in this visual essay on Englishness at home. But the dramatics, and the fantasy, are left to estates with names like Kedleston Hall (the Derby house of Viscount Scarsdale), about whose massy interior marble pillars Dr. Johnson complained: ''They take up too much room.'' Many of these dwellings, like enormous old oaks, are rooted in England's past, and there is often a melancholy about them that no amount of polishing can remove. Glass cases of curiosities - the collectibles of the outer world brought home by its ''civilizers'' - line the brocade walls of some rooms. In others, ranks of mounted heads stare toward extinction in a decorative fashion that to Evelyn Waugh owed ''more to the taxidermist than the sculptor or painter.'' Mr. Pick parses English style into individuality, eccentricity, love of light and craving for warmth. At Clouds Hill, T. E. Lawrence's Dorset retreat, the bedroom walls are lined in foil (for warmth or coolness) and the high wood bunk bed has a Shaker severity.
headline: DECORATED BY HISTORY

outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AT FREDDIE'S. By Penelope Fitzgerald. (Godine, $14.95.) What's to be said about a well-meaning book like this? We approach with respect the British novelist Penelope Fitzgerald's first work to appear in America; she won the prestigious Booker Prize for an earlier novel, ''Offshore.''

title: Out Of Order
author: Nicholas Capaldi
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OUT OF ORDER: Affirmative Action and the Crisis of Doctrinaire Liberalism. By Nicholas Capaldi. (Prometheus Books, $17.95.) With the Reagan Administration committed to ending affirmative action programs, the intellectual case underlying opposition to them is a timely topic.

title: Footfall
author: Larry Niven and Jerry Pournelle
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FOOTFALL by Larry Niven and Jerry Pournelle (Del Rey/Ballantine, $17.95) tries to serve two masters, and gets away with it. I'm not referring to the collaborators, both of whom are science fiction writers whose previous books have attracted a substantial readership. Their latest novel is a structural hybrid that shouldn't work but does. On the one hand, it is a big, fat ''crossover'' novel clearly aimed at an audience more familiar with the formulas of mass-market fiction, such as pop psychology and boudoir athleticism, than the conventions of science fiction. On the other hand, its science fiction elements are handled with a skill found only in the best of the genre.   The premise of ''Footfall'' is alien invasion. The intelligent creatures from outer space who come to conquer Earth, and almost succeed, look like small elephants with bifurcated, prehensile trunks. Though capable of independent action up to a point, they are essentially members of a herd whose allegiance to their peers and superiors goes far beyond the concept of loyalty. The strengths and weaknesses of this form of social organization are worked out in great detail by Mr. Niven and Mr. Pournelle, who succeed in conveying the aliens' point of view while leaving no doubt in the reader's mind about where the authors themselves stand -firmly in the anticollective camp.
headline: SCIENCE FICTION

author: Gerald Weales
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

author: Harlan Cleveland

pull_quote: THE KNOWLEDGE EXECUTIVE: Leadership in an Information Society. By Harlan Cleveland. (Truman Talley/ Dutton, $18.95.) Does successful leadership today require different qualities from leadership in the past? The management guru Harlan Cleveland, the dean of the University of Minnesota's Hubert H. Humphrey Institute of Public Affairs and the author of ''The Future Executive: A Guide for Tomorrow's Managers'' (1972) and other books, believes it does, and he devotes ''The Knowledge Executive'' to explaining why.

title: Amalgamemnon
author: Christine Brooke-Rose
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AMALGAMEMNON By Christine Brooke-Rose. 144 pp. New York: Carcanet Press. $14.95.      CHRISTINE BROOKE-   ROSE'S earliest books were always deft and alert fictions about love, loss, death, faith, about people and a continent of troubles. The manner was traditional, realistic. Then, with ''Out'' (1964), followed by ''Such'' (1965), ''Between'' (1968) and ''Thru'' (1975), the manner changed, becoming satiric, antic, fantastic. This author, however, is laconic only in her titles. She has also written several works of criticism, notably ''A ZBC of Ezra Pound'' (1971) and ''A Rhetoric of the Unreal'' (1981), well regarded among academics. Yet she remains obscure in her distinction. Why? I can address the question only in a certain slant of language. I say language because Miss Brooke-Rose is a confessed graphomaniac, and her later fiction, like so much of postmodern literature, takes a self-delighting, linguistic turn. That is, fiction, which has always attended to language, now makes it the center of its reflexive concern, and explodes in ludic, parodic, ironic forms. It is carnival time for the Logos, with all the anarchic exuberance that the 20th-century Russian critic Mikhail Bakhtin has invested in the term ''carnivalesque.'' But now, alas, the lights have begun to dim on such frolics.
headline: REVILLUSIONARY PUNORAMA

title: Last Wish
author: Betty Rollin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LAST WISH By Betty Rollin. 236 pp. New York: Linden Press/Simon & Schuster. $14.95.   THIS is the story of a life and a death. Both belonged to Ida Rollin - a successful entrepreneur at a time when few women worked, an early health food enthusiast, a fiercely devoted mother of the writer and television news correspondent Betty Rollin. Mrs. Rollin was the kind of mother who, when her daughter informed her over lunch at Schrafft's that she was planning to leave her first husband, quit her job and move to another city, replied with equanimity: ''You're not a boring daughter.''
headline: HELPING HER MOTHER DIE

title: Freud For Historians
author: Peter Gay
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FREUD FOR HISTORIANS By Peter Gay. 252 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $17.95.   IN ''The Next Assignment,'' his presidential address to the American Historical Association in December 1957, William L. Langer urged his fellow historians to deepen their understanding of history through the ''exploitation of the concepts and findings of modern psychology.'' By ''modern psychology'' he did not mean, as he made clear, ''classical or academic psychology'' but psycho-analysis ''and its later developments and variations as included in the terms 'dynamic' or 'depth psychology.' '' He added that despite the ''prodigious impact'' of psychoanalysis on many, perhaps even most, fields of knowledge, historians had ''maintained an almost completely negative attitude'' toward Freud and the teachings of psychoanalysis.

pull_quote: GOOD ENOUGH TO DREAM By Roger Kahn. 351 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $16.95. headline: A BASEBALL WRITER'S SHOESTRING CATCH

title: The Accidental Tourist
author: Anne Tyler
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE ACCIDENTAL TOURIST By Anne Tyler. 355 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.   IN Anne Tyler's fiction, family is destiny, and (nowadays, at least) destiny clamps down on one in Baltimore. For an archeologist of amnners with Miss Tyler's skills, the city is a veritable Troy, and she has been patiently excavating since the early 1970's, when she skipped off the lawn of Southern fiction and first sank her spade in the soil which has nourished such varied talents as Poe, Mencken, Billie Holiday and John Waters, the director of the films ''Pink Flamingos'' and ''Polyester.''   It is without question some of the fustiest soil in America; in the more settled classes, social styles developed in the 19th century withstand, with sporelike tenacity, all that the present century can throw at them. Indeed, in Baltimore all classes appear to be settled, if not cemented, in grooves of neighborhood and habit so deep as to render them impervious - as a bright child puts it in ''The Accidental Tourist'' - to everything except nuclear flash.

author: Paul Fleischman

pull_quote: COMING-AND-GOING MEN By Paul Fleischman. Illustrated by Randy Gaul. 147 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $11.50. (Ages 11 and up) THE car, the radio and the television set have gradually opened up the valleys of Vermont.

title: Return To Region
author: Juan Benet
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RETURN TO REGION. By Juan Benet. Translated by Gregory Rabassa. (Columbia University Press, $18.95.) ''Return to Region'' is a brilliant novel by one of Spain's major writers. The Region of the title is mythical and unforgettable. One imagines it in northern Spain, in the Pyrenees, a desolate, mysterious and sparsely populated place. Above it looms El Monje, a peak in the shape of a death mask; those who cross Region's river and climb into the mountains never return. There is a church called El Salvador (the Saviour) and a hotel-brothel run by an old woman named Muerte (Death). If Region is not hell, it is one of the circles on the road to hell. Old Dr. Sebastian lives in a wreck of a house, unattended but not alone. Upstairs, behind a padlocked door, sleeps his retarded godson, heavily sedated by the doctor who has an unwanted visitor, a woman who has just returned to Region, some 20 years after the end of the civil war, in the middle of Franco's long reign. The doctor and the woman exchange haunting stories of their lives in which characters appear who are common to both, and who merge, separate, become one again. The doctor has been blighted in love; the woman has had many lovers (the first a German volunteer to the Republic's cause during the Civil War), and has passed part of her time in Muerte's brothel. Underlying their respective tales is the Spanish Civil War, its fratricidal cruelties, its tragedies; their stories are haunted by fear, weighed down by guilt and impotence.

pull_quote: Not many women write tough-guy private-eye mysteries. Sara Paretsky is one who does. She appeared on the scene three years ago with ''Indemnity Only'' and followed it up two years later with ''Deadlock.'' Now comes the third in the series, KILLING ORDERS (Morrow, $15.95).   In each book the private eye is V. (for Victoria) I. (for Iphigenia) Warshawski. She works in Chicago. She used to be a lawyer. She is smart, attractive, outspoken, liberated and stubborn, with something of a temper. The author has been successful in portraying a woman in a man's world, and the emphasis is on ''woman.'' V. I. Warshawski is tough but never loses her femininity, and she is an altogether believable creation.

EVER since 1969, when the artist Judy Chicago donned boxing gloves and trunks to pose for an advertisement in Artforum proclaiming her new, nonpatriarchal surname, she has often stepped back into the ring to take on our tacit assumptions about the nature of art and of women.

title: Hugh Dalton
author: Ben Pimlott
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HUGH DALTON By Ben Pimlott. Illustrated. 752 pp. Manchester, N.H.: Jonathan Cape/Merrimack Publishers' Circle. $29.95.   HIS father was tutor to Queen Victoria's grandsons and Canon of Windsor. Hugh Dalton grew up - literally - in the shadow of the royal palace, leaving only for Eton, en route to King's College, Cambridge. Incongruous beginnings for ''the most socialist Chancellor of the Exchequer Britain ever had.'' But he was ''the first of the upper class renegades,'' as Ben Pimlott, who teaches politics at Birkbeck College, University of London, and is the author of ''Labor and the Left in the 1930's'' demonstrates in this sympathetic, judicious biography. For 30 years Dalton was the rogue elephant of British politics, happiest when trampling on Tory sensibilities. His enemies claimed he believed in redistributing wealth less because he sympathized with the poor than because he hated the privileged. His supporters, his biographer among them, view Dalton as a key figure in the evolution of Labor as a moderate, popular, democratic Socialist party.
headline: A TRAITOR TO HIS CLASS

title: In Country
author: Bobbie Ann Mason
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN COUNTRY By Bobbie Ann Mason. 245 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $15.95.   A SWATCH of western Kentucky near the Illinois border constitutes Bobbie Ann Mason's private literary terrain. Encountered three years ago in ''Shiloh and Other Stories'' and now revisited in an impressive first novel, her landscape is populated by K Mart clerks, gas station attendants, young grandmothers who read Harlequin novels, and other ''good country people,'' to borrow Flannery O'Connor's serviceable phrase. Light-years from the young professionals sipping margaritas on Columbus Avenue, this small corner of the South is a place where Shrimp Night at the Holiday Inn is an occasion rivaled by a visit to the mall in Paducah. Here, depicted without condescension, is a quintessential middle America whose icons are Phil Donahue and Phyllis George, Egg McMuffin and Ed McMahon.
headline: WINNING HER FATHER'S WAR

title: I Am One Of You Forever
author: Fred Chappell
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
I AM ONE OF YOU FOREVER By Fred Chappell. 184 pp. Baton Rouge: Louisiana State University Press. $14.95. KITE By Ed Minus. 278 pp. New York: Viking. $15.95. FRED CHAPPELL has written novels, stories, poetry, essays and reviews. Though perhaps best known as a poet - he was co-winner of this year's Bollingen Prize - he began his career in the early 1960's by publishing three novels in rapid succession, then a fourth a few years later. But ''I Am One of You Forever'' is his first novel in 12 years.

It is not, however, a conventional novel. Though it is told from the point of view of a single character, a boy named Jess, and though the entire book concerns him and his family - father, mother and grandmother - in the North Carolina mountains in the 1940's, it is actually a series of vignettes about people who visit the family and does not tell a continuous narrative. One character, an orphan named Johnson Gibbs, comes to work on the farm and figures in a number of the stories.
headline: COMING OF AGE IN CAROLINA

title: Torture
author: Edward Peters
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TORTURE By Edward Peters. 202 pp. New York: Basil Blackwell. Cloth, $24.95. Paper, $9.95.   THE thought of torture evokes the sound of screams and brings an appalling imagery to mind. How do the authorities who order these torments explain their decisions to themselves? How do societies legitimize such acts? Edward Peters speaks in a voice of scholarly calm as he addresses the subject of inflicted agony. The academic style is associated with the quiet libraries of universities, but in the restrained prose of ''Torture'' lies a passionate message about the intentional violation of the bodies of human beings, in our time and in the past.
headline: BRUTALIZATION IN THE SERVICE OF THE STATE

title: Victory Over Japan,
author: Ellen Gilchrist
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: VICTORY OVER JAPAN, by Ellen Gilchrist. (Little, Brown, $7.95.) This collection of 14 short stories about Southern women from World War II to the present won the 1984 American Book Award for Fiction. Last year Beverly Lowry wrote here that these stories are ''wonderful to tell aloud,'' though she found ''problems with a few. . . . But this is a writer who does not play it safe and so the risks and misses are bound to be there. The pay-off is definitely worth the ride.'' Little, Brown has also reissued the author's novel, THE ANNUNCIATION ($7.95). Its heroine is Amanda McCamey, who grows up on a Mississippi Delta plantation, marries money, rejects it and moves to a university town to work and make new friends. Reviewers praised the book as rich, evocative, intelligent and strikingly original. WHEN AND WHERE I ENTER: The Impact of Black Women on Race and Sex in America, by Paula Giddings. (Bantam, $8.95.) ''When and Where I Enter'' is a history of the dogged determination of black women to survive in America. Last year in The Book Review Gloria Naylor wrote of the author that ''by sorting through a vast amount of primary and secondary material, by reading innumerable novels and conducting exhaustive interviews, she compiled a narrative history of black women from the 17th century to the present, with particular emphasis on the black women's club movement of the 1890's to the 1940's. It was a labor of commitment and love - and it shows.''
headline: NEW & NOTWORTHY

title: The Oval Amulet
author: Lucy Cullyford Babbitt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE OVAL AMULET By Lucy Cullyford Babbitt. 243 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $13.50. (Ages 12 and up) FANTASY novels with young female protagonists have become quite popular in recent years, and deservedly so. Lucy Cullyford Babbitt's ''Oval Amulet'' is distinctive in that it looks beyond the basic question of sexual equality to show that the traditional differences between the acceptable behavior of men and that of women are not only artificial, but often limiting and harmful to both sexes.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Letter To Lord Liszt
author: Martin Walser
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LETTER TO LORD LISZT By Martin Walser. Translated by Leila Vennewitz. 149 pp. New York: Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $13.95.   THE most enduring and pervasive myth of the postclassical world is that of Faust, the tragical doctor who sold his soul to the Devil in return for power and knowledge. There seems to be hardly a poet, novelist or playwright (with the exception, strangely perhaps, of Shakespeare) who has not treated the theme in some form or other. However, the myth originated in Germany, appearing in print first in Frankfurt in 1587; it is a German genius, Goethe, who has laid strongest claim to the story; and it is Germany itself that followed Faust's example in this century and made a pact with the powers of evil. The reckoning, it appears, has now arrived, if we are to take as a true representation the picture of modern German life painted by Martin Walser in his novels.
headline: RISE AND FALL AT THE DENTURE WORKS

title: Caracole
author: Edmund White
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CARACOLE By Edmund White. 342 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $17.95.   TO go about in a mask is both to conceal and to insist upon one's own identity. The concealment is obvious; the insistence arises from the masquer's challenge to the rest of the world to see through the mask by intuiting or analyzing subtle clues. Sometimes, especially among the clever or decadent, this can be a tricky business. At the climactic masked ball scene in Edmund White's new novel, for example, there's a throwaway line about revelers dressed as dukes and duchesses who probably were dukes and duchesses.
headline: CHANGE PARTNERS AND DANCE

title: A Transparent Tree
author: Robert Kelly
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A TRANSPARENT TREE By Robert Kelly. 200 pp. New Paltz, N.Y.: McPherson & Company. Cloth, $20. Paper, $10.   THE literary task Robert Kelly has set for himself is succinctly stated in his 1975 book of poetry, ''The Loom'': ''Say it all / over again, / but say it all. / Write everything.'' An ambitious undertaking, to be sure, but in a career that now spans 25 years, Mr. Kelly has made a good start - 40 books published, mostly poetry, but also three volumes of essays and an unduly neglected novel, ''The Scorpions'' (1967). Readers familiar with this remarkable body of work will find in ''A Transparent Tree,'' Mr. Kelly's first collection of short fiction, many of the features of his work from the outset - a lyrical prose style that mixes eroticism and erudition, a focus on the act of perception and on the presentation of sensory stimuli and sexual impulses in highly charged images, a sense of shock, wonder and utter bewilderment that human consciousness exists at all and a primal urge to leave behind a mark of his own particular consciousness in sensuous language.
headline: EROTIC, EXOTIC AND CRAZED

title: The Good Terrorist
author: Doris Lessing
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GOOD TERRORIST By Doris Lessing. 375 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.   DORIS LESSING has returned to Earth, after years of voyaging in space in her ''Canopus in Argos'' series of novels. But it is not clear whether she is here to stay or only passing through. The London her new novel describes is not a place I would even want to visit.   Mrs. Lessing's good terrorist, otherwise soothed as ''the poor baby'' on the last page of the book, is Alice Mellings, 36, a college graduate with a degree in politics and economics, daughter of upper-middle-class parents in Hampstead. She maintains a liaison blanche with Jasper, whose interests are resolutely homosexual. While he goes out cruising, the poor baby tries to turn an abandoned house into a home fit to be inhabited by a floating group of radicals. Alice and her companions call themselves the Communist Centre Union, and they plan to join the Irish Republican Army in some vague capacity as an ''England-based entity.'' But most of the novel is concerned with Alice's struggle to live in the house, at 43 Old Mill Road, and save it from demolition. In the process she discovers, not surprisingly, that a middle-class background is immensely helpful when you have to deal with bureaucrats.
headline: ALICE, THE RADICAL HOMEMAKER

title: After The Reunion
author: Rona Jaffe
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AFTER THE REUNION. By Rona Jaffe. (Delacorte, $17.95.) When last heard from in ''Class Reunion,'' at least three-quarters of Rona Jaffe's select group of 1950's Radcliffe grads were still happily immersed in their college-romance marriages and, as expected, living comfortably as upper-class housewives and successful career women.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Kingdom Of The Wicked
author: Anthony Burgess
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE KINGDOM OF THE WICKED By Anthony Burgess. 379 pp. New York: Arbor House. $17.95.   SIMONE WEIL once noted an intractable literary problem: in literature goodness tends to appear banal, dull and colorless, and evil seems thrilling, fulfilling and rich - while in life it's just the reverse. This problem must necessarily be hardest to solve when the author sets, as Anthony Burgess does in his new novel, an enterprise of absolute, even divine, goodness against one of history's great examples of wickedness.
headline: ST. PAUL MEETS NERO

title: The Disappearance Of Gregory Pluckrose
author: Elizabeth Gundy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DISAPPEARANCE OF GREGORY PLUCKROSE. By Elizabeth Gundy. (Dial/Doubleday, $15.95.) You will probably find yourself picking out and stowing away your favorite lines from this curious, comic and thoroughly satisfying novel.

title: Greek Religion
author: Walter Burkert
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GREEK RELIGION By Walter Burkert. Translated by John Raffan. 493 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $30.   THE glory that was Greece'' conjures up for many of us visions of gleaming architectural masterpieces, superbly executed statues, great epic and dramatic poetry, the beginnings of democratic institutions and pioneering achievements in mathematics, science and philosophy. All these glories were connected more or less intimately with Greek religion, but what do we think of it? Though it entered deeply into all the other achievements of that remarkable civilization, Greek religion is less likely to excite our admiration. The many gods, the elaborate mythology, the sometimes bloody ceremonies are alien to us. While early Christian and Jewish writers were willing to learn from Greek philosophy, they were uniformly hostile to Greek religion, and that legacy of hostility has remained. But perhaps we have to try to reach a better understanding of the religion of Greece.
headline: CLEARING THE MISTS FROM OLYMPUS

title: Midair
author: Frank Conroy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MIDAIR By Frank Conroy. 149 pp. New York: Seymour Lawrence/E. P. Dutton. $15.95.   EIGHTEEN years ago Frank Conroy published his first book, a novel - or was it a memoir? -''Stop-Time,'' in which the narrator's fortunes (he was an ''I'' named ''Frank'') were presented in rich detail, with all the leisurely fullness one encounters in ''naturalist'' writers like Dos Passos (''Adventures of a Young Man'') or Sherwood Anderson (''A Story Teller's Story''). But ''Stop-Time'' also revealed a rare wit that showed, one felt, Mr. Conroy's most attractive qualities, as in a passage where his stand-in father explains to him about how a car can be a ''lemon,'' put together in such a way that ''everything goes wrong - little things at first and then bigger and bigger things.'' Suitably impressed, the boy meditates as follows:   ''The idea fascinated me. Watching the empty road ahead of us I turned the concept of lemon over and over in my mind. It seemed the perfect word - a bright yellow car mysteriously endowed among all its broth-ers with an individual fate. . . . Instead of spreading the mistakes equally over all the cars produced, cer-tain cars, known as lemons, were packed efficiently with everything that could possibly go wrong with an automobile. In this way one knew that the other cars were okay.''
headline: REASONS TO BE NERVOUS

title: Walk Through Cold Fire
author: Cin Forshay-Lunsford
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WALK THROUGH COLD FIRE By Cin Forshay-Lunsford. 205 pp. New York: Delacorte Press. $14.95. (Ages 12 and up) THREE years ago Delacorte Press announced a literary competition to encourage young adult fiction by previously unpublished novelists. ''Walk Through Cold Fire,'' the most recent prizewinner, is a tale in a time-honored tradition - a story of misunderstood adolescents. Written by an 18-year-old woman, the novel is described by its publisher as ''rich in autobiographical detail.'' Thus it is not surprising that, while also rich in melodrama, it has the ring of authentic adolescent angst.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Giacometti
author: James Lord
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GIACOMETTI By James Lord. Illustrated. 575 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $30.   ''A rose without thorns,'' is what Andre Gide called Switzerland, much to the irritation of the Swiss, who like to consider themselves a passably thorny lot. Take for example Alberto Giacometti, who was born in 1901 in the Bregaglia Valley, just north of the Italian border. If Gide in a botanizing mood had ever met the great sculptor, I am sure he would have found him wondrously thorny both as a man and as an artist. Giacometti seems to have been all thorn, a prickly maker of prickly statues, with a wiry build and spatulate fingers and hair standing on end. His first inportant works, executed in Paris in the late 1920's, when he fell under the influence of Surrealists, are perhaps less thorn than petal; the ''Spoon Woman'' of 1926 is almost as petal-like as spoonlike in shape. But as time wore on, Giacometti's sculptures shed more of their bulk. At length they turned into the elongated figures, rather shorter than life-size (and usually cast in bronze), that won him international acclaim in the '50's.
headline: A LIFE UNLIKE HIS ART

title: Stanley And The Women
author: Kingsley Amis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STANLEY AND THE WOMEN By Kingsley Amis. 256 pp. New York: Summit Books. $14.95.   THIRTY-ONE years ago, Kingsley Amis published ''Lucky Jim,'' a hilarious and sometimes brutal satire on academia in particular and the human quest for happiness. He attacked so many things - class structure, pomposity, hypocrisy, the debacle of modern education - that few noticed how particularly sharp and cruel was his attack on Margaret, the nervous, suicidal and unscrupulous academic spinster whose avocation was teaching, but whose profession was pursuing unattached men. Mr. Amis did not dissect Margaret; he vivisected her. As his career progressed, the cold war between men and women became increasingly central to Mr. Amis's work. Like Freud, he asked what women want. He also asked, compulsively and obsessively, what women are. ''Jake's Thing'' (1978) - his 13th novel to be published in the United States - chronicled an Oxford don's heroic attempts to resuscitate his fading libido, and his final, surprising conclusion that he was better off as he was: ''Jake did a quick run-through of women in his mind . . . their concern with the surface of things . . . with seeming to be better and to be right while getting everything wrong . . . their certainty that a view is the more credible and useful for the fact that they hold it, their use of misunderstanding and misrepresentation as weapons of debate, their selective sensitivity to tones of voice, their unawareness of the difference in themselves between sincerity and insincerity . . . their fondness for general conversation and directionless discussion, their preemption of the major share of feeling, their exaggerated estimate of their own plausibility, their never listening and lots of other things like that, all according to him.''
headline: ONLY TWO SEXES, BOTH CRAZY

title: The Marital Arts
author: Arthur Hoppe
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MARITAL ARTS By Arthur Hoppe. 206 pp. New York: Arbor House. $12.95.   MARRIAGE is a competition in suffering,'' the syndicated columnist Arthur Hoppe asserts in ''Marital Arts,'' a humorous look at the institution and traditions of marriage. He offers some sketches of modern marriages that are so embarrassingly accurate a reader has to blush and smile in self-recognition. The book captures the petty but preoccupying grievances between spouses that, far more than sex or money, supply most of the material for marital arguments. ''You put half your hangers backward in the closet, dear,'' a fictional case-study wife complains. ''I simply can't stand seeing your jackets facing each other every which way.''
headline: DOUBLE BEDS AND OTHER TORTURES

title: Luisa Domic
author: George Dennison
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LUISA DOMIC. By George Dennison. (Harper & Row, $14.95.) One of the happiest literary occurrences of the past several years has been the emergence of a surprising number of new novelists and short-story writers whose books celebrate rural life in contemporary America, yet at the same time transcend the limitations traditionally associated with regional fiction.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Oriental Tales
author: Marguerite Yourcenar
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
ORIENTAL TALES By Marguerite Yourcenar. Translated by Alberto Manguel in collaboration with the author. 147 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $12.95.

MARGUERITE YOURCENAR is one of the great scholar-artists. Her masterpiece, ''The Memoirs of Hadrian,'' an imagined autobiography by the second-century Roman Emperor, has riches for anyone interested in history, humanism or the psychology of power. But Miss Yourcenar's range is much wider than the classical scholarship of that book suggests. In ''Oriental Tales,'' first published in 1938, revised in 1982, and now translated for the first time, she ransacks many cultures - those of the Balkans in the Middle Ages, medieval Japan, Taoism, Hinduism - for the folklore that feeds the book's bewitched and esoteric stories of magic, dream, death, sex and transformation. Here is the scholar as Scheherazade.
headline: SCHOLAR AS SCHEHERAZADE

title: F.D.R.: A Biography
author: Ted Morgan
pull_quote: F.D.R.: A Biography. By Ted Morgan. 830 pages. Illustrated. Simon & Schuster. $22.95.   IN the acknowledgements with which he concludes this remarkable popular biography, Ted Morgan pays tribute to the five multivolumed works on Franklin D. Roosevelt ''from which every writer on F.D.R. benefits,'' and accordingly lists works by John Morton Blum, James MacGregor Burns, Frank B. Friedel, William E. Leuchtenburg, and Arthur M. Schlesinger whose proper citation here would consume an inordinate share of this review.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Workshop Of Democracy
author: James Macgregor Burns
pull_quote: THE WORKSHOP OF DEMOCRACY. By James MacGregor Burns. 671 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $24.95. AMONG the many virtues of James MacGregor Burns's masterful ''Workshop of Democracy'' is that he is unafraid to take the measure of some of America's revered icons. In relating the development of the country in his new book - from the Emancipation Proclamation to the start of the New Deal - he quotes Walter Lippmann, the columnist who sometimes made Presidents tremble, on literary and political matters. While Mr. Lippmann's ideas are given due respect, Mr. Burns also reveals cracks in his image under the searchlight of time.   For instance, writing about Franklin D. Roosevelt when the New York Governor was a Democratic contender for the Presidential nomination in 1932, Mr. Lippmann said that Roosevelt was ''no crusader. He is no tribune of the people. He is no enemy of entrenched privilege. He is a pleasant man who, without any important qualifications for the office, would very much like to be President.'' Not long after the New Deal got going, Mr. Lippmann dismounted from his high horse and admitted that the President was taking strong steps to pull the country out of the Depression.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Galapagos
author: Kurt Vonnegut
pull_quote: GALAPAGOS. By Kurt Vonnegut. 295 pages. Delacorte Press/Seymour Lawrence. $16.95. WITH ''Galapagos,'' the author's 11th novel, we're back in familiar Vonnegut territory: the subject is the end of the world (or at least the end of the world as we know it); the objects of lamentation are man's cruelty to man, contemporary society, modern technology and, of course, the horrors of war - World War II and Vietnam, as well as the more generic variety. Although there are no singsong refrains like ''hippity hop,'' ''hi ho'' or ''so it goes,'' the narrative voice still has the quality of a verbal shrug - flip, careless and willfully casual (''the people would eat up all the food, gobble, gobble, yum, yum, and it would become nothing but excrement and memories''), and the characters still bear more of a resemblance to cartoon figures than regular human beings. The narrator is a Vietnam veteran named Leon who happens to be the son of the erstwhile Kilgore Trout, the hero of ''God Bless You, Mr. Rosewater'' and ''Breakfast of Champions.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Mr Palomar
author: Italo Calvino
pull_quote: MR. PALOMAR. By Italo Calvino. Translated from the Italian by William Weaver. 130 pages. A Helen and Kurt Wolff Book. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $12.95. AT first, I thought I'd made a serious error while reading Italo Calvino's ''Mr. Palomar,'' a new novel by the distinguished Italian writer who died at the age of 61 only a week ago.   Near the beginning of this series of sketches about an anxious, neurasthenic man who, like the telescope whose name he bears, devotes his time to observing various phenomena around him, I was seized by an impulse to turn to the final pages of the book. There I discovered, of all things, an index to the novel, introduced by a note that begins as follows:   ''The numbers 1, 2, 3 that mark the titles of the index, whether they are in the first, second or third position, besides having a purely ordinal value, correspond also to three thematic areas, three kinds of experience and inquiry that, in varying proportions, are present in every part of the book.''

title: Table Of Contents
author: John Mcphee
pull_quote: TABLE OF CONTENTS. By John McPhee. 293 pages. Farrar Straus & Giroux. $15.95.   BACKWARD progress is the theme of the eight pieces by John McPhee collected in ''Table of Contents.'' Written for The New Yorker between 1981 and 1984, they bring news of old professions being rediscovered, of obsolete technologies becoming viable again, of endangered animal species repopulating their old habitats, and of people finding new ways to live in what remains of the North American wilderness.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Nuclear Age
author: Tim O'Brien
pull_quote: THE NUCLEAR AGE. By Tim O'Brien. 312 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95. Tim O'Brien's most recent novel, ''Going After Cacciato,'' published in 1978, was one of the finest books to emerge from the Vietnam War. Picaresque, mythic in dimension, ''Cacciato'' found, in the hallucinatory dreams of a renegade soldier, the perfect metaphor - and narrative strategy - for dealing with that most surreal and anomalous of wars. It made the reader both apprehend the ugliness of death and combat, and also viscerally experience the hero's panic and soft, eager longings for safety and escape.   In ''The Nuclear Age,'' Mr. O'Brien is addressing similar issues of war, death and existential terror - but he has turned from the battlefront in Southeast Asia to the battlefront at home. His hero, William Cowling, is a veteran of 1960's radicalism - ''ten years on the lam, hideout to hideout, dodging bombs and drafts and feds and all the atrocities of our machine-tooled age'' - who has more recently made a fortune in uranium speculation, and who now counts among his ''assets,'' ''a blond wife and a blond daughter, and expensive Persian rugs, and a lovely redwood ranch house in the Sweetheart Mountains.''
headline: PROPHET OF DOOM

title: Angels Unawares
author: T. S. Matthews.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ANGELS UNAWARES Twentieth-Century Portraits. By T. S. Matthews. 294 pp. New York: Ticknor & Fields. $17.95.   ALTHOUGH T. S. Matthews might be expected at the age of 84 to have fired off all his salvos, he had another shot in the locker. ''Angels Unawares'' is the second volume of his autobiography. The first one, ''Name and Address,'' published in 1960, saw him through St. Paul's School, Princeton and Oxford Universities and a career in journalism at The New Yorker, The New Republic and Time. It ended with his resignation from the editorship of Time in 1953 and his taking up permanent residence in England. (Mr. Matthews's best-known book is ''Great Tom,'' a biography of T. S. Eliot. Published in 1974, it drew mixed signals from the critics. Some praised it as a sensitive portrait of a poet writing in illness and pain; some found the long bow of conjecture drawn too far.) ''Angels Unawares'' is not a linear extension of Mr. Matthews's earlier memoir but a book of character sketches, portraits elaborately drawn or snapshots of people remembered from childhood on. Though it leans against the earlier volume on the bookshelf, it has its own value and interest: more than half the 40 or so sketches are beautifully written.
headline: AGEE AND OTHERS

title: Adventures In The Alaskan Skin Trade
author: John Hawkes
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ADVENTURES IN THE ALASKAN SKIN TRADE By John Hawkes. 396 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95. INNOCENCE IN EXTREMIS By John Hawkes. 92 pp. Providence, R.I.: Burning Deck. Cloth, $17.50. Paper, $8. THE new book by that veteran producer John Hawkes is the most accomplished meaningless novel I have ever read. I say ''meaningless'' partly in disparagement, but also partly as neutral description. ''Adventures in the Alaskan Skin Trade'' refers to nothing outside itself; it sets off, as you read it, none of those anticipations of significance you expect of serious fiction; it lacks the tug of profundity that pulls you through a book and amounts to a promise from the author that behind his story is his real subject and your task as a reader is to crack the narrative code disguising it. Imagine ''Moby-Dick'' as just - as only -what Hemingway called it, ''a fish story,'' and you have a model for understanding this often gorgeous prose poem to Alaska and to male camaraderie.

A GERMAN merchant of the 15th century asked an eminent professor where to send his son for a good business education. The professor responded that German universities would be sufficient to teach the boy addition and subtraction but that he would have to go to Italy to learn multiplication and division. Before you smile indulgently, try adding the Roman numerals CCLXVI, MDCCCVII, DCL and MLXXX without first translating them.   The Moroccan-born French mathematics professor Georges Ifrah relates this anecdote in ''From One to Zero: A Universal History of Numbers,'' which has been glowingly reviewed in France. The book is an exhaustive and at times exhausting history of numerals (number symbols) and numeration systems from prehistoric times to the Renaissance, when the Hindu-Arabic system we use today came to worldwide dominance. The heroes of his tale are the nameless scribes, accountants, priests and astronomers who discovered the principles of representing numbers systematically.

author: Ginny Foat with Laura Foreman

pull_quote:
NEVER GUILTY, NEVER FREE By Ginny Foat with Laura Foreman. 307 pp. New York: Random House. $17.95.

THE metamorphosis of a self-described ''worthless slut'' into a nationally prominent feminist ought to make for interesting reading. And, indeed, Ginny Foat's life, as she recounts it in ''Never Guilty, Never Free,'' is dramatic material. For example, Mrs. Foat recalls her extradition from California to Nevada in 1977 on a murder charge based on allegations by her vengeful former husband, Jack Sidote. '' 'We're not supposed to take off the handcuffs,' one of the deputies said, 'but if we do, do we have your word that you're not going to do anything?' . . . What was I going to do? Make a break for it in leg shackles in the middle of a desert? Or maybe brain them both with the thermos bottle.''
headline: AT THE MERCY OF 'ANY MAN'S WORD'

title: Against Racism
author: W. E. B. Du Bois. Edited by Herbert Aptheker. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
AGAINST RACISM: UNPUBLISHED ESSAYS, PAPERS, ADDRESSES, 1887-1961 By W. E. B. Du Bois. Edited by Herbert Aptheker. Illustrated. 325 pp. Amherst: University of Massachusetts Press. $25.

ALTHOUGH the name is familiar, one feels always the need to introduce W. E. B. Du Bois to American readers. Yet Du Bois (1868-1963) was one of the most outspoken and published Americans of his time. Many of his letters have appeared in the three-volume ''Correspondence of W. E. B. Du Bois,'' which, like ''Against Racism,'' was edited by Herbert Aptheker, who teaches ethnic studies at the University of Santa Clara and is the director of the American Institute for Marxist Studies. This volume reminds us that we never really knew Du Bois.

His life doesn't quite support the conventional view that intelligence and hard work at the service of worthy ends will result in progress. Rather, Du Bois's life and work force us to confront the paradoxes of democratic society - that it is unable to rid itself of irrational and self-destructive tendencies, and that it sometimes confines truly exceptional and original human spirits. We are not comfortable with these ideas, so it has been simpler to dismiss Du Bois as a curious black American who lived a life that always seemed off-center.
headline: A CAUTIONARY LIFE

ON the door of an inn in chalk was drawn a woman's face.   From a reliable source the turban-wearers heard the news. ''Woe to our faith,'' they said, ''people have seen a woman unveiled.'' Religion and order were indeed in danger when the pious arrived in haste. One brought dirt, another water with a veil of mud they covered the face and thus reassured returned to their homes religion and order were once more in order.
headline: MOSLEMS IN REVOLT

title: Sovieticus
author: Stephen F. Cohen.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOVIETICUS American Perceptions and Soviet Realities. By Stephen F. Cohen. 160 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $12.95.   STEPHEN COHEN, a professor of Soviet politics and history at Princeton University, is one of the most articulate American Sovietologists. This collection of articles, written for The Nation between 1982 and 1985, is clear and to the point, although the quality is somewhat uneven. Mr. Cohen's strength lies in his treatment of Soviet domestic rather than foreign affairs. When discussing the impact of World War II on Soviet society or the nature of the social contract between governors and governed, he provides an excellent corrective to the Manichaean vision of those who view the Soviet Union as the source of all evil and the West as the source of all good. His treatment of foreign affairs and the related issue of ''Sovietophobia'' is less convincing.
headline: EVENTS AND PHOBIAS

title: Mr Palomar
author: Italo Calvino
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MR. PALOMAR By Italo Calvino. Translated by William Weaver. 130 pp. New York: A Helen and Kurt Wolff Book/ Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $12.95.   Symetries and arithmetics have always tempted Italo Calvino's imagination to grow flirtatious and to begin its fantastic displays. Early on, he gave us some marvelous binary blarney in his tale ''The Cloven Viscount,'' a dual patterning of good and evil, a two-storied story that opened as fluently and knowingly as a zipper in a penthouse. That same allegorical impulse operated with equal freedom but with even more archness and architectural invention in ''Invisible Cities.'' Then came the cat's cradle narrations of ''The Castle of Crossed Destinies,'' regulated but not determined by the inner relations of the cards in the tarot deck. Now we ask ourselves, can he possibly get away with it again?   Mr. Calvino's new book has three main sections entitled ''Mr. Palomar's Vacation,'' ''Mr. Palomar in the City'' and ''The Silences of Mr. Palomar.'' Each main section has three subsections and each subsection three parts and Mr. Calvino has created a numbering system for them. ''The numbers 1, 2, 3 that mark the titles of the index,'' he writes, ''whether they are in the first, second, or third position, besides having a purely ordinal value, correspond also to three thematic areas, three kinds of experience and inquiry that, in varying proportions, are present in every part of the book.
headline: THE SENSUAL PHILOSOPHER

title: The Dialectical Biologist
author: Richard Levins and Richard Lewontin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DIALECTICAL BIOLOGIST By Richard Levins and Richard Lewontin. 303 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $20.   DURING the last two decades, Richard Levins, the John Rock Professor of Population Sciences at Harvard University's School of Public Health, and Richard Lewontin, a professor of zoology at Harvard's Museum of Comparative Zoology, have made extremely important experimental and theoretical contributions to biology. A distinguishing feature of these contributions is the authors' employment of a dialectical method of explication and analysis. As this book's dedication - ''To Frederick Engels, who got it wrong a lot of the time but who got it right where it counted'' - indicates, this dialectical method has its roots in the theories of Marx and Engels. In ''The Dialectical Biologist,'' Mr. Levins and Mr. Lewontin offer an explanation of this method, reasons for adopting it and examples of its application. Their main focus consequently is on philosophical aspects of biology - the nature of knowledge, the nature of the world and the inextricable connection between values and science.
headline: SCIENCE IN THE STYLE OF ENGELS

title: Recombinations
author: Perri Klass
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RECOMBINATIONS By Perri Klass. 283 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $17.95.   IN today's fictional world of deranged housewives and sex-starved careerists, Anne Montgomery, the heroine of ''Recombinations,'' is a lucky woman.   She has a cushy job in a bioengineering company in Manhattan, where not only is she not downtrodden, she's considered a rising star and given all sorts of plum projects. In addition to this pleasant career trajectory, for several years she has also been living unstressfully with a rather nice banker who has some special expertise in linguistics. He's becoming a little disappointing, mostly because he is doing more banking than linguis-tics, but life on all fronts is moving right along.

GREGOR VON REZZO=   RI'S massive, disquieting novel ''The Death of My Brother Abel'' is, like the author's earlier ''Memoirs of an Anti-Semite,'' an attempt to portray European society from the end of World War I to the late 1960's. author: Stephen Dobyns

In THE SAINT VALENTINE'S DAY MURDERS (St. Martin's, $12.95), she takes another look at the system. WHEN Julien Green was converted to   Roman Catholicism in 1916, he took as his baptismal name Francis in honor of St. Francis of Assisi. Now, nearly 70 years and 40 books later, he has at last written a biography of his patron saint. ''God's Fool'' is, unsurprisingly, a labor of love, a quest to discover the nature of a man who inspired the novelist so deeply in his youth and who has been an inspiration to so many, Catholic, non-Catholic and atheist, through the ages.

BY the year 2000 Sao Paulo is expected to be the second-largest city in the world - a megalopolis where 26 million people will be competing for food, shelter, clothing and jobs. It is difficult to imagine what it will mean to live in such a setting; already, with a population only half that size, the city seems ungovernable, and riven by the enormous disparities between its few rich and many poor. In ''And Still the Earth,'' the Brazilian novelist Ignacio de Loyola Brandao tries to envision what 21st-century Sao Paulo might be - a nightmare that exceeds anyone's worst fears for the future.
headline: LIFE UNDER THE MILI-TECHS

MEDICINE has always been an uncomfortable marriage between the scientific and the social. In medical school catalogues it is often described as ''the art and science'' of medicine. In fact, medicine is practiced in a specific socioeconomic context, and it is in this arena that the triumphs and glaring limitations of medical advances are most readily apparent.

With an Introduction by Polly Devlin. 320 pp. New York: Penguin Books/Virago Press. Paper, $6.95. THE wealthy English between the two World Wars - can so many have been the way we imagine? Wrought up and overwrought, malicious, alcoholic, infinitely decorative, highly sexed and nearly always on some edge. Perhaps it had something to do with the furniture, those Art Deco inventions whose last ambition was comfort of an ordinary sort, whose function was hidden behind some elaborate mimesis of the natural world. Consider this description in M. J. Farrell's ''Devoted Ladies'':   ''The bath was not a bath at all but a shallow pink shell, its grooved radiations like mild Beleek china made kinder to the naked body by a movable lining of green sorbo moss. The other half of the shell . . . opened backwards into the wall hollowed to fit it. . . . Of taps or plug there was no sign. Nothing so vulgar. The uninitiated might search in vain for any means of inflow or egress for the bath water, which . . . both welled up and ran out through a species of navel concealed beneath the sorbo moss.''

AS a general rule, feminists should probably not say mean things about each other when members of the enemy camp (some would say enemy sex) may be listening. Yet in the recent past the level of intrafeminist invective on one issue has sometimes threatened to surpass the antifeminist invective from the far right. The issue is pornography. One side would like to prohibit it, or at least rule that it is an infringement on women's civil rights. The other side has been, for the most part, not so sure.
headline: PORNOGRAPHY AS PARADOX

title: Bringing Up A Moral Child
author: Michael Schulman and Eva Mekler.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
BRINGING UP A MORAL CHILD A New Approach for Teaching Your Child to Be Kind, Just and Responsible. By Michael Schulman and Eva Mekler. 362 pp. Reading, Mass: Addison-Wesley Publishing. Paper, $12.95. Cloth, $19.95. HAD this book been written in 1885 it would have been well received, because it extols the moral virtues of kindliness, justice and responsibility so dear to Victorian hearts. Its prescriptions for instilling morality in children are pre-Freudian: they are based on the belief that parents can set good examples and that children are emotionally uncomplicated and responsive to loving correction.

The thesis of ''Bringing Up a Moral Child'' - that parents actually have power to influence character -will also be popular with parents of the 1980's, whose views of children are largely post-Freudian. Most experts tell today's parents that children are eager learners of a culture's shared beliefs and not to fear thwarting their little spirits by efficient potty training, demanding good manners or teaching moral principles. Contemporary parents believe that firmly enforced limits, appropriate to the child's developmental level, make for secure children rather than repressed ones. Michael Schulman and Eva Mekler, who are both psychologists, see the child as robust, resilient and responsive to parental guidance.

TRUTH being stranger than fiction, it shouldn't surprise anyone that the 19th-century naval incident recounted in ''Sea Dangers'' is the archetypal mutiny story, a ''Bounty'' in which the fathers win instead of the sons, a ''Caine Mutiny'' that doesn't cheat in its narrative viewpoint, a drama that Herman Melville would have borrowed if he hadn't been after bigger game, and even so he was gracious enough to acknowledge it in ''Billy Budd.''   But since fiction usually has the advantage of narrative freedom, one has to be impressed by ''Sea Dangers'' for the richness with which it reconstructs the Somers affair, which occurred in 1842 and involved the execution aboard ship of three suspected mutineers, one of them Philip Spencer, the wayward son of John Canfield Spencer, President John Tyler's Secretary of War.

title: The Inman Diary
pull_quote: THE INMAN DIARY. A Public and Private Confession. Edited by Daniel Aaron. Two volumes. 1,661 pages. Illustrated. Harvard. $39.95 until Dec. 31, $50 thereafter. WITH the appearance of this huge slab of self-revelation, space will have to be found for a new entry in the annals of American literature: Arthur Crew Inman (1895-1963). It is not the entry that Inman himself would ideally have chosen; he first set out to win fame as a poet, paid for the publication of several volumes of mediocre verse and clung to the conviction that although he was never mentioned by the critics who ''pedestalized'' Robert Frost, Carl Sandburg and the like, his time would eventually come. (''I am superbly patient in big things.'') But at some point in the 1920's he decided that his best chance of achieving immortality lay in the diary that he had begun keeping in 1919 - a personal record intended to be the most candid and inclusive ever written.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Back In The World
author: Tobias Wolff
pull_quote: BACK IN THE WORLD. By Tobias Wolff. 221 pages. Houghton Mifflin. $15.95.   ''WE used to talk about how when we got back in the world we were going to do this and we were going to do that,'' says a character in one of Tobias Wolff's fine, angular stories. ''Back in the world we were going to have it made. But ever since then it's been nothing but confusion.'' Though this happens to be a Vietnam veteran talking about the disillusion he experienced on returning home after the war, he might well be speaking for any one of Mr. Wolff's disaffected heroes. Frustrated, lonely and divorced from their youthful expectations, these people all drift through the present, trying to get by day to day, by telling assorted stories and lies. For them, as for Mr. Wolff, lying - in this case, fiction-making -represents a way of imposing a narrative order on their lives, as well as a means of connecting with others and with their receding dreams.

author: Tracy Kidder

His prose could make you visualize a borasnadafras doing a cherbstorg, if there ever were such things.

title: Vengeance. India After The Assassination Of Indira
author: Pranay B Gupte
pull_quote: VENGEANCE. India After the Assassination of Indira Gandhi. By Pranay Gupte. 368 pages. W. W. Norton. $16.95. PRANAY GUPTE'S ''Vengeance: India After the Assassination of Indira Gandhi'' reads more like a series of news dispatches than it does the big book on India Mr. Gupte thought he might write. A journalist with a Brandeis degree and 14 years at The New York Times behind him, Mr. Gupte was in India visiting his ailing father in Bombay when Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated. Foreign journalists had been barred from the Punjab, where terrorism had led to a military assault on the Golden Temple, the Sikhs' principal shrine, and army rule. Mr. Gupte, an Indian national, was asked to cover the most severe test since independence in 1947 of Indian unity and democracy.   The book is mostly about headline events - the assassination of Mrs. Gandhi by Sikh bodyguards; her 40-year-old-son, Rajiv, succeeding her as Prime Minister; the orchestrated and spontaneous killing of Sikhs in northern India; the triumph of terrorism over moderation in the Punjab; the rising tide of regional and agrarian politics; the decay of India's cities ands environment; Rajiv Gandhi's sweeping electoral victory in last December's parliamentary election.
headline: Books: Eyewitnesses in a Changing India

title: The Victim's Song
author: Alice R Kaminsky
pull_quote: THE VICTIM'S SONG. By Alice R. Kaminsky. 268 pages. Illustrated. Prometheus Books. $19.95.   ON the evening of Sept. 13, 1980, Eric Kaminsky, an exceptionally promising 22-year-old student at the Manhattan School of Music, was attacked and murdered shortly after entering the Eighth Avenue subway at 181st Street. His two assailants robbed him of $22; one of them stabbed him in the back, twisting the knife in the wound, and he was then thrown onto the track. Some young people who found him managed to lift him onto the platform before a train arrived, but his aorta had been pierced and he died in a matter of minutes.

title: Galapagos
author: Kurt Vonnegut
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GALAPAGOS By Kurt Vonnegut. 295 pp. New York: Seymour Lawrence/ Delacorte Press. $16.95. YES, American culture is more smart than wise. But Kurt Vonnegut, that clown-poet of homesickness and Armageddon, might be the rare American writer who is both. He dances the witty and informed dances of the literary smart, but while he does, he casts a wide eye about, and he sees. He is a postmodern Mark Twain: grumpy and sentimental, antic and religious. He is that paradoxical guy who goes to church both to pray fervently and to blow loud, snappy gum bubbles at the choir.   None of this, of course, is news to Mr. Vonnegut's fans, and neither is this: His most recent novels have not been his strongest. ''Jailbird'' was the most restrained and accomplished and contained Mr. Vonnegut's most memorable female characters. But ''Deadeye Dick'' suffered from a deadly narrative sprawl, and ''Slapstick'' floundered in silliness, exemplified by the irritating mantra ''Hi ho.'' Despite its courage and farsightedness, much of Mr. Vonnegut's recent work has seemed fatigued, marred by sloppy writing. It is prose that makes a beeline for a punch line - like a man for a water fountain, only to find it dribbling, not working right at all.

THIS book is the story of the building of a house, and it is told with such clarity, intelligence and grace it makes you wonder why no one has written a book like it before. In the way that a well-told story of a marriage, or of a love affair or of a child's coming of age fills you with a sense that you are reading about a fundamental human experience for the first time, so it is with ''House.'' title: Dwellers In The Land
author: Kirkpatrick Sale.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DWELLERS IN THE LAND The Bioregional Vision. By Kirkpatrick Sale. 217 pp. San Francisco: Sierra Club Books. $14.95.   THIS is a radical book - it says that most of us should give up orange juice for breakfast. According to the bioregionalist philosophy, the world should be divided not according to the artificial boundaries of nation-states, but according to natural regions defined by landforms and life-forms. Each region would be self-governing and self-sufficient - so people in non-citrus-growing regions would have to find other sources of vitamin C. Although Kirkpatrick Sale, the author of ''SDS,'' ''Human Scale'' and ''Power Shift: The Rise of the Southern Rim and Its Challenge to the Eastern Establishment,'' is proposing some radical ideas, he doesn't want to sound radical, far-out or utopian. Indeed, ''Dwellers in the Land'' sounds like inspirational literature. Its basic theme is mythological or even religious. Mr. Sale begins by singing the praises of Gaea, the primordial earth mother of Greek mythology. This one true mother-god was abandoned when ''somewhere, somehow, the poisons crept in.'' Humankind turned to a false scientific god and became obsessed with dictating to the environment rather than heeding its dictates. We have constructed an unhappy civilization based on the ''industrio-scientific paradigm'': large-scale organizations, a competitive and exploitative economic system, centralized and hierarchical politics and a polarized, violent society.
