SAUDI ARABIA The Ceaseless Quest for Security. By Nadav Safran. 524 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press. $25.

SAUDI ARABIA is an improbable nation - a meager population of perhaps seven or eight million, more than one-third of them foreign workers, living in a vast, indefensible area under whose barren deserts lie the world's largest reserves of easily accessible oil, and with a unique political system held together by Islamic tradition and a royal family several thousand strong. The reality is difficult to describe accurately. What has been presented to American readers is often deeply colored by the views and purposes of the presenter, who may be driven by the idea of building barriers against the Russians, intent on the need for Saudi oil (and thus for Saudi friendship) at almost any cost, worried about the security of Israel being threatened by Arab armies and terrorists backed by Saudi wealth, or merely desirous of titillating a reader's fancy with tales of this strange society of millionaires one step removed from the nomad's tent.

author: Yashar Kemal
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SEA-CROSSED FISHERMAN By Yashar Kemal. Translated by Thilda Kemal. 288 pp. New York: George Braziller. $16.95.   YASHAR KEMAL, Turkey's and perhaps the Islamic world's best living writer, again demonstrates his skill at braiding dramatic action with popular myth in ''The Sea-Crossed Fisherman.'' It is an intensely political book, its vision framed sometimes as beautifully written stream-of-consciousness dreams and sometimes as messages Samuel Goldwyn would have said were better sent by Western Union.
headline: ISTANBUL'S MIASMA

title: The Forms Of Violence
author: Leo Bersani and Ulysse Dutoit. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE FORMS OF VIOLENCE Narrative in Assyrian Art and Modern Culture. By Leo Bersani and Ulysse Dutoit. Illustrated. 136 pp. New York: Schocken Books. $19.95.

THE savage spectacles of war and lion hunting carved in stone by Assyrian sculptors nearly three millenniums ago have frequently struck observers as too emotionally inexpressive, rigidly hierarchic and nakedly celebratory of the carnage depicted to be wholly satisfying to modern esthetic sensibilities. In ''The Forms of Violence,'' however, Leo Bersani and Ulysse Dutoit, who teach French and film, respectively, at the University of California at Berkeley, reinterpret these ancient reliefs in a provocative, complex and elegant meditation on the relationship between narrative and violence. An expanded version of two essays that originally appeared in the journal October, the book is an impressive testimonial to the mutually enriching encounter of visual and literary studies with the theory of psychoanalysis.
headline: FRUSTRATING THE SPECTATOR

title: The Militarization Of Space
author: Paul B. Stares.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE MILITARIZATION OF SPACE U.S. Policy, 1945-1984. By Paul B. Stares. 334 pp. Ithaca, N.Y.: Cornell University Press. $25.

THE successful test of a United States anti-satellite (ASAT) device Sept. 13 against a still-functioning spacecraft has once again dramatized the controversy over the necessity and wisdom of developing weapons systems for use in or from space. We now have, in Paul Stares' book ''The Militarization of Space,'' a work that places recent events in a broad historical perspective. According to Mr. Stares, who is a research associate at the Brookings Institution, when Ronald Reagan entered the White House in 1981, ''the future development of ASAT weapons was still very much in the balance.'' This is no longer the case, Mr. Stares says. His ''depressing prognosis'' therefore is that, under President Reagan, ''the chance for a significant anti-satellite arms control agreement was lost - possibly forever.''
headline: THE GENSIS OF 'STAR WARS'

title: Field Of Blood
author: Gerald Seymour
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FIELD OF BLOOD. By Gerald Seymour. (Norton, $14.95.) ''An oath's an oath. An oath's a lifetime.'' Exactly what kind of havoc our oaths can wreak, and how perilous and abbreviated a lifetime in Belfast, Northern Ireland, can be, preoccupies this relentlessly grim suspense novel, Gerald Seymour's eighth in 10 years.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Mademoiselle
author: Bruno Monsaingeon. Translated by Robyn Marsack. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
MADEMOISELLE Conversations With Nadia Boulanger. By Bruno Monsaingeon. Translated by Robyn Marsack. Illustrated. 141 pp. New York: Carcanet. $14.95.

IN the film ''Love Story,'' millions of moviegoers heard the name of one of the 20th century's most influential musical pedagogues, when Ali MacGraw, as the harpsichord-playing heroine, protested to Ryan O'Neal, her would-be bridegroom, that she wasn't ready for marriage. She wanted to go to Paris, she said, to study with Nadia Boulanger.

It has been said that Boulanger was single-handedly responsible for nurturing several generations of American composers. It has also been said that she was single-handedly responsible for ruining several generations of American composers. Paul Valery called her ''the personification of music.'' Controversial or canonized, Nadia Boulanger taught music tirelessly for nearly 70 years, receiving pupils at her studio in the Rue Ballu, dressed in black or gray, until moments before her death in 1979 at the age of 92. An erudite elitist, she was honored by heads of state, decorated, filmed and televised, and on her 90th birthday, huge hot-air balloons were released in her honor into the skies over Fontainebleau.
headline: EVERYBODY'S MUSIC TEACHER

pull_quote: IS SALAMI AND EGGS BETTER THAN SEX? Memoirs of a Happy Eater. By Alan King and Mimi Sheraton. 218 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $15.95.   JOHNNY will definitely hold it up. headline: EATING FOR PLEASURE

title: Masks Of The Universe
author: Edward Harrison
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MASKS OF THE UNIVERSE By Edward Harrison. Illustrated. 306 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $18.95.   WE should get one thing straight at the beginning - although this book is written by a respected member of the scientific community, it is not a book about science. It is about those aspects of philosophy and theology that border on the scientific enterprise, which is quite a different thing. The book's title derives from Edward Harrison's central thesis - that there is a distinction between the Universe and various universes. The Universe is the real thing - everything that exists. It is also, according to Mr. Harrison, forever unknown and unknowable. A universe, on the other hand, is the conception people have of the makeup of the Universe at any given time -what most scientists would call a model of the Universe. It is this distinction between the Universe and our ideas about it that occupies the first section of the book. Mr. Harrison, who is a professor of physics and astronomy at the University of Massachusetts, sees human history as a long succession of universes, each representing a different mask behind which the true Universe hides.
headline: MAGIC, GOD AND QUANTUM PHYSICS

title: The Secrets Of Harry Bright
author: Joseph Wambaugh
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SECRETS OF HARRY BRIGHT By Joseph Wambaugh. 345 pp. New York: A Perigord Press Book/ William Morrow & Company. $17.95.   JOSEPH WAMBAUGH has been a best-selling author for long enough now that you'd think he'd know the club rules. You'd think one of the older members would have cautioned him against tackling such difficult subjects, putting so much energy into his prose style, making his books so different from one another and acting as if he were under an obligation to prove his talent anew each time out.

This handsome illustrated book proposes that some periodicals are worth putting on the shelf for future reflection.

author: Robert McCrum
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE FABULOUS ENGLISHMAN By Robert McCrum. 274 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $14.95.

A NOVEL of sad nostalgias, ''The Fabulous Englishman'' presents a rite of passage into what is presumably adulthood (or middle age) and acceptance of our present dreary realities. The word ''fabulous'' refers to the ability to create ambiguous stories about one's past, in this case the 1960's of revolution, sex, drugs and music. Robert McCrum is quite good at evoking the sense of that time.
headline: SHAKING OFF THE 60's

title: Badger On The Barge
author: Janni Howker.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BADGER ON THE BARGE And Other Stories. By Janni Howker. 201 pp. New York: Greenwillow Books. $10.25. (Ages 10 and up) OCTOBER smelled of bonfires, even in Alfred Street. Down by the canal the yellow leaves of the big conker trees flickered and rustled like burning newspapers. In the still canal water black leaves floated on Helen's reflection.'' These evocative words begin Janni Howker's first book, a collection of five stories, set in England, each one a memorable encounter between a young person and an old one.   With the prose style and skillful dialogue of a far more experienced writer, the writer gently reminds the reader that, in an era when the young reign supreme, the old, who are often lonely, sometimes forgotten, sometimes misunderstood, have plenty to offer. There is Helen, achingly sad in the quiet house where her parents mourn the death of her brother. She discovers Bad Bill, the badger on the barge, and better yet, feisty Miss Brady, the pet's owner (although in her words, ''he's no pet. . . . He's a trial and a torment, bless him.''). Miss Brady, however (alone but not lonely), says she does not want human companionship, yet it is her very aloofness that attracts Helen to her, and it is their somewhat gruff friendship that eventually gives Helen the courage to set her fragile family to rights.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: October Blood
author: Francine du Plessix Gray
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OCTOBER BLOOD By Francine du Plessix Gray. 253 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $16.95. THE peculiar world of high fashion is satirized in Francine du Plessix Gray's new novel, ''October Blood.'' It also sounds a lot like the literal truth.
headline: WHY NOT SET YOUR HAIR ON FIRE?

title: Vaulting Ambition
author: Philip Kitcher.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: VAULTING AMBITION Sociobiology and the Quest for Human Nature. By Philip Kitcher. 456 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: The MIT Press. $25.   A DECADE has passed since the publication of E. O. Wilson's ''Sociobiology: The New Synthesis'' - an event that is generally seen as marking the consolidation, if not the start, of a new field of biological and behavioral science. It was greeted with praise in The New York Review of Books by C. H. Waddington, a renowned English geneticist and lifelong progressive, and it was widely acclaimed as an encyclopedic summary of the evolutionary approach to animal, and human, behavior. However, it came under fire from many quarters. Such critics as Richard C. Lewontin at Harvard University, a leading mathematical geneticist, and Stephen Jay Gould, a leading paleontologist and naturalist who is also at Harvard, have devoted substantial time, energy and print to exposing its scientific flaws. They have also pointed out its dangerous political implications, arising from the inappropriate application of sociobiological principles to support racist and reactionary ideologies. Those implications have been puzzlingly ignored by many of the practitioners in the discipline.
headline: ONE GENE AT A TIME

title: An Evening Performance
author: George Garrett
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AN EVENING PERFORMANCE. By George Garrett. (Doubleday, $18.95.) Though best known for his historical novels - ''Death of the Fox'' and ''The Succession'' - George Garrett has also produced a large body of short fiction encompassing the American experience of the last 30 years. The stories collected here describe the conflicts of adolescence, romantic and domestic turmoil, life in small Southern towns, academic life and wartime experiences, and they range in manner from the naturalistic to the near-farcical. Never less than workmanlike, solidly traditional in form, Mr. Garrett's stories frequently sound the theme of human cruelty. ''Human beings are the foulest things in all creation,'' says a character in ''Wounded Soldier,'' while the boy-narrator of ''The Last of the Spanish Blood'' is made to confront his own potential for evil and violence. ''What's the Purpose of the Bayonet?,'' a powerful story of wartime, ends by indicting ''the whole inhuman race.'' This abiding misanthropy does, however, allow for the saving grace of humor. ''Bread From Stones,'' an amusing tale of a feckless gigolo, also forms a tiny critique of the American dream. Perhaps the best story in the volume, ''Texarkana Was a Crazy Town,'' tells of a likable former soldier who finds ''real life'' much more fearsome and wondrous than anything he had encountered in the military. With few exceptions, the stories seem defiantly ''unfashionable'' in style. In our age of pared-down realism, Mr. Garrett's flaws as a writer - a fondness for elaborate similes, an occasional straining after poetic effects and a general prolixity -are particularly noticeable.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Masters of Atlantis
author: Charles Portis
pull_quote: MASTERS OF ATLANTIS. By Charles Portis. 248 pages. Knopf. $15.95.   IT is typical of Charles Portis's wonderfully comic characters to go on quests. The hero of his first novel, ''Norwood'' (1966), went forth from Mr. Portis's home state of Arkansas to collect $70 owed to him by a marine buddy in New York. In ''True Grit'' (1968), young Mattie Ross hired Rooster Cogburn and LaBoeuf and tracked the dirty varmints who killed her Daddy. In ''The Dog of the South'' (1979), Raymond E. Midge of Little Rock, Ark., set out after Guy Dupree for running off with his wife, his Ford Torino, his Texaco and American Express cards, and his prized recording of Ole Miss's Dr. Buddy Casey giving his lecture on the Siege of Vicksburg.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Move Your Shadow
author: Joseph Lelyveld
pull_quote:
MOVE YOUR SHADOW. By Joseph Lelyveld. 389 pages. Times Books. $18.95. THE other day I was crossing Harvard Yard with the esteemed botanist Richard Evans Schultes, a vigorous man in his seventies who has spent years collecting plant specimens in the jungles of South America. When we came upon a group of undergraduate specimens carrying banners that said ''Divest Now,'' Mr. Schultes gave them a stare that stopped them in their tracks and boomed out five words: ''Why don't you grow up?''

Well, yes and no. There are sound arguments for and against divesting. But beyond that, Mr. Schultes felt that while South Africa was without doubt a worthy cause, the student protest was a cheap way to join the side of the angels, as were the demonstrations in front of the South African Embassy, where Congressmen and other concerned citizens were arrested and released. ''To do good is noble,'' Mark Twain said. ''To teach others to do good is nobler yet, and less trouble.''
headline: Books: On Apartheid

title: Dictionary Of American Regional English. Volume I
author: Frederic G Cassidy
pull_quote: DICTIONARY OF AMERICAN REGIONAL ENGLISH: Volume I - Introduction and A-C. Chief editor: Frederic G. Cassidy. 903 pages. Belknap/ Harvard. $49.95 until Dec. 31; $60 thereafter.   IT is nearly a hundred years since a group of leading philologists and language enthusiasts, among them such honored names as the Dante scholar Charles H. Grandgent and the ballad collector Francis J. Child, founded the American Dialect Society. One of the society's aims was to produce a comprehensive American dialect dictionary, along the lines of the dialect dictionary then being edited in England by Joseph Wright, but though a great deal of material was collected over the years that followed, and the position of editor of the dictionary was formally created in 1929, the project remained stalled for lack of funds and of adequate planning.

title: Fifty Years Adrift
author: Derek Taylor
pull_quote: THE limited edition has long been a practically foolproof way of making sure a work of art, a book or a recording will rapidly appreciate in value -and a favorite ploy for enabling the artist or publisher to sell his work at a price far above what it would fetch as a mass-produced item. There have not been many limited editions in the world of pop music, and for a good reason: many dedicated fans exist on modest incomes and have enough trouble saving up to buy a new album at regular or discount prices.   Still, there is something to be said for the idea of publishing an instant collector's item in the form of a limited edition, and this is what Derek Taylor has done with a new book describing his adventures as press agent for the Beatles and other rock stars of the 60's. ''Fifty Years Adrift'' ($350, Genesis Publications Limited) is an impressively weighty tome, beautifully bound in calf leather with gilt-edge pages, and it includes many previously unpublished pictures, full-color reproductions of concert tickets, stage passes, letters, postcards and the like, and more than 500 pages of text. Also included are some 15,000 words of margin notes by George Harrison, who expands on certain tales from the band's point of view and is said to have personally edited the manuscript.
headline: HEAVY LIMITED EDITION

title: Texas
author: James Michener
pull_quote: TEXAS. By James A. Michener. 1,096 pages. Random House. $21.95. BY now, James Michener has pretty much found his formula for the novel: whether the setting is Hawaii (''Hawaii''), Afghanistan (''Caravans''), South Africa (''The Covenant''), the eastern shore of the United States (''Chesapeake'') or, as now, the sprawling plains of Texas, the result is always a huge book, crammed to overflowing with facts, ideas and sociology - a sort of Baedeker to local civilization. This time, Texas seems the ideal subject: vast, sprawling, and eclectic in population and geography, the state has just the sort of larger-than-life history that lends itself to Mr. Michener's taste for multi-generational epics; and the story of its emergence - from frontier outpost to proud flagship of the New South - personifies the sort of old-fashioned American values that the author likes to examine in his fiction.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Jesus Through The Centuries
author: Jaroslav Pelikan
pull_quote: JESUS THROUGH THE CENTURIES.      His Place in the History of Culture. By   Jaroslav Pelikan. 270 pages. Illustrated. Yale University Press. $22.50.      ''J   ESUS CHRIST,'' we are told in the New Testament, ''is the same yesterday and today and for ever.'' But however immutable He may be in His theological essence, here on earth, under the shifting lights of history, He has assumed many different guises. Each age has tended to reinterpret his significance according to its own needs, and if some of the images men have formed of Him are complementary, others have been inconsistent or even sharply contradictory. As William Blake wrote, for example, rejecting the conventional piety of his day, The Vision of Christ that Thou dost see Is my Vision's Greatest Enemy.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Family And Friends
author: Anita Brookner
pull_quote: FAMILY AND FRIENDS. By Anita Brookner. 187 pages. Pantheon. $13.95. In the British writer Anita Brookner's four previous novels, a recognizable vision of society, of the interactions between men and women, has been elegantly mapped out. It's a vision of the world as a dangerous, predatory place, peopled by two sorts of individuals - sophisticates and innocents. And while Miss Brookner always sides with her naifs - in each case, a Pym-like spinster, diligent, correct and impeccably earnest -she also makes it clear that she regards them as losers in society's hypocritical games. It's the careless, tempestuous people who get ahead and who win the love of others - not her discreet little heroines, who seem doomed by their own good intentions.   In her finest work, in this reader's view, ''Look at Me,'' Miss Brookner has used her keen sense of irony to limn this deeply felt, if somewhat limited, theme with clarity and moral vigor; in such lesser performances as ''Providence'' and ''Hotel du Lac,'' a certain attenuation sets in; a tendency to identify too closely with her heroines leads Miss Brookner to slip, from time to time, into sentimentality and self-pity, and the solitary predicament of her characters also threatens to become predictable and routine.

title: Healing Song For The Inner Ear
author: Robert Bly
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOVING A WOMAN IN TWO WORLDS By Robert Bly. 78 pp. New York: The Dial Press/ Doubleday & Company. $12.95. HEALING SONG FOR THE INNER EAR By Michael S. Harper. 97 pp. Urbana: University of Illinois Press. Cloth, $12.95. Paper, $6.95. A POET who fashions an extreme individual style, as Robert Bly surely has done, may find he has forged his own manacles to a limited means of expression. Whatever his subject or emotions, his poems may melt together in a monochrome haze. The ostensible subject of ''Loving a Woman in Two Worlds'' is romantic love, but many of the poems - even those containing the phrase ''man and woman'' - are hard to distinguish from Mr. Bly's other poems of landscape and mystic reverie. The verses become creatures of a habit not necessarily their own. The problem is aggravated by the kind of idiom Mr. Bly has fabricated. So many lines weighted with reverent pauses, stolid with monosyllables, muffled by end stops, can make poems not suggestive but stonily incommunicative. There is too much easy Orientalism, as in ''The Turtle'': Rain lifts the lake level, washing the reeds. Slowly the milkweed pods open, the yellow lily pads. Through the mist man and woman see the far shore. The turtle's head rises out over the water. In ''The Roots'' and ''The Hawk,'' he is still playing Tarzan; and he still takes flying leaps - ''I float in the current, calm and mad as a sleepy cork.''

author: Djuna Barnes
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: INTERVIEWS By Djuna Barnes. Edited by Alyce Barry. Foreword and commentary by Douglas Messerli. Illustrated. 396 pp. Washington, D.C.: Sun & Moon Press. Cloth, $16.95. Paper, $10.95.   IT is a terrible thing that memories of great men die with their contemporaries,'' Djuna Barnes wrote in her 1917 interview of Frank Harris, whom she described as a short man with ''a mustache like a mural painting.'' Harris, the roguish sexual adventurer who chronicled his amatory exploits in the once suppressed ''My Life and Loves,'' is one of 40 individuals - some celebrated, some obscure, some forgotten - in these extraordinary conversational encounters dating from 1913 to 1931. Here, collected for the first time, are Barnes's pieces on James Joyce, Florenz Ziegfeld, Jack Dempsey, Diamond Jim Brady, D. W. Griffith, Mother Jones, Billy Sunday, Alfred Stieglitz, Alfred Lunt and Lynn Fontanne, Coco Chanel and others, plus an interview of the author by a man described here as a charlatan and pretender.

title: The Mind's New Science
author: Howard Gardner.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MIND'S NEW SCIENCE A History of the Cognitive Revolution. By Howard Gardner. 423 pp. New York: Basic Books. $22.50.   PSYCHOLOGISTS used to become famous for one of two reasons - either they ruthlessly banished common sense from their theories or they surreptitiously brought it back. B. F. Skinner, with his denial of mental processes, belonged to the first group; Edward C. Tolman, who at the height of the behaviorist movement insisted that rats formed cognitive maps, belonged to the second. In the 1930's and 40's there were many brave souls who stood out against behaviorism, but their theories lacked rigor and were often merely a reflection of common-sense views of the mind. The reason was that there were no rigorous concepts and no symbolism with which to describe mental activity. The digital computer has changed all that.
headline: THAT'S USING YOUR HEAD

title: Buildings For Music
author: Michael Forsyth. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BUILDINGS FOR MUSIC The Architect, the Musician, and the Listener from the Seventeenth Century to the Present Day. By Michael Forsyth. Illustrated. 371 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: The MIT Press. $30. MICHAEL FORSYTH'S ''Buildings for Music'' is a superbly illustrated and absorbing study of concert halls and opera houses built or conceived since the 17th century. It starts with the first rooms constructed in London particularly for the pleasure of ''lovers of musick'' and ends with 20th-century world's fair pavilions specially devised to house works by Edgard Varese and Karlheinz Stockhausen. In between it delivers a feast of revelations, like Friedrich Gilly's project for the Berlin Schauspielhaus, Ernst Haiger's Symphoniehaus or Harvey Lonsdale Elmes's titanic St. George's Hall in Liverpool, England, and of pleasures, like its thorough documentation of the Neues Gewandhaus in Leipzig, East Germany. Throughout it is sustained by an intelligent, engaging narrative remarkable for its knowledge of the history of musical composition and its command of the acoustical implications of design. Since Leo Beranek's ''Music, Acoustics and Architecture'' (1962) there are few books in its class.   This study by Mr. Forsyth, who teaches architecture at the University of Bristol, England, illustrates a basic thesis - composers are heavily influenced in what they write by the qualities of the spaces in which their works will be played, and that architects are heavily influenced in what they design by their vision of the musical purposes their buildings will serve.
headline: PAVILIONS OF HARMONY

title: Table Of Contents
author: John McPhee
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TABLE OF CONTENTS By John McPhee. 293 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $15.95.   THIS book collects eight essays originally published in The New Yorker between 1980 and 1984. Two pieces are about bears. One is about people who run small hydroelectric projects. One is about Circle City, Alaska, and its 17-subscriber telephone company. The longest and best focuses on the new breed of family doctors beginning to appear in small-town America. Another tells the story of John McPhee's interaction with a namesake he didn't know he had: a John McPhee who is an airborne game warden for the state of Maine. There is no common thread to ''Table of Contents'' at all - or at least no more of one than that all the people Mr. McPhee writes about are uncommonly nice, and also pioneers in one way or another. (The bears aren't pioneers, but Patricia McConnell, the woman who looks after wild bears for the state of New Jersey, surely is.) There is no law, of course, that says a book has to have a theme. And this book manages uncommonly well without one. Each essay, except perhaps the one that describes a day in the life of New Jersey Senator Bill Bradley, stands well on its own. Each, except perhaps that one, is a delight to read. Mr. McPhee is in top form, and his voice, fairly constant from piece to piece, provides sufficient unity.

author: Pam Durban.

pull_quote: ALL SET ABOUT WITH FEVER TREES And Other Stories. By Pam Durban. 211 pp. Boston: David R. Godine. $15.95.   IN a recent interview William Styron is quoted as saying, ''This, it seems to me, is an era of witnesses. We no longer trust the voice of the omniscient.'' But I think it is not so; I think that given any voice at all that has power and integrity, a reader will abandon his soul to it, and there is such a voice to be found in ''All Set About With Fever Trees,'' this first book of collected stories by Pam Durban.

title: The Tragedy Of Zionism
author: Bernard Avishai.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE TRAGEDY OF ZIONISM Revolution and Democracy in the Land of Israel. By Bernard Avishai. 389 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $19.95.

ISRAEL is loved and defended in the United States, but the passion often has about it something of the quality of John Donne's outcry to the lady of his dreams: ''For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love!'' It is a very strange experience to read the newspapers from Israel, even those of right-wing orientation, alongside the pro-Israel publications in the United States. What everyone in Israel knows as a matter of course is often denounced as false and subversive when quoted in America. So in June 1982, when Israel's army moved north into Lebanon, by the third day of the exercise, no one in Israel was in any doubt that the campaign had been conceived as going far beyond its announced target of cleaning out a ''security zone'' of 45 kilometers; military means were being used to remake the political face of Lebanon. Only reluctantly, and not before at least two years had passed, was there a kind of grudging acceptance in most pro-Israel circles in America of the fact that Gen. Ariel Sharon had not been drawn against his will to the gates of Beirut.
headline: WHAT SHOULD ISRAEL BE

title: Parrots' Wood
author: Erma J. Fisk.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
PARROTS' WOOD By Erma J. Fisk. 240 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company.  5.95.

IN ''Parrots' Wood,'' Erma Fisk constantly plays with our preconceptions. What appears to be a good-natured book about a spry older woman's participation in a bird-banding expedition in Belize is actually a deep, sweet meditation on aging, love, loneliness and hope.
headline: BANDING TOGETHER

title: Fdr
author: Ted Morgan
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FDR By Ted Morgan. Illustrated. 830 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $22.95.   NO American President has so dominated his times as Franklin Delano Roosevelt, and no President since Lincoln has been so much written about. There are multivolume biographies by James MacGregor Burns, Arthur Schlesinger Jr. and Frank Freidel, as well as innumerable books by those who were associated with Roosevelt, memoirs by journalists and studies by historians, political scientists and other scholars.   Now comes a popular one-volume biography that, without ignoring Roosevelt's political actions during the Great Depression or World War II, focuses more on the man - his chilhood, marriage, struggle with polio and relations with family, friends, enemies, subordinates and rivals. Ted Morgan, previously author of ''Churchill: Young Man in a Hurry 1874-1915,'' seems to have done his research for ''FDR'' as thoroughly as an academic historian; his notes on his sources are extensive, and he has interviewed many of the survivors of the Roosevelt years. What emerges is a fascinating three-dimensional portrait of this extraordinary man. Mr. Morgan's work is neither that of a slavish idolator nor of a hostile critic. The portrait he draws is of a great man with human frailties. To one who knew Roosevelt as a reporter, the portrait seems accurate.
headline: MANIPULATIVE, SECRETIVE AND GREAT

title: In Her Own Image
author: Anna Murdoch
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
IN HER OWN IMAGE By Anna Murdoch. 225 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $15.95.

THE author of this first novel - a romantic melodrama about family life on an Australian sheep farm - happens to be married to the newspaper magnate Rupert Murdoch. But one can safely put aside any prejudices or preconceptions about the wives of the wealthy and powerful (those women, one imagines, who approach writing as if it were the verbal equivalent of needlepoint). This is not a dilettantish effort. On the contrary, ''In Her Own Image'' suffers from a tendency toward unrelieved earnestness; humor is in shorter supply here than water during the Australian outback's driest month - December.
headline: CHRISTMAS IN THE OUTBACK

title: Little David
author: Elliott Chaze
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: There have been many mysteries and suspense novels in which classical music plays a major part. (Remember Helen Traubel's ''Metropolitan Opera Murders''?) But there doesn't seem to have been one set at an international music competition. In THE MUSIC WARS (Beaufort, $15.95), Gordon Pape and Tony Aspler tell the story of a brilliantly talented American violinist at the Tchaikovsky Competition in Moscow.   Many music professionals have been hinting for years that the Tchaikovsky Competition is stacked in favor of the Soviet Union and its satellites. Mr. Pape and Mr. Aspler do more than hint. Their premise is that the Russians will use any means short of actual murder to make things hard for foreign contestants. And Heaven help an American contestant who comes to the attention of the K.G.B.
headline: CRIME

title: Walking After Midnight
author: Maureen McCoy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WALKING AFTER MIDNIGHT By Maureen McCoy. 223 pp. New York: Poseidon Press. $14.95.   THE book takes its title from a Patsy Cline song; the story seems to take a cue from the Albert King blues classic, ''Born Under a Bad Sign,'' notably the part that goes: ''If it wasn't for bad luck, I wouldn't have no luck at all.''
headline: PLUCKY LOTTIE JAY

title: Notes From A Schoolteacher
author: James Herndon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NOTES FROM A SCHOOLTEACHER By James Herndon. 169 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $15.95.   JAMES HERNDON has been in the classroom since 1960. Now he teaches at Spanish Main Junior High School in a suburb near San Francisco. He has written about his trade in a number of books, notably those two splendid and funny works ''The Way It Spozed to Be'' (1965) and ''How to Survive in Your Native Land'' (1977).
headline: WHEN DOUGLAS BROKE THE WATER FOUNTAIN

title: What The Movies Made Me Do
author: Susan Braudy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WHAT THE MOVIES MADE ME DO By Susan Braudy. 233 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.   ONCE upon a time movie stars were larger than life. Their pinup photographs decorated the fuselages of warplanes; their marriages and divorces sold countless magazines; their offscreen appearances drew crowds as surely as spilled food draws ants. Now it's the rare star that one would cross a street for, and Elizabeth Taylor must be accounted the last of the traffic stoppers.
headline: LOVE ON LOCATION

title: Encounters With Qi
author: David Eisenberg with Thomas Lee Wright. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ENCOUNTERS WITH QI Exploring Chinese Medicine. By David Eisenberg with Thomas Lee Wright. Illustrated. 254 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $16.95.   ONCE when he was living in China, David Eisenberg relates, ''a group of schoolchildren gently took hold of my arms and walked me across the street. Having noticed my blue-gray eyes, they assumed I was totally blind and wanted to escort me through the traffic.'' But to judge by ''Encounters With Qi,'' a vivid glimpse of traditional Chinese medicine, Dr. Eisenberg is far from blind.
headline: BEYOND ACUPUNCTURE

title: King Bidgood's In The Bathtub
author: Audrey Wood
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: KING BIDGOOD'S IN THE BATHTUB By Audrey Wood. Illustrated by Don Wood. Unpaged. San Diego: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $12.95. (Ages 4 to 8) AUDREY and Don Wood seem to enjoy their work. In their book ''The Napping House'' and in this latest creation they express an exuberance that is quite infectious. ''King Bidgood's in the Bathtub'' is a short farce about a Renaissance King who one day refuses to leave his bathtub. Members of his royal staff (including the Queen) attempt to persuade him to perform his kingly duties. One by one they fail. As this dilemma builds to a tumultuous and bubbly climax, a clever Page, in a surprise gesture, finds an apt solution.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: American Falls
author: John Calvin Batchelor
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AMERICAN FALLS By John Calvin Batchelor. Illustrated. 570 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $16.95.   COMBINING obscure history and compelling fiction is always a difficult task. Fact and fiction wrestle mightily with one another and, in the ideal match, the result would be an amicable draw. If one overwhelms the other, vividness may be lost in a morass of unlived detail, or accuracy may be sacrificed to vision. In ''American Falls,'' John Calvin Batchelor struggles with epic material, the scheming and espionage that brought the American Civil War to a close. The author of two previous novels, ''The Further Adventures of Halley's Comet'' (1981) and the well-received ''The Birth of the People's Republic of Antarctica'' (1983), he has chosen to write in a heightened, old-fashioned theatrical style, so that the immense amount of historical fact may seem to be the intertitles of silent films. Overheated and yet distanced from anything resembling real human emotion, they presume upon our notions of history as melodrama to draw us into the plot.
headline: PAIRS IN BLUE AND GRAY

title: Reluctant Farewell
author: Andrew Nagorski
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RELUCTANT FAREWELL. By Andrew Nagorski. (New Republic/Holt, $16.95.) Before taking up his Newsweek assignment to Moscow, Andrew Nagorski talked to some of the reigning experts and was surprised, he says, by the dearth of empirical evidence for their theories about the Soviet Union.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Man Descending
author: Guy Vanderhaeghe.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
MAN DESCENDING Selected Stories. By Guy Vanderhaeghe. 230 pp. New York: Ticknor & Fields. Paper, $7.95.

IN the 12 stories of ''Man Descending'' we meet a tough farming widow with a waitress daughter and a sick grandson, a miner with a teen-age family, a Belgian immigrant salesman and some professional people, most of whom are retired or dying or unemployed. Guy Vanderhaeghe is a prizewinning young Canadian writer introduced here to American readers for the first time. He convincingly describes more kinds of people than most writers, and uses a variety of voices. When he writes in the authorial third person and lifts his eyes from his characters to the scenery his prose once or twice becomes pulpy and inflated, but usually it is careful and easy to read. And what the stories have in common, besides their mostly Canadian settings, is a special sort of rage and hatred, the chilled social sort called contempt. Few books have shown it working in so many ways.
headline: VARIETIES OF CONTEMPT

title: Moonshine
author: Alec Wilkinson.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MOONSHINE A Life in Pursuit of White Liquor. By Alec Wilkinson. 153 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.   MOONSHINE liquor is not the mountain nectar that country-music singers have made it out to be. It is usually nasty stuff, and often poisonous. And modern moonshiners, or bootleggers, are seldom the romantic outlaws of the stereotype. Rather, they are traffickers in a grotesque variety of human misery. Their main customers apparently are advanced-stage alcoholics among the rural poor -people who either cannot afford legal liquor or who live from drink to drink in one of those dry districts that still checkerboard much of the nation.
headline: RIDES WITH THE REVENOOER

title: The Tiger
author: Lisa St Aubin de Teran
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE TIGER. By Lisa St Aubin de Teran. (Franklin Watts, $16.95.) The third novel by this prize-winning young British author is her most ambitious and most imaginative. Like her first book, ''Keepers of the House'' (first published in the United States as ''The Long Way Home''), ''The Tiger'' unfolds against the decay and drought of an unforgiving Venezuelan landscape. But whereas ''Keepers'' and its successor, ''The Slow Train to Milan,'' dealt with a young Englishwoman married to a Venezuelan (as the author once was), ''The Tiger'' partakes less of autobiography and more of the mysticism and legend that are popular symbols of South America. Its protagonist, a German family scion born in 1911 and known simply as Lucien, grows up under the tutelage of his grandmother, Misia Schmutter, a despot who rules her Venezuelan estate as if she were a spider who spins a web not so much for killing (although she does this too) but for the fascination of power. She molds Lucien to her will, and after dying becomes a supernatural presence clinging to his back like the predatory tiger the boy once killed. But while her creed seems vaguely fascist, it is transmuted by Lucien's somewhat gentler spirit into a kind of existential obsession with pure action. This is, in fact, a story of obsession: Misia's for order and the will; Lucien's for architecture, gardens and gambling, and those of other characters, whose feelings range from love to bitterness.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Press And The Presidency
author: John Tebbel and Sarah Miles Watts.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PRESS AND THE PRESIDENCY From George Washington to Ronald Reagan. By John Tebbel and Sarah Miles Watts. 583 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $24.95.   ANYONE wanting a reasonably full and accurate chronicle of relations between United States Presidents and the press from 1789 to the present can turn to John Tebbel and Sarah Miles Watts's new book. The weaknesses of ''The Press and the Presidency'' should not make readers ungrateful for its strengths. Mr. Tebbel, a professor emeritus of journalism at New York University, and Mrs. Watts, a professor of journalism at the State University of New York College at Geneseo, have worked very hard. They are good at portraying individuals, an important part of their task. Every reader is likely to discover some new facts and some nuances.
headline: 200 UNEASY YEARS

title: Move Your Shadow
author: Joseph Lelyveld.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
MOVE YOUR SHADOW South Africa, Black and White. By Joseph Lelyveld. 390 pp. New York: Times Books. $18.95.

THIS extraordinary feat of reporting is unlike any other book about South Africa. It provides the kind of authentic evidence of the ordeals of black life that few white South Africans themselves discover. And it is superbly written, presenting characters and dialogue with the vividness of the great Russian novels, with a sense of careful observation that makes it hard to argue with - at least until the final political summing up.
headline: IN APARTHEID'S GRIP

title: India: A Guide For The Quality-Conscious Traveler
author: Louise Nicholson
pull_quote: India: A Guide for the Quality-Conscious Traveler By Louise Nicholson 270 pages. The Atlantic Monthly Press $19.95 Few visitors are neutral about India. They are either captivated by the contrasts in scenery, people and ways of life or repelled by the intense heat that blankets much of the country much of the year or by the crowds and noise in the cities, the dust and dirt, the political vituperation and the pervasive poverty. Some first-time visitors vow never to return, but others eagerly await opportunities to see India again and again and again.
headline: TRAVEL BOOKSHELF

title: Texas
author: James A Michener
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TEXAS By James A. Michener. Maps. 1,096 pp. New York: Random House. $21.95.   WELL, by heaven, you knew it had to happen sooner or later. James Michener, the fellow who writes the biggest books, has tackled the biggest state - Texas. Boy, has he cut a fat hog, as they say down home. Mr. Michener's ''Texas,'' at almost 1,100 pages, contains enough paper to cover several New England counties. The novel is so heavy you could probably leave it on a Lubbock, Tex., coffee table in a tornado and find it there when everything else was still in the air over Kansas City, Kan.   ''Texas'' is not literature in the classical sense, it is ''trotting'' journalism, history in a hurry. Admittedly, the history of the Lone Star State cries out for condensation - for all except true-blue Texans who can't get enough of it - but Mr. Michener has bitten off too much. People of various cultures and colors have been running around down there brawling and killing each other under one pretext or another since at least the 16th century, when our recorded knowledge of what is now known as Texas begins. Texans like to brag that their state has existed under six flags - those of Spain, France, Mexico, the Republic of Texas, the Confederacy and the United States. That's an awful lot of colorful characters to cram into one book, even a book as thick as this one.
headline: FOUR CENTURIES OF TEX ARCANA

title: You Can Fool All Of The People All The Time
author: Art Buchwald. Illustrated by Steve Mendelson.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
''YOU CAN FOOL ALL OF THE PEOPLE ALL THE TIME'' By Art Buchwald. Illustrated by Steve Mendelson. 332 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $16.95. MY aunt Emma called me from Sioux City, Iowa, to ask how Art Buchwald's new book, '' 'You Can Fool All of the People All the Time,' '' was doing in the nation's capital, so I went to a Washington cocktail party to check it out.

''It beats me,'' a man high in the Smithsonian was saying as I joined a group, ''how Buchwald's 26th book can turn out to be as fresh as his first.'' ''How do you mean, 'fresh'?'' I asked. ''Both ways,'' he said. ''Impudent and full of insights pristine as new-peeled eggs.''
headline: ART NOUVEAU

title: Betrayed
author: Nicholas Bethell
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
BETRAYED By Nicholas Bethell. Illustrated. 206 pp. New York: Times Books. $15.95.

IN ''My Silent War,'' Kim Philby gloated over the failure of the covert operations Britain and America mounted between 1949 and 1953 to subvert the Albanian Communist regime. But Mr. Philby, a Soviet spy in the British intelligence service, was indeed silent on the part he played in thwarting those operations. In the past quarter-century, bits and pieces of information about Mr. Philby's role have appeared in various publications, but the complete story of the Albanian operations has never been told, because the British and American secret services are reluctant to reveal the whole truth - or to confirm what Kim Philby told the Russians.
headline: KIM PHILBY AND THE ALBANIAN MISSION

title: The Divorce Revolution
author: Lenore J. Weitzman.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DIVORCE REVOLUTION The Unexpected Social and Economic Consequences for Women and Children in America. By Lenore J. Weitzman. 504 pp. New York: The Free Press. $19.95. ''UNEXPECTED'' is the crucial word in Lenore J. Weitzman's subtitle. It goes along with its mates - ''unintended'' and ''unfortunate'' - to describe the results of the new divorce laws. The laws, which began in 1970 with California's no-fault, no-consent statute and which every state but Illinois and South Dakota have since adopted in some form, were the work of people of good will. These men and women believed they were correcting an outmoded legal code that was degrading and humiliating to all parties involved in the process and often unfair to one party in the outcome. The new laws were intended to reduce accusation and acrimony, to remove marital misconduct (often manufactured) as the necessary grounds for divorce and to base monetary awards on need and ability to pay, rather than treating them as rewards for virtue or punishments for sin.
headline: VICTIMS OF REFORM

title: Honorable Men
author: Louis Auchincloss
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HONORABLE MEN By Louis Auchincloss. 278 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $15.95.   LOUIS AUCHINCLOSS is one of the few remaining heirs to what has been called the ''genteel tradition'' in American fiction, and no one is more aware of his literary predecessors than Mr. Auchincloss himself. His latest novel, ''Honorable Men,'' resonates with echoes of his distinguished ancestors; it even occasionally gives an explicit bow in their direction. Here is a young debutante reviewing a winter of discontent:   ''When I looked back over those months of futile activity, I had only a sense of hundreds of bland young faces, of lips forming inane compliments or feeble jokes, and of laughs, smiles, giggles, an endless bray of pointless jocosity. Where was the heart of fools? Of course, in the House of Mirth!''
headline: OVERBURDENED BY HIS VIRTUE

title: The Tree Of Life
author: Hugh Nissenson
pull_quote: THE TREE OF LIFE. By Hugh Nissenson. 159 pages. Harper & Row. $15.95. AT first, Hugh Nissenson's extraordinary new novel, ''The Tree of Life,'' appears to be a tour de force of realism, as well as a radical departure from the Jewish themes that have preoccupied him in his story collections, ''A Pile of Stones'' and ''In the Reign of Peace,'' and in his previous novel, ''My Own Ground.'' Taking the form of a diary or ''Waste Book'' written by an educated 43-year-old New Englander named Thomas Keene, ''The Tree of Life'' seems to be a documentary collage recreating life in the frontier community of Mansfield, Ohio, from July of 1811 until October of the following year.   Reading here and there at random, one comes across inventories of Keene's possessions, a running tally of his ''ready money,'' and laconic reports of communal events. Billy Stump wins second prize - cotton suspenders - in a ''shoot at the mark'' held in Mansfield's Central Park. ''My brother's to home, sickened of the pukes,'' says 11-year-old Sarah Cooper. ''Fanny, too.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Frank And Maisie. A Memoir With Parents
author: Wilfrid Sheed
pull_quote: FRANK AND MAISIE. A Memoir With Parents. By Wilfrid Sheed. 296 pages.   Illustrated. Simon & Schuster. $17.95. FOR many years Sheed & Ward was the pre-eminent Catholic publishing house in the English-speaking world. But the flesh and blood Sheed and Ward - the Frank and Maisie of their son's memoir - formed a more remarkable partnership still. They were tireless lecturers, doughty street-corner orators, gifted authors: Frank Sheed's theological writings earned him, layman though he was, a doctorate in theology from Rome itself (complete with the right to wear a four-pointed biretta), while Maisie Ward wrote biographies, notably her life of G. K. Chesterton, that are of lasting interest. The two of them were also unique personalities, very different in temperament and background, but bound together, as Wilfrid Sheed says, by ''a Siamese twin of a vocation which neither could have pursued solo.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Pride
author: William Wharton
pull_quote: PRIDE. By William Wharton. 288 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95. ''THERE is all kinds of pride, Dickie,'' says a character midway through William Wharton's new novel. ''There's real pride, like being proud of good work, like when we do a good job building a porch. Then there's false pride like when you think you're better than somebody else for no good reason; that's the sin one. Then there's the lion's pride, his family.'' Those disparate definitions of the word pride - which, not incidentally, happens to be the title of this novel -pretty much summarize what the book's about, and they're also about the only thing that ties its jumpy, hodgepodge narrative together.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Nothing Happens In Carmincross
author: Benedict Kiely
pull_quote: NOTHING HAPPENS IN CARMINCROSS. By Benedict Kiely. 279 pages. David Godine. $16.95. CARMINCROSS, where nothing happens, is a small town in Ulster. Mervyn Kavanagh is a wandering son of Carmincross (Catholic as opposed to Protestant Carmincross) who has been teaching in America, at a women's college in ''the semi-Deep South'' - a well-cushioned exile in ''a never-never land of dogwood and forsythia and chipmunks and young people.'' He has also acquired and then lost an American wife, who has left him and gone to live in New York, with a boyfriend in fitful attendance.   Now, at the outset of Benedict Kiely's new novel, Kavanagh is on his way home to attend the wedding of a favorite niece. When we meet him, he has just enplaned at Kennedy, with 10 brandy alexanders (''or brandies alexander'') inside him, and some whimsical speculations on who exactly Alexander might have been buzzing round in his head. A genial sort, Mervyn: a man in his 50's, ''big and fat and bald and Irish and cheerful.'' It isn't long before he ''nibbles or nipples'' at yet another brandy.

pull_quote: THE SHOPPING MALL HIGH SCHOOL Winners and Losers in the Educational Marketplace. By Arthur G. Powell, Eleanor Farrar and David K. Cohen. 360 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $16.95.   IMAGINE the typical high school as a kind of shopping mall, a place where students pick academic subjects the way a shopper wanders into one store or another and sifts through the merchandise for the best buy. For the student who does not want the English course on Shakespeare's tragedies, for example, there is an elective on sports literature; for the student who must take a year of mathematics but wants to avoid the rigors of algebra or geometry, there is the innocuous ''consumer mathematics.''

title: Advertising The American Dream
author: Roland Marchand. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ADVERTISING THE AMERICAN DREAM Making Way for Modernity, 1920-1940. By Roland Marchand. Illustrated. 448 pp. Berkeley: University of California Press. $27.50; $35 after Dec. 31.   MODERNITY'S town criers,'' Roland Marchand calls the advertising men and women of the 1920's, at the start of this fine social history of American advertising between the two great wars. By and large, they were a white-shoe lot. Having shaken off its earlier image as a lair of snake-oil salesmen, advertising was fast on its way to respectability. It was attracting bright young Ivy Leaguers with a proper suburban passion for golf. Two-thirds of New York copywriters had domestic servants. Women were paid high salaries for copy intended to be read by women but were generally excluded from management jobs in their agencies. Few advertising people were Jewish.

author: Patrick McGinley

pull_quote: FOXPRINTS By Patrick McGinley. 282 pp. New York: A Joan Kahn Book/ St. Martin's Press. $14.95.   THE joke has gone far enough,'' says Charles Keating, the sex-obsessed fugitive hero of Patrick McGinley's curious suburban fable. A puzzled reader sympathizes with Keating's complaint. Mr. McGinley, the talented Donegal novelist whose previous works, like ''The Trick of the Ga Bolga,'' have shown a wonderful eye for Irish landscape, seems less at ease in the Home Counties England he has invented for his shaggy-dog, or rather shaggy-fox, tale.

title: Back In The World
author: Tobias Wolff
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BACK IN THE WORLD By Tobias Wolff. 221 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $15.95.      ONE comes to Tobias Wolff's ''Back in the   World'' with dangerously raised expectations, for his two previous books, ''In the Garden of the North American Martyrs'' (a volume of short stories) and ''The Barracks Thief'' (a single long story), were exceptionally fine works of a fully mature writer. This collection of stories is mostly concerned with the inner lives of middle-class loners in the Sun Belt. They are lapsed materialists in a material world trying to ignite a spiritual flame despite being cut off from all traditional sources of the spirit - family, church, art, even politics. Most of Mr. Wolff's characters are motivated by unenlightened self-interest. They may be yuppies, but they are trapped and manipulated by the system, and that makes them sympathetic. Mr. Wolff views their entrapment as something to be both feared and pitied and their attempts at escape -through fantasy, drugs, exercise, electronic toys and casual sex - as dignified. These microchippers, real-estate speculators, compulsively exercising cocaine addicts and frantic adulterers are victims, not exotic objects of derision, and consequently one reads the stories with an open heart.

title: The Winning Performances
author: Donald K Jr Clifford

pull_quote: THE WINNING PERFORMANCE: How America's High-Growth Midsize Companies Succeed. By Donald K. Clifford Jr. and Richard E. Cavanagh. (Bantam, $19.95.) Clifford Jr. and Richard E. Cavanagh, both management consultants, describe as those with annual revenues of between $25 million and $1 billion.

title: The Story Of The Lost Reflection
author: Paul Coates.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE STORY OF THE LOST REFLECTION The Alienation of the Image in Western and Polish Cinema. By Paul Coates. 167 pp. Verso/Schocken Books. Cloth, $25. Paper, $9.95. DESCRIBING ''The Story of the Lost Reflection'' as a collection of unrelated essays would be misleading - though things do occasionally jell to good effect, the book is more a collection of unrelated paragraphs. Paul Coates displays a wide acquaintance with European culture, and one is pleased to find apposite references to Holderlin and Schiller in a film book. He also knows a lot about movies.   Perhaps his only real problem is that he writes too well and thus is frequently led to substitute style for considered thought. Words are heaped on words in the hope they will add up to something, and then the subject is abruptly changed. Bold assertion and clever paradox replace the homelier tasks of demonstration and argument.
headline: SHORT SUBJECTS

title: Jerusalem
author: F. E. Peters. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: JERUSALEM The Holy City in the Eyes of Chroniclers, Visitors, Pilgrims, and Prophets From the Days of Abraham to the Beginnings of Modern Times. By F. E. Peters. Illustrated. 640 pp. New Jersey: Princeton University Press. $35.   THIS book is in many ways a worthy tribute to a city that very few people can visit, or can ever have visited for hundreds or thousands of years past, without profound excitement and emotional turmoil. ''There is no other city like it,'' says F. E. Peters, ''so solemn yet modest, so attractive and so intelligible; so earthly, even provincial, and yet somehow spiritual and universal.'' But I query ''intelligible.'' Jerusalem is far too complicated to be that - which is why Mr. Peters's ''Jerusalem: The Holy City in the Eyes of Chroniclers, Visitors, Pilgrims, and Prophets From the Days of Abraham to the Beginnings of Modern Times'' is useful. Its author offers huge chunks of quotations from all epochs, which it is good to have because many of them are not readily accessible. Mr. Peters modestly suggests that he may have ''over-explained'' them. But he has not. Indeed his quotations from the Bible are scarcely explained at all, at least from the point of view of the historian; about Abraham, Moses, Solomon, about the responsibility for Jesus' crucifixion, Mr. Peters's critical analysis is sparse.
headline: A PLACE LIKE NO OTHER

title: Naomi
author: Junichiro Tanizaki
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NAOMI By Junichiro Tanizaki. Translated by Anthony H. Chambers. 237 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.   TO readers who know Junichiro Tanizaki (1886-1965) from ''Some Prefer Nettles'' or ''The Makioka Sisters,'' ''Naomi'' may come as a surprise. The familiar Japanese trademarks of shadowy tatami rooms and pale beauties in exquisitely colored kimonos are conspicuously absent. This is the sleazy world of 1920's Tokyo, where the moga (modern girls) and mobo (modern boys) fox-trotted in garish evening dress. Post-World War I cosmopolitanism gave rise to freewheeling ideological exchanges among serious minds, but the lost generation was more an object of fun to the journalists, who gave it the epithet ''ero-guro-nansensu'' (''erotic-grotesque-absurd''). For a time Tanizaki was that generation's laureate.
headline: HUMBERT HUMBERT-SAN

title: Socialism And America
author: Irving Howe
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOCIALISM AND AMERICA By Irving Howe. 225 pp. San Diego: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $17.95.   SOCIALISM is a dream from which many intellectuals would prefer not to awake. One of the exceptions is Irving Howe, who is fully awake and alert to the vast complexities of Socialism and so free of the soothing incantations of Marxist theory that one wonders whether his probing mind will ever find a moment of rest.   For the past two decades in America, the dream of Socialism has been nurtured by Marxism, which has come close to being the dominant ideology in the academic world. With the 1960's generation now ensconced in the university, studies of the working class have become a major scholarly industry for social scientists, while literary critics proceed to expose the delusions of ''bourgeois humanism.'' Today aspiring yuppie students listen patiently as professors lecture on Engels's version of 19th-century working conditions and the horrors of capitalism and the promises of Socialism. But eventually a question must be faced: if Socialism promises the glory and dream of the future, what happened to it in the past? In general, former Old Left writers like Seymour Martin Lipset seemed prepared to let the dream die, while younger scholars believed the subject warranted further study. In ''Socialism and America,'' Irving Howe, the editor of Dissent and author of ''The World of Our Fathers,'' stands between the Old Left and the New.
headline: WHY THE FUTURE NEVER HAPPENED

title: The Stories Of Muriel Spark
author: Muriel Spark
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE STORIES OF MURIEL SPARK By Muriel Spark. 314 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $18.95.   THE writings of Muriel Spark illustrate very clearly the idea, put forward by the Russian Formalists earlier in this century, that the function of art is to defamiliarize or ''make strange'' the world, to overcome the deadening effects of habit on our perceptions. It seems more than coincidental that the central consciousness of Mrs. Spark's best-known novel, ''The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie,'' is called Sandy Stranger (my emphasis), and that as a cloistered nun she writes a book called ''The Transfiguration of the Commonplace.''
headline: MARVELS AND NASTY SURPRISES

title: The Zero-Sum Solution
author: Lester C. Thurow.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE ZERO-SUM SOLUTION Building a World-Class American Economy. By Lester C. Thurow. 416 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.   LESTER C. THUROW, a professor of economics and management at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a sometime adviser to Democratic Presidential candidates, spells out in his latest book his solution to the dilemma he posed in ''The Zero-Sum Society'' (1980). He had argued that the United States was caught in a trap of sluggish growth from which it could not escape without making some politically powerful groups worse off in the short run, to make the nation as a whole better off in the long run.   The term ''zero-sum,'' taken from John von Neumann's and Oskar Morgenstern's theory of games, refers to that class of games, such as football or poker (and some wars), in which the total gains equal the total losses. A negative-sum game, a nuclear war, for example, is one in which everybody loses. A positive-sum game - good trade or a happy marriage - is one in which both sides win.
headline: REVERSING REAGANOMICS

author: Olivier Zunz
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RELIVING THE PAST The Worlds of Social History. Edited by Olivier Zunz. 334 pp. Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press. Cloth, $29. Paper, $9.95. IN 1973, Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie, exhilarated by the accomplishments of social history, proclaimed that ''tomorrow's historian will program computers or will cease to exist.'' It is reassuring to find, on reading ''Reliving the Past: The Worlds of Social History,'' that he was wrong.   True, in 1973, social historians had successfully adopted new methodologies and turned to new areas of research. Historians using quantitative analysis, and others as well, were writing history from the bottom up, often undertaking collective biographies of ordinary people in their research. Today even more scholars call themselves social historians, a swelling of the ranks that is due to the number of historians trained in graduate school in the halcyon days of the late 60's, to the development of a pluralistic vision of society (one that emphasizes the experiences of ordinary people) and to the influence of the social sciences.

title: Delorean
author: John Z. DeLorean with Ted Schwarz. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

By William Haddad. 193 pp. New York: Random House. $17.95.   AT last we get an answer to one of the most mystifying aspects of the John DeLorean story: that business with the cocaine and the undercover agents. Mr. DeLorean was acquitted of criminal charges, yes, but how did a titan of General Motors get so deeply involved in such a deal? In ''DeLorean,'' he tells us it was really the fault of his most trusted adviser: Sonja, a storefront fortuneteller. That's right. Mr. DeLorean claims that at the time his DeLorean Motor Company was heading into receivership, he fell under the spell of a palm reader and adviser.   Mr. DeLorean (who became a born-again Christian after his arrest) now believes Sonja used ''the wiles of the devil'' to cloud his mind: she was ''one of the most astute people with whom I had ever discussed my company,'' he writes. So when his company was going under and undercover narcotics agents offered him ''interim financing'' to rescue it, he plunged ahead on Sonja's advice. ''She had assured me everything would work out in my favor.'' In other words, the devil made him do it.

pull_quote: A SMALL TOWN By Shelby Hearon. 335 pp. New York: Atheneum. $15.95.   CHILDREN in a Chicago suburb were once charmed by a certain game, played with locked hands whose spired forefingers touched, into tireless repetitions of the chant, ''This is the church, this is the steeple; open the doors, and see all the people.'' Because the chant was unchanging, and nobody (no kid) was mocked by it (it wasn't like ''Liar, liar, pants on fire''), its charm had to be found in the reiterated gesture of unfolding, which never failed to work on us, never failed to mean something. We loved it that people - meaning adults - who thought they were hidden could be exposed so simply, through words.

title: The Art Of Biblical Poetry
author: Robert Alter
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE ART OF BIBLICAL POETRY By Robert Alter. 228 pp. New York: Basic Books. $17.95.   A PROFESSOR of poetry at Oxford in the 18th century made original and somewhat eccentric contributions to the study of biblical poetry. His work had an influence on the Prophetic Books of William Blake, and I imagine on the ''Jubilate Agno'' of Christopher Smart, poems written in madness. The professor, Robert Lowth, is remembered today only for these two splendid disciples, his lectures having been delivered in Latin. It is odd how little genuine progress has been made since. The best recent guide, as Robert Alter notices, is T. Carmi's ''Penguin Book of Hebrew Verse,'' with its full introduction and bibliography, and its invaluable note on the systems of Hebrew versification.

title: Watson's Apology
author: Beryl Bainbridge
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WATSON'S APOLOGY By Beryl Bainbridge. 222 pp. New York: McGraw-Hill Book Company. $14.95.   ALL the world loves a murderer. Victorian society, in particular, rationalized its morbid fascination with murderers by drawing uplifting moral lessons from their crimes. As early as 1827, Thomas De Quincey wrote on murder as a fine art, arguing that the murderer's passion was a heroic transcendence of a milquetoast age. Henry James greatly admired ''the dear old human and sociable murders'' chronicled by his contemporary William Roughead, for the light they shed ''on manners and conditions . . . the testimony to manners and morals.'' Jack the Ripper's rampages in the London slums of 1888 were subjected to intense scrutiny for their sociological pertinence, and, indeed, bloody Jack endures as a metaphor for all the evils of the industrial age.

THE WARNING The Coming Great Crash in the Stock Market. By Joseph Granville. 397 pp. New York: Freundlich Books. $18.95.


ON Jan. 6, 1981, Joseph

Granville dispatched an urgent message to his investment newsletter subscribers: ''Sell Everything!'' The next trading day, the Dow-Jones average obediently dropped 23 points. Although the market subsequently endured a series of ups and downs, it failed to crash. Mr. Granville was undeterred. In March 1983, he appeared on Ted Koppel's television news program, ''Nightline,'' and warned any worried viewer to ''flee for your life.'' As he concedes in ''The Warning,'' ''In the 1983-85 markets this writer was proved to be premature in his bearishness.'' Nevertheless, the 184 parallels, each carefully labeled, that he draws between 1929 and 1985 convince him that doom, though momentarily postponed, is certain to arrive sooner than many think.

pull_quote: THE NATURE AND LOGIC OF CAPITALISM By Robert L. Heilbroner. 225 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $15.95.   ROBERT L. HEILBRONER'S ''Worldly Philosophers'' is still by far the best book for students to inspire them with the excitement of that great drama - the history of economic thought. It is written with brilliance and charm, two virtues that may be looked at askance by members of the economics profession who are not noted for them. If ever an oratorio were written on the history of economic thought, Mr. Heilbroner, the Norman Thomas Professor of Economics at the New School for Social Research, would certainly be my nominee to write the libretto.   It was with great anticipation, therefore, that I turned to his new book, ''The Nature and Logic of Capitalism.'' But I regret to report that it did not really live up to its predecessors. Nor is it easy reading, though it does stimulate some hard thinking. Part of the problem is that Mr. Heilbroner might be described, perhaps a little unkindly, as a Unitarian Marxist, seeing in Marxism something of a revelation, but certainly not divine and not even very workable. There is a slight air of an apologia about this work, and some ambiguity about whether it is for capitalism or against it.

pull_quote: Lisa Goldstein's latest novel, THE DREAM YEARS (Bantam, $13.95) plays with the notion that reality is a kind of public dream. The situation that the author sets out in the opening chapters is enormously promising. The place is Paris, the year is 1924, the principal characters include Andre Breton, Louis Aragon and other writers, artists and hangers-on associated with the French Surrealist movement. It is the author's conceit that the Surrealists were not only devastating critics of the false and pretentious in the art of their day but reliable guides to effective political action and, quite literally, to the nature of the universe.   Robert St. Onge, a colleague of Breton's who appears in no history books but whom Lisa Goldstein skillfully brings to life, is briefly transported to a phantasmagoric future Paris where a mysterious woman adjures him to ''remember that your imagination is real.'' Only later does St. Onge find out what the reader immediately recognizes; the future from which this message comes is 1968, the year of the student revolt against the more conservative aspects of French society. The young revolutionaries have learned to open ''the avenues of time'' and they seek the help of the Surrealists, who proclaimed that in order to change the world, you must first change your dreams. But, as Breton later reminds St. Onge, ''dreams are dangerous things.''

title: The Fringes Of Power
author: John Colville
pull_quote: THE FRINGES OF POWER. 10 Downing Street Diaries 1939-55. By John Colville. 796 pages. Illustrated. Norton. $25. SIR JOHN COLVILLE was only 24 when he was seconded from the British Foreign Office to 10 Downing Street in 1939. He was to serve as private secretary to three British Prime Ministers - to Neville Chamberlain from 1939 to 1940; to Winston Churchill for the remainder of World War II, apart from a period of two years (1941-43) when he was a fighter pilot in the R.A.F.; to Clement Attlee for a few weeks after the 1945 election, and to Churchill once again from 1951 to 1955. Before returning to Downing Street for the last time he also served as private secretary to Princess Elizabeth, the present Queen.         At the beginning of the war, though it was strictly against regulations, he decided to keep a diary, of which he has now published a generous selection, complete with lively footnotes and an excellent biographical appendix. While the resulting volume may not contain any momentous revelations, it does round out the existing picture of the period in an urbane, highly readable manner. Its chief value lies in its intimate portrait of Churchill, but it also conveys the  flavor of day-to-day life in his entourage; and while the focus is naturally British, there are many passages that have a strong interest for American readers.
