title: Whole Earth Software Catalog
pull_quote: ONE of the most informative and refreshing books to emerge from the great computer publishing glut of 1984 was the Whole Earth Software Catalog, Version 1.0. The 1986 edition, Version 2.0, is now in the stores ($17.50, paperback, from Quantum Press/ Doubleday). Just as the most successful software programs improve with age, adding new features and refining old ones, so too has this compendium of pithy software reviews and wise computer advice.         Between editions, the computer industry fell into what analysts politely called a shakeout, in which weak companies fainted and strong companies wept. This shakeout has given consumers a much-needed respite from the dizzying pace of the first part of the 1980's. It used to be hard to keep up with the arrival  of new products; now it is hard to keep up with the departure of old companies.
headline: PERIPHERALS;ASSESSING SOFTWARE, VERSION 2.0

title: The Old Gringo
author: Carlos Fuentes
pull_quote: THE OLD GRINGO. By Carlos Fuentes.   Translated by Margaret Sayers Peden and the author. 199 pages. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $14.95. THE old gringo referred to by the title of Carlos Fuentes's latest book happens to be Ambrose Bierce, the American journalist and short-story writer who left for Mexico in 1913 - presumably to join Pancho Villa's revolutionary army - and who mysteriously disappeared. What Mr. Fuentes has done is to imagine Bierce's subsequent life - and death - there in the desolate desert reaches of northern Mexico, and in doing so, he has succeeded in welding history and fiction, the personal and the collective, into a dazzling novel that possesses the weight and resonance of myth.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Holy Days: The World Of A Hasidic Family
author: Lis Harris
pull_quote: HOLY DAYS: The World of a Hasidic Family. By Lis Harris. 266 pages. Summit. $16.95. IT is immediately obvious to the reader what a wonderful subject Lis Harris has found for her first book, ''Holy Days: The World of a Hasidic Family,'' most of which appeared in The New Yorker recently. Her prospects did not look promising at the start. When she first approached the world of Hasidic Jews, not even the traditionally more gregarious Lubavitcher Hasidim of Brooklyn's Crown Heights neighborhood seemed willing to open up to her.   But then, through the grapevine, she found the woman to whom she gives the pseudonym Sheina Konigsberg. Sheina had come to Hasidism from Bloomfield Hills, a suburb of Detroit, via Edgar Cayce and an obsession with reincarnation. Sheina owned a Betamax and drove a blue Cutlass Supreme with its license plates lettered MITZVOT. Sheina may sound outlandish, but we are lucky to have her, because it was the courage of her nonconformity that allowed her to welcome the author into her household and produce the touching book that ''Holy Days'' turns out to be.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Sacred Rage
author: Robin Wright
pull_quote: SACRED RAGE. By Robin Wright. 315 pages. Linden Press/Simon & Schuster. $17.95. EARLY in her volume on the fundamentalist crusade of modern Islam, Robin Wright quotes approvingly from Marvin Zonis, a Middle East expert at the University of Chicago: ''The message from Iran - no matter how bizarre or trivial it sounds on first, second, fourth or thirty-ninth hearing - is in my opinion the single most impressive political ideology which has been proposed in the 20th century since the Bolshevik Revolution.'' If that seems too large a statement at the beginning of the book, it does not seem so by the end, for Miss Wright weaves a skillful, disturbing tapestry of warning from the religious history, doctrine, terrorism, politics and social upheaval that have created and sustained the movement.
headline: Books: Islam Inflamed

title: The Lives Of Lee Miller
author: Antony Penrose
pull_quote: THE LIVES OF LEE MILLER. By Antony Penrose. 216 pages. Illustrated. Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $29.95. IN her heyday, Lee Miller was a legend - the beautiful Vogue model who was also an outstanding photographer, the muse of the Surrealists who went on to cover some of the most dramatic and devastating scenes of World War II as a photojournalist. In her later years, she faded from view, and by the time she died in 1977, she was pretty much a forgotten figure. But recently there have been renewed stirrings of interest in her, and the biographical study that her son has written, accompanied as it is by many examples of her work, now makes it possible for the first time to follow the full course of a remarkable career.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Foreign Land
author: Jonathan Raban
pull_quote: FOREIGN LAND. By Jonathan Raban. 352 pages. Viking. $16.95. George Grey, the hero of Jonathan Raban's new novel, has spent the better part of his life on the road - moving from city to city, country to country, one set of rented rooms to another. He believes that ''the safest way to live was to assume that your marching orders would arrive tomorrow,'' and having lived so many years ''a lodger in other people's houses,'' he's ''picked up the lodger's habit of passing through without leaving tracks. He'd been born in a rectory that belonged to the Church and gone on to Navy quarters and Company apartments; and he left each billet exactly as he'd found it.'' If such a restless life has freed him from responsibilities, however, George has also begun to realize that it's made him a stranger to his family and friends - he has become one of those unannounced, nervous-making guests who drop by in the night and then are gone the following morning. At the age of 60, he decides to leave Bom Porto, the small African nation where he's lived for the last couple years, and return home to England.
headline: PASSING THROUGH

title: They Sleep Without Dreaming
author: Penelope Gilliatt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THEY SLEEP WITHOUT DREAMING. By Penelope Gilliatt. (Dodd, Mead, $14.95.) Not all the characters in this collection are as dotty as the bag lady talking to herself in ''Purse,'' but all of them are eccentric - the kind who recite Latin verses while doing backbends or still use lorgnettes with ivory handles.
headline: IN SHORT:FICTION

title: New World, The. An Epic Poem
author: Frederick Turner.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE NEW WORLD An Epic Poem. By Frederick Turner. 182 pp. New Jersey: Princeton University Press. Cloth, $26. Paper, $9.95.

SCIENCE FICTION is a version of pastoral, more dependent on Theocritus than space travel. Like pastoral, its simplicities are deceptive. The attractive ease with which complex social ideas can be inserted into simple characters has ensnared many authors. In ''The New World,'' Frederick Turner has conceived a grand and grotesque ambition, an epic poem that fuses science fiction with medieval romance, finding in the future the grim corruptions of the present and from those corruptions forging an idyll.

The poem opens four centuries in the future, in the year of the sexcentennial of the United States. The oil and gas reserves, the uranium deposits and the mineral resources have been exhausted. The world has been depopulated by immigration to distant planets and the slaughter of the middle class. The great nation-states of the 20th century have been whirled into the vortex of history, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics collapsing into its ethnic groups, Japan into its company families, Europe into the catchment areas of its soccer teams. In the United States, now called the Uess, the cities have become Riots, lawless matriarchies that feed off the slave labor of the suburbs. Outside are only Mad Counties and Free Counties - the former, fundamentalist theocracies, constantly warring against the latter, Jeffersonian democracies.
headline: IN THE MEDIEVAL FUTURE

title: Eleni
author: Nicholas Gage
pull_quote: The small snapshot could be a tourist's memento. It shows several people sitting around a wooden picnic table in a Greek town. The sun is bright, and the vines and lush Mediterranean vegetation give the sense of an arbor in the garden behind. There are several older Greek women, their hair tied by scarves, peasant-style, their faces weathered and lined, and at least two apparent tourists, a man and a striking young woman with short blond hair.   The man is Nicholas Gage, whose book ''Eleni'' chronicles the torture and murder of his mother in 1948 by Communist guerrillas during the Greek civil war, and his own return to Greece some 30 years later to search for his mother's killers. Some of the village women are his relatives, peasants who still live in the village of Lia where his mother's martyrdom occurred. The blond woman is the actress Kate Nelligan, who joins the town's ranks temporarily to play Eleni, who gave her life so that her children might escape to freedom, in the film version of Mr. Gage's book. The film, in which John Malkovich co-stars as Mr. Gage, opens Friday at Cinema 1.
headline: 'ELENI' ENSHRINES ON FILM A MOTHER'S LEGACY OF LOVE

title: The Off-Season
author: Michael Covino
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE OFF-SEASON. By Michael Covino. (Persea, $14.95.) A collection can go for or against you. On the plus side there is the chance for the work to build, layer by layer, toward a fully realized fictional world.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Working Women
author: Arlene Carmen and Howard Moody.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WORKING WOMEN The Subterranean World of Street Prostitution. By Arlene Carmen and Howard Moody. 208 pp. New York: A Cornelia & Michael Bessie Book/Harper & Row. $16.50.   THIS book challenges the way society handles prostitution - the way it harasses and jails women, leaves their tricks and pimps virtually untouched, burdens police and courts, levies fines that prostitutes pay by working longer hours and makes a mockery of the law.
headline: JUST ANOTHER TRADE?

title: Sea Dangers. The Affair Of The Somers
author: Philip McFarland. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: The Affair of the Somers. By Philip McFarland. Illustrated. 308 pp. New York: Schocken Books. $19.95.    ON the first of December, 1842, aboard a naval ship in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, an 18-year-old midshipman was hanged along with two sailors, the three accused of conspiracy to mutiny. The young man was Philip Spencer, son of John Canfield Spencer, President Tyler's Secretary of War. The ship was the U.S.S. Somers, a brig ironically on a test cruise to improve methods of naval training and discipline. In command was Capt. Alexander Slidell Mackenzie, a naval officer who was also a successful author, a protege of Washington Irving, a friend of Longfellow, a man respected by influential friends in and out of the Navy - and one of the most enigmatic, intriguing and, finally, appalling personalities to emerge from the annals of pre-Civil War America.
headline: SEA DANGERS

title: The Pre-Raphaelite Sisterhood
author: Jan Marsh
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PRE-RAPHAELITE SISTERHOOD By Jan Marsh. Illustrated. 408 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $21.95.      THE women chosen by the   Pre-Raphaelite painters as models for the wide-eyed, wild-haired ''stunners'' who haunt their art were mainly working-class girls and prostitutes. Sitting for these young painter-poets, they were introduced into a bohemian and intellectual world much richer than the shops and streets from which they came. In ''The Pre-Raphaelite Sisterhood,'' Jan Marsh discusses six of these, the wives, lovers and models for the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood. The first she considers, Elizabeth Siddall, was a milliner who became D. G. Rossetti's wife. Before the marriage, she, too, began painting and writing. The eminent Ruskin was her champion, but her tortuous relationship with Rossetti and with laudanum, along with one of those mysterious ailments that haunted Victorian women, led to her suicide.
headline: MODELS FOR THEIR SEX

title: Hollyhocks, Lambs And Other Passions
author: Dee Hardie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HOLLYHOCKS, LAMBS AND OTHER PASSIONS. By Dee Hardie. (Atheneum, $15.95.) Dee Hardie has been chronicling her experiences on Thornhill Farm, in Maryland, in House Beautiful magazine for the last six years. Mrs. Hardie was inspired to write this memoir of life in the country as a legacy for her children and grandchildren.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Memory Of Fire: I. Genesis
author: Eduardo Galeano. Translated by Cedric Belfrage.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MEMORY OF FIRE: I. GENESIS Part One of a Trilogy. By Eduardo Galeano. Translated by Cedric Belfrage. 293 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $17.95.   LONG after Octavio Paz observed that the fragment is the form of our times, we know, with special reference to Latin America, that it is the content too. From its fractured map to its splintering factions and classes to its ruptured history, Latin America suggests identity drawn and quartered.
headline: DRAMAS THAT SCORCH

title: Shadow Dancing In The U.S.A.
author: Michael Ventura
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHADOW DANCING IN THE U.S.A. By Michael Ventura. 232 pp. Los Angeles: Jeremy P. Tarcher/St. Martin's Press. $14.95.    MICHAEL VENTURA should reassure diehards from the 1960's who fear that decade's most dearly held notions have evaporated in a welter of casual consumerism. The pugnaciously hopeful essays in ''Shadow Dancing in the U.S.A.,'' greatly expanded from Mr. Ventura's columns in the L.A. Weekly, display a tenacious belief in the Whitmanesque ideals that were supposed to form the underpinnings of a new community. The subjects range quite far, from posters of winged, fiery phalluses on the walls of Mexican cantinas and the first appearance of rock-and-roll dancing in Brooklyn in the 1950's (the author was born in New York City in 1945), to helping to keep a marriage between two strong-willed people on an even keel. But under all this topic-hopping there surges a rhythm, driving and impatient, of a calypso of contemporary life.
headline: HOT OVER 'THE BIG CHILL'

title: Wallace Stevens: A Mythology Of Self
author: Milton J. Bates. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
WALLACE STEVENS A Mythology of Self. By Milton J. Bates. Illustrated. 319 pp. Berkeley: University of California Press. $24.95.

WHEN asked to name the greatest French poet of the 19th century, Andre Gide replied, ''Victor Hugo - helas!'' Some American readers, if asked to choose their foremost modern poet, might echo Gide's perplexity by answering, ''Wallace Stevens, alas.'' For though Stevens ranks high among the most deserving candidates, he hardly offers Americans the sort of national poet they might like. Affluent, aloof and undemocratic, Stevens so deeply contradicted the available stereotypes of the American poet that for years bewildered critics inaccurately classified him as sui generis, an inexplicable hybrid of two seemingly irreconcilable sides of the American experience - business and poetry. That the two sides of Stevens' life never overlapped, that no trace of his office life ever appeared in his poetry and his literary career was hidden for decades from his fellow workers, only heightened the mystery of how this insurance lawyer with the body of a football player wrote some of the great modernist poetry in English.
headline: THE EMPEROR OF HARTFORD

title: Masters of Atlantis
author: Charles Portis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MASTERS OF ATLANTIS By Charles Portis. 248 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.   CHARLES PORTIS'S fourth novel, ''Masters of Atlantis,'' which chronicles 60 years in the life of a secret society called the Gnomons, should be a rich source of comedy. The last century has seen a proliferation of sects, cults and secret societies of every imaginable sort - the natural, historically documented corollary to a civilization in the throes of disintegration. In this instance the process has been exacerbated by an original factor - the forces responsible for the debacle insist upon calling it progress, obscuring what would otherwise be self-evident.
headline: PLETHO PAPPUS AND THE DOUGHBOY

title: Zone, The. A Prison Camp Guard's Story
author: Sergei Dovlatov. Translated by Anne Frydman.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE ZONE A Prison Camp Guard's Story. By Sergei Dovlatov. Translated by Anne Frydman. 178 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $14.95.

WHEN will Western publishers tire of prison camps and dissidents and give us some other aspect of Soviet life? At least ''The Zone'' is not about us, the inmates or victims, but about them, the guards. Moreover, its guards are not just puppets of the novelist - the account is based on Sergei Dovlatov's experiences as a guard assigned by the army to a maximum-security prison for criminals. In a prefatory note he declares with pride that ''the names, events, and dates given here are all real.''
headline: SOULS IN THE GULAG

title: Conversations With Isaac Bashevis Singer
author: Isaac Bashevis Singer and Richard Burgin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CONVERSATIONS WITH ISAAC BASHEVIS SINGER By Isaac Bashevis Singer and Richard Burgin. 178 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $15.95. IS there a Jewish sensibility? Anyone reading these interviews of Isaac Bashevis Singer by Richard Burgin, a professor of English at Drexel University in Philadelphia, would have to say yes. For Mr. Singer, character is ''the very essence of literature'' and is established through ''the language of deeds,'' while Yiddish is rich in descriptive idioms for character and behavior. He also assumes life is richer than art, and he always begins with real people.   Believing in the soul, sustained by the residues of religious tradition, he knows that the world he writes about - a world in large part vanished - is morally real. He repudiates the nihilistic tendency of modernism and its esthetic ideology, its ''forced originality,'' in favor of ''the originality of events.''
headline: A SKEPTICAL BELIEVER

title: Darlinghissima: Letters To A Friend
author: Natalia Danesi Murray
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DARLINGHISSIMA Letters to a Friend. By Janet Flanner. Edited and with commentary by Natalia Danesi Murray. Illustrated. 507 pp. New York: Random House. $24.95.      TEN years ago this autumn, Janet Flanner, The   New Yorker's Genet, wrote her final ''Letter From Paris.'' Half a century of them, regularly informed, various, passionate, curious, cosmopolitan, stately. I wish I could claim to have read all her published letters that came my way; I'm sure I'd have been the wiser for reading them. Like many Americans, I'm star-struck by the glamour (bogus or authentic) of Paris, but Flanner's appetite (bless it) for matters French - politics, painting, music, flora, food, architecture, the nation a to zed - could wear a reader down.

author: Martin H Greenberg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

(Ages 3 to 5) In this handsome adaptation of an African variation on ''the sky is falling,'' foolish rabbit, dozing under an apple tree, wakes to a crash and becomes convinced that the earth is breaking up.

author: Sheila Solomon Klass

pull_quote: THE BENNINGTON STITCH By Sheila Solomon Klass. 133 pp. New York: Charles Scribner's Sons. $12.95. (Ages 12 and up) AMELIA BLOOMER HAMILTON, known as Amy, may be the world's worst test-taker, and her SAT scores are too low to get her into a good college. This doesn't particularly upset Amy because she doesn't really want to go to college yet. She would rather take some time off after high school to figure out what to do with her life. Opposition comes from her mother, who has her heart set on Amy's attending Bennington College, the school she once hoped to attend.

author: Ronald M Clark
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WORKS OF MAN. By Ronald W. Clark. (Viking, $24.95; $29.95 after Dec. 31.) At a time lost in the mists of antiquity, someone looked at the two stone posts on either side of the doorway and wondered if and how the two might support a horizontal crosspiece.

title: Political Crisis/Fiscal Crisis
author: Martin Shefter.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: POLITICAL CRISIS/FISCAL CRISIS The Collapse and Revival of New York City. By Martin Shefter. 270 pp. New York: Basic Books. $21.95. TEN years ago, in an informal meeting at Gracie Mansion, several journalists confronted Mayor Abraham Beame with evidence of what was fast becoming an open secret - that New York City was teetering on the brink of bankruptcy. Mr. Beame, who rarely betrayed emotion, fidgeted in his seat and sipped a scotch-on-the-rocks as he listened politely but stone-faced. Then, in exasperation, he delivered a warmed-over lecture about how New York was unique, and why, in spite of the proliferating warning signs, it couldn't happen here.   In retrospect, it is arguable whether Mr. Beame was putting on his best face that night to keep dire predictions from becoming self-fulfilling or whether he genuinely believed that New York was immune to bankruptcy and that threats by the banks to cut off the city's credit were merely a ploy to increase and protect their profits. In any case, it was generally overlooked during the early stages of New York's fiscal crisis that not only could it happen here, but, in fact, it had happened before. And more than once.
headline: DARWIN AND GRACIE MANSION

title: The Magnificent Spinster
author: May Sarton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MAGNIFICENT SPINSTER By May Sarton. 384 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $16.95.   MAY SARTON has for decades been writing about the inner lives of thoughtful women. In an almost frightening number of novels, journals and volumes of poetry (over 40 at last count), she has indefatigably kept up what amounts to a lifelong investigation of women in work and in love.
headline: INVENTING WOMEN

title: The Mare On The Hill
author: Thomas Locker
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MARE ON THE HILL Written and illustrated by Thomas Locker. Unpaged. New York: Dial Books. $15. (All Ages) THOMAS LOCKER'S first book for children, ''Where the River Begins,'' was the story of a grandfather and his two grandsons who follow the river that flows past their house, hike up the foothills of a mountain and come at last to a small, still pond where the river originates. The story was a simple one, told in a straightforward, unelaborate fashion, but one that would strike a chord for any reader, child or adult, who ever tossed a leaf in a gutter and then waited for it to come out the other end of a drainpipe. It conveyed, wonderfully, the suspense a person can feel at the bend of a river (or the turn of a page), waiting to see what's on the other side.   The pictures were oil paintings rather than illustrations - deep, richly textured landscapes that might almost have emerged from the Hudson River School. The book established Mr. Locker nearly instantly as an important figure in the world of children's books. His new book, ''The Mare on the Hill,'' is also a beauty. We are back at the same big yellow house where Grandpa and the two boys live, at the edge of the same wide river, next to the same steep cliff. But this time, instead of journeying, we stay close to home.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: The American Occupation Of Japan
author: Michael Schaller.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE AMERICAN OCCUPATION OF JAPAN The Origins of the Cold War in Asia. By Michael Schaller. 351 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $22.50.   AS Michael Schaller recounts, two months before the end of the Pacific war, Asia specialists from the State Department sent a long report to the War Department full of foreboding about the future of the Far East. Japan, the report predicted, would be reduced to a smoldering ruin and would have to be garrisoned indefinitely by American troops. China, far from being President Roosevelt's cherished ''policeman of Asia,'' would fall victim to civil war and possible Soviet intervention. A wave of nationalism would sweep Southeast Asia and make it difficult or impossible for the European powers to reimpose colonial rule. Finally, a ''rising force'' of Soviet ideology throughout the Far East would threaten to close the entire region to Western influence.
headline: HWO HISTORY SURPRISED US

title: The Old Gringo
author: Carlos Fuentes
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE OLD GRINGO By Carlos Fuentes. Translated by Margaret Sayers Peden and the author. 199 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $14.95.   TEN years ago, Octavio Paz told an interviewer there was not one Carlos Fuentes, but two, the European voice and the Mexican voice. Since then, more have emerged. Carlos Fuentes has been the palimpsest of Mexican history and culture separated into its discrete layers: Indian, Spanish, French, revolutionary, aristocratic, leftist, centrist, expatriate. In this analyzed presentation of the person, this soul shown after the centrifuge, Mr. Fuentes demonstrates the complexity of the Mexican character and the artistic difficulties peculiar to the novelist born in the Navel of the Universe, which is where the Aztecs placed Mexico.   For the North American reader to appreciate the levels and enjoy the discoveries of the sensual and mind-pleasing new novel by Mr. Fuentes, it may be helpful to provide the context to a tale that is, on casual reading, an imagined conclusion to the life of Ambrose Bierce, the San Francisco writer of sentimental stories and misanthropic newspaper columns who disappeared in Mexico in 1914.
headline: TO WRITE, TO FIGHT, TO DIE

title: The Vampire Lestat
author: Anne Rice
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE VAMPIRE LESTAT By Anne Rice. 481 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.

THE vampires whose hungers Anne Rice chronicles are not the conventional undead; they are the truly alive. Her first novel, the wonderful ''Interview with the Vampire,'' is narrated by a tormented Victorian esthete named Louis who is scourged and glorified by his heightened vampire perceptions. Louis and his kind thirst to know the mystery of their origins as insatiably as they thirst for blood; they brood over the death of God and the unenlightenment of the average vampire. Crucifixes and garlic do not trouble them, but changing times are their bane; weary of endless adjustments to new centuries, they fall at last into suicidal inertia. Anne Rice brings a fresh and powerful imagination to the staples of vampire lore; she makes well-worn coffins and crucifixes tell new tales that compose a chillingly original myth.
headline: NO. 2 WITH A SILVER BULLET

title: A Mother's Work
author: Deborah Fallows
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A MOTHER'S WORK By Deborah Fallows. 243 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $16.95. I WON'T keep you in suspense: According to ''A Mother's Work,'' a mother's work is to stay home and raise her children. And if we are to believe Deborah Fallows's study of the world that working mothers have bought their children with their labors, the 50 percent of American mothers who think they can both work and raise happy kids are fooling themselves and harming their children.
headline: DAY CARE VS. BEING THERE

title: Shared Destiny
author: Abbott Gleason
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHARED DESTINY Fifty Years of Soviet-American Relations. Edited by Mark Garrison and Abbott Gleason. 167 pp. Boston: Beacon Press. $16.95.   BEFORE their summit meeting next month, the Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, and President Reagan could do worse than to read ''Shared Destiny: Fifty Years of Soviet-American Relations.'' This slim collection of essays, edited by Mark Garrison and Abbott Gleason, comes as a shaft of light - and no wonder, considering the caliber of the contributors.
headline: MAKING THE BEST OF IT

title: The Tree Of Life
author: Hugh Nissenson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE TREE OF LIFE By Hugh Nissenson. Illustrated. 159 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $15.95.   WHY are diaries so dear to us? The ones on the shelf nearest where I write are almost daily company to me: ''A Treasury of the World's Great Diaries,'' with its tidbits from Pepys and Stendhal and the clipper-ship captain Joshua Sears; magisterial volumes of Virginia Woolf; the indelible childhood epics achieved by Helena Morley of Brazil and Anne Frank of the Holocaust; the vivid jottings from the Oregon Trail and other westward journeys compiled by modern scholars such as John D. Unruh Jr. and Lillian Schlissel.
headline: A SETTLER'S OHIO, DAY BY DAY

title: Fletch Won
author: Gergory Mcdonald
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: When Gregory Mcdonald's ''Fletch'' appeared 11 years ago, it all but started a minor industry. The book sold like iced clams at the seashore; it sparked a movie and, of course, many Fletch follow-ups. Most of them were issued in paperback. But now comes FLETCH WON in hard-cover (Warner, $14.95).   Why the success of this series? For one thing, it appealed to the younger generation. Fletch -Irwin Maurice Fletcher - was young, smart, irreverent, honest and very mod, a symbol for his peers. His normal - and also formal - dress consisted of sneakers (through which poked a toe or two), blue jeans and a T-shirt. In some respects he was of the 60's generation, though not a part of the drug scene. He refused to kowtow to authority. Sham, pretension and hypocrisy were to be attacked. As a young newspaper reporter, Fletch immediately saw through things his more complacent or cynical colleagues shrugged their shoulders at. He marched to his own drummer, very much a rebel.
headline: CRIME

title: Sacred Rage: The Crusade Of Modern Islam
author: Robin Wright. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SACRED RAGE The Crusade of Modern Islam. By Robin Wright. Illustrated. 315 pp. New York: Linden Press/Simon & Schuster. $17.95.   THIS reporter's notebook of Moslem violence since the 1979 Iranian revolution is gripping.   The 1983-84 bombings of the United States Embassy and Marine headquarters in Beirut, Lebanon, are conveyed with the immediacy of the flash bulletins and banner headlines that announce such now-familiar terrorist actions as the recent hijacking of the Italian cruise ship. Robin Wright, who has been a correspondent for The Sunday Times of London and The Washington Post, traces the nurturing of Islamic fundamentalism under the Ayatollah Khomeini in Iran and its rise and spread throughout the Moslem world.
headline: ON THE TRACK OF THE MILITANT MULLAHS

title: Nothing Happens In Carmincross
author: Benedict Kiely
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NOTHING HAPPENS IN CARMINCROSS By Benedict Kiely. 279 pp. Boston: David R. Godine. $16.95.   THE main character in Benedict Kiely's new novel is a man named Mervyn Kavanagh, and when he is asked by a publisher to write a coffeetable history of Ireland, he thinks: ''I'll do it and welcome: anything to oblige and the money's good. I'll send them my plan here and now. Begin with the latest atrocity.''   He conceives of the dust jacket of the book depicting a man rushing madly out of a freshly bombed building, arms wide, on fire from head to toe, a flaming cross on the run. Doctorow's marvelous new novel, ''World's Fair,'' you shake your head in disbelief and ask yourself how he has managed to do it. ANY novel that opens with a man named Vito McMullen putting on a skull cap and sitting down to Passover dinner already has a claim on my affections. And since this is only the first of many incongruities in ''Family Business,'' one has to admire Vincent Patrick's restraint in not going for the easy laugh. Consider the temptations he puts in his own way. The novel presents the American family as an ethnic smorgasbord: the paterfamilias Jessie McMullen is half-Irish, half-Cherokee, his son Vito is half-Italian and his grandson Adam is half-Jewish. Living in New York with their wives or girlfriends, they carry what Vito ruefully calls a ''criminal gene.'' Because the gene is somewhat recessive in Vito, who is in the wholesale meat business, he's chary of Adam and Jessie's scheme to steal a plant cell from a California laboratory and sell it to a competitive genetic engineering company.

Alan Lelchuk's fisrt novel, ''American Mischief'' (1973), was a sprawling, energetic, sexual and intellectual Jewish carnival centered on a dean struggling against a student radical. His third novel, ''Shrinking'' (1978), was again a big, sexy case study of the hazards of Jewish writer's life in America. title: Foreign Land
author: Jonathan Raban
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FOREIGN LAND By Jonathan Raban. 352 pp. New York; Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $16.95.   Since its beginnings, the novel has had friendly relations with travel writing. Novels are often about traveling, and many novelists - from Defoe and Fielding through Dickens, Twain, James, and D. H. Lawrence, to Graham Greene, V. S. Naipaul, Paul Theroux and Bruce Chatwin - have also written travel books, to keep their gifts for seeing, hearing and self-displacement in shape and to find new material and some ready cash. In his first novel, the British writer Jonathan Raban applies the powers exhibited in his fine travel books, ''Arabia: A Journey Through the Labyrinth'' (1979) and ''Old Glory'' (1981), to the purposes of fiction, with impressive success.   To write a travel book you must of course leave (or escape from) home, but the book will secretly be about coming back. Even if, Like D. H. Lawrence, the writer never really returns, the writings do. Like personal letters, they may be enjoyed by outsiders, but to hear their full resonance once must know, or imagine, how they would sound back where the writer left from. The thoughtful traveler's question ''Who am I now and here?'' bears upon another one of equal difficulty: ''Who was I then and there?''

PAUL RAND: A DESIGNER'S ART By Paul Rand. Illustrated. 239 pp. New Haven. Yale University Press. $39.95.

IN our built environment and our civilization of manufactured objects, every product, every printed page, every urban corner has been designed, sometimes badly, sometimes well. Yet we have few opportunities to reflect on the ways designers work and to celebrate their accomplishments. Our painters, sculptors and architects are household names, but few people, apart from the members of the design community, are aware of the identities and the qualities of the principal shapers of the forms with which we are surrounded. Fewer still have an understanding of the thought processes or the intellectual preoccupations of the major designers of our time.

title: A Violent Life
author: Pier Paolo Pasolini
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A VIOLENT LIFE By Pier Paolo Pasolini. Translated by William Weaver. 320 pp. New York: Carcanet. Cloth, $18.50. Paper, $17.50.   IT begins as a guided tour of hell. Tommaso, the protagonist of ''A Violent Life,'' grows up in a stinking shantytown on the outskirts of Rome shortly after World War II. Half-starved children play in sand littered with human excrement beside a river foully polluted, their everyday speech a litany of curses, taunts and threats. As a young man Tommaso becomes a thief, a bully and a sometime hustler, a homosexual prostitute. He and his vicious companions rob at random, sometimes beating their victims, their goal being to get no more than a few thousand lire with which to buy food, drink or the company of a woman. They are without talent, ambition or hope. Even when Tommaso courts a respectable young woman, he seethes with resentment and hatred as he makes his crude advances in the darness of a cheap movie house - the same hatred he feels for the ''queens'' or ''faggots'' he tries to hustle, or for his companions who remain unimpressed with him no matter what he does. He is in fact a pathetically ordinary young man who elicits little or no interest from anyone save his mother and his lackluster girlfriend, and the indifference he endures is emphasized by the author almost as much as the hunger and poverty he suffers all of his life.

In the long encounter between Indians and Europeans on the American frontier, perhaps no figure is more alien to modern sensibilities than the missionary. Journeying sometimes hundreds of miles beyond the colonial settlements, the missionaries appeared at the edge of Indian villages and proclaimed the gospel of Christianity. To imagine what this must hve ben like for the Indians, one almost has to conjure up visions of space trvelers descending from flying saucers to announce that they bring a new sacred text and wish to share with us their God. One suspect that Indians accustomed to inhabiting a magical world filled with many gods and spiritual teachers handled such an event with more equanimity than we might, but they must have feld a strange mixture of fear, suspicion and exhilaration nonetheless.

Most actors are best observed in their fictional skins, and stories of their lives tend to be mere travelogues of living and loving arrangements between roles. ''A Remarkable Woman,'' Anne Edwards's biography of Katharine Hepburn, is a more substantial study, explaining the elements that originally formed Miss Hepburn's character: her admiration for her outspoken mother; her adoration of her father; and an insular childhood. The last, combined with disinterest in her peers, developed into perverseness on sage and an aversion to ensemble acting. At the age of 24, she was cast in ''The Animal Kingdom'' - and promptly fired for what her co-star Leslie Howard called ''outrageous posturings'' and ''insufferable bossiness.'' This was not unusual for the aspiring actess, and it was only with her first Hollywood triumph in ''A Bill of Divorcement'' (1932) that her talent and beauty were recongnized.

title: The City Of Joy
author: Dominique Lapierre
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CITY OF JOY By Dominique Lapierre Translated by Kathryn Spink. 464 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $17.95.   AN Indian proverb says that if a bag of Calcutta dust is put under the bed of a virtuous man or woman, he or she will become corrupt. But there are some, not a few, but millions, who must be exempt becuase they have no bed; they sleep on a plank laid on bricks or over a gutter, if they are lucky, or on the pavement or any space they can find. These are the refugees from Bangladesh, Bihar, Assam or the refugees from their own countryside, who flock into the city, adding themselves to its already swarming poor.   Calcutta was built for exploitation, but for farily benevolent exploitation, not virulent as it is now. ''If it was possible to steal the air we breathe, there'd be people in Calcutta prepared to do it,'' one character says, quoting Ram Chander. He is a wise and generous rickshaw puller, one of the innumerable lesser characters of ''The City of Joy,'' Dominique Lapierre's new book in the nonfiction historical genre he and Larry Collis, used in such popular successes as ''Is Paris Burning?'' about the liberation of Paris and ''Freedom at Midnight,'' about the partition of India.

Finding himself attracted to a director both 13 years older and sonsiderably more successful than he, Gabe, a frustrated Boston playwright making ends meet as a waiter, finds a way to this somewhat formidable woman's heart through her stomach. Cynthia Kagan has had her doubts about this klutzy, unpromising-looking 30-year-old (Gabe admits he has a ''soft belly that hangs over my shorts like the cap of a mushroom''). But harassed and exhausted while lecturing and giving interviews in Copenhagen, she finally gives in to Gabe when he conjures up a smorrebrod (a Danish hors d'oeuvre) of ''lobster meat crisscrossed with curls of red onion, and...halibut with peaks fo tartar sauce and diced black radish.''

WHEN I began covering Geraldin Ferraro's campaign for The New York Times in September 1984, her champagne days were behind her. She was in a bad mood and she had a cold. Her husband, John Zaccaro, was with her on the plane, looking miserable. Her approval ratings were sinking and the investigations into her family's background and finances were mounting.   ''She's like Cinderella with ashes in her mouth,'' another reporter said. The phrase stuck in my mind. Miss Ferraro's biggest asset as she danced off on her blind date with history had been ''the goose-bump factor,'' as the columnist Ellen Goodman called it. The Congress-woman from Queens had embodied the Cinderella myth, the American dream and the feminine mystique.

title: The Mystery Of Hermann Goering's Suicide
author: Ben E Swearingen
pull_quote: THE MYSTERY OF HERMANN GOERING'S SUICIDE. By Ben E. Swearingen. 253 pages. Illustrated. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $19.95.   AS Ben E. Swearingen reminds us in his intriguing piece of historical detective work, Hermann Goring's suicide was not just a bizarre and incidental footnote to history. title: Political Murder. From Tyrannicide To Terrorism
author: Franklin L Ford
pull_quote: POLITICAL MURDER. From Tyrannicide to Terrorism. By Franklin L. Ford. 440 pages. Illustrated. Harvard. $29.50.    ''POLITICAL murder'' can mean many different things - to a pacifist, war itself is a form of political murder - and in choosing the phrase for the title of his new book, Franklin L. Ford has taken advantage of its flexibility. He is primarily concerned with assassinations, as the word is commonly understood, and with tyrannicide, the slaying of an unjust or illegitimate ruler, in particular. But where appropriate he also feels free to discuss judicial murder and those forms of terrorism - bombings, hijackings and the like - that claim their victims more or less at random.

title: What's Bred In The Bone
author: Robertson Davies
pull_quote: WHAT'S BRED IN THE BONE. By Robertson Davies. 436 pages. Viking. $17.95. THE moderns, says a character in Robertson Davies's new novel, ''are painting the inner vision, and working very hard at it when they are honest, which by no means all of them are. But they depend only on themselves, unaided by religion or myth, and of course what most of them find within themselves is revelation only to themselves.'' Mr. Davies, by contrast, adheres to rather a more old-fashioned approach to art: drawing upon both Jungian myth and religious allegory, he has created a rich oeuvre of densely plotted, highly symbolic novels that not only function as superbly funny entertainments but that also give the reader, in his character's words, a deeper kind of pleasure - delight, awe, religious intimations, ''a fine sense of the past, and of the boundless depth and variety of life.''   In his latest - and perhaps most accomplished - novel to date, Mr. Davies relates the tale of one Francis Cornish, a wealthy Canadian provincial, who grows up to become a painter and one of the world's foremost patrons of art. Mr. Davies, of course, has rarely settled for telling a story straight-on - ''Fifth Business'' took the form of a super-long letter of grievance; ''The Manticore'' explored the personality of its hero through his experiences in psychoanalysis - and this book is no exception.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Piaf
author: Margaret Crosland
pull_quote: PIAF. By Margaret Crosland. 240 pages.   Illustrated. Putnam. $16.95. ON a house in a working-class district of Paris, there is a plaque - it was unveiled by Maurice Chevalier - stating that Edith Piaf was born on the steps outside ''in utter destitution.'' Piaf's birth certificate makes it clear that she was, in fact, born in a hospital. On the apartment building in a more fashionable quarter of the city where the singer lived during her final years, there is a plaque stating that she died there. That was what the radio announcements said at the time, and where else but in Paris could such a quintessential Parisian have breathed her last? But, in fact, she died in a village in Provence.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Collected Stories
author: Tennessee Williams
pull_quote: COLLECTED STORIES. By Tennessee Williams. 574 pages. New Directions. $19.95. ''For love I make characters in plays,'' wrote Tennessee Williams, in the preface to this volume. ''To the world I give suspicion and resentment, mostly. I am not cold. I am never deliberately cruel. But after my morning's work, I have little to give but indifference to people. I try to excuse myself with the pretense that my work justifies this lack of caring much for almost everything else. Sometimes I crack through the emotional block. I touch, I embrace, I hold tight to a necessary companion. But the breakthrough is not long lasting. Morning returns, and only work matters again.''   Afflicted by a ''morbid shyness,'' a fear of desiring or loving anything or anyone too much for fear of losing them, Williams tried, throughout his life, to break out of his ''solitary confinement'' by writing - by transforming his fears, his anger, his longings and his guilt into words, and the words into characters who might in turn transform the singular into the plural, the personal into the universal. He wrote every morning of his adult life - even when reeling from drugs and alcohol and loss - and he left behind an astonishing body of work, including the 49 stories collected in this volume.
headline: CONFLICTS OF THE HEART

title: Common Courtesy
author: Judith Martin.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: COMMON COURTESY In Which Miss Manners Solves the Problem That Baffled Mr. Jefferson. By Judith Martin. 70 pp. New York: Atheneum. $10.95.   TEN or 15 years ago, ''etiquette'' was a curse word. It meant all the phony things that untrustworthy people over 30, usually your relatives, wanted you to say and do. It was false, snobbish, finicky; it suggested a neurotic fixation on fish forks and placement and people who related to empty social roles and not as Real Warm Human Beings.   How completely the social climate has changed! Once my students at Cornell wanted to be married at dawn in a flowery meadow, with ''Hey Jude'' playing and the ceremony performed by a bearded minister in love beads. Now they send out engraved invitations and hold receptions at the yacht club. Etiquette, reborn as ''good manners,'' has swept the country, with Judith Martin, the self-designated Miss Manners, behind the broom - if it is possible to imagine someone of her wit and elegance wielding anything so drably proletarian.
headline: DOES POLITENESS LEAD TO VIRTUE

title: More Tales Of Amanda Pig
author: Jean Van Leeuwen
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MORE TALES OF AMANDA PIG By Jean Van Leeuwen. Illustrated by Ann Schweninger. 56 pp. New York: Dial. $8.95. (Ages 4 to 8) I LIKE Amanda Pig and her big brother Oliver. I like their mother and their father too. In a world - the world, that is, of the Read-It-Yourself books - peopled, or creatured, by rather too many wimps, goody-goods and falsehearted cutie-pies, with cipher parents who exist silently in the background representing order at its most coldblooded, the Pigs are an encouraging bunch. They are pleasingly compact in shape, as low to the ground as Bruegel peasants. They all have extremely cheerful ears which manage to be earthbound yet suggest potential holidayish flight. The younger Pigs are occasionally perfectly dreadful to each other. But remember, they are siblings, and one of the great values of these books is their ability to dramatize the ridiculous and trivial and sickeningly frequent fights that siblings engage in every day of their lives, and yet suggest the siblings' essential fondness for each other, their dependency, their mutual good will.
headline: PIG TALES

title: A World Of Secrets
author: Walter Laqueur.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A WORLD OF SECRETS The Uses and Limits of Intelligence. By Walter Laqueur. 404 pp. New York: Basic Books. $21.95.   IN recent months, there have been some dramatic revelations from the underground world of espionage. In New Mexico, a former C.I.A. officer vanished, presumably en route to Russia; in Rome, meanwhile, a senior K.G.B. officer suddenly defected to the C.I.A.; in Berlin, the head of West German counterintelligence crossed over to East Germany; in London, British intelligence announced that a K.G.B. agent there had been their double agent for more than a decade; and in Moscow, the K.G.B. reported the arrest of a C.I.A. mole. Even assuming the worst about betrayals, what is the net effect of this spy war on statecraft? Do nations get the answers they need from intelligence in order to conduct a rational foreign policy? And what are the limits - and costs - of such intelligence?
headline: HOW SPIES AVERT WARS

Ludwig Bemelmans, in his series of books devoted to Madeline and her 11 schoolmates and their mutual governess, Miss Clavel, did more for establishing Paris as an exotic, marvelous, romantic place than an army of minions working diligently for the French National Tourist Office.

author: Anita Brookner

pull_quote: FAMILY AND FRIENDS By Anita Brookner. 187 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $13.95.   A SHARP-WITTED spinster who loves the wrong man and lives on the memory ever after - the predictable Anita Brookner heroine resembles a Victorian maiden who has stepped into the present; she is plucky, but befuddled by the new rules of the sexual game. In four previous novels -notably ''Hotel du Lac,'' winner of last year's Booker Prize, and ''Look at Me,'' a drama of emotional string-pulling - we encounter women whose independence is a mask for stoicism, whose stoicism muffles an impulse to wail ''Poor, lonely me.'' So it is a relief that in ''Family and Friends'' the author has sent her characters back to the past, where most Anita Brookner people might feel more comfortable.
headline: SNAPSHOTS OF LOST INNOCENCE

title: Holy Days
author: Lis Harris.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HOLY DAYS The World of a Hasidic Family. By Lis Harris. 266 pp. New York: Summit Books. $16.95.   EARLY in her book about an ultra-Orthodox Jewish family, Lis Harris asks her Hasidic host, a man she calls Moshe Konigsberg, if he can recommend any books that will help her understand his world of observance, worship and devotion. ''There are no books,'' the Hasid says firmly, adding -quite accurately - that all attempts to portray Hasidic life have fallen far short of the mark.   Well, Mr. Konigsberg might be happy to know there is now such a book. It is called ''Holy Days,'' and it is Miss Harris's beautiful portrait of the world of Moshe and Sheina Konigsberg, a couple deeply committed to the way of life of the Lubavitcher sect of Hasidim in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn. To be sure, Mr. Konigsberg, who finds truth only in the Torah and Hasidic texts, might quibble with parts of Miss Harris's work. But to the secular reader, ''Holy Days'' is a treasure. With precision and elegance, Miss Harris, a staff writer for The New Yorker, tells the story of the center of Hasidic life - the family - and all the individuals and institutions that revolve around it - the synagogue, the rebbe, the ritual bath, the wigmaker, the schools, indeed, the entire Hasidic world.
headline: FOR TORAH, COMMUNITY AND REBBE

title: Once There Was A Tree
author: Natalia Romanova

(Ages 5 and up) SOVIET children's book illustration has lately enjoyed a degree of international recognition unsurpassed except during the heady Constructivist 1920's. In recent years Soviet artists have won the two most coveted honors open to illustrators worldwide, the Bratislava Biennale's Grand Prix and the Hans Christian Andersen Medal (sometimes called the ''Little Nobel Prize''). Gennady Spirin, a painter now in his mid-30's, is among the Russians to have brought home a Bratislava ''Golden Apple,'' or second prize. Yet scant news or evidence of his or his colleagues' accomplishments has so far reached the United States. The appearance here of ''Once There Was a Tree'' - first published in Moscow in 1983 and subsequently in West German and Greek editions - is therefore an event of considerable interest.

(All Ages) THERE is a sweetness of soul that illuminates Maurice Sendak's most frightening works, and that quality permeates his father Philip Sendak's posthumously published ''In Grandpa's House.'' Much of the book is a dreamlike set of legends - located in a Polish-Jewish shtetl - that Philip Sendak told his children when they were young. Then, when Philip was a lonely widower of 75, his son insisted that he commit them to paper. In that respect, the book is an inspiring act of filial love.   ''In Grandpa's House'' is really two stories. The first eight pages, which describe Philip Sendak's boyhood in Europe and life in America, will appeal to children and adults because they sound like the unembellished reminiscences of a very kind grandfather. The rest of the book is the story of a little boy named David whose beloved grandfather has died, whose parents have disappeared and who is guided through a series of scary, oddly comforting adventures by a magic bird that his grandfather has secretly sent. David's story is somewhat disjointed. But in its emotional flavor, it is very much like Mickey's story in ''In the Night Kitchen'' and Max's in ''Where the Wild Things Are.''
headline: WHERE THE WILD THINGS CAME FROM

author: Timothy Findley

NOT WANTED ON THE VOYAGE By Timothy Findley. 352 pp. New York: Delacorte Press. $17.95.

TIMOTHY FINDLEY'S new novel, ''Not Wanted on the Voyage,'' retells the story of the Flood in a way that is as appealing as those creatures invented by the author who never make the boat. The traditional two-by-two scenario, with the chosen captain welcoming all aboard, is just that - a simple base for a complex and highly imaginative tale. It is ''Tobacco Road,'' ''Monty Python,'' ''Mutiny on the Bounty,'' Disney animation and ''Charlotte's Webb,'' combining the Bible story with 20th-century dialogue and humor, evolution and fairy tales yet accurately depicting human nature and emotions. Mr. Findley, a Canadian who has written several well-received novels, offers us a cast of characters rich and imaginative enough to persuade the reader to suspend his disbelief.

ALMOST immediately after the 1968 election, politicians, journalists and academics, all conditioned by eight years of Democratic control of the White House, began asking if Richard Nixon's victory had been a fluke. Richard Reeves asks the same question about our current President and answers with the title of his book, ''The Reagan Detour.'' To Mr. Reeves, among the most perceptive and accessible of political analysts, the liberal consensus that guided the development of America's welfare state continues intact. President Reagan has been unable ''to change very much about America,'' the author says. Mr. Reeves's argument is supported by polls showing that Mr. Reagan was re-elected because people voted their pocketbooks rather than their ideology.

(Ages 8 to 12) THERE is something very moving about ''The Miracle Child'' in this year of great hunger in Ethiopia. It is the story of Tekla Haymanot, one of Ethiopia's great saints, who was popularly known as the saint who prayed on one leg, after his other had withered away. In fact he was one of the most able patriarchs of the Ethiopian Church and largely responsible for its 13th-century literary and monastic efflorescence. (Christianity came to Ethiopia in the fourth century, and the church there developed its own rich hagiographic tradition.) After Tekla's death, the monks at Debra Libanos, the monastery he founded, wrote down the stories they heard about him and illustrated them with brightly colored illuminations. His story incorporates themes from the Bible and saints' legends, but has its own distinct flavor.

FRANK AND MAISIE A Memoir with Parents. By Wilfrid Sheed. Illustrated. 296 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95.

FILIAL piety is hardly a conspicuous virtue these days, when hostile or disappointed offspring seem eager to give us the lowdown on Mommy Dearest or to reveal, with appropriate ruefulness, the hideous truth about Dad's sexual predilections. ''Frank and Maisie,'' Wilfrid Sheed's memoir of his ebullient Australian father and his downright and unconventional English mother, is redolent of this old-fashioned virtue; when not positively brimming over with affection, the book is saturated with respect - at once awed and humorous - for this doughty marital team, who, as the leading Roman Catholic publishers of their day, helped alter the countenance of the Catholic Church in the United States. Such piety is attractive, though it necessarily imposes certain limitations on the memoir's scope as biography or history.

author: Frank MacShane. Illustrated.

HAS any other modern American novelist received the barrage of bravos and brickbats accorded James Jones? Unlikely. His first novel, ''From Here to Eternity'' (1951), was universally cheered. The New York Times Book Review called it ''A major contribution to literature.'' His second, ''Some Came Running'' (1958), was called ''befuddled'' by Edmund Fuller and ''a monstrosity'' by Granville Hicks. And so it was throughout his writing career. It is just eight years since Jones's death, too early to predict accurately his place in American literature; but it seems safe to say that on the strength of his war trilogy, he will be seen as one of the significant writers of his generation.

title: God Save This Honorable Court
author: Laurence H Tribe
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GOD SAVE THIS HONORABLE COURT: How the Choice of Supreme Court Justices Shapes Our History. By Laurence H. Tribe. (Random House, $17.95.) Laurence H. Tribe, Harvard Law School's distinguished constitutional scholar, mentions William Howard Taft more than Ronald Reagan in this short study of the United States Supreme Court. Indeed, there are only seven references to President Reagan in the entire text. Even so, ''The Senate Save This Honorable Court From Ronald Reagan'' might have been a more appropriate and more candid title. Today's Supreme Court, Mr. Tribe notes in his prologue, is the first ever to have a majority of members over the age of 76. Mr. Tribe never comes out and says it, but his point is clear: President Reagan may remake the Court. Mr. Tribe does not talk explicitly about the President's judicial philosophy or the shape of a possible Reagan court. Instead, he combs the history of the High Court for a set of interesting but unstartling propositions that seem disconcertingly applicable to the situation at hand. A single Justice, he notes, can affect the Court profoundly. The narrow literal interpretation of the Constitution prized by conservatives is largely a myth. Most Supreme Court Justices, even Earl Warren, turn out to be pretty much what their benefactors wanted. Selecting Justices on the basis of a single issue - say, abortion or school prayer - is unacceptable. And, perhaps most important, the Senate has both a long tradition and constitutionally mandated duty to scrutinize all High Court nominees closely.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Use Of Pleasure
author: Michel Foucault. Translated by Robert Hurley.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE USE OF PLEASURE The History of Sexuality, Volume Two. By Michel Foucault. Translated by Robert Hurley. 293 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $17.95.

WHEN a serious and courageous thinker has died an untimely death, it is difficult to report that his last work is not only disappointing, but also a retreat from the principles that defined his career. It is more difficult still when, as in the present case, the work deals with the thinker's deepest personal and political concerns, and when the reviewer shares his belief in the importance of those concerns. With sadness, then, it must be said that ''The Use of Pleasure,'' the second of four volumes in Michel Foucault's ''History of Sexuality,'' is both mediocre and a departure from views about the inseparability of ideas from social institutions that have been his most valuable legacy to modern philosophy.

(Ages 5 and up) ONCE upon a time, when the world was young, the daily life of ordinary people was infused with spiritual meaning.   The gods walked invisibly among us, their presence acknowledged in ceremonies great and small. In this wise and beautiful book, Madhur Jaffrey invites us into the world of her Indian childhood, where that sense of immanence and ritual survives, where a child learns the way he is to live his life and face his death in the same way that he learns to walk or talk: by the loving encouragement of his family, and by significant play, much of it inspired by the myths, fairy tales, legends and fables passed down for generations within the family.

title: World's Fair
author: E. L. Doctorow.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WORLD'S FAIR By E. L. Doctorow. 288 pp. New York: Random House. $17.95.   WORLD'S FAIR'' by E. L. Doctorow is a peculiar hybrid of novel and memoir. Its hero, like Mr. Doctorow, is named Edgar, and grows up in the Bronx in the 1930's; his parents, like Mr. Doctorow's parents, are named Rose and Dave; his brother, like the author's brother, Donald. The family's last name is Altschuler. One is reminded of Renata Adler's novel ''Pitch Dark,'' in which the heroine, Kate Ennis, must choose a name similar to, yet slightly different from, her own, and decides on Alder; in both these works, the naming strategy seems to be a kind of tipoff, a way of telling the reader that the book at hand will unapologetically combine fiction and memory.

title: The Hard Knocker's Luck
author: William Murray
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE HARD KNOCKER'S LUCK By William Murray. 265 pp. New York: Viking. $14.95.   WILLIAM MURRAY'S skill - he is a staff writer for The New Yorker and the author of several novels and works of nonfiction -raises interesting questions about the place of such an entertainment as ''The Hard Knocker's Luck.'' Many readers look continually for the work of genius or at least of brilliance, deep compassion and understanding. Unless a reader is easily satisfied, he seems not to discover such novels very often after reaching the age of, say, 20. So we find ourselves disappointed, when perhaps it would be wiser to enjoy sane balance, quirky invention, shrewd observation, a touch of wit; in other words, we should be satisfied with competent professional skill while we wait for the occasional new masterpiece to shamble along.

title: The Story Of Mrs Lovewright And Purrless Her Cat
author: Lore Segal
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE STORY OF MRS. LOVEWRIGHT AND PURRLESS HER CAT By Lore Segal. Illustrated by Paul O. Zelinsky. Unpaged. New York: Alfred A Knopf. $12.95. (Ages 5 to 9) MRS. LOVEWRIGHT, in this brief, enchanting, alarming and funny-profound children's book by Lore Segal fails to extract coziness from her cat, hopefully christened Purrly, but presently, more appropriately, renamed Purrless. The story, illustrated by Paul O. Zelinsky, is likely to please both children and adults. Children prefer the vulgarity and energy of reality; the adults (who hand over the money and so usually win) like to have created, on the page, a discreet and beautiful world for the children to inhabit. Mr. Zelinsky manages both, with verve and skill, and I tell you it's delightful - if alarming.   In the course of a few pages the dreadful Purrless rips the puzzled Mrs. Lovewright's leg, bites her nose, blacks her eye and pushes her out of bed, all in his determination not to settle down, not to be cozy, not to be loved. She finally wins through to an uneasy truce: Purrless will never sit on her lap, never give her the satisfaction of hearing him purr, though she suspects him of doing it when she's not around. Well, I've known quite a few cats like that in my time - and quite a few husbands too, for that matter.

pull_quote: THE COLOR OF THE AIR Scenes From the Life of an American Jew, Volume One. By John Sanford. 301 pp. Santa Barbara, Calif.: Black Sparrow Press. Cloth, $20. Paper, $12.50. TOWARD the end of this packed and vivid memoir of his years from 1904 to 1927 - set forth in 171 numbered, titled and dated scenes - the author quotes a remark that was to transform his life and wake his psyche, like a fairy-tale princess, from a 12-year sleep: ''I'm writing a book, Nat Weinstein had said, and ever since, through the course of more than a year, the words had been in suspension near the surface of your mind.'' The year was 1926, and the mind was that of the 22-year-old John Sanford, who prefers in this narrative, despite a strong ego and distinctive opinions, to call himself ''you.'' The book Weinstein announced was published five years later as ''The Dream Life of Balso Snell.'' By then its author was known as Nathanael West.   Mr. Sanford and West had known each other as children playing in the streets of a still largely white Harlem. When they became close friends a decade later, Mr. Sanford was dazzled by West's wild imagination, his casual references to Beerbohm, Modigliani and Apollonius of Tyana.

JUDAISM, as a religion of law, is faced with many difficult questions. What is the relationship between the moral life as envisaged, say, by Aristotle or Kant and the life of a Jew loyal to God's law? title: All What Jazz
author: Philip Larkin.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ALL WHAT JAZZ A Record Diary 1961-1971. By Philip Larkin. 316 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. Cloth, $19.95. Paper, $9.95. PHILIP LARKIN once wrote a poem to Sidney Bechet that perfectly captures the response of a young English provincial to great jazz. Attending a concert, he is overwhelmed by the classic soprano saxophonist; both awestruck and liberated, the poet can only cry, ''An enormous Yes!'' ''All What Jazz'' records his search for the same enormous Yes! in the years since then. The search led to dissatisfaction during the English traditional jazz revival of the 1950's, then to increasing dismay as he heard the main lines of jazz's evolution, bop to hard bop to free jazz. Meanwhile, he became a novelist and poet - in fact, he has been a leading contender for poet laureate - and in 1961 he began hacking out monthly jazz record reviews for London's Daily Telegraph, a gig he held until 1971.

author: Helen Hooven Santmyer

title: The Year It Rained
author: Crescent Dragonwagon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE YEAR IT RAINED By Crescent Dragonwagon. 224 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $12.95. (Ages 12 and up) IN a way it's too bad that this particular novel is being reviewed on this particular page where it will go largely unnoticed by the older audience that should know about it. It would be ideal to read at age 17, but also at 30, and again at 45 when one's own children are circling 17 - it faces so unflinchingly the anguished and so often unsuccessful attempts to get past all the precious but heavy baggage of love between mother and child and on into some kind of mutual understanding that can set both free.   Seventeen-year-old Elizabeth and her mother -''the mother everyone wants'' - are the principal characters in an account, told by Elizabeth in first person and in chunks of flashback, of a year when everything comes apart for both of them. Elizabeth has tried three times in a confused and unfocused way to commit sui-cide, which has put her in and out of a variety of hospitals with attention from a variety of psychiatrists. Her parents, long antagonists, have separated and will soon divorce. Elizabeth takes the reader through, among and around these situations, looking hard at every person and every detail from a bittersweet present perspective of comparative calm - calm brought about by successful treatment with vitamins of what has finally been diagnosed as biochemically based schizophrenia.

title: The People Could Fly
author: Virginia Hamilton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PEOPLE COULD FLY American Black Folktales. Told by Virginia Hamilton. Illustrated by Leo and Diane Dillon. 178 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $12.95. (Ages 8 to 12) THOUGH best known for his dialect poetry, Paul Laurence Dunbar, who was born in 1872, wrote prose as well. In his novels and short stories he employed such a lofty writing style that one has to read between the lines to discern his harsh social criticism. At the University of Iowa, I once heard a critic translate Dunbar's prose so that his students could follow it. Late 19th-century Jim Crow society, when the cocked pistol and the lynch rope were ever present, was not conducive to the candor that we've come to expect from modern Afro-American writers.   Still earlier, slaves had to resort to allegory to release their anger toward the people who kept them in bondage, to impart moral values to their young and to entertain themselves.
headline: ALLEGORIES WITH ALLIGATORS

title: Junk On The Hill
author: Jeremy Pikser
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Here are two first novels, and let's start with THE COYOTE CRIED TWICE by Austin Bay (Arbor House, $14.95). It is the story of a drifter, a young man who was a helicopter pilot in Vietnam. Thumbing his way through Texas, he takes a ranch job to tide him over. Strange things happen in the desert at night - auto headlights where there should be none, low-flying planes on mysterious missions. Then murder. The man who gave him the job and now is his best friend is bushwhacked and killed. The drifter is promptly fired. But he has to find out what happened and is almost murdered doing so.   There may be nothing unusual about the ingredients of ''The Coyote Cried Twice,'' but there can be no denying the deftness with which the story is told. Mr. Bay displays unusual competence. His writing moves alertly along, with a minimum of padding. His characters are mostly men in a man's world, though a tough woman - his boss, who owns the ranch - is portrayed as having as much personality as the men. The drifter is no angel, but he is basically honest (even considering what he does in the last five pages) and is the kind of man you would want next to you in a dirty fight. There is no moral to the book, no ethics or weighty issues. It is a story meant to entertain, and entertain it does.

title: Foxybaby

pull_quote: FOXYBABY. By Elizabeth Jolley. 261 pages. Viking. $14.95. How, wonders the heroine of ''Foxybaby,'' has she got herself in such a ridiculous predicament? Here she is, Miss Alma Porch, novelist and lecturer, stuck in some Godforsaken little town in the middle of nowhere in Australia, trying to teach drama to a bunch of unhappy women, who are more intent on shedding a couple of pounds than thinking about art. Can she really use them as a sounding board for her latest work of fiction? Can she inspire them to create something vaguely artistic themselves? Can she find, here, a respite from her own boring life at home? Or failing all that, can she simply get through the semester without going mad?   Using this ludicrous situation as a springboard, Elizabeth Jolley gets her third novel off to a fine, bouncy start. ''Foxybaby,'' the reader eagerly thinks, may turn out to be a funny satire on academia like Kingsley Amis's ''Lucky Jim,'' or maybe a strange, black-humored account of a faraway sojourn, along the lines, say, of Evelyn Waugh's ''Ordeal of Gilbert Pinfold.''

title: More Letters Of Oscar Wilde
author: Rupert Hart-Davis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MORE LETTERS OF OSCAR WILDE Edited by Rupert Hart-Davis. 215 pp. New York: The Vanguard Press. $14.95. LORD ALFRED DOUGLAS By H. Montgomery Hyde. Illustrated. 366 pp. New York: Dodd, Mead & Company. $19.95.   IF there ever was a writer whose life is inseparable from his work that person is Oscar Wilde. Indeed it is not implausible to suggest that Wilde's writing (with the notable exception of ''The Importance of Being Earnest'' and a number of essays) constitutes the less important part of his life. This idea was recognized during Wilde's own lifetime; it was recognized by Wilde himself; and it became persuasively clear in 1962 when Rupert Hart-Davis published his monumental edition of ''The Letters of Oscar Wilde'' - now regrettably out of print, although many of the best letters can be read in his Oxford paperback ''Selected Letters of Oscar Wilde,'' which remains available.   Now Sir Rupert Hart-Davis has edited ''More Letters of Oscar Wilde,'' a slim collection of 164 newly discovered letters by Wilde, plus 10 full letters that appeared earlier only in abbreviated form, along with letters to and about Wilde and additional material of relevant interest. The book is thus a kind of supplement to the out-of-print ''Letters.''
headline: HE RESISTED EVERYTHING EXCEPT TEMPTATION

title: The Revenge Of The Philistines
author: Hilton Kramer.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE REVENGE OF THE PHILISTINES Art and Culture, 1972-1984. By Hilton Kramer. 445 pp. New York: The Free Press. $25.   HILTON KRAMER is a percipient, sophisticated and highly intelligent observer of the contemporary art scene. Readers of this paper, where he was chief art critic for some years, do not have to be reminded that as a day-to-day critic he is second to none. In this volume alone the essays on artists as varied as Frank Stella, Grant Wood, Edward Hopper, Max Ernst and Helen Frankenthaler, as well as some scattered paragraphs about the museum today or the nature of the retrospective, impose upon the genre new standards of precision and adequacy to the material. His best essays, like the art he admires most, are packed with content.   Of course Mr. Kramer has his limitations. He has a blind spot for wit in painting - and, for that matter, for wit generally, except as the handmaid of polemic; and when he starts to write about topics outside art, such as politics, his vision switches, like a defective television, into black and white. But these shortcomings should not, I believe, unduly disturb us. A more ecumenical critic might very well have less to tell us, and Mr. Kramer is not politically more insensitive than, say, Baudelaire or Ruskin.
headline: MODERNISM: SMOTHERED BY ITS FRIENDS

title: The Nuclear Age
author: Tim O'Brien
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE NUCLEAR AGE By Tim O'Brien. 312 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.   WHAT subjects! The probable end of the world, survival, madness. Whose madness? One-person madness or world-madness. Fear. When Tim O'Brien's new novel, ''The Nuclear Age,'' begins, the year is 1995 and a man is digging a deep hole in his backyard. Why? Because the world hasn't changed too much and neither has he. The world is still accumulating its thousands of nuclear death heads. And he, although he now owns the blonde wife and clever child any American male assumes is his due, is still the boy we meet in flashbacks. About 40 years earlier, William Cowling was a child suffering such extreme clear-sightedness that he was unable to put on the soft cloth of faith threaded with reason and common sense with which most children begin to dress their terror as soon as they hear the bad news we grown-ups have to tell them.

title: Prehistory Of Flight
author: Clive Hart
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: In these days of the Concorde and the space shuttle, it is astonishing to realize that, as Clive Hart's PREHISTORY OF FLIGHT (University of California, $35) reminds us, until a century ago ''by far the most voluminous notes on the theory of bird flight were made by Leonardo da Vinci.'' Mr. Hart, who teaches literature at the University of Essex in England, elegantly and lucidly explores thinking about flight and flying machines from preclassical times to the 18th century. ''The Prehistory of Flight'' is not, he tells us, a general survey of aviation - his ''Dream of Flight'' (1972) was about practical attempts at flying, and he promises a later book about the iconography of flight. Instead, this beautifully illustrated volume explores what sages through the centuries have thought about flying and how they have applied scientific principles to the problem of human flight. He tells us, for example, that some commentators, believing human flight to be inevitable, urged that all flying machines be owned or regulated by the state. Others predicted disaster and felt that if people could fly, no one would be safe from marauding aeronauts. Mr. Hart also examines several heavier-than-air inventions, including Burattini's flying dragon (whose landings, the 17th-century Italian engineer promised, would cause ''only the most minor injuries''), Swedenborg's flying saucer and Pierre Desforges's airborne gondola (which, unlike many others discussed here, was actually tested, in 1772; the pilot, the Abbe Desforges himself, escaped with only a bruised elbow).

Ford is forced to be selective, naturally, but his selections range from the halls of Montezuma to the shores of Tripoli and beyond, sparing us neither the dark and bloody shenanigans of Old Testament folk nor those of the Red Brigades. outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE AMERICAN CATHOLIC EXPERIENCE A History from Colonial Times to the Present. By Jay P. Dolan. 504 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $19.95.   FOR more than 100 years after 19th-century immigration changed Roman Catholicism from one of the smallest to the largest Christian denomination in the United States, members of the church made only modest contributions to the general intellectual life of the nation. Familiarity with poverty led most educated Catholics, and especially those in the secular world, to seek training in practical affairs. Life on the cultural margin of a hostile Protestant society led the others, and especially those in the clergy, to devote their minds to building institutional and apologetic bulwarks from which to defend their faith.   The expansion of economic and educational opportunity after World War II and the turning outward that followed the Second Vatican Council have dramatically improved Catholic intellectual life. Old allegations and fears that the Roman faith is incompatible with intellectual achievement are now belied by the evidence. Catholic scholars have emerged in all disciplines, and some of them have begun to examine their religious heritage with a proud but critical eye. They, as well as the general audience of readers inside and outside the church, will welcome the publication of ''The American Catholic Experience'' by Jay P. Dolan of Notre Dame University.
