Englewood Cliffs, N.J.: Prentice-Hall. $12.95. (Ages 7 and up) WINTER MAGIC By Eveline Hasler. Illustrated by Michele Lemieux. Unpaged. New York: William Morrow & Company. $11.75. (Ages 4 to 8) ANY parent who's discovered a groggy 2-year-old, the same child who might quite casually have witnessed the preparation of a lobster dinner, now screaming and literally climbing the walls to get away from a cribful of giant, writhing arthropods, knows that you don't read just any old book to your children before they go to sleep. What to read, when and what for, has been a bone of contention for decades, ever since psychologists began to suspect that books like the 19th-century ''Struwwelpeter'' (''Slovenly Peter''), in which children are graphically punished in both words and picture for various misdemeanors (such as sucking a thumb or refusing to eat supper) by having their thumbs cut off or eyes pecked out, are a form of child abuse. So what's a parent to do when we read to our children or tell them bedtime stories? Are we supposed to soothe, educate, moralize, or stupefy?
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: By The Open Sea
author: August Strindberg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BY THE OPEN SEA. By August Strindberg. Translated by Mary Sandbach. (University of Georgia, $15.95.) This odd novel, written in 1889 and 1890, when Strindberg had already produced some of his best-known plays, veers erratically from wooden, pedagogical prose to luminous descriptions of nature.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Illywhacker
author: Peter Carey
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ILLYWHACKER By Peter Carey. 600 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $18.95.   ARE we to read these 600 pages of sprawling invention as an allegory of modern Australia?   Yes, and then again, no. Peter Carey's previous novel, ''Bliss,'' was an engagingly unappetizing story of rank passions and seedy hopes in an unnamed place suspiciously like Brisbane, only clammier and even more of a remote outpost of American colonialism if that's possible. Written with enormous verve and malice and only halfheartedly prepared to toy with the notion of salvation through goodness, ''Bliss'' left one wondering what its author might achieve with less distaste and more ambition.
headline: DIRTY VERY OLD MAN

title: Along With Youth: Hemingway, The Early Years
author: Peter Griffin. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LONG WITH YOUTH Hemingway, the Early Years. By Peter Griffin. Illustrated. 258 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $17.95. HEMINGWAY A Biography. By Jeffrey Meyers. Illustrated. 644 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $27.50.
headline: COMING OF AGE, GOING TO PIECES

title: The Social Brain
author: Michael S. Gazzaniga. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SOCIAL BRAIN Discovering the Networks of the Mind. By Michael S. Gazzaniga. Illustrated. 219 pp. New York: Basic Books. $17.95.   DURING the last 25 years several dozen people with severe and otherwise untreatable forms of epilepsy have been subjected to a bold operation that - roughly speaking - splits the brain in two. The effects of this operation have in a few cases been so strange and perplexing that they now serve as irresistible showcase phenomena for those speculating on the mind and consciousness. Does the operation turn a single person into two people inhabiting one body? Is the ''person'' of the usually silent (right) hemisphere conscious? The facts, in their most unvarnished form, are complex and extraordinarily hard to interpret with any confidence, but few if any who have studied such ''split-brain'' patients would deny that one mind-boggling thing or another must be going on in them.
headline: MUSIC OF THE HEMISPHERE

title: Double Exposure
author: Joy Gould Boyum.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DOUBLE EXPOSURE Fiction Into Film. By Joy Gould Boyum. 287 pp. New York: A Plume Book/ New American Library. Paper, $10.95. MOVIES have long had a voracious appetite for narrative, stocking up on plays, novels, short stories, newspaper stories, biographies, fairy tales, poems, paintings, operas, popular songs, sex manuals. Film's free and easy interaction with other art forms is the subject of much theoretical writing, because theorists feel they can readily identify film's distinctive qualities by specifying how it differs from the other arts.   In ''Double Exposure'' Joy Gould Boyum, who reviews films for Glamour and is a professor of English and communications arts at New York University, explores movies adapted from major literary works and meticulously examines a wide range of theoretical texts on the problems of adaptation. She chooses to depart from earlier writings, however, with a curious theoretical position of her own. She writes, ''Far from being literature's antagonist, film is in a very real sense a form of literature itself.''
headline: ART IN THE DARK

title: The Therapy Of Avram Blok
author: Simon Louvish
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE THERAPY OF AVRAM BLOK By Simon Louvish. Illustrated. 328 pp. New York: Stein & Day. $16.95.   ACCORDING to the old joke, the difference between a schlemiel and a schlemazel is this: when a schlemiel makes a souffle, he puts the souffle in the oven, walks out of the kitchen and slams the door; when a schlemazel makes a souffle, he puts the souffle in the oven, and someone else walks out of the kitchen and slams the door. In ''The Therapy of Avram Blok,'' Simon Louvish has written the story of a schlemazel.
headline: PUNCH LINES FROM THE RUBBLE

title: Gardens
author: Holly Prado
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GARDENS. By Holly Prado. (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, $14.95.) Mother Kate is in the attic, painting. Daughter Sheila is in her bedroom, writing.

title: Doing Business
author: Olivia Vlahos
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DOING BUSINESS: The Anthropology of Striving, Thriving, and Beating Out the Competition. By Olivia Vlahos. (Franklin Watts, $18.95.) Pop history and a gung-ho appraisal of business today are sloppily thrown together in this book, which sets out to demonstrate how unfairly businessmen have been treated throughout the ages.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Brave New Workplace
critic: Herbert Mitgang Brave New Workplace. By Robert Howard. 224 Pages. Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $16.95
pull_quote: A SPATE (or, rather, glut) of books has come out about management and corporate life whose common message seems to be: How to overpower your rivals by guile. Reading as if they were stamped out by the same M.B.A. cookie-cutter, they offer advice about everything from dressing for success to applying military tactics in the company board room and marketplace. Their canny, commercial authors suggest that the product is less important than the hustle or hustler behind it, that the customer no longer comes first. On the highest levels, the new version of old-fashioned free competition now goes: Arbitrage thy neighbor.   By contrast, there is some cold comfort in a book that raises questions about life in the corporate Utopias. Robert Howard, a young scholar from Amherst and Cambridge who writes for several of the American opinion magazines, throws a monkey wrench into the winning-is-everything philosophy in ''Brave New Workplace.'' Looking at several of America's technological giants -among them A.T.& T., Eastern Airlines, Hewlett-Packard - he finds that their computerized operations cause human and, ultimately, corporate problems. Alluring on the surface, major companies have vestiges of what John Brooks, who chronicled the fate of the Edsel, has described as built-in self-destruct mechanisms. As for some of the new electronic wonders in California, Mr. Howard indicates that Silicon Valley resembles ''Death Valley Days.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Beyond Belief
critic: John Gross Beyond Belief: the American Press and the Coming of the Holocaust 1933-1945. By Deborah E. Lipstadt. 370 Pages. the Free Press. $19.95
pull_quote: DEBORAH E. LIPSTADT'S ''Beyond Belief'' is a valuable addition to recent studies of the Western response to the Holocaust. Inevitably it overlaps to some extent with a book like David S. Wyman's comprehensive account of American reactions during World War II, ''The Abandonment of the Jews''; inevitably, limiting itself as it does to the way Nazi enormities were covered by the press, it is more narrowly based. But that doesn't diminish its importance. It deals at one remove with deeds as well as words - the press may not make policy, but in a free society it certainly makes things easier or harder for those who do.   In the first half of the book Professor Lipstadt, who teaches at the University of California at Los Angeles, describes the darkening course of events from 1933 to 1939. The main landmarks are grimly familiar ones - the Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht, the Anschluss - but her account of what newsmen made of them at the time contains a good deal of rewarding new material. She has some particularly pertinent things to say about the difficulties put in the way of correspondents based in Germany by the Nazi authorities, and sometimes by their editors or proprietors as well.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Wine-Dark Sea
author: Leonardo Sciascia
pull_quote: THE WINE-DARK SEA. By Leonardo Sciascia. Translated from the Italian by Avril Bardoni. 142 pages. New York: Carcanet. $14.95. AS novelist and essayist, Leonardo Sciascia is the most authentic voice writing in Sicily today. He remains in Palermo, avoiding the literary mainstream in Milan and Rome, spinning stories that unfold so naturally they seem derived from folk tales. Some are; they can begin with a great-grandfather who ran through the streets of Palermo with Garibaldi's Thousand, and suddenly turn into a story on Mafia vengeance. The better-known Italo Calvino, who died two months ago at the height of his powers, also drew strength from old tales for his fabulist novels.
headline: Books: Darkest Sicily

title: Some American Men
author: Gloria Emerson
pull_quote: SOME AMERICAN MEN. By Gloria Emerson. 315 pages. Simon & Schuster. $17.95.      ''T   HIS is a book,'' Gloria Emerson writes in the prologue to this volume, ''suggesting why some men of different generations and class behave as they do, how they defend themselves and have made their own trails, what they fear and what they believe is required of them.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Amusing Ourselves To Death
author: Neil Postman
critic: Walter Goodman Amusing Ourselves To Death: Public Discourse In the Age of Show Business. By Neil Postman. 184 Pages. Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $15.95
pull_quote: TO call Neil Postman a critic of television would be as inadequate as calling Bishop Tutu a critic of apartheid or Jerry Falwell a critic of abortion. In Mr. Postman's view, the much-criticized medium is a peril to our society, our culture, our civilization. The theme of his 16th book, ''Amusing Ourselves to Death,'' is that television is bringing us speedily to the condition of the residents of Aldous Huxley's ''Brave New World,'' who were seduced into happy mindlessness. He writes: ''When a population becomes distracted by trivia, when cultural life is redefined as a perpetual round of entertainments, when serious public conversation becomes a form of baby-talk, when, in short, a people become an audience and their public business a vaudeville act, then a nation finds itself at risk; culture-death is a clear possibility.''   Mr. Postman, a professor of communications arts and sciences at New York University, emphasizes that what troubles him is not the widely lamented profusion of ''junk'' on television (''The best things on television are its junk, and no one and nothing is seriously threatened by it''), but the medium itself. This offspring of the union of the telegraph and the photograph, he maintains, is destroying the ''serious and rational public conversation'' that was sustained for centuries by the printing press. He warns in the tones of Jeremiah that the ''Age of Exposition'' is being displaced by the ''Age of Show Business.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: But First A School
author: Jennifer Dunning
critic: Nancy Goldner But First A School. the First Fifty Years of the School of American Ballet. By Jennifer Dunning. 242 Pages. Illustrated. Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $20
pull_quote: THERE is history, and there are anecdotes. ''But First a School,'' an account of the School of American Ballet since its founding in 1933 by George Balanchine and Lincoln Kirstein, takes the anecdotal route. In many ways this approach befits the subject splendidly. One would be hard put to find under any other roof the galaxy of colorful characters who work at the school. The book is replete with quotes from Russian emigre teachers who never had to learn good English; shrewdly, Jennifer Dunning, a dance critic and reporter for The New York Times, doesn't clean it up. She also has good informers. The dancer Jacques d'Amboise gets at the heart of the pre-Revolutionary style that students absorbed, and still do, from their teachers. Reminiscing about Pierre Vladimiroff, he says: ''He epitomized the Petipa school, the pre-Soviet manners, that are gone now. With the Soviets, everything is big. Up. For Vladimiroff, princes didn't look up.''
headline: Books: Dance Masters

title: Lyrics. 1962-1985
author: Bob Dylan
pull_quote: LYRICS. 1962-1985. By Bob Dylan. 524 pages. Illustrated by the author. Alfred A. Knopf. $21.95. ''You don't necessarily have to write to be a poet,'' Bob Dylan declared once. ''Some people work in gas stations and they're poets. I don't call myself a poet because I don't like the word. I'm a trapeze artist.'' Like so many of the gnomic, contradictory pronouncements he would make over the years, that statement attests to a decidedly equivocal attitude on Mr. Dylan's part - in this case, toward literature and the whole literary establishment.   Clearly the author of ''Tarantula'' - a melange of surreal nonsequiturs and stream-of-consciousness ramblings vaguely packaged as a novella - had always cherished certain literary ambitions, and over the years he had appropriated literary techniques with the same undiscriminating urgency as he had absorbed various musical styles. While too much was doubtless made of this during the 1960's, when college students routinely wrote theses dissecting his debt to Rimbaud, Celine and Whitman, the fact remains that his early work did help, in those formative years, make people aware of the possibilities of rock-and-roll as a potential forum for serious discussion, as a potential meeting ground for high and popular art.
headline: Books of The Times;   Times Are A-Changin'

title: We Are Talking About Homes
author: Lynne Sharon Schwartz.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WE ARE TALKING ABOUT HOMES A Great University Against Its Neighbors. By Lynne Sharon Schwartz. 175 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $15.95.   THE fire broke out on a workday in March 1983.   With most of the residents away at the time, there were no serious injuries, and most of the building was seemingly undamaged. But for tenants of the venerable building on Manhattan's Riverside Drive, the hurt, grief and struggle to regain their homes and to remain in their Morningside Heights neighborhood had just begun.
headline: COLUMBIA'S TENANTS

title: Victory Dances
author: Judith Brin Ingber
pull_quote: Modern dance is still so young an art form that a comprehensive history of its development has yet to be written. If the pioneers in the field are familiar, there are many dancers of lesser importance who stand to be lost to that history even if they were known in their own time.   In some cases, these choreographers and dancers made a special contribution that should be noted for its own value - and also as an element that explains aspects of modern dance's development. One of these dancers was Fred Berk, who died in 1980 and who was best known as a teacher of Israeli folk dances but who also started out as a modern dancer in his native Vienna and then was involved in American modern dance on many levels -dancer, choreographer, teacher and impresario.   Among his contributions were innovations such as a professional modern dance company aimed at children -the Merry-Go-Rounders - co-founded with Doris Humphrey and others. Still fewer people realize that in 1951, he originated the idea of a dance series at the Brooklyn Museum. The dancers performed in the museum's sculpture court. Since Merce Cunningham was on that series, it is very possible that the Cunningham ''Events'' - begun in a museum space in Vienna 13 years later - might have had their roots here.
headline: ONE MAN'S CONTRIBUTION TO THE HISTORY OF MODERN DANCE

title: Neuromancer
author: William Gibson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: I have to apologize for failing to review William Gibson's NEUROMANCER (Ace, Paper, $2.95) when it appeared last year. What put me off, I think, was the title, which struck me as an ungainly play on words, hinting at some trendy hybrid of sword-and-sorcery fantasy and high-tech adventure, with perhaps a bit of heavy-breathing sex thrown in. I was led to believe I had done Mr. Gibson an injustice when this novel (the author's first) won both of the important 1984 best-of-the-year awards in science fiction: the Nebula (voted by members of the Science Fiction Writers of America) and the Hugo (voted by the fans). Now that I have read the book, I would like to cast a belated ballot for Mr. Gibson.
headline: SCIENCE FICTION

title: In Summer Light
author: Zibby Oneal
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN SUMMER LIGHT By Zibby Oneal. 149 pages. New York: Viking Kestrel. $11.95. (Ages 12 and up) ZIBBY ONEAL'S heroines are cool, leggy and intelligent adolescent girls who struggle to unlock the repressed rage that blocks their growth to womanhood. Though the preoccupation seems narrow, the literary resolution grows more polished and mature with each novel. Miss Oneal's new book, ''In Summer Light,'' is also her most ambitious and coherent work to date.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Open Net
author: George Plimpton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OPEN NET By George Plimpton. Illustrated. 288 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $16.95. FOR his books to succeed, George Plimpton must fail. It would not do for him to actually triumph at what he calls participatory journalism. Everyman cannot become Superman.   He must train with professional athletes and wear their equipment and play against them, but he must not best them. They must remain giants. Why else would we admire them? Which is why many of Mr. Plimpton's books have self-deprecating titles - ''Out of My League,'' about baseball; ''Paper Lion,'' about playing football with the Detroit Lions; ''The Bogey Man,'' about golf; and now ''Open Net,'' about playing goalie for the Boston Bruins hockey team.
headline: PAPER GOALIE

title: Inside Warner Bros. (1935-1951)
author: Rudy Behlmer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: INSIDE WARNER BROS. (1935-1951). Edited by Rudy Behlmer. (Viking, $19.95.) Rudy Behlmer, the author of the fascinating 1972 ''Memo From David O. Selznick,'' has compiled a second look at Hollywood through memos, letters and telegrams. This time it doesn't work. ''Inside Warner Bros. 1935-1951'' is a jumble of memos by actors, writers, directors, producers and Harry and Jack Warner, the heads of the studio. ''Memo From David O. Selznick'' was shaped by that great producer's obsessions and spent, for example, more than 100 pages on ''Gone With the Wind.'' ''Inside Warner Bros.'' dips in and out of more than 100 movies, often in only one or two memos. The result is a hodgepodge that contains some nuggets but only rarely any depth. Most interesting are the sections on ''Casablanca,'' John Huston and the war between art and commerce in the making of Tennessee Williams's ''Glass Menagerie'' and ''Streetcar Named Desire.'' An exchange of letters between B. Traven, the reclusive author of ''The Treasure of the Sierra Madre,'' and Mr. Huston, who was to win Academy Awards for writing and directing a movie version of the novel, is compelling. One is struck also by numerous angry letters from Bette Davis, one of the few actors who expressed her dudgeon on paper, and such oddities as William Faulkner trying to get out of his screenwriting contract. One of the problems with ''Inside Warner Bros.'' is inherent in the material. Casting decisions on bad or forgotten movies seem trivial decades later.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Balanchine
author: Jennifer Dunning. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ''BUT FIRST A SCHOOL'' The First Fifty Years of the School of American Ballet. By Jennifer Dunning. Illustrated. 242 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $20. BALANCHINE Photo Album and Memoir. Photographs by Steven Caras. A Memoir by Peter Martins. 64 pp. New York: Rizzoli. Paper, $14.95.   THE School of American Ballet is now the national academy George Balanchine and Lincoln Kirstein always intended it to be - and more. Students flock there from around the world; hundreds more audition than are accepted. Graduates fill the ranks of the affiliated New York City Ballet and dance with myriad other troupes here and abroad. In the United States, 11 professional ballet companies are run by its alumni and associates. In '' 'But First a School' '' Jennifer Dunning, a dance critic for The New York Times, deftly chronicles the growth and growing pains of the School of American Ballet over its first five decades, as well as the development of the New York City Ballet.
headline: WHERE THE BOOM BEGAN

title: The Mammoth Hunters
author: Jean M Auel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MAMMOTH HUNTERS. By Jean M. Auel. (Crown, $19.95.) This is the third in the ''Earth's Children'' series about Ayla - the brilliant, beautiful, blond cavewoman.

title: Cold Dog Soup
author: Stephen Dobyns
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: COLD DOG SOUP. By Stephen Dobyns. (Viking, $15.95.) ''Cold Dog Soup,'' while often a clever, intriguing and verbally playful novel (its author is also a poet and mystery writer), seems to have been constructed to put off its readers.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Amusing Ourselves To Death
author: Neil Postman.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AMUSING OURSELVES TO DEATH Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business. By Neil Postman. 184 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $15.95.   FOR every television addict, there's a television critic. Neil Postman, the latest critic, is in many ways one of the best. He is also, in some ways, one of the worst. He writes so brilliantly that he cannot seem to stoop to those inconvenient qualifications that real life always requires. One senses in him a weakness for dichotomies and sweeping truths. In ''Amusing Ourselves to Death,'' he tends toward the kind of formulations people have difficulty living up or down to. In his wit and genius for quotation, he reminds us of the kind of beautiful complaint, flinging art in our faces, that Randall Jarrell used to write in the 1940's and 1950's.
headline: GOING DOWN THE TUBE

title: Nata
author: Helen V. Griffith. Illustrated by Nancy Tafuri.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NATA By Helen V. Griffith. Illustrated by Nancy Tafuri. 23 pp. New York: Greenwillow Books. $11.75. (Ages 2 to 5) WHATEVER adult fears that exist about a child's introduction to fairy tales - whether it is the goriness of some stories or the sexual stereotyping of passive princesses who must wait while heroic males do battle - at varying points in a child's development there is an appetite, perhaps even a need, for fairy tales. No other literature is as fierce or as eloquent in capturing our most primal fears and desires.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Still Life
author: Antonia Byatt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STILL LIFE By Antonia Byatt. 384 pp. New York: Charles Scribner's Sons. $16.95.   ANYONE who has read Antonia Byatt's three previous novels or her critical study of Iris Murdoch knows that this English writer has an acute, supple mind not always primarily interested in the narrative mode as such. She excels at finely attuned brooding and an emphatic introspection, which reveal so much of how it feels to be a certain character that we don't always care what the character does next. A psychological novelist, enthralled by the sensation of being alive, she is best when she works the vagaries of self-communing against the obstinacies of the appended body. She does what Dreiser called ''chemisms'' with the rippling, elated touch of a Virginia Woolf.
headline: SENSATIONS OF BEING ALIVE

author: Ed Mcclanahan
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FAMOUS PEOPLE I HAVE KNOWN. Ed McClanahan. (Farrar, Straus & Giroux, $13.95.) Before Vietnam, Woodstock, Watergate or Charles Manson, ''we had the swellest parties'' writes Ed McClanahan.

author: Paul Brodeur.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OUTRAGEOUS MISCONDUCT The Asbestos Industry on Trial. By Paul Brodeur. 374 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $19.95.      IN 1982 when the Manville   Corporation, with nearly $2 billion in assets, declared bankruptcy, Paul Brodeur got angry. In ''Outrageous Misconduct'' he shows why.

title: Classical Illusions
author: Jascha Kessler
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CLASSICAL ILLUSIONS. By Jascha Kessler. (McPherson, $14.95.) This volume of short fiction is a collective odyssey of the contemporary ruling class, with places as varied as Los Angeles, southern France and Central America the equivalents of classical settings.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: People Who Knock On The Door
author: Patricia Highsmith
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PEOPLE WHO KNOCK ON THE DOOR. By Patricia Highsmith. (Penzler Books, $15.95.) The gods seem to be napping in this master storyteller's new suspense novel.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Henry James: A Life
author: Leon Edel. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HENRY JAMES A Life. By Leon Edel. Illustrated. 740 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $24.95.   THERE are biographers whose careers are a succession of attachments, whether of love or hostility, admiration or contempt. They pass from one literary commitment to the next and cast no backward glances. And there are those who ''from an ample nation, choose one, then close the valves of [their]  attention like stone,'' in Emily Dickinson's words. Among such monogamists is Leon Edel, whose devotion to Henry James has been lifelong. Though other writers have sometimes interested him as an editor or essayist, one has had his devotion since 1932, when he wrote a dissertation in French at the Sorbonne on the then overlooked topic of James's playwriting. Perhaps not long afterward, he began the accumulation of research materials that was to form the basis of one of the most ambitious of modern life histories. A first volume was published in 1953, and the conclusion did not come until the fifth volume in 1972.
headline: THE ESSENCE OF THE MASTER

title: Where She Was
author: Anderson Ferrell
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WHERE SHE WAS. By Anderson Ferrell. (Knopf, $13.95.) Farm life has become fashionable again, to judge by movies such as ''Country'' and ''Places in the Heart,'' and by this precisely wrought first novel, ''Where She Was.''
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Sweetheart
author: Andrew Coburn
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: The world of big-time gambling occupies the major part of THE WINNING STREAK by Arnold Grisman (St. Martin's, $15.95). Goldberg is the central character; no first name is ever given. Now nearly 60 years old, he was a football hero at Yale University before an injury ended his career. He is now tired and disillusioned - and a professional gambler who consistently wins. When he is ready to go on a winning streak, he knows he can't lose. A female friend suggests he must work through extrasensory perception.   At Las Vegas, Nev., he streaks and walks away from the craps table with $147,000. He does not have the money very long. A woman who picks him up disappears with his winnings. Of course, he sets out to find her. Of course, he upsets a hornet's nest. Of course, there are attempts on his life. What distinguishes these rather commonplace ingredients is the size of the scam he and some old Treasury Department associates discover. For some years Goldberg was a T-man.
headline: CRIME

title: The Wine-Dark Sea
author: Leonardo Sciascia
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WINE-DARK SEA By Leonardo Sciascia. Translated by Avril Bardoni. 142 pp. New York: Carcanet. $14.95.      THE works of Leonardo   Sciascia have been written at different periods of his life and in different genres, but they seem to have a strong connecting element: the constant attempt to define what it means to be a Sicilian. Like American writers from the Deep South, who have been influenced by classical and European traditions yet are rooted in their own cultural and social heritage, Sicilian novelists are a mixture of provinciality and cosmopolitanism - a combination of self-deprecation and self-assurance. Among other traits in common, Sicilian writers from Giovanni Verga and Pirandello down to Elio Vittorini and Giuseppe di Lampedusa (the author of ''The Leopard'') reveal an iron pride even as they lament their people's fate.
headline: SICILIAN TALES

title: Let Truth Be The Prejudice
author: W Eugene Smith
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: W. Eugene Smith's images have changed the way we see history. LET TRUTH BE THE PREJUDICE (Aperture, $50) is a tribute to this master of photojournalism who, in a 40-year career, sacrificed health and personal life in the struggle to document human lives.
headline: IMAGES THAT TESTIFY

title: Sometimes A Shining Moment
author: Eliot Wigginton. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOMETIMES A SHINING MOMENT The Foxfire Experience. By Eliot Wigginton. Illustrated. 438 pp. New York: Anchor Press/ Doubleday & Company. $19.95.   IT is refreshing and inspiring to read Eliot Wigginton's history of the magazine and project called Foxfire, which he began as a teacher in a small public high school at Rabun Gap, Ga., two decades ago. Refreshing because the Foxfire project, a quarterly magazine about the culture and folk heritage of southern Appalachian mountain residents, is a highly innovative and successful experiment in high school English teaching. (And we have had in recent years little but criticism for our public schools, and the teachers in them, from either end of the political spectrum.) Inspiring because Mr. Wigginton is teaching with apparent undiminished energy and enthusiasm in the same school system he started teaching in 20 years ago.
headline: AND GLADLY TEACH

title: The Pushcart Prize X
author: Bill Henderson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

author: William Wharton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PRIDE By William Wharton. 288 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.   THE family has come in for remorseless bashing in the fiction of the last couple of decades. In bleak or hilarious novels about self-absorbed parents and confused children, it's often been hard to tell the grown-ups from the kids. So it should be comforting to pick up a nice, wholesome domestic portrait. And we've had several this year. I'm thinking of E. L. Doctorow's ''World's Fair,'' Ntozake Shange's ''Betsey Brown,'' Anita Brookner's ''Family and Friends'' and now, William Wharton's fifth novel, ''Pride.'' Tellingly, all these novels are set a generation or so ago - a golden age when fathers were strong, mothers tender and children were, well, children.   William Wharton - a pseudonym for an American who divides his own domestic life between a houseboat in Paris and a summer place in Cape May, N.J. - has been worrying over the family in all his novels. A typical Wharton hero is torn between nesting and flying the coop. ''Dad'' read like a combat report filed from the sex war. Even ''A Midnight Clear'' - a real war story -toyed with ideas of family: two of its main characters are soldiers nicknamed Mother and Father.

WENDELL BERRY'S poetry is a validation of his decision nearly 20 years ago to give up the literary life in New York and seek a deeper bond with his ancestral home, a hillside farm in Henry County, Kentucky, on the Kentucky River. His straightforward search for a life connected to the soil, for marriage as sacrament and family life, affirms a style that is resonant with the authentic. The lyricism is not forced, but clearly grows out of a deep bond with the earth and its generosity, with all of nature. He mocks little except man's arrogance and destructiveness, and he can be said to have returned American poetry to a Wordsworthian clarity of purpose. pull_quote: THE EVIDENCE OF THINGS NOT SEEN. By James Baldwin. (Holt, $11.95.) The worst two years in Atlanta's history were 1980 and 1981, when the bodies of dead black children turned up all over the city. In the atmosphere of panic and paranoia that grew with each horrible discovery, ''Atlanta became, for a season, a kind of grotesque Disneyland.'' So writes James Baldwin of the plague of unsolved murders that ultimately totaled 28, according to a police task force set up to investigate them. The ordeal in Atlanta, whose black leadership was slow to recognize the crisis being visited upon its poorest citizens, would seem an aptly challenging subject for a writer of Mr. Baldwin's gifts. But this slim volume will not satisfy many readers. Nor, one suspects, does it satisfy the author himself. ''I have never, in all my journeys, felt more of an interloper, a stranger, than I felt in Atlanta,'' writes Mr. Baldwin, who was on assignment for Playboy, where much of this book first appeared. There is far too much sermonizing here on the overall state of race relations in America and not enough digging into specific facts of the Atlanta murders. Nonetheless, when Mr. Baldwin steps down from the pulpit he can still bring passionate intensity to reportage, especially in an assessment of Wayne Williams, the failed music promoter whose 1982 conviction for two murders closed the Atlanta case. Mr. Baldwin derides the controversial fiber evidence that allegedly connected two victims with Mr. Williams's home in what the author terms ''an untidy trial,'' and he judges the verdict dubious.

Back in the days when golf was the preserve of the rich and the titled, cruising on big liners was also an upper-class affair relying on those who had the time and money to embark on a journey of frivolity or edification, usually both.   Over the last 50 years, and particularly with the coming of the jet age, cruising has become to passenger shipping what the municipal course has become to golf. In ''Liners to the Sun,'' John Maxtone-Graham has assembled a wealth of detail into an urbanely written volume on the cruise business, its past, its present and even its future.

His book provides us with a clearer, more detailed picture of how Churchill worked, thought and spoke in private than any yet published. Sir John began his work as secretary to the Prime Minister a convinced partisan of his predecessor, Neville Chamberlain. But after a few weeks he became one of Churchill's strongest admirers.

WHEN Gustave Flaubert and Ivan Turgenev first met at a favorite Left Bank writers' hangout in 1863, they were both accomplished writers, familiar with - and admiring of - each other's work: at the age of 41, Flaubert, the author of the controversial ''Madame Bovary,'' had just published ''Salammbo,'' and Turgenev, at 44, was already well known as the author of ''Hunting Sketches'' and ''Fathers and Sons.'' Although they would not start corresponding regularly for some five years, the two felt an immediate intellectual kinship and, as these letters demonstrate, they would remain in touch until Flaubert's death in 1880.

But in ''The Mammoth Hunters'' - as well as I can recall after having finished it more than an hour ago - she mostly kills a mammoth and has some steamy sex with both Jondalar and a dark-skinned ivory carver named Ranec, who also loves her.

BRYAN 3D'S first brush with glory was in 1917, when he rode in the same elevator as Jess Willard, the heavyweight champion. His next approach to it, in a somewhat modified fashion, was in 1934, when he got to know Arthur Samuels, the editor in chief of House Beautiful. By this time, Mr. Bryan himself was managing editor of Town and Country, but Samuels came trailing glamorous associations of a different order - his wife was a well-known actress and he had collaborated on the score of a musical starring W. C.Fields.   Even more than that, Samuels had the reputation of being a wit, a humorist, a joker, what you will. He belonged to a species that over the years was to provide Mr. Bryan with many of his closest friends, and he is the first of the 13 gentlemen (and one lady, Dorothy Parker) who are celebrated in this amiable collective memoir. The others include Robert Benchley, S. J.Perelman and - less predictably, in this connection -John Steinbeck; they range from well-remembered figures like Fred Allen and Marc Connelly to half-forgotten ones like the author Finis Farr and the mural-painter and dedicated practical joker Hugh Troy.

In ''Akenfield,'' his superb oral history of a Suffolk village, the British writer Ronald Blythe drew a minutely detailed portrait of life in the English countryside. By interviewing members of the community from all classes and professions - from an illiterate hermit to the blacksmith to the local justice of the peace - and allowing them to deliver their own monologues to the reader, Mr. Blythe was able strip away our nostalgic fantasies of a pastoral Eden, and replace them with an unsentimental picture of the repressive, fatalistic - and often stultifyingly provincial - way of life that still exists 100 miles from London.   In ''The Visitors,'' a collection of short stories belonging, the author points out, ''mainly to the first years of my writing life,'' Mr. Blythe takes on, in fictional terms, much the same territory he covered, as a journalist, in ''Akenfield.'' The setting, for the most part, is the rural England of his childhood - ''on the face of it,'' as he wrote in the earlier book, ''the kind of place in which an Englishman has always felt it his right and duty to live.'' And the dominant emotions, again, are a sense of suffocation, of lost innocence, and of time past intruding ineluctably upon time present.

LESS than 100 years ago, Augustus Saint Gaudens was more famous than Andy Warhol is today. In fact, in his own time this formidable sculptor's reputation rivaled and probably surpassed the notoriety of most of today's more publicized art stars. He rose to prominence in the post-Civil War years, when America was transforming itself from a provincial agrarian country into a modern industrial nation with a sophisticated culture of its own. Saint Gaudens provided the emerging American consciousness with its first indigenous and contemporary public monuments and supplied its influential families with exquisitely realistic bronze-relief portraits during an era when the rich turned to art collecting and embraced culture as an appropriate sign of their increased cultivation, power and wealth. Saint Gaudens combined an innate sculptural fluidity with the ability to integrate the diverse influences of the neoclassical, the Beaux Arts and even the Pre-Raphaelite style into a new naturalistic and romantic realism that suited the epoch.

pull_quote: A GRAND STRATEGY FOR THE WEST The Anachronism of National Strategy in an Interdependent World. By Helmut Schmidt. With an introduction by William P. Bundy. 159 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $12.95.   TEN years ago Helmut Schmidt was often rated the West's leading statesman. His close working relationship with President Valery Giscard d'Estaing of France had finally made the West German-French special relationship the motor for European cooperation that Konrad Adenauer and Charles de Gaulle had envisioned. On the surface, at least, trans-Atlantic diplomatic and even economic relations seemed unusually smooth.   The Chancellor's didactic and uncompromising political style made his popularity all the more impressive. Few subordinates or colleagues were spared the sting of his sarcastic wit. His authority came not from warm charisma but from the rational integrity of his arguments and policies. More than any other leader, he had made himself the embodiment of and spokesman for what had come to be taken as the enlightened postwar consensus. He was for the welfare state, but within a market economy disciplined by competition and fiscal balance. Loyal, if not uncritical, support of the alliance with America was coupled with a clear dedication to greater European cooperation and autonomy.

pull_quote: PUTTERING ABOUT IN A SMALL LAND. By Philip K. Dick. (Academy Chicago, $16.95.) Written almost two decades ago, this book was in manuscript form when unearthed by Philip K. Dick's literary executors - a bad move on their part, since the novel was obviously nowhere near readiness for publication.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: To Engineer Is Human
author: Henry Petroski
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TO ENGINEER IS HUMAN: The Role of Failure in Successful Design. By Henry Petroski. (St. Martins, $16.95.) Engineering, like all human endeavors, in-volves a chance of failure, and, as Henry Petroski writes in ''To Engineer Is Human,'' technological advances often come out of what we learn from failures.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Secret Generations
author: John Gardner
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SECRET GENERATIONS. By John Gardner. (Putnam, $17.95.) Every once in a while, a fragment of a decent spy novel peeks out from beneath the mound of cliches and unconvincing happenstance that make up ''The Secret Generations.''
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Made In America: His Own Story
author: Peter Ueberroth
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MADE IN AMERICA: His Own Story. By Peter Ueberroth, with Richard Levin and Amy Quinn. (Morrow, $17.95.) The man who headed the Los Angeles Olympic Organizing Committee from 1979 to 1984 - and who is now the commissioner of baseball - here offers us a first-person chronology of the dry diplomacy and elaborate social gavotte that shaped the 1984 Summer Games.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Dreadful Pleasures
author: James B. Twitchell. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DREADFUL PLEASURES An Anatomy of Modern Horror. By James B. Twitchell. Illustrated. 353 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $18.95.   FOR the time being,'' James B. Twitchell writes, around the middle of his chapter on vampires in ''Dreadful Pleasures: An Anatomy of Modern Horror,'' ''I have no interest in the art manipulation of the vampire myth. . . . I am interested in the unaffected and artless return of the vampire back into popular culture.'' A few paragraphs later he adds: ''Art renditions tend to make the saga socially relevant, allegorical, or atmospheric, rather than just letting it play itself out.'' His credo is shared by all appreciative critics of trash: the unselfconscious junkiness of pulp - B-movies, comics, and so forth - may sometimes reveal more than the traditional highbrow arts because there is less censorship going on.
headline: HERE BE MONSTERS

title: Ar'n'T I A Woman?
author: Deborah Gray White
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AR'N'T I A WOMAN? Female Slaves in the Plantation South. By Deborah Gray White. (Norton, $18.95.) ''I have plowed, and planted, and gathered into barns, and no man could head me -and ar'n't I a woman?'' asked the former slave Sojourner Truth at an 1851 women's rights convention in Akron, Ohio.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Monuments & Maidens
author: Marina Warner. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MONUMENTS & MAIDENS The Allegory of the Female Form. By Marina Warner. Illustrated. 417 pp. New York: Atheneum. $25.   DURING the early days of space exploration in the mid-60's a top-secret team at NASA conducted a search for a mythological figure to symbolize America's race to put a man on the moon. But if Diana, goddess of the hunt and mistress of that heavenly body, answered the casting call, despite her impressive credits and prior claim to the role, she failed the audition. The maiden with her bow and quiver and her retinue of nymphs and hounds didn't have the right stuff. Those in the space program with the power to name preferred to mix their celestial metaphors in the national interest, and called their moon shot Project Apollo.
headline: FINDING THE HER IN HEROIC

title: American Images: Photography 1945-1980
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AMERICAN IMAGES: PHOTOGRAPHY 1945-1980 (Barbican Art Gallery/Viking, Cloth, $35. Penguin Books, Paper, $16.95) appears to be a trick done with mirrors.
headline: LIFE THROUGH THE APERTURE

title: Beyond The Helix
author: Carol Kahn
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BEYOND THE HELIX: DNA and the Quest for Longevity. By Carol Kahn. (Times Books, $17.95.) Despite all our medical niceties, it is still practically impossible to live beyond the age of 110.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: First Figure
author: Michael Palmer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FIRST FIGURE By Michael Palmer. 79 pp. San Francisco: North Point Press. Paper, $8.50. MICHAEL PALMER'S ''First Figure'' is his fifth volume of poetry, not counting chapbooks. One of our finest poets at the height of his power, he brings together and unifies tendencies that have divided poets into opposing factions. The epigraph from Paul Celan, ''Niemandes Stimme, wieder,'' announces the book's theme even by the fact that it is left in German - ''nobody's voice, again,'' in a language the reader may not understand. We are entering a meditation on language that will not stay within the range of comfort: ''Once I could not tell of it / and now I cannot speak at all.''
headline: CALLING ALL ANTS

title: The Obedient Wife
author: Julia O'Faolain
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE OBEDIENT WIFE. By Julia O'Faolain. (Carroll & Graf, $17.95.) As the accomplished novelist Julia O'Faolain's sixth book begins, Carla Verdi - the Florentine wife of the title - waits in a rented Los Angeles house for her unfaithful husband's return from Italy.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: On The Perimeter
author: Caroline Blackwood
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ON THE PERIMETER By Caroline Blackwood. 117 pp. New York: Penguin Books. Paper, $5.95.   CAROLINE BLACKWOOD'S ''On the Perimeter,'' though it is perfectly dreadful considered as prose and as journalism, merits attention all the same for the strange emotional charge it carries. The surreal warping of syntax, the dotty preoccupation with mud and sex and rude odors, are the testament to an anxiety so intense as to have lost a clear sense of its occasion.   Miss Blackwood's subject is a long and famous vigil by a band of women at Greenham Common, an Amer-ican military base near Newbury, England, at which cruise missiles are deployed. Four years ago, in protest against their coming, a group of women and children walked 400 miles, from Wales, to establish a camp outside the base. Women are camped there still, maintaining a vigil notable for the extreme wretchedness of the conditions in which they live. Local authorities try to drive them away with bulldozers, midnight raids and confiscations. Local thugs set the surrounding bushes on fire. Still, women continue to live outside the gates of the base, in ''benders,'' tiny shelters made of branches and plastic, in defiance of hostility, tedium, cold and mud, sustained by the gifts of well-wishers - of whom there are a great many - and by the fact that their protest has become a sort of pilgrimage site for like-minded people from the ends of the earth.
headline: A LONG AND WRETCHED VIGIL

title: The World Of Thought In Ancient China
author: Benjamin I. Schwartz.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WORLD OF THOUGHT IN ANCIENT CHINA By Benjamin I. Schwartz. 490 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press. $27.50. ''THE Command of Heaven is not forever.'' This simple idea with far-reaching consequences was articulated in a court song commemorating the founding of the Chou dynasty in the middle of the 11th century B.C. It presumably was sung for centuries to remind Chou kings that their behavior still counted, just as the behavior of their ancestors counted, the founding kings who secured Heaven's revocable command to rule the world.   The idea was invented to help legitimize the new dynasty, which had usurped the power of its predecessor, but it perhaps inadvertently also broke apart the previous cozy arrangement in which a king's position was derived from his connection to his royal ancestors, who were in turn his connection to the high ancestral divinities, including even Heaven. Heaven now was influenced by performance, not just kinship ties expressed through rituals. This simple idea made possible the notion that leaders had moral responsibilities to perform in the interests of the welfare of the led.
headline: WHY BE MORAL?

title: The History Of Southern Literature
author: Blyden Jackson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE HISTORY OF SOUTHERN LITERATURE Edited by Louis D. Rubin Jr. with Blyden Jackson, Rayburn S. Moore, Lewis P. Simpson and Thomas Daniel Young. 626 pp. Baton Rouge: Louisiana State University Press. $29.95.   THIS vast enterprise attempts nothing less than a detailed account of Southern writing from Capt. John Smith's ''Generall Historie of Virginia, New England, and the Summer Isles'' in 1624 to Anne Tyler's ''Dinner at the Homesick Restaurant'' in 1982. It is the product of a committee headed by Louis D. Rubin Jr., a distinguished man of letters at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and to an admirable extent it refutes the old notion that no good book ever comes out of a committee. About 50 scholars have contributed some 70 articles to ''The History of Southern Literature.'' Some of these deal with general trends from period to period, and others give brief vignettes of major figures - Poe, Mark Twain, Faulkner, Wright, Robert Penn Warren and so on. They vary inevitably in quality, but there is a sufficiency of sound critical judgment and perspective, and among them the little army of commentators have highlighted the chief currents and the crucial changes in Southern imaginative expression over three and a half centuries.
headline: A CONFEDERACY OF GENIUSES

title: Emigrants And Exiles
author: Kerby A. Miller.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EMIGRANTS AND EXILES Ireland and the Irish Exodus to North America. By Kerby A. Miller. 684 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $35.   IN ''Emigrants and Exiles,'' Kerby A. Miller, an associate professor of history at the University of Missouri, presents a spirited and far-ranging synthesis on one of the oldest and best-studied immigrant groups in the United States, the Irish. It is a true work of trans-Atlantic history, for Mr. Miller has done original research and assessed carefully the published materials both on the cultural and economic circumstances of Ireland that caused more than seven million people to leave between 1607 and 1921 and on the nature of their subsequent experience in the United States and Canada. With the help of many people, including myself when I was the American Ambassador to Ireland, he has found thousands of letters and fragmentary memoirs written by immigrants. And he has made wider use than any previous American historian of materials written in Irish, aided by the graceful translations of Bruce Boling of Brown University.   Mr. Miller grapples with subtle and difficult questions. Why did so many Irish immigrants look upon America as a place not of opportunity or refuge but of forlorn exile? What was distinctive in the Irish culture and national character that shaped the attitudes of most immigrants? Did those attitudes assist or retard assimilation into American life? How, precisely, did Irish nationalism and Irish-American experience interact?
headline: WE WHO LEFT IRELAND

title: The Skaters' Waltz
author: Philip Norman
pull_quote: THE SKATERS' WALTZ. By Philip Norman. 331 pages. Linden Press/Simon & Schuster. $15.95. ONE of the things that distinguished ''Shout!,'' Philip Norman's collective biography of the Beatles, published in 1981, was his meticulous attention to detail. In that volume, exhaustive research, served up in dense, fact-filled prose, made for an informative, lively book - a book that lent the story of the Beatles' life and times a palpable weight and thrust. Now in ''The Skaters' Waltz,'' Mr. Norman tries to use a similar approach, in a novel, to evoke the vanished world of childhood in the 1940's and 50's.   The book is packed with lengthy passages memorializing everything from the taste of old-fashioned ice cream to the sensation of riding the train from Portsmouth Harbour. We are told what it's like for a young boy to go to London with his grandmother, and what it's like for that same boy, slightly older now, to visit the West Country with her. There are lengthy reminiscences about favorite boyhood sweets (Murraymints, Barker & Dobson fruit drops, Butter Brazils, Hooper Struve ginger beer and Peter's Original Milk Chocolate), and equally detailed reminiscences about favorite toys and cartoons.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: To A Violent Grave: An Oral Biography Of Jackson Pollock
critic: Christopher Lehmann-Haupt To A Violent Grave: An Oral Biography of Jackson Pollock. By Jeffrey Potter. 303 Pages. Putnam. Illustrated. $19.95
pull_quote: JACKSON POLLOCK (1912-1956) is very much alive again in the pages of this oral biography of the famous and controversial painter. Compiled and written by Jeffrey Potter, a friend of Pollock's who lived near him on the South Fork of Long Island, ''To a Violent Grave'' usefully supplements B. H. Friedman's admirable 1972 biography, ''Jackson Pollock: Energy Made Visible,'' which, as Mr. Friedman himself admits in these pages, failed to anticipate the enormous subsequent growth of Pollock's reputation.   In the pages of ''To a Violent Grave,'' we see the birth of the legend in perspective. Through the testimony of Pollock's family, friends, colleagues and neighbors, as well as Mr. Potter himself, who developed a typically complex relationship with the painter, we watch Pollock grow from the pampered youngest child of a mother-dominated family from the American West to the figure about whom it has been said, ''There was art and then came Pollock.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Pleasures Of The Belle Epoque
author: Charles Rearick
pull_quote: PLEASURES OF THE BELLE EPOQUE.   Entertainment and Festivity in Turn-of-the-Century France. By Charles Rearick. Illustrated. 240 pages. Yale University Press. $29.95. FEW golden ages feel golden at the time, and in the 30 years or so before 1914 no one in France seems to have gone around proclaiming that the country was living through a ''belle epoque.'' It was only in retrospect, after the dark divide of World War I, that the phrase came into use as a label for the prewar period. Once it had been applied, however, it stuck, and it still serves to sum up, as brightly and effectively as a Jules Cheret poster, the popular notion of French life in that era as a constant round of cafes, cabarets, strolls along the boulevard, sophisticated pleasures.   Historians have no trouble in showing how much of this is nonsense -partly the product of nostalgia, partly of publicity (not least, of course, of publicity for Paris as one of the world's great tourist centers). In reality, pre-1914 France was plagued by bitter political conflicts, festering social problems, harsh economic divisions; the beautiful epoch had some very ugly features.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Selected Poems
author: John Ashbery
pull_quote: SELECTED POEMS. By John Ashbery. 349 pages. Elisabeth Sifton Books/ Viking. $22.95. ''The words are only speculation/ (From the Latin speculum, mirror),'' writes John Ashbery. ''They seek and cannot find the meaning of the music./ We see only postures of the dream.'' The lines are from Mr. Ashbery's dazzling masterwork ''Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror,'' and like so much of his verse, they address not only the situation at hand in a given poem, but also the overall condition of his art - his relation, as a poet, to the reality around him. In this case, the lines also uncannily describe the effect of reading Mr. Ashbery's poetry - an effect not unlike that produced by listening to a piece of avant-garde music. Certainly his elliptical work frequently defies conventional attempts to impute meaning - most are vague about time, place and characters, as though external reality were quite beside the point; many constantly shift point of view, as though the idea of fixed character, too, were outmoded. And yet its meditative, allusive beauty retains a powerful ability to entrance, goading the reader to re-examine his own relationship to the world.
headline: WITH POETIC LICENSE

title: The Year They Sold Wall Street
author: Tim Carrington
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE YEAR THEY SOLD WALL STREET By Tim Carrington. 245 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $16.95 ''MAYDAY'' - killing off the New York Stock Exchange fixed-commission schedule in favor of negotiated rates - badly squeezed most retail-oriented brokerage firms. Many went out of business or merged. Then, as mutual funds, pension funds and insurance companies came to dominate the market, the average size of stock exchange transactions ballooned. Large blocks (10,000 shares and up) are half of total exchange volume, up from 5 per cent 20 years ago. A broker able to take a $10-million block of stock off a customer's hands into its own inventory, to distribute at leisure, can get the business away from one that offers to dribble the stock out for the customer over weeks or months. That, however, calls for substantial capital. To get it, some large brokerage houses floated their shares to the public or looked for merger partners.
headline: BUT THAT'S GREENMAIL!

title: Grace In The Wilderness
author: Aranka Siegal.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GRACE IN THE WILDERNESS After the Liberation 1945-1948. By Aranka Siegal. 220 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $11.95. (Ages 12 and up) ARANKA SIEGAL'S award-winning first book, ''Upon the Head of the Goat,'' detailed the harrowing story of the Davidowitz family's roundup by the Nazis and ended with four of the Hungarian Jewish children and their mother boarding a transport train for Auschwitz. This sequel begins with the liberation of Bergen-Belsen, which 15-year-old Piri Davidowitz and her sister Iboya have survived through luck and their deep, protective bond. What has happened between the train and the arrival of the Allied troops surfaces in an autobiography that reads more like fiction as the narrator recounts her postwar recovery and relocation to Sweden.   Because Piri is ill, the sisters are accepted for care by the Swedish Red Cross and leave the destruction of war behind to start a new life. As Piri's body and emotions stabilize, she experiences survival as a maze of confusion and displacement, with reminders of pain amid sudden plenty. Concentration camp ordeals come back as she is able to admit them in narrative flashbacks more subtle and telling than any direct account. However, the reader must wait patiently through scenes densely populated with characters from Piri's Swedish present to catch sudden glimpses of her past.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: State Of The Art
author: Pauline Kael
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STATE OF THE ART By Pauline Kael. 404 pp. New York: A William Abrahams Book/ E. P. Dutton. Cloth, $22.50. Paper, $12.95. PAULINE KAEL, the feisty film critic of The New Yorker, rouses such passion that the publication of a new collection launches a bloody biennial rite, Kael-bashing. But she is no innocent. She writes taunting, contentious prose that she knows will jangle nerves, and she can be uncharitable about anyone's opinion but her own. Still, if pugnacity and crabbiness were sufficient provocation, nearly every critic could foment the rage Pauline Kael calls down. The hostility to her runs deeper because her criticism has always struck deeper. It strikes the very hearts of cultural supremacists.   Even before she began writing for The New Yorker in 1967, Pauline Kael, like a sadistic dentist, knew precisely how to stab at her enemies' sensitivities and make them howl. Her enemies were (still are) all those custodians of taste who put popular culture in its place, a nether region far below Art. From the first, she anointed herself the liberator of American film criticism, freeing it from snooty academics who treated movies as weightless divertissements (unless, of course, you were talking about Ingmar Bergman) and from middlebrows who felt that commendable movies, like medicine, had to be good for you.
headline: HISS HISS BANG BANG

title: The Later Adventures Of Tom Jones
author: Bob Coleman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LATER ADVENTURES OF TOM JONES By Bob Coleman. 345 pp. New York: Linden Press/Simon & Schuster. $15.95.   KEEPING up with the Joneses - well, why not? Here we have Bob Coleman, Ph.D., a student of Henry Fielding's writings but at present a vice president of a San Diego small-business brokerage and consulting firm, who has decided to take a high flyer, since writing a sequel to Fielding's great ''Tom Jones'' (1749) is something like following W. C. Fields on the vaudeville stage. There is no safety net allowed in this sort of thing, and the audience is hoping you fail. Quel audace!  I put aside the temptation to reread Fielding's novel before opening Mr. Coleman's continuation -the only fair thing to do, so as not to immerse the review in boring comparisons. A masterpiece that has endured for more than two centuries is without compare, anyway, so why disturb Fielding's ghost? What we need to determine is, first, whether Mr. Coleman's sequel is worth reading on its own merits, and, second, what his higher purpose in bridging the centuries may have been.
headline: THE HISTORY OF A FOUNDLING, CONT.

title: The Fear Of Population Decline
author: Michael S. Teitelbaum and Jay M. Winter.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE FEAR OF POPULATION DECLINE By Michael S. Teitelbaum and Jay M. Winter. 201 pp. San Diego: Academic Press/ Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. Cloth, $34. Paper, $19.95. FOR many years now, public attention - and debate - concerning the world's ''population problem'' has largely focused on overpopulation. Demographers and pundits note that the world's population is still rising at an unacceptably high rate of about 1.75 percent a year, or an increase by the year 2000 from 4.9 billion to 6.2 billion. This means that sometime early in the next century, the world will contain some 9 billion people. And more than three-quarters of them will be packed into the economically struggling states of the third world, which can least afford high population growth.   But overpopulation is not a problem for most of the industrialized West, or for the Socialist states of Eastern Europe. These countries have been experiencing a flattening out of the postwar baby boom; many of them are now undergoing a net population decline as couples have fewer or no children, and as their populations age.
headline: THE BARREN LANDS

title: The Visitors
author: Ronald Blythe
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE VISITORS By Ronald Blythe. 239 pp. San Diego: A Helen and Kurt Wolff Book/ Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $16.95.   THAT Ronald Blythe, the author of ''Akenfield'' - that fine portrait of a Suffolk village - has published a book of stories, raises the immediate appetite for more East Anglian lore, and in this ''The Visitors'' does not disappoint us. In the major part of the 20 stories here, which date from the earliest years of Mr. Blythe's career, we are led into the lives of the folk of that region (or similar locales lying off the beaten track) who ask approval of no one. Eccentrics and anecdotes abound; ghosts put in frequent appearances; old relatives tell their individual stories; churches, brambly cottages and rundown mansions breathe esthetic and spooky delights.
headline: LOCAL HABITATIONS

title: Bronx In The Innocent Years, The. 1890-1925
author: Lloyd Ultan and Gary Hermalyn. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BRONX IN THE INNOCENT YEARS #1890-1925. By Lloyd Ultan and Gary Hermalyn. Illustrated. 164 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $19.95.   I AM not a reader who can resist a volume with such chapter headings as ''I Remember Tremont.'' ''The Bronx in the Innocent Years, 1890-1925'' has an ''innocence'' of its own as a publishing venture. This is a series of recollections by people who are not identified other than by name and who are possibly not professional writers. They write with simplicity and a sense of the pertinent detail about the years covered in the book, their words accompanied by some 80 delicious vintage photographs. Here is the Bronx as it was changing from an outlying rural section of the city to a subway-linked borough where newly arrived immigrants lived in distinct neighborhoods.
headline: NEW YORK PASTORAL

title: Response To Revolution
author: Richard E. Welch Jr.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RESPONSE TO REVOLUTION The United States and the Cuban Revolution, 1959-1961. By Richard E. Welch Jr. 243 pp. Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press. Cloth, $24. Paper, $9.95. SEVEN United States Presidents ago, Fidel Castro came to power in Cuba. This well-written book focuses on Washington's response to the Cuban revolution in the immediate aftermath of Mr. Castro's victory in Cuba in January 1959 until the consolidation of revolutionary rule after the defeat of the United States-backed exile invasion at the Bay of Pigs.   Richard E. Welch's book discusses three principal themes. The first is a succinct summary of the complex flow of events between the United States and Cuban Governments during these years. The second charts a path through the jungle of conflicting partisan as well as scholarly interpretations of the Cuban revolution and its relations with the United States. The third analyzes in some detail the American public's response to the Cuban revolution. The book's main weakness is its insufficient attention to Cuba's own foreign policy and its responses to the United States.
headline: AS WE SAW CUBA

title: Part Of My Soul Went With Him
author: Winnie Mandela
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PART OF MY SOUL WENT WITH HIM By Winnie Mandela. Edited by Anne Benjamin. Adapted by Mary Benson. 164 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. Cloth, $14.95. Paper, $5.95. THE name Mandela has been the symbol of the black liberation struggle in South Africa for more than a generation. Nelson Mandela, who is 67 years old and still unbowed after 21 years in prison, became prominent in the 1940's as a young leader of the African National Congress - the oldest black protest organization in South Africa. He spurred the organization to a radical course of mass civil disobedience and later sabotage. In 1958, six years before he was sentenced to life imprisonment, he married Winnie Madikizela, a young social worker who became a leader and symbol of defiance in her own right.
headline: SOUTH AFRICA'S 'POLITICAL BAROMETER'

title: Gentlemen On The Prairie
author: Curtis Harnack
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GENTLEMEN ON THE PRAIRIE By Curtis Harnack. Illustrated. 254 pp. Ames: Iowa State University Press. $19.95.   ''YESTERDAY a wilderness, today an empire,'' a Le Mars, Iowa, newspaperman wrote of his community in 1882. His boast was more than just small-town boosterism; an empire had indeed grown around him, built by people who knew something about empires - the British. That year, 135,000 acres of prime land in Iowa and Minnesota were under the control of recently arrived English colonists. In this splendid book, ''Gentlemen on the Prairie,'' Curtis Harnack traces their fortunes in the New World.
headline: PLAYING FIELDS OF IOWA

title: From The Ruins Of The Reich: Germany 1945-1949
author: Douglas Botting
pull_quote: FROM THE RUINS OF THE REICH:   Germany 1945-1949. By Douglas Botting. Crown. 341 pages. Illustrated. $17.95.   IT is not exactly as if the events described in Douglas Botting's ''From the Ruins of the Reich: Germany 1945-1949'' were obscure ones. The invasion of Nazi Germany by the Grand Alliance, the discovery of the death camps, the fall of Berlin and the end-game played out in the Hitler bunker, the Occupation and the four-power administration of Germany's remains, and, finally, the American and British merger of their zones and the Soviet response of blockading Berlin - these momentous occurrences are etched in the memory of anyone over the age of 50 with pain and awful wonder.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Poland Under Black Light
author: Janusz Anderman
pull_quote: POLAND UNDER BLACK LIGHT. By Janusz Anderman. Translated by Nina Taylor and Andrew Short. 131 pages. Readers International. $12.50. ''WHEN did it happen?   Could it have been in this country? When?''   It happened in Poland in December 1981, when, as Janusz Anderman describes the imposition of martial law, the police, party and army made war on the Polish people. What that meant is the theme of ''Poland Under Black Light,'' his book of grim and gritty vignettes from a crushed society.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: That Bowling Alley On The Tiber: Tales Of A Director
author: Michelangelo Antonioni
pull_quote: THAT BOWLING ALLEY ON THE TIBER: Tales of a Director. By Michelangelo Antonioni. Translated from the Italian by William Arrowsmith. 208 pages. Oxford University Press. $18.95.      ''TOWARD THE FRON=   TIER,'' one of the 33 sketches in this collection, reads like a kind of composite summary of every Antonioni movie you've ever seen. Four people, thrown together by circumstance, are traveling through a bleak landscape toward some unnamed border: the Italian director himself; a pretty German woman whom everyone calls Grethe, though Grethe is not her name; an American Army captain, and another young girl. They do not know each other very well, but they have in common a vague sense of alienation, a need to improvise their evenings together.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Preparing For Power: America's Elite Boarding Schools
author: Caroline Hodges Persell
pull_quote: PREPARING FOR POWER: America's Elite Boarding Schools. By Peter W. Cookson Jr. and Caroline Hodges Persell. 260 pages. Basic Books. $19.95. THE observation that inspired this book is not terribly startling. Like many other sociologists have done - professionals and amateurs alike - Peter W. Cookson Jr. and Caroline Hodges Persell noticed that when youngsters go into the elite boarding schools of America, they tend to be the children of rich and powerful parents. And when they come out of those schools, they are better prepared to take the place of those parents.   The interesting question they raise in ''Preparing for Power: America's Elite Boarding Schools'' is, what happens in between? Or as they put it, ''what happens in the 'black box' of the school itself?'' Obviously the elite boarding schools ''prep'' their students for the elite colleges, from where, in disproportionate numbers, graduates go on to the board rooms, the bar associations and the bureaucracies that run this country. And the authors explore how this process works. But isn't there more to America's boarding schools than their students' simply being there?
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Fdr: The New York Years 1928-1933
author: Kenneth S Davis
pull_quote: FDR: THE NEW YORK YEARS 1928-1933.   By Kenneth S. Davis. 512 pages. Random House. $19.95.    AS its title makes plain, the second volume of Kenneth S. Davis's biography of Franklin Delano Roosevelt carries its protagonist through his term as Governor of New York and into the White House. The subtitle might be ''The Composition of a President.'' Mr. Davis presents Roosevelt in his mid-40's as an unfinished man, possessed of surpassing charm, immense physical courage that sustained him in his struggle against polio, and instinctive political savvy. But he seemed wanting in commitment to any cause but his own and had only a shaky comprehension of the ideological depths into which he was being drawn.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: China
author: Hiroji Kubota
pull_quote: IN his book ''The Decisive Moment,''   Henri Cartier-Bresson raised questions about color photography that have troubled photographers for more than 25 years. Not only did he consider color films to be inflexible -allowing for little leeway in exposure and lighting - but he also expressed doubt about the quality of color reproduction. Indeed, Cartier-Bresson wondered whether we would ever see color pictures as powerful as those that existed in black and white.   With the publication of ''China'' by the photographer Hiroji Kubota, we may be able to set aside some of those fears. Many of the 185 color photographs reproduced in this book possess the power of the best of black and white.
headline: A POWERFUL COLOR PORTRAIT OF CHINA

title: I'm Not Making This Up, You Know
author: Anna Russell. Edited by Janet Vickers. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: I'M NOT MAKING THIS UP, YOU KNOW The Autobiography of the Queen of Musical Parody. By Anna Russell. Edited by Janet Vickers. Illustrated. 246 pp. New York: Continuum. $17.95.   ANNA RUSSELL, the English song parodist who started out 40 years ago as a kind of cross between Helen Traubel and Martha Raye and has evolved into an uncanny amalgam of Joan Sutherland and Phyllis Diller, here offers a certain length of breathless, scattershot reminiscence. A book like this, reaped in interview and parceled out by an editor in chronological sequence, is intended to give its subject's votaries a look inside the complex circuitry that galvanizes the performing clown.
headline: THEY LAUGHED WHEN SHE STOOD UP

title: Liberty
author: Leslie Allen
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STATUE OF LIBERTY: The First Hundred Years. By Christian Blanchet and Bertrand Dard. English-language version by Bernard A. Weisberger. (American Heritage/Houghton Mifflin, $29.95.) LIBERTY: The Statue and the American Dream. By Leslie Allen (The Statue of Liberty-Ellis Island Foundation/Summit Books, $32.95.) The tumultuous celebration next July 4 for the centennial rededication of the Statue of Liberty promises to make the adjective ''momentous'' emerge as an understatement. The same might be said for the sheer tonnage of books, films and assorted mementos the lady in New York Harbor is inspiring. If these two handsome, profusely illustrated volumes are gauges of what is to come, they augur well for high-quality birthday gifts. Bernard A. Weisberger's ''Statue of Liberty,'' based on a French version of the book by Christian Blanchet and Bertrand Dard, may well be one of the best in its treatment of the statue itself. As much picture as it is text, it offers a bright biography of this extraordinary figure, conceived during a dinner party by a group of influential republicans, as a gift of France in the name of liberty. We learn about its construction according to the most modern techniques applied by Frederic-Auguste Bartholdi, who created a genuine modern colossus. Although it was in a classic, old mold that many felt lacked artistic innovative genius, it has seized the imagination of the world. The story tells of the fund-raising, the commercialism, the idealism, the subsequent neglect that surrounded the statue during the 100 years since it was erected.
headline: TEETH, WONDER WOMAN AND THE SOUL OF BALI

title: Company Of Adventurers
author: Peter C. Newman. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: COMPANY OF ADVENTURERS Volume One. By Peter C. Newman. Illustrated. 413 pp. New York: Viking. $25. ONE long evening long ago in northern Canada an unhappy man named James Isham smashed a blood-bloated mosquito onto the page of his personal journal, right next to an anguished entry about the insect swarms that dominate summer life in that part of the world to this day.   His journal entry, one of thousands written with goose quill and frigid fingers over the centuries as the top of North America was being unlocked by enterprising traders, may or may not have been read by Isham's corporate sponsors in faraway London. But two-and-a-half centuries later, along comes Peter C. Newman, a professional writer of considerable curiosity, with a sharp eye for detail and a knack for storytelling. He uses this journal entry and others, combined with impressive independent research, to weave the fascinating tale of the Hudson's Bay Company, ''the oldest continuous capitalist corporation still in existence.''
headline: FROZEN ASSETS

title: Past Or Future Crimes
author: Elliott Currie.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CONFRONTING CRIME An American Challenge. By Elliott Currie. 326 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $19.95. PAST OR FUTURE CRIMES Deservedness and Dangerousness in the Sentencing of Criminals. By Andrew von Hirsch. 220 pp. New Brunswick, N.J.: Rutgers University Press. $25.   IN ''Confronting Crime,'' Elliott Currie fails to offer practical answers to America's crime problem, but his attempt adds ballast to a criminal-justice debate far too preoccupied with prison as the only response to crime. It is, Mr. Currie makes clear, a response that prevails in the absence of anything better. ''There is a pervasive sense,'' he writes, ''that older ways of thinking about crime have lost their usefulness and credibility; but no convincing alternatives have come forward to take their place.''
headline: JAIL: WHO GOES, FOR HOW LONG?
