title: Christopher Columbus
author: Gianni Granzotto
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CHRISTOPHER COLUMBUS By Gianni Granzotto. Translated by Stephen Sartarelli. Illustrated. 300 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $18.95.   GENTLE reader, beware! The quincentenary celebration of Columbus's ''discovery'' of America is only on the horizon, but Colombomania has already landed. Scholars armed with historical magnifying glasses are meeting to determine the exact site where the Admiral of the Ocean Sea first set foot on American soil; archeologists are actively searching for remains of the first Spanish settlement in Hispaniola; nautical buffs are preparing to sail full-scale replicas of the Nina, Pinta and Santa Maria across the Atlantic; museums, colleges and universities are vying in a race to commemorate this historic event, and books dedicated to the man responsible for this hoopla are beginning to reach the bookstalls.
headline: WAS CUBA PART OF CHINA?

title: That Bowling Alley On The Tiber
author: Michelangelo Antonioni. Translated by William Arrowsmith.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THAT BOWLING ALLEY ON THE TIBER Tales of a Director. By Michelangelo Antonioni. Translated by William Arrowsmith. 208 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $18.95.   ''ALL human happiness and misery take the form of action,'' Aristotle declared. It was probably some similar sentiment that led audiences at the 1960 Cannes Film Festival to hiss ''L'Avventura,'' Michelangelo Antonioni's film drenched in human misery (with scattered droplets of human happiness) but devoid of any action beyond the occasional enigmatic sigh. Flouting Aristotle - and getting hissed in the bargain - made Mr. Antonioni's reputation. But as his brand of swank anomie slid out of vogue (his last two features have not even been distributed here), his films began to look dated, mannered, even silly - they became a 60's joke.
headline: CINEMA DOODLES

title: Abc Et Cetera
author: Alexander Humez and Nicholas Humez.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ABC ET CETERA The Life & Times of the Roman Alphabet. By Alexander Humez and Nicholas Humez. 274 pp. Boston: David R. Godine. $17.50.      JUST as Alexander and Nicholas Humez used the   Greek alphabet in ''Alpha to Omega'' to explore the influence of ancient Greek civilization on our culture, they have now produced a companion volume, ''ABC et Cetera,'' on the Roman alphabet. The abecedarian organization of the book enables the authors to highlight one aspect of Roman civilization in each chapter; for example, ''L is for legal, legislate, and legitimate - all from Latin lex, legis (law).'' Depending on how many facts one can absorb, the reader will either relish or resent the exceedingly thorough descriptions of Roman family structure, government, gods, engineering, numbers, letters, theater, law, satire, war, festivals and medicine. Moreover, digressions into subjects not entirely Roman are frequent; the already overburdened reader may deem unwelcome these excursions into computerese, slogans, orthographic signs and the unicorn.
headline: DEAD LANGUAGE SPEAKS UP

title: The Bayeux Tapestry
author: David M Wilson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BAYEUX TAPESTRY. Introduced by David M. Wilson. (Knopf, $75.) Whoever designed the Bayeux tapestry nine centuries ago was one of the greatest narrators ever to tell a story. In pictures and words this embroidered linen strip 20 inches high and 230 feet long tells the story of the conquest of England by William of Normandy in 1066 so gracefully and clearly that few accounts of any historical event can match the swiftness of its narrative or its power over one's emotions. As a viewer watches the story unfold, the rich and tumultuous life of 11th-century nobles and their armies fills the imagination and when the Battle of Hastings finally comes into view the action becomes startlingly dramatic. The epic elevation and dignity of this great work lift the spirit; vanquished and conquerors alike move with energy one can feel across the centuries, they fight without treachery and their nobility endows the final battle with tragic grandeur. Brilliant photographs made several years ago when the tapestry was removed from its casing in its Bayeux museum for cleaning have been assembled in 146 consecutive pages by Sir David Wilson in a magnificent book that displays the tapestry in greater clarity, at times, than one can see it in the museum. Sir David, the director of the British Museum, also provides clear, brief commentaries on the events depicted in the tapestry as well as on the people and action in each picture. His appendixes on society, customs and buildings of the era convey his enormous learning with engaging good humor.
headline: TEETH, WONDER WOMAN AND THE SOUL OF BALI

title: What's Bred In The Bone
author: Robertson Davies
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WHAT'S BRED IN THE BONE By Robertson Davies. 436 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $17.95.   ''WHAT'S bred in the bone will not out of the flesh,'' says the old English proverb that serves as an epigraph to this novel by the Canadian author Robertson Davies. Certainly what is bred in the bone of Mr. Davies's hero, the painter-art forger Francis Cornish, is a fascinating and volatile mixture of contradictory qualities. Focusing on the life and career of an artist irresistibly drawn to the methods and symbols of a bygone era, ''What's Bred in the Bone'' also explores perhaps the central problem facing contemporary artists: how to retain the old-fashioned virtues associated with great art of the past (chiefly, art's ability to instruct and console by providing a coherent system for interpreting the world and our role in it) in a century whose twin allegiances - to a heartfelt but potentially chaotic subjectivism or to dehumanizing rationality - pose equal dangers to the artist. Mr. Davies ambitiously plunges headlong into these deep divisions and creates both a hero and a novelistic form designed to reconcile these oppositions. In the end, however, Mr. Davies may have produced a masterpiece that is so tied to the codes and methods of an earlier era that it becomes an anachronism.
headline: PAINTER, FORGER, MISER, SPY

title: The Epic Of Life
author: Idanna Pucci
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE EPIC OF LIFE: The Balinese Journey of the Soul. By Idanna Pucci. (Alfred van der Marck/Harper & Row, $60.) Balinese arts have been illustrated in large-size books throughout our century, but never has a particular visual creation from Bali been more beautifully captured than in this stunning volume. Classic court paintings there portrayed gods, heroes, demons and comic servants. The paintings were stored and then shown on occasions determined by taboos that helped regulate the iconography's power. One exception to this rule is this vibrant set of paintings, which illustrates the ''Bhima Swarga,'' the Balinese folk tale that describes a hero's journey into the afterlife. Set in the ceiling of the royal pavilion in Klungkung, a former royal capital, these fixed, painted surfaces became a monument to the legal system established after Klungkung fell to the Dutch in 1908. The panels depict Bhima, that most approachable high-born protagonist in the ''Mahabharata,'' witnessing punishments that characterize the Hindu hell: ordeals by fire, boiling, anal and genital mutilations and horrific battles. Along with the few remaining relics of Klungkung's once expansive palace area, the work has been preserved, occasionally restored and added to Bali's principal tourist sites. Idanna Pucci, a widely traveled freelance writer who has lived in Indonesia, organized this stately volume around splendid photographs, most of which were taken by Hans Hoefer, a publisher and photographer who lives in Singapore, before recent applications of acrylic paints to the panels. The book isolates individual scenes in extraordinarily subtle colors set off against surrounding panels left in black and white.
headline: TEETH, WONDER WOMAN AND THE SOUL OF BALI

title: The Encyclopedia Of Superheroes
author: Jeff Rovin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE ENCYCLOPEDIA OF SUPERHEROES. By Jeff Rovin. (Facts on File, $29.95.) In his introduction to this exhaustive listing of the hyperactive characters who have been a colorful part of the American scene for half a century, Jeff Rovin indicates that the superhero is not exactly a new boy on the block. Perhaps the first recorded superhero is in the Babylonian epic of Gilgamesh, circa 2000 B.C. Gilgamesh was the King of Erech, part god, part human. Other mythological old boys Mr. Rovin mentions are Neph, a ram-headed Egyptian; Husheng, a Persian monster-slayer, and Rama, an Indian archer and warrior. ''In the earliest days, we called them 'gods,' '' writes Mr. Rovin, a comic-book editor and television consultant. The true superhero, Mr. Rovin says, must have at least one superpower, must be ''neither vindictive nor selfish'' and ''must function like the secretary-general of the United Nations, working for the good of everyone.'' Merlin, Ulysses and John Henry fail to make the grade. Moses doesn't qualify because ''he stretched forth his hand over the sea [and]  there remained not so much as one'' Egyptian, while ''the Lone Ranger never killed a soul'' and ''is a saint.''

title: Karan
author: B. Wongar.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: KARAN By B. Wongar. 248 pp. New York: Dodd, Mead & Company. $16.95.   JUST when you think you have exhausted your hatred of militarists, along comes something else. For about 10 years, during the 1950's and 60's, the British secretly tested nuclear weapons in South Australia, a fact not disclosed until 1984. The area chosen for these tests is among the most desolate regions on earth. Nevertheless, some aborigines lived there. According to the author's preface, these experiments had ''a lethal effect on Aboriginal tribal man and his culture.'' This is the basis for a provocative novel. Its author, B. Wongar (a pseudonym), is the son of an aboriginal mother and a European father. He was educated in Europe, but later returned to Australia, where he married an aborigine. This explains why, although this book, like its predecessor, ''Walg,'' is written in English, it is not altogether the product of a Caucasian sensibility.
headline: ANAWARI FEELS RESTLESS

title: Cadillac
author: Stephen Salmieri
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CADILLAC. Photographs by Stephen Salmieri, hand-painted by Sydnie Michele Salmieri. Text by Owen Edwards. (Rizzoli, $50.) Consider the front view - or the face - of the 1955 Cadillac Fleetwood. The hood comes forward like the bulging forehead of a beluga whale. Slow, deep curves connect this forehead to fenders containing two hooded, saturnine eyes. A silver tusk juts from either side of the grinning, heavily chromed grill. Zoomorphic indeed. And this orgy of curved surfaces renders the aerodynamically sound boxes we drive today bland and soulless. In ''Cadillac,'' the Brooklyn-born photographer, Stephen Salmieri, displays the results of a 12-year search that took him and his wife, Sydnie Michele Salmieri, coast to coast through junkyards, ghettoes, deserts, auto shows, amusement parks and funeral homes in a pilgrimage for these living rooms on wheels. If your soul soars when you gaze on the winged, pachyderm sleekness of a '59 Cadillac -those vast fins, each attended by two bullet-shaped taillights - these 80 or so portraits, along with Owen Edwards's quirky, on-the-mark essay, may constitute nirvana for you. Some purists may balk at the colors Mrs. Salmieri used in hand-painting the black-and-white photographs - some of them never were and probably never will be available in Cadillacs - but the effect she achieves is mildly and pleasantly surrealistic. Mr. Edwards's essay is emphatically not just dressing. He peels back the layers of the American psyche and analyzes our love of the horseless carriage. He invokes the ghost of Harley Earl - the General Motors designer responsible for fins and grinning grills - and gets Keats, poltergeists and the Holy Grail into the discussion in meaningful ways.
headline: TEETH, WONDER WOMAN AND THE SOUL OF BALI

title: Blackberries In The Dark
author: Mavis Jukes
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BLACKBERRIES IN THE DARK By Mavis Jukes. Illustrated by Thomas B. Allen. Unpaged. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $10.95 (Ages 8 to 12) IN a complicated world where children often land at the bottom of the heap it is comforting to find a book about a child who participates in decisions and who makes crucial connections about events and emotions. ''Blackberries in the Dark,'' by Mavis Jukes, a Newbery Honor Book author, while sometimes overly subtle and flat, deals with some important issues, among them loss, loneliness and the need for tradition.

title: The Grasshopper Trap
author: Patrick F. McManus.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GRASSHOPPER TRAP By Patrick F. McManus. 214 pp. New York: Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $13.95.   PATRICK F. MCMANUS is a writer who makes people laugh out loud, hard. The first time I read his first collection of pieces, ''A Fine and Pleasant Misery,'' I was sitting by myself in a one-room house, and the experience gave me a chance to hear what my own laugh sounds like. I began to laugh on page 6, and as I went along I listened more closely. The sound was not ''ha ha ha''; I laughed with loud barks and high-pitched, wheezy runs and long, helpless relapses. I was like one of those Bag-o'-Laffs you buy in joke shops.
headline: FAST MEAN COWS AND SLOW MEAN COWS

title: Under Siege
author: Rashid Khalidi.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: UNDER SIEGE P.L.O. Decisionmaking During the 1982 War. By Rashid Khalidi. 241 pp. New York: Columbia University Press. $25.   AT one point during the 1982 Israeli siege of Beirut, Lebanon, I was interviewing the Palestinian guerrilla leader George Habash in his musty underground bunker. Surrounded by young acolytes, Mr. Habash spoke not of the Palestinians' parlous battlefield situation but of the fact that the guerrillas were still on the battlefield with the Israelis at all - longer than any Arab army had ever been. There was something about the passion of his remarks and the fury with which he pounded the table for emphasis that struck me then, and strikes me now, that here is a man who was finally getting a chance to fight the war his father never fought. Indeed, what took place in Lebanon during June, July and August of 1982 was the real Palestinian-Israeli war - just 34 years late.
headline: INSIDE THE PALESTINIAN BUNKER

title: The Donkey's Dream
author: Jean Rogers
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: KING ISLAND CHRISTMAS By Jean Rogers. Illustrated by Rie Munoz. Unpaged. New York: Greenwillow. $11.75 (Ages 5 to 8) THE DONKEY'S DREAM By Barbara Helen Berger. Unpaged. New York: Philomel. $12.95 (Ages 5 to 8) THAT mysterious thing, the spirit of Christmas, is brought heartily to life in ''King Island Christmas.'' There are no Christmas trees in this book, no Santa Claus, no reindeer, no Christ Child, but plenty of Yuletide cheer just the same.   The story is simple. When rough seas prevent the steamship North Star from setting ashore the new priest for the village church, the Eskimo islanders are disappointed. It is the ship's last trip to King Island before the ice closes in. Will the pulpit be empty until next year? Gallantly they achieve a solution. Setting off en masse to the other side of the island, they carry their walrus-skin boat up a steep hill and down again to the leeward shore where the sea is calmer. Bravely they start the outboard and go to meet the ship as it steams around the island. The priest is brought ashore to a joyful welcome and a grand Christmas feast.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Forgive Me
author: Cathleen Crowell Webb and Marie Chapian
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FORGIVE ME By Cathleen Crowell Webb and Marie Chapian. Illustrated. 220 pp. Old Tappan, N.J.: Fleming H. Revell Company. $15.95.   FOR three days last May, hundreds of reporters jammed the auditorium of the State of Illinois Center in Chicago to hear a New Hampshire woman tell Gov. James Thompson she had caused an innocent man to be sent to prison. In the glare of television lights, Cathleen Crowell Webb explained to the Governor and the Illinois Prisoner Review Board that eight years before, she had lied about being raped in an effort to conceal a teen-age sexual encounter she feared had made her pregnant. Now, she said, the man she had accused should go free.

title: On Being Blue
author: William H Gass
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A WORD is its uses, as William H. Gass shows in his rollicking conspectus, ''On Being Blue,'' although he might have ogled ''purple'' as well. Purple does seep into his bluebook, however, here tinting some ''spent body like a bruise,'' there leaving a ''lavender thumb''-print of ''broken veins.'' In fact, as well as being a book on the uses of ''blue'' - in talk, literature and the dictionary - ''On Being Blue'' is a prime, up-to-date example of purple prose, not so much a patch as it is a pyramid, a pandemonium, a seething nuclear pile of words.   Infatuated with ''blue,'' its optical resonance and its metaphorical range, Mr. Gass picks up samples from far and near, reveling in the word's every appearance, teasing and inciting and delving until the little tome glides off on its own like emancipated lava, announcing I Am Words, I Am Language, I Am Style. The book is elaborate without being ornate, ambulatory without being pedestrian, and, for those whose tastes run to purple, a definite joy. It reminds us that the almost lost art of phrasemaking attracts the scorn only of those who have never made up a stylish phrase in their lives, as if style had become taboo, a menace to people, gods and cars.
headline: IN DEFENSE OF PURPLE PROSE

OUR country and the American language finally have the long-awaited, definitive and fascinating Dictionary of American Regional English.   The publication of the first of this dictionary's five volumes (the rest to be published at intervals of a year or more) is an astounding achievement, a landmark for the American language and of American scholarship. The result of years of research, compilation and editing, the completed project will be a major reference and sourcebook for lexicographers, linguists, social historians and folklorists for generations to come, and one of the layman's most interesting and revealing books about our language and our country.

title: Politics
author: Edward I Koch
pull_quote: POLITICS. By Edward I. Koch. With William Rauch. 255 pages. Illustrated. Simon & Schuster. $17.95. IN a ''Last Word'' that he wrote especially for the paperback edition of his best-selling autobiography, ''Mayor,'' Edward I. Koch complained, albeit obliquely, about those critics who reviewed the author himself instead of the book he had written.   Well, here's another book by Mayor Koch, called ''Politics,'' which has been rushed from manuscript to finished book so fast that the flap copy on the dust jacket never got a chance to know the book's contents intimately. (The jacket refers to ''Koch's revealing'' portrait of ''President Carter who was shocked by him''; yet the book contains merely a passing reference to the former President that is incidental to an anecdote about President Nicolae Ceaucescu of Rumania.) So out of respect for Mr. Koch -who may conceivably succeed in his stated ambition to have his administration as New York's mayor ''surpass'' that of Fiorello H. La Guardia - and because the Mayor assures us in the introduction to ''Politics'' that it ''is not simply more of the same,'' one tries as hard as one can to consider the book as a book instead of as an extension of its author.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Burning Forest
author: Simon Leys
pull_quote: THE BURNING FOREST. Essays on Chinese Culture and Politics. By Simon Leys. 257 pages. A New Republic Book/Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $16.95.    SIMON LEYS is the pen name of Pierre Ryckmans, a Belgian-born scholar who teaches Chinese literature at the Australian National University in Canberra. Ever since the appearances of ''Chinese Shadows,'' his account of returning to China after the Cultural Revolution, it has been clear that he is one of the most incisive commentators on the contemporary Chinese scene, unsurpassed in his determination to strip away myths and misconceptions. What has been equally plain is that he writes out of deep affection for the Chinese people and deep admiration for Chinese culture - an admiration that gives him the measure of how much has been squandered or betrayed in the last 30 years.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Commonplace Book
author: E M Forster
pull_quote: COMMONPLACE BOOK. By E. M. Forster. Edited by Philip Gardner. 372 pages. Stanford University Press. $35.      ''T   HE cardinal fact in my life is my writing,'' E. M. Forster once declared. And even though the peculiar shape of his novelistic career implies a sharp cessation of literary labors in middle age - his first four novels, including the brilliant ''Howard's End,'' were written between the years 1905 and 1910, and his last, ''A Passage to India,'' in 1924 - he actually remained extraordinarily productive until his death in 1970 at the age of 90, turning out reviews, essays and as many as six letters a day to family and friends. While he no longer seemed able to make the imaginative transactions necessary for fiction, Forster could not relinquish the habit of trying to preserve ideas and observations in the clear amber of prose, and in 1926, he began keeping a ''commonplace book'' - a compendium of quotations, remarks and odd clippings from life. That book, issued in a limited facsimile edition in 1978, has now been made available to the general public by Stanford University Press.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Gerald's Party
author: Robert Coover
pull_quote: GERALD'S PARTY. By Robert Coover. 316 pages. Linden Press/Simon & Schuster. $17.95.   ''NONE of us noticed the body at first,'' begins the narrator of Robert Coover's latest novel, a hallucinogenic, phantasmagoric nightmare of mayhem and ecstasy named with ironic simplicity, ''Gerald's Party.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: William Marshal. The Flower Of Chivalry
author: Georges Duby
pull_quote: WILLIAM MARSHAL. The Flower of Chivalry. By Georges Duby. Translated from the French by Richard Howard. 155 pages. Pantheon. $15.95 WILLIAM MARSHAL was born around the year 1145, the son and grandson of men who had been household officials - marshals, in fact - at the Plantagenet court. If his name means little or nothing today, except to students of the period, he was a person of great importance in his time. A staunch supporter of Henry II and his heirs, he rose from his relatively obscure origins to become first a celebrated knight, and then one of the most powerful noblemen in the realm.   As Earl of Pembroke, he played a leading role during the turbulent reigns of King Richard the Lion-Hearted and King John; and eventually, when John's 9-year-old son, Henry, succeeded to the throne, he became regent, and led the forces that drove the invading French armies of Prince Louis out of the country.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Serpent & The Rainbow
author: Wade Davis
pull_quote: THE SERPENT & THE RAINBOW. By Wade Davis. 297 pages. Simon & Schuster. $17.95. It's immediately clear that Wade Davis, the author of ''The Serpent & the Rainbow'' - an account of his research in Haiti - fancies himself some kind of real-life Indiana Jones. He makes a point of interrupting his narrative to tell us that he went to see ''Raiders of the Lost Ark'' at a local movie theater in Haiti; and the ''about the author'' note accompanying his book does its best to play up the parallels. ''During his many expeditions,'' the note from Simon & Schuster reads, Mr. Davis ''was initiated into secret rites and ceremonies traditionally off-limits to whites; was caught in gunfire between soldiers and guerrillas; was mistaken for a Dutch gunrunner; he ate a lunch of fresh termites with warriors in loincloths; got lost among the Jivaro, the famed headhunters; flew an aging wreck of a DC-3 over the Andes when the pilot was hung over. He has survived high fevers, hepatitis, malaria and pains, ills, and diseases barely known in the so-called civilized world.''
headline: THE FRONTIER OF DEATH

title: Natives And Strangers
author: Louisa Dawkins
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NATIVES AND STRANGERS By Louisa Dawkins. 404 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $18.95.   IT is perhaps one measure of the strength of this novel that I began it with the wariness of the reviewer, asking: ''Who is Louisa Dawkins?* Why a pseudonym? Why that one? Why the romance title? Why African whites?'' and I ended with the curiosity of the reader, wondering: ''How will Marietta and Charlie fare in London? What will be his relation to Africa? Will Michael come? Will Michael and Marietta get back together, and if not, how will they bear being apart? And when will Catherine pop up next?'' I have cavils generated by the book itself - a little more of this here, a little less of that there - but they are only cavils. If a sequel appeared, I would read it immediately.   ''Natives and Strangers'' takes place primarily among white settlers in Kenya and Tanganyika from the mid-1950's to the early 1970's, the years of decolonization and independence. Virginia Hamilton, the daughter of British settlers, is an attractive, spirited widow who runs bush hotels, sleeps with her customers and even marries two of them. Her second husband, Neville Bilton, the intellectually inclined inheritor of a large estate, becomes particularly important to her fatherless daughter, Marietta.
headline: 'AND YOU CAN'T BE AFRICAN'

title: Public Philosopher
author: Walter Lippmann
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PUBLIC PHILOSOPHER Selected Letters of Walter Lippmann. Edited by John Morton Blum. 652 pp. New York: Ticknor & Fields. $29.95.   WHY should anyone bother to read over 600 pages of letters written by the same person, even so prominent a pundit as Walter Lippmann? In one sense, the answer is simple. In 1913, Walter Lippmann published his first book, ''A Preface to Politics.'' From then until 1971, almost four years before his death, through a steady stream of books and news columns, he acted as a learned and respected observer of governance and policy in America. Leaders often disagreed with Lippmann, but they almost always read him, as these letters demonstrate.   ''Public Philosopher'' is a chronological selection from the more than 20,000 letters in the Walter Lippmann papers at Yale University. The letters help us get beneath the vagueness and some of the detachment of his published books and columns, although detachment was a calculated part of the Lippmann style. Almost all the selections seem important. In part, that is because Lippmann rarely corresponded with any but the rich and famous - at least not in this sampling - and there is a certain fascination in that world of movers and shakers. In larger part, however, the significance of the letters is a tribute to Walter Lippmann's mind and John Morton Blum's hard work.
headline: DEAR RICH-AND-FAMOUS

title: Brave New Workplace
author: Robert Howard
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BRAVE NEW WORKPLACE By Robert Howard. 224 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $16.95.   IF Robert Howard's stark predictions about the effects of the transformation of work in the electronic age should prove to be only half accurate, the fall of the high expectations some have invested in our new technologies may well be complete. In ''Brave New Workplace,'' a well-written and broadly conceived book, he tries to put in perspective the heady claims that some experts have made for ''new technology as the harbinger of meaningful work,'' the corporate world as the model of a ''caring community,'' the workplace as ''a realm of self-fulfillment'' and business ''as the fundamental source of identity in modern society.''
headline: WHOSE COMPUTER REVOLUTION IS THIS, ANYHOW?

title: Outside The Magic Circle
author: Virginia Foster Durr
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OUTSIDE THE MAGIC CIRCLE The Autobiography of Virginia Foster Durr. Edited by Hollinger F. Barnard. With a foreword by Studs Terkel. Illustrated. 360 pp. University: The University of Alabama Press. $24.50.   IN the 1960's there were certain names that blew across the South, right across state lines, exemplars of bravery and immovability in the face of racism and redbaiting. Many were poor and black; others were white and ''wellborn.'' The urgencies of history had taken them all by surprise. While the majority of Alabamians considered Virginia and Clifford Durr traitors, not heroes, they represented to many of us the best of the white South, its native strength: they were sensible, outspoken, committed and only accidentally heroic.
headline: THE WELLBORN MAVERICK

title: Secular Love
author: Michael Ondaatje
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SECULAR LOVE By Michael Ondaatje. 126 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. Cloth, $14.95. Paper, $6.95. ELEGY ON INDEPENDENCE DAY By Arthur Smith. 50 pp. Pennsylvania: University of Pittsburgh Press. Cloth, $12.95. Paper, $6.95. THE TRIUMPH OF ACHILLES By Louise Gluck. 60 pp. New York: The Ecco Press. $13.50.      MICHAEL ONDAATJE'S new book, ''Secular   Love,'' is persistently and often intelligently obsessed with art. He cares more about the relationship between art and nature than any other poet since the Romantics, and more than most contemporary poets care about any ideas at all. Mr. Ondaatje is an oddity - a passionate intellect -and his book is alternatingly exasperating and beautiful. Most of the poems in it are about a fragmentary-seeming world, written from a fragmentary self. The result is that in too many cases there is a lack of ambition or accomplishment in the work. A few of the shorter poems, particularly, feel like ditties. Others have a raw, unfinished, lurching quality, skittering in fits and starts from place to place. In some of the longer poems, this scattered effect can be powerful, like the cumulative charge of fireworks. But even the longer poems, with a few happy exceptions, are seldom entirely satisfying or evenly gifted, and Mr. Ondaatje tends to indulge in posturing and nonsense: My tin ear would still play into your hand.

title: The Blood Seed
author: Andrew Ward
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BLOOD SEED. By Andrew Ward. (Viking, $17.95.) A rare Indian perspective on the last 100 years of the British raj is provided in this entertaining adventure novel, purportedly the memoir of Balbeer Rao, orphaned son of a Rajput widow.

title: A Simple Story
author: S Y Agnon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A SIMPLE STORY By S. Y. Agnon. Translated and with an afterword by Hillel Halkin. 246 pp. New York: Schocken Books. $14.95.   IT is something of a mystery why this understated masterpiece by S. Y. Agnon (1888-1970) had to wait 50 years to be translated into English. All the same, one must be grateful for its appearance now and for Hillel Halkin's skillful (if at times rather free) rendering of Agnon's elegantly stylized Hebrew.   This unrivaled major figure of modern Hebrew fiction, co-winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1966, had been writing stories and novellas for almost three decades when ''A Simple Story'' was originally published in 1935. It was his first real novel, since the long work of fiction he had produced four years earlier, ''The Bridal Canopy,'' is really a frame story containing a series of short tales. He would go on to write three more novels - only one of which, ''A Guest for the Night,'' has been translated into English - each bolder than the last in its sweep of symbolic invention and its plunge into strange worlds of revelatory fantasy.
headline: BLIND BEGGARS AND INCESTUOUS PASSIONS

title: Tomie Depaola's Mother Goose
author: Tomie Depaola
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TOMIE DEPAOLA'S MOTHER GOOSE Illustrated by Tomie dePaola. 127 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $17.95. (Ages 3 to 7) THE new edition of ''Mother Goose'' by Tomie dePaola is a mutedly colorful, well-designed and rich sampling of 200-plus rhymes and songs of childhood. Its selections, leaning heavily toward those emphasizing domestic animals - cows, pigs, ducks, hens, geese, cats and dogs - make this a Mother Goose decidedly aimed at the younger range of listeners. (It also results in an unavoidable sameness to some of the pictures, particularly in the early part.) The rhymes are told complete in most instances, with the texts taken from Iona and Peter Opie, the folklore specialists in Britain. The book includes such nontraditional rhymes as ''Three little ghostesses, / Sitting on postesses'' and '' 'I went up one pair of stairs.' 'Just like me.' '' (This ends with, '' 'And there I saw a monkey.' 'Just like me.' '') Here, as elsewhere in a markedly successful 20-year career in children's picture books, Mr. dePaola provides ingratiating, cheerful and intelligent illustrations, albeit perhaps too bland. His ''Mother Goose'' cuts a commendably wide ethnic swath with black, Hispanic, Oriental and gypsy characters taking full part in the verse happenings. Rhymes about time and weather are illustrated together inventively.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Learning To Heal
author: Kenneth M Ludmerer.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LEARNING TO HEAL The Development of American Medical Education By Kenneth M Ludmerer. 346 pp. New York: Basic Books. $21.95.   THOSE of us who teach undergraduates have formed a composite image of premed students. They are the ones who prepare diligently for class, sit in or near the front row, take copious notes and drop the course after the first test if they get anything less than a B plus. It is hard to blame them. They want to be admitted to medical schools in the United States, unquestionably the world's best. These schools choose the cream of the undergraduate crop.
headline: THE DOCTOR'S DIPLOMA

title: Destroying Democracy
author: James T. Bennett and Thomas J. DiLorenzo.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DESTROYING DEMOCRACY How Government Funds Partisan Politics. By James T. Bennett and Thomas J. DiLorenzo. 561 pp. Washington: Cato Institute. Cloth, $24.95. Paper, $11.95.   LONG before progressive taxes (and exemptions) helped the philanthropic impulse along, United States foundations aided the poor and supported universisites, hospitals, science and the arts. More recently, however, some foundations have behaved in ways that might surprise the original donors - promoting radical social reform. Henry Ford would be amazed by some of the uses - for example, leading the movement for such then-radical changes as community school boards in New York City in the 1960's - to which his money has been put by the Ford Foundation.
headline: TAX-EXEMPT TROUBLEMAKERS

title: On Extended Wings
author: Farley Mowat
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MY DISCOVERY OF AMERICA. By Farley Mowat. (Atlantic Monthly, $12.95.) When the Canadian writer Farley Mowat was barred from entering the United States last April, he wondered, naturally enough, why. Mr. Mowat's frequently hilarious book chronicles his quest to get a sensible answer from the Immigration and Naturalization Service. The author of ''Never Cry Wolf'' learned he and thousands of others are blacklisted under the McCarran-Walter Act of 1952, a law intended to keep Communists and anarchists out of the country. Given no further explanation from immigration officials, Mr. Mowat examined his conscience. Was the problem his book ''The Siberians''? On reflection he admitted he had ''treated the Soviets as human beings essentially like us.'' Or was it ''Sea of Slaughter,'' which condemned the butchery of wildlife along the United States and Canadian coasts? Neither, an anonymous immigration official finally explained. Mr. Mowat, he said, was a serious espionage risk and a threat to our armed forces. According to a 1968 newspaper clipping in a Government file, the author - no stranger to bluster - had said he took potshots with a .22 at United States bombers flying over Newfoundland. The way Mr. Mowat tells it now, the planes were visible only with binoculars - decidedly out of range for a rifle commonly used to hunt squirrels. Since he believed the aircraft carried hydrogen bombs, Mr. Mowat says he had even less reason to shoot. After he was refused entry and the Government was lambasted in newspapers across the nation, officials rigged an escape hatch for themselves: they would ''parole'' Mr. Mowat.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Cat Who Walks Through Walls, The. A Comedy Of Manners
author: Robert A. Heinlein.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CAT WHO WALKS THROUGH WALLS A Comedy of Manners. By Robert A. Heinlein. 382 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $17.95.   WRITING fiction set in the future is a troublesome business. For one thing, one tends not to be taken seriously as an artist. For another, one risks being taken seriously as a seer. Thus a number of important writers - H. G. Wells, George Orwell, Aldous Huxley - have seen some or all of their work first dismissed, both by serious critics and by pundits of popular taste, as ''mere'' science fiction, only to suffer jeers later because the worlds they invented did not literally come true (witness the circus a year ago when the news media made a straw man of Orwell's ''Nineteen Eighty-Four,'' as if, were Big Brother not extant by Jan. 1, 1985, we could all stop worrying about tyranny).

title: Amalgamation!
author: James Kinney
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AMALGAMATION! Race, Sex, and Rhetoric in the Nineteenth-Century American Novel. By James Kinney. (Greenwood, Cloth, $29.95. Paper, $12.95.) James Kinney's subject is race relations - in both the social and sexual senses. Mr. Kinney, who teaches English at Virginia Commonwealth University, traces the ways in which novelists from 1792 to 1914 dramatized miscegenation and participated in the struggle over slavery and racism.

title: Life In Sports
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Many of the most striking photographs in LIFE IN SPORTS (Harper & Row, $29.95) have appeared in Life magazine. Gjon Mili's photograph of a 1939 cockfight (shot at 1/100,000 of a second), George Silk's thrilling photo essay of the 1962 America's Cup race and Arthur Rickerby's violent images of football and lacrosse are unforgettable.

title: The Burning Forest
author: Simon Leys.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BURNING FOREST Essays on Chinese Culture and Politics. By Simon Leys. 257 pp. New York: A New Republic Book/ Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $16.95.   EVALUATING someone else's revolution from a distance can produce great argument among the outside observers, who tend to identify with one or another protagonist in the domestic conflict. This seems particularly true in the case of China, because Chinese culture and civilization have fostered so many interested constituencies abroad, all the way from Christian missionaries to businessmen, humanist scholars and social scientists. Simon Leys (actually Pierre Ryckmans, a Belgian art historian) is a well-qualified humanist. His 1977 book, ''Chinese Shadows,'' blew the whistle on the too-complacent Western acceptance of the Maoist cover-up of the horrors and atrocities of the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1969 and later. Mr. Leys's dire picture of the Maoist attack on Chinese intellectuals has since been filled in with a flood of gruesome details.
headline: DISSONANCE IN THE COSMIC HARMONY

title: Safe Houses
author: Lynne Alexander
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SAFE HOUSES. By Lynne Alexander. (Atheneum, $13.95.) The title of Lynne Alexander's first novel refers to both the real safe houses that sheltered refugees in World War II and the more elaborate safe houses of the imagination.

title: The Ratzinger Report
author: Joseph Ratzinger
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE RATZINGER REPORT An Exclusive Interview on the State of the Church. By Joseph Cardinal Ratzinger with Vittorio Messori. Translated by Salvator Attanasio and Graham Harrison. 197 pp. San Francisco: Ignatius Press. Paper, $9.95.   JOSEPH CARDINAL RATZINGER is the Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of Faith (once called the Holy Office), the Vatican bureau that has the duty of defending and promoting Roman Catholic orthodoxy. He has developed the habit of giving interviews, and this book publishes his most famous one, given to an Italian journalist last year. When excerpts from it appeared in an Italian magazine some months ago, they aroused a great deal of controversy. The book's title calls it a ''report,'' but it is really a collection of sometimes highly personal observations and evaluations offered by a man who occupies an extremely important post in the Roman Curia. It is not an official interpretation, but his private views, which have, therefore, roughly the same significance as the views of Chief Justice Warren E. Burger when he comments on the state of the legal profession today -not legally binding, but perhaps important as indications of how he might vote on issues that come before the Supreme Court.

title: Frederick's Fables
author: Leo Lionni
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FREDERICK'S FABLES A Leo Lionni Treasury of Favorite Stories. Written and illustrated by Leo Lionni. Introduction by Bruno Bettelheim. 132 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $16.95. (Ages 3 to 8) LEO LIONNI is a modern master of the picture book. Beginning with ''Little Blue and Little Yellow,'' in 1959, he has been an outstanding innovator. A distinguished art director and graphic artist, he is a minimalist for preschoolers. His influence has been pervasive in the field, traceable through the efforts of William Steig, Eric Carle, Elizabeth Cleaver and Robert Kraus, among many others. The little ''parables'' Mr. Lionni writes and illustrates generally concern misfits who, with just the right touch of imagination, transcend their sorry circumstances. The publication of ''Frederick's Fables,'' an anthology of 13 of his best-known picture books issued between 1960 and 1983, should be a cause for celebration.

title: Estrangement. America And The World
author: Sanford J Ungar
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ESTRANGEMENT America and the World. Edited by Sanford J. Ungar. 347 pp. New York: A Carnegie Endowment Book/ Oxford University Press. $19.95.   THE theme of this collection of essays, by authors who are predominantly American and liberal, is blazoned in the title. The word ''estrangement'' is a pregnant one, implying both that close and relatively harmonious links existed between two partners in the past and also that the parties are no longer in what the French call bon accord. The editor, Sanford J. Ungar, a senior associate at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, sums up this theme at the outset. The United States, he says, is ''separate, aloof, more alone than even the most cynical or pessimistic observers might have predicted in the heyday of American postwar power.''

pull_quote: THE NUCLEAR DEBATE: Deterrence and the Lapse of Faith. By Robert W. Tucker. (Holmes & Meier, Cloth, $24.50. Paper, $9.95.) Do we need to be reminded of how confused we are about nuclear weapons and the odds and ends of deterrence? Yes, in this case, we do.

IN the history of jazz, no period can match the 1940's in importance, mythography or sheer fascination. Be-bop, the avant-garde music spearheaded by Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, appeared and soon supplanted the swing sound entirely. At first decried, later described as a fad, by the 1950's be-bop had become the cornerstone of modern jazz, the mother tongue for a majority of jazzmen.

THIS book is a study of the American press and radio (principally daily newspapers) and how their generally uninformed coverage, with notable exceptions, of the rise of Adolf Hitler led to their uninformed reporting, again with notable exceptions, of the Holocaust. The title refers to the unwillingness of some but not all important dailies to publish reports of the Final Solution or to publish them prominently because they were ''beyond belief.'' A similar charge could be made about uninformed reporting in the American press about the rise of Joseph Stalin, the Soviet war against Russia's peasantry and the organization of the Soviet gulags.

author: Ian Frazier
pull_quote: DATING YOUR MOM. By Ian Frazier. 123 pages. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $11.95. THERE are flowers and pink ribbons on the cover of Ian Frazier's first book, ''Dating Your Mom.'' author: Agatha Christie

Dodd, Mead. $14.95.      ''A   CHRISTIE for Christmas'' -such was the heaven-sent slogan with which, once upon a time, Agatha Christie's publishers used to advertise her latest autumnal offering. Those days, of course, have gone forever; but this year - a year that has already seen the appearance of an excellent biography of Agatha Christie herself, by Janet Morgan - insatiable addicts can at any rate console themselves over the holiday season by reading a biography of her second most celebrated character.

title: Truman. The Rise To Power
author: Richard Lawrence Miller
pull_quote: TRUMAN. The Rise to Power. By Richard Lawrence Miller. 536 pages. McGraw-Hill. $19.95. THIS much everyone knows about Harry Truman: He made his way up in Missouri politics, and so into the White House, by courtesy of Tom Pendergast's machine. But even while consorting with some of the less wholesome elements of Kansas City, he managed to stay clear of the sort of activities that in time sent the boss and several of his cronies to jail. Richard Lawrence Miller's new book is not likely to change that assessment. What it does do, in rather more detail than the general reader may find absorbing or care to absorb, is to describe the future President's business and political dealings before anybody outside Missouri or many people in his own state had heard of him.   If ''The Rise to Power'' is not an expose, neither is it a revelation of character. The Truman here is the man we have met in previous biographies - a small-town striver, hard-working and self-educated, an energetic joiner, one of the boys at the poker table, a middle-level pol who was not above low-level deals, an unlucky businessman fated to build up debts and determined to pay them.

title: Pandaemonium
critic: John Gross Pandaemonium: the Coming of the MacHine As Seen By Contemporary Observers, 1660-1886. By Humphrey Jennings. Edited By Mary-Lou Jennings and Charles Madge. 376 Pages. Illustrated. the Free Press. $17.95
pull_quote: IN everyday speech, ''pandemonium'' has come to signify bedlam, cacophony, chaos. But the creation of the original Pandaemonium, the ''palace of all the devils'' in ''Paradise Lost,'' was anything but disorganized. On the contrary, it represented a heroic feat of mining and metallurgy, engineering and large-scale planning. What Milton shows us, as we watch the huge fabric take shape, is the Devil's energy being harnessed to audaciously constructive ends - although we are never allowed to forget that the result, however magnificent, is still the Devil's handiwork.   For Humphrey Jennings, Pandaemonium was a prophetic symbol of industrialism, and it provides not only the title but also the starting point of his attempt to chronicle ''the imaginative history of the Industrial Revolution.'' This was best done, he thought, by letting those who took part in the process speak for themselves, and Milton's lines usher in a collection of some 370 texts ranging from the 1660's to the 1880's - the testimony of scientists, artists, rich men, poor men and a great throng of miscellaneous witnesses. Between them, these passages (or ''images,'' as Jennings preferred to call them) are meant to provide a composite picture of how contemporaries experienced the triumph of the machine, how it transformed both their outward circumstances and inner lives.

title: The Building
author: Thomas Glynn
pull_quote: THE BUILDING. By Thomas Glynn. 371 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95. As many New Yorkers know all too well, apartment living can seem like a series of never-ending hassles: no water, not enough heat, broken radiators, temperamental elevators, noisy, obnoxious neighbors and irresponsible management. And if that weren't enough, the city often seems to add to all the frustrations with its own intractable conditions: dangerous subways, random violence, filthy streets, roving bands of nut cases, rip-off artists and con men. What Thomas Glynn has done in his first novel, ''The Building,'' is take all the grotesqueries of life in New York and reflect them through a fun-house mirror that distorts and magnifies all that is ugly and perverse. The result is a particularly nasty novel that strives to be taken as a hallucinatory epic about modern civilization - a novel that reads like a tabloid newspaper written by an assiduous student of Swift, Kafka and Marquez.   The building, as Mr. Glynn describes it, is ''huge, a grotesque magnificence'' - its apartments are vast, with parquet floors and oak doors; the lobby, gargantuan, with a marble floor, a gold-leaf ceiling and empty urns. Whatever grandeur it once possessed, however, has long since vanished: The courtyard is piled high with garbage; the floors are bloodstained from muggings; the structure itself, subject to electrical storms, floods and fires set by tenants.

title: The Unpublished Opinions Of The Warren Court
author: Bernard Schwartz
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE UNPUBLISHED OPINIONS OF THE WARREN COURT By Bernard Schwartz. 470 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $29.95.   ''THE facts of this case are unavoidably distressing. Needless, heedless, wanton and deliberate injury of the sort inflicted by Life's picture story is not an essential instrument of responsible journalism. Magazine writers and editors are not, by reason of their high office, relieved of the common obligation to avoid deliberately inflicting wanton and unnecessary injury. The prerogatives of the press - essential to our liberty - do not . . . confer a license for pointless assault.''   Abe Fortas made that stinging comment in an opinion written for the Supreme Court. ''The opinion of the Court,'' it was headed when Associate Justice Fortas circulated a draft to his colleagues on June 8, 1966, in the case of Time Inc. v. James J. Hill. But when the case was decided the following January, the opinion of the Court was by Associate Justice William J. Brennan Jr., and Justice Fortas dissented. The sharp words of his 1966 draft opinion were never published - until now.

He is one of only three or four World War II generals most of us can name. We know MacArthur, of course, then Eisenhower and finally perhaps Bradley, who lived so long. A FRIEND of mine, as a young man, showed every sign of feeling oppressed by an atmosphere of eminence at home. His family included many eminent men. His ancestors could hardly have been more eminent. There were times when I thought that gifted, indeed brilliant, though my friend was, this pressure to be eminent would prevent him from ever starting out in life. He couldn't stand the thought of an achievement that fell short of eminence.   My friend solved that particular problem of getting going by a ruse that was worthy of his ancestors. He embarked on a line of work so secret that neither his friends nor his family could inquire into its nature. Of course one must assume that within this line of work there were colleagues whose job it was to assess what my friend was doing - he had not put himself beyond the reach of criticism, but he had managed to make most people's opinion irrelevant to his work. It amuses me to think that if I tried now to assess my friend's achievement I could be arrested.

THE Italian immigrants to America were different from other ethnic groups, and nowhere is this more apparent than in literature. Even the poorest Jew treasured the sacred writings, and the Irish were English speakers with a tradition of storytelling. But the Italians, divided among themselves by regional dialects, sought to escape poverty by their labor, not their words. So few became writers that even today, nearly a century after the great waves of Italian immigration to this country began, perhaps the best known book by an Italian-American writer, about Italians, is a novel about organized crime.

A Roman Catholic priest of Croatian origin, he became in effect both the first Western expert on Russia and the first philosophic apologist for autocratic Great Russian nationalism. This excellent new English edition of his major work, the ''Politika'' or ''Discourses on Government,'' provides a rich analysis of Russia in the 1660's -and a prescription for its modernization that has never been followed, but may have relevance even today.

pull_quote: MYTHS OF GENDER Biological Theories About Women and Men. By Anne Fausto-Sterling. Illustrated. 258 pp. New York: Basic Books. $18.95.   BIOLOGY has frequently been invoked to sanction social inequalities, not least those associated with sex. A century ago, measures of head size and speculations about physiology were deployed to make the case that women were intellectually incapable of higher learning and physically unable to tolerate the strain of it. While these fallacies have long since been discredited, the invocations they represent remain alive, finding expression nowadays in the language of psychology, split-brain theory, endocrinology, genetics and sociobiology. Various scientists would have it that the structure of women's brains renders them, on average, less adept than men at spatial relations and mathematics; that they are victimized by their hormones into moodiness, passivity and volatility under stress; and that they have been fated by evolution to play social roles subordinate to those of men.   In ''Myths of Gender,'' an instructive and provocative book, Anne Fausto-Sterling, a developmental geneticist at Brown University, scrutinizes these claims and concludes that most of them are just so many scientifically baseless manifestations of the status quo. They owe their origins in the main to unconscious bias, she holds, for in the socially charged area of sex differences ''it is inherently impossible for any individual to do unbiased research.''

A FOUNDATION, Dwight Macdonald once remarked, ''is a large body of money completely surrounded by people who want some.'' According to the Internal Revenue Service, the United States has 28,468 philanthropic funds. Their assets total $50 billion, from which they hand out $4 billion every year to recipients of their choosing. Altruism apart, foundations flourish because they allow rich people to perpetuate their fortunes. Without this option, much of their money would go to governments in inheritance and estate taxes. Private benevolence should be encouraged, we are told, because it takes on tasks not covered by public programs. In ''The Golden Donors,'' Waldemar A. Nielsen finds that few foundations are delivering on that promise. This should be a matter of public concern. After all, one reason taxpayers must pay more every April is that wealth made over to foundations not only avoids inheritance levies but becomes tax-exempt in its new incarnation.

(Ages 3 to 6) MOST adults have trouble remembering how central size is to the world-view of children.   Their world is one of castlelike houses, hippo-size dogs and grown-ups who lumber about like Goliath come to crush David. A power estimate follows: big people command awesome power; little people must take heed. Children's humor tries to make light of this heavy situation. In some cases big people are cut down to size. In others little people grow even smaller. Like most humor, such jokes serve to prick the balloon of anxiety.

title: Gerald's Party
author: Robert Coover
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GERALD'S PARTY By Robert Coover. 316 pp. New York: The Linden Press/ Simon & Schuster. $17.95.   ROBERT COOVER has given us some of the most distinguished fiction of his generation. ''The Origin of the Brunists'' (1978), ''The Universal Baseball Association'' (1968) and long sections of ''The Public Burning'' (1977) are enduring works, demonstrating a total command of idiomatic American speech with a philosophical acuity rare in American literature. These are political and sexual parables at once deadly serious and deadly funny. In his most recent novel, however, Mr. Coover has both compressed and exploded his signature techniques well beyond comprehension. ''Gerald's Party'' is one we have all reluctantly been to, in both contemporary life and fiction, and the point is there will be no relief until it is over. A cranky courage is nevertheless operating here; as the narrator tells us, straight-faced: ''The mirror, as parodist, did not lie - on the contrary - but neither did it merely reflect: rather, like a camera, it created the truth we saw in it, thereby murdering potentiality.'' And of all the murders in this book, the novel's own self-slaying is the only one with clear motivation and ruthless intent.

Perhaps we no longer notice how startling such normality is because Spain today is so much like the rest of the West, unrecognizable, as the novelist Juan Goytisolo recently suggested, in terms of its own past cliches and popular images.

IN her first collection of short stories, Mary Flanagan writes about women and girls who are bad, but not in any conventional way. The great seductresses, the women who sell themselves body and soul, these are not her protagonists. Instead she writes about women who should lead normal lives - women of class, money and discontent. Women who have refinement, intellect and a large dose of emptiness. At times in their refinement, they feel too blase. They are hopelessly bourgeois, and their gestures toward liberation often become grotesque distortions of the bourgeois. These respectable housewives, gourmet cooks, guests of college roommates, mothers, artists and even a doctor tip over the edge at some point. IT is a morning in April 1941. In Dachau 500 prisoners in blue-striped uniforms - the inmates of the ''Jewish block'' of Camp Number Three - tensely await the new day's horrors. Some will be beaten to death, some shot. Others will be taken to the Bunker (''the sinister cave used for solitary confinement, where the tortures inflicted . . . were so cruel that they were kept secret even from the regular SS guards'') or sent to a torture table called the Bock (on which one would be bound and then struck with a bullwhip that had been soaked in water). The crematorium will receive its share. Groups of others will listlessly head off to do the camp's soul-destroying, physically punishing work, in the stone quarry or the swamp.

title: Good To Eat
author: John Gross
critic: John Gross Good To Eat: Riddles of Food & Culture. By Marvin Harris. 289 Pages. Simon and Schuster. $17.95
pull_quote: SCIENTIFICALLY speaking, Marvin Harris tells us, human beings are omnivores - between us we manage to consume an enormous number of different substances, animal, vegetable and mineral. But that doesn't mean that we all eat everything that is edible. Some of us eat some things, some of us eat other things, and one man's delicacy is quite likely to be another man's aversion.   In many cultures, such items as termites and cockroach eggs form part of the regular diet; rats, according to a recent survey, are eaten in 42 different societies; there are South American Indian tribes that particularly enjoy getting their teeth into a tarantula. On the other hand all over the world - not least in regions plagued by malnutrition - there are taboos forbidding the consumption of food that is both nourishing and readily available.

title: Anxiety
author: Donald W Goodwin
pull_quote: ANXIETY. By Donald W. Goodwin, M. D. 234 pages. Oxford University Press. $17.95. ''No Grand Inquisitor has in readiness such terrible tortures as has anxiety,'' wrote Soren Kierkegaard in ''The Concept of Dread,'' ''and no spy knows how to attack more artfully the man he suspects, choosing the instant when he is weakest, nor knows how to lay traps where he will be caught and ensnared, as anxiety knows how, and no sharpwitted judge knows how to interrogate, to examine the accused, as anxiety does, which never lets him escape, neither by diversion nor by noise, neither at work nor at play, neither by day nor by night.''   Kierkegaard, Donald W. Goodwin writes in his new book, ''discovered anxiety in 1844.'' Surely, there were individuals before that who suffered from the unfortunate afflictions of anxiety - what Rollo May called ''a nameless and formless uneasiness,'' a vague, persistent feeling of ''uncertainty and helplessness.'' In 1621, Robert Burton expounded upon similar varieties of psychic distress in ''The Anatomy of Melancholy''; in the same century, Pascal wrote of the despair that accompanies man's realization that his life is ''swallowed up in the eternity before and behind it.'' Still, it was with the progressive loss of faith in the old certainties of religion and reason, that anxiety -along with dread and alienation - became elevated into a philosophical concept used to define the condition of modern man.
headline: Books of the Times; Fears and Phobias

title: Reinhold Niebuhr. A Biography
author: Richard Wightman Fox
pull_quote: REINHOLD NIEBUHR. A Biography. By Richard Wightman Fox. 340 pages.   Pantheon Books. $19.95. BETWEEN the mid 1930's and the mid-1950's, Reinhold Niebuhr was America's most influential churchman. He would never be a popular figure in the manner of Billy Graham or Bishop Fulton J. Sheen, nor as esteemed among theologians as his brother, Richard, but in the world of political and social controversy, Richard Fox makes plain in his finely balanced biography, no one came close.

title: Dickens And The Social Order
author: Myron Magnet
pull_quote: DICKENS AND THE SOCIAL ORDER.   By Myron Magnet. 266 pages. University of Pennsylvania Press. $39.95. WHAT was Charles Dickens's social philosophy?   Did he even have one, beyond what one critic has called the ''philosophy of Christmas''? To the extent that Dickens can be given a political label, he has traditionally been seen as a splendid but piecemeal liberal reformer, a radical in the Victorian sense of the term who directed his anger against specific social abuses and then fell back on hazy appeals for a change of heart all round.

title: Nine Women
author: Shirley Ann Grau
pull_quote: NINE WOMEN. By Shirley Ann Grau. 204 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95. In such earlier books as ''The Black Prince and Other Stories,'' ''The Keepers of the House'' and ''The Wind Shifting West,'' Shirley Ann Grau not only established herself as a highly acclaimed writer, gifted with a highly tuned, authoritative style, but also as one of Faulkner's heirs - a Southerner whose stories remained firmly grounded in the places, as well as the gothicism and oral traditions of her native land.   In ''Nine Women,'' her latest collection of stories and her first book in eight years, Miss Grau moves beyond the more insistent regionalism of her previous work to delineate the lives of nine very different women living in widely disparate worlds - tony, blue-blooded summer resorts, ingrown Roman Catholic communities, poor black neighborhoods and isolated bayou towns. With a couple exceptions - an incident with a gun, and a portentously foreshadowed disappearance - Miss Grau's penchant for melodrama and violence has grown more muted; her taste for mythic symbolism a little more restrained.

title: Good To Eat. Riddles Of Food And Culture
author: Marvin Harris.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GOOD TO EAT Riddles of Food and Culture. By Marvin Harris. 289 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95.   WHY do we eat what we do, rapturous about one sort of food and loathing another? Why, to take one example especially odious in the Western point of view, do we despise dung beetles? In the 1930's a researcher working in Laos, where the beetles were prized, tried one and found that, toasted, it had ''a nice crisp exterior and soft interior of souffle consistency which is by no means unpleasant.'' Not so bad. But of course it is terrible, full of associations connoting filth and primal fear. To Westerners, anyway. The dung beetle, as the anthropologist Claude Levi-Strauss might put it, is ''bad to think.'' Mr. Levi-Strauss and a great many other scholars see in the food choices people make a panoply of symbols reflecting deep truths about human nature. But to Marvin Harris, a feisty anthropologist whose previous books include ''Cannibals and Kings: The Origins of Cultures,'' that emphasis on symbolism evidently seems precious and off the mark. In ''Good to Eat'' he counters it with the unromantic, common-sensical framework called cultural materialism that he has expounded in several books. Cultural materialism, he has written, asserts that ''human social life is a response to the practical problems of earthly existence.''

Buckley Jr. He just turned 60. His magazine, National Review, is 30, and his television program, ''Firing Line,'' is 20. He is a man who richly deserves praise. He is generous, erudite, witty and courageous, and he has performed a service to the whole nation, even to those who disagree with him. When the tide of intellectual and political history seemed headed inexorably leftward and the conservative movement was caricatured (not entirely unfairly) as a collection of segregationists, Babbitts and crackpot generals, Mr. Buckley had the temerity to uphold the cause of Toryism. He and his magazine nurtured the movement, helped it recover from the 1964 Goldwater debacle and gave it a rallying point and sounding board as it gradually gained the strength and respectability to win the Presidency. Conservatism is far from the dominant intellectual force in the country today, but neither is liberalism. There is now a balance between the movements, a permanent contest, and Mr. Buckley deserves credit for helping make it so.

(Ages 10 to 14) BEFORE I met Vera and Bill Cleaver, I could not imagine how two people could collaborate on something as individual and personal as a book. After I met them in the early 1970's, at a conference on the literature of Appalachia at which they were the featured speakers, I felt I understood. WHEN Reinhold Niebuhr died three weeks before his 79th birthday in 1971, obituaries identified him as the most influential American theologian of this century. That he surely was, but for Niebuhr himself the distinction might have seemed, to use one of his favorite words, ''ironic.'' He usually balked at calling himself a ''theologian'' (preferring in-stead ''teacher of social ethics''), and not a few academic theologians regarded his modesty as well grounded. When he joined the Union Theological Seminary faculty in 1928, his fellow teachers gave him a chilly reception. Niebuhr had never earned a doctorate, and some saw him as little more than a spellbinding preacher with rough-hewn Midwestern habits whom the seminary's president, Henry Sloane Coffin, wanted on the faculty because his popularity on the college chapel circuit and his visible activism in left-wing and pacifist causes might help recruitment.

In ''Mothers on Trial,'' she describes it as a birthright for them to defend jealously. This apparent change of heart coincides with changes in popular feminist priorities; children have become as politically correct as careers. It also reflects the harm done to women, particularly older, traditional homemakers, by ''enlightened,'' nonsexist family-law reforms. Women have been impoverished by no-fault divorce and low, short-term alimony awards. Now, according to Phyllis Chesler, courts are less likely to presume mothers make better parents, and women are beginning to lose their children.

IN what amounts to the prologue of Iris Murdoch's new novel, ''The Good Apprentice,'' young Edward Baltram, a college student living in a London bed-sitter, tricks his friend, Mark Wilsden, into taking a psychedelic drug, something Mark would never knowingly do. The resulting ''trip'' is a good one; Mark, in ecstasy, envisions the world as ''one . . . big . . . fish,'' sees God descending ''like a lift,'' and falls happily asleep. So Edward feels free to heed the sexual summons of a young woman he has recently met. But when he returns to Mark, he finds the room empty, the window open, and Mark's smashed body lying on the pavement below.   The official inquest pronounces Mark's death an accident. Edward is merely suspended from college for a year. But inside his head he descends into a black pit of guilt and self-loathing. At almost the same time, Edward's stepbrother, Stuart Cuno, decides to drop out of school, renounce his promising mathematics career and seek a pure life of service and celibacy. Thus the nearly biblical theme of Miss Murdoch's 22d novel is sounded: Is it possible to survive in the presence either of black evil or white goodness? Who has the better chance in the modern world, the good Samaritan or Cain?

title: The Riddle Of The Dinosaur
author: John Noble Wilford
pull_quote: THE RIDDLE OF THE DINOSAUR. By John Noble Wilford. Illustrated. 304 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $22.95. THE last dinosaur died 65 million years ago. For 160 million years they flourished, living on every major land mass with the possible exception of Antarctica. Some dinosaurs were grazing herbivores. Others were carnivores, fierce predators that hunted in packs. Some were small, no bigger than rabbits or crows. The bigger ones - diplodocus, brontosaurus, brachiosaurus - were the largest land animals that ever lived. They were the dominant animals in the time known as the Age of Reptiles. They saw the first flowers bloom 100 million years ago. None survived.   ''Dinosaurs live today only in the minds of the species that in all likelihood owes its existence to the dinosaurs' demise,'' writes John Noble Wilford, a Pulitzer Prize-winning science reporter for The New York Times, in ''The Riddle of the Dinosaur.'' ''If the dinosaurs had not become extinct, if their kind had continued to dominate the land, mammals might still be small rodentlike creatures foraging by night and hiding by day from the mighty reptiles. Or if the dinosaurs had lived on beyond the Cretaceous to become extinct in more recent times, the Age of Mammals might only be in its infancy, with no humans or even protohumans yet in sight. We have every reason, therefore, to be fascinated with dinosaurs, especially their extinction.''

His resuscitation is evident in the 1982 reissue of his autobiography, ''An Artist in America,'' by the University of Missouri Press, the big exhibition of his work organized last year by Bard College and the installation of his busy 10-panel mural, ''America Today,'' as the sole lobby adornment of the new Equitable Life Assurance tower on Seventh Avenue and 51st Street.
