pull_quote: THE ENDLESS GAME By Bryan Forbes. 309 pp. New York: Random House. $17.95.   ALEC LEAMAS, the spy who came in from the cold, would find no warm hearth in the England where Alec Hillsden, an angst-ridden secret agent, keeps playing an ''endless game.'' In Bryan Forbes's gripping, relentlessly chilling novel, modern London, like the characters we meet there in sleazy sauna clubs and crumbling Government corridors, is a burnt-out case. The center of an empire on which the sun has permanently set, the city has sunk to a dreary, decaying ghetto of concrete, rust, junk food and plastic flotsam. Immigrants live behind doors that are ''like rotten teeth in the mouth of a derelict.'' Brutal punks crucify cats for a thrill. Pay phones don't work, the subways are hellish, and nearly every day some group with a political grudge indiscriminately tosses a bomb at innocent bystanders.
headline: A DEEP FAITH IN OLD-FASHIONED EVIL

title: Sympathy And Science
author: Regina Markell Morantz-Sanchez.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SYMPATHY AND SCIENCE Women Physicians in American Medicine. By Regina Markell Morantz-Sanchez. 464 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $24.95.   WHAT difference does it make and to whom whether women can be physicians? Some of the trends in feminist scholarship of the 1980's might suggest that women's influence would transform medicine utterly and promote holistic healing, prevention and egalitarian doctor-patient relations. Evelyn Fox Keller and Ruth Bleier have argued in their books on gender and science that masculinity shaped what we know as science. Carol Gilligan has emphasized ways in which women are different from men and revived the belief of 19th-century feminists that women are morally superior. It has been argued that women's greater connectedness with others gives them less of an adversary relation with the objects of their study or treatment and that the incorporation of more women in science and the professions would change both fields substantially. But another feminist tradition emphasizes the essential similarity of men and women and criticizes American culture's exaggeration of gender difference.
headline: THE MASCULINIZATION OF MEDICINE

title: Prairie Songs
author: Pam Conrad
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
PRAIRIE SONGS By Pam Conrad. Illustrated by Darryl S. Zudeck. 167 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $11.50. (Ages 10 and up) DAKOTA DUGOUT By Ann Turner. Illustrated by Ronald Himler. Unpaged. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $10.95. (Ages 8 to 12) GROWING up with a computer and a video cassette recorder, it is hard for children to imagine life before technology transformed this country. In our urban society, few children have the opportunity to test themselves against the rigors of nature. The frontiers they dream of are the fantasy worlds of other planets, and they imagine facing them not with ax and plow but with robots and laser guns.

These two books look back a century to the prairies and the pioneers who first settled them armed with little but their own fortitude. It is Willa Cather country, a bleak but fertile literary landscape where, in Cather's memorable phrase in ''My Antonia,'' ''the grass was the country, as the water is the sea.'' Both books depict the the harshness and isolation of that land.
headline: CHILDRENS' BOOKS

title: Wrap It In Flags
author: Robert Terrall
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WRAP IT IN FLAGS By Robert Terrall. 339 pp. New York: Penguin Books. Paper, $6.95.   OVER the last few decades, most often pseudonymously (as MacLennan Roberts, Brett Halliday and others), Robert Terrall has written some 50 novels. ''Wrap It in Flags'' adds another to the brood, and a hybrid child it is.
headline: WAR GAMES

title: At Any Cost
author: Morton Mintz. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AT ANY COST Corporate Greed, Women, and the Dalkon Shield. By Morton Mintz. Illustrated. 308 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $17.95.   IN 1971 many women, frightened by bad publicity about the side effects of oral contraceptive pills, were delighted to hear of a new contraceptive alternative: the Dalkon Shield, a crab-shaped intrauterine device that the A. H. Robins Company in Richmond was marketing as ''modern'' and ''safe.'' The company quoted the developer, claiming the shield was without ''the actual and potential hazards of systemic medication for birth control.'' It quickly became the leading intrauterine device, with more than 4.5 million sold worldwide, before sales were suspended in the United States in June 1974.
headline: WHAT STANDARDS FOR CORPORATE CRIME?

title: Japan Solo: A Practical Guide For Independent Travelers
author: Eiji Kanno
pull_quote: Japan Solo: A Practical Guide for Independent Travelers By Eiji Kanno. 252 pages. Nitchi Map-Publishing Company. $12.50.   There is no need to bring along toothbrush and toothpaste to a Japanese hotel, Eiji Kanno suggests in his new guidebook, ''Japan Solo''; any good hotel provides them free of charge. But it is advisable, he cautions, to carry tissues and a handkerchief because many public restrooms do not have toilet paper, and almost none have paper towels.
headline: TRAVEL BOOKSHELF

title: A Door Into Ocean
author: Joan Slonczewski
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A DOOR INTO OCEAN by Joan Slonczewski (Arbor House, $17.95) starts so slowly that many readers may not get past the 40 leisurely pages of Part One. This would be a mistake. By the time the conflict she introduces so obliquely in Part One has moved to center stage, you not only know the antagonists intimately, you care passionately about the outcome. Two sister-planets, Valedon and Shora, harbor societies that appear to be mirror images of each other. On Valedon, an Earthlike world, the principal occupations are trade and war; those Valans who compete successfully are rewarded with wealth and power. On Shora, a water world with no dry land and no males, self-awareness and ecological awareness are so linked that the inhabitants refer to themselves as Sharers; whole-hearted participation in the planet-wide web of life is not an ideal or a goal for Sharers but a source of pleasure so intense that they have trouble believing that creatures who cannot ''share'' are human.
headline: SCIENCE FICTION

title: Swimming To Cambodia
author: Spalding Gray
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SWIMMING TO CAMBODIA. By Spalding Gray. (Theatre Communications Group, Paper, $7.95.) Theater critics have compared the actor-storyteller Spalding Gray to figures as diverse as Woody Allen, Mark Twain, Andy Warhol and Mr. Rogers - an indication of how difficult it is to categorize his work.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Good Apprentice
author: Iris Murdoch
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GOOD APPRENTICE By Iris Murdoch. 522 pp. New York: Viking. $18.95. AT the end of her first book, an enduring study of Jean-Paul Sartre published in 1953, Iris Murdoch prophetically lamented that Sartre's ''inability to write a great novel is a tragic symptom of a situation which afflicts us all.'' Her own inability has extended now through 22 novels, of which the best seem to me ''Bruno's Dream'' (1969), ''The Black Prince'' (1973), ''A Word Child'' (1975) and her latest, ''The Good Apprentice.'' So fecund and exuberant is Miss Murdoch's talent that many more novels may be expected from her. If ''The Good Apprentice'' marks the start of her strongest phase, and it may, then a great novel could yet come, rather surprisingly in the incongruous form of the 19th-century realistic novel. The age of Samuel Beckett and Thomas Pynchon, post-Joycean and post-Faulknerian, is set aside by Miss Murdoch's novelistic procedures, almost as though she thus chose to assert her own direct continuity with the major 19th-century Russian and British masters of fiction.
headline: A COMEDY OF WORLDLY SALVATION

title: The Seventh Secret
author: Irving Wallace
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SEVENTH SECRET. By Irving Wallace. (Dutton, $17.95.) ''Another book on Hitler? . . . It has become an industry,'' says a character in this novel about the ''real'' story behind Hitler's and Eva Braun's supposed suicides.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Taking Sides. The Education Of A Militant Mind
author: Michael Harrington.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TAKING SIDES The Education of a Militant Mind. By Michael Harrington. 278 pp. New York: Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $16.95.   MICHAEL HARRINGTON started in literature. As he says in the introduction to this collection of his essays, his mentor was T. S. Eliot, ''a self-proclaimed monarchist and classicist.'' But he came to be a liberal journalist, a theorist of democratic Socialism, and, above all, a political activist, and this book, collected from the writings of more than 30 years, consists for the most part of reports from the front, bearing the occasional reactions, self-accusations and justifications of someone who has constantly sought to explain himself, his changing commitments and alliances, to himself and to the world.   There are not only reports, but reflections. The book, divided by subject as well as by time, sets out his thoughts on a range of things from the politics of the Peace Movement to the political novel and the lessons that Disney World has for Socialists (a splendid piece). Some of the material comes from a long way away, or will now seem so to those younger or from a different place. Just occasionally the controversies of the day before yesterday become inaudible under coverings of discretion: ''For Mr. F., C. H., and others, there is a counterposition between political freedom and economic and social freedom. As Mr. F. writes . . .''
headline: RETHINKING SOCIALISM

title: Darkness
author: Bharati Mukherjee
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DARKNESS By Bharati Mukherjee. 199 pp. New York: Penguin Books. Paper, $5.95.   IN the story ''The World According to Hsu'' (which seems closest to the actual biography of the author, a Bengali immigrant married to a Canadian) a woman vacationing in a tourist island paradise undergoing a revolution listens to her husband read about geology and feels ''with effort she might become an expert on the plate tectonics of emotion.'' In this superb collection of short stories, ''Darkness,'' Bharati Mukherjee writes of the tearing off of old selves, the collisions of Eastern and Western lives, the wrinkling up of new forms of identity.
headline: BRIGHT MOMENTS OF DISAPPOINTMENT

title: When Light Pierced The Darkness
author: Nechama Tec.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WHEN LIGHT PIERCED THE DARKNESS Christian Rescue of Jews in Nazi-Occupied Poland. By Nechama Tec. 262 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $19.95. WITH the recent release of Claude Lanzmann's film ''Shoah,'' Nechama Tec's book comes out at a time when many people are thinking about the destruction of European Jews during World War II. Her book tells the story of Jewish survivors and their rescuers in Nazi-occupied Poland. Mrs. Tec herself lived through the war in Poland. Her family was assisted by a number of people, including the German manager of a factory the family had owned before the war.   They paid some of their helpers, not ransom money but agreed-upon fees for services. Others helped them without being paid. Since Mrs. Tec and her sister had what was called a ''good appearance'' (they didn't look Jewish), they could move around and even work, passing as non-Jewish. Mrs. Tec previously published a memoir, ''Dry Tears,'' describing her experiences, and even though her own biography is not incorporated into ''When Light Pierced the Darkness,'' the strongest points of the book derive from the author's personal knowledge of what it meant to be a Jew: ''In those days being different always suggested being Jewish - a dangerous possibility.'' The threatening wisdom of this sentence is worth many a sociological generalization about Nazi-occupied Poland.
headline: POLES WHO SAVED JEWS

title: A Writer's Time
author: Kenneth Atchity
pull_quote: A WRITER'S TIME. A Guide to the Creative Process, from Vision through Revision. By Kenneth Atchity. 194 pages. Illustrated. Norton. $12.95. FIRST, the good news. Kenneth   Atchity's ''Writer's Time'' is crammed with the sort of useful advice that it seems to take some people years to learn. ''Don't forget,'' Professor Atchity writes in a chapter on the subject of ''foreshadowing'' in novels and plays, ''that the audience doesn't want to be surprised any more than you do. It wants to know, in advance, that it's going to be surprised so it can worry itself to that point, imagining.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Bedside Manners
author: Edward Shorter
pull_quote: BEDSIDE MANNERS. The Troubled History of Doctors and Patients. By Edward Shorter. 316 pages. Illustrated. Simon & Schuster. $18.95. ONCE upon a time doctors were hopeless, and everyone knew it. Then, in the 19th century, they learned to understand the nature of disease, and enjoyed a dramatic rise in prestige. But while the new confidence they inspired was itself a valuable therapeutic asset, until some 40 years ago there was a strong element of myth-making, even bluff, in the image of streamlined progress that they projected. Despite a few limited advances, they were still unable to cure most of the illnesses they diagnosed.   It was only in the 1940's that the actual practice of medicine began to catch up with its full scientific pretensions. In particular, the revolution in drug therapy - signaled most obviously by the coming of antibiotics -enormously widened the range of effective treatment. But the triumphs have been achieved at a considerable cost. Doctors have tended to become technicians, their attention focused on the disease rather than the patient; gains in medical knowledge have all too often been accompanied by a decline in the quality of medical care. And patients in turn have become disaffected. Their trust has been eroded, and in many cases they have even reverted to the old attitude of seeing doctors as positive adversaries.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Collected Poems: 1948-1984
author: Derek Walcott
pull_quote: COLLECTED POEMS: 1948-1984. By Derek Walcott. 516 pages. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $25. ''I   HAD no nation now,'' Derek Walcott writes in ''The Star-Apple Kingdom,'' ''but the imagination.'' It's a statement that succinctly sums up the issues that have preoccupied this eloquent poet throughout his career - a career handsomely celebrated, at midpoint, with this magisterial new collection. Born in the West Indies to a family of English, African and Dutch descent, Mr. Walcott grew up a ''divided child,'' caught on the margins of different cultures, and from this mixed paternity, he has forged the themes of his verse, as well as that rare thing - an authentic poetic voice.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Wiseguy: Life In A Mafia Family
author: Nicholas Pileggi
pull_quote: WISEGUY: LIFE IN A MAFIA FAMILY.   By Nicholas Pileggi. 256 pages. Simon & Schuster. $17.95. NICHOLAS PILEGGI wasn't impressed when first approached by a lawyer and asked to write the story of Henry Hill, a gangster who had recently joined the Justice Department's Federal Witness Protection Program. In Mr. Pileggi's nearly two decades as a journalist he had ''gotten bored with the egomaniacal ravings of illiterate hoods masquerading as benevolent Godfathers.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Good Morning Blues
author: Count Basie, as told to Albert Murray
pull_quote: GOOD MORNING BLUES. By Count Basie, as told to Albert Murray. Illustrated. 399 pages. Random House. $19.95. IN the pantheon of jazz, Count   Basie is right up there with such other legendary band leaders as Duke Ellington and Benny Goodman. In ''Good Morning Blues,'' Basie's voice comes through like his piano - laid-back, yet self-assured. For his memoirs, the Count was fortunate to have as his co-author Albert Murray, an accomplished writer with a sense of history whose own books include ''Stomping the Blues,'' ''South to a Very Old Place'' and ''The Omni-Americans.'' Because Count Basie's life as a musician criss-crossed the country from Harlem to Kansas City and all the one-night whistle stops in between, and because the Basie band pioneered on the international road from London to Tokyo, his personal story ranks with the most telling accounts of the evolution of jazz from the 1920's to now. Basie, the epitome of swing, died at 79 in 1984, but not before sharing many hours of memories with Mr. Murray.
headline: Books: Jazz Nobility

title: Symbols Of America
author: Hal Morgan
pull_quote: SYMBOLS OF AMERICA. By Hal Morgan. 239 pages. Illustrated. Viking. $35. AT first sight ''Symbols of   America'' may seem a rather grandiose title for a book about trademarks. But if the business of America is business (as on the whole it is), why shouldn't the symbols of America be commercial (as on the whole they are)? At all events, Hal Morgan's compendium represents a veritable codebook of popular culture. The brand images he has assembled have not just served to sell products; for more than 100 years, they have also played an incalculable part in coloring American experience.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Bad Manners
author: Maggie Paley
pull_quote: BAD MANNERS. By Maggie Paley. 198 pages. Clarkson N. Potter. $14.95. There are New Yorkers who have evolved a sort of rarified life that takes place almost entirely on the phone. They conduct business meetings, therapy sessions and romances over the phone; they order groceries, pizza and Chinese food over the phone, and they plan parties, orchestrate affairs, and plot the course of their lives over the phone. To deal with all this, they've also developed their own complicated rules of etiquette and gamesmanship, involving the answering machine, the secretary and the multiple-line telephone. Who calls whom first, who keeps whom waiting, who leaves messages for whom and who puts whom on hold -all are indices of where one stands.   It's the one clever conceit of this first novel by Maggie Paley - a former editor at Life, the Paris Review and The Saturday Evening Post -that the entire narrative takes place on the phone; everything else happens off stage. What we read - or overhear - are the conversations between four inveterate telephone users: Violet, an over-sexed publicist, who's trying to choose between her devoted boyfriend and a hunky, not-so-bright movie star; Helena, a book publisher's somewhat prissy wife, who's having trouble conceiving; Alexandra, a radio talk-show personality, who's carrying on less than fulfilling affairs with an Italian playboy and a ''human potential'' expert, and Kitty, an ambtious entrepeneur who's vying with Alexandra for the attentions of the same men.
headline: INDICES OF MODERNITY

title: The Female Malady
author: Elaine Showalter. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE FEMALE MALADY Women, Madness, and English Culture, 1830-1980. By Elaine Showalter. Illustrated. 312 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $19.95.   FROM the 17th century to the present day, the number of women in psychiatric care has greatly exceeded the number of men. Elaine Showalter, in this feminist history of psychiatry in England from 1830 to 1980, has examined how far this preponderance can be regarded as a cultural phenomenon. Mrs. Showalter, the author of ''A Literature of Their Own: Women Writers from Bronte to Lessing,'' argues that feminine mental illness is a protest against feminine subjection and exploitation; that women have been labeled mad because mental illness has been defined and codified by male psychiatrists; and that changing social attitudes to women have affected psychiatric diagnosis and treatment.
headline: CRAZY BY DEFINITION

title: Benchley At The Theater: Dramatic Criticism, 1920-1940
author: Robert Benchley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BENCHLEY AT THE THEATRE: Dramatic Criticism, 1920-1940. By Robert Benchley. (The Ipswich Press, P.O. Box 291, Ipswich, Mass. 01938, $14.95.) The best dramatic criticism recalls theatrical occasions to vivid presence, reveals what is not obvious about their nature and workings and relates them to larger contexts of art and life.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Nietzsche: Life As Literature
author: Alexander Nehamas.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NIETZSCHE Life as Literature. By Alexander Nehamas. 261 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $17.50.   THE HUMANITIES have become uncertain of their way: recent discourse in philosophy and literary theory suggests that reason has undermined trust in reason; the traditional distinction between theory and literature, between philosophy and poetry, has blurred. Such uncertainty has renewed appreciation of Nietzsche's attempt to replace Plato's idealized Socrates, whose life and death celebrated confidence in reason, with his own ideal image of the philosopher, an idealization of himself as a poet-philosopher opening doors to a post-Socratic, postmodern culture. At issue is the future of philosophy. Philosophers and anyone interested in philosophy ought therefore to welcome Alexander Nehamas's elegant and challenging interpretation of this ''most writerly of philosophers.''
headline: THE WORLD AS A WORK OF ART

title: Pleasures Of The Belle Epoque
author: Charles Rearick. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PLEASURES OF THE BELLE EPOQUE Entertainment & Festivity in Turn-of-the-Century France. By Charles Rearick. Illustrated. 240 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $29.95.   ON a February night in 1899, the President of the French Republic, Felix Faure, died of a stroke, and rumor quickly spread that he had departed in a paroxysm of amorous pleasure that was hazardous to the health of an overweight bourgeois. The following year, across the Seine near the Ecole des Beaux Arts, Oscar Wilde suffered an acute brain inflammation and achieved a final, tragic blend of art and life; like his earnest rake, Ernest Worthing, he died in a Paris hotel room, oppressed, the legend goes, by ghastly wallpaper. Neither Faure nor Wilde appears in Charles Rearick's instructive and entertaining book, ''Pleasures of the Belle Epoque,'' but the Irish poet spoke for the age when he insisted that ''the only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it.''
headline: FRENCH BREAD AND CIRCUSES

title: The Progress Of A Fire
author: Robert Abel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PROGRESS OF A FIRE By Robert Abel. 509 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.   ''YOU know the story,'' Joe Turner says halfway through Robert Abel's second novel, ''The Progress of a Fire.'' ''Anything forty miles outside of Boston is on its own, except for paying taxes.'' Sawmills and sugarhouses, pickup trucks and pig farms: the western Massachusetts hill towns, where this novel is set, seem so far away in spirit from the city that calls itself the Hub that Turner isn't even sure the state fire marshal will bother to investigate the town of Lake Ecstasy's latest bit of arson. This time a barn belonging to the painter Chong Hu Lan has gone up. Everybody knows that ''The Club,'' a gang of swamp Yankee hoodlums, did it - but nobody will sign a complaint in a town where The Club outnumbers the police force.
headline: JIM AND CHONG FIND INNER PEACE

title: Fdr: The New York Years 1928-1933
author: Kenneth S. Davis.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FDR The New York Years. 1928-1933. By Kenneth S. Davis. 512 pp. New York: Random House. $19.95.   IN 1982 Congress appropriated $25,000 to underwrite a joint session of the Senate and House of Representatives to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the birth of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, the man who was President longer than any other. Two years ago there was no recognition by the Federal Government of the centennial of Eleanor Roosevelt's birth or of her years in the White House and the activities that earned her the appellation ''the first lady of the world.'' However, in 1974 Congress appropriated $7,500,000 for a proper remembrance of Herbert Hoover's birth. Kenneth S. Davis's book on Roosevelt's years as Governor of New York is a healthy corrective to such mindless official judgments.
headline: SIGNPOSTS TO WASHINGTON

title: The Moral Life Of Children
author: Robert Coles
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MORAL LIFE OF CHILDREN By Robert Coles. Illustrated. 302 pp. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. $19.95. THE POLITICAL LIFE OF CHILDREN By Robert Coles. Illustrated. 341 pp. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. $19.95. WHEN I was in grade school, Christmas time was a problem. We were always made to sing those mysterious carols, and although ''Jingle Bells'' was a piece of cake, most of the canon was fraught with danger for a Jewish boy. Harold Goldstein and I figured out a way to defend ourselves. We turned the line ''Deck the halls with boughs of holly'' into ''Deck the halls with rows of cholly,'' this last word being our rhymed distortion of ''challah,'' the delicious Jewish bread served on the Sabbath. No one actually heard us do this. We believed Christian ears would not suffer our defiance lightly, and so we silently mouthed the words rather than utter them. When we had done this, Harold and I always exchanged the kind of glance that might have passed between Kim Philby and Guy Burgess in the corridors of Whitehall.
headline: A SINGER OF THEIR TALES

title: Blind Trust
author: John J. Nance. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BLIND TRUST By John J. Nance. Illustrated. 416 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $17.95.   WHEN the domestic airline industry was deregulated in 1978, safety specialists worried that a rash of new airlines and an uninhibited scramble for business would bring about an increase in crashes. In ''Blind Trust'' John J. Nance, a lawyer, a former airline pilot and the author of ''Splash of Colors'' (about Braniff International Airlines), argues that deregulation has indeed created a ''national crisis'' in airline safety. To advance this thesis, he superbly details two pertinent accidents: one involving an Air Florida twin-engine Boeing 737 that crashed in January 1982 just after taking off from Washington National Airport in a snowstorm, and another in which an Air Illinois turboprop crashed in the fall of 1983 because its captain pushed on through murky weather after losing electric power from both engines.
headline: ALMOST PERFECT IS A FAILING GRADE

title: In The Penny Arcade
author: Steven Millhauser
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
IN THE PENNY ARCADE By Steven Millhauser. 164 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $14.95.
STEVEN MILLHAUSER'S first novel, ''Edwin

Mullhouse: The Life and Death of an American Writer'' (1972), was a playfully conceived, furiously written, quirky, richly metaphorical fiction. What an idea for a book! At the age of 10 Edwin Mullhouse produces the classic American novel ''Cartoons,'' all the while dogged by his best friend, biographer and dark-souled secret sharer, Jeffrey Cartwright. Edwin is a more or less ordinary child until he writes his book, yet his commonplace world of yellow raincoats, sugar dots, Viewmasters and pulpy kids' books is cast in a spectral, wondrous light. Jeffrey's description of ''Cartoons'' could be Mr. Millhauser's of his own novel: ''If, then, our first reaction . . . is that we have entered an unreal world, blissful or boring . . . gradually we come to feel that we are experiencing nothing less than the real world itself, a world that has been lost to us through habit and inattention, and that we are hereby being taught to repossess.''
headline: FIRST LOVE AND THE LAST AUTOMATONS

title: The Wand
author: Allan W. Eckert. Illustrated by David Wiesner.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WAND The Return to Mesmeria. By Allan W. Eckert. Illustrated by David Wiesner. 214 pp. New York: Little, Brown & Company. $14.95. (Ages 8 to 12) THIS sequel to ''The Dark Green Tunnel'' is a satisfying fantasy that can be compared with the Narnia books on one level and the ''Star Wars'' movies on another. It has just about everything a good fantasy ought to have: bright, enterprising, likable children; noble, heroic adults; all manner of exotic, imaginatively named creatures, some lovable, others loathsome; a beneficent sorceress and a wicked sorcerer; gentle humor; a colorful, compelling setting; wonderful illustrations; and a plot of high adventure culminating in eventual triumph for the forces of good.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Shenandoah: An Anthology
author: James Boatwright
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHENANDOAH An Anthology. Edited by James Boatwright. 512 pp. Wainscott, N.Y.: The Pushcart Press. $28.   ONE of the unexamined received ideas we seem to live with is that we have two modern literary cultures, one mainstream and one underground; one major and one minor. The first is supposed to work through big-time publications that pay in good money and fame. The second through the literary magazines, which pay in modest (or no) money and reputation. I think it's time this idea was put to rest.
headline: TAKE BACK YOUR MAINSTREAM

title: The Shortest Way To Hades
author: Sarah Caudwell
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: This column somehow missed ''Thus Was Adonis Murdered,'' Sarah Caudwell's first novel, a few years ago. But if it was as good as Miss Caudwell's second book, THE SHORTEST WAY TO HADES (Scribners, $12.95), the loss was ours.   In ''Hades'' the plotting is fairly traditional, down to the expected encounter between killer and investigator. But it's all in the telling, and the pseudonymous author tells her story in a kind of English that has not been around since the days of Oscar Wilde. Most of the characters speak in rounded periods, often with a touch of malicious wit. '' 'Vashti's?' said Ragwort, with austere disapproval. 'Vashti's has a most unsavoury reputation. I have heard it spoken of as a place frequented by females of unnatural propensity, seeking companions in disgraceful conduct.' '' To which Ragwort's friend Selena answers, ''I have heard it spoken of as an agreeable little establishment where single women may enjoy one another's company in relaxed and convivial surroundings.''   The narrator and amateur detective of this book is a legal scholar named Hilary Tamar. Basically he is a historian, and he describes his profession as ''speaking ill of the dead.'' He is questioning a young man who is terribly impatient with his parents and says some ill-advised things about them, concluding with the statement ''Parents can be very difficult.'' Tamar has only one comment: ''They have suffered a traumatic experience - you must make allowances.''
headline: CRIME

title: Fireside Tales Of The Traveller Children
author: Duncan Williamson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FIRESIDE TALES OF THE TRAVELLER CHILDREN Twelve Scottish Stories. Told by Duncan Williamson. Illustrated by Alan B. Herriot. 170 pp. New York: Harmony Books. $12.95. (Ages 8 and up) THE children of Scottish travelers, gathered around a campfire listening to tales told by their fathers, contrast sharply with American children transfixed by bright pictures and patter emanating from a television set. What children of all cultures and times share is the thirst for story and entertainment. The differences suggest how traditions, values and the role of the imagination have changed.   Duncan Williamson's fireside tales are of keen interest to the folklorist and scholar. Transcribed from taped recordings, these narratives - told for generations by clans of itinerant Highlanders - weave rich textures of sound with unusual syntax, idiom and abrupt tense changes, creating a sense of intimacy rarely found on the printed page. These 12 stories, chosen from more than 3,000 in Mr. Williamson's repertoire, range from variations on familiar themes such as ''Beauty and the Beast'' to fresh adventure, enchantment, Jack (or hero), anthropomorphic and burker -body snatcher - tales. Edited by Linda Williamson, the narrator's American wife, ''so far as to be comprehensible to a wide English audience,'' each story is appended with brief notes as to source and circumstance as well as comments on translation, idiom and syntax.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Hawksmoor
author: Peter Ackroyd
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HAWKSMOOR By Peter Ackroyd. 217 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $16.95.   AT the conclusion of Peter Ackroyd's ''Last Testament of Oscar Wilde'' - a work of fiction imagined in Wilde's own voice - the dying Wilde, exiled and dishonored, fantasizes entering into another man's heart as a way of salvation: ''In that moment of transition, when I was myself and someone else, of my own time and in another's, the secrets of the universe would stand revealed.'' At the conclusion of Mr. Ackroyd's new novel, ''Hawksmoor,'' this mystical transformation occurs as the spiritually exhausted Hawksmoor - a senior detective assigned to investigate a series of murders committed on the sites of certain 18th-century churches - enters into an alliance of sorts with the very murderer he seeks, a devil worshiper named Nicholas Dyer: ''And his own Image was sitting beside him . . . and when he put out his hand and touched him he shuddered. . . . They were face to face, and yet they looked past one another at the pattern which they cast upon the stone . . . and who could say where one had ended and the other had begun?'' It is a measure of the author's ingenuity (and, perhaps, his audacity) that while Hawksmoor is our contemporary, Dyer lived and died in the early 18th century. He is in fact the architect of the very churches in which the series of murders has occurred.
headline: 'THE HIGHEST PASSION IS TERROUR'

title: Greed And Glory On Wall Street
author: Ken Auletta. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GREED AND GLORY ON WALL STREET The Fall of the House of Lehman. By Ken Auletta. Illustrated. 253 pp. New York: Random House. $19.95.   INVESTMENT banking, ''doing deals'' in trendyspeak, is the new glamour job. Doing deals is cleaner than making things, better paid than doctoring or lawyering, more powerful than local politics. ''The reason I decided to go into investment banking,'' said Carol Bellamy, the former City Council President, of her decision to join Wall Street's Morgan Stanley & Company, ''is I want to do deals.''   Ken Auletta's ''Greed and Glory on Wall Street: The Fall of the House of Lehman'' is the story of a once proud investment banking firm whose partners did a deal on it and themselves - a riveting chronicle of the lust for money, power and reputation that drove a handful of Lehman Brothers' partners to liquidate at a bargain price Wall Street's oldest continuing partnership. The gist of the book appeared in The New York Times Magazine last year. The expanded form is invaluable for anyone interested in piercing Wall Street's glamorous veil, or in managing ''people-intensive'' businesses.
headline: CHARITY FOR NONE, AVARICE FOR ALL

title: Anatomy Of A War
author: Gabriel Kolko.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ANATOMY OF A WAR Vietnam, the United States, and the Modern Historical Experience. By Gabriel Kolko. 628 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $25.   UNTIL now, almost nothing of real importance has been written by Americans about the war in Vietnam. That is the opinion of Gabriel Kolko, who modestly describes himself as a ''critical, independent'' thinker. The reason, we are told, is that ''those in America who were opposed to the war have still written precious little about it, while those who were in favor of it or pretend neutrality . . . have yet to offer new insights, despite their privileged access to sources and funding.'' It is a measure of this book's objectivity that Mr. Kolko spends much of the preface thanking various research councils for their generous ''material support.''   Like many others, Mr. Kolko, a professor of history at York University in Canada, is determined to explain why the Communists won in Vietnam and why the Americans failed. Despite his wooden prose, the answers come easily. Mr. Kolko contends that the Vietnamese struggle against French colonialism produced revolutionary leaders who were tough, patient, selfless, responsive and shrewd. They could not have been anything less. ''The enthusiasm and power of the masses had brought to power a party which saw itself as both an agent of history and a creator of historical change.''
headline: SAINTS AND SINNERS IN SOUTHEAST ASIA

title: Immodest Acts
author: Judith C. Brown.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IMMODEST ACTS The Life of a Lesbian Nun in Renaissance Italy. By Judith C. Brown. 214 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $14.95.   IN every time and place, there are certain people who have an instinct for shaping the materials of their circumstances, however simple, into deeds that command attention. In her own way, Benedetta Carlini, a young nun and a religious mystic in the Tuscan town of Pescia at the beginning of the 17th century, was such a person. Although her era was not very sympathetic to the claims of common people, especially common women, Sister Benedetta, as she emerges in Judith Brown's fascinating and highly readable account, seems to have been exceptionally strong-willed and ambitious. Her quest for power, pursued by the limited means open to such a woman in Renaissance Italy, set her on the path to sainthood. Ambition, however, eventually led to downfall and disgrace in a clash with the church authorities.
headline: DIVINE VISIONS, DIABOLICAL OBSESSIONS

author: John D Campbell
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

author: Marcio Souza
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
MAD MARIA By Marcio Souza. Translated by Thomas Colchie. 390 pp. New York: Bard/Avon. Paper, $4.95.

As long ago as 1967, Carlos Fuentes argued that those steamy Latin American novels in which the hero was swallowed up by the jungle belonged to the past. He spoke too soon. The old story of civilized man succumbing to tropical atavism is alive and well.
headline: IT'S A JUNGLE OUT THERE

title: Freud's Discovery Of Psychoanalysis
author: William J. McGrath.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
FREUD'S DISCOVERY OF PSYCHOANALYSIS The Politics of Hysteria. By William J. McGrath. 336 pp. Ithaca, N.Y.: Cornell University Press. $25.

THERE is no better corrective to wild rumor and meanspirited speculation than the availability of facts. A case in point is this compelling new study of young Sigmund Freud, spanning childhood, adolescence and early adulthood. It is subtitled ''The Politics of Hysteria'' to convey William J. McGrath's conviction that to understand the roots of Freud's ideas in their richly layered, architectonic structure they must be put in historical context - Freud's cultural and sociopolitical environment in the broadest sense.
headline: AUSTRIA IN HIS DREAMS

title: Tender Offer
author: Nora Johnson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TENDER OFFER By Nora Johnson. 315 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95.   THIS is a lively if sometimes petulant novel about money and sex, but mostly money. Its narrator is James (Jamie) Winslow Ricklehouse, pampered daughter of J. S. Ricklehouse, scion of Ricklehouse & Ricklehouse, otherwise known as The Firm. Hers is the perfect, privileged Manhattan childhood: a Scottish nanny, the best schools, dancing lessons, riding lessons, summers in Connecticut and a blithe lack of awareness ''that the juice, the life-blood, the fuel that made the wheels not only turn but even exist was money . . . Oh, I got a peek at it occasionally. . . . It caused Daddy to shift his body in the restaurant chair to get the wallet out of his hip pocket. He'd ruffle it out half-hidden by the tabletop . . . and Mummy would look in another direction as though he were doing something not quite nice.''
headline: TWO NOT QUITE NICE THINGS

title: With The Contras
author: Christopher Dickey
pull_quote: WITH THE CONTRAS: A Reporter in the Wilds of Nicaragua. By Christopher Dickey. 327 pages. Illustrated. Simon & Schuster. $18.95. THE actual narrative of Christopher Dickey's ''With the Contras,'' a vivid if horrifying report on recent events in Central America, begins in San Juan del Sur, Nicaragua, on July 19, 1979. The civil war is over, the government of dictator Anastasio Somoza Debayle has collapsed, Somoza has left, the officers of his Guardia Nacional, or National Guard, have fled. But the rank and file remain, and the townspeople of San Juan del Sur, trapped between the Pacific Ocean and the guardsmen fleeing from the victorious rebel army, are bracing themselves.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: People Will Talk
author: John Kobal
pull_quote: PEOPLE WILL TALK. By John Kobal. 728 pages. Illustrated. Knopf. $25. IN ''People Will Talk'' the film historian John Kobal has written up 41 of the interviews with vintage Hollywood personalities that he has been taping since the early days of his career - the first of them, featuring such veterans of the silent era as Dorothy Gish and Colleen Moore, dating from 1964, the most recent of them recorded within the past year or two. Their documentary interest is obvious, and even if you can't take the minutiae of the movies quite as seriously as Mr. Kobal himself does, they make enjoyable and sometimes riveting reading.   More than half those interviewed are stars or former stars, all but one of them women. (The only god among the assembled goddesses is Joel McCrea.) But Mr. Kobal has also found space for the testimony of choreographers, designers, several directors, including Lewis Milestone and Henry Hathaway, a producer (Arthur Freed of the M-G-M musicals) and some of the men who took portrait photographs for the studios - a special interest of his, and one to which he has previously devoted a full-length book.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Entrances. An American Director's Journey
author: Alan Schneider
pull_quote: ENTRANCES. An American Director's Journey. By Alan Schneider. Preface by Edward Albee. Illustrated. 416 pages. Viking. $25. WHEN he died two years ago at the age of 66, Alan Schneider left behind a considerable body of theatrical work. He had worked on Broadway and off, in regional theaters and abroad, and he had earned a reputation as one of the pre-eminent American directors of work by Samuel Beckett, Edward Albee, Harold Pinter, Bertolt Brecht and Michael Weller. Nine days before he was struck and killed by a motorcycle in London, he turned in the manuscript of this book - the first volume of his autobiography, which chronicles his life up through 1966.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Fire In Heaven
author: Malcolm Bosse
pull_quote: FIRE IN HEAVEN. By Malcolm Bosse. 654 pages. Simon & Schuster. $18.95. THAILAND. 1948. A girl is watching frozen with fascination as a crocodile emerges from a pond and approaches her erect on its hind feet, gazing with a single ''round and gentle eye.'' She awakens from her nightmare, recalls the equally disturbing sight she once beheld of two women making love, and begins to describe the experience to an imaginary friend. One of the women was her mother, she explains, but you have to understand that she suffered greatly during the Russian Civil War, having had to walk ''thousands of kilometers across Siberia, when she was no older than we are.''   Oh, good, this reader thought. The mother has to be Vera Rogacheva. And the dreaming girl is Sonia, her daughter by Gen. Tang Shan-teh, the title character of Malcolm Bosse's previous novel, ''The Warlord.'' In fact, splendid! Because it means that ''Fire in Heaven'' is a sequel to ''The Warlord.'' And that novel, Mr. Bosse's eighth, so skillfully blended fictional action in the foreground with actual events in the background that the history of China from 1927 through 1939 seemed to come alive before our eyes.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Jonathan Swift, A Hypocrite Reversed
author: David Nokes
pull_quote: JONATHAN SWIFT, A HYPOCRITE REVERSED. By David Nokes. Illustrated. 427 pages. Oxford University Press. $24.95.   JONATHAN SWIFT died in 1745, and for the next 200 years he attracted a succession of legends - about his parentage (was he really the son of his patron, Sir William Temple?), about his relationships with women (did he really contract a secret marriage?), about the misanthropy and madness to which he was supposed to have gradually succumbed. The last 40 years, on the other hand, have seen a determined attempt by scholars to strip away the mythology and set him in the context of his age - an attempt that has found its fullest expression so far in the three-volume biography by the late Irvin Ehrenpreis.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Pandaemonium
author: Humphrey Jennings
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PANDAEMONIUM #1660-1886. The Coming of the Machine as Seen by Contemporary Observers. By Humphrey Jennings. Edited by Mary-Lou Jennings and Charles Madge. Illustrated. 376 pp. New York: The Free Press. $17.95. ORWELL, in ''The Road to Wigan Pier,'' laments the fact that ''Socialism, as usually presented, is bound up with the idea of mechanical progress . . . as an end in itself, almost as a kind of religion. . . . The Socialist is always in favour of mechanization, rationalization, modernization - or at least thinks that he ought to be.''   But the author of ''Pandaemonium'' was a very different sort of socialist, a romantic in the tradition of William Morris, whose troubled sense of the insidious effect of machines on human life is everywhere reflected in his book. Humphrey Jennings, a poet and documentary film maker, set out to depict ''the imaginative history of the Industrial Revolution'' in the form of quotations from the writings of scientists, poets, journalists, novelists and social observers. Asked by a friend shortly before his death in 1950 if he had deliberately chosen texts that reflected a particular viewpoint, Jennings answered that he ''found a theme emerging . . . almost spontaneously - that the coming of the Machine was destroying something in our life.''
headline: UNDER THE WHEELS OF PROGRESS

title: More Than Friend
author: Robert Browning
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MORE THAN FRIEND: The Letters of Robert Browning to Katharine de Kay Bronson. Edited by Michael Meredith. (Wedgestone Press, P.O. Box 175, Winfield, Kan. 67156, $25.)
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: I Been There Before
author: David Carkeet
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: I BEEN THERE BEFORE By David Carkeet. 314 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $18.95. IT is a well-known cosmic coincidence that Samuel Langhorne Clemens, better known as Mark Twain, was born during one visit of Halley's Comet to our solar system in 1835 and died during another in 1910. In his biography ''Mr. Clemens and Mark Twain,'' Justin Kaplan reports Clemens's version of what God was no doubt saying about Halley's Comet and Mark Twain: ''Here are these unaccountable freaks. . . . They came in together and they must go out together.'' Mr. Kaplan adds, ''Like his Connecticut Yankee, he was 'getting up his last effect': he was to die at sunset on April 21, one day after the comet reached its perihelion.'' Clemens did not exactly stop his breath and die; he was 75 years old and suffering from heart failure. Still, the coincidence, like Mark Twain himself, has all but passed into American folklore.   David Carkeet has taken the effect one step farther and documented Mark Twain's brief return to earth during the comet's 1985-1986 visit. ''I Been There Before'' (the title is the last line of ''The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn'') purports to be a collection of travel sketches, stories, letters and notebook entries written during Mark Twain's second sojourn on earth. These fragments are surrounded and augmented by an array of critical apparatus so awesome that it quickly raises the question of how far the fiction extends.
headline: RETURN OF THE COMET MAN

title: The Parable Of The Blind
author: Gert Hofmann
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PARABLE OF THE BLIND By Gert Hofmann. Translated by Christopher Middleton. 152 pp. New York: Fromm International Publishing. $14.95.   THE prizewinning West German playwright and essayist Gert Hofmann began publishing fiction in 1979, at the age of 47. He is so far known in this country by two novels, ''The Spectacle at the Tower'' (for which he won the coveted Alfred Doblin Prize in 1982) and ''Our Conquest'' (1984). They are long, grotesque studies in man's inhumanity to man, the former set in a desolate corner of modern Sicily, the latter in Germany on the spring day in 1945 that saw the end of the Nazi Reich.

title: Journals 1939-1983
author: Stephen Spender
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: JOURNALS 1939-1983 By Stephen Spender. Edited by John Goldsmith. Illustrated. 510 pp. New York: Random House. $19.95. COLLECTED POEMS 1928-1985 By Stephen Spender. 204 pp. New York: Random House. $19.95. IN February 1960 Stephen Spender - Sir Stephen   Spender since 1983 - was in Moscow, as he has been all over the world, on a cultural visit. There he was called on by the former English diplomat Guy Burgess, who had fled to Russia in 1951 after being exposed as a Soviet agent. Burgess was living near the still elegant National Hotel, where Mr. Spender was staying, and was in great good humor despite the suspected microphone to which he pointed in the ceiling of the hotel room as they talked. Burgess likened ''solid and expanding'' Russia to England in 1860, ''my favourite time in history, and no one feels frightened.''
headline: HALF A CENTURY OF POETRY, POLITICS, PEOPLE

title: Lie Down With Lions
author: Ken Follett
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LIE DOWN WITH LIONS By Ken Follett. 333 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $18.95.   ROMANTIC interest has always been a tricky proposition for spy thrillers. Some lighthearted brands of espionage, true, can cheerfully accommodate breezy, endearing affairs of the heart - or, in gaudier fashion, James Bond-style encounters with dragon ladies and pneumatic playmates. But the more substantial, ambitious sort of international suspense, which depends on a certain degree of tough-minded realism, often stumbles into mawkishness or damsel-in-distress twitterings when it gives central importance to romance.
headline: BETWEEN C.I.A. AND K.G.B. IN AFGHANISTAN

title: Wiseguy. Life In A Mafia Family
author: Nicholas Pileggi.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WISE GUY Life in a Mafia Family. By Nicholas Pileggi. 256 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95.   IN 1955 an 11-year-old of Irish-Sicilian parentage walked across the street from where he lived in Brooklyn into a dingy, mob-run cab company looking for after-school work. His energy, intelligence and what seems to have been a general likableness quickly started him on his way to becoming the kind of tough thief New Yorkers euphemistically call a ''wise guy.'' Henry Hill had both driving ambition and a talent for staying alive. He eventually became one of a group who, in his words, ''walked in a room and the place stopped. Everyone knew who we were, and we were treated like movie stars with muscle.''
headline: NOT-SO-ORGANIZED CRIME

title: The Storyteller
author: Harold Robbins
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE STORYTELLER. By Harold Robbins. (Simon & Schuster, $17.95.) Someday Harold Robbins is going to wash his mouth out with soap and call it quits, but until then, here comes ''The Storyteller,'' his 19th novel. There are 10 things you need to know before you purchase or don't purchase it, according to your custom. (1) It is possibly autobiographical, at least in part, because when the hero, Joe Crown, an aspiring novelist, is asked what he expects from his career, he replies, ''I want money.'' (2) Most of the words in the book have only one or two syllables (and four or five letters), but in the case of adverbs Mr. Robbins will stretch it to seven syllables or even eight (''unenthusiastically''). (3) The book boasts some hilarious lines, such as ''A good pimp has to be born, not taught.'' (4) This is an adult book in the sense that for plenitude and monotony of sex scenes it could be stocked wherever ''Adult Books'' are sold. (5) As Joe Crown travels from the Brooklyn of 1942 to Hollywood to Europe and the top of his profession -buying his way out of the draft, managing a high-class West Side bordello, climbing in and out of beds and bathtubs, writing in spare moments - he meets few women but many ''girls.'' (6) The only honor observed in the tale is among racketeers. (7) Mr. Robbins's women - well, girls - get slapped around plenty; as Joe explains, ''She probably wanted it.'' (8) Facts are treated cavalierly - in 1949, Audrey Hepburn was not an American movie star, nor were Sophia Loren and Carlo Ponti gossip column fodder. (9) Lesbians abound, but there are no male homosexuals. (10) A more appropriate title, since there isn't much in the way of storytelling, might be ''The Draft Dodger,'' ''The Pimp'' or ''The Best-Selling Author.''
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Bad Manners
author: Maggie Paley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BAD MANNERS By Maggie Paley. 198 pp. New York: Clarkson N. Potter/Crown Publishers. $14.95. IF forced to choose, many of us would surrender our television before our telephone. Telephone calls feel like palliatives for some kinds of modern isolation.   They are more soothing than Valium, easier than drop-in visits. However, telephone talk is disembodied. There is no need to smooth your skirt, nod, make eye contact, or look interested. Intimate telephone conversation is one step away from the psychiatrist's couch and dangerously close to being alone with yourself.
headline: REACH OUT AND SCRATCH SOMEONE

title: Wife Of...An Irreverent Account Of Life In Powertown
author: Sondra Gotlieb.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WIFE OF . . . An Irreverent Account of Life in Powertown. By Sondra Gotlieb. 208 pp. Washington: Acropolis Books. $12.95. THE Canadian Ambassador to the United   States, Allan Gotlieb, is the husband of Sondra Gotlieb, who, like Gen. Lew Wallace writing ''Ben Hur'' while stationed at a desolate frontier Army post, has found a constructive way to snatch her sanity from the jaws of government service.
headline: WASHINGTON PREPOSTEROUS

title: Time After Time
author: Allen Appel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TIME AFTER TIME By Allen Appel. 372 pp. New York: Carroll & Graf. $17.95.   WE'VE all played with the notion of traveling to the past and tinkering with events. Can you be your own grandfather? Can you see yourself coming and going? And which historical villain would you strangle in his cradle? Allen Appel takes up these conundrums, and in doing so has created a fine entertainment.

pull_quote: WILD BANANAS. By Sandra Thompson. (Atlantic Monthly, $15.95.) The year is 1966. Sally leaves New York City to lose her name and her identity when she marries Barry Feldman, a Jewish law student studying for the Florida bar exam in Birmingham, Ala.

title: Hear The Wind Blow. American Folk Songs Retold
author: Scott R. Sanders. Illustrated by Ponder Goembel.

pull_quote: HEAR THE WIND BLOW American Folk Songs Retold. By Scott R. Sanders. Illustrated by Ponder Goembel. 202 pp. New York: Bradbury Press. $14.95. (Ages 12 and up) TELLERS of folk tales, no matter how slender the bridge between their stories and the original material, must move in tune with their music.

title: The Building
author: Thomas Glynn
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BUILDING By Thomas Glynn. 371 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95. THOMAS GLYNN'S new novel is the get of monsters, an 80's offspring of 70's leviathans such as Thomas Pynchon's ''Gravity's Rainbow,'' Robert Coover's ''Public Burning'' and William Gaddis's ''JR,'' books that swallow a subject and the reader. Like them, Mr. Glynn's novel imitates in its form and style what it's about - a Brooklyn apartment house tenanted by the crazed - and comments on its own monstrosity: ''The Building is huge,'' runs the first sentence, ''a grotesque magnificence.''   Most of the book's 47 densely printed chapters take place within the Building, a once-elegant structure that could have been Henry James's many-windowed house of fiction but now resembles an urban ''House of Usher,'' decaying in its parts, threatening collapse into the fetid pond in its basement, exerting what Poe called a ''peculiar influence'' over its inhabitants. The Building's roof has been stolen by gypsies. Rivers run through its walls. Only fireflies live in one apartment. A room bleeds. The boiler, cursed by voodoo, disappears, then reappears. At times the whole edifice vibrates like a skeleton on a string.
headline: ONLY THE MAD KNOW BROOKLYN

title: Shakespeare Stories
author: Leon Garfield
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHAKESPEARE STORIES By Leon Garfield. Illustrated by Michael Foreman. 288 pp. New York: Schocken Books. $14.95. (Ages 12 and up) TELLING the story of a Shakespeare play is an exacting test of understanding and imagination.   It is far easier to recount ''The Iliad,'' the plays of most other playwrights, ''Don Quixote'' or even ''The Brothers Karamazov'' than to give someone an adequate narrative of ''Hamlet,'' ''The Merchant of Venice'' or ''The Tempest.'' In performance even the most complicated of Shakespeare's plays leave the impression that the emotions and actions of dozens of characters come together to give one a clear, direct comprehension of life. It is only when one tries to tell one of these well-known tales that he knows how subtle an artist, and how cunning an illusionist, Shakespeare was.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Napoleon 1812
author: Nigel Nicolson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NAPOLEON 1812 By Nigel Nicolson. Illustrated. 192 pp. New York: A Cornelia and Michael Bessie Book/ Harper & Row. $16.95.   NAPOLEON'S invasion of Russia is one of those episodes in history whose myth-making qualities raise them above their immediate significance. The attack on Russia, launched for no sound political reason, assured the decline of the French empire that had dominated most of Europe for nearly a decade. But the invasion is remembered more as the expression of one man's passion for violence and domination, as a clash between East and West that carried Russian power far into Central Europe, and for its terrible human and social costs. The burning of Moscow and the horrors of the French retreat have acquired epic stature in our historical imagination.
headline: DOOMED FROM THE START

title: Forms Of Feeling. The Heart Of Psychotherapy
author: Robert F. Hobson.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FORMS OF FEELING The Heart of Psychotherapy. By Robert F. Hobson. 318 pp. New York: Tavistock Publications/Methuen. $19.95. CAN you simply talk to someone and go away healthy? The claim that you can is not universally accepted. Some people believe you recover spontaneously and the psychotherapist takes the credit. Others say you are healed by the power of faith. Still others think the whole thing is a fraud. My respect for doctors persuades me that talking doctors must do something helpful. And whatever they do, it is not beyond human understanding.   Freud called it catharsis. In his version, the doctor leaves the talking to you. You are helped to bring traumatic experiences into consciousness, along with all the disturbing feelings they arouse. You are healed when you have ''worked through'' those experiences and lived out those feelings. The psychic energy previously needed to keep infantile emotion out of consciousness is freed to enrich your adult life.
headline: WHAT WE SAY AND WHAT WE MEAN

title: Entrances. An American Director's Journey
author: Alan Schneider. Preface by Edward Albee. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
ENTRANCES An American Director's Journey. By Alan Schneider. Preface by Edward Albee. Illustrated. 416 pp. New York: Viking. $25. ALAN SCHNEIDER died in London in May 1984. During a break in rehearsals of a play he was directing at the Hampstead Theater Club, he was about to step across a notoriously dangerous intersection to post a letter to Samuel Beckett when a motorcyclist ran into him. He was thrown on his head and received fatal injuries. He was 66 years old. A few days earlier he had delivered the manuscript of ''Entrances,'' the first volume of his autobiography, to his publishers.

Alan Schneider was the diametrical opposite to the stereotype of a successful director - casually dressed, stocky, round-faced, always wearing a visored cap (a red baseball cap in his earlier years, more lately a ''Russian student's cap''), he was immensely lively, intense, involved, articulate, brimming over with intelligence and ideas, and he was an outstandingly sensitive man of the theater. This fascinating man has left us a fascinating book.

Not merely a book of theatrical memories, it is also an American success story and, more than that, the record of a working life in an environment that reproduces more intensely than perhaps any other working milieu the human involvements, triumphs, disappointments and betrayals that inevitably beset any career. This theatrical life story thus becomes a heightened image of the crises and heartaches of everyone's working life.
headline: THE MAN WHO UNDERSTOOD BECKETT

title: Secrets Of Marie Antoinette
author: Olivier Bernier
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SECRETS OF MARIE ANTOINETTE By Olivier Bernier. 326 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $19.95. MARIE ANTOINETTE didn't brush her teeth properly, dressed badly, wrote sloppy letters and was generally frivolous, foolish, loose-tongued and dissipated. That is, according to her mother. Maria Theresa, Empress of Austria and an 18th-century Miss Manners, bombarded her teen-age daughter with advice on everything from politics to sex. No subject was too small or personal for the Empress's nagging solicitude, from the consummation of Marie Antoinette's marriage (it took Louis XVI seven years) to her reluctance to wear a corset or read a book. Their 10-year correspondence - selected and impecca-bly translated by Olivier Bernier, a popular writer on the 18th century, under the lurid title ''Secrets of Marie Antoinette'' - is a behind-the-scenes peek at Versailles avant le deluge and an account of a fraught mother-daughter relationship.

title: With The Contras. A Reporter In The Wilds Of Nicaragua

pull_quote: WITH THE CONTRAS A Reporter in the Wilds of Nicaragua. By Christopher Dickey. Illustrated. 327 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.   THE story of the anti-Sandinista guerrillas, the so-called contras, once a rag-tag band of 500 survivors of Anastasio Debayle Somoza's notorious National Guard of Nicaragua, now a force of more than 15,000 men - well-equipped, professionally trained and energetically looked after by its foreign patrons - is well worth telling. Until about two years ago the Sandinistas, keen on depriving their enemies of any claim to legitimacy, were apt to dismiss the contras as either mercenaries or diehard ''Somocistas.'' Champions of the contras, on the other hand, above all President Reagan, often consider them lineal descendants of America's Founding Fathers, valiant freedom fighters determined to deliver their countrymen from the tyrannical reign of Communist totalitarianism. While few people give credence to the Sandinista version - and indeed while the Sandinistas themselves have become increasingly realistic in their assessment of the rebels -the far more extravagant claims for them of the Reagan Administration continue to flourish.

title: Musings
author: Gunther Schuller
pull_quote: A critic, it has been said, is someone who conducts his education in public. That definition, which critics ought to accept without the least sense of shame, can also apply to prominent composers, whose progress or lack of progress is monitored at every step of their careers both by their peers and, if they are fortunate, by audiences. It takes a hard-shelled character to bear up under such continual and pitiless scrutiny, which is perhaps why so many composers (and critics) choose early on to fasten onto accepted ideas and skulk behind them.   Judging from ''Musings,'' a collection of Gunther Schuller's writings published by Oxford University Press, the 60-year-old composer, conductor and educator has never been one of the skulkers. These essays are the record of one artist's intellectual and artistic odyssey, beginning with a 1957 article entitled ''The Future of Form in Jazz'' and extending into the 1980's. Along the way, Mr. Schuller has tested his powers of analysis against an uncommonly diverse range of subjects, from jazz masters such as Whiteman, Ellington and Cecil Taylor to the austerities of musical form and esthetics.

THE AFFAIR The Case of Alfred Dreyfus. By Jean-Denis Bredin. Translated by Jeffrey Mehlman. Illustrated. 628 pp. New York: George Braziller. $24.95.

''ON all great subjects,'' Macaulay once declared, ''much remains to be said.'' Measured by words already expended, the Dreyfus affair must surely be a great subject. For almost a century now, there has been a steady flow of books about it, not to mention plays and films. How is one to justify still another detailed account of what the French call quite simply ''the Affair.''

After all, we know (or think we know) the essential facts of the case. Capt. Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish officer attached to the French General Staff, was accused of selling secrets to the Germans. Tried and convicted in 1894 by a court-martial on the basis of evidence withheld from the defense, he was sent to Devil's Island for life. His family vainly sought to find out what had brought suspicion on Dreyfus in the first place and then what happened at the trial - even resorting in desperation to the services of a clairvoyant (who apparently hinted at events that later really happened).

title: Flight Of Fancy. The Banishment And Return Of Ornament
author: Brent C. Brolin. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FLIGHT OF FANCY The Banishment and Return of Ornament. By Brent C. Brolin. Illustrated. 338 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $30. BRENT C. BROLIN writes that ''Flight of   Fancy'' is intended ''to understand why ornament, which had been an integral part of life for millenia, should have virtually disappeared at the beginning of this century.'' The explanation offered by Mr. Brolin, an architect and writer, is that the newly emergent European middle class of the 18th and 19th centuries, unlike the aristocratic patrons of the arts before, brought a largely uneducated taste to the marketplace its buying power created. Because of its penchant for decorative excess, however, the middle class alienated artisans from ornamentation. Starting with the English architect A. W. N. Pugin in the early 19th century, reformers tried to elevate middle-class taste levels by setting esthetics on a moral basis; they argued in favor of honesty of materials, function and structure. But without visible improvement after nearly a century, reformers and artisans began to seek refuge in abstract ornamentation, and finally, about the time of World War I, they escaped into an esthetic that bypassed ornament and the middle class altogether.

title: The Beethoven Sketchbooks

pull_quote: THE BEETHOVEN SKETCHBOOKS History, Reconstruction, Inventory. By Douglas Johnson, Alan Tyson and Robert Winter. Edited by Douglas Johnson. Illustrated. 611 pp. Berkeley: University of California Press. $75. BEETHOVEN was a slow worker. There could be years and even decades between the conception of a work and the finished product. He was constantly changing, restructuring, refining. In his studio and in his pockets were sketchbooks in which he jotted down ideas. He adhered to this practice much of his life and never threw a sketchbook away. Thus posterity has a very good idea of how Beethoven worked and of how, through the alchemy of his genius, he changed lead to gold.   When he died in 1827, his personal effects were auctioned off, among them more than 60 sketchbooks. One of his publishers, Domenico Artaria, purchased a large number. Some collectors who wanted a souvenir of der Meister picked up one or two. Before long the sketchbooks were dispersed all over Europe; later some reached the United States. The 19th century was not particularly historical-minded. Collectors or their heirs started selling the priceless objects. Or they even might cut single sheets from a sketchbook and give them away as presents. Today, of course, such vandalism is rightly condemned - especially by scholars, who have to reconstruct the originals and track down missing leaves all over the world.

Those same gifts, when employed in the short story form, however, tend to point up Mr. King's limitations as a writer: Whereas the novel derived a kind of energy from the author's emphatic narrative drive, the stories seem to suffer from a surfeit of plot twists, melodramatic flourishes and authorial high jinks. Like old-fashioned works by O. Henry, the stories in this volume are continually jabbing the reader with an elbow, as though to say: ''Look at this! See how ironic this ending is. See how blind the characters are. See how superior you and I are for realizing what they will never know.''

title: Gothic Stained Glass: 1200-1300
author: Catherine Brisac
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A ''privileged reflection of thirteenth-century Gothic art'' is the felicitous phrase this authoritative and fascinating book uses to describe the stained-glass windows produced in the century that was intellectually and artistically the most glorious of the Middle Ages. Louis Grodecki, the pre-eminent scholar of stained glass, mapped out GOTHIC STAINED GLASS: 1200-1300 (Cornell University Press, $75) with his assistant, Catherine Brisac, and the two wrote large sections of it before he died in 1982. She finished the project in the same quiet style that marked their work on Romanesque glass, ''Le Vitrail Roman'' (1977), to which this book is a sequel. That is a weak word for ''Gothic Stained Glass,'' translated by Barbara Drake Boehm. Stained glass of the 13th century is one of the greatest artistic achievements of Western culture and so much of it survives that many volumes many times the size of the one on Romanesque glass could be written about it. That the authors were able to give so much information and appraisal of more than 1,000 windows -mainly in France where the art flourished most, but also in Germany, Italy, Spain and England - in so brief and engaging a book is the best evidence of their mastery of the field. The systematic correlation of the windows with the architecture, painting and technology of the century, and with the dominant religious ideas as those are expressed in contemporary iconography gives order, directness and clarity to this history of an art that grew from hesitant beginnings to overwhelming grandeur in a few decades and came to be the dominant influence on all visual art by the end of the century.

THE majority of libel suits might never have been filed had the aggrieved parties had the chance to discuss their complaints with a sympathetic member of the offending institution of the media. This finding by three professors at the University of Iowa is illustrated by the opening story in ''Untended Gates'': at great personal cost, a successful young journalist quits newspapers to attend a graduate school of journalism because he has grown tired of everyone who phoned a protest to the newsroom being termed a ''crazy.'' For Norman E. Isaacs, a former editorial director of The Indianapolis Times and a former editor with The St. Louis Star-Times, The Louisville Times and The Louisville Courier-Journal, this newsroom attitude reveals ''journalism's greatest weakness'' -''newsroom mismanagement'' by the editors, or ''gatekeepers,'' in power.

title: The Military Life Of Frederick The Great
author: Christopher Duffy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MILITARY LIFE OF FREDERICK THE GREAT By Christopher Duffy. Illustrated. Maps. 407 pp. New York: Atheneum. $25.   THE Germans must be becoming a bit tired of anniversaries. Last spring they had to make up their minds about how to commemorate the 40th anniversary of the end of World War II in Europe, and long before May 8 had been reached, the debate had caused a political controversy of major proportions. This year marks the 200th anniversary of the death of Frederick the Great of Prussia, and while that is not likely to cause a repetition of last year's hullabaloo, it is not without awkwardness.   Which Frederick should be celebrated, the philosophe de Sans Souci or the victor at Leuthen and Liegnitz? The question caused great nervousness among those planning the Prussian Exhibition held in Berlin in 1981; there was concern lest any emphasis on Frederick's military skills might offend the public. It is unlikely that this ambivalence toward the Prussian monarch will disappear soon in a country that has a large and vocal peace movement, and so we shall probably hear more - at least in public ceremonies in Germany this year - about Frederick as a leading figure in the Enlightenment, and about his decree of tolerance and abolition of torture, his legal and administrative reforms and his role as an advocate of modernity, than about Frederick the soldier.

''IN art both agony and ecstasy are matters of stylization,'' Albert Murray reminded us in ''The Hero and the Blues.'' In ''Good Morning Blues,''   Mr. Murray lets Count Basie tell his life story with the economy and understatement one would expect of a hero reticent to promote himself. Basie - who by the time of his death in 1984 had spent nearly five decades leading one of the most important big bands in jazz history - preferred to promote his team. This was something he learned in the 1920's from Walter Page and his Blue Devils, the first big band the Count ever heard and the first one he played in:   ''Everybody seemed to be having so much fun just being up there playing together, and they looked good and sounded good to boot. There was such a team spirit among those guys, and it came out in the music, and as you stood there looking and listening you just couldn't help wishing that you were a part of it. Everything about them really got to me, and as things worked out, hearing them that day was probably the most important turning point in my musical career so far as my notions about what kind of music I really wanted to try to play was concerned.''

IN the reverberant days of the ''Boom'' in Latin American fiction a couple of decades ago, when literature was for a moment the region's headiest and most dangerous export, all the talk was of the pursuit of the ''total novel.''
