In the early years of the 20th century, Royce and his colleagues, who included such men as George Herbert Palmer, William James and George Santayana, first brought American philosophy to international notice. When Royce died in 1916, he was eulogized as one of the major philosophers of his time.
headline: CALIFORNIA PHILOSOPHIZING

title: The Paper Crane
author: Molly Bang
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PAPER CRANE Written and illustrated by Molly Bang. Unpaged. New York: Greenwillow Books. $13. (Ages 5 to 8) MOLLY BANG'S newest book derives its charm from illustrations composed of intricate paper constructions, yarn and fabric.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: To A Violent Grave
author: Jeffrey Potter. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TO A VIOLENT GRAVE An Oral Biography of Jackson Pollock. By Jeffrey Potter. Illustrated. 303 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $19.95.   JACKSON POLLOCK is probably the most famous, and certainly the most notorious, of that group of artists that came of age in the 1940's and 50's in New York, known as Abstract Expressionists. Many observers credit him with freeing American art from its tutelage to the European tradition and place him among the greatest painters of the 20th century, in the exalted company of Cezanne, Matisse and Picasso. But whatever one's judgment of Pollock's artistic stature, it is undeniable that he was instrumental in shifting the center of esthetic gravity in the art world from Paris to New York. Perhaps more than any of his colleagues, he epitomizes the Abstract Expressionists' celebration of unmediated impulse and feeling. In the vibrant canvases of his mature work, paint is dripped and poured and splattered in exuberant yet highly controlled bursts of lyrical abstraction.
headline: PAINTING ON THE EDGE OF MADNESS

title: Shackleton
author: Roland Huntford
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHACKLETON By Roland Huntford. Illustrated. 774 pp. New York: Atheneum. $29.95.   WHAT exactly were those eight Americans after when their airplane crashed in a fog off the coast of Antarctica on the last day of 1985? What could move eight men to spend roughly $1,000 each for 48 hours of dampness amid sea lions and penguins?   The answer dominates Roland Huntford's ''Shackleton,'' a vivid, thorough and rewarding biography of the relentless British adventurer Sir Ernest Shackleton (1874-1922). The answer is that bizarre but weighty word ''Antarctica.'' The breathless quest for the white desert ended horribly for those eight and their two crewmen, and in the end no less sadly for Shackleton, who died after two massive heart attacks at the age of 47 while sailing south on his fourth expedition for glory and fortune; nevertheless, the ice continent compelled them absolutely and against reason. If this quest suggests a boy's vision of the world, it is, and the commonplaces of life - debts, family, politics, heartbreak - cannot stop genuinely spectacular boys like Shackleton from pursuing a fantastic destiny at the bottom of the world.
headline: A MAN FOR COLD SEASONS

title: Soldiers In Hiding
author: Richard Wiley
pull_quote: SOLDIERS IN HIDING. By Richard Wiley. 199 pages. Atlantic Monthly Press. $14.95. ''IT gives me pleasure to hinder American tourists occasionally. It is a small pleasure, to be sure, but a real one, and it is so very un-Japanese.'' So goes the opening of Richard Wiley's ''Soldiers in Hiding,'' and its mischievousness seems reason enough to go on reading this unusual first novel.   But if there is any doubt remaining, just consider the story that develops from that opening. As the narrator, Teddy Maki, recalls his past, he tells how two young Japanese-Americans from Los Angeles - he and his friend Jimmy Yamamoto - were touring Tokyo with their dance band when the Japanese raided Pearl Harbor. Forced to enlist in Japan's army along with their Japanese agent, Ike, whose sister, Kazuko, Jimmy Yamamoto has married, they wind up in the Philippines sporadically waging jungle warfare against Filipino guerrillas.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Holocaust
author: Martin Gilbert
pull_quote: THE HOLOCAUST. A History of the Jews of Europe during the Second World War. By Martin Gilbert. Illustrated. 959 pages. Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $24.95. MARTIN GILBERT'S new book, ''The Holocaust,'' is as straightforward an enterprise as its title suggests. The history of the Holocaust bristles with controversial issues; Mr. Gilbert himself has devoted a previous book to one such problem, the Allied reaction (or lack of reaction) to Auschwitz while it was still possible to do something about it. But on this occasion he is concerned with the broad course of events as they affected Jews throughout Nazi-occupied Europe, and with telling the story of what actually happened, rather than with why it happened or what might have happened instead.   A straightforward task doesn't necessarily mean an easy task, and that Mr. Gilbert's chronicle should be as effective as it is represents a formidable achievement. As far as possible he has attempted to let the victims speak for themselves, drawing on an enormous amount of documentary research (much of it into sources that have only become available in recent years), and talking to numerous survivors. He has also used his professional skills as a historian - he is best known as the official biographer of Winston Churchill - to sort out and appraise his material, to strike a balance between different aspects of the story, and (not least) to weave the scattered and often fragmentary evidence into a seamless narrative.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Sorcerer's Apprentice
author: Charles Johnson
pull_quote: THE SORCERER'S APPRENTICE. By Charles Johnson. 169 pages. Atheneum. $9.95. ''WAS sorcery a gift given to a few, like poetry?'' wonders Allan, the aspiring magician in the title story of Charles Johnson's new collection. ''Did the Lord come, lift you up, then drop you forever? If so, then he was finished, bottomed out, bellied up before he even began. He had not been born among the Allmuseri Tribe in Africa, like Rubin, if this was necessary for magic. He had not come to New Orleans in a slave clipper, or been sold at the Cabildo, if this was necessary. He had only, it seemed, a vast and painfully acquired yet hollow repertoire of tricks, and this meant he could be a parlor magician, which paid well enough, but he would never do good.''

title: None But A Blockhead
author: Larry L King
pull_quote: NONE BUT A BLOCKHEAD. On Being a Writer. By Larry L. King. 322 pages.   Viking. $17.95. IT'S typical of Larry L. King to warn us at the start of this autobiographical work that though ''I do not instruct you to place this book back on the shelf if you are a mere reader, it is primarily'' for ''neophyte writers, struggling writers, would-be writers young or old,'' or any other blockhead. Mr. King has implicitly expanded Samuel Johnson's definition from anyone who would write for any purpose other than earning money, to anyone who would write for any purpose whatsoever.

title: Holy Smoke
author: C Cabrera Infante
pull_quote: HOLY SMOKE. By G. Cabrera Infante. 329 pages. Harper & Row. $16.95.   THE Cuban novelist G. Cabrera Infante was born in Gibara, a town in the northeast of the island built on the site of the village where Europeans first encountered Indians using tobacco. Columbus, taken there by one of his crew whom he had sent on ahead, virtuously declined the offer of a native cigar - thus becoming, as Mr. Infante says, ''the first declared non-smoker on record'' - but it is hard to picture Mr. Infante himself doing the same. He is an aficionado for whom a cigar is not merely a cigar but ''a burning passion,'' and in ''Holy Smoke'' he has produced a rich compendium of cigar lore and literature.

title: Rebel: The Short Life Of Esmond Romilly
author: Kevin Ingram
pull_quote: REBEL: THE SHORT LIFE OF ESMOND ROMILLY. By Kevin Ingram. 253 pages. E. P. Dutton. $22.50. During the 1930's, the English press referred to him as the ''Red Menace'' and Winston Churchill's ''Red Nephew''; his upper-class family and friends spoke of him alternately with irritation and affection as a romantic, a troublemaker and ''an impertinent little boy.'' Certainly Esmond Romilly enjoyed playing a variety of roles - schoolboy martyr, adolescent propagandist and Spanish Civil War volunteer - but for all his flirtations with leftist politics, he seemed to harbor few illusions about the sources of his rebellion. ''Sometimes,'' he wrote of his teen-age attempts to spread the gospel of Communism among his wealthy friends, ''I would persuade myself that my desire to change the conditions of my life was due to intellectual understanding; whereas, really it was probably due simply to the combination of a wish for change and excitement, with irritation and boredom.''
headline: UPPER-CLASS LEFTIST

outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BOOK OF ABSENT PEOPLE By Taghi Modarressi. 206 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $15.95.   DURING the tense days of the Iranian hostage crisis, there were no doubt many of us who pondered the paradox of stern mullahs sitting beneath the sensuous ceilings of Isfahan, and who asked ourselves in bewilderment: How? Why? What was the route from Persia the Magnificent to modern Iran? Rokni, 23-year-old son of the dying patriarch of the Heshmat Nezami family, and narrator of ''The Book of Absent People,'' embarks on a quest to solve those very riddles.

author: Shirley Ann Grau
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NINE WOMEN By Shirley Ann Grau. 204 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.   SHIRLEY ANN GRAU, whose novel ''The Keepers of the House'' was awarded a Pulitzer Prize, has published two collections of short stories - the first of which, ''The Black Prince'' started her literary career in 1955. To anyone whose initial exposure to her brief fiction is ''Nine Women,'' however, such news would probably come as a surprise. Because if this collection is a fair sample, it would seem that the short story is not Miss Grau's metier.
headline: LIVES IN SHORT

title: The Stories Of Denton Welch
author: Robert Phillips
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE STORIES OF DENTON WELCH. Edited by Robert Phillips. (Dutton, $24.95.) The typical Denton Welch story centers in a consciousness a little outside the accepted patterns of social order, usually that of an artist or writer (both of which Welch himself was) or a rucksack-carrying stranger seeking shelter in an unfamiliar countryside. Some contact, emotional or physical - as slight as the touching of a tongue to the brass fixtures of a Chinese houseboat or a lingering handclasp between two men - causes a shift of perception that subtly alters a relationship or simply brings a fresh vision. The best of these stories are autobiographical, with the narrator even named Denton in some, and the collection records (though not chronologically) Welch's pivotal moments of revelation. Born in 1915, as Robert Phillips states in his preface, Welch was ''knocked off his bicycle by a 'woman driver' (as he said) on June 7, 1935.'' Until his death in 1948 Welch had to deal with the consequences of this accident: a fractured spine that became tubercular, and crippling pain. Now that most of Welch's writing -which included novels, poems and journals - is appearing in American editions, Mr. Phillips suggests that these stories offer the easiest entry to Welch's work. This is true, but it would have been even more useful, considering the seemingly arbitrary shifts in locale, to add that Welch was born in Shanghai, the youngest of three sons, to an Anglo-American couple. His father and brothers were ''hearty'' types, the sons revealing nothing of their mercurial American mother.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: How The West Grew Rich
author: Nathan Rosenberg and L. E. Birdzell Jr.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
HOW THE WEST GREW RICH The Economic Transformation of the Industrial World. By Nathan Rosenberg and L. E. Birdzell Jr. 353 pp. New York: Basic Books. $19.95.

MARX and Engels wrote in 1848 that ''the bourgeoisie, during its rule of scarce two hundred years, has created more massive and colossal productive forces than have all preceding generations together,'' and on this we can agree. Since 1848 the bourgeoisie has gone on creating productive forces, with notable consequences. The typical great-great-grandfather of the typical American was very, very poor in food and housing and the material comforts of life. Statistically speaking, as Nathan Rosenberg and L. E. Birdzell note, ''more than 85 percent of the per-capita output 
[
of the United States
]
 in 1985 represented growth since 1885.'' We may ask why. Economic historians, influenced by Marx's strange notion that history matters, have been asking the question for a century, and have by now discovered pieces of the answer. Mr. Rosenberg and Mr. Birdzell assemble the pieces in ''How the West Grew Rich,'' a sweet and lucid tale.

title: The Crocus List
author: Gavin Lyall
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: British espionage fiction at its best is very stiff-upper-lippish. Oxbridge types speak elegant, if elliptical, English. Many of them are epicene. In their hearts lies a slumbering Shakespeare or Swift. Much of their conversation proceeds in soft, murmuring phrases tapering off in classical periods. Who is the hero, who the villain? The mole or the patriot? It is so hard to determine. So it is in THE CROCUS LIST by Gavin Lyall (Viking, $15.95). This is another Maj. Harry Maxim operation. He has to work with suave types in the Foreign Office or the various intelligence services. They are experienced bureaucrats, all of them, and they know well how to protect their flanks. When they feel threatened, they can be deadly.   But en famille they let their hair down: ''George, we have a little problem after today's evenements. My Minister is going to have to Make A Statement, and at the moment he can barely remember his own name. He was there, did you realise, and the thought that his own dear skin might have been punctured has quite unmanned him. Too pitiful for words. Never mind, it keeps him out of the way while we prepare a helpful submission which he really can't get wrong, unless he reads it upside down.'' In England, as anywhere else, it is the Old Boy network that runs the country.

title: People Will Talk
author: John Kobal
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PEOPLE WILL TALK By John Kobal. Illustrated. 728 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $25. THE celebrity interview is a business transaction. It usually occurs when a star has a project to plug and a journalist has a space to fill. But ''People Will Talk,'' a collection of 41 interviews with Hollywood figures, lacks the odor of commerce. Most of these actresses, directors, choreographers and photographers have their greatest achievements behind them. They stand to gain nothing accept a fan's affectionate attention.   The fan, John Kobal, has reproduced the naked musings of these perpetual oration machines in chapters that validate Mr. Kobal's status as an avid gossip and a certified nice guy. His adulation is a mood elevator for both the aging subjects and the reader.

title: Vincent Van Gogh
author: Bernard Zurcher. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
VINCENT VAN GOGH Art, Life and Letters. By Bernard Zurcher. Illustrated. 325 pp. New York: Rizzoli. $60.
IN March 1886, Vincent van Gogh left his native

Netherlands for Paris. This homely and tormented preacher's son had been a failure in business and in academic and missionary work. Failures in the ''real world'' often succeed at art, at least in retrospect, and van Gogh's case follows this mythic pattern. Given financial support by his younger brother Theo, an art dealer, he turned to drawing and painting as a way of leaving his mark on the world. In Paris he entered the arena of modernist theory and practice that he had avidly read about and mused over. The reality of Paris changed van Gogh and his painting style more than he had imagined it would. He met a group of young artists who were converting Impressionism into a more abstracted and expressionistic symbolism. He abandoned his Rembrandtesque chiaroscuro and brightened his palette dramatically. Soon he moved south to the town of Arles to found a new school of painting, one that would reintegrate nature and human society. He argued violently with Gauguin, whom he had persuaded to join him. He cut off part of his ear. The story becomes more and more like a fiction.
headline: THE MYTH BEHIND THE MAN

THE HOLOCAUST A History of the Jews of Europe During the Second World War. By Martin Gilbert. Illustrated. Maps. 959 pp. New York: Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $24.95.

ON Sept. 27, 1941, 3,400 Jews in the little Lithuanian town of Eisiskes, not far from Vilnius, were rounded up by special SS units, the Einsatzgruppen, aided by Lithuanian auxiliaries, and with utmost brutality were driven to the Jewish cemetery, where they were forced to strip and then shot at the edge of previously dug trenches. A 16-year-old named Zvi Michalowski fell into the pit unharmed, a split second before the bullets killed those standing with him, including his father. When night fell, he climbed out of the mass grave and ran naked, covered with blood, to the nearby house of a peasant. In response to the boy's anguished plea for asylum, the peasant shouted, ''Jew, go back to the grave where you belong!'' and slammed the door in his face. There was the same response at several other doors.
headline: IN THE WORDS OF THE SILENCED

title: Crown Cork Cafeteria
pull_quote: MORE than half of the 16 characters in William Wise's ''Crown Cork Cafeteria,'' at the Working Theater, lose something through the play's two acts. Another loses his wits over being suspended and has his bosses believing they are about to lose their lives at gunpoint. A cook loses her husband. The hint is that everyone in the plant has lost in the tawdry little games of sex and romance they all play; and finally an employee loses the world's greatest collection of damaged bottle caps when the box he is carrying them in drops its bottom and spills his treasure all over the cafeteria floor.

author: Stanislaw Lem

pull_quote: ONE HUMAN MINUTE By Stanislaw Lem. Translated by Catherine S. Leach. 102 pp. San Diego: A Helen and Kurt Wolff Book/ Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $13.95.   ALL books by this Polish master of intellectual science fiction should come with a label on the cover warning: ''Handle With Care.'' Mr. Lem is a moralist, an ironist, a man of wide erudition (in both science and literature) who has little patience with the shortcomings of his fellow man.

title: The Handmaid's Tale
author: Margaret Atwood
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE HANDMAID'S TALE By Margaret Atwood. 311 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $16.95.   SURELY the essential element of a cautionary tale is recognition. Surprised recognition, even, enough to administer a shock. We are warned, by seeing our present selves in a distorting mirror, of what we may be turning into if current trends are allowed to continue. That was the effect of ''Nineteen Eighty-Four,'' with its scary dating, not 40 years ahead, maybe also of ''Brave New World'' and, to some extent, of ''A Clockwork Orange.''   It is an effect, for me, almost strikingly missing from Margaret Atwood's very readable book ''The Handmaid's Tale,'' offered by the publisher as a ''forecast'' of what we may have in store for us in the quite near future. A standoff will have been achieved vis-a-vis the Russians, and our own country will be ruled by right-wingers and religious fundamentalists, with males restored to the traditional role of warriors and us females to our ''place'' - which, however, will have undergone subdivision into separate sectors, of wives, breeders, servants and so forth, each clothed in the appropriate uniform. A fresh postfeminist approach to future shock, you might say. Yet the book just does not tell me what there is in our present mores that I ought to watch out for unless I want the United States of America to become a slave state something like the Republic of Gilead whose outlines are here sketched out.

PYE has been a prominent figure for three decades in the social science establishment. author: Yoshiko Uchida

(Ages 8 to 12) IN the dark purple shadow of the sheer eastern face of the Sierra Nevada, near the hamlet called Independence, Calif., lies a desert plain. It is baking hot in summer, swept by freezing winds from the mountains in the winter and barren except for brittle clumps of tumbleweed. Here and there, half hidden by the blowing sands, are flat stretches of concrete, sealed-off drains, scraps of rusted barbed wire. At a discreet distance from the highway that passes through this stark landscape is a monument erected by the California State Park Service. ''May the injustices and humiliation suffered here as a result of hysteria, racism and economic exploitation never emerge again,'' it proclaims in bronze letters which have been nearly obliterated by vandals intent on denying our national disgrace. For this is the site of Manzanar, one of 10 relocation camps in which Americans of Japanese descent were interned during World War II.
