title: A Tough Act To Follow
author: Max Wilk
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
A TOUGH ACT TO FOLLOW By Max Wilk. 347 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $14.95.

''DYING is easy. Comedy is hard,'' the English actor Edmund Gwenn is supposed to have said during his final hours. This tidbit is offered by Jody Cassel, the central character in ''A Tough Act to Follow,'' Max Wilk's roman a clef about early television. It helps explain the trajectory of Jody's career in television comedy, and it might also define one of the book's major themes. Putting yourself on the line to make people laugh can cause a lot of heartache.
headline: HEEEEERE'S JODY

title: The Bold Experiment
author: Gerard T. Rice. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BOLD EXPERIMENT JFK's Peace Corps. By Gerard T. Rice. Illustrated. 349 pp. Indiana: University of Notre Dame Press. $15.95. ''ASK what you can do for your country,'' John Kennedy urged in what was probably the most oft-quoted phrase of his oft-quoted inaugural. For the surprising number of Americans who did ask that question, the clearest if not the only answer of the Kennedy Administration was a brand-new Federal agency called the Peace Corps. Despite initial misgivings, the idea touched a chord in the country and the Peace Corps went on to become one of the few concrete successes of Kennedy's Presidency.   ''The Bold Experiment,'' Gerard T. Rice's chronicle of the Peace Corps's early years, is a reminder of an era when idealism was in fashion and could gain public support. Indeed the Peace Corps's strong start gave it such continued impetus that President Reagan, for all his deep mistrust of Government-sponsored do-goodism, nevertheless felt obliged recently to mark the agency's 25th-anniversary year by officially reaffirming ''our nation's commitment to helping people in the devloping world help themselves.''
headline: WHEN IDEALISM WAS IN FLOWER

title: Time Out Of Mind
author: John R. Maxim. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TIME OUT OF MIND By John R. Maxim. Illustrated. 502 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $17.95.   WITH the very first page of his corking new novel, John R. Maxim establishes a mood of troubling urgency. It is snowing in Manhattan, and Jonathan Corbin is beginning to feel spooked. He's no stranger to snow, but he's felt uneasy about it ever since he moved to New York from Chicago. When it snows in New York, Jonathan Corbin sees things: horse-drawn wagons and trolleys and omnibuses, men and women wearing the clothes of the 1880's. And he not only sees a Victorian panorama - he's part of it, in the black of night, in a fearful blizzard, following the woman whom he knows he will murder.
headline: THE SNOWS OF YESTERYEAR

title: Soldiers In Hiding
author: Richard Wiley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOLDIERS IN HIDING By Richard Wiley. 199 pp. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. $14.95. TEDDY MAKI, the narrator and aging hero of Richard Wiley's first novel, ''Soldiers in Hiding,'' is the host of a popular Japanese television program called the ''Original Amateur Hour.'' The show always begins and ends with Maki's rendition of Duke Ellington's ''Mood Indigo'' on the guitar. He addresses his audience in both English and Japanese, although he reads the latter poorly and must have his cue cards written out in roman letters rather than ideographic characters. Maki delights in occasionally misdirecting lost American tourists. He has a son named Milo and a mistress named Sachiko, whose scarred torso recalls the blast that razed her hometown of Hiroshima when she was a little girl.
headline: WHOSE SIDE ARE YOU ON, TEDDY MAKI?

title: Providence
author: Geoffrey Wolff
pull_quote: PROVIDENCE. By Geoffrey Wolff. 217 pages. Elisabeth Sifton/Viking. $16.95. ''PROVIDENCE'' is the title of Geoffrey Wolff's fourth and latest novel, the earlier ones having been ''Bad Debts,'' ''The Sightseer'' and ''Inklings,'' all of which this new book easily surpasses. Providence is the Rhode Island city where the action of the novel is set, a ''runt town of 156,000, declining population,'' where on a typical evening in Mr. Wolff's story a pretty singer named Lisa with ''a batty smile'' tries to entertain the crowd at the 19th Hole, a Shriners' roadhouse.   ''The crowd wasn't listening, because the listeners couldn't hear. The place was wall-to-wall deaf people; they weren't inconsiderate; they weren't yammering above her ballads. These were silent people. Busy with their fingers, also smiling. Drunk conventioneers, handicapped persons putting out-of-town moves on one another. They'd picked Providence.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Her Majesty's Secret Service
author: Christopher Andrew
pull_quote: HER MAJESTY'S SECRET SERVICE. The Making of the British Intelligence   Community. By Christopher Andrew. 619 pages. Illustrated. Elisabeth Sifton/Viking. $25. IN the early 1870's, following the suppression of the Paris Commune, the authorities in Britain found themselves faced with urgent requests from foreign governments for information about the activities of newly arrived political refugees. With a touching faith that when in doubt you should consult the top man, they wrote to Karl Marx -could he possibly be of assistance? With a scarcely less touching readiness to oblige, he promptly supplied them with details of the Workingmen's International.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Arctic Dreams
author: Barry Lopez
pull_quote: ARCTIC DREAMS. Imagination and Desire in a Northern Landscape. By Barry Lopez. 464 pages. Scribner's. $22.95.   ''ARCTIC DREAMS'' is a book about the Arctic North in the way that ''Moby-Dick'' is a novel about whales. Though not a work of fiction, Barry Lopez's dazzling new volume resembles Poe's ''Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym'' and Ted Talley's ''Terra Nova'' in that it treats the distant, snowy world of the Arctic as a place that exists not only in the mathematics of geography, but also in the terra incognita of our imaginations. For Mr. Lopez, it is a land where ''airplanes track icebergs the size of Cleveland and polar bears fly down out of the stars,'' a land rich in imagery and metaphor, where the moon can shine for a week and the sun may disappear for days. It is his achievement in this book that he communicates to us a visceral sense of his own understanding and wonder, as well as an appreciation for this distant country that flickers insistently like a flashbulb afterimage in our minds long after we've finished reading.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: No Laughing Matter
author: Joseph Heller
pull_quote: NO LAUGHING MATTER. By Joseph Heller and Speed Vogel. 335 pages. Putnam's. $18.95.    A READER of ''No Laughing Matter,'' by Joseph Heller and Speed Vogel, finds himself in the position of Mr. Heller's older brother, Lee, who, as Mr. Heller wisecracks at one point, ''could conceive I was paralyzed,'' but ''could not believe I was unable to move.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Alexander Pope. A Life
author: Alexander Pope
pull_quote: ALEXANDER POPE. A Life. By Maynard Mack. Illustrated. 975 pages. Yale University Press in association with W. W. Norton. $22.50.   IT comes as something of a shock to be reminded by Maynard Mack that no full-scale life of Alexander Pope has appeared since 1900. During the 20th century, Pope's stock, among those who care about such things, has risen sharply; scholars have established a reliable text of his poems; his letters have been edited, his work has been analyzed by critics, there have been scores of studies bearing on different aspects of his career. On the other hand, all these labors also explain why a biography has not been forthcoming until now. Without them, it would probably have been beyond the powers of a single writer, even a writer as saturated in Pope as Mr. Mack.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Wider World, A. Portraits In An Adolescence
author: Kate Simon
pull_quote: A WIDER WORLD. Portraits in an Adolescence. By Kate Simon. 186 pages. Harper & Row. $14.95. In ''Bronx Primitive'' (1982), her first volume of memoirs, Kate Simon created an indelible portrait of immigrant life in post-World War I New York, and she also introduced a wonderfully spirited heroine - herself. Headstrong, curious, at once terrified and dazzled by the exigencies of life around her, little Kaila - or Kate, as she's soon called - possesses the quick, intuitive intelligence of Anne Frank, the artistic yearnings of the young Mary McCarthy (in ''Memories of a Catholic Girlhood''), and the end of that earlier volume sees her poised, at the age of 13, on the brink of womanhood and independence.   Now, in ''A Wider World,'' Miss Simon takes up the story of Kate's adolescence, giving us a portrait of the author as a young rebel - an eager would-be artist, by turns willful and hesistant, insecure and proud. Babysitting for a wealthy, cultured couple named the Bergsons, Kate listens to them invoke the magical names of such artists as Martha Graham, Alfred Stieglitz and James Joyce, and she dreams of one day inhabiting that same exalted, magical world.
headline: MEMOIRS OF INNOCENCE

title: Death's Midwives
author: Margareta Ekstrom
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DEATH'S MIDWIVES By Margareta Ekstrom. Translated by Eva Claeson. Preface by Nadine Gordimer. 149 pp. New York: Ontario Review Press/ Persea Books. Cloth, $17.95. Paper, $8.95.   ''THERE is so much money in this country that I almost go crazy,'' says a man at a bus stop in Margareta Ekstrom's story ''When We Are Home Alone We Dance All Around the House.'' The country is Sweden, but the man is not a Swede. With a foreigner's sharp eye for the telling quirks of a nation, he notices that despite their money and their advanced state of civilization, Swedes talk a lot about birds. ''They talk as though they were still living in some sort of primitive era in which they have to know all about the edibility of plants and the egg-laying periods of birds.''
headline: IN THE HEART OF THE HEART OF THE COUNTRY

title: Rat Man Of Paris
author: Paul West
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RAT MAN OF PARIS By Paul West. 180 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $15.95.   PAUL WEST'S 10th novel, ''Rat Man of Paris,'' addresses the large question of our time: How does one live one's daily life in the span between past atrocity and atrocity to come? What happens to the wound that does not heal, that will not scar over?   Paul West has imagined the mind and times of the historical Rat Man, who used to walk the boulevards of Paris several years ago, opening his coat to flash a live rodent in the faces of strolling Parisians and the tourists in the cafes. He has imagined Rat Man's childhood in an Alsatian village during the Second World War, the inside of Rat Man's room in a derelict Paris street - and he has imagined Rat Man's imagination in the act of producing his several symbolic street performances. The act in which Rat Man carries a picture of ''the Boche'' through the streets of Paris earns him a bullet, fired at him - is it from the right fringe or the left? But at the core of this wonderful book that is about atrocity, Paul West has also allowed Rat Man the goodness of reciprocal love.
headline: THE FLASHER OF THE APOCALYPSE

title: Preparing For Power
author: Caroline Hodges Persell
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PREPARING FOR POWER: America's Elite Boarding Schools. By Peter W. Cookson Jr. and Caroline Hodges Persell. (Basic Books, $19.95.) From Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who graduated from Groton, to George Bush, who went to Andover, a sizable segment of America's leaders have been shaped by their experiences in private boarding schools.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: We're Still Here
author: Jill Jonnes. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
WE'RE STILL HERE The Rise, Fall, and Resurrection of the South Bronx. By Jill Jonnes. Illustrated. 422 pp. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. $24.95. THERE are three periods in the history of the Bronx. The first was one of remarkable rise from bucolic farmlands to thriving urban community. The next, following World War II, was marked by rapid decay. The current period, as Jill Jonnes sees it in ''We're Still Here,'' is one of hope, a time when those who have remained have begun to conquer the forces of blight and to rebuild the South Bronx. Miss Jonnes, a freelance journalist, explains this complicated history with clarity.

When the Third Avenue elevated railway reached the West Farms station at the turn of the century, it opened the way for extraordinary growth and development. Early entrepreneurs built good housing, and the city provided the spectacular 10-lane Grand Concourse. Jacob Ruppert, the brewer who was one of the owners of the Yankees, built Yankee Stadium, which opened in 1923, and brought Babe Ruth to town to draw the crowds. A powerful, disciplined political machine emerged under the leadership of Edward J. Flynn, a friend of Gov. Al Smith and President Franklin D. Roosevelt.
headline: DECLINE AND TURNAROUND?

title: The Emancipist
author: Victoria Geoghegan Sweeney
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE EMANCIPIST. By Victoria Geoghegan Sweeney. (Simon & Schuster, $18.95). Victoria Geoghegan Sweeney has crammed every possible event into the 1,048 pages of this melodramatic novel.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Tenniel Illustrations To The 'Alice' Books
author: Michael Hancher
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE TENNIEL ILLUSTRATIONS TO THE ''ALICE'' BOOKS By Michael Hancher. Illustrated. 152 pp. Columbus: Ohio State University Press. Cloth, $45. Paper, $17.50. THE Alice books continue to fascinate us.   Written by a shy Oxford don, ''Alice's Adventures in Wonderland'' (1865) and ''Through the Looking-Glass'' (1872) were intended for the amusement of the Rev. Charles Lutwidge Dodgson's circle of young friends, and they still delight (and sometimes frighten) children today. Yet in the 20th century Lewis Carroll's reputation has taken a peculiar turn, for his sublime nonsense has been appropriated by philosophers, mathematicians, psychoanalysts and literary critics, all of whom have overinterpreted his texts with a vengeance. ''Everything's got a moral, if only you can find it,'' as the Duchess remarked to Alice.
headline: THE ROAD TO TWEEDLEDUM

title: A History Of American Law
author: Lawrence M. Friedman.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A HISTORY OF AMERICAN LAW Second Edition. By Lawrence M. Friedman. 781 pp. New York: A Touchstone Book/Simon & Schuster. Cloth, $29.95. Paper, $18.95. WHEN Lawrence M. Friedman's ''History of American Law'' was first published in 1973, it filled a deep, chronic need and captured the market, in part because it had no competition. Until then, if one surveyed the literature of American law, or even Anglo-American law, he would find few comprehensive books on the subject. On the English side, there was ''The History of English Law'' by Edward Pollock and Frederic W. Maitland - but it had the foreboding subtitle ''Before Edward III'' (he died in 1307); there was Sir William Holdsworth's endless ''Legal History'' in 15 volumes; and there was T. F .T. Plucknett's ''Concise History of the Common Law,'' a 900-page volume that essayed the whole range and depth of that wildly complex subject with magisterial command.
headline: WHO WRITES THE LAWS

title: Arctic Dreams
author: Barry Lopez. Maps.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ARCTIC DREAMS Imagination and Desire in a Northern Landscape. By Barry Lopez. Maps. 464 pp. New York: Charles Scribner's Sons. $22.95. IF you lowered a microphone into Lancaster Sound off Baffin Island in the Canadian Arctic on a summer day, you might hear all at once the tremolo moans of bearded seals, the baritone boom of a walrus, the high-pitched bark and yelp of ringed seals, the electric crackling of shrimp, the birdlike trills and clicks and other harmonics of white beluga whales and horned narwhals, and the elephantine trumpeting of huge bowhead whales. And it is this synchronous wealth of life - of all life - that Barry Lopez is celebrating in his jubilant new book. Among contemporary nature writers Mr. Lopez is especially a rhapsodist, and what he has done in this passionate paean to the Arctic and its cycles of light and darkness, its species of ice, its creatures and waters, is to present a whole series of raptures and riffs on the subject of musk oxen, ivory gulls, white foxes, polar bears, icebergs and sea cur-rents. Speaking of the effect of the Arctic upon an explorer, he describes how ''the land becomes large, alive like an animal; it humbles him. . . . It is not that the land is simply beautiful but that it is powerful. . . . Darkness and light are bound together within it, and the feeling that this is the floor of creation.''
headline: FROM THE LAND WHERE POLAR BEARS FLY

title: The Anthropic Cosmological Principle
author: John D. Barrow and Frank J. Tipler. Diagrams. Tables.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE ANTHROPIC COSMOLOGICAL PRINCIPLE By John D. Barrow and Frank J. Tipler. Diagrams. Tables. 706 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $29.95 EVER since Copernicus removed humankind from the center of the universe, scientists have tended to proceed on the assumption that we inhabitants of one tiny planet are nothing special and have little to do with the vasty workings of the stars. But in recent years this Copernican assumption has been challenged by researchers wielding what is called the anthropic cosmological principle - ''anthropic'' meaning ''of mankind'' and ''cosmological'' pertaining to the study of the universe as a whole.
headline: I THINK, THEREFORE THE UNIVERSE IS

title: No Laughing Matter
author: Joseph Heller and Speed Vogel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
NO LAUGHING MATTER By Joseph Heller and Speed Vogel. 335 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $18.95.

I HAVE a particular interest in reviewing this book. It is about an author who, to be rightly melodramatic, just escaped from the jaws of death. I am an author just escaped from the jaws of death, though that happened so long ago that the event has turned into mere myth. Literature, as Horace said, and Shakespeare after him, defies time as rocks defy the sea - it is aere perennius, more lasting than brass. But authors are flesh and subject to the Grim Reaper (there are states of being where only melodrama tells the truth). ''No Laughing Matter'' is so much about the approach of the Grim Reaper that it requires the combined strength of two authors to push him back.
headline: WITH A LOT OF HELP FROM HIS FRIENDS

title: Georg Lukacs
author: Mary Gluck. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
GEORG LUKACS And His Generation 1900-1918. By Mary Gluck. Illustrated. 265 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $25.

HISTORY sometimes effects a kind of reverse perspective in our perception of the past: the farther away things get, the larger they appear. What started out as a series of informal Sunday afternoon meetings of a group of mostly Jewish, mostly thirtyish intellectuals and artists in Bela Balazs's elegantly furnished apartment in Buda, during the early years of World War I, ends up in historical perspective as the breeding ground for much of what came to characterize 20th-century sociology, art history, film theory and revolutionary politics. The ''Sunday circle'' - or the ''Lukacs circle,'' so named after its leading spirit, the philosopher and literary critic Georg Lukacs - counted among its regulars the film theorist Balazs, the sociologist Karl Mannheim, the poet and artist Anna Lesznai, the art historians Arnold Hauser and Lajos Fulep; and among its visitors and colleagues, the composers Bela Bartok and Zoltan Kodaly.
headline: SUNDAY IN THE APARTMENT WITH GEORG

title: Life On This Planet
author: Matt Cohen.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LIFE ON THIS PLANET And Other Stories. By Matt Cohen. 182 pp. New York: Beaufort Books. $14.95.   MATT COHEN is a Canadian writer who, though he has published seven novels and previous collections of short stories, and though a story from this collection won the 1982 Canadian Fiction Award for best short story, seems little known in the United States. Margaret Atwood, in discussing the ways that Canadian fiction has been ignored or taken lightly in America, ruefully quoted an American editor's dismissal: ''Listen sweetie, Canada is death down here.''
headline: MELANCHOLY MEN, WANTON WOMEN

title: Bimwili & The Zimwi
author: Verna Aardema. Illustrated by Susan Meddaugh.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BIMWILI & THE ZIMWI A Tale From Zanzibar. By Verna Aardema. Illustrated by Susan Meddaugh. 32 pp. New York: Dial Books for Young Readers. $10.95. (Ages 4 to 8) INTRODUCING a folk tale to an alien culture is a challenging task, especially when it is for a picture-book audience. Verna Aardema has often met that challenge with her elegant, authentic-sounding versions of traditional African tales, including ''Why Mosquitoes Buzz in People's Ears'' and ''Bringing the Rain to Kapiti Plain.'' Her latest venture is a curious tale from Zanzibar (now part of Tanzania).
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Great Battlefields Of The World
author: John Macdonald
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Conventional maps have always made it difficult for armchair historians to understand the problems that terrain imposes on military leaders. In John Macdonald's lavishly illustrated volume, GREAT BATTLEFIELDS OF THE WORLD (Macmillan, $35), computer technology has created 9 1/2-by-12-inch three-dimensional maps of 30 famous battlefields that provide a much-enhanced perspective of the locales in which these battles were fought.
headline: TACTICS IN 3-D

title: Risk & Other Four-Letter Words
author: Walter B. Wriston.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RISK & OTHER FOUR-LETTER WORDS By Walter B. Wriston. 243 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $19.95. THE epigraph of the first chapter of my book ''The Bankers'' in 1975 was a quotation from Henry Harfield, a senior partner in the law firm of Shearman & Sterling, addressing a lawyers' group: ''Just remember this: If bankers were as smart as you are, you would starve to death.'' I am reliably informed that when a copy of this book crossed the desk of Walter B. Wriston, then chairman and chief executive officer of Citicorp, he put in a call to Shearman & Sterling, which is Citicorp's lead counsel, to inquire whether Mr. Harfield had really said that. As the quotation had been taken from the transcript of a meeting, Mr. Harfield could not disown it. ''I have a problem,'' Mr. Wriston is reported to have said. ''I can spell Sullivan, but I'm not sure how you spell Cromwell.''
headline: PHILOSOPHER-KING OF CITICORP

title: Musings
author: Gunther Schuller.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MUSINGS The Musical Worlds of Gunther Schuller. By Gunther Schuller. 303 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $22.50. WHEN, in the midst of ''Musings: The Musical Worlds of Gunther Schuller,'' you come upon the words ''I am not by nature a polemicist or a crusader,'' don't believe them for a minute. Whether or not Gunther Schuller was born to be a crusader, his life has been devoted to many causes, all working toward a common purpose - opening the ears and minds of Americans to the music of their time and land. By definition, it seems, an American composer has to be a fighter. But few have struggled on so many fronts so ceaselessly; Mr. Schuller not only promotes his own music and that of composer colleagues but embraces jazz with open arms and subscribes to what he terms ''a global view of music.''   In ways Mr. Schuller is the Henry Cowell of our day. Like that multifaceted musical pioneer and entrepreneur from the first half of our century, Mr. Schuller is a thoroughly integrated musician both in the kinds of music he admits as classical or serious and in the diversity of his own activities. Composer, conductor, editor, educator, publisher, recording artist and writer, in Cowell's famous phrase he reaches out to the ''whole world of music'' even while he involves himself in the whole world of music making in America.
headline: KLANGFARBENMELODIEN AND THE DUKE

title: Gathering Evidence
author: Thomas Bernhard. Translated by David McLintock.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GATHERING EVIDENCE A Memoir. By Thomas Bernhard. Translated by David McLintock. 340 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $19.95.   THOMAS BERNHARD is by far the most disturbing and original literary figure to have emerged in postwar Austria. At 54 he has produced a remarkable body of work, over 30 books of fiction and drama that focus with an immeasurable single-mindedness on the ill will, the continual betrayal and the self-doubt that inexorably motivate his characters to contemplate their self-destruction.   Now ranked with the foremost world authors, Mr. Bernhard writes novels that continue to incur a certain resistance on the part of the reader, for to read him is to enter a hazardous emotional maze singularly devoid of affection, love or pleasure not marred by the intrusion of death. The utter nihilism of a comment such as, ''The dead are more attractive than those who haven't yet reached that stage,'' by an eccentric aristocrat discussing suicide with his physician in ''Gargoyles,'' one of Mr. Bernhard's earlier novels, exemplifies not only the recklessness with which the author's often distraught characters tend to expose their innermost thoughts, but also their all-pervasive lack of expectation. Whatever writing may actually mean for Mr. Bernhard, one can read into it an indubitable delay, the postponement of an implacable ending of which his characters are all too aware.
headline: EMBRACED BY DEATH

title: Last Resorts
author: Clare Boylan
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LAST RESORTS. By Clare Boylan. (Summit, $16.95.) Clare Boylan's gift for stunning prose and unorthodox images is wonderfully evident in her second novel (her first, ''Holy Pictures,'' was highly praised). But she overburdens her central character, Harriet Bell, with more problems than even the strongest character could resolve in this novel. An unenviable sad sack, Harriet is chronically at sea, without the faintest notion of how to fulfill herself. Fittingly, she is vacationing in the Aegean with her three children on the none-too-subtly named isle of Keptos, which has kept her returning every year for a decade with its promise of idyllic stasis. This character without drive knows herself only in terms of her many unsatisfying relationships. Yet her children, noisy slobbering teen-agers, are not the monsters Harriet likens them to, just typical adolescents bumbling through one postpubescent trauma after another. She obsessively schemes to lure Joe Fisher, an unexceptional businessman, away from his wife, but doesn't see that his dalliance with her is a pathetic attempt to absolve himself of guilt about his dead daughter, who resembled Harriet. Even her imaginary childhood companion, the toothy Hawna Maroyle, keeps cropping up to taunt her. Harriet's estrangement from Joe and her children is just the beginning; she no longer recognizes her own vision of paradise, as Greek entrepreneurs set about modernizing Keptos and the neighboring island into tourist resorts. ''Last Resorts,'' although a third-person narrative, is too often told from the murky recesses of Harriet's mind.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Fifth Row Center: A Critic's Year On And Off Broadway
pull_quote: This article has been excerpted from ''Fifth Row Center: A Critic's Year on and Off Broadway, c 1986 by Benedict Nightingale, to be published Feb. 26 by Times Books, a division of Random House Inc. I've spent enough ink berating American dramatists for not quite managing to be capsule reincarnations of Shakespeare and Buchner, Ibsen and Brecht. Maybe it's time to acknowledge the difficulties they face at a time when the traditional center of their theater is so inhospitable to even their less serious efforts, let alone their more challenging ones. Nearly 15 years ago William Goldman complained in his book about Broadway, ''The Season'': ''We have not had a first-rate playwriting debut in almost a quarter of a century, and the wait is getting painful.'' Since he wrote that, the prospect of such a debut has become so slight, so slim that any sane person would give up the wait as hopeless. Indeed, the best may not be seen on Broadway at all. David Mamet's ''American Buffalo'' may have slipped past the sentries, but Sam Shepard, whom many would regard as the first among the first-rate, has yet to have a play produced there.
headline: WHY DRAMA FLOURISHES SO VIGOROUSLY IN BRITAIN

title: Providence
author: Geoffrey Wolff
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PROVIDENCE By Geoffrey Wolff. 217 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $16.95.   IN common parlance, the word ''providence'' is full of happy connotation. It refers to the use of foresight or to luck or, even, to the loving care of an attentive Supreme Being. ''Providence'' is the word theologians apply to God's relationship to His creation, how He foresees events and preordains them. Secular people get at the same cozy idea by affirming the inevitability of progress or the dialectical movement of history toward some utopia. But the idea of providence, whether the biblical version or the Enlightenment's or Marx's, is at bottom a tragic notion, for it implies that individual human choices count for nothing against the weight of an inexorable, overwhelming force, whether benign or cruel, whether known as God, History, Destiny, Progress or DNA.
headline: LAUGHING OUR WAY TO DEFEAT

title: The Vigil
author: Clay Reynolds
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE VIGIL. By Clay Reynolds. (Marek/St. Martins, $13.95.) This engrossing first novel revolves around a single incident: the mysterious disappearance of an 18-year-old girl traveling with her mother through a small Texas town.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Her Majesty's Secret Service
author: Christopher Andrew. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HER MAJESTY'S SECRET SERVICE The Making of the British Intelligence Community. By Christopher Andrew. Illustrated. 619 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $25.   IN Britain the activities of the intelligence and security services have always been regarded in much the same light as marital sex. Everyone knows that it goes on and is quite content that it should, but to speak, write or ask questions about it is regarded as exceedingly bad form. So far as official Government policy is concerned, the British security and intelligence services, M.I.5 and M.I.6, do not exist. Intelligence is brought by the storks, and enemy agents are found under gooseberry bushes. Government records bearing on intelligence activities are either industriously ''weeded'' or kept indefinitely closed. Members of Parliament who ask questions are listened to in icy silence and choked off with the most abrupt and inexplicit of replies. Serious historians, deprived of documentation, tend to accept the situation and do not ask questions to which they know they cannot provide the answers. The field is left to inquisitive journalists, disgruntled professionals and imaginative fiction writers - categories that confusingly overlap.
headline: COWBOYS, PLAYBOYS AND OTHER SPIES

title: Winning Back The Sky
author: David G Hubbard
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WINNING BACK THE SKY: A Tactical Analysis of Terrorism. By David G. Hubbard. (Saybrook, $14.95.) Today's terrorist is neither Superman nor Satan, says David G. Hubbard in ''Winning Back the Sky,'' a 140-page book that is slim on facts but fat on pronouncements. Dr. Hubbard, a Dallas psychiatrist who says he has interviewed hundreds of skyjackers and terrorists over the last 20 years, is a former consultant to the Federal Avia-tion Administration and author of an earlier book on skyjackers. Dr. Hubbard writes that the first skyjackers were usually personal failures who wanted to stage a dramatic act but were not necessarily great planners.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Conjugal Rites
author: Ellen Feldman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CONJUGAL RITES By Ellen Feldman. 236 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $15.95.   TO judge by ''Conjugal Rites,'' the primary business of the world - at least on Manhattan's Upper East Side - is getting divorced. The characters have already split and are facing off in acrimonious custody and settlement battles; or they are still coupled, but moving unawares, as if on a conveyor belt, toward dissolution; or they are hanging onto the marriage by their teeth. At whatever moment you catch them, these edgy people are so prone to split they can't enter a restaurant without checking all the exits.
headline: SETTINGS ASUNDER

title: Conflicts And Contradictions
author: Meron Benvenisti
pull_quote: CONFLICTS AND CONTRADICTIONS.   By Meron Benvenisti. 210 pages. Villard. $15.95. AMONG the conflicts referred to in the title of Meron Benvenisti's acutely thoughtful ''Conflicts and Contradictions'' are, most obviously, those between Israelis and Arabs in the Middle East, between Israelis and Palestinian Arabs in Jerusalem and on the West Bank of the Jordan River, and between Ashkenazi and Oriental Jews in Israeli society.   The contradictions are chiefly those that Mr. Benvenisti discerns between Israel's ideals and its actual policies, particularly toward the settlement of the occupied territories. If the result of those policies was no longer rationalized as a temporary, fluid situation capable of being reversed, and acknowledged as the fait accompli that the author believes it to be, then Israelis would be faced with unpleasant choices, he says.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: People Of Chance
author: John M Findlay
pull_quote: PEOPLE OF CHANCE. Gambling in American Society From Jamestown to Las Vegas. By John M. Findlay. Illustrated. 272 pages. Oxford University Press. $19.95. IN 1612, when the fortunes of its plantation at Jamestown were foundering, the Virginia Company in London fell back on the expedient of raising fresh capital by organizing a lottery. John M. Findlay takes this as a symbolic starting point for his study of gambling in American history. From the very outset, he maintains, the advancing frontier of American culture has been marked by an exceptional readiness to bet on the future - and to bet on lots of lesser things as well. So doggedly does he iterate this thesis (and, on the whole, so convincingly) that by the time you get very far into ''People of Chance,'' the spirit of the frontier and the spirit of gambling have come to seem virtually synonymous.   In the beginning, everything was frontier. Puritan New England and Quaker Pennsylvania might hold out against licensed gambling as long as they could, but in Virginia and elsewhere traditional nonpuritanical English attitudes prevailed, and betting flourished. At the same time, Colonial gambling was always more democratic and less tightly regulated than its English counterpart, a difference confirmed by the emergence of distinctively American forms of betting sport such as quarter-horse racing, which was ''informal, disorderly and backwoodsy.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Collaborators
author: Janet Kauffman
pull_quote: COLLABORATORS. By Janet Kauffman. 134 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.    ''MY mother rushes by,'' says the narrator of ''Collaborators,'' describing a dream she has just had, ''and the column of fire surges with images until these begin to link and move by, a long strip of separate scenes, many frames of a film, but each one developed, and moving upward as if the roll were being wound through the fire and burning there, and not being burned and not extinguishing. My mother sees the exchanges of mind, the collaborations of innumerable souls; they are drenched with fire and they roll and roll, nothing stops them.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Marya: A Life
author: Joyce Carol Oates
pull_quote: MARYA: A Life. By Joyce Carol Oates. 310 pages. William Abrahams/Dutton. $16.95. VIEWED from its narrowest perspective, Joyce Carol Oates's latest novel, ''Marya: A Life,'' could be described as a textbook psychological study of a feminist. Marya Knauer is abandoned by her parents early in her life. Because of her father's violent death in a labor dispute and her mother's unwillingness to raise their children alone, Marya and her brothers are dumped with relatives.   To this psychic injury is added the insult of sexual abuse by one of her male cousins as well as the stigma of being gifted intellectually in a lower-class rural setting where bookishness is scorned. Marya spends the rest of the novel competing successfully with men for the attention of surrogate fathers and mothers, and feeling persecuted for being a woman.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: An Unnatural Pursuit & Other Pieces
author: Simon Gray
pull_quote: AN UNNATURAL PURSUIT & OTHER PIECES. By Simon Gray. Illustrated. 244 pages. St. Martin's Press. $15.95. No doubt few American readers have seen Simon Gray's play ''The Common Pursuit,'' which had a few weeks' run at London's Lyric Theater, Hammersmith, a year and a half ago, and which has as yet received neither a West End nor a New York production. Inspired in part by the experiences of Mr. Gray's friend Ian Hamilton, who once ran a small but influential literary magazine, the play examines the unraveling lives, ambitions and dreams of five gifted Cambridge students, who leave behind the university, and their high-minded intellectual ideals, for the more pragmatic rewards and frustrations of the London literary world: talk-show appearances, petty journalistic assignments, lucrative book offers, as well as ''the routine stuff of English social comedy'' - ''love affairs, abortions, adulteries, treacheries, compromises, lingering deaths, sudden deaths.''
headline: A Playwright's Journal

title: Target: Cancer
author: Edward J Sylvester
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TARGET: CANCER. By Edward J. Sylvester. (Scribners, $17.95.) In an editorial three years ago, the science journal Nature raised hopes that the most fundamental causes of some cancers would be known by the end of 1983.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Stories Of Heinrich Boll
author: Heinrich Boll
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE STORIES OF HEINRICH BOLL By Heinrich Boll. Translated by Leila Vennewitz. 686 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $25. BORN into a liberal Roman Catholic family in Bonn in 1917, and the least military of men, Heinrich Boll was drafted into the German army in 1939 and eventually taken prisoner by the Americans. His first novel was published in 1949, and in 1972 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature for a body of work that, in its emphasis on life and a positive vision, fulfilled the ideals the prize is meant to honor. Possibly his sense of noblesse oblige induced him to serve as the quasi-official conscience of postwar Germany - who else was anything like as eligible? - and this function, one may surmise, proved a burden to him. How could so private a person, the ironic champion of the outsider and the lone wolf, feel comfortable as a spokesman on public issues and for large and sometimes simple-minded causes?
headline: WHEN THEY WERE WRONG THEY WERE RIGHT

title: Where They Are Now
author: Jill Abramson and Barbara Franklin.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WHERE THEY ARE NOW The Story of the Women of Harvard Law 1974. By Jill Abramson and Barbara Franklin. 323 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $17.95. IT was not until 1950 that Harvard Law School admitted women as students and not until the class of 1974 that women constituted more than 10 percent of an entering class. ''Where They Are Now'' is a breezy, sometimes affecting but ultimately unsatisfying account of how the 70 women who made up 12 percent of the Harvard Law School class of 1974 spent their first decade as lawyers.   ''There was no group of women more determined to 'have it all,' '' Jill Abramson and Barbara Franklin assert, but the goal proved elusive for most. By 10 years out of law school, barely a quarter of the women were partners in law firms, compared with just over half of their male classmates; while only a handful of the women had formally been rejected for partnership, many had taken themselves out of the race along the way and by their 10th reunion were no longer measuring themselves by the classic Harvard Law School model of a successful career in big-time corporate law.
headline: PORTIA FACES LIFE

title: Curranne Trueheart
author: Donald Newlove
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CURRANNE TRUEHEART by Donald Newlove. 394 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $17.95. DONALD NEWLOVE'S latest novel, ''Curranne   Trueheart,'' begins ''What could be more hopeless than a madwoman marrying a drunk?''   The speaker - Jack Trueheart - is too hard on himself. In fact, his alcoholism is cured quickly and permanently and the madness of his wife, Curranne, becomes the dominant subject - the obsession - of the book.
headline: GUILT ON HER FINGERS

title: The View From Nowhere
author: Thomas Nagel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE VIEW FROM NOWHERE By Thomas Nagel. 244 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $19.95. MANY people believe that in recent decades philosophy has lost its vocation and abandoned its inquiry into all the interesting and important questions that enthralled the great minds of its history. If you feel that way, you would do well to read this new book by Thomas Nagel, a professor of philosophy at New York University. He is as well versed as anyone in linguistic philosophy and is a fully competent practitioner of contemporary analysis, but no one can pick up his book without realizing that he stands in the mainstream of philosophical tradition and is grappling with the same problems that fascinated Kant and Nietzsche.   In a sense, ''The View From Nowhere'' is about a single problem - how to combine the perspective of a particular person inside the world with an objective view of the same world, including the person himself. But because this internal-external tension pervades human life, Mr. Nagel is able by studying it to cast light on four of the supreme topics of philosophy - the metaphysics of mind, the theory of knowledge, the possibility of free will and the nature of ethics.
headline: TACKLING THE BIG QIESTIONS

title: The Storm And Other Things
author: Eugenio Montale
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE STORM AND OTHER THINGS By Eugenio Montale. Translated by William Arrowsmith. 219 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. Cloth, $14.95. Paper, $6.95. WHEN Eugenio Montale received the Nobel   Prize in 1975 for five formidable volumes of poetry (of which ''The Storm and Other Things'' is the third, most difficult and most beautiful), no one doubted that the prize had gone to the poems, not the public persona. Montale generated no legend. No shred of gossip clung to his heavyset, almost invisible figure. His career illustrated, it seemed, the irrelevance of a poet's private life to his work. The tight, acoustically intriguing poems with their murky private allusions blocked all attempts to extract an autobiography. At most, the frequency with which they addressed women, unnamed and named - Esterina, Gertin, Dora Markus, Liuba, Vixen, Mosca and, above all, Clizia - allowed one to surmise that for Montale life, like art, was quintessentially speech to a woman.
headline: BETWEEN THE LOVE OF CLIZIA AND MOSCA

title: Moments Of Reprieve
author: Primo Levi
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MOMENTS OF REPRIEVE By Primo Levi. Translated by Ruth Feldman. 172 pp. New York: Summit Books. $14.95. RETURNING 40 years later to the scene of his first classic works about Auschwitz, ''Survival in Auschwitz'' and ''The Reawakening,'' Primo Levi has written a series of sketches and vignettes that vary in quality and focus. Mr. Levi worked as a chemist in a camp laboratory at Monowitz, a private camp near Auschwitz that belonged to I. G. Farben. He writes about the start of a day: ''When reveille sounds (and it's still pitch dark) first of all we put on our shoes, otherwise somebody will steal them and it is an unspeakable tragedy.'' This is Mr. Levi's characteristic tone in ''Moments of Reprieve'' - wry, understated, innocent, mordant and humorous. At its best, the mix makes for an illuminating method of comprehending the abyss of concentration camp experience.   In an interview with Mr. Levi in the British publication Literary Review, Germaine Greer wrote that he had traced an intellectual system based on four tenets: ''Human beings suffer unjustly, man is great notwithstanding; he is saved by understanding and by laughter.'' Perhaps this is too cheerful an assessment of the human condition to bear the weight of 20th-century experience. ''Moments of Reprieve'' may reflect this dilemma.
headline: SOME WHO SURVIVED

title: Coroner At Large
author: Joseph Dimona
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CORONER AT LARGE. By Thomas T. Noguchi with Joseph DiMona. (Simon & Schuster, $16.95.) A pajama top pocked with ice-pick holes convinces a jury that Jeffrey MacDonald murdered his pregnant wife and two daugh-ters.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: In These Promiscuous Parts
author: Menna Gallie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN THESE PROMISCUOUS PARTS. By Menna Gallie. (Joan Kahn/St. Martin's, $15.95.) Menna Gallie has created a colorful microcosm in her story of a small Welsh mining town where petty crimes and scandals are resolved in a humorous, humane manner.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: None But A Blockhead
author: Larry L. King.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NONE BUT A BLOCKHEAD On Being a Writer. By Larry L. King. 322 pp. New York: Viking. $17.95. LARRY L. KING'S ''None but a Blockhead'' is an amiable memoir marinated in hard lessons learned and not a little alcohol. In the narrative of his long career as a freelance writer that makes up most of the book, virtually no account of Mr. King's experiences omits booze - or its effects: ''I told Gutwillig let's have a beer or three''; ''after choking down a couple of bloody Marys''; ''it is mid-afternoon and I am mostly sober - only slightly pumped by four or five screwdrivers at lunch.'' The references are compulsive, and for 150 pages one wonders what Mr. King's attitude is toward his own thirst; then, abruptly, mid-paragraph, he finally mentions alcoholism and acknowledges the broader implications of his drinking. Toward the end there is a notebook entry from 1983, a brief ''sermon'' to readers, on the occasion of his newly won sobriety.   But this is not a book about drinking, nor is it a disguised polemic on the sins of the sauce. If it calls constant attention to drinking, it does so chiefly as a way of capturing the flushed color and flavor of Mr. King's career. Reading it is rather like listening, at considerable length, to the most interesting patron at your neighborhood bar. And this is both the book's appeal and its limitation.
headline: GOOD OL' FREELANCE

title: Commonplace Book
author: E. M. Forster. Edited by Philip Gardner.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
COMMONPLACE BOOK By E. M. Forster. Edited by Philip Gardner. 372 pp. California: Stanford University Press. $35. IN 1924 E. M. Forster found in the house in Surrey that he had inherited from an aunt, and where he was himself to live for over 20 years, a very large leather-bound notebook. This turned out to be a present from John Jebb, Bishop of Limerick - who had bought it in 1804 - to his chaplain, Forster's grandfather. John Jebb intended to use it as a commonplace book but had only made entries (mostly in Latin and Greek) filling 18 of its 400 pages.

Forster, then 46, wrote in the flyleaf, ''Continued it at Abinger Hammer, Wednesday October 21, 1925, E. M. Forster.'' In the facsimile edition (published in London by the Scolar Press), the effect of the pages covered with Forster's handwriting is a good deal calligraphic: the way in which the sentences are written on the page - sometimes in thick, sometimes in thin, strokes, sometimes indented, sometimes enclosed in boxes of drawn lines, sometimes a whole page given to a quotation or a few sentences. Philip Gardner, the editor of ''Commonplace Book,'' wisely does not attempt to reproduce such effects typographically. However, he helpfully provides a photographic illustration of a page of Forster's text.
headline: GOODBYE TO GREEN LINES

title: Architecture, Men, Women And Money
author: Roger G. Kennedy. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ARCHITECTURE, MEN, WOMEN AND MONEY In America, 1600-1860. By Roger G. Kennedy. Illustrated. 526 pp. New York: Random House. $35. BEHIND the creation of great houses there are always strong personalities - clients and architects whose self-images and notions of art and sensibility either flourish and thrive or struggle for survival within the cultural, artistic, economic and political contexts of the time. Whether it is in Renaissance Italy, Enlightenment Britain or colonial America, the same very human drama unfolds as a patron decides to build himself a house. Is there enough money? How does its source determine the house's role in the owner's psychology? How and from where do the owner and architect obtain their ideas? Later we wonder, with what sorts of moods and motives was the house conceived and built? Who were the protagonists and antagonists? How does this human drama relate to the larger events and movements of the time or to the past and future? And what can it tell us about the development of values of a particular country - in the case of this book, America?
headline: THEY WERE WHAT THEY BUILT

title: Sirens And Spies
author: Janet Taylor Lisle
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SIRENS AND SPIES By Janet Taylor Lisle. 169 pp. New York: Bradbury Press. $11.95. (Ages 10 and up) IN Janet Taylor Lisle's second book, ''Sirens and Spies,'' two sisters, Elsie Potter, 14 years old, and Mary, who is 15, and a music-loving derelict are the audience that focuses attention on the dramatic Miss Fitch. She is the local violin teacher in their southern Connecticut town and a figure of some flair and mystery.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Only The Dead Know Brooklyn
author: Newgate Callendar
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Carefully assembled and well written, Thomas Boyle's ONLY THE DEAD KNOW BROOKLYN (Godine, $15.95) is a gripping procedural. A psychotic killer is on the loose. To add to the problems of the police, a professor is abducted by an extremist group that announces he will be tried by a ''people's tribunal'' and found guilty unless his university announces a restructuring of its curriculum and its policy toward the underprivileged.   Eventually the two cases come together, culminating in a chase in New York Harbor. But ''Only the Dead Know Brooklyn'' has much more in it than the work of the Police Department. It is a gazetteer of the borough, it contains some acid comments about the deterioration of higher education in the city and it examines the disintegration of what was once a prosperous middle-class part of New York.
headline: CRIME

title: Dead Ground
author: Philip Kerrigan
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DEAD GROUND By Philip Kerrigan. 217 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $13.95. HAVING been an avid consumer - and occasional producer - of thrillers for decades, I recently became convinced, to my great sorrow, that I had wearied of the entire genre. I believed it impossible to find a new work that was both fresh and stirring.   I am delighted to confess to a grave error. In ''Dead Ground'' Philip Kerrigan, a 26-year-old Briton, offers aficionados of the genre (and the general reader) a thriller that is not only highly original but extremely moving. A first novel by Mr. Kerrigan, ''Dead Ground'' deals brilliantly with the men who kill, as they believe, to further their dream of a united Ireland.
headline: DANNY PARKER HAD TO DIE

title: The Lightning Of August
author: Jorge Ibarguengoitia
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LIGHTNING OF AUGUST By Jorge Ibarguengoitia. Translated by Irene del Corral. 117 pp. New York: Bard/ Avon Books. Paper, $3.95. When it was originally published in 1965 in Mexico, the late Jorge Ibarguengoitia's ''Lightning of August'' caused a considerable literary stir. Until then, the literature dealing with the Mexican revolution had been somber and solemn - its dominant tone set by the monumental saga of the conflict and the gigantic suffering of the community. History, these works implied, was a serious affair. And then suddenly, for the first time, a novel appeared proclaiming that this shattering, traumatic event was, with all due respect, a laughing matter. It had taken the Mexican revolution 55 years to produce its first satire.   Now, more than 20 years later, American readers can enjoy this funny, bittersweet book in a reasonable translation by Irene del Corral.
headline: THE CLOWNS COME TO THE REVOLUTION

title: Wider World, A. Portraits In An Adolescence
author: Kate Simon.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A WIDER WORLD Portraits in an Adolescence. By Kate Simon. 186 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $14.95.   THERE are stories so crucial for their audience that each fresh telling, and perhaps especially each fresh revision or debunking, only heightens the story's power. The American immigrant success story, for many of us, is such a story, as Kate Simon has demonstrated before in her previous autobiographical volume, ''Bronx Primitive: Portraits in a Childhood.'' This new book picks up where that one ended, as the author passes from childhood in the late 1920's. ''A Wider World: Portraits in an Adolescence'' continues into the Great Depression, and ends with harsh, even bitter emblems of rebirth and survival.
headline: LIFE LAY BEYOND THE BRONX

title: Rivers Of Empire
author: Donald Worster.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RIVERS OF EMPIRE Water, Aridity, and the Growth of the American West. By Donald Worster. 402 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $24.95. ''SOLITARY, singing in the West,'' chanted Walt Whitman, ''I strike up for a New World.'' From Thomas Jefferson through Whitman and Thoreau, down to Frederick Jackson Turner's famous essay of 1893, ''The Significance of the Frontier in American History,'' and even to the present day, the West has occupied a mythic niche in the American imagination. Jefferson conjured traveling westward as a journey backward in time to ''the infancy of creation.'' He expected that the acquisition of the enormous Louisiana Territory would create an empire of liberty where the American experiment in republicanism could be perpetually refreshened. Thoreau felt jacketed by convention in the settled East, but ''westward,'' he concluded, ''I go free.'' Expanding on Jefferson, Turner argued that the repeated experience of pushing the frontier line westward shaped the culture of American democracy by reinforcing republican virtues, especially ''that dominant individualism . . . that buoyancy and exuberance which come with freedom.''
headline: 'WE ENJOY PUSHING RIVERS AROUND'

title: A Loving Place
author: Mark Dintenfass
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A LOVING PLACE By Mark Dintenfass. 287 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $17.95. SEVENTY-FOUR-YEAR-OLD Murray Farber is a retiree whose primary occupation these days is to worry. He frets over his failing health, his sour marriage of 40 years, his withdrawn son and contrary grandson. He anguishes over his decision to leave Brooklyn - where he was considered the unofficial Mayor of Montgomery Street - for the sterility and boredom of a planned community in Florida. But one warm winter night at the Sunset Mall, Murray happens upon an old neighbor from Montgomery Street. This chance meeting draws his thoughts back through time to Brooklyn of the 1930's, back to a place that is not just a geographical location but a nearly mythological neighborhood, ''A Loving Place,'' as Mark Dintenfass's title suggests.   From his first encounter with his old neighbor until a reunion of relocated Montgomery Street residents at a crowded Chinese restaurant the following night, Murray is haunted by a collage of memories that alternately assault and comfort him. The present is carefully chronicled in great detail as we slowly follow Murray through the small rituals of his daily life: a walk across the golf course, a shower, a card game, several well-practiced arguments with his wife, Irene. But it is in the past, in a Brooklyn that is forever lost to Murray, that this novel finds its voice.
headline: ONLY THE RETIRED KNOW BROOKLYN

title: Adventures Of An Advertising Woman
author: Jane Maas
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ADVENTURES OF AN ADVERTISING WOMAN By Jane Maas. 227 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $15.95. DAVID OGILVY was already a legend on Madison Avenue and the author of the newly published ''Confessions of an Advertising Man'' when Jane Maas took her first advertising job, as a junior copywriter at Ogilvy & Mather in the early 1960's. She had the opportunity to learn from a master, and some of those lessons are evident in this book - not least its title. Mr. Ogilvy has only a walk-on part in ''Adventures of an Advertising Woman'' but is easily its most fascinating character. Unfortunately, both Mr. Ogilvy's creative genius and his flair for language have eluded Mrs. Mass. Without them, the craft of advertising that Mr. Ogilvy exalted is made to seem a trivial business in her book.   In 1982 Mrs. Maas, a copywriter turned account ex-ecutive, became president of Muller Jordan Weiss, a medium-size advertising agency. She is something of a first; most women who are agency presidents founded the agencies themselves. She is evidently a woman of considerable managerial talent and energy, which becomes clear from page one, where she describes her typical day (''5:30 A.M. Up to do warmups prior to our jog''). And she seems to be a thoroughly nice person, a worshipful wife and fond mother who, by her own description, is ''relentlessly cheerful; I've never recovered from being a cheerleader.''
headline: SHE  [ LOVES ]  MAD AVE.

title: Reasonable Doubt
author: Henry Hurt. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: REASONABLE DOUBT An Investigation into the Assassination of John F. Kennedy. By Henry Hurt. Illustrated. 555 pp. New York: Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $19.95. THIS is a compelling yet fundamentally calm analysis of the most important assassination in the United States since that of President Lincoln. More particularly, ''Reasonable Doubt'' examines the processes and findings of the official investigations conducted since Nov. 22, 1963, when John F. Kennedy was killed in Dallas.   For anyone who has not delved deeply into the immense literature on the subject, the book seems to demonstrate - the author contends the evidence is ''overwhelming'' - that Lee Harvey Oswald was a tool and probably a fall guy for some group of people who wanted Kennedy dead. But Henry Hurt has really done more of a job of showing that the case for Oswald as a lone assassin is flawed than of showing that Oswald was involved in a conspiracy.
headline: OSWALD AND OTHERS?

title: Huckleberry Finn
author: Samuel Langhorne Clemens
pull_quote: ''Persons attempting to find a motive in this narrative will be prosecuted; persons attempting to find a moral in it will be banished; persons attempting to find a plot in it will be shot.'' Clearly that famous prefatory note to ''Adventures of Huckleberry Finn'' has neither dissuaded generations of scholars from annotating the text, nor dissauded other persons from adapting, dramatizing, analyzing or, in one editor's words, ''enriching'' Mark Twain's celebrated epic. In the century following its publication, the classic has been issued and reissued (today there are more than 30 editions of the book available), amplified with introductions, bibliographies and criticism, and in one case even rewritten by a professor, who attempted to update it with contemporary slang, graphic sex and a heightened antislavery theme.   The performing arts, too, have eagerly seized upon the novel. Since 1920, five feature films, two television movies and various plays and musicals have been made of ''Huckleberry Finn''; and there are currently three dramatic presentations, based on the book or its characters, at hand: the Broadway musical ''Big River,'' ''The Adventures of Mark Twain,'' a recently released animated movie featuring Huck, Tom Sawyer and Becky Thatcher, and a four-part American Playhouse dramatization of the novel, the third segment of which airs tonight on Channel 13.
headline: ADAPTING AND REVISING TWAIN'S 'HUCK FINN'

title: Blessings In Disguise
author: Alec Guinness
pull_quote: BLESSINGS IN DISGUISE. By Alec Guinness. Illustrated. 238 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.    IF one happens to be an American, one thinks of Sir Alec Guinness primarily as a great film actor. So the first surprise in his charming and original autobiography, ''Blessings in Disguise,'' is that he scarcely mentions his movie career until the 15th of the book's 16 chapters.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Siege
author: Conor Cruise O'Brien
pull_quote: THE SIEGE. The Saga of Israel and Zionism. By Conor Cruise O'Brien. Illustrated. 798 pages. Simon & Schuster. $24.95. THERE is no shortage of books about Israel; there is unlikely to be any shortage of them in years to come. But ''The Siege'' is one of the very few that one would confidently predict is going to prove of enduring interest. It has a combination of qualities that sets it apart from the great mass of writing on the subject; its distinction is of the kind that doesn't get overtaken by events.   In the first place, it addresses itself to the essential issues of the Arab-Israeli dispute, without losing sight of the intricate forms that those issues have taken in practice. It is written out of deep personal conviction, but also from the point of view of an outsider, who maintains a certain inevitable (and valuable) distance, and makes illuminating use of his own concerns and experiences - those of an Irishman, in particular. It is the work of a liberal who disagrees with many of the prevailing liberal assumptions about the Middle East, and who engages unflinchingly with those points that most need to be argued in the current climate of opinion.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Sportswriter
author: Richard Ford
pull_quote: THE SPORTSWRITER. By Richard Ford. 375 pages. Vintage Contemporaries.   Paper, $6.95. FRANK BASCOMBE, the protagonist of Richard Ford's powerful new novel, is a sportswriter the way Walker Percy's famous hero, Binx Bolling, was a moviegoer. Frank admires athletes, regards them as ''people who are happy to let their actions speak for them,'' and he envies their capacity to live ''within'' themselves -''a basketball player who goes for his patented outside jumper,'' he observes, ''becomes nothing more than the simple wish personified that the ball go in the hole.'' As a young man, Frank himself possessed ''the lanky, long-loose-arm grace of a natural ball player,'' but he was never much good at the game, afflicted as he was by a crippling self-consciousness, ''an inbred irony'' that cramped his instincts and his timing. So today, Frank works as a writer for a glossy sports magazine - watching, observing and annotating the actions of others. It is a job, he tells us, that he rather enjoys, a job that teaches you ''there are no transcendent themes in life,'' that ''things are here and they're over, and that has to be enough.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Whites
author: Norman Rush
pull_quote: WHITES. Stories by Norman Rush. 150 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $14.95. ''WHITES.'' The title of   Norman Rush's first collection of stories has an abruptness bordering on a curse. The setting - the south African republic of Botswana (formerly Bechuanaland) - and Mr. Rush's credentials as a co-director of the Peace Corps there from 1978 to 1983 further suggest that we are in for at least a taste of ideology in what follows, one that is not likely to place white people in an especially favorable light.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Sound-Shadows Of The New World
author: Ved Mehta
pull_quote: SOUND-SHADOWS OF THE NEW WORLD. By Ved Mehta. 430 pages.   W. W. Norton. $17.95. IN the continuing multivolume story about himself, his parents, and the modern evolution of India, which may yet turn out to be longer than standard biographies of monarchs and presidents, Ved Mehta now moves to his adolescence in the United States. ''Sound-Shadows of the New World'' could be the most accessible book thus far in the saga of the Mehta family, relatives and friends. The title itself is revealing; it refers to the echoes and sensations that enable a blind person to penetrate the dark world around him.
headline: Books: Mehta, Cont'd

title: Marriage And Morals Among The Victorians
author: Gertrude Himmelfarb
pull_quote: MARRIAGE AND MORALS AMONG THE VICTORIANS. Essays by Gertrude Himmelfarb. 253 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $19.95. THE title of Gertrude Himmelfarb's new collection of essays is a little misleading. It is taken from the title of the opening piece, a dissection of Phyllis Rose's study of Victorian wedlock and deadlock, ''Parallel Lives''; but in the subsequent essays, though marital themes crop up from time to time, they are not a major preoccupation. Morals, on the other hand, are absolutely central to the book's concerns - not in the narrow sense, but in terms of an all-pervading ''moral imagination.''   That phrase is necessarily vague, just because its application is so wide; but it serves very well, Miss Himmelfarb argues, to sum up a set of characteristic Victorian convictions - a belief in human dignity, a respect for human complexity, a sense of common responsibility based on sympathetic insight rather than textbook rules.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Tender Passion
author: Peter Gay
pull_quote: THE TENDER PASSION: The Bourgeois Experience, Victoria to Freud. By Peter Gay. 490 pages. Oxford University Press. $24.95. In the first volume of his massive examination of bourgeois life during the 19th century, the historian Peter Gay took it upon himself to re-examine the sexual behavior and attitudes of the Victorians, both here and in Western Europe. ''Education of the Senses'' (1984), as that volume was called, proved to be a witty, erudite and controversial study that challenged many of the stereotypes commonly held about that not so distant era - besides arguing that the middle classes of that period were considerably more interested in sex than its genteel manners suggested, the book presented a thoroughgoing reassessment of the role and nature of Victorian women, persuasively arguing that the old image of them as repressed, frigid, anesthetic creatures was as inadequate as it was demeaning.
headline: VICTORIANS IN LOVE

title: Lovers And Fugitives
author: Gabriella Mautner
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOVERS AND FUGITIVES.   By Gabriella Mautner. (Mercury House, $16.95.) The lovers and fugitives of Gabriella Mautner's novel are David Held and Saskia Stark, young German Jews seeking a safe haven in the early years of World War II.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Winter's Tales
author: David Hughes
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WINTER'S TALES New Series: One. Edited by David Hughes. 189 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $13.95. AS I watched the mailman skid up my ice-covered walk, ''Winter's Tales'' in his gloved hand, I vowed to read the book slowly, reflectively - as a reviewer. But seven pages into the first story, Muriel Spark's ''Executor,'' when a woman haunted by her uncle's ghost prays, ''Make me strong, and guide and lead me as to how Mrs. Thatcher would conduct herself in circumstances of this nature'' - a prayer that perfectly sums up her character - I found myself gobbling up the feast of these fine stories.
headline: PUT OFF BY BEAUTY AND OTHER STORIES

title: On Becoming A Biologist
author: John Janovy Jr
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ON BECOMING A BIOLOGIST. By John Janovy Jr. (Harper & Row, $15.95.) In ''On Becoming a Biologist,'' John Janovy Jr. writes that biologists see the worth of a plant or an animal ''in its contribution to our understanding of life, not necessarily in our ability to convert it into money or prestige.''
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: One Is A Wanderer
author: Francis King
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ONE IS A WANDERER. By Francis King. (Little, Brown, $16.95.) Francis King's editors are not really his friends. Why, otherwise, would they allow this English novelist and critic to publish a collection of 21 stories so wildly uneven in quality? Mr. King's last novel, ''Voices in an Empty Room,'' showed him master of a subtle, melancholy style, rich and understated. At his best he achieves this in his short stories, but it occurs rarely in this collection. ''Indirect Method'' is a poignant story about an Englishwoman who returns to Japan and visits her family's former houseboy, now a married businessman, who had been her lover. The great chasm between them, and the failure of emotion to bridge it finally, is beautifully rendered, as it is in ''The Festival of the Dead,'' about an Englishwoman whose Japanese lover mourns the death of his young son. ''The Goat,'' an unsettling account of the death of an adored animal, and ''A Corner of a Foreign Field,'' about an old Japanese scholar of English literature, are both small jewels. But the rest of the stories are crude and heavily ironic, lacking depth, perception and finesse. We have the feeling that he is dashing these off. In three of the stories, for example, there appears a woman whose hair is ''an improbable shade of orange.'' Using the same trite phrase three times in the same book is not a criminal offense, but it makes the author's position clear: Mr. King simply can't be bothered to think up a new phrase, one that startles and delights and brings a character into vivid focus.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Coaster
author: George Foy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: COASTER By George Foy. 326 pp. New York: Viking. $16.95. JOHN PENROSE, the central figure in George Foy's complex thriller, is the owner-captain of a beat-up coastal freighter taking on a cargo of highly volatile coal dust at a Welsh port. En route to its destination, the cargo liquefies, shifts and sends Penrose's ship to the bottom of the English Channel. He makes a claim on a Lloyd's of London underwriter for insurance, the claim is denied, and Penrose finds himself launched on a series of hair-raising, frequently nightmarish adventures.
headline: COAL FOR DAVY JONES'S LOCKER

title: The Postponed Generation
author: Susan Littwin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE POSTPONED GENERATION: Why America's Grown-up Kids Are Growing Up Later. By Susan Littwin. (Morrow, $16.95.) What a dismal picture of the young! Pampered by their parents, intellectually stunted by poor education, made cynical by politics and boggled by changing sex roles, they respond by prolonging adolescence for 10 extra years.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Grania: She-King Of The Irish Seas
author: Sherie Posesorski
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GRANIA: She-King of the Irish Seas. By Morgan Llywelyn. (Crown, $17.95.) What becomes a legend most? ''Battle and murder''? ''Imprisonment and impoverishment''? Thus ponders Grania, legendary 16th-century Irish chieftain and self-proclaimed She-King of Ireland, as her life passes before her eyes in cinema verite detail.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Little People
author: MacDonald Harris
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LITTLE PEOPLE By MacDonald Harris. 299 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $16.95. RURAL England, which is surely now among the tamest and most conquered of landscapes, goes on being the setting for an improbably large number of stories that draw on the primeval forces of wild nature, the dark backward of gods and fairies, the old Druid forest and the barrow and megalith. MacDonald Harris is an American, and at first it seems that may be what makes his particular variant on the standard themes so strangely unreal; but no, it's more than that.
headline: NO SEX PLEASE -- WE'RE ELFISH

title: Conflicts And Contradictions
author: Meron Benvenisti
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CONFLICTS AND CONTRADICTIONS By Meron Benvenisti. 210 pp. New York: Villard Books. $15.95. IN A. B. Yehoshua's novella ''Facing the Forests'' (published in Israel in 1963), a young Israeli watchman, a forest scout, is haunted by the remains of an Arab village that was bulldozed to make way for a newly planted forest of slender pine trees. The watchman shares the solitude of the forest with an old Arab who cannot speak and an Arab child. The solitude is interrupted every now and then by groups of hikers who come to admire the work of the Afforestation Department. One such group of hikers turned up with a map and inquired as to the whereabouts of an Arab village. ''A village?'' the watchman asked. He knew of no such village: ''The map must be wrong, the surveyor's hand must have shaken.'' But the old Arab, in excited gestures, ''pointing fervently, hopelessly, at the forest,'' confirms that a village once stood there. The young watchman now wants the forest to burn down. Eventually, on the last night of his assignment, he looks away as the old Arab burns down the forest in a ''riot of horror and glee.'' And out of the smoke and haze, the ruined village appears before his eyes ''in its basic outlines as an abstract drawing, as all things past and buried.''
headline: LIVING AMONG THEIR ENEMIES

title: Marya: A Life
author: Joyce Carol Oates.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MARYA A Life. By Joyce Carol Oates. 310 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $16.95. WE punish Joyce Carol Oates for the crime of her productivity. A book a year, in some years two - we respond as if she did it just to make us look bad, the A student who hands in for a geography assignment not only a weather map of the Hawaiian Islands, but a papier-mache model of a volcano as well. Our sense of her work as a mass ready at any moment to engulf us makes us reluctant to read, as they come toward us, the individual works and to differentiate among them. Partly, we assume that if there are that many none can be any good, as if literature were a finite resource like, say, a soup meant to serve 10 which had been cynically thinned to fill the bowls of 36.
headline: THE LIFE AND HARD TIMES OF CINDERELLA

title: Krippendorf's Tribe
author: Frank Parkin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: KRIPPENDORF'S TRIBE By Frank Parkin. 192 pp. New York: Atheneum. $13.95. JAMES KRIPPENDORF, the protagonist of Frank   Parkin's first novel, is an unemployed anthropologist and beleaguered house-husband who does not know what to make of his screaming, brawling progeny. But just when the reader begins to think that perhaps a stew, House of Atreus style, might be nice, Krippendorf does manage to contrive a project: a fictional, anthropological study of an Amazonian tribe which will use his own children and their savage ways for fieldwork data. To substantiate his ''research,'' he will darken their skins, dress them up and take pictures of them in the backyard of his suburban London home. He will seduce the Ethiopian baby sitter and a Thai nurse and take pictures of them as well. This will save on expenses (the grant money which he spent long ago), and, if no one discovers his deception, will bring his career out of the broom closet. His research, he is told, could do for this ''Shelmikedmu'' tribe ''what Margaret Mead did for the Trobriand Islanders.''
headline: ONWARD AND UPWARD WITH THE SHELMIKEDMU

title: Decision In Philadelphia
author: Christopher Collier and James Lincoln Collier.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DECISION IN PHILADELPHIA The Constitutional Convention of 1787. By Christopher Collier and James Lincoln Collier. 331 pp. New York: Reader's Digest Press/Random House. $19.95. THE major anniversary of a great event in American history usually produces a flurry of books, needed or not. We need books about the creation of the Constitution, so we can look forward with anticipation to the bicentennial of its birth in 1987.   We need books about the making of the Constitution because professional historians all but abandoned the topic 20 years ago. Absorbed by the controversy over Charles Beard's thesis regarding the economic motives of the drafters of the Constitution, constitutional scholarship in the 1950's and early 60's became so disputatious and complicated that it intimidated even experts. Concurrently, the ascendancy of what has been called the new social history, which focuses on the activities of the humbler segments of society rather than ''great white men,'' practically proscribed the Constitution as a topic of investigation. As a result, many professional historians believe that they have ''no stake in the Constitution,'' a remark that passed without reproof from the members of the fraternity assembled at a recent conference. The passing of history from college curriculums because of its perceived irrelevance, documented by recent surveys, is surely related to the pervasiveness of such attitudes in the academy.
headline: JAMES MADISON, MINUS HALO

title: The Serpent And The Rainbow
author: Wade Davis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SERPENT AND THE RAINBOW. By Wade Davis. (Simon & Shuster, $17.95.) Zombies are more than legend, it seems. Haitian sorcerers actually use substances than can drastically reduce the body's metabolic rate and cause a condition of seeming death.

author: Mell Lazarus

pull_quote: THE NEIGHBORHOOD WATCH. By Mell Lazarus. (Doubleday, $16.95.) Loring Neiman, to turn Byron's phrase, awakes one morning to find himself destitute.
