title: Available Light
author: Ellen Currie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
AVAILABLE LIGHT By Ellen Currie. 297 pp. New York: Summit Books. $16.95.
''T

HIS is not trouble we're having, this is just life we're having,'' Eileen tells her sister, Kitty, who answers, ''I sincerely hope you are mistaken.'' They're both right. Life, as it happens in this first novel, isn't trouble-free or just. It's funny, menacing and more than a little skewed - as if Fra Angelico's ''Annunciation'' had been retouched by Salvador Dali and used as a backdrop for a rock video. This is a tall tale told with high good humor and respect for unshared but universal secrets.

At first ''Available Light'' seems straightforward enough: Kitty, a fashion stylist who rounds up ''the clothes and so on for the models and actors in print ads . . . and television commercials,'' wakes up one morning to find that her lover, Rambeau, a gambler, has left her. As the couple's paths separate, though, the story widens too, stretching familiar patterns of love into amazing events.
headline: RAMBEAU -- NOT RIMBAUD OR RAMBO

title: Walking On Glass
author: Iain Banks
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WALKING ON GLASS By Iain Banks. 239 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $15.95. THIS novel contrasts three different sets of fantasies: those of a young man in love with a woman who he (and everyone else) knows is already involved with someone; those of a paranoid workman who should be hospitalized; and, finally, the highly conventionalized fantasies regularly presented in works of science fiction and fantasy. Iain Banks has taken on an ambitious formal task.   The English art student Graham Park has fallen in love with Sara ffitch - yes, two lowercase f's. In five chapters and a coda, Graham reviews their meeting at a party, visits Sara at her flat and endlessly questions his friend Slater about her, while trying not to think too much about her estranged husband or her current lover, the leather-garbed, motorcycle-riding Bob Stock.
headline: IN LOVE WITH SARA FFITCH

title: The Man Who Mistook His Wife For A Hat
author: Oliver Sacks. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE MAN WHO MISTOOK HIS WIFE FOR A HAT And Other Clinical Tales. By Oliver Sacks. Illustrated. 233 pp. New York: Summit Books. $15.95. WHEN the Psalmist lamented the Jewish exile by the waters of Babylon he wrote:

''If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand lose its cunning and my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth if I remember thee not.'' The Psalmist's style differs somewhat from that of current medical journals, yet the writer is describing a neurological condition well known to the modern physician. Now, as then, many people who are unfortunate enough to suffer a cerebrovascular accident - a stroke - become paralyzed on the right side of the body and lose their command of speech. Many other examples of severe but relatively isolated disorders of perception, knowledge or skilled action consequent upon injury to the brain were described by scholars of the ancient world. For example, in his ''Natural History'' the elder Pliny tells how a man who fell from a high roof failed to recognize the faces of his mother and other close relatives and friends. Likewise Thucydides reports in his ''History of the Peloponnesian War'' how famine and typhus caused many people to be unable to recall recent events in their lives.
headline: IN THE REGION OF LOST MINDS

title: Peace, O River
author: Nancy Garden
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PEACE, O RIVER By Nancy Garden. 246 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $12.95. (Ages 12 and up) IN ''Peace, O River,'' a somewhat grim, unrelievedly message-driven novel, Nancy Garden uses the contemporary issue of nuclear waste to propel what is essentially a thinly veiled cautionary tale about class and social status.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Alexander Pope: A Life
author: Maynard Mack. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ALEXANDER POPE A Life. By Maynard Mack. Illustrated. 975 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $22.50. ALEXANDER POPE had a very long period of development as a poet; in fact, one could say it was lifelong. A modern reader new to his work, picking up, say, some close-printed one-volume edition and flicking through the pages, is apt to notice first that with very rare exceptions his poetry is composed in 10-syllable couplets and then to conclude hastily that it is all basically similar, as if one poem in couplets must be like another. In fact, Pope's gamut goes all the way from the prettiness of the early ''Pastorals,'' through the delicate fantasy of ''The Rape of the Lock'' and the surreal and savage burlesque of ''The Dunciad,'' to the calm and luminous irony of the ''Imitations of Horace,'' which discuss life and relationships very directly in a language stripped of ornament and staying very close to prose - though, thanks to the fineness of the poet's ear for rhythm and cadence, never becoming merely prosy. Pope had inherited from Renaissance literary culture the doctrine that literature naturally groups itself in genres, or ''kinds,'' and that there is an appropriate set of conventions and an appropriate linguistic level for each kind, so that training oneself for a fresh attempt on one is like learning a new language. He succeeded in so many kinds that his achievement is complex and not at all easy to assess beyond the simple remark that it is brilliant.
headline: A PROPER STUDY OF THE MAN

title: The New York Times World Of New York
author: Marvin Siegel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE NEW YORK TIMES WORLD OF NEW YORK: An Uncommon Guide to the City of Fantasies. Edited by A. M. Rosenthal and Arthur Gelb in association with Marvin Siegel.

title: In One Newspaper
author: Konstantin Simonov
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN ONE NEWSPAPER: A Chronicle of Unforgettable Years. By Ilya Ehrenburg and Konstantin Simonov. (Sphinx Press, $24.95.) Four decades after the end of World War II, much of the immediacy and the passion have gone from the articles that Ilya Ehrenburg and Konstantin Simonov wrote for the Russian Army newspaper, The Red Star.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Academic Festival Overtures
author: Daryl Hine
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ACADEMIC FESTIVAL OVERTURES By Daryl Hine. 189 pp. New York: Atheneum. Cloth, $20. Paper, $10.95. THE LONG APPROACH By Maxine Kumin. 80 pp. New York: Viking. $14.95. THE PAST By Galway Kinnell. 57 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. Cloth, $13.95. Paper, $5.95. DARYL HINE, celebrated for translations of the Homeric Hymns and Theocritus, has embarked on his own autobiography in classical disguise in ''Academic Festival Overtures.'' Though the poem is written in self-proclaimed alexandrines (by alternating 13 and 12 syllables), its indented patterning is suggestive rather of Ovid (part ''Tristia,'' part ''Amores''). The narrative impulse races through long paragraphs, while a rhyme scheme insistently coagulates internal elements into epigrammatic quatrains. It is a virtuoso achievement, as remarkable in its way as anything by Auden. It is also a remarkable record of a yearning, bookish and inhibited boyhood. Behind the metrical screen Mr. Hine imposes on his memoirs, he paces to and fro - as if watching from be-hind the self-imposed bars of his caged existence.
headline: REFUGE IN THE LIBRARY, ON THE FARM AND IN MEMORIES

title: Edith Stein: A Biography
author: Waltraud Herbstrith
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EDITH STEIN A Biography. By Waltraud Herbstrith. Translated by Bernard Bonowitz. Illustrated. 127 pp. San Francisco: Harper & Row. $15.95. PHILOSOPHER and mystic, Edith Stein began life in 1891 as a precocious, high-strung, intellectually flamboyant child in a strict Jewish family in prewar Germany. From the outset she was an obsessive, energetic scholar and in time she became passionately drawn to philosophy, especially phenomenology, the description and classification of phenomena, and went to learn from its master, Edmund Husserl, at Gottingen.
headline: JEWISH NUN AND MARTYR

title: Family And Nation
author: Daniel Patrick Moynihan.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FAMILY AND NATION The Godkin Lectures, Harvard University. By Daniel Patrick Moynihan. 207 pp. San Diego: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $12.95. CHILD poverty is epidemic in the United States. But poverty is unfashionable; most politicians struggle to show their unconcern with old-fashioned ''liberal'' issues. So Daniel Patrick Moynihan, the senior senator from New York, should be congratulated for devoting his 1985 Godkin Lectures at Harvard University, reprinted in this book, to a plea for concern. Children make up only 27 percent of the nation but 40 percent of the people in poverty; they are, Mr. Moynihan points out, ''the only age group over-represented in the poverty population.'' The situation is particularly alarming among minorities - in 1984 almost half of America's black and over a third of its Hispanic children lived below the poverty line. We are compromising our future as well as our humanity.
headline: 40% OF THE POOR ARE CHILDREN

title: Saturday Night
author: Doug Hill and Jeff Weingrad. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SATURDAY NIGHT A Backstage History of ''Saturday Night Live.'' By Doug Hill and Jeff Weingrad. Illustrated. 510 pp. New York: Beech Tree Books/William Morrow & Company. $17.95. IN the mid-1970's, satire changed from what closed on Saturday night to what people stayed at home to watch on Saturday night. For a time ''Saturday Night Live,'' like rock music before it, captivated a generation and attained a near-mythic status.   Maintaining that status is no easy task, as Doug Hill and Jeff Weingrad point out in ''Saturday Night.'' Mr. Hill, a staff writer for TV Guide, and Mr. Weingrad, an editor for Woman's World magazine, trace the evolution of ''Saturday Night Live'' and explain how the pressure of living up to a legend affected those who created the show. The book is packed with the kind of behind-the-scenes information that reveals the world behind the hoopla, besides having a special interest for those fascinated with the mechanics of production. Getting an extremely complex 90-minute show on the air live is a daunting job, and much of this book's most interesting material describes the chaotic but ultimately effective production process.
headline: CONEHEADS IN CAMELOT

title: Pretty Good For A Woman
author: D. A. Callard. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ''PRETTY GOOD FOR A WOMAN'' The Enigmas of Evelyn Scott. By D. A. Callard. Illustrated. 202 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $14.95. IT was 1929, and his publisher felt that the provocative but minor William Faulkner would need critical support if his new book was to to be well received. It was submitted to a better-known writer, and the result was a small pamphlet. It began: ''This essay by Evelyn Scott, whose recent novel 'The Wave' placed her among the outstanding literary figures of her time . . . is being distributed to those who are interested in Miss Scott's work and the writing of William Faulkner. 'The Sound and the Fury' should place William Faulkner in company with Evelyn Scott.''   Eleven years later, a very successful Faulkner was asked whether there were any good female writers. ''Well,'' he answered, ''Evelyn Scott was pretty good, for a woman.'' I'd say that was a shrewd tactical response, for if, as the comment makes clear, he didn't care to keep company with female writers at all, why not offer a few critical leavings to one whose career had declined so far that she no longer posed a threat? ''No memory of having starred / Atones for later disregard / (Or keeps the end from being hard),'' wrote Robert Frost in a vengeful little poem called ''Provide, Provide.'' He was right.
headline: SHE MIGHT HAVE HAD IT ALL

title: The God Of Mirrors
author: Robert Reilly
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GOD OF MIRRORS By Robert Reilly. 403 pp. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. $17.95. MAKING novels out of the lives of historical figures is always dangerous. This is particularly so for Oscar Wilde. Even 40 years ago, Richard Aldington could write, ''Almost everything that could be said about Oscar Wilde has been said already.'' Not quite. Definitive biographies and fictionalizations kept emerging, and Wilde himself spoke beyond the grave, for ''De Profundis'' was published uncut for the first time in 1960. The dangers in Wilde's case are further compounded by the fact that he self-consciously turned his own life into a fiction. One of his most persistent paradoxes, which he managed to make entirely convincing, was that life imitates art. His acquaintances all testified that Wilde's greatest art was his conversation. His disregard of facts was one of the primary facts about him.
headline: OSCAR WAS STRANGER THAN FICTION

title: The Dream Of Deliverance In American Politics
author: Mona Harrington
pull_quote: THE DREAM OF DELIVERANCE IN AMERICAN POLITICS. By Mona Harrington. 308 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $19.95.   MONA HARRINGTON, a lawyer and political scientist, asks a familiar but important question at the opening of her intriguing study, ''The Dream of Deliverance in American Politics.'' Why have so many Americans lost confidence in their system? Her answer is not much more startling. The American Dream has failed, she believes, because we have allowed ourselves to be seduced by what she calls the ''myth of the deliverance from evil,'' which, she argues, over the course of the past century or so, has been promoted by three primary but irreconcilable interest groups within the American economy.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Randlords
author: Geoffrey Wheatcroft
pull_quote: THE RANDLORDS. By Geoffrey Wheatcroft. 314 pages. Illustrated. Atheneum. $17.95. ONE of the countless changes that the triumph of the bourgeoisie brought with it in the 19th century was - relatively speaking - the democratization of diamonds. Where they had once been the prerogative of the very rich, in Europe and North America they became a familiar object of middle-class desire (the diamond engagement ring above all), and by mid-century potential demand had far outstripped the supply.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Transactions In A Foreign Currency
author: Deborah Eisenberg
pull_quote: TRANSACTIONS IN A FOREIGN CURRENCY. By Deborah Eisenberg. 214 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.   THE author of the highly acclaimed play ''Pastorale'' (1982), Deborah Eisenberg writes with a playwright's quick, bristling ear for dialogue and a painter's affection for nuance and image. In this, her first collection of fiction, she delineates her characters' lives with a full palette of colors, using not just the earth tones of fashionable alienation, but also the pastel brights of comedy and the darker, more luminous shades of an artist blessed with emotional wisdom. By turns magical, tender and funny, ''Transactions in a Foreign Currency'' makes for an astonishing debut.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Greatest Crusade
author: Richard Hough
pull_quote: THE GREATEST CRUSADE: Roosevelt, Churchill and the Naval Wars. By Richard Hough. Illustrated. 274 pages.   William Morrow. $17.95. THIS is the story of two men, two nations and two wars; the growth of the American-British Alliance from 1917 and the naval battles in the First and Second World Wars that did so much to achieve victory.
headline: Books: Wars at Sea

title: America In Europe
author: German Arciniegas
pull_quote: AMERICA IN EUROPE: A History of the New World in Reverse. By German Arciniegas. Translated from the Spanish by Gabriela Arciniegas and R. Victoria Arana. 298 pages. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $19.95. FROM the moment Europeans discovered America, it began to modify their lives, their politics, their economies, their ideas. Even more importantly, perhaps, by confirming their hopes, it raised fresh ones. It was a dream come true - not exactly in the way that had been anticipated, but palpably enough to hold out the possibility that many other dreams might come true as well.   In ''America in Europe'' German Arciniegas argues that the influence of the New World on the Old has been neglected by historians. In taking it as his subject, he has set himself a daunting task; to measure its full extent would indeed be to calculate the incalculable. But Mr. Arciniegas, a veteran Colombian man of letters, is too shrewd to let himself get drawn into attempting an exhaustive survey. Instead, he concentrates on a few major themes and episodes. His aim, as he says, is ''above all to promote another choice - a new perspective.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: A Family Madness
author: Thomas Keneally
pull_quote: A FAMILY MADNESS. By Thomas Keneally. 336 pages. Simon & Schuster. $17.95. The consequences of history fascinate Thomas Keneally - not so much history's abstract effects on nations and ideology as its impact on ordinary people; its cold, impersonal power to warp the shape of one's life and mold one's heart and mind. In ''The Chant of Jimmie Blacksmith'' (1972), he examined the tensions between white and aborigine cultures in turn-of-the-century Australia, through the story of a half-caste ''mission black'' who became an outlaw killer. In ''Confederates'' (1980), he looked at one summer's events during the American Civil War and their impact on four individuals. And in the award-winning ''Schindler's List'' (1982), he demonstrated how the horrors of the Holocaust inspired, in one man, a courageous moral passion that goaded him into heroic action.   Now, in his latest novel, ''A Family Madness,'' Mr. Keneally has again taken an actual historical situation -the plight of Byelorussia during World War II - and he proposes to demonstrate its lasting effects on a family and the people who cross its path.
headline: Books of The Times; Tyranny of the Past

title: In the Dark
author: R. M. Lamming.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN THE DARK By R. M. Lamming. 230 pp. New York: Atheneum. $13.95. Love, rarely a thing we can find by chasing it down, often comes from unexpected places; most often it sneaks up on our blind side. Arnold Lawson, age 84 and in surprisingly good health, has lived for 20 years with his taciturn but devoted housekeeper and his library of thousands of rare and scholarly books. He sees himself as a recluse and wants only to read his beloved books and be waited on by his hated housekeeper. His favorite pastime is berating her as she silently goes about the business of caring for him. ''She achieved the look of a perfect drudge - and an energetic one at that, the sort who glories in her slavery. Ancient Rome was probably full of them: offer them freedom, and they would purse up their lips at the insult.''
headline: AN OCTOGENARIAN'S CRUSH

title: Stairway C
author: Elvire Murail
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STAIRWAY C By Elvire Murail. Translated by M. L. Linden. 192 pp. New York: A Bard Book/Avon Books. Paper, $3.95. MY father told me about French women. ''No matter how homely, no matter how poor, the one thing they all have is style. They can walk down the street in the most ordinary dress and look like they just stepped out of Christian Dior. They do it with a touch of perfume, a scarf at the neck.''   This is what I kept thinking all through Elvire Murail's novel ''Stairway C'': she sure knows a lot of those ''scarf at the neck'' tricks. The book, Miss Murail's first, is full of the most harrowing obstacles an author can place in front of him- or herself, and she goes blithely bouncing right past them, refusing to acknowledge they even exist. That she manages to pull it off so well without making it look like a circus stunt is quite an accomplishment.
headline: GREENWICH VILLAGE MON AMOUR

title: Constitutional Reform And Effective Government
author: James L. Sundquist.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CONSTITUTIONAL REFORM AND EFFECTIVE GOVERNMENT By James L. Sundquist. 262 pp. Washington: The Brookings Institution. Cloth, $26.95. Paper, $9.95. THE bicentennial of the American Constitution takes place in 1987. Before the party begins though, it is legitimate to ask just which Constitution we will be celebrating. There is the original Constitution, which set out the powers and duties of the separate branches of the Federal Government, structuring our political institutions. There also is the document, cited frequently by many contemporary legal scholars and some jurists as the basis for judicial activism, that might accurately be described as the phantom Constitution, setting forth what ought to be the laws of the land. And then there is the unwritten Constitution, that body of arrangements and agreements subject to adaptation from time to time to meet changing circumstances, which enables the original Constitution to endure with little alteration over the years.
headline: IS IT BROKE? SHOULD WE FIX IT?

title: As Soon As It Rains
author: Kaylie Jones
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AS SOON AS IT RAINS. By Kaylie Jones. (Doubleday, $16.95.) Academic indecision, a difficult love, a semester abroad - these are familiar clippings from a college diary.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Let Us Know
author: Diane Vreuls
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LET US KNOW. By Diane Vreuls. (Viking, $14.95.) These 12 short stories range from brilliantly evocative fiction to experimental tales so laden with non sequiturs and symbolism that they threaten to collapse under their own weight.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Night Life
author: Liam Hudson. Diagrams.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NIGHT LIFE The Interpretation of Dreams. By Liam Hudson. Diagrams. 184 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $19.95. DO we still need to dream? This is the most original and provocative question that Liam Hudson, a professor of psychology at Brunel University in Uxbridge, England, asks in ''Night Life,'' a new book on a venerable subject - the interpretation of dreams. In our technological society, ''the dream is at risk,'' he announces with alarm. Comparing ours with ancient times, he has the impression that ''our dreams have become tame.'' He imagines scenarios that might threaten our very capacity to dream. Television, with its rapidly shifting images, its discontinuous narratives and its vicariously thrilling subject matter, may increasingly be doing our dreaming for us. And Mr. Hudson wonders whether the social uses of computers will expand to the point that their way of ''thinking'' will come to rule over our inner lives, forcing everything into rational channels, making all intelligence, in effect, into artificial intelligence. In that event, our imaginative powers might simply atrophy. Dreaming would no longer have an adaptive function in such a society, and if dreams continued to exist at all, they would be little more than a psychic vestige, a sort of mental appendix.
headline: LEAVE OUR DREAMS ALONE!

title: Life And Fate
author: Vasily Grossman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
LIFE AND FATE By Vasily Grossman. Translated by Robert Chandler. 880 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $22.50. AN important novel written in the Soviet Union will almost certainly prove unpublishable there, but it will usually find its way to the West sooner or later. In the case of Vasily Grossman's ''Life and Fate'' this has happened much later rather than sooner. Grossman's novel was completed in 1960. In other words it was written at about the same time as Boris Pasternak's ''Doctor Zhivago,'' the work with which the practice of smuggling out illicit writings began 30 years ago.

''Life and Fate'' hinges on the closing phase of the Battle of Stalingrad in the bleak winter of 1942-43, when the Soviet Army held and then routed the German invader on the Volga. But the action is by no means confined to that river. It also ranges through Soviet- and German-occupied Eastern Europe, giving detailed vistas of front and rear, depicting mass atrocities and penal procedures on both sides. The text is nearly 900 pages, and the named characters are legion.
headline: STALINGRAD AND STALIN'S TERROR

title: Painters And Public Life
author: Thomas E. Crow. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PAINTERS AND PUBLIC LIFE In Eighteenth-Century Paris. By Thomas E. Crow. Illustrated. 290 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $40. TO some readers, Thomas E. Crow's first book might suggest only another chronology of 18th-century French painting, beginning with Watteau and ending with Jacques Louis David. But to those more familiar with the revisionist methods of current art history, ''Painters and Public Life: In Eighteenth-Century Paris'' will represent the most comprehensive and valuable study of art and public life in that era now in print. Mr. Crow, an assistant professor of art at Princeton University, attempts, with much success, to investigate almost every manifestation of what might be considered public - public life, spaces, opinion, discourse, art and, finally, the public itself, which he sees as ''nothing more nor less than a series of representations.''
headline: OUT OF THE BOUDOIR AND INTO THE STREETS

title: Sound-Shadows Of The New World
author: Ved Mehta
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOUND-SHADOWS OF THE NEW WORLD By Ved Mehta. Illustrated. 430 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $17.95. PICTURE the skinny teen-age boy, blind, self-conscious with ambition, cramped in a musty broom closet - his mildewed, cobwebbed room of his own - dreaming of Shakespeare. ''Oh, my yearning is simply to become like this great man,'' he types in his journal (a journal he will never be able to read himself). ''I know that's impossible. But if one aims one's arrow at the sky, it will at least get to the top of the trees.''   There is something sweetly heroic about the boy in his broom closet as he painstakingly transforms the tiny, bare room (''close as a coffin'' and smelling of Ajax) at the Arkansas School for the Blind into a writer's studio, an electronic refuge stocked with typewriter, radio-phonograph, tape recorder, Talking Book player and earphones. There's something poignant about the young high school student from India, desperate for news of a world beyond Little Rock, excitedly recording and replaying Edward R. Murrow's daily broadcasts as a charm against his own isolation, ''almost like a boy on the moon.'' But youthful egotism, however delightfully expressed, can become a bit tiresome; announced ambition, however naive (''I would also like my views to be known widely - all over the world''), soon loses its appeal. And self-absorption, after a while, becomes claustrophobic - like being shut away in a dark, dusty closet.
headline: A DONKEY AMONG HORSES

title: The Bourne Supremacy
author: Robert Ludlum
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BOURNE SUPREMACY By Robert Ludlum. 597 pp. New York: Random House. $19.95. READING Robert Ludlum's latest thriller is a bit like watching a blacksmith forge a very long chain. The making of the first few links is interesting enough as an exercise in brute manipulation. What is lacking in finesse and artistry is made up for by lots of noise and energy. But after watching the smith link together a foot or so of chain, one perceives a certain sameness to the effort. The chief suspense is in how long the man will keep at it.   To be fair, in ''The Bourne Supremacy'' Mr. Ludlum does not simply create one chapter over and over again. He makes two. In the first kind of chapter a character explains the plot to another character. The second character expresses incredulity - ''This is nuts!'' - no matter how many times he has heard the scheme. The plot of this chapter does not vary, although teller and listener do become slightly more appalled at the consequences as they go along - ''You're crazy!''
headline: CHOPPING DOWN A FOREST OF BAD GUYS

title: Blanche And Nicky
author: Elliot West
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BLANCHE AND NICKY By Elliot West. 323 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $18.95. PROSTITUTES in fiction are rarely more than sentimental variations on cliches. Fanny Hill performed with as much emotional virtuosity as a pornographic film star, and even Emile Zola's Nana, who may be the most enduring fictional representative of her trade, seemed to be as much a victim of circumstances as a woman driven by her own passions.
headline: HER SINS AND HER SON

title: Forrest Gump
author: Winston Groom
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
FORREST GUMP By Winston Groom. 228 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $14.95. THIS novel is a tale told by an idiot (with an I.Q., he tells us, ''near 70'') who, in the course of his travels through three decades of American landscape, becomes a football star, a war hero, a Ping-Pong ace, a one-man band, a chess champion, a movie actor, an astronaut, a professional wrestler and a business tycoon. Forrest Gump also gets to visit China - he in fact saves Mao Zedong from drowning - and he spends four years in the jungles of New Guinea among cannibals. Winston Groom's picaresque novel is a kind of defanged ''Candide,'' an unabrasive satire of the idiocy of life in our time as manifested in various touchstone events and institutions.

Each of Mr. Groom's three earlier novels (''Better Times Than These,'' ''As Summers Die,'' ''Only'') is as different from the others as they are from the present work. Mr. Groom seems to be willing his fictions into existence rather than letting them emerge out of intractable necessity. Except for ''As Summers Die,'' the novels have a certain conviction, but together they sustain no coherent vision. ''Forrest Gump'' is an advance, in this sense, over its predecessors. It is the least tendentious of the books and comes out of a deeper and more mysterious source.
headline: 'A PRETTY INTERESTIN' LIFE'

title: The Fanciest Dive
author: Christopher M. Byron.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE FANCIEST DIVE What Happened When the Media Empire of TIME/LIFE Leaped Without Looking Into the Age of High-Tech. By Christopher M. Byron. 280 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $16.95. WHEN I worked for Time Incorporated I knew there was a 34th floor, somewhere up above, that commanded everything I was happy to ignore, which is to say everything on the corporate level. As I was of course opposed to that level on principle, I joined the Newspaper Guild -whose memos reflected as great an impertinence toward the actual business of writing a story as management's did. In practice, I stayed out of the 34th floor's way and it stayed out of mine.

I figured those guys up there could take care of the business end, keeping profits up so that I could continue to enjoy the admirable freedom of a Sports Illustrated writer. I never made more than $500 a week, but I could pretty much go wherever I felt a story led and could stay in a fancy hotel. I seldom had to go into the office, and when I did I could get drunk in excellent company and play golf in the halls. A hell of a job.
headline: ABLE WERE THEY ERE THEY SAW CABLE

title: Between Washington And Jerusalem
author: Wolf Blitzer.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BETWEEN WASHINGTON AND JERUSALEM A Reporter's Notebook. By Wolf Blitzer. 259 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $15.95. AMERICANS, Israelis and even Arabs derive endless fascination from scrutiny of the strange and - dare I say it? -special relationship between America and Israel. The topic is both simpler and more complex than is commonly supposed.   Simpler at its base: across generations of policy makers and successive administrations of both political parties, United States policy is simply pro-Israel, however distasteful this may be to moderate Arabs and their sympathizers in this country. More complex in the way the relationship operates: nothing happens automatically, and little happens by deliberate prearrangement. The alliance (in all but name) functions only through the most painstaking attention to detail by officials on both sides, senior and junior, who arrive at working arrangements from quite different starting points, for differing motives and, often, driven by quite different interests.
headline: BETTER THAN 5 C.I.A.'S

title: Rembrandt: His Life, His Paintings
author: Gary Schwartz. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: REMBRANDT His Life, His Paintings. By Gary Schwartz. Illustrated. 380 pp. New York: Viking. $50. IN his fascinating study of Rembrandt, Gary Schwartz is engaged in recovering the true likeness of the painter that lies beneath the mellow chiaro-scuro of his self-portraits, and the image that emerges is neither saintly nor endearing. From a thorough and careful study of documents, mostly concerning patronage, the author vividly characterizes Rembrandt as a repugnant and untrustworthy person. Greedy, vain, unsociable, boorish and arrogant, this Rembrandt hardly fits the stereotyped portrait of the kindly old grandfather who warms our hearts with his probing portrayals of man's humanity.
headline: ABOVE ALL, HE PLEASED HIS PATRONS

title: The Girl Who Would Be Russian
author: Willis Johnson.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GIRL WHO WOULD BE RUSSIAN And Other Stories. By Willis Johnson. 180 pp. San Diego: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $15.95. IN the early 1950's, Richmond, Me., a small town on the banks of the Kennebec River, became the site of a colony of White Russian immigrants still loyal to the memory of czarist days. These original immigrants are now old and dying, and their rich ethnic community is dying out with them. But Willis Johnson has made this colony the subject of his first book of fiction, ''The Girl Who Would Be Russian,'' a superb collection of seven traditionally realistic stories.   In the title story, the ''girl'' (she's actually 31, dangerously overweight and still living at home with her mother) decides to become a Russian because, unlike the familiar and faded natives, ''Russians, at least, looked like something.'' She affects Russian peasant dress, a Russian accent, learns to sing Russian folk songs and to play the ''bellyliker.'' She is finally and pathetically undone by her obsession with the exotic, and her story can be seen as the possible fate of the writer who seeks to deal with such material. But Mr. Johnson, a former Associated Press reporter who is neither Russian nor a native of Maine, achieves just the right balance between sympathetic understanding and ironic detachment.
headline: MOTHER MAINE

title: South Light: A Journey To The Last Continent
author: Michael Parfit.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOUTH LIGHT A Journey to the Last Continent. By Michael Parfit. 306 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $17.95. EVERY year, the National Science Foundation outfits five or six journalists in survival suits and bunny boots and sends them on a whirlwind tour of Antarctica to publicize United States scientific research programs there. Usually the results are newsy stories in the daily papers and the general interest magazines. Michael Parfit took the tour too - he saw the same scientists, the same antifreeze-producing fish, got the same briefing at the South Pole, even saw what may be the very same stiff dead seal I'd seen on my press tour a few years earlier. But Mr. Parfit stayed on. His ''South Light: A Journey to the Last Continent'' covers a whole season, from a harrowing whiteout landing in the early spring, when a supply plane touches down in a snowstorm so dense that air, sea and land have become indistinguishable, to a last-minute escape by icebreaker in the late fall.
headline: WHERE THE FISH HAVE ANTIFREEZE

title: Going To See The Leaves
author: Linda Collins
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GOING TO SEE THE LEAVES By Linda Collins. 197 pp. New York: Viking. $15.95. AS the American baby boomers begin to enter their 40s, perhaps the experience of middle age will become a more serious subject for our literature, and the midlife crisis will be recognized as more than a sociological chestnut dismissible by yet another Hollywood cackle. If so, the baby boom generation may have found a sympathetic interpreter in Linda Collins, whose work has appeared previously in many magazines, though this is her first collection of stories. ''Going to See the Leaves'' describes the trials and poignancy of transit into the middle years with sobering precision and shows evidence of a mature talent.
headline: THE HERO WAS PREGNANT

title: Transactions In A Foreign Currency
author: Deborah Eisenberg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TRANSACTIONS IN A FOREIGN CURRENCY By Deborah Eisenberg. 214 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95. IN this provocative debut collection of stories, ''Transactions in a Foreign Currency,'' Deborah Eisenberg's characters are exhaustingly fascinating, made to travel outside the native land of their inner selves into a world that appears astonishingly regulated, where ostensibly enlightened men collect women the way superpowers assert spheres of influence, where sexual diplomacy becomes a contest ''to adhere to the slippery requirements of distant authorities.'' Charlotte, the physically awkward narrator of ''Flotsam,'' is told by her fashionable roommate: ''You're lucky that you're so nice. . . . Men are going to treat you really well in your next life.'' Needless to say, niceness is a disability. Charlotte, alternately bludgeoned and ignored by romance, is a victim of her own inclination to be overwhelmed by beauty and by folks like those Padgett Powell describes in his novel, ''Edisto,'' as knowing ''the whole alphabet of worldly maneuver.'' How to survive in the midst of women who always win, men who always manipulate?
headline: A HIGHBROW LOVES A LOWBROW

title: Gentlemen In England
author: A. N. Wilson.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GENTLEMEN IN ENGLAND A Vision. By A. N. Wilson. 311 pp. New York: Viking. $17.95. MIXED with our nostalgia for the coziness of Victorian life is an impatience with all the things it left unspoken. If, as writers like Peter Gay and Steven Marcus have suggested, Victorians were not quite so repressed as we once thought, they nevertheless maintained the outward signs of repression, which almost amounts to the same thing. When they did exercise their sexuality, they denied it a full acknowledgment, a recognition of its place near the heart of things. To some of us this denial is intolerable, for it is the essence of the modern to say what one feels, to break an ancient silence into which we seem to have been shushed by church, state or society. More and more, we live by pronouncing ourselves.  In A. N. Wilson's novel ''Gentlemen in England'' the infinitely articulated manners of his Victorian men and women might be seen as a defense against understanding one another - or even the darker side of themselves. For a novelist, this defense has certain advantages: it gives a character privacy and allows his personality to develop as a pure distillation. As someone said, character is a secret psychosis - but in the 20th century we can't keep secrets.
headline: IN AND OUT OF LOVE AND FAITH

title: Free Spaces
author: Sara M. Evans and Harry C. Boyte.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FREE SPACES The Sources of Democratic Change in America. By Sara M. Evans and Harry C. Boyte. 228 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $16.95. IN an era when fighting for clean air or racial justice is interpreted as special-interest politics and when selling the Federal Housing Administration, the Grand Coulee Dam and the United States Postal Service to private interests is construed as the public good, it is hardly surprising that America's understanding of such terms as public and private should appear as more than a little warped. In fact, a continuing struggle over the meaning of public and private has been central to the nation's ideological battles of this century.
headline: WHERE WE LEARN DEMOCRACY

title: Home Front
author: Patti Davis with Maureen Strange Foster
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HOME FRONT. By Patti Davis with Maureen Strange Foster. (Crown, $15.95.) Despite its catalogue of flaws as narrative fiction, this roman a clef by President Reagan's daughter offers a tiny harvest of redeeming social value.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Bird Of Life, Bird Of Death
author: Jonathan Evan Maslow.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BIRD OF LIFE, BIRD OF DEATH A Naturalist's Journey Through a Land of Political Turmoil. By Jonathan Evan Maslow. 249 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95. ''I   F the Quetzal is confined in a cage, it dies. The Quetzal cannot live in captivity,'' says a poster quoted by Jonathan Evan Maslow in his second book, ''Bird of Life, Bird of Death.'' He then proceeds to document his uneasy, stubborn search for the legendary bird in the midst of Guatemala's past and present pain and violence. Bird of life and bird of freedom, familiar to the ancient Mayan kings and Guatemala's national symbol, it was the resplendent quetzal that drew Mr. Maslow into the ''wonder voyage'' recounted in this fine book. His fascination with the creature is palpable.
headline: QUETZAL AND MAN IN GUATEMALA

title: Plane Crazy: A Celebration Of Flying
author: Burton Bernstein
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PLANE CRAZY: A Celebration of Flying. By Burton Bernstein. (Ticknor & Fields, $16.95.) Didn't everyone in long-ago America spend the happiest hours of childhood hanging around the local airport, envying the freedom of the men and women who came and went in rackety little machines that mysteriously responded to their will? Well, I did, and so did Burton Bernstein.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The White House Mess
author: Christopher Buckley
pull_quote: THE WHITE HOUSE MESS. By Christopher Buckley. 224 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.   IT is Friday, Jan. 20, 1989, at the outset of Christopher Buckley's funny novel, ''The White House Mess.'' President-elect and Mrs. Thomas Nelson Tucker are waiting for President Reagan to join them in their limousine for the motorcade to Capitol Hill and the inauguration ceremonies. But President Reagan won't come. ''Have you spoken to him?'' the narrator, one Herbert Wadlough, asks Tucker, for whom he works as personal assistant and deputy chief of staff.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Maul And The Pear Tree
author: T A Critchley
pull_quote: THE MAUL AND THE PEAR TREE. The Ratcliffe Highway Murders 1811. By P. D. James and T. A. Critchley. Illustrated. 234 pages. The Mysterious Press. $17.95. >WAPPING is a very old part of London, a riverside district a little to the east of the City, with a main road called the Highway - formerly Ratcliffe Highway - running along its northern edge. Until recently it was hemmed in by docks, and at the beginning of the 19th century it was a region of marine store dealers, ships' victuallers, sailors' lodging houses, with a population depending almost entirely for its livelihood on the trade of what was then the busiest port in the world.   It was also a region that called up sinister associations - until the 18th century it had been the spot where pirates were hanged at the low water mark and left swinging ''till three tides had overflowed them.'' Then, in December 1811, it acquired a new notoriety, with a pair of interlinked crimes that form the subject of ''The Maul and the Pear Tree.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Gentlemen In England
author: A N Wilson
pull_quote: GENTLEMEN IN ENGLAND. By A. N. Wilson. 311 pages. Viking. $17.95. SEVERUS EGG, writes A. N. Wilson in his latest novel, ''recognized ruefully that he had been born some 20 or 30 years late. He had been but a lad when Byron died. But to have known Byron! As he now realised, Mr. Egg had been born just early enough to see the excellence, all the light, all the fun, and just late enough to watch it all evaporate, banished by lumpishness and self-righteous mediocrity.''   ''The century, like a young man whose features were once considered handsome, had grown thicker and more corpulently pompous once it had passed its middle thirties.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Thinking In Time
author: Richard E Neustadt
pull_quote: THINKING IN TIME: The Uses of History for Decision Makers. By Richard E. Neustadt and Ernest R. May. 329 pages. The Free Press. $19.95. IN explaining the other day why President Reagan was so insistent on offering Ferdinand E. Marcos haven in the United States, a State Department official said that Mr. Reagan was determined that the former Philippine leader not be treated ''as shabbily as the Shah of Iran.'' The official added, however, that Mr. Marcos was more concerned that he not end up like the former ruler of South Vietnam, Ngo Dinh Diem, who was killed during the coup that ousted him in 1963.   And, as the debate continues in Washington on whether to provide $100 million in aid, including $70 million in military assistance, to the rebels of Nicaragua, the critics in Congress are warning of ''slipping into another Vietnam.'' The White House, for its part, is warning that failure to provide the aid will hasten ''another Cuba'' in the hemisphere.
headline: Books: History Lessons

title: Children Of Light
author: Robert Stone
pull_quote: CHILDREN OF LIGHT. By Robert Stone. 258 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.   NEAR the opening of ''Children of Light'' - Robert Stone's fourth novel, after ''A Hall of Mirrors,'' ''Dog Soldiers'' and ''A Flag for Sunrise'' -Gordon Walker, badly hung over, strung out on cocaine, sick, panicked and lonely for the wife who has just left him, catches sight of himself in the mirror and quotes from ''King Lear.'' ''Thou art the thing itself,'' he declares. ''Unaccommodated man is no more than such a poor bare forked animal as thou art.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Wreck Of The Titanic Foretold?
author: Martin Gardner
pull_quote: THE WRECK OF THE TITANIC FORETOLD? Edited by Martin Gardner. Illustrated. 157 pages. Prometheus Books. $18.95.   MORGAN ROBERTSON (1861-1915) was the son of a Great Lakes ship captain who became a sailor himself and then turned to writing sea stories. He enjoyed considerable popularity in his own time, but he would scarcely be remembered today if it were not for a short novel that he published in 1898.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Objects Of Desire
author: Adrian Forty
pull_quote: OBJECTS OF DESIRE. Design and Society From Wedgewood to IBM. By Adrian Forty. 272 illustrations. 260 pages. Pantheon Books $24.95. Why did the Montgomery Ward catalogue of 1895 offer customers a choice of 131 different pocket knives? Why were wireless sets concealed inside pieces of furniture - like cabinets, desks and even chairs - during the early days of radio? Why did white replace red and brown as the favorite color of decorators at the turn of the century? These are just a few of the questions the British scholar Andrian Forty proposes to address in his fascinating new study of design.   As Mr. Forty sees it, design is not merely an indicator of esthetic taste, but a social phenomenon that both mirrors and shapes how we think. Whereas objects of art reflect the personal vision of their makers, manufactured goods - which are designed to be salable and profitable - tend to embody more generalized beliefs about society, and so ''can cast ideas about who we are and how we should behave into permanent and tangible forms.'' Modern office equipment in ''bright colours and slightly humorous shapes,'' for instance, can help perpetuate the myth that office work is fun; just as modern, streamlined kitchen appliances can underline the contemporary faith in progress and technological salvation.
headline: Books of The Times; Design for Living

title: Rommel And The Rebel
author: Lawrence Wells
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ROMMEL AND THE REBEL By Lawrence Wells. 415 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $17.95. FIVE German Army officers, traveling under assumed names, arrive in New York in June 1937, on their way to Oxford, Miss., where an R.O.T.C. professor of tactics at the University of Mississippi is to explain to them the fighting methods of the Confederate General Nathan Bedford Forrest. German officers openly visited United States military sites and even attended American military schools before the war, but in his novel, ''Rommel and the Rebel,'' Lawrence Wells packs this delegation with three future field marshals: Erwin Rommel, who would become ''the desert fox''; Walter Model, who succeeded von Rundstedt as the commander in chief in the west; and Ferdinand Schorner, later to head three different army groups in Russia.   To serve as translator the R.O.T.C. professor has summoned the young Lieut. Speigner, an ''Ole Miss'' graduate in German studies, now collecting information on future German commanders in an obscure office in the War Department. He already has a complete dossier on Rommel in his files.
headline: A NAZI AT OLE MISS

title: Tourist Season
author: Carl Hiaasen
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
TOURIST SEASON By Carl Hiaasen. 272 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $15.95. THE small puzzle Carl Hiaasen uses to lure one into ''Tourist Season'' fades away by page 80. By then it doesn't matter that we know who done it. What matters now is what is going to happen next to a very human (if slightly bizarre) cast of characters operating in a world that the author tilts a few degrees beyond reality. We're caught up in another remarkable example of what talented writers are doing these days with the mystery novel.

''Tourist Season'' is a lively story of a conspiracy intended to save Florida for the future by terrorizing tourists and thereby collapsing its superhyped condominium economy. In telling this almost plausible yarn, Mr. Hiaasen, a former member of the investigations team of The Miami Herald and now a columnist for that paper, displays a strength that I'd come to believe was exclusively British. Like Robert Barnard, Jack S. Scott, Evelyn Waugh and some of their English brethren, Mr. Hiaasen has us meeting folks who are bent, in varying degrees, out of plumb but who still come alive.
headline: TERRORISTS AND BEAUTY QUEENS

title: A Day At A Time
author: Margo Culley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A DAY AT A TIME The Diary Literature of American Women From 1764 to the Present. Edited by Margo Culley. 341 pp. New York: The Feminist Press at the City University of New York. Cloth, $29.95. Paper, $12.95. THIS anthology of ''The Diary Literature of
headline: SELF SPEAKS TO SELF

title: Hannie Richards
author: Hilary Bailey
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HANNIE RICHARDS. By Hilary Bailey. (Random House, $16.95.) Hannie Richards is a 34-year-old Englishwoman with a husband, two daughters and an old farm in Devon whose upkeep requires massive amounts of cash.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Break In
author: Dick Francis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BREAK IN By Dick Francis. 317 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $17.95. IT is ''winter and horses, the old song in the blood'' again for Dick Francis, whose last few books spooked some readers into thinking he had hung up his racing colors for good. Christmas (Kit) Fielding, the hero of Mr. Francis' 25th mystery adventure, is neither a computer systems analyst nor a banker nor an international kidnapping consultant nor a wine merchant - to identify the heroes of Nos. 21, 22, 23 and 24 respectively - but a bona fide professional steeplechase jockey. The man rides horses the way Mr. Francis' heroes used to before they began rooting in wine cellars and data banks. Furlong for furlong, ''Break In'' makes up in sheer track time for some of those lean years since ''Reflex.''   It's not surprising that Kit, as one of the most successful jump jockeys in England, should ride for royalty. Among the owners whose colors he wears is a middle-aged princess with porcelain skin, ''powerful femininity'' and a romanticized resemblance to the Queen Mother, whose horses Mr. Francis rode during the golden decade when he was himself a champion steeplechase jockey. Making the professional rounds for the princess and other owners, Kit travels from one racecourse to another every few days, riding mounts with beautiful names and compelling personalities.
headline: BACK ON THE TRACK

title: Children Of Light
author: Robert Stone
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CHILDREN OF LIGHT By Robert Stone. 258 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95. ROBERT STONE is the apostle of strung out. People in his novels have reached the end of the tether: alone, desperate, scared, doing a lot of hard liquor and drugs, they hit the road. And as they go they keep listening in the dark, against all odds, for something that might be a moral channel marker, or love, or God, or just a way to get through the night.   Critics have compared Mr. Stone to Conrad, Faulkner, Hemingway, Graham Greene, Malcolm Lowry, Nathanael West; all apt enough, but there's a James T. Farrell, Raymond Chandler, Dashiell Hammett strain as well - a hard-edged, lonely intelligence that sets bright promise off against stark failure and deals its mordant hand lightly. In ''A Flag for Sunrise'' (1981), an anthropologist observes: ''There's always a place for God. . . . There is some question as to whether He's in it.'' And near the end of ''Children of Light,'' a writer tells his lover: '' 'I would die for you.' . . . It was true, he thought, but not really helpful.''
headline: HEEBIEJEEBIEVILLE EXPRESS

title: The Puritan Conscience And Modern Sexuality
author: Edmund Leites
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PURITAN CONSCIENCE AND MODERN SEXUALITY By Edmund Leites. 196 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $17.50. SEX on bed linen usually surpasses sex on paper by such an order of magnitude that it's a wonder people write about the subject at all. Yet whenever scribblers do put sex into words, it is most often to make rules, an extremely bizarre approach considering how hard it is these days even to govern small islands, much less the national orgasm. Eastern ancients, like today's behaviorists, have written lessons on the sex act; medieval Western churchmen issued austere injunctions against earler pagan rhapsodies. Lately we've got into the habit of analyzing sex as we continue to cope with the efforts of those dark inquisitorial times, so far from the Garden of Eden.
headline: NEITHER SIN NOR DUTY

title: Thinking In Time
author: Richard E. Neustadt and Ernest R. May.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THINKING IN TIME The Uses of History for Decision-Makers. By Richard E. Neustadt and Ernest R. May. 329 pp. New York: The Free Press. $19.95. IN 1948 George C. Marshall, then President   Truman's Secretary of State, was concerned that the Communists seemed to be winning the civil war in China. He therefore asked Gen. Albert Wedemeyer, who had been the American commander in China at the end of World War II, to go to the Far East and see what, if anything, could be done. Upon his return, Wedemeyer recommended that Washington dispatch a few thousand military advisers. Attached to Chinese Nationalist forces, those advisers might well halt the Communist advances and perhaps even allow the Nationalists to win.
headline: FOREIGN POLICY WITHOUT TEARS

title: The White House Mess
author: Christopher Buckley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WHITE HOUSE MESS By Christopher Buckley. 227 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95. ANYBODY setting out to write a comic novel about the White House confronts an obvious problem. How do you top the material generated by the gagsmiths who've been running the country for the last couple of decades? You could people the place with bumbling Teutons who skulk around in false beards with bags of cash while their boss glowers and mutters over his afternoon glass of bourbon, but it's been done. You could go the zany relatives route - beer-swilling brothers, motorcycle-momma sisters - but ditto. Well, then, how about inventing a President who conducts meetings seated on the commode, or who can't seem to deplane without a spectacular pratfall, or who baffles visitors with irrelevant anecdotes culled from obscure right-wing newspapers? Boffo stuff, yes, but there might be copyright problems. Only a few authors - Philip Roth and Joseph Heller come to mind - have written White House burlesques that manage to exaggerate the seemingly unexaggeratable.
headline: RUNNING IN CIRCLES IN THE OVAL OFFICE

title: Isadora: Portrait Of The Artist As A Woman
author: Fredrika Blair
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ISADORA: Portrait of the Artist as a Woman. By Fredrika Blair. (McGraw-Hill, $24.95.) No dancer - perhaps no American performing artist - continues to exert as strong a pull on biographers as Isadora Duncan.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Peggy
author: Jacqueline Bograd Weld. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PEGGY The Wayward Guggenheim. By Jacqueline Bograd Weld. Illustrated. 493 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $24.95. THE life of Peggy Guggenheim, the pioneering art dealer and collector who died in Venice in 1979, was dominated by two major impulses: her promiscuous rebellion against the straitlaced hypocrisy of her parents' milieu, New York's German Jewish elite; and an inner drive that led her to become one of the most prophetic art connoisseurs of her generation. The most grievous flaw of Jacqueline Weld's book ''Peggy, The Wayward Guggenheim,'' along with its trite, cliche-ridden style, is that it exploits the more sensationalistic aspects of her private life at the expense of any solid insight into her artistic vision.   However, this biography is the only one to have been authorized by Peggy Guggenheim, whose compulsive sexual exhibitionism is amply evidenced in her own memoirs, ''Confessions of an Art Addict'' (1960). Mrs. Weld's access to her subject's private papers and to weeks of her ever ingenuous conversation enables her to dredge up many telling details of her subject's early years to which later eccentricities are traced. We see the young girl growing up under the tutelage of a series of sadistic German governesses and of a harebrained mother who was repeatedly abandoned by her philandering husband and who denied her daughters any formal education.
headline: TORTURED SEX, GREAT COLLECTION

title: Altered Harvest
author: Jack Doyle
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ALTERED HARVEST: Agriculture, Genetics, and the Fate of the World's Food Supply. By Jack Doyle. (Viking, $25.) Along with an astonishing amount of food, farming and its related businesses produce about a quarter of the nation's gross national product.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: In Southern Light
author: Alex Shoumatoff.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN SOUTHERN LIGHT Trekking Through Zaire and the Amazon. By Alex Shoumatoff. 239 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95. IT is easy to be interesting about travel in the third world. One can arrive in a country like Zaire and, simply by walking into a hotel bar or taking an internal airline flight and recording what one hears and sees, come up with something revealing about the place. Alex Shoumatoff, a writer for The New Yorker, does this in ''In Southern Light.'' He flies from Kinshasa to Isiro in Zaire. At the Isiro airport, he waits with his fellow passengers while baggage handlers dump their luggage onto the runway and then devote themselves to the more important task of loading valuable tusks, some of them from elephants killed by poachers, that are owned by a local government official. (Mr. Shoumatoff learns the provenance of the tusks from a Belgian coffee planter he meets on the plane.) Two hours elapse before ''an official announced that nothing was going to be done about the baggage, and we were al-lowed to walk past the soldier in spotted fatigues who had been guarding it with an automatic rifle and retrieve it ourselves.'' Clearly, we are not at O'Hare. This is a glimpse into another world.
headline: LONG SPEARS AND SHORTWAVE RADIOS

title: The Island Of The White Cow
author: Deborah Tall.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE ISLAND OF THE WHITE COW Memories of an Irish Island. By Deborah Tall. 234 pp. New York: Atheneum. $14.95. FEW of us have the chance to realize a dream. For Deborah Tall chance took the shape of a wild Celtic professor who whisked her off to find passion and her poetic self on a barely inhabited lump of rock just off the west coast of Ireland. ''The Island of the White Cow'' tells us the story of that time and of the lives that Miss Tall, her lover and the islanders made for themselves on its rocky and inhospitable shores. Miss Tall's narrative is divided into four main parts - ''The First Spring,'' ''Summer,'' ''Autumn'' and ''The Last Winter'' -and the device serves as framework for recollection of what was, in fact, a five-year stay.   The keynote is culture shock, and it would be hard to establish a scenario better calculated to induce it. The product of a comfortable Jewish middle-class Philadelphia home, Miss Tall finds herself, two weeks after graduation from college, en route to a community with no central heating, no piped water, no television, no sewers, a place where men and women lead lives of segregated propriety, determined as much by the demands of survival as the dictates of an ever present Roman Catholic Church.
headline: IT WASN'T PARADISE

title: The Good Life
author: Yi-Fu Tuan
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GOOD LIFE By Yi-Fu Tuan. 191 pp. Madison: The University of Wisconsin Press. $19.95. YI-FU TUAN, the John Kirtland Wright Professor of Geography at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, is a good man to whom nothing human is alien. Well, almost nothing. In ''The Good Life,'' he has undertaken an ambitious task. He explores answers to an old and unanswerable question: how should we live? He knows he cannot provide an answer to suit everybody but indicates the directions his own answers take. With modesty he suggests that his book may be ''best seen as an expedient for conversation.''   Good enough. It is the book's charm that it provokes back talk, the murmur of agreement and the rattle of protest. Like conversation, ''The Good Life'' is civilized, promoting values that are urban, nonviolent and liberal. (It is, of course, conservative to promote liberal values.) Also like conversation, the book is content to leave its terms vague, not to dissipate itself in the rigors of definition.
headline: CONTRADICTORY PLEASURES

title: This Well-Wooded Land
author: Phillip Drennon Thomas
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THIS WELL-WOODED LAND: Americans and Their Forests From Colonial Times to the Present. By Thomas R. Cox, Robert S. Maxwell, Phillip Drennon Thomas and Joseph J. Malone.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Trek
author: Ann Jonas
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE TREK Written and illustrated by Ann Jonas. Unpaged. New York: Greenwillow Books. $11.75. (Ages 5 to 9) DAYDREAMING is a private canvas on which we can all paint. The fantasies we sketch can get us into deep trouble or lift us even into the realm of genius.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: All Manners Of Food
author: Stephen Mennell. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ALL MANNERS OF FOOD Eating and Taste in England and France From the Middle Ages to the Present. By Stephen Mennell. Illustrated. 380 pp. New York: Basil Blackwell. $24.95. CULINARY history has come into fashion and is about to come of age.   Like such other new subjects as the history of gardening and the history of photography, it is beginning to find its rightful place in the academic world. Groups of devotees are assembling from Ann Arbor to Boston, London to Leeds, and erudite papers are exchanged on the tantalizing pleasures of early recipes and the more problematic pleasures of early kitchens. Learned symposiums have been held in Boston; Oxford, England; and Adelaide, Australia.
headline: HISTORY A LA CARTE

title: Love Is The Crooked Thing
author: Lee K. Abbott.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOVE IS THE CROOKED THING By Lee K. Abbott. 182 pp. North Carolina: Algonquin Books of Chapel Hill. $13.95. THE implicit code behind Lee K. Abbott's fiction seems to be: if you haven't gone too far, you haven't gone far enough. Or as a California comic put it back in the 1970's, ''There is a light within you - burn it out!''   Not that the lights in the lives of these 11 stories burn so brightly to begin with. Living in the author's native Southwest - a landscape of dry arroyos, of ''trees and buttes and colors from Mister Disney'' - Mr. Abbott's characters include a local rocker known as Dr. Filth, a coked-out college professor, a ''sissy'' outlaw, and assorted ''dipsticks'' and would-be smoothies.
headline: LINGUISTIC WHIZ-BANGS

title: Poland Under Black Light
author: Janusz Anderman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: POLAND UNDER BLACK LIGHT By Janusz Anderman. Translated by Nina Taylor and Andrew Short. Introduction by Stanislaw Baranczak. 131 pp. New York: Readers International/ Persea Books. $12.50. ''POLAND UNDER   BLACK LIGHT'' is a book one wants to like. The author and the book have noble histories.
headline: WRITERS IN THEIR CELLS

title: Make Way For Sam Houston
author: Jean Fritz. Illustrations by Elise Primavera.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MAKE WAY FOR SAM HOUSTON By Jean Fritz. Illustrations by Elise Primavera. 109 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $12.95. (Ages 8 to 12) SAM HOUSTON was the kind of larger-than-life hero about whom legends of Texan proportion have been woven. The ''Hero of San Jacinto'' and the first president of the Republic of Texas, Houston was a soldier, politician and statemaker. In the hands of the fine biographer Jean Fritz, Houston's life retains its drama and vigor.   Born in Virginia in 1793, Sam Houston migrated to Tennessee with his widowed mother. Adolescent impatience impelled him to escape to an Indian settlement, where he spent three years as the adopted son of a Cherokee chief. He subsequently enlisted under Gen. Andrew Jackson to fight the British. After the War of 1812, he followed Jackson into politics, read law, served in Congress and was elected governor of Tennessee at the age of 34.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: A Family Madness
author: Thomas Keneally
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A FAMILY MADNESS By Thomas Keneally. 336 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95. THE prolific Australian writer Thomas Keneally obviously likes to give himself tough assignments. Undeterred by the accidents of nationality or the hard facts of embryology, he has, in his recent fiction, chosen the American Civil War as the subject of one novel (''Confederates'') and a preternaturally sophisticated fetus as the narrator of another (''Passenger''). Still more ambitiously, he has written a gripping ''nonfiction novel'' of the Holocaust, ''Schindler's List,'' in which he tells the true story - embellished with an abundance of historical and imagined detail - of a Sudeten German industrialist and bon vivant, Oskar Schindler, who ingeniously and recklessly managed to snatch several thousand Jews from the very gullet of the Nazi death machine. ''Schindler's List'' won the Booker Prize in England, where it was published as a novel, and brought Mr. Keneally a wide audience in this country, where it was published as nonfiction. His new work, which seems to be in part a spinoff from the research undertaken for its predecessor, is again bold in its scope and its choice of subject.
headline: BREEZY, BOOZY AND BYELORUSSIAN

title: The Bourgeois Experience
author: Peter Gay. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BOURGEOIS EXPERIENCE Victoria to Freud. Volume Two: The Tender Passion. By Peter Gay. Illustrated. 490 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $24.95. THE second volume of Peter Gay's projected five-volume survey of middle-class culture in the 19th century is a less tidy affair than its predecessor. In ''The Education of the Senses,'' (1984), the first volume of ''The Bourgeois Experience: Victoria to Freud,'' Mr. Gay took issue with received wisdom about Victorian sexuality. Despite their exaggerated fears of masturbation and their insistence on confining sex to marriage, the Victorians, he argued, appreciated sexual pleasure and pursued it avidly. His exploration of 19th-century love (the ''tender passion'' of the title of this volume) yields no such sharply etched revisionist thesis. To be sure, his book contains an argument of sorts, and many telling insights, but it is often overwhelmed by biographical detail, textual commentary and psychoanalytic speculation whose significance for his general portrait is not entirely clear.
headline: LOVE, LOVE, HOORAY FOR LOVE

title: Dream Palace
author: Herbert Morris
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DREAM PALACE By Herbert Morris. 87 pp. New York: Harper & Row. Cloth, $16.95. Paper, $8.95. ALMA By Linda Gregg. 69 pp. New York: Random House. Cloth, $12.95. Paper, $7.95. ORRERY By Richard Kenney. 108 pp. New York: Atheneum. Cloth, $17.50. Paper, $10.95. HERBERT MORRIS is not a newcomer, though his first book, ''Peru,'' appeared just three years ago. He had been publishing poems for a quarter century before he was persuaded to collect them, and he had devised such a distinctive style that ''Peru'' was greeted with surprised acclaim by those unfamiliar with him. A strong style is like any other landmark - it seems always to have been there. And Mr. Morris is an original, in part because he is a throwback.
headline: LOVE, LUST AND THE PASSING OF SEASONS

title: Eclipse
author: William Stevenson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ECLIPSE By William Stevenson. 370 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $17.95. NO doubt about it, a terrific story awaits the first reporter who can get into Spandau Prison and wangle an exclusive interview with Hitler's onetime deputy, Rudolf Hess.   The same idea makes a solid premise for a thriller. So too does another historical puzzle William Stevenson places at the center of his novel, ''Eclipse'' - the disturbing questions of whether the Allies knew during World War II that the Nazis were exterminating Jews and, if they did, why they never bombed any of the death camps.
headline: WHO IS THE ENEMY?

title: Strangers In Their Own Land
author: Peter Sichrovsky
pull_quote: STRANGERS IN THEIR OWN LAND:   Young Jews in Germany and Austria Today. By Peter Sichrovsky. Translated from the German by Jean Steinberg. 165 pages. Basic Books. $14.95. A MIXTURE of curiosity and apprehension assails a reader making his way into the remarkable set of interviews that Peter Sichrovsky has put together in ''Strangers in Their Own Land: Young Jews in Germany and Austria Today.'' One is curious as to why the 13 people interviewed here would want to live where they do, which is mainly West Berlin and Vienna.   One is apprehensive that the answers will come too soon and that nothing will be left but the pain that Mr. Sichrovsky, himself a young Austrian Jew now living in Berlin, must surely have exposed if one reaction he cites in his introduction is a fair indication. A journalist told him that reading these interviews was like going to the beach with a friend you had always assumed was normal and happy. For the first time you see him stripped and his body is covered with scars from the neck down.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Samurai And Silk
author: Haru Matsukata Reischauer
pull_quote: SAMURAI AND SILK. A Japanese and American Heritage. By Haru Matsukata Reischauer. Illustrated. 371 pages. Harvard University Press. $20. HARU MATSUKATA   REISCHAUER'S mother was born in New York, the daughter of a Japanese entrepreneur named Rioichiro Arai who had made his home in America since 1876. When she married the son of a leading Japanese statesman in 1912 and went to live in Tokyo, she wrote to her brother, who was then at Harvard, saying that she was determined to do her best to adjust to Japanese ways - but the very phrase in which she expressed her resolve suggests how deep the process of Westernization had already gone. Her aim, she said, would be ''to do in Rome as the Romans do.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Rain Or Shine
author: Cyra Mcfadden
pull_quote: RAIN OR SHINE. By Cyra McFadden. 178 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95. WHEN Cy Taillon, the   ''Dean of Rodeo Announcers,'' died in 1970, he was memorialized as a man of the West, a gentleman cowboy who had come to personify both an ideal and a vanishing way of life. Newspapers compared his golden voice with the sound of a Wurlitzer, the man himself with John Wayne. Like Fitzgerald's Gatsby, the farm boy who tried to invent a self commensurate with his romantic image of life, Cy had succeeded in turning himself into a legend.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Acts Of War: The Behavior Of Men In Battle
author: Richard Holmes
pull_quote: ACTS OF WAR: The Behavior of Men in Battle. By Richard Holmes. Illustrated. 436 pages. Free Press. $19.95.   DESPITE its vague and slightly misleading title, Richard Holmes's ''Acts of War: The Behavior of Men in Battle'' was written with a specific and useful purpose in mind. As a student of war and the deputy head of the department of war studies at the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst, Mr. Holmes felt too little serious work had been done ''on the individual soldier's experience of battle.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Cats Of The Temple. Poems By Brad Leithauser
author: Brad Leithauser
pull_quote: CATS OF THE TEMPLE. Poems by Brad Leithauser. 70 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. Cloth, $14.95; paperback, $7.95. ''CATS OF THE TEMPLE'' is Brad Leithauser's second collection of poems. In an introductory note, he expresses the hope that readers will greet it as ''a sibling companion'' to his first collection, ''Hundreds of Fireflies.'' It is an understandable request, since the earlier book was exceptionally well received. It is also one that can be readily granted - in the new book, Mr. Leithauser both extends his range and confirms his promise, making it clear that he is one of the most gifted American poets to have come over the horizon in years.   To start with, he has the primary, indispensable quality, without which poetry wouldn't be poetry at all - a keen delight in language, in disclosing its hidden recesses and its as-yet unrealized powers. There is his fondness for near-punning effects, for example - the echo that mimics what it describes (so that animals like the fox and the tortoise that lend themselves to fables are ''didactically adaptable'') the tiny but somber shift from ''finely'' to ''finally'' as the view from a plane window fades away; the line break that momentarily misdirects us, so that the innocently hyperactive rabbit ''who's sharp on fun-'' turns out to be ''sharp on fun-/damentals'' as well.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Mating Birds
author: Lewis Nkosi
pull_quote: MATING BIRDS. By Lewis Nkosi. 184 pages. St. Martin's Press. $13.95. ''In a few days I am to die. Strange, the idea neither shocks nor frightens me. What I feel most frequently now is a kind of numbness, a total lack of involvement in my own fate, as though I were an observer watching the last days in the life of another man.'' So begins Lewis Nkosi's ''Mating Birds,'' and the echoes of ''The Stranger'' by Albert Camus that vibrate through these first sentences, it turns out, will be sustained throughout the novel.   Like Camus's Meursault, the hero of ''Mating Birds'' - one Ndi Sibiya - is a man condemned to death, a man who is spending his last days looking out at a piece of blue sky from his prison cell. Like Meursault, Sibiya is a sensualist, obsessed with his own physicality and that of the hot, sun-drenched world around him. And like Meursault, Sibiya seems strangely disconnected, nearly indifferent to his approaching execution and the fact of his own death.
headline: APARTHEID'S VICTIMS

title: Evolution As A Religion
author: Mary Midgley.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EVOLUTION AS A RELIGION Strange Hopes and Stranger Fears. By Mary Midgley. 180 pp. New York: Methuen. Cloth, $33. Paper, $11.95. This is a book from which one goes away to ponder without having to push back against philosophical bullying. In a genre in which polemics are the rule, the hallmark of Mary Midgley's style is civility. Her topic is ''the distortion that afflicts science when it is put into the place of religion.'' Her ruminations are cautionary: the Victorian impulse to define progress as the replacement of religion by science has led to overgeneralizations by scientists on nature, life and humanity that range from the sanguine or euphoric to the cynical or despairing - all of which are fatalistic attitudes.
headline: SCIENCE AND SELFISHNESS

title: Perfection Salad
author: Laura Shapiro. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PERFECTION SALAD Women and Cooking at the Turn of the Century. By Laura Shapiro. Illustrated. 280 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $16.95. LAURA SHAPIRO'S delightful new book has cast some light on one of the more peculiar mysteries of my adolescence. This was eggs a la goldenrod, the first lesson in eighth-grade home economics class, and it was prepared by hard-boiling an egg, separating the white from the yolk, stirring the chopped-up white into freshly prepared white sauce, pouring the white mixture over toast and topping the whole production artistically with the crumbled yolk. Since no one, to my knowledge, had ever eaten such a thing, it was unclear why anyone should be obliged to cook it -especially while the boys were off in shop learning useful things like carpentry and radio repair. For the first time I realized that puberty was not, after all, the nadir of human existence: if eggs a la goldenrod defined the business of womanhood, then the worst might be yet to come.
headline: WOMEN AND WHITE SAUCE

title: Keeping Hope Alive
author: F Robert Rodman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: KEEPING HOPE ALIVE: On Becoming a Psychotherapist. By F. Robert Rodman. (Harper & Row, $15.95.) This memoir is supposed to be a guide for prospective psychotherapists.
headline: IN SHORT

title: From My Father, Singing
author: David Bosworth
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FROM MY FATHER, SINGING By David Bosworth. 120pp. Wainscott, N.Y.: Pushcart Press. $13.95.   A MAN sits in a cabin in Maine, writing a letter to his son Robbie, back in New Jersey. It's a letter Robbie, who is 21 months old, won't be able to read for some time yet. And it's an apologia pro vita sua. the man talks about his job clerking in the general store in Johnson Mills.
