He goes on to explain why, two months ago, he quit his much better paid job in Trenton, left his family and fled to Maine. He reminisces about his parents. Then he gives brief accounts of God, sex and death. End of David Bosworth's first novel, ''From my Father, Singing.''
headline: ERUMPENT THINGS

title: Hunger Strike
author: Susie Orbach.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HUNGER STRIKE The Anorectic's Struggle as a Metaphor for Our Age. By Susie Orbach. 201 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $15.95. IN ''Fat Is a Feminist Issue'' (1978) Susie Orbach, a psychotherapist and co-founder of the Women's Therapy Center Institute in New York City, offered one of the first feminist analyses of women's obsessions with food and body size. In ''Hunger Strike: The Anorectic's Struggle as a Metaphor for Our Age,'' a cultural and clinical study of anorexia nervosa, Miss Orbach reads anorexia as ''a dramatic expression of the internal compromise wrought by Western women in the 1980s in their attempt to negotiate their passions and desires in a time of extraordinary confusion.'' She decodes the anorexic's emaciated body and iron control as ''at once an embodiment of stereotyped femininity and its very opposite.''
headline:
MIND/BODY/HEALTH;
THE NEW HYSTERIA

title: Confessions Of A Pregnant Father
author: Dan Greenburg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CONFESSIONS OF A PREGNANT FATHER By Dan Greenburg. 214 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $16.95. LIVES there a writer who, upon joining the ranks of fatherhood, hasn't felt the urge - no, the compulsion - to tell the world of his firstborn's arrival? Good sense or perhaps good editors fortunately prevail and temptation is set aside. These fond recollections are saved instead for family, friends and Lamaze class reunions.   Not so for Dan Greenburg, the humorist who wrote of amorous pursuits in ''Scoring'' and who, with his wife Suzanne O'Malley, wrote ''How to Avoid Love and Marriage.'' Mr. Greenburg has now written about the conception, gestation, delivery and early months of his son, Zack.
headline: ZACK A TO Z

title: The Sportswriter
author: Richard Ford
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SPORTSWRITER By Richard Ford. 375 pp. New York: Vintage Contemporaries. Paper, $6.95. MANY of our best novelists are obsessed with exploring the nature of the family, and for good reason. What is more fascinating than these disparate beings who inhabit the same households, breathe the same air, inspire hope and expectation and - all too often - cause disappointment? The disintegration of a family, particularly one in which a young child has died, moves us directly into a territory of sorrow. In fiction, the loss of a child is by definition an exploration of a loss of faith. For the novelist, it generates a mysterious, perhaps impossible equation with which to struggle: how much does such a death contribute to upsetting the precarious balance of a faltering marriage?
headline: A WIFE NAMED X, A POODLE NAMED ELVIS

title: Ringarra
author: Coral Lansbury
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
RINGARRA By Coral Lansbury. 220 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $15.95. GOTHIC fiction's appeal is rooted in the fear of -and attraction to - the irrational. Relying upon exaggeration and the macabre, the genre slips easily into self-parody (the plot of the first Gothic novel, Horace Walpole's 1764 ''Castle of Otranto,'' all but defies rational summation) and has long inspired such deliberate spoofs as Austen's ''Northanger Abbey'' and Peacock's ''Nightmare Abbey.'' In ''Ringarra,'' Coral Lansbury (Australian-born, now a professor of English at Rutgers University) has attempted to write a straight Gothic novel, undiluted by levity, but leavened by a strong infusion of literary and psychological self-consciousness.

Aware that the Gothic novel's obsession with the mystery of power has made it a favorite vehicle for exploring (and often exploiting) themes of sexual ambivalence, she has also chosen to evoke a larger-than-Gothic tradition that seems to begin with Charlotte Bronte, but has darker roots in Samuel Richardson's ''Clarissa Harlowe.'' ''Ringarra'' gives us Gothic romance with a feminist twist, pitting the clever, logical, suitably mated Katsie McLeod and her hearty, intelligent Australian fiance against the charismatic Michael Taverner, who manages Ringarra, the most valuable sheep ranch in Australia.
headline: AUSTRALIAN GOTHIC

title: You're Only Old Once!
author: Theodor Seuss Geisel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: YOU'RE ONLY OLD ONCE! Written and illustrated by Dr. Seuss. Unpaged. New York: Random House. $9.95. YOU can't arrest Arnold Schwarzenegger for trying to be an actor, or Mayor Koch for wanting to be Fiorello La Guardia, or Norman Mailer for attempting elder statesmanship, and certainly nobody wants to arrest kindly Dr. Seuss for trying to write and illustrate a book for adults. It's a free country.   Even long-time admirers of Dr. Seuss - I've been a fan ever since I first saw his commercial illustrations in the late 1930's - will be forced to ask themselves a very painful question: Is ''You're Only Old Once!'' really suitable to place in the hands of a sensitive adult?
headline: THE SHAPE THAT HE'S IN

title: Necessary Losses
author: Judith Viorst.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NECESSARY LOSSES The Loves, Illusions, Dependencies and Impossible Expectations That All of Us Have to Give Up in Order to Grow. By Judith Viorst. 447 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95. BACK in 1968, when the youthquake shook our land and anyone over 30 was deemed untrustworthy, Judith Viorst consoled an entire generation with her hilarious book of poems and perceptions, ''It's Hard to Be Hip Over Thirty and Other Tragedies of Married Life.'' A few years later, sensing the terror of those who would soon turn 40, Mrs. Viorst came to the rescue again, with ''How Did I Get to Be Forty and Other Atrocities.'' And so it has gone - through the years her many adult and children's books as well as her monthly columns in Redbook magazine have amused and instructed her readers as they struggle with the small and big challenges of everyday living.   Now Mrs. Viorst has moved in a new direction. ''Necessary Losses'' is a serious book that grew out of the author's person-al psychoanalysis and her six years of study and training at the Washington Psychoanalytic Institute.
headline: GAINING BY LOSING

title: Bohemian Paris
author: Jerrold Seigel. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BOHEMIAN PARIS Culture, Politics, and the Boundaries of Bourgeois Life, 1830-1930. By Jerrold Seigel. Illustrated. 453 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $25. FOR all its mystery and exoticism, bohemia has seemed definable - a place of free thinking and free love, where young and impoverished artists and poets flout middle-class pieties and conventions. Jerrold Seigel, a historian at Princeton University, sets out to challenge and deepen our thinking about this subject in ''Bohemian Paris,'' and he succeeds admirably.
headline: INDISCRETIONS OF THE BOURGEOISIE

title: Whites
author: Norman Rush
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WHITES By Norman Rush. 150 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $14.95. A CHILDHOOD spent on the Laguna Pueblo   Reservation in New Mexico brought me to the conclusion that the third world is not just poor, developing nations. The third world is any place dogs roam freely, howl and bark all night, and defecate and breed on the streets. Last autumn in southern China I discovered that the Chinese understand what dogs are good for - good for lunch, good for dinner, and tasty with noodles and greens. The way the Chinese explained it, European colonialists used to feed their pet dogs while Chinese starved. Plains Indian tribes had good dog recipes too, until Christian missionaries arrived with their sentimentality for their pets.
headline: GRACE ABOUNDING IN BOTSWANA

title: Home Health Care
author: Jo-Ann Friedman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HOME HEALTH CARE: A Complete Guide for Patients and Their Families. By Jo-Ann Friedman. (Norton, $22.50.) The very successes of modern medicine have, ironically, generated increasing demands for new forms of health care.
headline: IN SHORT

title: Fifth Row Center: A Critic's Year On And Off Broadway
author: Benedict Nightingale.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FIFTH ROW CENTER A Critic's Year On and Off Broadway. By Benedict Nightingale. 346 pp. New York: Times Books. $17.95. BENEDICT NIGHTIN=   GALE, ordinarily the theater critic of the New Statesman in London, spent the 1983-84 season in New York performing a similar function for the Arts and Leisure section of The New York Times and was deeply disappointed by what he saw and didn't see. He contemplates a future in which ''the Fabulous Invalid will increasingly resemble a gaudily painted clown, crazedly singing and dancing in a terminal ward, and off-Broadway will increasingly be thought of as an invalid, too, only not a very fabulous one.''
headline: A CHRONIC INVALID

title: Marriage And Morals Among The Victorians
author: Gertrude Himmelfarb.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MARRIAGE AND MORALS AMONG THE VICTORIANS Essays. By Gertrude Himmelfarb. 253 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $19.95. WHEN introducing Cambridge undergraduates to Victorian marriage and morality, I direct them first to Sir John Plumb's sparkling little piece ''The Victorians Unbuttoned'' for some flavor of the distinctive nature of the Victorian moral code and for some sense of the political, economic and social anxieties that led to the development of those remarkable moral attitudes. Thereafter I introduce them to the work of Martha Vicinus, Peter Cominos, Wanda Neff, Elaine Showalter, Keith Thomas, Lawrence Stone and Peter Gay, among others. When I now add Gertrude Himmelfarb's ''Marriage and Morals Among the Victorians'' to my list of recommended reading it will have to be with warning words of explanation and qualification.   Miss Himmelfarb has not been well served in the choice of her title. She is not - save for the first chapter - directly concerned with Victorian marriage and morals as usually understood. The two essays on Jeremy Bentham, the ones on William Godwin, Thomas Macaulay, Benjamin Disraeli, Sidney and Beatrice Webb and the philosopher Michael Oakeshott, and indeed the ones on social Darwinism, science and sociobiology, are not concerned with marriage or morals at all.
headline: DEFENDING 'ALL THE DECENT DRAPERY OF LIFE'

title: The Dog Is Us
author: Marcelle Clements.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DOG IS US And Other Observations. By Marcelle Clements. 338 pp. New York: Viking. $17.95. THIS is a collection of articles and essays reporting that surviving members of the 1960's ''youth movement'' are getting through their middle years only because psychotherapy and antidepressant drugs like Elavil are there to console them. Reading it, I kept thinking of the La Brea tar pits in Los Angeles, where eons ago animals of kinds that no longer exist went to drink and were trapped by the treacherous tar. I also kept envisioning Idealism and Intensity and Political Awareness and, especially, Social Conscience as large, innocent, unadaptable ungulates, sinking like future fossils into the merciless pits of Neurosis and Materialism.
headline: MUTANT ELITES

title: The Three-Pound Universe
author: Judith Hooper and Dick Teresi
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE THREE-POUND UNIVERSE By Judith Hooper and Dick Teresi. Illustrated. 410 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $25. MIND is such an odd predicament for matter to get into. I often marvel how something like hydrogen, the simplest atom, forged in some early chaos of the universe, could lead to us and the gorgeous fever we call consciousness. If a brain is just three pounds of blood, dreams and electricity, how does it manage to contemplate itself, worry about its soul, do time and motion studies, admire the shy hoofs of a goat, know that it will die, enjoy all the grand and lesser mayhem of love? What is mind, that one can be ''out of one's . . .''? How can a neuron feel compassion? What is a self if, as Judith Hooper and Dick Teresi observe, ''what our Victorian grandparents used to call 'character' is contained in an intricate matrix of speech centers, motor pathways, and minute electrical circuits''? Why did automatic, hand-me-down mammals like our ancestors somehow evolve brains with the ability to consider, imagine, project, compare, abstract, think of the future? If our experience of mind is really just the simmering of an easily alterable chemical stew, then what does it mean to know something, to want something, to be?
headline: DO NEURONS CRY?

title: Reckless Eyeballing
author: Ishmael Reed
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RECKLESS EYEBALLING By Ishmael Reed. 148 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $12.95. AN interloper ties up feminist writers at gunpoint, denounces them for defaming black men, shaves their heads and departs, leaving a chrysanthemum behind. The Flower Phantom's first victim is the playwright Tremonisha Smarts, at once lauded and despised for ''Wrong-Headed Man'' - a stage drama in which a black man batters and sodomizes his wife, commits incest and attempts unnatural acts with fish. Farther down the leather-clad avenger's list is Becky French, the queen archfeminist producer who controls the New York theater establishment, advocates castration of rapists and administers the ''sex list,'' a roster of male playwrights whose careers she keeps in ruin because their works are not politically correct. As the Phantom's attacks become commonplace, black men show their approval by wearing chrysanthemums on their lapels.
headline: MEDIA-LASHED AND SEX-LISTED

title: Born To Die?
author: Earl E. Shelp.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BORN TO DIE? Deciding the Fate of Critically Ill Newborns. By Earl E. Shelp. 250 pp. New York: The Free Press. $19.95. ''PARENTS bear the burden and authority, except in rare instances, to decide the medical care of severely defective newborns in the light of their moral values, commitments, principles, and norms.'' Earl E. Shelp's thesis in ''Born To Die? Deciding the Fate of Critically Ill Newborns'' may seem so obvious that one might reasonably ask: why is it necessary to write a book to defend it? The answer is that in the past several years parents' authority has been challenged, at least when their decision is to withhold or withdraw treatment.   Under the ''Baby Doe rule,'' passed by Congress in April 1985, the Federal Government has tried to remove discretionary power from parents - and from physicians - in deciding how to treat disabled newborns. Decisions to withhold ''medically indicated treatment'' (a term subject to various interpretations) may be considered child abuse and medical neglect. If the Supreme Court rules in favor of the Reagan Administration an earlier, even more restrictive rule will be reinstated.
headline: HARD CASES, HARD CHOICES

title: Fit For America
author: Harvey Green. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
FIT FOR AMERICA Health, Fitness, Sport, and American Society. By Harvey Green. Illustrated. 367 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $24.95. TWENTY years ago I heard a mildly funny story about the heyday of psychoanalysis in America.

An enthusiastic young woman had gone to a lecture on the psychology of her sex. Taking its predictable course, the lecture dwelled on the subject of anatomic envy. By the discussion period, the disciple's patience was exhausted. ''Why all this fuss about the penis?'' she blurted. ''It's just another phallic symbol.''

Grizzled and lame as the joke may be, it catches a certain truth about bodies. They often work better for us as metaphors than as flesh. They are, in the anthropologist Mary Douglas's phrase, ''natural symbols.'' Fears of pollution and disintegration; of illness precipitated by alien forces; countervailing hopes that prophylaxis or powerful cures can be achieved through right conduct or the right connections - these are standard stuff in the anthropological literature on tribal peoples.
headline:
MIND/BODY/HEALTH;
CHEW WELL AND SWALLOW WHOLE

title: Stolen Mind
author: Myrna Doernberg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STOLEN MIND: The Slow Disappearance of Ray Doernberg. By Myrna Doernberg. (Algonquin, $14.95.) The slowest deaths can prove the most painful, for sufferers and survivors alike.
headline: IN SHORT

title: Woodland Walks In Britain
author: Bayard Webster
pull_quote: Vidal in Venice By Gore Vidal. Edited by George Armstrong. Photographs by Tore Gill. 160 pages. Summit Books. $22.95.   In ''Vidal in Venice,'' Gore Vidal is pictured in a gondola on the Grand Canal, half-smiling back at the camera, looking as serene as one of the city's lions, but without the wings. Another illustration in this coffee-table book shows some flotsam below a street sign, Rio de San Vidal, a small canal that passes behind the Church of San Vidal. The floating rubbish is about the only visible touch of anything less than a picture-postcard view of Venice.
headline: TRAVEL BOOKSHELF

title: New Jerusalem
author: Len Jenkin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NEW JERUSALEM By Len Jenkin. 214 pp. Los Angeles: Sun & Moon Press. Cloth, $16.95. Paper, $10.95. LEN JENKIN has pulled off something striking here: with comic-book exaggeration and a cynical luridness, he has created a delicate, moving novel set in a blasted, despairing future, early in the 21st century. New Jerusalem is the bitter, mocking name given to an island prison where the dregs of the earth are dumped by an uncaring world government. Criminals and misfits are exiled here, but so are the indigent and the eccentric - in Mr. Jenkin's vision of the future, sympathy is an unaffordable luxury.
headline: LAND OF THIEVES AND KILLERS

title: Actual Minds, Possible Worlds
author: Jerome Bruner
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ACTUAL MINDS, POSSIBLE WORLDS By Jerome Bruner. 201 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $15. PITY today's generalist - or, for that matter, any scholar who aspires beyond the ever more narrowly drawn confines of his own specialty. Today, the degree of incomprehensibility to nonprofessionals seems almost a measure of the progress made within a given domain. And I'm not just speaking here of fields like relativistic quantum mechanics, which outsiders are quite prepared not to understand. I mean research even in the humanities, the study of literature, say, or philosophy, which not so very long ago an educated person might have regarded as his territory through a kind of inherited ownership. These areas too have become laden with theories dictating new forms of language, incrusted with technical terms that are necessary for the very formulation of the problems under consideration.   Pity then, but at the same time praise, those who yet make the attempt to hack their way through jargon-barbed thickets of theory - Jerome Bruner, for example, whose latest book is the result of just such a heroic expedition. In ''Actual Minds, Possible Worlds,'' Mr. Bruner, the director of the New York Institute for the Humanities at New York University, explores some recent currents in literary theory and philosophy and attempts to apply them to his own subspecialty, the psychology of learning and education.
headline: MIND/BODY/HEALTH

title: Vidal In Venice
author: Herbert Mitgang
pull_quote: Woodland Walks in Britain By Gerald Wilkinson. Illustrated. 320 pages. Holt, Rinehart & Winston. $19.95.   This is a comprehensive and beautifully packaged guide to the woodland walks of England, Scotland and Wales. It is not, however, aimed at the American who visits the British Isles and who has only a casual interest in the outdoors.
headline: TRAVEL BOOKSHELF

title: America's Health Care Revolution
author: Joseph A. Califano Jr.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AMERICA'S HEALTH CARE REVOLUTION Who Lives? Who Dies? Who Pays?. By Joseph A. Califano Jr. 241 pp. New York: Random House. $17.95. A REVOLUTION, precipitated by seemingly uncontrollable costs, is occurring in our system of medical care, and the battle is joined between those who provide the care and those who pay for it. This is Joseph A. Califano Jr.'s thesis in ''America's Health Care Revolution.'' He believes that the traditional control of health care by doctors and hospitals is shifting to large corporations and to the Government because those who ultimately pay the doctor bills can determine the way their money is spent if they wish to.   Mr. Califano says that when he was Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare from 1977 to 1979, he firmly believed that only the Government could solve the problem of rising medical costs, but his more recent experience in corporate America, and particularly with Chrysler Corporation as the chairman of its committee on health care, has led him to believe that the private sector must initiate the reforms that will be necessary to control costs.
headline: HOW THE BILLS GOT BLOATED

title: The Healer Within
author: Steven Locke
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE HEALER WITHIN The New Medicine of Mind and Body. By Steven Locke and Douglas Colligan. Foreword by Norman Cousins. 272 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $22.50. IF the title of this book is somewhat misleading -the authors are more concerned to document the effect of psychosocial factors on disease than to show us how we can heal ourselves - the subtitle is simply remarkable. For a very long time, it has been clear that the Cartesian separation of mind and body was a philosophical fiction. (In non-Western cultures, Descartes would have been laughed out of the room.) As a practical matter, dualism has been refuted by the successful use of biofeedback, faith healing, placebos, and hypnosis, among other things. But only recently has medical science begun to take official notice that attitude and temperament are intertwined with neurobiological phenomena. Thus the straight-faced reference to a new medicine of mind and body.   Despite their conviction that our medicine is insufficiently holistic, Dr. Steven Locke, who teaches in the psychiatry department at the Harvard Medical School, and Douglas Colligan, a senior editor at Omni magazine, are hardly iconoclasts. The reader of ''The Healer Within'' is cautioned immediately that ''all matters regarding your health require medical supervision''; the final chapters are disdainful of therapies not carried out under the supervision of physicians. In between, though, the authors present a review of research that must shake the faith of the most intransigent dualist.
headline: THE WHOLE HOLISTIC THING

title: Those Days
author: Richard Critchfield. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THOSE DAYS An American Album. By Richard Critchfield. Illustrated. 419 pp. New York: Anchor Press/Doubleday. $19.95. THIS powerful memoir begins with a wedding in the garden of an Iowa parsonage on April 19, 1913. Anna Louise Williams and Jim Critchfield, the author's parents, are married by the bride's father, the Rev. Hadwen Williams. Neighbors have filled the house with daffodils, tulips, violets, ferns and lilies of the valley; from the cellar come the creak and groan of grinding ice and salt muffled by a wet gunnysack: ''Anna Louise's brother, Hadwen, down from his teaching job in Minnesota, was cranking out some tutti-frutti ice cream in the freezer.''   This is an American Eden. But in the garden, among the lilacs, Anna Louise confesses to her father that Jim ''drinks a little,'' and Mr. Williams wounds his daughter forever by blurting out, ''I wish you were marrying Forrest instead.''   Forrest is Anna Louise's college classmate - a local boy. Jim farms in North Dakota. He's not a churchgoer. His mother was ''lace-curtain Irish.'' He's descended on his father's side from an English convict, a Virginia infantryman in the Continental Army, and an Ohio pioneer. Anna Louise, the preacher's daughter, is a Methodist who comes from New England Quakers. They went west in 1859, pursuing ''the vision of a purer, simpler society.''
headline: LIVE ONCE, AND BOLDY

title: Sexual Desire. A Moral Philosophy Of The Erotic
author: Roger Scruton.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SEXUAL DESIRE A Moral Philosophy of the Erotic. By Roger Scruton. 428 pp. New York: The Free Press. $25. ROGER SCRUTON is not a sexologist and this is not a sexy book. He is an English philosopher and a founder of the Conservative Philosophy Group, which advises the Thatcher Government. He views the Enlightenment as a perversion, and his goal in ''Sexual Desire'' is to dignify the sexual act of heterosexual lovers by restoring to modern consciousness a sense of original sin.   His book is illiberal, antifeminist, anti-Freudian, antiliberationist, antilibertarian, and anti-free market. Mr. Scruton defends the ''truths'' of traditional sexual morality - that fidelity, modesty and shame are virtues, that masturbation, promiscuity and homosexuality are vices - and he undertakes a mission to save ''sexual morality from the morass into which modern ways of thinking have enticed it.'' It is a stunning achievement that is bound to be viewed in the wrong light from both sides of the political spectrum.
headline: THE JOY OF ORIGINAL SIN

title: Damning The Innocent
author: Pierre Darmon. Translated by Paul Keegan.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DAMNING THE INNOCENT A History of the Persecution of the Impotent in pre-Revolutionary France. By Pierre Darmon. Translated by Paul Keegan. 234 pp. New York: Viking. $18.95. THIS is a very curious piece of book publishing. Consider, for example, the title: in the French original (and the British version) it was neutral and descriptive: ''Le Tribunal de l'Impuissance: Virilite et Defaillances Conjugales dans l'Ancienne France''; in the American edition it becomes shrill, a story of ''persecution'' and ''damning'' of ''the innocent.'' In defense of the new title, it has to be admitted that it fairly accurately describes the tone of Pierre Darmon's book, which is a polemical attack on the canon law and canon lawyers in early modern France -and by implication also against the plaintiff wives.
headline: SUING FOR ANNULMENT

title: The Moonlight Man
author: Paula Fox
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MOONLIGHT MAN By Paula Fox. 192 pp. New York: Bradbury Press. $12.95.(Ages 12 and up) ''WHERE was he?   Where was her father?'' For three weeks of the summer vacation Catherine Ames has been stranded at her Montreal boarding school, waiting for her father to come and get her. It's to be their first long time together since her parents divorced 12 years ago when she was 3. He finally calls, disarming, apologetic as always; and she crosses on the ferry to meet him in Nova Scotia, where they spend a month in a cottage near a seaside village.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: 20 Under 30
author: Debra Spark
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: 20 UNDER 30 Best Stories by America's New Young Writers. Edited by Debra Spark. 269 pp. New York: Charles Scribner's Sons. Cloth, $15.95. Paper, $7.95. DOESN'T it seem that commercial publishers are willing to open the window of opportunity a crack more to writers in their 20's or late teens than they were, say, a generation ago? The 1960's, when I was coming up, were certainly as fixated on youth as the 80's, but the publishing world still presumed it necessary for a young writer to go out and get Experience first. Perhaps the salutary dethroning of this macho ideal (the writer as ex-stevedore/mercenary) has made it possible to give more credence to the imaginations of the young; or perhaps this new generation is simply so preternaturally talented that it cannot be denied.   In any case, putting aside my initial grumpy envy, I took up ''20 Under 30: Best Stories by America's New Young Writers,'' and found to my surprise a wonderfully enjoyable reading experience. There are some knockouts here; and when one is in the midst of reading a great story with a mesmerizing prose style completely under control, the author's age scarcely enters one's thoughts.
headline: ALL THE YOUNG SPELLBINDERS

title: Inside Oscar
author: Mason Wiley
pull_quote: Like it or not, the odds are that tomorrow you'll be spending at least part of a long evening in front of a television set watching the 58th annual Academy Awards ceremonies (on ABC, starting at 9 E. S. T.). Any insurance man's actuarial tables will tell you so. You might tune in to see whether, after eight nominations, Geraldine Page finally wins her first Oscar (for ''A Trip to Bountiful''), and whether Steven Spielberg, who wasn't nominated, will show up to support his ''Color Purple'' colleagues, who were. It could be that your interest is in who gets the sound recording award. Possibly you're at home only because there's no one around to go bowling with. Whatever the reasons, you're part of the show's dizzy ratings.   Ever since the first Oscar telecast from the Pantages Theater on March 19, 1953, Hollywood's annual tribute to itself has drawn one of each year's biggest viewing audiences. Over the last three decades, movies have changed in size, shape, manners, cost and impact. Indeed, they aren't even the mass entertainment medium they once were - television is. Yet we continue to watch the Oscar show with an anticipation not always seemly in someone old enough to drive a car.
headline: OSCAR NIGHT CASTS ITS MAGIC SPELL

title: Paradise Postponed
author: John Mortimer
pull_quote: PARADISE POSTPONED. By John Mortimer. 374 pages. Viking. $17.95.   IT is with a familiar tableau that John Mortimer entices us into his thoroughly delightful new novel, ''Paradise Postponed.'' It is 1985. Simeon Simcox, 80-year-old rector of the English village of Rapstone Fanner, is ''approaching death, like most of the other events in his long life, with a puzzled good will under which lay a certain dogged persistence.'' ''I should like you to know that it hasn't been so simple,'' he tells his younger son, Dr. Fred Simcox, who is sitting at his bedside, reflecting on his affection for the old man. ''Not half so straightforward as it might have looked.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Power Of The Press
author: Thomas C Leonard
pull_quote: THE POWER OF THE PRESS. The Birth of American Political Reporting. By Thomas C. Leonard. Illustrated. 273 pages. Oxford University Press. $22.50. AMERICAN journalism has seldom been shy about proclaiming its own achievements, and a free press, we must all agree, stands high among the forces that have made the United States a working democracy. But how did journalists first acquire political power? What part did they play in creating a popular interest in politics? How did the conventions and emphases of political reporting develop, and how steep was the price that had to be paid for them? These are relatively neglected questions, and ones that can rarely have been raised as pointedly as they are by Thomas C. Leonard in ''The Power of the Press.''   Mr. Leonard, who is an associate professor of journalism at the University of California at Berkeley, has selected a number of key developments, from the first stirrings of an independent press in the early 18th century to the heyday of ''muckraking'' 200 years later. Some of the episodes he discusses, like the exposure of the Tweed Ring in the New York City of the 1870's, are familiar stories looked at in an unfamiliar light. Others represent largely uncharted territory -the long road that had to be traveled, for example, before journalists were able to perform the simple service of setting down what a politician actually said.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Another Marvelous Thing
author: Laurie Colwin
pull_quote: ANOTHER MARVELOUS THING. By Laurie Colwin. 130 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.   HAPPINESS and love, those two longed-for emotions of adult life, have served as the magnetic poles of Laurie Colwin's two novels (''Happy All the Time,'' ''Family Happiness'') and her short-story collections (''Passion and Affect,'' ''The Lone Pilgrim''), and not surprisingly, she returns to them again in this new volume of interlinked tales. Certainly those themes are commodious ones -more than roomy enough to sustain an entire career - but Miss Colwin seems to have already settled on a fairly formulaic approach, almost invariably blending together scenes of contemporary life (the well-heeled variety in which everyone seems to have attended a good school, gives dinner parties and knows two or more languages) with aphoristic observations on the nature of love, marriage and adultery.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Bohemian Paris
author: Jerrold Seigel
pull_quote: BOHEMIAN PARIS. Culture, Politics, and the Boundaries of Bourgeois Life, 1830-1930. By Jerrold Seigel. Illustrated. 453 pages. Elisabeth Sifton/ Viking. $25.   ''BOHEMIAN'' is the common French term for gypsy, a relic of the erroneous assumption that gypsies originated in Bohemia -much as the term ''gypsy'' itself enshrines the equally erroneous belief that they originated in Egypt. For centuries ''Bohemia'' was also synonymous with the Paris underworld. It was only in the 1830's that the name began to be applied to the world of unconventional young artists and picturesque dropouts, only in 1849, with the successful dramatization of Henry Murger's newspaper sketches about his Bohemian friends, that this became its predominant meaning, and ''la vie de Boheme'' began an international career that culminated in Puccini's opera.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Family Resemblances
author: Lowry Pei
pull_quote: FAMILY RESEMBLANCES. By Lowry Pei. 264 pages. Random House. $16.95.   The idea of ''Family Resemblances,'' Lowry Pei's first novel, is a lot like that of the movie ''The Summer of '42'': show one pivotal summer in which a teen-ager grows up -discovers love and sex, loses a few illusions, and basically learns something about the uncertainty of grown-up life. The tone is similarly nostalgic; the protagonist, similarly likable: bright without being a smart aleck, earnest without being drippingly sincere, innocent without being a goody-two-shoes.
headline: RITE OF PASSAGE

title: Japanese Business Etiquette
author: Diana Rowland
pull_quote: JAPANESE BUSINESS ETIQUETTE: A PRACTICAL GUIDE TO SUCCESS WITH THE JAPANESE. By Diana Rowland. 176 Pages. Warner Books. $8.95.   The glut of oil is probably exceeded only by the glut of books on Japanese business. Yet why do so many of these books seem the same, filled with overheated claims of having unlocked the supposed mystery of Japan's corporate thinking, with much ballyhoo about Zen management techniques, bellicose industrial policies and shadowy strategists?
headline: AID TO INNOCENTS ABROAD

title: The Randlords
author: Geoffrey Wheatcroft
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE RANDLORDS By Geoffrey Wheatcroft. Illustrated. 314 pp. New York: Atheneum. $17.95. IN the preface to his hard-to-put-down book, ''The Randlords,'' Geoffrey Wheatcroft, a talented British journalist and columnist for The Evening Standard of London, observes that the social and economic forces enveloping South Africa today relate directly to one industry - gold. Then he disclaims: ''A mighty book could be written on such a mighty theme. This is not that. What has emerged from my efforts is a modest little book with a good deal to be modest about. All that I have been able to do is to pick out some themes here and there and highlight them.''

In the first stanza of his poem ''Of Himself,'' William Cowper wrote: William was once a bashful youth, His modesty was such, That one might say (to say the truth), He rather had too much. That applies to Mr. Wheatcroft as well. His is not a book to be modest about. It is a literate, absorbing narrative about South African robber barons of the late 19th century, known as Randlords. They were ambitious, acquisitive predators and exploiters who milked land and labor and battled one another for diamonds, gold, corporations and political influence. Many of them later became actual barons. Their wealth and charitable giving entitled them when they settled in London and the British countryside. And being Jewish was not a bar to entitlement, though political discredit was.
headline: BLAMING GOLD FOR EVERYTHING

title: Angels Of September
author: Andrew M. Greeley.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ANGELS OF SEPTEMBER By Andrew M. Greeley. 451 pp. New York: A Bernard Geis Associates Book/ Warner Books. $17.95. ANDREW M. GREELEY is a caution, as my friend Mrs. O'Brien would say, that is, someone who astonishes or causes mild apprehension. Sociologist, Roman Catholic priest, syndicated columnist, college teacher, theologian - deeply concerned with the role of religion in modern life - he is the author of more than 100 scholarly and popular articles and dozens of nonfiction books (variously characterized as truculent, cantankerous, controversial, crotchety, contentious, argumentative, brilliant, lucid, reasonable, readable, witty), as well as a volume of poetry brashly called ''Women I've Met.''
headline: A PASSION BORN IN KINDERGARTEN

title: The Sorcerer's Apprentice
author: Charles Johnson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SORCERER'S APPRENTICE By Charles Johnson. 169 pp. New York: Atheneum. $9.95. CHARLES JOHNSON'S brief, highly concentrated ''Sorcerer's Apprentice'' has the feel of a good short novel rather than a collection of stories. These tales - or are they fables? - are realistic without strictly adhering to realism, fantastic without getting lost in fantasy. Mr. Johnson, a professor of English at the University of Washington, writes of truths that intersect and sometimes intercept our everyday trajectories.
headline: VOODOO AND SUBTLER POWERS

title: A History Of Modern Criticism: 1750-1950
author: Rene Wellek
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A HISTORY OF MODERN CRITICISM: 1750-1950 Volume Five: English Criticism, 1900-1950. 343 pp. Volume Six: American Criticism, 1900-1950. 345 pp. By Rene Wellek. New Haven: Yale University Press. $22.50 each. WE live in a time when literary criticism is dominated by the academy. The days of the great poet-critics or novelist-critics - of Dryden or Johnson, Coleridge or Arnold, Flaubert or James, Eliot or Pound - seem to be over. If such people still exist, and I see no sign of it, the chances are that they are employed by a university. The leading reviewers, who were once men of letters or men of affairs, from Hazlitt and Macaulay to Ford Madox Ford and Orwell, are now for the most part professors. Compare the contributors to the great earlier periodicals, from the Edinburgh and Quarterly Reviews to Eliot's Criterion, with those of modern quarterlies like The Sewanee Review or such papers as The New York Review of Books, the London Review of Books or The Times Literary Supplement.
headline: BEFORE THE PROFESSORS TOOK OVER

title: Paradise Postponed
author: John Mortimer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PARADISE POSTPONED By John Mortimer. 374 pp. New York: Viking. $17.95. EVER since Virginia Woolf and James Joyce dynamited the conventional English novel, those of us who love the old Victorian-Edwardian form have been looking for a modern-day equivalent. John Mortimer may well have provided one.   Yet ''Paradise Postponed'' is by no means a throwback to an earlier period of history (a feat of which Mr. Mortimer, who adapted ''Brideshead Revisited'' for television, would undoubtedly have been capable). The novel is set firmly in late 20th-century Britain, amid episodes ranging from the imposition of postwar rationing to the 1974 coal miners' strike, from the Mandy Rice-Davies scandal in Parliament to the recent antimissile demonstrations on Greenham Common. But the book has an appealingly old-fashioned quality, inherent in the author's solicitous attitude toward plot, character and language. And even the novel's topicality is itself a kind of Victorianism, since by employing history in this way Mr. Mortimer reverts to a theme rarely found since the days of Dickens, Conrad and E. M. Forster: the idea that private experience only gains its full meaning in the context of public experience. In fashioning an appealing novel from this 19th-century idea, Mr. Mortimer evades both the pitfalls of historical pastiche (as practiced, for instance, by John Fowles and A. N. Wilson) and the limitations of much contemporary fiction.
headline: THE RECTOR'S WILL AND OTHER MYSTERIES

title: I.B.M.'S Early Computers
author: John Savage
pull_quote: THE myth of a paperless office has by now been relegated to the scrapheap by all but the most diehard electronics fanatics. The reality behind the death of this dream is simple: Only copiers produce more paper than personal computers.   The number of magazines and books computer users ought to glance at if they are to remain au courant is equally staggering. Here the reality of the situation manifests itself in what I call the great shutout. More and more users simply say, ''That's it. I have my system up and running. I don't want any more problems to face, and I don't want anything more to read. Please cancel my subscription.''
headline: CATCHING UP ON SOME READING

title: Minsky's Burlesque
author: Morton Minsky and Milt Machlin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MINSKY'S BURLESQUE By Morton Minsky and Milt Machlin. Illustrated. 312 pp. New York: Arbor House. $15.95. WHO in the New York of the 1920's, that sunny world of lounge lizards and flappers, didn't know about Minsky's National Winter Garden on Second Avenue and Houston Street? The notorious downtown burlesque house packed into its seats such regulars as John Dos Passos, Robert Benchley, George Jean Nathan and Conde Nast. Even Hart Crane shared the Minsky experience; squinting through the smoke-filled air of the magenta hall, he hailed in verse the ''outspoken buttocks in pink beads.''   Now Morton Minsky, with the help of the veteran writer Milt Machlin, allows us to relive those rowdy early days in this nostalgic and frankly partisan history of burlesque. Morton - the youngest of the four Minsky brothers - joined the family firm in 1924, fresh out of New York University, and became the resident Minsky at their newly acquired Little Apollo Theater on 125th Street. For the next four years, the theater showed a weekly profit of $20,000 after payola. Despite the seaminess of cops on the take and gun-toting patrons, young Morton seemed to relish his work - and his enthusiasm is charming. He titled his sketches ''Julius Teaser'' and ''Panties Inferno,'' sprinkling high culture over his blunt enterprise like MSG.
headline: 4 BROTHERS -- COUNT 'EM -- 4

title: Rich And Poor
author: Jim Goldberg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RICH AND POOR By Jim Goldberg. Unpaged. New York: Random House. Paper, $15.95. IF Studs Terkel's ubiquitous tape recorder suddenly went dead and he relied on a camera instead, the outcome might resemble this collection of 78 black-and-white portrait photographs by Jim Goldberg, who offers these grainy pictures, taken over seven years, in support of the sociological conceit of his title. As he explains in his afterword, Mr. Goldberg discovered the subjects for his ambitious project in only two places: a transient hotel in San Francisco and on the board of trustees of an unnamed art school that he attended, also in San Francisco. He also warns us not to expect ''an 'accurate,' descriptive, educational tool about the issue of poverty and wealth in America.'' He should have said something earlier, perhaps in his title.
headline: A TOUCH OF TWO CLASSES

title: Gentleman Bear
author: William Pene Du Bois
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GENTLEMAN BEAR Written and illustrated by William Pene du Bois. 78 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $14.95. (Ages 8 and up) HAVE the tales of William Pene du Bois become increasingly arcane over the years, or have today's children - and perhaps their elders -simply lost the patience needed for his leisurely and delectably convoluted prose style?
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Ancient History
author: M. I. Finley.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ANCIENT HISTORY Evidence and Models. By M. I. Finley. 131 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/ Viking. $17.95. THE most influential writers of history in the Western world are the Greek and Roman historians, yet in the way we tend to think of history today, they were rarely, and then often inadvertently, historians. To write about ancient society in a form that modern historians would regard as history, scholars must try to construct an account from reluctant and elusive source materials: the fragments of stone and papyrus that have survived the ravages of earthquake, weather and vandalism; whatever literary evidence ancient writers chose to give us; and whatever facts can be gleaned from the scattered and partial evidence of archeology. If we now have some notion of the economic life and the underlying political motives of Greek and Roman society, it is largely because of Sir Moses Finley, the emeritus professor of ancient history at the University of Cambridge, who in his own books and through the works of his pupils has given economic and political factors the attention the ancients neglected to pay them.
headline: BEWARE GREEKS...

title: The Bobby-Soxer
author: Hortense Calisher
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BOBBY-SOXER By Hortense Calisher. 281 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $17.95. HORTENSE CALISHER'S 10th novel and 17th book, ''The Bobby-Soxer,'' begins as one kind of novel, the story of a bright, sensitive teen-age girl growing up in a New Jersey town in the 1950's. But as she learns more of her family's history, and as she gets to know a famous playwright who is mining that material for his new work, it turns from a Bildungsroman into a fairy tale for grown-ups, built on old lore that leaves the social world behind and tests the bounds of credibility. The novel is full of solidly observed details of small-town life, family conflicts and wild adolescent yearnings. But finally, it may be less about these things than about Hortense Calisher's odd, offbeat way of telling a story.
headline: LEARNING ABOUT LIFE FROM AUNT LEO

title: A Lesser Life
author: Sylvia Ann Hewlett. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A LESSER LIFE The Myth of Women's Liberation in America. By Sylvia Ann Hewlett. Illustrated. 461 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $17.95. A YOUNG lawyer friend of mine once worked out this response to the prospective employer's query whether marriage might conflict with her fast-track career: ''I'm so glad you asked. I believe that men have struck a perfect balance between personal and professional lives. Reasonable accommodation of private lives? Nonsense. Humanization of the work world? Who needs it? I've made it clear to my friends and family that love, affection, friendship and human emotion play a small role in the life of a real professional.'' And what if the interviewer asks about children? ''Not to worry. Test tube babies for me. That way I can wait until I'm 40, 50, even 60 before I start a family, until my career is really well established. I'm no fool.''
headline: HAVING IT ALL IS TOO MUCH

title: Pagoda, Skull & Samurai: 3 Stories
author: Chieko Irie Mulhern
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PAGODA, SKULL & SAMURAI: 3 STORIES BY ROHAN KODA. Translated by Chieko Irie Mulhern. (Charles E. Tuttle, $12.50.) The literature of Japan's Meiji period (1867-1912), the era when the nation first opened to Western ideas, remains surprisingly little known.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Libertation Of One
author: Romuald Spasowski
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LIBERATION OF ONE By Romuald Spasowski. Illustrated. 687 pp. San Diego: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $24.95. A WEEK after martial law came crashing down in Poland in December 1981, smashing Solidarity and the most far-reaching mass movement for freedom the Soviet bloc had ever seen, Romuald Spasowski, the Polish Ambassador to the United States, defected. At a crowded news conference in the State Department he read a dramatic and emotional message: he expressed support for Lech Walesa, called imprisoned Solidarity activists ''the best sons and daughters of the Polish nation'' and insisted he could no longer have any association with a regime capable of such brutality and inhumanity. ''A cruel night of darkness and silence was spread over my country,'' he lamented.   Two days later, Mr. Spasowski and his wife, Wanda, were ushered into the Oval Office for a 15-minute meeting with President Reagan. According to Larry Speakes, the White House spokesman, the couple wept and the President's eyes brimmed with tears. Afterward, the President walked with them through a cold rain to a waiting limousine. He held a black umbrella over them and when they reached the car, he put his right arm around his wife and hugged her. The photograph, like the defection, was front-page news.
headline: WAKING UP, GETTING OUT

pull_quote: LIFE DRAWING. By Emily Arnold. (Delacorte, $15.95.) With the return of figurative painting to the foreground of the contemporary art scene, the New York of the Abstract Expressionists assumes the archaic, tinted dignity of a daguerrotype.

title: Samurai And Silk
author: Haru Matsukata Reischauer. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SAMURAI AND SILK A Japanese and American Heritage. By Haru Matsukata Reischauer. Illustrated. 371 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $20. ''I TELL you, Mr. Arai, it is getting very hard to make money by Jap. business because as you know, in Japan there is not much necessary thing that we can export.'' This letter from one Japanese businessman to another, composed in English to express his international outlook, was obviously not written recently. It was sent in 1878. Mr. Arai was a silk merchant in New York, and the grandfather of the author of ''Samurai and Silk.'' Mrs. Reischauer's other grandfather, on her father's side, was Prince Masayoshi Matsukata, who was Prime Minister twice and Finance Minister for 15 years at the end of the 19th century. The story of these two gentlemen, an international businessman and a nation-builder, is meant to illustrate, as Mrs. Reischauer puts it, ''the reasons for Japan's economic success in modern times.''
headline: ANCESTORS AT HOME AND ABROAD

title: Saranac: America's Magic Mountain
author: Robert Taylor
pull_quote: SARANAC: America's Magic Mountain.   By Robert Taylor. Illustrated. 308 pages. Houghton Mifflin. $17.95. QUESTION: What do Ralph   Waldo Emerson and Marjorie Merriweather Post have in common - along with the writer Robert Louis Stevenson, the baseball player Lawrence (Laughing Larry) Doyle, the poet Sylvia Plath, the cartoonist Garry Trudeau and thousands of people who died of tuberculosis? Answer: They have in common the town of Saranac Lake, in New York State's Adirondack Mountains.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Great And Desperate Cures
author: Elliot S Valenstein
pull_quote: GREAT AND DESPERATE CURES. The Rise and Decline of Psychosurgery and Other Radical Treatments for Mental Illness. By Elliot S. Valenstein. Illustrated. 338 pages. Basic Books. $19.95. IN November 1935 a surgeon in   Lisbon drilled two holes in a mental patient's skull and injected absolute alcohol into the frontal lobes of her brain. The operation had been devised by a distinguished Portuguese neurologist, Egas Moniz, although on account of the gout from which he suffered he was unable to perform it himself; the object was to destroy the nerve fibers that Moniz believed were responsible for delusions and pathological anxieties.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: I The Supreme
author: Augusto Roa Bastos
pull_quote: I THE SUPREME. By Augusto Roa Bastos. Translated by Helen Lane. 438 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95.   HAVING taken part in the Paraguayan revolution against Spain, Jose Gaspar Rodriguez de Francia declared himself dictator of the country in 1814 and exercised absolute power until his death in 1840. Known as ''El Supremo,'' Francia tolerated little opposition: he suppressed the aristocracy, limited the power of the church, jailed and reportedly tortured his enemies, and effectively cut Paraguay off from the outside world. And it is his story that the exiled Paraguayan writer Augusto Roa Bastos attempts to reimagine and relate in this huge, Rabelaisian novel.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Japanese Automobile Industry
author: Michael A Cusumano
pull_quote: THE JAPANESE AUTOMOBILE INDUSTRY: Technology and Management at Nissan and Toyota. By Michael A. Cusumano. 493 pages. Council on East Asian Studies, Harvard University Press. $25.   IN 1947, when most of Japanese industry was struggling to recover from wartime damage and a frail economy, a self-taught engineer named Taiichi Ono was put in charge of a machining shop at the Toyota Motor Corporation's Koromo factory. He set out to help improve the company's fortunes by eliminating waste in the production process. Waste to Mr. Ono was more than rejected parts or metal shavings on the floor. He saw waste in a worker standing idle, even if only for a few seconds, or parts piled in inventory waiting to be used.
headline: Books: Industrial Coup

title: The Book Of Abraham
author: Marek Halter
pull_quote: THE BOOK OF ABRAHAM. By Marek Halter. 722 pages. Henry Holt. $19.95.   THE Jews, who get their title as People of the Book from their unique relationship to the Bible, inspire possibly a greater volume of writing than any other people. There is an endless profusion of Jewish literature, fiction and nonfiction, by Jews and others, for Jews and others, that almost daily deals with the sorrows, glories, failings and virtues of these people so dispersed and diverse and yet somehow sharing a common past and maybe even a common destiny.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Reckless Eyeballing
author: Ishmael Reed
pull_quote: RECKLESS EYEBALLING. By Ishmael Reed. 148 pages. St. Martin's Press. $12.95. The way ''Reckless Eyeballing'' starts off reminds you of a seedy 1940's detective novel gussied up with some contemporary bigotry and anger: a large man, wearing sunglasses and a raincoat, has been assaulting prominent feminists. He ties them up, shaves off their hair, chastises them for giving black men a bad name, and leaves a chrysanthemum behind as his calling card. His explanation is that this is what the Resistance did to whores who collaborated with the Nazis, and that women today who help perpetuate ugly stereotypes about black men deserve a similar punishment for their sins.   This is Ishmael Reed's seventh novel, and like much of his earlier fiction, it's a nasty, idiosyncratic blend of invective, satire and social criticism, served up with lots of narrative pratfalls and jokes. This time, he takes on what he sees as a cultural establishment bent on manufacturing and reinforcing racist cliches. And he goes so far as to imply that black men are currently being stereotyped and maligned in much the same way that the Nazis once treated the Jews.
headline: GALLERY OF THE REPELLENT

title: The Contentious French
author: Charles Tilly
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CONTENTIOUS FRENCH By Charles Tilly. Illustrated. 456 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press. $25.   IN February 1684 a large number of winegrowers from the region around Dijon assembled to the beat of the drum, elected sergeants and marched off in good order to trespass on a forest that belonged to a nearby monastery. There they gathered firewood and, on their return to the city, clashed with officials who had turned out to frustrate their illegal act. Although 12 of their leaders were placed in jail there was considerable local sympathy for an action taken to assert a traditional right that agents of the forest land's leaseholders had progressively eroded. Eventually the municipality brought suit to enforce the winegrowers' right to gather wood.   In May 1968 a large number of students formed militant bands in the Latin Quarter, occupied university buildings, built barricades and engaged in mutually violent conflict with the police. The precise causes of the student rebellion, its nature and even its consequences are still subject to conflicting interpretations. It is clear that the students acted as an autonomous force, on their own turf, and with regard to what they perceived as their collective interests as well as for larger goals.
headline: REBELS WITH MANY A CAUSE

title: High Jinx
author: William F. Buckley Jr.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HIGH JINX By William F. Buckley Jr. 261 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $16.95. THE language they speak in Albania is called Shqip and is divided into two dialects, Gheg and Tosk. More than one-third of the country is covered by forest, and there was no rail transport before 1948. On the face of it, this smallest member of the Communist community hardly seems a logical choice as the scene for mounting ''the most important countersalient since the beginning of the cold war.''   However, covert operations were in fact initiated by Great Britain and the United States in Albania between 1949 and 1953 on the assumption that Albania's isolation made it vulnerable to the West, and there is evidence that the British spy Kim Philby, who was a liaison officer in these operations, betrayed them. So it is on history that William F. Buckley Jr.'s new novel ''High Jinx'' is loosely based. British and American commandos are dropped at five strategic sites, but scarcely are they on the ground when the lot of them is captured, shot or hanged and an album of photographs sent back to the West to prove it. The question is, how did they know about the commandos' landing behind the Iron Curtain?
headline: OAKES AGAINST THE SPOOKS

title: Blessings In Disguise
author: Alec Guinness
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
BLESSINGS IN DISGUISE By Alec Guinness. Illustrated. 238 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.

BEFORE Alec Guinness began his career, he was forced to act, to pretend. ''A small, reddish-haired and very freckled child, makes his fearful entrance; upstage; centre,'' and from the first paragraph of his memoir Sir Alec's chameleon character fascinates the reader. He has a two-page scuffle with his Ego before he begins his story. He knows, he tells us, that he is ''not in the same class'' as Laurence Olivier, Ralph Richardson, John Gielgud or ''the other greats.'' His readers and audiences will be quick to add that Sir Alec is in a class by himself, not only as an actor, but as a writer as well.
headline: THE RECORD BOOK OF GUINNESS

title: An Earthquake In My Family
author: J. F. Federspiel. Translated by Eveline L. Kanes.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AN EARTHQUAKE IN MY FAMILY By J. F. Federspiel. Translated by Eveline L. Kanes. 249 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $17.95.   THE often powerful and enigmatic stories gathered in ''An Earthquake in My Family'' originally appeared in German as long ago as the early 1960's. Not one of them was published later than 1973. This means the collection forms more of a prequel than a follow-up to the arrival in English of J. F. Federspiel's recent, cruel, memorable novel, ''The Ballad of Typhoid Mary.'' Presumably the selection has been made to show what else the distinguished Swiss writer can do besides making scrupulous inquiries into the morality of the typhoid carrier. As it turns out, that is just what he does best; he is most satisfying when he is most somber.   He is the poet of anxiety and obsession, touched by Surrealism, crackling with black humor, but these strengths can be grounded by a leaden whimsy and dissipate themselves in perverse eccentricity. The group of stories about the volatile Dr. Paratuga, who is more of an extended quirk than a man or an idea, are elaborately artificial, strenuously fey, with the ungainly sprightliness of an elephant's polka - like cruel parodies of magic realism. Yet this writer can achieve extraordinary effects and has the capacity to move the intellect as forcefully as the heart.
headline: MISSING THE TITANIC, DROWNING IN THE BATH

title: The Unfinished Universe
author: Louise B. Young. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE UNFINISHED UNIVERSE By Louise B. Young. Illustrated. 239 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95.   A NUMBER of scientists have recently suggested that the observed order in the universe, and especially the order required to support life, cannot easily be explained within traditional science. In 1974, the physicist Brandon Carter embodied this notion in the ''Anthropic Principle,'' which, in some versions, states that if such fundamental physical constants as the forces in atoms were much different in strength, then atoms (and planets and people) could never have formed in the first place. Why should a universe care about making atoms, or life? In 1979, the biologist James Lovelock cast his version of the idea in the ''Gaia'' hypothesis, which claims that the entire earthly biosphere, including atmosphere and oceans and soil, is a self-regulating system, maintaining the delicate conditions for life against staggering odds. Why should our planet offer us such hospitality? These ideas, in broad terms, are centuries old; they have taken on new precision with the advances of science. Few scientists dispute the facts behind the Anthropic Principle or the Gaia hypothesis. The interpretation of these facts, however, is controversial.
headline: THE FORCE IS WITH US

title: The Diary Of Beatrice Webb
author: Jeanne Mackenzie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DIARY OF BEATRICE WEBB Volume Four: 1924-1943. ''The Wheel of Life.'' Edited by Norman MacKenzie and Jeanne MacKenzie. Illustrated. 519 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press. $25.   BEATRICE WEBB was a woman of natural spiritual temperament and applied political dedication. One of nine daughters of a prosperous Victorian railway magnate and industrialist, she was for her whole adult life a shining advertisement for the Fabian virtues of high thinking and plain living - virtues that her two ''children,'' the London School of Economics and the left-wing magazine the New Statesman, for many years loyally reflected. The corpus of her own work - intimidating tomes with titles like '' The History of Trade Unionism,'' ''Industrial Democracy'' or ''English Local Government'' - may nowadays be largely unread: instead, her enduring monument is to be found in the three volumes of ''The Letters of Sidney and Beatrice Webb'' and the four volumes of her diaries, of which this is the last.
headline: FABIAN MOTHER SUPERIOR

title: The Short Season
author: David Falkner.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SHORT SEASON The Hard Work and High Times of Baseball in the Spring. By David Falkner. 276 pp. New York: Times Books. $16.95.   Oh, what baseball does to literary types! Grab a poet who was once a 12-year-old listening to his Emerson the day Bobby Thomson hit his home run, or a novelist who wanted to make his mark in Wrigley Field long before he'd heard of the National Academy of Arts and Letters, and suddenly great stretches of Canadian pulpwood forest are imperiled by the omnivorous publishing industry.
headline: THE BOYS OF SPRING

title: A Porcupine Named Fluffy
author: Helen Lester
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A PORCUPINE NAMED FLUFFY. By Helen Lester. Illustrated by Lynn Munsinger. 32 pages. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $12.95. (Ages 4 to 7) WHEN I was growing up, I knew lots of children who hated their names. I certainly hated mine. ''It's a lovely name,'' my mother told me. '' 'Grave Alice' is from Longfellow's ''Children's Hour.'' Since I felt I had to live up to my name, I wished she had chosen ''Laughing Allegra.'' My problem was minor compared to Fluffy's! His proud parents rejected names like Spike and Lance and Needleroozer - any of which would have been easier for a porcupine to live up to. But oh, no. ''Let's call him Fluffy.'' they say. ''It's such a pretty name.'' And it doesn't take Fluffy long to realize that he isn't. ''He first became suspicious when he backed into a door and stuck fast. That was not a fluffy thing to do.'' So he tries to live up to his name. But it's not easy being a cloud when you're a porcupine - it's hard to stay up. And it's dangerous to pretend you're a fluffy pillow. ''When his mother sat on him, she was not pleased.''
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: C B Greenfield: A Little Madness
author: Lucille Kallen
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: C. B. GREENFIELD: A LITTLE MADNESS. By Lucille Kallen. (Random House, $14.95.) Charlie Greenfield, suburban news editor, has solved some murders, but only fine music can bring him to a state resembling animation.
