title: Arab Folktales
author: Inea Bushnaq
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ARAB FOLKTALES Edited and translated by Inea Bushnaq. Illustrated. 386 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $19.95.   THE introduction to ''Arab Folktales,'' an anthology of 130 stories collected and translated by Inea Bushnaq, begins with a comparison of the arts of embroidery and storytelling in the Arab world. The elaborate stitching that traditionally ornaments women's dresses throughout the eastern Mediterranean reveals both the unity and diversity of the region. The embroidered decoration of the gowns is widespread, but the patterns and designs reveal differences specific to given locales. From denser decorations on a dress, one can read that the young girl wearing it had ample time for sewing while she sat watching a flock of sheep or cattle; women who work in the fields have less time for adorning their dresses. The patterns as well are important in indicating the provenance of the wearer of the gown. Embroidery from Bethlehem or Beit Jala is immediately distinguishable from the designs worked in Nablus or Al-Bireh.
headline: ALL ABOARD THE FLYING CARPET

title: Japan's War: The Great Pacific Conflict 1853 To 1952
author: Edwin P Hoyt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: JAPAN'S WAR: The Great Pacific Conflict 1853 to 1952. By Edwin P. Hoyt. (McGraw-Hill, $19.95.) The kingdom of Japan, says Edwin P. Hoyt, suffered neither military defeat nor foreign occupation until 1945, making it the oldest government of its kind.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Next-To-Last Things
author: Stanley Kunitz.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NEXT-TO-LAST THINGS New Poems and Essays. By Stanley Kunitz. 130 pp. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. $17.95. THE sharp and seasoned good humor Stanley Kunitz brings to the poems, essays, interview and aphorisms in ''Next-to-Last Things'' is a tonic in our literary life. Mr. Kunitz, who is now 80 years old, was remarkably prescient about his own eventual reputation when he once wrote of E. E. Cummings that ''more than any other poet of his generation Cummings cherished and nurtured the image of himself as poet. . . . In a society of gladhanders and backslappers and self-advertisers he insisted not so much on his own uniqueness as on his right to be unique.'' The work of a much battered, ceaselessly active veteran of around 60 years of effort to keep bright his own and the world's esteem for poetry, this brief new book is strikingly youthful. A maxim in the section ''Seedcorn and Windfall'' puts it nicely: ''Be prepared for everything - even spontaneity.''
headline: PREPARED FOR SPONTANEITY

title: Stone Virgin
author: Barry Unsworth
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STONE VIRGIN By Barry Unsworth. 309 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $17.95.   JUST when I thought I couldn't stand to read another semi-autobiographical novel about a failing marriage, a blocked writer or a young man on drugs and the make, along comes the British novelist Barry Unsworth (''Mooncranker's Gift'') with a book that makes me think of that old ''Monty Python'' line ''And now for something completely different.'' ''Stone Virgin'' is certainly that. Set in Venice in three different centuries, it's the only novel I can think of besides ''The Picture of Dorian Gray'' whose central figure and most interesting character is a work of art - a late Gothic statue of the Virgin of the Annunciation that seems to glow, may have supernatural powers and is definitely associated with murder, treachery, vengeance and high erotic doings down through the ages. There are problems with having a statue upstage the human characters, and I'll get to them in a bit, but give Mr. Unsworth credit: one couldn't be farther from the Upper West Side.
headline: A SEXUAL RECTANGLE

title: I The Supreme
author: Augusto Roa Bastos
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: I THE SUPREME By Augusto Roa Bastos. Translated by Helen Lane. 438 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95.   In the fall of 1967 I happened to be in London at the same time as the Peruvian novelist Mario Vargas Llosa. We had both read, recently and with admiration, as well as a touch of envy, Edmund Wilson's portraits of the American Civil War in ''Patriotic Gore.'' Sitting in a pub in Hampstead, we thought it would be a good idea to have a comparable book on Latin America. An imaginary portrait gallery immediately stepped forward, demanding incarnation: the Latin American dictators.   Individuals such as Mexico's Santa Anna, the peg-legged cockfighter who lost the Southwest to President James K. Polk's Manifest Destiny; or Venezuela's Juan Vicente Gomez, who announced his own death in order to punish those who dared celebrate it; or El Salvador's Maximiliano Hernandez Martinez, who fought off scarlet fever by having street lights wrapped in red paper; or Bolivia's Enrique Penaranda, of whom his mother said, ''If I had known that my son was going to be president, I would have taught him to read and write'' - all of them pose tremendous problems for Latin American novelists: How to compete with history? How to create characters richer, crazier, more imaginative than those offered by history?
headline: A DESPOT, NOW AND FOREVER

title: An Unnatural Pursuit & Other Pieces
author: Simon Gray
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AN UNNATURAL PURSUIT & OTHER PIECES. By Simon Gray. (St. Martin's, $15.95.) Simon Gray, the witty author of ''Butley,'' ''Otherwise Engaged'' and other plays, is, he would have us believe, totally lacking in the equipoise of his leading characters.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Great And Desperate Cures
author: Elliot S. Valenstein. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GREAT AND DESPERATE CURES The Rise and Decline of Psychosurgery and Other Radical Treatments for Mental Illness. By Elliot S. Valenstein. Illustrated. 338 pp. New York: Basic Books. $19.95.   TO acquire ''a name and a fame,'' and to acquire them quickly, a physician must do ''some great and desperate cures.'' So said John Bunyan in 1668. Certainly there are other ways. But a goodly number of the protagonists in Elliot S. Valenstein's historical study took this short cut. Although ambition, quite naked at times, is not the only theme, it does figure prominently in this troubling chronicle.   The author traces the recent history of somatic treatments for mental disorders, but central among his accounts of ''great and desperate cures'' is the story of psychosurgery. It is not a pretty tale, but it is well told, even compellingly told. It is not the story of a medical aberration, but rather a cautionary tale. The complex factors that inform it have a tendency to recur in other guises.
headline: CRUEL AND UNUSUAL MEDICINE

title: The Book Of Abraham
author: Marek Halter
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE BOOK OF ABRAHAM By Marek Halter. Translated by Lowell Bair. 722 pp. New York: Henry Holt & Company. $19.95. ''BEING elsewhere,'' said the French writer Charles Peguy, ''is the great secret vice of the Jews, their great secret virtue, the great vocation of this people.'' In Marek Halter's spectacular novel, ''The Book of Abraham,'' the ''elsewhereness'' of one Jewish family pervades 100 generations succeeding one another over a period of almost 2,000 years. Mr. Halter, tapping in part the documented experience of his own forebears, has expanded Peguy's sentence into a saga.

The vice of being elsewhere. Never solidly here, never truly stable, safe or sure, forever thrashing the air (like the image in the Talmud: ''Man's shadow is not that of a tree swaying but that of a bird aflutter''), Mr. Halter's characters often have itineraries rather than lives. Here is a genealogy of flights from persecution without, from demons within; jagged trajectories that start with the sack of Jerusalem in A.D. 70, zigzag in ancient Carthage, travel through medieval Andalusia, cross Bourbon France, to end, after many a wheeling and looping, in the all-too-modern Warsaw ghetto, raked by the machine guns of the SS.
headline: SALVATION THROUGH MEMORY

title: The Mormon Corporate Empire
author: John Heinerman and Anson Shupe
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MORMON CORPORATE EMPIRE By John Heinerman and Anson Shupe. 293 pp. Boston: Beacon Press. $19.95. ONLY 156 years have passed since Joseph Smith   Jr. founded the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints on his claims that he had met God and Jesus Christ and had been led by the Angel Moroni to discover gold plates that he translated into the Book of Mormon. After a century as a small sect seen as a curiosity because of its early commitment to polygamy, the church has emerged in recent decades as a major political and economic force.
headline: LEDGERS OF THE LATTER-DAY SAINTS

title: Inventing Reality
author: Michael Parenti.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: INVENTING REALITY The Politics of the Mass Media. By Michael Parenti. 258 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $16.95. FREEDOM of the press, A. J. Liebling wrote, belongs to the man who owns one. Taking Liebling's maxim as his point of departure, Michael Parenti, the author of ''Democracy for the Few,'' has written a forceful though flawed critique of the American news media. By documenting patterns of conservative bias in a dozen major news stories in the printed and broadcast press, ''Inventing Reality'' provides a valuable rebuttal to the drumbeat of criticism of the news media from the right. Unfortunately, Mr. Parenti is so simplistic and doctrinaire in accounting for this bias that he makes his book easy to dismiss.   The function of the press, Mr. Parenti says, is to ''recreate a view of reality supportive of existing social and economic class power.'' Major newspapers and networks accomplish this by advancing the class interests of their corporate owners, who dictate the politics of the press. Only editors who share their outlook get promoted; reporters, eager to please editors, censor themselves. The result is news organizations that favor ''management over labor . . . the affluent over the poor, private enterprise over socialism . . . anticommunism and arms-race militarism over disarmament.'' Most of the news is little more than ''ruling class propaganda.''
headline: CAPITALIST CRUSADERS

title: The Maul And The Pear Tree
author: P. D. James and T. A. Critchley. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MAUL AND THE PEAR TREE The Ratcliffe Highway Murders 1811. By P. D. James and T. A. Critchley. Illustrated. 234 pp. New York: Mysterious Press. $17.95.   THE art of murder, in fact as in fiction, reached levels of accomplishment in 19th-century Britain rarely matched in subsequent times. Connoisseurs hark back to dusty British murders with fond admiration, and assuage any guilt over their morbid interest with the knowledge that the victims would all have been dead by now anyway and, but for their spectacular demise, completely forgotten as well.
headline: PLEASANTLY GHASTLY

title: Saranac: America's Magic Mountain
author: Robert Taylor. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SARANAC America's Magic Mountain. By Robert Taylor. Illustrated. 308 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $17.95.   BEFORE the story slips away, Robert Taylor, the chief art and book critic of The Boston Globe, has captured the way people from about 1860 to 1945 were drawn to Saranac Lake in northeastern New York State for health and recreation - and sometimes to die. Where Thomas Mann made fiction out of characters in a tuberculosis sanitarium on a Swiss mountain, Mr. Taylor records the lives of a score of men and women, most of them well known, who sought similar sanctuary in the Adirondack wilderness. Even though his portraits sometimes take him too far from his theme, he holds us with the richness of his story and the inherent drama of any struggle with an insidious disease. The central figure is Dr. Edward Livingston Trudeau, who, stricken by tuberculosis, came to Saranac Lake in desperation and stayed to establish a sanitarium that would in time attract patients from everywhere.
headline: WHAT BARTOK AND LEGS DIAMOND HAD IN COMMON

title: Judge Spencer Dissents
author: Henry Denker
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: JUDGE SPENCER DISSENTS. By Henry Denker. (Morrow, $17.95.) The action of this made-for-a-television-movie novel starts when the ''eccentric and unconventional'' Judge Harry Spencer hands down a legal opinion written in Spanish.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Louis Sullivan
author: Robert Twombly. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOUIS SULLIVAN His Life and Work. By Robert Twombly. Illustrated. 530 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $29.95.   THE life of the architect Louis Sullivan (1856-1924) was a curious combination of success and tragedy. One of the masters of the late 19th-century Chicago School of skyscraper architecture, Sullivan was acclaimed in his halcyon days as one of the world's greatest architectural designers. Yet by the time his life ended, he had slipped into poverty and neglect. In this long awaited biography, the historian Robert Twombly explores the architect's rise and fall with thoroughness and sensitivity.   Born in Boston of an Irish father and a Swiss mother, Sullivan experienced an apparently untroubled childhood in an artistically cultivated family. After secondary schooling in Boston, he studied for a year at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology before becoming a draftsman in the Philadelphia firm of Frank Furness. In 1873 he went to Chicago, where his parents had moved, and found work in the office of the fabled William Le Baron Jenney. Like most Chicago architects, Jenney's firm was engaged in rebuilding the city after the disastrous fire of 1871. In 1874 Sullivan decided to continue his education at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris, where he stayed for a year before returning to Chicago.
headline: GENIUS WAS NOT ENOUGH

title: The Killing Of Yesterday's Children
author: M. S. Power.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE KILLING OF YESTERDAY'S CHILDREN By M. S. Power. 264 pp. New York: Viking. $16.95.   SET in modern Belfast, this tale of ambush, intrigue and betrayal takes its title from the journals of its hero, Arthur Apple. That choice sets the tone for the entire tale, where the imaginary takes precedence over the all-too-real. Unlike other works in this vein, which, at their best and their worst, depend on meticulous descriptions - of weapons, places, personalities, actions - the narrative here seems to strive for streaks and blurs in a way reminiscent of Malcolm Lowry's ''Under the Volcano'' or, more aptly, Andrei Bely's hallucinatory rendering of assassination and patricide, ''Petersburg.''
headline: ONE BAD APPLE

title: The Aesthetic Experience
author: Jacques Maquet. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE AESTHETIC EXPERIENCE An Anthropologist Looks at the Visual Arts. By Jacques Maquet. Illustrated. 272 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $35. A LARGE and noble ambition informs ''The Aesthetic Experience'' by Jacques Maquet, a distinguished anthropologist, philosopher, art lover and sometime denizen of several Buddhist monasteries who teaches at the University of California, Los Angeles. It seeks to frame nothing less than a comparative science of esthetic experience. Mr. Maquet does not shilly-shally - he reckons there is a distinctively esthetic attitude, and he is happy to delineate its precise contours in broad, clear strokes.   For a while, the author teases the reader by appearing to dally with the theory, first adumbrated by the anthropologist Marcel Mauss, that the art world creates works of art by conferring a kind of social status on likely looking candidates, rather as the French Academy creates Immortals by electing them. But Mr. Maquet wisely resists this rather precious suggestion and plumps instead for the more challenging claim that artworks propose to engender a peculiar mode of consciousness in the onlooker.
headline: WHY THINGS LOOK GOOD

title: Nuclear Ethics
author: Joseph S Jr Nye
pull_quote: NUCLEAR ETHICS, by Joseph S. Nye Jr. 162 pages. Free Press/Macmillan. $14.95. THE main targets of Joseph S. Nye's ''Nuclear Ethics'' are people who purport to have the answers to the dilemmas of nuclear deterrence. He mistrusts the military strategists who see the hydrogen bomb as merely a variation on conventional weapons, but his heaviest attack is leveled at those he calls moral ''absolutists'' in the anti-nuclear camp.   Mr. Nye, who is the director of the Center for Science and International Affairs at Harvard University, attempts here to apply to the nuclear age the principles of ''just war'' theory that have offered guidance to moralists in other ages. His objective is clarity, which he obtains at some cost to felicity of expression. His language tends to be stiff and is sometimes simple to the point of simple-mindedness: ''Survival is not an absolute value, but it is important because it is a necessary condition for the enjoyment of other values.'' He has a weakness for unhelpful charts and lists. But in sum, he offers a lucid approach to a subject that has a way of attracting technological gobbledygook and puffy preachments.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Franklin Of Philadelphia
author: Esmond Wright
pull_quote: FRANKLIN OF PHILADELPHIA. By Esmond Wright. Illustrated. 404 pages. Harvard University Press. $25. BENJAMIN FRANKLIN sat for his portrait more often than any of his American contemporaries, and fashioned an even more durable image of himself in his writings. He was a man who thoroughly understood the arts of publicity - in fact it rather serves him right, you feel, that in 1956 the Poor Richard Club of Philadelphia should have marked his 250th anniversary by issuing a pamphlet entitled ''Benjamin Franklin, Patron Saint of Advertising.''   The image he presented was sturdy, humorous, stubbornly human. Among the illustrations to Esmond Wright's new biography are a pair of pictures, based on Fragonard, paying homage to ''le docteur Franklin'' in the best classical manner - one shows him being crowned by Liberty, the other takes its title from the sonorous tribute in which the French statesman Turgot summed up his achievements as scientist and American patriot: ''Eripuit caelo fulmen sceptrumque tyrannis'' (''He seized the lightning from the sky and the scepter from tyrants''). Both representations have their charm, both are unintentionally droll; of all the Founding Fathers, Franklin is the one whom it is hardest to cast in the guise of a demigod or a Roman hero, and the one who seems closest in spirit to the pragmatic, problem-solving, business-dominated America that didn't finally take shape until the following century.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The War
author: Marguerite Duras
pull_quote: THE WAR. A Memoir. By Marguerite Duras. 183 pages. Pantheon. $13.95.   WITH ''The Lover,'' published to critical acclaim and popular success in America last year, Marguerite Duras created a hypnotic story of love and death, set down in stylized, translucent prose. Though billed as a novel, ''The Lover'' actually looked back upon Miss Duras's own adolescence in French Indochina during the 30's; and in a sense, this memoir gives us a portrait of the author as that same heroine more than a decade later - grown to womanhood, living in war-ravaged France and working for the Resistance.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: A Perfect Spy
author: John Le Carre
pull_quote: A PERFECT SPY. John le Carre. 475 pages. Knopf. $18.95.   IN the charming yet ominous opening scene of John le Carre's latest novel of intrigue, ''A Perfect Spy,'' a man of ''powerful but stately'' build named Magnus Pym arrives ''in the small hours of a blustery October morning in a south Devon coastal town'' and makes his way to a Victorian boardinghouse marked ''No Vacancies.'' After hugging the old landlady, who is surprised but happy to see him -''Why Mr. Canterbury, it's you'' -and presenting her with a cashmere shawl from Harrods, he joins her for a cup of tea, explains that he'll be staying a while - ''I've a bit of heavy writing to do'' - and climbs the stairs to his room.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: A Father's Words
author: Richard Stern
pull_quote: A FATHER'S WORDS. By Richard Stern. 189 pages. Arbor House. $14.95.   THE father whose words keep coming at us in Richard Stern's new novel is Cy Riemer, a middle-aged intellectual, once of New York (where his own father ran a butcher shop on the Upper West Side), now of Chicago, where he has been editing and publishing a none too prosperous science newsletter for the past 30 years. For most of that time he was married to Agnes - an admirable wife and mother in her way, ''the great Smoother Over,'' but increasingly (in his eyes, at least) ''Mrs. Tedium Vitae,'' too boring to put up with.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Bigfoot Dreams
author: Francine Prose
pull_quote: BIGFOOT DREAMS. By Francine Prose. 280 pages. Pantheon. $16.95.   Vera, the heroine of Francine Prose's seventh novel, sees everything around her as a tabloid headline - it's kind of a nervous tic. A bum throws up in the lobby of her office, and she thinks ''Bridgeport Bandit Blows Lunch.'' A steam tunnel in Brooklyn makes a snakelike hissing noise, and she thinks ''Borough Boa Binds Brooklyn Baby.'' Rowdy kids disrupt her daughter's dance recital, and she thinks, ''Bandits Blast Baby Ballet.'' A friend tells her that she's dating a man who calls himself ''the Lizard,'' and she thinks ''I Married an Iguana.''
headline: Stranger Than Fiction

title: Games
author: Vera Cowie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GAMES. By Vera Cowie. (Doubleday, $16.95.) Under the best circumstances, it would be hard to take seriously a book whose chief male character answers to Brad Bradford.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Bess W Truman
author: Margaret Truman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BESS W. TRUMAN By Margaret Truman. Illustrated. 445 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $19.95.   MARGARET TRUMAN has written a refreshing, real and touching biography of her mother. Far from being a ''Mommy Dearest'' or even an uncomplimentary autobiographical novel like ''Home Front'' by Patti Davis, the daughter of President and Mrs. Reagan, ''Bess W. Truman'' is primarily about love.   Because Bess Truman always let her husband, Harry Truman, take center stage, she was well liked but little understood. She also had a tough act to follow - Eleanor Roosevelt. It was not Bess's style to take up a crusade that would become a trademark. In the public's view, the First Lady was gracious but in some ways grim. Revelations about her often had her taking her irrepressible husband to task for an epithet -spoken or written - that he had hurled in anger.
headline: THE WHITE HOUSE WASN'T LIKE HOME

title: The Wild Birds
author: Wendell Berry
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WILD BIRDS: Six Stories of the Port William Membership. By Wendell Berry. (North Point, $13.95.) Where could a country visitor to Prohibition-era Louisville, Ky., get his hands on a pint of whisky during a family emergency? Why would an elderly hill farmer deliberately venture so far down into a wooded gorge that he has to crawl out inch by inch at the risk of his life? How does a scrupulously honest small-town lawyer preserve what he knows is the true intention of a friend whose notion of a binding codicil is a ''slow, crooked legend'' in a tattered pocket notebook that says: ''Wheeler see the boy has his place''? These are some of the central considerations of Wendell Berry's six interconnected stories in this leisurely and engaging collection. In ''Thicker Than Liquor'' young Wheeler Catlett, just married and admitted to the bar, travels to Louisville to retrieve improvident Uncle Peach from his annual binge in the city. It is a hilarious and revealing odyssey through stockyards, train depots, fleabag hotels and hole-in-wall speak-easies. Later in his career, Wheeler has more complex commitments to honor. In a tale called ''It Wasn't Me,'' and again in the title story, his task is to unravel the underlying design of wills written to maintain the ''membership'' of a tight local network of relatives, friends and neighbors dedicated to one another and to their farms. Best known as an accomplished essayist, Mr. Berry sometimes slows down the narrative drive of his fiction with lengthy genealogies, anecdotes and explanations.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Another Marvelous Thing
author: Laurie Colwin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ANOTHER MARVELOUS THING By Laurie Colwin. 130 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.   MORE often than not, in real life the love affairs of one's friends are heartbreaking to watch, no matter where one's sympathies or loyalties may lie. When couples begin re-sorting themselves into ill-considered combinations, it is quite painful to watch the flailing about of the children and spouses left in their wake. But Laurie Colwin's new book chronicles a charmingly romantic love affair in which there are no dire consequences whatsoever. There are really no consequences at all other than the creation of a sweetly isolated slice of memory to be shared only by the two people involved.   ''Another Marvelous Thing'' is a collection of eight stories that tells the tale from beginning to end of an affair between a determinedly tough-minded young woman, Josephine (Billy) Delielle, and an unabashedly sentimental older man, Francis Clemens, called Frank only by his sharp-tongued and irreverent mistress.
headline: SWEET ADULTERY

title: Tracking Marco Polo
author: Tim Severin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TRACKING MARCO POLO. By Tim Severin. (Peter Bedrick Books, $15.95.) One of the most appealing kinds of travel literature is that in which ill-prepared but intrepid young men (or women) set off on peculiar vehicles in search of adventure in strange places.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Catholic
author: David Plante
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CATHOLIC By David Plante. 151 pp. New York: Atheneum. $11.95. WHERE I grew up, in North Cambridge, Mass., the local French-Canadian community produced boys who were ferocious ice hockey players while the girls - who usually attended the Francophone Catholic high school, Notre Dame, a feeder institution for the nuns - often seemed shy and pious. As a community, the French appeared somewhat claustral, rarely making a figure in local politics or involving themselves in such general cultural activities as offered, apart from sports.   All the more remarkable then that two of the most sophisticated American novelists of the generation coming of age in the late 1960's, both in their mid-40's, both at present and for some time domiciled in London, should have emerged from this very same French-Canadian population of southern New England. However, it is the sort of surprise that occurs in the American multiethnic, culturally diverse society with some regularity, and we should probably enjoy it without wondering too much about it.
headline: WHAT DANIEL TOLD ROBERTA ABOUT HENRY

title: Heroes And Hustlers, Hard Hats And Holy Men
author: Ze'ev Chafets.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HEROES AND HUSTLERS, HARD HATS AND HOLY MEN Inside the New Israel. By Ze'ev Chafets. 249 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $17.95.   THIS sharp-tongued book gives a voice to the new younger generation of Israelis. This generation, the author says, is convinced that the utopian dream of the founders of the state is dead and that Israel is now ''a real country with the flaws and weaknesses of real countries everywhere.'' The author and his generation do not believe in utopias. Of course, in Israel the flaws and weaknesses are seen as worse than normal; and hundreds of thousands of young people, battered by wars, economic troubles and claustrophobic anxieties, have deserted Israel in recent years. This book is the story of the majority who stayed behind, told by an American who joined them in what he loyally calls ''a good country in a bad neighborhood.''
headline: NEW KINDS OF PROMISE

title: Strangers In Their Own Land
author: Peter Sichrovsky
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STRANGERS IN THEIR OWN LAND: Young Jews in Germany and Austria Today. By Peter Sichrovsky. (Basic, $14.95.) Chancellor Helmut Kohl likes to describe himself to visitors as the first truly postwar West German leader, the implication being that his generation -teen-agers when the war ended - can no longer be held responsible for wartime atrocities, including the Holocaust.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Unbalanced Accounts
author: Kate Gallison
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: UNBALANCED ACCOUNTS. By Kate Gallison. (Little, Brown, $14.95.) An author treads on treacherous ground when trying to parody a style somewhat tongue-in-cheek to begin with.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Rain Or Shine
author: Cyra McFadden. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RAIN OR SHINE A Family Memoir. By Cyra McFadden. Illustrated. 178 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.   IT would be hard to imagine a more unexpected book by the author of the nimble and terrific comedy ''The Serial.'' ''Rain or Shine'' is a message in a bottle, sent with forlorn force to a dead father. That the father was the legendary voice of rodeo and therefore, to some extent, of town life in the West for 40 years does indeed seem to amplify the breadth and peculiarity of this tale of rodeo, open roads, motels and towns that, whether they border Canada or Mexico, are viewed as part of one region. In Miss McFadden's book, this is a remarkably unupholstered district where lives rise and fall, even respectable lives, with as much solitude as those of drifters.
headline: KING OF THE RODEO

title: Courting Fame
author: Karen Stabiner. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: COURTING FAME The Perilous Road to Women's Tennis Stardom. By Karen Stabiner. Illustrated. 254 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $16.95.   DEBBIE SPENCE is chubby, middle class and, at 16, America's top-ranked amateur tennis player in the 18-and-under girls' category. Unlike junior tennis prodigies such as Tracy Austin and Kathy Rinaldi, no agents pursue Miss Spence, no clothing or equipment companies contracts. She turns pro without fanfare shortly after her 17th birthday and earns $60,000 her first year on the tour - half of which is eaten up by expenses.
headline: LITTLE MATCH GIRL

title: The World Of Marcus Garvey
author: Judith Stein. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE WORLD OF MARCUS GARVEY Race and Class in Modern Society. By Judith Stein. Illustrated. 294 pp. Baton Rouge: Louisiana State University Press. $22.50.

MARCUS GARVEY occupies a central place in the pantheon of American black nationalist heroes. Garvey, who was born in Jamaica in 1887 and died in 1940, has been the subject of several biographies and his papers are being edited and published by Robert A. Hill, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles. Garvey, in short, is riding a new wave of popularity.
headline: THE BLACK MOSES AND HIS IMPERIAL DREAM

title: The Wrong Side Of The Tracks
author: Charles M. Haar and Daniel Wm. Fessler. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WRONG SIDE OF THE TRACKS A Revolutionary Rediscovery of the Common Law Tradition of Fairness in the Struggle Against Inequality. By Charles M. Haar and Daniel Wm. Fessler. Illustrated. 335 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.   IN 1971, Charles M. Haar and Daniel Wm. Fessler wrote a euphoric article, ''Beyond the Wrong Side of the Tracks,'' describing their victory in the case of Hawkins v. Town of Shaw, Miss. The case arose out of a class-action suit brought by poor black residents against the town under the Federal Civil Rights Act of 1964. The plaintiffs charged that municipal services were not equally provided and that the discrimination against them based on race and poverty was unconstitutional. The trial court dismissed the suit. The appellate court found that on one side of the town's tracks the population was predominantly white and middle class; on the other side of the tracks, the population was entirely black and predominantly poor. On the one side, white citizens received adequate public services, including water, sewage, electricity and paved streets. On the other, services were either totally lacking or grossly inadequate. The court held that the municipality had unconstitutionally denied the plaintiffs equal protection of the law.
headline: FOR EQUAL, IF SEPARATE, NEIGHBORHOODS

title: Half Laughing Half Crying
author: Malcolm Boyd
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HALF LAUGHING HALF CRYING. By Malcolm Boyd. (St. Martin's, $15.95.) The subtitle on this book's dust jacket - ''Songs for Myself'' - was obviously intended to relate Malcolm Boyd's items, prose or poetry, to the verse and personality of Walt Whitman.
