title: A Country Year
author: Sue Hubbell. Illustrations by Lauren Jarrett.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
A COUNTRY YEAR Living the Questions. By Sue Hubbell. Illustrations by Lauren Jarrett. 221 pp. New York: Random House. $17.95.

SUE HUBBELL lives in the Ozark Mountains, southern Missouri, on a farm, in an indigo bunting ghetto where she shares title to the land -more or less 100 acres - with coyotes, cardinals, turtles, buzzards, raccoons, skunks, opossums, dogs, cat, bobcat, copperheads, puff adders, brown recluse spiders, little brown bats, thousands of frogs and ''1,200,000 bee souls.'' She says she lives alone.
headline: COME MUDTIME, COME HONEYTIME

title: Dreaming In The Dust
author: Katherine Chrisman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: In DREAMING IN THE DUST: Restoring an Old House (Houghton Mifflin, $16.95), Katherine Chrisman shows us that the reality of replacing rickety handrails and redoing rooms is a difficult one. This two-year chronicle of one family's experience begins the day Mrs. Chrisman and her husband first visit the slightly tilting, 100-year-old Victorian mansion that will later become their home.
headline: OLD LAMPS FOR NEW, AND SO ON

title: Turning The Tide
author: Noam Chomsky.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TURNING THE TIDE U.S. Intervention in Central America and the Struggle for Peace. By Noam Chomsky. 298 pp. Boston: Sound End Press. Cloth, $30. Paper, $10.   TODAY, in the flush of the Reagan era, it is easy to forget America's debt to the New Left scholars and writers who have explored the dark side of American history, politics and foreign policy. This loosely knit band of thinkers has been much less successful, however, at turning its findings into a convincing wholesale indictment of current American public policies, much less a sound program for the future. The strengths and weaknesses of the New Left's approach are all showcased in ''Turning the Tide,'' a broadside against the United States record in Central America and around the world written by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology linguist and New Left stalwart Noam Chomsky.
headline: INSTITUTIONAL STRUCTURE BLUES

title: Night Kites
author: E. M. Kerr.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NIGHT KITES By E. M. Kerr. 216 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $11.50. (Ages 12 and up).   The Rudds' family life in an affluent Long Island community is the prototypical good life, American style. Dad stays in New York City during the week to run his prosperous brokerage firm, Mom stays at home and works at good causes and son Erick spends his days with high school, his all-American girlfriend Dill, and his lifelong best friend Jack, a good-natured jock who has fallen in love with his flamboyant, glitzy classmate Nicki.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Makers Of Modern Strategy
author: Gordon A Craig
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MAKERS OF MODERN STRATEGY From Machiavelli to the Nuclear Age. Edited by Peter Paret with Gordon A. Craig and Felix Gilbert. 941 pp. New Jersey: Princeton University Press. Cloth, $45. Paper, $12.95. WHO makes modern strategy? Have the theorists of war exercised much direct or indirect influence on the battlefield, or has their impact been overshadowed by that of the makers and wielders of weapons? Two hundred years ago, when resources were limited -both in numbers and kind - and goals no less so, and when the science of warfare was in its infancy, the answer to both these questions was fairly straightforward. Princes and generals were the big players in the war game; the most skillful practitioner won the laurels and intellectual application mattered little. Voltaire thought war a chancy business and regarded soldiering as one of a pair of bloody professions that had yet to come of age. ''The art of medicine, like that of war,'' he pronounced, ''is murderous and conjectural.''
headline: THE MEN IN THE SIZE 10 HELMETS

title: Selling Hitler
author: Robert Harris
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SELLING HITLER By Robert Harris. Illustrated. 402 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $18.95.   THE story of the bogus Hitler diaries is a study in obsessions. There is the obsession of Gerd Heidemann, the gullible, debt-ridden reporter for the West German magazine Stern who entered into an entranced relationship with living and dead adherents of the Third Reich and was apparently one of the last to grasp that his scoop of the century was one of its greatest hoaxes. There is Konrad Kujau, an ornately compulsive liar and small-time Nazi memorabilia dealer who went from forging minor Nazi documents and Hitler paintings to penning 60 volumes of Hitlerian banalities using cheap paper and a cramped gothic script that hardly anyone who vouched for the authenticity of the volumes could decipher. And there are the top managers of the publishing company of Gruner & Jahr, the owners of Stern, who ran the Hitler diary project as a cabal for several years without cutting in the professional journalists who might have saved them ignominy and $8.6 million.
headline: BROWN SHIRTS AND RED FACES

title: The Lifted Veil
author: George Eliot
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LIFTED VEIL By George Eliot. 91 pp. New York: Penguin Books/ Virago Press. Paper, $5.95.   GEORGE ELIOT didn't want this story (it is only a story, not a novel or even a novella) published separately. She was reluctant even to publish it under her name. Yet here it is, looking like a novel, published separately, and being offered as a serious work in its own right. Such are the vagaries of criticism, which since F. R. Leavis's writings in the 1940's has been resurrecting George Eliot (nee Marian Evans, 1819-1880) in spite of years of modernist contempt. Almost the least of George Eliot finds itself on the market.
headline: THE WIMP WHO KNEW TOO MUCH

title: Lionel Trilling And The Fate Of Cultural Criticism
author: Mark Krupnick
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LIONEL TRILLING AND THE FATE OF CULTURAL CRITICISM By Mark Krupnick. Illustrated. 207 pp. Evanston, Ill.: Northwestern University Press. Cloth, $21.95. Paper, $10.95. BY the time Lionel Trilling died in 1975 he no longer seemed the central figure in American intellectual life he had been in earlier decades.   Literary people who had been brought up on his classic essay collections of the 40's and 50's, particularly ''The Liberal Imagination'' and ''The Opposing Self,'' continued to recall affectionately his characteristic virtues, especially his lucidity and his extraordinary capacity to think against himself. But even his devout admirers knew that an emergent generation of critics and academicians nourished on the writings of European theorists like Roland Barthes and Walter Benjamin would find less and less to compel them in a writer more interested in establishing a respect for limits than in celebrating the joys of liberation. The Trilling who could speak without embarrassment of ''the rational intellect'' and reserve his highest praise for people who were ''decent'' and ''serious'' and committed to ''the best kind of truth'' was bound to seem a little quaint and out of touch to younger people trained to value fragmentation, experimentation, revolution and instability.
headline: TOO SMART TO BE CORRECT

title: The Price Of A Life
author: Tom Riley.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PRICE OF A LIFE One Woman's Death From Toxic Shock. By Tom Riley. 293 pp. Bethesda, Md.: Adler & Adler.  5.95.   THIS book is not so much about the death of a woman from toxic shock syndrome as it is about corporate greed, Government timidity and scientific compromise. It is also a warning that ''women will continue to die painful and terrorizing deaths'' from the tampon-related disease as long as big business puts profits before people and is unhampered by an apathetic Food and Drug Administration.
headline: CUSTOMERS AS VICTIMS

title: People Of Chance
author: John M Findlay
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PEOPLE OF CHANCE: Gambling in American Society from Jamestown to Las Vegas. By John M. Findlay. (Oxford University, $19.95.) John M. Findlay, who teaches history at Pennsylvania State University, sees the riverboat gambler and the Old West cardsharp as pioneers of the American frontier.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Vladimir The Russian Viking
author: Vladimir Volkoff
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: VLADIMIR THE RUSSIAN VIKING By Vladimir Volkoff. Illustrated. 384 pp. Woodstock, N.Y.: The Overlook Press. $18.95. THIS is an impressive biography of Vladimir I (960?-1015), the sainted ruler of Russia who brought Christianity to that pagan land by the force of his imperial power. Born the bastard son of Prince Svyatoslav of Kiev and a lady-in-waiting, he distinguished himself early for his uncommon wisdom, courage and guile in battle. He also distinguished himself for his prowess with women, and ''Vladimir the Russian Viking,'' by the novelist Vladimir Volkoff (''The Turn-Around'' and ''The Set-Up''), is to a great extent a lurching from gory battles to carnal sprees of gargantuan proportions.   Many of the earliest Russian princes were in fact Scandinavians, Vikings if you will, who moved east from their traditional homes to the land of the politically backward Slavs. Following the extensive river systems, they settled as far south as Kiev, and it is there that probable descendants of Rorik of Jutland ruled. Indeed, the name ''Rus'' itself is of Swedish origin, and in the ninth and 10th centuries its use referred to Norsemen rather than Slavs. These Norsemen, however, having settled in Slavic lands, eventually adopted the Slavic language, and the blood of these two vigorous peoples merged.
headline: PAGAN INTO SAINT

title: Handling Sin
author: Michael Malone
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HANDLING SIN By Michael Malone. 544 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $17.95.   OURS is a chaotic age, with few moral boundaries and fewer rules of social conduct; therefore, it's hard to be funny about everyday life.   Nature (or somebody) beats us to it. Even the sick, hurtful humor of the 1950's and 60's has assumed a ''so what?'' posture in our lives, where we find it daily in newspaper headlines and television broadcasts. To quote Molly's old line from radio's Fibber McGee and Molly, ''T'ain't funny, McGee.''
headline: FRUITCAKES IN THE CAROLINAS

title: Up Goes The Skyscraper!
author: Gail Gibbons
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: UP GOES THE SKYSCRAPER! Written and illustrated by Gail Gibbons. Unpaged. New York: Four Winds Press. $12.95. (Ages 5 to 8) UNLIKE ''The Little House,'' Virginia Lee Burton's 1943 classic story of a sweet little house that gets swallowed up by successive urban growth until it is finally rescued and moved back to the country where it can regain the bucolic countryside once again, Gail Gibbons's ''Up Goes the Skyscraper!'' presents a completely optimistic message about the development of the cityscape. There is no smog, no congestion, no suggestion that urban progress brings a loss of light and added density - only the exciting and unrelenting progress of a skyscraper being built just around anybody's corner.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: A Perfect Spy
author: John le Carre
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A PERFECT SPY By John le Carre. 475 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95.   FIRST, a small technical matter. Pains will be taken in this review to reveal nothing from the plot of ''A Perfect Spy'' that might take away from the pleasure of reading the book. Were I reading ''Great Expectations'' for the first time I would not, for instance, want some loudmouth to reveal the identity of the mysterious benefactor, thank you very much. Despite a few leaks about ''A Perfect Spy'' printed elsewhere, adherence to a literary equivalent of the Official Secrets Act seems appropriate because, whatever else it is, John le Carre's new book is a first-rate espionage novel, perhaps the best of his already impressive oeuvre. The author has gone to great lengths to create a tense balance between the narrative drive of the plot and the intelligent, artful richness of the style. I say tense because the book is a page-turner as well as a very satisfying read - you want to move fast so you can find out what will happen and you want to go slow so as to relish the writing. Out of respect for this remarkable achievement, discretion will prevail.
headline: SINS OF THE FATHER

title: Fifth Row Center
author: Benedict Nightingale
pull_quote: Fifth Row Center. By Benedict Nightingale. 346 pages. Times Books. $17.95. IN September 1983, Benedict   Nightingale, former theater critic for the New Statesman in London, came to New York to write about theater for The New York Times Arts and Leisure section. In June 1984, he left New York with the ''uneasy'' feeling that he'd ''never quite managed to find the New York theater.''
headline: Books: Offstage Journal

title: The Golden Gate
author: Vikram Seth
pull_quote: THE GOLDEN GATE. By Vikram Seth. 307 pages. Random House. $17.95.   JOHN is a young Silicon Valley executive, good-looking, hard-working and currently feeling lonesome, ''a linkless node.'' Janet Hayakawa is his former girlfriend - by day a sculptor, by night the drummer in a band ''well known and feared'' throughout San Francisco for the amount of noise it makes. Liz Dorati is a blond and comely lawyer whom John meets as the result of an advertisement Janet places in the personal columns on his behalf.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Golden Fire
author: Jonathan Fast
pull_quote: GOLDEN FIRE: A Novel of Ancient India.   By Jonathan Fast. 418 pages. Illustrated with map. Arbor House. $18.95.   THE ingredients of good historical fiction are all present in Jonathan Fast's ''Golden Fire,'' a story set in fourth-century India, about the rivalry of two half-brothers for the throne of the ancient kingdom of Magadha. Along with the exotic setting, we get colorful spectacle, plenty of authentic-sounding action, a wealth of information on the period and a story based on an incident deeply embedded in both Indian culture and the human imagination.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Private Life Of Axie Reed
author: John Knowles
pull_quote: THE PRIVATE LIFE OF AXIE REED.   By John Knowles. 214 pages. E. P. Dutton. $15.95.   IN ''A Separate Peace,'' his most famous novel, and in such lesser-known works as ''The Paragon'' and ''Morning in Antibes,'' John Knowles demonstrated a seemingly durable, if slender, talent for delineating the emotional geometry connecting members of certain rarefied worlds (prep school, Yale University, the Riviera) in deft, coolly-refined prose. ''The Private Life of Axie Reed'' also takes place against a backdrop of wealth and privilege -most of it is set in Southampton, L.I. - but it surprisingly evinces none of Mr. Knowles's usual gifts. The book is obvious, poorly written and perfunctory in both tone and execution. It reads like the sort of name-brand schlock novel one might buy at an airport, though it lacks the tarted-up sex scenes and epic length associated with that form.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Crabgrass Frontier
author: Kenneth T Jackson
pull_quote: CRABGRASS FRONTIER: The Suburbanization of the United States. By Kenneth T. Jackson. 396 pages. Illustrated. Oxford University Press. $21.95.   WHEN Kenneth T. Jackson's ''Crabgrass Frontier: The Suburbanization of the United States'' appeared last October, it was overlooked in this space. Superficially, it appeared that Professor Jackson's mourning over ''the loss of community'' that suburbanization has inflicted on America was an exercise that had been undertaken before. Moreover, his conclusion that the problems of suburban sprawl will eventually disappear of their own accord seemed shallowly optimistic.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Final Harvest: An American Tragedy
author: Andrew H Malcolm
pull_quote: FINAL HARVEST: An American Tragedy. By Andrew H. Malcolm. 320 pages. Times Books. $17.95. THIS is the dark side of Lake Wobegon. The victims and villains of ''Final Harvest'' are not stronger, smarter or above average. Like other Americans, they were swept up in the tornado of social and economic change in American agriculture. When the twister landed in homicidal fury on a 10-acre spread in southern Minnesota, the events provided Andrew Malcolm with a page 1 story in The New York Times and now this follow-up saga.   Mr. Malcolm's reporting skills transform the dreams and deeds of these people who seem so ordinary into an extraordinary American story. On Sept. 29, 1983, Jim Jenkins, a failed farmer, along with his son Steve, managed to entice the president of the Buffalo Ridge State Bank, Rudy Blythe Jr., and the bank's loan officer, Toby Thulin, onto a lonely farmhouse road. Mr. Jenkins murdered them both, then fled to Texas, where he walked into an open field, carefully took his eyeglasses off, put a shotgun into his mouth and pulled the trigger. His son later stood trial in Minnesota on accessory charges.
headline: Books: A Midwest Tale

title: William Shakespeare
author: Terry Eagleton
pull_quote: WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE. By Terry Eagleton. 114 pages. Basil Blackwell. $14.95. ANACHRONISMS abound in   Terry Eagleton's ''William Shakespeare,'' an example of revisionist analysis with a vengeance. Sometimes maddening, often turgid, always provocative, Mr. Eagleton does in print what directors regularly do on stage: change the century, stitch up new costumes, but preserve the story line and language. Miraculously, Shakespeare takes on all comers - including the author -and survives.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Selected Letters Of Charles Baudelaire
author: Rosemary Lloyd
pull_quote: SELECTED LETTERS OF CHARLES BAUDELAIRE. The Conquest of Solitude. Translated and Edited by Rosemary Lloyd. 268 pages. The University of Chicago Press. $24.95. The life of Charles Baudelaire quite blatantly contradicts Chesterton's famous observation that the artistic temperament is a disease afflicting amateurs. While his meticulously crafted work was strict, indeed almost classical in form, Baudelaire himself led a manic, disordered existence that sounds awfully like a grade-B movie parody of 19th-century bohemian life. Besides overindulgence in alcohol, opium and hashish, there were pernicious debts, syphilis -which resulted in assorted nervous disorders, dizzy spells and death at the age of 46 - noisy, fragmented relationships with women and incessant attacks of what the poet would call spleen. In fact, Baudelaire was almost always in a bad mood - either enraged by the horrors and indignities of the world around him, tormented by the loneliness of his self-inflicted solitude, or simply bored with himself and everyone around him.   ''What I do know,'' he wrote in 1863, ''is that I feel utterly disgusted with everything and particularly with all kinds of pleasure (that's no bad thing) and that the only feeling that convinces me I'm still alive is a vague desire for celebrity, vengeance, and fortune.''
headline: Books of The Times; A Poet's Complaints

title: On The Edge
author: Kenneth Koch
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ON THE EDGE By Kenneth Koch. 98 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. Cloth, $18.95. Penguin Books. Paper, $8.95. HURRICANE LAMP By Turner Cassity. 68 pp. Illinois: The University of Chicago Press. Cloth, $15. Paper, $6.95. ''IS there some way to ride to old age and to fame and acceptance,'' Kenneth Koch asks in a poem called ''The Art of Poetry,'' ''And pride in oneself and the knowledge society approves one / Without getting lousier and lousier and depleted of talent?'' He answers his question with an emphatic ''Yes,'' invoking the careers of Yeats and Sophocles as evidence.   I would be inclined to offer as supporting evidence the careers of John Ashbery, James Schuyler and Kenneth Koch. Mr. Koch's ''Selected Poems,'' published last year, reminded one of the remarkable diversity of his talent. He is the New York School's master of comedy, a fact that should not lead us to assume he is less serious than his colleagues. One might point out that he is also a poet of elegy, but, in any case, it should not be necessary to say that comedy itself is a serious business or that parody can result in major works of literature -witness the careers of Pope and Byron. Mr. Koch's ''Fresh Air'' is a ''Dunciad'' for our times, and his two book-length epics, ''Ko'' and ''The Duplications,'' pay homage to Byron's ''Don Juan.''
headline: A BRASH YANKEE AND A SOUTHERN DANDY

title: Tefuga
author: Peter Dickinson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TEFUGA Peter Dickinson. 256 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $14.95. IT isn't surprising that ''Tefuga,'' Peter Dickinson's amusing and elegantly structured tour de force about Nigeria, is very English. At the time of the recent PEN conference, Edward Hoagland pointed out on The New York Times's Op-Ed page the great deficiency of American writers in being so unconcerned about the rest of the world: ''I would guess that five times as many have been to Tuscany as to the whole continent of Africa; that more have visited Barcelona than all of South America. . . . Much of the extraordinary ignorance of most Amercans about what has been happening elsewhere . . . is due to the fact that their eyes and ears - their writers - have stayed home.''
headline: BEWARE THE UNDERDOG

title: High Hearts
author: Rita Mae Brown
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HIGH HEARTS. By Rita Mae Brown. (Bantam, $17.95.) This expansive novel of the Civil War contains what must surely be the first in-saddle marital squabble between two members of a Virginia cavalry regiment. Geneva Chatfield, tall for her 18 years and an excellent horsewoman, can't stand the idea of her new husband, Nash Hart, running off to the cavalry and leaving her back on the plantation. So she cuts off her hair, convinces her mother and her best slave friend, Di-Peachy, to stay quiet about it, and sneaks off to join up. Nash seems as much turned off as surprised by this, and that's where the conjugal discord begins. (She's a much better rider; he's in the Ashley Wilkes part, the unfortunate kind of soldier who quickly earns the nickname ''Piggy Woo.'') The war is also beginning, and here Rita Mae Brown's childhood fascination with Virginia battlefields -and her extensive research for this book - serve her well. She knows her horses, and the movements of a cavalry unit in the battles of First Manassas and the Seven Days are excitingly painted. Women did indeed dress as men and fight in the war, and this idea comes alive. While the story rides breathlessly in Geneva's saddle, all is well. But the author's intention is to render the larger story of women's roles in the war, to create, she says, a ''monument'' to them. After all the careful interweaving of feuding slaves, sainted mothers, gossiping Richmond hostesses and the inevitable gold-hearted madam, the sound of guns comes to seem a relief.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Deadwood
author: Pete Dexter
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
DEADWOOD By Pete Dexter. 365 pp. New York: Random House. $17.95.

PETE DEXTER'S wily, picaresque second novel is a spry yarn about the South Dakota town known, if at all, for Nuttall and Mann's Number 10 saloon and the August day in 1876 when Wild Bill Hickok was ''shot in the back by Jack McCall whilst holding aces and eights.''
headline: KILLED, HOLDING ACES AND EIGHTS

title: Main Street To Miracle Mile
author: Chester H. Liebs. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
MAIN STREET TO MIRACLE MILE American Roadside Architecture. By Chester H. Liebs. Illustrated. 259 pp. Boston: New York Graphic Society/ Little, Brown & Company. Cloth, $40. Paper, $19.95.

WRITERS on the architecture of the American roadside seem to choose a common literary style. Chester H. Liebs describes the experience of a highway:

''Holiday Inn, Ramada Inn, Texaco, Burger King, Wendy's, Arby's, Mobil. A quick glance in the mirror reveals the angry-looking grill of a tractor trailer pressing close behind . . . K Mart, Midas, 7-Eleven, Star Cafe, Nite-O-Rest Motel, Putt Putt Miniature Golf, Twilight Drive-In Theater. Gradually the bombardment of commercials diminishes, traffic picks up speed, and the road narrows to two lanes. A sense of relief takes over.''
headline: FROM STRIP TO SHINING STRIP

title: A History Of The Israeli Army
author: Ze'ev Schiff. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
A HISTORY OF THE ISRAELI ARMY #1874 to the Present. By Ze'ev Schiff. Illustrated. 274 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $25.

IT is virtually impossible to understand Israel or the Middle East without understanding Israel's military history and its security needs. There are many books that attempt to provide such a history, but Ze'ev Schiff's concise ''History of the Israeli Army'' is unquestionably the most successful. Although Mr. Schiff is an Israeli, and the military correspondent for the newspaper Ha'aretz, he writes with great objectivity and probes issues that most Israeli military writers prefer to dodge. Few Arab readers would be likely to quarrel with Mr. Schiff's facts or conclusions or with the balance he preserves in treating the long history of conflict between Israel and its Arab neighbors.

Mr. Schiff provides an excellent summary of the tensions between the Jewish settlers in Palestine and the Arab confrontation states. He makes it clear that, as he puts it, ''from the moment Jews decided to return to Palestine and cultivate their own lands the need to protect life and property became a major concern.'' He does not dodge the fact that Israel could come into existence only by conflict with the Arabs, but he provides a good picture of the forces that drove Jewish settlers to take up arms.
headline: CYCLES OF CONFLICT

title: The Rustle Of Language
author: Roland Barthes
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE RUSTLE OF LANGUAGE By Roland Barthes. Translated by Richard Howard. 373 pp. New York: Hill & Wang/Farrar Straus & Giroux. $25.

ONE reads Roland Barthes for the music of his rebellion and for phrases and insights, aphorisms, apercus, and for the portrait of Barthes, and for one's own memories of the era. One does not read him ''seriously.''

A professor of literary semiology at the College de France, Barthes began publishing in 1964 when he was already nearly 50. In the next 15 years he published 152 articles, 55 prefaces and contributions to miscellanies and 11 books (the figures are from his French editor's brief preface). That body of work amounts to an unofficial history of Sixties-isme, installments in a curious life-text documenting the most enthusiastic and profound (and most consequential) of all movements of thought and of feeling since the end of World War II.
headline: A TOTALITARIANISM OF PLEASURE

title: A Dangerous Place
author: Hugh Fleetwood
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A DANGEROUS PLACE By Hugh Fleetwood. 198 pp. North Pomfret, Vt.: Hamish Hamilton/ David & Charles. $22.50.   A MEXICAN journalist once recommended that, to write well about his country, a foreigner stay in Mexico less than two weeks or more than two years. In less than two weeks, his theory went, the outsider would not begin to see the complexities that make Mexico the unique society it is; and once he did, it would be two years before he could understand them.
headline: DOWN, MEXICO WAY

title: Making Europe Unconquerable
author: Gene Sharp.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MAKING EUROPE UNCONQUERABLE The Potential of Civilian-Based Deterrence and Defence. By Gene Sharp. 250 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Ballinger Publishing Company. Paper, $14.95.   IN the predawn of Aug. 21, 1968, Czechoslavakia was overwhelmed by a Soviet-led invasion meant to end a brave attempt to give Communism a less repressive face. Without warning, the country was engulfed by a half-million Warsaw Pact troops. Czechoslovak party leaders were kidnapped. Bewildered civilians awoke to confront tanks in city streets. Yet somehow, an improvised nonviolent resistance delayed the inescapable - the purge of the reformist Prague leadership - for nine months.
headline: PEOPLE POWER AND SUPERPOWERS

title: Lovers & Cohorts
author: Herbert Gold
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOVERS & COHORTS By Herbert Gold. 331 pp. New York: Donald I. Fine. $17.95.   THERE is no chronology offered for the 27 stories contained in ''Lovers & Cohorts,'' although in his introduction Herbert Gold tells us they were written over a 40-year period. He has had a prolific career, producing more than 20 other books, among them a collection called ''Love and Like,'' whose stunning title story is the most successful one included here. ''Love and Like'' is about the particular agonies of the husband in a failed marriage: the wrench of separation from his children, the relearning of bachelorhood and the ambivalence felt toward the recently beloved. ''But she was staring at him with enormous eyes turning black - as with anger, as with love - the pupils dilating and thick, congested hate squirting like black arterial blood from a deep wound over the thin face.'' This wife is unnamed, and not very lovable, but she's distinguished and redeemed by the protagonist's rueful compassion for her.
headline: FIRST TOGETHER, THEN APART

title: Final Harvest: An American Tragedy
author: Andrew H. Malcolm.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FINAL HARVEST An American Tragedy. By Andrew H. Malcolm. 320 pp. New York: Times Books. $17.95. WHEN the report of a double murder in rural Ruthton, Minn., broke in the press, readers responded viscerally. Although it has been over two years, the story has not been easy to forget, as the agricultural depression that began in the Midwest in 1981 has deepened and spread. Now, in ''Final Harvest,'' a native Midwesterner, Andrew H. Malcolm, has written a powerful and provocative account of the inexorable progression of events leading up to that cold, drizzly morning of Sept. 29, 1983, when Rudy Blythe, president of Ruthton's small Buffalo Ridge State Bank, and Toby Thulin, his chief loan officer, were called out to an abandoned, dilapidated 10-acre farm that the bank had earlier repossessed, where the farm's previous owner, James Jenkins, and his 18-year-old son, Steve, were waiting.
headline: DEATH AND THE FAMILY FARM

title: The Brave Little Toaster
author: Thomas Disch
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BRAVE LITTLE TOASTER By Thomas Disch. Illustrated by Karen Lee Schmidt. 78 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $10.95. (All ages) I'VE always had a ridiculous fantasy that book contracts were made on the basis of sudden bolts from the blue. A writer described an idea, an editor smacked his desk blotter and shouted ''I love it!'' and money changed hands. While that is not exactly the way it works in publishing, it is the way it works with ''The Brave Little Toaster.'' If you love the concept, you will love Thomas Disch's book. Quite simply, it is the story of five small appliances, living in a summer cottage, who set off to find their missing owner. It either tickles you or it doesn't.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: French Fascism
author: Robert Soucy. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FRENCH FASCISM The First Wave, 1924-1933. By Robert Soucy. Illustrated. 276 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $25. IN his new book on French fascism, Robert Soucy reminds us that, between the world wars, powerful conservative figures in France were not averse to supporting or associating with fascist movements in their efforts to defeat the left. Perhaps it is the memory of such associations that has led contemporary political analysts to watch with growing concern the emergence of Jean-Marie Le Pen's National Front, which won about 10 percent of the vote in last month's legislative elections, and to attend closely to Mr. Le Pen's flirtations with conservatives - the obvious candidates for political alliances with his ultranationalist organization.   Fascist movements in France posed a challenge when they emerged in the 1920's, not only to established parliamentary practices, but to the image historians and politicians had created of France as the most liberal nation in Europe. Of course, no fascist party ever captured the reins of government, as happened in Italy and Germany, but definably fascist organizations enlisted hundreds of thousands of followers and exercised significant influence at key moments during the interwar period. How did this happen?
headline: THE POLITICS OF VIRILITY

title: On Persephone's Island
author: Mary Taylor Simeti. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ON PERSEPHONE'S ISLAND A Sicilian Journal. By Mary Taylor Simeti. Illustrated. 329 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95.   THESE days, for a publisher to be caught without a subtitle is tantamount to indecent exposure.   Perhaps ''On Persephone's Island'' really did need that extra clue - ''A Sicilian Journal'' - to entice the reader of nonclassical bent. However, the book is much more than a daily record of happenings, and Mary Taylor Simeti is much, much more than an eager American junketing around with pen and wonder at the ready.
headline: WITH THE GODDESS IN HER SEASONS

title: The Soloist
author: Nicholas Christopher
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SOLOIST By Nicholas Christopher. 306 pp. New York: Viking. $17.95.   MUSIC has charms to soothe the savage critic, and concert-goers may well be entertained by ''The Soloist,'' Nicholas Christopher's first novel, if they do not take it as seriously as its author does. The hero is a self-absorbed piano virtuoso going through an early midlife crisis. Once a child prodigy accustomed to thunderous applause and glowing reviews, Max Randal suddenly observes, at the age of 29, that ''the music was dead off my fingers.'' His technical proficiency is still there, but the chemistry between him and his instrument is gone, along with ''that magical essential element'' of his performance - and he stops playing in public for four years.
headline: PLAY IT AGAIN, MAX

title: Mr Justice And Mrs Black
author: Hugo L Black
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MR. JUSTICE AND MRS. BLACK: The Memoirs of Hugo L. Black and Elizabeth Black. (Random House, $22.95.) Unfortunately for historians and students of the Supreme Court, Justice Hugo Black was 82 years old and only three years from death when he started writing his memoirs in 1968.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Iowa Baseball Confederacy
author: W. P. Kinsella.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE IOWA BASEBALL CONFEDERACY By W. P. Kinsella. 310 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $16.95.

W. P. KINSELLA loves fantasy. His characters do a lot of dreaming. His enjoyable first novel, ''Shoeless Joe,'' fantasized that baseball's great Joe Jackson was brought back to life and that J. D. Salinger was kidnapped to witness the glory of his return. In ''The Iowa Baseball Confederacy,'' Mr. Kinsella deals with the mystery of an amateur baseball league of the early 1900's of which there is absolutely no record, though the Chicago Cubs, the world champions of 1908, played an exhibition game against the league's all-stars.
headline: DID LEONARDO INVENT THE HOME RUN?

title: The Creation Of Patriarchy
author: Gerda Lerner
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE CREATION OF PATRIARCHY By Gerda Lerner. Illustrated. 318 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $21.95.

SINCE 1967 and the publication of her study on the abolitionist Grimke sisters, Gerda Lerner has established herself as one of the most distinguished historians of American women. Often collaborating with other scholars, she has worked to construct a theoretical framework for what she calls ''woman-oriented history.'' Exploiting the vast range of documents currently available, including women's diaries and letters, Mrs. Lerner's research has been dedicated to helping the American majority find its past.

Now Mrs. Lerner has turned her attention to the four millenniums preceding 400 B.C., in which, she claims, the patriarchal system emerged and became institutionalized. She links this development to changes in family relationships, in the economy, in government and in religion. She grafts Claude Levi-Strauss' theory that men's exchange of women is the principal cause of male dominance onto the evolutionary pattern developed by Friedrich Engels (which posits that the subordination of women resulted from the development of private property). However, Mrs. Lerner reverses Engels's cause and effect, arguing that women's reproductive power was the first private property amassed by men, and that domination over women provided the model for men's enslavement of other men.
headline: WHEN NO ONE WORE PANTS

title: Objects Of Desire
author: Adrian Forty
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: What manufactured goods look like is almost as important as what they do; that is the simplified argument of OBJECTS OF DESIRE. (Pantheon, $24.95), a book that looks at industrial design as the art of the 20th Century.
headline: APPEARANCE IS REALITY TOO

title: Family Resemblances
author: Lowry Pei
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FAMILY RESEMBLANCES By Lowry Pei. 264 pp. New York: Random House. $16.95.   FROM the opening paragraph of Lowry Pei's remarkable first novel, Karen's unmarried, 35-year-old Aunt Augusta cuts a formidable figure.   ''On the hottest days, my Aunt Augusta would drive around New Franklin with the windows rolled up, so that people would think the air conditioning still worked in the Buick she had inherited along with the house. Occasionally, when she got to an out-of-the-way place, she'd hit the four buttons by her left hand and all the windows would slide down at once to let in relief, but she may have done this only when I was with her, to accommodate my weakness and youth.'' Augusta's pride, her love of baseball and beer, her cowboy shirts and cutoff jeans, her insomnia, her eccentric regimen of gardening and hopeless repairs (the shutters, the summer house) will turn out to be bewildering enough for Karen, but what was really wrong with Augusta was ''the look in her eye, lonely and defiant. Fierce - but with no one to back her up, and she knew it.''
headline: HER DESIRE WON'T LET GO

title: Collaborators
author: Janet Kauffman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: COLLABORATORS By Janet Kauffman. 129 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.   ''MY mother has me surrounded. I must be hers.'' Janet Kauffman's stunning novel, ''Collaborators,'' explores the bonding between a mother and her young daughter. Andrea Doria, named for a sinking ship because her mother liked the sound of it, finds it impossible to recognize herself as separate from her mother. Her life is defined by her mother's actions, her mother's thoughts, even her mother's taste. After swimming in the ocean, her mother extends her arm and asks Andrea Doria to taste the salt. ''I feel on the tip of my tongue the trace of the hairs of her arm, a print of her sea-swimming arm. And I lick my own arm, which is a lifeless arm, not my own at all, not anyone's. I have nothing that isn't hers.''
headline: AT FIRST, MERGED WITH MOTHER

title: Death Of The Soul: From Descartes To The Computer
author: William Barrett
pull_quote: DEATH OF THE SOUL: From Descartes to the Computer. By William Barrett. 173 pages. Anchor Press and Doubleday. $16.95. WILLIAM BARRETT'S   ''Death of the Soul: From Descartes to the Computer'' is a defense of the uniqueness of the human spirit, obviously enough - an attempt to counteract what the author sees as Western culture's reductive attitude toward the ''spiritual status of the human person.'' It seems difficult to fault such an undertaking, for who would not prefer to believe that the human soul exists independent of matter, and that, like matter, it endures for eternity in one form or another?
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Collected Letters Of W B Yeats
author: William Butler Yeats
pull_quote: THE COLLECTED LETTERS OF W. B. YEATS. Volume I 1865-1895. Edited by John Kelly. Illustrated. 548 pages. Oxford University Press. $29.95. WHEN John Kelly and his colleagues set out to produce a collected edition of the letters of W. B. Yeats they envisaged it running to four volumes - something altogether more substantial than the one-volume edition (long out of print) that had appeared in 1954, 15 years after the poet's death. In fact they seriously underestimated the scope of their task; so many letters have come to light in the course of their researches that the project will now stretch to 12 volumes, if not more. In the first volume, which takes Yeats up to the age of 30, nearly half the letters are printed for the first time, and Mr. Kelly tells us that the proportion of new material will increase in every subsequent volume.   On the evidence so far the edition is clearly going to be an example of literary scholarship at its best. The notes are unusually detailed and informative without being allowed to clog the text; the editing is both tactful and thorough. And nobody is likely to dispute that a poet of Yeats's stature deserves the full scholarly treatment.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Good Mother
author: Sue Miller
pull_quote: THE GOOD MOTHER. By Sue Miller. 310 pages. Harper & Row. $17.95. A QUICK summary of the plot of ''The Good Mother'' tends to sound like a standard soap-opera scenario: woman gets divorced, woman meets new man in Laundromat, woman becomes involved in hot new romance, woman's 4-year-old daughter accuses woman's lover of sexual harassment, woman's ex-husband sues for custody, woman agonizes over relationship with lover, woman goes to court in effort to regain custody of daughter. In the course of these events, there are lots of steamy sex scenes, lots of melodramatic arguments and lots of painful goodbyes.   As it turns out, however, ''The Good Mother'' does not resemble a soap opera at all. Thanks to Sue Miller's gift for precise psychological detail, her sure sense of narrative and her simple compassion for ordinary lives, this powerful novel proves as subtle as it is dramatic, as durable - in its emotional afterlife - as it is instantly readable. In Anna, the ''good mother'' of her story, Mrs. Miller has created a hip, passionate narrator, a modern heroine, who suffers not from alienation and malaise - those staple afflictions of so many fictional characters today - but from a surfeit of feeling for two people in her life, her daughter and the man she loves.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Terrorism: How The West Can Win
author: Benjamin Netanyahu
pull_quote: TERRORISM: How the West Can Win.   Edited by Benjamin Netanyahu. 254 pages. Farrar Straus Giroux. $18.95.   THIS year marks the 10th anniversary of the Jonathan Institute, a research organization founded in memory of Jonathan Netanyahu, the Israeli officer who was killed leading the rescue mission at Entebbe. Among its other activities, the institute has organized two conferences on terrorism, in 1979 and again in 1984. ''Terrorism: How the West Can Win'' is a symposium based on the proceedings of the second of these gatherings. It is edited by Benjamin Netanyahu, Jonathan Netanyahu's brother; Mr. Netanyahu, who is at present the Israeli delegate to the United Nations, also contributes two papers himself, one of them - his concluding reflections -the most substantial in the book.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Story Of A Shipwrecked Sailor
author: Gabriel Garcia Marquez
pull_quote: THE STORY OF A SHIPWRECKED SAILOR. By Gabriel Garcia Marquez. Translated by Randolph Hogan. 106 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95.   The year was 1955, and Gabriel Garcia Marquez - who decades later would win the Nobel Prize for such works as ''One Hundred Years of Solitude,'' ''The Autumn of the Patriarch'' and ''In Evil Hour'' - was working as a newspaper reporter in Bogota, Colombia. One of his assignments that spring was to interview a sailor named Luis Alejandro Velasco - the sole survivor of a terrible accident at sea - and to ghostwrite an account of his ordeal as a 14-part series for the paper. The story, based on 120 hours of interviews, was first published in book form under Mr. Marquez's name in Spanish in 1970.
headline: Early Garcia Marquez

title: Among Birches
author: Rebecca Hill
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AMONG BIRCHES By Rebecca Hill. 323 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $17.95. REBECCA HILL'S first novel, ''Blue Rise,'' is prefaced by a quotation from Edna St. Vincent Millay that could apply to ''Among Birches'' as well: ''It's not true that life is one damn thing after another; life is the same damn thing over and over.'' In ''Blue Rise,'' Miss Hill's characters speak a near-perfect Deep Southern idiom. In this book, an otherwise engaging group lapses at times into an unfortunate psycho-rap. And while (as implied by her title) Miss Hill has this time left the Southern milieu behind, she has once more taken as her subject that nebulous, filamented and fragile relationship called marriage, that pairing in which man and woman become for each other lover, brother, sister, mother, father and friend. And she sets this alliance squarely where it belongs -within a context larger than the family of origin, the family of friends.
headline: THAT'S ASPERA TESTING THE ICE

title: Boston Boy
author: Nat Hentoff
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BOSTON BOY By Nat Hentoff. 176 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95. ''EATING a huge salami sandwich very slowly'' on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the day of fasting, while sitting on his family's porch overlooking the main street leading to the local synagogue, 12-year-old Nat Hentoff enjoyed not so much ''that awful sandwich'' as the experience of his first act of rebellion, and the knowledge of ''how it felt to be an outcast.'' Inquiring, exploring, observing, Mr. Hentoff grew up in the Boston of the 1930's and 40's, where he learned about prejudice first-hand from youthful gangs of ''Irishers,'' then learned how to fight anti-Semitism when he went to work at age 15 for a crusading young Irish Catholic editor, Frances Sweeney, to whom he dedicates this book.
headline: GROWING UP AT THE SAVOY

title: Veracruz
author: Rosalind Wright
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: VERACRUZ. By Rosalind Wright. (Harper & Row, $18.95.) Veracruz, Mexico's principal Caribbean port, provides a fabulous setting for this ambitious historical novel.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Kangaroo
author: Yuz Aleshkovsky
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: KANGAROO By Yuz Aleshkovsky. Translated by Tamara Glenny. 278 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $17.95. WITH due respect, and apologies, to Leonard Schapiro and Robert Conquest, the most searching histories about the Stalin era in the Soviet Union have been written by novelists like Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn and Arthur Koestler and memoirists like Nadezhda Mandelstam and Eugenia Ginzburg. In recent years, the novelist Vassily Aksyonov, Ginzburg's son, has joined this group, and now there is Yuz Aleshkovsky, another emigre from the Soviet Union to the United States, whose Schweikian novel ''Kangaroo'' - as obscene a book as I have read in years, and who can blame him? - uses laughter to reveal hell. The translation must have been unusually difficult, and is marvelously done by Tamara Glenny.   ''Kangaroo,'' which Mr. Aleshkovsky completed in 1975, will be called an absurdist satire by many, but anyone who has read Mandelstam and the others will know that it is in truth a realistic novel about the prison world that straddles the vast land between Leningrad and Vladivostok. It is the story of Fan Fanych, also known as Comrade Etcetera, pickpocket, scamp, madman and the only sane person other than his pal Kolya, whom he addresses throughout, to appear in the novel. The plot of ''Kangaroo'' is nothing less than the history of the Soviet Union from Lenin's time to the removal of Stalin from Lenin's tomb after Khrushchev's revelations about his regime in 1956.
headline: COMRADE ETCETERA'S REPORT FROM HELL

title: Tai-Pan
author: James Clavell
pull_quote: The history of American film and television production in China has been prickly from the start.   Not long after President Nixon made his breakthrough trip here in 1972, there was the well-known New York television producer who rejected a ''typical'' family chosen for her by the Chinese because one of the children had jug ears. And later -among other examples - there were a couple of ''Love Boat'' specials that featured American tourists behaving as though they had made their landfall in Miami rather than Peking.   Lately, the task of squaring American needs and Chinese sensibilities has fallen to the most ambitious project yet, a film version of James Clavell's epic novel ''Tai-pan.'' Nearly 20 years after Hollywood first considered the idea, the de Laurentiis Entertainment Group has committed $25 million to a big-screen version of Mr. Clavell's saga about the 19th-century swashbucklers who built commercial empires - and the colony of Hong Kong - out of the opium trade along the South China coast.
headline: 'TAI-PAN' CONTRASTS OLD CHINA AND NEW

title: Artists Against War And Fascism
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ARTISTS AGAINST WAR AND FASCISM Papers of the First American Artists' Congress. Introduction by Matthew Baigell and Julia Williams. Illustrated. 310 pp. New Brunswick, N.J.: Rutgers University Press. $23. THE American Artists' Congress, which came into existence in 1935 and for a few years enjoyed the support of a great many American artists, including some distinguished ones, was in certain respects a typical phenomenon of the 1930's. ''Artists Against War and Fascism,'' the book Matthew Baigell and Julia Williams have now produced on this organization and its activities, is similarly a typical product of the 1980's. For it is an entirely representative example of the kind of interest American academics nowadays take in the cultural history of the 30's. Mr. Baigell is a professor of art history at Rutgers University and Miss Williams is described as ''affiliated'' with Rutgers.
headline: THE BIG RED PAINTPOT

title: Hidden Agenda
author: Anna Porter
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HIDDEN AGENDA By Anna Porter. 322 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $14.95. I'M a sucker for opening sentences, and this book starts beautifully: ''No one likes to think about suicides. Least of all, the men who run the subways.'' There's a lead with legs. It would be tough for anyone to maintain that pace for the length of an entire novel, so I can't fault Anna Porter for seldom again quite reaching that Mach 1 of laconic hipness, but I do wish we'd been up there more often.
headline: EDITOR SAVES WORLD

title: Manhunt
author: Peter Maas
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MANHUNT By Peter Maas. 301 pp. New York: Random House. $17.95. ONE of Edwin P. Wilson's last acts as a free man, on a plane from the Dominican Republic carrying him to certain arrest in New York in June 1982, was to tear up a handwritten account of his assets and liabilities after 27 years working for the C.I.A., the Navy and himself in what might loosely be called the world of intelligence. An alert United States marshal on the plane recovered the list. From one point of view, you could say Mr. Wilson had done all right: his net worth was roughly $14 million. On the other hand, when the prosecutors were done with him he was in solitary confinement in a tough Federal prison, serving sentences totaling 52 years with no better than an outside chance of parole somewhere around the year 2000, when he would be 72.
headline: EASY MONEY AT THE C.I.A.

title: The Story Of A Shipwrecked Sailor
author: Gabriel Garcia Marquez
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE STORY OF A SHIPWRECKED SAILOR By Gabriel Garcia Marquez. Translated by Randolph Hogan. 106 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $13.95. THIS short piece of reportage was ghostwritten in 1955 by Gabriel Garcia Marquez for a young Colombian sailor named Luis Alejandro Velasco, who was swept off his destroyer into rough seas on a voyage from Mobile, Ala., to Cartagena, Colombia. He found himself next to a life raft and scrambled aboard. His four shipmates who fell into the sea at the same time were drowned as they struggled to join him. For 10 days Mr. Velasco drifted in the Caribbean Sea without food or fresh water. His spirits rose and fell like the waves around him - sinking as he heard the cries of his drowning friends, rising as he realized that he would soon be rescued, sinking again as airplanes flew overhead and their pilots failed to see him.
headline: THE HERO WHO LIVED TO REGRET IT

title: Major John Andre
author: Robert Mcconnell Hatch
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MAJOR JOHN ANDRE: A Gallant in Spy's Clothing. By Robert McConnell Hatch. (Houghton Mifflin, $17.95.) Before dawn on the morning of Sept. 22, 1780, in a cluster of fir trees atop a hill on the west bank of the Hudson, two men met to discuss a scheme that might have changed the outcome of the American Revolution. Brig. Gen. Benedict Arnold, hero of many a battle in the cause of independence, told Maj. John Andre, adjutant general to the British commander, that for $:20,000 he would arrange to turn over the crucial post at West Point and 3,000 rebel troops. Ten days later, in the village of Tappan, N.Y., a thousand American soldiers and residents of the neighborhood, all of them sad-faced and many of them weeping, watched as Andre died, gibbeted as a spy. Meanwhile, Arnold had slipped through the lines into British-held New York City to collect his reward. The story has been told many times before, but this is the first work to concentrate on Andre's career, making full use of the Andre family papers. Mr. Hatch presents a portrait of a most engaging young man -British-born of Huguenot ancestry, urbane, well traveled, possessing a flair for writing light verse and drawing. He was a charmer of women, among them the Philadelphia belle who became Mrs. Benedict Arnold. Mr. Hatch depicts him in a highly elegant style that frequently scants significant facts and names. To his credit, Mr. Hatch does make it clear that, although to his contemporaries, American as well as British, Andre was a tragic hero, his heroism had great flaws.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Good Mother
author: Sue Miller
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GOOD MOTHER By Sue Miller. 310 pp. New York:   Harper & Row. $17.95.   VERY once in a while, a first novelist rockets into the literary atmosphere with a novel so accomplished that it shatters the common assumption that for a writer to have mastery, he or she must serve a long, auspicious apprenticeship.   The novel arrives, all its parts gleaming, ticking, and we are filled with awe. However did the novice learn to build this thing? We marvel. But the question is beside the point, which is that the thing exists, has form, energy and power. This is the case with Sue Miller's ''Good Mother,'' the work of a writer who has thus far published only a handful of short stories.
headline: MEN, WOMEN AND CHILDREN FIRST

title: Women And Children Last
author: Ruth Sidel.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WOMEN AND CHILDREN LAST The Plight of Poor Women in Affluent America. By Ruth Sidel. 236 pp. New York: Viking. $16.95. RUTH SIDEL, a professor of sociology at Hunter College, has also been a psychiatric social worker whose clients were families trying to cope with serious economic and emotional problems. A major strength of ''Women and Children Last'' is that Mrs. Sidel draws deeply and equally from these two elements of her professional experience.   As a sociologist, she provides a concise, updated profile of the social and economic changes that have affected the lives of American women and children over the last 20 years, drawing on the best data available from the census and numerous surveys. But Mrs. Sidel knows from her firsthand contacts as a psychiatric social worker that such statistics present ''people with the tears washed off.'' Consequently, she has supplemented the statistical evidence with material from interviews she conducted with nearly 100 poor women and professionals who deal with the problems of the poor in 12 states. And it is the skillful weaving together of the statistics and the interviews that makes this book persuasive and moving.
headline: DESTITUTION IS JUST A DIVORCE AWAY

title: Ibm Vs. Japan
author: Robert Sobel.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IBM VS. JAPAN The Struggle for the Future. By Robert Sobel. 262 pp. New York: Stein & Day. $18.95. ROBERT SOBEL is a professor of business history at Hofstra University and a syndicated newspaper columnist with many books to his credit. In ''IBM vs. Japan,'' he discusses the looming battle for control of the computer industry between the International Business Machines Corporation and several Japanese competitors. He argues that the Japanese are going to have much more trouble in computers than they had in automobiles and consumer electronics, largely because of the strength of I.B.M. The computer giant has subdued all threats in the past and it is learning from the experience of the auto industry how to meet the Japanese challenge.
headline: THE CHIPS ARE DOWN

title: Stalin
author: Alex de Jonge
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STALIN. By Alex de Jonge. (William Morrow, $19.95.) Alex de Jonge, who teaches at Oxford University and has written biographies of Rasputin, Peter the Great, Dostoyevsky and Baudelaire, turns his considerable talents to a life of Stalin. Mr. de Jonge's work is largely one of synthesis, yet he draws so widely from the literature and blends his material so well that this eloquent, engrossing chronicle surpasses its genre and acquires a pulse and a point of view all its own.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Lisa And David Today
author: Theodore Isaac Rubin.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LISA AND DAVID TODAY Their Healing Journey From Childhood and Pain Into Love and Life. By Theodore Isaac Rubin. 146 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $14.95. IN case you didn't know, ''David and Lisa,'' that touching film of some 20 years ago about two deeply disturbed adolescents who reach out to each other, wasn't true. It was based on the novelette ''Lisa and David'' by Theodore Isaac Rubin, who has written a sequel. They are here published together as one novel.   The young David, overintellectual and compulsive, feared being touched; the childlike Lisa could speak only in rhymes, while her alter ego, Muriel, was speechless. In some ways Lisa and David were exaggerations of the sexual stereotypes of the early 1960's. Now Dr. Rubin brings us the stereotypes of the 80's as well.
headline: AFTER THERAPY, WHAT?

title: What Happened To Patrick's Dinosaurs?
author: Carol Carrick
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WHAT HAPPENED TO PATRICK'S DINOSAURS? By Carol Carrick. Illustrated by Donald Carrick. Unpaged. New York: Clarion Books/ Ticknor & Fields. $12.95. (Ages 5 to 9) WHY do kids love dinosaurs? They love how weird and scary they look and how much they resemble the monsters of their own imaginations. They love their fun-to-pronounce, crazy names and the number of different kinds and the fact that they lived (safely long ago) in a world that seems like a fantasy of outer space. When these things are combined, it becomes fun to imagine creatures so weird and so remote as part of your own world. It's also fun to imagine yourself as part of theirs.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Crabgrass Frontier
author: Kenneth T. Jackson. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CRABGRASS FRONTIER The Suburbanization of the United States. By Kenneth T. Jackson. Illustrated. 396 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $21.95. EVERYTHING conspired to make it happen: farmland was a drug on the market and crops were surplus commodities; gasoline was cheap and so were autos; Congress repeatedly subsidized interest rates for mortgages that encouraged an outward flow; cities accumulated blacks, debts and crime. And so it came about, the greatest exodus of city population into new suburbs in world history, coupled with the greatest expansion of suburban housing. From the end of World War II in 1945, this revolution ran unchecked until the oil embargo of 1973, and still continues in varying degrees into the 1980's. In ''Crabgrass Frontier,'' Kenneth T. Jackson, a professor of history at Columbia University, unfolds the comprehensive history of those forces behind the suburban boom and the implacable and virtually irresistible pressures that brought it about. (Whether it was inevitable is a question yet to be resolved.) He sets the stage for future revisionists with this ''essay,'' as he terms it - a history of authoritative scope, winner of the Francis Parkman Prize of the Society of American Historians and a Bancroft Prize in history, awarded by Columbia.
headline: JUST A COTTAGE SMALL BY A SHOPPING MALL

title: Plaintext
author: Nancy Mairs.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PLAINTEXT Essays. By Nancy Mairs. 154 pp. Tucson: The University of Arizona Press. $15.95. NANCY MAIRS has a way of dropping her bombshells casually, almost in passing.   ''A few years ago I almost died by my own hand, and when I woke from that disagreeable event, I recognized for the first time that I was fully and solely responsible for my existence,'' she writes at the beginning of her preface, and then goes on to express her gratitude to the people who helped her along the road to this book of essays; her suicide attempt is not discussed further there. Or, at the beginning of her first essay, ''On Having Adventures,'' she describes lunch with a friend in a California-style restaurant and goes on to remark, ''As an agoraphobe who, fifteen years ago, could not have crossed the sill of my apartment, and who even now suffers wayward attacks of breathlessness in movie theatres and lecture halls and even friends' homes, I find that conducting a relationship in a California-type restaurant contains a certain risk.'' The essay is not about agoraphobia.
headline: LIFE WITHOUT EUPHEMISMS

title: Nuclear Ethics
author: Joseph S. Nye Jr.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NUCLEAR ETHICS By Joseph S. Nye Jr. 162 pp. New York: The Free Press. $14.95. AT the height of the antinuclear emotions that gripped Western societies a few years ago this book could probably not have been written. That, after all, was the period in which nuclear weapons were debated in absolute terms by all and sundry, and each side - nuclear abolitionists and nuclear protagonists - pretended to possess the absolute truth. I remember a sense of profound uneasiness when, during weekend shopping in London's Hampstead Village, a woman next to me in a greengrocer's shop held a toddler on her arm who wore a big button on his little body inscribed ''Babies Against the Bomb.''   Yet perhaps it is because of the experience of those agitated years that Joseph S. Nye Jr. has written ''Nuclear Ethics.'' He has produced not only an excellent treatise on moral philosophy addressed to the complex issues of nuclear war, but also an important introduction to these very issues. Mr. Nye, an internationally respected Harvard professor of government and a Deputy Under Secretary of State during part of the Carter Administration involved in making nonproliferation policies, writes with insight and clarity. He shows himself to be an eminently reasonable man, a voice for balance and proportion.
headline: NEITHER HAWK NOR DOVE

title: Prodigal Sons
author: Alexander Bloom.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PRODIGAL SONS The New York Intellectuals & Their World. By Alexander Bloom. 461 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $24.95. READING this book I was continually thinking of a moment - perhaps a critical moment, though Alexander Bloom makes nothing of it -in the summer of 1965. Dozens of people had been flown in to New Brunswick, N.J., from all over, their tickets paid for by some vaguely benign foundation, to take part in a Partisan Review conference on the Future. Happy as we all were to attend this grand affair, few of us visiting firemen made much of a mark on the proceedings, which were dominated by a large contingent of the very persons Mr. Bloom has been studying, the New York Intellectuals; full of polemical vigor, contemptuously anti-Socialist, they allowed no consideration of courtesy to old or new acquaintances to qualify their freedom of expression.

There are the personal confrontations, complete with tears: ''The President's eyes were moist,'' writes Mr. Stockman at the opening of his prologue. ''It was unmistakable -they glistened.'' title: Talking Animals And Other People
author: Shamus Culhane
pull_quote: TALKING ANIMALS AND OTHER PEOPLE. By Shamus Culhane. Illustrated. 463 pages. St. Martin's Press. $24.95. SHAMUS CULHANE has had a long and varied career in animated movies, dating from 1924, when he was only 15. His first job consisted of punching holes in drawing paper, but by 1930 he had graduated to the ranks of the animators, developing his skills under Max Fleischer in the heyday of the Fleischer Studio's celebrated sexpot, Betty Boop. Subsequently he went on to work for Walt Disney and other leading studios, and also made his mark as a pioneer of television animation.   The filmography at the end of his memoirs, ''Talking Animals and Other People,'' is that of a man who has lived in the thick of his profession for nearly 60 years. It lists more than a hundred films on which he worked as animator, producer or director; along with some undisputed classics - ''Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs,'' ''Pinocchio'' - they include such less well-remembered items as ''Dippy Diplomat'' and ''Abou Ben Boogie,'' ''Technocracked'' and ''Mousie Come Home.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Heart's Desire
author: Gwyneth Cravens
pull_quote: HEART'S DESIRE. By Gwyneth Cravens. 259 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95. WHEN we first meet the three heroines of ''Heart's Desire,'' we're inclined to write them off, a bit condescendingly, as familiar, and not all that interesting types. There's Judy, Tommy Hammond's pert, devoted wife, who obediently cooks and cleans house for her handsome hubby and worries that she's unworthy of his attentions. Then there's Effie, Tommy's formidable mother, a spunky, ''can-do'' woman of the New West - you can picture her being played by an older Sally Field in the movie version of the novel - who's fond of dispensing chirpy, greeting-card encouragements like ''New York in the fall must be the most inspiring fantastic place for you to achieve every possible success in every way.'' And finally, there's Effie's daughter Nancy, a sweet, somewhat muddled girl, who comes across on first meeting as a variation on your standard-issue American teen-ager - narcissistic, insecure and obsessed with science fiction.

title: I'll Take Manhattan
author: Judith Krantz
pull_quote: I'LL TAKE MANHATTAN. By Judith Krantz. 437 pages. Crown. $18.95. THE thing to do is to be positive, to look for the good in Judith Krantz's new novel, ''I'll Take Manhattan.'' Don't go searching for blemishes. Never mind that on page 3 beautiful Maxime Emma Amberville is described as moving ''with the tadpole agility of the born New Yorker'' as ''she slapped her shoulder bag down on a customs table and looked around impatiently for an inspector.'' It makes perfectly good sense if you don't stop to think about it.   Never mind the implausibility of the 1945 scene in which Maxi Amberville's father demands a copy-boy job at The New York Times and is turned down by ''the Times receptionist,'' who suppresses ''a giggle'' when the applicant expresses his disappointment with an obscenity. I'm sure Judith Krantz has a couple of believable things to say about the New York publishing industry, providing you don't examine them too closely.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Selected Poems
author: Robert Bly
pull_quote: SELECTED POEMS. By Robert Bly. 213 pages. Harper & Row. Cloth, $18.95; Paper, $8.95. More than two decades have passed since the limpid, haiku-like poems of Robert Bly's first collection, ''Silence in the Snowy Fields'' (1963), appeared. In the ensuing years, the poet has changed directions several times - eschewing the realm of private emotions for noisy, public pronouncements on the Vietnam War in ''The Light Around the Body'' (1967) and ''The Teeth Mother Naked At Last'' (1970), and returning to a more pastoral mode in works like ''The Morning Glory'' (1975) and ''This Body Is Made of Camphor and Gopherwood'' (1977). What has remained constant in his work, as this new selection demonstrates, is Mr. Bly's interest in man's relationship with nature, and his commitment to an idiom built upon simplified diction and the free associative processes of the unconscious mind.
headline: Books of The Times; Man and Nature

title: A Man Of Letters
author: V. S. Pritchett.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A MAN OF LETTERS Selected Essays. By V. S. Pritchett. 305 pp. New York: Random House. $19.95.   ''I HAVE done, given my circumstances and my character, what I have been able to do and I have enjoyed it.'' So runs the concluding sentence to V. S. Pritchett's 1972 memoir, ''Midnight Oil,'' in which he declared himself ''an old man, though no one would think of telling me I am.'' A good thing no one thought to tell him that, since in the ensuing 14 years (and in addition to becoming Sir Victor Pritchett) he has continued to do what he has been able to do so well, and with no visible abatement of enjoyment. ''Collected Stories'' (1982) and ''More Collected Stories'' (1983); a biography of Turgenev (1977); and two collections of essays, ''The Myth Makers'' (1979) and ''The Tale Bearers'' (1980) - these are a few of his recent productions, the fruits of refusing to take it easy. Now comes this selection from his literary essays, the earliest of them dating from 1939, the most recent from 1984.
headline: CAN'T STOP NOW, NO TIME FOR THEORY

title: Fuel-Injected Dreams
author: James Robert Baker
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: Madison Bell: Madison Bell Is the Author of the Novelsthe Washington Square Ensemble'' and Waiting For the End of the World
pull_quote: FUEL-INJECTED DREAMS By James Robert Baker. 323 pp. New York: Plume/ New American Library. Paper, $5.95. E. P. Dutton. Cloth, $15.95. ''THIS is Scott Cochran, macho superstud, male feminist, and untreatable schizophrenic. You're listening to Radio Noir.'' ''Fuel-Injected Dreams'' takes off with the voice of its manic D.J. narrator, a voice James Robert Baker seems to capture very well. Cochran is a middle-aged casualty of several broken marriages, a loner living in a dumpy Los Angeles motel, who pours all his energy into a late-night radio slot that he fills with most of the mid-60's pop groups that ever existed and a few more that Mr. Baker has invented, his sets cemented together with a fast, self-parodying patter that includes the occasional visionary, apocalyptic gleam. ''I wanna get on a death trip'' is a line Cochran throws away casually on the airwaves, but soon enough he gets his wish.   ''In a megalopolis of psychopaths,'' says Cochran, ''a few were bound to crawl out of the fiberboard occasionally,'' and the one that crawls toward Cochran is Dennis Contrelle, a production whiz from the Phil Spector era who's lived in hermetic seclusion since the decline of his career at the end of the 60's. Offended by one of Cochran's cracks, he calls the station to deliver murky threats, and the next day apologizes. The queasy relationship that develops out of this encounter awakens memories in Cochran that are more than simply nostalgic.
headline: PSYCHOPATHORAMA

title: Mayday
author: Michael R. Beschloss. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
MAYDAY Eisenhower, Khrushchev and the U-2 Affair. By Michael R. Beschloss. Illustrated. 494 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $19.95.

ON May Day, 1960, an American U-2 reconnaissance plane was shot down over Sverdlovsk, in the Soviet Union, at a height of probably over 70,000 feet, on a secret intelligence flight from Peshawar, Pakistan, to Bodo, Norway. This incident becomes the centerpiece of a fascinating reconstruction of the American U-2 program, of relations and attitudes in the intelligence community, of politics and personalities around the Eisenhower White House, of the fit (or lack thereof) between American diplomacy and intelligence, of Soviet-American relations in the Eisenhower-Khrushchev years and a good deal more. Michael R. Beschloss, a historian at the Smithsonian Institution and the author of a well-received book, ''Kennedy and Roosevelt,'' has done an excellent job of asking good questions, digging for answers wherever he could and making his way through the shoals of complexity and contradiction.
headline: THE SUMMIT THAT FELL FROM THE SKY

title: Out Of Work
author: Alexander Keyssar. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: Alice Kessler-Harris: Alice Kessler-Harris, Who Teaches History At Hofstra University, Is the Author ofOut To Work: A History of Wage-Earning Women In the United States.''
pull_quote: OUT OF WORK The First Century of Unemployment in Massachusetts. By Alexander Keyssar. Illustrated. 469 pp. New York: Cambridge University Press. Cloth, $49.50. Paper, $14.95. RECENT headlines tell us that Texas now has an unemployment rate of over 15 percent. A few years ago, workers fled Detroit and the Northeast squirmed under unemployment rates that climbed to 25 percent in some urban areas and single-industry towns. Next year, high unemployment could even threaten Silicon Valley. This is the 1980's, but it could well be any decade of the last 15. For as Alexander Keyssar demonstrates in this fine book, though the policies with which we confront it have changed, the fact of unemployment has remained a feature of American life from the early industrial age.   ''Out of Work'' makes two important points about unemployment that extend the boundaries of the book's narrow framework - a study of unemployment in Massachusetts from the early 19th century to the 1930's. It demonstrates the tenacity of unemployment in the lives of working people, and it sustains the notion that job loss is an inevitable consequence of a free market economy. Both themes are woven into a narrative that finds more continuity than change between 1830 and 1930.
headline: LAID OFF IN GOOD TIMES AND BAD

title: Around The Day In Eighty Worlds
author: Julio Cortazar
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AROUND THE DAY IN EIGHTY WORLDS By Julio Cortazar. Translated by Thomas Christensen. Illustrated. 288 pp. San Francisco: North Point Press. $22.50.   FOR 20 bonus points and an extra turn around the game board, what do the following have in common: Marcel Duchamp and Louis Armstrong, Novalis and Jack the Ripper, graphology and speleology, Calcutta and St. Tropez, jaguars and chameleons and crocodiles and coleoptera and a cat named Theodor W. Adorno, a disembodied hand called Dg and a mad artist named Wolfi, cycling and furniture and eroticism, luggage and shadows and siestas, prowlings in European foreign ministries and strolls through the Auvergne, spheres and polygons and chests of drawers with magical properties, Jose Lezama Lima and Jelly Roll Morton? Stuck on square one or whizzing past ''go,'' they're all occasions for a diverting roll of the dice by Julio Cortazar. With this miscellany that's as challenging as an infinite exercise in connect-the-dots, a color-by-number landscape a la Salvador Dali, the late Argentine fabulist constructs yet another prototype of literature as schoolboy's amusement. This time his chosen avocation is not hopscotch or a model kit but a version of Trivial Pursuit in which profundity is the grand prize and the winner is the first player to disregard the rules altogether.

title: Hiroshima Joe
author: Martin Booth
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HIROSHIMA JOE By Martin Booth. 441 pp. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. $17.95. WHEN we meet the World War II veteran Joe   Sandingham in the spring of 1952, he is sickly and ''touched in the head,'' an unsightly fixture at a Hong Kong hotel, where the manager is wearying of his patronage. Periodically, Sandingham has to pay his overdue rent, and then he scavenges, picks pockets or runs errands for a Chinese crime lord. When he needs love, he turns to Lucy the prostitute, but that isn't satisfying, partly because he is addicted to opium and partly because he is homosexual. For years he hasn't had sufficient luck or resolve to find a male lover. His one proud habit is to pay the full fare for the Star Ferry from Hong Kong to Kowloon, which allows him to sit on the upper deck, as most Europeans do, rather than on the lower deck with the Chinese.
