title: I'll Take Manhattan
author: Judith Krantz
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: I'LL TAKE MANHATTAN By Judith Krantz. 437 pp. New York: Crown Publishers. $18.95.   JUDITH KRANTZ sounds tired, or as she might put it: exhausted - supremely, profoundly, uniquely exhausted. Her new novel, ''I'll Take Manhattan,'' follows the formula she devised for ''Scruples,'' ''Princess Daisy'' and ''Mistral's Daughter'' - lots of rich people, lots of designer clothes and a measured amount of brisk, clinical sex - but by now she seems to be having a hard time convincing even herself that she gives a damn. Very likely it was the setting that wore her out this time. ''Manhattan'' takes place in the magazine publishing world. And although God knows there's hardly a more glamorous profession, what with word processors glowing in every office and devastatingly attractive young editors poised here and there along the corridors, Mrs. Krantz does have to work harder than usual to get her characters popping in and out of swimming pools, yachts and casinos. Luckily, the heroine lives in the Trump Tower and does most of her editorial brainstorming in bed, ''pulling up the white mink throw'' so ''her knees made a little fur desk.''
headline: FROM THE LITTLE FUR DESK OF MAXI AMBERVILLE

title: A Concrete Atlantis
author: Reyner Banham. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: John Coolidge: John Coolidge, Professor of Fine Arts Emeritus At Harvard University, Is the Author of the Forthcoming Book, the Architectural Design of Some Twentieth Century Art Museums.''
pull_quote: A CONCRETE ATLANTIS U.S. Industrial Building and European Modern Architecture. By Reyner Banham. Illustrated. 266 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: The MIT Press. $25.   REYNER BANHAM, born in Britain and trained as an engineer, has taught the history of architecture at several American universities. He now teaches at the University of California, Santa Cruz. His primary interest has been the International style, which, as he has written, ''was intended to be and did indeed become the style of our times.'' He has concerned himself with what he considers overlooked or undervalued aspects of that style; every book by him is a report of some welcome discovery or a challenge to the reader to disagree with the author.   ''The Concrete Atlantis'' maintains, in a some-what discursive introduction, that there is ''a causal, cultural and conscious connection'' between such early masterworks of explicit modernism as Gropius's Fagus factory in Germany or Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye near Paris and certain American factories and grain elevators. Most of the latter were built between 1900 and 1920 - of reinforced concrete, as this book's title suggests.

title: More Fun With Dick And Jane
author: Marc Gallant
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: Maggie Paley: Maggie Paley Is the Author of the Recently Published NovelBan Manner.''
pull_quote: MORE FUN WITH DICK AND JANE Written and illustrated by Marc Gregory Gallant. 70 pp. New York: Penguin. Paper, $5.95. LEARNING to read is a thrilling experience. Once we can re-create in our own minds a story someone else wrote down at another time in another place, we can begin to control the information we take in. And yet our experience is limited at the time most of us learn; it's presumed we're fragile, and ignorant about meaning and nuance, and this is probably why the people who write the texts from which we learn make them so bland.   For example, these were among the first sentences many Americans who entered first grade between 1931 and 1965 were required to read in school: '' 'Help, help,' said Dick. / 'Come, Father, Come. / Come and help.' / 'Look, look,' said Sally. / 'See it go up. / See Spot run. / This is fun for Spot.' / 'Oh, Dick,' said Jane. / 'Spot can help you. / Funny little Spot can help.' '' They conclude a very short story, about a dog (Spot) who played with his master's (Dick's) kite, in the Scott Foresman & Company primer called ''Fun With Dick and Jane.''
headline: LOOK AT FATHER, HE IS GROSSED OUT.

title: My Beautiful Lanudrette And The Rainbow Sign
author: Hanif Kureishi
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MY BEAUTIFUL LAUNDRETTE AND THE RAINBOW SIGN By Hanif Kureishi. 111 pp. Boston: Faber & Faber. Paper, $8.95.   ''FROM the start I tried to deny my Pakistani self,'' writes the half English, half Pakistani playwright Hanif Kureishi at the start of ''The Rainbow Sign,'' the rich autobiographical essay published here with his script for the Stephen Frears film ''My Beautiful Laundrette.'' ''It was a curse and I wanted to be rid of it. I wanted to be like everyone else'' - particularly when, he says, he saw his school friends joining the marches of Enoch Powell's ''Paki-bashing'' National Front in the late 1960's. ''The Rainbow Sign'' describes the process through which Mr. Kureishi learned that he could never be like everyone else, in his mother's England, where he was born, or Pakistan from which his father had emigrated. ''We are Pakistanis,'' he's told on a visit to his father's family in Karachi, ''but you, you will always be a Paki.''
headline: HE COULD NEVER BE LIKE EVERYONE ELSE

title: Camping Out
author: Eleanor Clark
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
CAMPING OUT By Eleanor Clark. 223 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $16.95. SOME of my friends and I first came to Eleanor Clark's ''Rome and a Villa'' because our mothers pressed it on us with eager hands. Those aging sedentary housewives who had traveled largely in their imagination took vicarious joy in its opulence of experience and learning. For once we listened to them, and read a book they loved. Having begun, who could resist it? We too were enamored of its style and its stylishness, and have cherished Miss Clark ever since for the immaculate writer and intuitive witness that she is.

Witnessing: woman's role and art. What would we - all of us - lose if women succeeded in entering the arena as the equals of men, at the expense of that witnessing? From Jane Austen and Emily Bronte to Emily Dickinson and Marianne Moore, the view from the sidelines has produced a precious hoard. But Eleanor Clark is still witnessing, and recording the decline and fall of the West with a heated energy beyond despair.
headline: TWO WOMEN, TERRIFIED

title: Heart Of The Country
author: Greg Matthews
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: Donovan Fitzpatrick: Donovan Fitzpatrick Is A Contributing Editor of M.d. Magazine
pull_quote: HEART OF THE COUNTRY By Greg Matthews. 532 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $17.95.    Think of the Marquis de Sade writing a history of the West and you have an approximation of ''Heart of the Country,'' a big book about goings-on in the village of Valley Forge, Kan., in the last half of the 19th century. One of the few good guys is Joe Cobden, offspring of an Indian woman and a white ne'er-do-well. Blessed with a quick mind, Joe is a kind of prairie intellectual and iconoclast. He is also bitter because fate dealt him a low blow - he is deformed and ugly, and thus most people recoil from him. Unhappy, longing for affection, he becomes variously a bouncer in a bordello, a buffalo hunter, a wood chopper, a carver of cigar-store wooden Indians.
headline: BLEEDING KANSAS

title: The Flying Change
author: Henry Taylor
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE FLYING CHANGE By Henry Taylor. 55 pp. Baton Rouge: Louisiana State University Press. Cloth, $13.95. Paper, $6.95. SAINTS AND STRANGERS By Andrew Hudgins. 82 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. Cloth, $13.95. Paper, $6.95. PLACES/EVERYONE By Jim Daniels. 80 pp. Madison: The University of Wisconsin Press. Cloth, $12.50. Paper, $7.95. IN ''The Flying Change,'' which has just been given the Pulitzer Prize for poetry, Henry Taylor writes the poems of a country squire. Most of the time this country life is all too settled, predictable and complacent; the squire, after all, enjoys all the pleasures of a farmer's life with none of the risks. Indeed, the gentleman farmer may pursue pleasures for which the real farmer has neither time nor inclination, as in ''Evening at Wolf Trap'': Once, outside the theater's weathering walls, we sat on the grass with wine and cheese, French bread and fruit; and as we ate, our talk was sometimes interrupted by a small crowd farther down the hill, throwing a frisbee.   Happily, Mr. Taylor is aware of the danger of such inherently unintense, unpoetic material to his work, and that is why he calls his book ''The Flying Change.'' In the title poem he explains that this equestrian term refers to the changing of a horse's lead in mid-jump; as poet, it is his desire to ''hold myself immobile in bright air, / sustained in time astride the flying change.''
headline: LANDSCAPES AND STILL LIVES

title: The American Profile Poster
author: Stephen J Rose
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE AMERICAN PROFILE POSTER Who Owns What, Who Makes How Much, Who Works Where, and Who Lives With Whom. By Stephen J. Rose. Poster designed by Dennis Livingston and Kathryn Shagas. Illustrated. 37 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. Paper, $8.95.   THOUGH an economist, Stephen J. Rose is a man of imagination. In 1978, he, along with Dennis Livingston, designed a poster, ''Social Stratification in the U.S.,'' that graphically portrayed American incomes, occupations, family arrangements and racial composition. Instead of nodding over eye-glazing statistics, all a curious citizen needed to do was tape the gaily colored poster to a convenient wall and look carefully at the way the symbols - tiny human figures - distributed themselves as officially poor (according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics), struggling along on low budgets, keeping up appearances on medium budgets or living it up on high ones. The poster's ingenious design sorted out the varying fortunes of men and women; white, black and Hispanic Americans; and professionals, managers, clerks and blue-collar workers.

title: The Sardine Deception

BIG BANG means different things to different people, but to most cosmologists it means The Beginning. And because the interests of cosmologists and ordinary people coincide in curiosity about the origin of the physical universe, John Gribbin's ''In Search of the Big Bang'' (his 31st book ) will be widely read. It should be. It is a beautifully written explanation of why cosmologists, using the data gathered by astronomers of various kinds about the huge universe in which we find ourselves, now make common cause with scientists of a very different kind, those concerned with the structure of matter on the finest scale. The cosmologist's conviction is that a proper understanding of why the universe is the way it is will also prove to be an explanation of why matter turns up in precisely the forms we know, the atoms in our bodies in particular. So the search for the Big Bang is a search for a Universal Explanation.

THIS is a complex and extraordinary book, a collection of six narratives, four overtly autobiographical and two fictional, set in France at the end of World War II. Its title chapter is the most powerful text I have read about that period. Marguerite Duras describes the weeks of 1945 during which she waited to know if her husband had survived imprisonment in Germany, and her struggle to save his life after he returned from Dachau. The memories it relates are so harrowing that the author claims not to recall how or when she composed it. Its original draft, she tells us, was only discovered in 1984 in a cupboard in her country house. ''I found myself confronted,'' Miss Duras writes in her introduction, ''with a tremendous chaos of thought and feeling that I couldn't bring myself to tamper with, and beside which literary work was something of which I felt ashamed.'' The book's original French title was ''La Douleur'' (''Pain'').   Because it is equally sublime as a literary work and as an act of witness, because its style and theme so tightly encapsulate the last four dec-ades of this admirable writer's career, the first chapter of ''The War'' needs to be fully considered on its own merit, rather than as a prelude to the less accomplished texts that follow it.

THE literature that emerged from Latin America two decades ago was magical in its range of characters and incredible plots, impressive in its political and historical scope and distinctly male. It is not that women weren't writing and publishing in Latin America. They certainly were, but with very few exceptions - among them Isabel Allende, whose brilliant novel, ''The House of the Spirits,'' was published here last year - women were generally not making their way into translation, and those who did failed to achieve popular acclaim in this country. Some have suggested that the paucity of Latin American women writers in translation proves that there aren't any good ones. But this is simply not true. The reasons, rather, have to do with a complex blend of literary politics, the problem of machismo and other forms of cultural repression. Whatever the causes, the first major anthology of Latin American short fiction, ''The Eye of the Heart'' - published by Avon in 1974, in its significant Latin American literature series, and recently reissued - though otherwise excellent, contained only 5 stories by women out of more than 40.

AT the heart of good history, even the most rarefied and scholarly history, is a naughty little secret: good storytelling. A history that isn't implicitly a colorful, twisty yarn is at best fodder for other specialists - and not particularly nourishing fodder at that, for a historian's richest insights generally come when he asks himself what it would have been like to have been there, to have confronted the personalities, conditions and conundrums of which history is made. The British novelist and screenwriter George MacDonald Fraser understands all this, but he works from the opposite direction: at the heart of his vivid storytelling is plenty of solid history. In creating his justly celebrated Flashman novels, of which the rousing ''Flashman and the Dragon'' is the eighth, he seizes on a historical milieu and then hurls himself into it - or rather he hurls his dastardly alter ego, Sir Harry Flashman V.C., the self-avowed lecher, blackguard and coward whose military and amorous exploits Mr. Fraser has been chronicling since 1969.

pull_quote: LESS THAN ONE. Selected Essays. By Joseph Brodsky. 501 pages. Farrar Straus Giroux. $25.   IN 1984 Joseph Brodsky was invited to give the commencement address at Williams College. No doubt his listeners were hoping for something unusual -why else ask a poet? - but it seems unlikely that they were prepared for what they got. After warning them that in the course of their lives they were bound to come into direct contact with ''what's known as Evil,'' he offered them some subtle advice on how best to defend themselves, and urged them to make sure they understood the full implications of turning the other cheek. Finally he admitted to uneasiness about discussing such issues in public, above all because he was afraid of divulging strategic secrets to the enemy - and it was reasonable to assume that his youthful audience contained its share of potential evildoers as well as potential victims.

ALTHOUGH he is best known today as a writer on politics, Norman Podhoretz began his professional life as a literary critic, and in the essays gathered together in his latest book he partly resumes his original role. For the most part they are reports from what Lionel Trilling once called, in a phrase that gives the book both its title and subtitle, ''the bloody crossroads where literature and politics meet'' - bloody because writers have so often been the victims of political oppression, no less bloody because so many of them have encouraged or condoned that oppression.   The essays have a number of obvious and important virtues. They generally address themselves to the issues that matter most; they are blessedly serious, at a time when so much criticism is characterized by frivolous over-elaboration; they are crisp and well argued - almost too well argued, you feel, since they display some of the limitations as well as the strengths of intellectual neatness.

EVOKING both childish pretense and the act of compelling someone into belief, John Leggett's title, ''Making Believe,'' neatly implies the substance of his novel, reminding us how innocent an act of faith really is and how destructive it is to have to go along with something you don't believe in. ''Make'' stands for the creative, poetic aspect of belief and for coercion too.   The action starts in 1950, when the narrator, Ethan Soames, encounters Roy Train, a fellow student at an Episcopal seminary in Manhattan. Soames is even-tempered but impressionable, and he soon forms a liking for the irrepressible Train, who keeps questioning what their theological mentors tell them. Soon after they first meet, Train brings a lecture to a halt by challenging the idea of the Resurrection. ''That's the cornerstone of Christian thought, Mr. Train,'' says the long-suffering professor of contemporary theology, ''the conquest over death.'' No, says Train, the evidence is hearsay, and each disciple saw something different: ''That's a pretty wobbly cornerstone.'' At this point Soames begins to scold Train, invoking ''certain givens . . . certain beliefs that all Christians share.'' Train counters by asking if the Resurrection is historical fact or myth he is being asked to take on trust, and the lecture hall fills with noise. From then on Train has Soames in thrall.

THE proper method for scientific investigation has been a subject of disagreement for a long time. One view, put forward by Galileo, Francis Bacon and Newton, is that the most effective way to discover scientific laws is through experiment - by setting up controlled situations in which the basic elements of some phenomenon can be isolated and studied independently of complications. Another view, championed by literary figures such as Goethe, suggests that the direct study of almost any phenomenon in nature can lead to insights about fundamental natural laws. In the words of Tennyson: Little flower - but if I could understand What you are, root and all, and all in all I should know what God and man is.   The experimental method has had much the better of it in leading to the fundamental discoveries of modern science, especially in physics, chemistry and 20th-century biology. Only in sciences such as astronomy, where experiments are impractical, has the observation of natural systems held sway; and even there, much of the progress has come from the application of laws from other sciences.

THE second novel by the author of the much admired ''Water Castle'' is set in the Vienna of the last days of World War II and the early period of the Allied occupation, when, after its great upheaval, the European world lay undefined, indeterminate, awaiting interpretation. The success of the novel is in establishing and maintaining a sort of phenomenology of indeterminacy.   ''Vienna Girl'' describes a world in which old myths have been literally exploded and new ones are yet to take their place. Events and characters are developed through continual ironies and reversals that undercut any interpretation that might begin to seem tenable. These convolutions describe a miasmic interconnectedness in events and - for lack of a better word - ideas, which has a terrible feeling of truth about it. History is itself a narrative, and everything depends on who does the telling. The teller's ideas of plausibility and coherency become principles of selection, and unassimilable details drop away, ambiguities are nudged until they fall to one side or the other, and finally only a single account of things seems possible.

In about 50 spending categories the President could choose a ''nick,'' a moderate cut, or a ''whack.'' This wasn't at the beginning; this was two years into the Administration, when the deficit was running over $100 billion a year. ''The President enjoyed the quiz immensely,'' Mr. Stockman writes. ''He sat there day after day with his pencil.'' But in the end, thanks to too many nicks and not enough whacks, the President's report card showed a projected five-year deficit of $800 billion. Yet when Mr. Stockman then suggested it was time to think about a tax increase, President Reagan pounded his fist on the table. ''I don't want to hear any more talk about taxes. The problem is deficit spending!''

Hanawalt's book on the English peasant family in the late middle ages are its demands that the reader consider existential issues - one's place in history, the timelessness of familial relationships - and be interested in the subject for its own sake yet willing to think about the seemingly obvious in new ways.

JUST as women used to have hope chests, Edna O'= Brien has a hopelessness chest, where she treasures up material for her novels. In the early books, the hopelessness is bitter and destructive; in her middle and late period, it is flailing and ironical.   Published separately in the early 1960's, her first three novels are now reissued as ''The Country Girls Trilogy.'' As always, Miss O'Brien addresses the old misunderstanding between men and women. Her characters live in what Aldous Huxley called ''a hostile symbiosis,'' a deep, historical distrust. There is little friendliness or good will between the sexes in this village in western Ireland: each sees the other as a punishment for the ancient sin of desire.   This is the life that Kate, the narrator of the first two novels, and her friend Baba are born into. While Miss O'Brien underlines their isolation by more or less ignoring events outside the village, the time seems to be the 1930's or 40's. Women, including the girls' mothers, are swept into the corner by convention, by Irish Catholicism and perhaps by Miss O'Brien. Men repair -the word is apt - to the pub. Lower-class respectability breeds an everyday obscenity, a deep suspicion of human nature. Earthiness has decayed into vulgarity.

BIOGRAPHERS, Robert Skidelsky tells us, find themselves in a curiously defensive position: are they trying to tell a story or to explain something? It is a question that is bound to confront anyone who undertakes a life of John Maynard Keynes. Keynes was arguably the most influential economist since Adam Smith. He was also a public person with an extraordinary range of interests and influence - the chief economic representative of Great Britain during its negotiations with the United States at the end of World War II, a major architect of the postwar international monetary system, a director of the Bank of England, an entrepreneur in the theater and ballet, and a trustee of the National Gallery. THE excesses of the recent military regimes in South America have become the fountainhead of an angry, unforgiving literature. For a new wave of writers, the grotesque nature of dictatorships cannot be adequately conveyed even by the masterly surrealism of a Gabriel Garcia Marquez. These writers view themselves as scribes, faithful chroniclers of the many acts of torture, execution and psychological terror that are all too fresh to be relegated to the domain of allegory. The subject of Omar Rivabella's ''Requiem for a Woman's Soul'' is torture, described in such harrowing, unrelenting detail that none of it can be dismissed as a product of the imagination. Indeed, the author, an Argentine journalist and human rights advocate, has based his novel on the testimony of victims of repression in his country. More than once, the reader is tempted to put down this slim volume, lock it away, forget its stomach-churning passages. But to no avail. Sooner or later, the compul-sion to press onward, no matter how painful, becomes overwhelming.

THE motto of the Boy Scouts, ''Be Prepared,'' is not only a brisk exhortation; it also enshrines the initials of the movement's founder, Robert Baden-Powell - a fact that ''B-P'' himself more than once called attention to in the early days of Scouting, just in case anyone missed the point. The Scouts are a monument to Baden-Powell's ambitions no less than to his ideals, and to study the origins of the movement, as Michael Rosenthal has done in ''The Character Factory,'' is inevitably to study the life of the man who created it as well.   He was a curious blend, in some respects an innocent, in others a cool operator, a conventional late-Victorian soldier who was also a born showman. His father, who died when he was a child, was a professor of geometry at Oxford, and he grew up in the midst of the academic elite -when his mother was worried about his ability to draw equally well with either hand, she consulted Ruskin; when he failed to win a place at Oxford, he was turned down, so to speak, under distinguished auspices, by the classical scholar Benjamin Jowett (who was also his godfather) and by the mathematician Charles Dodgson, better known as Lewis Carroll.

pull_quote: MELANIE KLEIN Her World and Her Work. By Phyllis Grosskurth. Illustrated. 515 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $25.   ''My dear, don't make any mistake. I'm a Freudian, but not an Anna Freudian.'' - Melanie Klein   DURING the last decade of Freud's life, battle lines were drawn in a theoretical and personal struggle between two passionate and strong-willed women - Anna Freud and Melanie Klein - that would significantly mark the history of the psychoanalytic movement. Phyllis Grosskurth's remarkable biography of Melanie Klein shows the struggle as a case of sibling rivalry. For one woman, Sigmund Freud was father to the work that was more than her life's passion, it was her life. For the other, Frued was this and more: her father and her analyst.

WHEN Don Denkinger erred on what turned out to be a crucial ninth-inning call in last year's sixth game of the World Series between the Kansas City Royals and the St. Louis Cardinals, baseball fans spent a good deal of the winter discussing whether the umpire was responsible for the eventual outcome of the Series. title: The Great Pretender
author: James Atlas
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GREAT PRETENDER By James Atlas. 277 pp. New York: Atheneum. $15.95.   I MUST confess that my aging Jewish comedian's heart skipped a beat when I read the jacket blurb describing a book written by someone under 40 as ''the most important comic-Jewish novel since 'Portnoy's Complaint' '' (a summary that goes to the heart of the novel's anxieties, even though the blurb has disappeared from the final version). Scarcely any writers of that age who seem in any sense ''important'' these days are ''Jews.'' Indeed, I have long since decided that the Jewish-American novel is over and done with, a part of history rather than a living literature. To be sure, many of the Jewish-American authors whose newest work we used to await so breathlessly only a decade ago are still alive and writing. Moreover, they continue to be honored with prestigious awards, memorialized in adulatory biographies and mined for quotations on Ph.D. examinations. In part for this very reason, however, their more recent books have come to seem not merely irrelevant but posthumous. In any case, from the start the Jewishness of such laureates of Jewish-American life was already vestigial, approaching degree zero - and their exploitation of it has come to seem in retrospect a final act of assimilation into the homogenized, postethnic society that made them rich and famous. It was perhaps an awareness of this that impelled Saul Bellow to make the fictional alter ego of his latest novel for the first time not even a vestigial Jew but a goy.
headline: GROWING UP POST-JEWISH

title: Early Elkin
author: Stanley Elkin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EARLY ELKIN. By Stanley Elkin. (Bamberger Books, P.O. Box 1126, Flint, Mich. 48501, Cloth, $15. Paper, $7.50.) ''I was no prodigy,'' Stanley Elkin warns in his introduction to the odd assortment - three stories, one critique-cum-story, one memoir - that make up the 1950's wing of ''my little awful Elkin museum.'' But he would have us take this book to heart, regardless, as a sort of pep talk on the virtues of resolve, patience and desire in the making of a writer. Indeed, in the long story, ''The Party,'' it is difficult to see the wit or edgy tough-mindedness that would later distinguish such bravura performances as ''The Dick Gibson Show'' and ''The Franchiser.'' Instead we find ethnic sentimentality, clumsy flashbacks, portentous phrasings. Yet, even amid failures of technique and imagination, the Elkin sensibility struggles to its feet. ''That he was unhappy was his tragedy,'' he writes of the protagonist. ''Or rather that he was not happy made him unhappy and that was his tragedy.'' Similarly, ''A Sound of Distant Thunder,'' which gives us a Jewish shopkeeper in a failing urban neighborhood (the prototype, perhaps, for the extraordinary ''Criers and Kibitzers, Kibitzers and Criers''), has, despite its simplistic view of character and fate, a firm grip on the details of work and environment. The story reaches its climax with a sales spiel that anticipates the arias Elkin characters will deliver, to great effect, in the three decades following. In my opinion, the only wholly successful piece - aside from the wise, funny memoir, ''Where I Read What I Read'' - is ''Fifty Dollars,'' and it strikes me as an untypical effort, more somber and mannered than the mature work. Mr. Elkin, it appears, really wasn't a prodigy.

pull_quote: THE BLOODY CROSSROADS Where Literature and Politics Meet. By Norman Podhoretz. 221 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $16.95.   NORMAN PODHORETZ, editor of Commentary magazine and a leading neoconservative intellectual, occupies a position more extraordinary than these credentials might reasonably allow. Like many ambitious young writers starting out in the 1950's or before - in this he may be compared to Norman Mailer, James Baldwin and Gore Vidal, all of whom at one time or another were published in Commentary - he drove his first passions mainly along literary lines, and only later took on political heat. Unlike these erstwhile colleagues, whose appetites frequently divided between imaginative and polemical writing, Mr. Podhoretz has remained a consistent essayist. And unlike Mr. Mailer and Mr. Vidal, he has not run for public office. His influence - a source of controversy and of more than controversy - derives chiefly from the quiet clamor of print.

You'll be just another highly intelligent, talented, rich writer, the literary hope of the nation, lost to Hollywood. THE JONATHAN INSTITUTE, a private research institute based in Jerusalem and concentrating, among other things, on terrorism, sponsored a conference in Washington in June 1984, from which this volume emerged. The institute's ''main purpose,'' we are told, is to demonstrate that terrorism is ''part of a much larger struggle, one between the forces of civilization and the forces of barbarism, and that, if left unchallenged, terrorism would continue to spread with disastrous consequences.'' title: Cat's Grin
author: Francois Maspero
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: Herbert R. Lottman: Herbert R. Lottman'S Latest Book, the Purge,On the Punishment of Collaborators In France After World War II, Will Be Published This Summer
pull_quote: CAT'S GRIN By Francois Maspero. Translated by Nancy Amphoux. 295 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.   IN my early years in Paris, Francois Maspero's bookstore was a Left Bank landmark of a particular kind. His specialties were liberation movements and revolution, and Mr. Maspero himself was the publisher of many of the incendiary titles sold in his shop. This was at a time - the early 1960's - when France was still trying to remain a colonial power the hard way (it has since become a soft colonial power). The police sometimes seized Mr. Maspero's books before they left the printers, and I remember that in response to a publishing directory questionnaire he noted with irony that his house was founded in 1959 - ''legally.'' (The founder was then 27 years old.) The first bookstore in Paris to stay open evenings, Mr. Maspero's shop eventually became a victim of its own success when too many late-night browsers, in ultimate protest against the consumer society, bypassed the cash register on their way out. At least this was the reason given by the press for the closing, although I suspect that the real cause of the failure and the sale of the Maspero publishing house was the disaffection of France's yuppie generation from radical solutions. That was when the leftist militant Regis Debray was exchanging his worship of Che Guevara for a position in President Francois Mitterrand's Socialist Government.

title: Table Money
author: Jimmy Breslin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TABLE MONEY By Jimmy Breslin. 435 pp. New York: Ticknor & Fields. $17.95.   IT is impossible to approach a work by Jimmy Breslin without a preconceived notion of it. His voice, gruff and glib at once, has been familiar now for decades. In his newspaper columns, for which last month he won a Pulitzer Prize, and in his books (''The Gang That Couldn't Shoot Straight,'' ''World Without End, Amen'' and ''How the Good Guys Finally Won,'' to name his most popular), he has chronicled the experience of his New York as deftly as Woody Allen or Louis Auchincloss have theirs. No one speaks for ethnic American urban working people, particularly Irish, with more authority than he does. From this dean of big-city blue-collar columnists, we almost always get that peculiar mix of old-fashioned Democratic liberalism, reflexive compassion for underdogs and victims, a naif's contempt for figures of authority who abuse their trust, combined with a worldly-wise cynicism that expects them to - all served up with savvy, offhand spontaneity in which seriousness is sometimes sacrificed to wisecracks. We know, in other words, what to expect from Mr. Breslin.

title: Burning Houses
author: Andrew Harvey

pull_quote: BURNING HOUSES By Andrew Harvey. 214 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $16.95. IN Andrew Harvey's book of verse ''No Diamonds, No Hat, No Honey,'' a self-conscious young man, Fernando, and a worldly-wise woman named Lydia carried on a poetic and philosophic dialogue. In Mr. Harvey's new novel, ''Burning Houses,'' dialogue is once again his chosen vehicle, in this case between Charles, a 31-year-old English novelist and travel writer raised in India (Mr. Harvey was born in India and educated in England), and Adolphe, a 67-year-old extraordinarily flamboyant transvestite and internationally known film director whom Charles describes as ''pug-faced, chubby-cheeked, Empress of the Demi-Monde, spiritual adviser to cardinals and princesses, pimps and taxidrivers.'' Their conversations, which take place in Adolphe's lavishly eccentric 18th-century Parisian palazzo on the Place St.-Sulpice, center on Charles's reading of his new novel, ''A Burning House.'' Yet long before we get to that title within a title in a novel within a novel, we become aware that we are being drawn into a narrative in which the distinction between life and art is deliberately being blurred.

title: Mating Birds
author: Lewis Nkosi
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
MATING BIRDS By Lewis Nkosi. 184 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $13.95. LEWIS NKOSI will always be remembered at Harvard University as the Nieman Fellow who could not go home. Mr. Nkosi, who began his career as a journalist in South Africa in the mid-1950's, left Johannesburg for Cambridge, Mass., in 1961 on a one-way permit. He has been barred from returning ever since. A professor of literature at the University of Zambia, Mr. Nkosi is a highly regarded literary critic whose works ''Home and Exile'' (1965) and ''Tasks and Masks'' (1981) are standards. As a playwright and short-story writer, he is also the most subtly experimental of the black South African writers, many of whom are caught in the immediacy of the struggle against apartheid.

''Mating Birds,'' his first novel, confronts boldly and imaginatively the strange interplay of bondage, desire and torture inherent in interracial sexual relationships within the South African prison house of apartheid. His play ''The Rhythm of Violence'' and his short story ''The Prisoner'' explored related themes. The treatment of miscegenation as a political indictment of a racist South Africa is not without its literary dangers and risks, however, and Mr. Nkosi's novel does not entirely escape them.

title: The Hour Of The Star
author: Clarice Lispector
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

pull_quote:
THE HOUR OF THE STAR By Clarice Lispector. Translated, and with an afterword by Giovanni Pontiero. 96 pp. New York: Carcanet. $15.95.

BRAZIL is scrutinized daily by economists and bankers, but Brazilian literature is subsumed into ''Latin American writing,'' which usually means written in Spanish. But Brazil possesses the strongest literary tradition in Latin America; the Spanish Americans we read come from many lands, while Brazilian writers are isolated in one nation and the Portuguese language. There are women among the Latin American writers, of course, but precious few, and once again in recent years it is Spanish American women like Isabel Allende, Luisa Valenzuela and Rosario Ferre who have stolen the show. Clarice Lispector, the author of ''The Hour of the Star,'' is the premier Latin American woman prose writer of this century, but because she was a woman and a Brazilian, she has remained virtually unknown in the United States.
headline: FALLING DOWN IN RIO

title: Debt And Danger
author: Harold Lever and Christopher Huhne.

pull_quote:
DEBT AND DANGER The World Financial Crisis. By Harold Lever and Christopher Huhne. 160 pp. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. $16.95.

THIS provocative book on the international debt crisis argues persuasively what most analysts and government officials only whisper in back corridors: debt default is becoming a logical economic and political option for developing countries. ''Debt and Danger'' also makes a strong case that developed countries can no longer afford a policy of muddling through and must take significant, coordinated steps. In fact, there are some signs that the industrialized countries are moving in this direction; the recent Tokyo summit urged progress toward a ''cooperative debt strategy'' based on a central role for the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
headline: WINNING BY DEFAULT

title: The Lion Of Pescara
author: George MacBeth

pull_quote: THE LION OF PESCARA By George MacBeth. 256 pp. Topsfield, Mass.: Jonathan Cape/Merrimack Publishers' Circle. $14.95. IN childhood I had nightmares about executions: hangings, electrocutions and decapitations. My parents blamed my comic books, because the final - and often the most lurid -panels showed criminals suffering hideous retributions. EARLY in his career Ernest Hemingway devised the writing strategies he would follow for life: when composing a story he would withhold mention of its central problem; when writing a novel he would implant it in geography and, insofar as possible, he would know what time it was on every page; when writing anything he would construct the sentences so as to produce an emotion not by claiming it but by rendering precisely the experience to cause it. What he made of all this was a rigorous art of compressive power, if more suited to certain emotions than others. He was unquestionably a genius, but of the kind that advertises its limits. Critics were on to these from the very beginning, but in the forward-looking 1920's, they joined his readers to make him the writer for their time. His stuff was new. It moved. ONLY in the peaceable kingdoms of art and Eden are the relationships of humans and animals innocent and harmonious; here and now they are complex, uneasy, often cruel and always profound. CHRISTINA STEAD, the Australian-born author of 13 novels and, if we include this new volume, two collections of short stories, lived from 1902 to 1983. With some stretching she could be seen as a female counterpart to D. H. Lawrence. Like him, she grew up amid great hardship, fought free of her binding family, wrote copiously with the natural ease of a born novelist, recycled her own childhood and adult experiences into radically transposed fictions, traveled widely, won renown but lived outside the literary establishment - and shocked her contemporaries with the unsmutty high seriousness with which she treated the sexual relations between men and women.   Like Lawrence, she saw sex as, at its best, a means of exaltation, transcendence and intimate accord and, at its worst, a degrading enslavement. Unlike Lawrence, she recognized that women are as complex and varied as men: she once wrote in a note to a correspondent, ''I often felt that quite well known writings lacked truth, and this was particularly so of the pictures of women, I felt, not only because women took their complete part in society but were not represented as doing so, but because the long literary tradition . . . had enabled men completely to express themselves, while women feared to do so.''

Shcharansky was being released from a Soviet prison last February, the British historian Martin Gilbert was completing a life of the 38-year-old Jewish dissident. A prolific writer and the official biographer of Winston Churchill, Mr. Gilbert had been working on the project for three years, sifting through dissidents' documents, culling Mr. Shcharansky's letters from prison and interviewing his friends in Moscow and abroad. The result is a book written in a tone of quiet outrage, obviously conceived as a protest over Mr. Shcharansky's imprisonment; it now serves a happier function as a fine introduction to a man from whom we are likely to be hearing a good deal.   Anatoly Shcharansky may prove to be the most interesting figure to come out of the Soviet prison camps since Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn. Rarely has such a noble actor and perceptive witness confronted Soviet authoritarianism with Mr. Shcharansky's keen sense of the absurd, his impish appreciation for the truths contained in comedy. Just as Mr. Solzhenitsyn emerged from Stalin's gulag to record the system's violations in novels, histories and plays, Mr. Shcharansky will find his own way and his own voice; he is now beginning to write his own account of his nine years in prison.

Since law, like the elephant of the parable, is a large phenomenon, there are many perspectives from which it can be viewed, and so there are many ways in which it can be generalized. ''Law's Empire'' by Ronald Dworkin, a professor of jurisprudence at the University of Oxford and a professor of law at New York University, is a strong statement of general ideas about law from a leader in the current dialogue about how legal issues should be resolved by judges. pull_quote: UNHEALED WOUNDS France and the Klaus Barbie Affair. By Erna Paris. Illustrated. 252 pp. New York: Grove Press. Cloth, $17.50; Paper, $7.95.   GREAT enthusiasm greeted Erna Paris's examination of the Klaus Barbie affair upon its publication in Paris last year. But the French critics had a difficult time explaining their enthusiasm, perhaps because her analysis was not so much of Mr. Barbie's role as the Gestapo chief in Lyons during World War II as of France. And the story she told in ''Unhealed Wounds'' was not that of a historical accident in the evolution of France - which is how the last war is generally viewed in France - but of an obsession that has divided France since the Revolution of 1789, divided it during the war and divides it today.
headline: LYONS HAS SEEN A GHOST

title: Our Aging Society: Paradox And Promise
author: Alan Pifer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OUR AGING SOCIETY: Paradox and Promise. Edited by Alan Pifer and Lydia Bronte. (Norton, $22.95.) For some time now we have been put on notice that our nation will soon be blundering into demographic terra incognita.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Her Native Colors
author: Elisabeth Hyde
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HER NATIVE COLORS. By Elisabeth Hyde. (Delacorte, $15.95.) In one of Aesop's fables, a country mouse visits a city mouse for dinner; his friend's hectic urban life gives the country mouse indigestion and he abruptly leaves, vowing to be content with the familiar comforts of his own hole.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Spirit Of Survival
author: Gail Sheehy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: Eden Ross Lipson: Eden Ross Lipson Is An Editor of the Book Review
pull_quote: SPIRIT OF SURVIVAL By Gail Sheehy. Illustrated. 400 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $17.95. IN her wildly successful book, ''Passages,'' Gail Sheehy, a New York journalist, seemed to capture a fragment of the self-interested, self-absorbed 1970's and make stages of personal growth understandable to readers who found their lives in flux. Her new book, ''Spirit of Survival,'' is a far less structured and very personal account of lives in crisis that may even baffle Miss Sheehy's most faithful admirers.   The author says she intends a meditation on ''an examined life,'' principally meaning the horribly eventful experiences of her adopted Cambodian daughter, Mohm Pat. The book is a pastiche of recent histories -a report on political events in Cambodia, a first-person narrative by the child who survived the Khmer Rouge and who at age 12 became the author's daughter, as well as accounts of Miss Sheehy's own crises and, to a lesser but intrusive degree, those of her natural daughter, a college student, and Clay Felker, a New York editor, now her husband. There is also some theoretical glue about the kinds of personalities that survive against the odds. Unfortunately, the journalistic design that was meant to yield counterpoint often yields cacophony.
headline: MOHM PAT IN AMERICA

title: The China Card
author: John D Ehrlichman
pull_quote: THE CHINA CARD. By John Ehrlichman. 523 pages. Simon & Schuster. $18.95. John Ehrlichman's ''China Card'' is a suspense thriller about the rapprochement between the United States and China that was effected by President Nixon and his national security adviser, Henry A. Kissinger, in 1971 and 1972. Where, you may wonder, is the suspense in this, since we know from the outset that Mr. Nixon will end up going to Peking? Where is the thrill?   Aha! What you didn't know is that in the autumn of 1966, a young graduate of Harvard Law School named Matthew Thompson went to work for the law firm of Nixon, Mudge, Rose, Guthrie & Alexander. Through his father, an Orientalist at Whittier College, Matt Thompson knew Richard Nixon, who was gearing up to run for the Presidency in 1968. Also through his father, Matt had contact with certain key people in the circle of China's leadership who began to cultivate him as a secret lobbyist in the Nixon camp. Matt was willing because he deeply believed that the United States and China should be friends once again.
headline: East-West Intrigue

title: The Life And Legend Of Jay Gould
author: Maury Klein
pull_quote: THE LIFE AND LEGEND OF JAY GOULD. By Maury Klein. Illustrated. 595 pages. The Johns Hopkins University Press. $27.50. THERE were no opinion polls in the 19th century, but if there had been, they would probably have shown that Jay Gould was the most hated American of his time. Regularly execrated by the press while he lived, unmourned at his death, he has come down to posterity as a symbol of the robber barons at their worst - a pure predator, wholly unscrupulous and unrestrained in his greed.   This is the legend that Maury Klein has set out to overturn in his huge new biography of Gould. A tough assignment - but Mr. Klein, a professor of history at the University of Rhode Island, has delved deep into archives that most previous writers on Gould have ignored, and is able to back up his revisionist assertions with a multitude of telling details.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Beachmasters
author: Thea Astley
pull_quote: BEACHMASTERS. By Thea Astley. 185 pages. Viking. $14.95.   ''THE heat, the wet had become components of their minds as well as their skins,'' writes Thea Astley in her fierce new novel. ''They made money and they lost money and still they stayed. It was the tug of the Pacific that clutched them, the idea of it, the leisurely drawl, the casualness, the supremacy of ruling their own three, four, five thousand acres of colonnaded palms with the cattle dawdling beneath.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Lionel Trilling And The Fate Of Cultural Criticism
author: Mark Krupnick
pull_quote: LIONEL TRILLING AND THE FATE OF CULTURAL CRITICISM. By Mark Krupnick. 207 pages. Illustrated.   Northwestern University Press. $21.95. ELEVEN years after his death, Lionel Trilling still exerts great influence on the landscape of American culture. Yet even discounting the frequent abstractness and digressiveness of his writing style, Trilling remains a somewhat elusive thinker. One person's Trilling is the radical anti-Stalinist of the 1930's; another's is the genial book-club belletrist of the 1950's; still another's is the critic of the 1960's counterculture who refused to join the neoconservative movement that so many of his intellectual brethren embraced.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Oxford Dictionary Of Popes
author: J N D Kelly
pull_quote: THE OXFORD DICTIONARY OF POPES. By J. N. D.Kelly. 347 pages. Oxford University Press. $24.95. WHO exactly was St. Silverius? ''Born at Frosinone, son of Hormisdas, he was, unprecedentedly, only a subdeacon when, news of Agapitus I's death at Constantinople having reached Rome, Theodahad, last Ostrogothic king of Italy (534-6), terrorized the clergy into electing him pope.'' Within less than a year, however, he was deposed by the Emperor Justinian's General Belisarius and sent into exile, dying not long afterward as a result of his sufferings.   The first thing you are liable to feel on dipping into the Oxford Dictionary of Popes is what a lot of history there is, and how little of it most of us are ever likely to know. For those who accept his authority, a pope holds the highest of offices, which makes him someone of great consequence for everyone else as well. Yet many of the popes of the past remain shadowy figures, and unless you are a specialist even the most notable of them can often be hard to sort out.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Success Stories
author: Russell Banks
pull_quote: SUCCESS STORIES. By Russell Banks. 183 pages. Harper & Row. $15.95. In his last book, ''Continental Drift,'' Russell Banks created a visionary epic about innocence and guilt, and in doing so, he also set down a shattering portrait of contemporary American society. His story of one man's doomed attempts to reinvent his life became a dark mirror of the American dream: As we watched Bob Dubois set off for Florida with entrepreneurial visions of glamour dancing in his head, then witnessed the smashing of all his ambitions and his hopes, we were made aware of the terrible consequences that the false promises of success can have on the lives of ordinary workingmen.
headline: American Dreamers

title: The Character Factory
author: Michael Rosenthal. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CHARACTER FACTORY Baden-Powell and the Origins of the Boy Scout Movement. By Michael Rosenthal. Illustrated. 335 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $22.95.   PERHAPS unfairly, I've always found scouting faintly ludicrous. My only two personal experiences of it were a bit odd and not really conducive to respect. Also, I can remember as a boy those photographs of King George VI - ridiculous, like all adult Scouts, in baggy shorts and wide-brimmed hat - looking as if he couldn't tie a knot to save his life.   Robert Stephenson Smyth Baden-Powell, first Baron Baden-Powell, the subject of Michael Rosenthal's new study, could tie knots. Born in 1857, he went to Charterhouse school in 1870. Typical of his period, he despised work - ''often sleeps in class'' - and loved games. Two hints of the future: he was a successful schoolboy actor; he was a solitary, who loved creeping about the Godalming countryside having fantasies that he was an American Indian or a trapper.
headline: BEACH BLANKET BOOK BAG

title: The Professor And The Prostitute
author: Linda Wolfe. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PROFESSOR AND THE PROSTITUTE And Other True Tales of Murder and Madness. By Linda Wolfe. Illustrated. 228 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $16.95. IN a rather curious, autobiographical introduction to the nine true stories in ''The Professor and the Prostitute,'' Linda Wolfe informs the reader that she is a ''psychological'' writer whose interest is in ''people who inhabit the middle class . . . people I, and many others like me, might know, entertain, work beside.'' She had hoped to become a novelist, but, concluding that her imagination was ''impoverished,'' decided to ''try using fictional techniques to fuel nonfiction'' -as she seems to see it, to go slumming with style.   In the title story, Miss Wolfe's reminder that such writers as Heinrich Mann, Dostoyevsky, Somerset Maugham and Zola all demonstrated an interest in ''the love of reputable males for reprobate females'' is unnecessary. The story of how and why William Henry James Douglas, a professor of anatomy and cellular biology at Tufts University's School of Medicine in Boston, became obsessed with, and later murdered, a comely prostitute named Robin Benedict in 1983 is fascinating on its own terms.
headline: WHEN THE MIDDLE CLASS SNAPS

title: The Funeral Makers
author: Cathie Pelletier
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE FUNERAL MAKERS By Cathie Pelletier. 247 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $16.95.   A BLURB on the back cover of this latest in a growing number of wild and crazy novels from Maine claims this may ''well be the first Northern Southern Novel.'' It has been suggested before that there is a similarity between recent Maine fiction and the tough and earthy, often sensational yet sensitive, fiction known as Southern Gothic written from the 1930's on by such authors as William Faulkner, Erskine Caldwell, James Dickey and Flannery O'Connor. Last year ''The Beans of Egypt, Maine,'' Carolyn Chute's popular first novel, was compared to (among other novels) Faulkner's chronicles of the Snopeses, and there are other, lesser-known Maine writers such as Lucy Honig, Willis Johnston, Fred Bonnie and S. T. Colby who have produced fine fiction that includes elements of the regional grotesque. The similarity should really come as no surprise; even though ''Tobacco Road'' and ''God's Little Acre'' are set in the South, folks around here have speculated for some time that Mr. Caldwell may have gleaned a lot of his local color from the area around Mount Vernon, Me., where he lived from 1925 to 1932. Local legend also has it that the actual setting of Mr. Dickey's 1970 novel ''Deliverance'' was South Solon, Me., the river the upper Kennebec.
headline: BEACH BLANKET BOOK BAG

title: Educational Myths I Have Known And Loved
author: Baird W. Whitlock.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EDUCATIONAL MYTHS I HAVE KNOWN AND LOVED By Baird W. Whitlock. 115 pp. New York: Schocken Books. $12.95. LABELED A to Z, the 26 brief essays in Baird W. Whitlock's book purport to demolish 26 educational ''myths.'' What are some of these myths? One is that faculty members in the Northeast are ''more liberal than faculties in the rest of the country.'' Mr. Whitlock's argument: schools and colleges in the Northeast are actually conservative in their unwillingness to experiment with new programs. Another myth is that artists are ''more sensitive'' than the rest of us. Mr. Whitlock's argument: some of the artists with whom he has served on faculties were actually very insensitive to their colleagues or students.   Since one may fairly assign a political meaning to ''liberal'' and a self-referential meaning to ''sensitive,'' Mr. Whitlock's mythology quickly comes to seem more of a gimmick than a meaningful organizing principle. And since eight of the essays have already been published in an educational journal, one also suspects that Mr. Whitlock has had to strain to use the whole alphabet for ''Educational Myths I Have Known and Loved.''
headline: TALES OUT OF SCHOOL

title: Enter Talking
author: Joan Rivers with Richard Meryman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ENTER TALKING By Joan Rivers with Richard Meryman. Illustrated. 398 pp. New York: Delacorte Press. $17.95. ENTER talking? In this era of the hype, Joan Rivers's title wins hands down as the year's greatest understatement. She does not merely talk, she takes aim, begins to fire and rakes her audience - 373 pages plus index, acknowledgements, and last but far from least, a heartfelt dedication ''To Edgar  [ her husband ]  who made this book happen, and to Johnny Carson, who made it all happen.''   Years ago, while investigating what made great comedians tick, I interviewed the great ''Perfect Fool,'' Ed Wynn. He had a simple formula for success. ''I come out and in the first couple of minutes I make friends with the audience,'' he said. ''After that, I can do anything with them, and they'll accept and love me.''
headline: BEACH BLANKET BOOK BAG

title: The Patient Has The Floor
author: Alistair Cooke
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PATIENT HAS THE FLOOR By Alistair Cooke. 204 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.   EVERYBODY knows Alistair Cooke. He's that cordial English gentleman who guides us weekly through the polished parlors (and equally polished sentences) of the British upper classes. Were it not for Mr. Cooke, would we appreciate the stiffness of a lady's gown or the delicacy of her gossip? Would we assume a link between good literature and good leather or admire a Scotsman who knows his place? At the same time, Mr. Cooke has brought us his masterly television series, ''Alistair Cooke's America,'' in which he seemed to know all about the huddled masses who came to the United States from such places as Latvia and Italy. Yet he told their stories so compassionately it was hard to discern whether he actually believed in the American dream or was simply fascinated by it.
headline: BEACH BLANKET BOOK BAG

title: Flowers And Fruit
author: Colette
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FLOWERS AND FRUIT By Colette. Edited by Robert Phelps. Translated by Matthew Ward. 163 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $14.95. NO one has written better about gardens than Colette. Her mother, Sido, gardened passionately above and below their house at Saint-Sauveur-en-Puisaye. Colette, her youngest child, was left to moon and dawdle around the plants as much as she liked. Plants were her earliest and most faithful companions; she looked into them as deep and hard as only a child can, and she never forgot what she learned. Of each she remembered the mode and the imprint, as well as the way it behaved in garden society. The gardens she liked least were the ones she herself had to make from scratch; she entered fully into the atmosphere of gardens already existing, complete with their animals and insects. Each crumbling wall, with its rampant stragglers and tangled blooms attended by ragged butterflies, worked its way into her memory.
headline: LOVE OF BLOOMS

title: Misadventures Of A Fly Fisherman
author: Jack Hemingway. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MISADVENTURES OF A FLY FISHERMAN My Life With and Without Papa. By Jack Hemingway. Illustrated. 326 pp. Dallas: Taylor Publishing Company. $17.95.   ''I SPENT the first fifty years of my life being the son of a famous father,'' Jack Hemingway says with an almost audible sigh near the end of this friendly memoir, ''and am now spending the last fifty as the father of famous children.'' Neither a famous father nor famous children are known for being easy to deal with, but Mr. Hemingway's ''Misadventures of a Fly Fisherman'' is some proof of the good spirit with which he has not only weathered but enjoyed the experience.
headline: LIFE IS WHAT INTERRUPTS FISHING TRIPS

title: Soda Poppery
author: Stephen N. Tchudi. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SODA POPPERY The History of Soft Drinks in America. By Stephen N. Tchudi. Illustrated. 148 pp. New York: Charles Scribner's Sons. $13.95. (Ages 10 to 14) I AM, I confess, my dentist's dream patient, when I can afford to see him or pay his bills. I consume 64 ounces of a particular soft drink a day, which adds up to 23,360 ounces every year or 700,800 ounces over the span of my adult life to date.
