pull_quote: NOT SO FAST SONGOLOLO Written and illustrated by Niki Daly. Unpaged. New York: Margaret K. McElderry/Atheneum. $11.95. (Ages 5 to 8) THE names in ''Not So Fast Songololo'' should be read aloud or sung.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: The Outside Story
author: Richard Brookhiser.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE OUTSIDE STORY How Democrats and Republicans Re-elected Reagan. By Richard Brookhiser. 298 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $17.95. EVER since Theodore H. White wrote ''The   Making of the President 1960,'' journalists have competed furiously to get the gossip on how key staff members on Presidential campaigns get along with one another and to explain the intricacies of how convention delegates are won. Above all, the reporters work hard to keep up a steady flow of novelistic detail. Richard Brookhiser, managing editor of National Review, has chosen not to play that game. In his new book on the 1984 Presidential campaign, he has instead sought ''to focus on what the candidates and their supporters say and do in public; to leave the green room and the wings and go out front, and attend, with respect, to the performance.'' By listening to what the candidates had to say and analyzing its impact on voters, Mr. Brookhiser was able to piece together what he calls, with mild irony, ''The Outside Story.''
headline: THE LIBERAL SHIPWRECK

title: Sometimes I Live In The Country
author: Frederick Busch
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOMETIMES I LIVE IN THE COUNTRY By Frederick Busch. 218 pp. Boston: David R. Godine. $15.95. WHEN first seen, Petey, the 13-year-old protagonist of Frederick Busch's vivid, moving novel, is playing Russian roulette. Having stuffed the cold barrel of his father's handgun into his mouth, he is about to pull the trigger when he remembers to open his eyes. ''He didn't want to miss anything.'' This is suicide-as-sideshow, and Petey is a true American adolescent - entertained by his own despair.   The entertainment of despair has two primary tones, sorrow and comedy, and in ''Sometimes I Live in the Country'' Mr. Busch mixes them with generally effective results. He has transplanted that perennial character, the American boy, from this particular boy's original home in Brooklyn to the rural wilds of upstate New York, and given him an affectionate, alcoholic ex-cop father, known throughout the novel only as Pop. As the novel opens, Petey's mother is, somewhat unaccountably, missing. And as the story develops, the mystery of Petey's broken family is placed next to the mystery of Northern rural racism, including the gradual uncovering of a Ku Klux Klan chapter in the neighborhood, headed by a mad book-banning fundamentalist preacher, the Reverend Staynes.
headline: PETEY AMONG THE CORNHEADS

title: Playing God In Yellowstone
author: Alston Chase.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PLAYING GOD IN YELLOWSTONE The Destruction of America's First National Park. By Alston Chase. 446 pp. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. $24.95.   IF the national parks are the cathedrals of American civilization, as they are sometimes called, then Yellowstone is our Chartres. The biggest national park at 2.2 million acres, it is a land of scenic splendor, spectacular thermal features such as Old Faithful and rich, varied wildlife that includes some of the last grizzly bears in the 48 contiguous states.
headline: CAN WE STILL TRUST RANGER RICK?

title: The Woman Who Escaped From Shame
author: Toby Olson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WOMAN WHO ESCAPED FROM SHAME By Toby Olson. 324 pp. New York: Random House. $16.95. THREE sailors discharged and on the loose in San Diego. Not for me a promising beginning; I await the false heartiness of self-conscious vernacular, the blurry, beery onslaught of the so-called Real. We find ourselves hooked by it again, these days. I think: but Toby Olson is a poet, and a good one - what is he doing in these conventional alleyways?   The answer is interesting and comes soon. He is getting us out of town. Going south. Mexico. Into the heart of the story. He takes his start right in the middle of the ordinary, as a good writer always will, and worries his material and struggles with it to make it reveal the splendors and austerities our fantasies try to persuade us do proliferate from every common act.
headline: ORDINARY SPLENDORS

title: Good-Bye To The Low Profile
author: Herb Schmertz with William Novak.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GOOD-BYE TO THE LOW PROFILE The Art of Creative Confrontation. By Herb Schmertz with William Novak. 242 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $16.95. HERB SCHMERTZ, Mobil Oil's vice president for public affairs, has written a lively and often humorous book telling businessmen how they should face - and face down - the press. As Mr. Schmertz revels in his many confrontations with the news media, he also slips in evidence to support the conclusion that he is a most ingenious and important corporate public relations man.   Mr. Schmertz was aided by William Novak, whose writing skill helped make Lee Iacocca's autobiography a blockbuster. ''Good-bye to the Low Profile'' should do very well in business and public relations circles, but it will not be another ''Iacocca.'' While Mr. Schmertz tells us that ''the real leaders in any society are not afraid of showing who they are,'' we come away knowing little about his personal motivations, except that he always seems to be looking for a good fight.
headline: PLAYING HARDBALL WITH THE PRESS

title: The Last Film Of Emile Vico
author: Thomas Gavin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LAST FILM OF EMILE VICO By Thomas Gavin. 403 pp. New York: Viking. $17.95. THIS complex, ambitious and sometimes surreal second novel by Thomas Gavin has as many layers as an onion - a description that also perfectly suits the brilliant auteur, Emile Vico, as he is perceived by the narrator, his cameraman, Griswold Farley. At first, the novel appears to be a murder mystery set in 1930's Hollywood, with an ambiance as authentic as a reel of Movietone News. But more is going on here than the disappearance of a famous author/director/star and the subsequent police investigation of Vico's beautiful, estranged second wife, Lisa, and Farley. Was it murder, suicide, or was the actor -as one old-timer suggests - simply eaten up by the camera? (''Want to find Vico? . . . Look in that last can of film.'') Is Farley himself the killer, or is it his elusive alter ego, the untrustworthy Spyhawk? Or is there some more serious hidden meaning here?
headline: HE IS A CAMERA

title: Driving The Body Back
author: Mary Swander
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
DRIVING THE BODY BACK By Mary Swander. 81 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. Cloth, $14.95. Paper, $8.95. SOURCE By Fred Chappell. 57 pp. Baton Rouge: Louisiana State University Press. Cloth, $13.95. Paper, $6.95. SWAN'S ISLAND By Elizabeth Spires. 56 pp. New York: Holt, Rinehart & Winston. Paper, $8.95.
MARY SWANDER'S ''Driving the Body

Back'' is a long poem that develops over the time it takes to drive the body of the first narrator's mother back to the town where she was born. Its novelistic form is direct and interesting. A butcher, a bootlegger, a one-eyed cigar smoker, a midwife and a country doctor are among those whose tales of heartbreak, desolation and grim truth also contain a gentle humor: Uncle George smoked short cigars and the night he died, flicking ash on the floor, said, ''Reach under the cot, honey, pull me out a beer.'' Because he weighed only three pounds at birth, Grandma kept him in the oven for warmth, and you still use the cake pan she lay him in.
headline: BOOTLEGGERS, KNEEWALKERS AND ACROBATIC DOLLS

title: A Taste Of Liberty
author: Bulat Okudzhava. Translated by Leo Gruliow.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A TASTE OF LIBERTY (Poor Avrosimov). By Bulat Okudzhava. Translated by Leo Gruliow. 223 pp. Ann Arbor, Mich.: Ardis. Cloth, $29.50. Paper, $9.95. I MET Bulat Okudzhava, the author of ''A Taste of Liberty,'' in January 1960 on my first visit to Leningrad. A group of poets from Moscow invited me one evening to the Oktyabr Hotel, where they were to read their new poems. Mr. Okudzhava is both a writer and a singer. To a simple guitar accompaniment, he performed the ballads that were to make him famous when he began singing them in public. We were all spellbound. Mr. Okudzhava was slender, elegant, dark-eyed. Though his performance was low-key, his ballads were full of lyric power. There was a slightly conspiratorial intensity to that evening; the poets present were all young, and their hopes for a freer, more humane Soviet Union were running high. They were not unlike the characters in ''A Taste of Liberty'' - the Decembrists, the young army officers who dreamed of a bright future for Russia in the 1820's, only to be banished or executed when their rebellion was crushed.
headline: REVENGE IN ST. PETERSBURG

title: The Cambridge Apostles
author: Richard Deacon
pull_quote: THE CAMBRIDGE APOSTLES: A History of Cambridge University's Elite Intellectual Secret Society. By Richard Deacon. 214 pages. Illustrated. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $19.95.   THE first thing a reader might want to know about Richard Deacon's social history, ''The Cambridge Apostles,'' is, Who were the members of this ''elite intellectual secret society,'' as the book's subtitle describes it? Well, the men who in 1820 founded what was originally called the Cambridge Conversazione Society were Edward Brice, Henry Thompson, John Punnett and so forth; there were 12 of them at first (hence the nickname ''apostles''), and, according to Mr. Deacon, they were ''somewhat undistinguished students,'' nearly all ''evangelical in that they sought to propagate the Gospels in some detail.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Against All Hope
author: Armando Valladares
pull_quote: AGAINST ALL HOPE. By Armando Valladares. Translated by Andrew Hurley. 381 pages. Illustrated. Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95.   ARMANDO VALLADARES was a 23-year-old civil servant when he was arrested by the Cuban political police early in 1961 and charged with ''acts of public destruction and sabotage.'' In effect, he was being put on trial for his beliefs, since the prosecution didn't and couldn't produce any evidence of ''public destruction'' beyond the fact that he had frequently spoken out against Communism, rejecting it as a system that went against his religious convictions and what he calls ''some of my more idealistic notions of the world.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Death Valley & The Amargosa
author: Richard E Lingenfelter
pull_quote: DEATH VALLEY & THE AMARGOSA: A Land of Illusion. By Richard E. Lingenfelter. 664 pages. University of California Press. $39.95.   DEATH VALLEY and its landmarks, Coffin Peak, the Funeral Mountains, Deadman Pass, Dry Bone Canyon, Dante's View; the names alone conjure up terrible images of suffocating heat, parched land and death by thirst and exposure. ''It is a pit of horrors - the haunt of all that is grim and ghoulish,'' observed one writer at the turn of the century. Another refered to it as an inferno inhabited by creatures ''conjured up by Satan''; and even that circumspect journal Scientific American once referred to it as the ''puit d'enfer'' - the pit of hell - into which ''very few persons have ever gone . . who returned to tell the tale.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Blessed Assurance
author: A G Mojtabai
pull_quote: BLESSED ASSURANCE: At Home With the Bomb in Amarillo, Texas. By A. G. Mojtabai. 256 pages. Houghton Mifflin. $16.95.   WITH time and freedom at last to work on a novel called ''Enter Fleeing'' - it would have been her fifth, after ''Mundome,'' ''The 400 Eels of Sigmund Freud,'' ''A Stopping Place,'' and ''Autumn'' - A. G. Mojtabai found herself in the fall of 1981 restless, depressed, and preoccupied with an article she had read and clipped about a company called Pantex in Amarillo, Tex., whose business was not foundation garments but the final assembly of all nuclear weapons in the United States.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Semites And Anti-Semites
author: Bernard Lewis
pull_quote: SEMITES AND ANTI-SEMITES: An Inquiry Into Conflict and Prejudice. By Bernard Lewis. 283 pages. W. W. Norton. $18.95. STRICTLY speaking there are no such people as Semites, only people who speak one or another of the Semitic languages. The term, as Bernard Lewis explains in his powerful new study, is a classification devised by philologists in the 18th century, and though it has often been misappropriated by racial theorizers it has nothing to do with race in the anthropological sense.   Anti-Semites, on the other hand, indubitably exist. Their defining characteristic is their hatred of Jews, which means that in principle (contrary to the argument sometimes advanced, which rests on a confusion of categories) it is perfectly possible for Arabs to be anti-Semitic, even though they speak a Semitic language. But what bearing does anti-Semitism actually have on the Arab-Israeli conflict?
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMS

title: Sweet Soul Music
author: Peter Guralnick
pull_quote: SWEET SOUL MUSIC. Rhythm and Blues and the Southern Dream of Freedom.   By Peter Guralnick. Illustrated. 438 pages. Harper & Row. $24.95 cloth. $14.95 paper. Soul music, as the critic Peter Guralnick defines it in his compelling new book, is something very specific - it's Southern in origin, gospel-based in sound and uncompromised in its visceral appeal to the emotions. Whereas Gerri Hirshey devoted a considerable portion of her recent study (''Nowhere to Run - The Story of Soul Music'') to the Detroit sound, Mr. Guralnick - who tends to shrug off Motown as a pop ''industry aimed specifically at reaching the white market'' - has chosen to focus his book on the music that developed after the initial success of Ray Charles and Sam Cooke in the mid-50's, and came into its own in the early and mid-60's with hits by such artists as Otis Redding, Solomon Burke, James Brown, Wilson Pickett, Percy Sledge and Aretha Franklin.
headline: RHYTHM AND BLUES

title: Selected Essays Of R. P. Blackmur
author: Denis Donoghue
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SELECTED ESSAYS OF R. P. BLACKMUR Edited, and with an introduction, by Denis Donoghue. 372 pp. New York: The Ecco Press. $17.50. THE critic R. P. Blackmur relished language and made close attention to its intricacies the hallmark of his intellectual life. What he wrote of Melville's achievement also says much about his own: ''Words, and their intimate arrangements . . . bring meaning to birth.''   In the years since Blackmur's death in 1965, literary criticism has changed significantly. Partly in reaction to the 30-year sway of formalist New Criticism exemplified by Blackmur, John Crowe Ransom and Allen Tate, it has become fashionable to embrace structuralist and poststructuralist literary theory in an effort to shift attention from the art object and the artist's voice to the cultural and linguistic systems or codes that govern discourse. ''Signifier'' and ''signified'' have replaced ''point of view'' and ''tone'' in the critical vocabulary. In the process, R. P. Blackmur has become a piece of literary history, respected but unread. Now, with the generous sampling of ''Selected Essays'' -carefully edited and perceptively introduced by Denis Donoghue, himself one of our best-informed and keenest critics of modern writing - readers may discover or rediscover Blackmur's impressive independence and insight.
headline: A MASTER OF CLOSE READING

title: Letters To Judy: What Your Kids Wish They Could Tell You
author: Judy Blume.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LETTERS TO JUDY What Your Kids Wish They Could Tell You. By Judy Blume. 284 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $17.95. JUDY BLUME is probably the most widely read author of novels for teen-agers, and the most widely criticized. She writes about things like menstruation and first sexual experience - issues that don't sit well with some adults. But these unmentionable topics are just the things that are on young people's minds.
headline: TAKING ADOLESCENTS SERIOUSLY

title: An Artist Of The Floating World
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AN ARTIST OF THE FLOATING WORLD By Kazuo Ishiguro. 206 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $15.95. IT is not unusual to find new novels by good writers, novels with precise wording, witty phrases, solid characterizations, scenes that engage. Good writers abound - good novelists are very rare. Kazuo Ishiguro is that rarity. His second novel, ''An Artist of the Floating World,'' is the kind that stretches the reader's awareness, teaching him to read more perceptively.   As the retired gentleman Masuji Ono chats with the reader, the words are simple, but where is the reality? Postwar Japan is a world of shifting values, of behavior complicated by polite formalities, of undeserved pride or unnecessary humility, of memories that swell to smug importance or disappear to suit convenience. The ''floating world'' of the title is the Japanese term for night life in the pleasure districts. But its meaning grows.
headline: AFTER THE WAR WAS LOST

title: Freddy And The Perilous Adventure
author: Walter R. Brooks. Illustrated by Kurt Wiese.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FREDDY AND THE PERILOUS ADVENTURE By Walter R. Brooks. Illustrated by Kurt Wiese. 245 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. Paper, $3.95. (Ages 7 to 12) FREDDY the pig, the hero of Walter R. Brooks's series of books first published in the 1940's, can talk. Which isn't surprising, since he lives on the Beans' farm in upstate New York, where all the animals - from Mrs. Wiggins the cow, to Eek, Quik, Meenie and Cousin Augustus, the mice - speak acceptable, if sometimes addled, English.   Freddy is a detective of some renown, who keeps a wardrobe of disguises in the tack room of the barn. He is a poet, and if the odes are, as his friend Breckenridge the eagle puts it, a bit ''high-flown,'' it is, as Samuel Johnson said of whistling dogs, enough that he does it at all. Freddy has adventures, not always willingly (he would, for example, never have gone up in a balloon were it not for some caramel candy that stuck his teeth together at the wrong moment) but always stout-heartedly.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Against All Hope
author: Armando Valladares. Translated by Andrew Hurley. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AGAINST ALL HOPE The Prison Memoirs of Armando Valladares. By Armando Valladares. Translated by Andrew Hurley. Illustrated. 381 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95. IN 1958, Jean-Paul Sartre helped rouse the conscience of France by writing an introduction to ''The Question'' by Henri Alleg, a small book that recounted the torture of a French opponent of the Algerian war in Algerian prisons. One had to decide, Sartre wrote, ''whether to be the torturer or the tortured.'' Alleg suffered the fate of all those tortured, Sartre wrote, and he showed ''the calm courage of the victim,'' as well as a modesty and lucidity ''which wake us and show us the truth.''   Now Armando Valladares, a Cuban poet, awakes us to the same task and truths. How ironic that a year after Sartre wrote these words, he visited Cuba and proclaimed to the world that Fidel Castro was motivated above all by a hatred for injustice, and that he had brought about the liberation of Cuba from despotism. It has taken us 25 years to find out the terrible reality -Mr. Castro has created a new despotism that has institutionalized torture as a mechanism of social control.
headline: SURVIVING CASTRO'S TORTURES

title: Democracy And Capitalism
author: Samuel Bowles and Herbert Gintis.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DEMOCRACY AND CAPITALISM Property, Community, and the Contradictions of Modern Social Thought. By Samuel Bowles and Herbert Gintis. 244 pp. New York: Basic Books. $16.95. HOW does one reconcile liberty, socialism and democracy? With an optimism all the more remarkable for its buoyancy in current political tides, two radical economists, Samuel Bowles and Herbert Gintis, present a case for ''postliberal democracy.'' In such a society, the visions of Locke, Marx and the radical democrats would all at last be realized. The authors argue that any other social order is inherently contradictory, hence unstable. Indeed, much of the book explores the contradictions among the rights classical liberals defend against the unlawful intrusions of others, the Marxists' call for economic justice and the democrats' vision of participation as the means to autonomy and self-realization. Mr. Bowles and Mr. Gintis, both professors of economics at the University of Massachusetts at Amherst, propose instead a ''visionary-historical conception'' of a world in which the claims of personal freedom, economic efficiency and popular sovereignty could all be simultaneously attained.
headline: POSTLIBERAL VISION

title: Mata Hari
author: Russell Warren Howe. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MATA HARI The True Story. By Russell Warren Howe. Illustrated. 292 pp. New York: Dodd, Mead & Company. $17.95. MARGARETHA GEERTRUIDA MACLEOD (nee Zelle), alias Mata Hari, was a preposterous fraud: a dancer during the Belle Epoque and a spy in World War I whose contributions to both dance and espionage were of negligible importance. Her mysterious blend of sex and spying, combined with her death at the hands of a firing squad, have made her, nonetheless, a household name.   Mata Hari first attracted public attention with her uniquely pretentious variety of striptease, which masqueraded as a form of religious devotion. In place of her unremarkable Dutch bourgeois origins she invented an exotic Oriental upbringing as a sacred dancer in a Hindu temple on the Ganges. By the time she began her dancing career in Paris she was also masquerading as Lady MacLeod, the daughter of an English lord. This capacity for fraudulent invention made her a star. Her well-connected audiences could assure themselves that they were witnessing not the vulgar titillation of the cancan but the sacred mysteries of the Orient performed by a refined artiste of aristocratic birth.
headline: SHE BLEW A KISS TO THE FIRING SQUAD

title: The Tolerant Society
author: Lee C. Bollinger.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE TOLERANT SOCIETY Freedom of Speech and Extremist Speech in America. By Lee C. Bollinger. 295 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $19.95. IN 1977 a neo-Nazi group applied for a permit to march in Skokie, Ill., a suburb of Chicago whose large Jewish population includes survivors of German concentration camps. When the permit was denied, the American Civil Liberties Union filed suit, arguing that the free speech clause of the First Amendment protected the group's right to march. The issue stirred up a broad national controversy; 30,000 A.C.L.U. members resigned in protest. Ultimately, the courts said the Nazis could march in Skokie. (They didn't, but held a brief demonstration in downtown Chicago instead.) Whether the Constitution should protect speech that defames religious and racial groups or advocates totalitarian government has long been controversial. Neither the language of the First Amendment nor the history surrounding its adoption answers these and other difficult questions concerning its scope and application. Rather, courts have muddled along as they do in most areas of law, their doctrines both relying on and giving rise to theories, or models, of the amendment. In ''The Tolerant Society,'' Lee Bollinger, a professor at the University of Michigan Law School, criticizes two standard theories and proposes a third.
headline: HOW FREE DO WE WANT TO BE?

title: Weapons In Space
author: Donald Hafner
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WEAPONS IN SPACE. Edited by Franklin A. Long, Donald Hafner and Jeffrey Boutwell. (Norton, $16.95.) President Reagan's desire for a space-based defense against Soviet missiles came as an equal surprise to defense analysts and the public.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Peep Show
author: David Black
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PEEP SHOW. By David Black. (Doubleday, $16.95.) David Black's third novel suffers from an acute case of literary schizophrenia. Its focus is the impact of a 16-year-old nymphet on a tired marriage, but its animus lies entirely in the lively digressions of an otherwise listless narrator.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Going For It!
author: Victor Kiam
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GOING FOR IT! How to Succeed as an Entrepreneur. By Victor Kiam. (Morrow, $16.95.) After generously sprinkling his text with the word ''entrepreneur,'' Victor Kiam no doubt wondered what additional spin was needed to move this account of his business exploits. Mr. Kiam, president of Remington Products, bought Remington and appears in the television commercials for the company's electric shaver.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Italian Baroque And Rococo Architecture
author: John Varriano
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ITALIAN BAROQUE AND ROCOCO ARCHITECTURE. By John Varriano. (Oxford University, Cloth, $27.95. Paper, $16.95.) A fashionable as well as scholarly work, this comprehensive study of Italian architecture from 1600 to 1750 should be of interest not only to those in the profession but to architecture buffs too. Mr. Varriano, a professor of art history at Mount Holyoke College, devotes separate chapters to three major Baroque architects - Francesco Borromini, Gianlorenzo Bernini and Pietro da Cortona - and discusses the genesis of various design schemes and the role that personal connections, papal patronage and church politics played in determining style and commissions.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: America Can Win
author: Gary Hart with William S. Lind.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AMERICA CAN WIN The Case for Military Reform. By Gary Hart with William S. Lind. 301 pp. Bethesda, Md.: Adler & Adler. $17.95. THE timing of this book could scarcely be better.   After five years of the largest peacetime arms buildup in its history, the United States military can no longer excuse its shortcomings as the product of budgetary neglect or Presidential weakness. And pressure to reduce the Federal deficit will insure that Congressional scrutiny of new military spending is severe.
headline: BATTLE PLANS

title: Red
author: Ira Berkow. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RED A Biography of Red Smith. By Ira Berkow. Illustrated. 302 pp. New York: Times Books. $17.95. PEOPLE expect an awful lot from their newspapers, and the news isn't the half of it: they also expect the Last Word on practically everything. Thus the poor drudges who blunt their taste at bad plays night after night, and the drones who have to master two books a week - books of a kind that most people put aside a whole summer to read - are assumed to be the most important critics in town, while the hurry-up sages of the editorial pages may be the only voice some people will ever hear on the Middle East or the decline of the yen. (All the above, by the way, is supposed to be done entertainingly.) It's a lot to ask for 30 cents, but certain hardy souls devote their lives to bucking the odds and making newspapers just that good; and of these, none delivered the goods more consistently than Red Smith, the subject of Ira Berkow's skillful biography. Un-initiates might object right off that sportswriting is too slight and easy to count in the Sisyphus League, but it is easy only in whatever sense six-day bicycle racing is easy. The sports guy merely has to pump his way round and round the same old sports calendar ''making it new,'' in Ezra Pound's words, every time around. To do this, he is advised to maintain, or simulate, the fresh heart and clear eye of a rookie - not to mention the zest for motel rooms of a political candidate -until he drops.
headline: A PRETTY NICE WAY TO MAKE A LIVING

title: Expensive Habits
author: Maureen Howard
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EXPENSIVE HABITS By Maureen Howard. 298 pp. New York: Summit Books. $17.95. IN ''Facts of Life'' (1978), Maureen Howard told the story of her childhood and self-education in Bridgeport, Conn., among Irish-American Catholics. Now, her fifth novel opens with an echo of the blunt priestly send-off from a confessional: ''Go and sin no more.'' The second word of this novel's title resonates with the word for a nun's outfit, but ''habits'' spreads a wider net than costume can define.   The habit for which Maureen Howard's protagonist, Margaret Flood, has paid dearly is less a show of style than a principle of feeling. Her scarab-hard carapace of manner reveals hardheartedness, and Margaret Flood's combat against her meaner reflexes of thought and feeling provokes the friction that provokes the heat of a smart, sharp novel that might have - given a smaller purpose than Miss Howard's - been cold.
headline: HARDHEARTED MARGARET

title: Blessed Assurance
author: A. G. Mojtabai.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BLESSED ASSURANCE At Home With the Bomb in Amarillo, Texas. By A. G. Mojtabai. 255 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $16.95. ''Y   OU know,'' Ronald Reagan told a pro-Israeli lobbyist in 1983, ''I turn back to your ancient prophets in the Old Testament and the signs foretelling Armageddon, and I find myself wondering if - if we're the generation that's going to see that come about, I don't know if you've noted any of these prophecies lately, but believe me, they certainly describe the times we're going through.''   The President's interest in Armageddon - reflected in several remarks over recent years - became an issue in the 1984 campaign, leading some critics to wonder whether Mr. Reagan wasn't predisposed toward nuclear apocalypse as the ultimate showdown between good and evil.
headline: THE RAPTURE AND THE BOMB

title: Suing The Press
author: Rodney A. Smolla.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SUING THE PRESS By Rodney A. Smolla. 277 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $18.95. CHARLES HORMAN, a young American writer, was in Chile in 1973 when a military coup overthrew Salvador Allende's Government. Two days later he disappeared. His father came to look for him - and became convinced that the American Embassy was obstructing the search, perhaps because his son had learned something about a United States role in the coup. Charles Horman's body was later found in a cemetery in Santiago.   The movie ''Missing'' was based on the story of the Hormans. It was directed by Constantin Costa-Gavras, and like his other films it was political in tone and angry at official inhumanity. Three United States officials took it personally and sued for libel. Nathaniel Davis, who had been Ambassador to Chile at the time, and two of his colleagues claimed they were damaged by a false implication of United States complicity in the murder of Charles Horman. They asked for $150 million. The Davis lawsuit is an example of a remarkable contemporary phenomenon: the thinning of the American skin. Public officials and public figures of all kinds are taking furious offense at published comments and are suing for libel - generals, governors, senators, ambassadors, judges. They seek damages in the hundreds of millions, although many, like former Ambassador Davis, might find it hard to show that they have been hurt in the pocketbook at all.
headline: THE RISKS OF REPORTING

title: Collected Writings
author: John Cornford
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: COLLECTED WRITINGS By John Cornford. Edited by Jonathan Galassi. 203 pp. New York: Carcanet. Paper, $10.50. AMERICAN COMMANDER IN SPAIN Robert Hale Merriman and the Abraham Lincoln Brigade. By Marion Merriman and Warren Lerude. Illustrated. 255 pp. Reno: University of Nevada Press. $16.95. THIS year marks the 50th anniversary of the start of the Spanish Civil War. Franco has been dead for a decade, Spain is a democracy once again, and as the passions of that time gradually ease, these two books are fitting commemoratives for the internationalists who went to the defense of the republic. One is ''Collected Writings'' by John Cornford, the English poet who was killed in 1936, leaving behind a truncated oeuvre, some political exhortations and a handful of letters from the Aragon front. The second, ''American Commander in Spain,'' is a personal recollection by his wife of Robert Hale Merriman, a young teacher at the University of California, Berkeley, who became chief of staff of the Abraham Lincoln Battalion and died in the retreat from Belchite in 1938. (As Mrs. Merriman notes, the organization was a battalion and only much later became popularly known as the Abraham Lincoln Brigade.) The charismatic Merriman may have been Hemingway's inspiration for Robert Jordan in ''For Whom the Bell Tolls.'' The two men met briefly in Madrid, and Hemingway was deeply impressed.
headline: CASUALTIES OF A 'PURE WAR'

title: A Funny Dirty Little War
author: Osvaldo Soriano
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A FUNNY DIRTY LITTLE WAR By Osvaldo Soriano. Translated by Nick Caistor. 108 pp. New York: Readers International/ Persea Books. Cloth, $12.50. Paper, $6.95. MOST of the Argentine literature that has made its way into English is associated with the work of Jorge Luis Borges and other fantasists, his spiritual children. But there is another kind of imagination at work in the Babel of Buenos Aires, feisty and brawling, rooted in the reality of the nation and its frequently noxious political atmosphere. Very often the writer looks with jaundiced eye at the repressive power structure that dominated the nation from the military coup of 1930 until the comic-epic encounter with Britain over the Falklands. None of the generals, now happily toppled, would be happy with Osvaldo Soriano's mordant vision of Juan Peron's dictatorship and that of his numerous successors.
headline: INNOCENCE UNDER SIEGE

title: Hidden Pictures
author: Meg Wolitzer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
HIDDEN PICTURES By Meg Wolitzer. 294 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $16.95. BOY meets girl. Boy marries girl. Boy loses girl. In light of standard publishing policies, this topic would have been thrown into the wastebasket along with stories about an Airedale biting a postman. But when boy loses girl - to another girl - and for good measure she takes along their 3-year-old son, we're talking news and what lies at the heart of Meg Wolitzer's second novel, ''Hidden Pictures.'' It is a challenging scenario, demanding an intense re-examination of our views on lesbianism, parenting and the structure of the traditional family. And it's a challenge that Meg Wolitzer, more often than not, meets.

Laura Giovanni is cut straight from the fiber of the Middle American farmlands. She's gone to the right schools, married the right man (a Yale Medical School graduate) and, after they've moved to New York City, even had the right child, named Ian. She has the perfect setup for balancing career and family - working at home as a freelance illustrator for children's magazines. It couldn't be better, except that Laura finds herself unhappy with her present life. She never discovers why, and neither does the reader.
headline: IAN'S MOTHER LIVES WITH JANE

title: Winter In Jerusalem
author: Blanche d'Alpuget
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WINTER IN JERUSALEM By Blanche d'Alpuget. 269 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $16.95. HER deliciously Princess-of-Cleves-type name notwithstanding, Blanche d'Alpuget is an Australian born and bred, the author of a vivid biography of that country's Prime Minister Bob Hawke among other books, and, as ''Winter in Jerusalem'' proves, a writer of talent and feistiness.   It is no news that the Middle East as a whole and Israel in particular are afflicted by perpetual tension and hostilities. By and large, the intricate issues involved in the Arab-Israeli conflict are also familiar, even if not always fully understood, and have received, to put it mildly, much exposure.   What is less known, trickier to write about, are the internal debates that have gone on for at least 3,750 years, which is the length of time since the Jews began their seemingly endless arguments with one another, with their neighbors and, most vociferously, with God. Bear in mind that in Hebrew the name Israel means ''He who struggles with God.'' Pared to their essence, these arguments concern the sort of people the Jews should be, the sort of state they should form, the sort of relationship they should sustain with their Creator.
headline: IN EXILE FROM THE PROMISED LAND

title: Tone Deaf And All Thumbs?
author: Frank R. Wilson.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TONE DEAF AND ALL THUMBS? An Invitation to Music-Making for Late Bloomers and Non-prodigies. By Frank R. Wilson. 210 pp. New York: Viking. $15.95. FOR those who were not prodigies, the lure of being able to make music has strong appeal. The usual alibi is, ''It's already too late. I'm too old to start now.'' In ''Tone Deaf and All Thumbs?'' Frank R. Wilson, a physician, delivers a refutation that is a blend of scientific analysis, personal experience and enthusiastic encouragement. He presents an analysis of the brain and the muscular system; considers the neurological basis of auditory perception; describes the biology of timing, rhythm and tempo; explores the visual system and its application to musical notation; discusses principles of learning theory; confronts the problem of stage fright; and offers advice on getting started.
headline: IS THERE A MUSICIAN IN THE HOUSE?

title: The News From Ireland
author: William Trevor.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE NEWS FROM IRELAND And Other Stories. By William Trevor. 285 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $16.95. TEN novels, six story collections and numerous dramatic writings have already come to us from William Trevor, and in this his seventh book of short fiction he proves once more that he is best when writing about his native land. Born in County Cork and educated in Dublin, he now lives in Devon. That England has been his home for a long time can be surmised from the quantity of fiction he has written about the English - country English, village English, London English, the English abroad. Mr. Trevor is a sturdy writer of clear and satisfying prose, who knows how to seek out the fictionally viable character and how to catch the pulse beat in a relationship or the secret strain within a heart. Yet his English stories seem strangely ''produced,'' planned instead of crying to be written. It is the news from Ireland that, wander where he will, he is always returning to give voice to - and these are the stories with flow and power.
headline: FRENCH LESSONS WHILE THE NEIGHBORS STARVE

title: The Outside Story
author: Richard Brookhiser
pull_quote: THE OUTSIDE STORY: How Democrats and Republicans Elected Reagan. By Richard Brookhiser. 299 pages. Doubleday. $17.95.   PRESIDENTIAL election seasons go on nonstop now, without even the brief breathing spaces available to fans of other sports. Before Ronald Reagan was renominated in 1984, observers were busy analyzing how Bob Dole, Howard Baker and George Bush were already positioning themselves for 1988. Even as Mario Cuomo was getting cheers at the Democratic convention that would anoint Walter Mondale, thoughts flew ahead to what role Mr. Cuomo would play at the convention four years later. And now, to confuse matters, as we are comfortably settled, watching the hopeful players suit up for the next tournament, along comes a book that takes us back to 1984.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Selling Of The Royal Family
author: John Pearson
pull_quote: THE SELLING OF THE ROYAL FAMILY: The Mystique of the British Monarchy. By John Pearson. 350 pages. Illustrated. Simon & Schuster. $17.95. THE worldwide fascination with the British royal family has become such an obvious fact of life in recent years that it is tempting to take its growth for granted - how could it have been otherwise? Yet in reality there was nothing inevitable about it. As Britain's standing in the world declined, the monarchy could easily have dwindled into a faded minor attraction, of largely local interest. That it should have evolved instead into one of the greatest shows on earth remains a much more extraordinary business than is commonly acknowledged.   This is the phenomenon that John Pearson has taken for his subject in ''The Selling of the Royal Family.'' He is concerned not so much with the well-worn repertory of royal stories as with the story of those stories -the ways in which they have been presented, and their public impact. A seasoned journalist, whose previous books include biographies of Ian Fleming and the Sitwells, Mr. Pearson combines shrewd judgment with a keen eye for social nuance; he has succeeded in pursuing his researches into regions where facts are still frequently elusive, and by virtue of his approach he holds your interest even when dealing with dramas that you might well have felt you never wanted to read about again.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Triumph Of Pierrot
author: Martin Green
pull_quote: THE TRIUMPH OF PIERROT. The Commedia dell'Arte and the Modern Imagination. By Martin Green and John Swan. Illustrated. 297 pages. Macmillan. $25. WHAT do Stravinsky, Degas, Chaplin, Isak Dinesen, Meyerhold, Monty Python and T. S. Eliot have in common? What do such disparate works as Picasso's ''Family of Saltimbanques,'' Bergman's ''Sawdust and Tinsel,'' Waugh's ''Put Out More Flags'' and Pirandello's ''Six Characters in Search of an Author'' share? As Martin Green and John Swan persuasively argue in their new book, all have been influenced by the Italian commedia dell'arte.   No doubt most of us are familiar enough with commedia's main characters as described by Mr. Green: ''Pierrot, at least in modern times, wears a black skullcap, white floppy pants and jacket, a pale, gaunt makeup. Harlequin wears tights, designed in contrasting diamonds of color, often spangled, and carries a stick. Columbine is sumptuously and sensually adorned. The naive, defenseless, moonstruck Pierrot adores the lovely Columbine, who has wit and feeling enough to appreciate his worth but is too light-minded to resist the coarse and brutal Harlequin, who is himself bound to Pierrot in a mocking, rueful, treacherous comradeship.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Hot Properties
author: Rafael Yglesias
pull_quote: HOT PROPERTIES. By Rafael Yglesias. 408 pages. Dutton. $16.95.   WE meet the main characters of ''Hot Properties'' at the New York City dinner party with which Rafael Yglesias opens his new novel. They have labels coming out of them like those spikes you stick in the soil to distinguish the tomatoes from the pole beans. There is Fred Tatter, the dumpy sportswriter turned aspiring novelist; Patty Lane, the sexy blonde who carries around her brain like a concealed weapon; David Bergman, the youngest senior writer at Newstime magazine, and Tony Winters, the playwright prodigy whose Hollywood parents lived through the McCarthy era.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Prodigy
author: Amy Wallace
pull_quote: THE PRODIGY. By Amy Wallace. Illustrated. 297 pages. E. P. Dutton. $18.95. FAME came early to William   James Sidis, while he was still a small child - but then how much of a childhood can he be said to have had? Not long after he was born, in 1898, his parents, in keeping with their belief that ''a baby is never too young to start learning anything,'' hung alphabet blocks over his crib. By his second year he was spelling, reading and counting; at the age of 3 he taught himself Latin and Greek.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Delirium Eclipse And Other Stories
author: James Lasdun
pull_quote: DELIRIUM ECLIPSE AND OTHER STORIES. By James Lasdun. 200 pages. Harper & Row. $15.95. James Lasdun loves metaphors. This sparkling new collection of stories by this young British writer absolutely bristles with them - as well as extended similes, striking descriptions and hallucinatory images. A college professor finds himself lost in a subway maze that reflects his own disordered state of mind. An ambitious writer watches a former mentor die of a wasting illness that reminds him of his own disloyalty to his ex-teacher's ideas. An unhappy child indulges in an orgy of eating and destruction that mirrors the torment he feels over his mother's burgeoning romance with a divorced man.   Such thumbnail sketches tend to make these tales sound somewhat contrived, mechanical even, and there are moments in this volume when the reader feels bloated with a surfeit of coincidence: in the title story, for instance, a solar eclipse heralds the hero's descent into illness, which in turn serves as a metaphor for the feverish jealousy he feels toward his wayward girlfriend. Other stories pivot around all-too-ironic twists of fate. In ''The Siege,'' a young woman finds her wary indifference toward her employer turning into passion, even as her long-term wish - to be reunited with her missing husband - is miraculously granted. And in ''Heart's Desire,'' a provincial teen-ager's fascination with a group of upper-class decadents abruptly sours, as soon as he has a chance to make contact with them.
headline: Tales of Anxiety

title: Cecil Beaton: A Biography
author: Hugo Vickers. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CECIL BEATON A Biography. By Hugo Vickers. Illustrated. 656 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $25. CECIL BEATON, who died six years ago at the age of 76, was an English photographer, set designer, illustrator, portraitist and writer. Critics used to argue over whether he was a true artist in any of these pursuits or merely slick. But on one point everybody, tout le monde, agreed. Cecil Beaton was a great snob. He was not just a big snob but a great snob, an ingenious snob and a daredevil on top of that, a perfect snob and a snob clear through. So much so, that this book by Hugo Vickers, the biographer Beaton chose shortly before he died, turns out to be something Beaton may not have envisioned: an enormous, sloughing, tireless, unsparing, inch-by-inch trench-warfare chronicle of an English snob's progress through the 20th century.   Snob is a purely English term. There is no direct translation of the word in any other language. The French were reduced to importing it intact as le snob. Rightly so; le snobisme is a supremely English talent. A snob is someone who judges all things, from shoes and dinner parties to love and beauty, according to their social rating. And there you have Cecil Beaton. This book is not ''Vanity Fair,'' although it is nearly as long, but Beaton is the Becky Sharp of the 20th century.
headline: SNOB'S PROGRESS

title: To The Ends Of The Earth
author: Michael Talbot
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH. By Michael Talbot. (Knopf, $18.95.) Basing his novel on the settlement of Australia by British convicts in the late 18th century, Michael Talbot assembles a diverse crew of voyagers, mostly credible if not especially engaging. For Commodore Arthur Phillip, who leads a convoy of semiseaworthy vessels into partly uncharted seas, the venture is a desperate race against the French for territorial expansion. For the prisoners below decks, it is an unexpected alternative to the gallows. The narrative shifts from group to group, bringing into focus varying backgrounds and perspectives through some singular character types: Phillip, a bootstrap tough, a born risk taker; Kitty Brandon, whose credentials include some onstage triumphs and an offstage murder; Joe Cribb, a former soldier turned loose to live by his wits amid the London low life; Levi, a onetime peddler and medical quack in whom Messianic fervor is at war with practical experience. Although he knows that nothing can be had for nothing, he dreams of Australia's Botany Bay as an earthly paradise for the lost tribes of Israel. The Anglican cleric Richard Johnson disdains a land of milk and honey; what he wants is a harvest of Christian souls. By the end of the book part of the fleet has reached Botany Bay, but since this is the first in Mr. Talbot's projected series of novels about the founding of Australia, journey's end is only a beginning. The author (under a pseudonym) of spy novels and thrillers, he knows how to keep readers engrossed in the drama and brutality of naval exploration.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

author: W Andrew Achenbaum
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOCIAL SECURITY: Visions and Revisions, By W. Andrew Achenbaum. (Cambridge University, $19.95.) Many politicians and some actuaries say the Federal Government solved the financial problems of the social security system, at least for the rest of this century, when it passed a bill to prevent the bankruptcy of the giant pension program in 1983.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Off For The Sweet Hereafter
author: T. R. Pearson.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OFF FOR THE SWEET HEREAFTER By T. R. Pearson. 283 pp. New York: Linden Press/Simon & Schuster. $17.95. IT'S been just a year since the publication of T.R. Pearson's first novel, ''A Short History of a Small Place,'' in which he did his best to explain why an elderly woman in Neely, N.C., leaped backward off the town water tower. Our ribs have barely stopped aching when he's at it again, this time trying to sum up the ramshackle career of Neely's very own Bonnie and Clyde.   That his narratives are more often attempts at narratives, proposing to tell a certain story but veering helplessly at every fork in the road to scoop up other stories that strike him as equally worthwhile, is partly what makes them so funny. Like one of his own characters, he can't present the simplest occurrence without a preliminary ''two or three dozen laps all roundabout the dilemma.''
headline: HE DID IT ALL FOR JANE ELIZABETH FIRESHEETS

title: A Father's Words
author: Richard Stern
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A FATHER'S WORDS By Richard Stern. 189 pp. New York: Arbor House. $14.95. IN his new novel, ''A Father's Words,'' Richard   Stern gives us snapshots, through the eyes of Cyrus Riemer, of a comfortable middle-class man's divorce, his long-suffering former wife (who joins the Peace Corps at 55), his girlfriend (who talks in code and baby talk), the world of gamy personal ads, death, birth, grief, the body petering out and unexpected moola coming in. Most of all, Mr. Stern gives us a glimmer of fatherhood and how it goes to the marrow of one's bones. He gives us Riemer and his son Jack.
headline: SON OF A SAD SACK

title: Shallow Graves: Two Women And Vietnam
author: Wendy Wilder Larsen and Tran Thi Nga.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHALLOW GRAVES Two Women and Vietnam. By Wendy Wilder Larsen and Tran Thi Nga. 291 pp. New York: Random House. $16.95.   WENDY WILDER LARSEN, an American poet, spent 1970-71 with her husband, a journalist, in Saigon, South Vietnam, where she met Tran Thi Nga, the bookkeeper in her husband's office. ''Shallow Graves,'' begun after the two women were reunited in the United States in 1975, tells Wendy Larsen's own story of her year as a teacher of English literature, as well as Tran Thi Nga's life story, beginning with her birth in China in 1927 and ending with her present life in Cos Cob, Conn., where she and her family maintain an uneasy relationship with American culture. The book was written in English as a verse novel, or truyen, a Vietnamese form, and though at first the enterprise seems a curious amalgam of choices, this reader was soon won over. Mrs. Nga's story reads like a Shakespeare play; the people in it are reflected to us in both everyday and tragic dimensions, as they adapt - or fail to - to the larger demands of history and change.
headline: VIETNAM, EAST AND WEST

title: The Garish Day
author: Rachel Billington
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GARISH DAY By Rachel Billington. 335 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $17.95.   HARRY HAYES-MIDDLETON is a perfect product of the British class and educational system. With his ''sallow European looks'' and ''acute, well-ordered intelligence'' at the service of an extreme desire to satisfy anyone and no one, it's almost inevitable that he'll end up as a ''composed, clever member of the Foreign Office.'' After all, his father, the amiably pompous but womanizing Lionel, has steadily climbed the diplomatic service ladder until, by sheer effort of mediocrity, he has become British Ambassador to Washington. And Harry hasn't any objections to following in his father's - or anybody else's -footsteps. There are lots of amiably brilliant nincompoops like Harry around. ''They all,'' says an observer in Rachel Billington's odd but compelling novel, ''had a slightly dazed expression masked under an air of independence and competency.''
headline: SPIRITUALLY REORGANIZING HARRY

title: On The Meaning Of Victory: Essays On Strategy
author: Edward N. Luttwak.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ON THE MEANING OF VICTORY Essays on Strategy. By Edward N. Luttwak. 315 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.   EVEN the finest writer on public policy occasionally sets down words he would dearly love to take back. Assembling a collection of articles, as Edward N. Luttwak does in ''On the Meaning of Victory,'' may indicate the courage to have one's declarations tested by time, or the vanity to think one's every utterance worth preserving, or a little of both. Usually it's a little of both, and this case is no exception.   The author, a military affairs analyst affiliated with Georgetown University's Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington think tank, has three distinctions. First, Mr. Luttwak is a self-described hawk quite popular in conservative political circles, yet he argues tirelessly that the Pentagon is a bureaucracy run wild: it is out of touch with actual conditions, its weapons are unreliable, its tactics muddled by lowest-common-denominator committee structures, its strategic vision absent altogether. Second, in spite of all this, Mr. Luttwak also serves as a Pentagon consultant.
headline: HAWK VS. PENTAGON

author: Peter Evans
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ARI: The Life and Times of Aristotle Socrates Onassis. By Peter Evans. (Summit, $19.95.) Shortly before his death in 1975, Aristotle Onassis boasted to the British journalist Peter Evans that his life would make ''one hell of a story.''

title: Consuming Passions: The Dynamics Of Popular Culture
author: Judith Williamson. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CONSUMING PASSIONS The Dynamics of Popular Culture. By Judith Williamson. Illustrated. 240 pp. New York: Marion Boyars. $19.95.   JUDITH WILLIAMSON is a 32-year-old British journalist, critic and film maker whom the New Statesman has called ''the most incisive pop culture commentator presently at work in the left press.'' In ''Consuming Passions,'' a collection of 21 essays divided into sections on feminism, photography, film and politics, she argues that a consumer society channels our needs, desires and strong emotions into the marketplace. Her essays examine the ways in which popular culture recycles our passions and sells them back to us in familiar, but sometimes deceptive, forms. ''We are consuming passions all the time,'' observes Miss Williamson - ''at the shops, at the movies, in the streets, in the classroom.''

title: Reversal Of Fortune: Inside The Von Bulow Case
author: Alan M. Dershowitz. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: REVERSAL OF FORTUNE Inside the von Bulow Case. By Alan M. Dershowitz. Illustrated. 276 pp. New York: Random House. $19.95. ALAN M. DERSHOWITZ begins ''Reversal of   Fortune,'' his book on the von Bulow case, with a remark from one of the prosecutors involved:   ''This case has everything. It has money, sex, drugs; it has Newport, New York and Europe; it has nobility; it has maids, butlers, a gardener.'' It has in addition several other compelling characteristics, including a cast of thoroughly unappealing characters, a crime (if there was a crime) that millions of unhappily married people have contemplated and a lawyer with a book contract. The case has everything, in fact, except a hero, but that is where Mr. Dershowitz comes in, at least in his version of the story.

title: Semites And Anti-Semites
author: Bernard Lewis.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
SEMITES AND ANTI-SEMITES An Inquiry Into Conflict and Prejudice. By Bernard Lewis. 283 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $18.95.

BERNARD LEWIS wrote this provocative book to sound the alarm against what he sees as the deepest and most dire consequence of the Arab-Israeli conflict - the growth of anti-Semitism in the Islamic world. Mr. Lewis, who as the Cleveland E. Dodge Professor of Near Eastern Studies at Princeton University and a member of the Institute for Advanced Study is an acknowledged authority on Islam, devotes a good half of the book, however, to a history of Western anti-Semitism, in which he is dependent, for the most part, on the work of others. And yet, derivative though it is, Mr. Lewis's discussion of Western anti-Semitism is necessary to set off the story that he has come to tell, that anti-Semitism in the Islamic world, past and even present, is historically different from, and less virulent than, this hatred in the Christian West, where it is rooted in the Gospel accounts of the Christ story. But anti-Semitism in the Arab world, he believes, is now growing alarmingly.

title: A Conspiracy Of Cells
author: Michael Gold.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A CONSPIRACY OF CELLS One Woman's Immortal Legacy and the Medical Scandal It Caused. By Michael Gold. 170 pp. Albany: State University of New York Press. Cloth, $29.50. Paper, $10.95. TWO of President Nixon's laudable aims in the early 1970's were detente with the Soviet Union and the conquest of cancer. Both objectives were impeded in strange ways by a living legacy from a Baltimore woman who died of cancer many years earlier. ''A Conspiracy of Cells'' is the fascinating and troubling story of what has happpened to her cancer cells since she died.   The central character is Walter Nelson-Rees, an expert in the study of human and animal cells growing in laboratory culture flasks, who worked for many years for the University of California at an Oakland laboratory. Cell cultures are crucial to the growth of viruses and all manner of biological research; they have contributed to major advances in cancer research and molecular biology.

title: Within The Labyrinth
author: Norman Lewis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WITHIN THE LABYRINTH By Norman Lewis. 258 pp. New York: Carroll & Graf. $16.95.   HAVE you ever been to the mountainous outback of Southern Italy? Probably not. Neither had a young British sergeant named Manning, who is the protagonist of Norman Lewis's ''Within the Labyrinth.'' After a dreary war, years in Iraq filing useless intelligence reports, his posting to Italy is his chance to do a good job and retrieve his self-respect.
headline: BETWEEN THE MARSHAL AND THE MARCHESA

title: Half The Way Home: A Memoir Of Father And Son
author: Adam Hochschild.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HALF THE WAY HOME A Memoir of Father and Son. By Adam Hochschild. 198 pp. New York: Viking. $15.95.   The only child of older parents leads an unreal life. From the start he is worshiped like the Christ Child; he has made his parents, by his very birth, prodigious. The mother stands out among her equals, a living river of fecundity that mocks the curse of age. The father can be seen by his coevals as the man they fear they can no longer be. The child is long awaited, or a windfall for which his parents never dared to hope. He is the subject of enormous expectations and fears. He looks with awe at the parents of his friends: less kind perhaps, less patient, certainly less tired. A father coaching Little League, a mother running down a hill become for him the emblems of a glamorous and easy joy. He sees how his friends need not fear quite as he does for their parents; mortality does not brush quite so near these others, nor the glaring eye of fate so certainly approach. The pressures exhaust him, and yet only with his parents is he truly happy; try as he may he is not himself among the commoners. Yet he envies his friends their easy lot, as Isaac must have envied the sons of others, not led up the mountain, not the living symbols of their fathers' worth before the Lord.
headline: LOVE IN HEAVY ARMOR

title: Milk And Honey
author: Elizabeth Jolley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: Peter Ackroyd: Peter Ackroyd'S Most Recent Book Is the NovelHawksmoor.''
pull_quote: MILK AND HONEY By Elizabeth Jolley. 185 pp. New York: Persea Books. Cloth, $14.95. Paper, $8.95. IT has often been said of Australian fiction that its style is essentially baroque - certainly its extravagant conceits, its mannered exuberance and its perverse comedy have struck an entirely new note in English writing since World War II. And there is a sense in which Elizabeth Jolley's latest novel, ''Milk and Honey,'' reflects this interesting development - even though she is an Australian by choice rather than by extraction. She was born in England, brought up in a German-speaking household, and did not immigrate to the other hemisphere until 1959 (at the age of 36); that is perhaps why the cultural landscape of this novel is essentially a European one, despite its Australian setting.   It is written in the form of a monologue - the voice that of Jacob, a quondam cellist whose hand has been so badly charred in an accident that he is now forced to earn a precarious living as a door-to-door salesman. The mood of the book, therefore, is one of bleakness and frustration, and almost at once Jacob's unhappy narrative reverts to ''the shuddering, muttering, mocking nightmare which belongs with childhood.'' This is a nightmare from which he has never been able fully to awake, however, and the opening sequences cast their shadows across the entire novel.
headline: TWO CULTURES, ONE TRANSPLANTED

title: Gender Justice
author: David L. Kirp, Mark G. Yudof and Marlene Strong Franks.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GENDER JUSTICE By David L. Kirp, Mark G. Yudof and Marlene Strong Franks. 246 pp. Illinois: University of Chicago Press. $19.95.   HERE is a book about sexual equality that supports collective bargaining for ''comparable worth'' wage equity; that supports sex-neutral cash grants to the parents of young children and opposes government supervision of the private lives of the recipients; that supports vigorous government efforts against discrimination in employment; that opposes the exemption of women from jury duty and perhaps even from combat duty in the armed forces. Feminists will probably welcome ''Gender Justice'' - but not necessarily.
headline: LIBERTY AND AUTONOMY FOR ALL

title: Ulysses
author: James Joyce
pull_quote: JAMES JOYCE'S classic novel ''Ulysses'' has daunted many potential readers with its intellectual mystique. Even dedicated fiction-lovers often shy away from it, fearing that its dense allusions and knotty puns might prove impenetrable. One alternative approach to ''Ulysses'' is by ear. When the novel is properly read aloud, Joyce's fascination with language extends beyond meaning into a kind of literary music.   The sounds of Joyce will pour from two local stages tomorrow evening on the 82d anniversary of Bloomsday -June 16, 1904, the fictional day in Dublin on which all the events of ''Ulysses'' take place. Tomorrow evening, Symphony Space's fifth annual Bloomsday celebration, ''Bloomsday on Broadway V,'' will present six hours of readings from Joyce, from 7 P.M. to 1 A.M. Among the 70 participating actors, many of them veterans of previous Bloomsday celebrations, are Peggy Cass, Henderson Forsythe, Tammy Grimes, Jonathan Hadari, David Margulies, Frank McCourt, Malachy McCourt, Marian Seldes, Lois Smith, Maria Tucci and Fritz Weaver. ''Bloomsday on Broadway V'' will also be broadcast live, on WBAI-FM (99.5) in New York, as well as on more than 30 public radio stations nationwide.

JOSEF BERNHARDT was a 16-year-old mathematical whiz kid when he was banned from school in Berlin during the Third Reich because of his Jewish mother. He was sent, for his own protection and by grace of his genius and his family connections, to the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute. This neurological institute, the core and substance of Elly Welt's flawed but provocative second novel, ''Berlin Wild,'' was set up to conduct genetic research on fruit flies on the lower floors and collect the Aryan brains of downed Luftwaffe fliers on the upper floors.

title: The Not-Just-Anybody Family
author: Betsy Byars
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE NOT-JUST-ANYBODY FAMILY By Betsy Byars. Illustrated by Jacqueline Rogers. 149 pp. New York: Delacorte Press. $13.95. (Ages 10 to 14) ABOUT two-thirds of the way through Betsy Byars's new novel for children, ''The Not-Just-Anybody Family,'' a kindly bus driver says to 12-year-old Maggie Blossom, ''You take care of yourself. You the only member of your family doing all right. Everybody else in jail, in the hospital.''   Everybody else includes 11-year-old Vern, who has busted into jail to be with his grandfather Pap, who was arrested for firing his shotgun on Spring Street after two teen-agers in a Toyota purposely ran over his collection of 2,147 beer and pop cans, scattering them all over the road, and 7-year-old Junior, who has broken both legs trying to fly off the top of the Blossoms' barn (he was wearing wings; they just didn't work). Then there is the family dog, whose name is Mud, lost in the shuffle when Pap is taken away to jail, the subject of a humanitarian all-points bulletin as he tries to make his way back home across the busy city. The Blossom children's mother, Vicki, a rodeo trick rider, is away on the circuit while all this is going on; the children's father was killed a few years ago by a runaway steer in a rodeo accident in Nebraska.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Hitler's Games: The 1936 Olympics
author: Duff Hart-Davis. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HITLER'S GAMES The 1936 Olympics. By Duff Hart-Davis. Illustrated. 256 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $16.95.   FOR the Western democracies, the 1930's were years of economic depression and domestic turmoil, and it is understandable that their governments and peoples found it difficult to think seriously about matters beyond their own boundaries. Hence the failure to come to grips at an early stage with the menacing new regime that took power in Germany in January 1933. To the majority of Americans, Hitler was not a source of concern until the very end of the decade, when they reacted to his existence almost with surprise, like the woman in James Thurber's 1938 cartoon who asks, ''Who is this Hitler and what does he want?'' In Britain, the Hitler problem was held at bay by irony and humor - as in David Low's endless strip ''Hit and Muss,'' about the adventures of two vaguely familiar dictators who own a tandem bicycle, and in J. C. Squire's mocking verse: What's the use of Goering?
headline: ATHLETICS AS USUAL

title: Farce And Fantasy
author: Robert M. Isherwood. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FARCE AND FANTASY Popular Entertainment in Eighteenth-Century Paris. By Robert M. Isherwood. Illustrated. 324 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $29.95.   TO see a city en fete is to observe the place and its culture in their most precise and concentrated form. Urban festival culture, in all its variety, is not a world apart, but rather a highly condensed and intensified representation of the ''ordinary'' world of everyday urban experience, focused, refracted and sometimes even reversed by the powerful lens of the festive occasion. An engraving like the aerial view of the St.-Germain fair included in Robert M. Isherwood's study, ''Farce and Fantasy: Popular Entertainment in Eighteenth-Century Paris,'' simultaneously documents the permanent buildings of the fair, the fair itself at the height of its commercial activity and, in the foreground, a typical theatrical platform with performance in progress.
headline: PARISIAN BLOCK PARTIES

title: The Dream Of Deliverance In American Politics
author: Mona Harrington
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DREAM OF DELIVERANCE IN AMERICAN POLITICS By Mona Harrington. 308 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $19.95. ''THE American promise is in trouble,'' Mona Harrington warns in this ambitious and intriguing book. We face social and economic problems of great danger and staggering complexity; yet we deal with those problems by relying on simplistic and inadequate assumptions. Above all, we are crippled by our attachment to a longstanding and, in Miss Harrington's view, dangerous myth: the belief ''that human relations are, by their nature, harmonious, that serious conflict in human societies is unnatural and unnecessary,'' and that a series of relatively simple adjustments can establish a ''beneficent natural order'' in which all discord will be peacefully resolved ''without loss to any legitimate interest.''

title: Hirohito: The War Years
author: Paul Manning
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HIROHITO: The War Years. By Paul Manning. (Dodd Mead, $16.95.) Much of the history and biography in Paul Manning's ''Hirohito'' has already been covered in William Manchester's ''American Caesar'' and the diaries of the Marquis Kido, Lord Privy Seal in the Imperial Government during World War II and after. Mr. Manning's problem is that the prewar Emperor was a divine, aloof being whom few Japanese even saw.
