title: The Underground Empire
author: James Mills
pull_quote: THE UNDERGROUND EMPIRE: Where Crime and Governments Embrace. By James Mills. 1,165 pages. Doubleday. $22.95.   NEVER mind the enormous length of James Mills's new book, ''The Underground Empire: Where Crime and Governments Embrace'' - an astonishing five-year investigation into international drug traffic. This is one of those all-too-rare books that is both thick and substantial, and despite its size, I found myself reading every word of it for several days, savoring its remarkable mix of characters and subplots.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Who Goes Out In The Midday Sun?
author: Benedict Allen
pull_quote: WHO GOES OUT IN THE MIDDAY SUN? An Englishman's Trek Through the   Amazon Jungle. By Benedict Allen. Illustrated. 249 pages. Viking. $18.95.    ''WHEN I first heard its name,'' writes Benedict Allen, ''Amazonia was a land of steaming jungle on the equator inhabited by naked savages. All the savages were headhunters and most would eat each other given half the chance. The fiercest of them were tribes of women warriors who cut off their right breasts to fire their arrows with greater ease. Their targets were mainly explorers, who roamed the forest in search of gold. But amongst these primitives were some Good Indians, and because explorers gave them presents of salt (hard to get in the jungle) they guided the white men through the wilderness.'' That's how Mr. Allen saw the Amazon when he was 10 years old, and a dozen years later, still hungry for adventure, he satisfied his curiosity by going there and making a 1,000-mile trek through the jungle on foot. This book - the latest of several on the Amazon published this spring - is an account of that journey.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Last Blossom On The Plum Tree
author: Brooke Astor
pull_quote: THE LAST BLOSSOM ON THE PLUM TREE. A Period Piece. By Brooke Astor. 244 pages. Random House. $16.95. 8420THE characters in this charming new comedy of manners like to use phrases like ''top drawer'' and ''good blood'' and ''well bred.'' They ride about in Crane Simplexes and Hispano-Suizas; vacation in Monte Carlo and Baden-Baden; go dove-shooting in South Carolina and hunting in Kenya, and they live in homes with names like Villa Contenta and Bella Vista. When in London, they stay at Brown's; in New York, at the Ritz; in Rome, at the Hassler. They get their clothes from Paris, their butlers from England. The men refer to their girlfriends as mistresses; the women worry about what the servants will think.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Men's Lives
author: Peter Matthiessen
pull_quote: MEN'S LIVES: The Surfmen and Baymen of the South Fork. By Peter Matthiessen. Illustrated. 339 pages. Random House. $29.95.   ONCE upon a time, over three centuries ago, the South Fork, at the eastern end of Long Island, was a land of plenty. According to the text that Peter Matthiessen has written for this haunting documentary record, there were whales of many types in the waters, half-ton sturgeon bursting with roe, lobsters that often weighed between 10 and 20 pounds, flounders as big as serving plates, and enough other varieties of fish and mollusks to keep men busy catching them all the seasons round.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: War Without Mercy
author: John W Dower
pull_quote: WAR WITHOUT MERCY: Race and Power in the Pacific War. By John W. Dower. 399 pages. Illustrated. Pantheon Books. $22.50. FOUR and a half decades after   Pearl Harbor, ''War Without Mercy'' is one of the most original and important books to be written about the war between Japan and the United States. More than any official history and beyond any novel written by American or Japanese authors, John W. Dower's book explains how the prejudices and deceptions of racial and national pride - in both countries - were an underlying cause of the Pacific War.
headline: Books: Of Bias and War

title: Storm Center
author: David M O'Brien
pull_quote: STORM CENTER: The Supreme Court in American Politics. By David M. O' Brien. Illustrated. 384 pages. W. W. Norton. $18.95.   LIKE the centers of real storms, the Supreme Court is a tranquil area. Despite clashes of ideology and personality and the occasional testy exchange, it operates by a set of rituals, traditions and customs developed over decades that make it a more orderly and courteous place than its coequal branches of Government. Nonetheless, as David M. O'Brien shows in his timely and illuminating analysis, from the appointment of Justices to their choice of cases to the phrasing of decisions, the High Court is as subject to the political weather as Congress and the executive branch. He demonstrates, in an undemonstrative way, that the power of America's pre-eminently anti-democratic and countermajoritarian institution rests upon the approval or acquiescence of the nation.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Half The Way Home
author: Adam Hochschild
pull_quote: HALF THE WAY HOME. A Memoir of Father and Son. By Adam Hochschild. 198 pages. Viking. $15.95. To the world, Harold Hochschild was not only an enormously successful businessman (the head of Amax Inc., one of the largest mining concerns in the world) but also the consummate gentleman - charming, generous and fluent in the worlds of business, politics and the arts.   To his son, Adam, however, Harold Hochschild seemed a fearsome presence - a judgmental patriarch, the threat of whose disapproval hung darkly over his entire childhood; and as he recounts in this memoir, he would spend his entire life trying to come to terms with him.
headline: Coming to Terms

title: Good Behavior
author: Donald Westlake
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Dortmunder is back - hurray! - in GOOD BEHAVIOR by Donald E. Westlake (Mysterious Press, $15.95). John Dortmunder, a veteran thief, is a combination of Napoleon and the Sad Sack. If only fortune would smile on him! He is a brilliant strategist. He plans everything painstakingly. He tries to take all contingencies into account. But something unforeseen always happens, and Dortmunder flaps around and gasps like a beached flounder.   So it is in ''Good Behavior,'' one of the wackiest in this wacky series. By a combination of circumstances, Dortmunder takes refuge in a New York City convent when one of his capers explodes on him. The nuns come up with a proposition. They won't turn him in if he will kidnap a girl for them. Seems that a rich father had spirited his daughter out of the convent and is holding her prisoner in what amounts to a fortress in the city. Dortmunder recruits some of the most remarkable characters since the great days of Damon Runyon and sets to work.
headline: CRIME

title: The China Card
author: John Ehrlichman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CHINA CARD By John Ehrlichman. 523 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95. IN reading John Ehrlichman's new espionage novel, ''The China Card,'' one is reminded of how out-of-date the updated maxim ''Politics is the last refuge of a scoundrel'' has become. Many in the White House class that graduated into political oblivion after Watergate along with their President, Richard Nixon, lost little time in recycling themselves directly into the writing profession. In the years since, they have produced a blizzard of books capitalizing on both their experiences in office and their well-known, albeit variously besmirched, names. And now, like an unexploded mine from this period, one of the most prolific, Mr. Nixon's former adviser on domestic affairs, John Ehrlichman, has produced yet another offering, this time a thriller about the opening of diplomatic relations with China, a central event of the Nixon Administration.
headline: BOY GETS GIRL, CHANGES WORLD HISTORY

title: Brothers In Arms: A Journey From War To Peace
author: William Broyles Jr.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
BROTHERS IN ARMS A Journey From War to Peace. By William Broyles Jr. 284 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.

WILLIAM BROYLES JR. isn't the first combat veteran to seek out his old battlefield with questions about war -why some men die in battle and others live. But he is among the first combat veterans to journey back to Vietnam and a war that is still defined by questions that, even a decade after the last shot was fired, are unanswered: Why did we fight there? Why did we lose?
headline: GRASS ON THE BATTLEFIELD

title: Socrates And The Three Little Pigs
author: Tuyosi Mori
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOCRATES AND THE THREE LITTLE PIGS By Tuyosi Mori. Illustrated by Mitsumasa Anno. Philomel. $12.95. (Ages 7 and up) Another in the developing series of books on mathematics and logic by the Japanese illustrator and winner of the Hans Christian Andersen Prize.
headline: Bookshelf

title: Success Stories
author: Russell Banks
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
SUCCESS STORIES By Russell Banks. 183 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $15.95.

WITH his new collection, ''Success Stories,'' Russell Banks has published nine books of fiction - five novels and four volumes of stories - in the past 20 years. Yet until the appearance last year of ''Continental Drift,'' the first of his novels to win relatively large attention, he seemed destined to become a permanent member of that considerable company of American writers, many of them clearly gifted, who publish regularly but are reviewed sparsely if at all, and so remain little known even to the sophisticated reading public.

Part of Mr. Banks's problem is that his work has seemed dramatically out of phase with the most influential developments in postwar American fiction. Where Joseph Heller, John Barth, Thomas Pynchon, John Updike, Saul Bellow and others in the literary establishment have produced a fiction - often in the form of black humor or parodic fabulation - that is primarily concerned with the manifold anxieties and absurdities of affluent middle-class life, Mr. Banks is in no sense innovative or experimental, and he has shown no interest in the expensive tribulations of the urban world.
headline: BLUE-COLLAR ENIGMAS

author: Roger Warner
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

author: Ray Maloney
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE IMPACT ZONE By Ray Maloney. 246 pp. New York: Delacorte Press. $14.95. (Ages 12 and up) TO surfers, the place on a wave where the water is just about to collapse and explode is ''the impact zone'' - the spot of greatest danger, but also the greatest potential for thrilling achievement. For 15-year-old Jim Nichols, in Ray Maloney's fine first novel, it is a symbol of the way he is beginning to live his life.

The metaphor works so well that one wonders why surfing has not been used as the background for a coming-of-age novel more often. The only other that comes to mind is Kem Nunn's ''Tapping the Source.'' A lifelong resident of the southern California beach town of Ventura and a surfer since he was 10 - Mr. Maloney may be unique. He is able to free himself from the stereotypes of Gidget and beach party movies and write with a sure passion about the discipline and obsession as well as the excitement of the sport-art of surfing. Yet this is not a surfing novel any more than Walter Tevis's ''Queen's Gambit'' is a chess novel.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Feminism On Trial
author: Ellen Hawkes.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FEMINISM ON TRIAL The Ginny Foat Case and the Future of the Women's Movement. By Ellen Hawkes. 420 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $18.95.   GINNY FOAT'S arrest for murder in January 1983 sent shock waves through the National Organization for Women and made headlines everywhere. But by November of that year, when a Louisiana jury found her not guilty of bludgeoning an Argentine businessman to death outside New Orleans in 1965, the former barmaid who had become the president of the California chapter of NOW was not only a feminist heroine, her future career was assured. Her accuser had been the second of her four former husbands, John Sidote. On the witness stand, Mrs. Foat told the jury she was the helpless victim of his beatings. Since winning her case, Mrs. Foat has published her autobiography, ''Never Guilty, Never Free,'' optioned her life story to a television producer and crisscrossed the country speaking as a representative battered woman born again through the women's movement.
headline: SORORICIDAL WARFARE

title: Who Profits. Winners, Losers, And Government Regulation
author: Robert A. Leone.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: Robert D. Hershey Jr. Is An Economics Reporter In the Washington Bureau of the New York Times
pull_quote: WHO PROFITS Winners, Losers, and Government Regulation. By Robert A. Leone. 248 pp. New York: Basic Books. $17.95.   AT a time when so much economic analysis seems detached from reality - why do people think computers can forecast the gross national product three years hence if they can't give two weeks' notice of a collapse in oil prices? - it is refreshing to find something as thoughtful and practical as Robert A. Leone's treatment of the complex relationship of business and government. Not only has he avoided writing another soporific treatise on the subject, he has actually produced a book of considerable cogency.
headline: KEEP YOUR EYE ON THE SMALL PICTURE

title: Strength For The Fight
author: Bernard C. Nalty. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STRENGTH FOR THE FIGHT A History of Black Americans in the Military. By Bernard C. Nalty. Illustrated. 424 pp. New York: The Free Press. $22.50.   FOR black Americans, progress toward equality in the armed forces has usually required the stimulus of war. This is the unhappy but hardly unexpected conclusion that emerges from ''Strength for the Fight,'' Bernard C. Nalty's able overview of blacks in the American military. Sometimes the stimulus was applied directly by the enemy, who by enlisting blacks frightened white Americans into allowing black enlistments also. Early in the American Revolution, on Nov. 2, 1775, John Murray, fourth Earl of Dunmore, the royal governor of Virginia, offered freedom to slaves and indentured servants who would join with British troops in restoring the colony's loyalty to the crown. He organized an Ethiopian Regiment about 300 strong. A conference between Gen. George Washington and his principal subordinates on Oct. 8, 1775, had produced a decision to ban black enlistments in the Continental Army, but Dunmore's activities may have helped precipitate decisions by Washington and the Continental Congress to reverse course - to the extent of permitting re-enlistment of blacks already serving.
headline: THE RIGHT TO BE IN COMBAT

author: Ralph Beer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BLIND CORRAL. By Ralph Beer. (Viking, $16.95.) The West, as writers like Sam Shepard are quick to point out, is the West no longer. Today it is filled with shopping malls, trailer parks and yuppie bars.

JUST a few years ago business bookshelves overflowed with studies that found America's industrial talents wanting, at least in comparison with Japan's. Then, spurred by ''In Search of Excellence'' and the flag-waving 'Iacocca'' came a slew of books offering the reassuring news that, if proper attention is paid to business fundamentals, no one can touch America's mix of manufacturing might and ingenuity.

title: Dreams Of An Average Man
author: Dyan Sheldon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DREAMS OF AN AVERAGE MAN By Dyan Sheldon. 312 pp. New York: Crown Publishers. $15.95.   OUTRAGE and delight in a curious rich mix distinguish Dyan Sheldon's fiction. Her ear is tuned, her eye is clear, she is smart and generous, tough and funny. Her second novel, ''Dreams of an Average Man,'' was originally published in England, where this native New Yorker now lives, but it is a New York sort of book. So good that it's bound to be about a lot of things, it's mainly about getting another, firmer handhold on life's rough, slippery line as it grows ever shorter in your grasp. Her characters have come to the place where large, grand questions have cooked down to a single piercing one: What about me? Urban, sharp, impudent and unrelenting, they confront, a ''summer of self-assessment and reckoning'' all among ''the restless drumbeats and languid violence of Manhattan.''

pull_quote: JERUSALEM, JERUSALEM. By Lesley Hazleton. (Atlantic Monthly, $16.95.) When Lesley Hazleton arrived in Jerusalem she was a young woman of 20 years, innocent and in love.

title: Brazil
author: Errol Lincoln Uys

pull_quote: BRAZIL By Errol Lincoln Uys. 1,005 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.   COWBOYS and Indians and rugged explorers braving the trackless backlands; slaves and colonial plantations and harsh, whip-wielding overseers. All the stuff of a historical saga reminiscent of James Michener's ''Texas'' or ''Centennial'' is here, and in abundance. The setting this time out is Brazil and the author Errol Lincoln Uys, but no matter. Mr. Uys, a South African journalist and editor now living in Massachusetts, was a researcher for Mr. Michener on ''The Covenant.'' He has written a sprawling novel very much in the Michener style, with all the strengths and shortcomings that implies.

title: Breaking The Silence
author: Walter Laqueur and Richard Breitman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BREAKING THE SILENCE By Walter Laqueur and Richard Breitman. Illustrated. 320 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95. IN August 1942 an astonishing report reached London and Washington from Switzerland. A major German industrialist had disclosed during a visit to Zurich that the Nazi regime planned to slaughter the millions of Jewish men, women and children in the vast territories it controlled. Among the means being considered, the report indicated, was wholesale gassing. Like numerous subsequent reports, this news encountered disbelief among Allied officials. As Supreme Court Justice Felix Frankfurter explained at the end of 1942 to an eyewitness from Poland who described the details of one extermination center, it was simply impossible to believe such horrendous crimes were possible. Yet even before the first report came via Switzerland, the Holocaust was well under way.
headline: HERR S.'S SECRET

title: One Way Or Another
author: Peter Cameron
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ONE WAY OR ANOTHER By Peter Cameron. 181 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $15.95.   MANY things worth doing are worth doing quickly. Like plays (and souffles), short stories rise rapidly, form themselves around a single governing premise and are as suddenly finished - after upsetting and revising the environment in which they occur and which they created.
headline: BETWEEN JUMPING AND DIVING

title: Men's Lives
author: Peter Matthiessen. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MEN'S LIVES The Surfmen and Baymen of the South Fork. By Peter Matthiessen. Illustrated. 339 pp. New York: Random House. $29.95.   IN March 1961 a northeasterly gale tore through the beach resorts and summer homes of the Hamptons on eastern Long Island. The wind blew whole sand dunes back into the sea, exposing a surface of rutted peat on which were printed the cart tracks and the hoofmarks of the oxen of the first colonial settlers. The fishermen and farmers were just one wild morning away from the 20th century. It's tempting to see a message in the gale -that history is at once tenaciously near at hand and very easily dispersed. In this magnificent and somber portrait of the fishing community of the South Fork, Peter Matthiessen shows a stubbornly surviving culture being carelessly exterminated. ''Men's Lives'' is fired, as Mr. Matthiessen's best work always is, by love and indignation in equal parts. (His text is complemented by scores of historical and contemporary photographs.) The remaining fishermen of the Hamptons can put names to the owners of the 17th-century oxcarts. The Millers and Lesters gossip with Mr. Matthiessen about their ancestors' dealings with the Montauk and Shinnecock Indians as if they were talking about grandma and grandpa, with all the ''great-great-greats'' left out. They have been clam dredging, lobster potting, launching dories into the surf, setting traps and nets and lines, in an unbroken family chain that reaches all the way back to the original Dutch and English colonization of the island.
headline: THIS IS THE WAY A WORLD ENDS

title: The Opposing Shore
author: Julien Gracq
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE OPPOSING SHORE By Julien Gracq. Translated by Richard Howard. 292 pp. New York: Columbia University Press. $19.95. AT last, 35 years after its first publication in French, Julien Gracq's major novel, ''Le Rivage des Syrtes,'' is available in English. Richard Howard's translation retains all of the novel's verbal magnificence and its full grip on the imagination.   Syrtis Major was the ancient appellation of the Gulf of Sidra. Long before being named the ''Death Zone'' by Col. Muammar el-Qaddafi, the gulf was reputed perilous to ships. Virgil called it ''inhospitable Syrtis,'' not only for its strong currents and shifting sands but for its wild shores and the nomadic tribes of the bordering country. In different ways, the French title ''Le Rivage des Syrtes'' and its English counterpart, ''The Opposing Shore,'' conjure up this old image of an alien coast, clearly still vivid in the Western imagination.
headline: THE BECKONING GHOST

title: In Search Of The Trojan War
author: Michael Wood
pull_quote: In Search of the Trojan War,By Michael Wood. Illustrated. 272 pages. Facts on File. $22.95.   Any traveler who has searched for the world of Homer around the Mediterranean Sea discovers that the poems and the legends are fixed but many of the places themselves are more watered-down than wine-dark. Without the literature, the landmarks would be almost meaningless. It is essential to turn to the stories so that the imagination can fill in the locales that have been looted or have disappeared after thousands of years.
headline: TRAVEL BOOKSHELF

title: The Cult Of Information
author: Theodore Roszak.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CULT OF INFORMATION The Folklore of Computers and the True Art of Thinking. By Theodore Roszak. 238 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $17.95.   HELL, for Theodore Roszak, is a place where information takes the place of ideas, a corporate colossus of data processing companies floods the schools with small computers, video graphics pass for art and bit manipulation passes for thinking. Needless to say, we're almost there. ''There may soon be no one left in the high-rise ziggurats of our cities but a small elite of top-level decision makers surrounded by electronic apparatus,'' Mr. Roszak writes. ''They will be in touch around the globe with others of their kind, the only decently paid work force left in the information economy, manipulating spreadsheets, crafting takeover bids, transferring funds from bank to bank at the speed of light, arranging 'power lunches.' ''
headline: FUNKY BITS, FUNKY BITES

title: Beachmasters
author: Thea Astley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BEACHMASTERS By Thea Astley. 185 pp. New York: Viking. $14.95. WITH nine works of fiction that preceded ''Beachmasters,'' Thea Astley achieved an awesome repute in Australia, winning the coveted Miles Franklin Award three times for novels described by critics as ''scathing visions.'' If the novels recently published here by Penguin and Viking are exemplary, the description is accurate. Miss Astley's visions of society in backwater Queensland or in the South Seas are scathing indeed. Yet they are compassionate in an oblique way, and they feature striking pages of rather heavy lyricism. The extent to which American readers will respond to her talent will depend very much on their appreciation of her idiosyncratic language and, in this novel, on the ready sympathy they bring to the subject of the rulers and the ruled in a Pacific Ocean colony.   As a text for an earlier work, Miss Astley employed a quotation from Simone Weil: ''There will be no hope for man until he returns to the caves.'' This stifling contention is modified in ''Beachmasters'' by a vestigial if palpable hope of self-determination in the hearts of the Kristi islanders. A 13-year-old boy, Gavi, who looks white, threads the several episodes from beginning to end, and at the last - coming of age through an encounter with death - he faces his mixed ancestry, therewith choosing his role at a future time when independence will again, and more resolutely, be attempted.
headline: REVOLUTION AMONG THE FLAME TREES

title: Herbert Von Karajan. A Biographical Portrait
author: Roger Vaughan.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HERBERT VON KARAJAN A Biographical Portrait. By Roger Vaughan. 274 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $16.95.   THE authorized biographies of living icons are usually bland affairs - gushy, anecdotal and dumb. There are whiffs of dumbness about ''Herbert von Karajan,'' the authorized biography of one of our best-known conductors. But in the end we are left with a fascinating, distinctly unflattering and, finally, unfair picture of its subject. Mr. Karajan is portrayed as a cold, calculating workaholic, self-obsessed to the point of parody (after days in the dark editing films of himself conducting, he says, ''Making this review of my music is like a religion for me''). According to Mr. Vaughan, Mr. Karajan distrusts people in the music world (those he controls and especially those he can't control) and admires expertise in other areas. Hence, when Mr. Vaughan, an American yachting expert, showed up in 1981 to write about Mr. Karajan's huge and fearsome sailboat, Mr. Karajan enlisted him for this book. What he got was an author who can write such things as, ''By the age of seventy-three (in 1981) his ego had become blinding, colossal.''
headline: 'GENERAL MUSIC DIRECTOR OF EUROPE'

title: The Big Boys
author: Ralph Nader and William Taylor.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BIG BOYS Power and Position in American Business. By Ralph Nader and William Taylor. 571 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $22.95.   HERE are nine long-playing profiles of accomplished capitalists, a compilation that evidently was not calculated to bring the authors standing invitations to the power tables at ''21.'' At a time when too much business journalism seems a celebration of mega-wealth, Ralph Nader and William Taylor have approached their subjects - the chief executive officers or leading principals of the United States Steel Corporation, General Motors, Dow Chemical Company, Lazard Freres & Company, Cargill Inc., Northrop Corporation, MCI Communications, Control Data Corporation and a Washington lobbying firm - in a manner that seems almost quaint. That is, they have conducted their research in a tirelessly thorough manner, along the way cataloguing every discernible wart and scar.
headline: RAIDED, GRADED AND UPBRAIDED

title: The Idea Of The Good In Platonic-Aristotelian Philosophy
author: Hans-Georg Gadamer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE IDEA OF THE GOOD IN PLATONIC-ARISTOTELIAN PHILOSOPHY By Hans-Georg Gadamer. Translated, and with an Introduction, by P. Christopher Smith. 182 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $20.

WITH the passage of time, conceptual distinctions that may once have provoked arguments, fights or even wars seem to coalesce. Many come to appear as manifestations of a single, coherent point of view. Though they may grate on learned ears, expressions like ''the Greco-Roman outlook,'' ''the Elizabethan world picture'' or ''the values of the Enlightenment'' are constantly used to describe such presumed unities.

Plato and Aristotle, however, seem to provide a remarkable exception to this commonplace. From our perspective, they stand close together in time, but seem philosophically worlds apart. Time has opened an immense gap between them - a constantly expanding space, large enough to contain the whole of the rest of philosophy within it.
headline: GREEK ON GREEK AND EYE TO EYE

title: The Straw Giant
author: Arthur T Hadley
pull_quote: THE STRAW GIANT. Triumph and Failure: America's Armed Forces. By Arthur T. Hadley. 314 pages. Random House. $19.95. IF you happen to care about the adequacy of the United States' armed forces, then ''The Straw Giant'' is discouraging in the way that most recent critiques of America's military strength are discouraging. Arthur T. Hadley - a veteran reporter who has served as consultant to the Joint Chiefs of Staff and has written seven books, among them ''The Nation's Safety and Arms Control'' - begins by reminding us in painful detail of the catastrophic 1980 hostage-rescue operation in the desert of Iran.   He next identifies six ''basic themes'' that ''helped create the disaster at Desert One.'' First among these is what he terms ''the Great Divorce,'' or ''the less-than-amicable separation of the military from the financial, business, political, and intellectual elites of this country, particularly from the last two.'' Second is the destructive twins, ''Interservice Rivalry,'' and, less well known but almost as damaging, ''Intraservice Rivalry.'' Third is ''Flawed Organization,'' a dull subject, but then ''the dull ax is the one most apt to glance off the log and remove your foot.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Kate Vaiden
author: Reynolds Price
pull_quote: KATE VAIDEN. By Reynolds Price. 306 pages. Atheneum. $16.95. IN this, his 14th book, Reynolds   Price returns again to the hill country of North Carolina that he mapped out so persuasively in his first work of fiction, ''A Long and Happy Life'' - the novel that established him as one of the most promising heirs of the Southern Renaissance two and a half decades ago.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Across
author: Peter Handke
pull_quote: ACROSS. By Peter Handke. Translated by Ralph Manheim. 138 pages. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $14.95.   ''ACROSS,'' the resonant, if curt, title of this novel, rather bluntly refers to the book's dominant theme -the crossing of what the narrator, Andreas Loser, likes to call ''thresholds.'' And in the course of this story, he encounters quite a lot of them: as an amateur archeologist, he specializes in the social and architectural significance of ancient house, church and temple thresholds; and as student of his own psyche, is obsessed with transition states, emotional borderlines and spiritual frontiers. One day, Andreas commits an impulsive, but deliberate, murder - he stones to death a man who has been painting swastikas on trees - and he finds that the act places him on what may be the most important threshold of his life.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Hornes: An American Family
author: Gail Lumet Buckley
pull_quote: THE HORNES: AN AMERICAN FAMILY. By Gail Lumet Buckley. Illustrated. 262 pages. Knopf. $18.95. ''I AM a Horne, too,'' writes   Gail Lumet Buckley near the opening of her unusual memoir ''The Hornes: An American Family.'' ''I was born Gail Horne Jones in the winter of 1937. It was the year that my grandfather, Teddy Horne, saved a menu from the Joe Louis Training Camp Restaurant - where the filet mignon was seventy-five cents. He also saved a registered-mail envelope printed 'Fly United to the Fight on New Douglas Mainlines - None Faster, Lower Fares.' (The sporting crowd was ahead of everyone in air travel.) Teddy was Lena's father. I am Lena's daughter. My daughters are her granddaughters. Family faces are magic mirrors. Looking at people who belong to us, we see the past, present, and future. We make discoveries about ourselves and them. Forms, faces, skin, stature all form a circle of existence. If you spin us we become a glittering chain of life.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Outlands: Journeys To The Outer Edges Of Cape Cod
author: Robert Finch
pull_quote: OUTLANDS: Journeys to the Outer Edges of Cape Cod. By Robert Finch. 175 pages. David R. Godine. $15.95.   IN the very best of the dozen and a half essays in Robert Finch's ''Outlands: Journeys to the Outer Edges of Cape Cod,'' the author doesn't ruminate on nature and draw lessons, as too many heirs of Henry David Thoreau have an unfortunate tendency to do. Instead Mr. Finch describes an action - like following deer tracks on a snowy night (''Nighttracking''), or visiting the site in Wellfleet Harbor where 65 pilot whales have beached themselves and died (''Cutting In''), or surprising a herd of seals at the tip of Jeremy Point (''The Seals of Jeremy Point'') - and lets the drama of the action speak for itself.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Margaret Bourke-White. A Biography
author: Vicki Goldberg
pull_quote: MARGARET BOURKE-WHITE. A Biography. By Vicki Goldberg. Illustrated. 426 pages. Harper & Row. $25.95. No doubt the reader is already familiar with her photographs, images imprinted on the national consciousness by Life magazine, Fortune and her own numerous books: a monumental view of the Fort Peck Dam as a massive feat of engineering, dwarfing the two tiny figures of workmen in the foreground; a close-up shot of plow blades as gleaming, abstract images of technology; a picture of flood victims, standing in line before a billboard (''There's no way like the American Way'') as a dark commentary on Depression-age America; a portrait of Gandhi, looking ascetic and otherworldly as he sits reading on the floor.
headline: A Life in Pictures

title: The Marksman
author: Sergey Yuryenen
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MARKSMAN. By Sergey Yuryenen. Translated by Roger and Angela Keys. (Quartet/Salem House, $14.95.) The plot of Sergey Yuryenen's novel is sturdy and simple.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Second Creation
author: Robert P. Crease and Charles C. Mann.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SECOND CREATION Makers of the Revolution in Twentieth-Century Physics. By Robert P. Crease and Charles C. Mann. 480 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $25.   THE authors of ''The Second Creation'' acknowledge their debt to Horace Freeland Judson's ''Eighth Day of Creation,'' the gossipy, perceptive and monumental account of the development of modern biology that appeared seven years ago. Robert P. Crease and Charles C. Mann have set out to tell the story of the development of modern physics in the last century by weaving a web of anecdote, explanation and physicists' personal recollections. Their task is inherently more difficult than was Mr. Judson's. Their book is a good hard read (in which phrase, both adjectives count).   The canvas is vast. It has its beginning in the 15 turbulent years at the end of the 19th century when the complacent conviction that physics had become a closed book - Newton's book with appendixes - was challenged by observation (the discovery of X-rays and radioactivity, for example) and by theorists, for whom the notion that empty space is filled with an intangible but material substance called the ether became a kind of scandal. It ends right now, or rather two years ago, with the discovery of three new particles of matter, called - strangely, as these things tend to be - the intermediate vector bosons.
headline: SEARCHING FOR THE 'THEORY OF EVERYTHING'

title: A Dolphin Summer
author: Gerard Gormley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A DOLPHIN SUMMER. By Gerard Gormley. (Taplinger, $14.95.) Fifteen years ago the author, a marketing consultant, was cruising off Gloucester, Mass., when he found himself in the midst of 15 finback whales who lolled and played alongside his boat for the next seven hours.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Barrier Island
author: John D Macdonald
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BARRIER ISLAND. By John D. MacDonald. (Knopf, $16.95.) John D. MacDonald's latest novel features dozens of characters, an ever-thickening plot, a modicum of sex and violence and a narrative propelled mostly by dialogue, which bears Mr. MacDonald's lively, gritty stamp.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Complete Works Of Captain John Smith
author: Philip L Barbour
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE COMPLETE WORKS OF CAPTAIN JOHN SMITH (1580-1631). In Three Volumes. Volume One, 448 pp. Volume Two, 488 pp. Volume Three, 513 pp. Edited by Philip L. Barbour. Illustrated. Chapel Hill: The Institute of Early American History and Culture/ The University of North Carolina Press. $150.   EVERY American schoolchild knows Capt. John Smith as the dashing hero of early Virginia who was saved from certain death by Princess Pocahontas. From there on, the picture blurs. Did Smith marry Pocahontas? Were they the progenitors of the innumerable Smiths who pervade American history? Was Smith a monumental liar who invented the Pocahontas story and other dramatic episodes to gain wealth and glory? The answer to each question is, of course, no. Smith was a hero of early Virginia all right, and Pocahontas probably saved his life - though it may have been in less jeopardy than he claimed. Pocahontas married John Rolfe (she was only about 12 years old when Smith was in Virginia, though he said he could have married her) and died in England in 1617. Her son, Thomas Rolfe, had many American descendants; John Smith, a bachelor, had none. And while most of this information comes from Smith's numerous publications, which have often been challenged as self-serving fabrications, most modern authorities - especially Philip L. Barbour, editor of the first edition of Smith's works in more than a century - accept the captain's accounts as fundamentally truthful.
headline: BEYOND POCAHONTAS

title: Kate Vaiden
author: Reynolds Price
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: KATE VAIDEN By Reynolds Price. 306 pp. New York: Atheneum. $16.95.   ''I'D caused their deaths.'' Every writer who has produced a large body of work has themes that play as relentlessly as a ground bass beneath the changing melody of plot and character; every book could yield up a single sentence from the center of the author's obsession. Reynolds Price has shaped many of his novels around the lives of children whose mothers have died giving birth to them, or whose conception is in some other way clouded - children, that is, who feel or are treated as if they are guilty from their first breath.   ''Kate Vaiden,'' which teems with orphans and murderous and suicidal generations - all the expected passions of a Price book - is nonetheless different from the North Carolina novelist's other work. It is a forgiving, immensely readable story, set mainly in the early 1940's, almost light in feeling (although its tale of early death and frustrated passions is hardly frivolous). But the voice of Mr. Price's heroine blows like fresh air across the page. ''Kate Vaiden'' even looks different from its eloquent but frequently ponderous predecessors, typographically dense from margin to margin.
headline: TRAVELS WITH A DANGEROUS WOMAN

title: House Mother Normal: A Geriatric Comedy
author: B S Johnson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HOUSE MOTHER NORMAL: A Geriatric Comedy. By B. S. Johnson. (New Directions, Cloth, $16.95. Paper, $7.95.) The British writer B. S. Johnson created a large and formidable body of work before his suicide in 1973, including six novels, two collections of poetry, as well as drama and essays.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Life And Legend Of Jay Gould
author: Maury Klein
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE LIFE AND LEGEND OF JAY GOULD By Maury Klein. Illustrated. 595 pp. Baltimore: The Johns Hopkins University Press. $27.50.

IN his own time Jay Gould was considered one of the worst stinkers in American business, and the label has persisted after his death. Most accounts of his career have dwelled more on the scandals than on the rationale of Gould's business maneuvers. Maury Klein's admirably detailed biography, ''The Life and Legend of Jay Gould,'' instead examines at length the financial and business architecture of Gould's railroad and other operations, while placing the bribery, insider stock manipulation and betrayals in the context of the seamy ethics of the day. This was, after all, the era of the Tweed Ring, the ''Black Horse Cavalry'' of corrupt Albany legislators and the scandal-racked Grant Administration. Gould, like Cesare Borgia, took the measure of the world around him and plunged in: he put Boss Tweed on his Erie Railroad board of directors, outbid Commodore Vanderbilt in buying the people's representatives in Albany and paid off Grant's brother-in-law to gain access to the President and to learn his intentions on government gold sales.
headline: 'MOST HATED MAN IN AMERICA'

title: Elegant Inn, The. The Waldorf-Astoria Hotel
author: Albin Pasteur Dearing. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE ELEGANT INN The Waldorf-Astoria Hotel, 1893-1929. By Albin Pasteur Dearing. Illustrated. 250 pp. Secaucus, N.J.: Lyle Stuart. $16.95.

THE inn as an allegory for the world is an enticing approach; and Albin Pasteur Dearing deals with the old Waldorf-Astoria Hotel with something of this in mind. He sees the fabulous hostelry as a reflection of its times. He is at considerable pains to picture the 1890's in America, intimating that the Waldorf was a highly innovative experiment, breaking with many social customs and expectations, and also that it was the legitimate (or illegitimate) child of the Age of Opulence. This is perhaps the most interesting aspect of his book, for even well-told tales about the eccentricities of the hotel's guests, and the obsequious measures by which the staff catered to them, do not always seem as amusing as perhaps once they did.
headline: 2,200 BEDS ON FIFTH AVENUE

title: The Spanish Ulcer
author: David Gates. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SPANISH ULCER A History of the Peninsular War. By David Gates. Illustrated. 557 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $29.95.   THE disastrous French adventure in Spain between 1808 and 1813 probably had as much to do with Napoleon's ultimate downfall as his invasion of Russia. Generations of Britons and most Americans tend to see the Spanish conflict as a wholly British affair in which the figures of the Duke of Wellington and Gen. Sir John Moore and the activities of their armies dominate the war. David Gates, a British historian, has put the war in perspective in ''The Spanish Ulcer,'' as Napoleon called the war.
headline: BASHING THE FRENCH

title: Impostors
author: George V. Higgins.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IMPOSTERS By George V. Higgins. 362pp. New York: Henry Holt & Company. $16.95.   GEORGE V. HIGGINS has put his bold and realistic narrative gifts to a new test in his 15th book, ''Imposters'' - a determinedly contemporary novel of sex, corporate politics, real estate scheming and getting away with murder.
headline: BOSTON BAKED SEX

title: Our Tempestuous Day: A History Of Regency England
author: Carolly Erickson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OUR TEMPESTUOUS DAY: A History of Regency England. By Carolly Erickson. (Morrow, $18.95.) Regency England was like a compulsive bon vivant whose nightly overindulgence is matched each morning by the equally excessive appeasement of his Puritan soul. The historian Carolly Erickson, author of ''Bloody Mary,'' has spun out a lively and thoroughly enthralling account of this paradoxical age - 1810 to 1820 - whose gods were Byron and the Duke of Wellington (Napoleon's conqueror) but whose all-too-human ruler was a puckish, overweight boy-man given to wide mood swings and overdoses of laudanum and fast women. When his father, George III, began to recede into his own mad dream world, Parliament appointed the Prince of Wales, later George IV, as Regent. George both repelled and fascinated his subjects: they regularly castigated him for his profligacy and his very public battle to divorce his promiscuous wife, Caroline. But thousands of them also stood in line for hours just to glimpse his private chambers at Carlton House - and the remains of his legendary all-night ball. According to Miss Erickson, the excesses of the melancholy young Byron, both romantic and literary, took on symbolic power, dramatizing what she calls the ''diseased and violent'' undertow of the age, the sense that there was a ''canker at the root of things.'' Hannah More, a stern Christian evangelical, agreed and in her best-selling tracts exhorted Britain to cleanse itself of worldliness, encouraging the rise of a ferociously pious army of reformers.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Mountain Of Truth
author: Martin Green. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MOUNTAIN OF TRUTH The Counterculture Begins: Ascona, 1900-1920. By Martin Green. Illustrated. 287 pp. Hanover, N.H.: University Press of New England. $19.95.   AT the beginning of the 20th century, advocates of a free life made an especially deep impact on German-speaking Europe with visions based on feminism, sexual liberation, nature worship, the rejection of authority, vegetarianism and cultural renewal. It was a heady brew, whose ingredients have been drawn on many times since, though not always happily. One of the problems Martin Green confronts in his engaging group portrait of figures and movements from the German counterculture is that, along with innocents and victims, there appear not a few whose ideas contributed to Nazi practice, and even some who were willing to cooperate with it.
headline: GERMANS IN THE TREETOPS, WAY UP HIGH

title: Collected Letters Of W. B. Yeates
author: W B Yeates
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE COLLECTED LETTERS OF W.B. YEATS Volume One: 1865-1895. Edited by John Kelly with Eric Domville. Illustrated. 548 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $29.95. THESE letters from the first 30 years of William Butler Yeats's life are the statements of an obsessive mythmaker whose sense of purpose is casual and passionate and whose determination to gather material for his poetry from every possible source is so implacable that it verges on the predatory.   From the beginning, Yeats was obsessed with certain ideas, places, themes and people. These early letters show him tentatively but energetically exploring his ideas on legend, mythology, history, Ireland and Irish writers, fairy tales, theosophy, theater, folklore, ballads, ghosts, County Sligo, magic and the supernatural. As a young writer, he was ardent and clumsy, feeling his way through the rich darkness of his imagination, trying to define his own position as a poet, learning from others and also working on their behalf, a vigilant listener, a furious talker, a nonstop worker constantly hammering out his own esthetic.
headline: PASSIONS OF A SHY WARRIOR

title: The Underground Empire
author: James Mills
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE UNDERGROUND EMPIRE Where Crime and Governments Embrace. By James Mills. 1,165 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $22.95.   IN every reporter there is a desire to know everything - to be set free of having to perceive the world through interviews and press briefings and to be able instead to watch the real action as it unfolds in private. More than six years ago James Mills was given such an opportunity: the head of a small Federal antidrug strike force called Centac decided to grant him a spectacular degree of access to its operations. Mr. Mills was apparently even allowed to accompany agents into the field, not to mention being privy to nearly everything that went on back at headquarters.
headline: BIGGIES, BUREAUCRATS AND THE WORLD DRUG TRADE

title: The End Of Life
author: James Rachels.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE END OF LIFE Euthanasia and Morality. By James Rachels. 204 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $17.95.   MORE than 5,500 people die every day across this country, one every 16 seconds or so. But there is something dramatically new in many of these deaths (no one knows exactly how many) - they are negotiated, arranged, even scheduled by doctors, families and the dying patients themselves.
headline: CHOOSING TO DIE

title: Wallis And Edward
author: Michael Bloch
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WALLIS AND EDWARD Letters 1931-1937. The Intimate Correspondence of the Duke and Duchess of Windsor. Edited by Michael Bloch. Illustrated. 367 pp. New York: Summit Books. $19.95.   SHE was beautiful, brilliant, charming, virtuous and unselfish, and although she was but a poor American commoner, modestly protesting against such elevation, the handsome prince fell madly and irrevocably in love, valuing her hand in marriage beyond any honors and riches the world had to offer. Just a minute, please. What is that snickering?  Who is rude enough to suggest that Wallis Simpson was none of the above, but a dime-a-dozen divorcee, and the prince a fool for his pains? Is that a proper attitude to take about a real-life fairy tale? You people who melted with sentiment over the current Prince of Wales's unexceptionable courtship and wedding: Where are your hearts? How little it usually takes for you to endow even the most ordinary royal match with beauty and courage and virtue and sacrifice - the ingredients of storybook romance. By contrast, history's reaction to the love story of Edward VIII and Wallis Simpson, which really did contain the elements of drama, including a classic test of love that he unflinchingly passed by trading his kingdom for a wife, is, ''What on earth could he see in her?''
headline: GOOD MEESEL, MRS. SIMPSON

title: War Without Mercy
author: John W. Dower. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WAR WITHOUT MERCY Race and Power in the Pacific War. By John W. Dower. Illustrated. 399 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $22.50.   INDUSTRY flacks keep trying to persuade us that Japan and the United States are again at war in the Pacific. But so far World War IIB has amounted only to a few salvos of grade-B hype. The snubs and slurs seem wimpish by comparison with the robust disgust volleyed from both sides of the ocean in the early 1940's. Even inept reruns of wartime vilification, however, are ''ominous,'' says John W. Dower, because they might unshackle ur-impulses to commit genocide. Mr. Dower, who is a professor of Japanese studies at the University of California, San Diego, argues that the Pacific war was whipped into its final frenzy by racial hatreds that were more primal than the ideological motivations behind the war in the Atlantic. The results, on both sides, was a hidden holocaust whose horrors have yet to be fully acknowledged.
headline: IMAGES OF THE ENEMY

title: The Last Blossom On The Plum Tree
author: Brooke Astor.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE LAST BLOSSOM ON THE PLUM TREE A Period Piece. By Brooke Astor. 244 pp. New York: Random House. $16.95.

ASPIRING - but no longer young - novelists can take heart from the example of Brooke Astor. Undaunted by the tepid critical response to her first novel, ''The Bluebird Is at Home,'' published in 1965, the distinguished philanthropist and patron of the arts went on to write a successful autobiography, ''Footprints,'' the 1980 sequel to her earlier ''Patchwork Child.''
headline: YOU'RE NEVER TOO OLD TO BE LOVESICK

title: Ghosts
author: Paul Auster. The New York Trilogy, Volume Two.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GHOSTS By Paul Auster. The New York Trilogy, Volume Two. 96 pp. Los Angeles: Sun and Moon Press. $12.95.   THOSE of us who have an insatiable passion for mystery novels know that this appetite has very little to do with the love of literature in general.
headline: THE MAN SHADOWING BLACK IS BLUE

title: Sentries
author: Gary Paulsen
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SENTRIES By Gary Paulsen. 165 pp. New York: Bradbury Press. $11.95. (Ages 14 and up) PART ode to the incredible luck of being alive, part cry of alarm, wholly a plea that life go on, Gary Paulsen's new book, ''Sentries,'' is strange, hard to pigeonhole. Unlike his ''Dogsong,'' a 1986 Newbery Honor Book, this collection of short fictions isn't exactly a novel. It has seven main characters, yet they don't know one another. Their paths don't cross, yet their stories produce a unified effect.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: The Ambassador
author: Andre Brink
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE AMBASSADOR By Andre Brink. 288 pp. New York: Summit Books. $16.95. ''I WAS born on a bench in the Luxembourg Gardens in Paris, in the early spring of 1960,''   Andre Brink has written. He was in his mid-20's at the time. He was born again in 1968, during a second visit to Paris, when he was ''caught up'' in the student demonstrations. These Parisian rebirths, in Mr. Brink's own formulations, were political, literary, metaphysical and sexual, the outcome of a ''romantic love-affair'' with the city. When he first arrived in Paris, fresh from South Africa, he was comfortable with his Afrikaner convictions, stiffened by his religion and its puritanism; but then, as he puts it, he was transformed by ''that great metropolis where every single thing I had taken for granted now had to be tested, explored, validated - or rejected.''
headline: A PIPSQUEAK'S OBSESSION

title: Open Road
author: Phil Patton. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OPEN ROAD A Celebration of the American Highway. By Phil Patton. Illustrated. 304 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95.   LADY BIRD JOHNSON has a lot to answer for, according to Phil Patton in his intriguing new book ''Open Road.'' Armed with the smug conviction that bushes are better for the American tourist than billboards, concrete dinosaurs, giant tar-paper trout and the whole mad gaggle of roadside come-ons that used to lend a certain aura of exoticism and spine-chilling pseudodanger to cross-country treks, she got the Highway Beautification Act passed in 1965.   The full force of law banished the eye-popping menagerie to a distance of 600 feet from the center line, and with it those attendant congeries of signage promising almost unimaginable delights at the next interchange. But if you look very closely at Lady Bird's bushes strung out along the 600-foot mark - especially in the wintertime, when the foliage is sparse, or toward sunset, when the light takes on that peculiar power of penetration - you can catch glimpses now and then of the aged critters, lurking back there, massing for another assault on a highway grown longer and duller and wearier in their absence.
headline: ONCE, ALL THOSE BILLBOARDS MADE YOU WINCE. THIS BOOK EXPLAINS WHAT'S HAPPENED SINCE.

title: The American Newness
author: Irving Howe.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE AMERICAN NEWNESS Culture and Politics in the Age of Emerson. By Irving Howe. 99 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $12.50. IS America a success? The way to find out, said Henry Adams in a famous passage Irving Howe quotes early in this little book, is by asking whether American ''social power'' is being transformed into ''the higher forms of thought.'' Is the country giving ''new life to religion and art''? Are we creating and maintaining ''in the mass of mankind those habits of mind which . . . hitherto belonged to men of science alone''? In Adams's opinion nothing less than a revolution of spirit - a far-ranging democratization of culture - would be necessary for complete American fulfillment.   In Mr. Howe's opinion Ralph Waldo Emerson is the chief American spokesman for such a revolution; in ''The Poet,'' ''The American Scholar'' and other permanent utterances, Emerson envisioned cultural complements to democratic political institutions - ways of giving new life to religion and art. ''The American Newness,'' three essays based on the Massey Lectures that Mr. Howe delivered last year at Harvard University, examines the nature, background and influence of these components.
headline: ENGAGEMENT WITH THE OVERSOUL

title: Colette: A Passion For Life
author: Colette
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ''If I cannot have too many truffles, I will do without truffles,'' Colette once declared, illustrating what might have served as her motto: ''All things in excess.'' The doted-on little girl grew up to be a jealous lover, a pitifully dependent wife and then an indomitable woman, and in time one of France's most loved and finest writers.
headline: LUST FOR YOU NAME IT

title: The Embassy House
author: Nicholas Proffitt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE EMBASSY HOUSE By Nicholas Proffitt. 399 pp. New York: Bantam Books. $16.95.   WAR is the handmaiden of mythology, and the prevailing myth of American war novels has been, appropriately enough, an egalitarian one: our heroes tend to be amateurs. The platoon traditionally has been a model populist legislature of citizen soldiers representing various ethnic factions, where democratic consensus is achieved after struggle and misunderstanding; at which point the men ''come of age'' on the battlefield and return home better for the experience.
headline: THE CONSCIENCE OF A GREEN BERET

title: A Cast Of Killers
author: Sidney D Kirkpatrick
pull_quote: A CAST OF KILLERS. By Sidney D. Kirkpatrick. Illustrated. 301 pages. E. P. Dutton. $17.95.   IN Sidney D. Kirkpatrick's nonfiction crime thriller ''A Cast of Killers,'' the film director King Vidor solves the mystery of who murdered his fellow director William Desmond Taylor on the evening of Feb. 1, 1922. You may ask the obvious question, ''Who cares who killed the film director William Desmond Taylor?'' The answer is, ''Anyone who indulges the pleasure of reading Mr. Kirkpatrick's intriguing book.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Play Of The Eyes
author: Elias Canetti
pull_quote: THE PLAY OF THE EYES. By Elias Canetti. Translated by Ralph Manheim. 329 pages. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $22.50.   FIRST the tongue, then the ear, now the eyes. ''The Play of the Eyes'' is the third installment of the memoirs of Elias Canetti, who was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1981. Two previous volumes, ''The Tongue Set Free'' and ''The Torch in My Ear,'' were largely devoted to the author's struggle to escape from a domineering mother, and to his emergence as a writer in the Vienna of the 1920's. By 1931, when the new volume opens, he had already completed what was to be his only novel, ''Auto-da-Fe,'' although it had not yet found a publisher.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Murrow: His Life And Times
author: A M Sperber
pull_quote: MURROW: His Life and Times. By A. M. Sperber. Illustrated. 795 pages.   Freundlich Books. $25. IF an author's effort could produce a good biography, ''Murrow'' would be a masterpiece. A. M. Sperber seems to have read everything by and about the widely admired radio-television journalist Edward R. Murrow, who died in 1965, and to have talked with everybody who knew him. Unfortunately, her devotion overwhelms her discrimination. The research, which reportedly took 12 years, has been exhaustive; the printed results, some 700 pages not counting the index, are exhausting. There is much interesting material here from an eventful life, but it is submerged in a welter of anecdotes, quotes and excerpts, many of them tangential or repetitious.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Why The South Lost The Civil War
author: Herman Hattaway
pull_quote: WHY THE SOUTH LOST THE CIVIL WAR. By Richard E. Beringer, Herman Hattaway, Archer Jones and William N. Still Jr. Illustrated. 582 pages.   University of Georgia Press. $29.95. WHEN a university press book arrives from Georgia 121 years after the surrender at Appomattox Court House and bears the title,''Why the South Lost the Civil War'' (rather than ''Why the South Lost the War Between the States''), it suggests that the Stars and Bars is finally being hauled down. This news may not be greeted with approval by the good old boys who flaunt the Confederate flag for fun and games; but to Civil War scholars it is a signal of changed attitudes.
headline: Books: Blue and Gray

title: The Lyrical Left
author: Edward Abrahams
pull_quote: THE LYRICAL LEFT: Randolph Bourne, Alfred Stieglitz and the Origins of Cultural Radicalism in America. By Edward Abrahams. Illustrated. 265 pages. University Press of Virginia. $20. THE Greenwich Village writer   Floyd Dell once spoke of the year 1912 as the ''Lyric Year.'' For artists and intellectuals, it was a time of brave beginnings; in the avant-garde excitements of the period and the hammering out of new social ideals, many of them foresaw nothing less than the imminent transformation of society itself. This confident early phase of modern cultural radicalism forms the subject of Edward Abrahams's book - though rather than attempting a general survey, he tries to get ''the Lyrical Left'' into focus by concentrating on the careers of two of its foremost representatives, Randolph Bourne and Alfred Stieglitz.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Nemesis Affair
author: David M Raup
pull_quote: THE NEMESIS AFFAIR. A Story of the Death of Dinosaurs and the Ways of Science. By David M. Raup. Illustrated. 220 pages. W. W. Norton. $14.95.   David M. Raup is a distinguished paleontologist and a professor of geophysical sciences at the University of Chicago. During the past three years he has also become widely known as a proponent of the theory that many of the mass extinctions of species that are known to have occurred in the prehistoric past were brought about by comets colliding with the earth, and that these collisions have taken place at regular intervals of some 26 million years. He has now written a gripping account of how the theory evolved, one which also offers some instructive insights into the workings of the scientific community.
headline: Books of The Times; Cycles of Destruction

title: Hot Properties
author: Rafael Yglesias
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HOT PROPERTIES By Rafael Yglesias. 408 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $16.95. BARRY SCHWARTZ, a professor of psychology at Swarthmore College, has written a lengthy polemic against three academic schools of thought that are based, as he sees it, on the assumption that self-interested motives dominate human beings as well as other living creatures. The three schools are neoclassical economics, with its postulate of rational economic man; evolutionary biology, asserting the universal competition of organisms to repro-duce; and Skinnerian behaviorism, treating both human and animal behavior as shaped by the ''reinforcement'' of responses producing pleasurable outcomes. In ''The Battle for Human Nature,'' Mr. Schwartz contends that these three schools add to one another's plausibility, even though they obviously differ in subject matter and method. Their underlying kinship is certainly not immediately apparent, considering that economists see human actions as guided by rational intelligence, evolutionary biologists give priority to inborn impulses and behaviorist psychologists concentrate on habit formation.

AT first sight, Czeslaw Milosz's most recent collection seems to be a poet's scrapbook rather than a book of poems. It reminds one of the silva rerum, a ''forest of things,'' the 17th-century term for a fascicle containing loosely arranged notes, occasional poems, copies of letters and memorable quotations. In the same way, ''Unattainable Earth'' consists only in part of Mr. Milosz's own poems. The rest of the volume is filled with his prose notes or aphorisms, letters from his friends and what he calls ''inscripts'' - fragments from sources as diverse as ''Corpus Hermeticum,'' Casanova's memoirs, Zen philosophy, the Russian emigre philosopher Lev Shestov, the poet Oscar Milosz and the French philosopher Simone Weil. There are even several poems by Walt Whitman and D. H. Lawrence, translated by the author into Polish in the book's original edition and here restored to their English versions and included as ''an homage to tutelary spirits.''

THE magic realism of Amitav Ghosh's first novel, ''The Circle of Reason,'' is a genre much developed in Latin America, a continent where the condition of the people is not conducive to novels of rational cause and effect. India, with its pullulating poor and its superstitions, has recently given us, though the book was written in London, Salman Rushdie's ''Shame,'' which belongs to the tradition of Gabriel Garcia Marquez and Mario Vargas Llosa. Mr. Ghosh, who teaches in the sociology department of the Delhi School of Economics, follows the same line of extravagance in the service of truth.   His title would seem to disclaim any magical content, though the contradiction in it cancels the rational in favor of the cyclical. His characters think they are walking a straight line, but they are going round, powered by hope, in that nonproductive circle that life too often imposes on the poor.
headline: A LITTLE DEMENTIA IN THE NAME OF PROGRESS

A DISTINGUISHED black lawyer, an official in the Department of Housing and Urban Development during the Nixon Administration, once identified the precise moment when he realized American society had experienced a major transformation: ''I was watching the Harvard-Yale football game on television. Yale substituted a black quarterback, and I was astounded. I didn't know his family!''

In ''The Hornes,'' Gail Lumet Buckley argues that in the century between emancipation and the civil rights movement America's black bourgeoisie - a small, privileged class dependent for identity upon superior achievement, strong leaders, light skin and ''favored slave'' origins - created an ''ideal world'' that mirrored white values. This world came to an end, Mrs. Buckley believes, with the rise of equal opportunity, which created political, educational and economic possibilities that ''go far beyond anything even imagined by the old bourgeoisie.''

MORALITY, REASON, AND POWER American Diplomacy in the Carter Years. By Gaddis Smith. 296 pp. New York: Hill & Wang. $18.95.

EVEN with hindsight, the Carter Administration's foreign policy seems curiously elusive, although Gaddis Smith has made a serious attempt to distill and assess its basic character, but he has not altogether succeeded. He leaves out too much, above all the critical economic dimension. And the questions around which he builds his assessment -morality versus power, or global versus national interests - are not the real issues, in my opinion.

As might be expected from Gaddis Smith, an accomplished scholar who teaches the history of American diplomacy and foreign policy at Yale University, the book is well organized and well written. It finds the Carter years ''among the most significant in the history of American foreign policy in the twentieth century'' because ''a fundamental debate about how the United States should behave in international affairs was waged with unusual clarity.'' The Administration tried to an unusual degree to make decisions for a lasting and universally beneficial world order rather than for short-term advantage over the Russians. But it lost its vision and reverted to America's traditional nationalist combativeness.

AMERICAN soldiers used to tell me a story about the invasion of Grenada in 1983. A Spanish-speaking supply sergeant named Ontiveros was persuaded to volunteer to be dropped with the first paratroopers, so they could communicate with Grenadian civilians. Ontiveros was invariably described as rotund, frightened yet game. The story went that he jumped, came under fire and spent invasion morning shouting, ''Que pasa?'' at uncomprehending Grenadians. Finally, went the tale, Sergeant Ontiveros realized, ''These people speak English, not Spanish! I've volunteered for nothing!'' I wanted badly to report that story, but could never meet Sergeant Ontiveros, nor anyone who had ever met Sergeant Ontiveros. There was no Sergeant Ontiveros listed in the American invasion force. Yet it was still a sterling story, as it reflected the feelings of enlisted soldiers toward the officers who had planned the invasion.

MURROW His Life and Times. By A. M. Sperber. Illustrated. 795 pp. New York: Freundlich Books. $22.95.

''HELLO America, this is London calling.'' It was 1938 and the voice was Edward R. Murrow's. The cadenced words came nightly through the shortwave static across the Atlantic to the living rooms of America. ''You burned the city of London in our houses and we felt the flames that burned it,'' Archibald MacLeish said of Murrow and those broadcasts. ''You laid the dead of London at our doors and we knew that the dead were our dead . . . were mankind's dead . . . without rhetoric, without dramatics, without more emotion than needed be. . . . You have destroyed . . . the superstition that what is done beyond 3,000 miles of water is not really done at all.''

Those radio reports marked the beginning of the career of the most important broadcaster of our time. Murrow was then, at the age of 30, a pioneer of radio journalism. Later he became the most prominent figure in the new medium of television news. Then he undertook a second career in government, serving in President Kennedy's Administration before dying of cancer in 1965 at 57.

IN his later years Henry Adams enjoyed thinking of himself as a failure. Now his ghost will have to learn to live - quizzically, no doubt - with the burden of incontestable success. After being out of print for several decades, Adams's monumental history of the Jefferson and Madison Administrations has been reissued, as the latest publication of the Library of America - the surest sign the present age has to offer that it is a certified classic.   Even so, most readers are likely to wonder whether it is really worth giving it the time it requires - and it runs to some 2,700 pages. Sooner or later, after all, even the finest historical work is bound to be overtaken by subsequent research; what are the qualities that nonetheless give this particular specimen, originally published nearly 100 years ago, its enduring attraction?

pull_quote: THE TRIUMPH OF PIERROT The Commedia dell'Arte and the Modern Imagination. By Martin Green and John Swan. Illustrated. 297 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $25.   THE commedia dell'arte originated in Renaissance Italy as a lowbrow parody of the commedia erudita (''learned comedy'') that dominated the polite stage. The ''art'' in the label meant skillful performance, not poetry; settings were minimal and the untrained actors often improvised their lines. Because the early commedia dell'arte was both plebeian and unwritten, we possess few records of it, though we know it flourished in Italy into the 19th century and was established as early as 1576 in France, where it strongly influenced the higher-toned comedies of Moliere. Some of its stock characters - wistful Pierrot, fickle Columbine, tricky Harlequin - became cliches of popular culture, even in countries that had little contact with the commedia itself.

title: Ford: The Men And The Machine
author: Robert Lacey. Illustrated.

pull_quote: FORD The Men and the Machine. By Robert Lacey. Illustrated. 778 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $24.95.   HENRY FORD was an authentic American folk hero, the humbly born son of Irish immigrants, self-taught and self-made, who struggled valiantly against adversity, like Ragged Dick or any other of Horatio Alger's characters. He didn't invent the car, as Edison invented the incandescent lamp, but he made it available to the masses, a fine and democratic (not to say profitable) thing to do.   What Henry Ford did invent was the notion that society could be bettered by running it along the lines of an industrial plant. In his soul he wasn't a businessman but a social engineer. Why couldn't people be more like Model A's, reliable, trustworthy, economical, good performers capable of improvement. His gospel was Emerson, whose oblique Darwinian message reconciled the idealist and the entrepreneur. Each man had to live up to his potential, said the sage of Concord, for each man had God in him. You could not be ''leaning willows.'' You had to cultivate self-reliance and be guided by your own light, however dim, and not that of others. Ford recognized himself in Emerson's description of ''a class of men . . . endowed with insight and virtue,'' ''usually received with ill-will because they are new.''

LESS THAN ONE Selected Essays. By Joseph Brodsky. 501 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $25.

FOR those of us who still follow the faint trajectory of contemporary Russian letters, Joseph Brodsky's selected essays come as an event both valedictory and anticipatory. Their appearance on the horizon, like that Roman candle or ''shower of light'' of which Marina Tsvetayeva spoke in her well-known essay on Pasternak, makes the surrounding darkness more palpable. These studies of poets and prose writers, reminiscences and ethical and esthetic musings are shot through with an intensely lived native (though by no means narrow or local) culture many of us have been looking in vain for in the otherwise talented members of the so-called Third Wave of Russian emigre writers. What left others, like Tsvetayeva and Vladislav Khodasevich, beached like leviathans in the backwaters of emigre politics was their lack of English and of access to a readership worthy of the name.

THE title suggests a riddle: where do you place ''The John Foster Dulles Book of Humor'' in a bookstore? Between ''Dean Rusk's Favorite Recipes'' and ''George Shultz's Ten Best Party Tricks''? Those who never knew, or hardly remember, the austere Presbyterian Dulles, President Eisenhower's Secretary of State and the man for whom the homburg hat must have been invented, might initially suspect that ''The John Foster Dulles Book of Humor'' is a deliberate oxymoron. The image problem was once addressed by Dulles himself: ''Anyway, I know that in some ways I am a cold fish, and that I'm afraid is that.'' Also, it was Prime Minister Anthony Eden of Britain who used to joke about ''dull, duller, Dulles.''   As Dulles's security officer for five years until the diplomat died in 1959, Louis Jefferson has compiled the sort of personal recollections and press-club-bar war stories that require amplification with age. The old patrician was really a card, Mr. Jefferson seems to be telling us, but as is often the case with anecdotes, being there is half the fun.

title: Microcosmos
author: Lynn Margulis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MICROCOSMOS Four Billion Years of Evolution From Our Microbial Ancestors. By Lynn Margulis and Dorion Sagan. Foreword by Lewis Thomas. Illustrated. 301 pp. New York: Summit Books. $17.95.   IT is frustrating not to be able to praise ''Microcosmos'' unreservedly. This collaboration between a very distinguished biologist and a very talented writer (the last phrase may be inadequate) attempts to present the whole history of life on earth. If it had stopped there, it might have been possible to say it is the one book to read about that history, a masterpiece. Unfortunately, Lynn Margulis, a professor of biology at Boston University, and Dorion Sagan, a science writer, did not stop there but added a number of things more dubious and idiosyncratic, making the book much narrower in interest. Still, annoying though this is, most of ''Microcosmos'' is a sheer delight to read, a feast.
headline: BACTERIAL COLONIES LIKE US

title: The Landing
author: Haynes Johnson and Howard Simons
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LANDING By Haynes Johnson and Howard Simons. 319 pp. New York: Villard Books. $17.95.   ALTHOUGH it starts like one, ''The Landing'' is not a traditional World War II suspense novel. It attempts to be a serious examination of American racial attitudes in Washington during the early months of the war. This relatively high-minded approach to the construction of a thriller is both a principal strength of the novel and its most debilitating weakness. ''The Landing'' is an eminently laudable work. Its intentions are honorable, and it reflects well upon its authors' social consciousness. It carries an important message, and I desperately wish I liked it more.
headline: THE PLOT TO START A RACE WAR

title: The Straw Giant
author: Arthur T. Hadley.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE STRAW GIANT Triumph and Failure: America's Armed Forces. A Report From the Field. By Arthur T. Hadley. 314 pp. New York: Random House. $19.95.   AS the French would say, ''Arthur T. Hadley deserves well of the Republic.'' At a critical moment in the history of the American military he has written a clear, incisive account of its strengths and many weaknesses. The author has two advantages: he served in the United States Army in World War II, and since then he has been tireless as a reporter and as a consultant to the Joint Chiefs of Staff - attending NATO exercises, visiting ships, air bases and remote Army posts. Few writers have as profound a knowledge of the armed services, their virtues and faults, as Arthur Hadley.
headline: WHAT'S WRONG WITH THE MILITARY MIND

pull_quote: KILLING FOR COMPANY: The Case of Dennis Nilsen. By Brian Masters. (Stein & Day, $18.95.) In British criminal history, Dennis Nilsen holds a double distinction.

pull_quote: RITES: A Guatemalan Boyhood. By Victor Perera. (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, $15.95.) Take a young Portnoy, clean up his act a bit and plop him down in Guatemala.
