title: Lasalle
author: John Vernon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LA SALLE By John Vernon. 240 pp. New York: Viking. $17.95.   THIS small seamless novel concerns four moments in the life of the explorer Robert Cavelier, sieur de La Salle: his successful 1682 voyage down the ''Messipi'' River, his attempts in Paris two years later to finance another expedition, his disastrous return to what would eventually be Texas, and his cartographer's long trek from there to Canada to recount his master's fate.
headline: DOWN THE CRAZY RIVER

title: Cats Of The Temple
author: Brad Leithauser
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
CATS OF THE TEMPLE By Brad Leithauser. 70 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. Cloth, $14.95. Paper, $7.95.

STARS PRINCIPAL By J. D. McClatchy. 81 pp. New York: Collier Books/Macmillan Publishing Company. Cloth, $16.95. Paper, $9.95.

DIFFICULTY By William Logan. 64 pp. Boston: David R. Godine. Cloth, $12.95. Paper, $8.95. BRAD LEITHAUSER'S first book of poems, ''Hundreds of Fireflies,'' was greeted with unusual critical acclaim, and deservedly so. It was accomplished, unpretentious and - rare among books of poetry - readable. His novel, ''Equal Distance,'' while weak in plot, pacing and characterization, was dazzling in its use of language and particularly pleasing in its imagery and power of sensory evocation. It was, in short, a poet's novel. Mr. Leithauser's second book of verse, ''Cats of the Temple,'' is a letdown. It disappoints because it represents no artistic growth, no broadening of poetic vision beyond what was evident in the first book.
headline: DRAGONFLIES AND HEGEL'S COWS

title: I Am Having An Adventure
author: Perri Klass
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: I AM HAVING AN ADVENTURE By Perri Klass. 253 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $17.95.   WHAT constitutes an adventure? A move from the semicomfortable present to the unknowable future, along with the thrill that comes from exposing oneself to the possibility of danger. The stories in Perri Klass's first collection (her novel, ''Recombinations,'' was published last fall) are risky, but things happen to the people in them.
headline: BORED? TAKE OFF WITH A STRANGER

title: Gilbert Green: The Real Right Way To Dress For Spring
author: Frederick Ted Castle
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GILBERT GREEN: The Real Right Way to Dress for Spring. By Frederick Ted Castle. (McPherson, $16.95.) If you were in New York in the late 1960's and spent your time rubbing shoulders with Andy Warhol at Max's Kansas City, rushing off in cabs to catch the latest Charles Ludlam play or participating in endless improvisational 16-millimeter epics, then Frederick Ted Castle's ''Gilbert Green'' - written in 1968 but only now unveiled - will probably set you reeling with the shock of recollection.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Lights, Camera, Action!
author: Louis Goldman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Cocky, baby-faced Warren Beatty jabs a bossy finger at Robert Rossen, the aging, infirm director of ''Lilith''; Dustin Hoffman hisses an eloquent obscenity at Robert Redford, who has just flubbed a line during the filming of ''All The President's Men''; the most macho of maestros huddles with a permed-blond transvestite on the set of ''Fellini-Roma.'' These historic yet private off-camera moments have been captured on film by a sly, omnipresent still-photographer named Louis Goldman, as you will joyfully discover while leafing through LIGHTS, CAMERA, ACTION! Behind the Scenes, Making Movies (Abrams, $35). Mr. Goldman has not been content, however, to stuff the 216 pages of this tome with gloriously printed black-and-white remembrances of his colorful past.
headline: NO, BUT I SAW THE STILLS

title: The Malady Of Death
author: Marguerite Duras
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MALADY OF DEATH. By Marguerite Duras. Translated by Barbara Bray. (Grove, $9.95.) The success last year of ''The Lover'' enhanced critical celebration of Marguerite Duras.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Contract
author: J. W. Rhoads.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CONTRACT By J. W. Rhoads. 108 pp. New York: Henry Holt & Company. $12.95. MONSIEUR BAUDOIN buys an apartment. What else is new? He buys it in Paris. And?   It is a viager - a very different matter! The story of one's viager is sure to interrupt the most heated political discussion at any dinner party.
headline: WAITING FOR MADAME

title: The Agency: The Rise And Decline Of The Cia
author: John Ranelagh. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE AGENCY The Rise and Decline of the CIA. By John Ranelagh. Illustrated. 847 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $22.95. IT looked like the spectacular finale to a Fourth of July fireworks extravaganza. Several hundred feet above the Pacific coast, near Vandenberg Air Force Base, a huge Titan rocket carrying a spy satellite exploded in a brilliant starburst. The loss last April of the Titan and its cargo, coupled with the earlier loss of the space shuttle and the later loss of a Delta rocket, has thrown the United States intelligence community, grown precariously dependent on space and high technology, into one of the most severe crises in its history.   The long and sometimes bitter war over whether intelligence gathering is better done by men or machines is one of the many subjects addressed by John Ranelagh's comprehensive examination of the Central Intelligence Agency, ''The Agency: The Rise and Decline of the CIA.'' Unlike most books on the nearly 40-year-old spy organization, ''The Agency'' is not a diary of old war stories or a flashy expose; it is a thoughtful analysis of the C.I.A. from gestation to middle age.
headline: KEEPING INTELLIGENCE SMART

title: Family Secrets
author: David Leitch.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FAMILY SECRETS A Writer's Search for His Parents and His Past. By David Leitch. 242 pp. New York: Delacorte Press. $17.95.   IN his previous memoir, ''God Stand Up for Bastards,'' David Leitch, well known as a writer for such British publications as The Sunday Times, The Guardian and the New Statesman, sent out the literary equivalent of a smoke signal: ''Mother,'' he asked, ''where are you?'' The title of that book suggests the problem; at the age of 8 days, the infant David had been given away by his natural mother, to a prosperous couple who answered her advertisement in The London Daily Express. (It is appropriate, perhaps, that the fate of so prominent a journalist should have been decided by a newspaper.) He never really expected to see his mother again, but a year after his book's anguished inquiry, she answered. ''Family Secrets'' is the subsequent account of one man's journey toward his unknown parents, which was essentially a journey toward his unknown self. It is one of the oldest stories in the world, at least as old as Telemachus, who set out to find his father, Odysseus, after the Trojan War, and it has survived so long precisely because of its power. But even though that familiar search has been the material of epic and fairy tale, in ''Family Secrets'' it becomes a much more problematic and unsettling business. The ''secrets'' of Mr. Leitch's title have to be extracted painfully, from people who are often confused, difficult and, in certain respects, unlovable.
headline: NOTES OF AN INVESTIGATIVE SON

title: Flannery Row
author: Karen Ackerman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FLANNERY ROW By Karen Ackerman. Illustrated by Karen Ann Weinhaus. Unpaged. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. $12.95. (Ages 3 to 8) TELEVISION'S ''Sesame Street'' has made the old alphabet book all but obsolete. Yet nothing can discourage the children's book publishing industry from producing some unusual, ambitious examples from time to time. No recent work has superseded C. B. Falls's classic ''ABC Book'' (1957) in so effectively teaching a child his letters, but the latest is worthy of sharing a shelf with ''Ashanti to Zulu'' (1977) by Leo and Diane Dillon and ''On Market Street'' by Anita and Arnold Lobel (1981). ''Flannery Row'' is not just another alphabet book; in it Karen Ackerman has invented a charming memory game.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: The Catalogue Of The Universe
author: Margaret Mahy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CATALOGUE OF THE UNIVERSE By Margaret Mahy. 185 pp. New York: A Margaret K. McElderry Book/ Atheneum. $11.95. (Ages 14 and up) IN a literature for young adults overpopulated with innocuously pretty girls, Margaret Mahy, a prize-winning author from New Zealand, presents us with a heroine, deceptively named Angela May, who is unsettlingly beautiful. Her mother, Dido, unable to convince her Aeneas to stay (''he's too fond of his first family to run any risks'') has taken their daughter to live in a rundown cottage atop Dry Creek Road, above the city.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: For Sylvia
author: Valentine Ackland. Foreword by Bea Howe.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FOR SYLVIA An Honest Account. By Valentine Ackland. Foreword by Bea Howe. 135 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $13.95.   ONE might think that an account of growing up lesbian in England during the 1920's would make a quaint tale of persecution, something remote and historical; but key aspects of Valentine Ackland's wispy yet trenchantly told story may be amply found in today's lesbian literature: the horror of parents when learning of their daughter's ''aberration,'' the pressures to conform, the threats and punishments, the need for secrecy, the flight of the daughter into some brief unhappy marriage or into drugs, alcohol, obsessive travel, indiscriminate sex - these are familiar contingencies described in any recent work of the genre. Equally familiar are the strong avowals of pleasure in knowing another woman intimately, the sense of rightness and of happiness in love, despite social opposition. Miss Ackland's story has it all.
headline: HERSELF EXPLAINED

title: The Vietnamese Gulag
author: Doan Van Toai and David Chanoff
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE VIETNAMESE GULAG By Doan Van Toai and David Chanoff. Illustrated. 351 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.   TEN years after the Communists' almost unopposed but dramatic capture of Saigon, the Vietnam War continues to produce shelves of books, mostly written by Americans. Only recently have the Vietnamese begun to write of the war and, perhaps more significant, of its aftermath.   A few Communist authors have published military accounts, notably about the ''Ho Chi Minh campaign,'' which has as its climax Saigon's fall; a considerable number of novels and short stories as well as diaries and essays have appeared in Vietnamese, some of which have been translated. Very few Southerners, however, except for a handful of old-regime officers, have written anything of consequence since they fled Vietnam after April 1975. And even less has come from those who believed in the revolution and initially stayed behind.
headline: RETHINKING THE REVOLUTION

title: East And West
author: Gerald Green
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EAST AND WEST By Gerald Green. 476 pp. New York: Donald I. Fine. $18.95.   WAS that Kipling's ghost snorting? In the passionate flesh of Julie Varnum and Kenji Tamba, Occident and Orient not only meet, they merge and multiply. With Pearl Harbor just six months away, their eyes lock on the U.C.L.A. campus. Before you can say Papa Hemingway, the earth moves for the all-American girl and the brilliant Japanese student. They become man and wife. The union is beset by personal and geopolitical strains. Both families are upset for traditional reasons. How can a red-haired campus belle prefer a bowing Japanese to the fine young marine next door? How dare the second son of a civil servant at Emperor Hirohito's court wed a shallow, round-eyed foreigner? But there it is. The advent of war in the Pacific carries Julie and Kenji first to a detention camp and then to Japan, where the clash of cultures is soon complemented by deprivation and the crash of American bombs.
headline: KANJI LOVES JULIE

title: Home: A Short History of an Idea
author: Witold Rybczynski
pull_quote: HOME: A Short History of an Idea. By Witold Rybczynski. Illustrated. 256 pages. Viking. $16.95. IN the opening chapter, ''Nostalgia,'' of this delightful, intelligent book about the idea of the home in Western culture, Witold Rybczynski dilates on the subject of Ralph Lauren as a ''total fashion designer'' and ''an orchestrator of images.'' By and by he arrives at an amusing description of the four exhibition rooms at Bloomingdale's Ralph Lauren Home Furnishings boutique, which were designated ''Log Cabin,'' ''Thoroughbred,'' ''New England'' and ''Jamaica.'' His point, almost incidentally, is that these rooms are completely innocent of clock radios, electric hair dryers or video games. ''The mechanical paraphernalia of contemporary living has been put away, and replaced by brass-cornered gun boxes, silver bedside water carafes, and leather-bound books.''   Much later, near the end of ''Home,'' Mr. Rybczynski makes the point that nostalgia ''for the past,'' such as is revealed by the Ralph Lauren rooms, ''is often a sign of dissatisfaction with the present.'' After all, we don't pine for period cuisine or drive antique cars. Yet ''if department stores or home-decorating magazines are any indication, most people's first choice would be to live in rooms that resemble, as much as their budgets permit, those of their grandparents.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: All Of Us Here
author: Irving Feldman
pull_quote: ALL OF US HERE. By Irving Feldman. 81 pages. Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. Cloth, $17.95; paper, $8.95. IRVING FELDMAN made his name 25 years ago with his first collection of poems, ''Works and Days.'' Since then he has advanced steadily from volume to volume, establishing himself as one of the most gifted and intelligent American poets of his generation; but nowhere before has he broken new ground quite as boldly as he does in his new collection, ''All of Us Here'' - or rather in the title poem that makes up a good half of the book.   ''All of Us Here'' - the title poem, that is - opens with a hubbub of mixed reactions. We are in a museum, at an exhibition of work by the contemporary American sculptor George Segal, and visitors are offering their comments on Mr. Segal's creations, everything from ''God, sometimes I feel just the way they look.'' to ''Do you have any idea what plaster does to a rug?'' Then someone complains that ''It's starting to get crowded in here,'' and the voices fade away with somebody else asking: ''Who are all these people?''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Tombee: Portrait Of A Cotton Planter
author: Theodore Rosengarten
pull_quote: TOMBEE: PORTRAIT OF A COTTON PLANTER. By Theodore Rosengarten. 750 pages. William Morrow & Company. $22.95.   IF further evidence is needed about why the nonnegotiable institution of slavery made the Civil War inevitable, it can be found in Theodore Rosengarten's ''Tombee: Portrait of a Cotton Planter.'' Tombee was the name of a plantation on St. Helena Island, in South Carolina, run by a quite ordinary man named Thomas B. Chaplin. The only thing extraordinary about him was that he had some sense of destiny and kept a journal between 1845 and 1861.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Iron Eagle: The Turbulent Life Of General Curtis Lemay
author: Curtis Lemay
pull_quote: IRON EAGLE: The Turbulent Life of General Curtis LeMay. By Thomas M. Coffey. Illustrated. 449 pages. Crown Publishers Inc. $18.95. CURTIS LEMAY was an   American original. He came from the wrong side of the tracks. He was always laconic, often rude. He held strong, right-wing opinions. He was also a genius in aerial bombardment who played a leading role in devising the tactics that enabled American day bombing to succeed over Germany and the B-29's to reduce Tokyo and other Japanese cities to ashes.
headline: BOOKS: BOMBING GENIUS

title: Red Storm Rising
author: Tom Clancy
pull_quote: RED STORM RISING. By Tom Clancy. 652 pages. Putnam's. $19.95.    ''ONCE more unto the breach, dear friends, once more.''   It's time for World War III in Tom Clancy's second novel, ''Red Storm Rising,'' his first having been the phenomenally successfully ''Hunt for Red October'' about a race between the United States and the Soviet Union to capture a defected Russian nuclear submarine.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Henry Flagler
author: David Leon Chandler
pull_quote: HENRY FLAGLER: The Astonishing Life and Times of the Visionary Robber Baron Who Founded Florida. By David Leon Chandler. Illustrated. 324 pages. Macmillan. $22.50. HOW many people - at least outside Florida, the state he did so much to develop - could readily identify Henry Flagler today? Yet he was one of the more remarkable of the major carnivores who stalked the American economy in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He merits a biography, and David Leon Chandler's is only the second to be published in the 73 years since his death.   Flagler was born in upstate New York in 1830, the son of an itinerant minister. His parents separated when he was a child, and he was brought up by his mother; at 14 he struck out on his own and headed for Ohio, where his half brother ran a country store. He made money as a grain merchant and lost it as a salt manufacturer; then, after the Civil War, he moved to Cleveland, became caught up in the burgeoning oil industry and joined forces with the owner of a small refinery who had previously acted for him as a commission agent in the grain business, John D. Rockefeller.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Oskar Kokoschka: A Life
author: Frank Whitford
pull_quote: OSKAR KOKOSCHKA: A Life. By Frank Whitford. Illustrated. 221 pages. Atheneum. $21.95. Oskar Kokoschka was born a hundred years ago this year in a small town in Austria called Pochlarn. Shortly after his birth a fire broke out, threatening to engulf the entire town, and he was carried to safety in a hay cart. Or so his mother told him, and so he always believed - though Frank Whitford assures us in his new biography of the artist that the fire almost certainly never took place. No matter; the important thing is that the story meant so much to Kokoschka that it reinforced him in his belief in portents and in his sense of being reserved for an exceptional destiny.
headline: ARTIST AS OUTSIDER

title: Slave
author: William Malliol
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SLAVE. By William Malliol. (Norton, $16.95.) A comic novel about slavery? One has to admire the author's audacity, even if he doesn't pull it off.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Fantomas
author: Marcel Allain and Pierre Souvestre
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
FANTOMAS By Marcel Allain and Pierre Souvestre. With an introduction by John Ashbery. 324 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $17.95. IN 1911 a French publisher covered the walls of Paris with posters depicting ''Fantomas, Master of Dread, Torturer, Emperor of Crime,'' and created a minor myth even before readers had purchased the first volume of his adventures. Within weeks Fantomas had become a popular hero, a fashionable hero, a Dadaist hero, the hero of the intellectual elite.

Fantomas's success was due to the very nature of the character. Where literature had been high-minded, now this purely criminal hero inflamed imaginations as exquisite as those of Jean Cocteau and Guillaume Apollinaire as he violated society women and left their delicately slashed bodies for the servants to find.
headline: SOCIETY WOMEN, DELICATELY SLASHED

title: Margaret Bourke-White
author: Vicki Goldberg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MARGARET BOURKE-WHITE By Vicki Goldberg. Illustrated. 426 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $25.95.   MARGARET BOURKE-WHITE (1904-71) never had herself fired from a cannon or tried to seduce Joseph Stalin. But nobody who reads this book will doubt that she would have done these things without a moment's hesitation had either promised to provide a handsome photograph or enhance her reputation as a glamorous photojournalist with access to power.   First and foremost what emerges from this thoroughgoing but ambivalent biography are Bourke-White's extraordinary courage and concern for image - her own as well as those she trapped with her lens -not to mention her extreme manipulativeness. She could and did cry on cue whenever anyone stood in the way of a picture. In a man's world she also learned, as Vicki Goldberg explains, not as it turns out with total accuracy, to ''promise what she had no intention of delivering.''
headline: SHE WAS ABOVE SELF-REPROACH

title: The Prodigy
author: Amy Wallace
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PRODIGY. By Amy Wallace. (Dutton, $18.95.) At the age of 3 William James Sidis learned Latin as a gift to his father; at 11 he was admitted to Harvard College and gave a lecture to the mathematics club.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Mythmaker
author: Hyam Maccoby.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MYTHMAKER Paul and the Invention of Christianity. By Hyam Maccoby. 237 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $17.95. THE line of Hyam Maccoby's argument in ''The   Mythmaker'' is clear: Jesus was a Pharisee who regarded himself as the Jewish Messiah, a human leader who would restore the Jewish monarchy by calling on God to drive out the Roman invaders and establish an independent Jewish state. Believing that God would perform this liberating miracle on the Mount of Olives (as foretold by Zechariah), Jesus went to Jerusalem, only to find that His utopian dream was not fulfilled. The Romans perceived His plan, arrested Him and tried and executed Him; they had done this earlier to other leaders of Jewish liberation movements, as Mr. Maccoby points out in his earlier book, ''Revolution in Judea.''
headline: A GENTILE IN SPITE OF HIMSELF

title: The Compleat Violinist
author: Yehudi Menuhin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE COMPLEAT VIOLINIST: Thoughts, Exercises, Reflections of an Itinerant Violinist. By Yehudi Menuhin. (Summit, $15.95.) In this little book, intended for the violin student and yet frequently relevant to all musical activity, the master violinist alternates panegyrics to the musical life with practical, yogalike exercises for shaping the musician's body.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The War Of The Two Emperors
author: Curtis Cate
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WAR OF THE TWO EMPERORS: The Duel Between Napoleon and Alexander. Russia, 1812. By Curtis Cate. (Random House, $24.95.) In 1812 Russia stood alone in Europe against Napoleon, victor of Austerlitz, Wagram, Jena and all those other battlefields whose names are known to anyone who has trudged the tourist's Paris.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Gorbachev
author: Zhores A. Medvedev.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GORBACHEV By Zhores A. Medvedev. 272 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $15.95.   THE main grist of Kremlinology has always been the civic rites of the Soviet state - or, more precisely, deviations from those rites. More so than any other political system, the Soviet system has sought throughout much of its history to subsume politics in an elaborate cycle of public events. The lineup of leaders at the Nov. 7 celebration of the Russian Revolution, the annual May Day demonstration, the slogans carried by the bused-in public, the elections at which 99.8 percent of the populace approves a single slate of candidates, the toasts at banquets for visiting heads of state when Soviet leaders review world affairs, the debates at Supreme Soviet sessions or at party congresses, the order of signatures on an obituary, the wording of official announcements, even the funerals of party leaders all follow a precisely ordered script. It is a routine that is supposed to give a reassuring sense of continuity, immutable order, unanimity.
headline: THE SEARCH FOR GORBACHEV

title: Social Disease
author: Paul Rudnick
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOCIAL DISEASE By Paul Rudnick. 195 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $14.95.   THE scene is ''the fabulous Club de,'' the hottest nightspot this week, and outside are the requisite desperate throngs shrieking for admittance.   Those inside - the lucky, the chic, the rich and the sordid - are a crowd of markedly ambiguous sexuality and well-rehearsed style. It is a world of aging debutantes and professional dilettantes where the unwritten code is ''Don't call me before noon'' and the only sin that surpasses that of showing any sincerity is the wearing of synthetics.
headline: EIGHT MILLION TRENDS IN THE NAKED CITY

title: King Matt The First
author: Janusz Korczak
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: KING MATT THE FIRST By Janusz Korczak. Translated by Richard Lourie. Introduction by Bruno Bettelheim. 332 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $15.95. (Ages 10 and up).   ON Aug. 5, 1942, the director of an orphanage for Jewish children on Warsaw, Henryk Goldszmit, known throughout Poland under his pen name Janusz Korczak, accompanied more than 200 orphans to the main railroad station. Their destination was the Treblinka concentration camp. Although influential Polish friends had secured escape routes, he refused to abandon his young wards: he boarded the train with the orphans and was annihilated with them. However, the Nazis were never able to annihilate the record of Korczak's deed and his remarkable contributions to the fields of child psychology and children's literature.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: The Irish Signorina
author: Julia O'Faolain.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE IRISH SIGNORINA Divertimento. By Julia O'Faolain. 187 pp. Bethesda, Md.: Adler & Adler. $15.95.
A YOUNG woman, Anne, travels to

Florence from her native Ireland after her mother's death, the better to understand her mother's life. The mother, at nearly the same age, served as au pair to an aristocratic Italian family and, discovered in a romantic adventure, was dismissed. Sweet memories sharpened by loss were to color the rest of her days, and the sensibilities of her young daughter as well. The father, also dead, never counted, never shared in the mother's erotic daydreams or the intimacies conveyed to the daughter. ''Passion, in Mummy's book, excused all, but without a high, hot blaze of it sex was tawdry.'' ''Mummy's reluctance to acknowledge disappointing truths had left Anne leery of fantasy - especially Mummy's.'' Anne comes, finally, to absorb ''a horror of the unlived life.''
headline: MUMMY'S EROTIC DAYDREAMS

title: The Legacy Of Ladysmith
author: John Kenny Crane
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LEGACY OF LADYSMITH By John Kenny Crane. 398 pp. New York: Linden Press/Simon & Schuster. $17.95.   IT is to the Boer War, that ferocious turn-of-the-century contest between two British colonies and two Dutch-French nations, that the bleeding patchwork of the Republic of South Africa owes its dubious existence. One of the war's most harrowing episodes, the siege of a British garrison town in Natal, provides the dramatic basis for ''The Legacy of Ladysmith,'' an exceptionally ingenious first novel by John Kenny Crane.
headline: JASON GLASS UNDER THE LOCH

title: Stealing The Language
author: Alicia Suskin Ostriker.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STEALING THE LANGUAGE The Emergence of Women's Poetry in America. By Alicia Suskin Ostriker. 315 pp. Boston: Beacon Press. $19.95. THE subtitle is misleading. The first chapter of ''Stealing the Language: The Emergence of Women's Poetry in America'' simply gallops through women's poetry from 1650 to 1960 - 44 pages for more than 300 years. The remaining chapters focus on women's poetry from 1960 to the present, with only occasional reference to women poets as ''historical'' as H.D. In that accelerated first chapter, some extraordinarily interesting poets are given short shrift, among them Edna St. Vincent Millay, Amy Lowell and Emma Lazarus. (Lazarus is mentioned in one sentence acknowledging late 19th-century poets who ''wrote on humanitarian issues.'') This is all the more unfortunate in light of Alicia Suskin Ostriker's wonderful analysis of Emily Dickinson's poetry. Mrs. Ostriker is brilliant at close reading, but she rarely puts her talent for it to work in this book. I would have been interested to read her at length about other long-lost poets, like Frances Osgood, who is tantalizingly quoted but given only brief attention here. ''The Emergence of Women's Poetry in America'' would indeed be a book worth writing, but it is not the book Mrs. Ostriker has produced.
headline: THE POWER OF VICTIMS

title: Dear Diego
author: Elena Poniatowska
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
DEAR DIEGO By Elena Poniatowska. Translated by Katherine Silver. 87 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $10.95.
WHEN Diego Rivera left Paris for his native

Mexico in 1921, the young Russian exile and painter Angelina Beloff, who had been his common-law wife for seven years, waited for him to send for her as promised. She took comfort in the jacket he had left hanging in the entryway. It retained the shape of his ample body, and she did not dare to dust it for fear that it would lose the imprint of his presence. But the celebrated artist never returned to fill its sleeves.

title: Sink The Rainbow!

pull_quote: SINK THE RAINBOW! An Enquiry Into the ''Greenpeace Affair.'' By John Dyson with Joseph Fitchett. Illustrated. 192 pp. North Pomfret, Vt.: Victor Gollancz/David & Charles. $19.95.   AFTER France and New Zealand accepted United Nations mediation in their dispute over the ''Greenpeace affair'' aftermath, the two French intelligence agents imprisoned in New Zealand for their role in the sinking of the Rainbow Warrior last July are being released.

title: Act Of Will
author: Barbara Taylor Bradford
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ACT OF WILL. By Barbara Taylor Bradford. (Doubleday, $17.95.) This book's title raises a question: Is the ''act of will'' Audra Crowther's struggle to give her daughter Christina a charmed life? Is it Christina's struggle to build a fashion empire to repay her mother for all she has done? Or is the most remarkable act of will exerted by the reader who gets to the last page of this book? Barbara Taylor Bradford, the phenomenally best-selling author of ''A Woman of Substance'' and ''Hold the Dream,'' gives us Audra Kenton, orphaned from a once-wealthy family, who works as a Yorkshire nurse until she is swept off her feet by Vincent Crowther.

author: Bernard Drew
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HARD-BOILED DAMES: Stories Featuring Women Detectives, Reporters, Adventurers, and Criminals From the Pulp Fiction Magazines of the 1930's. Edited by Bernard Drew. (St. Martin's, $16.95.)

title: The Mexican Pet
author: Jan Harold Brunvand
pull_quote: THE MEXICAN PET: More ''New''   Urban Legends and Some Old Favorites. By Jan Harold Brunvand. Illustrated. 221 pages. W. W. Norton. $13.95.   THERE are some entertaining whoppers in Jan Harold Brunvand's latest collection of ''urban legends,'' the title of which, ''The Mexican Pet,'' refers to the absolutely true story, told by the inevitable friend of a friend - or F.O.A.F. - about an American woman who smuggled home from Tijuana, Mexico, what she thought was a friendly Chihuahua, only to learn from a veterinarian that she'd adopted a dying sewer rat.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Purge
author: Herbert R Lottman
pull_quote: THE PURGE. By Herbert R. Lottman. 332 pages. William Morrow. $19.95.   IN World War II, during the Nazi occupation of France, Frenchmen who collaborated with the enemy were left in no doubt, either by the Free French - broadcasting from London - or by the underground press, that once the country had been liberated they could expect to face a day of reckoning. Well before the liberation, in fact, the Resistance had begun meting out its own brand of justice, and plans were being drawn up by the Gaullist government-in-waiting for an official epuration - a purification or purge.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: A Girl Of Forty
author: Herbert Gold
pull_quote: A GIRL OF FORTY. By Herbert Gold. 254 pages. Donald I. Fine. $16.95. IN ''A Girl of Forty,'' Herbert   Gold has created a California Holly Golightly, and more. But instead of breakfasting at Tiffany's, she has dinner on the grass. Grass, recreational drugs, trendy veggies, avocado dips and other nutrients that she and her friends consider good for one's life style and karma are consumed. Eating, drinking and smoking do not simply satisfy hunger and habit; they are food for thought and soul. Like Cyra McFadden's pitch-perfect ''The Serial,'' Herbert Gold is a master of San Francisco Speak, that foggy lingua francaof the laid back on both sides of the Golden Gate Bridge.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Jesse Owens: An American Life
author: William J Baker
pull_quote: JESSE OWENS: An American Life. By William J. Baker. Illustrated. 289 pages. Free Press/Macmillan. $19.95.   UPON reading the final pages of Prof. William J. Baker's remarkable biography of Jesse Owens, the great black athlete, we feel a little as if we'd just witnessed some breathtaking sleight of hand. How did he do that?, we want to know. How did he manage to tell two contradictory stories, yet leave the reader feeling as if he'd learned a single truth?
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Spring Jaunts
author: Anthony Bailey
pull_quote: SPRING JAUNTS: Some Walks, Excursions & Personal Explorations of Town, Country & Seashore. By Anthony Bailey. 239 pages. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $16.95.   ANTHONY BAILEY likes traveling, particularly walking, and he likes to write about his expeditions. In ''Spring Jaunts'' he has gathered together five travel pieces, reports from the Isle of Wight and the River Severn in Engand, from the River Boyne in Ireland, from New Hampshire and the Cote d'Azur.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Celebrating The Wild Mushroom: A Passionate Quest
author: Sara Ann Friedman
pull_quote: CELEBRATING THE WILD MUSHROOM: A Passionate Quest. By Sara Ann Friedman. Illustrations by Diana Jacobs. 265 pages. Dodd, Mead. Hardcover, $18.95; paperback, $10.95. Why would anyone want to look for, let alone eat, fungi? For any number of reasons, according to this entertaining celebration of wild mushrooms by Sara Ann Friedman. They can be delicious, a far sight better than the bland commercial variety. They are fascinating to hunt and study, especially the rare ones like the morel, which many mycophiles consider the Moby Dick of mushrooms. And they are sensual and erotic, not only in their appearance but often, too, in their taste, texture and smell.   But the more interesting question that Ms. Friedman addresses in ''Celebrating the Wild Mushroom: A Passionate Quest'' is, Why would anyone not want to hunt and devour fungi? The answers here seem more compelling, at least on the printed page. Wild mushrooms are dangerous: you can get poisoned to death if you get careless. They are repellent: as Ms. Friedman observes, in some minds, everything putrescent and dangerous is associated with fungi. ''In a dazzling display of etymological virtuosity,'' she writes, a retired banker named Gordon Wasson has ''uncovered a kinship between fungi, toadstools, poison, frogstools, witchcraft, Satan in all his disguises, imps, filth, foulness, toadstools and stools of another sort, udders, sponges, and finally to the source of all life - the womb.''
headline: Fervent for Fungi

title: Seven Summits
author: Dick Bass and Frank Wells with Rick Ridgeway
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SEVEN SUMMITS. By Dick Bass and Frank Wells with Rick Ridgeway. (Warner, $19.95.) What would motivate two middle-aged businessmen, strangers with little climbing experience, to spend four years attempting to climb the highest mountain on each of the seven continents? Were Frank Wells, president of the Walt Disney Company, and Dick Bass, a ski resort owner, compelled to climb Everest, McKinley, Kilimanjaro and the others by some profound force, a deep need to test themselves? ''Seven Summits'' doesn't say.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Survivng The Flood
author: Stephen Minot
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SURVIVING THE FLOOD. By Stephen Minot. (Second Chance Press, $18.95.) This wry novel belongs to that category of books whose purpose is to set the historical record straight.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Metropolis
author: Jerome Charyn.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: METROPOLIS New York as Myth, Marketplace, and Magical Land. By Jerome Charyn. 304 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $18.95. IN ''Metropolis,'' Jerome Charyn has written a love song to cities in general and to New York City in particular. It is also a passionate invocation of his own life and of the earlier immigrant days of Ellis Island. (Someone - I cannot believe it is the author -has given the book the foolish subtitle ''New York as Myth, Marketplace, and Magical Land.'' Just ignore the cheap alliteration.) The best things about this roller coaster-written, hypnotic, ambitious, often brilliant, often utterly wrongheaded and fascinating book are its author's voice and its beautifully lived-in subject. In the invisible place where subjects and authors are mysteriously joined, a fortunate meeting has occurred between a ''Bronx Iroquois'' and the anarchic city he has soaked up through his nerve endings, a pairing that extends here to the borders of poetry, mythology and politics. This last category, in my opinion, takes Mr. Charyn onto tricky ground; he occasionally lurches and retrieves his footing mainly by the sheer energy of his language and poetic drive.
headline: ROXY, SPINOZA AND OTHER URBAN GREATS

title: Storm Center
author: David M. O'Brien. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STORM CENTER The Supreme Court in American Politics. By David M. O'Brien. Illustrated. 384 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $18.95. THIS is no time to deny that the Supreme Court is a political institution. Throughout history the Court, which is three years away from its 200th birthday, has been a vital actor on the political scene even when trying to float majestically above it. Often, as today, the Court is fought, or fought over, by the other two, more overtly partisan branches of Government as they seek to control the direction of the law. Just as often the Court has been engaged in telling Presidents and Congresses how to behave - or deciding to disclaim the right to interfere with elected officials. At all times the Court must interpret not only the Constitution but also a multitude of laws that order the lives of all citizens, a task that demands political wisdom no less than legal learning.   So much for what everyone knows and political science keeps discovering. David O'Brien, who teaches that subject at the University of Virginia, has amassed much useful evidence for the real debate: What kind of political institution should the Supreme Court be? How do we want it to function? Is it functioning well?
headline: REHNQUIST'S INHERITANCE

title: In The Green Morning
author: Francisco Garcia Lorca
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN THE GREEN MORNING Memories of Federico. By Francisco Garcia Lorca. Translated by Christopher Maurer. Prologue by Mario Hernandez. Illustrated. 258 pp. New York: New Directions. Cloth, $23.50. Paper, $12.95. TOWARD the end of his days as a student of law at the University of Granada, the poet Federico Garcia Lorca stopped showing up for exams. The faculty was hesitant to throw him out, however. He had published a book of poems, and he was cultured and widely read. If not the poet, then the university might gain honor from the young man's degree. So, when he failed to appear for the examination in penal law, the committee sought him out in the courtyards, led him to their chambers, asked his opinion of the death penalty and waved him on. Civil and private law, canon law, public finance - one way or another he passed each one. Then came the last, and again no candidate. Again, allowances were made, a special session arranged. The topic was mercantile law; what exactly, the examiners asked the poet, was a merchant? Garcia Lorca knew that. They gave him his degree.
headline: THE ANDALUSIAN BROTHERS

title: Days Like This
author: Phyllis Gillis.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DAYS LIKE THIS A Tale of Divorce. By Phyllis Gillis. 302 pp. New York: McGraw-Hill Book Company. $15.95. PHYLLIS GILLIS had been a good wife, almost a Stepford wife, the kind of woman who fills up her appointment book with her husband's business engagements. At her husband's urging, she had given up a promising career to devote herself more single-mindedly to his. ''He means well,'' she told her feminist friends, and at least his Type A strivings brought in enough income to position them squarely in the exurban tennis-and-cocktail set. Then one night he came home late, silently strode over to the television set Phyllis was watching, pressed the off button, and announced, ''I'm leaving you. . . . I will be moving in the morning.'' This is the beginning of the two years of legal terrorism recounted in ''Days Like This,'' as Ms. Gillis fights to hold on to her home, her son and her depleted supply of self-confidence.   If this were the prototypical divorce story of the 1970's, she would have been through her six-figure-a-year sleazeball of a husband on page one, thrown him out with the help of her consciousness-raising group before the first chapter was over, and plunged into a fulfilling profession, multiple relationships and evenings of est. ''Kramer vs. Kramer'' (1979), for example, featured a footloose wife bent on ''growth'' and a bereft husband who triumphs over the twin burdens of heartache and domestic ineptitude.

pull_quote: FIGURES OF ENCHANTMENT. By Zulfikar Ghose. (Harper & Row, $15.95.) This odd, alluring novel explores what Zulfikar Ghose calls ''fantastic reality'' by following the related journeys of two spiritually desperate men in a fictional South American country.

title: Travels In Hyperreality
author: Umberto Eco. Translated by William Weaver.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TRAVELS IN HYPERREALITY Essays. By Umberto Eco. Translated by William Weaver. 307 pp. New York: A Helen and Kurt Wolff Book/ Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $15.95. IN ''Reports From the Global Village'' - falling roughly halfway through the sequence of essays and articles which Umberto Eco has gathered together under the general title ''Travels in Hyperreality'' - the wily and witty Italian philosopher, historian, semiotician and author of the best-selling novel, ''The Name of the Rose,'' offers a surprising proposition: ''All the professors of theory of communications, trained by the texts of twenty years ago (this includes me), should be pensioned off.'' Mr. Eco is only kidding, of course; and the reader who has followed him that far knows it instantly, being already experienced in the rhetorical stances, several kinds of ambiguity and stylistic fun and games Mr. Eco employs to consider almost everything under the sun - holography, wax museums, ''The Return of the Middle Ages,'' Superman and ''Casablanca,'' Federico Fellini and Michelangelo Antonioni, the survival of ancient African religious sects and cults in contemporary Brazil, Jim Jones and his murderous temple, the Red Brigades and terrorism in general, Marshall McLuhan and Charles Manson, Woody Allen and St. Thomas Aquinas, the social and personal implications of snug-fitting blue jeans and the secret meaning of spectator sports.

author: Roger Franklin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

title: The Purge
author: Herbert R. Lottman.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PURGE By Herbert R. Lottman. 332 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $19.95. IN the fateful years between the armistice of June 1940 and liberation in the summer of 1944, French men and women faced an anguished choice. They could take their lead from Charles de Gaulle in London, resist the Germans and create disruptions and diversions until, with outside aid, the occupying army was expelled. Or they could follow the lead of Marshal Philippe Petain and his government in Vichy, which by collaborating promised to shield France from even harsher enemy treatment.   The advocates of collaboration, of course, often acted from far less honorable motives. Some, by word or deed, openly supported the Nazi new order as a bastion against Communism or as an ideology preferable to democratic liberalism, which they had long denounced as the tool of Communists, Socialists, Freemasons, Jews and pacifists. ''The worst of our defeats,'' wrote the die-hard reactionary Charles Maurras, who at least had the virtue of having held to his convictions ever since the Dreyfus affair, ''has had the good result of getting rid of our democrats.''
headline: THE PURIFICATION OF FRANCE

title: The Soviet Paradox
author: Seweryn Bialer.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SOVIET PARADOX External Expansion, Internal Decline. By Seweryn Bialer. 391 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $22.95. SEWERYN BIALER has done it again. He has rewritten the penetrating, often brilliant analysis of the Soviet regime and its policies that he has produced at intervals over the last decade. This time his stimulating, updated synthesis of his own views and those of others is wider-ranging than before. He gives more space to futurology, the international context, the Soviet policy of the United States, and his own prescriptions for policy. Unlike his book ''Stalin's Successors'' (1980), the new work is aimed more at lay readers than at scholars.
headline: GETTING STRONGER, GETTING WEAKER?

author: William Heyen
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: VIC HOLYFIELD AND THE CLASS OF 1957. By William Heyen. (Available Press/Ballantine, Paper, $4.95.) Most of us develop some feeling of nostalgia for our high school years, especially as those years recede.

title: Across
author: Peter Handke
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ACROSS By Peter Handke. Translated by Ralph Manheim. 138 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $14.95. BETWEEN 1966 and the early 70's, the Austrian   Peter Handke made his reputation as an important writer with a fierce, icy set of plays and novels: ''Offending the Audience,'' ''Kaspar,'' ''The Ride Across Lake Constance,'' ''The Goalie's Anxiety at the Penalty Kick'' and ''Short Letter, Long Farewell.'' Oblique yet startlingly immediate, these works embodied in fresh fictional and dramatic forms concerns that seemed particularly postmodern, notably an obsession (indeed, a disgust) with the way language itself defines and constricts human possibilities.

title: Red Storm Rising
author: Tom Clancy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RED STORM RISING By Tom Clancy. 652 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $19.95. TOM CLANCY'S first novel, the best-selling ''Hunt for Red October,'' was a superior example of the technological thriller, a genre that awards equal billing to human actors and state-of-the-art computers, missiles, devices of detection and deception, spy satellites, nuclear submarines and Mach 2 or Mach 3 fighter planes. Men, and even an occasional woman, prevail when they outwit their opponents with better deployment of exotic tools, not necessarily superior in design to those in the enemy arsenal. Skilled spinners of such au courant tales, among them Mr. Clancy, appeal simultaneously to the universal appetite for individual heroics and the special American affection for high tech.   ''The Hunt for Red October'' focused on the attempted defection of a single Soviet submarine. Success has increased Mr. Clancy's ambition. His new theme is nothing less than World War III. The conflict begins in western Siberia one starry night when a band of Moslem extremists ignite a huge oil refinery complex and eliminate a third of the Soviet Union's crude oil production for as many as three years. How is the Politburo to cope with this?
headline: VIRTUOUS MEN AND PERFECT WEAPONS

title: Red Dawn At Lexington
author: Louis Birnbaum
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RED DAWN AT LEXINGTON: ''If They Mean to Have a War, Let It Begin Here!'' By Louis Birnbaum. (Houghton Mifflin, $18.95.)

title: Fiela's Child
author: Dalene Matthee
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FIELA'S CHILD By Dalene Matthee. 350 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95. SET in rural South Africa in the 19th century, Dalene Matthee's novel ''Fiela's Child'' deals with a white foundling raised by a black family. One night in 1865 Fiela Komoetie, the family's matriarch, awakes to find a young boy standing at her back door. Nine years later, the boy, now known as Ben, has become an integral part of the Komoetie farm, Wolwekraal. The family explains the difference in his skin color to neighbors by little more than the fact that he is ''his parents' hand-child. Like the hand-lamb the ewe does not want that has to be hand-fed.'' ''If you took a lamb and reared it, who's going to tell you whose sheep it is?'' Fiela Komoetie asks when the question of the real mother is raised.
headline: THE FOUNDLING OF THE LONG KLOOF

title: Q Clearnace
author: Peter Benchley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Q CLEARANCE By Peter Benchley. 340 pp. New York: Random House. $16.95. AWHITE HOUSE speechwriter, Timothy Burnham - wearer of plaid boxer shorts, gobbler of multivitamins, disciple of Samuel Johnson -reluctantly vaults from the contented obscurity of siring 400-word toasts and forgettable proclamations to become the President's confidant. His abrupt transit was not sought, nor is it smooth. Within days Burnham gains Q clearance - access to nuclear secrets - loses his politically pious wife, becomes amorously entwined with a honey-haired Soviet spy and defuses a Cuban crisis of sorts by cutting a deal with a transsexual in-law. Not your average bureaucrat's 8 to 4:30 tour, but then Burnham is not your average bureaucrat. He is profane, well-read, insubordinate, creative when pressed and certainly funnier than most foot soldiers in the long gray flannel line. At the top he becomes predictably pixilated with power, though, happily, he does not dull out before his equally predictable fall.
headline: PLEASE PASS THE FETTUCCINE ATOMICO

title: God Dies By The Nile
author: Nawal el-Saadawi
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
GOD DIES BY THE NILE By Nawal el-Saadawi. Translated by Sherif Hetata. 138 pp. Totowa, N.J.: Zed Books/Biblio Distribution Center. Cloth, $13.95. Paper, $6.95. NAWAL EL-SAADAWI, the Egyptian physician, civil servant, feminist, political detainee (under Sadat) and novelist, writes in a tradition that ascribes to fiction the duty of social inquest and takes for granted the intersection of literature and politics. Born, like her characters in this book, in a village by the Nile, she bears down on social issues with directness and passion, transforming the systematic brutalization of peasants and of women into powerful allegory.

This directness may put off American readers. Ms. Saadawi is not a mediator. She doesn't try to make postcolonial Egypt's problems familiar to the West. She is impatient with psychology and motivation; her villagers are who they are because they have been betrayed by history and by religion.
headline: BETRAYED BY BLIND FAITH

title: Perelman, S J: A Life
author: Dorothy Herrmann
pull_quote: S. J. PERELMAN: A Life. By Dorothy Herrmann. Illustrated. 337 pages. Putnam. $18.95.   PREDICTABLY, the clown turns out to have been weeping behind his mask. And so a large portion of this first biography of S. J. Perelman (1904-1979) must inevitably be devoted to unhappy aspects of the humorist's life.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Here Lies. An Autobiography
author: Eric Ambler
pull_quote: HERE LIES. An Autobiography. By Eric Ambler. Illustrated. 234 pages. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $16.95.   A CAR spins off the autoroute between Lausanne and Geneva and lands in a ditch.   The driver, an English author who lives in Switzerland, had fallen asleep at the wheel, overcome by fumes; he is lucky to be alive. But when the police get him to a hospital, he is found to be suffering from partial amnesia. He tries desperately to remember what he had been thinking about before the accident . . .
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Wartime Writings 1939-1944
author: Antoine de Saint-Exupery
pull_quote: WARTIME WRITINGS 1939-1944. By Antoine de Saint-Exupery. Translated by Norah Purcell. 256 Pages. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $12.95. IN the middle of war, Antoine de Saint-Exupery turned his mind to peace. He envisioned a time when the guns, including those on his P-38 Lightning, would be silent and the real challenge would begin for France and other democratic nations. War was only a momentary blip on his mental radar screen.   Having a large vision - seeing the small world beneath the cockpit of his plane - did not always make the famous flyer and author a popular character around the Mediterranean theater of operations. His ego, as well as his sense of grandeur and literary elegance, comes through in ''Wartime Writings 1939-1944.'' Occasionally, a querulous tone that is unattractive interrupts these posthumous essays, letters and autobiographical fragments. Yet his unguarded frankness adds a certain intimacy for the reader.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Alphabet Effect
author: Robert K Logan
pull_quote: THE ALPHABET EFFECT: The Impact of the Phonetic Alphabet on the Development of Western Civilization. By Robert K. Logan. 272 pages. Morrow. $16.95. IT is Robert K. Logan's not entirely original theory that ''of all mankind's inventions, with the possible exception of language itself, nothing has proved more useful or led to more innovations than the alphabet.'' Not only has it ''contributed to the development of codified law, monotheism, abstract science, deductive logic, and individualism, each a unique contribution of Western thought,'' the alphabet ''has also served as a model for classification.'' More significantly still, ''it has provided us with a conceptual framework for analysis and has restructured our perceptions of reality.'' As Mr. Logan concludes: ''These effects take place independent of what we read. The information that is coded is not important; it is the act of coding itself that has been so influential and acted as a springboard for new ideas.'' In other words, the medium of the alphabet has been the message.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Tenth Muse
author: Ronald B Parker
pull_quote: THE TENTH MUSE: The Pursuit of Earth Science. By Ronald B. Parker. 221 pages. Scribner's. $15.95.   ANNE BRADSTREET, the first American poet of consequence, called her collection of poems ''The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America.'' The title had no particular connection with earth science, but Ronald B. Parker has borrowed the idea of a tenth muse to personify the spirit that watches over geology. It seems a rather defensive move, as though geology had become a Cinderella in need of a fairy godmother; and it is probably true that among laymen it no longer enjoys the prestige that it once did, that it is widely regarded as prosaic, intellectually undemanding, a science with its heroic days behind it.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Jane Austen Companion
author: J David Grey
pull_quote: THE JANE AUSTEN COMPANION. Edited by J. David Grey, A. Walton   Litz and Brian Southam, with ''A Dictionary of Jane Austen's Life and Works,'' by H. Abigail Bok. 511 pages. Macmillan. $27.50. Don't be put off by the title. The idea of a literary ''companion'' may well suggest a rather routine handbook, but ''The Jane Austen Companion'' is a great deal more than that. Along with an index of people and places, such as you might expect, it contains 65 short essays covering an unusually wide span of topics connected with Jane Austen's life and work. It is very much a book designed to be read, not just consulted.
headline: ILLUMINATING JANE AUSTEN

title: Korea: The First War We Lost

UNFORTUNATELY for scholars and serious fans of Ralph Ellison, there is little in this volume that has not been published before. In fact, at first glance ''Going to the Territory'' - a mix of occasional pieces, essays, speeches, interviews and reviews, many of them two decades old - bears a disquieting resemblance to ''Shadow and Act,'' a collection of Ralph Ellison's nonfiction writings published in 1964. Both books evaluate Richard Wright's stature as a writer, elaborate the intricate interplay between Afro-American fiction and folklore, explore the novel as a vehicle for moral and ethical truth, worry the notion of American identity and consider the craft of fiction as discipline and vocation. ''Going to the Territory'' is best viewed as a continuation of the project begun when Mr. Ellison introduced ''Shadow and Act'' as ''an attempt to transform some of the themes, the problems, the enigmas, the contradictions of character and culture native to my predicament, into what Andre Malraux has described as 'conscious thought.' Maps. 368 pp. New York: Columbia University Press. $30.   IN the 18th century the most dazzling jewel in the crown of France was the city of Paris, the scene of rapid social mobility and fusion, where the nobility and the bourgeoisie shared the same turf with merchants and shopkeepers, artisans and laborers. Paris spawned a heterogeneous society that was permeated by the written word. Parisians of all stripes, educated or not, burned with the fever to write on many topics, including themselves. ''Infected by the craze for life in the great city,'' one aspirant wrote, ''the disease overcame me, and I became an author too.'' People distributed broadsheets, posters, pamphlets and treatises throughout the city. Literate Parisians (around 66 percent of men, 62 percent of women) transmitted news to less literate cohorts, bridging the gap between elite and popular culture. In this heady milieu, a glazier, Jacques-Louis Menetra, wrote and rewrote ''Journal of My Life'' between 1764 and 1802. Despite his disclaimer (''Journal of my life written for me''), Menetra too courted the amorphous public.

title: The Birth And Death Of The Miracle Man
author: Albert Wendt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BIRTH AND DEATH OF THE MIRACLE MAN. By Albert Wendt. (Viking, $18.95.) The modern Samoans in Albert Wendt's stories are dutiful Christians, their children training to be government clerks on the mainland. But the shades of ancient island gods and ancestors still swirl around their heads, binding them to the mysteries - of nature, mortality and clan honor - that form the background for these gentle but powerful tales. In ''Prospecting,'' several villagers and their European boss pan for gold and unearth the skeletons of a whole town whose inhabitants were slaughtered in a long-ago battle. The prospectors fall into deep grief, which is assuaged only when their boss agrees to bury the skeletons, with complete funeral rites, in their own churchyard. Mr. Wendt also makes room in the teeming Samoan universe for private, solitary rites of passage. In ''The Balloonfish and the Armadillo,'' he describes the hardened pain of a middle-aged man whose father was wrenched away from him as a child. The pain now manifests itself as a chronic migraine he envisions as a spiky Samoan blowfish inflated to its full, menacing size. After his father's death, the hero uncovers the truth about him - reading through his letters, hurling books into a bonfire - which makes it possible to continue his own life. Mr. Wendt generously dusts his stories with ironic, knowing playfulness. In ''I Will Be Our Saviour From the Bad Smell,'' a village is suddenly enshrouded by an abominable smell which unsettles everyone but the hero, for whom the Bad Smell is a precious gift.

Alienated creatures who think they're alive and simulate life's activities but who are dimly aware that all their passions and desires are counterfeit. As George Romero suggested in his wickedly funny movie, ''Dawn of the Dead,'' these zombies are all around us. They haunt our shopping malls, riding escalators and listening to background music, emptily searching for the next bargain item; they sit in our suburban ranch-style homes, mesmerized by images and slogans that engage their fake emotions and programmed longings. author: Sherley Anne Williams
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DESSA ROSE  By Sherley Anne Williams.  236 pp. New York:  William Morrow & Company. $15.95.    TWO things can happen when poets venture into fiction. They can approach the business with the arrogant (or naive) assumption that they already understand the purposes and problems of fiction, and end up producing books which, while sometimes pyrotechnic in terms of poetry, are duds in terms of prose. This, alas, is the usual case. Sometimes, however, a gifted poet comes to the novel with a humble determination to do what fiction has to do: tell a story worth telling. The product in this case is not only good fiction, but fiction enlivened by symbolic connections and daring imagery - elements that those who write only prose often neglect. It must have been with such a desire that Sherley Anne Williams, whose ''Peacock Poems'' was nominated for the 1976 National Book Award, began her first novel, ''Dessa Rose.'' For what she has written is an absorbing fusion that is both elegant poetry and powerful fiction.

author: Tim Winton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHALLOWS. By Tim Winton. (Atheneum, $14.95.) Australia is so far beyond the exclusive claims of either the Old World or the New that it may be impossible to live there as anything but a stranger. In this fine second novel by Tim Winton, the 1984 winner of Australia's Miles Franklin Award, a young woman named Queenie Coupar, fifth-generation inhabitant of an Australian whaling town called Angelus, abandons her job as a local tour guide and joins a group of foreign environmentalists who have come to shut down the town's commerce. Thus, for reasons buried and unnamed, she alienates herself from even the common strangeness of her own people. Her grandfather, Daniel, who raised Queenie as his own daughter, broods on the distant lies surrounding his wife's death and nurtures the bitterness of a youthful rebellion that came to naught. Queenie's husband, Cleve, is generally despised as dim and ineffectual. During his night watch on the town pier he reads a journal written a century and a half earlier by Daniel's ancestor - a whaler and maritime deserter who speaks to Cleve's evolving comprehension of the things which make men guilty and survive. Mr. Winton is not always in control of the material. His metaphors are relentlessly literary, from the symbolism of the whales to the sexual sterility of ruthless and decadent tycoons; and the narrative sometimes lingers over pastoral moments while cascading across crucial ones -such as Cleve's search for the journal's missing years - in fewer than two pages.

IT suited someone to title this book, ''Home: A Short History of an Idea,'' but it is about comfort and the source and spread of domesticity as much as it is about ''home,'' a word which stands for a loosely bagged collection of concepts more complex and distantly historical than this book is prepared to deal with. Nor is it about an idea, really, because there is no treatment of what people have thought about private housing, or the homeland, or alienation or nationality or personal identity. It is devoted to social practices, not social theories. There is little analytic penetration of its principal notions, either, although a term like ''comfort'' badly needs it. Rather the book treats of cultural values like privacy as they became current, or conditions such as cleanliness as they began to be striven for, of feelings toward what is called the cozy or the snug, of relations of intimacy as they were increasingly sought, as well as of the significance of materials, building types, and furnishings in the service of what would become ''home, sweet home'' - including its female rulers, the habits they encourage, the objects they enshrine in their domain.

Then there's the abundance of energetic creatures who populate this book: bulls and billy goats; runners and wrestlers; the author's 86-year-old grandmother and an Egyptian pyramid guide with an endless supply of hustles.   Then there's Mr. Kesey's prose, which if nothing else is energetic. Here is the protagonist of his book, Devlin Deboree, remembering Houlihan (in reality Neal Cassady), ''that lightning-mouthed character Kerouac had called Dean Moriarty in On the Road and that John Clellon Holmes had named Hart Kennedy in Go.'' Houlihan ''was Lenny Bruce, Jonathan Winters, and Lord Buckley all together just for starters. He couldn't have helped but been a hit. But a nightclub format would have pinched his free-flying mind, and no stage in the world could have really accommodated his art - his hurtling, careening, corner-squealing commentary on the cosmos - except the stage he built about himself the moment he slid all quick and sinewy under the steering wheel of a good car: the bigger, the boatier, the more American, the better.''

pull_quote: THE BLOOD OF KINGS. Dynasty and Ritual in Maya Art. By Linda Schele and Mary Ellen Miller. Illustrated. 335 pages. George Braziller/Kimbell Art Museum. Cloth, $45; paper, $28. NOW that they've been deciphered, the beautiful, cold stone walls of the Mayan ruins offer up some bloody and grotesque stories: a woman threads a rope of thorns through her tongue; a man lacerates his penis with a stingray spine, a captured soldier is methodically scalped and disemboweled.   For a long time, though, observers insisted that these images were either abstract sketches of gods engaged in mysterious rituals or decorative doodling produced by fevered artistic minds. The images, after all, are stylized ones - rendered in voluptuously abstract lines and ornate curlicues; and for years, they resisted interpretation.

''O NE wondered how with so little work to show he had come by his lofty reputation,'' Elias Canetti writes about a Viennese poet and dramatist now entombed in Austrian literary history. Seeing that Mr. Canetti's reputation is a good deal loftier - he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1981 - the question is even more puzzling in his own case. Part of the answer may well lie in the fact that he is modern European literature's greatest adept at recycling his own products. These consist of one large novel, ''Auto-da-Fe'' (1935), one large work of philosophical anthropology, ''Crowds and Power'' (1960), a travelogue, three post-Expressionist plays hardly ever performed on the professional stage and several volumes of essays and reflections, some of which are commentaries on the novel or reformulations of the arguments of the philosophical book. In his autobiography, of which ''The Play of the Eyes'' is the third volume, the lofty reputation is taken for granted, and we are presented with some of the personal and literary circumstances upon which it is based. ''Non multa sed multum'' was the motto Schopenhauer chose for his collected works: Mr. Canetti gets a lot of mileage out of a compact set of themes.

FEMININITY and slavery were the central preoccupations of ''Sally Hemings,'' Barbara Chase-Riboud's best-selling 1979 novel about the slave woman some think was Thomas Jefferson's mistress. In ''Valide,'' Ms. Chase-Riboud returns to those themes, this time against a drastically different backdrop. Exploration of the complex institution of slavery in another culture - the sultan's harem of the Ottoman Empire during the late 18th and early 19th centuries - has prompted some interesting changes in Ms. Chase-Riboud's thinking. ''Sally Hemings,'' whose heroine was bound to her master and lover even more securely by her feelings than by the laws of Virginia, suggested that for women, love itself is a form of slavery. Ms. Chase-Riboud's second novel makes a broader and more radical point: love is impossible in a slave society, where absolute power over other human beings poisons all personal relationships and eliminates the possibility of free choice that is at the root of all real love.

TO Joseph Hone's father and godfather, Africa represented what the American West represented to the early pioneers: it was a new frontier, a place of possibilities, a colonial escape-hatch where they might leave behind their dreary lives in England and begin glorious new lives in the sun. They spoke of hunting fabulous wild game there, of starting a farm in some secluded Happy Valley, of leading dangerous expeditions into the continent's interior.   And to young Joseph, too, Africa held out the promise of high romance. Well versed in the classic texts of Edwardian adventure literature (from ''King Solomon's Mines'' to bound copies of the ''Boys' Own Paper''), he came to picture the continent as a ''place of pulsating, ultimate adventure, of liberating space and freedom from the confines of a restricted, almost Victorian childhood.'' In the hours before sleep, he would conjure up this mythical land, speaking to himself in made-up African tongues, and playing, in his imagination, with the props of ''a boy's Africa - witch doctor's masks, long barbed assegais, poisoned arrows, old black powder Martini-Henry rifles.''
