author: Lydia Davis
pull_quote: BREAK IT DOWN. By Lydia Davis. 177 pages. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $14.95.   IN the title story of this collection, the hero is looking back over a spoiled love affair and trying ''to break it down.'' ''The ticket was $600,'' he says to himself, ''and then after that there was more for the hotel and food and so on, for just ten days. Say $80 a day, no, more like $100 a day. And we made love, say, once a day on the average. That's $100 a shot. And each time it lasted maybe two or three hours so that would be anywhere from $33 to $50 an hour, which is expensive.'' On the other hand, he goes on, he enjoyed his lover's company every waking hour - roughly 16 hours a day, and ''sixteen into a hundred would be $6 an hour, which isn't too much.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Names
author: Paul Dickson
pull_quote: NAMES: A Collector's Compendium of Rare and Unusual, Bold and Beautiful, Odd and Whimsical Names, by Paul Dickson. Illustrated. 282 pages. Delacorte. $15.95.    TO be sure, at the heart of this latest extravaganza by Paul Dickson, there is a ''Collector's Showcase,'' featuring items from the John Q. Raspberry Memorial Collection of Names. Here we find everyone from Preserved Algar to Trougout Zumm, including such old friends as Magdalena Babblejack, Sibyl Bibble, Urbin Bowels, Rotten Earp, Eloise Tittlekitty, and Vera Zero - all real, as far as can be determined, and all collected in North America and the British Isles.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Adam's Task: Calling Animals By Name
author: Vicki Hearne
pull_quote: ADAM'S TASK: Calling Animals by Name. By Vicki Hearne. 274 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.    As kids, a lot of us grew up reading such dog and horse stories ''Lad, a Dog,'' ''Black Beauty'' and ''The Black Stallion''; and from the movies and television, we were familiar, too, with the stories of Lassie and Rin Tin Tin. They were stories in which a brave dog or horse helped rescue someone in trouble, or stories in which a troubled child and an endangered animal saved and redeemed one another. For Vicki Hearne, those stories are not simply sentimental tales concocted for children, but fictions that reveal the possiblities of communication between domestic animals and man; and in this provocative new book, she expounds further on the intricate moral relationship that can develop between dogs, cats, horses and human beings.
headline: Not So Dumb Animals

title: The Moon Pinnace
author: Thomas Williams
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MOON PINNACE By Thomas Williams. 374 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $17.95.    SINCE colonial days the remote outposts and half-forgotten hamlets of rural New England have been peculiarly fertile sources of material for some of the most unorthodox American writers. The past decade or so has witnessed another vigorous flowering of fresh, daring talent from the pre-cincts north of Boston. Some of these writers have rooted their work deeply in the often forbidding regions of northern New Hampshire and Maine. Others have used the same territory as what north country hunting and fishing guides call a jumping off place - a starting point from which they strike out in so many different directions that the term ''regional'' seems to have no application to their work at all.
headline: DORY LOVES JOHN, JOHN GOES TO CALIFORNIA

title: The Peopling Of British North America
author: Bernard Bailyn.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PEOPLING OF BRITISH NORTH AMERICA An Introduction. By Bernard Bailyn. 177 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.    BERNARD BAILYN has already had two careers - as one of Harvard's most distinguished teachers, whose proteges have carried his word throughout the universities of the United States, and as the author of ''The Transforming Radicalism of the American Revolution,'' the famous introductory essay to his first volume of ''Pamphlets of the American Revolution: 1750-1776.'' In the essay he demonstrated that the Founding Fathers drew their radical political ideas largely from the reading of the Leveler and Dissenting literature of 17th-century and early 18th-century England. This thesis has now become the prevailing interpretation of the causes of American separation from Britain. For many in the profession all this would be fame enough.
headline: WHEN EUROPE PULLED UP STAKES

title: Her Living Image
author: Jane Rogers
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HER LIVING IMAGE. By Jane Rogers. (Doubleday, $16.95.) Jane Rogers often writes beautifully in her second novel, which consists of two alternate versions of the same character's story.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Something Sleeping In The Hall
author: Karla Kuskin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SOMETHING SLEEPING IN THE HALL Written and Illustrated by Karla Kuskin. 64 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $8.95. (Ages 5 to 8)    WRITING for the new reader is a particular challenge. The words and concepts must be simple and yet engaging.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Here Lies
author: Eric Ambler. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HERE LIES An Autobiography. By Eric Ambler. Illustrated. 234 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $16.95.    IN a sense, reviewing an autobiography is the literary equivalent of passing judgment on someone's life. A touchy business, made even touchier when the autobiographer is a writer by profession, for then his life story can be evaluated in terms of form as well as content. This, in turn, could lead to such improbable verdicts as: a dreary life beautifully told.
headline: CODE NAME ERIC

title: Keelhauled
author: Doug Riggs. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: KEELHAULED Unsportsmanlike Conduct and the America's Cup. By Doug Riggs. Illustrated. 308 pp. Newport, R.I.: Seven Seas Press. $19.95.    WHEN the Australians removed the America's Cup from this country, they left behind a number of suspicions about the legitimacy of their victory -not their victory on the water, which was both convincing and almost absurdly dramatic, but their triumph ashore over the New York Yacht Club, guardians of the Cup for 132 years. Even so, with the Cup in Perth, Western Australia, the controversies of 1983 seem thoroughly moot, so what is the point of this book?
headline: LOSERS STILL WEEPERS

title: The Long Walk
author: George La Fountaine
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LONG WALK. By George La Fountaine. (Putnam, $17.95.) Although badly wounded by infelicitous prose, melodrama, implausibilities so large they're almost daring and characters who burst into polemic as if it were song, this Vietnam War novel still manages to pull itself along on sheer narrative bravado.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: My Life With Chagall
author: Virginia Haggard. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
MY LIFE WITH CHAGALL Seven Years of Plenty With the Master as Told by the Woman Who Shared Them. By Virginia Haggard. Illustrated. 190 pp. New York: Donald I. Fine. $18.95. 

WE seem to be experiencing in our culture a re-emergence of some ancient forms of powerful goddess-energy that are causing women's images of themselves, previously defined by the dominant patriarchal consciousness, to change. Perhaps it is this phenomenon that makes Virginia Haggard's memoir of her life with the painter Marc Chagall seem so dated in its awe for the mystique of famous artists and their work. Although I very much enjoyed reading ''My Life With Chagall,'' with its irresistible frankness and unpretentious writing, I did find myself out of sympathy with Chagall's exploitative ego and lavish self-importance.
headline: MENDING THE MASTER'S SOCKS

title: When Brooklyn Was The World: 1920-1957
author: Elliot Willensky
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: The Golden Age of Athens lasted three decades. Brooklyn's outlasted that by seven years - and what a zesty age it was, according to Elliot Willensky in his book WHEN BROOKLYN WAS THE WORLD: 1920-1957 (Harmony, $19.95).
headline: Betrayed by Walter O'Malley

title: Digging Up The Mountains
author: Neil Bissoondath
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DIGGING UP THE MOUNTAINS By Neil Bissoondath. 247 pp. New York: Viking. $15.95.    THE superb short stories in Neil Bissoondath's first collection are alive with movement and flight, leaving and returning, insecurity and impermanence. Peopled by exiles and immigrants, deracines and runaways - perhaps the true representatives of the mobile 20th century - these are tales of two worlds, usually the Caribbean and Canada - and of those who are stretched between the two.
headline: ALISTAIR RAMGOOLAM DOES WELL TO BE UNEASY

title: Behind The Forbidden Door: Travels In Unknown China
author: Tiziano Terzani
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BEHIND THE FORBIDDEN DOOR: Travels in Unknown China. By Tiziano Terzani. (Holt, $17.95.) This work grows out of the genre started by Simon Leys, another European and disillusioned Sinologist who finds the Communists have destroyed much of what was grand about China and replaced it with a cultureless totalitarianism.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Almost Midnight
author: Don Belton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ALMOST MIDNIGHT By Don Belton. 213 pp. New York: Beech Tree Books/ William Morrow & Company. $14.95.    ''A ND at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh.'' This biblical text resonates through Don Belton's first novel, ''Almost Midnight.'' It chronicles conflicting attempts to determine the truth about the legendary Daddy Sam Poole, the white-skinned black preacher, who built his million-dollar Metaphysical Church of the Divine Investigation ''out of the scraps and broken furniture hanging out in the back of his mind.'' Who is this man who used his church to front for prostitution and drug rings? Is he God or the Devil? If there is an answer, it is entangled in the lives of Daddy Poole and his women. For some of them, arriving at an answer seems a simple process, but for others it is as difficult as drawing a straight line between good and evil, love and hate, truth and lies, as difficult as untangling long, intricately enmeshed threads without ending up in knots.
headline: ALL THE PREACHER'S WOMEN

title: How Real Is The Federal Deficit?
author: Robert Eisner
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HOW REAL IS THE FEDERAL DEFICIT? By Robert Eisner. 240 pp. New York: The Free Press. $17.95.   THE DEFICITS How Big? How Long? How Dangerous? By Daniel Bell and Lester Thurow. 142 pp. New York: New York University Press. $15.    ON Nov. 5, 1980, the day after Ronald Reagan was elected President and just four years after America's 200th birthday, the national debt - the sum total of all its past deficits - stood at about $900 billion. Had a dispirited Jimmy Carter predicted that under his successor the national debt would more than double to about $2 trillion ($2,000 billion) in just five years, he would have been accused of everything from sour grapes to downright silliness.
headline: BIGGER AND WORSE

title: And Venus Is Blue
author: Mary Hood
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AND VENUS IS BLUE By Mary Hood. 293 pp. New York: Ticknor & Fields. $15.95.    IN ''After Moore,'' the first story in this marvelous collection by Mary Hood, a difficult, 15-year marriage begins ''with her wanting someone, and him wanting anyone. Love was all they knew to call it.'' A young wife in ''Desire Call of the Wild Hen'' holds out against her husband's unhappiness. '' 'I love you, baby,' she never tired of saying, even when she knew he'd only reply 'Yeah,' with that look in his eyes like a glutted steer in a feedlot.'' In ''The Goodwife Hawkins,'' a bitter marriage ends as the story begins: ''He hadn't thrown her a word or a look since he'd refused breakfast - some whole days passed like that - but as soon as she touched Hawk's cold shoulder she knew he was good and dead, not sulking.'' Love offers no solace to the characters in Mary Hood's fiction, a tough, unrelentingly real bunch of Southerners. At best, it is inconsequential (''I guess I stll love him,'' says Rhonda in the first story, ''but so what?''); at worst, it is attended by cruelty and violence.
headline: LOVE WAS ALL THEY KNEW TO CALL IT

title: The Shaping Of America
author: D. W. Meinig. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SHAPING OF AMERICA A Geographical Perspective on 500 Years of History. Volume One: Atlantic America, 1492-1800. By D. W. Meinig. Illustrated. 500 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $35.    IT has been nearly 40 years since anyone dared attempt a book like this - a comprehensive historical geography of North America - and no one before D. W. Meinig has embarked on such a project with so large an ambition. ''The Shaping of America'' will ultimately fill three large volumes, covering the periods 1492-1800, 1800-1915 and 1915-1990. It aspires to be nothing less than ''a new map . . . of the American past,'' made possible by what Mr. Meinig calls the geographer's ''special way of looking at the world.'' Whatever its problems, there is little doubt it will remain a standard work in its field.
headline: THE LANDSCAPE OF OUR PAST

title: A Question Of Sedition
author: Patrick S. Washburn.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A QUESTION OF SEDITION The Federal Government's Investigation of the Black Press During World War II. By Patrick S. Washburn. 296 pp. New York. Oxford University Press. $19.95.    THE position of blacks in America has contained no irony more painful than this: Denied the full rights and privileges of citizenship, blacks have yet been required to display as much patriotism toward the Republic as their white brethren, who have never been so denied. It isn't surprising that this irony helped shape the character of the black press, to influence its stance on national issues, to present it with a dilemma quite similar to the one in which its readers have found themselves.
headline: THE CRACKDOWN THAT NEVER WAS

title: The Headhunters
author: John A Byrne
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE HEADHUNTERS. By John A. Byrne. (Macmillan, $19.95.) In this book, executive recruiters - commonly known as headhunters - stalk their prey in the corporate jungle.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Regrets Only
author: Sally Quinn
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: REGRETS ONLY By Sally Quinn. 556 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.    THE meanspirited souls who licked their chops over Sally Quinn's short, overpromoted television career won't find much to gloat over here.   The prose is workmanlike, even a bit stuffy, and the Marie Antoinettish spirit finds a suitable outlet in some rather imperious characters in Washington's Presidential and newsgathering circles. On the other hand, ''Regrets Only'' will never be read twice by anyone except a proofreader, and even as a once-through, it's not what you'd call an easy read.
headline: SUNNY (KIR) VS. SADIE (CHAMPAGNE)

title: Shattering The German Night
author: Annette E. Dumbach and Jud Newborn.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SHATTERING THE GERMAN NIGHT The Story of the White Rose. By Annette E. Dumbach and Jud Newborn. 259 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $17.95.    INSIDE Germany those who worked against the Nazi regime usually did so alone, undertaking isolated deeds, such as harboring Jews. There were cells of resisters, particularly in the army, the trade unions and the universities, but these cells were disparate and discrete units and did not amount to an organized movement. Even the unsuccessful attempt on Hitler's life in July 1944 was not the work of a na-tional underground but of an alliance of elites, including disaffected army officers, theologians, leftist ideologues and intellectuals.
headline: STUDENTS AGAINST THE REICH

title: Freud And His Father
author: Marianne Krull
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FREUD AND HIS FATHER By Marianne Krull. Translated by Arnold J. Pomerans. Illustrated. 294 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $18.95.    MARIANNE KRULL'S ''Freud and His Father'' looks at Sigmund Freud's life at a crucial time, the period of his renunciation of the seduction theory, which held that neurosis resulted from sexual seduction at an early age. In her words, she is ''trying to assess the scientific import of Freud's reorientation, and then looking at that reorientation against the background of his ties to his father.'' The year is 1897, an important time for Freud historians, since two events mark this period: one in his life, the death of his father; the other in his work, a shift in theory.
headline: HONOR THY FATHER, AND THEN SOME

title: Virtue Under Fire
author: John Costello. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: VIRTUE UNDER FIRE How World War II Changed Our Social and Sexual Attitudes. By John Costello. Illustrated. 309 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $17.95.    ''T HE moral life of America is in danger,'' Herbert Hoover warned the country shortly before a mighty Allied armada landed triumphantly on the beaches of Normandy. The former President was inclined to glumness, but he certainly had a point. By the third year of American involvement in World War II, the juvenile crime rate in the United States had doubled, the divorce rate had soared, and infidelity was rampant. Teen-age prostitution was particularly dismaying. Since Pearl Harbor it had risen 70 percent, the F.B.I. reported, for wherever G.I.'s gathered, ''good-time girls'' could be found in droves - so many that New York City had to set up a special Wayward Minors Court to handle the heavy traffic in underage sin. In the factory towns of the war boom, according to The Washington Post, women factory workers were making hash of family values ''after a lifetime of being home slaveys.'' In both America and Britain the war's assault on prewar morality was indeed pervasive, and it forms the main theme of ''Virtue Under Fire,'' John Costello's intriguing ''sexual history of World War II.''
headline: MORALITY: MISSING IN ACTION

title: Nancy Mitford
author: Selina Hastings. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NANCY MITFORD A Biography. By Selina Hastings. Illustrated. 274 pp. New York: A William Abrahams Book/ E. P. Dutton. $19.95.    NANCY MITFORD'S lover Gaston Palewski said ''La famille Mitford fait ma joie,'' but Americans may take a different view. Her biographer calls the United States ''the one nation on the face of the earth Nancy loathed above all others.'' John Wilkes Booth was her favorite figure in history. Surprisingly, her books have sold well here, including the snobby but droll ''Noblesse Oblige'' (recently reprinted), with its careful discrimination between ''U'' (upper-class lingo) and ''non-U.'' But success in the United States did not please Nancy (although the royalties did): ''Either praise or blame from govs  [ Americans ]  leaves ONE cold.'' Definitely not a democrat, she thought Utopia was ''cottagers, happy in their cottages while I am being happy in the Big House.'' Nor will feminists relish her sentiment that ''in every satisfactory union it was the man who kept the upper hand.''
headline: O BRAVE U WORLD

title: The Fabulous Lunts
author: Jared Brown. Foreword by Helen Hayes. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE FABULOUS LUNTS Biography of Alfred Lunt and Lynn Fontanne. By Jared Brown. Foreword by Helen Hayes. Illustrated. 523 pp. New York: Atheneum. $24.95.    WHEN I was a young actress from Brooklyn looking for a job on Broadway, I used to meet my theater pals each Tuesday to share a common thrill: from a 55-cent seat in the second balcony of an old Broadway house we would watch intently the performances of the leading stage stars of the day. We hoped that by observing the greats we would assimilate their glamour and style, and be transported to another realm.
headline: LIVES OF THE GREAT COUPLES AND UNCOUPLES

title: The Powers That Be,
author: David Halberstam
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE POWERS THAT BE, by David Halberstam. (Dell, $5.95.) David Halberstam examines the recent history of four important news-gathering organizations - The Los Angeles Times, The Washington Post, Time Inc. and CBS - in what Richard Rovere, writing in these pages in 1979, called an ''important and admirable book.'' It is, he said, ''a prodigy of research and tendentious but sharply focused narrative and analysis.'' For a different perspective on the press, Quill/Morrow has reissued THE OTHER SIDE OF THE STORY ($7.95), in which Jody Powell, former press secretary to President Carter, takes aim at the White House press corps. ''It is a lively performance, full of spleen and not a little gall,'' Lester Bernstein said in The Book Review in 1984. LOVE ALWAYS, by Ann Beattie. (Vintage, $5.95.) A main character in Ann Beattie's third novel is Nicole Nelson, a 14-year-old soap opera star who comes to spend the summer in Vermont with her Aunt Lucy. ''Miss Beattie is one of the most graceful writers we have,'' Alice Hoffman said here last year; ''at times her prose is nothing short of exquisite. It is such sheer pleasure to read the dialogue in 'Love Always,' we almost don't care what the characters say to one another. But when we really do listen, the absence of desire is more than unsettling - it's chilling.'' THE LIFE OF HENRY BRULARD, by Stendhal. Translated by Jean Stewart and B. C. J. G. Knight. (University of Chicago, $12.95.) Stendhal (Marie-Henri Beyle) wrote this autobiography, calling himself Henry Brulard, in 1835-36, but it lay forgotten until 1890, when it was found in an attic.
headline: NEW AND NOTEWORTHY

title: Home Ground
author: Lynn Freed
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HOME GROUND By Lynn Freed. 273 pp. New York: Summit Books. $15.95.    FROM its title to its final ambiguous paragraph, this absorbing novel charts a network of ironies and poses a question: In what sense can South Africa be claimed as ''home ground'' by any of those who happen to be born there? Black South Africans, treated as chattel, scarcely feel at home. Indian merchants are homesick - for Oxford. The transplanted Europeans cluster in exclusive and supercilious enclaves. As for Ruth Frank, growing up Jewish in Durban, the sense of South Africa as home is possible only when she is safely on a plane, fleeing to England and freedom. ''How lucky you are to have all this to leave behind,'' a famous actress, visiting from England, tells her without intentional irony.
headline: EXIT, PURSUED BY SOUTH AFRICA

title: The Chimpanzees Of Gombe: Patterns Of Behavior
author: Jane Goodall
pull_quote: THE CHIMPANZEES OF GOMBE: Patterns of Behavior. By Jane Goodall. Illustrated. 673 pages. Harvard University Press. $30.   IN 1960, Jane Goodall went into the interior of Tanzania to study the behavior of chimpanzees, genetically the closest living relatives of humans. She became something of a celebrity: the young Englishwoman who plunges into Africa, spends the days and years in communion with chimpanzees, shows up trim and cool in photographs in the popular press and National Geographic, falls in love and marries a photographer who came calling, dispatches occasional learned reports and keeps right on studying the animals she finds so fascinating.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Beet Queen
author: Louise Erdrich
pull_quote: THE BEET QUEEN. By Louise Erdrich. 338 pages. Henry Holt. $16.95.    ''W HERE did everything go?'' a character named Mary in ''The Beet Queen'' wonders as she and a friend drive home across the windy fields of North Dakota. ''The flat fields unfolded, the shallow ditches ran beside the road. I felt the live thoughts hum inside of me, and I pictured tiny bees, insects made of blue electricity, in a colony so fragile that it would scatter at the slightest touch. I imagined a blow, like a mallet to the sheep, or a stroke, and I saw the whole swarm vibrating out.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: My Life Between Japan And America
author: Edwin O Reischauer
pull_quote: MY LIFE BETWEEN JAPAN AND AMERICA. By Edwin O. Reischauer.   Illustrated. 368 pages. Harper & Row. $22.50.    JAPAN figures so prominently in the American consciousness that it is easy to forget that until recently this was not so. Edwin O. Reischauer's autobiography is a useful reminder. It is also an uncommonly informative one, although that should come as no surprise, given the source. Over many decades, through a distinguished career as a scholar, an author and a diplomat, Mr. Reischauer has taught Americans much of what they know about Japan and the rest of the Far East.
headline: EAST AND WEST

title: It
author: Stephen King
pull_quote: IT. By Stephen King. 1,138 pages. Viking. $22.95.   THE drain. Things down there in the drain. Things down there in the drain that might reach up and get you. The awful necessity of having to go down the drain to face those things. These are the essential fantasy-fears that underlie ''It,'' Stephen King's latest, longest and most complicated novel of terror to date. If drains ever bothered you, then ''It'' is going to suck you right in. If not - well, the story's other compensations may or may not suffice.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Strength For The Fight
author: Bernard C Nalty
pull_quote: STRENGTH FOR THE FIGHT: A History of Black Americans in the Military. By Bernard C. Nalty. 424 pages. The Free Press/Macmillan. $22.50.    This is a success story. A success achieved largely by blacks aided by farsighted whites, men like John J. McCloy, Gen. James H. Doolittle, Adm. Elmo R. Zumwalt, Gen. Matthew B. Ridgway. The story also mirrors the long, often agonizing struggle of the black in the military, which is part of our society, to achieve equality, which basically means a readiness to fight and die for the Republic on the same terms as white warriors.
headline: Books of The Times; Jim Crow in Uniform

title: The Limits Of Vision
author: Robert Irwin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LIMITS OF VISION By Robert Irwin. 120 pp. New York: Dedalus/Viking. $12.95.    DIRT, grime, dust, sludge - the villains of Robert Irwin's third novel are the soldiers of Mucor, the Spirit of Uncleanliness, sprung from the Temple of Evil to do combat with Marcia, a South London housewife whose heroes in the battle are Lawrence of Arabia, Sir Philip Sidney and the Spartan boy who stuffed the fox up his shirt. But the subject of ''The Limits of Vision'' is not housework but the imagination, that rash dancer that spins a Taj Mahal in the air above the pup tent of reality.
headline: DUST TO DUST? NOT FOR MARCIA

title: Stranger In Two Worlds
author: Jean Harris
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STRANGER IN TWO WORLDS By Jean Harris. Illustrated. 388 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $18.95.    IN the introduction to ''Stranger in Two Worlds,''   Jean Harris, the convicted murderer of Dr. Herman Tarnower, refers to herself as ''the instrument'' of her lover's death. In a typical qualification she adds: ''To be the instrument of death and to be a murderer are two quite different things.'' But are they? The book tosses the reader into a mixture of tormenting ambiguities, thus upsetting questions of truth, of justice, of crime and punishment and, yes, of love and retribution. Mrs. Harris dares us to rethink the self-accommodating positions we so comfortably embrace. Her inconsistencies are characteristically provoking, but that's another story. The news is that her book moves the reader, not just emotionally, but intellectually, and in startling new directions.
headline: THOUGHTS AFTER THE UNTHINKABLE

title: Stardust: The David Bowie Story
author: Henry Edwards
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STARDUST: The David Bowie Story. By Henry Edwards and Tony Zanetta. (McGraw-Hill, $17.95.) David Bowie first attracted attention in the early 70's during a lull in pop music.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Invisible Weapons
author: Michael Wolfe
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: INVISIBLE WEAPONS. By Michael Wolfe. (Donald S.Ellis/Creative Arts, Paper, $8.95.) Imagine sitting in a bar one night with a bunch of cronies.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Who Profits: Winners, Losers And Government Regulation
pull_quote: Who Profits: Winners, Losers, and Government Regulation, by Robert A. Leone. Basic Books, N.Y. 248 pages, $17.95.    ONE problem with economics, according to the economist who wrote this book, is that it has become preoccupied with questions of macroeconomics: ''What should we do about the Federal deficit? Is the money supply expanding too rapidly? Is Keynesian economics dead? Should 'supply-siders' control Federal fiscal policy?''   They are all important questions, but the economic challenges most of us face are at the level of individual industries, individual companies and governmental agencies. Thus, this book concentrates on the microeconomy - individual enterprises competing in individual markets and dealing with public policy initiatives.
headline: Spotting the Real Costs of Regulation

title: Interest Rates, The Markets, And The New Financial World
author: Henry Kaufman
pull_quote: Interest Rates, the Markets, and the New Financial World, by Henry Kaufman. Times Books, N.Y. 258 pages, $22.50.    WHEN he joined Salomon Brothers in 1962, Henry Kaufman recalls, financial life proceeded at a leisurely pace. Only a handful of people on Wall Street tracked the daily and weekly operations of the Federal Reserve and the Treasury, and only a few academicians followed fluctuations in the money supply.
headline: More Warnings From Dr. Doom

title: My Life Between Japan And America
author: Edwin O. Reischauer. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
MY LIFE BETWEEN JAPAN AND AMERICA By Edwin O. Reischauer. Illustrated. 369 pp. New York: A Cornelia and Michael Bessie Book/ Harper & Row. $22.50. 

NOT long ago, in a master's thesis she submitted to Columbia University, the daughter of a longtime United States Foreign Service officer argued that the adage ''home is where the heart is'' has unsettling implications for Americans whose youth was largely spent abroad. Such people, she asserted, have strong emotional ties to communities outside the United States and, as a result, face identity problems of a kind unfamiliar to those of us whose formative years were entirely spent in this country. That is a judgment in which I generally concur. In his autobiography, ''My Life Between Japan and America,'' Edwin O. Reischauer, a professor emeritus at Harvard University, offers powerful support for a more positive version of the same proposition - that the psychological bifurcation undeniably produced by an expatriate childhood can be of great constructive value not only to the individual who must live with it but to the diverse societies that command a place in his heart.
headline: LOOKING BOTH WAYS

title: Sicilian Uncles
author: Leonardo Sciascia
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SICILIAN UNCLES By Leonardo Sciascia. Translated by N.S. Thompson. 205 pp. New York: Carcanet. $15.95.    LEONARDO SCIASCIA is a cool and sedate Sicilian, one of those Sicilians we are asked to admire in ''Sicilian Uncles'': Sicilians ''who speak little ... who don't get excited ... who worry deep inside and suffer.'' Fully aware of the evil forces at work in history and society, they cling to ''the fragile, silent hope of the best Sicilians. . . . a hope that's afraid of itself, that fears words and has death instead as a neighbour and familiar.''   Sicily has been for Mr. Sciascia a main source of inspiration and a constant concern. With shrewd and unimpassioned eyes he can see its historical weaknesses thrive and expand in today's political climate; he can see its tortuous ways and corruption, its Mafia, spread over the boundaries, invade Italy and blight all hope of renovation. Nothing can be spared the tangle of corruption and compromise, the heavy cloak of conformity and hypocrisy, the web of complicity and self-interest. Yet the writer's task is to reason things out, to see through the web, to bring peripheral testimony.
headline: JUSTICE, VENGEANCE, HEROES AND MAFIOSI

title: A Hollywood Education
author: David Freeman.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A HOLLYWOOD EDUCATION Tales of Movie Dreams and Easy Money. By David Freeman. 268 pp. New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons. $17.95.    BY the time one finishes ''A Hollywood Education'' by the screenwriter and journalist David Freeman, it has become easy to forgive this short-story collection's periodic awkwardness and relish its several virtues. Mr. Freeman's 17 stories, lightly (and in some ways gratuitously) cemented by a journalist-turned-script-polisher narrator, tell the tales of various Hollywood types, from a studio production executive who specializes in wrapping Porsches around trees, to gag writers for Bob Hope, to teen-age hustlers. This is tawdry territory whose landmarks are drugs, deals, dreams, adrenaline and German cars. F. Scott Fitzgerald, Nathanael West and others have been here before, but Mr. Freeman works the soil in his own deadpan manner. These stories reveal the stereotypes behind the stereotypes before proceeding to reveal the bruised humanity behind all this high-priced hubris. Which is to say that Mr. Freeman's triumph - more apparent the deeper one gets into the book - is to dryly depict the pathos without depriving his less sympathetic subjects of their genuine shallowness.
headline: LAST PLACE BEFORE THE SUN SETS

author: Jane Goodall. Illustrated.

When Dr. John Doolittle, Hugh Lofting's fictional English country doctor turned animal linguist -- sailed for Africa, his dog, Jip, navigated the ship by sniffing the wind. Both Jane Goodall and I were inspired by Africaa through a childhood love of Lofting's fantasy ethologist. Indeed it is in studying the expressive bahavior of animals that ethologists usually begin their research.   Miss Goodall celebrates in this book 26 years of research on perhaps the most fascinating of all African primates -- the chimpanzee. Her careful documentation puts the necessary flesh on much that has been merely speculation and corrects earlier accounts of chimpanzee behavior. Human beings are of course not direct evolutionary descendants of this primate, but our taxonomic relationship is so close that ''The Chimpanzees of Gombe'' should become a prime source for material on which theories of human evolution are based.
headline: AN UNDAUNTED 'STARER AT ANIMALS'

JOHN SINGER SARGENT is considered by some to be the greatest artist - or at least the greatest portraitist - of the Edwardian era. He was certainly among the most prolific. In addition to painting well over 600 portraits, he finished more than 2,500 other works, including landscapes, genre paintings, watercolors, murals and architectural decorations. ''For him,'' Stanley Olson writes in his engrossing new biography of the painter, ''life was not a transit up and down the scale of emotions; it was employment. author: Richard E. Lingenfelter. Illustrated.

pull_quote:
DEATH VALLEY & THE AMARGOSA A Land of Illusion. By Richard E. Lingenfelter. Illustrated. 664 pp. Berkeley: University of California Press. $39.95. 

THE desert reveals itself to us reluctantly.

To appreciate it fully we need guidance. A naturalist can show us that the desert is a place rich in exotic plants and wildlife. Now a physicist turned historian, Richard Lingenfelter, has examined the human history of Death Valley and the surrounding Amargosa Basin in the seemingly barren, sun-blasted border country of southwestern Nevada and southeastern California, and in ''Death Valley & the Amargosa'' he reveals the region to be one of the liveliest places on earth.
headline: HEAT, LIES AND FANTASIES

title: Money Talks: The 2,500 Greatest Business Quotes
pull_quote: Money Talks: The 2,500 Greatest Business Quotes from Aristotle to Iacocca, edited by Robert W. Kent. Pocket Books, N.Y. 341 pages, $7.95 (paper).    NOT many editors would try to find a pattern in the remarks of Aristotle and Lee Iacocca, to say nothing of Gypsy Rose Lee and Peter Drucker, or Frantz Fanon and David Sarnoff. But apparently, they and hundreds of other disparate people have from time to time had interesting things to say about the conduct of business through the ages. This book pulls those quotes together, providing a chuckle to those addicted to pithy, thoughtful, irreverent or outrageous remarks.
headline: Plumbing the Past for Business Quotes

author: Anita T. Sullivan. Illustrations by Sarah Bienvenu.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SEVENTH DRAGON The Riddle of Equal Temperament. By Anita T. Sullivan. Illustrations by Sarah Bienvenu. 104 pp. Lake Oswego, Ore.: Metamorphous Press. $12.95.    ''A RT steps in when Nature fails'' is the way a corset advertisement in a 19th-century newspaper put it. Anita T. Sullivan, who invokes the aphorism in this meditation on piano tuning, puts the sentiment this way: ''A piano is full of suppressed desires, recalcitrance, inhibition, conflict. Yet because its opposing forces are carefully balanced, they are still. And the still place, though small, is where music can spin its way through into our dimension.''
headline: EVERY PIANO IS A SOCIETY

title: Nicobobinus
author: Terry Jones
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
NICOBOBINUS By Terry Jones. Illustrated by Michael Foreman. 175 pp. New York: Peter Bedrick Books. $16.95. (Ages 10 and up) 

IMAGINE monks who are also pirates and who, when they want to dispose of someone without directly killing him, suspend him over a cliff at the end of a rope being gnawed by hungry rats. Or imagine a chorus line of daisy-carrying dragons, whose leader responds to a lack of gratitude by saying, ''What else do you want . . . an embroidered tea-towel?'' Whereupon another dragon adds, ''It could say: 'Thank you for saving us - love from all the Dragons.'c'' Or imagine a ship captain - or at least a man who claims to be the captain of a ship that, incidentally, steers and cooks by itself -wearing ''a very short skirt which I suppose we would nowadays call a tu-tu, but which in those days simply didn't exist.'' And if you think you're in Monty Python territory, you're not far wrong.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Security Or Armageddon
author: Louis Rene Beres
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SECURITY OR ARMAGEDDON Israel's Nuclear Strategy. Edited by Louis Rene Beres. 242 pp. Lexington, Mass.: Lexington Books/D.C. Heath & Company. Cloth, $25. Paper, $12.95.    NO Israeli government has ever acknowledged the possession of nuclear weapons, yet here is a collection of wide-ranging and probing essays by a dozen academics on ''Israel's nuclear strategy.'' In actuality, it has long been assumed that Israel has a nuclear weapons capacity, a ''bomb in the basement'' consisting, perhaps, of components that could be assembled on relatively short notice. Much of the debate in ''Security or Armageddon,'' therefore, is concerned with the question of the pros and cons of a possible declaration by Israel that it has the bomb.
headline: BRINGING THE BOMB UP FROM THE BASEMENT

title: Tongues Of Flame
author: Mary Ward Brown
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TONGUES OF FLAME By Mary Ward Brown. 162 pp. New York: Seymour Lawrence/E.P. Dutton. $15.95.    ''W ITH a small foot in a neat black oxford, Miss Emma pushed the front-porch swing back and forth. She meant to go ahead and decide about the tombstone now, this afternoon, so she could forget it. Cliff's grave had been on her conscience long enough.'' It had been on her conscience 15 years, in fact, for it had taken her and her four sons that long to pay off the debts their abusive father had left them when he unexpectedly died. Now, having earned her comfort and her rest, at 65 Miss Emma has eyes that ''might have belonged to a veteran of some long, major war. Through gold-rimmed glasses she examined the swing, settee, the porch chairs on which she had put new coats of paint last week. The cushion covers were all freshly washed and ironed. Her potted ferns, lined against the wall, were dark, healthy, and bristling with fronds.
headline: GOOD FAMILY RECIPES

title: France, Fin De Siecle
author: Eugen Weber
pull_quote: FRANCE, FIN DE SIECLE. By Eugen Weber. Illustrated. 294 pages. Harvard University Press. $20. A HUNDRED years ago, the   French had already started referring to the epoch in which they were living as the fin de siecle. By the 1890's the term had become commonplace, and where it might originally have implied nothing more than ''up to date,'' the connotations it now carried -they were by no means without their glamour - were those of decadence and moral anarchy. In 1888, Eugen Weber tells us, one of the plays put on in Paris was called ''Fin de Siecle''; it was a story of shady deals, loose morals and murder. In 1890, when someone founded a weekly called ''Le Fin de Siecle,'' the main fare it offered its readers was the lowdown on current financial scandals.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Roger's Version
author: John Updike
pull_quote: ROGER'S VERSION. By John Updike. 329 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.    ONE October day in 1984, a young computer hacker named Dale Kohler walks into Roger Lambert's office at the divinity school and makes a noisy announcement. God not only exists, he insists, but He won't be able to hide much longer: already scientific evidence points to His existence, and soon, very soon, someone will extract His presence from the statistics of high-energy physics - they'll succeed in pulling ''the divine rabbit from the cosmic hat.'' It's a proposition that Roger, a lapsed minister, finds esthetically and ethically repulsive - ''aesthetically because it describes a God Who lets Himself be intellectually trapped, and ethically because it eliminates faith from religion.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Entrepreneurs Of The Old West
author: David Dary
pull_quote: ENTREPRENEURS OF THE OLD WEST. By David Dary. 368 pages. Illustrated. Alfred A. Knopf. $22.95.   NO reader interested in the sad history of the broken arrows and treaties on the Great Plains of the American West can soon forget Evan S. Connell's ''Son of the Morning Star.'' In his nonfiction narrative that appeared a season or two ago, the novelist offered far more than a tale of the egomaniacal General Custer and the annihilation of his troops by Indian warriors at the Little Big Horn. By unearthing the deeper reasons behind that single defeat, Mr. Connell exposed the shards of shame in the treatment of peaceful tribes by legendary Indian fighters, the cover up of their atrocities by former Civil War commanders in postwar Washington, including Generals Sherman and Sheridan, and the perils of everyday life on the plains.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Digging Up The Mountains
author: Neil Bissoondath
pull_quote: DIGGING UP THE MOUNTAINS. By Neil Bissoondath. 247 pages. Viking. $15.95.    IN one of the stories in ''Digging Up the Mountains,'' a man stares out of a window, chilled by the thought that he lives in a world where everyone is a refugee: ''He saw the earth, as from space, streams of people in continuous motion, circling the sphere in search of the next stop which, they always knew, would prove temporary in the end.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: O-Zone
author: Paul Theroux
pull_quote: O-ZONE. By Paul Theroux. 527 pages.   G. P. Putnam's Sons. $19.95.    Adept at writing in a variety of genres and forms - from the novel to the travel essay to the short story - Paul Theroux has established himself as one of the most nimble writers around, a writer capable of assimilating - and reinventing - some of our most durable literary traditions. ''The Family Arsenal'' reverberated with echoes of Conrad's ''Secret Agent'' and ''The Mosquito Coast'' with ''Robinson Crusoe'' and ''Lord of the Flies.'' Now his latest novel, ''O-Zone,'' seems meant to recall such satiric portraits of the future as Huxley's ''Brave New World'' and Orwell's ''Nineteen Eighty-Four.''
headline: A Shocking Future

title: Trial By Fire
author: Gerry Spence
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TRIAL BY FIRE: The True Story of a Woman's Ordeal at the Hands of the Law. By Gerry Spence. (Morrow, $18.95.)    Gerry Spence, a Wyoming attorney, wears a white hat. Like all Western heroes he listens not to the odds but to a higher sense of good. Mr. Spence's weapons are the law and his potent courtroom presence -tall hat and all. He pokes fun at this Western imagery and exploits it to the advantage of his client. The client here is Kim Pring, the 1979 Miss Wyoming and a champion baton twirler. Her life changed forever when Penthouse magazine published a short story about a baton-twirling Miss Wyoming, remarkably similar to Miss Pring, whose facility at oral sex caused men to levitate. Asserting that the story damaged her reputation, Miss Pring sued Penthouse and the story's author for libel. The Wyoming jury found for Miss Pring, awarding her $26.5 million in damages from Penthouse. An appelate Court reversed the decision, holding that if a reasonable person would not believe the story to be describing ''actual facts,'' then there could be no libel. Levitation, it seems, had set Penthouse free. The United States Supreme Court refused to hear the case. ''History cannot remember a time when we did not hate our women,'' writes the converted feminist Mr. Spence, who makes passionate and convincing arguments about the unfair - even degrading - ways our legal system treats women: ''Should a woman dare come before our law seeking justice, what is offered is all that any system based on precedent has to offer - namely a hash of leftovers from past iniquities.'' Mr. Spence's conclusion is that the law's attitude toward women has changed little in 500 years.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Bitburg In Moral And Political Perspective
author: Elise O'Shaughnesy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
BITBURG IN MORAL AND POLITICAL PERSPECTIVE. Edited by Geoffrey H. Hartman. (Indiana University, Cloth, $29.95. Paper, $9.95.) 

Little more than a year after President Reagan visited the Kolmeshohe military cemetery - the burial site of several soldiers of the Waffen SS in Bitburg, West Germany -the journey is mentioned most frequently as one in a series of mistakes that failed to stick to the ''Teflon President.'' But, in ''Bitburg in Moral and Political Perspective,'' essays by 10 writers -Primo Levi, Raul Hilberg and Jurgen Habermas among them - are used to explore some very knotty questions about the brief controversy that exploded in May 1985: Who has the right to forgive? How can we sustain memory? What is the value of symbol? And how have the Germans, the Americans, and the Christian community dealt with their complicity and involvement in the Holocaust? The essays are accompanied by a compilation of primary sources - press reports of the visit, speeches made by various sides during the controversy, editorials, cartoons and photographs - which recapture the hot debate over President Reagan's gesture of reconciliation. In his introduction, Geoffrey Hartman, Karl Young Professor of English at Yale University, concedes that ''there are some who feel that an unfortunate incident was inflated into a cause celebre. Bitburg, they say, cannot retain its significance.'' In the end, Bitburg had a significance very different from that intended by President Reagan and Chancellor Helmut Kohl - it raised the specter of what Primo Levi terms ''the deformation of memory.''
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Dostoevsky
author: Joseph Frank. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DOSTOEVSKY The Stir of Liberation 1860-1865. By Joseph Frank. Illustrated. 395 pp. New Jersey: Princeton University Press. $29.50.    IT may not be stretching a point to say that being sent to prison was the best thing that ever happened to Fyodor Dostoyevsky. The alternative, death by firing squad, was certainly less appealing. And most observers have agreed that the years Dostoyevsky spent in Siberian imprisonment and exile from 1850 to 1859 were beneficial to his development as a man, writer and thinker, transforming him from a rather vain and hypersensitive prima donna flushed with overnight literary success (following the publication of his Dickensian novel ''Poor Folk'') into a serious and confident artist. What Dostoyevsky gained in prison - a remarkable breadth of tragic vision and a painful new understanding of the violent, irrepressible human impulse toward self-expression - he later injected into the novels he started writing soon after returning to civilization: ''Crime and Punishment,'' ''The Possessed,'' ''The Idiot'' and ''The Brothers Karamazov.'' Dostoyevsky's experiences in Siberia haunted him for the rest of his life and provided an inexhaustible stock of material that both inspired and terrified him. They also gave him lifetime membership in the distinguished club (still thriving, unfortunately) of Russian writers and intellectuals rewarded for their heretical political, philosophical or esthetic views with an unplanned sabbatical in the Eastern steppe.
headline: HOW SIBERIA CONCENTRATED HIS MIND

title: Wartime Writings 1939-1944
author: Antoine de Saint-Exupery
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WARTIME WRITINGS 1939-1944 By Antoine de Saint-Exupery. Translated by Norah Purcell. With an introduction by Anne Morrow Lindbergh. 237 pp. San Diego: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $12.95.    THERE are certain rare individuals (most often poets) who by the mere fact of their existence put an edge on life, their ceaseless astonishment before its possibilities awakening our own latent sense of renewal and expectation. No one ever stood out more conspicuously in this respect than the French aviator and author Antoine de Saint-Exupery. In an era when devastation and defeat forced the French people to lower their sights, he dared to fix his eye on the future long enough to warn us that ''we feel less human; somewhere we have lost our mysterious prerogatives.''

title: Roger's Version
author: John Updike
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ROGER'S VERSION By John Updike. 329 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.    THE language of fiction is a medley. The novelist, unlike the lyric poet or essayist, must command many styles and speak to us through a plurality of borrowed or imitated discourses as well as in what passes for his or her own voice. Four of them will be familiar to readers of his previous novels, but the fifth is, I believe, a new development, or acquisition, and a remarkably interesting one.

title: Brideshead Benighted
author: Auberon Waugh
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BRIDESHEAD BENIGHTED By Auberon Waugh. 221 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $16.95.    AUBERON WAUGH'S new book revisits a decade of opinions (1976-1985) first recorded while he was political correspondent for the British weekly The Spectator. title: Midterm Report
author: David Wallechinsky. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MIDTERM REPORT The Class of '65: Chronicles of an American Generation. By David Wallechinsky. Illustrated. 418 pp. New York: Viking. $19.95.    I'VE always suspected the 60's were somewhat of a fraud ever since I was in graduate school and the two big student radicals were Chiang Kai-shek's niece and the heiress to an enormous rubber fortune. My suspicions deepened when I visited one of those communes in California. You know what they were eating? Canned cat food. The hippies couldn't get it together enough to go out and gather food.
headline: GRANOLA OF THE MIND

title: Kenya
author: John Halkin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: KENYA. By John Halkin. (Beaufort, $17.95.)    This first novel reads suspiciously like a story outline for a television miniseries.
