title: The Fifties: From Notebooks And Diaries Of The Period
author: Edmund Wilson. Edited by Leon Edel. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE FIFTIES From Notebooks and Diaries of the Period. By Edmund Wilson. Edited by Leon Edel. Illustrated. 663 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $25.    ''J UDGE the work and not the man.'' This piece of advice, issued to students of literature for many decades now, is ostensibly sound. But like other bits of ostensibly sound advice - ''be good'' and ''have fun'' come contradictorily to mind - it is rather easier said than done. Can one read Oscar Wilde without considering the homosexuality that was central not only to Wilde's fate but to his artistic sensibility? Can one read Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn without recalling his years in a Soviet slave labor camp and his self-imposed task of setting straight Russian history? Even if one could do so, what does it profit a reader deliberately to blinker out the facts of a writer's life? In fact, one cannot do it. Philip Larkin was absolutely on target in this matter when he wrote: ''A writer's reputation is twofold: what we think of his work, and what we think of him. What's more, we expect the two halves to relate: if they don't, then one or other of our opinions alter until they do.''
headline: NEVER WISE- BUT OH, HOW SMART

title: The Beet Queen
author: Louise Erdich
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE BEET QUEEN By Louise Erdich. 338 pp. New York: Henry Holt & Company. $16.95. 

MIDWESTERN writers have to do the best they can with their inheritance of flat rhythms. One could say that for settlers, pressure from savage winters, dry summers, lack of neighbors and constantly breaking tools pressed immigrant language into the practical lobe. There it thinned. Midwestern spoken language tends to communicate secular information more than sacacred music. As children in the Midwest we don't hear long, looping sentences, mingling pereception and zaniness that Eudora Welty grew up with, stewed in leisure and peppered with the playfulness of sweet malice. A friend of mine heard a Midwestern farmer say to another last winter, ''I was sorry to hear about your wife, and how are the roads?'' If the novelist reports exactly what he or she hears, the mind turns it to satire, believing that no person inheriting thousands of years of feeling, since the earliest Sumerian poets, could speak in such a flat way. It is hard to write poetry or fiction with the worm of flatness coiled around the house since childhood. In ''The Beet Queen' Louse Endrich plays well with the demon of flatness and often wins.
headline: ANOTHER WORLD BREAKS THROUGH

title: The United States Navy
author: Edward L. Beach. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE UNITED STATES NAVY 200 Years. By Edward L. Beach. Illustrated. 564 pp. New York: Henry Holt & Company. $24.95.    WRITTEN by a retired Navy captain, ''The United States Navy: 200 Years'' is a highly personal, informal, affectionate history of the service. A submariner during World War II, Capt. Edward L. Beach regards that war as the climax toward which all the main tendencies in American naval history aimed. Without any pretense of writing a complete, balanced account, he stresses those forces and incidents that he believes pointed most clearly toward that climax. Optimistically, he anticipates that nuclear weapons such as finally punctuated that ending will never be used in war again, so that World War II will always seem the culmination of American naval history, and his book will remain a narrative of a drama essentially completed.
headline: ORGANIZATION SAILORS

title: New School
author: Peter M. Rutkoff and William B. Scott. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
NEW SCHOOL A History of the New School for Social Research. By Peter M. Rutkoff and William B. Scott. Illustrated. 314 pp. New York: The Free Press. $22.50. 

JUST a few years short now of 70 years old, the New School for Social Research in New York City has gone through at least four lives in its brief career, but it has preserved throughout, if only by a thread, something of a unifying identity. That identity was given at its founding in 1919 by two progressive historians, Charles A. Beard and James Harvey Robinson, who had resigned from Columbia University in protest at the firing of two professors who had opposed the war, and who found in Herbert Croly, the editor of The New Republic, and Dorothy Whitney Straight, its chief backer, support and financing for a unique institution. Beard and Robinson hoped to combine a research center and a school of adult education, expressing a progressive, rational and scientific outlook on society and its problems. The school would provide lectures for ''grown and responsible men and women'' and freedom for a group of social scientists, untrammeled by grades, degrees, departments and academic organization.
headline: A HOME AWAY FROM HITLER

title: The Spirit Of Mediterranean Places
author: Michel Butor
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SPIRIT OF MEDITERRANEAN PLACES By Michel Butor. Translated by Lydia Davis. 147 pp. Marlboro, Vt.: The Marlboro Press. $15.95.    IN England and America, Michel Butor's reputation as a major contemporary French avant-garde writer still rests mainly on the translations of a few of his earlier novels, such as ''Passing Time'' and ''A Change of Heart.'' Before being translated, these had already been widely acclaimed, both in France and abroad, as outstanding examples of a much publicized new school of French fiction, the so-called nouveau roman. Nearly 30 years have gone by since the original French publication of most of these novels, and the nouveau roman has meanwhile been absorbed, like a kind of foreign body, by the more traditional tissues of French fiction. Nobody in Paris now finds the earlier works of Mr. Butor, Alain Robbe-Grillet or Nathalie Sarraute very puzzling or innovative. Some of their novels even strike younger French readers as rather pedantic and boring.
headline: LE NOUVEAU TRAVELOGUE

title: I See A Long Journey
author: Rachel Ingalls.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: I SEE A LONG JOURNEY Three Novellas. By Rachel Ingalls. 141 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $14.95.    THE three novellas in ''I See a Long Journey,'' by the author of the novel ''Mrs. Caliban,'' are ice and fire - they take you to places you don't usually go. Rachel Ingalls, an American living in England, seems to have found the ideal form in which to exercise her astonishing imagination, and in at least one of these stories (the last) has managed to supply something Nabokov demanded of fiction, namely, ''esthetic bliss.''
headline: BROTHER ANSELM, IN A FAMILY WAY

title: Diary Of A Yuppie
author: Louis Auchincloss
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DIARY OF A YUPPIE By Louis Auchincloss. 215 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $16.95.    LOUIS AUCHINCLOSS'S ''Diary of a Yuppie'' is the story of Robert Service's quick rise to the top in the world of New York law. Service's father was a permanent associate - that is, as a young attorney he was passed over for promotion to partner but remained with his firm in a lesser role. Service is ashamed of his father's failure and intends to succeed. As the novel opens, he is a specialist in corporate takeovers and about to be made a partner at Hoyt, Welles & Andrew, a law firm with 36 partners and a hundred clerks. But Service worries that it is too pedestrian, aristocratic and moralistic to be competitive in the long term. Sensing that decay has set in, he establishes a rival firm, stealing both business and the best associates away from Hoyt, Welles. As he expands his new firm, he deals harshly with rivals and obsequiously with clients. His ethics disturb his wife, who leaves him. After an infatuation with Sylvia Sands, a beautiful, viperish widow, Service manages to win back his wife, all the while keeping his mind on business and opportunistically picking up clients when he can. ''Diary of a Yuppie'' is more than an ordinary story of ambition because of the moralists Service confronts along his way. There is Branders Blakelock, the aging sage at Hoyt, Welles, ''toting a bag of puritan principles,'' who refuses to sacrifice individuals for the benefit of business gain; Alice Service, Robert's wife, who chides him for ''looking down on poor scrapping mortals'' and forgetting the poet in his soul; and Cy Hawkins, a prep school teacher with an interest in theology who expounds on the ideas that suffering can be an honor and martyrdom a connection with God.
headline: PEOPLE WHO SNIFF AT SUCCESS

title: The Anti-Soviet Soviet Union
author: Vladimir Voinovich
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE ANTI-SOVIET SOVIET UNION By Vladimir Voinovich. Translated by Richard Lourie. 325 pp. San Diego: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $19.95.    IN the midst of these droll essays and vignettes, Vladimir Voinovich pauses to observe that ''there are secrets galore in the Soviet Union, but the principal and most carefully guarded state secret is the daily life of Soviet people.'' For decades the great failure of Western social scientists was their inability to penetrate this mystery. Instead, they plugged in ready-made topics drawn from the study of New Haven or Peoria, turgid exercises on such anemic themes as ''interest group articulation'' and ''elite formation.'' Or they chewed over tired conundrums such as whether Stalinism grew naturally from Leninism. Such questions kept the Sovietological industry grinding along while protecting the veil that obscured daily life in the Soviet Union.
headline: LAUGHING ALL THE WAY TO THE BORDER

title: Wilson And His Peacemakers
author: Arthur Walworth
pull_quote: WILSON AND HIS PEACEMAKERS:   American Diplomacy at the Paris Peace Conference, 1919. By Arthur Walworth. 618 pages. W. W. Norton. $35.    After all the millions of casualties in the trenches, the dethroning of monarchs, the rise of irredentist aspirations and of revolutionary causes, the Paris peace conference after World War I began as far more than an end to hostilities. It was a lightning-rod for every human and political dream that floated in the air over all the continents. The peacemakers and people everywhere in the world turned to President Woodrow Wilson to bottle the lightning of change.
headline: 1919 Peace Conference

title: The Frenzy Of Renown: Fame And Its History
author: Leo Braudy
pull_quote: THE FRENZY OF RENOWN. Fame and Its History. By Leo Braudy. Illustrated. 649 pages. Oxford. $27.50. SOCRATES is famous and Pia Zadora is famous, and anyone who sets out to write a history of fame, as Leo Braudy has done in ''The Frenzy of Renown,'' is committed to surveying an immense and immensely varied territory. Admittedly Mr. Braudy, who teaches at the University of Southern California, doesn't try to be comprehensive, which would have been attempting the impossible; he is primarily concerned with the idea of fame, the ways in which it has been defined and the ways in which it has evolved. But that still leaves him with an enormous subject on his hands.   Where he might easily have been overwhelmed, however, he has succeeded in producing a well-knit and compelling narrative. Key figures take their appointed place in the story - Alexander the Great, Augustus, Augustine, Charlemagne, Elizabeth I, Louis XIV, Washington, Byron, Barnum, Lindbergh, scores of others. Lesser figures are used to illuminate changing social ideals. The methods of promulgating fame, from coins to engravings, from epic poems to gossip columns, are kept firmly in view.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Progress Of Love
author: Alice Munro
pull_quote: THE PROGRESS OF LOVE. By Alice Munro. 309 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95. FOR the people in ''The   Progress of Love,'' storytelling is a way of seeing and remembering, a mundane but necessary art. In the title story, the narrator recounts how her father watched her mother burn her unwanted inheritance in the kitchen stove; though probably untrue, the story serves as a testament to what she believes about them and the nature of love. Another woman tells a story about how she met her first husband while singing madrigals at college, a neat story of destiny between ''a skinny innocent bit of a lad with a pure sweet tenor'' and ''a stocky little brute of a girl with a big deep alto.'' And a third speaks of how she and her husband ''invented characters'' for their children, casting each daughter in a specific role.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: God's Snake
author: Irini Spanidou
pull_quote: GOD'S SNAKE. By Irini Spanidou. 252 pages. Norton. $15.95.   ''THE first snake I saw was dead,'' reads the opening of Irini Spanidou's fervent, visionary first novel, ''God's Snake,'' ''and so were those of a long time after, but that first snake my father brought home and threw at my feet saying, 'A dead snake.' His orderly Manolis picked it up with some tongs and carried it out of the house, and I went back to my homework. It was an unusual occurrence, but that would be that, I thought. Not so.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Operation Garbo
author: Nigel West
pull_quote: OPERATION GARBO: The Personal Story of the Most Successful Double Agent of World War II. By Juan Pujol with Nigel West. 205 pages. Illustrated. Random House. $17.95. DURING World War II, British intelligence set up a body known as the Twenty Committee to coordinate its use of double agents. (''Twenty'' was a little joke - in Roman numerals it is XX, a double cross.) In 1972 the former chairman of the committee, Sir John Masterman, published a history of the double-cross system in which he singled out for special praise the work of the agent known as Garbo, and since then other accounts of deception during the war have confirmed Garbo's importance. But until 1984 his identity remained a closely guarded secret.   In May of that year, Nigel West, a British writer who specializes in books about espionage and who had been trying to track Garbo down for more than a decade, established that he was a Spaniard called Juan Pujol, now in his 70's and living in Venezuela. He agreed to meet Mr. West and subsequently to collaborate with him on ''Operation GARBO,'' in which he himself describes his life in Spain while Mr. West recounts his wartime exploits in London.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Lover Of Horses
author: Tess Gallagher
pull_quote: THE LOVER OF HORSES. By Tess Gallagher. 184 pages. Harper & Row. $16.95.    As a poet, Tess Gallagher has written movingly of damaged relationships, misplaced selves and the losses incurred by time and death; and those same themes surface again in this, her first collection of fiction. Ms. Gallagher is a strict, highly disciplined writer, and the tensile quality of her prose often reinforces the sense of danger - emotional, spiritual and physical - that lingers over these stories. Reading them, one begins to fear that something will happen (a drunken fight will erupt, a crackpot will fire his Smith & Wesson, a boyfriend will abscond with his former wife), or even worse, that nothing at all will occur, leaving the characters to stew, alone, in their disconsolation.
headline: A Sense of Peril

title: Saints And Strangers
author: Angela Carter
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SAINTS AND STRANGERS By Angela Carter. 126 pp. New York: Viking. $13.95.    ANGELA CARTER might easily be marketed as an eccentric English author, a fabulist and a feminist. But her writing transcends nationality and critical labels, genre and gender. ''Saints and Strangers'' is not only immensely readable in itself but should send readers to her other work - two collections of stories; a translation of the fairy tales of Charles Perrault; two works of nonfiction, ''The Sadeian Woman'' and ''Nothing Sacred: Selected Writings''; and eight novels, among them ''Nights at the Circus,'' published last year, and ''The Infernal Desire Machines of Dr. Hoffman,'' just reissued by Penguin. Ms. Carter's is an absolutely unique voice, intensely literary without being precious, deep without being difficult, indifferent to formulas without being ''experimental,'' and funny without being superficial or cruel. The sense of humor in this volume is a distinctive and healthy blend of English distance and American wackiness.
headline: A MAKER OF MAGIC SOUFFLES

title: An American Music
author: Barbara L Tischler
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AN AMERICAN MUSIC: The Search for an American Musical Identity. By Barbara L. Tischler. (Oxford University, $24.95.) It's difficult to define what qualities make a piece of music sound ''American,'' so American composers gradually abandoned the quest for a musical nationalism in favor of helping to create an international modernism.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Iron Curtain
author: Fraser J. Harbutt.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE IRON CURTAIN Churchill, America, and the Origins of the Cold War. By Fraser J. Harbutt. 384 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $24.95.    WHO started the cold war? The old answer was that the Russians did. Two decades ago, the revisionists began to blame the Americans. In recent years what the historian John Lewis Gaddis has called a postrevisionist consensus has tended to depict the cold war as a product of inevitable antagonisms. Under that view, the controversy has softened. But throughout the sometimes wearying argument, the issue was always whether the Soviet Union or the United States was responsible. Fraser J. Harbutt maintains in this tightly argued book that the British played a major role. In effect, he believes, an unrelentingly anti-Bolshevik Churchill, even after he left the office of Prime Minister in July 1945, enlisted the United States to support Britain's geopolitical battles. Stalin, Mr. Harbutt writes, played into Churchill's hands by stubbornly delaying the withdrawal of Soviet forces from Iran in the spring of 1946, thus confirming the dire warnings of the former Prime Minister's famous ''Iron Curtain'' speech at Westminster College in Fulton, Mo., on March 5 of that year. Harry Truman is off the hook. In his most useful analytical contribution, Mr. Harbutt, an associate professor of history at Emory University, substitutes a triangular diplomacy among Britain, the United States and the Soviet Union for the usual conflict between the two superpowers. As World War II drew toward its end, Stalin and Churchill both wooed Franklin Roosevelt.
headline: LAYING THE BLAME ON BRITAIN

title: Oskar Kokoschka: A Life
author: Frank Whitford. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: OSKAR KOKOSCHKA A Life. By Frank Whitford. Illustrated. 221 pp. New York: Atheneum. $21.95.    IN 1954, when he was already nearly 70 years old and settled in Switzerland after years of wandering, Oskar Kokoschka painted a triptych called ''Thermopylae.'' Though it is by no means among his greatest pictures, it can be seen as his testament -as an artist and as a man. After all, to paint a major figural composition when abstraction reigned supreme showed a healthy and continuing contempt for the fashions of Paris and New York by an artist who had first made his reputation in the German-speaking world. More important, it reaffirmed Kokoschka's lifelong conviction that ''the real, central issue'' of painting is the human image.
headline: THE WILD MAN OF VIENNESE ART

title: China And The Christian Impact
author: Jacques Gernet. Translated by Janet Lloyd.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
CHINA AND THE CHRISTIAN IMPACT A Conflict of Cultures. By Jacques Gernet. Translated by Janet Lloyd. 310 pp. New York: Editions de la Maison des Sciences de l'Homme/ Cambridge University Press. Cloth, $49.50. Paper, $17.95. 

ONE of the most furiously debated intellectual battles in 17th-c and 18th-century Europe was the Chinese rites controversy. Confronted by a culture in China that was in nearly all respects the equal of Europe's and in some ways its superior, Christian missionaries divided into two camps. Accommodationists, led by the Jesuits, argued that it was possible to blend Christianity with Confucianism, while purists argued that Confucianism was irreconcilable with Christianity and conversion of the Chinese would require fundamental cultural change. These divisions spread to Europe, where they polarized Christians and intellectuals, because accommodation would require not only that the Chinese make modifications in their culture but also that European Christians modify certain of their fundamental concepts.
headline: JESUS IN THE CONFUCIAN TEMPLE

title: The Cabalist
author: Amanda Prantera
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CABALIST. By Amanda Prantera. (Atheneum, $12.95.) Amanda Prantera's second novel examines the final weeks in the life of Joseph Kestler, a magician and scholar in the occult arts of the cabala.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Korean War
author: Burton I. Kaufman. Maps.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE KOREAN WAR Challenges in Crisis, Credibility, and Command. By Burton I. Kaufman. Maps. 381 pp. Philadelphia: Temple University Press. $34.95.    THE Korean conflict did for the cold war what the Japanese bombing of Pearl Harbor did for World War II - globalized it. Before the Korean War, the only American political or military commitment outside the Western hemisphere had been the North Atlantic Treaty in Europe. By 1955, the United States had several hundred bases in 36 countries. As a result of the Korean War, the United States began to perceive the struggle with the Soviet Union as broad and global rather than in terms of Europe alone.
headline: WHY WE WERE IN INCHON

title: The Harvard Century
author: Richard Norton Smith. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE HARVARD CENTURY The Making of a University to a Nation. By Richard Norton Smith. Illustrated. 397 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $22.95. 

WE seem, from the outpouring of books on its 350th anniversary, long past the days when, as Henry Adams recalled, ''no one took Harvard College seriously.'' Of course, now we all do, if not necessarily for the reason recently advanced by its fund-raisers -that ''institutions of higher education all across the country look to Harvard to set the pace.'' And because we all pay attention to Harvard, we can only welcome ''The Harvard Century.''
headline: THE IMPERIAL ACADEMY

title: The Frenzy Of Renown
author: Leo Braudy. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE FRENZY OF RENOWN Fame & Its History. By Leo Braudy. Illustrated. 649 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $27.50.    THERE is a Victorian audacity about an attempt to trace the history of fame in Western culture without neglecting (and this is only a partial list) Alexander the Great, Cicero, Julius Caesar, Jesus, St. Augustine, Dante, Chaucer, Elizabeth I, Shakespeare, Voltaire, Benjamin Franklin, P.cT. Barnum, Abraham Lincoln, Emily Dickinson, Walt Whitman, Charles Lindbergh or Ernest Hemingway. This is clearly an impossible task - one that invites charges of chutzpah on every page - but Leo Braudy manages to pull it off.   It is a serious measure of Mr. Braudy's success that ''The Frenzy of Renown: Fame & Its History'' forces a reader back to some of the greatest works of Western literature - that it makes one think about famous people, deeds and ideas in a new way. His exploration is rich in original insights and - considering the fact that its characters are, after all, inescapably familiar - surprisingly free of received opinion.
headline: FIFTEEN MINUTES IS NEVER ENOUGH

title: Bad Karma
author: Deborah Blum
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BAD KARMA: A True Story of Obsession and Murder. By Deborah Blum. (Atheneum, $17.95.) This is a routinely written account of the disturbing events that led to the 1969 shooting and stabbing death of Tanya Tarasoff, a freshman at the University of California, Berkeley.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: On Fiji Islands
author: Ronald Wright
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ON FIJI ISLANDS By Ronald Wright. 257 pp. New York: Viking. $19.95.    IN the 19th century, when the Fiji Islanders converted to Christianity under British pressure, they adapted some of the rituals of their old faith to the new religion. That tactic was commonplace among conquered indigenous peoples from Africa to the Arctic. But the Fijians, or at least some of them, developed an idea of their own. They came to believe that not only the people of Fiji but the old Fijian gods had become Christians.
headline: THERE'LL ALWAYS BE A FIJI

title: Obbligati
author: Anthony Hecht
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Anthony Hecht introduces his collection with a figure-in-the-carpet gambit. Though each of its essays was written for a separate occasion -- the earliest in 1962, the most recent year this year -- the volume displays, he says, ''an unexpected coherence, the more surprising in that it was not planned. As to what this coherence consists in,'' he adds, however, ''I had better leave it to others to say.''   ''Obbligati'' opens with a lecture the poet delivered two years ago at the Library of Congress (where he was consultant in Poetry from 1962 to 1984) on ''The Pathetic Fallacy.'' This lecture turns a critque of Ruskin's phrase for the illegitimate projection of human emotion onto objects (''the willful fountain sings, and the kindly flowers rejoice'') into a wide-ranging defense of metaphor as ''not merely the gadget of poets,'' but ''virtually unavoidable as an instrument of thought.''
headline: A METAPHOR IS A TERRIBLE THING TO WASTE

title: Death Of The Soul: From Descartes To The Computer
author: William Barrett.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DEATH OF THE SOUL From Descartes to the Computer. By William Barrett. 173 pp. New York: Anchor Press/Doubleday & Company. $16.95.    CURRENT philosophical teaching in the United States, William Barrett suggests in ''Death of the Soul:   From Descartes to the Computer,'' is that the mind is nothing more than a first-rate computer. We should reject this view, he argues, because it represents thinking as essentially passive, atomistic and fragmented, a set of errors that comes to us from David Hume - whom the Cambridge legal scholar Philip Allott calls ''that evil genius of modern consciousness.''
headline: HOW THE MIND LOST ITSELF

title: Two Women In One
author: Nawal el-Saadawi
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TWO WOMEN IN ONE. By Nawal el-Saadawi. Translated by Osman Nusairi and Jana Gough. (Seal Press, $14.95.) This short, impressionistic novel provides glimpses of the life and feelings experienced by its 18-year-old heroine, Bahiah Shaheen, who rejects her everyday identity.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Singular Rebellion
author: Saiichi Maruya
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SINGULAR REBELLION By Saiichi Maruya. Translated by Dennis Keene. 412 pp. New York: Kodansha International. $19.95.    IN the late 1960's, Eisuke Mabuchi, a widower and upward-bound employee of a small Tokyo electronics firm, falls in love with Yukari, a fashion model 20 years his junior. Mabuchi is in every way an ordinary man, but his eventual marriage to Yukari, an unusual if not rebellious act, leads him into an ever-tightening knot of comic events that highlight ''Singular Rebellion.'' The novel, which won the Tanizaki Prize in 1972, is the first by the Japanese writer and critic Saiichi Maruya to be translated into English.
headline: MARRIED FOR HIS MAID?

title: No Earthly Notion
author: Susan Dodd
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
NO EARTHLY NOTION By Susan Dodd. 216 pp. New York: Viking. $15.95. 

THIS is an utterly engaging story of a 31-year-old woman who initially seems only timid, long-suffering and given to guilt feelings - little more, in fact, than a plucky caretaker. We first see Murana Bill as a plain, orphaned child from a tiny Kentucky town who spends her girlhood caring for her scurvy little brother, Lyman Gene. He spends his boyhood and his manhood, what there is of it, grabbing everything he can. Never a cooperative kid brother, Lyman Gene becomes a true problem when he returns from Vietnam in psychic shock. He can't speak. He can't or won't take care of his body except to overfeed it. Their life together consists of Murana's cooking food and Lyman Gene's wolfing it all down.
headline: MORE GRATITUDE THAN MONEY

title: Anna Delaney's Child
author: John Thorndike
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ANNA DELANEY'S CHILD. By John Thorndike. (Macmillan, $17.95.) ''Lord keep my memory green!'' pleads Charles Dickens's hero in the story ''The Haunted Man,'' after his wish to forget all ''sorrow, wrong, and trouble'' has been granted.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Capitalist Revolution
author: Peter L. Berger.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CAPITALIST REVOLUTION Fifty Propositions About Prosperity, Equality, and Liberty. By Peter L. Berger. 262 pp. New York: Basic Books. $17.95.    ''T HE insight that an enduring human community requires a belief in its essential rightness,'' Peter Berger writes, ''long antedates modern social science.'' c''Capitalism, as an institutional arrangement,'' he adds, ''has been singularly devoid of plausible myths.'' Mr. Berger believes that if capitalism is to survive, people must believe that capitalism is ''right,'' and his book, ''The Capitalist Revolution,'' is an attempt to fill the gap between the two previous propositions - to demonstrate that capitalism is ''right'' and therefore worthy of positive myths. If one wants a nondogmatic, rational, reasonable, never shrill, balanced argument that capitalism as it is broadly practiced in Japan, Europe and the United States is better than what Mr. Berger and people in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe call socialism (but what most of the rest of us would call Communism), then this is a very good book. Few, even among those who call themselves socialists, would argue empirically with the proposition that ''industrial capitalism has generated the greatest productive power in human history. To date, no other socioeconomic system has been able to generate comparable productive power.'' Marx was clearly wrong when he predicted that capitalism would create falling real wages and sharply rising inequalities.
headline: WHO STAYS UP WITH THE SICK COW?

title: Hollywood: Legend And Reality
author: Michael Webb
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: I'm wary of books that scrutinize Hollywood myths; they have a sinister tendency toward psychobabble and sociological truisms. Luckily, HOLLYWOOD: Legend and Reality, edited by Michael Webb (N.Y. Graphic Society/Little, Brown, Cloth, $39.95.
headline: Behind the Mask

title: Suspects
author: William J Caunitz
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SUSPECTS. By William J. Caunitz. (Crown, $17.95.) To most of the world, Lieut. Joseph P. Gallagher is the ultimate cop, a hard-driving, glad-handing Irish-Catholic gumshoe who's everybody's pal.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: My Life With Goya
author: Andrew Potok
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MY LIFE WITH GOYA. By Andrew Potok. (Arbor House, $17.95.) ''My Life With Goya,'' is a novel rich in elegance and butchery, lucidity and insanity, love and cruelty.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Reaping The Whirlwind
author: Robert J. Norrell. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
REAPING THE WHIRLWIND The Civil Rights Movement in Tuskegee. By Robert J. Norrell. Illustrated. 254 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $19.95. 

ONE picture in this history of the civil rights movement in Tuskegee, Ala., shows the bronze statue of Booker T. Washington on the campus of Tuskegee Institute. The caption identifies the statue as ''ambiguous,'' referring no doubt to the suggestion by the Tuskegee graduate Ralph Ellison in ''Invisible Man'' that while Washington seems to be lifting a veil of ignorance from a kneeling slave's head, he might instead be lowering the hood more firmly into place. The story of civil rights in Tuskegee is also a study in ambiguity, for it is a history at once unusual and typical of the Southern black belt. Robert J. Norrell, an assistant professor of history at Birmingham-Southern College, explores both the unusual and the typical in this story, and for most of ''Reaping the Whirlwind,'' he presents the viewpoints of the major participants fully and sympathetically.
headline: WHAT VOTES CAN'T BUY

title: An Academic Question
author: Barbara Pym
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
AN ACADEMIC QUESTION By Barbara Pym. 182 pp. New York: E.cP. Dutton. $15.95. 

EVER since Barbara Pym was ''rediscovered'' in 1977 after 14 years of unmitigated neglect, we have been treated to a stream of her gentle yet sharp-witted fiction - her late, somberly beautiful masterworks, ''Quartet in Autumn'' and ''A Few Green Leaves,'' reissues of a half-dozen delightful earlier books (all but one previously unpublished in this country) and the pair of splendidly funny, surprisingly dissimilar novels written during her wilderness years, ''An Unsuitable Attachment'' and ''The Sweet Dove Died.'' Most recently, we have seen an edition of her letters and diaries.
headline: A COOLER, TOUGHER WOMAN

title: Lilian's Story
author: Kate Grenville
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LILIAN'S STORY By Kate Grenville. 227 pp. New York: Viking. $16.95.    THIS novel from Australia is a work of considerable beauty and power. Written in the first person in a sumptuous style, it flows easily, unobstructedly from the birth of its heroine, Lilian Una Singer, to her old age and approaching death (the time is the early half of this century). ''Lilian's Story,'' Kate Grenville's first novel, has an uncompromising vision behind it, and is told with honesty and virtuosity.
headline: LUNACY AMONG THE TEACUPS

title: Through A Glass Darkly
author: Karleen Koen
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THROUGH A GLASS DARKLY By Karleen Koen. 743 pp. New York: Random House. $19.95.    ONE of the great joys of writing a historical novel is the permission it gives to immerse oneself in the sights, sounds and smells of a vanished world. When readers marvel at the masses of research involved, it is difficult to explain that the research is really the easy part. Sitting in a library reading about costumes, coaches, cuisine, one is suspended in a place outside of time where worries about nuclear war, the environment, even one's own family problems, do not intrude.   But research is not the only thing a historical novel requires. One must create vivid characters, a compelling story, and above all one must tell a tale that can be set only in that particular epoch. There is a reason why certain writers are drawn to certain eras - Mary Renault to ancient Crete and Greece, Gore Vidal to ancient Rome or the United States in its formative years. Those epochs either cast light on our own time or tell us some-thing about the history of ideas, religion, politics.
headline: BETRAYED BY A GORGEOUS CAD

title: High Art
author: Rubem Fonseca
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HIGH ART By Rubem Fonseca. Translated by Ellen Watson. 345 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $17.95.    THE mass media, print and video, stole their best tricks from literature. A few contemporary novelists are now returning the favor. The most celebrated example is Umberto Eco, whose ''Name of the Rose'' - a hybrid medieval thriller, adventure novel and erudite entertainment - proves that intelligence, learning and esthetic experimentation can be yoked with 19th-century feuilleton devices: suspense, digression, violence, outrageous coincidence and spectacular historical panoramas.   In Latin American literature, the writer Manuel Puig exemplifies this stealing from the mass media. Mr. Puig was inspired by cinema - as were Guillermo Cabrera Infante and, to a lesser degree, Carlos Fuentes. The author of ''Kiss of the Spider Woman,'' Mr. Puig found in films not only themes and an inexhaustible supply of myths but, more important, a narrative technique. Like screenplays, his books - simultaneously visual and spoken - make rapid jumps to the past and the future. Their cinematic allusions constitute a utopian alternative, a fantasy world where people can escape the degradation of their lives.
headline: THUGS WHO KNOW THEIR GREEK

title: Adam's Task
author: Vicki Hearne.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ADAM'S TASK Calling Animals by Name. By Vicki Hearne. 274 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.    WHY do automobiles bear animal names such as ''Falcon,'' ''Mustang'' and ''Jaguar''? Most of us know practically nothing about these animals, whereas we all know something about cars and most of us actually drive them. What new information can possibly be added by using such labels? Yet we feel much is added, as though we had been brought up chasing mustangs or hunting jaguars. Human relations with animals are mysterious, profound and passionate. Vicki Hearne's book, written with a philosophical purpose in mind, illuminates one relation - that of a skilled trainer to dogs and horses -but also adds to the mystery and the passion.
headline: YOUR DOG IS SIZING YOU UP

title: The House Of Kanze
author: Nobuko Albery
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE HOUSE OF KANZE. By Nobuko Albery. (Simon & Schuster, $17.95.) The stately, ritualized Noh plays of Japan are not for theatergoers who succumb easily to the fidgets.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Enchantment
author: Daphne Merkin
pull_quote: ENCHANTMENT. By Daphne Merkin. 288 pages. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $16.95.   WHEN Hannah Lehmann was 10 years old, she went to summer camp.   Desperately homesick, she sent her mother a succession of tear-blotched letters: ''I love you so much. I miss you terribly. Please let me come home.'' Her mother tore up the first of the letters and sent it back to her with an accompanying note: ''This is what I will do with each and every one of these letters.'' Hannah persisted, even so, and in the end the family driver came to collect her in an enormous car - the talk of the camp. When she got back, her mother wasn't home.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Me And Dimaggio
author: Christopher Lehmann-Haupt
critic: Roy Blount Jr.: Roy Blount Jr.'S Latest Book Is A Collection of Humorous Pieces EntitledNot Exactly What I Had In Mind.''
pull_quote: ME AND DIMAGGIO. A Baseball Fan Goes in Search of His Gods. By Christopher Lehmann-Haupt. 303 pages. Simon & Schuster. $17.95. ''WHAT are you doing here?'' Red Smith asks The New York Times book reviewer Christopher Lehmann-Haupt at spring training in 1979.   ''I'm supposed to be writing a book about baseball,'' says Mr. Lehmann-Haupt.
headline: Books: On Baseball

title: Eisenhower: At War 1943-1945
author: David Eisenhower
pull_quote: EISENHOWER: AT WAR 1943-1945. By David Eisenhower. 977 pages.Random House. $29.95.   ''LET'S leave it to the historians,' Dwight D. Eisenhower once said when, as president of Columbia University, he was discussing the still lively controversy over his broad-front strategy during the closing months of World War II. The latest historian of this and Eisenhower's other battles is his grandson, David. Ike, at least, would be satisfied with the book.
headline: Books: Ike in Command

title: The Target Is Destroyed
author: Seymour M Hersh
pull_quote: ''THE TARGET IS DESTROYED.'' What Really Happened to Flight 007 and What America Knew About It. By Seymour M. Hersh. Illustrated. 282 pages. Random House. $17.95. IN a positive sense, Seymour Hersh's highly anticipated book about the shooting down of Korean Air Lines Flight 007 is something of an anticlimax, if only because it fails to confirm any of the more extreme speculation about what might have happened in 1983 when a civilian airplane apparently flew into Soviet airspace over Sakhalin Island and was destroyed by a Soviet interceptor.   As readers may know by now from a portion of '' 'The Target Is Destroyed' '' that appears in the current issue of The Atlantic Monthly, Mr. Hersh - principally through extensive investigation of American intelligence sources and through interviews with high officials of both the Soviet Union and Japan - has put together an account and explanation of what really happened on the night of Aug. 31-Sept. 1.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Wallace Stevens: The Early Years
author: Joan Richardson
pull_quote: WALLACE STEVENS: The Early Years, 1879-1923. By Joan Richardson. Illustrated. 591 pages. Beech Tree Books/ William Morrow. $21.95. To readers of his shimmering, musical verse, Wallace Stevens appeared in a variety of antic disguises - he was Peter Quince or Crispin the Comedian or the Man with a Blue Guitar. To his fiancee, Elsie Moll, he was Pierrot or Tom Folio or her favorite jongleur - wearing ''cap and bells'' as he tossed epiphanies about brightly in the empty air. Yet the poet saw himself simply as ''a most inappropriate man/In a most unpropitious place'' - a ''thinking stone'' who garbed his insecurities in a luminous cloak of words.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Lost Language Of Cranes
author: David Leavitt
pull_quote: THE LOST LANGUAGE OF CRANES. By David Leavitt. 319 pages. Knopf. $17.95. THE LOST LANGUAGE OF   CRANES,'' David Leavitt's skillful first novel (he has published a collection of stories, ''Family Dancing'') is about a New York City family in crisis. Owen Benjamin, admissions director of a private boys' school, has for years been routinely unfaithful to his wife, but now, as the novel begins, his growing sexual appetite is beginning to threaten their marriage. His wife, Rose, a copy editor for a publishing house, responds by retreating into her work, and into solving acrostic puzzles, to which she is addicted.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Obbligati: Essays In Criticism
author: Anthony Hecht
pull_quote: OBBLIGATI: Essays in Criticism. By Anthony Hecht. 330 pages. Atheneum. $18.95.   MOST good poets are also good critics, and Anthony Hecht is very much a case in point. But while he published his first collection of poetry more than 30 years ago, he has waited until now to put together his first collection of criticism. ''Obbligati'' consists of 10 essays, most of which began life as lectures or reviews; the topics range from large general themes - the pathetic fallacy, the poetry of architecture -to considerations of contemporary or recent poets such as Richard Wilbur and Robert Lowell.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Progress Of Love
author: Alice Munro
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PROGRESS OF LOVE By Alice Munro. 309 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.    STORYTELLING is shaped by two contrary, yet complementary, impulses - one toward brevity, compactness, artful omission; the other toward expansion, amplification, enrichment. The one, practiced most scrupulously, yields ever briefer and ever more abstract or parablelike fictions; the other, of course, yields the novel or the epic. Some storytellers experiment endlessly while others, having found their voices early on, and having developed (or appropriated) the most pragmatic structures to contain them, are content to work in more or less the same tradition throughout their careers. When the work is good no one is likely to lament the writer's lack of interest in experimentation. When the work is very good no one is likely even to notice it.
headline: CHARACTERS DANGEROUSLY LIKE US

title: The New England Soul
author: Harry S. Stout.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE NEW ENGLAND SOUL Preaching and Religious Culture in Colonial New England. By Harry S. Stout. 398 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $29.95.    THERE is a story in Cotton Mather's great compendium of New England history, the ''Magnalia Christi Americana,'' that tells of a minister of Massachusetts Bay who journeys north to spread the Gospel to one of the outlying settlements. Urging the folk he finds there ''to approve themselves a Religious People'' lest ''they . . . contradict the main end of Planting this wilderness,'' he is greeted with this insolent reply: ''Sir, you are mistaken, you think you are preaching to the people of the Bay; our main End was to catch Fish.''
headline: FISHERS OF MEN

title: Cadillac Desert
author: Marc Reisner. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CADILLAC DESERT The American West and Its Disappearing Water. By Marc Reisner. Illustrated. 582 pp. New York: Viking. $22.95.    IT'S unlikely that most taxpayers will read ''Cadillac Desert: The American West and Its Disappearing Water,'' but they should. It's a revealing, absorbing, often amusing and alarming report on where billions of their dollars have gone - and where a lot more are going.
headline: WHEN THE BILL FOR THE MARVELS FALLS DUE

title: Adieu, Volodya
author: Simone Signoret
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ADIEU, VOLODYA By Simone Signoret. Translated by Stanley Hochman. 418 pp. New York: Random House. $18.95.    THE actress Simone Signoret, who died in 1985, became a writer by chance, when she published a memoir in 1976 based on a six-day-long tape-recorded interview with a French journalist. She said the memoir gave her the idea ''to interrogate myself, after the fact, in silence and in solitude.'' She called it ''Nostalgia Isn't What It Used to Be,'' taken from graffiti she saw on a wall in Manhattan, and compared writing it to going underwater, ''diving slowly, to bring up the corals and the flotsam that lie at the bottom of one's memory.'' The memoir gave Signoret the impetus to continue writing, and ''Adieu, Volodya'' is her first novel and last published work.
headline: INTO MEMORY, SLOWLY

title: Eisenhower: At War 1943-1945
author: David Eisenhower
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EISENHOWER: AT WAR 1943-1945. By David Eisenhower. Illustrated. 977 pp. New York: Random House. $29.95.   FOR David Eisenhower, who was born in 1948, the events he depicts in ''Eisenhower: At War'' are as distant as World War I was to my generation. But Mr. Eisenhower's personal ties to those remote events are uniquely close. His grandfather was Supreme Commander of the Allied Forces in the European Theater of Operations. His father, John Eisenhower, served in the Army in the E.T.O. Both grandfather and father have written notable books about the European war. As a boy, David Eisenhower met Allied leaders - Churchill, Montgomery, Alexander, de Gaulle. One of his favorite spots in the White House was the second-floor room where President Eisenhower displayed his decorations and swords. Though his grandfather rarely discussed military decisions in his presence, David Eisenhower grew up in an atmosphere filled with memories of war.   Still, ''Eisenhower: At War'' is not, David Eisenhower tells us, the book he intended to write. He initially envisaged a book about his grandfather's second Presidential term. But he discovered that he could not treat the second term without examining the first term. Eventually he decided that he could not treat the White House years at all without examining the way World War II had prepared Eisenhower for the Presidency. ''Eisenhower: At War'' is, in consequence, the first of three projected volumes on the age of Eisenhower.
headline: No Headline

title: A Woman's Place
author: Marita Golden
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A WOMAN'S PLACE. By Marita Golden. (Doubleday, $16.95.) ''A Woman's Place'' is a female coming-of-age-into-one's-own tale told through a smoked glass three-way mirror.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Mostly True Confessions
author: Jean Gonick.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MOSTLY TRUE CONFESSIONS Looking for Love in the Eighties. By Jean Gonick. 201 pp. New York: Random House. $14.95.    ROMANTIC love is ephemeral and occasionally unavoidable, some feel, like the viral flu. It is given, it is borne away. All you can do is wait until it wanes, leaving you depleted and - if you're lucky - a little thinner. Some think it better to invest all that energy in something like building muscles, flossing teeth or reading the three-volume version of Proust.
headline: HEARTS AND SLEEVES

title: Confessions Of A Parish Priest
author: Andrew M. Greeley.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CONFESSIONS OF A PARISH PRIEST An Autobiography. By Andrew M. Greeley. 507 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.    ANDREW M. GREELEY, a Roman Catholic priest, social scientist and best-selling novelist, must be chuckling over the red flag of his title. To critics who have clucked about the sexual content of his fiction, wondering how a priest could possibly know, he offers the titillating possibility of ''confessions.'' To those who think he has abandoned his vocation, he proclaims he is, in fact, a parish priest (whose parish is his mailbox). ''What do the priests out there working in the trenches think of you?'' he reports Phil Donahue asked him. ''The trenches are everywhere,'' Father Greeley comments, ''including on the Phil Donahue show.''
headline: DON QUIXOTE IN THE TRENCHES

title: Right Turn
author: Thomas Ferguson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RIGHT TURN: The Decline of the Democrats and the Future of American Politics. By Thomas Ferguson and Joel Rogers. (Hill & Wang, $19.95.)
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: God's Snake
author: Irini Spanidou
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GOD'S SNAKE By Irini Spanidou. 252 pp. New York: W. W. Norton & Company. $15.95.    CHILDHOOD seems to be the almost inevitable subject of contemporary first novels. What the child saw and felt and suffered, how the future author gradually discovered artistic sensibility and vision - these have been the commonplace materials of first novels at least since Joyce wrote ''A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.''
headline: A RAW RECRUIT NAMED ANNA

title: To Be Free!
author: Ron Martin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TO BE FREE! By Ron Martin. (Vanguard, $14.95.) In this novel about ''the bloody maw'' of the Vietnam War, the protagonist, Jack Ramsey, is a prisoner of war saturated in symbolism.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Fools: And Other Stories
author: Njabulo Ndebele.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FOOLS And Other Stories. By Njabulo Ndebele. 280 pp. New York: Readers International/Persea Books. Cloth, $14.95. Paper, $7.95.    THE five tales in Njabulo Ndebele's ''Fools and Other Stories'' all have their setting in the African township near Johannesburg where the author was brought up. South Africa has produced a number of gifted writers but those best known to the rest of the world have been white. Most of the country's black writers have the problem that they are writing in a second language, but more strange to us is the fact that they are in the vanguard of a revolutionary situation: they cannot dodge the expectation that what they write will advance the cause, and anything else will be regarded as self-indulgence.
headline: TIN ROOFS AMONG THE PEACH TREES

title: The Master Terrorist
author: Yossi Melman. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MASTER TERRORIST The True Story of Abu Nidal. By Yossi Melman. Illustrated. 215 pp. New York: Adama Books. $16.95.    ''I AM the evil spirit of the secret services. I am the evil spirit which moves around only at night causing them nightmares,'' Sabri al-Banna once said, referring to the clandestine world of secret agents and subversives in which the terrorist lives. He has also said, ''I am Abu Nidal - the answer to all Arab suffering and misfortunes.''
headline: ON THE BLODDY TRAIL OF SABRI AL-BANNA

title: Carnival For The Gods
author: Gladys Swan
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CARNIVAL FOR THE GODS By Gladys Swan. 229 pp. New York: Vintage Contemporaries/Vintage Books. Paper, $6.95.    IN ''Carnival for the Gods,'' Gladys Swan's poetically elegant but uneven first novel, she follows the Southwest Odyssey of six burned-out carnival people as they make a final, desperate effort to salvage their roadshow and restore magic to their lives. Led by Alta, a former trapeze artist, and her husband, Dusty, whose ambitions for his circus outstrip his means, this troupe includes a sex-starved giant, a philosophical midget, a failed magician and a snake dancer with the unfortunately transparent name Grace.
headline: A GIANT ENSLAVED, A MIDGET MISPLACED

title: Me And Dimaggio
author: Christopher Lehmann-Haupt.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ME AND DIMAGGIO A Baseball Fan Goes in Search of His Gods. By Christopher Lehmann-Haupt. 303 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95.    At last count, Christopher Lehmann-Haupt had written four million two hundred and twenty-four thousand four hundred and seven book reviews for this newspaper. He had not himself committed a book. Maybe he should quit whle he is ahead. For ''Me and DiMaggio'' is another eccellent hymn to the joys of baseball. Good prose seems to thrive on afection for this game.
headline: ASK YOUR QUESTION AND DUCK

title: Life In Windy Weather
author: Andrei Bitov
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LIFE IN WINDY WEATHER By Andrei Bitov. Edited by Priscilla Meyer. 371 pp. Ann Arbor, Mich.: Ardis Publishers. Cloth, $19.50. Paper, $8.95.    IT was seeing Fellini's movie ''La Strada'' that helped Andrei Bitov decide to chuck the detested career of geologist for that of writer. He says in an autobiographical note at the beginning of this volume, ''For the first time I was witness to the possibility of the contemporary expression of contemporary reality.'' Like many other Soviet prose writers who started out in the 1960's, Mr. Bitov avoided such topics as World War II, social heroics, political corruption and labor camps, exploring instead the mundanities of daily life. A Leningrader, born in 1937, he has produced one novel, ''Pushkin House'' - scheduled for publication here next year - and several volumes of stories. Now we have the first collection of his work ever published in English, well translated by various hands. It reveals a writer of impressive power, subtlety and originality.
headline: ONE PLUS ONE EQUALS TWO ONES

title: Blood Libels
author: Clive Sinclair
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BLOOD LIBELS. By Clive Sinclair. (Farrar, Straus & Giroux, $14.95.) Jewish guilt as a literary theme is now off the market. With ''Blood Libels,'' Clive Sinclair, the literary editor of London's Jewish Chronicle, wraps up Jewish guilt like a corned beef sandwich and takes it home - along with Jewish paranoia and Jewish self-torment.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Only The Little Bone
author: David Huddle
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ONLY THE LITTLE BONE By David Huddle. 217 pp. Boston: David R. Godine. $15.95.    DAVID HUDDLE'S excellent new book of linked short stories, ''Only the Little Bone,'' is not just another tale of growing up south of the Mason-Dixon line. Its real interest, even when the narrator is still a young boy, lies in the depiction of the lines of power within the family, the community, the industries that support the community - and of the kind of men these institutions produce.
headline: A GENE FOR FLAWED COMPETENCE

title: Freedom
author: Leslie S Rowland
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FREEDOM A Documentary History of Emancipation, 1861-1867. Selected From the Holdings of the National Archives of the United States. Series I, Volume I: The Destruction of Slavery. Edited by Ira Berlin, Barbara J. Fields, Thavolia Glymph, Joseph P. Reidy and Leslie S. Rowland. Illustrated. 852 pp. New York: Cambridge University Press. $39.50.    LONG after Appomattox, the Civil War would be relived in the American imagination. With the passage of time, however, memories become increasingly selective. Monuments erected by Southern whites, for example, suggest that most blacks during the war rendered faithful service to a cause committed to their perpetual enslavement. That thought comforted several generations of whites. In ''Gone With the Wind,'' - the classic embellishment of white myths, fears and fantasies - slaves appeared invariably as faithful and passive, emancipated blacks as primitive and dangerous. ''Like monkeys or small children turned loose among treasured objects whose value is beyond their comprehension,'' Margaret Mitchell wrote of the freed slaves, ''they ran wild - either from perverse pleasure in destruction or simply because of their ignorance.''
headline: A DIFFERENT WAR

title: The Right To Die
author: Derek Humphry and Ann Wickett.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE RIGHT TO DIE Understanding Euthanasia. By Derek Humphry and Ann Wickett. 372 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $18.95.    FEW situations in life are more emotionally wrenching and morally perplexing than those in which the setting and manner of a person's death, either one's own or that of a loved one, are foreseen. Technology and pharmacology are at a stage of development where physicians are able to cure people of diseases that formerly would have been fatal. They can also deprive a person in the terminal phase of an illness or in a persistent vegetative state of the peace of death. In opposition to the dogma that human life must in every instance be sustained and never surrendered, whether by one's own act or with the help of a friend, Derek Humphry and Ann Wickett argue for the right of terminally ill people to be delivered from their condition.
headline: WHEN IS LIFE NOT WORTH LIVING?

title: A Machine That Would Go Of Itself
author: Michael Kammen. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A MACHINE THAT WOULD GO OF ITSELF The Constitution in American Culture. By Michael Kammen. Illustrated. 532 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $29.95.    WHEN Chief Justice Warren E. Burger recently announced that he would step down from the Supreme Court to head the bicentennial celebration of the Constitution beginning next year, irreverent critics assumed that his new position amounted to little more than a sinecure and that his resignation from the Court was deftly timed to enable President Reagan to appoint additional Justices. But sympathy will flow out to Mr. Burger from readers of Michael Kammen's book, ''A Machine That Would Go of Itself.'' They will understand that Mr. Burger's assignment to play schoolmaster to the American people about the significance of their Constitution is a task that will make his oft-complained-of workload crisis on the Court seem trivial.
headline: REVERENCE, IGNORANCE AND BLAZING APATHY

title: France, Fin De Siecle
author: Eugen Weber
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FRANCE, FIN DE SIECLE By Eugen Weber. Illustrated. 294 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: The Belknap Press/ Harvard University Press. $20.    HISTORY is clearly becoming more fun. In Eugen Weber's ''France, Fin de Siecle,'' statesmen and treaties are set aside in favor of the stuff of everyday existence. We learn about bathing, smells, sanitation, domestic quarrels, underwear, sexuality and the bicycle as they evolved during the last two decades of the 19th century. ''Profound realities may stir the imagination, but most of life passes on the surface,'' Mr. Weber writes. His attention is engaged by a mass of vital trivia, culled from the police blotter and the popular arts, statistics on the number of water closets and the price of railway tickets, as well as from memoirs of all sorts. Mr. Weber's book belongs to an ever-growing number of historical studies - particularly in France - devoted to dailiness, to the way our ancestors got through the day and the night.
headline: DECADENCE WAS ONLY SKIN-DEEP

title: O-Zone
author: Paul Theroux
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: O-ZONE By Paul Theroux. 527 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $19.95.    AT the beginning of ''The Mosquito Coast,'' before the soon-to-be-psychotic Allie flees what he believes is an imminently doomed America, Paul Theroux describes his protagonist's philosophy: ''It's the empty spaces that will save us. No funny bunnies, no cops, no crooks, no muggers, no glue sniffers, no aerosol bombs.'' Mr. Theroux, it seems, has an equally intense faith in the redemption of empty spaces, and O-Zone, ''the large sealed-off territory in the midwest,'' a supposedly uninhabitable zone created after a disastrous leakage of nuclear wastes, is one of those empty spaces and gives its name to his new novel.
headline: NERD OF PARADISE

title: Re-Making Love
author: Barbara Ehrenreich, Elizabeth Hess and Gloria Jacobs.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RE-MAKING LOVE The Feminization of Sex. By Barbara Ehrenreich, Elizabeth Hess and Gloria Jacobs. 228 pp. New York: Anchor Press/Doubleday. $15.95.    IT was women - it wasn't men - whose sexual attitudes and behavior drastically changed within the past two decades. The sexual revolution, Barbara Ehrenreich, Elizabeth Hess and Gloria Jacobs compellingly argue, is actualy women's sexual revolution. Thus the counterrevoluton, the sexual backlash that emerged in the early 1980's, is primarily directed against women and is a threat to women's achievements in ''the remaking and reinterpretation of sex.''
headline: ROLLING BACK THE LUST FRONTIER

title: Anastasia Has The Answers
author: Lois Lowry
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ANASTASIA HAS THE ANSWERS By Lois Lowry. 123 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin. $12.95. (Ages 10 and up)    ANASTASIA KRUPNIK is still hopeless with her feet. She walks just fine, but she could not cope with ballet and now she cannot climb the ropes in her seventh grade gym class. That humiliates and embarrasses her in front of the person she admires more than any other in the whole world, her tall, lanky physical education teacher Wilhelmina Willoughby. In ''Anastasia Has the Answers'' the title character comes to grips with her problems.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: We Irish
author: Denis Donoghue
pull_quote: WE IRISH. Essays on Irish Literature and Society. By Denis Donoghue. 275 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95. WHO speaks for Ireland? ''We Irish,'' the title   Denis Donoghue has chosen for his collection of essays on Irish themes, argues a common heritage and suggests at least the possibility of a collective voice. But although the phrase may look like one that Mr. Donoghue might have picked up anywhere, it has a history: Mr. Donoghue found it in Yeats, Yeats found it in Bishop Berkeley, and in the light of its pedigree it bristles with ironies.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Perfume: The Story Of A Murderer
author: Patrick Suskind
pull_quote: PERFUME: The Story of a Murderer. By Patrick Suskind. Translated from the German by John E. Woods. 255 pages. Knopf. $16.95. HOW can you help being intrigued by the title of this first novel, ''Perfume''; or by the subtitle, ''The Story of a Murderer''; or by the painting of the nude woman on the dust jacket, a detail from Watteau's ''Nymphe et Satyre''; or by the jovial yet ironic voice of the narrator? ''In eighteenth-century France,'' he begins, ''there lived a man who was one of the most gifted and abominable personages in an era that knew no lack of gifted and abominable personages.'' He continues, ''His story will be told here. His name was Jean-Baptiste Grenouille, and if his name . . . has been forgotten today, it is . . . because his gifts and his sole ambition were restricted to a domain that leaves no traces in history: to the fleeting realm of scent.''   Combined, these various elements offset each other in such a teasingly incongruous way that one of the first attractions of Patrick Suskind's remarkable fable is simply to watch the pieces of the puzzle fit together.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Seven Rivers West
author: Edward Hoagland
pull_quote: SEVEN RIVERS WEST. By Edward Hoagland. 319 pages. Summit books. $18.95 If confirmation were needed of Edward Hoagland's distinction as a travel and nature writer, his new novel would provide it. ''Seven Rivers West'' is a virtuoso display of imagination grounded in affection and respect for the wild. The muscular prose penetrates the ways of the animals and plants, the rivers and mountains that confronted and confounded men moving west into the unknown toward the end of the 19th century. Unfortunately, the men are not as vividly realized as the forces of nature. They seem slight amid their awesome surroundings, and their desires seem transient and a little foolish compared to the basic responses they encounter. Perhaps that is what Mr. Hoagland wants to get across, but it works against his novel, his first in 20 years.
headline: Books: Into the Wilds

title: From The Realm Of Morpheus
author: Steven Millhauser
pull_quote: FROM THE REALM OF MORPHEUS. By Steven Millhauser. 370 pages. William Morrow. $17.95.    STEVEN MILLHAUSER'S third novel, ''From the Realm of Morpheus,'' begins precipitously one fine summer day when Carl Hausman, a disaffected young man who's been sleepily watching a baseball game, chases a foul ball into a woodland thicket and tumbles down a hole into a hidden world. Whether he's slipped into a reverie is never really clear; in any case, he soon finds himself going down a staircase to a stone chamber, where he finds a key sitting on a little table. The key opens a door, which leads - surprise, surprise - to the secret realm of Morpheus, the god of sleep and dreams.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Crossing The Line: A Year In The Land Of Apartheid
author: William Finnegan
pull_quote: CROSSING THE LINE: A Year in the Land of Apartheid. By William Finnegan. Illustrated with maps. 418 pages. Harper & Row. $22.95. EARLY in 1980, a young Californian named William Finnegan made his way from Sri Lanka to Cape Town, partly to escape the tropical rigors of traveling in South Asia and partly to pursue the surf and pizza parlors of a comparatively developed country. Intending to set out on a journey over the fabled ''Cape to Cairo'' route through East Africa, Mr. Finnegan found himself low on money and managed to finagle himself a job teaching in a high school for ''colored'' students on the Cape Flats outside Cape Town.   The trip to Cairo never did come off, but by working ''in the land of apartheid'' for the year that followed, Mr. Finnegan - if one may judge from the book, ''Crossing the Line,'' that came out of his experiences -managed to travel at least as far in a different direction.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: When The War Was Over
author: Elizabeth Becker
pull_quote: WHEN THE WAR WAS OVER: The Voices of Cambodia's Revolution and Its People. By Elizabeth Becker. Illustrated. 502 pages. Simon & Schuster. $19.95.   FOR all the attention that was focused on it during the 1970's, Cambodia is still a country about which little is known in the world at large. There are no standard modern histories, Elizabeth Becker tells us, either of the country itself or of the Khmer Rouge; old misconceptions linger on, and for most of us the course of the Cambodian revolution remains easier to deplore than to understand.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Group Sex
author: Ann Arensberg
pull_quote: GROUP SEX. By Ann Arensberg. 175 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.    In her last book, the highly acclaimed first novel ''Sister Wolf,'' Ann Arensberg created a disturbing fairy tale of sexual infatuation and jealousy - a peculiar tale about a woman who loved animals and the dangerous consequences of her passion for a certain man. While its tone vacillated between the gothic and the comic, the stylized and the naturalistic, the novel possessed an almost incantory power - the reader was drawn into Marit's story by its very strangeness and by the richness and wit of Ms. Arensberg's prose.
headline: Laughable Literati

title: Thunder In America
author: Bob Faw and Nancy Skelton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THUNDER IN AMERICA. By Bob Faw and Nancy Skelton. (Texas Monthly, $16.95.) For a political reporter nowadays, there probably is no public figure more difficult to write about objectively than Jesse Jackson. Bob Faw, a CBS news correspondent, and Nancy Skelton, who covered Mr. Jackson's 1984 Presidential campaign for The Los Angeles Times, haven't done it perfectly. But their book sheds more light on Mr. Jackson and his remarkable adventure in American politics than several other recent works, which seemed aimed at proving the entire affair was all sound and fury, signifying nothing. In conventional political terms, Mr. Jackson's impact probably was minimal; at best, it was ambiguous. As one N.A.A.C.P. official observed, revulsion for Ronald Reagan probably did more to boost black voter registration than Jesse Jackson did. What's more, black gains were more than offset by increases in white registration, the result of a backlash inspired by fear and hatred of Mr. Jackson. But the Jackson campaign never was conventional, not in style or purpose or measures of success. And the differences are traceable ultimately to the peculiar character of the candidate. The strength of this book is that Mr. Faw and Ms. Skelton appreciated this central fact. They seek not to debunk but to come to terms with Jesse Jackson and so are able to penetrate his character in a way others have not. Race and racism - his own and others' - are only one part of the puzzle.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

Maud Malone Devlin, the heroine, is nine months pregnant at the beginning of the story - is, in other words, nine months ''gone.'' When Maud suddenly finds her husband, Jack, irrefutably guilty of having lapsed into a one-night stand with Xenia Olssen, their Swedish dish of a ''painless birth'' instructor - a day or so before Maud goes into emphatically painful labor - Maud derails, takes off on a several-months-long nervous breakdown, and is thus doubly ''gone.'' Finally, there is the invocation to another, vastly different Irish-Catholic heroine, Maud Gonne, romantic patriot and muse to Yeats, through whose shining spirit the author implicitly - though without pretensions - hopes to obtain some measure of affiliation with an illustrious literary confederation. If not directly with Yeats, Synge and Joyce, Ms. Lawrence clearly wishes to be in league with their American nieces - writers such as Mary McCarthy, and especially Mary Gordon, who have turned the stuff of Catholic girlhoods into a home-grown, full-blown genre.

SAY the name James Ewell Brown Stuart to anyone and most likely you will get a blink of incomprehension; say ''Jeb Stuart'' and the chances are pretty good your listener will remember the man as he has been remembered for a century and a quarter now: the gallant young cavalier cantering through the summer weather with his matchless Confederate horsemen, heading north on a daring raid. He is, in the popular imagination, more than just a cavalry leader; he is all the boldness of the Old South, casting his heedless glamour on that ghastly combination of 18th-century field surgery and 20th-century firepower that was our Civil War. Emory Thomas has chosen to call his excellent study ''Bold Dragoon'' because that is just what Stuart said he wanted to be back when he was a cadet at West Point. And it is a particularly appropriate title, because Stuart set about creating the image he bears to this day with all the deliberation of a sculptor chipping away at a block of marble.

THERE is more than one miracle in ''The Miracle of Intervale Avenue.'' Moishe Sacks - the feisty, indomitable rabbi of the last surviving Jewish congregation in the South Bronx - does not find it astonishing that the Intervale Jewish Center continues to exist: what is truly miraculous, he says, is that a minyan (a religious quorum) is maintained. The members of the congregation are elderly; they die, or are removed by their children - but new congregants continually turn up to take their places. Some are survivors from other, defunct, Bronx congregations; some are street people who claim to be Jewish and are accepted as such. Mr. Sacks welcomes anyone who finds his or her way through the rubble-strewn streets and into the repeatedly vandalized but still-living synagogue. He needs a minimum of 10 men to hold a proper service, and he will accept anyone God sends - including a policeman with a gun strapped to his side, or the visiting anthropologist, Jack Kugelmass. In a pinch, he will throw open the sacred ark and announce that God Himself is the 10th member of the minyan.

title: Seven Rivers West
author: Edward Hoagland
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SEVEN RIVERS WEST By Edward Hoagland. 319 pp. New York: Summit Books. $18.95.    THE heroes of many novels are dreamers. Hardy's tragic stonemason, Jude Fawley, is in love with his tantalizing cousin; that he can't have her merely serves to fuel his obsession. The gulf between the stonemason's dreams and his reality provides ''Jude the Obscure'' with an atmosphere of acute melancholy - for aren't we always moved when we encounter society's indifference to human longing? Nature can be indifferent, too. The doomed turtle fishermen in Peter Matthiessen's ''Far Tortuga'' are stalked by the sea they sail on - death pursues them more masterfully than they hunt down their green sea turtles; ''the narrative itself,'' Robert Stone wrote in these pages, ''is the recapitulation of a cosmic process.'' The novel has long been enriched by stories of dreamers and their obsessions, wishful-thinking heroes whose illusions and delusions seem real and huge - to themselves - but whose private schemes are relatively tiny and absurd; these dreamers are ignored by society's larger plans, or overlooked by the vast arrangements of nature.

THE essays and reviews in Denis Donoghue's ''We Irish'' hardly deliver a coherent portrait of the Irish or an exhaustive survey of Irish writing. But behind them we can discern a more or less stable complex of values and convictions that tell us a good deal about a certain kind of Irish mind and temper. Whether he is discussing ancestral houses in Yeats or the dubious accomplishment of a Roman Catholic civil servant who made good in Northern Ireland, Mr. Donoghue is ever alert to questions of memory and identity: What does it mean for an Irishman to remember and invoke the past? What is the relation between dream and reality in Irish thought and writing? How is an Irishman to know what he is when the very notion of identity has been powerfully challenged by the contemporary writers one most admires? Such questions are addressed again and again in ''We Irish,'' and it is a tribute to the penetration of Mr. Donoghue's intelligence that they never seem stale or obvious.

pull_quote: PERFUME The Story of a Murderer. By Patrick Suskind. Translated by John E. Woods. 255 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.    PATRICK SUSKIND'S novel is a book of smells - the odors of history, in fact - and on the first page 18th-century Paris is anatomized into its component stinks. In its most fetid spot, beside a mephitic cemetery and beneath a fish stall, the hero of ''Perfume,'' Jean-Baptiste Grenouille, is born. But the point, the miraculous point, is that he has no smell at all. He is an orphan whose absence of body odor turns him, also, into an outcast - both damned and blessed, pariah and magician.   Grenouille himself is haunted by smells. He recognizes the odors of separate stones and of the varieties of water; he can locate even the most tremulous perfume from miles away; he can separate the simplest stench into its various elements - that of a human being, for example, being composed of cat feces, cheese and vinegar. As a child and young man, he survives as an outsider only through some stubborn instinct - deciding ''in favor of life out of sheer spite and sheer malice'' -but this means that in 18th-century France, in an age of ''reason'' and a time of ''progress,'' he is a barbaric intruder. For him, this is a world stripped bare of its more elegant trappings and organized around the one fundamental principle of smell.
headline: A KILLER, HAUNTED BY SMELLS

THE NEW AMERICAN GRANDPARENT A Place in the Family, A Life Apart. By Andrew J. Cherlin and Frank F. Furstenberg Jr. 278 pp. New York: Basic Books. $17.95. 

AT the turn of the century, surviving grandparents were in short supply. A child born in 1900 had one chance in four of having four grandparents alive, and a mere one chance in 50 of having all four survive until he reached the age of 15. Now, owing to striking increases in adult life expectancy, there are many more grandparents around. Accord-ing to Andrew J. Cherlin and Frank F. Furstenberg Jr., authors of ''The New American Grandparent,'' a statistical analysis carried out in 1976 indicated that the typical 15-year-old had better than one chance in two of having three grandparents alive, and one chance in six of having all four of them alive.

title: Fumble
author: James Kirby
pull_quote: FUMBLE: Bear Bryant, Wally Butts, and the Great College Football Scandal. By James Kirby. Illustrated. 248 pages. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $16.95. IT still seems a little crazy, at least to someone old enough to recall the incident, which occurred nearly a quarter of a century ago. As Prof. James Kirby reconstructs it in his lucid and absorbing ''Fumble: Bear Bryant, Wally Butts, and the Great College Football Scandal'': on the morning of Thursday, Sept. 13, 1962, an Atlanta businessman named George Burnett tried to telephone one of his partners. Through some electronic mix-up, he suddenly found himself eavesdropping on a conversation between Paul (Bear) Bryant and Wally Butts, respectively the University of Alabama football coach and the athletic director at the University of Georgia.   Though Mr. Burnett didn't know much about football, it sounded to him as if Mr. Butts were giving Mr. Bryant vital information about the Georgia team, which was to play Alabama nine days later. Troubled, he told his two business partners what he'd heard, and at first followed their advice to keep silent, even when Alabama trounced Georgia, 35 to 0. But the following January, he confided what he knew to a friend of the Georgia coach, who was at odds with Mr. Butts and felt he'd been set up by the athletic director.

title: Fdr: The New Deal Years 1933-1937
