pull_quote: FDR: THE NEW DEAL YEARS 1933-1937. By Kenneth S. Davis. 756 pages. Random House. $29.95. WITH the third volume of his biography of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, ''FDR: The New Deal Years 1933-1937,'' Kenneth S. Davis arrives at the White House and the period of Roosevelt's great domestic achievements. Taking office at a time of nationwide suffering, the Roosevelt Administration set about the task, energetically if somewhat disjointedly, of aiding farmers and protecting workers, bringing jobs to the young and security to the aged, and establishing controls over financial institutions. In fits and starts, the New Deal began to put together what a half-century later would be accepted even by conservatives as a necessary safety net for the down and out.

THE world delineated in Peter   Taylor's highly acclaimed stories - and in ''A Summons to Memphis,'' his first novel since the brief ''A Woman of Means'' in 1950 - belongs to a nearly vanished past. It's a very definite world, genteel and circumscribed, and set in the Upper South of Memphis or Nashville, where the gentry pass their time fox hunting and attending debutante parties. An accent is enough to establish someone's background here (''I knew at once from his voice,'' a character says, ''not only that he was from Memphis but that he was from somewhere between Cooper and Crosstown and in the Anandale section of town''), and clothes - a choice of shoes or a fedora - instantly betray one's class and social standing.

Events of marginal importance in Israel or on its borders are chronicled in nightly newscasts and daily newspaper reports, but paradoxically there have been few in-depth studies on the subject of the Jews and Palestinians, and David Shipler's new book is a rare exception.

author: Robert McCrum, William Cran and Robert MacNeil
pull_quote: THE STORY OF ENGLISH. By Robert McCrum, William Cran and Robert MacNeil. Illustrated. 384 pages. Elisabeth Sifton/Viking. $24.95.   WHERE might you hear someone speaking like this? ''A no wahn a ting tu du wid yu bika yu kom . . . lang taym an yu no kom luk fu Titi'' - meaning, ''I want nothing to do with you because you have not come for a long time to see Titi.'' Answer: in Nicaragua, among the Miskito Indians. And what exactly is this? ''Oure vaader fho yarth ing heaveene, ee-hallowet bee t'naame.'' The opening of the Lord's Prayer in Yola, a form of speech used by the descendants of Anglo-Norman settlers in County Wexford, in the southeast corner of Ireland, that survived until the middle of the 19th century. CAROL BILLMAN'S lively study sheds some welcome new light on the enormously successful fiction factory known as the Stratemeyer Syndicate, an organization that has given new meaning to the term ''publishing phenomenon'' over the eight decades it has flourished as a major source of children's series. Founded by the prolific writer Edward Stratemeyer in the early 1900's, when he turned to assistants to flesh out the synopses of stories he had no time to complete himself, the syndicate has produced over 1,300 titles, with total sales estimated at 200 million copies. Its output has been staggering by all statistical measures - 125 series issued by 38 publishers in the United States alone, translations into 14 languages, plus adaptations into films and television programs and a host of commercial spinoffs.
headline: THE ROVER BOYS PASSED THE TORCH

title: The Defense Game
author: Richard A. Stubbing with Richard A. Mendel.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

BY the end of President Reagan's first term, the United States had expanded its defense spending by 50 percent over the 1980 level - adding $330 billion in real growth for the Pentagon. The Reagan buildup is unparalleled in peacetime. Even in the post-Sputnik hysteria of the late 1950's, the defense budget grew by a mere 10 percent over a five-year period. What did we get for our money? In 1983, the conservative Heritage Foundation found the results ''sadly below expectations,'' and in 1985 the Congressional Budget Office concluded that with a few exceptions, such as personnel quality, most defense indicators ''have not increased markedly.''
headline: NOT WITH A BANG BUT A DOLLAR

pull_quote: ONE LAST WALTZ By Ethan Mordden. 196 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $13.95.    ETHAN MORDDEN's ''One Last Waltz'' is an unnerving mixture of quaint language and bitter deeds. In this family story, set in Ireland and New York City in this century, Mr. Mordden writes that ''the King of Tara had three sons: a warrior, a mason, and a poet. The warrior died in battle. The poet told lies. But the mason made the world.'' By using such language, Mr. Mordden hopes to enlarge to mythic stature the world of Dublin Johnny Keogh, an immigrant who fathers three sons: a violent criminal, a homosexual writer of hit songs and an ironworker who helps build the skyscrapers of New York.

When world historians assess the second half of the 20th century, they are likely to focus on two great issues - the management of the superpower rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, and the drive of the poorer countries for economic and social development. In a very real sense, the world's future depends on the progress made on these two issues over the remainder of this century; yet surprisingly little has been written that attempts to grapple with them in a fundamental way, perhaps because the issues are so big.

She is a down-and-out American trapped in Managua and through her Mr. Johnson creates a vision bleaker than the madness and murder of his first novel, ''Angels,'' more desperate than the postapocalyptic world of his second, ''Fiskadoro.'' What better setting for such pessimism than the political and moral morass of 1980's Nicaragua? Here, as the narrator says, is ''the hyper-new, all-leftist future coming at us at the rate of rock-n-roll,'' where she finds no usable past or hopeful future, just a torturous present of ramshackle McDonald's and starving children.

LIKE an earlier generation of eminent academics, Ralph McInerny has a talent for the ingenuity of the detective story. As might be expected from a professor of medieval studies and director of the Jacques Maritain Center at Notre Dame University, Mr. McInerny's popular series features a sleuth who is also a Roman Catholic priest, the hard-headed, kind-hearted, irresistible reformed drunk, Father Dowling. Nearly all the inhabitants of Dowling's fictional Middle Western city - victims, villains, cops and mobsters - are as Catholic as Cork and Naples, and in these books commitments to faith tangle constantly with commitments to crime, or to preventing it. The characters in most of Mr. McInerny's 10 other novels, including ''Leave of Absence,'' are also predominantly Middle Western Catholics; their crimes, however, are felonies of the heart, and the mysteries in their lives are mysteries of belief and desire and pain, to which there are no tidy solutions.

Illustrated. 1,152 pp. Hanover, N.H.: The Norman Rockwell Museum at Stockbridge/ The University Press of New England. $170; $195 after Jan. 1, 1987.    WITH as much right as Poussin, Norman Rockwell might have expressed a retrospective complacency regarding his achievement as an artist by saying ''Je n'ai rien neglige'' - ''I have neglected nothing.'' The preparation for one of his Saturday Evening Post covers -''Fixing a Flat,'' say, of Aug. 3, 1943 - entailed as much preparation in the selection of models, costumes, authentic site and precise props as anything Poussin was required to assemble for the ''Rape of the Sabines'' (in any case, not altogether suitable as a cover idea for the Post). Rockwell painted with the luminous clarity and obsessive, detailed exactitude of a Flemish master; his April Fools' Day cover (April 2, 1943) is crammed with as many joking allusions as one of Bruegel's puzzle pictures. And he was full of the self-referential wit that is the cachet of postmodernist sensibility; his ''Triple Self-Portrait'' of Feb. 13, 1960, is a complex of mirrored conundrums unmatched since ''Las Meninas'' of Velazquez, and it drops as many art-historical references as a Whitney Museum biennial.

DURING the late 1940's and 1950's, several hundred college professors were questioned by Congressional committees about their political beliefs and associations. Most of them were former Communists or left-wing radicals, and many refused to cooperate. Although few of these recalcitrant professors were cited for contempt, the vast majority of them were punished by their employers. Some were censured or placed on probation; others were fired, then blacklisted for years. ''No Ivory Tower'' by Ellen Schrecker is both a history of the purges and a sounding board for the victims, many of whom Ms. Schrecker has diligently tracked down. Their vivid recollections are the best part of an otherwise familiar story.

IN a sendup of magazineland, one expects a little flash and dash - a long, gossipy lunch at a power restaurant, say, overwrought editors screaming at temperamental writers (or vice versa), an atmosphere of continual crisis. Possibly even a ride in a balloon. Peter Warner, whose personal experiences are in book publishing, has stayed at ground level in his funny but sometimes forced novel about the takeover of a magazine. There are world-class puns: ''putsch came to shove,'' ''a cuisine that is served without fear or flavor.'' There are inspired lines: ''no American President's valediction has urged the citizenry to beware of the media/communications complex.'' The author satirizes everything in sight, from the hoteliere Leona Helmsley's royal hospitality (this palace is called Malmaison) to a flaky minister who thinks he can cure mental disease through faith healing. But the book is funny in the way that a stand-up comic is funny. The characters are cardboard, the plot is creaky, and choosing an ordinary, well-behaved man for a hero is really making things difficult for yourself. The trouble is, life is more preposterous than ''Lifestyle.''

DESPITE mythology, the state of Maine was not settled by folk singers, New York writers or even Leon Leonwood Bean. The simple truth is splendidly related in this small and charming novel by the longtime Maine chronicler John Gould. A chap named David Ingram was among several men put involuntarily ashore in Mexico in 1568 by the privateer Capt. John Hawkins, who had too few supplies to get all of his men back to England. David's sole desire was to get back home, so he started walking north, through woods, across rivers, angling toward a place he'd heard the Indians speak about - the golden city of Bashaba, the lost Atlantis, in fabled Norumbega, home of the Pentagoet River. This beautiful, untamed spot was soon to be known as the Maine and scrimmaged over for the better part of two centuries by the French and British.

ROBERT SHAPLEN came to Indochina sooner than most of us, and he has stayed with it longer than most of us, too. He first visited Saigon in 1946 for Newsweek magazine; he was among the last Americans to leave the city in 1975, with the Communists at its gates; and he was permitted by the authorities in Hanoi to spend five weeks traveling in Vietnam and a week traveling in Cambodia in the autumn of 1984. ''Bitter Victory'' is an account of what he saw and heard on that journey, reporting for The New Yorker, as well as an analysis of the complex political and economic situation in Southeast Asia. It is enriched by the kind of perspective that few writers and even fewer policy makers can bring to the subject.
headline: WHAT HAVE THEY DONE WITH THEIR PEACE?

title: Group Sex
author: Ann Arensberg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: GROUP SEX By Ann Arensberg. 175 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.    FRANCES is a 27-year-old blond person, an editor at a small publishing company, and also a familiar type of American woman - a real loser/victim. In other words, Frances, a member of an oppressed minority that is actually the majority, is, or is trying to be, a nice person. This means that in college she was the sort who spent her evening hours giving foot massages to the more popular girls, and now that she is an adult she takes abuse from her various authors (all of them - it doesn't matter whether they write mysteries or Gothic trash or poetry about trees) and her co-workers. Taking abuse is what her days consist of. At night she goes home to her apartment, the top floor of a brownstone owned by her friend Madeline.
headline: FRANCES THE DOORMAT

title: The Nazi Doctors
author: Robert Jay Lifton.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE NAZI DOCTORS Medical Killing and the Psychology of Genocide. By Robert Jay Lifton. 561 pp. New York: Basic Books. $19.95. 

THE horrifying story of the Nazi extermination policy, under which millions of innocent men, women and children were systematically murdered, should be well known by now. In addition to the official documentation on it, many books have been published and movies and television programs have made it known to people everywhere. Reading ''The Nazi Doctors,'' Robert Jay Lifton's account of the crimes committed by physicians in the German concentration camps, painfully revived my memories of the time I had spent in two of them - memories of which I am unable to free myself, as no survivor of them ever can.
headline: THEIR SPECIALTY WAS MURDER

title: Ernie's War
author: David Nichols
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ERNIE'S WAR The Best of Ernie Pyle's World War II Dispatches. Edited with a biographical essay by David Nichols. Foreword by Studs Terkel. Illustrated. 432 pp. New York: Random House. $19.95.    THE book endured until the last time we moved, about three years ago, and then it just disintegrated. The binding broke, the cheap paper used during World War II came apart in great, yellow flakes, and, reluctantly, I gave up my paperback copy of Ernie Pyle's ''Brave Men.''
headline: OUR BOYS

title: Letters From Prison
author: Adam Michnik
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LETTERS FROM PRISON And Other Essays. By Adam Michnik. Translated by Maya Latynski. Foreword by Czeslaw Milosz. Introduction by Jonathan Schell. 354 pp. Berkeley: University of California Press. $25.    IN his recent Jefferson Lecture, the Polish philosopher Leszek Kolakowski said, ''We learn history not to know how to behave or how to succeed, but to know who we are.'' This viewpoint lies close to the heart of the present generation of intellectuals in Poland, where national self-discovery was one of the foremost goals of the Solidarity movement, and uncensored history one of its great passions. In 1966, when Mr. Kolakowski headed toward a life of exile by publicly criticizing the Communist regime, a young history student took his first step toward a life of persecution by joining in the discussion. Twenty years later, the master, Mr. Kolakowski, regularly jets between Oxford and Chicago. The disciple, Adam Michnik, who calls Mr. Kolakowski one of the ''creators of contemporary Polish culture,'' was recently released from his sixth major period of incarceration as a political prisoner. (Not long afterward, in a surprising and sweeping amnesty, the regime freed all 225 political prisoners.) Mr. Michnik stayed in Poland by choice. He had every inducement from the authorities to emigrate. But he chose to stay, ''out of the fear that by saving my neck I may lose my honor.''
headline: TRUE TO HIMSELF AND HIS HOMELAND

title: Females Of The Species
author: Bettyann Kevles. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FEMALES OF THE SPECIES Sex and Survival in the Animal Kingdom. By Bettyann Kevles. Illustrated. 270 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $20.    FOR much of the past century, scientists largely ignored the female role in evolution. For them, males were the true stars in the drama of natural selection. But as Bettyann Kevles correctly points out in ''Females of the Species,'' less biased modern investigators have discovered a very different reality. Although ''there is still some resistance to recognizing the powerful role of the female in the evolutionary process,'' she writes, most reputable observers increasingly acknowledge that a very active cooperation between the two sexes is essential to a species' success.
headline: Be Glad Your Mother Is Not an Emu

title: Drunk With Love
author: Ellen Gilchrist
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DRUNK WITH LOVE By Ellen Gilchrist. 239 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $15.95.    ONE'S first impression on reading Ellen Gilchrist's stories is of a world alive with numerous distinctive characters: Traceleen the maid and her employer, the eminently Southern Miss Crystal; Rhoda Manning, whom we meet as eccentric child, rebellious teen-ager and disappointed adult; Annalisa Livingston, The New York Times's religion critic, commenting weekly on the esthetics and morality of local churches; Nora Jane, the pregnant flower child, and her two boyfriends, Sandy and Freddy. Even Nora Jane's unborn twins have names and personalities: They become Tammili and Lydia the moment amniocentesis is performed.
headline: HOME MOVIES

title: Cold Spring Harbor
author: Richard Yates
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: COLD SPRING HARBOR By Richard Yates. 182 pp. New York: Delacorte Press/Seymour Lawrence. $16.95.    RICHARD YATES'S ninth book, ''Cold Spring Harbor,'' takes place mainly during a moment in American life that has come to be gilded with a certain nostalgia - the period surrounding this country's entry into World War II. But this novel is anything but nostalgic about the summer of 1942; its portrait of that period is ironic to the point of hostility.
headline: THE POWER OF WEAKNESS

title: The Advancement Of Science, And Its Burdens
author: Gerald Holton. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE ADVANCEMENT OF SCIENCE, AND ITS BURDENS The Jefferson Lecture and Other Essays. By Gerald Holton. Illustrated. 368 pp. New York: Cambridge University Press. Cloth, $39.50. Paper, $12.95.    IN the drugstore that serves as the center of the campus town at my university, there is a display of posters for sale. The members of the pantheon are sometimes predictable - Clark Gable as Rhett Butler, roguishly looking over the top of his hand of cards; Humphrey Bogart, dressed to kill in a dark suit set off by a Smith & Wesson. And between Marilyn Monroe and James Dean is Albert Einstein. Lesser stars have come and gone, but the physicist's friendly face has been a constant.
headline: The Most Beautiful Theories Are The Truest

title: Rca And The Videodisc: The Business Of Research
author: Margaret B W Graham
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RCA AND THE VIDEODISC: The Business of Research. By Margaret B. W. Graham. (Cambridge University, $19.95.) In high-technology companies there is often little correlation between a good idea and a good product.
headline: IN SHORT: SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY

title: A Loss For Words
author: Lou Ann Walker. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A LOSS FOR WORDS The Story of Deafness in a Family. By Lou Ann Walker. Illustrated. 208 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $15.95.    ''MY parents are deaf. I can hear.'' A book with that line has cried out to be written: how two deaf people get along in a world held together by speech and hearing, and how sharing their ghetto, helping them cope with it, has stressed their hearing, speaking daughter's life.
headline: THE GHETTO OF UNHEARING

title: Was Einstein Right?
author: Clifford M. Will. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WAS EINSTEIN RIGHT? Putting General Relativity to the Test. By Clifford M. Will. Illustrated. 274 pp. New York: Basic Books. $18.95.    MANY who fall under the spell of Albert Einstein's vision often feel a little like Alice in Wonderland: The universe begins to look ''curiouser and curiouser.'' Matter turns out to be frozen energy (E - mc#2); objects shrink as they accelerate toward the velocity of light, the speed limit of the universe; and gravity is no longer a mysterious force, but rather a curvature in the four dimensions of space and time. Space, Einstein told us in 1915 with his general theory of relativity, is like a boundless rubber sheet, and large masses indent this flexible mat, causing any passing rocket, planet or light beam to follow the natural depression.
headline: Cosmic Cornerstone

title: Machinery Of The Mind
author: George Johnson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MACHINERY OF THE MIND: Inside the New Science of Artificial Intelligence. By George Johnson. (Times Books, $19.95.) If a computer can be made to execute any precisely described process, and if human thought is a process that can be precisely described, a computer can be made to think.
headline: IN SHORT: SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY

title: Poison Pen
author: George Garrett. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: POISON PEN Or, Live Now and Pay Later. By George Garrett. Illustrated. 258 pp. Berkeley, Calif.: Stuart Wright/Small Press Distribution. $20.    GEORGE GARRETT is an insightful, technically adroit writer, but the quality of his novels has varied, partly because of his eclecticism.
headline: FROM THE DESK OF A DIRTY OLD MAN

title: Eustace And Hilda
author: L. P. Hartley. With an introduction by Lord David Cecil.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EUSTACE AND HILDA A Trilogy. By L. P. Hartley. With an introduction by Lord David Cecil. 736 pp. New York: Stein & Day. $24.95.    WHEN the British novelist L. P. Hartley died in 1972, Joseph Losey's film version of ''The Go-Between'' had just won the grand prize at the Cannes Film Festival, seeming to promise more than the professional respect Hartley had received during his long career. Perhaps this first American edition of ''Eustace and Hilda'' will accomplish what Losey's film did not. On the surface, ''Eustace and Hilda'' appeals to the same nostalgia that helped revive ''Brideshead Revisited.'' Like Waugh's novel, this trilogy rotates hugely around a grand country house, moving to Oxford and Venice before coming home again to rest. In this case, though, the circular movement is more clearly pathological and the return is not bittersweet but cold and deadly.
headline: WORSHIPING SIS

title: The Body Quantum
author: Fred Alan Wolf
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BODY QUANTUM: The New Physics of Body, Mind and Health. By Fred Alan Wolf. (Macmillan, $19.95.) The theme of this interesting but sometimes exasperating book is that the rules and ambiguities of quantum physics are crucial to understanding health and disease, the control the mind exerts over the body, the nature of life and its evolution.
headline: IN SHORT: SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY

title: The Prose Works Of Alexander Pope
author: Rosemary Cowler
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PROSE WORKS OF ALEXANDER POPE Volume II: The Major Works, 1725-1744. Edited by Rosemary Cowler. 529 pp. Hamden, Conn.: Archon Books. $49.50.    EXACTLY 50 years ago the first volume of this edition of Alexander Pope's prose works was published, most of it containing the essays he contributed to The Spectator and The Guardian. They show how neatly he could adapt his wit and good nature to the periodical essay, the form perfected by Addison and Steele. In this second volume we have the fallout from his personal and literary controversies. For busy as he was with writing, publishing and revising his poetry, he found time for multifarious activities whose byproducts he expressed in prose. Unlike the prose writings of such poets as Dryden and Johnson, however, his prose works represent a distinctly minor phase of his genius.
headline: BREAKING BUTTERFLIES

title: The Nature Of Reality
author: Richard Morris
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE NATURE OF REALITY. By Richard Morris. (McGraw-Hill, $16.95.) Modern people are supposed to laugh at Ptolemy and the epicycles he postulated to prop up the idea that the sun revolves around the earth.
headline: IN SHORT: SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY

title: Taking The World In For Repairs
author: Richard Selzer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TAKING THE WORLD IN FOR REPAIRS By Richard Selzer. 239 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $15.95.    IN Vienna early in this century, the Expressionist poet and surgeon Dr. Gottfried Benn, who most often worked on prostitutes in a morgue, once found a drowned truck driver awaiting his knife. Some joker had stuck a lavender aster in the man's rigid mouth. As Benn conducted his autopsy, the aster tumbled free, and Benn sewed it inside the man's chest along with the excelsior. Later, he wrote a poem about the event, which ends: ''Drink yourself full in your vase! / Rest softly, / little aster!'' I can picture Richard Selzer right at home in that landscape of clinical horror and poetic surge. A New Haven surgeon who moonlights as a writing teacher at Yale University, he knows better than anyone the rigors of mortis. As he reminds us, ''There is only the eternal eloquence of the wound.'' But few are so eloquent about it.
headline: Palpatating For Meaning

title: Women's Ways Of Knowing
author: Mary Field Belenky
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WOMEN'S WAYS OF KNOWING The Development of Self, Voice, and Mind. By Mary Field Belenky, Blythe McVicker Clinchy, Nancy Rule Goldberger and Jill Mattuck Tarule. 256 pp. New York: Basic Books. $19.95.    BEFORE 1982, psychologists routinely studied groups of men and generalized their results to women. When women were tested by male-based criteria, they were often accused of behaving like developmentally warped or retarded men, It was no wonder, given the standards the psychologists were using. The situation changed when Carol Gilligan's ''In a Different Voice'' exploded on the psychological world with its clear argument explaining how women make moral judgments differently from men. Ms. Gilligan's studies revealed that women make moral decisions within a web of concerns over relationship and responsibility, while men are inclined to lean on such pillars as impartiality and ''blind justice'' in their judgments.
headline: THEY HEAR DIFFERENT VOICES

title: The Wisdom Of Science
author: Hanbury Brown
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WISDOM OF SCIENCE: Its Relevance to Culture and Religion. By Hanbury Brown. (Cambridge University, Cloth, $32.50. Paper, $13.95.) Hanbury Brown, an Australian physicist, looks on the world with a heavy heart.
headline: IN SHORT: SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY

title: The Oxford History Of The Classical World
author: John Boardman, Jasper Griffin and Oswyn Murray
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE OXFORD HISTORY OF THE CLASSICAL WORLD Edited by John Boardman, Jasper Griffin and Oswyn Murray. Illustrated. 882 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $39.95.    CICERO paraphrases a late Greek philosopher as saying that people who do not know the past must remain always children. In our case, orphans. For the Greeks and Romans were the parents of all of us in the West, but try as we may, we can find out all too little about them. Thucydides' account of Pericles will not stand cross-examination; the reliable facts about Alexander the Great that survive can be jotted down on a page; even the autobiographies of Augustus Caesar and Hadrian have been lost. Hadrian did leave something like his real voice, possibly the most authentic one remaining from the ancient world. In a North African inscription recording his remarks to a legion, the forceful adverbs and verbs ring out as he commends the soldiers for their agility in throwing spears while clad in armor or the cavalry for its speed in finishing vast ramparts and then surging into battle. This is a great soldier talking soldiers' talk, and hearing it brings on suspicion about the formal language of all the surviving writings and makes one's heart ache over the silence surrounding it.
headline: HOMER, CATULLUS AND THE OX IN THE STAIRWELL

title: Apprentice To Genius
author: Robert Kanigel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: APPRENTICE TO GENIUS: The Making of a Scientific Dynasty. By Robert Kanigel. (Macmillan, $19.95.) Robert Kanigel's narrow subject is ''mentoring networks . . . in the highest ranks of science''; his broad one, how ''important'' science is done.
headline: IN SHORT: SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY

title: The Calculating Passion Of Ada Byron
author: Joan Baum
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CALCULATING PASSION OF ADA BYRON By Joan Baum. Illustrated. 133 pp. Hamden, Conn. Archon Books/The Shoe String Press. $21.50.    IN their zeal, new movements can choose the wrong heroes as easily as the wrong victims. For some years now Ada Byron, the daughter of the outrageous Romantic poet, has been seen as an object lesson in ''herstory,'' a mathematical innovator whom history ignored for more than a century because of the misfortune of her sex.   More recently has come the backlash. Does Ada Byron, the Countess of Lovelace, really deserve her posthumous title: the world's first computer programmer? Or should she instead be viewed as a 19th-century hypochondriac, an aristocratic amateur, muddled, conceited, hopeless at calculus and not foolproof in math?
headline: Byronic, Despite Everything

title: The Peak Of Success And Other Stories
author: Yury Nagibin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE PEAK OF SUCCESS AND OTHER STORIES By Yury Nagibin. Edited by Helena Goscilo. 409 pp. Ann Arbor, Mich.: Ardis Publishers. $29.50. 

AMONG the noteworthy Russian writers of today, Yury Nagibin is an anomaly in almost every respect. Neither a dissident nor an official writer, he is basically apolitical, nonmetaphysical and relatively uninterested in the great issues of either the Russian past or the Soviet present. He is detached in manner, wide-ranging in subject matter and (rarest of all) brief in treatment. Though he has been popular in the Soviet Union for nearly three decades, he is generally neglected by his fellow writers and undervalued by critics. His name was totally absent from the discussions of writers at the most recent Congress of Soviet Writers (as transcribed at length in the official literary publication, Literaturnaya Gazeta). Nor is he discussed in important Western surveys such as N. N. Schneidman's ''Soviet Literature in the 1970's.''
headline: CHEKHOVIAN LIVES IN SWAMP AND LAB

title: Raven's Wing
author: Joyce Carol Oates
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RAVEN'S WINGS By Joyce Carol Oates. 305 pp. New York: A William Abrahams Book/E. P. Dutton. $17.95.    SOMETIMES fictional characters reveal with startling directness one of the secrets of the artist who made them. In Joyce Carol Oates's latest collection, ''Raven's Wing,'' such significations occur often. The story ''Harrow Street at Linden'' begins ominously with a college student named Katherine Stickney - aware that she has been married exactly 108 days - surprising her husband with his ear to the wall as he listens to the couple in the next apartment. She is perplexed, concerned, intrigued - what, exactly, is happening? Later, near the end of the story, she takes notes during a lecture: ''It is the improvised nature of human life that accounts for the prevalence of unhappiness.''   This ''improvised nature'' accounts for anxiety too, along with suspense and the hunger for self-knowledge - materials of which stories are made. Katherine's unhappiness is characteristic of most of the troubled and limited people in this collection. Her insecurity is the obverse of her fascination with the possibilities of life, a fascination shared and reflected by her husband. They become obsessed with the sounds made by the couple next door and from these fragments of evidence try to re-create some sense of what their neighbors must be. Why do they need to know? Why should they care? Because we are always mirrored by others - a truth that is celebrated throughout the stories in ''Raven's Wing.''
headline: 108 DAYS OF MARRIAGE, AND COUNTING

title: Sewall Wright And Evolutionary Biology
author: William B. Provine. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SEWALL WRIGHT AND EVOLUTIONARY BIOLOGY By William B. Provine. Illustrated. 545 pp. Illinois: The University of Chicago Press. $30.    MODERN evolutionary thought is constructed around a deeply quantitative body of theory and observation known as population genetics. The scientific agenda for the field was largely determined from 1915 through 1960 by R. A. Fisher and J. B. S. Haldane in Great Britain and Sewall Wright in the United States. This was the period of the evolutionary synthesis, when scientific details were sought to flesh out Darwin's theory of evolution and speciation by natural selection. During that time, particularly after 1931, Sewall Wright established himself as the most important American evolutionary theorist of the 20th century.
headline: How Chance Leads of Change

title: The Stones Cry Out
author: Molyda Szymusiak. Translated by Linda Coverdale. Maps.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE STONES CRY OUT A Cambodian Childhood, 1975-1980. By Molyda Szymusiak. Translated by Linda Coverdale. Maps. 245 pp. New York: Hill & Wang. $17.95. 

THIS book is the true and horrifying story of a Cambodian girl who survived the barbaric regime of Pol Pot and his Khmer Rouge fanatics, which, backed by the Chinese, lasted from 1975 through 1978. ''The Stones Cry Out'' (in an uneven translation from the French) is told through the experiences of Comrade Peuw - the Communist name assumed by the author, which kept her from being labeled an aristocrat - and begins on April 17, 1975, when Pol Pot's troops storm the capital. The author, who writes under her adoptive name, Molyda Szymusiak, was 12 at the time, the daughter of a high official.
headline: SURVIVING POL POT

title: The Control Revolution
author: James R. Beniger.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE CONTROL REVOLUTION Technological and Economic Origins of the Information Society. By James R. Beniger. 493 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $25. 

AS systems involving people and machines increase in size, complexity and speed of operation, they confront recurring problems of coherence and control. The chemical catastrophe at Bhopal, India, the explosion of the Challenger space shuttle and the Russian nuclear accident at Chernobyl are cases in which well-planned systems suddenly went haywire and there was no ready handle to set them right. Studies done in the aftermath of such events typically locate the malady in some mechanical flaw, human error or both. But these findings offer little solace. There is no guarantee that any repairs will eliminate lethal glitches buried in similar mechanisms.
headline:
SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY;
Keeping Track of All We Know

title: Mayflower Madam
author: Sydney Barrows with William Novak.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
MAYFLOWER MADAM The Secret Life of Sydney Biddle Barrows. By Sydney Barrows with William Novak. 291 pp. New York: Arbor House. $17.95. 

AN ''escort service'' is not a house and therefore not a home, but with enough rarefied WASP touches it can be a boarding school. A descendant of Elder William Brewster, a leader of the Mayflower flock, Sydney Biddle Barrows - who ran the Cachet escort service in Manhattan until her arrest in 1984 for promoting prostitution - shares her illustrious ancestor's concern about what to pack when venturing forth to new and unknown worlds. The 17th-century settlers needed to remember to take along a keg of gunpowder and a Bible, which produced that WASP idiosyncrasy, the Old Kit Bag complex. Race memory tells us never to go anywhere without emergency supplies, which is why every well-raised WASP girl is always laden with those packets of needles, pins and thread that our housemothers call ''tailor's friends.''
headline: CALL ME ENTREPRENEUR

title: Descartes' Dream
author: Philip J. Davis and Reuben Hersh. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DESCARTES' DREAM The World According to Mathematics. By Philip J. Davis and Reuben Hersh. Illustrated. 321 pp. Boston: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $19.95.    ON Nov. 10, 1619, Rene Descartes, following a prolonged period of intense concentration, had a vision of the unification of all science through the power of reason. That night his sleep was interrupted by three successive dreams of nightmarish quality. Believing them to be of divine origin, Descartes, who was then 23 years old, vowed to pursue his vision, and he worked for 18 years to produce his celebrated treatise, ''Discourse on Method,'' which laid out the foundations of a rational philosophy of science and life. Mathematics lay at the heart of Descartes's method, for he imagined that in time all knowledge could be harnessed to the rigors of deductive analysis.
headline: Shall We Take Arms Against a Sea of Digits?

title: The Lost Language Of Cranes
author: David Leavitt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LOST LANGUAGE OF CRANES By David Leavitt. 319 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.    AT 25, David Leavitt is one of the stars of the literary youth movement. His story collection, ''Family Dancing,'' was praised for its tenderness and craft. Now he has taken the leap into novel writing, and, to his credit, ''The Lost Language of Cranes'' reads like a real novel: Mr. Leavitt's sense of pacing, his graceful sentences and his storytelling ability dovetail nicely. On the other hand, the book feels young - experientially thin, intellectually timid, contrived, erratic and, understandably, not yet wise.   In this after-college novel, Philip, its 25-year-old hero, holds a lowly editing position in a Manhattan ''bodice-ripper'' publishing house. He has no particular interest in his work; his energies are engaged in looking for love. Mr. Leavitt has elected to lyricize his hero's lovelorn impatience on its own reverent terms, rather than take the safer, ironic course. When, in a flashback to college, Philip's first partner says, ''It must have been a long time since you had sex,'' and he replies woefully, ''My whole life,'' it seems a rather melodramatic pronouncement for an 18-year-old.
headline: SEXUAL POLITICS, FAMILY SECRETS

title: Under The Cloud
author: Richard L. Miller. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
UNDER THE CLOUD The Decades of Nuclear Testing. By Richard L. Miller. Illustrated. 547 pp. New York: The Free Press. $24.95. 

IN his precedent-setting opinion in the case of Irene Allen v. United States, Judge Bruce Jenkins, finding in favor of the plantiffs, held that ''in its conduct of open-air atomic testing, and its off-site radiation programs - including its public information activities - the government was bound by a legal duty to act with the highest degree of care in light of the best available scientific knowledge.'' The suit was filed in 1979 in the Federal District Court in Utah by 24 people, the first of almost 1,200 ''downwinders'' to seek remedial action for injury resulting from negligence in this country's conduct of nuclear weapons tests that released radiation into the atmosphere. That the question of a government's obligation to act responsibly in conducting nuclear tests concerns not only the past was evident at a recent meeting of the International Atomic Energy Agency called to write a convention on early notification of nuclear accidents. Both the United States and the Soviet Union wanted to exclude from reporting requirements radioactive pollution from nuclear tests or accidents involving a nuclear weapon.
headline:
SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY;
Are We All Downwinders?

title: Life Above The Jungle Floor
author: Donald Perry
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LIFE ABOVE THE JUNGLE FLOOR By Donald Perry. Illustrated. 170 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $16.95.    TREE CLIMBING is primarily a childhood activity, and with good reason. When we become adults, our bodies are heavier than our bones are strong, and we are more likely to be injured in a fall than we once were. Sooner or later, every human being who climbs trees does fall out of one, principally because the human body is no longer designed for an arboreal existence. Our hands are still designed for grasping but not our feet. Our big toes are a shadow of the thumbs they once were. Our soles have been thickened and flattened by the pressures of walking upright. In short, evolution has clipped our wings as certainly as it has the ostrich's.
headline: Visiting the Great Potoo

title: Supply Of Heroes
author: James Carroll
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SUPPLY OF HEROES By James Carroll. 403 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $17.95.    IN 1915, when the masterful face and pointing finger of Lord Kitchener on the posters was not bringing in enough recruits, when the defense of small nations did not entirely seem a strong enough reason to disappear forever into Europe's trenches, the British Government prepared to introduce the Compulsory Military Service Act. Conscription was begun for the first time in the country's history - if you don't count serfdom and press gangs. The oratory was splendid, the arguments eloquently put by those who would never have to face the mud, the uncertainty, the chlorine gas and the high-pitched commands of frightened officers.
headline: A STATELY HOME IN REVOLUTIONARY IRELAND

title: The Harvest Of Sorrow
author: Robert Conquest
pull_quote: THE HARVEST OF SORROW. Soviet Collectivization and the Terror-Famine.   By Robert Conquest. 412 pages. Illustrated. Oxford. $19.95. BETWEEN 1929 and 1933 the   Soviet Government introduced measures that were responsible for the deaths of a huge number of peasants. In the view of Robert Conquest, who has arrived at the figure after a careful examination of telltale Soviet census returns and other data, the final death toll probably amounted to 14.5 million. Admittedly this includes some 3.5 million victims who were arrested during the period in question but who didn't die in labor camps until later; on the other hand, Mr. Conquest warns us that it is a conservative estimate.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Cities On A Hill
author: Frances Fitzgerald
pull_quote: CITIES ON A HILL. A Journey Through Contemporary American Cultures. By Frances FitzGerald. 414 pages. Simon & Schuster. $19.95.    THE title of Frances FitzGerald's new book comes from a declaration John Winthrop, the founder of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, made to his followers some four centuries ago: ''We must consider that we shall be a City Upon a Hill,'' he said, ''the eyes of all people are upon us.'' As Ms. FitzGerald argues in these pages, such visionary impulses not only helped found this country, but they have also endured in Americans' continuing efforts to reinvent themselves, their untarnished belief in the possibility of starting over.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Letters From Prison And Other Essays
author: Adam Michnik
pull_quote: LETTERS FROM PRISON AND OTHER ESSAYS. By Adam Michnik. Translated by Maya Latynski. 354 pages. University of California. $25. IF the struggle for a ''democratic alternative'' in Poland stands as one of the nobler political expressions of our time, it is owing to men such as Adam Michnik. Now 40 years old, Mr. Michnik has devoted most of his adult life to trying to find a way out of the Communist rule imposed on his country by the Soviet Union. In his part of the world, such a commitment often means jail, and so we have the gloomy title of this important collection of essays.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: His Way: The Unauthorized Biography Of Frank Sinatra
author: Kitty Kelley
pull_quote: HIS WAY: The Unauthorized Biography of Frank Sinatra. By Kitty Kelley. Illustrated. 575 pages. Bantam Books. $21.95.   FRANK SINATRA has been accustomed to the glare of publicity for some 45 years, and to the glare of bad publicity for nearly as long. Even in an era when celebrities tended to be better shielded from exposure than they are today, he had a reputation for rough stuff; the stormiest part of his legend, his readiness to consort with criminals, first became a national issue as far back as 1947, when he paid his respects to Lucky Luciano in Havana, and over the years the damaging stories have just kept rolling along.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: To Skin A Cat
author: Thomas Mcguane
pull_quote: TO SKIN A CAT. By Thomas McGuane. 212 pages. E. P. Dutton/Seymour Lawrence. $16.95. Thomas McGuane's men would like to be Hemingway heroes - if they could. They cultivate the manly arts of hunting and fishing, drinking and swearing, and they're constantly getting involved with women who mess up their lives. But while the America they inhabit still boasts patches of pristine wilderness, it's hardly the testing ground for manhood that it was in simpler times - the frontier ethic is dead or dying in Mr. McGuane's America, and it's been replaced by a nasty new code of survivalism and cant. Cut off from their own nobler instincts and surrounded by despicable Snopesian rednecks -it's no wonder that McGuane characters suffer from a ''sadness-for-no-reason,'' a feeling of being ''superfluous'' and outdated.
headline: Books of The Times; Haunted Characters

title: Going Solo
author: Roald Dahl
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
GOING SOLO By Roald Dahl. Illustrated. 208 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $14.95. 

IREMEMBER that when I was very young and curious, with my mouth doubtless as open as a nestling's, I asked an older cousin of mine what it had been like to fight in World War II (he had been involved in many epic events, including the Normandy landing), and he told me it had been ''all right.'' When I would not let it go at that, he tried to put me off with some trivial story about a street urchin selling him a fake Swiss watch in North Africa, and when I still persisted, he took me out and bought me an ice cream bar from a Good Humor man, and that finally shut me up.
headline: YOUNG MAN, OLD EMPIRE, BAD WAR

title: The Life Of Helen Alone
author: Karen Lawrence
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LIFE OF HELEN ALONE By Karen Lawrence. 260 pp. New York: Villard Books. $15.95.    THERE is a good question at the heart of this first novel: ''Where does a woman find a home?'' It's one we thought we had answered, but nowadays a panic is rising, in magazines and on television specials - Were we wrong?
headline: MALE VEGETABLES?

title: Alabama Showdown
author: Geoffrey Norman. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ALABAMA SHOWDOWN The Football Rivalry Between Auburn and Alabama. By Geoffrey Norman. Illustrated. 238 pp. New York: Henry Holt & Company.$18.95.    THIS shrewd, smoothly written book by Geoffrey Norman is a history of college football's version of the feud between the Hatfields and the McCoys. If you're unlucky enough never to have sat among 70,000 delirious fans on a crisp autumn Saturday afternoon yelling, ''Roll, Tide,'' or ''War Eagle,'' as the teams poured out of the tunnel and onto the field, Mr. Norman will make you feel what it means to be in Birmingham the two weeks before the Alabama-Auburn game, weeks that rearrange life in the city to a degree that even those who have lived through World Series and Super Bowls can't imagine.
headline: BEYOND SUPER BOWLS

title: All Of Us Here
author: Irving Feldman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ALL OF US HERE By Irving Feldman. 81 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. Cloth, $17.95. Elisabeth Sifton Books/Penguin Books. Paper, $8.95.  DREAM WORK By Mary Oliver. 90 pp. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. Cloth, $14.95. Paper, $8.95.  DOMINION By Brooks Haxton. 107 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. Cloth, $14.95. Paper, $8.95.
headline: No Headline

title: The Autobiography Of Henry Viii
author: Margaret George
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE AUTOBIOGRAPHY OF HENRY VIII. By Margaret George. (St. Martin's, $19.95.) In her first novel, Margaret George asks us to believe that Henry VIII wrote an extensive memoir, discovered posthumously and annotated by his erstwhile fool and companion, Will Somers.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Freud Scenario
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE FREUD SCENARIO By Jean-Paul Sartre. Edited by J.-B. Pontalis. Translated by Quintin Hoare. 549 pp. Illinois: The University of Chicago Press. $24.95.    JEAN-PAUL SARTRE liked going to the movies because it was an unstuffy, proletarian thing to do, but when it came to writing for the movies he showed himself as intellectually lordly as ever and produced a scenario that was quite brilliantly unmakable. Asked in 1958 to do a script about Freud by the director John Huston, Sartre wrote a synopsis of some 95 typed pages; this Mr. Huston accepted, and Sartre went to work (or to town) on a shooting script. Like the synopsis, it was on the long side; had it been shot it would have worked out at some seven hours of screen time, and seven unusually exhausting hours for simple moviegoers, untrained for the fiercely cerebral and ambiguous story Sartre had to tell. He was asked to chop and to change this first version, which he did with his usual freedom, with the result that the revamped version was longer still. He and Mr. Huston could anyway not get on together, and by the time a film was finally made Sartre had moved on; he asked not to be credited, even though it seems that ''Freud,'' the second-rate outcome of their doomed collaboration, still showed faint signs of his boisterous work on the script.
headline: M. SARTRE GOES TO HOLLYWOOD

title: Making Hay
author: Verlyn Klinkenborg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MAKING HAY By Verlyn Klinkenborg. Illustrated by Gordon Allen. 157 pp. New York: Nick Lyons Books. $14.95.    VERLYN is a good name for a Middle Western farm boy. Never mind that this one, Verlyn Klinkenborg, grew up to earn a Ph.D. in English at Princeton and now teaches at Fordham University. A part of his sensibilities seems always to have stayed in the Middle West, where his aunts, uncles and cousins still farm. And so he went there to make hay with his uncles. Verlyn Klinkenborg likes hay.
headline: THE JOY OF ALFALFA

title: Wits, Wenchers And Wantons
author: E. J. Burford. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WITS, WENCHERS AND WANTONS London's Low Life: Covent Garden in the Eighteenth Century. By E. J. Burford. Illustrated. 260 pp. Topsfield, Mass.: Salem House. $22.95.    HOW much fun could a young rake have in Georgian London? Plenty, says this zesty and informative book, but he might wake up fleeced, in jail and with syphilis - or at least with nits in his wig. Eighteenth-century Covent Garden, outside the City of London, was a town of brothels, gaming dens, homosexual ''Mollies clubs'' and dissolute baths, with two theaters promoting further riot. In ''Wits, Wenchers and Wantons,'' E. J. Burford writes that social distinctions were blurred in Covent Garden. The women ranged from starving prostitutes to sexpot actresses out to get an earl to the blue-blooded Pharaoh's Daughters, who ran illegal card games. Habitues included William Hogarth, who here sketched subjects for his satirical paintings, and the Prince of Wales (later George IV). Wits and literati crowded to the Shakespeare's Head Tavern, which featured female wrestling matches and meetings of an Eton Old Boy's society.
headline: THAT WILL BE 20 SHILLINGS, MR. CASANOVA

title: The Life Of Langston Hughes
author: Arnold Rampersad. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LIFE OF LANGSTON HUGHES Volume One: 1902-1941. I, Too, Sing America. By Arnold Rampersad. Illustrated. 468 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $22.95.    WHAT was Langston Hughes? An overwhelmer. Long ago I felt it was proper to say he had ''a long reach / strong speech / remedial fears / muscular tears.'' I gave him titles: ''Helmsman, hatchet, headlight.'' And I suggested: ''See / one restless in the exotic time! and ever, / till the air is cured of its fever.''   Well, the time is still exotic. The air is not cured of its fever. Hughes is not here to be restless, but his product is here, still restless and capable of quite an agitation, a continuing agitation. Schoolchildren, elders, laborers, maids, doctors, nurses, filing clerks, miners, computer dabblers, salespeople at Macy's and Marshall Field's have heard of Langston Hughes and his compulsions - and many can quote from his poetry. An increasing number of scholars and textbook builders find him interesting to study.
headline: THE DARKER BROTHER

title: Cities On A Hill
author: Frances FitzGerald.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CITIES ON A HILL A Journey Through Contemporary American Cultures. By Frances FitzGerald. 414 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $19.95.    ''WHAT is the good of history?'' the skeptical historian Carl L. Becker once asked a correspondent. Frances FitzGerald, although she is not an academic historian, seems not to question its usefulness. Her first book, ''Fire in the Lake,'' drew heavily on the history of Vietnam; her second, ''America Revised,'' was given over entirely to a critical evaluation of American history textbooks. Thus it is not surprising that in her latest book, ''Cities on a Hill,'' she turns again to history in seeking to identify and understand the alterations in American society over the last decade or so. Rather than look at broad, national movements like the New Right or feminism, she has elected to investigate four rather discrete and limited groups of Americans.
headline: THE GROUPING OF AMERICA

title: One Woman Lost
author: Abigail McCarthy and Jane Gray Muskie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ONE WOMAN LOST By Abigail McCarthy and Jane Gray Muskie. 321 pp. New York: Atheneum. $15.95.    THE premise seems intriguing enough. It is 1992 in Washington. Barricades snake through the city, an ominous reminder that terrorists are striking the United States steadily - bombing the Capitol, the State Department, the Washington Monument, a revival meeting in Kansas City, a riverboat in St. Louis.
headline: NITROGLYCERIN IN THE HAND CREAM

title: The Prince Of Tides
author: Pat Conroy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PRINCE OF TIDES By Pat Conroy. 567 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $19.95.    THE Southern-boy protagonists of Pat Conroy's fiction have twin obsessions - oppressive fathers or father figures, and the South. Against both they fight furiously for selfhood and independence, yet they never manage to secede from their seductive entrappers. Some fatal combination of nostalgia and loyalty holds them back; they remain ambivalent sons of their families and their region, alternately railing against, then shamelessly romanticizing, the myths and strictures that imprison them.
headline: ROMANCING THE SHRINK

title: Rediscovering Love
author: Willard Gaylin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: REDISCOVERING LOVE By Willard Gaylin. 288 pp. New York: Viking. $15.95.    TWENTIETH-CENTURY objective science has fostered blind faith in itself that has diminished, not enhanced our understanding about the nature of man. Once the romantic element is forcibly removed from this understanding, we are left alone to discover the purposelessness of modern life, drifting evermore rapidly into ''joyless narcissism.'' Dr. Willard Gaylin, ''an optimist and a romantic,'' declares that we must reinstate love to its central position in human experience.
headline: BETTER THAN PLEASURE

title: From The Realm Of Morpheus
author: Steven Millhauser
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FROM THE REALM OF MORPHEUS By Steven Millhauser. 370 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $17.95.    STEVEN MILLHAUSER'S first novel, ''Edwin Mullhouse,'' was a work of great originality that seemed, at the time, magically familiar. In ''From the Realm of Morpheus,'' he seems bent on reversing that equation, producing a strange sport of a book, wholly odd yet purposefully unoriginal.
headline: UNDERGROUND WITH MIRRORS AND MERMAIDS

title: The Leading Edge
author: Walter J Boyne
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Why would anyone but the most insatiable aeronautics buff want another photo-and-text history of human flight? Walter J. Boyne, in THE LEADING EDGE (Stewart, Tabori & Chang, $29.95), has anticipated that query and approached his task from an unusual perspective. The author focuses not on those famed for their piloting or on the captains of industry, but on the inventors whose ideas cut past apparent limits to extend the airplane's capabilities.
headline: THE WILD BLUE DRAWING BOARDS

title: Straight Cut
author: Madison Smartt Bell
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STRAIGHT CUT By Madison Smartt Bell. 230 pp. New York: Ticknor & Fields. $15.95.    THE best thing about this odd, old-fashionedly hard-boiled novel is its assured depiction of the vagaries of a freelance life. The hero, Tracy Bateman, is a sometime film editor, and the only constants in his existence are bad, impromptu meals, erratic hours, wild bouts of alcohol and nicotine abuse, bedridden sieges with unnamed viruses and a prevailing sense of undefended, uprooted stupefaction that suggests an almost total severance from reality.
headline: KNIFE-WIELDING HOODS, UNSTABLE FEMME FATALE

title: Looking For Hogeye
author: Roy Reed
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOOKING FOR HOGEYE By Roy Reed. 132 pp. Fayetteville, Ark.: The University of Arkansas Press. Cloth, $13.95. Paper, $7.95.    ROY REED, once a national and foreign correspondent for The New York Times, is now a professor of journalism at the University of Arkansas and, in his own heart at least, a farmer. ''Looking for Hogeye'' breaks no new literary ground, but with this collection of 21 essays Mr. Reed has raised a fine crop of staples.
headline: HOT SUMMERS AND THICK GRAVY

title: Mermaids
author: Patty Dann
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MERMAIDS By Patty Dann. 147 pp. New York: Ticknor & Fields. $13.95.    CHARLOTTE FLAX, the fragile yet indomitable narrator of this short tale, is the neglected 14-year-old daughter of a promiscuous, nomadic mother and a seemingly nonexistent father. She and her little sister invent their own fantastic worlds in order to cope with the ceaseless cross-country moves, their mother's weird dating habits and her menus. Mrs. Flax, as Charlotte calls her mother, has a repertoire of meals consisting solely of hors d'oeuvres. Tentatively ensconced in their latest home in Grove, Mass., Charlotte falls in love with the troubled young man who is the caretaker of a nearby convent.
headline: CHARLOTTE IN SEARCH OF ORDER

title: Resident Alien
author: Clark Blaise
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RESIDENT ALIEN By Clark Blaise. 184 pp. New York: Penguin Books. Paper, $5.95.    FOR anyone who immigrated to this country the title of Clark Blaise's new book has a magical sound. But it also implies diagnosis of a defect - resident, yes, but alien still, with citizenship the only remedy. The Canadian phrase ''landed immigrant'' is less pedantic, evoking as it does landed fish or something completed, final, with nothing held back; perhaps it suggests a new phrase, resident immigrant. You never know. In the popular ''Alien'' movies aliens arrive not through Immigration Service checkpoints, but, with a brutal squeak, from the chest of a hapless earthly host. Alien is a word with one too many uses.
headline: OUTSIDER BACK INSIDE

title: Higher Learning
author: Derek Bok
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HIGHER LEARNING. By Derek Bok. (Harvard University, $15.) The most important point Derek Bok makes in this book is that the undergraduate college ought to retain a central place within a major research university.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Establishment Clause
author: Leonard W. Levy.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: Lawrence M. Friedman: Lawrence M. Friedman, the Marion Rice Kirkwood Professor of Law At Stanford University, Is the Author ofA History of American Law.''
pull_quote: THE ESTABLISHMENT CLAUSE Religion and the First Amendment. By Leonard W. Levy. 236 pp. New York: Macmillan Publishing Company. $16.95.    LEONARD LEVY, one of the best of our constitutional historians, picks up a theme in his latest book that has concerned him for many years: the ''wall of separation'' between church and state. At the very end, he remarks that, ''Robert Frost notwithstanding, something there is that loves a wall.'' Mr. Levy is one of those who love the wall, though he is no extremist on the subject; and this excellent study was written in praise of the wall and against those who chip away at its structure.
headline: MENDING THE WALL

title: Funny Sauce
author: Delia Ephron.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FUNNY SAUCE Us, the Ex, the Ex's New Mate, the New Mate's Ex, and the Kids. By Delia Ephron. 191 pp. New York: Viking. $14.95.    WHEN they were growing up, did Delia Ephron and her sister Nora get enough to eat? Both writers seem obsessed with food as a metaphor for . . . well, food. Both like to give their books food-focused titles: Nora's ''Crazy Salad'' and ''Heartburn,'' Delia's ''How to Eat Like a Child'' and her latest, ''Funny Sauce.'' It's a pleasure to report that ''Funny Sauce'' won't lead to heartburn, despite the acid wit that's one of its ingredients - only to chortles and nods of recognition.
headline: SHARPER THAN LOTS OF SERPENTS' TEETH

title: Where You'll Find Me
author: Ann Beattie.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
WHERE YOU'LL FIND ME And Other Stories. By Ann Beattie. 191 pp. New York: Linden Press/Simon & Schuster. $14.95. 

THOUGH most of the stories in Ann Beattie's new collection, ''Where You'll Find Me,'' are pretty terse, one of them, called ''Janus,'' is sufficiently open and worked out to give convenient access to the materials from which they all are made. In ''Janus,'' Andrea, a successful suburban real-estate agent of a certain age, uses a glazed bowl of her own to provide a special touch of elegance to the houses she shows for sale. It is ''both subtle and noticeable - a paradox of a bowl,'' and Andrea is sure that it brings her professional luck. Once, when she forgot to remove it when she left a house, she felt as if she'd forgotten a friend, or a child (though she has no child). Her husband, a stockbroker, thinks it ''pretty'' but pays it no special attention, since he no longer takes particular pleasure in the possessions they have acquired ''to make up for all the lean years when they were gradu-ate students.''
headline: A GLAZED BOWL OF ONE'S OWN

title: Calculated Kindness
author: Gil Loescher and John A. Scanlan.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CALCULATED KINDNESS Refugees and America's Half-Open Door, 1945 to the Present. By Gil Loescher and John A. Scanlan. 346 pp. New York: The Free Press. $22.50.    FEW issues have attracted more propaganda, sanctimony and ignorance than those surrounding refugees and, more generally, immigration. The goal of ''Calculated Kindness'' is to explore the rationales and politics of United States refugee policy since World War II.
headline: WHO GETS IN, AND WHY

title: A Jockey's Life
author: Dick Francis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A JOCKEY'S LIFE: The Biography of Lester Piggott. By Dick Francis. (Putnam, $18.95.) There can be little argument that Lester Piggott, who won more than 5,000 races in a career that spanned almost four decades, was a successful jockey.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: It Seems Like Only Yesterday
author: John Bartlow Martin.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IT SEEMS LIKE ONLY YESTERDAY Memoirs of Writing, Presidential Politics, and the Diplomatic Life. By John Bartlow Martin. 345 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $19.95.    AT 71, John Bartlow Martin is a survivor of a virtually extinct breed of journalists who thrived in the glory days of ''the big slicks'' - one of the best of some 50 freelancers prolific enough to earn a living writing ''heavy fact'' pieces for The Saturday Evening Post, Collier's and other mass magazines in the 1940's and 1950's. He is also (not quite obsolete) a devoutly liberal Democrat, unabashed and unregenerate. Catching his first sight of Eleanor Roosevelt on a Manhattan street in the mid-1950's, he stood at attention and put his hat over his heart. And he worked as a speechwriter for all of his party's Presidential candidates from Adlai Stevenson to George McGovern.
headline: 2 CENTS A WORD

title: The Monkey's Wrench
author: Primo Levi
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE MONKEY'S WRENCH By Primo Levi. Translated by William Weaver. 174 pp. New York: Summit Books. $15.95. 

AN Italian Jewish chemist who is a survivor of Auschwitz and was for 30 years the manager of a paint factory has in his quiet way turned out to be one of the most valuable writers of our time. After 10 months in Auschwitz, Primo Levi was carted off to the Soviet Union before his liberators could manage transportation for him back to Italy. By the time Mr. Levi got home to Turin, he had experienced so much degradation and exile that it is astonishing to find in his books ''Survival in Auschwitz'' and ''Moments of Reprieve'' writing consistently objective, sober, all-observant and even witty. In the tormented literature of the concentration-camp universe, Mr. Levi represents something rare and astringent: his training as a scientist, the reflex resistance to evil offered by a man with nothing on his side but an indestructible belief in reason.
headline: LIFE AND STEEL: A RIGGER'S TALE

title: No Direction Home
author: Robert Shelton. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NO DIRECTION HOME The Life and Music of Bob Dylan. By Robert Shelton. Illustrated. 573 pp. New York: Beech Tree Books/ William Morrow & Company. $17.95.    BY 1966, Bob Dylan had transformed himself from a would-be Woody Guthrie into a rock-and-roll avatar. Having awakened the conscience of a generation with ''Blowin' in the Wind,'' he was discovering new ways to write, to sing, to shape the mind-blown spirit of the 60's into song. He had moved from the social realism of ''Only a Pawn in Their Game'' to the wild surrealism of ''Tombstone Blues,'' from the concerned commitment of ''The Times They Are A-Changin' '' to the bitter cynicism of ''Positively Fourth Street.''
headline: DYLAN'S LIVES

title: Second To None
author: Robert C Christopher
pull_quote: SECOND TO NONE: American Companies in Japan, by Robert C. Christopher. 258 pages. Crown. $16.95.   AMERICANS are gradually realizing that the United States has a lot to answer for when it comes to its huge trade imbalance with Japan. There's little quarrel, for instance, that many of Detroit's woes are traceable to complacency and poor quality that offended American drivers at the same time Japanese companies like Toyota, Honda and Nissan were courting them. Nor can anyone deny that a self-imposed ban on exporting Alaskan oil adds $2 billion to the deficit by preventing the Japanese from buying an American product they would love to have.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Theodore Dreiser: At The Gates Of The City, 1871-1907
author: Theodore Dreiser
pull_quote: THEODORE DREISER: At the Gates of the City, 1871-1907. By Richard Lingeman. Illustrated. 478 pages. Putnam. $22.95. READING Theodore Dreiser's own story is a little like reading a Dreiser novel. It looms up, a heavy and forbidding prospect; but as soon as you get into it, you are carried along by its stubborn power. Or you are if it is told as well as it is by Richard Lingeman in the first volume of his new biography.   Dreiser was the ninth child of a German Catholic immigrant. He was born at an inauspicious time; five years earlier his father had suffered an accident at work that according to family legend led to him losing his position as manager of a woollen mill and precipitated his decline into poverty. As Mr. Lingeman shows, the legend exaggerated, but it contained ''a core of truth.'' By the time Dreiser was growing up his father had been reduced to working at whatever menial job was available and had retreated into a rigid piety, while the family - held together by his wife -drifted from one Indiana town to another.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Mohawk
author: Richard Russo
pull_quote: MOHAWK. By Richard Russo. 418 pages. Vintage Contemporaries. Paper, $6.95. ''IT occurs to him that he had allowed himself to get more keyed up over the operation than he should've,'' writes Richard Russo of his hero, Dan Wood. ''The resulting disappointment was as slow and subtle in coming as the realization that, yes, once again he'd somehow gotten his hopes up. His grip on reality had always been a point of pride with him, and he felt a little like a backsliding AA member for losing that grip. Hope was a luxury he could not afford - a cruelty, really.''   Though Dan's dilemma is especially cruel - he's been paralyzed in an automobile accident - the same might well be said of most of the characters in ''Mohawk.'' Theirs are not terribly eventful lives - few have ever left the small upstate New York town of Mohawk; and their dreams are hardly extravagant - just the ordinary ones of love and work and family. And yet all of these people have begun to realize that their most deeply cherished hopes have already slipped out of reach, that resignation or acceptance are their two remaining choices.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Chicago
author: Studs Terkel
pull_quote: CHICAGO. By Studs Terkel. Illustrated. 148 pages. Pantheon. $15.95. NOBODY seems to be writing prose poems to the city of New York these days. With the sometime exception of Allen Ginsberg, there's no Walt Whitman around to sing the praises of (as he called the island) Mannahatta. Even one of the city's juiciest scandals has to get out of town in a hurry and be tried before a New Haven jury.
headline: Books; Big Shoulders

title: The Tears Of The White Man
author: Pascal Bruckner
pull_quote: THE TEARS OF THE WHITE MAN:   Compassion as Contempt. By Pascal Bruckner. Translated by William R. Beer. 244 pages. Free Press. $17.95. PASCAL BRUCKNER is a prodigy of polemic. In ''The Tears of the White Man,'' his first book to be published in the United States, the French writer exercises his gifts on members of the intelligentsia who go gaga over the third world while denigrating the West. Although his examples are drawn from his own country, beginning with Jean-Paul Sartre, his case has applicability to the United States as well, as William R. Beer, who did the translation, points out in an introduction. Mr. Beer notes that lacking a colonial past to feel guilty about, a portion of the American left has used American Indians, blacks, young people and women in much the way that some French leftists have used the inhabitants of their former colonies as weapons in an assault on Western values and culture.   Mr. Bruckner, who confesses he was for a time one of the ''third worldists'' whom he batters here, draws on his own experience to support his argument. He identifies three overlapping types of third worldist: those who profess solidarity with the entire Southern Hemisphere and take a ''we're all in it together'' position; those who ooze compassion, which he calls the ''put ourselves in their place'' line, and those who adopt a ''we are just like them'' pose.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The House On Moon Lake
author: Francesca Duranti
pull_quote: THE HOUSE ON MOON LAKE. By Francesca Duranti. Translated by Stephen Sartarelli. 181 pages. Random House. $15.95.   MONTAIGNE says that there are more books about books than about any other subject, and in recent years it has sometimes seemed that there are more novels about novels. Anyone who casts an eye over the reigning fashions in fiction - fiction with serious literary pretensions, that is - can hardly help being struck by the proliferation of fables that fold in on themselves, stories that escape from their fictional frame, novels designed to remind us (as though we were in danger of supposing anything else) that a novel is only a novel, and not a slice of reality.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Anagrams
author: Lorrie Moore
pull_quote: ANAGRAMS. By Lorrie Moore. 225 pages.   Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.    One of the best things about Lorrie Moore's new novel is its title - ''Anagrams.'' It's a reference, of course, to her heroine Benna's habit of ''trying to make anagrams out of words that weren't anagrams'' (moonscape and menopause; gutless and guilts; lovesick and evil louse), her tendency to mis-hear and jumble sentences spoken by friends (''I never want to see you again'' becomes ''I want to see again''). At the same time, it's also an allusion to Benna's efforts to reinvent herself, to become someone else through fantasy and imagination - and in that sense, it's an allusion as well to the fiction-making process as practiced by Ms. Moore.
headline: Jokers Wild

title: My Daddy Was A Pistol And I'm A Son Of A Gun
author: Lewis Grizzard
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MY DADDY WAS A PISTOL AND I'M A SON OF A GUN. By Lewis Grizzard. (Villard, $14.95.) Lewis Grizzard, a columnist for The Atlanta Constitution, writes humor books with mock country-western titles like ''Elvis Is Dead and I Don't Feel So Good Myself.''
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION
