author: Jeannette Haien
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE ALL OF IT. By Jeannette Haien. (Godine, $14.95.) The fictional landscape of ''The All of It'' is the west of Ireland, an area known for its lush, fertile farmland, its excellent salmon fishing and its small, country villages - such as Jeannette Haien's Roonatellin - where Roman Catholicism is a strong and sobering force.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Dark Victory: Ronald Reagan, Mca, And The Mob
author: Dan E Moldea
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DARK VICTORY: Ronald Reagan, MCA, and the Mob. By Dan E. Moldea. (Viking, $18.95.) ''Dark Victory'' is an ambitious book that sheds some light on past events but falls short in showing that old ties make for current scandal.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Enchanter
author: Vladimir Nabokov
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE ENCHANTER By Vladimir Nabokov. Translated by Dmitri Nabokov. 127 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $16.95.    THIS book is being billed as the European ''Lolita,'' and indeed ''The Enchanter'' is a short story on a related theme that Vladimir Nabokov wrote in Russian in 1939 in Paris. He then sailed for the United States, where, 10 years later, the real Lolita, our Lolita, first began to make her presence felt to him. The story, discovered in the Nabokov archives, has been impeccably translated by the author's son, Dmitri, who also contributes an entertaining commentary on the history and significance of the text.
headline: IMAGINE LOLITA AS A NERD

title: Children At Risk
author: Paula Hawkins.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CHILDREN AT RISK My Fight Against Child Abuse -A Personal Story and a Public Plea. By Paula Hawkins. 191 pp. Bethesda, Md.: Adler & Adler. $16.95.    WHEN Senator Paula Hawkins was a child, she and neighborhood friends often played at the home of an elderly couple in Long Beach, Calif., while the children's parents were away on errands. The couple and their home were greatly trusted by the children and their families. But that trust was lost forever. When Paula was 5 years old, the man of the house - a respected, grandfatherly type - lifted her onto his lap and handed her a piece of candy. His other hand ''went immediately down into my panties,'' says Senator Hawkins in ''Children At Risk.''
headline: THE PROBLEM BEGINS AT HOME

title: H G Wells
author: David C. Smith. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
H. G. WELLS Desperately Mortal. A Biography. By David C. Smith. Illustrated. 634 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $29.95. 

PERCHED upon the soapbox of his storytelling genius, H. G. Wells was more preacher than novelist, more prophet than scientist. Spurred by a rabbity randiness, he fashioned thinly veiled apologias into utopian fantasies that combined his biological and technological dreams - and nightmares - with societies in which love was unfettered. His novels of contemporary life were even more personal.
headline: INSPIRED BY RANDINESS

title: The Great Chinese Revolution: 1800-1985
author: John King Fairbank. Maps.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GREAT CHINESE REVOLUTION: 1800-1985 By John King Fairbank. Maps. 396 pp. New York: A Cornelia & Michael Bessie Book/ Harper & Row. $20.95.    FOR more than two decades, one of the leading texts in many college Chinese history courses around the country has been ''East Asia: The Modern Transformation,'' of which John King Fairbank was a co-author. In its own way, the text is a synoptic masterpiece, though critics have noted that the word ''revolution'' is conspicuously absent from the title, and they have claimed that the book overemphasizes the impact of the West on China and Japan. Mr. Fairbank's latest history of modern China redresses that balance. Not only has the doyen of United States-China studies made revolution the title and ''class struggle'' one of the themes of his new book, but he also has stressed the ''historical continuity and distinctive culture'' of a China that is centered on itself and - until very recent times - apparently impervious to the waves of modernization that have broken against its shores from without.
headline: THE LATEST THING IN EMPERORS

title: Quiet Rage
author: Lillian B Rubin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: QUIET RAGE: Bernie Goetz in a Time of Madness. By Lillian B. Rubin. (Farrar, Straus & Giroux, $16.95.) No one, says Lillian B. Rubin, is quite sure who Bernhard Goetz really is.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: In The Hollow Of His Hand
author: James Purdy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN THE HOLLOW OF HIS HAND By James Purdy. 254 pp. New York: Weidenfeld & Nicolson. $16.95.    IT'S as if Cormac McCarthy with his dark genius and Edward Bulwer-Lytton with his overblown prose style had joined hands to rewrite ''Joseph Andrews,'' sending their young protagonist forth across a landscape provided by Louis L'Amour. In this grimly antic antipicaresque, the passive young half-Indian Chad - instead of setting out on a traditional quest to find his own father - is kidnapped repeatedly by potential fathers eager to adopt him. And yet, many of the conventions of the picaresque are observed: the importance of coincidence; the totally episodic nature of the journey itself; its consequent lack of cause and effect; the stock characters who never develop; the bawdy encounters; the use of talismans.
headline: KIDNAPPED BY EVERYONE

title: Hope In Hard Times
author: Paul Rogat Loeb.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HOPE IN HARD TIMES America's Peace Movement and the Reagan Era. By Paul Rogat Loeb. 322 pp. Lexington, Mass.: Lexington Books/D. C. Heath & Company. Cloth, $24.95. Paper, $10.95.    THE American people elected Ronald Reagan in part because they wanted to ''walk tall.'' But in an era of unimaginably powerful nuclear arms and computerized weapons systems - and with the memory of defeat in Vietnam still fresh - ''tall'' soon seemed too tall to substantial numbers of people who were alarmed enough to want to learn as much as they could about the arms race, or Central America, or both -and, once informed, to become active, at least for a while.
headline: VILLAGE ACTIVISTS

title: A Summons To Memphis
author: Peter Taylor
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A SUMMONS TO MEMPHIS By Peter Taylor. 209 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.    PETER TAYLOR is a novelist and short-story writer who for almost half a century has produced fictions about a distinctive world of Southern inland cities, and about a characteristic stratum of society whose members are both provincial and urbane, descended from plantation-owning stock but very comfortably ensconced in the finest neighborhoods of Nashville and Memphis. They marry their own kind and honor the leisurely rituals of their caste, careful stewards of their own good fortune. These are not the tormented souls we are accustomed to finding in literature of the South. The motive force in most of these lives is complacency, the genial expectation that the young will succeed to the quiet privileges that their parents, in enjoying them, have preserved.
headline: THE FAMILY GAME WAS REVENGE

title: Masterpiece
author: Thomas Hoving
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MASTERPIECE By Thomas Hoving. 321 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $17.95.    THE masterpiece in question - the painting at stake in this first novel by Thomas Hoving, the former director of the Metropolitan Museum of Art - is a previously unknown, suddenly discovered picture by the 17th-century Spanish master Diego de Velazquez. Indeed, it is no less than the flip side, as it were, of Velazquez' supremely famous so-called Rokeby Venus, the languid nude on display at the National Gallery in London, her back turned to the viewer, her cloudy visage framed in a mirror held up by an attending Cupid.
headline: VENUS PERSUED

title: The Devil In The Dooryard
author: Gregory Blake Smith
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DEVIL IN THE DOORYARD By Gregory Blake Smith. 336 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $17.95.    FROM the moment the Pilgrims set foot on Plymouth Rock, preaching freedom and practicing bigotry, the American soul has been riven to the root. America presents an intellectual paradox, an endless source of fascination and tenure for sociologists and historians.
headline: J.J. AND THE INDIANS

title: Ecological Imperialsim
author: Alfred W. Crosby. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
ECOLOGICAL IMPERIALISM The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900-1900. By Alfred W. Crosby. Illustrated. 368 pp. New York: Cambridge University Press. $22.95. 

FOR most of us who live in the Americas, the colonization of the New World that inevitably followed the epic voyage of Columbus must stand as one of the great events of world history. And so, in 1982, as we approached the 500th anniversary of that voyage, it seemed uncontroversial for Spain and several other countries of Western Europe, together with virtually every independent state of the Western Hemisphere, to submit United Nations Draft Resolution A/37/ L.36, calling for the ''Observance of the Quincentenary of the Discovery of America'' in 1992.
headline: SPOILED PARADISES

title: Heart Of The Order
author: Tony Ardizzone
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HEART OF THE ORDER By Tony Ardizzone. 314 pp. New York: Henry Holt & Company. $16.95.    THIS baseball novel, its allegorical trumpets blowing, is about Danny Bacigalupo, who comes from a working-class family in Chicago. In the first half of the book, which seems to be set in the 1950's, Danny accidentally kills a playmate, Mickey Meenan, with a line drive to the Adam's apple. He also falls in love with a fat girl named Grace. Danny and Grace are freaks -he because of the accident and she because of her obesity - and the two have a whirlwind romance, which is never dramatized at all. The second half, which seems to be set in the 60's, involves a ''revelation.'' A priest tells Danny that he is alive to play for Mickey, and Danny becomes so confused by this pronouncement that he starts to think he is Mickey.
headline: PINCH-HIT FOR MICKEY

title: Niccolo Rising
author: Dorothy Dunnett
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NICCOLO RISING. By Dorothy Dunnett. (Knopf, $18.95.) A historical novel set in 15th-century Europe would seem to be mostly an adventure story, but this book is about the rise of international commerce.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: To Skin A Cat
author: Thomas McGuane
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
TO SKIN A CAT By Thomas McGuane. 212 pp. New York: Seymour Lawrence/E. P. Dutton. $16.95. 

THE downward spiral from prosperous, snug and well-adapted to despairing and outcast seems nowhere as uncannily seductive as in the fiction of Thomas McGuane. The abrupt blurring of normal into absurd occurs elsewhere in American writing - in the grim waywardness of reality in the work of Tim O'Brien, for example, or in Flannery O'Connor's fine-clawed cruelties - but Thomas McGuane seems driven by the settled, the moneyed, the suburban-serene aspects of American life into a kind of high, infuriated escapism all his own.

Nobody, not even a reader, had better feel too comfortable in a McGuane novel, where certainties are born to be sabotaged. A fluently burlesquing dread and flights of coolest lyricism coexist in his books; grotesque events unfold in classically evocative language, as if Mr. McGuane meant to revive the possibly threadbare beauties of naturalism with the most ambitious absurdities he could dream up. The volatile unease in this mix of lyricism and incongruity fueled his six previous novels as it does the 13 short stories collected in ''To Skin a Cat.''
headline: THE SIGN OF LIFE IS MAYHEM

title: Making A Difference
author: Milton Viorst
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MAKING A DIFFERENCE The Peace Corps at Twenty-Five. Edited by Milton Viorst. Foreword by President Ronald Reagan. 218 pp. New York: Weidenfeld & Nicolson. $16.95.    WITH a name like Peace Corps, a Federal agency might reasonably be suspected of some grand Orwellian deception. But the brief, sometimes colorful essays and reminiscences in ''Making a Difference'' by former Peace Corps sympathizers, directors and volunteers betray little ideological consistency. Quite the reverse. To President Reagan, the Peace Corps is ''the American Way'' of self-help; to Harris Wofford, past director in Ethiopia, it is an expression of the same American ''comic spirit'' that once floated Huck Finn down the Mississippi; to Senator Christopher J. Dodd, Democrat of Connecticut, it was a rocky road through ''a hot blast of reality'' in the Dominican Republic; to Paul Theroux, self-proclaimed draft-dodger, it was the start in Malawi of an expatriate career ''at the sharp end.''
headline: HUCK FINN IN MALAWI

title: Portrait Of Delmore
author: Elizabeth Pollet
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PORTRAIT OF DELMORE Journals and Notes of Delmore Schwartz 1939-1959. Edited, and with an introduction, by Elizabeth Pollet. 663 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $35.    YIDDISH, I am told, has 26 words for ''genius,'' several of these no doubt fashioned to the likeness of Delmore Schwartz, poet, writer of fiction and philosopher-critic, to whom such disparate writers as Robert Lowell, John Crowe Ransom (in his criticism) and John Berryman recognized their abiding debts.
headline: SEARCHING FOR GOD IN THE NEXT APARTMENT

title: Dancing On My Grave
author: Gelsey Kirkland with Greg Lawrence. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DANCING ON MY GRAVE An Autobiography. By Gelsey Kirkland with Greg Lawrence. Illustrated. 286 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $17.95.    GELSEY KIRKLAND, just turned 18, was dancing the Sugar Plum Fairy in George Balanchine's production of Tchaikovsky's ''Nutcracker'' when Clive Barnes wrote of her in The New York Times, ''There is already such authority and breeding that you can hardly wait to see the dancer she must surely develop into in a few more years.''
headline: THROUGH THE FLAMES ON THIN SOLES

title: A Missing Plane
author: Susan Sheehan
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
A MISSING PLANE By Susan Sheehan. Illustrated. 201 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $18.95. 

MARCH 22, 1944, was a free day for the United States Army Air Force's Second Lieut. Robert Allred, 27, and his B-24 crew. They were on temporary duty in Port Moresby, New Guinea, to train Australian pilots to fly the aircraft, but on this day there were no Australians to train. It had been nearly three weeks since they left their base at Nadzab, 190 miles away, and it would be at least another week before they would be transferred back. It had not been a pleasant assignment. The weather in Nadzab, on the other side of the Owen Stanley Range, was an agreeable combination of hot sunny days and cool nights, but in Port Moresby it rained constantly. Worse, for Allred's nose gunner, Port Moresby was ''chow lousy.'' The day off was a chance for the Americans to pick up their mail and return in the afternoon.
headline: A CLOUD WITH A ROCK IN IT

title: Small Claims
author: Jill Ciment
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SMALL CLAIMS. By Jill Ciment. (Weidenfeld & Nicolson, $14.95.) Fresh Youth storms the Big City to make it as Artist: recently, short stories have teemed with gullible waifs transported to the metropolis.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The City As A Work Of Art
author: Donald J. Olsen. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE CITY AS A WORK OF ART London, Paris, Vienna. By Donald J. Olsen. Illustrated. 341 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $35. 

THIS enthralling book is the latest product of the new climate of thought that has sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic since the recent widespread collapse of support for the buildings of the Modern Movement and the theories that sustained them. Donald J. Olsen believes that this shift in opinion may be as significant as the one that underpinned the Romantic Movement in Europe in the early 19th century. Now that many of the hated tower-blocks that have disfigured British cities since the 1960's are being demolished because of their social and functional failure, envious eyes are being cast back to the once-despised Victorian streets the tower-blocks replaced.
headline: THE CENTURY OF THE STREET

title: Fidel: A Biography Of Fidel Castro
author: Peter G. Bourne. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FIDEL A Biography of Fidel Castro. By Peter G. Bourne. Illustrated. 332 pp. New York: Dodd, Mead & Company. $18.95.    PETER BOURNE, a psychiatrist who served in the Carter Administration, was initially attracted to the Cuban revolution because of its idealism. He now describes Cuba as the ''personal fiefdom'' of Fidel Castro, run according to Mr. Castro's philosophy and wishes. Despite Dr. Bourne's disillusionment, he says he tried ''to avoid a reflex condemnation'' of Mr. Castro's Cuba. In the process, he has written a book that tilts in the opposite direction.
headline: WAS COMMUNISM AN AFTERTHOUGHT?

title: Sailing With The Wind
author: Thomas Locker
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SAILING WITH THE WIND Written and illustrated by Thomas Locker. Unpaged. New York: Dial Books. $15. (Ages 5 to 9)    THOMAS LOCKER'S first book, ''Where the River Begins,'' portrayed the simple story of the journey of two boys and their grandfather upcountry to find the source of a river in a high mountain pool. The masterly painting of its illustrations astonished readers, and it was named one of the 10 best illustrated children's books of 1984 in The New York Times Book Review. It was followed in 1985 by ''The Mare on the Hill'' and now by ''Sailing With the Wind,'' which tells the complementary story of a young girl's voyage down a river to the sea.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: One More Time
author: Carol Burnett
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ONE MORE TIME. By Carol Burnett. (Random House, $18.95.) Like all great clowns Carol Burnett has a profound respect for both the sentimental and the grotesque. She begins this affecting memoir of her childhood as an extended letter to her three daughters to explain ''just how your mom turned out to be the kind of hairpin she is.'' Raised only a block or so away from where Nathanael West placed ''The Day of the Locust,'' her family life was the very model of instability. Mother was an alcoholic. Her big dream was to write for the fan magazines but she spent most of her time in bed with a bottle and the shades pulled down. Father also drank; he sold things door-to-door when he could and died in a charity ward. This left Carol's upbringing to her maternal grandmother and it is the bond between the gawky, insecure little girl and the eccentric old woman that makes this book special. Nanny (Mabel Eudora Creighton) comes vividly to life: we see her in the one-room apartment the two of them shared, taking out her teeth to amuse the 3-year-old Carol or checking under the bed each night to make sure a man wasn't lurking. Nanny was subject to strange ailments, most particularly her ''hissy fits'' during which she clutched Mary Baker Eddy's ''Science and Health'' with one hand and downed phenobarbitals with the other. This woman is clearly just beneath the surface of all those wonderfully neurotic characters Miss Burnett created during the heyday of her television show.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Eagle's Nest
author: Charlotte M. Porter. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE EAGLE'S NEST Natural History and American Ideas, 1812-1842. By Charlotte M. Porter. Illustrated. 251 pp. University: The University of Alabama Press. $24.95.    WHEN Benjamin Silliman, a 22-year-old lawyer completely unschooled in the sciences, was appointed to the first professorship of natural science at Yale University, he immediately set off for Philadelphia. To Silliman in 1802, Philadelphia ''presented more advantage to science than any other place in our country.'' Soon thereafter William Maclure, ''father'' of American geology and an early president of the Academy of Natural Sciences, became the dominant figure within Philadelphia's considerable population of naturalists. The Philadelphia circle justly serves as a focus for ''The Eagle's Nest: Natural History and American Ideas, 1812-1842,'' Charlotte M. Porter's study of early American forays into natural history.
headline: CLAIMING THE ANIMALS

title: The Reckoning
author: David Halberstram
pull_quote: The Reckoning. By David Halberstam. 752 pages. William Morrow. $19.95.   THE president of the company blew a chance to buy a bargain-priced stretch of land for a new factory, and his indecision gave his competitors an immense advantage. Then, when a new plant was built, he let a statue of himself be erected there, in testimony, apparently, to his prescience.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Fortunes Of Mitchell Kennerley, Bookman
author: Matthew J Bruccoli
pull_quote: THE FORTUNES OF MITCHELL KENNERLEY, BOOKMAN. By Matthew J. Bruccoli. Illustrated. 337 pages. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $24.95. MITCHELL KENNER=   LEY was one of the more enterprising publishers in New York in the years before World War I, and a leading figure in the book auction world in the 1920's. In themselves, those achievements may not sound as though they warrant a full-scale biography; but his story turns out to have been curious enough to justify Matthew J. Bruccoli's decision to write about him at length. It also constitutes a valuable footnote to a vanished phase of cultural history.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Staying At The Top: The Life Of A Ceo
author: Sonny Kleinfield
pull_quote: STAYING AT THE TOP: The Life of a CEO. By Sonny Kleinfield. 298 pages. New American Library. $17.95. About a year ago, N. R. (Sonny) Kleinfield profiled Hicks Waldron, the chief executive of Avon Products, at length - great length - in The New York Times Magazine. In one of the most memorable anecdotes of the piece, Mr. Waldron spots several ''not overly offensive scraps of litter'' on the carpet in a reception area where a photographer is taking his picture. Mr. Waldron ''seems flustered and alarmed, as if there were several dead rats supine on the floor.''   ''Turning briskly to the receptionist,'' the account continued, ''he says coolly, 'Get someone up here with a vacuum cleaner. This shouldn't be.' ''
headline: Books; Executive Life

title: Paradise
author: Donald Barthelme
pull_quote: PARADISE. By Donald Barthelme. 208 pages. G. P. Putnam's Sons. $16.95. SIMON, the hero of Donald Barthelme's third novel, is a 53-year-old architect, prominent enough to be featured in ''Progressive Architecture'' and vain enough to think that his work could drive Louis Kahn's ghost mad with jealousy. As a student he once submitted a plan to redo Rockefeller Center in pickled pine, and he's apparently still partial to vaguely eccentric, avant-garde structures -transforming armories into schools and designing churches out of steel and glass blocks. Although he's always wanted ''to be a hearty, optimistic American, like the President,'' he's long since settled ''for being a competent, sometimes inventive architect with a tragic sense of brick.''   For readers of Mr. Barthelme's previous novels and short stories, Simon's practice of architecture may sound an awful lot like a tongue-in-cheek version of the author's own approach to fiction. Like Simon's buildings, his prose is stylized and formalistic, and it's marked by a similar sense of playfulness and sadness. What's more, the accusations leveled at Simon in his private life echo criticisms Mr. Barthelme's own work has received: as various characters put it, Simon is unserious, he doesn't care about people as individuals and his ''cheapo irony'' reduces people's emotions to the status of glib jokes. ''You worry about the way I say things,'' a woman tells him, ''but you don't worry about what I mean.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: A Taste For Death
author: P D James
pull_quote: A TASTE FOR DEATH. By P. D. James. 459 pages. Knopf. $18.95.   WE find dead bodies, excitingly enough, in the opening sentence of P. D. James's 10th and latest novel, ''A Taste for Death'' - bodies ''discovered at 8:45 on the morning of Wednesday 18 September by Miss Emily Wharton, a 65-year-old spinster of the parish of St. Matthew's in Paddington, London, and Darren Wilkes, aged 10, of no particular parish as far as he knew or cared.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Alone Together
author: Elena Bonner
pull_quote: ALONE TOGETHER. By Elena Bonner.   Translated by Alexander Cook. Illustrated. 270 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95. WHILE in the United   States for medical treatment early this year, Yelena G. Bonner wrote what she calls a chronicle of her years in exile in Gorky with her husband, Dr. Andrei D. Sakharov. ''Alone Together'' is an account of their battle against ill health, loneliness and constant harassment by Soviet officials for their efforts on behalf of their fellow citizens' human rights.
headline: Books; The Sakharovs

title: To The Land Of The Cattails
author: Aharon Appelfeld
pull_quote: TO THE LAND OF THE CATTAILS. By Aharon Appelfeld. Translated by Jeffrey M. Green. 148 pages. Weidenfeld & Nicolson. $14.95. IT is the summer of 1938. A mother and her son have made their way eastward from Austria to Bukovina, traveling first by train, then by horse and carriage. The mother, Toni, is a woman of 34. Seventeen years ago she ran away from a traditional Jewish home in the region together with a non-Jew; once they reached Vienna, they married and had a child, Rudi, but by the time she was 20 she was divorced. Now, after coming into a legacy from one of her many lovers, she has been seized by an urge to revisit her native village and see the parents with whom she has lost touch, taking Rudi with her.   In terms of nature, Toni is obeying a deep homing instinct. In terms of history - but perhaps she has no choice in the matter - she is traveling in a disastrously wrong direction.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Mother's Recompense
author: Edith Wharton
pull_quote: THE MOTHER'S RECOMPENSE. By Edith Wharton. Introduction by Louis Auchincloss. 272 pages. Charles Scribner's Sons. Cloth, $15.95; paper, $8.95. ''The Mother's Recompense,'' first published in 1925 and out of print for more than 30 years, recapitulates many of the themes mapped out in Edith Wharton's better-known works: the tension between domestic entrapment and rootless freedom; the dues exacted by family and society, and the costs of illicit passion in the highly stratified, manner-conscious world of the American upper class. Though one might dispute Louis Auchincloss's contention that the novel ''is really the last of her major fictions'' - it marks a precipitous falling off from ''The Age of Innocence,'' published five years earlier - it does stand as a sort of transitional piece between her masterly early work and the trite, blowsy effusions that were to follow.
headline: Books of The Times; Daughters and Lovers

title: Staying At The Top
author: Sonny Kleinfield.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STAYING AT THE TOP The Life of a CEO. By Sonny Kleinfield. 298 pp. New York: New American Library. $17.95.    IF you ever wondered what a chief executive officer eats for breakfast, this is the book for you. ''Staying at the Top'' is an exhaustive examination of the day-to-day doings of Hicks Waldron, the chief executive officer of Avon Products. Sonny Kleinfield, a reporter for The New York Times, tracked Mr. Waldron in his office, in his home and on his corporate jet in an attempt to make clear to the rest of us what, exactly, a C.E.O. does. ''The world of the chief executive officer is a mysterious one, rarely penetrated by anyone but those who live in it. The chief executive fills a range of roles: coach, politician, diplomat, Sun King, and Roman god,'' Mr. Kleinfield writes.
headline: Very Nice. Lovely, What's the Next Meeting?

title: Dreamgirl: My Life As A Supreme
author: Mary Wilson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DREAMGIRL My Life as a Supreme. By Mary Wilson with Patricia Romanowski and Ahrgus Juilliard. Illustrated. 292 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $16.95.    EARLY in her autobiography about her years with Motown's premier hit makers of the 1960's, Mary Wilson recounts how as a child she was beaten for soiling her aunt's gowns while playing dress-up. Punishment from authority figures hammered home a lesson - ''maintain peace, no matter what the cost'' - that Ms. Wilson retained even when the gowns were provided by Berry Gordy Jr., the founder and owner of Motown Records, who intended to promote the glamour of the ascendant Supreme, Diana (formerly Diane) Ross. Every successful musical group needs members who hold the act together, who feel without question they are part of an operation greater than themselves. Ms. Wilson was the adhesive of the Supremes, the group that symbolizes Motown for many people. In the triumphant afterglow of Motown's 25th-anniversary television special, various general histories of the company (Nelson George's ''Where Did Our Love Go?'' remains the most coherent and thoughtful) have appeared. But never has a Motown veteran spoken out as a first-person witness from inside Hitsville. Ms. Wilson, who lives in Hollywood and works as a singer, took the title of this book from the Broadway musical ''Dreamgirls.'' (She has called the play ''dead on''; Miss Ross resisted seeing it, claiming it was a distortion.) Despite obvious temptations, Ms. Wilson keeps nostalgic gush and embittered polemic to a minimum.

ANTON CHEKHOV'S father was an unsuccessful grocer in Taganrog, a somnolent seaport in southern Russia that by the mid 19th century had lost whatever prosperity it had once enjoyed. He was also a domestic tyrant who beat his children virtually every day, in the conviction that he was carrying out the will of God, and who forced them to spend long hours toiling in his grimy little shop under dismal conditions - on one occasion, when a rat drowned in a barrel of oil, he sent for a priest to recite a purification ritual so he could continue offering the oil for sale.   In spite of all this he was not without his affectionate impulses or his abilities (he taught himself to play the violin, for instance), and later in life his famous son was able to look back at him with remarkably little resentment. But at the same time Chekhov's childhood was overshadowed by hardship and fear; and the family's situation became even more wretched during his adolescence when it moved to Moscow (where his father had decamped to avoid being thrown into prison for debt).

(Ages 5 to 9)    PERSONALLY, I've never wondered what it would be like without a bellybutton. Even though one of my first, pleasant memories is of a game I played with my father - he'd tickle me and say, ''Button, button. Who's got the button?'' and I'd giggle -it never occurred to me that he might have been talking about bellybuttons. (I'll have to ask him.) Sure, I've compared bellybuttons. I've noticed that some people, like me, are innies; others are outies. I've decided, as have other innies, that ours are better - rounder, cuter, neater. I've even felt sorry for outies. But that's the extent of it, and you may think I've spent far too much time on the subject as it is. William Kennedy and his son Brendan have spent considerably more time - enough to collaborate on a story about what would happen if you woke up one day and discovered that your bellybutton was missing! WHENEVER he replied to an inquiring stranger that, yes, he was Vladimir Nabokov, the novelist in turn would ask, ''And what do you do?'' as though ''Nabokov'' were a vocation. The well-rehearsed role he played so well - urbane, polymath emigre, playful yet aloof - is nicely documented in Andrew Field's unauthorized life, ''VN,'' his third book about the writer. Mr. Field's efforts to get past the public persona, however, have been less successful. There is a telling moment in one of the earlier books when he observes Nabokov enter a room while putting on a tie and hears him speak to his wife: '' 'Darling, can I really not write about him?' . . . Then he suddenly saw me. - 'Oh, I'm terribly sorry, Andrew. I didn't realize you were still here.' The word stress was strangely out of place.'' This was apparently one of the few times Mr. Field saw the author with his guard (and necktie) down; had he witnessed such spontaneity more often, his analysis of the private man would almost certainly be more penetrating.

And true, the joys and sorrows abounding here have a lot to do with shoe sales, hip size, screenwriting contracts and an elusive crowd known as ''boyfriends'' - not exactly the issues that once ignited revolution. But Ms. Heimel's sensibility, like that of most feminists over the years, is anchored in life, not politics. SO much has been and is still being written about Voltaire that his own works are probably less often read than are the books discussing them. Lytton Strachey, whom A. J. Ayer is fond of quoting, remarked about Voltaire more than 80 years ago: ''Everyone, it is true, has heard of him; but who has read him? It is by his name that ye shall know him, and not by his works.'' It would therefore be unreasonable to expect that this rather short essay by a nonspecialist, and intended for a nonspecialized audience, should add much to what has already been said many times about Voltaire and his works. Nor can the book claim much originality for having been written by an Englishman, since Voltaire's well-known indebtedness to England has been more than amply repaid by England's disproportionately large contribution to Voltaire scholarship. Much more is yet to come. The Voltaire Foundation of Oxford University - where Sir Alfred was educated and where he long occupied a distinguished chair of philosophy -is sponsoring the gigantic endeavor of bringing out a new edition of the ''Complete Works of Voltaire,'' the first such in more than a century.

TO subtitle a biography, as William Griffin does, ''A Dramatic Life'' makes for great expectations - Lord Byron's wenching, or the South African poet Roy Campbell's buckaroo spirit, or D. H. Lawrence's flight with Frau Baronin Frieda von Richthofen. C. S. Lewis -scholar, novelist, science fiction fantasist and Christian apologist - by contrast lived the timorous life of an Oxford don. Drama is remarkable to his existence for having been absent from it. ''I love the monotonies of life. . . . I never 'want things to happen,' '' he confessed to a newspaper in 1946. And, tellingly, Lewis loathed ''Childe Harold'' and ''Don Juan''; he was once cruel to Campbell (about which Mr. Griffin misinforms us); and he thought ''Lady Chatterley's Lover'' paganism redivivus, which perhaps it was. Lewis wasn't the least interested in Mozart or Monteverdi (''that detestable art which humans called music''); he developed a puritan aversion to the cavalier poet John Betjeman (a pupil); and his great intelligence may come to be seen as mostly the fortunate affliction of photographic memory: ''I remember everything I ever read, and bits of it pop up uninvited.''

AT first glance a history of smell seems an amusing, if not trivial, pursuit, one of those characteristically French luxury items we might enjoy but for which there is little practical use. In fact, that is not at all the case with Alain Corbin's book ''The Foul and the Fragrant: Odor and the French Social Imagination,'' translated by Miriam L. Kochan with the assistance of Roy Porter and Christopher Prendergast. It is not only serious, but interesting and important; one of those studies that profoundly alter both our understanding of social life and of history. It exemplifies an epistemological position that French scholars have had a leading role in articulating, one that insists on the historically constructed (and therefore relative) meaning of all phenomena, including those seemingly natural functions such as eating and childbearing, those purely biological sensations such as taste and smell.   Uncovering the history of supposedly natural experiences provides, according to this outlook, crucial insight into the workings of social power. For social power depends on the ability to define and impose meaning - the meaning of behavior, of physical characteristics, of relationships among different groups. In addition, debates about meaning, differences of opinion and interpretation, are forms of social conflict; reading them provides a key to contests for power in any age.

AHARON APPELFELD'S habitual strategy as a writer haunted by the Holocaust is to concentrate on its historical margins, either prelude or aftermath. ''IT was years later too that I realized Buddy had used the wrong word,'' says the narrator of one of Margaret Atwood's new stories. ''It wasn't an identity bracelet, it was an identification bracelet. The difference escaped me at the time. But maybe it was the right word after all, and what Buddy was handing over to me was his identity, some key part of himself that I was expected to keep for him and watch over.''   As it turns out, this narrator, who fancies being the trustee of Buddy's identity, is herself struggling to define an appropriate self (she even tries to disguise her family's penchant for rustic living so as to appear more ''normal'') and most of Ms. Atwood's characters find themselves in similar predicaments. For them, identity is not a given or a neat package of attributes and accomplishments, but rather an elusive, mysterious thing, made up of other people's impressions and a select anthology of one's own actions and imaginings. It can be thrust upon one unwittingly by friends and lovers, but it can also be chosen - or affirmed - as an act of will.

IT was the peculiar genius of Paul Celan to be able to strip language of its normal socioeconomic occasions without cutting the lines that lead language to the heart. For all the celebrated difficulty of Celan's poems - dense constellations of morphemes, word elements packed like molecules - they are hard only when you try to think about them. At first touch (what William Carlos Williams called, in a noble phrase, the poem's ''intention to impress'') Celan's poems come to us from a warm sense of life, of paying attention and taking care.
headline: A LOVE AFFAIR WITH SILENCE

title: Bad Man Ballad
author: Scott R. Sanders.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BAD MAN BALLAD By Scott R. Sanders. 241 pp. New York: Bradbury Press. $14.95. (Ages 12 and up)    SCOTT SANDERS likes American legends. In ''Hear the Wind Blow,'' his last book for children, he fashioned elegant stories from old folk songs, retelling some and altering others to suit himself. The result was lively, irreverent and good for reading aloud - or, as the School Library Journal helpfully said of it, ''effective for oral sharing.''
headline: An Orphan Tracks a Giant

title: Hugh Pine And The Good Place
author: Janwillem van de Wetering
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HUGH PINE AND THE GOOD PLACE By Janwillem van de Wetering. Illustrated by Lynn Munsinger. 64 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $10.95. (Ages 5 to 9)    IN this age of dreary sequels, Hugh Pine's return is triumphant. Here, the wise and gentle porcupine is in search of The Good Place, somewhere he can live undisturbed by the strife between gray and red squirrels, the wearying incompetence of rabbits and the playful games of baby foxes. From his favorite pine tree on Maine's coast, Hugh Pine sees a tiny island, a dollop of land afloat in Sorry Bay, hardly big enough to accommodate its one tree. The place seems magical, far but near, familiar but venturesome, and it beckons with a promise of tranquil isolation. Hugh wants to get there, away from his role as peacemaker and troubleshooter, to live in misanthropic bliss.
headline: People's Porcupine

title: The Stranger
author: Chris Van Allsburg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE STRANGER Written and illustrated by Chris Van Allsburg. Unpaged. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $15.95. (Ages 4 and up)    CHRIS VAN ALLSBURG'S magnificently illustrated books have been receiving awards since 1979, when he created ''The Garden of Abdul Gasazi'' because, he wrote, he was ''interested in applying fine-art drawing style and sensitivity to the problems of illustration.'' Text and pictures have dazzled readers as Mr. Van Allsburg has moved from rich and muscular black-and-white drawings to a cool palette that sometimes suggests the Pointillist masterpieces of Georges Seurat.
headline: Jack Frost's Amnesia

title: After The Last Sky
author: Edward W. Said. Photographs by Jean Mohr.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AFTER THE LAST SKY Palestinian Lives. By Edward W. Said. Photographs by Jean Mohr. 174 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. Cloth, $22.95. Paper, $14.95.    WHEREVER the Palestinians dwell, they are outsiders, defined not by their qualities or by their own perception of self, but by their otherness. On their ancestral lands they are the ''non-Jews'' or the ''Arabs of Judea and Samaria,'' labels imposed by their conquerors. Among their fellow Arabs, except in Jordan, they are aliens. In the West, they are regarded at best as refugees, at worst (and more widely) as terrorists.
headline: ACTS OF CONTINUANCE

title: Populuxe
author: Thomas Hine
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: POPULUXE By Thomas Hine. Illustrated. 184 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $29.95.    THE endpapers of ''Populuxe'' might almost have been peeled from the walls of a once-posh guest suite at the Eden Roc Hotel in Miami Beach or salvaged, perhaps, from the ruins of the over-applianced model kitchen in which Richard Nixon debated Nikita Khrushchev in 1959. The hideous stuff is thick, deeply embossed with a random assortment of dimples and dots and overprinted in a loud pattern of yellow, salmon and poison green that combines asteroids (or are they satellites?), a parody of an International Style grid, and boomerangs aligned in such a way as to conjure up a vision of an infinity of 11-inch television screens looking out for customers from the windows of a suburban strip showroom back when baby boomers were in diapers. That style - a sort of bowl-o-rama moderne out of the futuristic cartoon show ''The Jetsons'' - has never really had a satisfactory name, much less a cogent apologia.
headline: DO THE CALIFORNIA DIP

title: Peeping In The Shell
author: Faith McNulty. Illustrated by Irene Brady.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PEEPING IN THE SHELL A Whooping Crane Is Hatched. By Faith McNulty. Illustrated by Irene Brady. 58 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $10.95. (Ages 8 to 12)    THE story of the fight for survival of whooping cranes in America is probably, along with the story of the bald eagle and DDT, the most stirring example of environmentalism. Both illustrious birds - one the winged spirit of our national liberty, the other the ancient Oriental bird of life itself -have been swept to the purlieus of extinction by the shortsightedness of Industrial Age America. And both have been the beneficiaries of powerful popular movements to save them.
headline: In The Purlieus of Extinction

title: The Railway Station
author: Jeffrey Richards and John M. MacKenzie. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE RAILWAY STATION A Social History. By Jeffrey Richards and John M. MacKenzie. Illustrated. 440 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $22.50.    THIS is the first book to identify and begin to come to terms with a worldwide phenomenon: whenever a big-city or small-town railroad station from the glory days of railroading is either demolished or replaced by something less magnificent, an extraordinary number of people in the area unexpectedly experience a great sense of loss. As the authors of ''The Railway Station,'' Jeffrey Richards and John M. MacKenzie, both historians at the University of Lancaster in England, put it, ''What was it about the station that was so fascinating?'' Once asked, the implications of the question are obvious enough - is this nostalgia, meaning that people are clinging to objects or ideas that serve little or no purpose? Or do stations have functions, not yet clearly identified, perhaps, that go beyond providing a place for getting on and off trains?
headline: POINTS OF DEPARTURE

title: Rembrandt Takes A Walk
author: Mark Strand
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: REMBRANDT TAKES A WALK By Mark Strand. Illustrated by Red Grooms. Unpaged. New York: Clarkson N. Potter/Crown Publishers. $14.95.    TO please his mother, Tom goes off to spend the night at his wealthy but eccentric Uncle Morton's. Although he's got ''tons of money,'' Uncle Morton dresses like a bum and lives in a decrepit mansion where the creepy hallways are illuminated by a single light bulb. Dinner chez Morton is half a hamburger and a few forkfuls of canned peas; Tom is additionally put out to discover that not only is Uncle Morton's refrigerator devoid of snacks but his (black-and-white) television seems permanently on the fritz.
headline: No TV, But Check Out The Paintings

title: The Random House Book Of Mother Goose
author: Arnold Lobel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE RANDOM HOUSE BOOK OF MOTHER GOOSE Selected and illustrated by Arnold Lobel. 176 pp. New York: Random House. $14.95. (All ages)    THE coming together of a gifted artist and a great children's classic is always interesting. If the union is successful the work will be reinterpreted, given not only new life but a subtly different meaning. It may even be, essentially, reborn, rising like a new-fledged phoenix from the ashes of its earlier incarnations.
headline: Roly-poly Fun and Feasting

title: How Nato Weakens The West
author: Melvyn Krauss
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
HOW NATO WEAKENS THE WEST By Melvyn Krauss. 271 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95. 

INTO the often surreal and overcomplicated world of scholastic foreign policy studies has come the economist Melvyn Krauss, of New York University and the Hoover Institution at Stanford University, with a simple solution to the problems of American foreign relations: ''The United States must abandon NATO.'' In his view, this will unite and electrify the Europeans, end their destructive defense dependency and provide them the incentive to halt their appeasement of the Soviet Union. Only if forced into greater self-reliance will they abandon the welfare statism that has crippled their defense efforts, and only in the absence of the American shield will they have a real need to pull together rather than apart.

According to Mr. Krauss, such a move not only will awaken Europe but will save the United States $150 billion per year, revitalize everyone's economy (everyone's, that is, except the Russians') and give Americans more resources and a free hand for sorting out problems in the third world, without the paralysis attendant on multilateralism.
headline: IS SEPARATE STRONGER?

title: The Invisible Bar
author: Karen Berger Morello. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE INVISIBLE BAR The Woman Lawyer in America 1638 to the Present. By Karen Berger Morello. Illustrated. 271 pp. New York: Random House. $19.95.    IN the last 13 years, the number of women who practice law in the United States increased nearly tenfold, from 12,000 to 116,000. And in the last 20 years, the proportion of women in law schools rose from 4 percent to over 40 percent. If this trend continues, by the close of the century half of all the attorneys in America will be women -though women were virtually excluded from the profession during the three preceding centuries.
headline: DO NOT APPROACH THE BENCH MIRACLE ON GRUB STREET

title: Style And Substance
author: Judith Martin.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STYLE AND SUBSTANCE A Comedy of Manners. By Judith Martin. 274 pp. New York: Atheneum. $15.95.    AS Miss Manners, Judith Martin has often warned us not to boast. With the title of her novel, Mrs. Martin compels us to compare the book to another comedy of manners, Jane Austen's ''Sense and Sensibility.'' Against such rough competition, Mrs. Martin is bound to seem the weaker sister. On the other hand, there are worse fates than failing to be as witty or wise as Jane Austen.
headline: ALWAYS READY FOR THE RIGHT WRONG MAN

title: Autonomy And Solidarity
author: Peter Dews
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AUTONOMY AND SOLIDARITY Jurgen Habermas Interviews. Edited by Peter Dews. 219 pp. New York: Verso/Schocken Books. Cloth, $27.95. Paper, $9.95.    One of the major ironies of contemporary thought is surely the fact that a champion of enlightened rationality is now more likely to speak German than French. No one represents this reversal of roles more clearly than the Frankfurt philosopher and sociologist Jurgen Habermas. Vigorously defending what he calls the ''uncompleted project of modernity'' as an emancipatory learning process, he has come squarely into conflict with French poststructuralists such as Jacques Derrida and Jean-Francois Lyotard. Mr. Habermas's targets, to be sure, have also been domestic, as evidenced by his courageous intervention in the German debate following President Reagan's visit to Bitburg cemetery over the ''normalization'' of the Nazi past by certain German historians. But in the main, he has taken aim recently at the postmodernist, poststructuralist onslaught from Paris, whose repercussions have been felt in the British-American world as well.
headline: STANDING UP TO PARIS AND BITBURG

title: The Flame Bearers
author: Kim Chernin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE FLAME BEARERS By Kim Chernin. 276 pp. New York: Random House. $16.95.    IN Kim Chernin's Jewish feminist Creation myth, Chochma, the Bride, also called Mother Compassionate, has been displaced by her son, Shaddai the Almighty, and goes ''out of heaven to live only with the earth, to console the women and men she made with sparks from her own fire.'' A sect of Jewish women known as the Flam-Trogers, the Flame Bearers, has secretly carried on her traditions, her work on this earth through the ages. The women can light candles by cupping their hands and commanding the flame, an incarnation of the heylige ikra, or sacred spark. The women await Ha Melamed Gadol, the Great Teacher, whose arrival will bring about an end of days, an end of human suffering.
headline: DAUGHTERS OF THE ISRAELIS

title: Rumpelstiltskin
author: Brothers Grimm
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RUMPELSTILTSKIN By the Brothers Grimm. Adapted and illustrated by Paul O. Zelinsky. Unpaged. New York: E. P. Dutton. $12.95. (Ages 4 and up)    THE pleasures of Paul Zelinsky's newly retold and illustrated ''Rumpelstiltskin'' are much like those of showing a medieval Book of Hours to a favorite child. Adult and child can delight together in the richness of color, gilt and detail, those crenelated castles, magical landscapes, patterned interiors and, above all, in the sheer quantity of human and animal life, the range of experience captured in such art.
headline: Spin Me Some Gold!

title: Paper Doll
author: Jim Shepard
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PAPER DOLL By Jim Shepard. 228 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $15.95.    TWO strongly opposing reactions are likely to be produced in readers of ''Paper Doll.'' The first is admiration: Jim Shepard, who has been much praised for his first novel, ''Flights,'' confirms here that he is a superb literary technician. The second is bafflement: Why did he want to write this novel?
headline: THE DEATH OF THE BALL TURRET GUNNER

title: Pageant
author: Kathryn Lasky
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PAGEANT By Kathryn Lasky. 221 pp. New York: Four Winds Press. $12.95. (Ages 12 and up)    FOR anyone who lived through the Kennedy years, the dreams and glory of that time are tough to communicate, especially to younger people. Kathryn Lasky, in her lovely new novel, ''Pageant,'' has finally done it. Her heroine, 14-year-old Sarah Benjamin, has strong opinions. The black stableboy statues decorating the yards at the edge of her wealthy Indianapolis neighborhood are ''racist.'' The only possible man to support for President, despite her mostly Republican eighth-grade schoolmates, is John Kennedy. And when things get tough, the only reliable person, the only one who can give her a phrase to get her writing project started or an idea to inspire her science experiment, is her big sister Marla.
headline: Wanting the World to Be Different

title: The Return Of The Indian
author: Lynne Reid Banks
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE RETURN OF THE INDIAN By Lynne Reid Banks Illustrated by William Geldart. 189 pp. New York: Doubleday & Company. $12.95. (Ages 8 to 12)    ILIKE the way Comanche Indians speak of love.   When a Comanche wants to say ''I love you,'' he says, ''My mind cries for you.'' When a Comanche wants to say something is ''lovable'' or ''beautiful,'' he says it is ''mind-cry-able.''
headline: Small Is Mind-cry-able

title: Truman
author: Roy Jenkins
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TRUMAN By Roy Jenkins. Illustrated. 232 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $17.95.    ANYONE who reads this latest book by one of Britain's most renowned politician-writers must wonder what we Americans have done wrong not to have the participation of eminent scholars in our own political life. Roy Jenkins, current M.P., former Chancellor of the Exchequer and a founder of the Social Democrats, is the author of a dozen books. This biography of Harry S. Truman is based on secondary sources, and by no means did the author survey all the secondary literature. But to criticize the book for that reason is to miss its strength, for Mr. Jenkins has produced a short, well-written, intelligent biography that doesn't grind any axes but is refreshingly opinionated in the British style.
headline: A PROFESSIONAL'S OPINION

title: The Dallas Titans Get Ready For Bed
author: Karla Kuskin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DALLAS TITANS GET READY FOR BED by Karla Kuskin. Illustrated by Marc Simont. 41 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $11.95. (Ages 5 to 9)    THIS is a neat, funny book. But it's a much better book for boys than for girls, which is the fault of football, not of the author, Karla Kuskin, or the illustrator, Marc Simont. ''The Dallas Titans Get Ready for Bed'' is the second book by the Kuskin-Simont team, based on the wonderful premise that even the most awesome adults have to get dressed - and undressed, in the case of the football team. People in a state of undress are of course vulnerable, here, endearingly vulnerable. They are not heroic, frightening, dignified or awesome. Which is doubtless why coaches are so fond of the saw, ''They all put their pants on one leg at a time.''
headline: Bedtime For Hulks

title: Working Space
author: Frank Stella
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WORKING SPACE By Frank Stella. Illustrated. 177 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. Cloth, $30. Paper, $14.95.    FRANK STELLA'S ''Working Space'' is a mass of exciting art talk teetering perilously on a narrow conceit: a strained parallel between the formal problems of Italian Mannerist painting four centuries ago and those of abstract painting today. So much about the analogy is fishy that a book longer than Mr. Stella's could be written in rebuttal, but it would be a foolish book. In the operations of critical intelligence, major artists are special agents, most effective when granted a license to kill. Genius's gaze is partial, but what it sees stays seen.
headline: SLAMMING VISION INTO HIGH GEAR

title: Dinosaurs Divorce
author: Laurene Kransy Brown
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DINOSAURS DIVORCE A Guide for Changing Families. Written and illustrated by Laurene Krasny Brown and Marc Brown. Boston: The Atlantic Monthly Press. $13.95. (Ages 4 and up)    FOR the child buffeted by divorce, this book could serve as a portable psychotherapist equipped with a whimsical sense of humor. Through a gaggle of side-splitting dinosaurs, it offers children aged roughly 4 to 8 (but appealing to older children and even adults) a working definition of divorce. And it charts the rocky passage they must negotiate after daddy (or, in these times, mommy) has moved out. By skillfully leavening the child's viewpoint with professional wisdom, this ''Guide for Changing Families,'' as it is somewhat euphemistically subtitled, will instruct beleaguered grown-ups too.
headline: After Brontosaurus Moves Out

title: Quest For The Real Samoa
author: Lowell D. Holmes. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: QUEST FOR THE REAL SAMOA The Mead/Freeman Controversy & Beyond. By Lowell D. Holmes. Illustrated. 209 pp. South Hadley, Mass.: Bergin & Garvey. $29.95.  IN 1983 Derek Freeman published his book ''Margaret Mead and Samoa: The Making and Unmaking of an Anthropological Myth,'' in which he claimed to have exposed what he has called a wholesale deception unmatched in the history of the behavioral sciences. He was referring to Mead's fledgling field study that won popular fame as ''Coming of Age in Samoa'' (1928). Systematically demolishing Mead's methods, findings and characterization of Samoan culture, Mr. Freeman drew a portrait of an aggressive, violent, sexually inhibited Samoa that contrasted dramatically with Mead's version. His purpose in this had less to do with understanding Samoa than with the unmasking of the ''cultural determinism'' supposedly perpetrated by Franz Boas on all of American anthropology - and on the public at large. By undermining the details of Mead's classic case illustrating how culture can shape the experience of adolescence, Mr. Freeman professed to be restoring the balance in the nature-nurture debate.
headline: MEAD'S MEANING

title: Ellen Bray
author: Jane Julian
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ELLEN BRAY. By Jane Julian. (Morrow, $16.95.) One wants to praise a novel as readable and energetic as ''Ellen Bray.'' Set in a copper-mining community in 19th-century Cornwall, the story evokes time and place and treats the miners' hardscrabble lives seriously.
headline: FICTION: IN SHORT

title: Theodore Dreiser
author: Richard Lingeman. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THEODORE DREISER At the Gates of the City 1871-1907. By Richard Lingeman. Illustrated. 478 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $22.95.    THIS first volume of Richard Lingeman's two-part biography of Theodore Dreiser reaches only seven years beyond the initial publication of ''Sister Carrie,'' when, in the wake of early neglect, the book was successfully reissued. Its 1907 revival - and victorious arrival - is an appropriate biographical climax. A first novel by the son of a German Catholic immigrant, ''Sister Carrie'' is also the first recognizably ''American'' novel - American in the way we feel it now. Springing up in a period when the novel's tone was governed chiefly by aristocrats of English-speaking stock - William Dean Howells, Edith Wharton, Henry James - Dreiser's driven prose uncovers the unmistakable idiom of a raw Chicago and the New York of dumbwaiters and flophouses. To find one's way into the streets and flats of Dreiser's two cities is to experience the unfolding of literary history - to see how the English novel, itself an immigrant, finally pocketed its ''papers'' and became naturalized.
headline: MIRACLE ON GRUB STREET

title: The Purple Coat
author: Amy Hest
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PURPLE COAT By Amy Hest. Illustrated by Amy Schwartz. Unpaged. New York: Four Winds Press. $12.95. (Ages 5 to 9)  A NEW COAT FOR ANNA By Harriet Ziefert. Illustrated by Anita Lobel. Unpaged. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $10.95. (Ages 5 to 9)

author: David Hughes
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

THE JOKE OF THE CENTURY By David Hughes. 223 pp. New York: Taplinger Publishing Company. $14.95.

Bunter, the rebel who was always defeated within a just set of traditions ''inexplicable to infants or foreigners or women,'' be-came the imaginative pattern by which generations of English boys formed their world view. ]
 risking punishment by going out of bounds to meet a national crisis, were rushing to the rescue in tugs and steamers and having the time of their lives.''

author: Laura Geringer

pull_quote: MOLLY'S NEW WASHING MACHINE By Laura Geringer. Illustrated by Petra Mathers. 32 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $11.95. (Ages 4 to 8)    AFTER seeing Laura Geringer's book ''A Three Hat Day,'' with its rich playfulness of language, and Petra Mathers's ''Maria Theresa,'' with its distinctive pictorial style, one naturally has high hopes at the prospect of an exciting collaboration between them.
