headline: Misappliance

title: Just Barbara
author: Barbara Woodhouse. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: JUST BARBARA My Story. By Barbara Woodhouse. Illustrated. 189 pp. New York: Summit Books. $16.95.    WALKIES! Come along now, all you dog owners and PBS watchers! Heads up, choke chain collar on, off we go, nose by the left heel, ears up, eyes bright. Don't mess about there, the man with the Yorkshire terrier, keep him alert!
headline: A WOMAN'S BEST FRIEND

title: Rising From The Plains
author: John Mcphee
pull_quote: RISING FROM THE PLAINS. By John McPhee. 214 pages. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $15.95. It would almost be unfair to make notes while reading one of John McPhee's fascinating books that explore some out-of-the-way corner of the American landscape and its inhabitants. They are comparable to Joseph Mitchell's model writing on the Mohawk Indians or the bottom of New York Harbor or any other subject that he has mined for nuggets of information. Among professional writers, there is an added pleasure in watching how authors in their class construct their factual narratives. By covering New York and America like some foreign country, they set a very high standard of originality for writers and readers.   Mr. McPhee's facts are delivered so artfully that attempting to record all the felicitous language would take too long and break the mood he creates. Obviously, an author's hand is behind the sentences; but the machinery is hardly visible, and it neither creaks nor seems too well oiled. As he demonstrates in ''Rising From the Plains,'' his latest excursion into uncharted territory, even when handling complex material, good prose need never be prosaic. The book is part of his series on geology and geologists that began with ''Basin and Range'' and continued with ''In Suspect Terrain.'' The series has come together as a unified theme in The New Yorker, where the text originally appeared, under the title, ''Annals of the Former World.''
headline: Books: Plains Geology

title: Maus
author: Art Spiegelman
pull_quote: MAUS: A Survivor's Tale. By Art Spiegelman. Illustrated. 159 pages. Pantheon. Paper, $8.95. ART SPIEGELMAN'S ''Maus:   A Survivor's Tale'' is a Holocaust memoir with a remarkable difference. True, one thread of it recapitulates the all-too-familiar story of the Spiegelman family in Poland from 1935 to 1944 struggling to avoid the inevitable fate of Auschwitz. There are the loss of property, the dawning sense of peril, the black markets, the ''selections,'' the cellar hiding places, the briberies, the betrayals and finally the truck to the gate with the sign over it reading, ''Arbeit macht frei.''   But there are four unusual innovations to the way Mr. Spiegelman has told his story. In ascending order of surprise, these are as follows: First, he explores the relations of the surviving generation and its children, especially the guilt visited by the former upon the latter. The adventures of the Spiegelmans in Poland are told by Vladek, the surviving family member, to his grown-up son, Artie, who begins his narrative: ''I went out to see my Father in Rego Park. I hadn't seen him in a long time - we weren't that close. He had aged a lot since I saw him last. My Mother's suicide and his two heart attacks had taken their toll.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Voyagers To The West
author: Bernard Bailyn
pull_quote: VOYAGERS TO THE WEST. A Passage in the Peopling of America on the Eve of the Revolution. By Bernard Bailyn, with the assistance of Barbara DeWolfe. Illustrated. 668 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $30. AT the time of the Declaration of Independence nearly one American in 10 had arrived in British North America within the previous 15 years. After the war of 1756-60, with French rivalry no longer a threat, there had been a sharp increase in the rate of immigration to the American Colonies: the figure of some 221,500 new arrivals for the period 1760-75 compares with an estimated 700,000 for the entire century and a half before 1760.   This flow of population was a historical fact of major importance. As Bernard Bailyn observes in ''Voyagers to the West,'' it has been overshadowed by the political struggle of the same period, leading up to the American Revolution, but even without that struggle it would inevitably have altered the relationship between Britain and America.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Emily Dickinson
author: Cynthia Griffin Wolff
pull_quote: EMILY DICKINSON. By Cynthia Griffin Wolff. Illustrated. 641 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $25.    ONLY one photograph of Emily Dickinson is known to exist. It's a daguerrotype, taken in 1847 or 1848, when the poet was about 17; and it shows a plain, skinny girl, reticent and somewhat ill at ease in aspect - a girl whose air of mystery would nurture all the legends that have accumulated around her name: the old maid of Amherst, doomed to spinsterhood by the demands of her tyrannical father; the lovelorn ''poetess,'' grieving over a doomed affair with an unavailable man; the dotty recluse, given to dressing in white and adamant in her refusal of transactions with the outside world.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Chekhov
author: Henri Troyat
pull_quote: ANY contemporary playwright who thinks he is alone in feeling paranoiac should read ''Chekhov,'' Henri Troyat's masterly new biography (published by E. P. Dutton). Though Chekhov could withstand physical deprivation and severe illness, in one area he was extremely vulnerable, and that was in his attitude toward the judgment of others about his art. He took everything to heart, especially rejection.   When a famous actress turned down his first play, ''Platonov,'' he destroyed the manuscript. A theater company rejected his second play, ''The Wood Demon,'' ''for want of effects, situations, and interesting characters,'' and he announced that he would never write another play. After the first production of ''The Sea Gull'' proved to be disastrous, he reaffirmed his abdication: ''If I live 700 years, I'll never give a theater another play. When it comes to theater, I'm doomed to failure.''
headline: THE THIN-SKINNED ANTON CHEKHOV

title: The Cycles Of American History
author: Arthur M Jr Schlesinger
pull_quote: THE CYCLES OF AMERICAN HISTORY.   By Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr. 498 pages. Houghton Mifflin. $22.95. DON'T be put off by the fact that ''The Cycles of American History'' is a collection of essays. Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr.'s new book is not one of those exercises in self-regard and drawer-cleansing in which writers of note have been known to indulge. Mr. Schlesinger has a thesis or two or 20 about the nature and workings of the American polity that link these eloquent pieces and give them historical weight and contemporary urgency.   His pattern here is to take an enduring issue - say, the tension between the principles of ''free enterprise'' and ''affirmative government'' - put it in historical perspective and then offer his analysis of where we are today and his opinions on where we ought to be. His sympathies remain mainstream liberal.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Learned Pigs & Fireproof Women
author: Ricky Jay
pull_quote: LEARNED PIGS & FIREPROOF WOMEN. By Ricky Jay. Illustrated. 340 pages. Villard Books. $29.95.    THERE are more ways than one of earning your living.   You can stand on a galloping horse, for example, with your face covered with a swarm of bees, or cram yourself into a crate -by the look of it, scarcely big enough to contain a small child - along with six dozen bottles. Alternatively you can drive a tractor through the streets of a strange town while you are blindfolded. Or perhaps you would find more job satisfaction in lying down, arching your back and supporting a piano on your stomach, while the pianist stands on your thighs and accompanies you as you sing ''Ireland Must Be Heaven 'Cause My Mother Came From There.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Collected Stories, 1948-1986
author: Wright Morris
pull_quote: COLLECTED STORIES, 1948-1986. By Wright Morris. 274 pages. Harper & Row. $17.95. ''In the taxi to Manhattan,'' writes Wright Morris in one of the best stories in this volume, ''Hazlitt was moved to chat a bit with the driver, but the Plexiglas barrier between them seemed intimidating. Through the tinted windshield, as they approached the city, the October evening skyline was like the opening shot of a movie. Hazlitt had often told his wife that if the sun never rose he might like city living. In the car lights the streets glittered like enamel. It pleased him to note, as they drew near the Plaza Hotel, the horse-drawn hacks lined up along the curb. One of the drivers was a young woman with pigtails, frail as a waif. She held a leather feed bag to the muzzle of her horse, whose pelt shone like patent leather where the harness had worn off the hair.''
headline: Books of The Times; Troubled Relationships

title: Dancing On My Grave
author: Gelsey Kirkland, with Greg Lawrence
pull_quote: DANCING ON MY GRAVE by Gelsey Kirkland, with Greg Lawrence. Illustrated. 286 pages. Doubleday. $17.95. Gelsey Kirkland's ''Dancing on My Grave'' is the talk of the dance world.   Miss Kirkland drags a number of reputations into the dust with her's as she tells the story of her life in dance and her battle with drugs. Some of the gossip in the book -which Miss Kirkland wrote with Greg Lawrence, her husband - is very funny, though hardly surprising. But scandal aside, ''Dancing on My Grave'' may be one of the saddest stories ever written.
headline: Books; Out of Pain

title: The Endless Short Story
author: Ronald Sukenick
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE ENDLESS SHORT STORY By Ronald Sukenick. 132 pp. New York: Fiction Collective. Cloth, $13.95. Paper, $6.95.    ONCE again Ronald Sukenick's peripatetic hero, Ronald Sukenick, is on the road, revisiting his childhood kingdom of Brooklyn, as well as the more exotic landscapes of Paris and California. The postromantic Mr. Sukenick, who teaches English at the University of Colorado, Boulder, still yearns for imaginative transcendence in a world grown violent and banal. ''The Endless Short Story,'' however, unlike his other books, is a more interiorized journey, and Mr. Sukenick's inquiries into the relation of imagination to reality are now fully integrated into his social and cosmic concerns. The ESS (his abbreviation) is a beautiful and poetic work, funny, intellectually challenging and unexpectedly moving.
headline: UNBOOGALOOABLE

title: Moon
author: James Herbert
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MOON. By James Herbert. (Crown, $14.95.) Jon Childes isn't looking for trouble, but he can't help seeing it. Each time he is made faint by dreamy, ghastly images of a corpse being desecrated or a body hacked up, Childes reads in the next morning's paper about just such wretchedness taking place exactly the way he sensed it.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Modern Romances
author: Judy Lopatin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MODERN ROMANCES. By Judy Lopatin. (Fiction Collective, Cloth, $15.95. Paper, $7.95.) Judy Lopatin's first collection of stories trains a quirky, agile intelligence on the New York-Paris axis, locating romance in hospitals, opium dens, law firms, movie theaters.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Wrestling Princess: And Other Stories
author: Judy Corbalis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Additional titles of interest:   ONCE UPON A TIME . . . : Celebrating the Magic of Children's Books in Honor of the Twentieth Anniversary of Reading Is Fundamental. Putnam. Cloth, $14.95.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS: BOOKSHELF

title: The Life And Times Of Congressman John Quincy Adams
author: Leonard L. Richards.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE LIFE AND TIMES OF CONGRESSMAN JOHN QUINCY ADAMS By Leonard L. Richards. 245 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $19.95. 

NO former President has served the United States more dramatically than John Quincy Adams. Denied re-election to the White House by Andrew Jackson in 1828, Adams came back to Washington in 1831 as a member of the House of Representatives where he persistently and zealously championed antislavery measures until he collapsed at his desk and died in 1848. The Southern leader John C. Calhoun called Adams ''a mischievous, bad old man,'' a Northern colleague graced him with the Miltonic epithet ''Old Man Eloquent'' and cheering crowds offered him the public acclaim that neither he nor his father had received in their Presidencies.
headline: OLD MAN ELOQUENT

title: The Well
author: Elizabeth Jolley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WELL By Elizabeth Jolley. 176 pp. New York: Viking. $14.95.  WOMAN IN A LAMPSHADE By Elizabeth Jolley. 229 pp. New York: King Penguin/Penguin Books. Paper, $6.95.    ELIZABETH JOLLEY seems to have a lot of fun when she writes. She lets herself go, laughs a lot, cries a lot, dances every chance she gets (women - women of all ages -dancing, dancing properly or crazily, most often crazily, or at least in delicious uninhibited celebration, is a profoundly Jolleyan motif), gets playfully inventive, then spooks herself with the uncanny, celebrates outrageous behavior and eccentric voices, mocks Paradise, eats an apricot, throws a goofy wedding party, commits a murder or two, hovers about hospitals and old folks' homes because she loves the people there, loves people everywhere, to tell the truth, though there's no hope for them, sadly enough, crippled as they are with guilt and poverty and stupidity and mortality, no hope and not all that much dignity either, but they are a treat to listen to. And what an ear she has for them!
headline: DOTTY AND DISORDERLY CONDUCT

title: Redeeming The Time
author: Page Smith
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: REDEEMING THE TIME: A People's History of the 1920s and the New Deal. By Page Smith. (McGraw-Hill, $34.95.) With this eighth volume of ''A People's History of the United States,'' the historian Page Smith ends his sweeping chronicle of America, told in terms of the people who shaped events and those who only lived through them.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Africans
author: Ali A Mazrui
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE AFRICANS: A Triple Heritage. By Ali A. Mazrui. (Little Brown, $29.95.) In spite of its title, the companion volume to the current PBS series of the same name is not an overview but an argument.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Private Scores
author: Anne Tolstoi Wallach
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PRIVATE SCORES By Anne Tolstoi Wallach. 354 pp. New York: NAL Books/New American Library. $17.95.    TODAY'S parents, having waited longer to have children, demand their money's worth from their issue. The downside of the $150 name-brand stroller is the cram course to prepare 4-year-olds to be tested for private schools. But children, unlike attache cases and running shoes, are nonreturnable.
headline: WHEN LIVVIE CAN'T READ

title: The Little Virtues
author: Natalia Ginzburg
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE LITTLE VIRTUES By Natalia Ginzburg. Translated by Dick Davis. 110 pp. New York: Seaver Books. $13.95. 

NATALIA GINZBURG, a glowing light of modern Italian literature who should be more widely and fervidly known by American readers, was brought up in Turin, the daughter of a shoutingly opinionated and dictatorial father in the combined combustible styles of Jewish patriarch and Italian tyrant, but (and this is one of Ms. Ginzburg's magics) an enchanting man. Her mother was a bubblingly optimistic, cultivated Protestant Italian. The pair and their children, as given us in the author's best-known work, ''Lessico Famigliare'' (translated as ''Family Sayings''), were a heady, attractive brew of Mediterraneanisms. The author began writing in childhood and was first published at the age of 17. In 1938 she married Leone Ginzburg, a professor of Russian literature and an ardent anti-Fascist who was forced into exile with his wife and their three small children to a lost hollow of the Abruzzi. He returned to Rome to continue printing and disseminating anti-Fascist broadsides, was caught and tortured by the Germans and died in a Roman prison.
headline: A CONTEMPT FOR DANGER

title: Blundering Into Disaster
author: Robert McNamara.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BLUNDERING INTO DISASTER Surviving the First Century of the Nuclear Age. By Robert McNamara. 212 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $14.95.    FROM 1961 to 1968 Robert McNamara dominated United States security policy, serving Presidents Kennedy and Johnson as Secretary of Defense. His reputation before his arrival at the Pentagon was as a manager rather than as a strategic thinker. He depended on the quality of his bright young staff to help him formulate his policies. These ''whiz kids,'' as they were not so affectionately known, came from the universities and research institutes such as Rand, full of the new analytical skills and lines of argument that had been developing during the late 1950's in an attempt to come to grips with the demands of the nuclear age.   Mr. McNamara was not the source of many of the ideas that came to be associated with his name, but, in line with his managerial philosophy, he made them systematic and precise. In his presentation of United States policy, especially in the area of nuclear strategy, there was a sense of irresistible logic. The possible options had all been identified and exhaustively assessed against all the possibly relevant criteria; there could be no appeal against the eventual choice.
headline: WHAT ARE NUCLEAR WEAPONS GOOD FOR?

title: Medical Care, Medical Costs
author: Rashi Fein.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MEDICAL CARE, MEDICAL COSTS The Search for a Health Insurance Policy. By Rashi Fein. 240 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. $20.    RASHI FEIN'S economic analysis of the American health care system, ''Medical Care, Medical Costs,'' has two virtues rarely found in such works: it is written with uncommon grace, in a limpid style devoid of jargon; and it is pervaded by a fine but firm sense of morality and ethics.
headline: THE RICH GET BETTER

title: Zorina
author: Vera Zorina
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ZORINA By Vera Zorina. Illustrated. 311 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $25.    VERA ZORINA was the woman who in the years just before World War II personified the glamour of the Russian Ballet - that exotic aura of demure, yet invincible womanly charm - for American theater and moviegoers. Ironically, Vera Zorina wasn't really Russian: she was a dark-blond German-Norwegian with wide eyes, a gently cleft chin and a lean, yet voluptuous body -born Eva Brigitta Hartwig in Berlin in 1917. The Russian name came from her stint as a dancer in the mid-1930's in Col. W. de Basil's Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo. The renown came from her migration from the ballet stage to the musical comedy stage - in the 1937 London production of Rodgers and Hart's ''On Your Toes''; thence to the movies as a protegee of Samuel Goldwyn, who featured her in his 1938 ''Goldwyn Follies''; then on to Broadway to play the sweetly comic angel in the Rodgers and Hart 1938 Broadway hit, ''I Married an Angel.''
headline: I MARRIED A GENIUS

title: The Cycles Of American History
author: Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CYCLES OF AMERICAN HISTORY By Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr. 498 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $22.95.    IN the years between the National Recovery Act of 1933 and the Civil Rights Act of 1964, America experienced its liberal epiphany. Although interrupted by two soporific Eisenhower terms, and ended by a Presidential assassination and the societal splintering brought about by the civil rights revolution and the Vietnam War, the liberal decades marked by Roosevelt, Truman and Kennedy exuded a vitality and public promise America had scarcely seen since its founding, and recast the shape of American politics.
headline: AMERICA AS A MONUMENTAL GAMBLE

title: Reel Power
author: Mark Litwak. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: REEL POWER The Struggle for Influence and Success in the New Hollywood. By Mark Litwak. Illustrated. 336 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $18.95.    AN attorney associated with Ralph Nader for a number of years, Mark Litwak left Albany in 1979 to make his fortune in Hollywood. As he writes in the preface to ''Reel Power,'' ''I didn't know anyone in show business, rarely went to the movies and had not watched television in ten years.'' Yet he was determined to break into moviemaking, and his naivete proved to be a boon. The studio executives whom he phoned were so intrigued by his background and by his brash approach that they agreed to meet with him. A few weeks later he had a deal with one of the studios (which he does not identify) to produce movies for television.
headline: ONCE, HE WAS CHIC

title: My Mother's Sabbath Days. A Memoir
author: Chaim Grade
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MY MOTHER'S SABBATH DAYS A Memoir. By Chaim Grade. Translated by Channa Kleinerman Goldstein and Inna Hecker Grade. 416 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $19.95.    THIS memoir begins with an old man's funny apology for living so long: ''Layb the innkeeper is older than I - a lot older.'' But Chaim Grade, a central figure in that great generation of Yiddish writers that includes I. J. Singer and his brother, Isaac Bashevis Singer, is not merely performing a charming turn and doing Sholem Aleichem variations here. In ''My Mother's Sabbath Days'' - a long and dense chronicle written after World War II, in which he describes his own survival, or partial survival, of the Holocaust - Grade means to cheat the angel of death with more than sentimental evocation of his destroyed universe. His memory grows dense and muscular because history demands it of him. As always, a writer's best work comes when there are no alternatives.
headline: ONCE UPON A TIME, THERE WERE MONSTERS

title: Loop's Progress
author: Chuck Rosenthal
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOOP'S PROGRESS. By Chuck Rosenthal. (Weidenfeld & Nicolson, $15.95.) In this, the year of the immigrant, Chuck Rosenthal offers a decidedly unromantic version of the American melting pot.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Injured Party
author: Susan Fromberg Schaeffer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE INJURED PARTY By Susan Fromberg Schaeffer. 309 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $16.95.    IN two of her previous six novels - ''Falling,'' her first, and ''Mainland,'' the book that preceded ''The Injured Party'' - Susan Fromberg Schaeffer described, respectively, the progress of a romantic relationship and the dilemmas of a modern wife. In both books, a backdrop of ancestral voices (and even the echoes of those voices within the protagonist's mind) functioned as a kind of extended family whose presence served to enrich these tales. ''The Injured Party,'' by comparison, suffers from its near-exclusive focus on one woman's midlife obsession.
headline: DINNER IN THE CRYPT

title: Architecture, Anyone?
author: Ada Louise Huxtable
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ARCHITECTURE, ANYONE? By Ada Louise Huxtable. (Random House, $27.50.) In 1982, after serving as architecture critic of The New York Times for many years, Ada Louise Huxtable, then a member of the editorial board, was appointed a MacArthur Fellow.
headline: Books From The Times

title: The Exile Of Sergeant Nen
author: Stephen Fleming
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE EXILE OF SERGEANT NEN By Stephen Fleming. 186 pp. North Carolina: Algonquin Books of Chapel Hill. $14.95. 

SINCE 1965, when the first marines landed in Danang, there has been a legion of books about the Vietnam War written by or about the American soldiers who fought that bloody war. Most of the books have focused on the American role; few, if any, have been written from the Vietnamese perspective. Now we have Stephen Fleming's first novel, ''The Exile of Sergeant Nen,'' the story of a 40-year-old Vietnamese paratrooper who fought with both the French and the Americans until the chaotic last days of Saigon.
headline: A WAR FOUGHT TWICE

title: On Acting
author: Laurence Olivier
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ON ACTING By Laurence Olivier. Illustrated. 397 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.    OF this book Lord Olivier writes, ''This is not a book for the gossips; it is purely and simply about acting, and about how I feel it has come about for me.'' It is the work everyone hoped we would have from him, and just because he tries to stay away from the sensational stuff, he gets, for the first time, into the sensational stuff. The story of the opening night of ''Richard III'' in Paris and, in its aftermath, of the near murder of Lord Olivier in his hotel room by Ralph Richardson will shock the reader as much as, in the event, it did the author. To theater people it will confirm again how close to the horns its great practitioners sometimes work. Richardson's remark the next morning, ''We were both very foolish,'' amazed Lord Olivier, who thought himself innocent; to some readers it may seem justified.
headline: AY, EVERY INCH A KING

title: The New Heartland
author: John Herbers.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE NEW HEARTLAND America's Flight Beyond the Suburbs and How It Is Changing Our Future. By John Herbers. 228 pp. New York: Times Books. $19.95.    FORT COLLINS, Coeur d'Alene and Mountain Home may not yet be household words. However, these communities - in Colorado, Idaho and Arkansas, respectively - and others like them are among the fastest-growing in the United States. While most large cities continue to decline and many suburbs are marking time, small towns and rural areas are in fact attracting people. Perhaps this was bound to happen. After all, surveys have consistently shown that almost half of all Americans say they would like to live in such settings. And, as John Herbers shows in ''The New Heartland,'' growing numbers are now able to realize that wish. Indeed, he points out in this engrossing and probing book, ''a large proportion of Americans have never felt comfortable with the structure of the modern metropolitan area.'' They find the suburbs sterile, and cities - well, they're not even nice places to visit anymore. Nor do all young professionals aspire to fast-track careers. More and more people with college degrees are opting for ''simplicity of life and rural atmosphere.'' Moreover, this trend has political implications, notably in a fundamentalism that has an agenda for the nation as a whole.
headline: THESE PIONEERS WANT CABLE TV

title: Lillian Hellman
author: William Wright
pull_quote: LILLIAN HELLMAN: The Image, the Woman. By William Wright. Illustrated. 507 pages. Simon & Schuster. $18.95.    IN the epilogue to his new biography, ''Lillian Hellman: The Image, the Woman,'' William Wright (''Pavarotti: My Own Story'' and ''The Von Bulow Affair'') recounts how, once having contracted for his book, he wrote to his famous subject in the slim hope that she might cooperate. Within days, Mr. Wright's editor got an angry telephone call from Ms. Hellman, newspapers received an announcement appointing William Abrahams as her official biographer, and two dozen or so of Ms. Hellman's friends got notes asking them not to talk to Mr. Wright.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Complete Prose Of Marianne Moore
author: Marianne Moore
pull_quote: THE COMPLETE PROSE OF MARIANNE MOORE. Edited and with an introduction by Patricia C. Willis. 723 pages. Elisabeth Sifton/Viking. $24.95.    DURING Marianne Moore's lifetime a number of her essays and reviews were reprinted in a volume called ''Predilections'' and in the ''Marianne Moore Reader'' published in 1961; but these pieces represent only a small fraction of the material that Patricia C. Willis has assembled in ''The Complete Prose of Marianne Moore.'' No one who has read Marianne Moore's poetry will need to be reassured about the new volume's distinction - or indeed about its variety, since her poems reveal a writer notable for the range and quirkiness of her interests. But admirers are likely to be surprised, even so, to learn just how much prose she wrote, and over just how many topics her imagination played.
headline: BOOK OF THE TIMES

title: Idols Of Perversity
author: Bram Dijkstra
pull_quote: IDOLS OF PERVERSITY. Fantasies of Feminine Evil in Fin-de-Siecle Culture.   By Bram Dijkstra. Illustrated. 453 pages. Oxford University Press. $35.    MERMAIDS, vampires, sirens, bacchantes, maenads - what do these creatures have in common? What about such mythological women as Circe, Lilith, Salammbo, Medusa, Leda, the Sphinx and Delilah? In fin-de-siecle culture, Bram Dijkstra argues in ''Idols of Perversity,'' all represented demonic images of women - images of women as evil temptresses, bent on turning men away from their spiritual destiny and corrupting them with the fleshly pleasures of sin.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Sports Spectators
author: Allen Guttmann
pull_quote: SPORTS SPECTATORS. By Allen Guttmann. 236 pages. Columbia University Press. $24.95. IN recent years sporting events have often been marred by outbreaks of hooliganism, but modern spectator violence pales in comparison with the kind of bloodshed that chariot-racing provoked in the Byzantine Empire: in the worst recorded instance - the rioting in Constantinople in A.D. 532 - an estimated 30,000 lives were lost. Nowadays sport attracts an immense amount of publicity, but it was hardly suffering from neglect in 1869, when The New York Times devoted all but one of its front-page columns to reports of a boat race in London between crews from Harvard and Oxford (which was said to have been watched by around a million people).   One way of clarifying a subject is to get it into historical perspective, and in ''Sports Spectators'' Allen Guttmann has opted for a mixture of history and sociology. Current problems and controversies are very much on his mind in the book, but he begins by going back to the Greeks and proceeds to trace the history of sports-watching (as best he can - for the facts are often hard to come by) from antiquity to the present.
headline: BOOKS CF THE TIMES

title: El Yanqui
author: Douglas Unger
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EL YAQUI By Douglas Unger 300 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $16.95.    DOUGLAS UNGER'S highly praised first novel, ''Leaving the Land,'' was set in an 18-mile stretch of the western Dakotas. He wrote of a small world, believable and recognizable even to a reader who has never set foot in the Middle West. His second book is a terrifying leap into a nightmare, with a story set largely in Argentina and briefly in New York City and on Long Island. ''El Yanqui'' reeks of desperation, and the reader, finding the work an ordeal to read, sympathizes with the author. It must have been that much more of an ordeal to write.
headline: AWAKE IN A NIGHTMARE

title: One Big Bed
author: John Krich
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ONE BIG BED. By John Krich. (McGraw-Hill, $16.95.) Early middle-aged radical Berkeley film critic finds happiness with young, wise, barely English-speaking Chinese artist in this Zeitgeist-busting novel that invokes enough film references to warrant description as ''The Big Chill'' meets ''Morgan!'' Despite some very funny lines (''Sex with Darlinda was a bit like haggling over a rug with an Afghan trader''), the effect of this inordinately busy novel, peppered throughout with non sequiturs posing as aphorisms and a constantly ticking narrative clock, is more wearying than kaleidoscopic.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Sixth Continent
author: Iain Finlayson.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE SIXTH CONTINENT A Literary History of Romney Marsh. By Iain Finlayson. 240 pp. New York: Atheneum. $15.95.    WHILE the Victorian Age was sickening and dying, and the poets of the English decadence were declaiming their delicate fevered verse in London, writers of a sturdier genius were reinventing literature 60 miles south of the capital, in the vicinity of a place called Romney Marsh. It was decidedly not a group effort: Henry James and Joseph Conrad and Ford Madox Ford and Stephen Crane did not put their heads together and decide to give birth to 20th-century consciousness.
headline: SCRIBBLING IN SUSSEX

title: Selected Poems. 1958-1984
author: John Wieners
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SELECTED POEMS #1958-1984. By John Wieners. Edited by Raymond Foye. Foreword by Allen Ginsberg. Illustrated. 317 pp. Santa Barbara, Calif.: Black Sparrow Press. Cloth, $20. Paper, $12.50.    THE poetry of John Wieners has an exceptionally human beauty - as if there ever were any other. There is in it such a commonness of phrase and term, such a substantial fact of a daily life transformed by the articulateness of his feelings and the intensity of the inexorable world that is forever out there waiting for any one of us. Charles Olson spoke of it as ''a poetry of affect,'' by which I took him to mean a poetry that is the process of a life being lived, literally, as Keats's was, or Hart Crane's, or Olson's own. In other words, the art becomes the complex act of ''making real'' all that one is given to live, and whatever in them may be style or fashion, the poems are so otherwise committed, so intensely a gesture of primary need and recognition, that their survival becomes the singular value, and their immense beauty.
headline: 'HOW IS IT FAR IF YOU THINK IT?'

title: The Deal Of The Century
author: Steve Coll.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DEAL OF THE CENTURY The Breakup of AT&T. By Steve Coll. 400 pp. New York: Atheneum. $18.95.  BIG BLUE IBM's Use and Abuse of Power. By Richard Thomas DeLamarter. 393 pp. New York: Dodd, Mead & Company. $22.95.    JAN. 8, 1982, was by any account a red-letter day in antitrust history. In the morning, the Justice Department won its eight-year quest to break up the world's largest phone company. In the afternoon, the Government abandoned its almost 13-year-old suit against the world's largest computer corporation. These two books argue that neither action furthered the public interest.
headline: GIANTS AND GIANT-KILLERS

title: Steamboat In A Cornfield
author: John Hartford
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STEAMBOAT IN A CORNFIELD By John Hartford. Illustrated. Unpaged. New York: Crown Publishers. $10.95. (Ages 8 and up)    EARLY in this century a reasonable way to get from Pittsburgh to Cincinnati was to travel the Ohio River on the palace steamer Virginia, a 235-foot, 1,200-ton riverboat. There were no dams or locks on the river yet, so when the water didn't flow, a captain and his passengers just had to wait for nature's help.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: The Fabric Of Mind
author: Richard Bergland
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE FABRIC OF MIND By Richard Bergland. Illustrated by Kati Bromley. 202 pp. New York: Viking. $16.95. 

FOR the better part of this century, mental illness was regarded as an expression of internal psychological conflict caused by developmental experiences and the effects of unpredictable, traumatic life events. The therapeutic flip side of this psychosocial model was psychotherapy, a treatment that helped patients resolve emotional issues by studying and understanding their psychic origins.
headline: PSYCHOCHEMISTRY

title: Hoosiers: The Fabulous Basketball Life Of Indiana
author: Phillip M Hoose
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HOOSIERS: The Fabulous Basketball Life of Indiana. By Phillip M. Hoose. (Vintage Books, Paper, $7.95.) In Indiana residents vie for positions on the local school board so they can dismiss a losing basketball coach.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Ceremony
author: Nigel Barley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CEREMONY: An Anthropologist's Misadventures in the African Bush. By Nigel Barley. (Holt, $15.95.) These days the popular American conception of tropical Africa seems to derive from either the romanticized landscapes in the film version of ''Out of Africa'' or television footage of the desperate confinements of the Ethiopian famine camps.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: The Bachelor's Bride
author: Stephen Koch
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BACHELORS' BRIDE By Stephen Koch. 270 pp. New York: Marion Boyars. $18.95.    SET in the New York art world of the 1960's, ''The Bachelors' Bride'' is a tour de force that hovers between satire and infatuation, gossip and art criticism. With a narrative that veers from neo-Dada to amyl nitrates, from androgyny to the Supremes, it can be tricky to tell whether the author of ''Night Watch,'' Stephen Koch, is seduced by the 60's or scoffing at them in his second novel. The narrator is a young art historian, Jason Phillips - ambitious, self-doubting and self-conscious - who is writing a dissertation about the Surrealist and Dadaist artist Marcel Duchamp, to be called ''The Bachelors' Bride.''
headline: NUDES ASCENDING A TRIANGLE

title: Emily Dickinson
author: Cynthia Griffin Wolff
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: EMILY DICKINSON By Cynthia Griffin Wolff. Illustrated. 638 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $25.    FOR a poet whose life was so uneventful (and hence enigmatic), Emily Dickinson has been relatively well served by her biographers.   George Frisbie Whicher's ''This Was a Poet'' (1938) remains an excellent general introduction, particularly to the work. Thomas H. Johnson, who published ''Emily Dickinson: An Interpretive Biography'' in 1955, the same year his definitive variorum edition of the Dickinson canon came out, provided another responsible overview of both the life and work and emphasized the Puritan background of Dickinson's themes and metrics. When Richard B. Sewall published his two-volume ''Life of Emily Dickinson'' in 1974, the biographical pursuit of the recluse of Amherst, Mass., seemed complete.
headline: THE PAGAN OF AMHERST

title: The Collected Essays Of Christopher Hill
author: Christopher Hill.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE COLLECTED ESSAYS OF CHRISTOPHER HILL Volume Three: People and Ideas in 17th Century England. By Christopher Hill. 340 pp. Amherst: University of Massachusetts Press. $27.50.    CHRISTOPHER HILL, whose contributions to the history of 17th-century England span more than 40 years, was an early member of what was to become the most important and influential group of historians in Britain after World War II. This illustrious body, England's left-wing equivalent of the Annales school in France, emanated not from an academic institution but a political party. Apart from Mr. Hill himself, who was to become the master of Balliol College, Oxford, the Historians' Study Group of the British Communist Party included many luminaries, perhaps the best known of whom are Eric J. Hobsbawm, the author of ''Bandits,'' and E. P. Thompson, who wrote the magisterial and much read ''The Making of the English Working Class.''
headline: GOD, SEX AND PIRATES

title: The Common Good
author: Marcus G. Raskin.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE COMMON GOOD Its Politics, Policies and Philosophy. By Marcus G. Raskin. 369 pp. New York: Routledge & Kegan Paul. $22.50.    MARCUS RASKIN, one of the reigning spirits at the ultra-liberal Institute for Policy Studies in Washington, has written an ambitious book. It is nothing less than a far-reaching program of ''social reconstruction.'' The book describes ''a new social covenant'' that would reduce material inequities in the United States; assure minimum income, health care, education and shelter to everyone; submit virtually all large-scale economic enterprises to public control by workers, consumers and communities; embark on a sweeping initiative for general disarmament; and reconstruct United States defense policy and international politics on the basis of United Nations mechanisms, tenacious local defense and overseas economic development.
headline: UP WITH THE GRASS ROOTS

title: Bluebeard's Egg
author: Margaret Atwood.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BLUEBEARD'S EGG And Other Stories. By Margaret Atwood. 281 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $16.95.    WE have been spoiled, perhaps, by the renaissance of the short story as a fashionable, and indeed salable, literary form.   Confronting a collection by, say, Raymond Carver or Alice Munro or Amy Hempel, we expect the thoughtfully selected and arranged components to produce a whole with a certain shapeliness of its own, a consistency of voice and tone, of subject matter and treatment. No such sense of a whole is to be found in Margaret Atwood's second collection, ''Bluebeard's Egg,'' which first appeared in a Canadian edition last year; instead, she has given us a book of unmatched parts, an assemblage of short memoirs, fictionalized character studies and a handful of stories that seem almost willful in their nonconformity to any of the current patterns of that genre. But once the unshapeliness is accepted, admirers of one of Canada's most accomplished writers will find plenty to entertain and interest them.
headline: OLD-FASHIONED VIRTUES, BOHEMIAN VICES

title: Lillian Hellman
author: William Wright. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LILLIAN HELLMAN The Image, the Woman. By William Wright. Illustrated. 507 pp. New York: Simon & Schuster. $18.95.    LILLIAN HELLMAN brought out the knee-jerk in almost everyone. To her admirers, she was a paragon of integrity during a ''scoundrel time'' - a tough-minded writer who refused to cut either her civil libertarian's conscience or her premodernist literary style for the sake of fashion or survival. To her detractors, she was a holier-than-thou opportunist - a hypocritical Stalinist whose dishonest, self-aggrandizing memoirs adroitly snookered the public into retroactively anointing her the St. Joan of the Joseph McCarthy era. By her death in 1984, Hellman's supporters included a goodly number of the show business and intellectual elite, but her enemies list was as long as, and more eclectic than, that of an archnemesis, Richard Nixon. She had not only been attacked by the expected conservatives and neoconservatives but had also provoked varying degrees of fire, for varying reasons, from a heterogeneous array of liberals, including Elizabeth Hardwick, Irving Howe, Alfred Kazin, Murray Kempton, Diana Trilling and, of course, Mary McCarthy. It was Miss McCarthy who sparked Hellman's final act of Dickensian litigation by telling the television interviewer Dick Cavett in 1980 that ''every word'' Hellman wrote was ''a lie, including 'and' and 'the.' ''
headline: SLAMMING THROUGH LIFE

title: Italia Perversa
author: Richard Appignanesi
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ITALIA PERVERSA. Part One: Stalin's Orphans. By Richard Appignanesi. (Quartet/Salem, $17.95.) Only a supremely self-confident or foolhardy novelist would dare start a trilogy with his protagonist's funeral.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Frieze
author: Cecile Pineda
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FRIEZE. By Cecile Pineda. (Viking, $16.95.) Call it karma or original sin, but for Cecile Pineda's characters, the given of life is suffering, and deliverance is possible only through the violent dismembering of the worldly self. Her elegiac first novel, ''Face,'' nominated for a 1985 National Book Award, told of a barber from a Brazilian slum whose face is grotesquely mutilated, and the solitary anguish of reconstructing it. The major character of her new novel is Gopal, a stone carver in 10th-century India, whose dissolution of self is more gradual at first and thus more deceptive. After losing the wife he cherishes to the shadows of her own dream world, he is conscripted by a dynastic prince to travel to Java to carve 120 friezes of Buddha's life for the shrine of Borobudur (still standing today), whose construction devoured the lives of thousands of laborers. Ms. Pineda is convincing in her description of the passion and hubris that fuel Gopal's carving of the sacred friezes but also blinds him to the close, hot breath of danger around him; she makes the act of savagery that forces him to recast his life both horrifying and believable. Unfortunately, the novel suffers from her insistence that Gopal lead a pointedly metaphorical life: she names his first, dreamily seductive wife Maya, the Sanskrit term for the illusions from which we must detach ourselves to gain true enlightenment; Borobudur is a not too subtle symbol for the pridefulness and cruelty of this world.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: The Principle Of Hope
author: Ernst Bloch
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PRINCIPLE OF HOPE By Ernst Bloch. Translated by Neville Plaice, Stephen Plaice and Paul Knight. 1,420 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: The MIT Press. $95.    ERNST BLOCH'S ''Principle of Hope'' is a masterwork of the ancient religion known as Marxism. The vast three volumes constitute the most extravagant argument for Marxism ever assembled. A philosophy of history, nature and culture; a logic, an epistemology, a politics, a theology; a practical technique of action and a prophetic plan for the end of days - all this, and more, is Marxism in the mind of Bloch. It was a mind under the spell of paradise. For all its mercilessly dense system of theory, Bloch's book is an intellectual's tribute to a millenarian thrill. For all its solidarity with the masses, it is the lonely communication of a vision, a sober and anti-Romantic exercise in dialectical materialism that culminates in an intoxicated and Romantic dream of the healing of all contradictions and the last wholeness of nature and history, matter and spirit. Bloch's Marxism even includes an obscure assurance about overcoming death.
headline: UNDER THE SPELL

title: A Midwife's Story
author: Penny Armstrong and Sheryl Feldman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A MIDWIFE'S STORY By Penny Armstrong and Sheryl Feldman. 228 pp. New York: Arbor House. $15.95.    I'VE always suspected that birth is the search for a larger apartment. ''A Midwife's Story'' confirms this suspicion. Penny Armstrong describes her profession to Sheryl Feldman in a book that celebrates each individual pushing out into the larger world. Concisely and in a clear voice, Mrs. Armstrong, an American, recalls her rigorous nursing and midwife training in Scotland in the 1970's, her hospital deliveries in the harshness of Philadelphia's inner city and her pitched battle with the medical establishment.
headline: BIRTH WITHOUT DOCTORS

title: The Pilgrims Of Plimoth
author: Marcia Sewall
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Additional titles of interest:   THE PILGRIMS OF PLIMOTH. Written and illustrated by Marcia Sewall. Atheneum. $14.95. (Ages 8 to 12) The rich text to this handsome book about the arrival and daily life of the first Pilgrims is written conversationally, and includes a glossary of terms.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS: BOOKSHELF

title: The Critical Legal Studies Movement
author: Roberto Mangabeira Unger
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CRITICAL LEGAL STUDIES MOVEMENT By Roberto Mangabeira Unger. 128 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. Cloth, $17.95. Paper, $7.95.    ''CRITICAL legal studies'' is a term laden with emotional overtones and mystery. The general public has been introduced to it - obliquely, anyway - in The New Yorker, for which Calvin Trillin wrote a piece, ''The Law at Harvard.'' At fairly regular intervals The New York Times has carried stories - battlefield communiques, as it were, from Cambridge, Mass. C.L.S. lies at the root of wild rumors of departures from Harvard Law School and of a faculty too divided even to make appointments. Making the subject all the more intriguing, Paul D. Carrington, the dean of the Duke University Law School, proclaimed that C.L.S. law teachers are morally bound to resign, for it is immoral, at best, to profess to teach a subject, law, in which one does not believe. (Is it appropriate, he asked, for an atheist to teach theology? Or for someone who denies that sociology is a legitimate academic subject to be a member of a sociology faculty?) The movement has become a kind of latter-day bogyman. As such, it has its own appeal.
headline: TOWARD A 'SUPER LIBERAL STATE'

title: No Hero For The Kaiser
author: Rudolf Frank
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
NO HERO FOR THE KAISER By Rudolf Frank. Translated by Patricia Crampton. Illustrated by Klaus Steffens. 222 pp. New York: Lothrop, Lee & Shepard. $13. (Ages 10 and up) 

RUDOLF FRANK, who was mustered into the German artillery in August 1914, described ''No Hero for the Kaiser'' as ''an anti-war novel to warn young people.'' Published in 1931 under the puzzling title ''The Skull of Sultan Mkwawa,'' it had been reprinted several times by 1933 when Hitler came to power. Rudolf Frank was arrested in March of that year and his novel was burned with other ''un-German'' works at the great book burning of May 10, 1933. In 1979, shortly before Frank's death, in Switzerland, it was republished in Germany with great success.
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Chaim Weizmann
author: Norman Rose. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CHAIM WEIZMANN A Biography. By Norman Rose. Illustrated. 520 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $24.95.    CHAIM WEIZMANN might be called a biographer's dream. Born in 1874 to a lower-middle-class Jewish family in an obscure corner of the Russian Empire, he died in 1952 as the first president of Israel - a state that he, perhaps more than any other single person, had ushered into existence. En route he lived as a student in Germany and Switzerland (where he debated socialism and Zionism with Georgi Plekhanov, the father figure among Russian Marxist exiles), as a scientist in England (where he made important scientific contributions to the British war effort during World War I), and thereafter as a peripatetic diplomat, a one-man foreign ministry of the Jewish people, flitting incessantly among London, Paris, Geneva, Jerusalem and, especially in later years, Washington.
headline: ZION'S GREAT PERSUADER

title: Foundation And Earth
author: Isaac Asimov
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FOUNDATION AND EARTH (Doubleday, $16.95) is Isaac Asimov's 340th or 3,400th book, or something like that. I suspect that no one, including Mr. Asimov, really knows how many books of fiction and nonfiction he has created in his 66 years, although I am inclined to believe Doubleday's claim that this new novel is the hundredth Asimov title to appear under that imprint. More important than mere numbers, anyway, is the ambitious feat of creation that Mr. Asimov has embarked on in recent years. In novels like ''Foundation's Edge'' (1982), ''Robots and Empire'' (1985) and now ''Foundation and Earth'' he has been linking his most important science fictions - the Foundation trilogy, the stories of detection set in the early Galactic Empire and the robot stories - into a single time- and space-spanning work of epic proportions. This would be a titanic labor under any circumstances; it is made still more remarkable by the fact that Mr. Asimov is returning to pick up threads of plot and nuances of character that he dropped, in some instances, as far back as four decades ago.
headline: SCIENCE FICTION

title: Jujitsu For Christ
author: Jack Butler
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
JUJITSU FOR CHRIST By Jack Butler. 208 pp. Little Rock, Ark.: August House. $14.95. 

THIS first novel is by a Baptist preacher's son from Alligator, Miss., who now lives in Little Rock, Ark., where he is a statistical analyst for the state Public Service Commission. I almost did not want to read the novel after relishing the promise of the title and the biographical blurb, which between them sum up the whole strange world of the postsegregation South, a place simmering with previously undreamed-of possibilities, a place so weird that Baptist preachers' sons from Mississippi can become statistical analysts and write novels called ''Jujitsu for Christ.'' Hot, as they say down here, damn!
headline: BLACK, WHITE, MEAN AND LOONY

title: Rising From The Plains
author: John McPhee
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RISING FROM THE PLAINS By John McPhee. 214 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $15.95.    IN ''Basin and Range'' and ''In Suspect Terrain,''   John McPhee accompanied geologists on field trips in the hope that ''something illuminating'' might occur. They were good books, and Mr. McPhee must have enjoyed himself because ''Rising From the Plains'' is similar and just as good.
headline: SNAPSHOT OF A BILLION YEARS

title: The Afternoon Sun
author: David Pryce-Jones
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE AFTERNOON SUN By David Pryce-Jones. 214 pp. New York: Weidenfeld & Nicolson. $15.95. 

WHEN the ''Vienna 1900'' show opened at the Museum of Modern Art in July, thoughtful observers wondered about the fascination that time and that place have for our time and place. Not only Klimt, Kokoschka and Schiele but also Schnitzler, Freud, von Hofmannsthal, Mahler - why do they seem so close? None of them appear in ''The Afternoon Sun,'' David Pryce-Jones's concisely written, historically accurate account of one family for over a hundred years, but we feel them watching.
headline: GNOME OF VIENNA

title: City Of Nets
author: Otto Friedrich. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CITY OF NETS A Portrait of Hollywood in the 1940's. By Otto Friedrich. Illustrated. 495 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $25.    THE ''tragedy of these men was that nothing in their lives had really bitten deep at all,'' F. Scott Fitzgerald once jotted about the Hollywood movie moguls. Fitzgerald was probably revealing less about the moguls than he was about the American literary imagination. Hollywood has always been an irresistible, prefabricated metaphor for the crass, the materialistic, the shallow and the craven, and the metaphor's blade was sharpened by the natural antagonism between writers, who were seldom regarded as much more than retainers there, and executives, who were the community's royalty. Writers could never seem to fathom why they weren't in charge and why these vulgarians were, but they gained a measure of revenge by carving Hollywood, now and forevermore, in our imaginations as something both absurd and unholy.
headline: THE TOWN EVERYBODY LOVES TO HATE

title: Sudden Fiction: American Short-Short Stories
author: Robert Shapard
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SUDDEN FICTION: American Short-Short Stories. Edited by Robert Shapard and James Thomas. (Gibbs M. Smith/Peregrine Smith, $18.95.) It has been widely reported that ours is a society with a diminishing attention span, that modern culture caters to an audience wanting instantaneous entertainment.

title: Joe & Marilyn: A Memory Of Love
author: Roger Kahn
pull_quote: JOE & MARILYN. A Memory of Love. By Roger Kahn. 269 Pages. William Morrow. $16.95. WHEN Roger Kahn was covering the Brooklyn Dodgers for The New York Herald Tribune, a pitcher named Billy Loes was famous for his theory that he never wanted to win 20 games in one season because then everybody would expect it of him all the time.   Roger Kahn had the literary equivalent of a 20-victory season with the classic ''The Boys of Summer,'' a memory of his Brooklyn roots and visits with ''the boys of summer'' when autumn had set in for all of them. Mr. Kahn's style was perfect for reminiscing with George Shuba in Ohio or Carl Erskine in Indiana about What It All Meant.
headline: Books; Crossed Stars

title: Bearing The Cross
author: David J Garrow
pull_quote: BEARING THE CROSS: Martin Luther King, Jr., and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. By David J. Garrow. 800 pages. William Morrow. $19.95. DAVID J. GARROW'S huge   ''Bearing the Cross'' begins on Dec. 1, 1955, with a tired Rosa Lee McCauley Parks deciding she would prefer not to move to the back of a Montgomery, Ala., bus. It ends on April 4, 1968, with a minister named Samuel (Billy) Kyles standing over the body of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis. ''Kyles looked down and thought he could see the color of King's complexion change right before his eyes. He turned away and sobbed.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Salvador Dali: A Biography
author: Salvador Dali
pull_quote: SALVADOR DALI: A Biography. By Meryle Secrest. Illustrated. 307 pages. Dutton. $22.50.    LATE in her lively biography of the Spanish surrealist painter Salvador Dali, Meryle Secrest reveals that in 1984, upon being invited by the Spanish Government to design his own monument, the 80-year-old artist sketched an enormous dolmen 60 to 70 feet high. (''Even with modern technology,'' Ms. Secrest observes, ''to move a single piece of stone of these dimensions into place would be no small undertaking.'') No doubt Dali's long and complex life will one day inspire a biography of similarly megalithic dimensions. But happily, this book is not it. Quite the contrary, Ms. Secrest's life of Dali is brisk, anecdotal and selective, and attempts above all to cut through the squidspray of mythology that Dali has over the years so tirelessly spread about himself. Indeed, the author has proceeded with such economy of movement that Dali's life unfolds almost as if in a stop-time film.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: My Mother's Sabbath Days
author: Chaim Grade
pull_quote: MY MOTHER'S SABBATH DAYS. By Chaim Grade. Translated from the Yiddish by Channa Kleinerman Goldstein and Inna Hecker Grade. 397 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $19.95. CHAIM GRADE was one of the foremost Yiddish poets and novelists of his generation. (A number of his books have been translated into English, most recently the group of three novellas entitled ''Rabbis and Wives.'') He was born in Vilnius, in Lithuania, in 1910, and won a name for himself as a writer while still in his 20's. When the Germans invaded Lithuania - which had not long before been annexed by the Soviet Union - in 1941, he set out for the Russian interior but decided that it would be safer for his wife to stay behind; they both shared what was then a commonly held illusion that however grievous a threat the Nazis posed to able-bodied Jewish men, they would at least spare women and children. His widowed mother also remained in Vilnius.   Grade's journeyings in the Soviet Union took him deep into Central Asia. After surviving many ordeals, he returned home at the end of the war only to find that both wife and mother (in common with almost everyone else he knew) had been killed. In 1948 he came to the United States; he died here in 1982.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: A Missing Plane
author: Susan Sheehan
pull_quote: A MISSING PLANE. By Susan Sheehan. Illustrated. 201 pages. G. P. Putnam's   Sons. $18.95.     Surely this is one of the most remarkable books of the year. Susan Sheehan has written what is at once a war story, a tale of scientific detection and a picture of Middle America in the Depression and at war, and she has woven these strands into an entrancing report. For although the book has the pace of a novel, it is clearly the result of the most thorough research and analysis; it is a product that makes one proud to be in the same profession.
headline: Books: An Old Mystery

title: The Mechanic Muse
author: Hugh Kenner
pull_quote: THE MECHANIC MUSE. By Hugh Kenner. 136 pages. Oxford University Press. $13.95.     With such works as ''The Pound Era,'' ''A Homemade World'' and ''The Invisible Poet,'' Hugh Kenner has earned a well-deserved reputation as our pre-eminent expert on modernism in English. Fluently written and packed with odd, thought-provoking observations, his books combine biography, history and critical analysis to give us portraits of seminal literary figures and to situate their work in a larger social and cultural context.
headline: Levers and Wheels

title: Rainbow Drive
author: Roderick Thorp
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: RAINBOW DRIVE. By Roderick Thorp. (Summit, $18.95.) Twenty years after the publication of his best seller, ''The Detective,'' Roderick Thorp has put together another gritty police novel that plunges the reader into the underbelly of crime in Los Angeles - a frightening world of corrupt politicians, drug dealers and addicts, sold-out cops, pornography and white slavery.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Fidel: A Critical Portrait
author: Tad Szulc.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FIDEL A Critical Portrait. By Tad Szulc. 703 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $19.95.    ''THIS is not a definitive biography, principally because President Castro is alive and has not completed his labors,'' Tad Szulc writes of the man he first interviewed in 1959, shortly after the 32-year-old revolutionary seized power, and saw last in February 1985, before Mr. Castro turned 60. But there is another reason - the ''cocoon of oblivion'' in which Mr. Castro chooses to hide as much as possible of his childhood and early youth. As a result, more than two-thirds of the book deals with the period that precedes the triumph of Mr. Castro's revolution in January 1959. This is too bad, not only because there is a great deal of repetition and an excess of detail in those first two-thirds, but also because the focus shifts from Castro the rebel and revolutionary to the history of Cuba under Mr. Castro's leadership, a shift that makes the vivid and complex personality of the leader more remote than it ought to be.
headline: POWER UNSHARED AND TOTAL

title: Louhi: Witch Of North Farm
author: Toni De Gerez
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOUHI Witch of North Farm. A Story From Finland's Epic Poem the ''Kalevala.'' By Toni de Gerez. Illustrated by Barbara Cooney. Unpaged. New York: Viking Kestrel. $12.95. (Ages 3 to 8)
headline: CHILDREN'S BOOKS

title: Northrop Frye On Shakespeare
author: Northrop Frye
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
NORTHROP FRYE ON SHAKESPEARE By Northrop Frye. Edited by Robert Sandler. 186 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press. $17.95. 

ALTHOUGH Northrop Frye has never strayed for long from his native Canada during his academic career, intellectually he has always been a fabulous voyager. Born in Quebec 74 years ago, Mr. Frye took his first degree at the University of Toronto and (following three years of theology, ordination as a minister in the United Church of Canada and a stint at the University of Oxford) chose to join the faculty of his alma mater, which he has served with extraordinary distinction and devotion for almost half a century, as, among other things, principal and then chancellor of Victoria College. For a while he edited Canadian Forum, and from 1950 to 1960 he wrote an annual critical and bibliographical survey of Canadian poetry. But the whole literary imagination is Mr. Frye's turf. Mythical, anthropological, folkloristic and archetypal critical strategies engage him; he is concerned with the social context of literary criticism.
headline: UP THE WALL WITH HAMLET

title: Service For The Dead
author: Robert A Anderson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SERVICE FOR THE DEAD. By Robert A. Anderson. (Arbor House, $16.95.) Robert A. Anderson, a Vietnam veteran whose previous novel, ''Cooks and Bakers,'' was also about the war, competently depicts combat situations, especially when he is patrolling a landscape of booby traps and snipers.

title: The Memoirs Of Frederic Mistral
author: George Wickes
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MEMOIRS OF FREDERIC MISTRAL. Translated by George Wickes. (New Directions, Cloth, $22.95. Paper, $10.95.) Frederic Mistral (1830-1914) is now almost unknown in America, but he was the bard of the French Midi in his own time.

title: Ike: His Life And Times
author: Piers Brendon. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IKE His Life and Times. By Piers Brendon. Illustrated. 478 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $21.95.    THIS witty, perceptive one-volume biography of Dwight D. Eisenhower contains very little new or startling in the way of fact; inevitably, large segments of it are summaries of more comprehensive treatments elsewhere. What is new and arresting in ''Ike'' is the author's moral penetration and his concentration on gathering evidence to show Eisenhower's chronic vacillation and remarkably opaque moral standards. Piers Brendon, a British biographer of Winston Churchill, among others, writes from a center-left perspective and gives some evidence of how inherently difficult it is for a foreigner to master the arcane ramifications and intransigencies of American politics. He occasionally oversimplifies and is once or twice guilty of a non sequitur. Nevertheless, this is a telling analysis that is bound to have an impact on the current debate over Eisenhower's proper place in history.
headline: MODERATE TO A FAULT

title: Torquemade
author: Benito Perez Galdos
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: TORQUEMADA By Benito Perez Galdos. Translated by Frances M.Lopez-Morillas. 569 pp. New York: Columbia University Press. $25.    THE emotive name that Benito Perez Galdos (1843-1920) gave to his memorable moneylender evokes Tomas de Torquemada (1420-98), during whose period as Spain's Inquisitor General 2,000 heretics were burned alive and 17,000 mutilated. The name hangs over the novels about Don Francisco Torquemada like a leaden cloud, but no direct parallel is drawn; indeed, we are dealing with a character more complex and far more interesting.   Don Francisco first appears in Galdos's novel ''El Doctor Centeno'' as ''a fierce, cold man, with the face of a sacristan, who used to lend money to students.'' He reappears briefly in ''Lo Prohibido'' and, sleeker and richer but still wearing that ''certain clerical air,'' in ''La de Bringas.'' A detailed account of his early life and methods can be found in the intimate epic ''Fortunata y Jacinta,'' a work that towers over the rest of the Spanish literature of the 1880's as ''Bleak House'' towered over the English novel of the 1850's and ''Our Mutual Friend'' over the 60's.
headline: SENOR URIAH HEEP

title: The Complete Prose Of Marianne Moore
author: Patricia C. Willis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE COMPLETE PROSE OF MARIANNE MOORE Edited, and with an introduction, by Patricia C. Willis. 723 pp. New York: Elisabeth Sifton Books/Viking. $24.95.    ''I THINK books are chiefly responsible for my doggedly self-determined efforts to write, books and verisimilitude,'' Marianne Moore surmises in one of the hundreds of essays, reviews and miscellaneous pieces that make up this monumental collection. Of the major American poets born in the 1880's - including Moore, William Carlos Williams, Ezra Pound, Hilda Doolittle and T. S. Eliot - Pound and Eliot are regarded as eminent critics. Now ''The Complete Prose of Marianne Moore,'' indefatigably edited by Patricia C. Willis, the curator of literature for the Rosenbach Museum and Library in Philadelphia, demonstrates that Moore was another of the superlative critics. With inevitable exceptions but with resolute continuity, she tracks poetry from ''The Wild Swans at Coole'' by William Butler Yeats in 1918 to a posthumous collection of Randall Jarrell's poems in 1967, and she covers many novels, biographies and critical studies over five decades.
headline: A GUSTO FOR DUMBO AND BALANCHINE

title: Salvador Dali
author: Meryle Secrest
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SALVADOR DALI By Meryle Secrest. Illustrated. 307 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $22.50.    DO we really want to hear again about the career of Salvador Dali, the once gifted painter whose life and art have been merged in a Surrealist saga of superhype? He himself wrote an autobiography (mendacious, to be sure), and others - among them Fleur Cowles, Robert Descharnes and Carlton Lake - have given their own readings of the Dali legend. Now, in ''Salvador Dali,'' Meryle Secrest presents still another version.

IN ''Understanding Media'' (1964), Marshall McLuhan looked forward to a time when technology might convert the divided world into ''a global village.'' RONALD BLYTHE'S specialty is painting with words; his subject is the English landscape, with figures. His best-known book is the one he refers to here as ''the personal rural experience which I called 'Akenfield,' '' an investigation of village life in his own county of Suffolk. title: Bearing The Cross
author: David J. Garrow.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BEARING THE CROSS Martin Luther King, Jr., and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. By David J. Garrow. 800 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $19.95.    ONE Sunday morning in 1957, Martin Luther King Jr., a young preacher who still had the open, unformed face of a boy, found an unexploded dynamite bomb on his front porch in Montgomery, Ala. Within hours he was in his pulpit saying, ''I'm not afraid of anybody this morning. Tell Montgomery they can keep shooting and I'm going to stand up to them; tell Montgomery they can keep bombing and I'm going to stand up to them. If I had to die tomorrow morning I would die happy because I've been to the mountaintop and I've seen the promised land and it's going to be here in Montgomery.''   The language, of course, anticipates that of the more famous speech King gave in 1968 in Memphis on the eve of his assassination, and the similarity underscores the central miracle and mystery of his life. Early and late, this man was able to summon a moral and physical courage that was, let us not forget, a new force on the stage of Southern history.
headline: DRIVEN TO MARTYRDOM

title: A Voyager Out: The Life Of Mary Kingsley
author: Katherine Frank. Illustrated.

pull_quote: A VOYAGER OUT The Life of Mary Kingsley. By Katherine Frank. Illustrated. 333 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $18.95.    MARY KINGSLEY is a most unlikely heroine - a 19th-century English spinster who became an explorer of Africa of such insouciance that Rudyard Kipling remarked, ''Being human, she must have feared some things, but one never arrived at what they were.'' Before I read ''A Voyager Out,'' most of what I knew about her came from a 1979 essay by Rosellen Brown (who has written the preface to this book) that explained how she had once intended to write a novel about Kingsley, then changed her mind. It is fortunate that Katherine Frank did not similarly retreat, for she has written a quietly beautiful biography that reveals not only the outer life of an extraordinary traveler but something of her inner life as well.
headline: 'I BELONG TO THE NONHUMAN'

CHRISTINE STANSELL'S ''City of Women'' is a colorful and vivid account of the lives of New York's working women and the challenges they posed to the middle class from 1789 until the eve of the Civil War. As the author puts it, in a characteristic blend of sympathy and admiration, ''This book is about the misfortunes that laboring women suffered and the problems they caused.'' Ms. Stansell writes about people who left behind no memoirs, letters or journals. She takes us into the slums where mothers, factory workers, servants and prostitutes struggled to make a living in tiny, dark rooms.

title: The Last Extinction
author: Les Kaufman and Kenneth Mallory
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE LAST EXTINCTION Edited by Les Kaufman and Kenneth Mallory. Illustrated. 208 pp. Cambridge, Mass.: The New England Aquarium/ The MIT Press. $16.95. 

ALTHOUGH extinction is a natural process it is one that, like death, we don't like to face. The six essays in ''The Last Extinction'' are united by the authors' passionate commitment to preserving the natural diversity, both genetic and esthetic, of the earth's myriad plant and animal species. Interspersed with quantitative science, such as Norman Myers's projection that 100 species will become extinct per day by the year 2000, is biblical imagery of the Ark and Paradise lost. The book contends that the biosphere is now experiencing a mass extinction at least as severe as that of the Cretaceous Period, in which the dinosaurs were eliminated. ''Over the past few centuries and in the century to come, just a geological instant,'' David Jablonski, a University of Chicago paleontologist, writes, ''our species will probably cause the worst disaster in the past 65 million years for life on this planet.'' Mass extinction, in which many kinds of organisms disappear at once, differs from ''background extinction,'' the steady dropping off of species which normally accompanies evolution. But unlike past mass extinctions, which Mr. Jablonski suggests may have been caused by meteorite impacts, glaciations, climatic deterioration, sea regression or combinations of these, the present crisis is one of our own making.
headline: MAN THE MESS MAKER

RICHARD HALLORAN is too modest in billing ''To Arm a Nation'' as primarily a layman's guide to the decline of the American military.   The New York Times military correspondent also broaches inescapable truths too often forgotten by the Government officials and private experts who dominate the national defense debate. The rebuilding of the United States military forces needs to be guided by a realistic set of missions, and these in turn require a realistic set of foreign policy goals. Without a sensible idea of what America's armed forces should be doing, the vital tasks of straightening out military command structures, rationalizing the defense budget, cleaning up the defense industry and even improving readiness will add up to so much wheel spinning.

IN 1975, after more than a decade of exile in Paris, the ''whitish'' (his term) Afrikaans-speaking poet and painter Breyten Breytenbach returned to South Africa incognito in order to help organize white resistance to apartheid. Arrested and convicted, he spent seven years in prison, two of them in solitary confinement. It is probably thanks to this involuntary sojourn - a story told with freshness and modesty in ''The True Confessions of an Albino Terrorist'' (1985) - that we now have ''End Papers,'' a collection of 50-odd addresses, analyses, poetico-political fragments and essays by Mr. Breytenbach, together with extensive notes on their occasions.

title: Robert Frost Himself
author: Stanley Burnshaw
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ROBERT FROST HIMSELF By Stanley Burnshaw. Illustrated. 342 pp. New York: George Braziller. $19.95.    THE greatness of poets is a topic much in abeyance these days. Audiences, teachers and most critics concentrate on what Gerard Manley Hopkins liked to call quiddity or inscape, at the expense of ''the roll, the rise, the carol, the creation'' that he thought is the essence of poetry - its ability to exalt, transfigure and regenerate. It's no wonder that few people realize how open the question of Robert Frost's nature and magnitude as a poet still remains. One remembers the concluding sentence of his note of thanks to Lionel Trilling for a dramatically disturbing speech at Frost's 85th birthday dinner: ''No sweeter music can come to my ears than the clash of arms over my dead body when I am down.''
headline: 'NOT JUST CONFUSED, JUST WILD'

title: James Brown: The Godfather Of Soul
author: James Brown
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: JAMES BROWN: The Godfather of Soul. By James Brown with Bruce Tucker. (Macmillan, $18.95.) Along with Chuck Berry, Little Richard and Ray Charles, James Brown is one of the most influential shapers of contemporary popular music. And in this surprisingly reserved autobiography he charts his life from the meager beginnings in rural Georgia to his induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame earlier this year. Born in Barnwell, S.C., in 1933, Mr. Brown, after his mother left when he was 4, was raised by his father and, later, an aunt who lived in Augusta, Ga. He was a better-than-average athlete but music became his early obsession and he formed his own trio by the age of 12. Poverty and a less than hospitable environment (his aunt ran a brothel), however, led him into a life of petty thievery, and at 16 he was sent to the Georgia Juvenile Training Institute. Released in 1952, he began to earnestly pursue musical ambitions. His career peaked in the late 60's, declined rapidly in the 70's with the advent of disco and numerous personal problems, then took off again recently with his exposure in movies such as ''Rocky IV.'' In recounting his story, Mr. Brown avoids lurid connections of drugs and sex with rock music. Instead he concentrates on the black performers' struggle to move from ''race'' recordings and the ''chitlin' circuit'' into the entertainment mainstream, the stress and excitement of extended tours (he sometimes played 350 one-nighters a year, thereby earning the sobriquet ''the hardest working man in show business'') and his friendships with legendary performers like Little Willie John, Elvis Presley and Jackie Wilson.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Departures: Memoirs
author: Paul Zweig. Introduction by Morris Dickstein.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DEPARTURES Memoirs. By Paul Zweig. Introduction by Morris Dickstein. 219 pp. New York: Harper & Row. $16.95.    IN his memoirs collected in ''Three Journeys'' (1976), the poet and critic Paul Zweig, who died in 1984, identifies himself with an image from Hieronymus Bosch: a figure sealed inside a transparent globe who floats serenely above the world. For Zweig it is an image of the artist, one who ''possesses everything, and also nothing. He has been offered a key to the myth, but the vehicle of his vision is also his prison.'' A similar image appears in Zweig's ''Departures,'' only this time the image of encapsulation and isolation defines a considerably more existential condition:   ''One morning I woke up with the impression that I was locked under a thickness of glass. The impression was so strong, I could virtually see the glass a few inches from my face. It was like a waking dream; I saw my feelings instead of experiencing them, as if my kidnapped body had excreted from it this secret of sidereal space, this smothered distance, which now flowered into one of those overused images the psyche loves: a glass dome.''
