title: American Talk
author: Robert Hendrickson
pull_quote: AMERICAN TALK. The Words and Ways of American Dialects. By Robert Hendrickson. 230 pages. Viking. $18.95. ''IT seemed to me that regional speech is in the process of disappearing, not gone but going,'' wrote John Steinbeck, describing a trip he took across America in the early 1960's. ''Forty years of radio and twenty years of television must have this impact. Communications must destroy localness, by a slow, inevitable process. I remember a time when I could almost pinpoint a man's place of origin by his speech. That is growing more difficult now and will in some foreseeable future become impossible.''   A quarter of a century has passed since Steinbeck made that observation, and it's true that the mass media have had their homogenizing - and pasturizing - effects. According to longtime Texas observers, Houstonites have steadily been losing their accents, and around the country, immigrants from ''da Bronx, Uppuh Manhattan, Toity-toid and Toid, Staten Oi-land, Lunk-Guylan, and Joisey'' have signed up with speech pathologists to learn how ''to sound like a person who comes from nowhere.'' Executives and clerks on the corporate fast-track attempt to jettison the verbal mannerisms that might betray their blue-collar roots, while teen-agers, from New York to Los Angeles, try to hone a kind of Valley Girl intonation that sounds ''rilly'' cool.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Between The Woods And The Water
author: Patrick Leigh Fermor
pull_quote: BETWEEN THE WOODS AND THE WATER. On Foot to Constantinople From the Hook of Holland: The Middle Danube to the Iron Gates. By Patrick Leigh Fermor. 248 pages. Elisabeth Sifton/Viking. $18.95. IN 1933 Patrick Leigh Fermor decided to see the world. He was 18 years old at the time, hanging around in London; two years earlier he had been expelled from his English public (i.e., private) school, after which he had drifted from preparing for a career in the army to playing around with the idea of pursuing a career as an author. Then, suddenly, he had an inspiration - he would tramp across Europe on foot, all the way to Constantinople.   The journey lasted 18 months; it was to be followed by many other journeys and long spells spent outside England, and in due course by a series of books - on Greece, the Caribbean and elsewhere - which would establish Mr. Leigh Fermor as the preeminent English travel writer of his generation. It was not until more than 40 years later, however, that he began writing an account of his original European trek, relying partly on old notebooks but still more on fabulous powers of recall.

title: November
pull_quote: NOVEMBER. By Janet Hobhouse. 198 pages. Vintage Contemporaries. $6.95.     Janet Hobhouse's people are all narcissists. That doesn't mean they're unlikable, shallow sorts - actually, they're more intelligent, more articulate and more charming than average. What it does mean is that they're constantly assessing their happiness, monitoring their emotional damage and charting their ability to take spiritual and sexual risks. And perhaps as a consequence, they spend most of the time being miserable - lonely, isolated and pretty much paralyzed when it comes to making important decisions about their families and their lives.

LAST May the Pace Gallery in New York assembled an exhibition featuring 45 of the 175 sketchbooks Picasso left to his heirs. Many of the sketchbooks were being shown for the first time and the show traveled to several major museums. Its title, and that of the accompanying book, comes from the cover of a 1907 sketchbook Picasso altered to read: ''Je suis le cahier appartenant a Monsieur Picasso peintre'' - ''I am the sketchbook belonging to Mr. Picasso the painter.'' (That sketchbook, however, is not one of those included in ''Je Suis le Cahier.'') Since Picasso was one of the most prolific artists of this century and his development was so changeable and refractory, only a selection of sketchbooks could be included in a single volume. Marc and Arnold Glimcher reproduce six sketchbooks in ''Je Suis le Cahier,'' and give samples from the remaining 169.

Paper, $4.95    In the title story of the collection, ''Postcards from Surfers,'' a young woman visiting a tacky seaside resort with her parents recalls being shown an idyllic postcard of Rio de Janiero by a Brazilian friend and asking him why he didn't live there, since it was so beautiful. ''Because,'' he had replied, ''right behind the beach there is a huge military base.'' Later on the character writes a series of postcards synopsizing her vacation (and her past) to a former lover, although she no longer knows his address and in the end throws the postcards away. Persistence in attempting to communicate despite belief in its impossibility is typical of the Australian writer Helen Garner's characters, as well as obliviousness to what postcard-pretty pictures don't show.

HIGHLY ranked among our sustaining mythologies is that of the dedicated physician who lived and labored not for the buck but, wonder of nostalgic wonders, for his patients. He even made house calls. This paragon performed not only in our collective memories but throughout our popular literature, which is a symptom of how much we treasured him. ''Interns Can't Take Money,'' ''Men in White,'' ''The Citadel'' come readily to mind. Young Kildare and old Gillespie, with hearts of gold, have flowed across the screens of our lives for 50 years. But, and there is always a ''but'' with such a myth, the hero (and it was invariably a hero and not a heroine) has, alas, dwindled down to the pygmy status of ''General Hospital'' and the public perception (true, false or in between) of young medicos on the make.

INSIDE By Helene Cixous. Translated by Carol Barko. 136 pp. New York: Schocken Books. $14.95. 

AFIRST novel that won the prestigious Prix Medicis in 1969, ''Inside'' is a daughter's account of her passionate attachment to her father and the violent separation caused by his premature death. It also tells the story of the emergence of the woman writer, a process Helene Cixous will later call a ''sortie,'' a ''coming-to-writing.'' Readers engaged in the complexities of those mother-daughter interactions so powerfully articulated by recent feminist authors - Ms. Cixous among them - might well be surprised by this affirmation of the father's importance to the woman writer. Yet ''Inside,'' now available in Carol Barko's excellent translation, exhibits important continuities with the author's later, more radically feminist and explicitly maternal works.
headline: FATHER OWNS THE WORDS

title: Bad Guys
author: Elizabeth Arthur
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BAD GUYS By Elizabeth Arthur. 262 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.    ISEE from the jacket copy that Elizabeth Arthur teaches writing to college students. My guess after reading ''Bad Guys'' is that she is very good at explaining how a novel works - technically. This one is a model of craft, at once intricate and economical, braiding together its two narrative strands with a practiced turn of the wrist. Descriptive touches - Ms. Arthur was praised for her rendering of the natural world in her previous novel, ''Beyond the Mountain'' -are here accurate but unobtrusive. And we can see her characters moving without a hitch to their appointed places. Alas, getting all the elements to work in concert is one thing, and bring-ing a world to life is quite another. That requires a kind of alchemist's intuition that can neither be taught nor learned.

Yet farming and, specifically, haying have stayed in his system, partly because he never completely understood the process and partly because it summoned ''all the epiphanies I have ever had'': ''They occurred while I stood on the edge of a field across a railroad spur line, my back to a small town, staring at farmsteads off in the distance.'' As Mr. Calvin, a neurobiologist at the University of Washington, explores such natural wonders as fossils, waterfalls, rapids and stars, he visits nearly every popular science topic - from genetic engineering to the aquatic-ape theory to artificial intelligence to sociobiology, the destruction of tropical rain forests and overpopulation. author: Martin Gilbert
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WINSTON S. CHURCHILL Volume Seven: Road to Victory 1941-1945. By Martin Gilbert. Illustrated. 1,417 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $40.    ''HOW does one seduce the elephant?'' asked the acolyte. ''First you must make yourself small, then you must make yourself clever,'' answered the wise man. Winston Spencer Churchill is a figure of elephantine proportions in history, lore, image. He was more than just the prime minister who happened to lead Britain and her empire during World War II; he gave the kind of leadership that inspired women and men to survive, struggle and eventually prevail. Martin Gilbert has tried to seduce, or at least embrace, the elephant by wrapping his arms all the way round. The seventh volume of his biography covers the era from the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor through the surrender of Hitler's Germany on May 8, 1945. That is approximately 1,350 pages of text, divided into 69 chapters, an average of around three weeks per chapter or one page for each day.   Stephen Oates, the biographer of Abraham Lincoln and Martin Luther King Jr., has suggested three categories of the genre - critical biography, which analyzes the subject; ''pure biography,'' which humanizes history by narrating a life story; and the chronicle, which recites the facts in dry, detached, lifeless prose. Mr. Gilbert's vast study is more than a chronicle, it falls short of pure biography and it avoids critical analysis.

Ms. Hobhouse, who has also written ''Everybody Who Was Anybody: A Biography of Gertrude Stein,'' looks at redemption through art and love and involvement. Zach arrives in London without plan or project and visits his brother, Michael, and sister-in-law, Helen. DID you know that if you fold a map of the United States in half lengthwise, Nebraska is on the center line? However much this seems unlikely, especially to Easterners, it is true; geographical fact does not invite opinion on the matter. Wright Morris, author of 19 novels, four collections of essays, three memoirs and five remarkable and original ''photo-texts'' that combine photographs and words in an assortment of ways, is from Nebraska. And even when his subjects depart from that setting, as they frequently do, the writer's unique voice - a touch irritable, adorned almost affectionately with his characters' cliches, unsympathetic to pretension, quirkily independent in the face of received opinion - belongs to the Middle Western farm people among whom he spent his early years. It is speech that is rarely elevated but too cunningly manipulated to be banal. ''The grain of the vernacular,'' Mr. Morris has said in an essay, ''naturally slopes downward. . . . The language leads and the writer follows where it leads.''

NO moderately curious browser will be able to resist picking up this book, if only to discover what the title refers to. Between these covers is the most satisfying array of oddities, marvels and novelties that has been gathered together in a blue moon.

The lucky owner of Ricky Jay's ''Learned Pigs & Fireproof Women'' will soon become familiar with Willard, the Man Who Grows, and various men and women who, to the great satisfaction of their adoring patrons, went through life gobbling down stones, swords, snakes and other treats. Brought before us for examination, along with the porcine wonders and resistant ladies of the title, is Harry Kahne, an artist who could write five different words - chosen by his audience - on five different blackboards simultaneously, holding pieces of chalk with each hand, each foot and his mouth. Kahne has hardly taken his bows before we are beguiled by the story of Blind Tom, born to slave parents in 1849, who was one of the most remarkable musical prodigies ever known, though he was sightless and mentally defective in most other respects. Among more recent miracle-workers included in this book is Kuda Bux (''The Man With the X-Ray Eyes''), who rode his bicycle after being blindfolded by a dedicated committee and actually walked on red-hot embers.

EARLY in the 19th century it was intellectually respectable to justify one's belief in God by arguing from design. The theologian William Paley presented one version of that argument in his ''Natural Theology'': Suppose we find a watch. We cannot imagine a watch arising without a watchmaker. And because organisms are vastly more complicated than watches, it is even harder to imagine them arising without an organism-maker.   The young Charles Darwin, when he was preparing to become a clergyman, occupied what were said to have been Paley's rooms in Christ's College, Cambridge. He later remarked that he had greatly admired Paley's works, though he had failed to pay much attention to the validity of the premises. In ''The Origin of Species'' (1859), Darwin revealed to the world that the so-called watchmaker is actually a purely natural process.

IN a recent golf tournament a veteran player called a penalty on himself when his ball moved imperceptibly after he had addressed his putt. Asked why he did this when no one else could have seen the ball move, he said he couldn't imagine the game being played any other way. He went on to win the tournament.

I was reminded of this incident while reading through Philip Booth's selected poems, intrigued by his slant on ''things as they are,'' the way he allows himself to use only available light, his refusal ever to cheat; rigorous habits of mind give his work an added tension and dimension. Titles like ''Weathers and Edges,'' ''Margins'' and ''Available Light'' evoke with philosophic accuracy the boundaries of his project. What can he quarry for himself from the real before night falls or the tide eats away the shoreline or the light fails or he falls asleep? He is no stranger to this condition.

pull_quote: MISHIMA A Vision of the Void. By Marguerite Yourcenar. Translated by Alberto Manguel with the author. 152 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $14.95.    IN November 1970, after haranguing an assembled mass of Japanese soldiers about their betrayal of their nation's glory, the writer Yukio Mishima, aided by unflinching friends, committed seppuku, a form of ritual suicide that involves disemboweling, decapitation and an almost unthinkable mixture of discipline, pain and mess. Was he mad, as the Japanese Prime Minister of the day suggested? Was he offering startling proof of loyalty to a defunct tradition? Before he died he shouted, ''Long live the Emperor,'' but can only have meant an ideal emperor, a once and future dream, and not the modest, historical Hirohito, who had disappointed Mishima by officially renouncing divine status. Did Mishima hope to drive a god to resurrection? Is this suicide intelligible to Westerners? Was it intelligible, in 1970 or after, to the Japanese? Can the act even be considered without dubious fascination or fancy theory? We shouldn't rush to answer these questions, and perhaps shouldn't answer some of them at all.
headline: UNABLE TO WAIT FOR THE GODS

title: The Complete Short Stories Of L P Hartley
author: L P Hartley
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE COMPLETE SHORT STORIES OF L. P. HARTLEY Introduction by Lord David Cecil. 760 pp. New York: Beaufort Books. $24.95.    HAD it not been for a film adaptation by Harold Pinter and Joseph Losey of his best-known novel, ''The Go-Between,'' L. P. Hartley (1895-1972) might have drifted into the gentle oblivion of a purely academic reputation. His novels - there are 18 of them, including ''The Hireling'' and ''Eustace and Hilda'' - often invoke the Edwardian age, that almost preternatural hush in time on the brink of World War I. Like Henry James, his most obvious literary forebear, Hartley examines the nuances of morality with a shimmering exactness, focusing on characters like Leo, the narrator of ''The Go-Between,'' caught between natural impulses and the social conventions that would thwart them. The short stories, just published in a massive volume, explore much the same territory, though readers familiar with the novels may be disappointed by these pieces, which - with wonderful exceptions - seem overconventional by comparison, even stunted, as if Hartley's imagination required more room to breathe than the shorter form permits.
headline: THAWED BY GHOSTS

title: Unspeakable Acts
author: Jan Hollingsworth
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: UNSPEAKABLE ACTS By Jan Hollingsworth. Illustrated. 592 pp. New York: Congdon & Weed. $18.95.    OF Susan, a parent who suspects that her child has been sexually abused, ''Unspeakable Acts'' tells us: ''Susan said she couldn't rest until she knew the truth. She wouldn't rest afterward, either.'' Readers of Jan Hollingsworth's account of a widely publicized Florida child-abuse case may feel the same. In its lurid details, its frustrating complexity and in the agony of the children and families who were victimized, this case would seem to be the paradigm of incidents in Minnesota, California and elsewhere that have surfaced in recent years. A startling difference, though, is the outcome: the molester was convicted and sentenced to life in prison.
headline: NIGHTMARE IN COUNTRY WALK

title: Washington
author: James Reston
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WASHINGTON. By James Reston. (Macmillan, $17.95.) This collection of columns by James Reston, who writes the Washington column on the Op-Ed page of The New York Times, ranges through five Presidencies, China, sports, universities, Congress and the press, among other subjects.
headline: IN SHORT: BOOKS FROM THE TIMES

title: Hotel Savoy
author: Joseph Roth
pull_quote: HOTEL SAVOY. With ''Fallmerayer the Stationmaster'' and ''The Bust of the Emperor.'' By Joseph Roth. Translated from the German by John Hoare. 183 pages. The Overlook Press. $16.95.    WORLD WAR I has been over for a couple of years. An Austrian soldier named Gabriel Dan is returning from captivity in Russia, making his way home to Vienna. First, however, he decides to break his journey in an unnamed town in Eastern Europe where some relatives live. For the most part the town is raw, dirty, blighted by smoke from its factory chimneys. But it also boasts a palatial hotel, the Savoy; and as soon as Gabriel checks in there, he feels he is at last back at ''the gates of Europe.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Before She Met Me
author: Julian Barnes
pull_quote: BEFORE SHE MET ME. By Julian Barnes. 174 pages. McGraw-Hill. Paper, $4.95. IN his most recent novel, the dazzling ''Flaubert's Parrot,''   Julian Barnes focused on a cuckolded scholar's obsessive attempts to come to terms with his idol, Gustave Flaubert; and in doing so, he not only reinvented old questions about the relationship of life to art, but also forced his protagonist -and his readers - to reassess the possibility of retrieving a biographical (or, for that matter, imaginary) past. Is it possible, he forced us to wonder, to truly imagine the life of another? And what sort of role does misinterpretation play in the relationship between writers and readers, historical figures and latter-day scholars?
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: A World Of Watchers
author: Joseph Kastner
pull_quote: A WORLD OF WATCHERS. By Joseph Kastner. With Illustrations by Louis Agassiz Fuertes. 241 pages. Knopf. $25.    ACCORDING to ''A World of Watchers,'' a certain ornithologist once defined bird watching as ''a mild paralysis of the central nervous system which can be cured only by rising at dawn and sitting in a bog.'' The remark is amusing but vague. It doesn't begin to explain why there are millions of bird watchers in America today, some 450,000 of whom are enrolled in various affiliates of the National Audubon Society.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Widow Claire
author: Horton Foote
pull_quote: OF course, almost nothing happens in ''The Widow Claire,'' the latest Horton Foote play to reach a New York stage. In keeping with his writing habits of four decades, the author of ''The Trip to Bountiful'' and ''Tender Mercies'' whisks us into the fictional small Texas town of Harrison and sets his characters about their diurnal business. ''The Widow Claire,'' a 95-minute anecdote in one act, describes only a single long summer night of 1911. Horace Robedaux (Matthew Broderick), a poor but ambitious 21-year-old about to enroll in a six-week business course in Houston, spends the eve of his departure courting the title character (Hallie Foote), a 27-year-old widow with several suitors and two rambunctious kids. Daybreak brings Horace's leave-taking and an exchange of farewells so formal one might wonder whether the couple had in fact stolen a few chaste kisses under the new moon of the night before.
headline: STAGE: 'WIDOW CLAIRE,' FROM HORTON FOOTE

title: Mission To Civilize: The French Way
author: Mort Rosenblum
pull_quote: MISSION TO CIVILIZE: The French Way.   By Mort Rosenblum. 470 pages. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $19.95.    THE French have been exporting civilization for a long time, and in the days when they ruled a vast empire their standard was that they were engaged on a civilizing mission. Nor was it only publicists and propagandists who proclaimed the belief, but many of their finest spirits. In his new book, ''Mission to Civilize,'' two of the most ardent apologists for the 19th-century conquest of Algeria quoted by Mort Rosenblum - both of them depicting it as a triumph of progress over barbarism - are Alfred de Vigny and Victor Hugo.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: My Dog Tulip
author: J R Ackerley
pull_quote: MY DOG TULIP. By J. R. Ackerley. 160 pages. Poseidon Press. $7.95.    Virginia Woolf wrote a biography of Flush, Elizabeth Barrett Browning's cocker spaniel. And John Steinbeck wrote a book about traveling across America with his French poodle Charley. Lesser known - to Americans, at least - is the story of Tulip, an Alsatian belonging to the writer J. R. Ackerley, who immortalized her in ''My Dog Tulip'' - an odd, charming and utterly English memoir, praised by E. M. Forster and Elizabeth Bowen, that has long been unavailable in this country.
headline: A Man and His Dog

title: Wallace Stevens
author: Joan Richardson. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: WALLACE STEVENS The Early Years 1879-1923. By Joan Richardson. Illustrated. 591 pp. New York: Beech Tree Books/ William Morrow & Company. $21.95.    IT'S hard to conjure up a picture of the young Wallace Stevens. As a poet, he was a late bloomer - 35 years old when he began to write the poems in his first book, ''Harmonium,'' and 44 when it was published in 1923. In the best-known glimpses we have of him he is already the imposing, remote vice president of the Hartford Accident and Indemnity Company composing verses in his head as he walks to work. Even the famous story of his fist fight with Hemingway comes from his later years - he was close to 60 when he threw those drunken punches. No youthful high jinks there.
headline: A POET: BOLD AND FEARFUL

pull_quote: THE GOOD WOMAN. By B. J. Chute. (Vanguard, $14.95.) Long before the homeless became headlines, the image of the bag lady had taken root in fantasy.

PRESIDENTS' SECRET WARS CIA and Pentagon Covert Operations Since World War II. By John Prados. 480 pp. New York: William Morrow & Company. $22.95.    THERE is nothing that can damage a reputation - or a Presidency - like a secret war. And now Ronald Reagan has his.

title: Children's Island
author: P. C. Jersild. Translated by Joan Tate.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CHILDREN'S ISLAND By P. C. Jersild. Translated by Joan Tate. 288 pp. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press. Cloth, $25.95. Paper, $11.50.    REINE LARSSON, the voluble narrator of this essentially picaresque tale originally published in Sweden in 1976, is a boy with a mission. This insatiably curious urban 10-year-old who loves language, life and the idea of independence wants answers to the great existential questions. But he hasn't got much time. Any morning now, he'll make his daily inspection of his ''male member,'' and instead of blond fuzz he'll find a real hair. Once this happens, it's curtains. ''The day he reached puberty, all was lost. . . . Imprisoned in horniness and other mucky things, your thoughts would never again be pure. All your energy would go on getting sex, and there would be nothing left to solve problems.'' He has seen lust wreak havoc. And he's read Freud - in his encyclopedia. He imagines adolescence as an ''insane . . . pornographic fair,'' where ''everywhere, on the Ferris wheel, on the rollercoaster, in the fun house . . . on the railing around the dance floor, thousands of youths were all sitting blind to their surroundings,'' masturbating ''like monkeys.''
headline: OH NO, - NOT PUBERTY!

title: The Century's Daughter
author: Pat Barker
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE CENTURY'S DAUGHTER By Pat Barker. 284 pp. New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons. $16.95.    IN her new novel, Pat Barker is concerned with two kinds of death - the transient one-time-only death of the flesh, and the living death of long-term unemployment. Her setting, as in her first two novels, ''Union Street'' and ''Blow Your House Down,'' is along working-class streets in the north of England. But she is no provincial writer working in a narrow or marginal genre. Her vision is worldly and in the grand tradition of political fiction that she has entered so ambitiously.
headline: LIZA TOUGHS IT OUT

author: Andre Dubus.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LAST WORTHLESS EVENING Four Novellas & Two Stories. By Andre Dubus. 214 pp. Boston: David R. Godine. $15.95.    IN Andre Dubus's fine story ''Rose,'' a nameless former Marine Corps lieutenant muses in a bar: ''We like to believe that in this last quarter of the century, we know and are untouched by everything; yet it takes only a very small jolt, at the right time, to knock us off balance for the rest of our lives.'' That could be the keynote of the four novellas and two short stories in ''The Last Worthless Evening,'' dealing mainly with ordinary people whose common bond is a kind of ecstasy of despair, which can also be their source of strength.

pull_quote: THE EARTH ABIDETH. By George Dell. (Ohio State University, $14.95.) ''The Earth Abideth'' is a novel both of and from another time.

title: American Musicians
author: Whitney Balliett.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: AMERICAN MUSICIANS Fifty-six Portraits in Jazz. By Whitney Balliett. 415 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $22.95.    Whitney Balliett, the jazz columnist for The New Yorker, has been writing biographical pieces about jazz artists since 1962, and this book collects all 49 articles (and 56 portraits) in one place at last. Of Mr. Balliett's 11 previous books - mostly shorter collections -''American Musicians'' makes at least three entire volumes plus hunks of several others obsolete. His biographical articles are his best, so this is his most valuable book. All of Mr. Balliett's subjects are American instrumentalists except for three Frenchmen, including the violinist Stephane Grappelli, and the Belgian-born guitarist Django Reinhardt.   Books about jazz seem to proliferate these days - especially books about jazz before the 1950's, when it was among America's most popular musics. That era attracts readers, perhaps because the music is receding into the past, surviving largely in memory, on reissued records and less satisfactorily in revival performances. Among the subjects of these 56 portraits, only the Modern Jazz Quartet and a dozen others are wholeheartedly ''modern'' musicians - that is, post-Charlie Parker. In fact, the majority are past the age of 65 - or would be if they were still alive - and only two are younger than 55.

author: Joseph Nocera
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

title: Cradle Song
author: Jane Rawlinson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CRADLE SONG By Jane Rawlinson. 174 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $12.95.    THIS surreal, impressionistic tale set in colonial Kenya explores a young British mother's irresistible desire to claim her housemaid's black son and the consequences of the extraordinary bond that grows between them. Isaac calls Ursula ''Mummy''; she calls him ''son.'' Ursula feels almost relieved at the sudden and unexplained deaths of her own baby daughter and husband, which leave her a lone white memsahib on a barren plantation surrounded by what she feels are conniving, irresponsible black servants and her beloved Isaac, with whom she even shares her bed. Ursula teaches Isaac to paint, count and read, and dresses him in her dead child's clothes, while her servants look on in perplexity and white neighbors glance away in horror and disgust.
headline: BLACK-AND-WHITE KALEIDOSCOPE

author: William C Jr Ketchum
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

Ketchum Jr. takes a colorful, spirited look at the handmade objects he calls ''America's glory.'' Geared toward collectors, but avoiding the this-is-how-much-it-costs approach of collecting guides, Mr. Ketchum's book is a personalized journey through the distinctively American themes and symbols that have occupied our collective imagination.

author: Benjamin J. Cohen.

Arguably - at least until the recent crisis over arms sales to Iran - the attention of President Reagan has been focused more closely on Mexican debt, the United States trade deficit, the depreciation of the dollar and other financial and commercial issues than on arms control and strategic defense.

(Ages 3 to 8)    THOUGH children and art museums are fairly incompatible, they should, I suppose, occasionally be exposed to each other. Such exposure is the theme of ''Visiting the Art Museum,'' which portrays a family trip to an institution that suggests both the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Modern Art in New York City.

FOR nearly two decades ''objective data'' have been tossed about to prove that drugs are everything from a demonic force unleashed in the heartland of America to an innocent avocation of artists and youth, evil only in the minds of government propagandists.

title: Mission To Civilize. The French Way
author: Mort Rosenblum.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
MISSION TO CIVILIZE The French Way. By Mort Rosenblum. 470 pp. San Diego: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $19.95. 

THE French and the Americans have a fascination with each other that reaches back to their ancien regime and our colonial times. This awareness of family resemblance has led a host of commentators in successive generations to attempt explanations of one culture to the other. In this tradition, Mort Rosenblum's ''Mission to Civilize: The French Way'' is a good introduction to contemporary high-tech France, the France of Ariane rockets, the train a grande vitesse, the Pompidou Center and military interventions in Chad and Togo. Anyone for whom the term ''French'' evokes only Chartres, Chateau Rothschild or Catherine Deneuve selling Chanel perfume will discover here that France is the world's third-ranking exporter of arms, produces two-thirds of its electricity in atomic power plants, maintains an independent force de frappe that includes four nuclear submarines, and has over 1,000 members of its armed forces stationed permanently in Africa.
headline: LOSE THE COLONIES, KEEP AN EMPIRE

title: Marilyn
author: Gloria Steinem. Photographs by George Barris.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MARILYN By Gloria Steinem. Photographs by George Barris. 182 pp. New York: Henry Holt & Company. $24.95.    ON June 1, 1962, her 36th birthday, Marilyn Monroe began what would be her final attempt to tell her story. Lies had been told about her, she insisted, and she was going to set the record straight. In addition to the biographical information she had contributed in interviews over the years, she had launched a previous full-scale autobiography in conjunction with the novelist and playwright Ben Hecht. Minus the name of its co-author, ''My Story,'' as that unfinished manuscript was called, was published in 1974 and reissued in paperback this year.   For her new venture Marilyn Monroe also had a collaborator, a photojournalist, George Barris. Mr. Barris was obviously a sympathetic co-adjutant. Through June and July Marilyn talked and posed - and drank champagne. Mr. Barris took many soft gentle pictures of her, in bathing suit, towels, beach robe, sweater. But this project, too, was not completed. On Aug. 4 Marilyn Monroe died of an overdose of sleeping pills. More than two decades later, Mr. Barris turned over his photographs to Gloria Steinem for use in her present thoughtful and absorbing biography of the actress.
headline: 'PLEASE DON'T MAKE ME A JOKE'

title: Felix Mendelssohn: A Life In Letters
author: Rudolf Elvers
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FELIX MENDELSSOHN: A Life in Letters. Edited by Rudolf Elvers. (Fromm International, $22.50.) ''Dear silent Schleinitz: Can such a thing be plausible? Isn't your own hair standing on end? That I, the worst correspondent in the kingdom, am writing for the second time already, and you, one of the best, have yet to write one at all. . . . Oh Schleinitz! This is atrocious beyond all atrocity; I am writing this entire letter con fuoco.''
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Thursday's Universe
author: Marcia Bartusiak
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THURSDAY'S UNIVERSE By Marcia Bartusiak. Illustrated. 306 pp. New York: Times Books. $19.95. 

A HEADLINE in the Oct. 12 New York Times read, ''2 Stars Offering Study of Gravity''; the story announced the discovery of a pair of burned-out stars orbiting around each other in a frantic 11-minute dance of death. Readers intrigued by such hints of cosmic mystery, who puzzle over the latest news from out there but don't know quite where it all fits in, will welcome ''Thursday's Universe,'' Marcia Bartusiak's authoritative new book. But read it with dispatch, for the frontiers of modern astrophysics are a region, like the checkerboard land of ''Through the Looking Glass,'' in which one has to move quickly to stay in the same place. A scant week after I began reading ''Thursday's Universe,'' as new research results appeared in journals and newspapers and on bulletin boards in astrophysics labs, it had already begun to show its age. Yet for a few years at least this will be a book that can render the arcana of astrophysical research understandable to the public.
headline: A GRAIN OF SAND WOULD FALL LIKE AN ATOM BOMB

pull_quote: THE JOURNAL OF NICHOLAS THE AMERICAN. By Leigh Kennedy. (Atlantic Monthly, $16.95.) This story of a first-generation Russian-American is anything but what one expects, and therein lies much of its appeal.

title: The New Maginot Line
author: Jon Connell
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE NEW MAGINOT LINE By Jon Connell. 348 pp. New York: Arbor House. $18.95. 

JON CONNELL, a correspondent for The Sunday Times of London, contends that NATO in general and the United States in particular have adopted a ''magic weapon mentality.'' NATO, seeking to offset its inferiority to the Warsaw Pact in conventional warfare by exploiting its technological advantages, Mr. Connell says, is buying weapons that are too complicated to perform effectively on the battlefield and too expensive to be deployed in sufficient numbers. In ''The New Maginot Line,'' Mr. Connell views NATO's reliance on first use of nuclear weapons as a similarly misplaced dependence on technology, arguing that the impossibility of fighting limited nuclear wars invalidates NATO's strategy of using nuclear weapons as a cheap substitute for adequate conventional forces. Finally, he condemns President Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative, popularly known as ''Star Wars,'' as the ultimate in illusory technological fixes.
headline: GUNS THAT DIE OF EMBARRASSMENT

title: Women-Church
author: Rosemary Radford Ruether.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
critic: Susan Schnur Is A Rabbi and Writer Who Teaches Religion At Colgate University
pull_quote: WOMEN-CHURCH Theology and Practice of Feminist Liturgical Communities. By Rosemary Radford Ruether. 306 pp. San Francisco: Harper & Row. $16.95.    FLANNERY O'CONNOR once wrote, ''To the deaf, you must shout! And to the near-blind, you must draw large, wild pictures.'' Sometimes it seems as though Rosemary Radford Ruether thinks all of us are deaf and near-blind. But then one must remember to whom Ms. Ruether is used to talking: the Roman Catholic Church - an institution not renowned, as far as feminists are concerned, for its ability either to hear or to see. Ms. Ruether, a professor of theology at Garret-Evangelical Theological Seminary in Evanston, Ill., and author of many books, including ''Sexism and God-Talk,'' deserves a good deal of credit for simply staying in dialogue with this church over the 25 years in which she has taught, lectured and written. It's no wonder, perhaps, that in the process she has lost a measure of moderation.
headline: SING TO HEAVEN A NEW SONG

title: Memories Of Mistresses
author: Luigi Barzini
pull_quote: MEMORIES OF MISTRESSES. Reflections From a Life. By Luigi Barzini. 311 pages. Collier Books/Macmillan. Paper, $12.95. ''MEMORIES OF MIS=   TRESSES'' is a collection of 22 essays by Luigi Barzini, who died in 1984. The title is not only deplorable but actively misleading as well, and there is no indication where or when any of the pieces originally appeared; but in other respects the publisher deserves a wholehearted vote of thanks. Barzini was one of the outstanding journalists of his time, and most of the articles and sketches that have been salvaged display the same sparkle that he brought to his celebrated account of his countrymen, ''The Italians.''
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: Anywhere But Here
author: Mona Simpson
pull_quote: ANYWHERE BUT HERE. By Mona Simpson. 406 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95.    MONA SIMPSON'S stunning first novel opens simply with a glimpse of a mother and a daughter driving westward in a Lincoln Continental. They are driving from their hometown of Bay City, Wis., to California so that the girl - Ann - can become a child star. In lieu of eating at restaurants, they steal vegetables from convenient farm trucks, and they use a borrowed credit card to charge gasoline and one-night stays at cheap motels. Behind them, to the east, is their old life, a life of modest expectations, modest comforts and modest rewards; ahead lies California, and all the glittering promises of that golden land.
headline: BOOKS OF THE TIMES

title: The Secret House
author: David Bodanis
pull_quote: EVER wonder what your house is up to when you're not looking? According to David Bodanis, a British science writer, that seemingly sedate structure of brick, wood or stucco shimmers, breathes, melts, hisses and otherwise is often up to no good. His book ''The Secret House: 24 Hours in the Strange and Unexpected World in Which We Spend Our Nights and Days'' (Simon & Schuster, $18.95) zooms in relentlessly on the mundane matters of modern life, proving once again that the difference between the ordinary and the exotic is only your point of view.   It's nothing short of astounding, the things we routinely ignore. That annoying static on your radio as you hunt for the right station may be lightning striking on distant continents.
headline: A Microscopic Look at the Home and Other Exotic, Hidden Worlds

title: Frank Norris: Novels And Essays
author: Donald Pizer
pull_quote: FRANK NORRIS: Novels and Essays. Edited by Donald Pizer. 1,232 pages. Library of America. $27.50. There is a fairly straight line in the American naturalistic novel from Frank Norris to Theodore Dreiser to John Steinbeck. Some of the themes they tackled through their characters first appeared in nonfiction form at the turn of the century, when the muckraking magazine journalists examined the excesses of various industries, from the stockyards to the oilfields. Looking at the popular books published today, it's hard to imagine that powerful works of fiction and fact that exposed unsafe conditions in the mines or the travails of migratory workers once led to legislative changes.   Few modern novelists grapple with such issues affecting everyday lives in the manner of the influential naturalists; when they sometimes attempt to do so, critics with narrow historical vision reproach these authors (or dramatists or scenarists) and brand their work agitprop. One need hardly add: how shortsighted and discouraging to present-day writers who have something significant to say.
headline: Books of The Times; The Naturalistic Novel

title: Boswell: The English Experience, 1785-1789
author: Frederick A Pottle
pull_quote: BOSWELL: THE ENGLISH EXPERIMENT, 1785-1789. Edited by Irma S. Lustig and Frederick A. Pottle. Illustrated. 332 pages. McGraw-Hill. $24.95.    IN November 1785, when ''The English Experiment'' opens, James Boswell was 45 years old. Samuel Johnson had died the previous December, and Boswell, who had just published his account of the tour that he and Johnson had made to the Hebrides, was getting ready to start work on a full-scale biography. Over the next three years or so he completed a first draft, and at the same time continued keeping the journal that was eventually, after coming to light in the 20th century, to give him a secondary but substantial claim to lasting fame.

title: The Broom Of The System
author: David Foster Wallace
pull_quote: THE BROOM OF THE SYSTEM. By David Foster Wallace. 467 pages. Viking. Cloth, $18.95; paper, $7.95.   This novel, chosen by Viking to kick off its new series of contemporary American fiction, was written by a 24-year-old graduate of Amherst College who is working for his M.F.A. at the University of Arizona. It's an unwieldy, uneven work - by turns, hilarious and stultifying, daring and derivative - but at the same time, it's a novel that attests to the publishers's committment to risky new fiction and its young author's rich reserves of ambition and imagination.

title: Chekhov
author: Henri Troyat
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CHEKHOV By Henri Troyat. Translated by Michael Henry Heim. Illustrated. 364 pp. New York: E. P. Dutton. $22.50.   WITH the publication in English of his study of Anton Chekhov, the Russian-born Henri Troyat has once again demonstrated that he is an excellent biographer. Whether his subject is one of Russia's despotic rulers, like Ivan the Terrible or Catherine the Great, or one of its complicated writers, such as Pushkin, Dostoyevsky, Gogol or Tolstoy, Mr. Troyat has a storyteller's skill for dealing with real-life characters. Their intimate worlds, their defeats, pains and triumphs, become the reader's. Mr. Troyat refrains from cluttering his biographies with mountains of details; instead, he selects only those events - large and small - that contribute to the whole picture. The academically inclined might like to know more about an event or person, but Mr. Troyat refuses to comply if he feels it would impede the dramatic flow of his story. Unobtrusive and seductive, his biographies read like novels. And that's no small achievement.
headline: LOOK AT YOUR BAD, BORING LIVES

title: Rock Of Ages: The Rolling Stone History Of Rock & Roll
author: Ed Ward, Geoffrey Stokes and Ken Tucker. Illustrated.

pull_quote: ROCK OF AGES The Rolling Stone History of Rock & Roll. By Ed Ward, Geoffrey Stokes and Ken Tucker. Illustrated. 649 pp. New York: Rolling Stone Press/Summit Books. Cloth, $24.95. Paper, $14.95. WE never did outgrow it, this hopped-up musical hybrid, this raucous noise that ultimately made all of popular culture march to its beat. When rock first began to shake, rattle and roll its way across the American consciousness, we children of the 1950's were told that it was at best a freakish fad - the musical equivalent of the Hula-Hoop or Davy Crockett's coonskin cap. At worst, it was the sound of the civilized social fabric unraveling. By the end of that decade, there were signs that this rude, frenzied musical aberration had spent its energy.   When the Beatles gave rock-and-roll a much-needed jolt, the moptops were generally regarded as a sociological phenomenon of a particularly silly season. We would soon leave this awkward age behind, we were assured. We would outgrow rock and adolescence together, and if we listened to music at all it would be good music, adult music. Guy Lombardo. Jerry Vale. Broadway show tunes. We would reflect on that loud, crazy music of old and laugh at the follies of youth.

outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE BUTCHER'S WIFE. By Li Ang. Translated by Howard Goldblatt and Ellen Yeung. (North Point, $14.95.) In Taiwan this first novel by Li Ang won a major literary award in 1983 and outraged a number of critics and government officials who considered it little more than pornography. ''The Butcher's Wife'' is not pornographic, but it omits few details or four-letter words in describing the brutalization of young Lin Shi by her much older husband, Chen Jiangshui, who treats her like the pigs he butchers in his slaughterhouse. Based on a homicide in Shanghai in the 1930's, the novel begins with two fictional press accounts of Lin Shi's harrowing murder of her husband. These reports are dismissive of her motives, but in the ensuing story of her life before the killing, in the small superstitious town of Lucheng, the author is wholly sympathetic to Lin Shi. Her fate, meant to be both shockingly singular and representative of oppressed women, is certainly among the most pathetic in recent world literature. Orphaned at 9, Lin Shi is forced to live with her unscrupulous uncle until he marries her off at 20 to Chen Jiangshui. His numbing mistreatment of her begins on their wedding night and escalates until the moment of her impulsive revenge. The story is simple, uncluttered and powerful in its way but is undermined by its repetitious scenes of sexual violence. Lin Shi is such a naive, defenseless victim and Chen Jiangshui such a vicious, unmotivated monster that our interest eventually wanes.

GET out your calculators, please. Take the number of stars in the universe and multiply it by the number of planets per star; subtract those that are too cold, hot, wet or dry to support life; take into account the lifetime of a typical alien civilization; correct for the inconvenience of interstellar travel (''assume ten tons of spaceship per colonist'') and don't forget that the travelers might have to zigzag; consider also U.F.O.'s, the Anthropic Principle and the Garbage Hypothesis; and you arrive at the probability that someone out there is trying to get in touch. If your answer is somewhere between impossible and certain, you know as much as the scientists debating this question, and you probably know as much as anyone will know in your lifetime. Unless, that is, the international coterie of astronomers now engaged in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) finally does ''answer the greatest long-distance call in history,'' as Thomas R. McDonough hopes and expects.

LAST year American readers were introduced to the British writer Julian Barnes with the publication of ''Flaubert's Parrot,'' a book that virtually created its own genre. Labeled a novel by its author, it was actually more like a literary improvisation on the life and art of Gustave Flaubert, combining stylistic elements of works as wildly disparate as the critical biography, the medieval bestiary and the train-spotter's guide. The result was an irreverent hodgepodge that, for all its playfulness, had serious and provocative things to say about our fascination with the elusive figures of our past.

Bruce Lincoln, a professor of Russian history at Northern Illinois University, has adapted the concept to his seventh book on Russian history, a sequel to his 1983 survey ''In War's Dark Shadow'' and an extension of his earlier studies, ''The Romanovs'' and ''In the Vanguard of Reform.'' pull_quote: MATISSE The Man and His Art, 1869-1918. By Jack Flam. Illustrated. 523 pp. Ithaca, N.Y.: Cornell University Press. $75.   THE life of Henri Matisse doesn't offer much in the way of drama, and Matisse's painting and sculpture, though radiant with feeling, are just a tad impersonal. The Olympian clarity of his art depends on a certain denial of the autobiographical impulse. Matisse is one of those artists - more in the line of Raphael than of Michelangelo - who are reluctant to leave shreds of undigested feeling hanging around. In the midst of his gigantic achievement, it may seem foolish to regret the absence of a more personal note; but Matisse can sometimes project the off-putting, holier-than-thou aura of one of those great writers who have burned - or have meant to burn - all their personal papers. Matisse would probably be glad to know that more than 30 years after his death the relationship between his art and his life looks as elusive as ever. The basic paradoxes remain: he is still the timid slow starter who went farther than almost any other artist of his age; he is still the conventional-mannered bourgeois - people called him ''Professor,'' ''Doctor'' - who smashed every convention of bourgeois art.

ELEVEN years after victory, Vietnam lurches in the company of the world's poorest nations, far behind its non-Communist neighbors in Southeast Asia. Its 60 million people live in conditions not much better, and in some cases worse, than prevailed during the 30 years of war. While unable to produce enough food or goods, the Hanoi Government maintains the world's third-largest standing army (after the Soviet Union and China), and uses it to subjugate its neighboring country, Cambodia - just the way the big boys used to treat Vietnam. The successors of the legendary Ho Chi Minh have made Vietnam a pariah among nations, almost entirely dependent on parsimonious Soviet patronage and continually threatened by its ancestral enemy, China.

title: After The Fires
author: Peter Demetz
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MEDICAL IMPLICATIONS OF NUCLEAR WAR Institute of Medicine/ National Academy of Sciences. Edited by Fredric Solomon and Robert Q. Marston. Foreword by Lewis Thomas. 619 pp. Washington: National Academy Press. Cloth, $43.50. Paper, $33.50. THE title of this collection of papers, ''The Medical Implications of Nuclear War,'' suggests a discussion cast in narrow clinical terms. In fact, the volume offers a comprehensive survey of the consequences of a major nuclear exchange, ranging from the carnage caused by blast, fire and radiation to long-term effects on the environment and on human society. This marshaling of the work of experts in many scientific fields creates a harrowing prospect, a kind of multidisciplinary vision of doomsday.   On scientific grounds, the work shares the weaknesses, as well as the strengths, of such assessments. The reliability of the source is not in question; the volume is based on a symposium organized by the ultraresponsible National Academy of Sciences' Institute of Medicine. The catch is that credibility in science depends on verifiability. Until a nuclear war occurs, the results remain hypothetical. And who would want the hypothesis tested?
headline: THE DOOMSDAY HYPOTHESIS

title: The Complete Notebooks Of Henry James
author: Lyall H Powers
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE COMPLETE NOTEBOOKS OF HENRY JAMES Edited by Leon Edel and Lyall H. Powers. Illustrated. 633 pp. New York: Oxford University Press. $30.   NEAR the end of his life Henry James destroyed many of his personal papers. Probably without intending to, he left behind nine notebooks or journals now deposited at Harvard's Houghton Library. Except for one small notebook, they resemble the old composition books, about 6 by 8 inches, which would have cost him only a few pennies each. They were not meant for posterity. They were a place where, in entries dated by James between 1878 and 1911, he could jot down the ''germs'' - things picked up at dinner parties or in his reading - that eventually would become novels or tales. Some notes are skeletal, others develop into full scenarios, and all are far more concerned with his possible method or treatment than with an ostensible subject. The notebooks became a workshop both for his fiction and for his subsequent commentaries on it in the prefaces to the New York Edition of his works, later collected in ''The Art of Fiction'' by R. P. Blackmur, who called them ''the most eloquent and original piece of literary criticism in existence.''

MAKOTO UEDA, the editor of this noteworthy anthology of modern Japanese short stories, has divided the book into five sections: the Maiden, the Wife, the Mistress, the Mother and the Working Woman. It is an indication that the influence of roles, even with the changes in postwar Japan, is still felt. The authors are all established -among them, the 1968 Nobel laureate Yasunari Kawabata and other popular writers such as Kobo Abe, Kafu Nagai and Fumiko Enchi - and include an almost equal number of men and women writers. (Readers be warned that the table of contents lists the authors in the traditional Japanese order, with surnames first.) The surface of these stories, mostly written since World War II, is often deceptively placid. The writing is spare. Because the stories have various translators -all, in fact, students of Mr. Ueda (who teaches at Stanford University) - it is hard to measure how much of the voice and style of a story is the author's own. Some are smoother than others. Still, throughout the placid prose there is strong emotion. In ''A Woman to Call Mother'' by Taiko Hirabayashi, a daughter's failure to visit her dying mother is ''an indication that their emotions were too strong.'' By refraining from frenzied description, the writer renders the drama in a story all the more powerfully.

THOMAS SHEEHAN is a philosopher whose effort to construct a ''postmodern and postliberal'' interpretation of the meaning of Jesus aroused considerable debate even before ''The First Coming'' was published. Along with many other works of modern theology, this book provides an interpretation of the Gospels that supports and legitimizes secular philosophical thought in the context of theological debate, in this case the ''hermeneutical'' method. In what represents a more radical pattern of exegesis, the work joins a growing corpus of contemporary Catholic treatments of Jesus that finds in the Gospels no basis for major elements of Catholic dogma. ''The First Coming'' endorses the disarray within Catholicism as a hopeful sign that the Church - and the distinction between God and man - will dissolve to usher in the Kingdom that Jesus actually proclaimed. Expertly documented and compellingly written, it is likely to be stimulating even for those who, on account of some stubborn, sentimental or superstitious attachment to the idea of Jesus as the Christ, cannot respond to the sound of this trumpet.

headline: FADED GLORY, VANISHED HOPES By John Logue. 230 pp. Boston: Little, Brown & Company. $16.95.    DREAMS of bygone glory dominate the lives of a diverse group of Alabamians in John Logue's intriguing novel, set in the capital city of Montgomery in 1967. The populist Governor, Jesse Stuart, recalls his youthful hopes that his gifts as a baseball hero would lift his family from rural poverty. A cynical newsman, Jack Harris, yearns for the passion and commitment that had distinguished his coverage of the famous bus boycott. A black clergyman, James Boone Jr., guiltily regrets his loss of faith; his parishioner, Arabella Jackson, whose son has died in Vietnam, wants to bury him on a beloved hillside, now annexed to the city's whites-only cemetery. In covering this dramatic story, Jack Harris runs into an even more explosive one: the Governor is secretly selling criminal pardons to secure his family's fortune before news of his mortal illness becomes public.   There is material here for several novels. Mr. Logue, who is the creative director of Southern Living magazine, nicely catches the inky ambiance of the newsroom before the computer terminal took over, and he has created a persuasive narrative voice for Jack Harris, the editor-narrator. Yet the author allows Harris to tell only portions of the story, disconcertingly shifting in and out of third-person narration in ways that sever the dramatic links his complicated tale requires. Moreover, perhaps his experience as the author of three mystery novels has led Mr. Logue to take technical shortcuts in which violent action substitutes for acuity in characterization.   The story is set precisely in January 1967, yet the mood of the novel seems distinctly late 1970's. Harris walks in front of Martin Luther King Jr.'s church on Dexter Avenue, musing about ''a movement now as forgotten as the river,'' without mentioning the great Selma march past that very spot not two years before. Boone complains that the burial of a black soldier shouldn't cause an uproar because ''nobody here wants to think about this war anymore,'' a sentiment that seems totally wrong for Alabama in 1967. Similarly, the police are stern with the surprisingly small number of redneck opponents of the soldier's burial and astonishingly courteous to the black mourners.   As the soldier's family watches his internment, an angry white family scrambles in the clay to remove a coffin from the adjacent plot. Having failed to rouse a violent protest, they have obtained a court order allowing them to open the grave rather than allow their mother to be buried near a Negro. Despite the historical discontinuities of the mood, Mr. Logue has written a powerful epitaph for the social conflict that still gripped Alabama in 1967.

title: Of Love And Shadows
author: Isabel Allende
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LEAD:  OF LOVE AND SHADOWS
headline: EROS MAKES WAR By Isabel Allende. Translated by Margaret Sayers Peden. 274 pp. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $17.95.    FEW literary legends can compare to that surrounding ''The House of the Spirits,'' Isabel Allende's family-chronicle-cum-history of her native Chile. Her very first novel, published when she was in her early 40's, rose to best-sellerdom. Reviewers were indulgent. Here was a beautiful, humane, talented woman who happened to be the exiled niece of the martyred Chilean President Salvador Allende. The troublesome secret was that in prose and format the book was mostly imitation Garcia Marquez.   Happily, Ms. Allende is no longer the novice in ''Of Love and Shadows,'' a suspenseful thriller. Set in the terrorized Chile of Gen. Augusto Pinochet (himself an occasional character), it tells of the love that grows between Irene Beltran - feisty, innocent, marginally upper-class and a reporter for a women's magazine - and Francisco Leal, son of impoverished Spanish Republican exiles, an unemployed psychologist and sometime political activist who casually drifts into Irene's office as a freelance photographer. Together they cover a variety of beats, but something clicks when they start investigating Evangelina, a 15-year-old peasant girl and fabled miracle worker. During a brutal army search of her family's house, Evangelina, in a trance, singlehandedly lifts up a cruel lieutenant and hurls him out the door.   Soon thereafter Evangelina ''disappears''; through journalistic tips and footwork the hero and heroine locate the girl's corpse in an abandoned mine shaft, where bodies of dozens of the regime's opponents are also decaying. Francisco takes photos; word spreads; a scandal ensues. Then someone sprays Irene with bullets from a passing car. She survives in the hospital but is obviously marked for Government liquidation. With help from friends she and Francisco assume disguises, quietly flee Santiago and cross the Andes into Argentina, ready to fight the dictatorship from exile. ''We will return,'' they say. LOVE and struggle a la ''Casablanca'' - it's all there. Ms. Allende skillfully evokes both the terrors of daily life under military rule and the subtler forms of resistance in the hidden corners and ''shadows'' of her title, particularly in the churches or in simple unsung acts of solidarity. At the same time the author ably captures the voices of the regime's apologists - the complex lies and cliches of its proud male foot soldiers and the pat false phrases of its rich lady cheerleaders. A journalist herself, Ms. Allende renders with expert detail such offbeat worlds as the professional routines of a hairdresser, the range of types in a private nursing home or the operations of the Santiago city morgue. While her prose at times verges on soap opera, that is also one of its charms. She can just as deftly depict loving tenderness as convey the high fire of eroticism. And when you've successfully mingled sex and politics with a noble cause, how can you go wrong?   While the translation by Margaret Sayers Peden is at times awkward (for example, ''pythoness'' and ''chiromancy'' instead of ''fortune teller'' and ''palmistry'') and could use more colloqualisms and contractions, on the whole it's a supple piece of work.

title: Skinny Legs And All
author: Tom Robbins
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SKINNY LEGS AND ALL By Tom Robbins. 422 pp. New York: Bantam Books. $19.95. By Joe Queenan WITH the retirement of Ronald Reagan, the demise of Drexel Burnham Lambert and the collapse of the Japanese stock market, it is generally agreed that the 1980's are over. The 1960's, however, are still very much with us - not only in the presence of porky, recidivist rock stars but in the continuing literary efforts of Tom Robbins, who is back with yet another surrealistic, phantasmagoric, free-association novel that makes you want to dust off those old Firesign Theater records and don those frayed, tie-dyed bell bottoms one last time.   Although Mr. Robbins made his name in the 1970's with his zany novels "Even Cowgirls Get the Blues" and "Still Life With Woodpecker," these were very much products of a laid-back, anti-establishment, 1960's mentality. Pastiches of wisecracks masquerading as literature, these gagfests were very funny affairs: flickering signs of gaiety and hope in a doomed culture that was already capitulating to the sinister Ann Beattie and others of an aggressively maudlin disposition.   Mr. Robbins is still a very funny guy, but he - and we - are getting a bit old for comic books. Which is not to say that "Skinny Legs and All" started out as a laugh riot; seemingly Mr. Robbins intended this compendious compendium to address all the major questions of human existence: Religion, Art, the Future of the Middle East, the War Between the Sexes, the Meaning of Life. Sad to say, Mr. Robbins is not yet ready for the big leagues; he has shown that he can hit the fastball, but he still has plenty of trouble with the curve.   Mr. Robbins begins "Skinny Legs and All" with his trademark pyrotechnics - ludicrous similes and rivetingly inane dialogue - and as long as the fireworks keep coming, things are just fine. In the first 25 pages we are introduced to Ellen Cherry Charles, an aspiring artist and waitress who is a member of the Daughters of the Daily Special, whose hair "did its own stunts" and who declares: "Some marriages are made in Heaven. . . . Mine was made in Hong Kong." She is driving across the heartland of America, in a vehicle redesigned to look like a roast turkey, with Boomer Petway, her welder husband, who is a native of Colonial Pines, "a suburb without an urb," and who has a penchant for asking cowboys whether the proper terminology for their line of work is not, in fact, "bovine custodial officers." So far, so good.   However, when he turns from one-liners to the daunting themes of art and religion, Mr. Robbins is seriously outgunned. After Boomer and Ellen arrive in the Big Apple, the welder becomes the darling of the art crowd, with the fowl vehicle fetching a king's ransom at Boomer's first exhibition. Sending up the downtown arts scene is a conceit so shopworn that one wonders what the Seattle-based Tom Robbins was thinking of. (Maybe he was thinking of downtown Seattle.) In addition to modern art, Mr. Robbins also dislikes organized religion, which he, mirabile dictu, has identified as an enemy of wild and crazy guys such as Boomer, Ellen Cherry Charles and himself. This results in a pointless and anachronistic tirade against a bunch of fundamentalist Christians who are plotting to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, in the hope of provoking the Messiah into a second - or perhaps it's a third - coming. All of this is tied in with an Arab and a Jew who build a restaurant across from the United Nations, and with a talking can of beans, a talking spoon and a talking sock, which have survived in some form since the time of Solomon and have many controversial theories about biblical events. The tin can, the spoon and the sock are all a good deal less funny than the humans, with the exception of the mysterious New York belly dancer Salome, who is not funny at all. (Of course, neither was her biblical forerunner; just ask St. John the Baptist.) Mr. Robbins is at his best when he is being snide, witty or downright juvenile, and at his worst when he is being profound. He is clearly on to something when he has Boomer declare, "If God didn't prefer for us to drink at night, he wouldn't have made neon!" And he makes a very valid point, overlooked by many anthropologists, when he notes that the switch from B.C. to A.D. in the time of Jesus Christ must have caused many Israelites to miss their dental appointments.   But when Mr. Robbins gets on his high horse, the results are pure bunkum. "As long as a population can be induced to believe in a supernatural hereafter, it can be oppressed and controlled," he pontificates. "People will put up with all sorts of tyranny, poverty, and painful treatment if they're convinced that they'll eventually escape to some resort in the sky where lifeguards are superfluous and the pool never closes." Oh, hush your tongue, Tommy, this is pure mush, as a look at the Peasants' Rebellion during the Reformation, the life of Oliver Cromwell or the voyage of the Mayflower can attest. What's more, it's not even your mush; it's stolen from Gibbons's "Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire."   Mr. Robbins should take a tip from Peter De Vries and mass-produce the kind of short, witty books that do not get confused with "Anna Karenina." When you can write lines such as "She knew the dark side of the moon like the back of her hand. She shopped there," you should write them. But you shouldn't write them for 422 pages. Readers, after all, have other chores.

title: Under God
author: Garry Wills
pull_quote: Under God Religion and American Politics By Garry Wills 445 pages. Simon & Schuster. $24.95.   It is the thesis of Garry Wills's new book that "nothing has been more stable" in American history "than religious belief and practice," that "religion has been at the center of our major political crises," and that "the willed ignorance about religion" on the part of political reporters and historians reflects "a refusal to see the connection between Christian doctrine and politics."   In the course of setting up this argument, Mr. Wills writes at length about the tendency of intellectuals to discount the importance of religion in this country. He notes that the same commentators who reported on the "death of God" fad that swept certain divinity schools in the 1960's have ignored or played down the potency of the evangelical movement. He points out that reporters focused on President Ronald Reagan's skills as a communicator, rather than on the fact that he was communicating religious attitudes. And he argues that "the 'educated' part of America" mistakenly assumed that the Scopes trial in 1925 was a victory for the evolutionary point of view -- when, in fact, Darwinism did not make a strong showing in textbooks until the 60's, when the Sputnik-generated rivalry with the Soviet Union focused new attention on the teaching of science in American schools.   Among the writers Mr. Wills singles out for their historical myopia are Henry Steele Commager and Arthur Schlesinger Jr., both of whom have written about the essential secularity of the American mind. "Commager and Schlesinger are to American history what Michael Dukakis was, in 1988, to American politics," Mr. Wills writes. "Much of American (indeed, of human) experience is off their mental maps. They have a serene provincialism, dismissive of the ordinary torments of people less optimistic, irreverent, and pragmatic than they."     But while Mr. Wills presents many of his arguments in this book as a kind of intellectual heresy, those views often represent a synthesis of other scholars' work in this same area. The historian Sydney Ahlstrom has made a strong case for Americans' sense of themselves as a "religious people"; Henry May has suggested that the vigor of American culture stems from the country's dialectic between secular and religious thought; and Richard Hofstadter has illuminated the links among fundamentalism, anti-intellectualism and right-wing politics in American life.   More recently -- last year, in fact -- two books appeared that underscored the hold that religion continues to exert on Americans' lives: Andrew Greeley's "Religious Change in America" (Harvard University Press) and "The People's Religion: American Faith in the 90's" by George Gallup Jr. and Jim Castelli (Macmillan). Indeed, Mr. Wills draws heavily upon the Gallup-Castelli study for statistics demonstrating the extent and nature of American piety:   Nine out of 10 American say they have never doubted the existence of God.   Eight out of 10 Americans say they believe in a Judgment Day.   Seven out of 10 Americans say they believe in life after death.   Thirty-seven percent of Americans say they believe in the Devil.   Forty percent of the American population attend church in a typical week.  Instead of trying to explain the social and historical reasons that make the United States the most religious nation in the developed world, Mr. Wills launches into a discursive -- and highly arbitrary -- discussion of the interplay between politics and religion in American life.     Considerable space is devoted to James Madison's and Thomas Jefferson's efforts to protect religion by separating church and state (a subject with which Mr. Wills seems fully at ease, having already set forth detailed examinations of both men's works in two earlier books, "Inventing America" and "Explaining America"), but such pivotal events as the Great Awakening are completely ignored. The Scopes trial and the current debates over abortion and pornography are held up to the light, but the issue of school prayer is mentioned only in passing. The bulk of this book consists of somewhat dated profiles of candidates in the 1988 Presidential race -- profiles that apparently represent amplified versions of stories Mr. Wills wrote for various periodicals during the campaign.   In these profiles, Mr. Wills tries to look at the candidates' own attitudes toward religion and the role that public attitudes toward religion played in shaping their campaigns. In the case of Jesse Jackson and Pat Robertson, this sort of examination yields fairly obvious insights: the very fact that these two men, representing the extremes of Left and the Right, were ordained ministers forces the reader to acknowledge "the broad stratum of religion underlying American culture."    With the other candidates, this approach devolves into more generalized assessments of character. Mr. Wills ends up reciting what are now familiar arguments about Gary Hart's lack of roots and a moral vocabulary, Michael Dukakis's lack of passion, and George Bush's successful exploitation of the themes of patriotism, religion, and law and order. When he tries to come up with a more original take on these men's personalities, the results tend to feel strained and pretentious.   He compares Mr. Hart to Don Giovanni, as someone who lives insistently in the present, unable to connect the future and the past. ("Donna Rice is the Zerlina of our story," he writes.) In another chapter, he even more incongruously compares Mr. Dukakis to Hippolytus, Racine's ascetic hero who runs afoul of the gods. (Of the Dukakis aide John Sasso's fall from grace over campaign improprieties, Mr. Wills writes, "Dukakis's need for a Sasso, for some escape hatch from his own self-containment, is like Hippolytus' involvement, against his nature, with Phaedra, the stepmother who falls in love with him.")     Fortunately, these sorts of passages do not occur frequently in "Under God." For the most part, the writing in this volume is intelligent and fiercely logical. Mr. Wills gives a surgical, if highly debatable, analysis of Mario M. Cuomo's stand on abortion (privately against it, publicly pro-choice), and he reveals the ironies contained in the religious Right's opposition to the strict separation of church and state.   Such controversial insights, however, do not add up to a cohesive book. In the end, "Under God" is a hodgepodge of thoughtful historical analysis and dated journalism, strongly articulated opinions and popularized recyclings of other people's research.
