title: Fragile Glory
author: Richard Bernstein
pull_quote: Fragile Glory A Portrait of France and the French By Richard Bernstein Maps. 349 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $24.95.   At a reception for the Goncourt prize a few years back, one could have seen a tallish man, over-elegant for the occasion, a note pad conspicuously in hand, moving among the guests to question them about this curious Parisian rite: a prestigious award no one believes in, since it's an open secret that the author jurors vote for their own publishers' candidates. The man, who, with his starched collar and unadorned spectacles, resembled a young Leon Blum (in his pre-political years as a literary critic), was in fact Richard Bernstein, then the Paris bureau chief of The New York Times, digging deeper than a Times correspondent need do for his daily news file.    We have the product of that deeper probing in the book before us. Mr. Bernstein was obviously moonlighting on The Times. During his three-year Paris stint, as in his student days and on frequent return visits, he threw himself into what may appear a hopeless endeavor: trying to make sense of the French, and not only of Parisians. For he knew something a less vigilant observer might not: that every Frenchman cultivates his down-home origins. And to understand the French, who tend to cluster in Paris and to do most of their business and politicking there, one necessarily travels to the hinterlands, to La France Profonde. Mr. Bernstein did that, again and again, and put it all down in the most penetrating account of contemporary France we're ever likely to own.    In looking for clues to French character, the author explores everything from wine culture to cultural politics, movies, food and the higher eroticism, with the same punctiliousness. One can imagine a harassed tourist picking up this book and letting it drop out of his hands. Too big to carry on a visit to France, "Fragile Glory" is to be read before and especially afterward. One hopes (vain hope?) that people in the State Department responsible for our European policy will read it, and you can bet that business executives bracing for an approach to the Common Market will consult this primer early on.      Is it giving away the plot to reveal Mr. Bernstein's conclusion that French civilization is a success? The nation is up front not only in life's treats like foie gras but also in the development of such contemporary artifacts as the world's first supersonic passenger plane, the fastest regularly operating railway train and a nuclear-energy network in working order. No longer a first-class power, France makes up for that with a superiority complex; one can travel far on myth, and Mr. Bernstein has penetrated this "France of the mind." Mr. Bernstein's Paris "has more of everything -- more museums and movies, more book stores and restaurants, more intellectuals per square inch, more distinguished men and beautiful women, more shops selling designer clothing, more grand monuments and historic places than just about any other urban conglomeration in the world."   And Mr. Bernstein shows us how Paris achieved that position. He borrows from the historian Fernand Braudel the notion that Paris owed its military advantage, which soon enough became political and spiritual superiority, to the raising of oats, allowing the Carolingians to feed horses, which, when used with newly invented stirrups, guaranteed victory in battle. Despite Paris, France remains a nation of peoples, and could easily have become a federation, like Yugoslavia, rather than the centralized nation we know. Mr. Bernstein takes us on a rapid tour of what the French proudly call their hexagon, with snapshots of landscapes, and insights on regional particularities. He also lets us visit Paris with him, quarter by quarter, the way a Michelin Guide cannot (Michelin eschews the dark side).    "Fragile Glory" addresses itself without flinching to the matter of French decline, Paris no longer being the place where things happen first. Mr. Bernstein finds redeeming qualities all the same, as in the passionate way Parisians defend their cultural heritage both monumental and literary. If Parisians are no longer at the top of the heap, they'll continue to act as if they were. The author deals evenly with French-American relations, which are never as good as one expects them to be (considering how the United States helped to save France in two World Wars and one cold war). Americans, Mr. Bernstein shows, are often lumped together with the British, the neighbor the French seem to detest more than they do the Germans. He offers a tongue-in-cheek description of the belligerent French campaign -- laws and all -- against use of the English language (obviously a sign of a culture unsure of itself). "Lurking behind" the language crusade, Mr. Bernstein writes, is "the longing for national glory," and an underlying anti-Americanism.     The author characterizes President Francois Mitterrand as "an opportunist, in the great French tradition of political opportunism," which is almost too kind, for of course Charles de Gaulle twice removed himself from power because he refused to be an opportunist, and Mr. Mitterrand's chief rival, Jacques Chirac, enmeshed in principles slightly out of step with his times, is losing his last crack at the throne because of them. Perceiving his countrymen's essential suspicion of things foreign, even of allies, Mr. Mitterrand has adopted some of the characteristics of Gaullist aloofness. Significantly, in the prudent manner of this author, Mr. Bernstein never comes out flatly against Mr. Mitterrand's "royalist habits," preferring to sum up the arguments of others.    Perhaps it is just as well; it makes "Fragile Glory" a compendium of the best and most useful    French    thinking about France. Mr. Bernstein is almost too conscientious in trying to explain everything while covering all exceptions and variants. But it is nice to have so scrupulous a reporter around when the subject is as complicated as this one: a people not quite ready to sit still for a portrait.
headline: The French as They See Themselves

title: Prosperity Lost
author: Philip Mattera
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: PROSPERITY LOST.  By Philip Mattera. (Addison-Wesley, $19.95.) Ronald Reagan got himself elected President in 1980 by asking Americans if they were better off than they had been four years earlier. The wonder is that after the subsequent two terms of radical, greed-driven economic policy -- Philip Mattera calls it a coup d'etat born of an unprecedented alliance of business, the Federal Government and the political right -- George Bush was able to convince American voters they were a prosperous lot. "Prosperity Lost" meticulously chronicles the downward plunge in the American standard of living, mostly during the Reagan years, an erosion that affects all but the wealthiest among us. Median income in 1987 was $30,853, just $33 above the adjusted 1973 figure. Meanwhile, real estate prices soared -- making the 1980's the first postwar decade in which home ownership rates declined. Many who can afford to buy homes emulate an unnamed southern California employee of a defense contractor mentioned by Mr. Mattera who sleeps in his car several nights a week instead of making the two-hour commute to an affordable home. The cost of a private college education rose by 50 percent in the 1980's (public college costs went up by about 33 percent), partly as a result of the colleges picking up the slack from cuts in Federal student aid. As manufacturing jobs have diminished, high-paid union workers have no option but to take low-paying, low-benefits service-industry jobs -- or even to become part of the contingency work force of short-timers, temps or sub-minimum-wage homeworkers. One result: some 31 million Americans are without any form of health insurance; about 40 percent of those who work are not included in employment-based health insurance. To support these endless statistics, Mr. Mattera, a former reporter for Fortune, includes anecdotes, many of them drawn from Congressional testimony, so the effect of "Prosperity Lost" is a rude awakening from the American dream. The major culprits: two Republican Administrations and big business. As his Administration was cutting housing subsidies, Mr. Mattera charges, Mr. Reagan was portraying homelessness as an unfortunate side effect of deinstitutionalization. Meanwhile, corporations were demanding wage concessions from labor unions that even some businessmen publicly admitted were unnecessary. Mr. Mattera calls for a return to the days when the Government better addressed the social needs of its citizens with average and below-average incomes and kept business in line. In the end, he suggests some options that he admits are utopian, such as establishing a "maximum wage" to control the excessive accumulation of wealth at the top; encouraging the development of aggressive labor unions in the third world to shore up global wages; offering some relief for domestic debtors; and that near-forgotten ideal, giving everyone a guaranteed income.

"How do you get to Carnegie Hall?" asks the old chestnut, to which the answer is, of course, "Practice, practice, practice." In "Grit, Guts, and Genius," the USA Today business reporters John Hillkirk and Gary Jacobson asked the equivalent question of a number of successful executives in business, sports and entertainment. The authors found eight common themes: "Trust your gut," "Make the complex simple," "Tap the power of every individual," "Sell fantasy and reassure people," "Tap the power of information," "Master quality," "Target, target, target" and "March at a slow and steady pace." Despite these catchy phrases, many of the answers that come through in the 27 relentlessly upbeat profiles gathered here aren't particularly complex. The key ingredients seem to be talent, old-fashioned hard work, detailed planning and an emphasis on quality, along with a can-do attitude, a good sense of timing, an ability to gauge calculated risks and a little luck. Some of the most interesting figures included are offbeat choices: New York City Police Commissioner Lee Brown; the educator Peter Kline; the Pulitzer Prize-winning Philadelphia Inquirer investigative reporters Donald Bartlett and James Steele, and Tom Galla, who coached his Trumbull, Conn., All Stars to the Little League World Series championship. Arnold Harris is the kind of managerial authority one imagines Leona Helmsley consulted. "Someone once said, 'You learn from your mistakes,' " he says. "He doesn't work here any more." Harris is a real capitalist's capitalist: he chomps on his cigar, he bellows memos, and come Christmas Eve he wheedles a deal out of Santa. The protagonist of "Two-Fisted Management," Harris is the cartoonist Mark Marek's embodiment of the combined corporate and personal profit motive that rings through every how-to business book. "You'll learn how to survive and succeed with just your own two hands (and the sweaty hands of those who work under you)," he promises. "I guarantee it or your money ba . . . well, I guarantee it." Harris comes equipped for class war. To bully employees out of a raise, he counsels you to stare at them silently for seven cartoon frames. ("Mind over money," he says.) To dress for success, he recommends you wear a decoy contract up your sleeve and a semiautomatic staple gun on your hip. To decorate the power office, he advises you hide metal detectors, cameras and strategically located land mines. When he commandeers a bus to get to a meeting (the driver won't stop in the financial district), Harris tells a worried employee: "This isn't a game, Davis. This is free enterprise! You're gonna have casualties." Harris is adaptable; he calls business in the 90's "New Age Moneygrubbing," in which "we are one (in all but salary)." Um, well, yes. Exactly. As Mr. Marek -- I mean Arnold Harris -- so aptly puts it: "Buy it, read it, and I'm sure you will profit from it. I know I will."

pull_quote: MOUNTAINS OF DEBT: Crisis and Change in Renaissance Florence, Victorian Britain, and Postwar America.  By Michael Veseth. (Oxford University, $29.95.) Both Florence and Britain were, at different times, the most admired economic powers in the world. Yet both tumbled off their pedestals. Why? In his academic study, "Mountains of Debt," Michael Veseth, an economist at the University of Puget Sound, points to public debt and government tax policies. Renaissance Florence not only borrowed from its citizens to finance wars and government services but even established a dowry fund to insure the marriageability of their daughters. Eventually the government had to pay such high interest rates that Florentines found it more profitable to invest in public debt than in the productive economy. Meanwhile, a tax loophole discouraged private savings and encouraged spending on lavish homes. Ironically, some of the great art of the Renaissance was made possible in part by this misguided tax policy. By the 1630's, Florence's economy was shattered. Victorian Britain's problem, Mr. Veseth contends, was precisely the opposite: a "compulsive need to achieve fiscal balance." As a result, the Government clung to a tax policy with what he calls one "fatal flaw." Because it made no provision for capital depreciation, it stunted the growth of modern industries. By the 1870's, he contends, Britain was no longer a major economic force. Both Florence and Britain, Mr. Veseth writes, could have prevented their falls had they acted at a critical point. He sees the debt-laden United States at just such a point, teetering on its economic pedestal. Among his recommendations: raise individual tax rates, remove tax incentives that encourage borrowing and establish a national sales tax. The new taxes would go toward reducing the budget deficit, improving education and building a high-quality service sector -- the nation's last, best hope for remaining competitive.

This mild-mannered book is a cousin to the megatrendy future studies popularized by John Naisbitt and Ken Dychtwald. The central tenet of Charles Handy's philosophy is that society in general, and the work place in particular, are in the grip of "discontinuous" changes, transformations so basic and so profound that the past is of no use in preparing for the future. The useful thing about this approach, of course, is that it permits one to dispense with entire boxcars of historical experience that might muddle one's arguments. Perhaps people in the past tended to behave a certain way -- tilling their own fields more assiduously than their landlords', for example, or seeking power at the expense of their neighbors. But come tomorrow, Mr. Handy, a visiting professor at the London Business School, says in "The Age of Unreason," we are all going to start behaving differently, because of the inevitable side effects of such profound changes as the telephone line, which permits people in scattered locations to work together. But is the advent of the telephone truly "discontinuous" change? Or is it just another stage in an organic continuum that began with drumbeats and smoke signals? If it is the latter, perhaps some small clues to where we are headed can be found by examining where we have been. It is this historical sextant that is lacking in Mr. Handy's various visions of our economic and social future. The result is that his musings, while compassionate and sometimes imaginative, soon begin to seem like just so much cotton candy: inoffensively sweet, briefly entertaining, but far too insubstantial to chew on.

pull_quote: Sexual Intercourse By Rose Boyt 181 pages. Random HouseAdvance Publications+. $17.95.    Are preoccupations and artistic styles handed down generation to generation? In the case of Rose Boyt -- whose first novel, "Sexual Intercourse," appeared to critical acclaim in England -- some interesting familial affinities emerge. Like her great-grandfather Sigmund Freud, she is obsessed with sexual relationships and the secret, taboo workings of the psyche. And like her father, the painter Lucian Freud, she brings to her work an ardent detachment -- an objectivity tinged with anxiety that imbues her work with a lingering sense of bizarreness and alienation. title: Images Of War
author: Hamilton Darby Perry
pull_quote: Images of War The Artist's Vision of World War II  Selected and edited by Ken McCormick and Hamilton Darby Perry  Illustrated. 453 pages. Orion Books. $65.     Photographers and soldier-cartoonists left the most important pictorial record of World War II. Robert Capa, Margaret Bourke-White, Peter Paris and scores of other photographers focused on the war fronts. The two unforgettable cartoonists who got closest to the real lives and thoughts of soldiers were Sgt. Bill Mauldin, creator of "Up Front," featuring the unshaven Willie and Joe, which appeared in the Mediterranean editions of Stars and Stripes, the Army newspaper, and Sgt. George Baker, creator of the bedraggled little enlisted man called the Sad Sack in a strip of the same name that ran in Yank, the Army magazine. Sergeants Mauldin and Baker exposed the harsh realities of combat and the frustrations of military life from the inside with sardonic humor and poignancy.    During the same period in the 1940's, an untold number of Allied and Axis illustrators and painters put their pens and brushes to work in the service of their countries and their art. Most of them were civilians whose work did not appear in the military publications, which seldom printed in color. Some were already well-known artists; some worked as propagandists in paint for the benefit of the state and armed services; some were moved to portray the lives of beleaguered people in and out of uniform so that the events would never be forgotten. Whether for patriotic or personal reasons, they felt wartime was no time to paint bowls of fruit.      These overlooked artists are now represented in a highly original and historic work, "Images of War," which provides a rare worldwide portrait of the home and war fronts. The book is edited by Ken McCormick, former editor in chief of Doubleday, and Hamilton Darby Perry, an author and editor who served on a PT boat during the Normandy invasion. In a moving foreword, John Hersey, who saw some of these artists at work while a war correspondent in the Pacific and Mediterranean theaters, tells why it is necessary to portray and remember the human side of war to this day:    "In the din of all the discussion of weaponry in the years since World War II -- talk of ICBM's, B-1's, Stealth bombers, Soviet XX-25's, MX missiles, Pershings, the hypothetical hardware of Star Wars and all the rest -- we have become inclined to think of warfare as something buyable, abstract, high-tech, mechanized, more or less automated. The images presented here, of moments in the last great war as seen through the eyes of highly individuated artists on both sides of the conflict, remind us that war is not fought by machines, and that the cost is not to be reckoned in dollars of national debt. War, these very human artists remind us, is fought by human beings. The cost is in human values and human lives."    What makes "Images of War" a rare assemblage of art and text is that it is international in outlook and well-balanced in its presentation. That could happen only after the passage of decades; it says something about the changed world that "Images of War" happens to be printed in Japan. Insofar as it is possible to be evenhanded about a war that included German concentration camps and harsh Japanese prison camps (not to mention the relocation camps that held thousands of Americans of Japanese descent in the Western United States), Mr. McCormick and Mr. Perry have succeeded in being "nonpolitical and nonnationalistic" in selecting these paintings.      Some 200 artists from 12 countries are represented in "Images of War." The book includes 50 Soviet paintings, most not seen before in the West, from state museums in Leningrad, Moscow and Kiev. Japanese paintings come from the National Modern Art Museum in Tokyo; German paintings from the Bavarian Army Museum; Italian paintings from three national museums in Milan; war museums in London, Ottawa and Canberra contribute paintings by British and Commonwealth artists. A major source of the American paintings -- which include works by such well-known artists as Thomas Hart Benton, Joseph Hirsch, George Biddle and Tom Lea -- are the combat art collections maintained by all the services in Washington.    Surprisingly, there is only one painting by Henry Moore, "Women and Children in the Tube," from the Imperial War Museum in London. It is by no means the best of the brilliant series of "shelter drawings" he did of families huddled together in the Underground during the bombings of civilian targets in London by the Luftwaffe. What is particularly commendable is that all through the book -- in the spirit of "The 'Good War,' " by Studs Terkel -- there are excerpts by war participants that supplement the paintings.    Speaking of the Blitz, a Royal Air Force fighter pilot says, "Victory was not in sight, yet the thought of defeat never entered our young minds." And a Luftwaffe pilot officer says: "You rarely acknowledge the fact that you have killed a human. It blunts the senses. I didn't like the feeling of the victim having an identity, a name."    "Images of War" covers nearly all the theaters: from the blitzkrieg in 1939 to the battles in North Africa, the island invasions and carrier wars in the Pacific, the final offensives on the Russian and European fronts, the liberation of the death camps and the Nuremberg trial of German war criminals. Like the drawings by Sergeants Mauldin and Baker, the paintings by these artists do not glorify war. The impression left by these realistic paintings is that of a sobering statement against war.

pull_quote: THE LOVER OF HISTORY.  By Jonathan Dee. (Ticknor & Fields, $19.95.) In his first novel, "The Lover of History," 28-year-old Jonathan Dee has much to say, as well as a story to tell. Conjuring up a vividly evoked Manhattan where "yellow taxis darted in and out of each other's company like fish," Mr. Dee constructs a cat's cradle of connections out of three characters' relationships to one other, to their personal histories and to events unfolding in the world around them. Diane Kendall and her roommate, Robert Warner (always referred to by their last names), live a cold existence where "eating alone seemed the norm." Although they've occupied a thinly partitioned bedroom for two years, they barely know each other. Kendall hates her job as an engineer at an all-news radio station and grows weary of her lover Julian's lack of ambition to move beyond singing advertising jingles. Then the American Secretary of State is assassinated in the tiny island nation of Colozan and the United States declares war -- and the murder and its formulaic reportage in the media become catalysts for varying degrees of growth in each character. Julian, the innocuous charmer who signs petitions without reading them, grows least. Kendall, however, sees links between her alienation from her personal history and her estrangement from the larger currents of life; she recognizes that "the source of things might be found outside herself" and starts edging beyond Julian's sphere. Most intriguing is the high-minded if sanctimonious Warner, the lover of history of the title, a teacher who urges his pampered prep-school students to see their role in and responsibility for the larger world, yet is himself adrift in time and place. Some of Mr. Dee's pre-Iraq political gambits now seem obsolete, but more often they prove prophetic. This gifted young author, acutely aware of how lives intersect with history, himself weds art to wisdom with admirable authority.

In "PowerShift," as in his earlier books "Future Shock" and "The Third Wave," the provocative social thinker Alvin Toffler urges us to contemplate, anticipate and act upon the extraordinary economic, social and political changes we face at the end of the 20th century. Mr. Toffler sees wide-ranging connections among the many separate events taking place in all these spheres. Thus the breakup of the Communist bloc, Michael Milken's exploitation of junk bonds and the increasing influence and sophistication of computer networks are all only symptoms of a larger "powershift" throughout the world. Bit by bit, in nations and in giant corporations alike, Mr. Toffler argues, the vast stores of information generated and made widely available by computer technology and by the mass media have taken power away from the centralized few at the top and given more to consumers, voters, workers and small businessmen. This has coincided with the growth of what Mr. Toffler calls our "super-symbolic" economy, one that is primarily based not on the production of goods but on the creation and dissemination of information, images and ideas. "PowerShift" is dense with jargon and buzz words: "For the new fact is that, as nations make the transition toward the advanced, super-symbolic economy, they need more horizontal self-regulation and less top-down control." And as is almost inevitable with an attempt at so sweeping a synthesis, some readers may grow uncomfortable with Mr. Toffler's relentless barrage of generalizations. These flaws should not overshadow his larger contribution, however. By placing the accelerated changes of our current information age in the larger perspective of history, Mr. Toffler helps us to face the future with less wariness and more understanding.

"The problem for Liebling and    The New Yorker   ," Joyce Carol Oates wrote in "On Boxing," "must have been to sell a blood sport like boxing to a genteel, affluent audience. . . . It is a problem that, for all his verbal cleverness, Liebling never entirely solves." One is tempted to reply that, in fact, A. J. Liebling is the only boxing writer who ever worked his way around this contradiction. The reason -- as readers of "A Neutral Corner," a collection of Liebling's previously uncollected boxing essays edited by Fred Warner and James Barbour, who teach English at the University of New Mexico, are quick to discover -- is that he was a great journalist. Unlike the celebrated boxing writers of today, Liebling went to a prize fight to report it, not experience it. Ms. Oates, Norman Mailer and others who cover only an occasional heavyweight championship fight always seem to be groping for the meaning of boxing; Liebling found meaning    in    boxing. Of course Liebling, who died in 1963, was fortunate enough to have lived in the last era when there were enough good fighters around to sustain interest in boxing more than once every two or three years. Not that he was all that taken with the era that inspired his best boxing pieces: "Nineteen-fifty was no Golden Age of boxing, but, compared to 1960, it was at least gold-plated." (But then, as he himself cautioned, "the exact period at which it was better . . . varies in direct ratio with the age of the fellow talking about it.") Liebling managed to find just enough gold, and, like Pauline Kael writing about bad movies, when his subjects were dull he turned lead into gold.

pull_quote: In February 1982, National Geographic published a cover photo of the Great Pyramids of Giza, one of which had been repositioned by means of a new computer graphics technology. The earth moved in the world of photography. Although photographs had been altered in various ways almost from the beginning, the degree of manipulation possible had increased dramatically. One could efficiently add, subtract or move parts of a photographic image without leaving any evidence. Fred Ritchin, in his illustrated book of essays, IN OUR OWN IMAGE. The Coming Revolution in Photography: How Computer Technology Is Changing Our View of the World (Aperture, Paper, $15.95), explains how this technology works and speculates on the ways it will evolve; its implications for photography and, in particular, for photojournalism concern him deeply. Mr. Ritchin, a former director of photography for The New York Times Magazine and the founding director of the photojournalism program at the International Center for Photography, makes it clear that the ethical and esthetic issues involved affect all of us. If we can no longer rely on photography as our witness of time and place, he writes, then what we perceive as reality is suddenly malleable. Mr. Ritchin sees potential harm -- an almost infinite capacity for deception -- in the use of these technologies, as well as a great opportunity for the renewal of a medium that he feels has lost much of its power in recent years. Mr. Ritchin brings to his discussion a passionate interest in the social role of photography -- which, he says, should challenge our easy assumptions about the world by reflecting its complexity and richness.
headline: The Camera Does Lie

title: Final Approach
author: John J Nance
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: FINAL APPROACH.  By John J. Nance. (Crown, $19.95.) John J. Nance, a lawyer and a former airline pilot, has made something of a career cataloguing the flood of changes that airline deregulation has brought to the industry and the traveling public. His first book, "Splash of Colors," depicted the bankruptcy of Braniff Airlines. "Blind Trust," Mr. Nance's best-selling second book, argued that deregulation has led to an erosion of safety margins. Now, in his first novel, Mr. Nance offers a behind-the-scenes look at the political jockeying that follows the crash of an airliner on a rain-soaked runway in Kansas City, Mo. In particular, he dissects the workings of the National Transportation Safety Board, the independent Government agency that, he suggests, is not so independent after all. Politically hungry officials at the Federal Aviation Administration, the Air Force and the fictional North America Airlines all try to sway the board's investigation. "Final Approach" is at its best as a gripping aeronautical whodunit. But the book seems overly ambitious, with a cumbersome plot that includes the possible assassination of a Congressman (a diversion Mr. Nance never fully resolves), a military cover-up and no fewer than two intra-office love affairs. The result is a sometimes turbulent read. Mr. Nance has gone to considerable pains to be technically accurate, and the novel occasionally bogs down in the fine points of flight-control systems or Federal rules that govern flying. But for the most part, "Final Approach" goes down smoothly, leaving readers something to chew on next time they board an airplane.

author: R M Koster
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: IN THE TIME OF THE TYRANTS. Panama: 1968-1990.  By R. M. Koster and Guillermo Sanchez. (Norton, $22.95.) Latin American armies have earned an evil reputation in the 20th century by corrupting the soldier's traditional role of protector into that of oppressor. Panama, though never an exemplary democracy, came relatively late to this unhappy situation. In 1968, its colonels engineered a coup d'etat that placed one military leader or another in control for the next 21 years. R. M. Koster, an American who teaches English at Florida State University's Panama Canal branch, and Guillermo Sanchez, a Panamanian journalist and the premier columnist of the opposition newspaper La Prensa, have joined forces to write a scathing history of these two decades of humiliation and corruption that is full of enough scoundrels, fools and genuine heroes to stock an old-time melodrama -- Omar Torrijos, for example, whose blend of charisma and radical slogans charmed Fidel Castro, the domestic Communists and naive intellectuals like Graham Greene, while his moderate actions reassured the United States. The authors, however, see in Torrijos the roots of the disasters that followed his accidental death in 1981, disasters such as the ascent of Manuel Noriega, whose limitless greed resulted in Panama being turned into a narco-military state. Opponents like Hugo Spadafora, who threatened Noriega's control, were murdered, preferably through torture; nearly everyone else was bought off. Looming over this catastrophe was, of course, the Colossus of the North, the United States, whose fears of instability and subversion led to a policy marked by callous stupidity, the end result of which was last December's invasion. "In the Time of the Tyrants" must read much as Mr. Sanchez' columns did: sarcastic, angry, witty, erudite and full of rumor, innuendo, insights and genuine news. It is by turns entertaining and horrifying, but always provocative.

title: Pushcart Prize Xv, The. Best Of Small Presses
author: Elizabeth Spires
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PUSHCART PRIZE XV: Best of the Small Presses. Edited by Bill Henderson with the Pushcart Prize editors: William Heyen, Elizabeth Spires, Anthony Brandt. (Pushcart Press/Norton, $27.95)    According to this 15th annual report on the state of America's small presses and little magazines, things are in pretty good shape. Well, perhaps the nonfiction could be punched up a bit, despite fine work from Barry Callaghan and especially Natalie Kusz; the same could be said for the essays, but then people have complained about the condition of the American essay at least since Mencken's time. The verse that's scattered through these pages, on the other hand, nearly always satisfies. An American voice of huge excess and a British one of cloistered modernism are cleverly played off by Lynne McMahon in her poem "Hopkins and Whitman." In another poem, Michael Collier measures Plato "and the limited technology/of his cave" against the American family with the video tools to test its worldly suppositions in slow motion and instant replay. Despite such pleasures, however, most of us read "The Pushcart Prize" for the fiction, and here the news is particularly good. Writers seem to be willing to explore larger territory than they have in previous years; in Joseph Geha's "Through and Through," even God Himself suggests this tactic to a hit man on the lam: "Do not blow town, My child. Blow the whole country." Sometimes, though, while they're probing for edges, characters hit limits. In Laura Kalpakian's impressive story, "The Battle of Mania," an old woman keeping alive the flame of memory for a dead son finally admits that "There's only living and dying and laughing and grieving, and you do them over and over like the seasons." Even if they accept such constraints, the writers in "The Pushcart Prize" continue to push against them. The command and authority displayed at almost every turn are enough to convince us, once again, that these yearly volumes feature much of the best writing available in this country -- and to make us thankful for them.

author: George Tames
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: For just about a half century, George Tames behind the lens of a camera has been a fixture in Washington. That    rarissima avis   , a native Washingtonian, he was born to Greek immigrant parents and grew up in the shadow of the Capitol. Government and those who run it were an early and constant source of fascination. Franklin D. Roosevelt, a Tames household hero, was the first President to be a subject ("I didn't know whether to light a candle, kiss his ring, or chant the Kyrie Eleison," Mr. Tames writes). Mr. Tames had an easy way with his subjects, and was close enough so that he could catch asides and offhand remarks that the political leaders would not have made if reporters were within earshot. EYE ON WASHINGTON: The Presidents Who've Known Me (HarperCollins, $35) is a kaleidoscope of pictures made with cameras and with words, rich in detail and anecdote. In a time when Presidents enjoyed a closer rapport with the press than their present-day handlers will allow, Mr. Tames, who spent 40 years in the Washington bureau of The New York Times, could put them at their ease and make great photos. One, showing a solitary John F. Kennedy hunched over his desk during the Cuban missile crisis, says more about the burdens of office than thousands of photos of men in dark suits holding meetings. Another, depicting Richard M. Nixon in golf togs putting his socks on at Burning Tree Country Club, captures self-conscious informality to a fare-thee-well. "Eye on Washington" is an affectionate look at the corridors of power by one who has prowled them for five decades.

pull_quote: ELVIS DON'T LIKE FOOTBALL: The Life and Raucous Times of the NFL's Most Outspoken Coach.  By Jerry Glanville and J. David Miller. (Macmillan, $18.95.) Jerry Glanville, formerly the head coach of the Houston Oilers and now with the Atlanta Falcons, has been over the course of his career a controversial figure who fancies himself something of a rebel. His book, "Elvis Don't Like Football," is dedicated to "Jerry Jeff Walker, Kris Kristofferson and John Cougar Mellencamp, the last true rebels of our time." Like many self-proclaimed rebels, Mr. Glanville, perhaps best known for his cloyingly precious habit of leaving tickets at the box office for deceased notables like Elvis Presley and James Dean, complains that he is misunderstood. For example, his football teams don't play dirty, they just play tough. With the help of J. David Miller, a contributing editor of Sport magazine, Mr. Glanville has produced what amounts to little more than an apologia for his professional life, as well as a comfortable perch from which he can snipe at his detractors; most notably, he settles scores against other coaches, including Chuck Noll of the Pittsburgh Steelers and Sam Wyche of the Cleveland Browns, who once proclaimed that Glanville's teams "are the dumbest, most stupid, undisciplined teams we've ever played." Others who come in for the Glanville chop block include sportswriters and broadcasters and assorted aides and players who were either disloyal to Mr. Granville or did not measure up to his code of ethics. On those rare occasions when he does stoop to discuss football philosophy, he often shoots himself in the foot. "Defenses get beat by mental errors. I don't believe you win a game with cerebral ideas. Your players have to know what they're doing. They have to react, not think." Say what? For the most part this is a rambling, sophomoric, self-indulgent book marked by feeble and tasteless attempts at humor, such as his description of one of his nonunion players during the strike of 1987 as "so fat he would've turned queer for a chocolate sundae." Curiously missing from this book is any mention of the Oiler quarterback Warren Moon, who most certainly had something to do with the success of the team while Mr. Glanville was at the helm. Or did he? In any case, it is hard to imagine who the audience for this book would be, other than Atlanta Falcon fans who might want a peek into the future of their team.

pull_quote: DESTINY OF DREAMS.  By Michael Bowler. (Poolbeg/Dufour Editions, Paper, $14.95.) The richness of daily life in rural County Kerry in the 1950's is evoked in exquisite detail in this first novel by Michael Bowler, a Kerry native himself. Mr. Bowler captures well the acute sensitivities of his narrator, an adolescent whose failed attempt, at age 10, to run away with tinkers in a horse-drawn caravan does little to staunch his melancholy and his sense of longing for life beyond the emigration-bled village of Cahirciveen. Young Michael's best friend is Johnny Coffey, the tinker's son, a slow-witted child who suffers endless cruelties at the hands of the priest who teaches the boys' form in the local primary school. "A big country footballer who taught like he played football -- by fear and favour," the teacher "would murder the spirit of a child," notes Michael, who observes that, unlike himself, the teacher's pet student is called "by his first name along with any other boy whose father had clean hands." With rituals of dailiness, time passes, "slow as a wet week." Michael's Mam, who often sits by the window after second Mass on Sundays, "having a peep," is forever serving up meals of bread and eggs and potatoes; his father, with whom, after a violent episode, the son barely speaks, reads the paper after tea "under the bulb." The limited experience and the cautions that abound in rural village life are unfurled in large and small moments, as when Michael is called "an obliging boy" by a neighbor for whom he does errands and the family looks "obliging" up in a dictionary, "in case it had two meanings." Mr. Bowler is a dab hand when it comes to the turn of a phrase, rendering with precision what has been said, just so, while at the same time evoking all that goes without saying.

By Louis A. Frank with Patrick Huyghe. (Birch Lane, $21.95.) "I live on the plains of Iowa, drive a pick-up truck, and build instruments for satellites that study the Earth," Louis A. Frank, a professor of physics at the University of Iowa, begins his story. "I am conservative in the way I dress, in the way I lead my life, in the people I vote for, and in the way I do science." "The Big Splash," written with Patrick Huyghe, the author of "Glowing Birds," tells how a respected physicist became a heretic and was pilloried by the establishment. In 1982 Mr. Frank discovered mysterious dark spots on satellite photographs of the atmosphere; he eventually concluded that the earth was being bombarded by small comets at the amazing rate of 20 times a minute, or 10 million times a year. (The spots were clouds of water vapor left as the comets, 100-ton house-sized blocks of ice, burned up in the atmosphere.) Among other things, that would be enough comets, over history, to account for all the water on earth. If Mr. Frank was right, grumbled one scientist, "we would have to burn half the contents of the libraries in the physical sciences." Mr. Frank's publication of his discovery led to three grueling years of warfare in the pages of the journal Geophysical Research Letters. His account has a wounded, ingenuous air; one famous scientist after another takes him on and, according to Mr. Frank, misses the point. When an astronomer finally photographs the supposed comets streaking across the sky, the evidence is disallowed. This is a savage tale of how science works, but lacking the other side of the story the reader has no way to decide whether Louis A. Frank is a martyr to truth or just bullheaded -- or both.

title: The Germans: A People At The Crossroads
author: David Marsh
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE GERMANS: A People at the Crossroads.  By David Marsh. (St. Martin's, $22.95.) There is a hint of pretentiousness about books on whole nations that are titled with a "the" -- as in "The Germans" or "The Russians." But let us see -- does the author deliver? David Marsh, chief German correspondent of the London Financial Times, has updated the 1989 British edition of his book, "The Germans," with some cutting and pasting to bring us beyond the fall of the Berlin wall, the collapse of the Communist system in East Germany and the express-train rush toward unification of the two German states. His thesis is that "Germany's destiny will shape the future of Europe" either to the Continent's benefit or to its risk. So far, so good, although I think one could argue with equal force that Europe's destiny will shape the future of Germany, as it has increasingly in recent decades. But to propose to inform readers about the nation and then largely or completely ignore the women of Germany, the writers of Germany, the film makers of Germany and even some of the major postwar politicians like Herbert Wehner or Theodor Heuss who played central roles in shaping modern Germany is to leave yawning gaps. "The Germans" is further marred by sloppy and turgid writing, awkward usages like "ecumenicalism" -- to describe the role of a church in northern Germany -- and an excess of material taken over unrevised from the previous edition that is now obsolete or irrelevant. On the plus side, Mr. Marsh has dealt at some length with the still unresolved problem of German national identity, which is the core of understanding this strange people, and with demography -- the peculiarity of a declining birth rate for the Germans themselves and the burgeoning of foreign-born people in their midst, now exceeding 5 million in what was West Germany. The best material in this book may be the lengthy quotations the author has assembled in the course of numerous interviews with politicians, bankers and some less extraordinary Germans. They at least give a sense of how contemporary Germans think about themselves and their world. Mr. Marsh is far less eloquent than his subjects.

title: Becoming The Butlers
author: Pamela Brandt
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
BECOMING THE BUTLERS. By Pamela Brandt. (Bantam, $19.95)

 Pamela Brandt's first novel begins originally and unpredictably. In a snappy, wisecracking voice, Rachel Harris, the 15-year-old heroine and narrator, tells of her mother's reckless flight to Spain with the superintendent of the family's apartment building on Manhattan's Upper West Side. Rachel and James, her devastated and drunken father, follow the runaways to Madrid, fail to bring them back, and return together to make what they can of their sadly incomplete domestic life. Rachel's father invites the super's helpless, Spanish-speaking wife and many noisy children to move into the Harris apartment; he seems to hope that, by adopting the super's family, he might somehow be transformed into the super. Rachel, obsessed with the two perfect children of a family named Butler, classmates at the private school they all attend, tries to become one of them. For Rachel is just as misguided as her father, believing that all her problems will be solved if she can be as rich, blond, poised and perfectly groomed as the Butlers. Needless to say, both James and Rachel learn the emptiness of strategies. "So I never did become a Butler," Rachel tells us at the novel's close, "and James couldn't change himself into a Spanish painter and woo my mother back. We never became what we hoped to be, but instead became better versions of ourselves." This insight is, unfortunatley, typical of Rachel; it is hardly new or surprising, and it is delivered in a voice of remarkable flatness. The smart and sassy girl we met at the beginnning of "Becoming the Butlers" soon becomes a very ordinary adolescent whose faith in the banal is expressed in bland and boring teen-age talk. The unpredictable and mad flight to Spain that begins the novel promises something new -- but the tame passages that follow it, and the sane compromise that ends it, fail to deliver on that promise.

"Had I known, as a young man, that someday I would want to write my autobiography, I assure you that I would have gone out of my way to have at least two or three great love affairs." Imagine those words delivered in Jack Benny's distinctively dry voice and you have some idea of the charm of "Sunday Nights at Seven." Unfortunately, this is    not    Jack Benny's autobiography, at least not entirely; it is an odd and rather disjointed literary hybrid in which the great comedian's own memories alternate with those of his daughter, Joan. Ms. Benny explains in her introduction that her father's words are excerpted from a manuscript of almost 400 pages that she discovered in 1984, a decade after his death. What she does not explain is why she has published only a fraction of that manuscript, fleshing out the book with her own reminiscences. Whenever the words are Jack Benny's, which is about half the time, "Sunday Nights at Seven" (the title refers to the time slot of his classic radio show) is a delightful book. His passages may be a bit short on depth and on details of his personal life, but they are long on warmth and wit, and they are full of perceptive -- and refreshingly immodest -- observations about the art and craft of comedy ("It has many times been written that I am a master of timing. I would agree to some extent. I am a master of    my    kind of timing"). His daughter, not being a brilliant comedian -- or, for that matter, much of a writer -- provides a far more prosaic and less insightful slant on things. She has a few good stories to tell, some of them funny and some of them touching. But she has very little to say about her father, or about growing up in Hollywood, that has not been said before.

title: Big Time
author: Phil Berger
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BIG TIME.  By Phil Berger. (Dryad Press/Jefferson Street Press/Taylor Publishing, $15.95.) In the early 1950's, college basketball was shaken by a point-shaving scandal. One of the most talented players of the era was Columbia University's Jack Molinas, a brilliant man compelled to live life on the edge. Drafted by the Fort Wayne Pistons of the National Basketball Association, he played in only 29 games before being banished from the league for placing bets on his own team. Several years later, after becoming a lawyer, he was convicted for his role in another college point-fixing scheme. After his release from prison, Molinas drifted into some shady deals and was eventually shot to death as he and a girlfriend sunbathed in his backyard in the Hollywood Hills. It is upon the life of Jack Molinas that the sportswriter Phil Berger has based his latest novel. Jake Cardoza is a kid from the Bronx who uses his brains as well as his enormous athletic ability to hoist himself out of the slums. Unfortunately, he's got the obligatory tragic flaw: a need to circumvent the rules. While others get caught in a college point-shaving conspiracy of which he is a part, Cardoza lucks out and winds up in the N.B.A., playing for a fictional team called the Rockbridge Stars. Naturally, character equaling destiny, Cardoza soon succumbs to his baser instincts, and therein lies this tale. Mr. Berger, who reports on boxing for The New York Times, knows his subject well and goes to great lengths to give the reader a sense of his story's time and place. Sometimes, however, he tries too hard; the early parts of the novel, for example, are overloaded with brand names and landmarks, an excess of detail that becomes wearisome, even irritating. In addition, Mr. Berger has set a difficult task for himself by trying to weave a fictional story that's more interesting than the real one on which it is based. Although he makes a valiant effort, in the end he isn't quite up to it. Instead, "Big Time" serves to whet the appetite for a book on the genuine article, rather than a pale imitation.

"It was June 1984," he writes, "and I had just been forced to file for bankruptcy. The newspapers were saying that I had lost eight million dollars and that much of it had gone up my nose. . . . My band, Fleetwood Mac, once one of the biggest groups in the world, hadn't played together in two years." In "Fleetwood," a blithe, slapdash memoir written with Stephen Davis, the author of "Hammer of the Gods," Mr. Fleetwood makes the rock musician's life seem cliched and ho-hum: he needed to play music, he made too much money, he took too many drugs. Fleetwood Mac, begun in England in the summer of 1967, has undergone several incarnations over the last two decades in both its music and its personnel. However, the most significant change came in 1975, when Mr. Fleetwood hired the singer-songwriters Stevie Nicks and Lindsey Buckingham. This edition of the band -- "more powerful than ever," Mr. Fleetwood writes -- would produce a string of best-selling albums. The downside was that the band began to abuse cocaine. "Until then, Fleetwood Mac hadn't had much experience with this Andean rocket fuel," he writes. "Now we discovered that a toot now and then relieved the boredom of long hours in the studio with little nourishment." Mr. Fleetwood, the band's manager as well as its drummer, says he felt compelled to get the other members to carry on with their work. After he recouped his financial losses in 1985, Mr. Fleetwood and the band gave it one more go, and in 1987 they released one last hit album before Mr. Buckingham left. Mr. Fleetwood has since recast the band yet again and looks forward to more life on the road. "I'll keep playing forever," he writes. "I'm going to be an eighty-year-old rocker, and they'll have to take me out and shoot me to get me to stop."

author: Anita Pollitzer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOVINGLY, GEORGIA: The Complete Correspondence of Georgia O'Keeffe & Anita Pollitzer.  Edited by Clive Giboire. (Touchstone, Cloth, $24.95; Paper, $14.95.) "Lovingly Georgia" is more than the complete correspondence between Georgia O'Keeffe and Anita Pollitzer, a friend and fellow artist with whom O'Keeffe exchanged letters for 53 years. It is also the story of a friendship broken after years of affinity and trust. O'Keeffe and Pollitzer met at Columbia University in 1914. Over the next several years, as O'Keeffe took teaching jobs in Virginia, South Carolina and Texas, the two corresponded almost weekly. Lonely and at times depressed, O'Keeffe found in Pollitzer's exuberant letters a link to the world she had left behind. Pollitzer sent books, photographs, art supplies and the latest avant-garde magazines, shared her thoughts on writers and critics, and described plays, art exhibits and lectures she had seen. O'Keeffe was equally expressive, though her letters spoke not of social events or of art ideas but of the huge Texas sky or a lightning storm at night on the prairie. She wrote of her daily schedule, of being lost in her work, unsure of her sanity. In Pollitzer she found not only a sympathetic ear but also an ardent supporter, critic and agent. O'Keeffe periodically sent Pollitzer rolls of drawings, to which she responded with unabashed enthusiasm. "It screams like a maniac & runs around like a dog chasing his tail," she exclaimed of one picture. "They've gotten past the personal stage into the big sort of emotions that are common to big people," she wrote of other works. Both women thought that the most important place to show art was at Alfred Stieglitz' gallery. Without telling her friend, Pollitzer took O'Keeffe's drawings to Stieglitz, whose now legendary response, "Finally a woman on paper," would change O'Keeffe's life. Stieglitz showed O'Keeffe's work and later married her. In 1950, with O'Keeffe's approval, Pollitzer began work on a biography. As the last of the letters in "Lovingly, Georgia" shows, the project came to a bad end after 18 years. (The book, edited by Clive Giboire -- who is also the editor of this volume -- was posthumously published in 1988 as "A Woman on Paper: Georgia O'Keeffe.") "I cannot approve it . . . in any way," wrote O'Keeffe. "It is a very sentimental way you like to imagine me," she observed. "It reads as if we . . . didn't understand one another at all." Yet to judge from the depth and candor of these fascinating letters, O'Keeffe's disavowal seems not only cruel but a denial of the rapport these two women so obviously shared.
headline: Georgia on Her Mind

title: The Plains Of Passage
author: Jean M Auel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PLAINS OF PASSAGE.  By Jean M. Auel (Crown, $24.95.) Prehistory buffs may be the only readers who'll have fun with Jean M. Auel's latest epic, "The Plains of Passage." In this fourth installment of the Earth's Children series, the adventure begun in "The Clan of the Cave Bear" continues, with Ayla of the Mamutoi and Jondalar of the Zelandonii undertaking a long and tortuous journey on horseback across the wind-swept grasslands of Ice Age Europe in search of Jondalar's kin. Will the two travelers ever reach the camp of the Zelandonii and, if they do, will Jondalar's fellow clansmen recognize him after so long an absence? These questions haunt Jondalar and Ayla throughout the novel, but a more pressing challenge is posed by the natural world that surrounds them, which sets a host of dangers in their path. Although Ms. Auel's descriptions of this world are fairly uninspired, the steamy love scenes between Ayla and Jondalar afford some compensation. Yet these interludes are few and far between, and it's unlikely that all but the most devoted readers will follow them to the book's end. Prehistory buffs with any savvy will also find Ms. Auel's feminist portrayal of the blond, blue-eyed Ayla somewhat hard to swallow. Here is a multilingual woman who, among other talents, is clever enough to invent a contraceptive, in an era when human reproductive capabilities were apparently still a mystery to mankind. Such skills may enhance Ayla's status in the novel -- but among readers they're apt to raise a few eyebrows.

title: The Dwarfs
author: Harold Pinter
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DWARFS.  By Harold Pinter. (Grove Weidenfeld, $17.95.) It comes as little surprise to discover that Harold Pinter's only novel is composed almost entirely of dialogue. "The Dwarfs" was completed in the early 1950's, before Mr. Pinter wrote any of his plays, before he established himself as one of the most influential voices of his generation. The delayed appearance of "The Dwarfs" is certainly a literary event. Nevertheless, it's easy to see why the novel has taken over 30 years to arrive, and why Mr. Pinter himself told The Paris Review in 1967 that it was "not good enough to be published, really." While some of the original material has evidently been cut and rearranged, what remains can be ferociously vague at times and woefully sophomoric at others. To be sure, a calculated ambiguity combined with a wealth of non sequiturs and a dearth of action emerge as powerful aspects of Mr. Pinter's theater of menace, and scholars will enjoy finding signs of his later work in this preliminary exercise. But such techniques do not make for a compelling novel. (Nor did they succeed, as Mr. Pinter also once acknowledged, when he based a play on "The Dwarfs" in 1960.) The story, if it can be called that, hovers around four characters. Pete, the catalyst, is a reluctant moralist given to internal musings a la Joyce and Beckett. He apparently works in some kind of an office, perhaps involved with "literary research." Though we learn that Virginia is a teacher, that Mark is an actor and a Lothario, and that Len works in an industrial setting, such information is outside Mr. Pinter's existential concerns. In its relentlessly dialectical unfolding, "The Dwarfs" aims to capture nothing less than "this whole bloody racket" called life. As the novel progresses, Mr. Pinter's characters might be accused of simply evaporating -- if they'd ever come into focus in the first place. Throughout, they remain blurry figures, four characters in search of the playwright Mr. Pinter would become, and in need of actors to embody the inflated ideas they represent.

title: Real Life Drama
author: Wendy Smith
pull_quote: Real Life Drama The Group Theater and America, 1931-1940 By Wendy Smith Illustrated. 482 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $24.95.   Many memoirs have been written about the theatrical company that in the 1930's tried to revolutionize American culture. The best known of them are probably "The Fervent Years: The Story of the Group Theater and the 30's" (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich), by Harold Clurman, one of the company's three founding directors, and "Elia Kazan: A Life" (Knopf), by the Group's most famously successful graduate.   But never before has the whole story been told as meticulously and objectively as Wendy Smith has done in her exhaustive "Real Life Drama: The Group Theater and America, 1931-1940." Recognizing in the Group's passionate intensity the sense of political commitment she herself felt in the turbulent 1960's, Ms. Smith has immersed herself in her subject's yearnings and traced its chronicle from start to finish. Unfortunately, her zeal outpaces her ability to breathe life into her story.      The Group Theater's history comprised some two dozen Broadway productions of wildly varying success, annual summer retreats to the country during which the Group members worked at their stage techniques, and endless tergiversation.  Luckily for the content of "Real Life Drama," two of the Group's founders, Harold Clurman and Lee Strasberg, stood for important dramaturgical ideals that tended toward opposing poles. (This is in no way meant to slight the third founder, Cheryl Crawford, who somewhat too selflessly took on most of the practical details of sustaining the Group's existence.)   As Ms. Smith summarizes one of Harold Clurman's early "rambling, impassioned lectures": "From his statement of principles, Clurman drew two main conclusions. They had to do with the twin imperatives of art -- form and content -- and it was typical of the sharply contrasting personalities of the two men who pulled their group in often uneasy tandem for seven years that form was Strasberg's bailiwick and content was Clurman's."   Form was essentially acting style, which Strasberg permanently changed in America. Drawing on the techniques developed by Konstantin Stanislavsky in his Moscow Art Theater, Strasberg taught the Group's actors how to build a stage character from their psychic interiors rather than depend on the illusion of physical gesture. Fittingly enough, as Ms. Smith observes, Strasberg's acting revolution came to fruition with the Method style of the self-absorbed 1950's, long after the socially committed 30's. It is a style from which audiences continue to benefit in the best of contemporary cinematic acting.     Content, on the other hand, had to do with the material that the actors performed. Clurman dreamed of turning the Group into a school for content, an institution that would not only embody the political and cultural issues of the day but also develop playwrights to dramatize those issues. Alas for American theater history, all he got for his trouble was Clifford Odets.   True, the passages describing Odets's work with the Group provide the few exciting moments of "Real Life Drama." On the night in January 1935 when his famous taxi-strike play, "Waiting for Lefty," opened, the playwright, the actors and the audience achieved the "near-religious communion" of which Clurman dreamed. And subsequent productions of Odets's "Awake and Sing!" and "Paradise Lost" must have come as close as anything the Group experienced to what the Moscow Art Theater achieved in its productions of the plays of Chekhov.   But the fact of the matter is that the best of Odets falls far short of Chekhov. Had the Group come up with even a Eugene O'Neill, its history might have been different. Perhaps to have produced a great playwright was impossible, given the stridently political issues of the times.  Whether to go on strike is hardly material for important drama. But in any case the Group didn't, and without a major artist to lead it, it was bound to falter.     Ms. Smith admits "that many of the Group's most famous efforts haven't aged well." She adds: "It's possible to read 'Lefty' and still be moved by its passion, but it's doubtful that it could be performed today with any credibility. The other Odets plays    can    be done, . . . but too often they're turgid and stagy, with the actors and directors unable to find any living significance in scripts written 50 years ago."   But she neglects to imagine what the nurturing of a great playwright might have meant to the Group, how the birth of a native Sophocles, Shakespeare, Moliere, Ibsen or Brecht might have lifted the company with an innovative, visionary body of drama. Instead she blames the fragility of human relations, and documents their failure endlessly in earnest but drab prose.   Was the Group's work worth all the trouble? On balance, it seems to have been. As Ms. Smith sums up: "A distinguished list of productions offered over 10 years; an acting technique that remains enormously influential; a new emphasis on ordinary experience -- these were the Group's specific contributions to the American theater, and they weren't trivial ones."     And as Eunice Stoddard, an original member of the Group, eloquently testifies: "Everybody had their frustrations. I stayed because it was more interesting theater than anywhere else. Rehearsals were always so exciting: the whole analysis of the play, of the parts, of what the play was saying in terms of our era, was just so much more stimulating than anything you'd ever get on Broadway. You didn't want to leave that for what you knew you'd be getting outside, which might satisfy your ego as an actress but not necessarily create very interesting theater. It was a very difficult choice."   But "Real Life Drama" doesn't live up to its author's passion for her subject. Her zealous devotion comes through, but it remains by and large uninspired and uninspiring.

title: Pheasants Of The Mind
author: Datus C Proper
pull_quote: Pheasants of the Mind  By Datus C. Proper  Illustrated. 154 pages. Prentice Hall Press. $18.95.     The subject is birds, seasonably enough, though it is pheasants not turkeys that Datus C. Proper would kill and dress and cook for his Thanksgiving table. Or his Christmas table. Or his table in any season of the year, as he testifies eloquently in "Pheasants of the Mind: A Hunter's Search for a Mythic Bird."   A retired Foreign Service officer who now lives in Bozeman, Mont., Mr. Proper (rhymes with roper) is a writer who hunts, not the other way around. On a typical day described in "Pheasants," he will be typing away when Huckleberry, his "domesticated wolf" will wriggle his muzzle under his elbow and let him know that "an ear-rub would be welcome." The ear-rub soon leads to a fetched boot and a dance "on crooked hind legs, like the god Pan."   "Huckleberry wants to go hunting," Mr. Proper writes. "He wants it because it is in his genes. I want it because it is in my genes. The hunting game makes no sense, these days, but it still feels as if it ought to." Pheasants are the author's game because they are to birds what the brown trout is to fish, which is important, as readers of the author's earlier book, "What the Trout Said" (Alfred A. Knopf), will understand.     As Mr. Proper explains in his new book: both pheasants and brown trout "had been learning about civilization for centuries before arriving in this country.   "Both species flaunted their knowledge. The old-world trout would sip real insects while refusing the angler's flies. The old-world bird would stand in a field looking heroic, then disappear when the hunter got out of his car."    But you can catch a fish and put it back. A shotgunned pheasant doesn't live to flush another day. As Alexander Pope wrote in "Windsor Forest":     See! from the brake the whirring pheasant springs,   And mounts exulting on triumphant wings:   Short is his joy; he feels the fiery wound,   Flutters in blood, and panting beats the ground.      What would make a writer and fisherman want to kill a bird?   Mr. Proper replies: "I want to give the cock a better death than he might get from other predators. Call it a deal: I deprive him of time, spare him from being eaten alive. He would not take the deal if he had a choice, but it's the best I can offer."     Some deal. But the author goes to lengths to make one understand. The pheasant is charming to his eye: "The cock's coat of many colors is also a nature jacket. His habitat is bronze grass, green leaves, bright shafts of light, and deep shadows. His colors are an elegant solution.   "Looking at all of the American upland birds without sentiment (a kind of apostasy), I reckon now that the cock pheasant is the most beautiful. He is a trompe-l'oeil masterpiece of a kind that even nature does not often produce."    So pheasants haunt his mind. His mind works something like this, if one may elide a subtle argument. Hunting is walking; walking is thinking; thinking is language; language is a beat. "By the time you hear the beat," Mr. Proper writes, "the thing that caused it has become important.  It    must    be important to have done this to you. Therefore you try very hard to shoot the bird when your chance comes. You try even if you were not eager when you started walking. If you have not had the experience, you may find this baffling, but I imagine the long-distance hunters nodding yes, yes."     Even if this is baffling, Mr. Proper discourses upon the habitats in which pheasants should be hunted, the right dog to point them, the right weapon to carry, the right clothes to wear, the right way to cook the bird once you have brought him home.   For him pheasants are also dragons:    "When I slay the pheasant, I kill, first, the dragon in me, which is the ugly one appearing in most Western art. . . . I clutch this reality as an antidote to indifference. We think of hunting and fishing as escape, and they are. They are escape from a society of escapism: from pervasive complacency, from media pitched to the lowest common denominator, from trivialization of thought, from the politics of blandness, from gladiators, celebrities, entertainment, scandals, the life synthetic. A hunter chasing pheasants feels everything except anomie."   Well, this is putting quite a burden on what is basically a gaudy chicken.  But between his flights of prose Mr. Proper keeps coming back to genes:   " '. . . one kills in order to have hunted' (Ortega y Gasset)'   'One eats in order to have killed' (Proper)."     So perhaps "Pheasants of the Mind" is simply a necessary book, one that beautifully explains why people and game birds are the way they are. It certainly is attractively designed, and handsomely illustrated by Eldridge Hardie. And intriguing to read. Though on the whole I'd prefer the author stuck to the sport of fishing.

title: Nordi's Gift
author: Clyde Rice
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NORDI'S GIFT.  By Clyde Rice. (Breitenbush Books, $21.95.) Is man meant to spend life with only one mate? Can a literate person satisfy his intellect through the exhilaration of outdoor physical labor? Clyde Rice tussles with these questions throughout "Nordi's Gift," the sequel to his first volume of autobiography, "A Heaven in the Eye." In this volume, the author, now 87 years old, recounts his experiences from 1934 to 1955, and his vivacious writing conveys the passion and immediacy of his younger years. Mr. Rice revels in jobs that demand muscle -- he chopped and sold cordwood, repaired ships, built a boat and fished for tuna, opened a lumber mill. The book's most enthralling passages are devoted to the author's family. His strong voice and remarkable memory combine to produce finely wrought portraits of his wife, Nordi, and her niece, Virginia, with whom Mr. Rice fell in love. Readers may wonder about and even condemn some of the author's decisions. He divorced Nordi to marry Virginia; Nordi later lived with the new couple. (If that sounds strange, imagine working on and off, as Mr. Rice did, for a stepmother who despises you and a father easily swayed by his spouse.) As a social history of the American Northwest (Mr. Rice is a native of Oregon), "Nordi's Gift" makes for engrossing reading -- with one caveat. Adept with an ax, Mr. Rice cuts trees more easily than he cuts through prose. Too many technical descriptions of logging and shipbuilding impede his story. Yet Clyde Rice is good company and has written an inspiring book about a thoughtfully considered life.

title: I Hear Voices
author: Paul Ableman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: I HEAR VOICES.  By Paul Ableman. (McPherson, Cloth, $18; Paper, $10.) Paul Ableman, an esteemed British playwright and critic, originally published this arresting and brilliant travesty 30 years ago. His first novel (Mr. Ableman has published four more since), "I Hear Voices" originally appeared on the list of the Olympia Press, the Paris house that first brought out "Lolita" and "Naked Lunch." It may be read as one long wake-up call -- the protagonist never entirely makes it out of bed. The delivery of his breakfast egg is a recurrent set piece, and would be a symbol in a less explosive exercise. But Mr. Ableman must constantly break his eggs, fragment his abbreviated roundabout world. His unnamed narrator -- who, one quickly suspects, is a schizophrenic -- tumbles through a series of encounters that flare with offhand intensity, including a number of party scenes that seem startlingly canny about social give and take, despite their strangeness. Along the way, poetic tangents fly off in every direction: "There were far reports and others that leapt from brain to brain so that the sunset was pricked with doubt and signaled a spectrum of confused acknowledgement." Is this in fact the mind of a madman? There are scenes that suggest psychiatric counseling, but whatever grasp on reality they might offer is laughingly undone by the narrator's phantoms and leitmotifs. Mr. Ableman's best effect is a breathtaking precision about states of mind, played off against a hilarious vagueness about physical reality. His unchaptered slice of dream (occasionally reminiscent of Donald Barthelme) is another example of the wild freedoms embraced by European fiction since 1945, freedoms still only fitfully understood on this side of the Atlantic.
headline: The Breakfast Egg

title: The Woman Who Read Novels And Peacetime
author: Constance Urdang
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WOMAN WHO READ NOVELS AND PEACETIME.  By Constance Urdang. (Coffee House Press, Paper, $9.95.) Constance Urdang, the author of five previous novellas as well as five books of verse, clearly displays a poet's sensitivity and depth of feeling in these two wonderfully crafted novellas. Leaning stylistically toward the experimental (though not tilting as far as the avant-garde), Ms. Urdang's crisp, angular prose explores the complexities of both loneliness and intimate relationships. "The Woman Who Read Novels," which is set in New York City, wanders between the past and present experiences of an elderly woman named Ruby, whose broken engagement to her cousin, Leo, has shadowed her life since she was barely past her teens. Alive with sadness, this novella depicts the chilling figure of a soul isolated and in despair. In contrast, the second novella -- titled, somewhat ironically, "Peacetime" -- presents the stories of several baby boomers who, while nostalgic for the 1960's and their idealized days as student activists, find their present-day marriages and close friendships enveloped in a fog of incompetence, violence and dread. Whereas "The Woman Who Read Novels" ends on a clearly pessimistic note, the very sense of failure felt by the characters in "Peacetime," their struggle to make satisfying contact with others, propel them forward in a heroic attempt to find, and define, the meaning of their lives.
headline: IN SHORT/SMALL PRESSES: FICTION

title: Eco-Warriors
author: Rik Scarce
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ECO-WARRIORS: Understanding the Radical Environmental Movement.  By Rik Scarce. (Noble Press, Paper, $11.95.) The direct-action wing of the environmental movement has garnered both widespread praise and opprobrium. An overwhelming groundswell of support transformed Greenpeace from a daring but ragtag band of eco-guerrillas into the largest environmental organization in the world in barely over a decade. Yet last spring's bombing incident in Oakland, Calif., involving two organizers of the group Earth First! exposed an underlying bias in the news media. Despite strong evidence to the contrary, many reporters unquestioningly accepted police and Federal Bureau of Investigation charges that the two activists had themselves planted the device. In "Eco-Warriors" the journalist Rik Scarce examines the controversial world of radical environmentalism, providing a sympathetic and fascinating look inside the hearts and minds of those who would meld Gandhi with King Ludd. Much of the book is devoted to Earth First!, the best known of the dozen or so direct-action groups now operating around the world. Mr. Scarce charts the rise of the group, from its founding in 1980 by a quintet of wilderness advocates fed up with Secretary of the Interior James Watt's prodevelopment "sagebrush rebellion" and the increasing bureaucratization of the country's leading conservation groups. The author also details the arguments over tactics, strategies and goals that have begun to splinter the group, arguments reminiscent of those that divided the New Left. In addition, the blow-by-blow accounts of assorted acts of sabotage in defense of the environment by the Sea Shepherds and animal liberationists make intriguing, if sometimes disturbing, reading. Mr. Scarce occasionally weakens his superb reporting with superficial analysis, but on the whole this is a fine account for anyone looking for insight into the global environmental movement.

title: The Look Of Horror
author: Jonathan Sternfield
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LOOK OF HORROR: Scary Moments From Scary Movies.  By Jonathan Sternfield. (Courage Books/Running Press, $14.98.) Covering a genre of movies that runs from "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari" to "Little Shop of Horrors," "The Look of Horror" is a compressed history that is long on images and short on words, a well-illustrated, smartly written recap of some of the more frightening moments in movie history -- and the faces that make those moments memorable. This is a fan's book and never pretends to be a groundbreaking study of horror films. No long-winded theories or footnotes about What It All Means, just page after page of the bright, fantastic visions from the classics we know so well (and some we may have forgotten). Jonathan Sternfield, a freelance writer and photographer, breaks his study into different sections, covering aliens, creatures, ghosts and the demons among us -- the bad seeds, the ordinary people who can be the most terrifying monsters around. The author wisely keeps his opinions short, crisp and to the point. His text amounts to plot summaries and critical commentaries on the quality of the films. What animates this book are the photos of these scary monsters and super freaks. Mr. Sternfield has some interesting inclusions: in a book rife with werewolves, blobs and tarantulas the size of 747's, for example, he has included "Fatal Attraction" as a horror film for a new generation. We cover the gamut here, from monsters alien and otherwise to seemingly innocent demonic devices (the car in John Carpenter's "Christine," the red-headed doll in "Child's Play"). Mr. Sternfield delivers what he promises and does it in a loose, readable style. And the coffeetable format makes it effective; the pictures are large and lurid -- the better to frighten you with, my dear.
