title: A Darling Of The Twenties
author: Madge Bellamy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A DARLING OF THE TWENTIES.  By Madge Bellamy. (Vestal, Paper, $19.95.) Although her name is now generally unknown, Madge Bellamy was a star of the silent screen. While most of her 57 movies may have been mediocre, and many remain hard to locate or lost forever, a handful possess cult interest, such as "Lorna Doone" or "The Iron Horse," which was directed by John Ford. (At the height of her popularity, fans could purchase a "Lorna Doone" cape and a Madge Bellamy cap.) Though she tried to shed an ingenue image and to negotiate the transition into talking pictures, Bellamy never really accomplished either. In her lavishly illustrated memoir, "A Darling of the Twenties," completed before her death in January (when she was probably 90 years old), Bellamy wants desperately to understand and explain what she calls her "Cinderella story in reverse." But in trying to account for a crucial moment when she turned down the lead in "The Trial of Mary Dugan," Bellamy exclaims, "Why did I do this? A thousand sleepless nights haven't solved the puzzle for me." In one embarrassing passage after the other, Bellamy betrays the naivete that apparently retarded both her career and her personal development. She says more than once, "I wish that I had gone to a psychiatrist, but I never did." Bellamy lived out most of the second half of her pathetic life "in abject poverty" with her "stage and screen identity undisclosed," and she last captured headlines for a few days in 1943, when she took a gun to a longtime companion, the lumber magnate A. Stanwood Murphy, after he abruptly married another woman. As the film historian Kevin Brownlow writes in his introduction, this poignant autobiography is "the dramatic and touching case history" of one of Hollywood's "victims." Whatever else it has to tell us about the shabby methods of the silent film industry, it inadvertently demonstrates that the firmament is fickle and that some stars are a lot less immortal than they may at first appear.

title: Greenways For America
author: Judith M Labelle

pull_quote: GREENWAYS FOR AMERICA.  By Charles E. Little. (Johns Hopkins University, $22.95.) Our system of land use may have lost much of its legitimacy and the planning profession may have few new ideas to offer, but Charles E. Little sees greenways as a grass-roots source of positive change. Greenways are protected natural areas; most are used for recreation such as hiking or biking, although some are designed primarily to protect environmental resources. Central to the greenway concept is the idea of linkage: creating connections among recreational resources, natural resources and communities. Mr. Little, whose previous books include "Challenge of the Land" and "Green Fields Forever," sees such networks as providing the framework for regional planning. "Greenways for America" makes clear that greenways have provided recreation, environmental enhancement, economic stimulus and civic pride in widely varied situations. Mr. Little concludes that to make a greenway is to make a community. The projects that the author visited are located across the country, from the San Juan Islands in Washington to the Hudson River Valley, and are "as rich and diverse as human ingenuity and topographic opportunity could make them." Mr. Little is an enthusiastic journalist with both an eye and an ear for local history and politics. With a few colorful strokes he brings to life the unconventional people he met along the way. His text ranges from the history of the greenway concept to an examination of the types of greenways he identified. During his greenway reconnaissance, Mr. Little found the tenacity and ingenuity that we want to believe continue to define the American character. And he provides many practical ideas for people who would follow suit.

title: Words With Power
author: Northrop Frye
pull_quote: Words With Power Being a Second Study of "The Bible and Literature" By Northrop Frye 342 pages. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $24.95.   In his new book, "Words With Power," the distinguished literary theorist Northrop Frye examines the role of myth and metaphor in the Bible, showing how many of its central themes and images reverberate throughout Western literature. His conclusion is that "the organizing structures of the Bible and the corresponding structures of 'secular' literature reflect each other," that a finite number of species of myths (including myths of creation, fall, exodus, destruction and redemption) provide the narrative sources of literature.    Such ideas, of course, have been suggested by Mr. Frye before -- most notably in his famous 1957 study, "Anatomy of Criticism." In fact, "Words With Power" serves as both a sequel to his earlier study of the Bible and literature, "The Great Code: The Bible and Literature" (1982), and as a summing up and restatement of his overall critical views. As a result, some of this book (particularly its theoretical first half, which deals with different idioms of linguistic expression and the social function of literature) feels turgid and overly pedantic, as though Mr. Frye were simply reworking earlier assertions, while trying to answer questions raised by other critics.      It is the second part of the book, which actually deals with specific myths and archetypes found in the Bible (and their reinvention in modern Western literature), that will be most accessible to the nonspecialized public that Mr. Frye says he hopes to reach. Clearly the reader may question his methodology in this section: Mr. Frye's choice of examples is highly selective, sometimes even random, and his discussions of individual works can feel similarly arbitrary. In addition, many of his observations relating biblical stories to classical and primitive myths will be familiar to readers of Robert Graves's "White Goddess," James George Frazer's "Golden Bough" and Joseph Campbell's studies of mythology.   Still, this portion of "Words With Power" intermittently makes for lively and provocative reading. Drawing on his vast reading, Mr. Frye helps the reader recognize some of the recurring myths that connect religious and secular literature, and he shows how ideological and social changes can cause changes in the interpretation and emphasis of those myths. While early hard-line Christians regarded parallel classical myths as "demonic parodies of the true biblical ones," he adds that later, more liberal Christians came to regard classical mythology as a kind of "supplement or counterpoint to the Christian one."      As Mr. Frye sees it, the idea of the axis mundi -- the vertical line postulated by the ancients as running through the cosmos, connecting heaven to earth and earth to hell -- underlies many of Western literature's central myths, providing writers with a wealth of metaphors and images. Those images, he notes, tend to fall into two categories: ascent and descent. Images of ascent, which symbolize man's longing for heavenly perfection, include Jacob's ladder, the purgatorial mountain in Dante's "Divine Comedy," the turning staircase in T. S. Eliot's "Ash Wednesday" and the towers and spirals that recur in Yeats's poetry.    The reverse movement -- downward into death or damnation -- has yielded equally powerful images. Christ's descent to earth echoes Adam's fall from innocence, while Adam's expulsion from the garden is mirrored by the exile of Cain. Whereas Mr. Frye sees downward movements in Dante and Milton as "simply descents to death and hell," he argues that they can take on more creative aspects in other writers's work.   Proserpine's descent every winter into the nether world is a necessary prelude to her ascent in the spring -- and the earth's renewed fertility. Prometheus is punished by Zeus for bringing fire down from heaven but is heralded as the liberator of mankind. Ahab descends into madness as he searches for the great white whale but in doing so becomes a symbol of man's eternal quest for wisdom.      For Mr. Frye, the lower depths represent not only death or hell; they can also stand for "whatever in human nature is subordinated in the traditional structures." In Freud, this comes to signify the unconscious promptings of the id; in Marx, the energetic strivings of the proletariat. For such revolutionary thinkers, Mr. Frye says, "the initiative comes from below" and "the response to it is normally a journey of exploration downward."    In the course of "Words With Power," Mr. Frye also discusses other recurrent literary themes, like the wheel of fortune (which brings together images of ascent and descent into an endless cycle), the "purgatorial vision" of Exodus (a three-part narrative that moves from the bondage in Egypt to the wandering in the wilderness to the entry into the Promised Land), the Virgin Birth and the Garden of Eden.    His discussions of these themes, like the ones noted above, tend to be discursive, peremptory and quite often reductive. Darwin, Schopenhauer, Kierkegaard as well as Marx and Freud are dealt with in a couple paragraphs, and Blake's idiosyncratic mythology (once the subject of an entire book by Mr. Frye) is summarized in several pages. As a result, the reader finishes this volume hungry for more details and deeper analysis. Indeed, one can only surmise that that was one of Mr. Frye's objectives in writing "Words With Power" -- to send the reader back to other books, to other volumes of criticism, as well as to the Bible and other works of literature.

Since we have heard little else about him these last few years, there is a tendency to view Bo Jackson as living the athletically charmed American life: a versatile athlete, a standout at Auburn University, a Heisman Trophy winner, husband, father, hitter of tape-measure home runs, able to leap tall obstacles with a single bound. "Bo Knows Bo," Mr. Jackson's autobiography (written with the sports journalist Dick Schaap), gives a personal view of this man with many helmets. Growing up black in the South presented challenges that athletics could not answer; not everything in Mr. Jackson's life has been sweetness, light and Nike endorsements. This affecting and brightly written memoir tells us that Vincent Edward Jackson, born in 1962 in Alabama, had an angry, tempestuous spirit. As a child he was called "Bo'-hog," soon shortened to Bo; he was a bully who could steal anything from lunch money to bicycles but "couldn't steal a father." Mr. Jackson speaks with savvy eloquence and is refreshingly matter-of-fact. For example, he says that "too many athletes allow colleges to mislead them. . . . It takes the dignity out of college athletics when you have a guy playing football who can't spell football." Clearly and guilelessly, he gives a rueful, heartfelt message about children. "I always want to be somebody they can look up to," Mr. Jackson says. "I wish I'd had somebody to look up to when I was a kid." Clearly, Bo knows writing, too.

pull_quote: THE BEST AMERICAN ESSAYS 1990.  Edited by Justin Kaplan and Robert Atwan. (Ticknor & Fields, $19.95.) It is hard to imagine any essay published last year more moving than Natalie Kusz's account of being mauled by a dog at the age of 7, or as grotesquely hilarious as Ann Hodgman's description in Spy magazine of taste-testing different brands of dog food, or as insightful as Stephen Jay Gould's examination of the origins of baseball -- which somehow comes to be a commentary on the abortion debate. The biographer Justin Kaplan and Robert Atwan, the editor of the "Best American Essays" series, have brought together 21 distinctive essays that make fair claim to being the year's best. Choosing, Mr. Atwan says, "public, rather than personal, essays" by writers who "move between the topical requirements of an article and the literary demands of an essay" -- or, as Mr. Kaplan puts it, "between stunt flying and scheduled air traffic" -- the editors have achieved an eclectic blend of the solemn and the laid-back, the incisive and the discursive. Here we have Joseph Epstein on the value of envy, Sue Hubbell on Elvis sightings in Kalamazoo, Leonard Michaels on the "R" word (relationships), Michael Pollan on lawn care -- or, rather, lawn neglect. Mr. Kaplan and Mr. Atwan have found writers with a gift for the memorable phrase ("My existence," says Anatole Broyard after learning he has cancer of the prostate, "had taken on a kind of meter, as in poetry, or in taxis") and for the memorable incident: Stanley Elkin describing his meeting with Hubert Humphrey, Randy Shilts describing a roomful of uneaten salads. Probably the hallmark entry in the book is the final one, Tom Wolfe's piece for Harper's on the American novel, which Mr. Kaplan describes as "surely one of the noisier literary events of 1989." Provocative, self-serving, eminently refutable (printed here, unfortunately, without the letters Harper's received in response), Mr. Wolfe's is a piece that can best be described as effective. As all these essays are, each in its own way.

Their black-and-white brilliance shows more than a century of exuberant children riding homemade go-carts, raising pigeons, jumping rope and unleashing fire hydrants. A block at a time, a stoop at a time, a face at a time, several generations of artists and photographers have captured a startling diversity of children and amusements, documenting the street as both playground and "test kitchen for new urban cultural forms." pull_quote: DISTANT FRIENDS.  By Greg Johnson. (Ontario Review Press, $17.95.) The short stories in this debut collection by Greg Johnson have a breathtaking cumulative power. Beginning with "Crazy Ladies," in which an 11-year-old boy's encounter with a locally renowned eccentric illuminates the puzzling changes overtaking his seemingly conventional family, the author establishes an elegiac tone that carries throughout the entire volume.  Many of the stories in "Distant Friends" are retrospective looks at unsettling, even brutal, childhood experiences. An outstanding example is "The Burning," which opens with an adult narrator recalling himself as a 10-year-old boy -- in a hospital bed recovering from numerous broken bones, his face "so swollen with bruises that it resembles an overripe plum." The narrator traces the events leading up to his battering, citing his father's progressive detachment from the family as an early omen. "There was no particular, unmistakable sign," he recalls, "just a gradual change in the atmosphere -- the way the air will seem to thicken, and even become eerily visible, as a prelude to bad weather." While such inchoate understanding of the dangers of the adult world is typical of all the young protagonists in these stories, not all the book's children appear as wounded innocents. In "El Paso" and "Passion Play," for example, they assume the role of protector, yet in both stories they are doomed in their attempts to shield those who are more vulnerable than themselves. Compassionate adults also pay a price, as in "Wildfires," the story of the wife of a Vietnam veteran who loses herself to her husband's suffering. In the final story, which tells of a man's aborted effort to comfort friends whose child has died, Greg Johnson crystallizes his grim but affecting vision with the ironic suggestion that the closest friends may in fact be those who manage to stay at arm's length.

title: The Man Who Changed The World
author: Mikhail S Gorbachev
pull_quote: The Man Who Changed the World  The Lives of Mikhail S. Gorbachev  By Gail Sheehy  Illustrated. 401 pages. HarperCollins . $22.95.    Gail Sheehy promises much in "The Man Who Changed the World," a biography of Mikhail S. Gorbachev that grew out of a portrait of the Soviet leader that Ms. Sheehy wrote for Vanity Fair magazine.   Taking off from the perception widely held in the Soviet Union that there are many sides to her subject's character, Ms. Sheehy subtitles her book "The Lives of Mikhail S. Gorbachev" and formulates a theory of his "incarnations" based on one of her previous books.   "The theory in my book 'Passages,' " she writes, "is that each of us develops throughout adulthood by stages. Between each stage are points of decision between progress and regression where we are challenged to shed a protective structure, and when we do we are left exposed and vulnerable, capable of stretching in ways we hadn't known before. For exceptional individuals, like Gorbachev, such passages assume the dimensions of deep personal transformations -- they become in some ways different people."      She hints ominously about one of these sides of Mr. Gorbachev when in the third paragraph of her text she quotes a former senior Soviet analyst for the State Department who has studied Mr. Gorbachev for a decade: "I think he's capable of a great cruelty."    But Ms. Sheehy delivers somewhat less than she promises. Her idea of cruelty is summed up in a remembrance by Andrei Brezhnev, who describes his grandfather, Leonid, taking pleasure in keeping pigeons and doves and hitting their cage to see them all fly around, terrified. This seems mild compared with Nikita S. Khrushchev's purported adolescent penchant for bashing cats' heads against stone walls, not to speak of Stalin's unspeakable sadism. As examples of Mr. Gorbachev's cruelty Ms. Sheehy offers us no detail. Nothing.   As for his multiple "lives," she tells us little more than what is surely self-evident to any reader, namely that Mr. Gorbachev is mercurial, intuitive, adaptable, capable of walking a tightrope and turning on a dime, and no longer in control of the revolution he began.     It is too bad that Ms. Sheehy lets her readers down so, because despite all its huffing and puffing her book is enlightening in many ways. She never got to interview Mr. Gorbachev himself, but she did manage to visit his home village, Privolnoye, and to pick up a trail of his friends and associates that led from the girl next door right to the top of his Government command.   From these contacts she has learned much about Mr. Gorbachev's family background: that his ancestors were Cossacks who "had pushed down from the Ukraine and the Don area in search of virgin soil and religious freedom, settling in the southernmost wilds of the territory of Stavropol known as the Caucasus"; that the women in his family were strong and outspoken; that his maternal grandfather, the family patriarch during Mr. Gorbachev's childhood, was chairman of the local collective farm, or kolkhoz, which made him the most important person in the village; and that by contrast his paternal grandfather was arrested and deported to Archangel in 1937, purportedly for having hidden 40 pounds of grain for his family from the collective's harvest.     From this background Ms. Sheehy draws plausible enough conclusions: that the strong women around him in his childhood explains why Mr. Gorbachev concedes so much power to his wife, Raisa, who has even been his instructor at times and whom he regards as a full partner, referring to her as "my General." And that the conflicting roles that his grandfathers played -- with one participating in Stalin's regime and the other becoming its victim -- account for the division in Mr. Gorbachev's character that allowed him to rise to the top of the ruling establishment and then to turn around and destroy it.   Unfortunately, she too often trivializes these perceptions with the style in which she presents them. Writing of Mr. Gorbachev's youth as if she were there present to observe it, she intones: "Driving the harvester every day, choking in the sworls of dust from the steppe, sweat streaming from his face, a continual trilling in his ears, he worked like a demon and waited for the Party to take notice." Characters variously "gush," "squeal" and "rhapsodize" where it would have perfectly adequately served for them simply to "say." At one point, she describes Mr. Gorbachev as "a brilliant chameleon," which seems an inapt way of saying what she is trying to convey, namely that Gorbachev is cleverly adaptable.     But the book's biggest shortcoming is its failure to dramatize Mr. Gorbachev's changes. Though she titles her various sections "First Gorbachev: Country Cossack 1931-1949," "Second Gorbachev: First-Generation Apparatchik 1950-1977" and so forth through "Sixth Gorbachev: Red Star Falling Spring 1990," she is only able to convey the startling contrast between Mr. Gorbachev as a genius on the world stage and Mr. Gorbachev as a failure at home.   What his problem finally comes down to, at least in Ms. Sheehy's view, is that despite the halting moves he has made toward a market economy, Mr. Gorbachev at heart still believes in socialism. As she quotes the image of a cabbage used by the writer Olas Adamovich: "Gorbachev believes that if he takes off the decayed leaves there will be a healthy cabbage inside. The apparatchiks know it's dangerous to strip off the leaves, because it's rotten inside, it will all have to be thrown away. Gorbachev is the last romantic socialist."   The wonder of Ms. Sheehy's book is that it goes through such a complicated dance to make such a simple point.

title: Love And Its Place In Nature
author: Jonathan Lear
pull_quote: Love and Its Place in Nature  A Philosophical Interpretation of Freudian Psychoanalysis  By Jonathan Lear  243 pages. Farrar, Straus & Giroux . $18.95.    It is commonly thought that in a typical psychoanalysis, the analyst eventually discovers, perhaps through a reported dream or a slip of the tongue, what is troubling the unconscious mind of the analysand. The analyst then announces the new-found insight and brings the patient in a single leap to the mountaintop of understanding. Eureka! The sufferer has been cured.   But those who have actually been through analysis report that it is a slow and tortuous process, more like climbing a mountain a few inches at a time, with each tiny step gaining a vantage point to see just a little farther.    In his profound new book, "Love and Its Place in Nature: A Philosophic Interpretation of Freudian Psychoanalysis," Jonathan Lear reveals that, surprisingly enough, early in his career, Sigmund Freud held a modified version of the former view. In his deep commitment to a 19th-century scientistic interpretation of the new discipline he was evolving, he believed that hysterics expelled the "foreign bodies" of their traumatic memories in a process of catharsis that resembled some law of thermodynamics.   It was only later and gradually that he came to understand that some primitive form of mental functioning underlay conscious thought and that it could only be coaxed to the surface gradually by an interpretation just one step ahead of the patient's understanding, not shouted down from the mountaintop, as it were. Moreover, the process of bringing the material to the surface involved not a strictly scientific procedure, but instead a form of love.   What Mr. Lear sees in these discoveries is a revolution that went much further than even Freud himself anticipated. In Mr. Lear's words, this revolution "contained three related elements whose significance we have only begun to understand: a science of subjectivity; the discovery of an archaic form of mental functioning; the positing of Love as a basic force in nature." He adds: "To take these ideas seriously would be to view the world very differently than we do now." In "Love and Its Place in Nature," he strives for that altered world view.   It is not a simple book to read. Aside from being a clinical associate of the Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis, the author is a professor of philosophy at Yale University and the author of "Aristotle: The Desire to Understand" and "Aristotle and Logical Theory." His thesis is so closely reasoned and rigorously worded that in a footnote in Chapter VI he feels compelled to remind us that "I began to discuss the distinction between accepting responsibility and holding responsible in Chapter II," as if his readers can't be expected to remember what they have already read.   The author sticks closely to Freud's own writing, so that his development of the master's ideas is done in the context of such works as "Studies in Hysteria," "The Interpretation of Dreams," "The Ego and the Id," "Beyond the Pleasure Principle" and "Civilization and Its Discontents," as well as many of Freud's less familiar works. Not incidentally, following a suggestion made by Bruno Bettelheim in his book "Freud and Man's Soul" (Knopf, 1983), he substitutes the words "I" and "it" for "ego" and "id," so that Freud's most famous statement reads "Where It was, there I shall become."    He explores the philosophical implications of psychoanalysis and compares his conclusions with those of thinkers like Kant and Nietzsche, finding both of them, and others, disappointingly limited in their views of the mind. In general he blames modern philosophy for its "tendency to investigate the structure of the human soul in isolation from any consideration of how that structure came about."    But a careful reading of "Love and Its Place in Nature" yields valuable rewards. He makes one understand how psychoanalysis works not only on the therapist's couch but also as a condition of being alive. He writes: "Psychoanalysis, Freud once said, is a cure through love. On the manifest level, Freud meant that psychoanalytic therapy requires the analysand's emotional engagement with the analyst and the analyst's empathic understanding of his patient. But the latent content of this remark, which Freud only gradually discovered, and then through a glass darkly, is that psychoanalysis in its essence promotes individuation. In that sense, psychoanalysis is itself a manifestation of love. And the emergence of psychoanalysis onto the human scene must, from this perspective, be part of love's developmental history."   Is psychoanalysis dying as a practical therapy? Mr. Lear asks in his Introduction. And answers: "To my mind, the issue is not whether psychoanalysis is obsolete, but whether the individual is." For all their immense value in relieving human suffering, he writes, "there is no evidence that drugs, surgery or electroconvulsive therapy can treat more than the grossest of psychic phenomena. That there will be marvelous advances in neurology and pharmacology is beyond question; that they will solve the conflicts inherent in living    this    particular life is fantasy."   He goes on: "And however valuable it may be to jump-start someone out of a depression, from the point of view of our commitment to the individual, the all-important question is: what happens next? Does the person use the relief from crippling pain as an opportunity to work through the meanings and conflicts inherent in his life; or is he 'relieved' of that opportunity? This is ultimately the question of whether a person is freed    to    become an individual -- or 'freed'    from    that possibility."   Mr. Lear disdains self-help books, because "selves are not that easy to help." He adds, "An individual requires a kind of nurturing and growth that goes far beyond aerobics and quick-fix therapy." Yet "Love and Its Place in Nature" may be the ultimate self-help book. It not only offers a form of spiritual nutriment for the self, it also defines that self with a clear profundity that few readers will have encountered before.
headline: Books of The Times; Psychoanalysis as a Step in the Evolution of Love

title: Road Song
author: Natalie Kusz
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ROAD SONG  By Natalie Kusz. 258 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $18.95.    THE author of this memoir has suffered so much in her 27 years that writing about it involved a risk. "Road Song" could have been a saccharine tract about the triumph of the human spirit or such a painful tale that even reading it would hurt. Instead it's a calm, reflective affirmation of family love.   Natalie Kusz was 6 years old when her parents moved with their four children from Los Angeles to Alaska, pursuing the dream of a freer life. For years her Polish-born father had told his wife and children about the woods he'd known as a boy, until his longing to get back to the land became theirs. "My mother, and then we all, had turned nostalgic for places we'd never seen, countries full of trees and cold rivers and neighbors far apart." In 1969 they sold their house and most of their belongings and headed north in their unreliable car, pulling a small trailer full of supplies.   On the trip, in keeping with family tradition, they harmonized on road songs -- " 'Wayfaring Stranger,' 'My Lord, I'm on My Journey,' and every Russian and Polish verse my father had ever taught us." The "true and unmuffled phrasings" blended and soared "until our very bones and their hollows resonated and increased with the joy of them." Music is as essential to the Kuszes as food. It gives voice to joy, consoles and even heals, seeing them through times that seem to go only from bad to worse.   The journey itself holds great promise. Away from big cities, the travelers encounter a "fresh sort of kindness" and make friends who share their dream. In Alaska, however, their money runs low, a brutal winter comes on and there are no jobs. Along with others in similar straits, they scrounge for food and warm clothing at the dump outside Fairbanks and camp on a river bank.   A relative helps them buy a piece of land, wild and remote and with no road in. Because it's too late in the year to build, they tack a makeshift room onto the trailer. By the time Ms. Kusz's father finds work as a carpenter, a job that takes him a long way from home, stove oil and groceries are all but gone. Waiting for his first paycheck to arrive, the family pawns its cherished musical instruments. Less intrepid people would cut their losses and leave, but the tougher the going gets, the tougher the Kuszes get too.   Then Natalie is attacked by a neighbor's sled dog (vicious because it's underfed) and injured so massively she's not expected to live. The attack costs her an eye and years of misery -- reconstructive surgery, infections, skin grafts that won't take and the attentions of "emotional sightseers," ghouls who want to hear every detail. Yet she insists that her family, especially her mother, suffered more. "The truth is, I think, that the casualties among us include not just those who are dying, or bleeding, or recovering from injury, but also the caretakers around the edges whose selves fall sacrificed to their charges."   More blows follow, including both parents' illnesses, the loss of a house that they manage to build and the medical horrors that Natalie endures. The family rallies again and again, sustained by friends, religious faith and rueful humor. "Someday," Natalie's mother tells her and her sisters, "some guy will say to you, 'Let's run away to the wilderness and live like pioneers. . . .' And you'll look back at that man and tell him, 'Get lost, buddy, I've done my time.' " Reality can vanquish romanticism, but not Natalie's spiritual sturdiness.   Ms. Kusz sings her own song of this tortuous road in a true voice, with no self-pity whatsoever. If her prose sometimes shades into lyrical overkill, becoming self-consciously biblical, its pitch is more often perfect. "Adversity," she observes, is "the small, hard seed of courage." Of all people, she ought to know.   Ms. Kusz took a college teaching job in Minnesota two years ago. She still gets lost easily driving around St. Paul, disoriented by freeways. To head true north to Alaska, where most of her family still lives, she needs no compass but her heart.
headline: 'Get Lost, Buddy, I've Done My Time'

title: The Man Who Thought He Was Messiah
author: Curt Leviant
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE MAN WHO THOUGHT HE WAS MESSIAH.  By Curt Leviant. (Jewish Publication Society, $18.95.) Hasidism appears profoundly conservative to modern eyes, but it was once a vibrant, radical, even revolutionary, movement. Breaking from the Judaism of the period, which they regarded as elitist, the Hasidic teachers of the 18th century sought to bring the gift of transcendence to the common man; through singing, dancing and fervent prayer, Hasidim aspired to mystical communion with God. Among the greatest of the Hasidic teachers was Rabbi Nachman of Bratslav, famous for the wisdom of his storytelling. In his enchanting, magical third novel, Curt Leviant becomes a modern Nachman and summons up a world suffused with a tangible spirituality, a world where trees or dreams or numbers might speak prophecy, where God is ever immanent behind the thin veil of the printed word. Sensual and intriguing, "The Man Who Thought He Was Messiah" shows us Reb Nachman in 1800, his incredibly eventful final year. It begins with God's whisper, a hint of Messianic destiny: Nachman might bring salvation to the scattered nation of Israel. Despite the presumption of this notion, Nachman seeks to prove himself worthy, but fails: he falls in love with Lizabeta, a young peasant "more beautiful than the alphabet." In fitting punishment, Nachman loses his ability to read; to atone for their liaison, he must leave Bratslav. Thus he travels to Vienna and studies composition with a proud but likable Beethoven; returning home with his new language of music, he finds his literacy partly restored. Setting out again, this time for the Holy Land, Nachman stops in Constantinople and, in a storybook scenario, cures the sultan's daughter of a storybook ailment. In Palestine divine tests await, and Nachman must probe his deepest values. Exquisitely written, Mr. Leviant's engaging exploration of the spirit will seduce and delight readers of any faith -- or lack thereof.

title: The Distant Friend
author: Claude Roy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DISTANT FRIEND.  By Claude Roy. Translated by Hugh A. Harter. (Holmes & Meier, $19.95.) Although Claude Roy has published many volumes of fiction, poetry, essays and art criticism in his native France, little of his work has appeared in English translation. "The Distant Friend," then, will probably introduce Mr. Roy to most American readers. This slim novel, which was first published in France in 1987 and has now been ably translated by Hugh A. Harter, takes the form of a wandering, elegiac memoir. The narrator, Etienne, has lived a life of sacrifice and postponement. Confining himself to the family estate in the provinces, where he cares for his invalid mother and balances the accounts, Etienne doggedly accepts his solitude: "I was born a bachelor and would remain a bachelor." His greatest consolation lies in his friendship with Stefan Stein, a German Jewish refugee he first met when they were both teen-agers. Unlike Etienne, this doppelganger is rootless, polyglot and, by nature of his Jewish ancestry, positioned at the tragic center of 20th-century history. Their two destinies diverge rather quickly. While Etienne putters around the farm, Stefan flees France in 1939 for Argentina, becomes an eminent lawyer and writer and, 40 years later, finds his life threatened by Peronist thugs. According to Etienne, their friendship has taught him the "luxury of existing in the eyes of someone else through and for myself." Before long, however, this pairing of Etienne with his opposite number begins to feel like a literary contrivance, one the author has festooned with a string of cliches about politics, history and friendship. As an attempt, in Etienne's words, to preserve memories "suspended at the edge of the abyss of time where oblivion will swallow  [ them ]  up," "The Distant Friend" falls sadly short.    Engage    it is, engaging it isn't.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Dazzle
author: Judith Krantz
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DAZZLE.  By Judith Krantz. (Crown, $21.95.) Anyone who has ever read and drooled over a Judith Krantz novel -- or been forced to confess, "No, but I saw the mini-series" -- will not be disappointed in "Dazzle." Its scrumptious heroine, Jazz Kilkullen, is a brilliant photographer of celebrities, based in Venice, Calif. She is the daughter of a Swedish actress, Sylvie Norberg, and a rancher, Mike Kilkullen, to whom she has been completely devoted since her mother's death when Jazz was 8. Jazz works at Dazzle, the name of the studio she owns with her two partners, Mel and Pete, who specialize, respectively, in food and cars. Sharing the same space is the ever ambitious, avaricious Phoebe Milbank, their representative. An enviable number of men orbit around Jazz, who is a study in gold tones, with rich golden skin, golden brown hair and golden eyes. Jazz's admirers include Sam, an Australian actor whose unimaginable gorgeousness puts him at a painful social disadvantage, and a photojournalist named Gabriel, who first seduced Jazz when she was 18 -- by flicking his tongue over the tips of her eyelashes. Finally, there is the good guy, Casey Nelson, an investor turned cow boss, who works for Jazz's father at the family ranch, 100 square miles of coveted undeveloped coastal real estate between Los Angeles and San Diego. But the people who provide the true drama of "Dazzle" are those who plot to get the precious Kilkullen ranch sold off to developers: Mike's bitter, scheming first wife, Liddy, and Jazz's two half sisters, Valerie, a dry, sexless interior decorator, and the precocious Fernanda. The latter, having experienced her first orgasm at age 3, spends the next 36 years trying to find a lover as good as herself. I wouldn't dream of revealing how this search, or the struggle to save the ranch, ends. "Dazzle," if not perfectly dazzling, is appropriately entertaining. Closet Krantz enthusiasts will find that it fits nicely into the jacket of "Rabbit at Rest" and can be read comfortably on the train.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Mexican Voices/American Dreams
author: Marilyn P Davis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MEXICAN VOICES/AMERICAN DREAMS: An Oral History of Mexican Immigration to the United States.  By Marilyn P. Davis. (Holt, $29.95.) This oral history follows a familiar format: numerous personal accounts arranged by topic, with short introductory sections by the author. Marilyn P. Davis, an independent scholar, draws on the experiences of a wide variety of Mexican immigrants (both legal and illegal), from field hands to professors, from those who stay only briefly in the United States to third-generation American citizens. Inevitably, the stories of immigrants who have adapted to life in    el norte    and have attained successful middle-class careers in this country are the least interesting and do not seem appreciably different from similar stories involving other immigrant groups. The portrayal of the broader Mexican experience, on the other hand, is fascinating. The economic motives for Mexican immigration to the United States are well known, but "Mexican Voices/American Dreams" shows that there are also deep cultural ramifications. For many Mexican children, stories about "over there" take on the aura of myth and exert a pull independent of economic necessity, so that immigration has become a rite of passage for Mexican youth. The separation of parents from children and husbands from wives -- often for years -- can devastate families, as some of Ms. Davis's most poignant pages show. An excellent chapter covers what is in effect an underground railroad for crossing into the United States; illegal immigration has become a major service industry along parts of the border. The book's major disappointment is that it lacks the lyric quality that characterizes the best oral histories. Nevertheless, "Mexican Voices/American Dreams" provides a welcome contrast to the depersonalization characteristic of some treatments of Mexican immigration, which all too often is considered only from the viewpoint of the American border patrol.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Human Rights In Iraq
author: Middle East Watch
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HUMAN RIGHTS IN IRAQ.  By Middle East Watch. (Human Rights Watch/Yale University, $19.95.) This cogent study offers grim details of the systematic repression of its citizens by the Iraqi Government over the last two decades of rule by the Baath Socialist Party and since 1979 by the regime of Saddam Hussein. During this period, according to "Human Rights in Iraq," the 16 million inhabitants of this oil-rich but troubled land have been subject to arbitrary arrest, imprisonment, torture, deportation, expulsion and execution. The often rebellious Kurdish minority (about 20 percent of the population) has suffered a crueler fate: thousands have been massacred, most recently by poison gas attacks, and some 500,000 have been resettled, no one is sure where, since the end of the Iran-Iraq war in 1988. These charges by Middle East Watch, a group that monitors human rights practices in the region, are based on witnesses' corroborated testimony and other research; all the charges have been denied by Baghdad. Although there appears to be no opposition to Saddam Hussein's regime outside the Kurdish areas -- those who conform are offered peace and prosperity -- the Government refuses to admit any human rights investigative body into the country. This study also examines how the United States has applied human rights criteria in its dealings with Iraq. Before Mr. Hussein's invasion of Kuwait, the record was not exemplary. Despite widely circulated State Department reports on Iraq's dismal record, this country offered financial aid and allowed exports of technology, some of it military, to the regime that now threatens the entire Middle East with bloodshed. Once known as the cradle of civilization, the Tigris-Euphrates valley has become a caldron of violence and terror.

title: Squandering The Blue
author: Kate Braverman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: SQUANDERING THE BLUE.  By Kate Braverman. (Fawcett Columbine, $18.95.) If, as they say, beauty is in the eye of the beholder, it stands to reason that horror, too, lurks deep within the optic nerve. How else to explain the lushly menacing imagery in the poet and novelist Kate Braverman's latest book? Never have the gaudy tropical flora of Los Angeles and Hawaii produced such gorgeously poisonous fruit. The stories in "Squandering the Blue," Ms. Braverman's first collection of short fiction, take place "on the border between death and the Mardi Gras," a sinister, forbidding and unpredictable region of the mind where even the leaves on the trees seem to wear camouflage and carry Uzis. Flowers are the color of "bruises, violence and disaster." A sunset metastasizes above the cliffs. The rain doesn't stop, it merely goes into remission. In the feverish imaginations of Ms. Braverman's characters -- many of them former or current substance abusers -- danger is everywhere, particularly in the mirror. If the book seems excessive at times, the characters' crazed outlooks and histrionic predicaments aren't the only cause. Ms. Braverman has a penchant for repetition: identical phrases recur in several stories, and in one 16-page stretch the word "blue" appears 85 times. While this is clearly designed to evoke the hysterical frame of mind of a woman on the verge of a nervous breakdown, it runs the risk of driving readers to distraction en route. Overall, though, the women in "Squandering the Blue" are fitting representatives of the walking wounded, tropical Cassandras with a taste for flashy destruction. Dancing hypnotically on the lip of the volcano, they pour florid language into the fire to create brief, spectacular moments of illumination.

title: Arthur Rackham: A Biography
author: James Hamilton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Anyone who remembers Arthur Rackham's classic illustrations as just treacly pictures of fairies is probably repressing the scarier aspects of childhood. Rackham's supernatural landscapes and their inhabitants enchant us with equal measures of grace and terror. For each rosebud princess, he drew a fearful wolf, witch or mountain peak. In ARTHUR RACKHAM: A Biography (Arcade/Little, Brown, $40; after Dec. 31, $45), the art historian James Hamilton suggests that the Stamford House garden, across the street from Rackham's childhood home, might have been the source of his fantastic arborial people and anthropomorphic trees. Unfortunately the biography, though conscientious and affectionate, gives more insight into Rackham's finances than his imagination. Partly this is due to Mr. Hamilton's effort to correct the view of Rackham as "some kind of busy little gnome, acquainted with the fairies." Born in London in 1867, Rackham supported himself first as a clerk in an insurance office, then as a magazine illustrator. He married a portrait painter and had one daughter. From 1905, when his illustrated edition of "Rip Van Winkle" was gobbled up by the public and the critics, until his death in 1939, Christmas wasn't Christmas without a new Rackham book. Among the more familiar are "Peter Pan in Kensington," "A Midsummer Night's Dream," "The Pied Piper of Hamelin" and fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen and the Grimm brothers; perhaps the best loved is his last, "The Wind in the Willows," published in 1940. Mr. Hamilton's biography invites you to lose yourself among hundreds of pictures selected from Rackham's books.

pull_quote: THE ROSE THIEVES.  By Heidi Jon Schmidt. (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, $18.95.) "When you had expression, you were safe at any speed," observes a young piano student in Heidi Jon Schmidt's first collection of stories. "You could turn pain to understanding like straw into gold." And in this book Ms. Schmidt effects just such alchemy. "The Rose Thieves" is a collection of pieces that reveal an intimate portrait of the storms and intermittent calms of a somewhat eccentric family living in rural Connecticut. If forced to name a central character, it would certainly be Kate, the eldest daughter of the Vanderwald family. For it is through Kate that readers meet her mother (volatile, passionate, dissatisfied with her life) and her father (a relentless optimist with a spent trust fund and an erratic income in futures trading), as well as her two sisters, Audie and Grace, the family peace-keepers. When a grown-up Kate reassures a friend that "love without difficulty could hardly be called love at all," she speaks from experience. But while the personal pain of Ms. Schmidt's characters is palpable, it is never burdensome. Using language that is precise and descriptive, she maintains a sense of the absurd throughout. However, what is perhaps most striking is the uncompromisingly honest yet forgiving nature of Ms. Schmidt's approach. Although Kate wishes she could stay at a distance from the histrionics of her parents, she finally accepts, and is even comforted by, the knowledge that one never outgrows one's family. "For a moment I had stepped inside their circle and felt its narcotic comfort," says Kate in the final story, in which her grandmother faces death. "I was glad, suddenly, to be home, to be sharing the glory of disaster." "The Rose Thieves" is a graceful journey into the individual life of a young woman and the collective life of a family -- and a fine debut.

These 35 short narratives by Arturo Vivante are aptly presented as tales, experiences told, with the double force of memory and invention. The variously named protagonists, like the first-person narrators, appear to be avatars of the author, remembering and touching up significant places in his life. Most frequently these are the landscapes of Italy, chiefly the Siena countryside, the scene of Mr. Vivante's childhood and early youth. The book's most vivid figure is the philosopher-father, perceived in the story called "The Orchard" almost as a fertility god, an extravagant planter of fruit trees, sustained by peaches and perhaps even more by the sight of the young women who gather them. The other side of his nature -- the aloof, crotchety parent -- emerges in "The Soft Core," in which, nevertheless, the son finally moves him to an affectionate response. The wrench of these father-son encounters is not the only tender spot in the collection, which also pays tribute to the gallantry and creative spirit of Mr. Vivante's mother and sister. There is recurrent homage to the English poets as well, and to Keats in particular, shown most clearly in "The Nightingale," a small parable of the writer's longing to express the inexpressible. Although some of the selections in "The Tales of Arturo Vivante" draw upon the many years the author has spent in the United States as a writer and teacher, it is the older, Italian memories that hold the imagination. Versions of all but one of these narratives, a selection from more than 30 years' work, have been printed separately before. It is a pleasure to find them here together.

FLAWLESS JADE.  By Barbara Hanrahan. (University of Queensland Press/International Specialized Book Service, 5602 Hassolo Street N.E., Portland, Ore. 97213, Paper, $12.95.) In her latest novel, the Australian writer Barbara Hanrahan reveals her concerns with life's contradictions and the nature of memory, particularly memories of childhood. But while her previous books have featured women in Australian and English settings, in "Flawless Jade" she turns to the Far East of the 1940's and 50's, as seen through the eyes of a young Chinese girl, Wing-yee. Born during "the Japanese War," Wing-yee lives through Mao Zedong's overthrow of Chiang Kai-shek and the Communist occupation of Canton. After fleeing with some of her family to an ostensibly better life in Hong Kong, she works as a servant, an embroiderer and, at 13, an usherette at the Golden Dragon Cinema. As time passes, Wing-yee's fantasies of returning to Canton gradually dissolve. She also experiences her first love -- and her first heartbreak. When she is 15, her mother crushes her aspirations to become an actress (she has sent a photograph to a movie company, using the name Flawless Jade), insisting that "unless you sold your body you couldn't become famous." Wing-yee's story is a modest 

Bildungsroman

, a poetic account of political and personal tumult and the human will to survive, of its heroine's efforts to make "even my bitter memories . . . somehow sweet." Ms. Hanrahan's book credibly portrays the stratified, male-dominated culture in which Wing-yee lives, a society in which, as she explains without self-pity, "a boy was better than a girl. . . . Girls were regarded as really quite useless." Its plain, straightforward style affectingly conveys the menace and futility of her world. At the book's conclusion, though years have passed, Wing-yee still waits hopefully for her "better future" to begin, studying English and dreaming of Hollywood. While this future appears doubtful, the story she tells assures that she will transcend it. For, as Ms. Hanrahan implies, by expressing ourselves we can triumph over the constraints of both culture and history.

Although the league's coverage from its inception on a Friday the 13th in 1967 to its demise in 1976 was minuscule, tales of prowess on the court and mishaps off (and on) it have become legendary. Like Julius Erving's revolutionary dunks and the Indiana Pacers' Boston Celtics-like championship esprit de corps. Great stuff for a book, right? Except that Terry Pluto throws up a brick by not even bothering to write a book. Instead, Mr. Pluto, a sportswriter for The Akron (Ohio) Beacon-Journal, has collected interviews with dozens of A.B.A. survivors (though he did not talk to several key figures who are talked about by the others), chopped them into paragraphs and strung them out in "Loose Balls." If Mr. Pluto's literary effort had an equivalent on the basketball court, he wouldn't have even made the Anaheim Amigos. Or the Minnesota Muskies.

Wayne Johnson's first novel illuminates the lives of a group of Ojibwa and Chippewa Indians in the lake country of northern Minnesota from the 1950's to the 1980's, revealing a world of guns and taverns and too much liquor, of grown men's anger turned on sons, wives and friends. Each of the 19 chapters takes place in a different year, and each focuses on different incidents in the lives of the novel's characters. Mr. Johnson uses both first- and third-person voices to tell their many stories. Among the most successful are his account of young Red Deer, who uses his skills as a baseball pitcher to vent his rage, and of Eli, whose pride in his welding skill enables him to transcend personal tragedies. But don't expect to find any levity in "The Snake Game," or to meet any women of substance. Dominated -- sometimes beaten -- by their men, the women wait meekly for drunken lovers, conjure spells to seduce objects of sexual desire or arrive in boatloads to service carousing fishermen from the city. Because Mr. Johnson writes so well, I wish he'd had a crankier editor -- to take care of puzzling lines like "The horn jabbed him like electricity" and to question bits of unfinished plot. Any author would be challenged by the prospect of inhabiting the lives of so many characters, and sometimes Mr. Johnson fails to bring all of them equally to life. He is most at ease when writing about a young outsider named Marty Sorenson, who seems to be something of an alter ego. Yet even when Marty and the others falter as characters, it is clear that Mr. Johnson cares for them and feels deeply the pain of their lives.

There are few who would deny that Broadway's greatest gift to the world has been the musical comedy, and perhaps fewer still who would dispute that this decidedly American concoction reached its peak in the middle of this century. Among its many other virtues as a comprehensive research tool, or just as a delight for theater aficionados, "Opening Night on Broadway" by Steven Suskin, a theatrical producer and manager, confirms that the critics were definitely aware something special was happening on the Great White Way at the time. As Brooks Atkinson wrote about "Finian's Rainbow," which opened in 1947, four years after the pivotal "Oklahoma!": "If the American musical stage continues to improve, it will no longer be necessary for anyone to speak dialogue on the stage. Everything essential can be said in song and dancing." From "Alive and Kicking" to "Ziegfeld Follies of 1957," this collection of excerpts from the daily reviews constitutes a galvanizing parade of the peacocks as well as the turkeys. Though the era encompassed practically every great musical our generation knows by name (including "Guys and Dolls," "How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying," "The Music Man," "My Fair Lady," "The Pajama Game," "West Side Story" and "Hello, Dolly!"), typically it was the less successful shows that inspired the wittiest comments. Consider the cavalcade of puns on titles, including Walter Kerr's "Anyone can whistle, but nobody can sing"; Robert Coleman's "Lerner, Loewe, and Hart spent so much to mount    Camelot    that the wisecrackers have been calling it 'Costallot' "; Howard Barnes's response to "Let's Make an Opera": "Let's not!"; and Louis Kronenberger's revised name for "The Girl From Nantucket": "The Girl From Death Valley." In response to this last woebegone offering, Wilella Waldorf of The New York Post was even more vicious: "If the producers wish to lift something from this review for advertising purposes, they may quote us as saying, 'It lacks everything.' title: Ludwig Wittgenstein: The Duty Of Genius
author: Ray Monk. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LUDWIG WITTGENSTEIN  The Duty of Genius. By Ray Monk. Illustrated. 654 pp. New York: The Free Press. $29.95.    Ludwig Wittgenstein was the greatest philosopher of the 20th century. Many books have been written about his philosophy. Ray Monk's "Ludwig Wittgenstein" is the first substantial biography of his whole life. It is not a book to which one would turn to learn about Wittgenstein's thought, but enough is said about the philosophical writings to make intelligible the story of the philosopher's life. And the story is well told; the narrative is vivid, clear, sympathetic and credible.   Wittgenstein's great-grandfather was a land agent named Moses Maier, who in 1808 took the name of his princely employers, the Wittgensteins. His father, Karl, a friend of Johannes Brahms, was the most acute industrialist in the Austrian steel industry; he made the family the Austrian equivalent of the Carnegies or Rothschilds. He had five sons and three daughters by a Roman Catholic wife, and baptized all of them into the Catholic faith. He set out to educate the sons in a very severe regime which would turn them into captains of industry. He did not succeed. Three of the sons committed suicide; the fourth, Paul, became (despite the loss of an arm in World War I) a concert pianist; the fifth, the youngest child, born in Vienna in 1889, was the philosopher.   Ludwig Wittgenstein attended the Realschule in Linz, where he was a contemporary of Adolf Hitler. He was a poor scholar, teased by his peers. At school he also lost his faith. The major intellectual influences on him in his youth, apart from the philosophical works of Schopenhauer, were the physicist Ludwig Boltzmann (suicide 1906) and the psychologist Otto Weininger (suicide 1903).   Mr. Monk believes that Weininger's bizarre book "Sex and Character" was of fundamental importance in shaping Wittgenstein's career. According to Weininger -- a homosexual -- all human beings are bisexual, a mixture of male and female. Woman is nothing but sexuality: every woman is a mixture of prostitute and mother. Men must choose between the masculine and feminine elements within themselves; the ideal for a man is to free himself from sex. "The choice that Weininger's theory offers is a bleak and terrible one indeed: genius or death," says Mr. Monk. "If . . . one cannot free oneself from sensuality and earthly desires -- then one has no right to live at all."   For Wittgenstein, to acquire genius became a categorical imperative. He once described Beethoven greeting a friend on completion of a new fugue: he "came to the door, looking as if he had been fighting the devil, and having eaten nothing for 36 hours because his cook and parlour-maid had been away from his rage. That's the sort of man to be."   It was in Cambridge in 1911 that Wittgenstein first gave evidence of genius in philosophy, and it was Bertrand Russell who first recognized it. Wittgenstein was, Russell wrote, "perhaps the most perfect example I have ever known of genius as traditionally conceived, passionate, profound, intense, and dominating." Russell was already well known as the author of powerful, original work in logic and mathematics; he soon realized that Wittgenstein's gifts were greater than his own, and he devoted himself with great generosity to their development. In 1912 he told Wittgenstein's sister, "We expect the next big step in philosophy to be taken by your brother."   The expectation was fulfilled, but Wittgenstein's philosophical message was not given to the world until after World War I. During that war he served in the Austrian Army on the Eastern and Italian fronts, and much of the material that later appeared in his masterpiece, "Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus," was written while on active service. At the front Wittgenstein showed conspicuous courage and was commended and decorated; he was also converted, by the reading of Tolstoy, to an intense though idiosyncratic Christianity. "Perhaps the nearness of death," he wrote in his diary, "will bring me the light of life. May God enlighten me. I am a worm, but through God I become a man. God be with me. Amen."   After the war, having inherited a share of his father's fortune, he found himself one of the wealthiest men in Europe. Within a month of returning from the army he gave all his money away. For some years he supported himself as a gardener or as a schoolmaster in rural Austrian schools. He believed, for a while, that he had already solved all the problems of philosophy in his "Tractatus," which appeared (after great difficulty in finding a publisher) in German in 1921 and in English in 1922. The book quickly became famous; though it was itself metaphysical and almost mystical, as well as austerely logical, it was most admired by the anti-metaphysical positivists of the Vienna Circle.    It was at Vienna that Wittgenstein returned to the study of philosophy, when his career as a schoolmaster came to an unhappy end after allegations of cruelty to his pupils. Eventually he returned to Cambridge and during his years there in the 1930's he became the most influential teacher of philosophy in Britain. The philosophy he taught in this period differed from that published in the "Tractatus"; it was not presented in print until "Philosophical Investigations" was published posthumously in 1953.   After the Anschluss, Hitler's forced unification of Austria and Germany in 1938, Wittgenstein became a British citizen. During World War II he worked as a paramedic, and in 1947 he resigned his Cambridge chair. He continued to write philosophy and to communicate philosophical thoughts to close friends and disciples. After a period of solitary life in Ireland, he stayed in the houses of various friends in Oxford and Cambridge until his death in 1951 at the age of 62. He left a mass of philosophical papers, many of them still awaiting publication.   Wittgenstein's genius is patent to any philosopher who will take the time and trouble to come to grips with his profound but difficult writings. His life, as described by Mr. Monk, seems to have been a lonely and tragic one. He was often tormented by temptations to suicide, and was sometimes on the verge of mental illness. He regarded his life as a professor as "a living death," and held many of his colleagues, in the various callings he pursued, in loathing and contempt. His only philosophical peer was Russell, and the relationship between the two soured after Wittgenstein's return to Cambridge. Many of his philosophical disciples loved him, but it was a love mixed strongly with fear.   Four times in his life, according to Mr. Monk, Wittgenstein fell deeply in love. Three of his loves were male and one female. (Sensational stories have been told of Wittgenstein's passion for rough homosexuals picked up in Vienna parks; Mr. Monk examines the evidence patiently and convincingly and concludes that any such encounters took place only in Wittgenstein's own fantasy.) David Pinsent, to whose memory the "Tractatus" was dedicated, accompanied Wittgenstein to Norway and Iceland in the prewar period; he was killed in 1918. Francis Skinner, who came up to Cambridge as a student in 1930, had an all-absorbing relationship with Wittgenstein in the 30's; and in 1946 Wittgenstein fell in love with a Cambridge medical student, Ben Richards, 40 years his junior.   MANY readers will be surprised to learn from Mr. Monk's book that there was a time when Wittgenstein had plans to marry. From 1926 to 1931 he had a friendship with a Swiss woman, Marguerite Respinger. For a period he wrote to her almost daily, and he sculpted a bust of her. An entry in his diary for 1930 reads: "Arrived back in Cambridge after the Easter vacation. In Vienna often with Marguerite. Easter Sunday with her in Neuwaldegg. For three hours we kissed each other a great deal and it was very nice."   Once it became clear that Wittgenstein wanted to marry her, Marguerite drew back -- especially as it transpired that what the philosopher had in mind was a Platonic, childless union.   Faith in God was important to Wittgenstein; but his faith seems to have been a somber one. God was perhaps no more than Fate. If He was to be thought of as a person, it was solely as a severe judge. Yet Wittgenstein's last words were, "Tell  [ my friends ]  I've had a wonderful life." Ray Monk's book has succeeded remarkably in portraying some of its wonders.    HE WELCOMED THE BOMB    Wittgenstein's hostility towards professional philosophy and his dislike of Cambridge remained constant throughout his academic career, but in the years . . . that followed the Second World War, they seemed to become fused with a kind of apocalyptic vision. . . .   What links this apocalyptic anxiety with his hostility to academic philosophy is his detestation of the power of science in our age, which on the one hand encouraged the philosopher's "craving for generality," and on the other produced the atomic bomb. . . . He even welcomed the bomb, if only the fear of it could do something to diminish the reverence with which society regarded scientific progress. . . . The most pessimistic view, for him, was one which foresaw the triumph of science and technology: "Science and industry, and their progress, might turn out to be the most enduring thing in the modern world. Perhaps any speculation about a coming collapse of science and industry is . . . nothing but a dream; perhaps science and industry, having caused infinite misery in the process, will unite the world -- I mean condense it into a single unit, though one in which peace is the last thing that will find a home. pull_quote: PIZZA IN PUSHKIN SQUARE: What Russians Think About Americans and the American Way of Life.  By Victor Ripp. (Simon & Schuster, $18.95.) Victor Ripp, an American academic of Russian descent, employs the travelogue genre to track down the misconceptions that, glasnost notwithstanding, continue to cloud the Soviet view of America. In his travels, Mr. Ripp meets a schoolboy who asks about the cowboys and Indians in today's Texas. He meets a Moscow woman who at first seems well informed about America, but then assumes that Mr. Ripp's home in Hopewell, N.J., is a summer    dacha.    And he finds himself in a great number of awkward situations caused by cultural misunderstandings between him and his Russian friends. All of this is amusing, albeit for the most part predictable. Unfortunately, the two elements in Mr. Ripp's scheme -- the misconceptions and the historical roots of these misconceptions -- do not fall together into a uniform narrative, and the sarcastic tone of "Pizza in Pushkin Square," while initially amusing, quickly becomes an annoyance. The author's tendency to jump to unjustified, sweeping conclusions is even more irritating. A decade or two ago, casual observers seemed to have little trouble noting undiscovered traits of Russian character and style. Today, with everybody Moscow-bound, even informed travelers like Mr. Ripp seem to be hard pressed to bring back anything of value.

In HOLLYWOOD GOTHIC: The Tangled Web of "Dracula" From Novel to Stage to Screen (Norton, $39.95), the novelist David J. Skal tracks Transylvania's most popular vampire with dry wit and the skills of a fine detective. He follows the efforts of Stoker's widow, Florence, to consign to flames every existing print of "Nosferatu," F. W. Murnau's unauthorized 1922 silent film version of the story (at least one of which, mercifully, escaped her clutches). He stalks "Dracula" from London to the Broadway stage, where the bloodthirsty Count claimed the body of a Hungarian actor named Bela Lugosi, making him forever captive to the role. Mr. Skal reveals the heretofore hidden intrigues that landed Stoker's novel in Hollywood, where Lugosi's heirs would eventually lose their 16-year struggle with Universal Pictures to possess their father's image beyond the grave. But the author is most satisfying when he reveals his discovery, in a Cuban film vault, of the missing reel of a Spanish-language "Dracula" that was filmed in tandem with Tod Browning's 1931 American release. Filled with charming and unusual illustrations, the volume includes a handy chronology ("Dracula at a Glance") and many incisive observations about the terror and appeal of mixing sex with immortality. Yet Mr. Skal wisely treads lightly over the meaning of "Dracula," leaving its essential mystery undisturbed. Indeed, those who cannot find their own reflection in Bram Stoker's still-living creation are surely the undead.

Availing himself of his rich family history, Terry Kay uses his fourth novel to tell an admittedly autobiographical story in which he celebrates his parents' marriage. "There was a grand romance of life between them," Mr. Kay states in an author's note at the end of the book, "and my father's loneliness following the death of my mother was a terrible experience for him." The novel explores how 81-year-old Sam Peek, hobbled by a bad leg and dependent on a walker, manages to carry on after the death of Cora, his wife of 57 years. Feisty and determined, Sam continues to drive his rattletrap truck to his pecan grove to tend the trees. He makes plans to travel to a nearby town in Georgia for his 60th college reunion. He keeps a journal. And he tries to outwit his two daughters, worrywarts whose mollycoddling grows irritating even to the reader. What ultimately saves Sam, though, is a magnificent and mysterious white dog -- perhaps the manifestation of Cora's gallant spirit -- whose companionship eases his loneliness and thus encourages him to maintain his independence. Despite a few monotonous characterizations and some banal journal entries, "To Dance With the White Dog" is a deftly shaped and vivid book. In this memorable novel, Terry Kay has created a tender and bracing tale of an octogenarian fighting to live a connected and purposeful life.

pull_quote: The First Amendment, Democracy and Romance  By Steven H. Shiffrin  285 pages. Harvard University Press.   One of the first surprises law students encounter in their course on constitutional law is that the First Amendment, as interpreted over the years by even the most liberal judges, doesn't give someone an absolute right to speak or write freely. Long before entering law school, most students have heard that free expression doesn't allow a person to shout "Fire!" in a crowded theater falsely. In addition to reasons of public safety, other limitations have been imposed by statutes and the courts, including laws against libel, invasion of privacy, blackmail and fraud.    A few more surprises are in store for readers of Steven H. Shiffrin's "First Amendment, Democracy and Romance." The biggest one is that his First Amendment exemplars aren't such history-making United States Supreme Court justices as Oliver Wendell Holmes and William J. Brennan but Walt Whitman and Ralph Waldo Emerson.

author: William Herrick
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BRADOVICH.  By William Herrick. (New Directions, $18.95.) In many ways, William Herrick's 10th novel conforms to the Pop Fiction Code. Stephen Bradovich, a craggy, widowed football player turned sculptor, lives in a city that purports to be New York but feels, with its cozy neighborliness and broad boulevards, like a dream. Here the hero is pursued by a supernaturally effective enemy called "The Authority." But instead of being the homage to Franz Kafka that the author clearly intended, the novel equally suggests Judith Krantz, featuring the sort of writing in which meals are described to the last crumb, yet logic evaporates at will. (Thwarted when he tries to book his escape at a travel agency or by phone, our hero never thinks simply to get in a bus, train or taxi, to rent a car or take himself directly to an airport.) Although it's a suspense novel, "Bradovich" is not intended to be commercial fiction; its dropped names are not those of brands beloved by Best-Selling Authors but those adored in our universities. And Mr. Herrick's pages are peppered with philosophizing about Life's Meaning and paeans to Great Art. So the really scary thing about this book is not the depredations capriciously wreaked by "The Authority," not the whipping, incest, bestiality, rape, mutilation and kinky sex that keep popping up, not death and its injustice, but rather the fact that New Directions, a house renowned for publishing writers like Jorge Luis Borges, Delmore Schwartz, Kay Boyle, Tennessee Williams and Jean Cocteau, is now offering thinking readers novels as meretricious as this one.

pull_quote: WATER BABY: The Story of Alvin.  By Victoria A. Kaharl. (Oxford University, $21.95.) This is a fascinating history of Alvin, the world's first deep-diving submarine. The three-person craft, which opened the ocean depths to exploration in the mid-1960's, has shown scientists strange and previously unknown worlds and in the process helped alter our understanding of planet Earth. "Water Baby," by the science writer Victoria A. Kaharl, is, however, much more than a story about a titanium sphere with a curious name. It is also about the men and women who, during dives so deep it takes hours to surface, must trust that Alvin will protect them from thousands of pounds of pressure on each square inch of the hull. There is heroism as well as humor: stories of pilots jockeying the craft free from fissures more than 8,000 feet down, for example, and a running account of the motley crew of Alvin's mother ship, including a man nicknamed Bare Bear who slept in his bunk with a teddy bear. The best parts of "Water Baby" are the vivid descriptions of trips to the sea floor. Early in its career, Alvin had shown scientists that the deep ocean was not barren, as had been believed, but was teeming with life. However, even veterans of deep diving were surprised at the lushness of marine oases at the bottom of the Pacific, which they viewed in the mid-70's, courtesy of Alvin. "Water Baby" does bog down in places, but the information overkill is clearly the result of the author's extensive research and love for the subject. In the end, Ms. Kaharl's enthusiasm proves to be irresistible.

pull_quote: LANDSCAPE: MEMORY.  By Matthew Stadler. (Scribner's, $19.95.) The year is 1915. Nine years after the great earthquake, San Francisco is hosting a world's fair, Model T's and trench warfare have captured the popular imagination and the hero of Matthew Stadler's first novel is coming of age. "Landscape: Memory" is a portrait of the artist as a painfully sensitive young man, a richly impressionistic tale told in the form of a private journal and illustrated with Mr. Stadler's renditions of the narrator's painting-in-progress. Young Maxwell Kosegarten is a survivor of the great 1906 earthquake. He and his best friend, Duncan, brought together by the disaster, now spend their days exploring a changed San Francisco. They trace the quake's path along the coast, wander through the glittering fair at night and puzzle over their own shared recollections of the past. The process of memory is Max's true fascination: he struggles to fix dynamic events and impressions in his journal just as he yearns to capture a changing landscape in paint. The book remains a bit sketchy and disorienting until Max succeeds in bringing the reader closer to his private world. But the outside world is always interesting, as Mr. Stadler subtly weaves accurate historical details into Max's accounts of his daily experiences. This vivid narrative scene-painting brings a lost era to life, encompassing the thrill of a first automobile ride, the increasing horror of news from the European front and a child's terror as the earth rips apart. Max's memory of the earthquake unfolds late in the book, but it finally allows us to enter his emotional landscape, even as human figures begin to appear in his painting. When Duncan comes closer too, becoming lover as well as friend, the stage is set for passion and tragedy. "Landscape: Memory" is an unusual and impressive debut, a book that takes both a young man and his city through pain toward maturity.

title: Bloomsbury Reflections
author: Alen Macweeney
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Vanessa Bell once said that the subject matter of photography should be a little absurd. By this, Bell may have been thinking of her great-aunt, the Victorian photographer Julia Margaret Cameron, "who posed her sitters in a 'high-art' mode, and whose aim was not merely to 'take' photographs but to immortalize those dragooned into posing for her," writes Frances Spalding in her brief, discerning foreword to BLOOMSBURY REFLECTIONS (Norton, $39.95), a collection of photographs of the friends and descendants of the Bloomsbury group. Likewise, Bell would have appreciated the photographer Alen MacWeeney's slightly absurd -- though exceptionally beautiful -- photographic portraits. Each, despite its appearance of spontaneity, has been composed with great artifice. Each of his pictures is a collage of allusions, a reference to the past, while at the same time a frozen moment revealing something essential about the sitter's character. To this end he makes use not just of color and light, but of the furniture, decorative objects and paintings of Bloomsbury. Among the book's most memorable photos, in fact, are his eerily evocative shots of such Bloomsbury haunts as Monk's House, where Virginia Woolf did much of her writing, and Charleston, the country home of Clive and Vanessa Bell. Unfortunately, while the photographs draw us in, the text, which largely consists of a brief reminiscence of Bloomsbury by each sitter, is far less absorbing. Even readers who normally subscribe to the cult of Bloomsbury will question the value of such banal revelations as that of Cecil Woolf, who recalls seeing his Uncle Leonard pick up a piece of chocolate from the floor of a theater and "pop it in his mouth," or Henrietta Garnett, who remembers that her grandmother Vanessa Bell was so frugal that she served "dessert at lunch, but none at dinner." The problem with most of these pieces, written by Sue Allison, a reporter at Life magazine, is that the speakers are of a different generation from the principals of Bloomsbury. With the exception of Quentin Bell, who speaks engagingly of life at Charleston, their memories are at best fragmentary, at worst too subjective to be revealing. Fortunately, Mr. MacWeeney's strangely canny photographs work independently of the text. While "Bloomsbury Reflections" reveals little of the actual stories behind these often guarded faces, it is a stunning visual record of what was once the spirit of Bloomsbury.
