author: David Walton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: The life and work of the Italian photographer Tina Modotti (1896-1942) have become fodder for such a variety of causes that Sarah M. Lowe's vow to write Modotti's "cultural biography" and "dislodge her from the center of her legend"  may cause cynics' eyebrows to arch in suspicion. Yet, as the author's intelligent introductory essay to the 150 elegant duotone photographs reproduced in TINA MODOTTI: Photographs (Philadelphia Museum of Art/Abrams, $45) soon makes clear, Ms. Lowe means what she says. She has done extensive research about the political, social and cultural contexts of Modotti's many whereabouts. Tina  Modotti was an uneducated working-class girl in turn-of-the-century Italy and a  sophisticated actress, muse and femme fatale in Hollywood before spending the years from 1923 to 1930 in Mexico, where she became an increasingly political photographer; later, among other activities, she was a relief worker in the Spanish Civil War. Ms. Lowe, an art historian and curator, puts the facts of Modotti's life in illuminating perspective, tracing the artist's esthetic development, her ties to the Modernist movement and her awareness of the conflict between making art and making politics. If "Experiment in Related Form" (1924) -- a double exposure of five glasses of differing sizes whose rims seem to float, intersect and shine all at once -- means freedom from the austere esthetic of Edward Weston, Modotti's lover and teacher of photography, the sea of sombreros in "Workers Parade" (1926) marks Modotti's first expression of her  disappointment with the unfulfilled promises of the Mexican revolution and her commitment to a new social order. From portraits of Aztec mothers with their infants to "Mella's Typewriter" (a close-up of a Communist lover's instrument of intellectual and political activity), Modotti's tight cropping and still-life esthetic excelled at melding Mexican culture and Modernist photography.   CHRISTINE SCHWARTZ HARTLEY

pull_quote: In the mid-1930's, a young French ethnographer named Claude Levi-Strauss ventured by rail, truck, canoe and horseback into the Brazilian interior to document the cultural habits of tribal groups whose numbers and customs were still somewhat protected by their relative isolation. Equipped with a Leica and  "an oval-shaped miniature 8-mm. camera whose name I have forgotten," the anthropologist, feeling ambivalent about the use of photography in such a setting, nonetheless created a rare visual record of archery contests, funeral rites, face painting and other traditional customs, some of which have long since been abandoned. The photographs of the Nambikwara, the Bororo and the Caduveo form the centerpiece of Mr. Levi-Strauss's SAUDADES DO BRASIL: A Photographic Memoir (University of Washington, $39.95), skillfully translated from the French by Sylvia Modelski. There are also images of Sao Paulo in the 1930's when it was a frontier city of "singular beauty" and not yet one of the industrial capitals in the world, and of pristine Brazilian landscapes that now, in large or small part, bear the scars of mining and logging as well as other ravages of modernization. The reader might be surprised at the remarkable, if rueful, candor with which the renowned anthropologist introduces the volume: "The photographs leave me with the impression of a void, a lack of something the lens is inherently unable to capture." Although Mr. Levi-Strauss, a chief architect of structural anthropology, declares that he is not a photographer, "not even an amateur," the images here are skillful and compelling. But it is not the quality of the photographs he is apologizing for; it is history. And his apology is not directed at us so much as at the ghosts of his tribal subjects, "the last escapees from the cataclysm" of European colonialism and its aftermath.   SUZANNE MacNEILLE

pull_quote: In 1946, a young American photographer named John Vachon was sent to Poland by the recently formed United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration to document that agency's aid efforts in a country suffering from the catastrophic ravages of World War II. Vachon (1914-75), who had been part of a distinguished photographic team working for the Farm Security Administration in  the 1930's, did not much relish doing official publicity shots, and most of the pictures he took in Poland were put away in archives without being published; but, as they are collected in POLAND, 1946: The Photographs and Letters of John Vachon (Smithsonian Institution, $39.95), they bring back, with  a startling poignancy, a time that for most of us is a forgotten historical zone. In Poland, perhaps more than in most of Europe, the war didn't really finish with its official end; and in his trips across the country, Vachon everywhere found the evidence of a continuing battle for survival, of massive social rearrangement and of still-seething political conflicts. Cities in rubble, children with rickets, villages burned to cinders by underground units fighting the newest Soviet domination, inhabitants of formerly German cities being deported, repatriates from Eastern territories being transported in filthy boxcars: this could be a terribly depressing record -- and yet, oddly, it isn't. In his letters to his wife, Vachon, despite his political naivete, wrote with great understanding not only about the hardships he witnessed, but also about the courage and dignity of the people he encountered -- and his images convey this fundamental sympathy. In the many faces of strangely grown-up children, in  the eyes of repatriates looking up with stubborn gravity, in the haunting melancholy of lone figures among ruins, in a family of peasants against a moody  rural landscape or a row of women salvaging bricks from a crumbled building, Vachon repeatedly caught both the pain of what had happened and the sense of fierce life reasserting itself. These impressionistic and somberly beautiful photographs constitute a deeply affecting portrait of a place and a people struggling to emerge from a terrible war into an uneasy peace.   Eva Hoffman

pull_quote: It was time," says the octogenarian photographer Eve Arnold, "to make an archive . . . to make order out of the chaotic files that have been my life." For a photojournalist who has published eight previous books and accumulated more than 40 years' worth of slides, negatives and prints, that is a tall order. EVE ARNOLD: In Retrospect (Knopf, $50) is a chronological memoir of Ms. Arnold's professional life along with the photographs by which she wants to be remembered. From images of Malcolm X, Marilyn Monroe and Margaret Thatcher to those of anonymous veiled Afghan women and of toddlers in a Chinese nursery, the shots she has chosen show not only the high points but also the broad sweep of her undertakings. Throughout her career, she has worked for Magnum, the photographers' cooperative founded by Robert Capa, Henri Cartier-Bresson, George Rodger and David Seymour, usually on assignment for publications like Life and London's Sunday Times. Her style, despite her confession to "dithering and nerves," is authoritative and humanist -- energized, as she says, by the unfamiliar. Being there is paramount to a photojournalist's success, and Ms. Arnold gives a lively account of the obstacles she surmounted -- rough terrain,  illness, intractable bureaucrats. Although few of the book's images hold the transcendent power of her color picture of an old Chinese woman whose beautifully lined face emerges from the textured black of her clothes and the surrounding shadow, all attest to her enterprise and tenacity, along with her ability to establish rapport with her subjects. As Ms. Arnold looks back, she seems justifiably pleased with her accomplishments and wonders about her next project. Now that she has achieved order, she might try another kind of memoir,  a distillation of her memories that brings more of the woman herself into focus.   Rosemary Ranck

Milne (Free Press, $24) briskly examines the authors of five classics of British children's literature and offers shrewd assessments of those profoundly eccentric men and their great works. Each of the writers, Ms. Wullschlger says, "needed a child as muse to trigger the adult imagination into creating an extraordinary fantasy. Once locked into this magical world, however, each drew on his own peculiarly strong affinity with childhood." The key there is "peculiarly," because, as she  discreetly puts it, "all shared a reluctance to engage in conventional behavior  and relationships." The creation of those fantasy lands, she argues, was made possible by, and in turn reflected, "the confidence and prosperity of Britain between 1860 and 1914." It was a confidence that "lasted until the First World War, when to die ceased to be the awfully big adventure that Peter Pan had expected." Ms. Wullschlger, a literary critic and feature writer at The Financial Times in London, thinks that A. A. Milne's work from the 1920's belongs with the others because it was "a throwback" and "nostalgically desperate" for what had been lost. While she is insightful and clear about all five writers, she is particularly good on Edward Lear. She does not hesitate to  address Lear's homosexuality, but she insightfully notes that his relationships  with children "had none of the anguished, knowing intensity of Carroll's or Barrie's." Lear, she says, "made child-friends and then let them go, as easily and carelessly as a child on holiday would." "The Owl and the Pussycat," that most beloved nonsense lyric about "two odd, sexless, cozy lovers," was written shortly after Lear was talked out of making a proposal of marriage to a much younger woman, she observes, and it is a poem of "hopeful escape." pull_quote: A HISTORY OF FASCISM, 1914-1945 By Stanley G. Payne. Illustrated. 613 pp. Madison: The University of Wisconsin Press. $39.95.    IS fascism a thing of the past? The question has both a theoretical and a practical interest. On the theoretical side we are curious whether fascist movements and regimes are so linked to the conditions of Europe between the world wars that nothing having their peculiar combination of features can be found in other historical contexts -- such as our own. Practically, we are anxious about the future of liberal democracy. We wonder if the increase in economic insecurity that affects almost all of us -- but particularly the middle classes, for whom it remains in some ways a novel experience -- may not provoke  a revival of movements of the kind that swept away fragile democracies in the 1930's. Looking at the world around us, it seems that powerful fascist movements do belong to the interwar period and pose no major danger to us now. Except perhaps for Russia, where Vladimir Zhirinovsky's bizarrely misnamed Liberal Democratic Party has evoked comparisons with Hitler's National Socialists in Weimar Germany, no democratic state faces anything that could reasonably be described as a fascist threat. Most democracies contain small groups that are estranged from democratic institutions, some of them -- like those who inspired  the Oklahoma bombing or those who daubed European synagogues with anti-Semitic slogans -- willing to resort to terrorist violence. Yet none of these groups are in a position to mount a challenge to a democratic state. Can we then safely write off fascism as largely banished from the world?

title: Saving Graces: Images Of Women In European Cemeteries
author: David Robinson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: They wilt, they swoon, they languish. What's more, they're naked, or mostly naked, or at least some of them are. In his afterword to SAVING GRACES: Images of Women in European Cemeteries (Norton, cloth, $25; paper, $14.95), a collection of more than 100 of his black-and-white photographs of marble, stone  and bronze maidens in various degrees of distress, David Robinson notes that these statues, most of them made in the mid- to late 19th century, serve as surrogate mourners and embody the Romantic notion of the link between love and death. And who can say him nay, especially after seeing the uninhibited figure from Genoa's Staglieno cemetery, passed out backward in apparent ecstasy, barely draped and with a posy of roses tucked in her armpit? Ecstatic, too, is the fully draped maiden in Pre Lachaise in Paris, about to be raised to heaven by a  well-muscled angel who is hovering above her with a display of more than brotherly (or perhaps sisterly -- it's hard to tell) interest. But the high-relief carving of a kneeling nude in the Staglieno, roses held strategically in her lap, is as unemotional and non-erotic as could be. And how  about the figure of the draped young girl in Paris's Passy cemetery who looks not only demure but totally unconcerned about such matters as love and death? No roses, but her attributes include a Greco-Etruscan helmet and a carved replica of a Bernard Palissy ceramic platter, which leads one to wonder whose monument this is, and why these particular artifacts are to the point. But why quibble? The photographs are beautiful, and beautifully reproduced.   Sarah Ferrell

These markets provide the book's true focus, as Zola chronicles the vigorous, greedy intrigues of butchers, fishwives, poultry sellers and butter dealers, all of whom feel first irritated, then threatened by the sight of this morose, idealistic, skinny young man. To Florent, the markets "appeared symbolical of some glutted, digesting beast, of Paris, wallowing in its fat and silently upholding the Empire" that has treated him so cruelly. Clearly that's also how they appeared to Zola, who, in Ernest Alfred Vizetelly's translation, minutely describes this "colossal belly" -- from the damp, odorous fish stalls to the mountains of fleshy produce in the vegetable and fruit pavilions. As Florent becomes increasingly repelled by Louis Napoleon's mercantile Paris and begins to plot an ill-fated insurrection, these descriptions turn monstrous. Never before  has cheese seemed so sinister: "A Livarot was swarming with life; and in a fragile box behind the scales a Grom flavored with aniseed diffused such a pestilential smell that all around it the very flies had fallen lifeless on the  gray-veined slab of ruddy marble." The novel's appeal lies, of course, in Zola's descriptive brilliance, his ability to paint this brutal, teeming world of food  with the confidence of a Dutch master. But the political conflict, personified by scrawny Florent and the overfed shopkeepers, is artfully rendered as well. This is not a book for dieters -- or those with delicate stomachs.   Suzanne Berne

author: Laura Goldstein
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: In the years following the Civil War, emancipated slaves poured into the nation's capital, often ending up in cramped and hidden alley neighborhoods. Overcrowding and lack of sanitation attracted reformers, and by the turn of the  century a movement to eradicate these pestilential areas was under way. Reform legislation, urban planning schemes, two wars and documentary photographers like Lewis Hine came and went before the neighborhoods were finally razed in a redevelopment effort in the 1950's. In 1943, a social worker named Godfrey Frankel (1912-95) took his camera and rode a bicycle into one of these alleys, ready to expose the capital's squalid underside. To his surprise, what he discovered during repeated afternoon forays was something richer and more complex -- a community and its children, which are portrayed in IN THE ALLEYS: Kids in the Shadow of the Capitol (Smithsonian, cloth, $55; paper, $24.95), with text by Laura Goldstein, a freelance Washington journalist, and a foreword by the photographer Gordon Parks. Mr. Parks also visited the alleys in the early 1940's, and describes them as dirty, disgruntled and gloomy, but Frankel's images portray a more benign environment. The sun raking across the uneven brick passageways and peeling wooden steps where troops of small children gather suggest stability and warmth. When Frankel's subjects face his camera, their expressions range from grave to gleeful, their integrity never in doubt. Ragged  clothes become symbols of pluck and resourcefulness rather than despair. Ms. Goldstein provides an affectionate biography of Frankel and a history of the Washington alleys. By including comments by middle-aged survivors of alley childhood, she adds depth to this record of an eradicated past.   Rosemary Ranck

title: Rumpole And The Angel Of Death
author: John John Clifford Mortimer Mortimer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: First-rate comic writing is often more difficult to produce than the serious  stuff, and real pros are few and far between. One of these is John Mortimer, an  Englishman best known in this country for his mystery stories starring the comic and gallant barrister Horace Rumpole. Mr. Mortimer knows his territory, and his  comments on the vagaries of the English legal system and the small value it places on common sense and moral standards are as sharp as ever in RUMPOLE AND THE ANGEL OF DEATH (Viking, $22.95), the 10th volume of stories in the series. In Rumpole, Mr. Mortimer has created a wonderfully durable and attractive character, henpecked as a husband but masterful with a jury, an honest man whose only cause is "preventing the conviction of the innocent." Rumpole's true home is the courtroom, but we are also made privy to life in the gloomy flat in Froxbury Mansions where he exists in pitiful thralldom to his wife, Hilda, otherwise known as She Who Must Be Obeyed. This moniker notwithstanding, the forbidding Hilda has occasional moments of decency, and Rumpole fans will be amused to find one story narrated by Hilda herself, in which she reveals surprisingly romantic yearnings as she contemplates an affair with a smarmy colleague of her husband's. In his happy ability to play a seemingly infinite number of diverting variations on the same theme, in the fluidity and panache of his prose, his combination of high intelligence and low foolery, John Mortimer is worthy of comparison to P. G. Wodehouse. "Rumpole and the Angel of Death," like all of the preceding Rumpole volumes, makes for ideally civilized light reading.   Brooke Allen

title: Robert Doisneau: A Photographer's Life
author: Peter Hamilton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Near the end of ROBERT DOISNEAU: A Photographer's Life (Abbeville, $75), Peter Hamilton explains that his book was "supposed to be the 'definitive' monograph" about the French photographer, born in 1912, who spent his life documenting the sometimes lonely beauty, enduring romance and comic contrasts he found in Paris and its suburbs from the 1920's to the 80's. A sociologist, Mr. Hamilton was clearly able to understand that Doisneau's art was deeply rooted, reflecting both his pride of place and his humanism. A typical photograph from the 30's shows carefree boys watching a merry-go-round. A shot of a coal ration  card against a snow-covered Paris Opera illustrates the hardships of the occupation. A photograph of unkempt children in an empty, cobblestoned Paris square speaks of France's dreary 50's; and new suburban concrete overpasses and  modern apartment buildings show up in Doisneau's late pictures. Doisneau's death in 1994, before the book's completion, obviously came as a personal loss for the author. "Robert Doisneau: A Photographer's Life" is less exhaustive than it appears, for all its nearly 400 dense, oversized pages, with almost as many striking duotone and color reproductions, and the appendixes and interviews. For one thing, many of the book's pages could have been better used to show photographs and to provide details about projects only mentioned in passing, rather than to describe Doisneau's very static life (he inhabited the same suburban apartment from 1937 on and almost never traveled abroad). Most important, Mr. Hamilton eschews any real discussion of Doisneau's frequent use of models, actors and mises-en-scne in order to re-create scenes of daily life.  His world-famous 1950 photograph "Baiser de l'H/tel de Ville," for instance, was far from being documentary; it was staged. Without an exploration of the practice of presenting as candid something that isn't, and of the ethical and photo-historical questions it raises, a monograph about Doisneau can't be definitive.   Christine Schwartz Hartley

title: The Silent City
author: Erez Yakin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Between the world wars, wordless picture novels were produced by visionary artists like Lynd Ward and Frans Masereel, both of whom were masters of the art  of turning iconic images into acerbic narratives about human folly. After a period of decline, wordless novels have recently enjoyed a small revival as an offshoot of so-called graphic novels, which are themselves offshoots of comic books. Since the wordless novel relies so strongly on visual shorthand, it is often a difficult genre in which to express complex ideas and emotions. THE SILENT CITY (Kitchen Sink Press, paper, $24.95), Erez Yakin's story of the plight of individuals in an industrial totalitarian state, is by no means graphically simplistic; in fact, as Yevgeny Yevtushenko writes in his introduction, "Erez Yakin screams with the silence of his drawings." It is indeed remarkable that such powerfully and exquisitely rendered pictures -- reminiscent of George Grosz and Otto Dix's post-World War I antiwar prints -- were made in 1988, when the artist was just 18 years old. But it is no surprise  that each image is more effective individually than as an element of a complete  story. Mr. Yakin finds it difficult to keep his theme of totalitarian oppression from being a shrill echo of George Orwell's "Nineteen Eighty-four," replete with the common visual clichs of fascist brutality. Nevertheless, "The Silent City" is remarkable for its horrific portrayals of unbridled, demonic power, as well as for the difficult, oppressive darkness of its pictures, which makes them at times barely reproducible. "The Silent City" may not have pushed the limits of the wordless novel beyond what was accomplished in the 1930's, but it proves that Erez Yakin is a virtuoso image maker, a gifted artist at the beginning of what might well be a brilliant career.   Steven Heller

title: Vital Dust: Life As A Cosmic Imperative
author: Christian de Duve.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: VTAL DUST Life as a Cosmic Imperative. By Christian de Duve. 362 pp. New York: Basic Books. Paper, $14.    WHEN Charles Darwin wrote the "Origin of Species," he deliberately refused to speculate about the first beginnings of life, claiming he hardly knew enough to  make any lasting contribution, and he held back from discussing what he really thought about the mental world of human beings, the highest point of the evolutionary process. Caution was necessary. Excited talk about spontaneous generation of insects occurring after electricity was run through overripe cheeses, and inflammatory, tub-thumping sermons on the miracle of divine creation, made the first stirrings of life on Earth the most perplexing and fascinating problem of the era. Similarly, to discuss the human mind as if its action were nothing more than the mechanical product of the brain might invite a storm of protest. Darwin therefore kept his evolutionary proposals inside strict self-imposed limits -- and was aghast when the hurricane that gathered raged around the very issues he studiously ignored. It is extraordinary how much more  is now known about these mysterious beginnings and endings, the parts of the evolutionary panorama that Darwin left out. Over the last 30 years or so the whole emphasis of research has shifted toward opening up the world of the minute, the vibrant hidden frontiers of life. Christian de Duve's "Vital Dust,"  published in 1995 and now reissued in a welcome paperback format, provides an astonishingly full account of this new story about life, as lucid and engaging as the "Origin" itself. Here is the entire sweep of what is known about living matter.
headline: Stirrings

title: Infamous
author: Joan Joan Henrietta Collins Collins
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: No, INFAMOUS (Dutton, $23.95) isn't that manuscript -- the one Joan Collins's former Random House editors recently described to a Manhattan jury as uneditable piffle. "Infamous" is a later oeuvre, one that Rosemary Cheetham, a top English  editor, proudly offered the same jury as proof that Miss Collins's writing could indeed be redeemed, albeit with extraordinary editorial effort. Having read "Infamous," I now know that Ms. Cheetham committed esthetic perjury, which carries the cruel and unusual sentence of having to read the unpublished Random  House manuscript. Aloud. "Infamous" (on which Ms. Cheetham testified she spent an enormous amount of work) is moderately coherent, all right, but whatever sense of salacious fun Miss Collins may have brought to the manuscript has been  lost. The writing just isn't cheesy enough. With metronome-like dutifulness, "Infamous" tracks the endless travails of Katherine Bennet, an actress popular for her role as a wealthy villainess on a nighttime television soap opera and an obvious stand-in for Miss Collins, who played Alexis Carrington Colby on "Dynasty." If Katherine Bennet is the poisonous Georgia Skeffington on the small screen, everywhere else she is a long-suffering victim -- generous, loving, faithful nad constantly betrayed. But who wants to read a "Gone With the Wind" as told by Melanie Hamilton? By the last 100 pages, it is clear that Ms. Cheetham's insistence that Miss Collins's work can be made readable is just flat-out wrong. The final episodes, in which Katherine realizes that her fabulous new husband is a full- blown psychopath, are so execrably written that  they threaten to give popcorn fiction a bad name. Even the obligatory sex scenes are undercooked.   JAN HOFFMAN

title: Rabbits Everywhere
author: Alicia Ezpeleta
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Alicia Ezpeleta has written that rare rabbit book for adults that does not feature the words "with brown gravy" anywhere. Instead, she has produced a delightful compendium of lagomorph lore, profusely illustrated with reproductions of artworks and artifacts culled from a vast array of world cultures -- from ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics to 20th-century American cartoon characters. "Rabbits have represented almost every emotion, ideal, foible and personality trait known to humanity," she writes in RABBITS EVERYWHERE (Abrams,  $24.95), and she goes on to explore the rabbit's role as a symbol for such things as sexuality, fertility, purity, luck and cunning in various societies. The text not only touches on the best known of the literary long-ears -- the Easter Bunny, Peter Rabbit, the March Hare, Br'er Rabbit -- but delves into the  lives of the less publicized as well, including the heroic hares of both Buddhist and African fables. Despite the rabbit's affectionate place in the hearts of many, Ms. Ezpeleta, an interior designer, reveals that a few cultures  weren't very fond of them: the Vikings lumped them in the same category as sea monsters, and the ancient Celts assumed that rabbits purposely lived underground because of their affiliation with darker powers. The giant demon-bunny absconding with a young maiden carved into a portal of the Chartres Cathedral is a little unsettling compared with the familiar images of Bugs and Thumper, and the author even manages to link similar medieval notions of evil to the role of  killer rabbit in the movie "Monty Python and the Holy Grail." Ms. Ezpeleta takes a grand hop through rabbit history, noting along the way that the same creatures used to represent immortality and rebirth in the old Chinese, Greek and Roman legends can be seen even today fulfilling the same role in television's Energizer Bunny commercials.   J. D. BIERSDORFER

author: Mark Jacob
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: George Brace is the type of photographer and baseball fan who concerns himself less with capturing frantic moments on the diamond than with collecting  and sorting vast stores of arcane data and images. In THE GAME THAT WAS: The George Brace Baseball Photo Collection (Contemporary, $35), Richard Cahan and Mark Jacob, two editors at The Chicago Sun-Times, have taken photos from Mr. Brace's collection of hundreds of thousands of negatives (most of them made by Mr. Brace himself) and organized them into the kind of offbeat categories -- sluggers, players wearing glasses, players with funny names -- that card collectors love. The authors chose only black-and-white images taken from 1929 through 1960, and they provide ample baseball lore in their captions. Mr. Brace, who was born in 1913, documented many aspects of baseball, but his portraits and his grand views of the Chicago baseball parks, where he was based, hold the most interest. His best portraits are distinguished by the openness and humor of the  players' faces; his images are suggestive of rural America of years past. In his close-ups, the visors of the head-hugging baseball caps serve to frame the faces, drawing the viewer into the animated exchange between photographer and subject. Yogi Berra becomes all grins and ears, Carl Hubbell's intense stare is  riveting, and the young Ted Williams radiates self-assurance. When Mr. Brace turned his viewfinder toward Wrigley Field and Comiskey Park, the ball fields were rendered as vast, almost sacred places. Altogether, the book has the feel of a family album -- an intimate and glowing view of a comforting past.   Rosemary Ranck

author: Antoine Volodine
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: In his clever and incisive novel, NAMING THE JUNGLE (New Press, $18.95), the  French writer Antoine Volodine follows the remembered and invented lives of Fabian Golpiez, a man "rich in cowardice," as he struggles to get by in the post-revolutionary society of Puesto Libertad, a prototypical Latin American city surrounded by jungle and mystery. Since his survival strategy involves feigning mental illness, Fabian must undergo a unique therapy at the not-too-gentle hands of Dr. Gonalves, a combination shaman and psychiatrist who  practices in the requisitioned office of a "disappeared" dentist. Sitting in the dental chair, surrounded by drills and other implements of the trade, the patient spins out tales that are part memory and part contrivance, all designed  to maintain his status as "a psychotic with severe and intractable disabilities." It is not easy work, for the doctor demands quality stories: "These standard hallucinations! Vibrating canoes, anacondas! Old hat! Rivers fermenting beneath their cargo of leaves. . . . Always the same junk! Sexual symbolism for half-wits!" Obediently, Fabian digs deeper, inventing and reinventing himself, winding his way through love affairs, shootouts and voyages of exploration and discovery until finally, traveling upriver toward the source  of his imaginings, he appears to invent Dr. Gonalves himself. In Linda Coverdale's spirited translation, "Naming the Jungle" (which is the first of Mr. Volodine's books to be published in English) emphasizes the uncertainties of the characters and their jumbled lives by placing them in an especially well-defined world. The therapy Fabian goes through to maintain his supposed craziness involves establishing an Indian identity by naming the plants and creatures of the jungle. Only the people remain hard to pin down. But that uncertainty, that  refusal to locate themselves, Mr. Volodine suggests, is precisely what makes them worth caring about.   James Polk

WE live, Julian Barnes suggests in an earlier book, in "a pragmatic and knowing century"; we are also, he says in another, "modern and ignorant." Can we really be all these things? Of course. Knowingness is not knowledge, and pragmatism and modernity are two of our favorite boasts about ourselves. But who is making this diagnosis? In the first case it is Geoffrey Braithwaite, the grieving, widowed doctor and ardent Flaubert fan who tells the story of "Flaubert's Parrot"; in the second, it is the deviser of the brilliant exploration of Gricault's "Raft of the Medusa" in "A History of the World in 10  Chapters." These characters are not exempt from the condition they describe, they are symptoms of it: wry, witty, belated, supposedly practical, often helpless. Behind them hovers the shadowy figure of Julian Barnes himself, who is just as wry, witty and belated, maybe as practical, and presumably quite a bit less helpless. I'm not so sure, though. Style and intelligence, which Mr. Barnes has in abundance, can focus helplessness and allow us to think about something else, but they can scarcely make it go away. Would we want it to go away, in all cases? "How do we seize the past? How do we seize the foreign past? We read, we  learn, we ask, we remember, we are humble; and then a casual detail shifts everything." This is Braithwaite, and "the foreign past," for him, as for Barnes and for us, is delicately weighted with a double meaning: the past of a foreign  scene or a foreign writer, and the past of our own life or marriage or love, which, as L. P. Hartley famously said, is a foreign country. Braithwaite's answer is more than modest, but his initial metaphor is surely too greedy, full  of the promise of failure. We don't seize the past. At best we get a picture of  it, and a couple of chances to revise the picture. And the past, in Mr. Barnes's fiction, becomes a figure for a whole series of separations and gaps, places where the mind or the memory can't quite reach the other side, as if the ferry were becalmed, or the tunnel not complete: between then and now, of course, but  also between there and here, between them and us, between her and him, between any event and the chance of our understanding it.

pull_quote: At a cliffside restaurant in a swanky Caribbean resort, wealthy vacationers pause between spoonfuls of passion-fruit sorbet to monitor the progress of a lone swimmer as she sidestrokes out to sea, faithfully escorted by her three Irish setters. Is she crazy? the diners ask one another with a mix of fascination and horror. Doesn't she know about sharks? The swimmer's name is Adele, and by some standards she must be crazy: not so long ago, she turned her back on a pampered, privileged life in the Connecticut countryside to fly off to India and worship at the feet of a tyrannical guru. Narrated in part by one of Adele's acquaintances, THE WOMAN WHO WALKED ON WATER (Riverhead, $21) unfolds in brief, elegantly written chapters, keeping its distance as it traces  this restless, enigmatic woman's attempts to lose herself in something greater.  Seen from the narrator's detached perspective, Adele's headlong pursuit of enlightenment proceeds inexorably, like a 10-car pileup viewed in slow motion far in the distance. As she steadily recedes from her earthly existence, Adele sacrifices not only her autonomy and her material possessions but also a chorus  of bewildered family and friends. She loses weight, her hair becomes streaked with gray, she suffers from mysterious illnesses. But could she be exchanging these mundane measures of health for a deeper spiritual well-being? Is Adele's flight from her former life transcendent or tragic? As it explores these questions, Lily Tuck's second novel emerges as a haunting, strangely perplexing  meditation on the quest for higher meaning -- and the steep price that seekers (not to mention those around them) must pay.   Sarah Ferguson

title: Frank Stella: An Illustrated Biography
author: Frank Frank Philip Stella Stella
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Frank Stella first caught the attention of the New York art world in 1958, at the age of 22, when his austere "black paintings" marked him as an uncompromising, inventive artist. At 34, Mr. Stella had his first retrospective  at the Museum of Modern Art. Both talented and well connected, Mr. Stella got himself included in the canon of American abstraction with precocious speed. Although his later works -- huge, multipart metallic constructions replete with gaudily colored French curves and graffitilike brushstrokes -- are now most visible as fixtures of corporate lobby art, Mr. Stella has secured a legacy as a masterly interpreter of space, someone who pushed the boundaries of painting. This kind of achievement merits more than the treatment it receives in FRANK STELLA: An Illustrated Biography (Rizzoli, $75). Sidney Guberman, an artist and  Mr. Stella's classmate at Princeton, is diligent about quoting from the best of  what has been previously written about his subject, neither cowed by nor dismissive of what has gone before. But from a close friend -- and well past the halfway mark of Mr. Stella's career -- we expect something extra. Mr. Guberman has plenty of anecdotes from the time he has spent with Mr. Stella over the years, but most of them are not very illuminating. He is at his best when he addresses the art directly, as in his explanations of the relatively complicated working techniques that Mr. Stella used to make his irregular frames and surfaces of serious sculptural depth.   Ted Loos

title: Women In Their Beds: New And Selected Stories
author: Gina Berriault
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: As an alternative to those trivial compendiums of literary opening passages sold near bookstore cash registers, how about a collection of last lines from Gina Berriault's very short stories, WOMEN IN THEIR BEDS: New and Selected Stories (Counterpoint, P.O. Box 65793, Washington, D.C. 20035, $25)? Consider this stand-alone triumph: "He lay facedown under the tree and bit off some grass near the roots, chewing to distract his smile, but it would not give in, and so he lay there the entire day, smiling into the earth." Or: "She heard his breath take over for him and, in that secretive way the sleeper knows nothing about, carry on his life." Ms. Berriault is nothing if not consistent. In these  35 stories, one struggles to find a sentence that is anything less than jewel-box perfect. And the author uses her gift for language to do more than show us the world through her characters' eyes; we are also forced to think about it from their point of view -- no small feat for someone who favors third-person narration. These are complex characters, and although many stories  run only a few pages Ms. Berriault never falls back on cliches: an aging male librarian, for example, is no shrinking violet; instead, he sports "a Borsalino  fedora" and "English boots John Major would covet." Most of Ms. Berriault's characters are caught at moments of divergence: in "Soul and Money," a lapsed Communist confronts God and Mammon in Las Vegas; in "Lives of the Saints," the son of a famous religious artist undertakes his own sort of pilgrimage, visiting his father's works, and discovers that life is more lasting than art. Yet in the smooth flow of Ms. Berriault's writing, few of these people manage to register the emotional pitch needed to transcend their crises. It is not a matter of stoicism; instead, most seem dizzyingly unaware of the option to act on their own behalf. Thus the stories, so exquisite to wend through, leave one a little cold. Like their characters, they seem trapped by the perfection of Ms. Berriault's prose.   Tobin Harshaw

title: Mother
author: Judy William George Wegman Olausen
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: What William Wegman has done for his dogs, Judy Olausen, a photographer who lives in Minneapolis, has done for her mother. But while Mr. Wegman's subjects,  being Weimaraners, look mostly soulful, doleful or moderately embarrassed, Vivian Olausen, a housewife now in her 70's, can personify any affect you can name. And what a game gal she is! In MOTHER (Penguin Studio, $24.95), she allows herself to be dressed up in frumpy housedresses and ratty furs, bedraggled hats and hideous wigs, and, in more than 50 deliriously funny pictures, submitted to any number of indignities. There is a program here: many of the images are a commentary on the lot of women in the 1950's, a period when, Ms. Olausen believes, depressed housewives dragged themselves to the cocktail cabinet or medicine chest for relief (see "Mother's Little Helpers," with Mother spaced out on Valium). Mrs. Olausen, on the other hand, remembers the decade as  one in which she had fun pottering around the house and entertaining, and everyone drank (see "Mother as Enabler"). But while the pictures of Mother carrying a huge wooden cross through the supermarket or chained to an ironing board or, best of all, in pink baby-doll pajamas and marabou mules (pace Marabel Morgan) make a feminist point, others transcend dogma to attain an almost Monty  Pythonesque lunacy. Only consider "Mommy Deer," in which Mrs. Olausen, antlered  and befurred, is tied to the roof of a car. Worth noting, too, that the car is a Plymouth Volare, one of a vast number of authentic, and frequently covetable, props and artifacts that repay careful study. (Remember Ike buttons? Cookie jars in the shape of French poodles? Paint-by-numbers sets?) Pass this book around among your friends, and watch them have conniptions.   Sarah Ferrell

pull_quote: Rosanne Cash was born with a microphone in her hand. The daughter of Johnny Cash, she released her first album in 1979 and was immediately recognized as one of country music's freshest singer-songwriters. Those familiar with her much-publicized private life (her marriage to the country star Rodney Crowell, which ended in divorce four years ago, was tabloid manna) will spot bits and pieces of it scattered throughout her first collection of stories and sketches, BODIES OF WATER (Hyperion, $19.95), some of which reads more like autobiography than fiction. But there is no angry score-settling in this pensive book, which takes as its subject the landmarks of a woman's life: love, marriage, childbirth, disillusion, renewal. Unusually for a lyricist, Ms. Cash has a straightforward, sharp-eyed prose style ("I was 22 years old, and my feet  were a little too big for my body. . . . I had two cats -- a serious mistake --  as I had been looking for an image and thought they might help") and, despite a  few awkwardly self-conscious patches, her first book reads like the work of a far more experienced writer. This is not "celebrity" fiction: it is a collection of stories that happens to have been written by a celebrity, and it is very good.   Terry Teachout

pull_quote: Once a barefoot beggar child, the heroine of the poet Marly Youmans's second  novel, CATHERWOOD (Farrar, Straus & Giroux, $20), is brought to live with a noble family in the years after the English Civil War. Something between an indentured servant and an adopted daughter, Catherwood is eventually married off to Gabriel Lyte, who takes her across the Atlantic to a world "fresh and curious" that appears to be "just league after league of woods and swamp and wild river." Feeling herself "the newest of all created things," the young woman confronts her new home, outside Albany, with a keen eye for the "lovely-fierce"  sensuousness of nature. Then one day she and her infant daughter become lost in  the wilderness, and for months they wander about, trying to find their way. Through her harrowing ordeal, Catherwood learns to divest herself of sentiment and fear, including the fear of "man judgment," until she comes to understand that there are "many roads through wilderness, many paths to the city." In describing this process, Ms. Youmans's language is trenchant, graceful and, in places, sumptuously archaic, filled with a richness that provides more than just period color. Her prodigious powers of description render with acuity both small moments and large: the sea crossing, childbirth, snowfall, the slitting of a fawn's throat, the "rammish" stench of a trapper. Ms. Youmans has written a subtle, intelligent novel about one of the most enduring issues in the American  experiment: how to embrace "the world and God" as "better" than men dream.   Philip Gambone

title: From Peep Show To Palace
author: David Robinson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Compared to today's special-effects-laden blockbusters, early cinematic efforts seem like a yawn. But their eerie realism was so startling to audiences  a century ago that their viewing often incited panic. In FROM PEEP SHOW TO PALACE: The Birth of American Film (Columbia University, $29.50), David Robinson, a film historian, provides a diligent overview from the moment cinema  was just a flicker in a magic lantern to the golden years between 1893 and 1913, when scientists and technicians laboriously fitted together the "pieces in a puzzle" and created feature films. Mr. Robinson's chronology is painstakingly  thorough, if at times tedious, and he dissects the various stages of motion picture development with scholarly zeal. His portrayals of the great cinematic innovators Thomas Edison, the Lumiere brothers and Georges Melies provide some vivid accounts of publicity mongering, patent wrangling and ego interference as  the race for notoriety accelerated. But, finally, the book seems to need a slightly more humorous approach to a subject brimming with pratfalls, and leaves the casual reader craving more anecdotes about the personalities that catapulted the entertainment into the pre-eminent American art form. As he says in A CAST OF FRIENDS (Taylor, $22.95), written with Tom Ito, a freelance journalist, Mr. Hanna and Joe Barbera knew they were a winning combination from their first meeting, in 1937. In short order, their collaboration produced Tom and Jerry, the classic cat-and-mouse team. When they founded Hanna-Barbera Productions in 1957, the two were pioneers gambling that their new limited animation techniques would enable cartoons to move from movie screen to television. Huckleberry Hound, Yogi Bear and Boo Boo, the Flintstones and the Jetsons, among many others, were the result. Now 85, still happily at work in his "cartoon quarry," Mr. Hanna pays tribute to wife, family, animation colleagues and employees while giving his two children and seven grandchildren credit for helping him bridge the generation gap. To this day, he watches pencil sketches evolve into exuberant cinematic fantasy and always finds the result "somewhat astonishing." He takes the reader  backstage and lets him feel that excitement. "Cartoons," he says, "symbolize enchantment." The fellow who obligingly screeched and yowled on cue to give voice to Tom and Jerry in the early years has never lost sight of the grand vision that captivated him as a youngster. pull_quote: Even the air is palpable in TUMBLING (Morrow, $24), Diane McKinney-Whetstone's engaging first novel about a 1950's community threatened with gentrification. In the working-class black Philadelphia neighborhood that serves as the book's setting, the woeful plaint of Mahalia Jackson records mingles with the perfume of backyard honeysuckle. But the city's insidious attempts to buy out homeowners eventually spill into the domestic world of Herbie and Noon, a young couple whose lives have already been rerouted after not one but two little girls are abandoned on their doorstep. Herbie and Noon are more successful as parents than as spouses and they salve their marital wounds independently: Herbie in a nightclub singer's bed and Noon in her church and in  her fight against the city's plans. But they are true partners in the love and care of their children, especially Fannie, who came first and who charms and frightens them with her occasional clairvoyance. Though the book's end is bluntly forecast from early on and more than a few events are puzzlingly unexplained, the story moves forward on the power of Ms. McKinney-Whetstone's characters. Herbie and Noon's neighbors -- from the meanspirited petty bureaucrat across the street, desperate to protect her meager authority, to the  well-intentioned but miscalculating local pastor, who falls prey to his own pride -- are never merely props. Through these and other deftly portrayed individuals, whose wrongdoing stems more from fallibility than intent, Ms. McKinney-Whetstone captures the formidable struggle to protect both a community  and a family. THE British novelist, playwright and journalist Angela Huth's lovely new book, "Land Girls," is a war story about the real heroes of World War II: not the generals but the ordinary citizens who left their workaday lives and fought  for their country as best they could. The girls of the title were young women who joined Britain's Land Army; they left the safe, tea-cozy world of traditional female jobs -- university student, hairdresser, sweetheart -- and went off to take up the exhausting, dawn-to-darkness labor of agricultural work  so the male farm workers could take up arms. At first blush, there is nothing exceptional about the three main characters. When gentle, cerebral Agatha, romantic Stella and fluff-brained Prue first assemble for their tour of duty on  the Lawrence farm in Dorset, the reader might be deceived into thinking this is  going to be yet another banal three-girls-meet-somewhere-and-become-friends novel, the sort in which there is inevitably one suicide, one ghastly abortion,  a slew of beastly men and a great display of passive aggression. pull_quote: No painter has been so hallowed by his fellow artists as Paul Cezanne. Picasso called him "the father of us all," Klee "the supreme master," Matisse "a kind of benevolent god of painting." Yet despite a century's influence and an abundance of literature that has successively denounced, extolled and interpreted his work, Cezanne remains an enigmatic artist, his impact on subsequent generations more quantifiable than his artistic intentions. In the introduction to CEZANNE (Philadelphia Museum of Art/Abrams, $75), an exceptionally handsome catalogue raisonne produced in conjunction with a traveling exhibition currently at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, Francoise Cachin, director of the Musees de France, and Joseph J. Rishel, a curator of European painting at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, make no claims to providing new interpretations of either the artist or the man. Instead they concentrate on the shifts of Cezanne's critical fortunes. The result is a fascinating patchwork of opinions that illustrates not only how Cezanne has been reinvented as the patron saint of each successive movement from Fauvism to Cubism to early abstraction, but how monumentally important he remains. Each reproduction is accompanied by a short text that provides the provenance of the work, bits of biography, excerpts from letters and occasional anecdotes, as well as details about Cezanne's technique. More academic and less accessible is Pavel Machotka's CEZANNE: Landscape Into Art (Yale University, $45). Mr. Machotka, who teaches psychology and art at the University of California, Santa Cruz, has photographed the sites of Cezanne's landscape paintings, with an eye to approximating the spot and precise time of day that Cezanne painted each scene. He then attempts to analyze Cezanne's way of working, noting the correspondences as well as the changes between place and painting. The result is fascinating to look at, though frequently pedantic. THE German occupation of France and its factious fallout provide the raw material of Brian Moore's powerful new novel. Between 1940 and 1944, more than one in four of the 330,000 Jews living on French territory were deported. The majority were identified, arrested and shipped off by French administrators and  the French police, without whose zealous cooperation German forces in France would have been unable to carry out the job. In a time of want, fear and national humiliation, few of the French cared about what happened to the Jews. While many individuals helped them (otherwise three in four would not have survived), many also denounced, pursued and robbed them. She became friends with a circle that included Imogen Cunningham and Ansel Adams, and for a time ran a successful portrait business. During the early years of the Depression, when breadlines and picket lines formed in San Francisco, she began  to photograph trouble in the streets. By her choice of perspective, use of gesture and framing, Lange's photographs convey her empathy and passionate belief in human dignity. The book, with text by Keith F. Davis, who has written extensively on American photography, reflects Lange's taste with its spare presentation of 85 reproductions and accompanying quotations or comments, a device Lange often used herself. Color somehow defangs even the most heinous of the bunch, like Heinrich  Himmler and Julius Streicher. author: Alan King
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Right off the bat, Alan King tells us what not to expect in NAME-DROPPING: The Life and Lies of Alan King (Scribner, $23), the scrappy memoir he has written with Chris Chase. "This book is not going to be heavy drama -- I don't want Robert De Niro playing my life," he says. "I'm not going to remember the bad stuff, I'm only going to remember the singing and dancing." True to his word, this most quick-witted of comedians nimbly sidesteps his fractious childhood as Irwin Kniberg -- a "very angry, very tough kid" who was thrown out  of every high school in Brooklyn -- to get to the good parts, which began when he was 15 and landed his first job as a comic in the Catskills. Mr. King tells priceless stories about Bugsy Siegel (his patron during the Las Vegas days, "when everybody I worked for got killed"), Frank Sinatra (who was declared the winner of their tomato sauce cookoff by judges named Willie the Nose and Morey the Mouth), and a host of other beloved old cronies including Jack Benny, Joe E. Lewis, Milton Berle and Sammy Davis Jr. But like the cocky street fighter he once was, Mr. King has an instinct for someone's weak spots, so the stories that really floor you are about wounded comrades like Dean Martin and Judy Garland. As for his own underbelly, Mr. King allows as how he's got a rotten temper and carries around a load of rage. (But he has nothing but compassion for his father, a Jewish immigrant embittered by real poverty and imagined failure.) "Most comedians are angry, it's their edge," he says. "When I get angry, I'm better." Mr. King leaves it to his wife, in a sweet and unaffected chapter called "Jeanette's Turn," to bring up uncomfortable subjects like the comedian's jaw cancer and certain unspecified problems with their children. We always knew  that Alan King was a funny guy; now we know what made him so keen and caustic.   Marilyn Stasio

pull_quote: At the outset of Mary Kay Zuravleff's engaging first novel, THE FREQUENCY OF  SOULS (Farrar, Straus & Giroux, $23), we learn a crucial piece of information about its hero, an electrical engineer named George Mahoney. It seems that from  the time he built his first radio set "from glass tubes and a spool of lead," George has been convinced that "the universe was soldered together with logic."  So it isn't surprising that he reacts with "fatherly embarrassment" to his new junior office mate's revelation that she experiments with radio frequencies in order to listen for the dead. In fact, George knows that Niagara Spense, who is  partly deaf in one ear, has difficulty hearing many things. What is surprising -- most of all to George himself -- is that, despite his disbelief, Niagara inspires in him "a burning curiosity that had not flared in some 20 years." And  in no time curiosity becomes obsession. When he awakens his wife, Judy, yelling, "Niagara," she replies, "You had better be screaming about vacation." For George, who has had no complaints or extramarital liaisons during his largely unexamined 16-year marriage, Niagara is an improbable love object. Ungainly, untidy and chaotic, she is the antithesis of Judy, "a Georgia brand of Southern  belle." But Niagara's presence makes George aware of the fine line between contentment and stagnation. As he explains it, "If you leave a car parked long enough, the tires go flat and the battery won't hold a charge." By the end of the novel, when Niagara and her research have enabled George to recapture a few  sparks, Ms. Zuravleff's insightful yet gentle rendering of the absurd has also allowed readers to connect fully with her quirky and endearing characters. pull_quote: Eric Lax, the author of a biography of Woody Allen, has turned his attention  to Paul Newman with a big book of pictures and text. He faithfully recounts the  facts about Paul Leonard Newman, born in 1925 and reared in comfort in Shaker Heights, an affluent suburb of Cleveland: the year in the Navy during which he catapulted six inches, up from 5-foot-4; his 38-year marriage to Joanne Woodward, with whom he fell in love when he was already married, with three young children; the Academy Award for "The Color of Money" (1986) and the eight  other Oscar nominations; the car racing; the salad dressing; the spaghetti sauce; the popcorn; the drug-education foundation in memory of the eldest of his six children, Scott, who died in 1978 of an accidental overdose of drugs and alcohol at the age of 28; the camps for ill children. There is a story here, but, as Mr. Lax writes in PAUL NEWMAN: A Biography (Turner, $29.95), "He has always been guarded about his personal life, especially his marriages." Mr. Lax  sums up at one point, "We are left to our private wonder." He also quotes Mr. Newman on his problems with alcohol: "I don't know why those times should be for public consumption." We don't need to be dragged through the mud with Mr. Newman, who seems to be an extraordinarily decent man; however, it would have been helpful to try going behind those baby blues to reach into the soul instead of simply sliding over the surface. But, oh, these pictures are divine! There's  Paul, on the cover, as the title character in "Hud": sexy. And there's Paul in his 20's, whose face, as Mr. Lax describes it, "was something from an ancient coin." And Paul at 71, who "has aged gracefully, and now his face has the finely etched look of someone on a postage stamp." Coins, stamps, whatever. title: Mr. Bumble
author: Kim Kennedy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MR. BUMBLE. By Kim Kennedy. Illustrated by Doug Kennedy. Hyperion. $15.95. (Ages 4 to 8) Here's the fanciful story of a clumsy bumblebee -- the one who always stumbles and spills. He gets trapped in a distant patch of clover, is rescued and tutored by the fairies who live there and becomes a fine racing bee. Very pretty illustrations, in which the flowers have faces and the fairies have instruction books.    COWBOY BUNNIES. By Christine Loomis. Illustrated by Ora Eitan. Putnam. $15.95. (Ages 3 to 5) Short verses tell about the adventures cowboy bunnies might have -- roping cows, tossing hay, calling cattle, dancing jigs in the moonlight. They are charmingly illustrated by an Israeli artist who paints on panels of whitewashed wood.     STAY! Keeper's Story. By Lois Lowry. Illustrated by True Kelly. Houghton Mifflin. $15. (Ages 7 to 12) The narrator, our hero, was ''born in the gutter and grew up in poverty.'' In true Dickensian style, albeit much more briefly, he confronts and surmounts obstacles bravely, discovers poetic talent and is finally reunited with his lost sister. Keeper is, of course, a dog. His story is entertaining but filled with shrewd social observations and judgments about human, as well as animal, behavior.     AESOP'S FABLES. Retold and illustrated by Jacob Lawrence. University of Washington. $18.95. (All ages) In 1970 this distinguished American artist published a collection of 18 illustrated fables, although he had completed 23. They are all included in this handsome new edition.     GABRIELLA'S SONG. By Candace Fleming. Illustrated by Giselle Potter. Anne Schwartz/Atheneum. $16. (Ages 3 to 8) Venice is a city of music as well as water, and in this pretty storybook a little girl named Gabriella goes about her errands singing sweetly. The melody drifts up to a composer who uses it in his next symphony and acknowledges the debt. The illustrations give a hint of the famous sun-drenched or fog-shrouded Venetian palette.     FIRST PALM TREES: An Anancy Spiderman Story. By James Berry. Illustrated by Greg Couch. Simon & Schuster. $17. (Ages 5 and up) A distinguished Jamaican-born British writer tells an original trickster story about the time a king offers a prize for whoever can create a palm tree that will yield palm wine. Greed drives Anancy, but he is compelled to collaborate with various gods. Anancy is shown as both spider and man, with eight eyes (his own and three pairs of glasses) and eight limbs that appear in the folds and angles of his robes.     ZOOM! ZOOM! ZOOM! I'M OFF TO THE MOON! Written and illustrated by Dan Yaccarino. Scholastic. $15.95. (Ages 3 to 5) A little boy's great adventure, told with wonderfully economical but accurate text and exuberant, intensely colored illustrations. It's an entire journey -- suiting up, lifting off, rocket separation, lunar landing -- but it gets him home in time for bed.     The House You Pass On the Way. By Jacqueline Woodson. Delacorte. $14.95. (Ages 12 and up) Staggerlee (she doesn't use her given name) is an appealing young heroine who deals with many complex issues in a slender novel. She is the child of a mixed-race marriage; she copes with her parents' celebrity and the death of her grandparents. And now a cousin she has never met is coming for the summer to the place she has always considered her sanctuary, and she is filled with anxiety.

pull_quote: SANJI AND THE BAKER. By Robin Tzannes. Illustrated by Korky Paul. Oxford. $14.95. (Ages 5 and up) The setting is an exotic bazaar, but the funny story about greed and common sense could take place anywhere. Sanji, the upstairs tenant, tells the baker below how much he enjoys the smells wafting up, and the baker tries to charge him for the pleasure. The judge turns the tables. If you look closely at the comic drawings, there seem to be some modern characters -- a typist and an artist -- who could be the author and illustrator.    YOUNG, BLACK, AND DETERMINED: A Biography of Lorraine Hansberry. By Patricia C. McKissack and Fredrick L. McKissack. Holiday House. $18.95. (Ages 10 and up) The American playwright was just 28 years old when ''A Raisin in the Sun'' was produced on Broadway and only 34 when she died in 1965. This thoughtful biography places her life and work in the political context of the changing times in which she lived. Useful time-line appendix.    ALICE AND ALDO. Written and illustrated by Alison Lester. Walter Lorraine/Houghton Mifflin. $15. (Ages 2 to 5) Here's a day in which Alice and her stuffed donkey, Aldo, do perfectly delightful, ordinary things, like have breakfast in bed, get clothes from the closet, leap in a leotard, paint a pink picture and yawn in their yogurt. Each alphabet-related activity is surrounded by other illustrated words starting with the appropriate letter. Aldo's a charmer.    GOOD-BYE, CHARLES LINDBERGH: Based on a True Story. By Louise Borden. Illustrated by Thomas B. Allen. Margaret K. McElderry. $16. (Ages 5 to 9) On a spring afternoon in 1929 in rural Mississippi, a boy on horseback was doing an errand for his mother when a sleek biplane set down in a field. Col. Charles A. Lindbergh was on his way from Mexico to New York City, and bad weather forced him to land and spend the night. This is the modest and engaging story modeled on that real boy, Harold Rea Gilpin, and the aviation hero. The soft colored-pencil illustrations capture the heavy weather, the storm and the bright morning that followed.    SMACK. By Melvin Burgess. Holt. $16.95. (Ages 12 and up) This grim and cautionary novel about Tar and his girlfriend, Gemma, runaway teen-agers and heroin use won the prestigious Carnegie Medal and the Guardian Prize for fiction. The story is set in and around Bristol, England, during the 1980's.    WHO'S WHOSE? Written and illustrated by Jan Ormerod. Lothrop, Lee & Shepard. $16. (Ages 5 to 8) In an urban neighborhood with relaxed adults and lots of children of companionable ages, the permutations on who is where, doing what and with whom, and just what is whose are delightful. For starters, there are four parents, one granny, a total of eight children, a dog and a guinea pig. There is also a very independent cat.    RETURN TO HAWK'S HILL. By Allan W. Eckert. Little, Brown. $15.95. (Ages 12 and up) More than a quarter of a century after ''Incident at Hawk's Hill,'' that exciting novel set on the Canadian prairie in the 1870's, here is a sequel involving Ben MacDonald and George Burton, the evil trapper. Ben drifts down the Red River and into Lake Winnipeg in a rowboat without oars.    JUST A MINUTE! By Anke Kranendonk. Illustrated by Jung-Hee Spetter. Front Street/Lemniscaat. $14.95. (Ages 2 to 6) Mommy really ought to have paid attention to Piggy, who just wanted to hear a story or to play, because when Mommy finishes her household chores she discovers that Piggy has made a really glorious mess. Funny illustrations.

pull_quote: INCUBUS  By Ann Arensberg.  322 pp. New York:  Alfred A. Knopf. $24.    IN the spring and summer of 1974, the little hamlet of Dry Falls, Me., suffers some oddities. They begin trivially enough, with herbs found strewn in the graveyard, candles stolen from the altar. Then an August heat wave descends in April. Stillbirths, false pregnancies and monstrous births occur among the farm animals. The crops parch, lettuce and spinach seed prematurely, peaches wizen, even the pond grasses wilt. Marriages likewise wither and deform. One after another the men fall into sexual malaise, and one after another their wives come to Henry Lieber, rector of the Episcopal church of St. Anthony the Hermit, for the psychotherapeutic counseling expected of a modern pastor.

title: The Tesseract
author: Alex Garland
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
THE TESSERACT
By Alex Garland.
273 pp. New York:
Riverhead Books. $24.95.

 FANS of Alex Garland's hugely popular first novel, ''The Beach,'' might feel slightly tricked by the fact that his complex, virtuosic second novel begins with a very familiar figure: a young, chain-smoking Englishman named Sean, who closely resembles Richard, the main character in ''The Beach.'' And that's not all: both books are set in Southeast Asia; both open in seedy hotel rooms; both are poised for thriller-caliber suspense. But then, just as Garland's fans are settling into what feels like a sequel, Sean is left wallowing in an open sewer and ''The Tesseract'' becomes a radically different sort of book.
headline: Square Root of a Hypercube

author: Cheng Ching-wen

THREE-LEGGED HORSE
By Cheng Ching-wen.
Edited by Pang-yuan Chi.
226 pp. New York:
Columbia University Press. $22.95. 

 IT is simply a law of evolution: the longer the time that elapses, the more the mutations, the more abnormality settles into normality. Thus China developed its foot-binding fetish; Egypt fixated on elaborate mummification rituals; ancient Hindus, facing each rising sun, solemnly mixed their urine tonic; and the Mayans smoked their narcotics when New York City was still a wide expanse of marsh. The 12 short stories in ''Three-Legged Horse,'' by Cheng Ching-wen, a Taiwanese writer, add new examples to the list.
headline: Disorientations

title: Chocolat
author: Joanne Harris
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: CHOCOLAT  By Joanne Harris.  242 pp. New York:  Viking. $22.95.    ''CHOCOLATE, I am told, is not a moral issue.'' Such, at least, is the opinion of Vianne Rocher, one of the two narrators of Joanne Harris's accomplished novel, which opens with the arrival of Vianne and her young daughter in the small French town of Lansquenet-sous-Tannes at the beginning of Lent. When Vianne transforms a defunct bakery into a chocolate shop called La Celeste Praline, the story echoes those folk tales in which the Devil, disguised as an amiable stranger, seduces the upstanding citizens of a village by awakening their appetite for pleasure. But in ''Chocolat,'' Harris plays a variation on this theme, illuminating the awful things that can happen when we neglect the satisfactions of this world for the promise of a better one. Her amiable stranger stands on the side of earthly angels.
headline: Let Them Eat Candy

author: James Howe

pull_quote: HORACE AND MORRIS BUT MOSTLY DOLORES. By James Howe. Illustrated by Amy Walrod. Atheneum. $16. (Ages 4 to 8) The adventures of three happy ''now-and-forever'' friends are halted when Horace and Morris form a boys' club, saying, ''A boy mouse must do what a boy mouse must do.'' Never fear; Dolores finds a way for fine friendship to win out. The collage-and-paint illustrations of the mice are droll.     OUR ONLY MAY AMELIA. By Jennifer L. Holm. HarperCollins. $15.95. (Ages 9 and up) Here's an engaging first novel based on the life of the author's great-aunt, the first Finnish-American girl born on the Naselle River in Washington in 1887. After seven boys, she was considered ''a miracle.'' Filled with details of farm life and the Finnish community; illustrated with historic photographs.     THE LANDRY NEWS. By Andrew Clements. Simon & Schuster. $15. (Ages 8 to 12) Mr. Larson's fifth-grade classroom is like a ''giant educational glacier,'' where nothing happens. Mr. Larson has effectively stopped teaching, leaving his students to fend for themselves. Then Cara Landry, who loves to read newspapers, starts her own, The Landry News, with a scathing editorial about her teacher. It becomes a class project and a political issue. While the story gallops along and celebrates journalism with the motto ''Truth and Mercy,'' the good humor makes the message palatable.     LOVE AS STRONG AS GINGER. By Lenore Look. Illustrated by Stephen T. Johnson. Anne Schwartz/ Atheneum. $15. (Ages 5 to 9) The author's Chinese immigrant grandmother worked in a Seattle cannery cracking crab in the 1960's and 70's. This loving anecdotal tale about going with her to the factory, about her labors and her heavenly cooking, about the hot bath needed to wash the chiubungbung -- the very bad crab smell -- from hair and skin, has been delicately illustrated in pastel and watercolor.     TWO SUNS IN THE SKY. By Miriam Bat-Ami. Front Street/Cricket. $15.95. (Ages 12 and up) In this novel set at the end of World War II, a family of Yugoslavian Jews in Rome is sent to a war refugee shelter in upstate New York, and there Adam Bornstein meets Chris Cook, a bright, bored local girl. The romance is predictable, but their families and the refugee camp are interesting, and a note at the end gives historical background.     WHATEVER HAPPENED TO HUMPTY DUMPTY? And Other Surprising Sequels to Mother Goose Rhymes. By David T. Greenberg. Illustrated by S. D. Schindler. Little, Brown. $14.95. (All ages) The obvious answer to the question in the title is ''omelets,'' but there was a problem with the king's blender -- he forgot the lid. Similarly gross consequences befell other familiar characters, including Mother Goose, the Pumpkin Eater and Mary's lamb, but the illustrations are surprisingly delicate and droll.     RAISING SWEETNESS. By Diane Stanley. Illustrated by G. Brian Karas. Putnam. $15.99. (Ages 5 to 9) In this sequel to ''Saving Sweetness,'' the reader is returned to Possum Trot, where the sheriff who rescued Sweetness and the other orphans is faced with taking care of all those children. What's wanted, Sweetness realizes, is a mom.     WHAT! CRIED GRANNY: An Almost Bedtime Story. By Kate Lum. Illustrated by Adrian Johnson. Dial. $14.99. (Ages 3 to 7) Patrick poses a hilarious set of problems and complaints to Granny; they keep him from having to go to bed.

title: Night Lights
author: Steven Schnur
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NIGHT LIGHTS. By Steven Schnur. Illustrated by Stacey Schuett. Frances Foster/Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $16. (Ages 3 and up) Here's a counting book in the form of a bedtime ritual as one little girl, Melinda, counts the lights each night, starting with her night light and moving out of her room into the world and the dark sky. Lush, dark illustrations.    MILTON. Written and illustrated by Hayde Ardalan. Chronicle. $7.95. (All ages) An autobiographical celebration of an ''exceptional'' black-and-white cat named Milton, told in 110 words of text and simple, stylish illustrations. Milton is highly pleased with himself and very amusing.    DARKNESS OVER DENMARK: The Danish Resistance and the Rescue of the Jews. By Ellen Levine. Holiday House. $18.95. (Ages 10 and up) There are several fine, widely read novels for young readers about the remarkable Danish resistance during World War II, so this well-researched nonfiction account, which includes interviews with participants Jewish and not, is particularly welcome. There's a chronology and an excellent bibliography.    GERSHON'S MONSTER: A Story for the Jewish New Year. By Eric A. Kimmel. Illustrated by Jon J. Muth. Scholastic. $16.95. (Ages 5 to 9) Gershon, a wealthy but childless baker, pitches his rudeness and misdeeds into the cellar and each year, instead of repenting, tosses them into the sea. With the help of a wise rabbi, precious children are born, but under a spell. This Hasidic story of how the baker learns t'shuvah -- repentance -- is beautifully told and illustrated.    THE DEMONS' MISTAKE: A Story From Chelm. By Francine Prose. Illustrated by Mark Podwal. Greenwillow. $15.95. (Ages 5 and up) The invisible demons of Chelm, that Polish town where the people are so simple, decide to go to America, where the streets are said to be paved with gold. The shrewdly imaginative story about what demons might do in today's New York City is illustrated with delicate, abstract pastels. Worth reading aloud.    NIGHT HOOPS. By Carl Deuker. Houghton Mifflin. $15. (Ages 12 and up) The Abbotts and the Dawsons live across the street from each other, and both Nick Abbott and Trent Dawson play basketball. That's all they seem to have in common. But nothing is as it seems, except the actual basketball games. A taut psychological novel.    COMES A WIND. By Linda Arms White. Illustrated by Tom Curry. Melanie Kroupa/DK Ink. $15.95. (Ages 4 to 8) Clement and Clyde promise Mama that for her birthday they will behave nicely. They sit on the porch boasting, cowboy style, till a real wind comes up and they have to cooperate to rescue their mother.    BATTLE DRESS. By Amy Efaw. HarperCollins. $15.95. (Ages 12 and up) The author of this first novel graduated from West Point in 1989. The heroine, Andi Davis, is sure that because her home life has been so miserable, she will be able to survive the hazing and the discipline of the military academy. In fact, it's a terrible struggle. There's a glossary of cadet slang and military terms.    NO DINNER! The Story of the Old Woman and the Pumpkin. Written and illustrated by Jessica Souhami. Marshall Cavendish. $15.95. (Ages 5 to 9) No Red Riding Hood, either. Instead, here's a skinny Indian granny who goes through the forest to visit her granddaughter and then returns. They are both very clever, outwitting the wild beasts who would attack the old woman.

author: Roni Schotter

pull_quote: F IS FOR FREEDOM. By Roni Schotter. Illustrated by C. B. Mordan. DK Ink. $15.95. (Ages 7 to 10) This short, exciting novel for lower-grade readers, set in 1850, vividly explains the Fugitive Slave Law and some of the background of the Civil War. It begins with the nighttime arrival of some mysterious sacks at Amanda's home. She learns that her house is a stop on the underground railroad when Hannah and her family, runaway slaves, emerge from the sacks.    I WILL NEVER NOT EVER EAT A TOMATO. Written and illustrated by Lauren Child. Candlewick Press. $15.99. (Ages 5 to 8) Clever Charlie tells us how he tricks Lola, his very finicky little sister, into eating orange twiglets from Jupiter (carrots), rare green drops from Greenland (peas) and even moonsquirters (tomatoes). If the plot is unsurprising, the illustrations are surely not. They are wildly patterned mixed-media collages, including vegetable photographs, and very funny indeed.    RADIO RESCUE. Written and illustrated by Lynne Barasch. Frances Foster/Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $16. (Ages 5 to 8) The author's father became the youngest licensed amateur radio operator in the United States in 1923, when he was 10. His ''station'' was in his family's apartment on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. With his fluency in Morse code, the boy was able to help rescue a family in Key Largo, Fla., during a hurricane in 1926. Great story.    IT'S SIMPLE, SAID SIMON. By Mary Ann Hoberman. Illustrated by Meilo So. Knopf. $15.95. (Ages 3 to 8) A boy named Simon is challenged to growl by a dog, to stretch by a cat, to jump by a horse -- and then is tricked by a tiger. The tiger has dinner plans, but Simon outwits him. Enchanting watercolor illustrations.    GHOST BOY. By Iain Lawrence. Delacorte. $15.95. (Ages 12 and up) The hero of this unusual and affecting novel about acceptance and belonging is an albino. Harold -- people call him Ghost -- runs away from home, from the taunts and teasing, from the meanspirited stepfather, and joins the circus passing through his prairie hometown, Liberty. Ghost makes friends with the Cannibal King, himself an albino, and becomes an elephant trainer. Eventually he is brave enough to go home.    THE EGG. Written and illustrated by M. P. Robertson. Phyllis Fogelman. $15.99. (Ages 5 to 9) George knew from the size of it that the egg was something different. He took it to his room and read to it for three days until it hatched and a little baby dragon called him ''Mommy.'' A responsible fellow, George taught it flying, fire breathing and damsel distressing. He continued to read it bedtime stories until time came for the dragon to fly away. Sweetly told.    DEAR MR. PRESIDENT: Thomas Jefferson. Letters From a Philadelphia Bookworm. By Jennifer Armstrong. Winslow Press. $8.95. (Ages 8 and up) Fictional but well-researched and handsomely illustrated exchanges between the president and a 12-year-old girl on subjects from a yellow fever epidemic to firefighting. This and other books in the ''Dear Mr. President'' series have footnotes to interactive Web sites for resourceful readers.
